fact_base: Excerpt content: two groups report conflicting pressure drop values for the same material class; the excerpt weighs their test conditions. The excerpt reaches a limited preference and states the condition on which it rests.
input:
When the reported values for the benchmark material are placed side by side, it becomes apparent that the two sets of pressure drop values stand apart by considerably more than the scatter that either group reports within its own runs, and it would seem that the gap follows the test conditions rather than the material itself. It should be emphasised that both groups were working with the same class of material, and neither set of values can simply be set aside as a measurement error on the face of the reports as they stand.

Looking more closely at the conditions, these differ in the state of the bed and in the flow through it, both of which are factors of some importance in this context. One of the groups measured its values on a bed that had been packed for the test and reported the packing alongside the results, whereas the other group took its values under conditions carried over from an earlier programme, with the bed state described only in part. Since the pressure drop across a packed bed answers to both of these factors, a value that is moved from one set of conditions to the other inevitably carries the difference along with it.

The preference that is reached here is, it must be said, a limited one. Where a design case happens to run near the conditions of the first group, the first group's values would appear to be the better basis, essentially because the bed state behind them is known and the flow range covers the case in question. The preference rests, in other words, on that closeness of conditions. It does not extend to cases run under the second group's conditions, and it settles nothing about the benchmark material beyond the range that the first group covered.

fact_base: Excerpt content: a staffing gap of 7 weeks is reported with its cause; the excerpt proposes one mitigation and its owner. The excerpt does not open or close the memo and does not restate its subject line.
input:
The project is currently facing a staffing gap that now stands at 7 weeks, and it is important to understand both how this gap has arisen and what is being done in response. The gap has been opened by departures from the engineering team, and the remaining workload has continued to be carried by the same team without any corresponding reduction in scope, which has placed sustained pressure on the staff who remain. The gap falls on the design work that feeds the EPC contractor, and each additional week that it persists effectively moves the affected packages by the same amount, creating a knock-on effect that is difficult to recover later in the programme.

Recovery through overtime working has broadly reached its limit, given that the team is already working extended hours and that the board has been clear that the quality of the issued drawings should not be traded for speed. The mitigation that is therefore proposed is the engagement of a contract engineer through the existing framework, assigned to the project manager, who owns the recovery plan and reports progress to the project board. The contract engineer would take on the checking and revision work that currently queues behind the design engineers, thereby releasing the design engineers for the packages on the critical path. The arrangement would run until the gap closes and would be reviewed at each board meeting against the recovery plan.

Recruitment for the vacant posts is continuing in parallel under its own process, although its outcome does not change the mitigation set out above, which has been sized on the gap as it currently stands. Should the departures continue, the gap would widen beyond the figure stated here, and the mitigation would then need to be revisited by the project board.

It is worth emphasising that the corrosion allowance forms an integral part of this figure, in the sense that the allowance has been included in order to ensure that the wall retains adequate thickness throughout the service life of the vessel as material is gradually lost to corrosion. The same allowance rule has been applied in the corresponding subsections that deal with the absorber and with the lean solvent pump, so a consistent basis is maintained across the section as a whole.

Attention now turns to the selection of the gasket material for the compressor joints, where a comparison has been carried out between the two candidate materials purely on the basis of temperature limit. Other properties that might in principle be relevant to the selection, such as chemical compatibility or mechanical behaviour, have not been compared at this stage, and the comparison should therefore be understood as resting on the temperature limit alone. On that basis, the material with the higher temperature rating is preferred, since it provides the greater margin between the rated limit and the conditions that the joint is expected to experience in service.

input:
The lifetime values that have been reported for the benchmark material by the two groups differ to a marked extent, and this disagreement is not readily explained by experimental scatter alone. A closer examination of the conditions under which the respective measurements were obtained suggests that the difference may be attributable, at least in part, to the test conditions that were employed. In one case the material was tested under conditions that departed in important respects from the conditions of the intended application, whereas in the other case the conditions were chosen so as to correspond more closely to those of the application in question.

On balance, and with the reservations that such a comparison necessarily entails, a limited preference is expressed for the values obtained under the conditions that match the intended service, although this preference is expressly conditional on that match holding for the application that the reader has in mind. Where the service conditions differ from both sets of test conditions, neither set of values can be adopted without further justification, and the disagreement between the two groups remains, for those cases, unresolved.

One group tested under conditions removed from the intended service; the other tested under conditions matched to it, and the matched conditions are the ones whose values survive the comparison of methods. Scatter within a group's own runs measures the repeatability of that group's method. It does not measure the distance between two methods, and a difference that exceeds both scatters is a difference of method or of condition, not of chance.

The weighing therefore turns on condition. The group whose conditions match the intended service has run the test the application asks for; the other group has run a test whose relation to the application has to be argued, and the argument is not supplied in the report.

The values from the matched test conditions are preferred, and the condition on which the preference rests is the match itself: the service in view must be the service the test reproduced. Where the intended service departs from both sets of conditions, neither value carries over, and the disagreement stands for that case. fact_base: An operating-manual chapter for a centrifugal pump, in four sections: start-up, normal operation, alarms, and shutdown. The alarms section lists two alarms and the operator action for each; no other alarms are introduced. The chapter addresses the operator directly and uses imperative verbs for actions.
input:
## Start-up

Before you start the pump, you should take some time to prepare it properly. You should inspect both the pump and the motor, and you should confirm that the coupling guard is in place and that no tools or loose material have been left near the rotating parts. You should also check the bearing housing and confirm that the oil is standing at the mark on the sight glass. Where the coupling is accessible, you should turn the shaft by hand, and you should satisfy yourself that it turns freely, without any scraping or tight spots. If you find any defect at all, you should report it and leave the pump stopped until such time as the defect has been fully cleared.

The next stage is to fill the pump. You should open the vent at the top of the casing, and you should then open the suction valve slowly so that the suction line and the casing fill with liquid. You should keep the vent open until liquid that is free of air is flowing from the vent, at which point you should close the vent. It is worth remembering that a casing which still holds air will not deliver its discharge pressure, and the pump should on no account be started while it is in that state. You should also confirm that the discharge valve is closed, since a centrifugal pump is started against a closed discharge valve in order to keep the motor load low during the run-up period.

You may then start the motor. As the pump comes up to speed, you should watch the discharge pressure gauge carefully, as the pressure should rise promptly and then hold steady. Once the pressure has risen, you should open the discharge valve slowly and bring the flow up gradually, in stages. As the flow rises, you should check both the pump and the motor, looking for any leaks at the casing joints and at the seal, and listening for any scraping, rattling or knocking. If the pressure fails to rise, or if a leak opens up, or if abnormal noise or heat makes an appearance, you should stop the pump at once, and you should report the fault before any second attempt at starting is made.

## Normal operation

During normal operation, you should run the pump with a steady suction supply, and you should make sure that the casing remains full of liquid at all times. You should never run the pump dry, and you should never attempt to throttle the suction valve in order to control the flow. Flow should instead be controlled at the discharge valve, and every valve change that you make should be made slowly, because a fast change sends a pressure shock through the line which can damage both the pump and the pipework.

Throughout the shift, you should keep a watch on the discharge pressure and on the flow indication, both of which should hold near their normal values for the duty in hand. If the discharge pressure falls while the valves remain untouched, this points towards a loss of suction supply, a blockage, or wear inside the pump itself, whereas a rising pressure points towards a restriction downstream. You should treat either of these changes as a fault that is in the process of developing: you should reduce the flow, check the suction supply first, and report the change together with the readings that show it.

You should also make rounds of the pump at regular intervals, during which you should record the discharge pressure along with any other readings that the log requires. On each round, you should look for leaks at the joints, the flanges and the seal, and you should clear up any liquid that has been spilled. You should listen to the pump and to the motor, comparing the sound that you hear with the sound of the pump when it is in normal service, and you should check the bearing housing for heat and confirm that the oil mark is still showing on the sight glass. You should keep the area around the pump clear and dry, and you should report defects as and when you find them, since a defect that is reported early is merely a repair, whereas the same defect left running becomes a failure of the pump in service.

You should hand the pump over in a known state at the end of your shift. You should tell the next operator which duty the pump is on, whether there has been any change in its readings, and whether any defect is under report, and you should enter exactly the same points in the log. The next operator should not be left in the position of having to discover the state of the pump from the pump alone.

## Alarms

Two alarms are fitted to this pump, and each of them demands the action stated under it, in the order stated. On no account should you simply silence an alarm and carry on running the pump regardless.

Low suction pressure. This alarm comes into operation when the pressure at the pump suction falls below the level that the pump requires in order to stay full of liquid. When it acts, you should stop the pump and close the discharge valve. You should then check the suction supply and the suction line for a valve that has been left closed, a blockage, or a supply that has run empty. You should not restart the pump until the supply has been restored, the casing has been refilled and vented, and the suction pressure is standing normal while the pump is still stopped. You should report both the alarm and the cause that you found.

High bearing temperature. This alarm comes into operation when the temperature of a bearing rises above its normal working level. When it acts, you should stop the pump, and you should close the discharge valve followed by the suction valve. You should leave the pump to cool down, and you should not attempt to turn the shaft while the bearing remains hot. Once the pump is safe to approach, you should check the bearing housing for oil, and you should record the state of the oil exactly as you found it. You should not restart the pump until the cause of the heating has been found and cleared. You should report the alarm, together with the readings that were taken and the state in which the oil was found.

An alarm which acts without any fault being found should still be regarded as a fault in itself. You should report the alarm, the checks that were made and the readings that were taken, and you should leave the decision as to whether the pump returns to service to the supervisor on duty. You should, in addition, enter every alarm in the log, together with the action that was taken and the readings at the time, since the log entry forms part of the action rather than an optional addition to it.

## Shutdown

To shut the pump down, you should bring it down in broadly the reverse order of the start. You should close the discharge valve slowly, bringing the flow down in stages, and you should stop the motor once the discharge valve has been closed. You should then close the suction valve. At this point the pump will be standing full of liquid, isolated from the line on both sides.

You should next open the vent and confirm that the pressure within the casing has fallen away. In cases where the pump is going to be opened up, or where it will be standing out of service through a period of cold weather, you should drain the casing, and you should close the vent and the drain again once the draining has been completed. You should wipe up any liquid that has been spilled, bearing in mind that a pump which is left wet and dirty tends to hide the first signs of the next leak.

Where the stop is only a short one, and the pump will be returning to service on the same duty, you may leave the casing full and leave the valves exactly as they have been described above. Where the stop is a long one, you should drain the casing in the manner described. Whichever applies, the state in which the pump is left is the state that is recorded, and the start-up procedure should always begin from that recorded state rather than from memory.

You should leave the pump in a stated condition. You should record the shutdown in the log, including the state of the valves, whether or not the casing was drained, and any defect that is under report. You should tell the next operator the state of the pump at the handover. Where a pump is to be opened for work to be carried out, it must be handed over drained, vented and isolated, with its state entered in the log and stated at the handover, and no part of the pump is to be opened until that state has been confirmed by the person who will actually be doing the work.

subtype: worked example with equation: friction loss
fact_base: Water at 293 K flows in a horizontal pipe. The density $\rho$ is 998 kg m-3. Mean velocity $v$ is 0.8 m s-1, pipe diameter $D$ is 0.08 m, pipe length $L$ is 44 m and the Darcy friction factor $f$ is 0.02. The friction pressure drop is 3.5 kPa.
input:
In this worked example, we are going to look at how the friction pressure drop can be determined for water flowing through a horizontal pipe. The water is at 293 K and has a density $\rho$ of 998 kg m-3, while the mean velocity $v$ is 0.8 m s-1, the pipe diameter $D$ is 0.08 m, the pipe length $L$ is 44 m and the Darcy friction factor $f$ is 0.02, and the result that we obtain for the friction pressure drop is 3.5 kPa.

It is important to note that the friction pressure drop $\Delta P$, expressed in Pa, is calculated from the Darcy friction factor $f$, the pipe length $L$ in m, the pipe diameter $D$ in m, the density $\rho$ in kg m-3 and the mean velocity $v$ in m s-1, using the well-known relationship given below:

$$\Delta P = f \frac{L}{D} \frac{\rho v^2}{2}$$

where, as noted above, every quantity is used in the unit that has been stated with it. Because the pipe is horizontal, the pressure drop consists of friction loss alone, and no elevation term needs to be included. The friction factor $f$, for its part, is simply a stated input to the example, and its value is taken as given throughout.

The substitution itself can conveniently be carried out in stages. The ratio $L/D$ works out at 550, which is essentially a dimensionless count of how many pipe diameters fit into the length. The square of the mean velocity, $v^2$, comes to 0.64 m2 s-2, and the dynamic pressure $\rho v^2 / 2$ is thus 319.36 Pa. Substituting $f$, $L/D$ and the dynamic pressure into the equation then gives $\Delta P$ as 3512.96 Pa, corresponding to the stated result of 3.5 kPa at the precision of the inputs.

Finally, a useful dimensional check can be applied to the result. Since the ratio $L/D$ is dimensionless and $f$ is dimensionless as well, the unit of the product is simply the unit of $\rho v^2 / 2$, namely the pascal. The computed drop should therefore be understood as a friction loss for the stated length at the stated velocity; a longer pipe or a higher velocity would raise it through the same relation, and the example does not state any value outside the given conditions.

fact_base: A tutorial passage explains representative sampling of a powder blend. The passage covers where samples are taken, how many increments form one sample, and why a single grab sample misleads. No numerical limits are quoted; regulatory limits belong to the site's permit, not to the passage.
input:
A sample of a powder blend represents the batch only when the material in the sample has the same makeup as the material in the batch. A blend is not uniform by default. Its components differ in particle size and in density, and handling moves them apart: fine material settles through coarse material, and light material gathers where the blend has been poured or carried. Any one place in the batch can therefore differ from the batch as a whole.

Sampling answers that unevenness by spreading the taking across the batch. Increments are taken from points spread over the whole batch, from the top, the middle and the bottom of a container, and from across its width, and the increments together form one sample. No single increment is the sample. The sample carries the makeup of the batch because every part of the batch has contributed to it.

A single grab sample has no such defence. Taken from the surface, it reports the makeup of the surface, which settling and pouring have already separated from the bulk. A result from a grab sample can be precise and still wrong for the batch: the measurement is sound, and the material measured is not the material the result is applied to.

fact_base: A drug in solution decomposes by first-order kinetics with rate constant $k$ = 0.141 min-1. After 76 min the fraction remaining $C / C_0$ is 0. The rate constant was measured at one temperature; no activation energy is available.
input:
In this example, we consider a drug in solution that decomposes in accordance with first-order kinetics, and we seek to determine what fraction of the drug remains after a specified period of time has elapsed. The rate constant $k$ for the decomposition has been determined to be 0.141 min-1, and the time of interest is 76 min. For a first-order process, the fraction of the substance that remains is related to the rate constant and the elapsed time through the integrated rate equation, which can be written as follows:

$$\ln\frac{C}{C_0} = -k t$$

In this relationship, the fraction remaining is expressed as the concentration at the time of interest divided by the initial concentration, and the negative sign reflects the fact that the concentration decreases as time progresses. Substituting the values given above into the equation and evaluating the resulting expression, it is found that the fraction of the drug remaining after the stated time is 0, which is to say that, for practical purposes, the decomposition has proceeded essentially to completion over this interval. It is also worth noting, by way of an important qualification, that the rate constant employed here was measured at one temperature only, and no activation energy is available for this system. Consequently, the result that has been obtained is applicable strictly to the temperature at which the measurement was made, and it cannot be extended to other temperatures by means of a temperature correction, since the information that would be required in order to perform such a correction is simply not available.
target:
A drug in solution decomposes by first-order kinetics with rate constant $k$ of 0.141 min-1. The task is the fraction of drug remaining after 76 min.

For first-order decomposition the fraction remaining, the concentration at time $t$ divided by the initial concentration, follows the integrated rate equation

$$\ln\frac{C}{C_0} = -k t$$

The equation is the integrated form of the rate law for a process whose rate is proportional to the amount present. Each equal interval of time removes the same fraction of what remains at its start, so the fraction falls by multiplication rather than by subtraction, and the logarithm in the equation is the step that converts that repeated multiplication into a quantity proportional to time. The negative sign records direction: the fraction decreases as time increases, and at the start of the interval the fraction is the whole amount, by the definition of the ratio the equation carries.

Substitution of the rate constant and the time gives a fraction remaining of 0. At the precision of the stated value, no drug remains undecomposed after the interval: the exponential term has carried the concentration below any figure the data can express. The result is a statement about the stated interval only, and it does not require the concentration to be exactly zero at any earlier time. A shorter interval would return a fraction the data could express, and the equation, not the stated result, is the means of obtaining it.

The rate constant was measured at one temperature, and no activation energy is available. The result therefore holds at the measurement temperature. A value at any other temperature cannot be obtained from the data given, because the correction would require the activation energy that is missing, and the single measured rate constant contains no information about how the rate changes with temperature.

fact_base: A review passage on membrane separations for solvent recovery, in four parts: scope, established results, disagreements, and gaps. The review covers 45 papers from the last 12 years. The disagreements part names the quantity on which reports conflict; the gaps part names the measurement nobody reports.
input:
Scope

This review is concerned with the rapidly developing field of membrane separations for solvent recovery, an area in which a membrane is used to separate a solvent from a dissolved solute, from a second solvent, or from a more complex mixture, so that the solvent in question can be returned to the process that produced the stream in the first place. In total, the review covers 45 papers that have been published over the course of the last 12 years. Work is included where the membrane operates on a liquid process stream and where the objective is the recovery of the solvent for the purposes of reuse. By contrast, work on desalination and on gas separation falls outside the boundary of the review, as does work in which the solvent is recovered only as a product of a reaction work-up rather than from a stream that the process generates on a continuous basis. The literature can be divided according to membrane material and according to the separation that is demanded of the membrane, and the review follows this division throughout: polymeric membranes and ceramic membranes are treated as separate bodies of work, reflecting the fact that their behaviour in organic solvents differs in kind and not merely in degree. It should also be noted that terminology is not uniform across the field, and the review accordingly uses the terms of each individual paper where a result is reported, before any comparison is drawn between results.

Established results

It is now well established that the separation of solvents from dissolved solutes by means of membranes can be achieved at laboratory scale across a wide range of solvent and solute pairs. Membranes that are capable of retaining the solute while at the same time passing the solvent have been reported for feeds that would damage a large proportion of the polymeric materials that are in common use, and the work that has been carried out on ceramic membranes demonstrates that solvent resistance, which represented the first major obstacle in the field, can be overcome, in the sense that there are materials on both sides of the material division that are able to withstand the solvents in question. Performance is defined by flux and rejection taken together, and the pattern that emerges from the reported results is essentially a trade-off between the two: a membrane that is tightened in order to raise its rejection will pass solvent more slowly, and the reported results arrange themselves along this trade-off rather than above it. Solvent stability, it is important to appreciate, is reported as a test outcome rather than as a service record; membranes that are described as stable have been exposed to the solvent under test conditions for the duration of a trial, and what the result establishes is behaviour over that period of exposure. Finally, the concentration of a solute by the removal of solvent is established as a unit operation at laboratory scale, with the membrane step placed either ahead of, or in place of, a thermal separation, and the energy comparison that motivates the field as a whole rests on the avoidance of the phase change that a thermal step would require.

Disagreements

It is in the area of the rejection of dissolved solutes that the literature is most clearly in disagreement with itself, and this disagreement represents the largest open question to emerge from the material reviewed here. The same class of membrane is reported in one body of work as retaining a solute almost completely, and in another body of work as passing a substantial proportion of it, under conditions that the papers themselves describe in broadly similar terms. Unfortunately, the disagreement does not resolve on a closer inspection of the reported conditions, because the conditions that actually decide rejection are not the conditions that the papers report most carefully: the feed composition at the membrane surface, the state of the membrane following its exposure to the solvent, and the duration over which the rejection was measured all differ from one report to another, and each of these factors is capable, on its own, of moving the figure that is obtained. Conditioning, in particular, is reported in a highly uneven fashion. A membrane that is measured after prolonged contact with the solvent is not in the same state as a membrane that is measured on first contact, and those papers that do not state the conditioning that was applied leave their rejection figures effectively unanchored. The conflict should therefore be understood as a conflict of method rather than as a conflict of material: until such time as rejection is reported against a stated conditioning and a stated measurement duration, the literature will continue to contain two different values for one and the same quantity, with no agreed means of choosing between them.

Gaps

Perhaps the most striking gap in the literature is the measurement that nobody appears to report, namely the performance of a membrane over extended continuous operation. Papers routinely report the flux and the rejection of a membrane at the start of a trial, and some go on to report the same pair of quantities again at the end of a trial, but the course of performance between those two points, and indeed beyond the longest trial that has been reported, is essentially absent from the literature that has been reviewed. This is a significant omission, because a recovery unit in an actual process runs continuously, and its membrane is purchased on the expectation that its performance will persist over time; the literature offers the initial value and, at best, a final value, and nothing whatsoever on the trajectory that connects the two, or on the point at which replacement of the membrane becomes necessary. A second gap follows directly from the first: because extended operation remains unmeasured, the effect of cleaning on a membrane that has been run in solvent service is likewise unreported, and no paper in the set establishes whether performance that has been lost in operation can be recovered by cleaning or whether that loss is, in fact, permanent. In summary, the field is in a position to state what its membranes do when they are new; it is not yet in a position to state what they do in service, and it is precisely that measurement that the next body of work will need to supply if the field is to move forward.

fact_base: A shell-and-tube exchanger heats crude oil in a refinery preheat train. Duty is 954 kW. Hot stream: 95 °C in, 70 °C out. Cold stream: 25 °C in, 40 °C out. The log-mean temperature difference is 49.8 K and the installed area is 66.9 m2, giving an overall coefficient of 286 W m-2 K-1. Fouling was assessed from a single 90-day run; no cleaning cycle has been completed.
input:
A shell-and-tube exchanger heats crude oil in a refinery preheat train at a duty of 954 kW. The hot stream enters at 95 °C and leaves at 70 °C; the cold stream enters at 25 °C and leaves at 40 °C. The log-mean temperature difference for the exchanger is 49.8 K and the installed area is 66.9 m2, giving an overall coefficient of 286 W m-2 K-1. The coefficient is a derived figure, computed as the duty divided by the product of the installed area and the log-mean temperature difference, on the values stated above.

Fouling was assessed from a single 90-day run, and no cleaning cycle has been completed. The figures therefore describe the exchanger in its assessed state, under the conditions of the run from which the fouling assessment comes. Each stream temperature is a terminal value for the exchanger as a whole; no distribution of temperature through the passes is reported, and none is implied by the figures above. A cleaned exchanger would return a different coefficient, and the present figures cannot say by how much, because the comparison they rest on has not been run.

The duty is heat passed from the hot stream to the cold stream inside the one exchanger, and the exchanger is reported as a single item of equipment.

fact_base: A gravity settler removes sand from a process stream. Design overflow rate is 0.53 m h-1 at a throughput of 104 m3 h-1, giving a plan area of 196 m2. The overflow-rate basis is a vendor rule for this solid; no settling test on the actual slurry has been run.
input:
In this passage, we will look at the sizing of a gravity settler that is intended to remove sand from a process stream, and we will see how the required plan area is arrived at. The settler needs a plan area of 196 m2, based on a throughput of 104 m3 h-1 together with a design overflow rate of 0.53 m h-1. It is worth bearing in mind that the overflow rate can be understood as the throughput divided by the plan area, so the area follows from the throughput and the rate taken together: at the stated rate, each square metre of plan area passes 0.53 m3 h-1, and the stated throughput accordingly sets the area at 196 m2.

A helpful dimensional check can also be applied to the sizing, providing further reassurance about the result. A throughput expressed in m3 h-1, divided by an overflow rate expressed in m h-1, gives an area in m2, and the stated values do indeed return the stated area. It should also be noted that no other quantity enters into the sizing at this stage: the area is fixed by the two stated values and by nothing else in the design.

Turning to the basis of the rate, this is a vendor rule for this solid, which is a point that deserves careful attention. No settling test on the actual slurry has been run, which means that the overflow rate cannot be regarded as a measured property of the material that the settler will actually treat. The plan area of 196 m2 therefore holds on that basis: while the arithmetic is exact for the stated rate, the rate itself rests on the vendor rule rather than on a test of the actual slurry. Any design that needs the rate to be confirmed would need the settling test first, and the sizing as stated does not include that confirmation.

Overall, then, the settler enters the design at 196 m2 of plan area, sized on a vendor overflow rate of 0.53 m h-1 for a throughput of 104 m3 h-1, with the test on the actual slurry still outstanding. It is, in the end, a sizing figure: it settles the area that the design carries forward, while settling nothing about how the settler will perform in service.

A lower ramp was considered during the preparation of the proposal, but it was felt that a lower figure would leave the project exposed during the period in which the workload rises most steeply, since the work that the ramp is intended to cover does not arrive evenly and cannot readily be deferred. fact_base: Staffing review for a dispatch office: 8 full-time staff, overtime at 6% of paid hours last year. Replacing half the overtime with one additional hire costs $60k per year fully loaded. Overtime is concentrated in two seasonal peaks; a hire is paid for the full year.
input:
This staffing review takes a detailed look at the position in a dispatch office that currently employs 8 full-time staff, and it considers whether an additional hire should be made in order to reduce the office's reliance on overtime. Over the course of last year, overtime stood at 6% of paid hours, and it is interesting to note that this overtime was not spread evenly across the year but was instead concentrated in 2 seasonal peaks. Replacing half of the overtime with 1 additional hire would cost $60k per year on a fully loaded basis, and it is this option that the review weighs up in what follows.

When the trade-off is examined more closely, a number of considerations come into view. The hire would cost $60k for the full year in order to remove 3% of paid hours, which is to say half of the 6% overtime share, and those hours arise in 2 seasonal peaks rather than across the year as a whole. Outside the peaks, in other words, the additional hire would be paid for hours that the office does not really need to have covered.

Overtime, by contrast, is bought only in the weeks that actually need it, which is one of its principal attractions in this context. The current arrangement pays for cover in the 2 peaks and pays nothing towards cover in the rest of the year. At the same time, however, its weakness lies in concentration: it is the same 8 staff who carry the peaks, and a peak that grows, or a peak that happens to coincide with absence, falls on a fixed team with limited room for manoeuvre.

Taking all of this into account, the position that emerges is a fairly narrow one. Staffing stays at 8, overtime continues to carry the 2 peaks, and the case for 1 additional hire would be reopened only when the overtime share rises above 6% of paid hours or the overtime begins to spread outside the peaks. On the figures for last year, it has to be said that neither of those conditions is met.
target:

The evidence base is last year's paid hours: overtime stood at 6% of paid hours, concentrated in 2 seasonal peaks. 1 additional hire, at $60k per year fully loaded, would replace half of that overtime, and the dispatch office manager should hold the hire until overtime spreads beyond the peaks.

The trade-off stands in one comparison. The hire costs $60k for the full year to remove 3% of paid hours (half of the 6% overtime share), and those hours arise in 2 seasonal peaks rather than across the year. Outside the peaks, the additional hire is paid for hours the office does not need covered.

The mismatch is one of timing. Overtime follows the work: it is available in the peak weeks and absent in the quiet weeks, at no standing cost. A hire reverses the pattern, at a standing cost in every week, quiet weeks included. The figures in this review fix the cost of the hire and the size and placing of the overtime, and the placing is the point.

fact_base: Excerpt content: the analogy between the transfer processes is stated, then qualified by the case where it fails. The excerpt works one short numerical check with numbers given inside the excerpt itself. The excerpt assumes the chapter's earlier definitions and adds none.
input:
The Chilton-Colburn analogy, which has been introduced in the preceding material, expresses a correspondence between the transfer processes, to the effect that $j_D$ is related to $f$ in such a way that the one quantity may be estimated from the other. A short numerical check may be used in order to illustrate the relationship in concrete terms. For the flow that is under consideration here, $f$ takes the value 0.02, and applying the analogy in the form $j_D = f/2$ leads directly to a value of 0.01 for $j_D$, which is the value that the analogy requires if it is to hold for this flow.

It is, however, necessary to qualify the analogy at this point, because the correspondence that it asserts is not universal in its application. Where the properties of the fluid vary appreciably across the layer through which the transfer takes place, the symmetry on which the analogy rests is weakened, and the estimate that it provides can no longer be relied upon to the same extent, since the conditions that were presupposed in arriving at the relation are no longer satisfied by the flow itself.

The correspondence is not a definition of either quantity. It is a statement that the layer at the surface treats momentum and mass alike, and its content is exhausted by that statement.

A short check fixes the relation in numbers. For the flow under consideration, $f$ is 0.02, and the analogy in the form $j_D = f/2$ returns 0.01 for $j_D$. The check is the analogy's own arithmetic; a value returned by substitution shows that the relation has been applied as stated, and nothing more.

The qualification follows at once. The analogy presumes that the fluid properties are effectively constant across the layer through which transfer takes place. Where the properties vary appreciably across that layer, the symmetry the analogy asserts is absent from the flow, the estimate loses its basis, and the number it returns is unsupported. The failure is in the correspondence, not in the arithmetic.

fact_base: Goal: compute the Reynolds number for water in a pipe and state the flow regime. The Reynolds number Re (dimensionless) is computed from density rho (kg m-3), mean velocity v (m s-1), pipe diameter D (m) and dynamic viscosity mu (Pa s) by Re = rho v D / mu. Water at 293 K: rho = 998 kg m-3, mu = 1.00 x 10-3 Pa s. Pipe diameter D = 0.025 m; mean velocity v = 0.9 m s-1. Worked result: Re = 22500 (computed as 998 x 0.9 x 0.025 / 0.001). Flow is laminar below Re = 2300 and turbulent above Re = 4000; between the two values the regime is transitional and is not assigned by the number alone.
input:
The goal of this worked example is to compute the Reynolds number for water flowing in a pipe and, on the basis of the value obtained, to state the flow regime that applies. The Reynolds number Re is a dimensionless quantity that is computed from the density rho (kg m-3), the mean velocity v (m s-1), the pipe diameter D (m) and the dynamic viscosity mu (Pa s) by means of the relation Re = rho v D / mu. For water at 293 K, the values of the properties are rho = 998 and mu = 1.00 x 10-3, and the pipe diameter D is 0.025 while the mean velocity v is 0.9, all in the units stated with the symbols above.

Substituting these values into the relation gives Re = 998 x 0.9 x 0.025 / 0.001, and evaluating this expression yields a Reynolds number of 22500. In order to state the flow regime, the computed value is compared with the conventional thresholds: flow is laminar below Re = 2300 and turbulent above Re = 4000, while between the two values the regime is transitional and is not assigned by the number alone. Since the value obtained in this case, 22500, stands well above the upper of the two thresholds, the flow in the pipe is classified as turbulent, and the classification is not a marginal one, because the transitional band that lies between the thresholds has been passed by a considerable margin.
target:
The Reynolds number for water in the pipe is 22500, and the flow is turbulent.

The Reynolds number Re is computed from the density rho (kg m-3), the mean velocity v (m s-1), the pipe diameter D (m) and the dynamic viscosity mu (Pa s) by Re = rho v D / mu, and Re is dimensionless. Water at 293 K has rho = 998 and mu = 1.00 x 10-3 in the units stated, the pipe diameter D is 0.025 and the mean velocity v is 0.9. Substitution of these values in Re = rho v D / mu gives Re = 998 x 0.9 x 0.025 / 0.001. The numerator collects the density, velocity and diameter terms, and division by the viscosity removes the units. Thus Re = 22500, and the Reynolds number is dimensionless because the units in the numerator and the denominator cancel.

The regime is read from the thresholds. Flow is laminar below Re = 2300 and turbulent above Re = 4000; between the two values the regime is transitional and is not assigned by the number alone. The computed value stands above the upper threshold by a wide margin, in the range the thresholds assign to turbulent flow. No part of the transitional range is involved, and the assignment does not rest on the number alone in the way the transitional case would. The check on the result is the threshold comparison itself. A value inside the transitional range would have left the regime unassigned on the number alone, and the example would then have turned on conditions the calculation does not contain. That case does not arise here, and the assignment is complete as stated.

subtype: worked example with equation: Arrhenius ratio
fact_base: Rate constants for a polymer cure were measured at two temperatures. With activation energy $E_a$ of 40 kJ mol-1, raising the temperature from 300 K to 330 K multiplies the rate constant $k$ by 4.3. The estimate holds the pre-exponential factor $A$ constant over the interval.
input:
Rate constants for a polymer cure were measured at two temperatures, and the purpose of this example is to determine by how much the rate constant increases when the temperature is raised across the interval in question. The temperature dependence of the rate constant $k$ is described by the Arrhenius equation, which relates the rate constant to the temperature $T$ through the activation energy $E_a$ and the pre-exponential factor $A$, and which takes the following form:

$$k = A \exp\left(-\frac{E_a}{R T}\right)$$

For the polymer cure under consideration, the activation energy $E_a$ is 40 kJ mol-1. Forming the ratio of the rate constants at the two temperatures, the temperature is raised from 300 K to 330 K, an increase of 30 K, and the evaluation of the ratio shows that the rate constant $k$ is multiplied by 4.3 over this interval. In other words, the cure proceeds a little more than four times as fast at the higher temperature as it does at the lower temperature, according to this estimate. It should be borne in mind that the estimate has been obtained by holding the pre-exponential factor $A$ constant over the interval, which is the assumption on which the calculation rests; if the pre-exponential factor were itself to vary with temperature, the ratio obtained would be modified accordingly.

It is also instructive to consider what the ratio does and does not depend upon. Because the ratio is formed from the rate constants at the two temperatures, any influence that affects both rate constants in the same proportion divides out of the ratio, and what remains is the effect of the temperature change itself, expressed through the activation energy. The measured rate constants at the two temperatures are consistent with the ratio that has been obtained, in the sense that the calculation and the measurements describe the same interval in the same terms, and the result may therefore be used for the cure in question across the interval that has been studied, subject always to the assumption that has been stated.
target:
Rate constants for a polymer cure were measured at two temperatures. The rate constant $k$ depends on the temperature $T$ through the Arrhenius equation

$$k = A \exp\left(-\frac{E_a}{R T}\right)$$

where $A$ is the pre-exponential factor, $E_a$ is the activation energy and $R$ is the gas constant. For the cure in question $E_a$ is 40 kJ mol-1. Raising the temperature from 300 K to 330 K, an interval of 30 K, multiplies the rate constant $k$ by 4.3. The ratio comes from the equation written at the two temperatures with $A$ held constant: the pre-exponential factor cancels in the ratio, and the exponential term carries the whole effect of the temperature change.

The estimate holds $A$ constant over the interval. That condition is part of the result, not a detail behind it: a pre-exponential factor that varied with temperature would change the ratio, and the measurements at two temperatures provide no means of separating such a variation from the exponential term. Within the stated condition, the cure at the higher temperature runs at the stated multiple of the rate at the lower, and the figure is a ratio of rate constants at the two stated temperatures and at no others.

The ratio has a direct reading for the cure. A process whose rate constant rises by the stated factor over the interval reaches a given state of cure correspondingly sooner at the higher temperature, and a cure schedule set at the lower temperature cannot be transferred to the higher without the correction the ratio supplies. Outside the interval, the same equation would return a figure, but the figure would rest on the activation energy holding beyond the range in which the measurements support it, and on the pre-exponential factor remaining constant over a range in which it has not been examined. The estimate is therefore an interval result. Its conditions are the two temperatures, the constant pre-exponential factor, and the activation energy as measured, and a statement of the ratio that drops any of those conditions states more than the calculation gives.

fact_base: Excerpt content: the analogy between the transfer processes is stated, then qualified by the case where it fails. The excerpt works one short numerical check with numbers given inside the excerpt itself. The excerpt assumes the chapter's earlier definitions and adds none.
input:
Before the analogy is put to work, it is as well to be clear about the case in which it can be expected to fail, since an estimate that is used outside its range of validity is worse than no estimate at all. The Chilton-Colburn analogy asserts that the transfer processes correspond to one another in form, so that $j_D$ and $f$ are connected, and knowledge of the one can be used in place of a measurement of the other. The correspondence depends on the layer adjacent to the surface behaving in the same way for each process, and it is precisely this condition that is liable to break down in practice.

A numerical check shows the analogy being applied in the manner intended. For the flow that is being considered, $f$ has the value 0.03, and the relation $j_D = f/2$ then gives 0.015 for $j_D$, which is the figure that a measurement would be expected to approach if the analogy holds for this flow. The check is deliberately short: its purpose is to fix the form of the relation, not to validate the analogy itself, which no single substitution is capable of doing.

The case in which the analogy fails is the case in which the properties of the fluid are not effectively constant across the transfer layer. A strong variation of properties across the layer affects the transfer of momentum and the transfer of mass differently, and once that happens the correspondence between the processes, which is the entire content of the analogy, has been lost. The estimate may still be computed, and it will still return a number, but the number is no longer supported by the reasoning that produced the relation, and it should not be carried into a design calculation on the strength of the analogy alone.
target:
The qualification belongs at the front of the analogy, not after it. The Chilton-Colburn analogy asserts a correspondence of form between the transfer processes: $j_D$ follows $f$, and either quantity can stand in for the other. The correspondence rests on one condition, that the layer at the surface behaves in the same way for each process. Where that condition fails, the analogy fails with it, and the failure is silent: the arithmetic still returns a number.

The numerical check is short and fixes the form only. For the flow under consideration $f$ is 0.03, and the relation $j_D = f/2$ gives 0.015 for $j_D$. That is the value the analogy requires; a measurement near it supports the application, and a measurement far from it withdraws the support. The check validates nothing by itself, because substitution into a relation cannot test the relation, and a writer who presents the check as a test has claimed more than the arithmetic contains.

Properties that vary strongly across the transfer layer break the condition. Momentum and mass respond differently to the variation, and the correspondence that is the whole content of the analogy is gone. An estimate computed in that state of affairs has no basis in the analogy, whatever its numerical value, and a design calculation that takes it up takes up an unsupported figure. The analogy is used where its condition holds and set aside where the condition fails, and the distinction is made on the properties of the layer, not on the plausibility of the result. A plausible result from a broken correspondence is still an unsupported result, and it is the more dangerous for looking sound. The distinction matters most where the result is convenient, because a convenient number is the one least likely to be questioned before it is used.

fact_base: Staffing review for a maintenance crew: 15 full-time staff, overtime at 9% of paid hours last year. Replacing half the overtime with one additional hire costs $74k per year fully loaded. Overtime is concentrated in two seasonal peaks; a hire is paid for the full year.
input: In this staffing review, we take a closer look at the current resourcing arrangements for the maintenance crew and explore whether there might be scope to adjust the balance between overtime working and established staffing levels. The maintenance crew currently consists of 15 full-time members of staff, and during last year overtime accounted for 9% of paid hours, which is by no means an insignificant share of the total hours worked. It is important to note, however, that this overtime is not distributed evenly across the year; instead, it is concentrated in two seasonal peaks, when the demand for maintenance work is at its highest. One potential option that has been identified is replacing half of the overtime with one additional hire, and it has been estimated that this would cost $74k per year on a fully loaded basis. That said, it is equally important to bear in mind that a hire is paid for the full year, so the additional capacity would be in place throughout the year, including during quieter periods when the overtime requirement is much lower. This creates an interesting dynamic, because overtime is inherently flexible and can be dialled up or down as circumstances require, whereas the cost of an additional hire is essentially fixed once the appointment is made. Ultimately, decision-makers will want to weigh a range of factors, including the $74k per year fully loaded cost of the hire, the 9% of paid hours currently worked as overtime by the 15 full-time staff, and the fact that this overtime is concentrated in two seasonal peaks, before coming to a view on the best way forward for the maintenance crew.
target: The maintenance crew review turns on a mismatch of timing, and the figures state it plainly. The crew has 15 full-time staff. Overtime stood at 9% of paid hours last year. Replacing half of the overtime with one additional hire costs $74k per year fully loaded. The overtime is concentrated in two seasonal peaks. A hire is paid for the full year. Set side by side, the two options buy different things: overtime buys hours inside the two seasonal peaks, where the demand stands, and the hire buys hours spread across the full year, including the long stretches between the peaks when no overtime is worked. The cost of the hire, $74k per year fully loaded, is therefore not compared against the overtime it replaces alone; it is compared against peak cover bought at a year-round price. Half of the overtime would remain in place under the proposal, so the peaks would still carry an overtime element, and the crew would carry the additional hire through every non-peak week as well. The proposal also changes the form of the cost before it changes the amount of cover: a cost that now rises and falls with demand becomes a cost that runs at one level in every week of the year, peak and non-peak alike. The figures support a narrow conclusion. Where the need is peak cover only, the hire is the more expensive way to buy it, because its cost runs for the full year while the need runs for two seasonal peaks. Where cover is short outside the peaks, the case changes, but nothing in last year's figures (15 full-time staff, overtime at 9% of paid hours) speaks to a shortfall outside the peaks. A decision to hire should therefore rest on evidence about non-peak cover, which this review does not contain.

fact_base: An amine absorption unit was tested at pilot scale on gas from a cement kiln. Over 45 days at 11 t of carbon dioxide per day, the unit captured 89% of the carbon dioxide in the treated gas. Steam demand was 3.8 gigajoules per tonne of carbon dioxide captured; solvent loss was 2.2 kg per tonne captured. Beyond 45 days, the effect of kiln dust on the solvent is untested.
input: An amine absorption unit has been tested at pilot scale on gas from a cement kiln, and this passage reports the principal results of that testing programme in some detail. Over a period of 45 days, operating at a rate of 11 t of carbon dioxide per day, the unit captured 89% of the carbon dioxide in the treated gas, which represents a strong level of capture performance sustained over the duration of the trial. In terms of the associated resource requirements, the steam demand was found to be 3.8 gigajoules per tonne of carbon dioxide captured, while the solvent loss was 2.2 kg per tonne captured, and both of these quantities are important considerations when the overall performance of the process is being assessed. It should be noted, however, that the testing extended over 45 days in total, and beyond 45 days the effect of kiln dust on the solvent remains untested, which is a significant caveat that should be borne in mind when these results are interpreted. Taken together, the results show that the unit achieved a capture level of 89% over the 45 days of testing at 11 t of carbon dioxide per day, with a steam demand of 3.8 gigajoules per tonne of carbon dioxide captured and a solvent loss of 2.2 kg per tonne captured, although the longer-term behaviour of the solvent when exposed to kiln dust has yet to be established. For ease of reference, the headline figures can be restated as follows: a capture level of 89% maintained over 45 days, a steam demand of 3.8 gigajoules per tonne of carbon dioxide captured, and a solvent loss of 2.2 kg per tonne captured, with a further 45 days of operation needed before any longer-term trend in performance could be identified.
target: An amine absorption unit tested at pilot scale on gas from a cement kiln captured 89% of the carbon dioxide in the treated gas. The test ran over 45 days at 11 t of carbon dioxide per day. Steam demand was 3.8 gigajoules per tonne of carbon dioxide captured, and solvent loss was 2.2 kg per tonne captured. The figures form one result with one boundary: each was measured over the same 45 days, and the boundary of the result is the length of the test. Beyond 45 days, the effect of kiln dust on the solvent is untested. The solvent loss of 2.2 kg per tonne captured is therefore a figure for solvent that has seen 45 days of kiln gas, and it carries no information about loss rates once kiln dust has accumulated in the solvent over a longer campaign. The capture figure has the same limit in the other direction: 89% was the capture held across the test as run, and a solvent changed by kiln dust may not hold it. Steam demand, at 3.8 gigajoules per tonne of carbon dioxide captured, is the one figure with no stated dependence on solvent condition, and it too was measured only within the 45 days. At its tested scope, the result is a pilot unit capturing 89% of the carbon dioxide in cement-kiln gas at 11 t of carbon dioxide per day, with a steam demand of 3.8 gigajoules per tonne captured and a solvent loss of 2.2 kg per tonne captured; performance beyond 45 days, where kiln dust acts on the solvent, is unmeasured.

fact_base: Carbon dioxide and hydrogen react over a copper-zinc oxide catalyst to give methanol. Space-time yield is the mass of product per unit catalyst volume per hour (kg L-1 h-1). Test conditions: 280 °C, 40 bar, feed ratio H2/CO2 = 3, one feed composition. Structured catalyst: space-time yield 0.89 kg L-1 h-1, pressure drop 0.22 bar, activity loss 8% after 100 h. Pellet catalyst: space-time yield 0.49 kg L-1 h-1, pressure drop 1.31 bar, activity loss 15% after 100 h. No sulfur-bearing feed was tested. Yield and pressure drop are seldom reported for the same catalyst charge.
input: Carbon dioxide and hydrogen react over a copper-zinc oxide catalyst to give methanol. Two catalyst forms were compared on space-time yield, pressure drop and activity loss under one feed composition. Space-time yield is the mass of product per unit catalyst volume per hour (kg L-1 h-1). Test conditions were 280 °C and 40 bar, with a feed ratio H2/CO2 = 3. The structured catalyst gave a space-time yield of 0.89 kg L-1 h-1, a pressure drop of 0.22 bar, and an activity loss of 8% after 100 h. The pellet catalyst gave a space-time yield of 0.49 kg L-1 h-1, a pressure drop of 1.31 bar, and an activity loss of 15% after 100 h. On the three measures together, the structured catalyst stands ahead at the conditions tested: yield 0.89 against 0.49 kg L-1 h-1, pressure drop 0.22 against 1.31 bar, activity loss 8% against 15% after 100 h. Each comparison is a comparison of the same two charges under the same test conditions (280 °C, 40 bar, feed ratio H2/CO2 = 3), so the differences belong to the catalyst form and not to the duty. The comparison rests on one feed composition, and no sulfur-bearing feed was tested, so the ranking is established for the tested feed only and carries no finding for a feed that bears sulfur. Yield and pressure drop are seldom reported for the same catalyst charge; both stand here for the charges tested, with the activity loss over the same 100 h, and that shared basis is the ground on which the comparison rests.

fact_base: Capital appraisal for a warehouse extension: installed cost $485k, expected net saving $117k per year for 8 years. At a discount rate of 10% the present value of the savings is $624k and the net present value is $139k. Savings are vendor and utility estimates; no saving has yet been measured on a comparable installation.
input: This capital appraisal considers a proposed warehouse extension and sets out the financial figures that have been assembled in support of the investment. The installed cost of the extension has been put at $485k, and the expected net saving has been estimated at $117k per year over a period of 8 years. Using a discount rate of 10%, the present value of the savings works out at $624k, which in turn gives a net present value of $139k for the project as a whole. On the face of it, this is a positive result, since the present value of the savings, at $624k, exceeds the installed cost of $485k by a comfortable margin. It is important to note, however, that the savings underpinning this appraisal are vendor and utility estimates, and no saving of this kind has yet been measured on a comparable installation, so there is inevitably a degree of uncertainty surrounding the saving figure. Decision-makers will therefore wish to consider not only the headline net present value of $139k, but also the basis on which the expected net saving of $117k per year for 8 years has been arrived at, before reaching a final view.
target: Recommendation: proceed with the warehouse extension, on the strength of the appraisal and with its basis stated plainly. The installed cost is $485k. The expected net saving is $117k per year for 8 years. At a discount rate of 10%, the present value of the savings is $624k, and the net present value is $139k. The margin is the difference between the two present figures: savings worth $624k in present terms against an installed cost of $485k, a difference in the project's favour. The basis of the appraisal is estimates. The savings are vendor and utility estimates, and no saving has yet been measured on a comparable installation, so the net present value of $139k is an appraised figure whose accuracy is the accuracy of estimates that have never been checked against a measured case. The decision the figures support is approval of the warehouse extension as appraised. They do not remove the need to treat the $117k per year as an estimate in the first years of operation, to compare the measured saving against it year by year over the 8 years, and to hold the appraisal answerable to that comparison. The appraisal period and the discounting are stated on the face of the figures, and the recommendation accepts both as given; what the recommendation does not accept without remark is the habit of treating an estimate as though it were a measurement.

fact_base: Excerpt content: the analogy between the transfer processes is stated, then qualified by the case where it fails. The excerpt works one short numerical check with numbers given inside the excerpt itself. The excerpt assumes the chapter's earlier definitions and adds none.
input: It is also worth pausing to consider the Chilton-Colburn analogy in a little more depth, because it provides an extremely useful bridge between the transfer processes that have been discussed so far. In essence, the Chilton-Colburn analogy tells us that the mass-transfer factor $j_D$ is equal to half of the friction factor $f$, and this simple relationship can be very powerful in practice. To illustrate this, we can work through a short numerical check using some values that are already in hand. Suppose, for example, that we are dealing with a Reynolds number of 20000 and a measured friction factor $f$ of 0.0064; applying the analogy then gives us $j_D$ = 0.0032, which is simply half of the friction factor, and the mass-transfer coefficient can then be obtained from that figure by following the route that was set out earlier in the chapter. It is important to note, however, that this equality is by no means universal, and there are situations in which it begins to break down. In particular, where form drag makes a contribution to the friction factor, the friction factor effectively includes an element that has no real counterpart on the mass-transfer side, and under those circumstances $j_D$ will tend to fall below $f$ / 2. Similarly, where the transfer rate becomes high enough to alter the boundary layer itself, the equality can again be expected to fail. So the check that has just been worked, with $f$ = 0.0064 and $j_D$ = 0.0032 at a Reynolds number of 20000, really only confirms the arithmetic of the analogy on that one pair of values, and it should not be taken as extending the analogy into cases involving form drag or high transfer rates.
target: The Chilton-Colburn analogy sets the mass-transfer factor $j_D$ equal to half the friction factor $f$, and the equality is the working form in which the analogy is used for design. A short check shows the arithmetic on values already in hand. At a Reynolds number of 20000, a measured friction factor $f$ of 0.0064 gives $j_D$ = 0.0032, half the friction factor, and a design calculation takes the mass-transfer coefficient from that figure by the route set out earlier in the chapter. The three transfer processes fall under one analogy because each is carried across the same boundary layer: momentum crosses it by friction, and mass crosses it by diffusion and convection together, so a measurement of the one process can be made to speak for the other wherever the layer behaves alike for both. The equality is not a law, and its range is the range of the conditions that produced it. The analogy rests on the boundary layer behaving the same way for momentum and for mass, and it fails where that behaviour separates. Where form drag contributes to the friction factor, $f$ carries a part that has no counterpart in mass transfer, and $j_D$ falls below $f$ / 2. Where the transfer rate is high enough to change the boundary layer itself, the equality again fails, in the same direction: the friction factor describes the flow that was measured, and the mass transfer is no longer the transfer of that flow. The check above therefore has a narrow use. It verifies the arithmetic of the analogy on one pair of values ($f$ = 0.0064, $j_D$ = 0.0032 at a Reynolds number of 20000); it does not extend the analogy to any case where form drag or a high transfer rate is in play, and a calculation that meets either condition needs its mass-transfer factor from measurement or from a correlation built for that case.

fact_base: Excerpt content: two groups report conflicting pressure drop values for the same material class; the excerpt weighs their test conditions. The excerpt reaches a limited preference and states the condition on which it rests.
input: Turning to the question of pressure drop, it is interesting to note that the picture presented by the literature is far from settled, and two groups working in this area report pressure drop values for the same class of material that are, quite frankly, difficult to reconcile with one another. Each set of results appears to be internally consistent and carefully obtained, and yet the two sets simply do not agree, which raises some important questions about what is actually being measured. Part of the difficulty is that pressure drop across a bed of the benchmark material is not really a property of the material in isolation; rather, it depends on how the bed has been packed and on the basis on which the gas flow has been stated, as well as on the condition of the feed, and the two reports differ in precisely these respects. A set of values measured on a loosely settled bed and a set measured on a consolidated bed are, in a very real sense, measurements of two different beds. It is also worth mentioning that IAST comes into the comparison only indirectly, through the loadings that the groups report alongside their pressure drop data, and it has nothing to say about the pressure drop itself, so the discrepancy would remain even if everyone agreed on the adsorption side of things. On balance, the most sensible reading is probably a conditional one: where the design case in question resembles one group's test conditions, that group's values are the ones to use, whereas where it resembles neither set of conditions, the honest position is that the benchmark material does not yet have a pressure drop measured for the duty in question.
target: Two groups report pressure drop values for the same material class, and the values conflict: each set, taken on its own terms, is consistent, and the sets do not agree. The disagreement is not resolved by counting papers or by averaging the sets, because the sets were not measured in the same way. Pressure drop across a bed of the benchmark material is a property of the bed as packed and of the gas as supplied, not of the material alone, and the reports differ on exactly those points: the packing of the bed, the basis on which the gas flow is stated, and the condition of the feed. A set measured on a loosely settled bed and a set measured on a consolidated bed are measurements of two different beds, and the conflict between them is in part a conflict of conditions. IAST enters the comparison only through the loadings the groups report alongside their pressure drops, and it defines nothing about the pressure drop itself; the discrepancy survives any agreement on the adsorption side. The preference the evidence supports is limited and rests on a stated condition. Where a design case resembles one group's test conditions (the packing and flow basis of the intended bed), that group's values govern, because they were measured on a bed of that kind. Where the design case resembles neither, neither set governs, and the benchmark material still lacks a pressure drop measured for the duty in question.
