fact_base: A flat firebrick wall of thickness 20 mm separates two process streams. Thermal conductivity of the wall is 1.1 W m-1 K-1 and the measured temperature difference across it is 332 K. Steady one-dimensional conduction gives a heat flux of 18260 W m-2. Surface (film) resistances are excluded from this estimate; including them lowers the flux.
input: In this worked example, we consider a flat firebrick wall with a thickness of 20 mm that separates two process streams, and our goal is to determine the steady heat flux passing through the wall. The thermal conductivity of the firebrick wall is 1.1 W m-1 K-1, and the temperature difference that has been measured across the wall is 332 K, which is a substantial driving force for heat transfer. Under steady, one-dimensional conditions, the heat flux can be calculated by multiplying the thermal conductivity by the temperature difference and dividing the result by the wall thickness. Converting the thickness into metres gives us 0.02 m, and substituting the values into the expression gives the heat flux as 1.1 × 332 / 0.02 = 18260 W m-2. It is important to note that this figure is obtained on a conduction-only basis. The surface (film) resistances on either side of the wall have been excluded from the estimate, and if they were included, the flux would be lower, because the films would add further resistance in series with the wall itself and the temperature difference of 332 K would be shared across a greater total resistance. So the calculated value of 18260 W m-2 should be understood as the flux associated with the 20 mm firebrick wall on its own, under the measured temperature difference of 332 K, rather than as the flux that would necessarily be observed across the complete boundary between the two process streams.
target: A flat firebrick wall of thickness 20 mm separates two process streams, and the worked quantity is the steady heat flux through the wall. The thermal conductivity of the wall is 1.1 W m-1 K-1. The measured temperature difference across the wall is 332 K. For steady one-dimensional conduction, the heat flux is the conductivity multiplied by the temperature difference and divided by the thickness. The thickness in metres is 0.02 m, and substitution gives the heat flux as 1.1 × 332 / 0.02 = 18260 W m-2. The result is a conduction-only figure. Surface (film) resistances are excluded from this estimate; including them lowers the flux, because each film adds a resistance in series with the resistance of the wall, and the same temperature difference of 332 K would then be shared across wall and films together. The heat flux of 18260 W m-2 therefore belongs to the wall alone, across the full 20 mm of firebrick, under a temperature difference of 332 K applied across the wall itself. A flux for the wall as it stands between the two streams, films included, would be smaller, and the size of the reduction is set by film resistances that this example does not carry. The example closes on the wall value, and the wall value is the one its inputs determine.

fact_base: A flat stainless steel wall of thickness 150 mm separates two process streams. Thermal conductivity of the wall is 16 W m-1 K-1 and the measured temperature difference across it is 248 K. Steady one-dimensional conduction gives a heat flux of 26453 W m-2. Surface (film) resistances are excluded from this estimate; including them lowers the flux.
input: In this worked example, we turn our attention to a flat stainless steel wall with a thickness of 150 mm that separates two process streams, and the quantity we are aiming to determine is the steady heat flux through the wall. The thermal conductivity of the stainless steel is 16 W m-1 K-1, and the temperature difference measured across the wall is 248 K, so we have all of the information we need in order to carry out the calculation. Assuming steady, one-dimensional conduction, the heat flux is obtained by multiplying the thermal conductivity by the temperature difference and then dividing by the thickness of the wall. The thickness expressed in metres is 0.15 m, and putting the numbers into the expression gives 16 × 248 / 0.15 = 26453 W m-2, which is the answer to the problem. It is worth emphasising that this is once again a conduction-only figure. The surface (film) resistances have been left out of the estimate, and including them would reduce the flux, since the films would sit in series with the wall and would absorb part of the overall temperature difference themselves. It is also worth noting that for a metal wall this particular exclusion can matter a great deal, because the wall's own resistance is comparatively small, so a film resistance of ordinary size represents a relatively large share of the total resistance. Consequently, the value of 26453 W m-2 really needs to be read as the flux for the 150 mm stainless steel wall under the 248 K temperature difference applied across the wall itself, and not as the flux that would arise across the assembled boundary between the two process streams, which would be noticeably lower.
target: A flat stainless steel wall of thickness 150 mm separates two process streams. The thermal conductivity of the wall is 16 W m-1 K-1, and the measured temperature difference across the wall is 248 K. The worked quantity is the steady heat flux through the wall under one-dimensional conduction. The heat flux is the conductivity multiplied by the temperature difference and divided by the thickness. With the thickness taken as 0.15 m, substitution gives 16 × 248 / 0.15 = 26453 W m-2. The figure is large because both factors that set it are large in the same direction: a high conductivity carries heat readily, and the full temperature difference is applied across the wall without sharing. The figure is a conduction-only figure. Surface (film) resistances are excluded from this estimate; including them lowers the flux, since the films stand in series with the wall and take part of the overall temperature difference. For a metal wall the exclusion matters more, not less: the wall's own resistance is small, so a film resistance of ordinary size is a larger share of the total, and the flux between the two streams as they stand would fall further below the stated value, in proportion, than the same exclusion would cause in a wall of low conductivity. The stated flux of 26453 W m-2 is therefore the value for the 150 mm stainless steel wall under a 248 K difference across the wall itself. No part of it should be read as the flux of the assembled boundary between the streams, where the films take their share of the difference and the wall takes only what is left. The example also fixes the meaning of its own answer: the flux belongs to the temperature difference stated for the wall, and any other difference, shared with films or measured at another place, belongs to a different calculation with a different result and a different use.

fact_base: A tutorial passage explains the Prandtl number to second-year students. Definition in words: the Prandtl number is the ratio of momentum diffusivity to thermal diffusivity. The passage must state what a value near 1 means and what a large value means, without inventing numerical examples.
input: The Prandtl number is a dimensionless quantity that plays a central role in heat transfer, and it can be defined as the ratio of momentum diffusivity to thermal diffusivity. To understand what this really means, it helps to think about what each of these diffusivities actually does. Momentum diffusivity is essentially a measure of how rapidly a difference in velocity is smoothed out within a flowing fluid, while thermal diffusivity is a measure of how rapidly a difference in temperature is smoothed out. The Prandtl number therefore brings these two tendencies together into a single figure that allows them to be compared directly. If the value is close to 1, this tells us that the two diffusivities are of a similar size, so momentum and heat spread through the fluid at broadly comparable rates, and the velocity field and the temperature field develop in a broadly similar way. At the other extreme, if the Prandtl number is large, momentum diffusivity is much greater than thermal diffusivity, which means that momentum spreads much more readily than heat does; the velocity field is smoothed out over distances over which the temperature field changes hardly at all, and a temperature difference can persist within a comparatively thin layer. It is important to note that, because the Prandtl number is a ratio, it does not by itself say anything about the actual size of either diffusivity, and two different fluids could in principle share the same Prandtl number while differing in both of the underlying diffusivities quite considerably. A Prandtl number of exactly 1 would represent the special case in which the two diffusivities are identical, and values progressively further above 1 represent cases in which the momentum diffusivity is progressively more dominant over its thermal counterpart.
target: The Prandtl number is the ratio of momentum diffusivity to thermal diffusivity. Momentum diffusivity measures how fast a velocity difference is evened out within a fluid; thermal diffusivity measures how fast a temperature difference is evened out. The Prandtl number compares the two rates for one fluid under one set of conditions. A value near 1 means the two rates are close: momentum and heat spread through the fluid at comparable speeds, and the velocity and temperature fields develop together, so a disturbance in either is smoothed over much the same distance. A large value means momentum diffusivity is much the larger of the two. Momentum then spreads far more readily than heat; the velocity field is evened out over distances across which the temperature field is barely smoothed, and a temperature difference persists in a layer much thinner than the layer across which the velocity changes. The number is a ratio, and it states nothing about either diffusivity on its own: two fluids can share a Prandtl number while differing in both diffusivities, because the number fixes only the proportion between them. What the proportion governs is the relative shape of the velocity and temperature fields, and that is the whole content of the definition. Read in that way, the Prandtl number sorts fluids by behaviour rather than by size: near 1, the two fields are alike in extent; well above 1, the temperature field is the confined one, and the velocity field reaches across ground the temperature field does not.

fact_base: Goal: compute the Reynolds number for water in a pipe and state the flow regime. The Reynolds number Re (dimensionless) is computed from density rho (kg m-3), mean velocity v (m s-1), pipe diameter D (m) and dynamic viscosity mu (Pa s) by Re = rho v D / mu. Water at 293 K: rho = 998 kg m-3, mu = 1.00 x 10-3 Pa s. Pipe diameter D = 0.05 m; mean velocity v = 1.9 m s-1. Worked result: Re = 94800 (computed as 998 x 1.9 x 0.05 / 0.001). Flow is laminar below Re = 2300 and turbulent above Re = 4000; between the two values the regime is transitional and is not assigned by the number alone.
input: In this example, we are going to calculate the Reynolds number for water flowing in a pipe, and then use the result to say what the flow regime is. The Reynolds number Re (dimensionless) is calculated from the density rho (kg m-3), the mean velocity v (m s-1), the pipe diameter D (m) and the dynamic viscosity mu (Pa s) by means of the expression Re = rho v D / mu. For water at 293 K, the density is rho = 998 kg m-3 and the viscosity is mu = 1.00 x 10-3 Pa s. The pipe diameter is D = 0.05 m and the mean velocity is v = 1.9 m s-1. If we substitute these values into the expression, the numerator works out at 998 x 1.9 x 0.05 = 94.81, and dividing this by the viscosity, taken as 0.001 Pa s, gives us Re = 94800. To decide the flow regime, we compare this value with the usual thresholds: the flow is laminar below Re = 2300 and turbulent above Re = 4000, while between these two values the regime is transitional and cannot be assigned from the number alone. Since our calculated value of 94800 is very much greater than 4000, the flow in this case is clearly turbulent, and the transitional band between 2300 and 4000 does not come into the decision at all. So the answer to the example is that the Reynolds number comes out at 94800 and the regime is turbulent, the value of 94800 lying far above the transitional band that begins at 2300.
target: The Reynolds number for water in a pipe is 94800, and the flow is turbulent. The Reynolds number Re (dimensionless) is computed from the density rho (kg m-3), the mean velocity v (m s-1), the pipe diameter D (m) and the dynamic viscosity mu (Pa s) by Re = rho v D / mu. Water at 293 K has rho = 998 kg m-3 and mu = 1.00 x 10-3 Pa s; the pipe diameter D is 0.05 m and the mean velocity v is 1.9 m s-1. Substitution gives the numerator as 998 x 1.9 x 0.05 = 94.81, and division by the viscosity, taken as 0.001 Pa s, gives Re = 94800. The regime is read from the thresholds. Flow is laminar below Re = 2300 and turbulent above Re = 4000; between the two values the regime is transitional and is not assigned by the number alone. The computed value, 94800, stands above the upper threshold by a wide margin, so the assignment does not rest on the transitional range at all: the value is in the turbulent region under the stated thresholds, and no part of the check depends on behaviour between 2300 and 4000. The check on the result is the threshold comparison itself. A value below 2300 would be laminar, a value between the thresholds would stay unassigned, and the value obtained, 94800, is turbulent. The example also shows the order in which such a check is made: the number is computed from the four stated quantities, each with its unit, and only then compared with the thresholds, because the thresholds are values of the same number and the comparison is meaningless until the number stands on the same basis. The threshold that decides this case is the upper one, 4000, and the computed value clears it without qualification.

fact_base: A food plant uses 1852 MWh of electricity per year in refrigeration. A heat-recovery retrofit is projected by the equipment vendor to save 16% of that use, a derived saving of 296 MWh per year at the vendor figure. Capital cost is $374k. At an electricity price of $0.1 per kWh, the derived annual saving is $30k and the derived simple payback is 12.5 years. The saving figure is a vendor projection and was not measured at this plant; refrigeration load in the summer peak month was not modelled. The recommendation is a metered trial on one of the three refrigeration lines before any capital decision. The plant engineer owns the trial.
input: This executive summary looks at a possible heat-recovery retrofit at a food plant and considers whether the project is ready to move forward. The plant currently uses 1852 MWh of electricity per year in refrigeration, which represents a very substantial part of its overall energy picture. According to the equipment vendor, the retrofit is projected to save 16% of that electricity use, which works out at a derived saving of 296 MWh per year at the vendor figure. The capital cost of the retrofit is $374k, and at an electricity price of $0.1 per kWh, the derived annual saving is $30k, giving a derived simple payback of 12.5 years, which is a long time over which to recover an investment of this size. It is important to note that the saving figure is a vendor projection and has not been measured at this plant, and it is also worth noting that the refrigeration load in the summer peak month has not been modelled, so there are open questions on both the size and the shape of the projected saving of 296 MWh per year. In light of all of this, the recommendation is that a metered trial should be carried out on one of the three refrigeration lines before any capital decision is taken, so that the projected saving can be tested against measured data; in other words, the plant would be committing $374k of capital in return for a derived annual saving of $30k, which is precisely why the payback stretches to 12.5 years and why the figures are being treated with some caution at this stage. The plant engineer owns the trial.
target: Recommendation: run a metered trial on one of the three refrigeration lines before any capital decision; the plant engineer owns the trial. The food plant uses 1852 MWh of electricity per year in refrigeration. A heat-recovery retrofit is projected by the equipment vendor to save 16% of that use, a derived saving of 296 MWh per year at the vendor figure. The capital cost is $374k. At an electricity price of $0.1 per kWh, the derived annual saving is $30k and the derived simple payback is 12.5 years. The payback states the weakness of the case as projected: 12.5 years is a long recovery for a figure that has not been measured. The saving is a vendor projection and was not measured at this plant, and refrigeration load in the summer peak month was not modelled, so the 296 MWh per year carries two open questions, its size at this plant and its shape across the year. A metered trial on one of the three refrigeration lines answers the first question on measured data and bounds the second, because a line under meter shows both the saving it makes and the months in which it makes it. Until the trial reports, the decision the figures support is the trial itself, not the retrofit. The capital decision would commit $374k against a derived annual saving of $30k that rests on a projection; the trial converts the projection into a measurement on one line before the commitment is made, and the plant engineer's ownership of the trial puts the measurement in the hands of the engineer who will have to run the retrofit if it follows.

fact_base: Excerpt content: the analogy between the transfer processes is stated, then qualified by the case where it fails. The excerpt works one short numerical check with numbers given inside the excerpt itself. The excerpt assumes the chapter's earlier definitions and adds none.
input: The Chilton-Colburn analogy is a very handy result at this point, because it allows us to connect the mass-transfer behaviour we are interested in with the friction behaviour that we already know about. What the Chilton-Colburn analogy says, in essence, is that $j_D$ is equal to half of the friction factor $f$, and we can quickly check the arithmetic of this on some values that are already in hand. At a Reynolds number of 20000, for instance, a friction factor $f$ of 0.0064 leads straight to $j_D$ = 0.0032, which is just half the friction factor. It is important to remember, however, that this equality only really holds where the boundary layer treats momentum transfer and mass transfer in the same sort of way. If form drag is contributing to $f$, then the friction factor contains an element that has no counterpart on the mass-transfer side, and $j_D$ will fall below $f$ / 2; and if the transfer rate is high enough to start changing the boundary layer itself, the equality will break down once again. So a check of this kind does no more than confirm the arithmetic on that single pair of values, and it certainly does not extend the analogy into any new territory.
target: The Chilton-Colburn analogy sets $j_D$ equal to half the friction factor $f$, and the equality is the form in which the analogy does its work. On values already in hand the arithmetic is direct: at a Reynolds number of 20000, a friction factor $f$ of 0.0064 gives $j_D$ = 0.0032. The equality holds only where the boundary layer treats momentum and mass alike. Where form drag contributes to $f$, the friction factor carries a part with no mass-transfer counterpart and $j_D$ falls below $f$ / 2; where the transfer rate is high enough to change the boundary layer, the equality fails again, for the same reason in another dress: the measured friction no longer describes the layer across which the mass is moving. A check of this kind verifies the arithmetic on one pair of values. It extends the analogy to no new case, and a case with form drag or a high transfer rate takes its mass-transfer factor from measurement, or from a correlation built for that case, rather than from the friction factor it happens to have. The analogy is used inside its range or not at all, and the statement of the range is part of the result the excerpt leaves on the page.

fact_base: Cost review of a returns flow: 737 km per trip at $1.6 per km, 857 trips per year. Annual transport cost is $1011k. Costs are carrier invoices for the last 12 months; empty running is included in the trip count.
input: In this cost review, we take a detailed look at the transportation costs associated with the returns flow, drawing on the carrier invoices from the last 12 months in order to build a comprehensive picture of what this flow is costing the business on an annual basis. The returns flow involves a substantial amount of vehicle movement: each individual trip covers a distance of 737 km, and the carrier charges a rate of $1.6 per km, which means that the derived cost of a single trip works out to $1179.2. Over the course of a full year, the business undertakes a total of 857 trips of this kind, covering a derived total distance of 631609 km, and when all of these elements are brought together, the annual transport cost comes to $1011k. It is important to note that the trip count on which this figure rests includes empty running, so the annual total does not relate solely to vehicles carrying returned goods; vehicles travelling empty are also captured within the 857 trips and are charged at the same $1.6 per km. Overall, the figure of $1011k therefore represents the full invoiced cost of operating the returns flow over the last 12 months, reflecting the combined effect of the distance per trip, the rate per kilometre, and the number of trips undertaken.
target: Returns transport costs $1011k a year. The figure comes from the carrier invoices for the last 12 months and covers the returns flow in full: 857 trips a year at 737 km per trip and $1.6 per km. Distance accounts for most of the total. The 857 trips cover a derived 631609 km a year, and each trip carries a derived cost of $1179.2. Three quantities set the total, and each stands on the invoice base: the trip count, the distance per trip, and the rate. A change in the annual figure has to enter through one of the three. The per-trip cost is the unit figure in the review: any comparison between carriers, or between the returns flow and an alternative arrangement, is made on that figure and on the trip count it multiplies. The trip count includes empty running. Empty kilometres are therefore paid for at the same $1.6 per km as loaded kilometres, and the $1011k is the cost of the returns flow as operated, not the cost of moving returned goods alone. No split of the total into a loaded part and an empty part can be read from the trip count. The evidence base is one year of carrier invoices. The review states the level of the cost over the last 12 months at the invoiced distance and rate. With no earlier period in the base, the review shows what the returns flow costs and not whether that cost is rising or falling.

fact_base: A continuous stirred-tank reactor runs a hydrolysis that is first order in the limiting reactant. The rate constant is 0.279 min-1 at the operating temperature and the mean residence time is 86 min. Steady-state conversion for an ideal CSTR is 96%. The estimate assumes perfect mixing and constant density; tracer tests on the actual vessel have not been run.
input: This worked example considers a continuous stirred-tank reactor, commonly referred to as a CSTR, which is being used to carry out a hydrolysis reaction that is first order in the limiting reactant. At the operating temperature, the rate constant for the reaction has a value of 0.279 min-1, and the mean residence time of the material inside the reactor is 86 min. When these values are applied to the ideal CSTR model, the steady-state conversion that is obtained is 96%, which represents a very high degree of conversion of the limiting reactant. It is worth bearing in mind, however, that this estimate is built on a set of idealising assumptions, in particular the assumption of perfect mixing throughout the vessel and the assumption that the density of the reacting mixture remains constant. In practice, real vessels can depart from this ideal behaviour, and it should be noted that tracer tests, which would reveal how the actual vessel behaves, have not been run on the vessel in question. The figure of 96% should therefore be understood as the conversion predicted for an ideal CSTR under the stated conditions, rather than as a measured performance figure for the real equipment.
target: Conversion in a continuous stirred-tank reactor (CSTR) running a hydrolysis that is first order in the limiting reactant is 96% at steady state. The rate constant (0.279 min-1 at the operating temperature) and the mean residence time (86 min) set the result: for first-order kinetics in an ideal CSTR, a rate constant and a residence time of this size leave only a small fraction of the limiting reactant unconverted, and the steady-state conversion follows from the two values together. Conversion here is the fraction of the limiting reactant consumed between the reactor inlet and the reactor outlet. Two assumptions carry the estimate. Mixing is taken as perfect, so the composition everywhere in the vessel equals the outlet composition, and the density is taken as constant along the reaction path. Perfect mixing is a statement about the vessel rather than the reaction: the incoming feed is dispersed through the vessel contents at once, and no part of the vessel holds material of a different age or composition from any other part. Both assumptions are built into the ideal CSTR model behind the estimate. Against the actual vessel, the estimate is unchecked. Tracer tests on the vessel have not been run, so its residence time distribution is unmeasured and any departure from perfect mixing is unknown. The 96% conversion is valid for the ideal CSTR at the stated rate constant and residence time; the conversion of the installed vessel stands or falls with mixing behaviour that has not been measured.

fact_base: A tutorial passage explains the pump affinity laws for a centrifugal pump at varying speed. The passage states the three proportionalities in words: flow with speed, head with speed squared, power with speed cubed. A worked check is included: doubling speed multiplies power by 8. No other numbers are introduced.
input: The pump affinity laws are a set of extremely useful relationships that describe how the performance of a centrifugal pump changes when its rotational speed is varied, and they are widely used by engineers who need to predict what a pump will do at a speed different from the one at which it was originally tested. In essence, the laws consist of three simple proportionalities. The flow delivered by the pump varies in direct proportion to the speed, so that if the speed is increased, the flow increases in exactly the same ratio. The head produced by the pump varies with the square of the speed, meaning that a change in speed has a considerably more pronounced effect on the head than it does on the flow. The power absorbed by the pump varies with the cube of the speed, which means that the effect on power is more dramatic still. A simple worked check helps to bring this point home: if the speed of the pump is doubled, the power does not merely double in line with the flow; because the power follows the cube of the speed, doubling the speed actually multiplies the power by 8. This is a striking result, and it underlines why even relatively modest increases in pump speed can have surprisingly large consequences for the power that has to be supplied.
target: Pump speed changes move flow, head, and power by fixed proportions, and the affinity laws state the three proportions for a centrifugal pump run at varying speed. Flow varies in direct proportion to speed: at twice the speed the same pump delivers twice the flow, and at half the speed half the flow. Head varies with the square of the speed, so a doubling of speed multiplies the head by the square of the doubling, a steeper response than the flow gives to the same change. Power varies with the cube of the speed, and the cube makes power the most speed-sensitive of the three quantities. The cube is not an accident of the set: power is built from flow and head together, since the pump does work on the flow it delivers against the head it raises, and a quantity formed from the other two carries the speed factors of both and a further factor of its own. A worked check fixes the size of the power effect. Doubling the speed multiplies the power by 8, the cube of the doubling applied to the power at the original speed. Flow and head from the same change grow by the doubling itself and by its square, and neither grows as fast as the power. Each proportion links corresponding operating points of the one pump: the impeller, the casing, and the liquid stay unchanged, and only the speed moves. Read that way, the laws answer a practical question directly. The duty of a known pump at a new speed follows from the duty already measured at a tested speed, with the power term setting the cost of any speed increase.

fact_base: Excerpt content: two groups report conflicting pressure drop values for the same material class; the excerpt weighs their test conditions. The excerpt reaches a limited preference and states the condition on which it rests.
input: It is also worth noting that the two groups whose results are discussed here report pressure drop values for the benchmark material that are in clear conflict with one another, and this disagreement cannot simply be brushed aside. On closer inspection, however, it becomes apparent that the conditions under which the two sets of measurements were obtained were by no means identical. In one case, the pressure drop was measured across a bed that had been freshly packed for each test, so that the reported values relate to the bed of the benchmark material itself, whereas in the other case the reported pressure drop was taken across the assembled contactor as a whole, meaning that the fittings and end sections through which the gas enters and leaves are also included within the figure. It should also be said that neither group appears to have been careless in its work, since each set of results is thoroughly consistent within itself, and the disagreement only emerges when the two sets are placed side by side. Given this difference, it is perhaps unsurprising that the second set of values sits consistently above the first. Taking these considerations into account, there is a reasonable case for preferring the first set of values when the purpose in hand is the design of a packed bed, although this preference clearly depends on the configuration to which the values are going to be applied.
target: Against that reading, the conflict in the reported pressure drop values for the benchmark material follows the test conditions rather than the material. Within its own runs each group reproduces its values closely, and the disagreement lives between the groups rather than inside either set of measurements. Neither set of values carries an obvious measurement fault; the two sets differ because the quantity measured was not the same quantity. One group packed a fresh bed for each test and took the pressure drop across the bed alone, so its values belong to the benchmark material in packed form. The other group took the pressure drop across the assembled contactor, and its values include the entry and exit fittings through which the gas passes before and after the bed. A drop measured over bed and fittings together stands above a drop measured over the bed alone, and the gap between the two reports has the size and the direction that difference in arrangement predicts. For design of a packed bed, the bed-only values are the safer basis: the fittings of a new design are the designer's own, and a figure that already contains another contactor's fittings cannot be separated after the fact. The preference is limited to that use. Where the contactor as assembled sets the pressure drop, the whole-contactor values are the relevant ones, and the bed-only set understates what the gas meets in service.

fact_base: A tutorial passage explains feedback control through a temperature loop on a process vessel. The passage covers the sensor, the controller, the final element and the sign of the feedback, in that order. No tuning numbers are given; the passage explains structure, not settings.
input: Feedback control can be understood very clearly by looking at a temperature loop on a process vessel, in which a number of distinct elements work together in order to keep the temperature of the vessel at the desired value. The first element in the loop is the sensor, which is responsible for measuring the temperature inside the vessel and for turning that measurement into a signal that can be used by the rest of the loop. This signal is passed to the controller, which compares the measured temperature with the set point and works out how far the temperature has drifted away from where it ought to be. Acting on that difference, the controller sends an instruction to the final element, which is typically a valve that adjusts the flow of the heating or cooling medium, thereby changing the amount of heat being added to or removed from the vessel. A particularly important feature of the arrangement is the sign of the feedback, which is negative: the action taken by the loop opposes the change that triggered it, so that when the temperature rises above the set point the loop responds by reducing the heating, and when the temperature falls it responds by increasing it. The present passage is concerned with the structure of the loop rather than with its settings, and no tuning numbers are involved. It is this continuous circulation of information and action around the loop, running from measurement through comparison to correction and then back again to a fresh measurement, that distinguishes feedback control from a simple one-off adjustment carried out by an operator and left at that.
target: A temperature loop on a process vessel shows the structure of feedback control in its smallest complete form: a sensor, a controller, and a final element, joined so that the loop's action opposes the change it detects. The sensor measures the temperature inside the vessel. Measurement is the loop's only contact with the process, and the signal the sensor sends onward stands for the vessel temperature in everything the loop does next. The controller receives the measurement and compares it with the set point, the temperature the vessel is to be held at. The comparison gives a difference, in size and in direction, and the controller's output is set by that difference: no difference, no call for action; a growing difference, a stronger call. The comparison is continuous rather than occasional: the measurement keeps arriving, the difference keeps being formed, and the output keeps changing for as long as any difference remains. The final element acts on the vessel. In a temperature loop the final element is a valve on the line that supplies the heating or cooling medium, and the valve's movement changes the heat flow into the vessel in the direction the controller has called for. The valve does not simply switch the heat flow on and off; it takes the position the controller's output sets, and the vessel temperature answers through the process itself. The sign of the feedback closes the loop. Feedback here is negative, meaning the action opposes the deviation that produced it: a temperature above the set point draws a reduction in heating, and a temperature below it draws an increase. Opposition is what makes the arrangement a control loop rather than a sequence of adjustments, because each action works against the error that remains. The loop's settings, how strongly the controller answers a given difference, belong to tuning and are a separate matter from the structure set out here.

fact_base: Adsorption of a dye from water on a zeolite 13X sample was measured in batch tests at 298 K. The fitted Langmuir capacity was 212 mg of dye per gram of adsorbent at pH 5. At an adsorbent dose of 0.8 g L-1, removal after 120 min was 87% of the initial dye concentration of 50 mg L-1. The Langmuir fit is reported for pH 5 only; capacity at other pH values was not measured.
input: Adsorption of a dye from water on a zeolite 13X sample was measured in batch tests at 298 K. In a batch test a known mass of adsorbent is held in contact with the dye solution and the concentration is followed as uptake proceeds, so each test gives both the rate at which the dye leaves the water and the loading the adsorbent reaches. The fitted Langmuir capacity was 212 mg of dye per gram of adsorbent at pH 5. The capacity is a parameter of the Langmuir fit, not a single measured loading: it is the loading the fitted relation approaches as the concentration rises, and it summarises the whole set of equilibrium points at pH 5 in one number. Removal in a single test depends on how much adsorbent is present. At an adsorbent dose of 0.8 g L-1, removal after 120 min was 87% of the initial dye concentration of 50 mg L-1. The two figures answer different questions. The capacity states what the zeolite 13X can hold at equilibrium under the fitted relation, while the removal states what one dose achieved in 120 min from one starting concentration. The Langmuir fit is reported for pH 5 only; capacity at other pH values was not measured. The 212 mg g-1 figure is therefore a pH 5 result, and adsorption performance away from pH 5 is not established by these tests.

fact_base: A tutorial passage explains absolute and relative error through a flow measurement. Worked figures: reading 175 units, tolerance 0.5% of reading, so the absolute error is 0.88 units. The passage distinguishes error from uncertainty and does not merge the two terms.
input: When a flow measurement is made, it is very important to have a clear understanding of the error that may be present in the reading, and this example uses a flow measurement in order to explain the difference between absolute error and relative error, as well as the way in which both of these differ from uncertainty. The absolute error is simply the size of the difference between the reading given by the instrument and the true value of the flow, and it is expressed in the same units as the measurement itself. Suppose, for example, that the reading is 175 units and that the tolerance on the instrument is 0.5% of the reading; the absolute error is then given by 0.5% of 175, which comes to 0.88 units. The relative error, by contrast, expresses that same error as a fraction of the reading, and in this case it is 0.5%. Uncertainty is a rather different idea, and it should not be confused with error, even though the two words are often used interchangeably in everyday speech. Whereas error belongs to one particular measurement and describes how far that reading lies from the true value, uncertainty describes the spread of values that could reasonably be associated with the measurement, and it characterises the doubt that remains about the result even when the measurement has been carried out with great care. To put the matter concretely, the absolute error of 0.88 units attached to a reading of 175 units is the very same error that the relative form describes, and stating the error as 0.88 units ties it to that particular reading and to no other.
target: Error in a flow measurement comes in two forms, absolute and relative, and a single worked case fixes both. Error is the difference between the reading an instrument gives and the true value of the flow. The absolute error states that difference in the units of the measurement itself. The relative error states the same difference as a fraction of the reading, most often as a percentage of the reading. A reading of 175 units from an instrument with a tolerance of 0.5% of reading carries the two forms together. The tolerance gives the relative error directly, 0.5% of the reading. The absolute error is 0.5% of 175 units, which is 0.88 units. One error, stated twice: as a percentage it travels from one reading to another of the same instrument, while as 0.88 units it belongs to the reading of 175 units and to no other. Uncertainty is a separate term and is not merged with error here. Error attaches to a single measurement and names its distance from the true value, a distance that cannot itself be measured once the reading is taken. Uncertainty attaches to the result as a statement of spread: the range of values that could reasonably be assigned to the flow, given the instrument and the conditions of the measurement. An error is a difference; an uncertainty is a dispersion, and the worked case's 0.88 units is an error, not an uncertainty. The distinction matters whenever readings are reported together, because a percentage can be carried from one reading of an instrument to the next, while an absolute figure stays behind with the reading it came from.

fact_base: A tutorial passage explains representative sampling of an effluent stream. The passage covers where samples are taken, how many increments form one sample, and why a single grab sample misleads. No numerical limits are quoted; regulatory limits belong to the site's permit, not to the passage.
input: In order for a sample of an effluent stream to be genuinely useful, it must be representative of the stream as a whole, and achieving this is by no means a trivial matter. A great deal depends, first of all, on where the sample is actually taken from. If the sample is drawn from a stagnant side tap, or from a quiet corner where the effluent is barely moving, what ends up in the sample bottle may bear very little resemblance to the effluent that is flowing through the main line, and a sampling point located in a well-mixed, flowing part of the stream is therefore strongly to be preferred. Just as importantly, a single sample is not usually collected in one go; instead, one sample is built up from a number of separate increments that are taken over the period which the sample is intended to represent and then combined together. The number of increments that form one sample depends on how variable the stream is expected to be, with a more variable stream calling for more increments spread more widely across the period. A single grab sample, taken at one moment and in one place, can be seriously misleading, because the composition of an effluent stream changes over time as production varies and as batch operations come and go; a grab sample may catch the stream at an unusual peak or in an unrepresentative trough and then present that moment as if it were the whole picture. Finally, it should be noted that no numerical limits are quoted in this passage, since regulatory limits of that kind are set by the permit for the individual site rather than by any general discussion.
target: A sample of an effluent stream has one job: to stand for the stream over the period the result will be applied to. Representativeness is fixed by three choices, where the sample is taken, how its increments are spread, and what a single grab sample is never asked to do. The sampling point belongs in the flowing, mixed part of the stream. Effluent drawn from a stagnant side tap or a quiet corner of a channel has sat apart from the flow, and its composition is the composition of that corner, not of the discharge. A point in the main line, where the stream is moving and mixed, gives the increments a chance to match the stream they represent. One sample is built from increments. Each increment is a small portion taken at its own moment, and the increments are combined into the single sample that goes for analysis. How many increments form one sample follows the variability of the stream: a steady stream needs few, a stream that swings with production needs increments spread across the whole period, so that peaks and troughs enter the sample in proportion to their duration. A grab sample misleads by construction. One portion, taken at one moment, records the stream as it was at that moment, and an effluent stream changes from hour to hour as batches discharge and processes start and stop. The grab sample may land on a peak or in a trough and be reported as the stream's normal state. No numerical limits are quoted here; regulatory limits for an effluent are set in the permit for the site, and the permit is not part of this passage.
