fact_base: A vapour-compression unit serves a process chiller, evaporating at -25 °C and condensing at 35 °C. The Carnot coefficient of performance between these temperatures is 4.13; the installed unit achieves 1.8. The achieved value is from the manufacturer's test at full load; part-load performance is not stated.
input: This worked example looks at a vapour-compression refrigeration unit that serves a process chiller, evaporating at -25 °C and condensing at 35 °C, and it compares the performance that the unit actually achieves with the best performance that could possibly be achieved between the same two temperatures. The best possible performance is given by the Carnot coefficient of performance, 4.13 in this case, and in order to calculate it the temperatures must first of all be converted to the absolute scale. Adding 273 to each temperature gives 248 K for the evaporating temperature and 308 K for the condensing temperature, a difference of 60 K between them. The Carnot coefficient of performance is the evaporating temperature divided by this difference, so it comes to 248 divided by 60, which is 4.13. The installed unit, by comparison, achieves a coefficient of performance of only 1.8, a figure that is taken from the manufacturer's test carried out at full load. It can be seen that the achieved value of 1.8 lies well below the Carnot value of 4.13, as it must do, since no real machine can exceed the Carnot limit. Finally, it should be noted that the manufacturer's figure relates to full-load operation only, and the performance of the unit at part load is not stated, so nothing can be said about how the unit performs away from the full-load condition. It is the 1.8 from the manufacturer's test, and not the ideal figure, that a designer would carry into an estimate of the chiller duty, and the shortfall of the 1.8 below the ideal value is the margin absorbed by the losses of the real machine.
target: A vapour-compression unit serving a process chiller evaporates at -25 °C and condenses at 35 °C. Between those two temperatures the Carnot coefficient of performance (COP) is 4.13, and the installed unit achieves 1.8. The coefficient of performance states the duty obtained for the work supplied: the heat removed at the evaporating side, divided by the work the compressor takes in. A higher figure means more cooling bought with the same work, and the measure allows machines of different sizes to be compared on equal terms, because both the duty and the work scale with the size of the unit while their ratio does not. The Carnot figure is calculated on the absolute scale. Adding 273 to each temperature gives an evaporating temperature of 248 K and a condensing temperature of 308 K, a difference of 60 K. The Carnot COP is the evaporating temperature divided by the difference between the two temperatures: 248 divided by 60, which is 4.13. No machine working between the same temperatures can exceed that value. The achieved COP of 1.8 comes from the manufacturer's test at full load. Set against the Carnot value, the comparison checks the result before it is used: 1.8 lies below 4.13, as the second law requires, and the gap between the two values is the performance the real cycle loses to the irreversibilities the Carnot cycle does not have. The scope of the achieved figure is narrow. Part-load performance is not stated, and the manufacturer's test says nothing about operation away from full load. The 1.8 is a full-load value for the stated evaporating and condensing temperatures; a duty at other temperatures, or at part load, needs its own figure and does not inherit this one. For the chiller duty the figure to carry forward is the achieved one, with its full-load condition attached to it. The Carnot value serves as the reference the achieved figure is judged against, and the two values are not interchangeable in a duty calculation.

subtype: worked example with equation: friction loss
fact_base: Water at 293 K flows in a horizontal pipe. The density $\rho$ is 998 kg m-3. Mean velocity $v$ is 1.6 m s-1, pipe diameter $D$ is 0.08 m, pipe length $L$ is 70 m and the Darcy friction factor $f$ is 0.02. The friction pressure drop is 22.4 kPa.
input:
In this example we are going to work through the calculation of the friction pressure drop for water flowing through a horizontal pipe. The water is at 293 K, and the relevant data are as follows: the density $\rho$ is 998 kg m-3, the mean velocity $v$ is 1.6 m s-1, the pipe diameter $D$ is 0.08 m, the pipe length $L$ is 70 m, and the Darcy friction factor $f$ is 0.02. Because the pipe is horizontal, there is no change in elevation to take into account, and the pressure drop is due to friction alone. The relationship that is used for this calculation is the Darcy relation, which is written as

$$\Delta P = f \frac{L}{D} \frac{\rho v^2}{2}$$

where $\Delta P$ is the friction pressure drop, $f$ is the Darcy friction factor, $L$ and $D$ are the pipe length and diameter, $\rho$ is the density, and $v$ is the mean velocity. It is helpful to evaluate the separate parts of the expression before bringing them together. The ratio of length to diameter, $L$ divided by $D$, comes to 875, and the square of the velocity, $v$ squared, is 2.56, so that the dynamic pressure, $\rho$ multiplied by $v$ squared and divided by two, works out to 1277.44 Pa. Finally, multiplying the friction factor 0.02 by 875 and by 1277.44 Pa gives the friction pressure drop, which is 22.4 kPa. The value of 22.4 kPa is therefore the pressure that has to be supplied in order to overcome friction in this pipe under the stated conditions.
target:
The friction pressure drop for water in a horizontal pipe is 22.4 kPa. The density $\rho$ is 998 kg m-3 for water at 293 K, the mean velocity $v$ is 1.6 m s-1, the pipe diameter $D$ is 0.08 m, the pipe length $L$ is 70 m, and the Darcy friction factor $f$ is 0.02. The pipe is horizontal, so the pressure drop is friction loss alone and no elevation term enters. The Darcy relation gives the drop as

$$\Delta P = f \frac{L}{D} \frac{\rho v^2}{2}$$

where $\Delta P$ denotes the friction pressure drop, $f$ the Darcy friction factor, $L$ the pipe length, $D$ the pipe diameter, $\rho$ the density, and $v$ the mean velocity, each in the unit stated with it above. The two grouped factors are evaluated before the product is taken. $L$ divided by $D$ is 875. The dynamic pressure, $\rho$ times $v$ squared over two, is 1277.44 Pa, with $v$ squared equal to 2.56. Substitution gives $\Delta P$ as 0.02 multiplied by 875 and by 1277.44 Pa, which is 22.4 kPa. The relation also shows where the size of the result comes from: the length-to-diameter ratio multiplies a dynamic pressure set by the velocity, so the velocity is the term a change of duty moves first and most strongly, acting through its square, while a longer pipe raises the drop in simple proportion to the length added. The result holds for the stated velocity and pipe; a longer pipe or a higher velocity raises the drop through the same relation.

fact_base: Liquid-liquid extraction recovers acetic acid from an aqueous stream into an organic solvent. The distribution coefficient (organic over aqueous) is 0.53 at 25 °C and the design uses 7 countercurrent stages. Predicted recovery is 99% of the acetic acid in the feed. The prediction assumes equilibrium stages and negligible mutual solubility; neither has been checked on the actual solvents.
input: Liquid-liquid extraction is a widely used separation technique, and in the case considered here it is being applied in order to recover acetic acid from an aqueous stream by contacting the stream with an organic solvent into which the acetic acid preferentially passes. One of the key quantities that characterises the system is the distribution coefficient, which is defined as the ratio of the concentration of acetic acid in the organic phase to its concentration in the aqueous phase when the two phases are in equilibrium with one another. For this system the distribution coefficient has a value of 0.53 at 25 °C, which means that at equilibrium the concentration in the aqueous phase is actually the higher of the two. The design that has been developed for this separation makes use of 7 countercurrent stages, and the predicted recovery that is obtained from the design calculation is 99% of the acetic acid present in the feed, which is a very high level of recovery. It is important to appreciate, however, that this prediction rests on certain assumptions that have been built into the calculation, most notably the assumption that every stage behaves as an equilibrium stage and the assumption that the mutual solubility of the two liquid phases is negligible. Neither of these assumptions has yet been checked against the actual solvents that would be used, and so the predicted figure should be treated with an appropriate degree of caution. With a distribution coefficient of 0.53, the solvent does not take up the acid strongly in any single contact, and a recovery of 99% is an ambitious figure to reach on that basis; the predicted 99% depends entirely on the staging delivering what the equilibrium assumption promises at every step.
target: Liquid-liquid extraction recovers acetic acid from an aqueous stream into an organic solvent. The distribution coefficient, the concentration of acetic acid in the organic phase divided by its concentration in the aqueous phase at equilibrium, is 0.53 at 25 °C. A coefficient below unity fixes the character of the separation: at equilibrium the aqueous phase holds the higher concentration, and recovery has to be built from repeated contact rather than from a strong preference of the solute for the solvent. The design uses 7 countercurrent stages. Across the stage sequence the predicted recovery is 99% of the acetic acid in the feed. Countercurrent contact is what makes a high recovery compatible with a coefficient of 0.53, because the leanest solvent meets the most depleted aqueous stream and the driving force is held up along the whole cascade. Recovery here is a fraction of the feed: it states how much of the acetic acid entering in the aqueous stream leaves in the organic stream, and the part not recovered leaves with the treated aqueous stream. A design can therefore be read at two levels, the coefficient fixing what one contact can do and the stage count fixing how far the sequence of contacts carries the separation. The prediction carries its assumptions with it. Every stage is treated as an equilibrium stage, and the mutual solubility of the two phases is treated as negligible. Under those two assumptions the stage calculation gives 99%. Neither assumption has been checked on the actual solvents. A real stage that falls short of equilibrium, or a solvent pair with appreciable mutual solubility, moves the recovery away from the predicted value in a direction the calculation does not test. The 99% recovery is a model result for the stated coefficient, temperature, and stage count; performance of the extraction on the actual solvents is unmeasured.

fact_base: The rate constant k (s-1) of a first-order liquid-phase reaction was measured at two temperatures. At 300 K, k = 0.077 s-1. At 340 K, k = 2.091 s-1, computed from the Arrhenius relation with activation energy 70 kJ mol-1 as a derived value. Each temperature was measured in triplicate; the relative standard deviation of k was 4%. Above 340 K the solvent evaporated during sampling, so no rate constant is reported above 340 K.
input: The rate constant $k$ (s-1) of a first-order liquid-phase reaction was measured at two temperatures, namely at 300 K and at 340 K, in order to establish how the constant responds when the temperature at which the reaction is carried out is changed. At 300 K, $k$ = 0.077 s-1. At 340 K, $k$ = 2.091 s-1, and it should be made clear that this second value was computed from the Arrhenius relation with an activation energy of 70 kJ mol-1, so that it is presented as a derived value. Each temperature was measured in triplicate, and the relative standard deviation of $k$ was 4%, which gives an indication of the consistency that was obtained across the repeated measurements at each of the temperatures studied. It is also important to highlight that above 340 K the solvent evaporated during sampling, and because of this difficulty no rate constant is reported above 340 K. The consequence of this limitation is that the results which are available relate only to the temperatures that could actually be studied, and anyone wishing to use these figures should be aware that the behaviour of the reaction at temperatures beyond the studied interval has not been characterised here and cannot be inferred from the reported pair of values without stepping outside the evidence that the measurements provide. The triplicate measurements, for their part, serve to show that the values obtained at each temperature were not isolated readings but were reproduced across repeated measurements under the same conditions.
target: The rate constant $k$ (s-1) of a first-order liquid-phase reaction was measured at 300 K and at 340 K. At 300 K, $k$ = 0.077 s-1. At 340 K, $k$ = 2.091 s-1; the value at the higher temperature is a derived value, computed from the Arrhenius relation with an activation energy of 70 kJ mol-1 and presented as a derived value. Each temperature was measured in triplicate, and the relative standard deviation of $k$ was 4%. Above 340 K the solvent evaporated during sampling, so no rate constant is reported above 340 K. The pair of values therefore rests on different footing at its two ends. The lower value is a direct measurement, repeated in triplicate, with the stated relative standard deviation. The upper value carries that measurement forward through the Arrhenius relation at the stated activation energy, and its standing depends on the relation and on the activation energy as much as on the measurement itself. The evaporation limit is a limit on sampling, not on the reaction: the reaction continues above the studied interval, but the sampling method fails there, and the record stops where the method stops. A user of these figures who needs a constant beyond the interval must obtain it by another sampling route, because the present record offers no measured point against which an extrapolation could be checked. The record is also silent on the direction in which sampling failed first: evaporation during sampling is stated as the operative difficulty, and the passage does not separate the effect of the solvent loss on the sample from any effect on the reaction mixture itself. What the record supports is the pair of constants, the precision attached to the measurements, the derived standing of the upper value, and the stated reason for the absence of any higher point.

fact_base: A tutorial passage explains the Nusselt number to second-year students. Definition in words: the Nusselt number is the ratio of convective to conductive heat transfer at a surface. The passage must state what a value near 1 means and what a large value means, without inventing numerical examples.
input: The Nusselt number is a dimensionless quantity that is widely used in the study of heat transfer, and it can be understood as the ratio of convective to conductive heat transfer at a surface. What this means, in practical terms, is that the number provides a way of comparing how effectively heat is carried away from a surface by the movement of a fluid with how effectively that same heat would be transferred by conduction through a stationary layer of fluid resting against the surface. When the Nusselt number has a value near 1, it tells us that convection and conduction are contributing at roughly comparable levels, so the moving fluid is not enhancing the transfer very much beyond what conduction alone would be able to achieve. When, on the other hand, the Nusselt number takes a large value, it indicates that convection is the dominant mechanism, and that the movement of the fluid is responsible for the great majority of the heat transferred at the surface, with conduction through the near-surface layer playing a comparatively minor role. It is worth keeping in mind that the number, being a ratio, is concerned with the relative importance of the two mechanisms, and it does not by itself say anything about how large either rate of transfer actually is in absolute terms, which is a point that is often overlooked by students who are meeting the quantity for the first time.
target: The Nusselt number is the ratio of convective to conductive heat transfer at a surface. Convection is transfer by a moving fluid; conduction is transfer through a stationary layer. The Nusselt number compares the two rates for the same surface. A value near 1 means the two rates are comparable: the moving fluid transfers heat at about the rate conduction alone would give, and fluid motion adds little to the transfer at the surface. A large value means convection dominates: the moving fluid carries most of the heat transferred at the surface, and conduction through the near-surface layer accounts for a small part of the total. The number is a ratio, and a ratio states a balance, not a magnitude. A surface can show a large Nusselt number while the absolute rate of transfer at that surface is low, because the conductive rate it is compared against is lower still. A surface can equally show a modest value while the absolute rate is high, because both mechanisms are then contributing strongly and the comparison between them stays close. The teaching point of the number is the identification of the governing mechanism. Where convection dominates, an account of the transfer stands or falls on its description of the fluid motion. Where the two mechanisms are comparable, the conduction description of the layer next to the surface carries the same weight, and neglecting it misstates the transfer even if the convection description is exact. The number also disciplines comparison between cases: two surfaces are compared through it only when the comparison is restated as a comparison of balances, never as a comparison of rates.

fact_base: A flat firebrick wall of thickness 12 mm separates two process streams. Thermal conductivity of the wall is 1.1 W m-1 K-1 and the measured temperature difference across it is 147 K. Steady one-dimensional conduction gives a heat flux of 13475 W m-2. Surface (film) resistances are excluded from this estimate; including them lowers the flux.
input: In this worked example, we consider a flat firebrick wall that has a thickness of 12 mm and that separates two process streams from one another. The thermal conductivity of the wall is 1.1 W m-1 K-1, and the measured temperature difference across the wall is 147 K. If the conduction through the wall is assumed to be steady and one-dimensional, the heat flux can be calculated from these quantities, and the calculation gives a heat flux of 13475 W m-2. It is important to note, however, that surface (film) resistances have not been included in this estimate, and if those resistances were in fact taken into account, the heat flux would come out lower than the value reported here. The example is therefore concerned only with the resistance that the wall itself offers to the passage of heat, and the temperatures that are used are the temperatures at the two faces of the wall rather than the temperatures of the streams on either side of it. Anyone applying the result should keep that distinction in mind, because the streams themselves are separated from the wall faces by the very films that the calculation sets aside, and the temperature drop across those films is additional to the drop across the wall that the example evaluates. It should also be appreciated that the example treats the wall as a slab of uniform material with the same properties throughout its thickness, and it treats the temperatures at its faces as though they were uniform over the whole of each face, neither of which is exactly true of a real installation, where the streams may not wash every part of the surface evenly and where the brickwork itself may vary from place to place in its composition and in the condition of its joints.
target: A flat firebrick wall of thickness 12 mm separates two process streams. The thermal conductivity $k$ of the wall is 1.1 W m-1 K-1, and the measured temperature difference $\Delta T$ across the wall is 147 K. For steady one-dimensional conduction, the heat flux $q$ is $k$ multiplied by $\Delta T$ and divided by the wall thickness, and substitution gives $q$ = 13475 W m-2. Surface (film) resistances are excluded from this estimate; including them lowers the flux. The result is the flux carried by conduction within the brick, at the measured difference between the wall faces. The two assumptions carry the calculation. Steadiness means the face temperatures and the flux do not change with time, so the value describes a wall that has settled into its operating state, not a wall still warming or cooling. One-dimensional conduction means the heat flows straight through the thickness, with no sideways spreading, which holds where the wall is wide compared with its thickness and the face temperatures are uniform. The films excluded from the estimate stand between the streams and the faces. In a complete calculation they appear as further resistances in series with the wall, the same flux passes through each element, and the temperature difference available to drive heat across the brick is then smaller than the difference between the streams. The stated flux is therefore an upper value for the assembly as a whole, reached only in the limit where the films offer no resistance at all. The check on the calculation is internal: the flux, the conductivity, and the temperature difference stand in the proportion the relation requires for the stated thickness, and a reader who divides the product of conductivity and temperature difference by the thickness recovers the stated flux from the stated inputs. The example makes no claim about the streams. Their temperatures, flow, and surface state belong to the film calculation set aside, and the flux in service is set by wall and films together, each taking its share of the overall temperature difference.

fact_base: Project proposal for a rooftop solar installation, in four sections: case, costs, schedule, and decision requested. Capital cost is $1031k with a 7-year appraisal horizon. The schedule section gives a start one quarter after approval; no contractor is named. The decision requested is approval to proceed to detailed design, not to construction.
input:
# Rooftop solar installation: project proposal

## Case

This proposal sets out the case for installing a rooftop solar installation on the building, and it is intended to provide the reader with a comprehensive overview of the background to the project, the reasoning that supports it, and the various considerations that have ultimately led to the recommendation that is being put forward here. The building has a roof that is currently not being used for the generation of electricity, and it is felt that this represents something of a missed opportunity, in the sense that the same roof area could potentially be used to generate electricity on the site where that electricity is used. Rooftop generation of this kind has the advantage that the electricity is produced at the point of use, and the installation makes use of an existing surface rather than requiring additional land to be taken up for the purpose. The case, therefore, is essentially that the site already possesses a suitable surface, that the technology for generating electricity on such a surface is well established and widely deployed, and that a project of this nature would allow the organisation to generate a portion of its electricity on its own premises rather than relying entirely on supplies brought in from outside. It should also be noted that the case being made at this stage is a case for proceeding with the next stage of work on the project, and it is not being suggested that every detail of the installation has already been settled or that the organisation is in a position to commit itself to the construction of the installation on the basis of the information that is currently available. A considerable amount of further work would still need to be undertaken before any such commitment could responsibly be made, and the purpose of the material that follows is to explain what that further work is and why it is considered to be worth doing.

## Costs

In terms of the costs of the project, the headline figure that has been arrived at at this preliminary stage is a capital cost of $1031k, and this figure should be regarded as the central figure around which the financial appraisal of the project has been structured. The appraisal of the project has been carried out over a 7-year appraisal horizon, and this horizon provides the frame within which the costs of the proposal have been considered for the purposes of this document. It is worth emphasising that the capital cost quoted here is the figure that is available at this early stage of the project's development, and figures of this kind are inevitably subject to refinement as the design of the installation is developed in greater detail and as the various elements that will make up the installation are specified more precisely. For that reason, the costs section of this proposal should be read as presenting the order of the financial commitment that the detailed design stage would be working with, rather than as presenting a final and fixed price for the completed installation. The purpose of setting out the capital cost and the appraisal horizon together is to give the reader a clear sense of the scale of the proposal, and to make it possible to judge whether a commitment of this scale is one that the organisation wishes to explore further through the detailed design work that is being requested. It is also intended that the detailed design stage, if it is approved, will return to the question of costs and will present them in a more developed form, at which point a further decision can be taken in the light of that more detailed information.

## Schedule

Turning to the question of the schedule for the project, the intention is that work would be able to start one quarter after approval is given, and this timing should be understood as the planned starting point for the next stage of the work rather than as a guaranteed date that has been fixed with any external party. At this stage of the proceedings, no contractor is named in this proposal, and no commitment has been entered into with any contractor in relation to this project, so the schedule that is presented here is necessarily expressed in terms of the organisation's own approval process rather than in terms of dates that have been agreed elsewhere. The interval of one quarter between approval and the start of work is intended to allow the necessary internal arrangements to be put in place in an orderly way, so that the detailed design work, when it begins, can proceed on a properly prepared footing. It should be appreciated that the schedule beyond that starting point has not been developed in detail in this document, precisely because the detailed sequencing of the work is itself one of the products that the detailed design stage would be expected to produce. The reader is therefore asked to note the proposed starting interval, and to treat the remainder of the programme as a matter that will be reported back once the detailed design has been undertaken and the associated planning has been carried out.

## Decision requested

In conclusion, the decision that is being requested by this proposal is approval to proceed to detailed design, and it is important to be clear that what is being asked for is not approval to proceed to construction. These are two quite separate decisions, and the distinction between them is a significant one, because the detailed design stage is the stage at which the open questions that have been identified in this document can be worked through and at which the costs and the schedule can be placed on a firmer footing. By approving the move to detailed design, the reader would be authorising the next stage of investigation and development work, and would not be committing the organisation to building the installation, which would remain a matter for a separate and subsequent decision taken in the light of the detailed design and its findings. It is hoped that the material set out above provides a sufficient basis for that decision to be taken, and the recommendation is therefore that approval to proceed to detailed design be granted, with the question of construction reserved for a later stage once the detailed design work has been completed and reported.
target:
# Rooftop solar installation: project proposal

## Case

Approval is requested to proceed to detailed design for a rooftop solar installation. Construction is not requested. The building has a roof that is not used to generate electricity. Generation on that roof would produce electricity at the point of use and would use an existing surface; no additional land is required. The case for the next stage rests on those two properties of the site and on the state of the design: the surface is available, the technology is established, and the open questions are questions of design detail rather than of principle. The case is not a case for construction. The installation is not yet specified in detail, the costs stand at a preliminary figure, and the schedule is expressed relative to approval. Each of those items is a product of the detailed design stage. The proposal therefore asks for the stage that settles them, and it holds the construction decision separate, to be taken on the detailed design and its costs when they are reported. Nothing in the case depends on a benefit that the detailed design has not yet established. The roof area, the point of use, and the absence of a land requirement are properties of the site as it stands. The generation that the installation would deliver, the layout that the roof can carry, and the connection arrangements are not properties of the site as it stands, and this proposal does not state them. A reader who accepts the case accepts a narrower proposition than a reader who approves a construction project: that a site with an unused roof at the point of use justifies the cost of a detailed design. The alternative to the detailed design is a decision taken on preliminary figures, and the preliminary figures in the costs section show why that alternative is weak. The capital figure is a single estimate at an early stage. The appraisal horizon is stated so that the scale of the commitment can be judged, not so that a return can be asserted. Where a proposal of this kind is refused at the design stage, the refusal is normally on scale or on priority, and both grounds are visible in this document: the scale is stated in the costs section, and the priority judgement is the reader's. The case section adds one further ground for proceeding. Electricity generated on the roof is generated behind the site's own point of use, so the installation's output displaces supply that the site would otherwise take in. That property does not depend on the detailed design either. It follows from the location of the generation, and it holds for any layout the detailed design may settle on. The case, stated in full, is that the site offers a suitable surface at the point of use, that the remaining questions are design questions, and that the design stage is the proportionate next step for a commitment of the stated scale. A further consideration supports the same step. A detailed design is reversible in a way construction is not. If the design returns figures the organisation does not accept, the project stops at the design report, and the loss is the design work alone. The structure of the request is therefore staged: a bounded commitment now, the information that a construction decision requires, and the construction decision itself reserved until that information exists. Proposals that merge the two decisions force the reader to judge construction on design-stage evidence, and the separation maintained here is the reason the request can be decided on the material in this document.

## Costs

Capital cost is $1031k. The appraisal horizon is 7 years. The capital figure is the figure available at this stage and it is preliminary: the design is not yet developed, the elements of the installation are not yet specified, and a figure set before specification is refined as specification proceeds. The figure is stated so that the scale of the commitment can be judged before the detailed design is approved. It is the number the detailed design will work from and the number it will replace with a developed cost. The horizon performs the same function for time. The appraisal period bounds the comparison the reader is asked to make: costs and benefits beyond the horizon are outside the appraisal as presented, and a reader who appraises over a longer period is making a different comparison from the one this document sets out. No return figure is stated in this proposal. A return would require a generation figure, and generation depends on the layout, the orientation in detail, and the equipment the detailed design selects. Stating a return on the preliminary capital figure would present a precision the project does not yet have. The costs section therefore states what is known (the preliminary capital cost), the frame in which it is appraised (the horizon), and what is not yet stated (any return, any operating figure, any breakdown of the capital sum). The breakdown belongs to the detailed design, which will present the cost by element, on a specified design, and will return the question of construction to the reader with that breakdown in hand. The decision requested at this stage is priced by the capital figure only in scale. Approval of detailed design commits the organisation to the design work, not to construction at the stated capital scale, and the distinction is stated again in the decision section because the two commitments are easily confused. The capital cost is the scale of the project that the design would define. It is not the cost of the approval being requested.

## Schedule

Work starts one quarter after approval. No contractor is named. The schedule is stated relative to the approval because no commitment exists outside the organisation's own process: there is no agreed date with any external party, and a calendar date would imply one. The quarter between approval and the start of work is the interval for internal arrangements, so that the detailed design begins on a prepared footing. No programme beyond that start is stated. The sequencing of the design work, its stages, and its reporting points are products of the work itself, and a programme set out now would be a programme for a design that has not been specified. The detailed design will report its own schedule for the stages that follow it, including the schedule on which a construction decision could be taken and the schedule construction would follow if approved. The reader is asked to fix one interval only: approval, then one quarter, then the start of design work. That interval also protects the decision itself. A start tied to approval rather than to a date means a deferred decision defers the start by the same amount, and the project does not drift into work that the decision has not yet authorised.

## Decision requested

The decision requested is approval to proceed to detailed design. Approval to proceed to construction is not requested and is not given by this decision. The detailed design will settle the layout the roof can carry, the equipment, the connection arrangements, a developed cost by element, and a programme for the stages after design. On that report, construction becomes a separate decision, taken on specified figures. Approval at this stage authorises design work. It commits the organisation to that work and to nothing beyond it.

fact_base: A tutorial passage explains the Nusselt number to second-year students. Definition in words: the Nusselt number is the ratio of convective to conductive heat transfer at a surface. The passage must state what a value near 1 means and what a large value means, without inventing numerical examples.
input: In the field of heat transfer, the Nusselt number is a dimensionless parameter that plays a central role in describing what is happening at a surface where a fluid is in contact with a solid. It is defined as the ratio of convective to conductive heat transfer at a surface, and this definition means that it essentially compares two different mechanisms by which heat can leave or arrive at that surface. When the value of the Nusselt number is near 1, it can be understood that the convective contribution and the conductive contribution are roughly in balance with one another, so that the fluid motion is not, in this situation, producing a dramatic improvement in the rate at which heat is transferred. By contrast, in situations where the Nusselt number assumes a large value, it is clear that convection has become the dominant mechanism, and the overwhelming majority of the heat that is transferred at the surface is being carried by the moving fluid rather than being conducted through the thin layer of fluid that is immediately adjacent to the surface itself. Students encountering this quantity for the first time sometimes assume that a bigger number automatically implies a bigger rate of heat transfer in absolute terms, but the ratio by itself is really about the relative importance of the two mechanisms rather than about the absolute magnitude of either one of them, and keeping that distinction clear is essential to using the quantity correctly in any subsequent analysis or discussion of the behaviour of the surface and the fluid that is in contact with it.
target: Heat transfer at a surface proceeds by convection and by conduction. Convection is transfer by the moving fluid at the surface; conduction is transfer through the stationary layer of fluid next to the surface. The Nusselt number is the ratio of convective to conductive heat transfer at a surface, and it compares the two mechanisms for the same surface and the same temperature difference. A value near 1 means the mechanisms contribute at comparable rates. Fluid motion then adds little to the rate conduction alone would give. A large value means convection contributes the greater part of the transfer, and conduction through the near-surface layer contributes a small part. The ratio carries no information about the absolute rate. A large Nusselt number can occur where both rates are small, provided convection exceeds conduction by a wide factor; a value near the lower end of the scale can occur where both rates are large, provided they remain close. The number therefore answers a question about mechanism, not about magnitude. It tells the reader which mechanism to model with care: where the value is large, the description of the fluid motion governs the result; where the two contributions are comparable, the conduction description of the near-surface layer carries equal weight, and a calculation that treats that layer casually misstates the transfer even if its convection description is sound. The comparison the number makes is local to the surface. It does not rank two different surfaces, two different fluids, or two different duties against one another, because each comparison is between the two mechanisms acting at the same surface under the same conditions. Read in that way, the number is a diagnostic for the model the reader should build, and its size directs effort: towards the flow where convection dominates, and towards the layer where it does not.

subtype: worked example with equation: radiative exchange
fact_base: A blackened plate at 800 K faces surroundings at 300 K. Its emissivity $\varepsilon$ is 0.9. Net radiative heat flux $q$ is 20.5 kW m-2, with the Stefan-Boltzmann constant $\sigma$ = 5.67 x 10-8 W m-2 K-4. The estimate treats both surfaces as large and parallel; view factors for the real geometry are not included.
input:
A blackened plate that is held at a temperature of 800 K faces surroundings that are at a temperature of 300 K, and the aim here is to estimate the net radiative heat flux exchanged between the plate and those surroundings. The emissivity of the plate, denoted by $\varepsilon$, is 0.9. The governing relation is the Stefan-Boltzmann relation, in which $\sigma$ is the Stefan-Boltzmann constant, 5.67 x 10-8 W m-2 K-4, and the relation is written as follows:

$$q = \varepsilon \sigma (T_1^4 - T_2^4)$$

In this relation, $T_1$ is the plate temperature (800 K) and $T_2$ is the surroundings temperature (300 K), and when these values are substituted the net radiative heat flux $q$ is obtained as 20.5 kW m-2. It should be noted, however, that the estimate treats both surfaces as large and parallel, and that the view factors appropriate to the real geometry have not been included, so the flux that has been calculated is the flux for that idealised arrangement rather than a description of an arrangement in which the surfaces might only partially face one another. It may also be observed that radiation of this kind depends very strongly on temperature, considerably more strongly than the modes of transfer that depend on a simple difference of temperatures, and this is one of the reasons why the plate, which is much the hotter of the two bodies involved in the exchange, contributes so overwhelmingly to the outcome of the calculation. The surroundings, for their part, also radiate towards the plate, and the net character of the flux that has been reported reflects the fact that both directions of exchange have been taken into account, with the emission from the plate exceeding the emission from the surroundings by the margin that the temperatures and the emissivity together produce. The treatment of the plate surface through its emissivity is likewise a simplification, in that the emissivity of a real surface can depend on the condition of the surface and on the direction in which the radiation leaves it, none of which has been gone into in the present estimate.
target:
A blackened plate at 800 K faces surroundings at 300 K. The emissivity $\varepsilon$ of the plate is 0.9. The net radiative heat flux $q$ follows from the Stefan-Boltzmann constant $\sigma$ = 5.67 x 10-8 W m-2 K-4 through the Stefan-Boltzmann relation:

$$q = \varepsilon \sigma (T_1^4 - T_2^4)$$

In the relation, $T_1$ is the plate temperature (800 K) and $T_2$ is the surroundings temperature (300 K). Substitution gives $q$ = 20.5 kW m-2. The estimate treats both surfaces as large and parallel; view factors for the real geometry are not included. The stated flux is therefore the exchange under the large parallel-surface idealisation, and an arrangement whose surfaces see each other only in part exchanges less, by the view factor the estimate omits. Radiation differs from the other modes in the temperatures it depends on. The relation takes each temperature to the fourth power, so the hotter body dominates the exchange out of proportion to the difference in kelvin: the plate term exceeds the surroundings term by a wide factor even though both bodies radiate, and a small change in the plate temperature moves the flux far more than the same change in the surroundings temperature. The emissivity scales the whole exchange. A surface that radiates less effectively than the plate considered here, at the same temperatures, exchanges proportionally less, while the temperatures themselves fix the ceiling that the emissivity scales down from. The estimate also holds both temperatures fixed, as the relation requires: it is an instantaneous flux for the stated pair of temperatures, not an average over a period in which the plate cools. A plate losing heat by radiation alone moves towards the surroundings temperature as it cools, and its flux falls steeply along the way, so the stated value describes the start of such a process and not its course. The estimate is likewise a statement about the pair of surfaces as arranged. Move the same plate to surroundings it faces only obliquely, or screen part of its view, and the exchange falls even though every quantity named in the relation keeps its value.

fact_base: Performance of a mechanical-draft tower at a chemical site was logged over one summer month. Mean wet-bulb temperature was 25 °C, the approach was 4 K and the range was 8 K. Performance outside the logged month, in particular at winter wet-bulb temperatures, was not measured.
input: The performance of a mechanical-draft tower located at a chemical site was logged over the course of one summer month, in order to build up a picture of how the tower behaved under warm-season operating conditions. Over the period covered by the logging, the mean wet-bulb temperature was 25 °C, the approach was 4 K and the range was 8 K. It is important to appreciate, however, that the performance of the tower outside the month that was logged was not measured as part of this work, and this applies in particular to the performance the tower would deliver at the winter wet-bulb temperatures experienced at the site during the colder part of the year, for which no corresponding measurements are available in the material that has been gathered. The figures that are reported should consequently be read as describing the behaviour of the tower during the single month in which the logging took place, and they should not be taken as representing the behaviour of the tower across the year as a whole, since the conditions under which the tower operates are known to vary with the seasons even though the extent of that variation has not been captured here.
target: Performance of a mechanical-draft tower at a chemical site was logged over one summer month. Mean wet-bulb temperature was 25 °C, the approach was 4 K, and the range was 8 K. Performance outside the logged month was not measured, in particular at winter wet-bulb temperatures. The three reported values describe the tower under the wet-bulb conditions of that month. The approach is the difference the tower held between its cooled-water outlet temperature and the wet-bulb temperature of the entering air, and the range is the cooling the water underwent across the tower in the same period. Both are operating results for the logged conditions, not ratings for the year. A cooling tower works against the wet-bulb temperature of the air it draws in, and that temperature is at its highest in summer, so a summer month presents the tower with its most demanding common condition at the site. The logged month is in that sense a severe test. It is not, however, a complete one: the tower's behaviour in cold air, where the wet-bulb temperature falls and the cooling duty changes character, stands outside the measurement, and no winter figure can be read off from the summer record. The record also fixes the meaning of the two differences. The approach is measured against the wet-bulb temperature of the entering air, so it moves if that temperature moves; the range is measured on the water alone. A reader comparing towers must compare approach with approach at a stated wet-bulb temperature, not either value without its reference.

fact_base: Staffing review for a dispatch office: 12 full-time staff, overtime at 16% of paid hours last year. Replacing half the overtime with one additional hire costs $87k per year fully loaded. Overtime is concentrated in two seasonal peaks; a hire is paid for the full year.
input: A dispatch office employs 12 full-time staff. Overtime was 16% of paid hours last year. The recommendation is to replace half the overtime with one additional hire, at $87k per year fully loaded, with the staffing decision held by the office's management. Overtime is concentrated in two seasonal peaks. A hire is paid for the full year, including the months outside the peaks, and the $87k cost stands on that basis. The comparison is therefore between overtime paid at peak periods only and a salary paid across the whole year. Half the overtime is replaced, not all of it: cover at the peaks still draws on overtime after the hire, and the remaining overtime stays available for the weeks when demand exceeds the pattern of the previous year. The case for the hire rests on the share of hours involved. At 16% of paid hours, overtime is a standing feature of the office's staffing, not an occasional supplement, and a standing share of that size is the part of the pattern a permanent post can carry. The office also gains cover independent of existing staff working additional hours at the peaks, where an overtime pattern is most exposed. The retained overtime still depends on such willingness, so the exposure is reduced, not removed.

fact_base: A flat firebrick wall of thickness 20 mm separates two process streams. Thermal conductivity of the wall is 1.1 W m-1 K-1 and the measured temperature difference across it is 127 K. Steady one-dimensional conduction gives a heat flux of 6985 W m-2. Surface (film) resistances are excluded from this estimate; including them lowers the flux.
input: Consider, by way of a worked example, a flat wall constructed from firebrick, having a thickness of 20 mm, which serves to separate two process streams that are at different temperatures. The thermal conductivity that characterises the wall material is 1.1 W m-1 K-1, and measurements indicate that the temperature difference maintained across the wall amounts to 127 K. If the conduction process is treated as steady in character and as taking place in one dimension only, the corresponding heat flux through the wall can be evaluated, and the value that emerges from the evaluation is 6985 W m-2 under the stated conditions. One point that deserves to be emphasised in connection with this result is that surface (film) resistances have been left out of the estimate altogether, and were those resistances to be brought into the picture, the consequence would be a heat flux lower than the one reported here, so the figure should be read as relating purely to the wall itself. The example also takes the temperature difference as the difference between the two faces of the brick, which is the difference the wall actually experiences, and not as the difference between the bulk temperatures of the two streams, which would be larger once the films are taken into account. It should be understood that the purpose of an example of this kind is to isolate the behaviour of the wall itself, and it achieves that purpose precisely by leaving to one side the complications that attend the transfer of heat from a stream to a surface and from the surface into the stream on the far side, complications that would need to be addressed in full in any calculation that was intended to predict the performance of an actual installation rather than to exhibit the conduction step in isolation.
target: Steady one-dimensional conduction through a flat firebrick wall gives a heat flux of 6985 W m-2 at the stated conditions. The wall thickness is 20 mm, the thermal conductivity $k$ of the firebrick is 1.1 W m-1 K-1, and the measured temperature difference $\Delta T$ across the wall is 127 K. The flux follows from the conductivity and the temperature difference divided by the thickness: the thickness is the length the heat crosses, and it sets the scale of the result together with the difference driving it. Surface (film) resistances are excluded from this estimate; including them lowers the flux. The reported figure is thus the conduction flux within the brick, stated without the two surface resistances that a complete wall calculation places in series with it. The series arrangement fixes the direction of the correction without fixing its size. The same flux passes through film, brick, and film in turn, the total temperature difference divides among them in proportion to their resistances, and the share falling across the brick is smaller than the whole. How much smaller depends on film coefficients this example does not state, so the example reports the brick alone and names what it omits. The steadiness assumption does the same kind of work as the film exclusion: it limits the claim. A wall still changing temperature stores or releases heat as it changes, the flux entering one face differs from the flux leaving the other, and no single flux describes the wall. The stated value belongs to the settled state, in which the temperature profile through the brick is fixed and the flux is the same at every plane within it. The profile in that state is a straight line between the face temperatures, because the conductivity is taken as constant and no heat is generated within the wall, and the flux can be read from the steepness of that line as directly as from the stated formula.

subtype: worked example with equation: Ergun pressure drop
fact_base: Gas flows through a packed bed of 1 mm particles. The void fraction $\varepsilon$ is 0.5, the superficial velocity $u$ is 0.32 m s-1 and the bed length is 3 m. The Ergun equation gives a pressure gradient of 2.6 kPa m-1, or 7.8 kPa over the bed. Particle diameter $d_p$ is 1 mm; gas density is 1.2 kg m-3 and viscosity is 1.8 x 10-5 Pa s.
input:
Gas is flowing through a packed bed made up of particles having a diameter of 1 mm, and the purpose of this example is to estimate the pressure drop associated with that flow. The void fraction of the bed, denoted by $\varepsilon$, is 0.5, the superficial velocity $u$ of the gas is 0.32 m s-1, and the length of the bed is 3 m. The relation used for the estimate is the Ergun equation, which is written in the following form:

$$\frac{\Delta P}{L} = \frac{150 \mu (1-\varepsilon)^2}{\varepsilon^3 d_p^2} u + \frac{1.75 (1-\varepsilon)}{\varepsilon^3 d_p} \rho u^2$$

In the equation, the particle diameter $d_p$ is 1 mm, the density $\rho$ of the gas is 1.2 kg m-3, and the viscosity $\mu$ is 1.8 x 10-5 Pa s. When the equation is applied to the conditions specified here, it gives a pressure gradient of 2.6 kPa m-1, and multiplying that gradient by the length of the bed gives a pressure drop of 7.8 kPa over the bed, which is the figure that characterises the resistance the bed presents to the gas flowing through it under the conditions of the example. It may be noted that the velocity used throughout is the superficial velocity, that is to say the velocity the gas would have if it occupied the whole cross-section of the bed, and the properties of the gas are the properties at the conditions within the bed rather than at some other reference state. The gradient that the equation produces is therefore a local statement about the bed at the specified velocity and with the specified packing, and it should not be carried over without question to beds packed with different particles or operated under different conditions from those set out here.
target:
Gas flows through a packed bed of 1 mm particles. The void fraction $\varepsilon$ is 0.5, the superficial velocity $u$ is 0.32 m s-1, and the bed length is 3 m. The Ergun equation gives the pressure gradient in terms of the void fraction, the particle diameter $d_p$, the viscosity $\mu$, the density $\rho$, and the superficial velocity:

$$\frac{\Delta P}{L} = \frac{150 \mu (1-\varepsilon)^2}{\varepsilon^3 d_p^2} u + \frac{1.75 (1-\varepsilon)}{\varepsilon^3 d_p} \rho u^2$$

For this bed, $d_p$ is 1 mm, the gas density $\rho$ is 1.2 kg m-3, and the viscosity $\mu$ is 1.8 x 10-5 Pa s. The equation gives a pressure gradient of 2.6 kPa m-1, or 7.8 kPa over the bed. The two terms of the equation carry the two regimes of flow through the bed. The first term is linear in the velocity and rests on viscous losses at the particle surfaces; the second is quadratic in the velocity and rests on inertial losses as the gas threads the voids. At low velocity the first term dominates and the gradient rises in proportion to the velocity; at high velocity the second dominates and the gradient rises with its square. At the stated velocity, the gradient is the sum of the two contributions at that point, and neither regime alone describes the bed. The total over the bed follows from the gradient by multiplication because the bed properties and the velocity are uniform along its length: each metre of bed presents the same resistance, and the pressure falls by the same amount across each. A bed whose packing changed along its length would need the gradient evaluated section by section, with each section carrying its own properties, and the single product used here would not hold.

fact_base: A shell-and-tube exchanger heats cooling water in a refinery preheat train. Duty is 1467 kW. Hot stream: 180 °C in, 130 °C out. Cold stream: 25 °C in, 40 °C out. The log-mean temperature difference is 121.7 K and the installed area is 41.4 m2, giving an overall coefficient of 291 W m-2 K-1. Fouling was assessed from a single 90-day run; no cleaning cycle has been completed.
input: A shell-and-tube exchanger is used to heat cooling water as part of a refinery preheat train, and the performance of the exchanger is described by the figures that follow. The duty of the exchanger is 1467 kW. On the hot side, the stream enters at 180 °C and leaves at 130 °C, while on the cold side the stream enters at 25 °C and leaves at 40 °C. The log-mean temperature difference for the exchanger works out at 121.7 K, and the installed area is 41.4 m2, which together give an overall coefficient of 291 W m-2 K-1. It is worth pointing out that fouling was assessed on the basis of a single 90-day run, and that no cleaning cycle has been completed for this exchanger as yet, so the picture available in relation to fouling behaviour is necessarily a limited one, resting as it does on the experience of a single period of operation rather than on a comparison between the condition of the exchanger before and after any cleaning operation has been carried out on it. The coefficient that is reported should accordingly be understood as the coefficient of the exchanger in the condition in which it was assessed, and it would not be safe to assume that the same value would be obtained once the exchanger had been cleaned and returned to service in a clean condition, since the whole burden of the fouling observation is that the state of the surfaces is part of what the coefficient describes.
target: A shell-and-tube exchanger heats cooling water in a refinery preheat train. Duty is 1467 kW. Hot stream: 180 °C in, 130 °C out. Cold stream: 25 °C in, 40 °C out. The log-mean temperature difference is 121.7 K and the installed area is 41.4 m2, giving an overall coefficient of 291 W m-2 K-1. Fouling was assessed from a single 90-day run; no cleaning cycle has been completed. The coefficient therefore describes the exchanger as it stood over the assessed run, with the fouling that run represents and without a post-cleaning measurement for comparison. A cleaned exchanger would present a different coefficient, and the record contains no value for that state. The temperature programme fixes the driving force the stated area works against. The log-mean difference follows from the four terminal temperatures, and the duty, the area, and that difference together fix the coefficient: at the stated duty, an exchanger with less area would need a higher coefficient to close the same balance, and the installed area is the quantity that was actually provided. The single-run basis of the fouling assessment bounds what the passage can say about time. Fouling grows with service, the run covers one interval of that growth, and the coefficient over a longer interval, or after a cleaning cycle that resets the surface, stands outside the record. The passage therefore reports a working exchanger at a stated duty, in a stated fouling condition, on a stated temperature programme. It does not report a design point for a clean exchanger, and it does not report a fouling rate, because neither a clean measurement nor a second fouled measurement exists in the record against which such figures could be set.

fact_base: Excerpt content: a seal replacement takes about 24 min with the unit isolated; the excerpt gives the isolation steps only. The excerpt warns once about stored pressure and does not repeat the warning.
input: Once the relevant arrangements have been put in place, the isolation of the duty pump should be carried out in accordance with the steps that are set out below. The suction and discharge valves of the duty pump are to be closed in the first instance, and the pump is to be stopped and isolated from its electrical supply so that it cannot be started inadvertently while the work is in progress. It is extremely important at this stage to be aware that stored pressure may still be present within the casing and the associated pipework even after the valves have been closed, and the casing should therefore be vented and drained in a controlled manner before any attempt is made to disturb the seal housing. With the isolation in place, the standby pump is brought into service so that the duty of the system continues to be met while the duty pump is out of operation, and the PTW arrangements covering the work are completed and displayed at the point of work. The branch connections are blanked as required, the isolated section is proved drained and depressurised, and the isolation is recorded so that everyone involved in the task is working to the same picture of the plant state. Carried out in full, in the sequence described, the isolation takes about 24 min with the unit isolated, at the end of which the pump is in a condition where the seal replacement itself can be begun by the maintenance team.
target: Close the suction and discharge valves of the duty pump. Stop the duty pump and isolate it from its electrical supply, so it cannot start during the work. Stored pressure remains in the casing and the connected pipework after the valves close: vent and drain the casing before the seal housing is disturbed. Bring the standby pump into service in place of the duty pump, so the duty the duty pump was carrying continues while it stands isolated. Complete the PTW documentation for the work and display it at the point of work. Blank the branch connections as required. Prove the isolated section drained and depressurised. Record the isolation, so that the state of the duty pump is fixed in the record and not held only in the memory of the team carrying out the work. Each step removes one route by which the pump could present a hazard to the seal work: the closed valves remove the process connection, the electrical isolation removes the possibility of a start, the venting and draining remove the stored pressure, and the proving step confirms that the removals have taken effect rather than assuming them from the valve positions alone. The order matters in one place above all. The casing is vented before the seal housing is disturbed, because the stored pressure has no other release path once the housing is opened, and a housing opened against stored pressure releases that pressure at the opening. With the unit isolated, the isolation steps take about 24 min. The duty pump then stands stopped, drained, depressurised, and electrically isolated, with the standby pump carrying the duty, and the seal housing can be opened.

topic: tut:phase:a pure component at its boiling point
fact_base: A tutorial passage explains phase equilibrium for a pure component at its boiling point. The passage states the equilibrium condition in words (equality of chemical potential across phases) before any equation is named. No numerical data are introduced; the passage is conceptual.
input:
It is important to note that phase equilibrium is a truly fundamental concept in thermodynamics, and understanding what happens when a pure component reaches its boiling point provides a foundation for many separation processes. At the boiling point, the liquid and vapour phases coexist in a state of balance, meaning that molecules pass from liquid into vapour while others return from vapour into liquid, the two opposing flows cancelling out. The system settles into a dynamic equilibrium in which the composition of each phase remains completely unchanged over time, provided that both phases are still present.

The formal condition that captures this state can be expressed in words, before any equation is introduced, as follows: equilibrium holds when the chemical potential of the component is the same in both phases. Chemical potential can be thought of as a measure of how strongly a component tends to escape from the phase it currently occupies. If the chemical potential in the liquid is higher than that in the vapour, molecules will tend to move from liquid to vapour and boiling will proceed; if it is lower, vapour will tend to condense back into liquid. Only when the two values are exactly equal does net transfer come to a halt, highlighting the central role that this equality plays in defining the boiling point itself.

Pressure also plays a significant role in this picture. Raising the pressure means that the vapour has to be compressed further before its chemical potential can rise to match that of the liquid, so equality is reached only at a higher temperature, whereas lowering the pressure allows equality to be reached at a lower temperature instead. A boiling point is therefore never a fixed property of a substance in isolation, and it should always be reported together with the pressure at which it applies, underscoring the close interdependence of temperature and pressure in phase behaviour.

Finally, it is worth emphasising that boiling a pure component does not change the composition of either phase, since each phase contains one and the same component. Boiling can change the relative amounts of liquid and vapour present, but it cannot enrich or purify anything, which is why separation by boiling has nothing to gain from a pure component.
target:
Phase equilibrium for a pure component at its boiling point is the condition in which liquid and vapour coexist without net change: molecules leave the liquid and return to it at equal rates, and the composition of each phase stays constant while both phases remain present. The condition is stated in words before any equation is named: at equilibrium, the chemical potential of the component has the same value in the two phases. Equality of chemical potential across the phases is the equilibrium condition, and the boiling point is the temperature at which that equality holds for the liquid and vapour of the pure component at the given pressure.

Chemical potential measures the tendency of a component to leave the phase it occupies. Where the chemical potential in the liquid stands higher than in the vapour, transfer runs from liquid to vapour and boiling continues; where it stands lower, transfer runs the other way and vapour condenses. Net transfer stops only where the two values meet, and the meeting of the two values is what the boiling point records. Boiling is not a one-way release of vapour: both directions of transfer continue at equal rates.

Temperature and pressure fix where equality can hold for a pure component. At a higher pressure, equality is reached at a higher temperature, because the vapour must be compressed further before its chemical potential rises to meet that of the liquid. At a lower pressure, equality comes at a lower temperature. The boiling point is tied to the pressure imposed on the component, and a statement of a boiling point without its pressure is incomplete.

The condition also bounds what boiling can do to a pure component. Transfer between the phases changes how much liquid and vapour are present, and it changes neither phase's composition, because each phase holds the one component only. Purity is preserved through boiling, and separation by boiling has no purchase on a pure component. Equality of chemical potential is the whole content of equilibrium here: a balance of tendencies to transfer, struck at the temperature the pressure selects.

fact_base: A continuous stirred-tank reactor runs a neutralisation that is first order in the limiting reactant. The rate constant is 0.239 min-1 at the operating temperature and the mean residence time is 81 min. Steady-state conversion for an ideal CSTR is 95.1%. The estimate assumes perfect mixing and constant density; tracer tests on the actual vessel have not been run.
input:
A continuous stirred-tank reactor, or CSTR, carries out a neutralisation reaction that is first order with respect to the limiting reactant, meaning that the rate is directly proportional to the concentration of that reactant. The rate constant at the operating temperature is 0.239 min-1, and the mean residence time is 81 min, the mean residence time being the average time a portion of feed spends inside the vessel, obtained by dividing the reactor volume by the volumetric flow rate through it.

For an ideal CSTR at steady state, the conversion achieved is governed by the product of the rate constant and the mean residence time. Multiplying the two together gives 19.359, a dimensionless quantity that compares the time available for reaction with the characteristic time the reaction requires. Because this product is considerably larger than unity, only a small proportion of the limiting reactant passes through the reactor without reacting. Dividing this product by one plus itself, as the steady-state relationship for an ideal CSTR requires, gives a conversion of 95.1%.

The result can be checked against the expected limiting behaviour. If the residence time were zero, no conversion at all would be achieved, while if the product of rate constant and residence time were to grow without limit, the conversion would approach completeness, and the value obtained here sits close to the complete end of that spectrum, as a product of this magnitude would lead one to anticipate. The estimate rests on two assumptions: perfect mixing throughout the vessel, so that the composition everywhere is the same as at the outlet, and constant density, so that the residence time is the same for every portion of feed. Tracer tests on the actual vessel have not in fact been carried out, so the perfect-mixing assumption remains unverified for the vessel in question, and the figure should properly be regarded as the ideal-CSTR value corresponding to the stated rate constant and residence time.

Mean residence time is the reactor volume divided by the volumetric flow through it, and it fixes how long a portion of feed spends in the vessel on average.

The check on the result is the limiting behaviour. A residence time of zero would give no conversion, and a product growing without bound would drive conversion toward completeness; the stated conversion sits close to the complete end of that range, as a product of this size requires. The estimate assumes perfect mixing, so every part of the vessel holds the same composition as the outlet, and it assumes constant density, so the residence time is the same for every portion of feed. Tracer tests on the actual vessel have not been run, so the perfect-mixing assumption is unverified for the vessel in question, and the conversion stands as the ideal-CSTR value at the stated rate constant and residence time.

fact_base: A shell-and-tube exchanger heats crude oil in a refinery preheat train. Duty is 561 kW. Hot stream: 150 °C in, 110 °C out. Cold stream: 35 °C in, 50 °C out. The log-mean temperature difference is 86.9 K and the installed area is 24.4 m2, giving an overall coefficient of 265 W m-2 K-1. Fouling was assessed from a single 90-day run; no cleaning cycle has been completed.
input:
This passage reports a shell-and-tube heat exchanger used to heat crude oil within a refinery preheat train, the sequence of exchangers through which crude oil passes to raise its temperature before the downstream processing units. The duty of the exchanger, the rate at which heat is transferred from the hot stream to the crude oil, is 561 kW. The hot stream enters the exchanger at a temperature of 150 °C and leaves it at 110 °C, while the crude oil itself enters at 35 °C and leaves at the somewhat higher temperature of 50 °C, having been heated as required.

The log-mean temperature difference for the exchanger, the appropriately averaged driving force for heat transfer along the unit, allowing for the way the local temperature difference varies from one end to the other, is 86.9 K. The installed heat-transfer area is 24.4 m2, and when the duty, the area and the log-mean temperature difference are combined together, they yield an overall heat-transfer coefficient of 265 W m-2 K-1. This overall coefficient bundles the thermal resistances of the films on both sides of the tubes with the resistance of the tube wall itself, all expressed with reference to the installed area, and it characterises this particular exchanger at this particular duty, rather than describing either stream in isolation.

Finally, the question of fouling deserves mention. Fouling was assessed on the basis of a single 90-day run, and no cleaning cycle has yet been completed on the exchanger. This means that the assessment reflects only the fouled condition that happened to prevail during that one run: the reported coefficient is the value for a fouled exchanger at some unrecorded point between cleanings, and there is no clean-surface coefficient available against which it might meaningfully be compared. Both the performance that would be obtained immediately after cleaning and the rate at which fouling would build up again afterwards remain unmeasured.

fact_base: Adsorption of a dye from water on activated carbon was measured in batch tests at 298 K. The fitted Langmuir capacity was 153 mg of dye per gram of adsorbent at pH 6. At an adsorbent dose of 0.7 g L-1, removal after 120 min was 79% of the initial dye concentration of 50 mg L-1. The Langmuir fit is reported for pH 6 only; capacity at other pH values was not measured.
input:
Adsorption of a dye from water on activated carbon was measured in batch tests at 298 K. In a batch test, a fixed mass of adsorbent is contacted with a fixed volume of solution and the concentration is followed as uptake proceeds. The fitted Langmuir capacity was 153 mg of dye per gram of adsorbent at pH 6. Langmuir capacity is the dye mass taken up per gram of adsorbent at saturation under the Langmuir model, in which uptake rises with concentration and levels off as the surface fills; the fit reports the levelled value, not the uptake at any one concentration.

At an adsorbent dose of 0.7 g L-1, removal after 120 min was 79% of the initial dye concentration of 50 mg L-1. Adsorbent dose is the adsorbent mass per litre of solution treated, and removal is stated against the initial concentration, so the figure compares the dye removed from solution with the dye present at the start of the test. Each value is tied to its conditions where it is stated: temperature with the tests, pH with the capacity, and dose and contact time with the removal.

The Langmuir fit is reported for pH 6 only. Capacity at other pH values was not measured, so the capacity and the removal figure describe the dye and carbon pair at the stated pH and temperature. Neither value carries to a different pH, where the charge on the dye and on the carbon surface, and with them the uptake, can differ. The reported removal is a batch-test result at the stated dose; a different dose changes the share of dye removed without changing the capacity the fit returns.

fact_base: 214 pumps run at the plant. Maintenance records for 12 months show 1119 h of unplanned downtime; bearing failures account for 40% of the downtime hours. A sensor set for all 214 pumps is quoted at $386k installed, plus $65k per year. In a vendor trial on a comparable unit, the sensors cut downtime by 28%; the figure is a vendor figure and was not measured at this plant. A pilot on 20 pumps costs $31k over three months. Spare-part lead times are unchanged by the sensors. The memo recommends the three-month pilot; the reliability engineering group owns the pilot and reports before the March capital review; the decision on full installation is held until the pilot results are reported.
input:
This memo recommends a three-month pilot of bearing condition sensors on 20 pumps, at a cost of $31k, before any decision about a full installation across the whole fleet. The pilot would be run by the reliability engineering group, and the decision on full installation held until the pilot results are reported, in time for the March capital review, when the decision can be taken on evidence gathered at this plant rather than figures supplied by others.

There are 214 pumps running at the plant, and the maintenance records covering the last 12 months show 1119 h of unplanned downtime. Bearing failures account for 40% of the downtime hours, which works out, as a derived figure, at 447.6 h attributable to bearing failures over the period. This concentration of downtime in a single failure mode makes bearing monitoring an attractive candidate, since a sensor package aimed at bearings is directed at the largest single identified contributor to lost running time.

A sensor set covering all 214 pumps is quoted at $386k installed, plus a further $65k per year. In a vendor trial on a comparable unit, the sensors cut downtime by 28%, although this figure is a vendor figure, generated elsewhere, and was not measured at this plant. It indicates the possible scale of the prize, but it does not by itself demonstrate what would actually be achieved here. Spare-part lead times are unchanged by the sensors: the sensors improve detection but do not shorten supply, so any benefit still depends on parts being available when a deteriorating bearing is identified.

The pilot is a measured next step. For $31k, three months on 20 pumps will show how the sensors perform on this plant's pumps, records and crews, and the reliability engineering group will report before the March capital review. The decision on full installation is held until that evidence is available, rather than prejudged in either direction.
target:
