The plant runs 214 pumps. Maintenance records for 12 months show 1119 h of unplanned downtime, and bearing failures account for 40% of the downtime hours, a derived 447.6 h. Unplanned downtime is running time lost outside a planned outage. The bearing share makes bearings the largest single named cause in the record, and a sensor set aimed at bearings addresses that share rather than downtime in general. The record is a count of hours, not of events, so a cause that stops a pump for long periods weighs more heavily in it than a cause that stops pumps often but briefly.

Full installation is quoted at $386k installed for all 214 pumps, plus $65k per year. In a vendor trial on a comparable unit, the sensors cut downtime by 28%; the figure is a vendor figure and was not measured at this plant, so it sizes the prize without evidencing the saving here. Spare-part lead times are unchanged by the sensors: detection improves, supply does not, and downtime avoided still depends on parts being on hand when a bearing is flagged.

The pilot bounds the commitment. Three months on 20 pumps tests detection on this plant's pumps, records and crews at $31k, against a full-installation decision that is held, not pre-judged, until the reliability engineering group reports. The March capital review then decides with plant data in place of the vendor figure, and the quoted full-fleet cost stands unchanged as the figure that decision will weigh. The pilot also fixes what the vendor trial cannot: whether the warning the sensors give arrives early enough, on this plant's bearings, for a repair to be planned rather than improvised.

fact_base: Cost review of a regional delivery route: 394 km per trip at $1.99 per km, 651 trips per year. Annual transport cost is $510k. Costs are carrier invoices for the last 12 months; empty running is included in the trip count.
input:
This review examines the cost of a regional delivery route, whose total cost is $510k per year. The route covers 394 km per trip at a carrier rate of $1.99 per km, so each trip costs, as a derived figure, $784.06. Over a year the route runs 651 trips, and the per-trip cost taken over that number of trips produces the annual total.

The figures are drawn from carrier invoices covering the last 12 months, so the annual cost records what was actually paid, rather than an estimate projected from a published tariff. Empty running is included in the trip count: trips made without a load are counted alongside loaded trips, so the annual figure covers loaded and empty kilometres together.

Because the total is assembled from a rate per kilometre, a distance per trip and a number of trips, the annual cost can be moved through any one of these components: a change in the negotiated rate would alter the cost of every kilometre, a change in the route would alter the distance on each trip, and a change in the schedule would alter the number of trips run. What the review reports, however, is the position as invoiced over the period covered, with each component standing at the value it actually took during that period.
target:
A regional delivery route costs $510k per year. The route runs 394 km per trip at $1.99 per km, a derived $784.06 per trip, over 651 trips per year. The annual figure is the per-trip cost taken over the trip count, and it is built from carrier invoices for the last 12 months, so it records what was paid rather than what a tariff card would predict.

Empty running is included in the trip count. The count is a count of journeys made, loaded or not, and the distance is the distance of the route as driven. The annual cost covers loaded and empty kilometres together, and a reduction in empty running lowers the trip count or the distance per trip without any change in the rate per kilometre. The rate, the distance and the count are the three components the figure contains, and the invoice base fixes each at last year's value: a renegotiated rate changes the cost per kilometre, a route change changes the distance, and a schedule change changes the count.

No other cost of the route is in the figure. The total is transport as invoiced, at the stated rate and distance, over the stated year, and it changes only when one of its three components changes.

subtype: worked example with equation: radiative exchange
fact_base: A furnace wall at 1000 K faces surroundings at 350 K. Its emissivity $\varepsilon$ is 0.85. Net radiative heat flux $q$ is 47.5 kW m-2, with the Stefan-Boltzmann constant $\sigma$ = 5.67 x 10-8 W m-2 K-4. The estimate treats both surfaces as large and parallel; view factors for the real geometry are not included.
input:
This example calculates the net radiative heat flux leaving a furnace wall facing much cooler surroundings. The quantity we are interested in is the net radiative heat flux, denoted by $q$ and expressed in kW m-2, and it depends on the emissivity of the wall surface, denoted by $\varepsilon$, on the Stefan-Boltzmann constant, denoted by $\sigma$, which has the value 5.67 x 10-8 W m-2 K-4, and on the temperatures of the wall and of the surroundings, denoted by $T_1$ and $T_2$ respectively. In the present case, the wall is at a temperature of 1000 K and the surroundings are at 350 K. The relationship connecting all of these quantities to one another is the following equation:

$$q = \varepsilon \sigma (T_1^4 - T_2^4)$$

The emissivity of the wall surface is 0.85, a value which reflects the fact that the surface does not radiate quite as effectively as a perfect emitter would at the same temperature. Substituting all of the values into the equation and carrying out the calculation gives a net radiative heat flux of 47.5 kW m-2. The result is dominated by the wall temperature because each temperature enters the equation raised to the fourth power, so the contribution from the hot wall is much larger than that coming back from the cooler surroundings, and the net flux is the difference between a large emitted term and a small received term. It should be borne in mind, however, that this estimate rests on a simplifying treatment in which both surfaces are regarded as large and parallel, so that every part of each surface faces the other. View factors for the real geometry are not included in the calculation, and in an actual furnace, where parts of the wall may face surfaces that are shielded or colder, the exchange that takes place could well be less than the value that has been obtained here.
target:
The net radiative heat flux $q$ (kW m-2) from a furnace wall is calculated from the wall emissivity $\varepsilon$ (dimensionless), the Stefan-Boltzmann constant $\sigma$ (5.67 x 10-8 W m-2 K-4), the wall temperature $T_1$ (1000 K) and the surroundings temperature $T_2$ (350 K) by

$$q = \varepsilon \sigma (T_1^4 - T_2^4)$$

Net flux is emission less return: the wall radiates toward the surroundings and receives radiation back, and $q$ is the difference. The wall emissivity is 0.85, the share of perfect-emitter radiation the surface achieves at its temperature. Substitution gives $q$ = 47.5 kW m-2. Each temperature enters at the fourth power, so the hotter temperature dominates the exchange and the return from the surroundings offsets only a small part of what the wall emits; at equal temperatures the two terms would cancel and the net flux would vanish, which is the check the stated value has to pass in direction. The constant carries the units it does because the flux it scales is an energy flow per unit area, and the fourth-power law leaves it no simpler form.

The estimate treats both surfaces as large and parallel, so every part of each surface faces the other. View factors for the real geometry are not included, and a wall part facing shielded or colder surfaces would exchange less than the stated flux. The value is the large-parallel-surface result at the stated temperatures and emissivity. Emissivity is the one property of the surface in the calculation, and it enters as a simple multiplier: a surface that emits less freely gives a proportionally smaller flux at the same temperatures.

fact_base: A textbook chapter section on distillation, in four parts: principle, equipment, a worked example, and limits. The worked example uses only the numbers given in the principle part; no new data appear later in the chapter. The limits part states where the simple model fails, in plain terms, without new equations.
input:
## Principle

Distillation is a widely used separation technique, based on a simple idea: when a liquid mixture is boiled, the vapour that is produced is not identical in composition to the liquid from which it came, but is instead richer in the component that boils more readily, the more volatile component. Condensing that vapour gives a liquid enriched in the more volatile component relative to the original mixture, and a degree of separation has been achieved. A single boiling and condensing achieves only a limited enrichment, however; the power of distillation comes from repeating the process, so that the enrichment is compounded stage by stage until the desired separation is reached.

The vapour differs in composition from the liquid because the components differ in volatility, their tendency to pass into the vapour phase. At a given temperature, the more volatile component escapes the liquid more readily and contributes a disproportionately large share of the vapour formed. As a boiling mixture is heated, the more volatile material passes over preferentially at first, which is why the vapour, and its condensate, start out enriched, while the liquid remaining in the boiler becomes steadily depleted in the volatile component and enriched in the less volatile one. Separation by distillation is therefore possible only because, and only to the extent that, the components differ in volatility; a mixture whose components were identical in volatility would yield a vapour of exactly the same composition as its liquid, and no separation could be brought about at all, however many times the operation might be repeated.

In a working distillation, the enrichment is not left to separate boilings in separate vessels. Vapour rises through the apparatus while liquid flows back down, and the two streams are brought into contact again and again along the way. Wherever rising vapour meets descending liquid, material passes between them in both directions: the less volatile component condenses out of the vapour into the liquid, while the more volatile component vaporises out of the liquid into the vapour. Each such contact therefore improves both streams at once, enriching the vapour in the volatile component as it rises, and enriching the liquid in the less volatile component as it falls. The descending liquid that makes this exchange possible is reflux, produced by condensing part of the vapour that reaches the top and returning it to the apparatus rather than drawing it all off as product.

A qualitative illustration fixes the principle. Consider a mixture of two components, one more volatile than the other, heated in a boiler until it boils. The vapour that leaves the boiler is richer in the more volatile component than the liquid remaining behind. Condensing that vapour gives a liquid of the vapour's enriched composition; boiling the condensate in its turn gives a vapour richer again. Repetition moves the collected material steadily toward the more volatile component at one end and toward the less volatile component at the other, and this compounding of many small enrichments builds a substantial overall separation from a modest difference in volatility.

## Equipment

The apparatus is the distillation column, a vertical vessel in which rising vapour and descending liquid are brought into contact. Contact is provided either by trays, horizontal plates arranged one above another up the column, or by packing, a filling of shaped material that spreads the liquid into films over a large surface. Vapour passes upward through the trays or the packing voids, bubbling through or flowing past the liquid, while liquid passes downward from tray to tray or trickles over the packing under gravity, so the exchange of the principle proceeds along the whole height.

At the foot stands a reboiler, the heat exchanger that boils the liquid collected at the bottom and generates the vapour rising through the column. At the top stands a condenser, which condenses the vapour from the topmost contact; the condensate divides into a portion returned to the column as reflux, on which the internal exchange depends, and a portion withdrawn as the overhead product, the distillate. Liquid withdrawn from the bottom is the bottoms product. The feed is introduced at an intermediate point, at a height chosen so its composition matches the streams it joins there. The section above the feed point enriches the vapour in the more volatile component; the section below strips that component from the descending liquid so it is not lost in the bottoms.

## Worked example

The column's operation can be followed through a two-component mixture, keeping to the qualitative picture of the principle. The feed enters partway up the column and divides there: its vapour joins the vapour rising from below, and its liquid joins the liquid descending from above, so that the feed is worked on by both sections of the column at once. Above the feed point, the rising vapour passes from contact to contact, giving up less volatile component to the descending liquid and taking up more volatile component in exchange. The vapour that finally reaches the condenser is therefore rich in the more volatile component, and the distillate drawn off from the condensate shares that enriched composition, although it is not, in general, the pure component, since each contact achieves only a partial exchange. Below the feed point, the descending liquid passes from contact to contact, giving up more volatile component to the rising vapour and taking up less volatile component in exchange. The liquid that finally reaches the reboiler is therefore depleted in the more volatile component, and the bottoms drawn off are enriched in the less volatile component, though again not completely pure. The two products are drawn toward opposite ends of the composition range by one internal traffic of vapour and liquid, maintained by heat supplied at the reboiler and removed at the condenser, and the separation depends on how many effective contacts the traffic passes through and how generously reflux is supplied.

## Limits

The picture presented is simplified, and its limits need stating. The treatment assumes that at every contact the vapour and liquid leaving one another have come fully into equilibrium, so each contact achieves the whole exchange equilibrium allows. Real trays and packing fall short: contact time is finite, mixing is imperfect, and the streams leave partway toward the equilibrium compositions, so a real column requires more height, or more trays, than the ideal picture suggests for the same separation. The treatment also takes the volatility difference as fixed, whereas in real mixtures it can shift with composition and operating pressure, and some mixtures form a constant-boiling combination at which vapour and liquid have the same composition; there enrichment stops, and simple distillation cannot carry the separation past it. Finally, the picture counts only compositions and contacts: it says nothing about energy consumed at reboiler and condenser, nothing about pressure drop of the rising vapour, and nothing about components that react or decompose at the boiling temperature. Within its limits the model guides; beyond them it must be supplemented before use in design.
target:
## Principle

Distillation separates a liquid mixture by volatility. When the mixture boils, the vapour formed is richer than the liquid in the more volatile component, the component with the greater tendency to pass into the vapour. Condensation of that vapour gives a liquid enriched in the same component, and repetition of boiling and condensing compounds the enrichment until the separation required is reached. A single boiling enriches once and modestly; separation is the product of many enrichments in sequence.

Reflux makes the sequence continuous rather than batchwise. Without a descending liquid, vapour rising from the boiler would meet nothing, exchange with nothing, and leave with the composition the boiler gave it; the column would add height without adding separation. The returned liquid supplies, at every level, a stream already enriched in the less volatile component, against which the rising vapour is repeatedly corrected. The correction has a price: part of the condensed product is sent back instead of withdrawn, so the column produces less at the top than it condenses, and the separation is bought with that returned share.

Volatility difference is the whole basis of the method. At a given temperature the more volatile component escapes the liquid more readily and contributes a disproportionate share of the vapour, while the liquid left behind is depleted in that component and enriched in the less volatile one. A mixture whose components had the same volatility would give a vapour of the liquid's own composition, and no repetition would separate it.

In a working column the repetition is internal. Vapour rises and liquid descends through the same vessel, and where the two meet, material passes both ways: the less volatile component condenses from the vapour into the liquid, and the more volatile component vaporises from the liquid into the vapour. Each contact enriches both streams at once. The descending liquid is reflux, made by condensing part of the vapour at the top and returning it instead of drawing it all off as product. A qualitative example fixes the idea: vapour from a boiling two-component mixture, condensed and boiled again, gives a second vapour richer again in the more volatile component, and repetition moves material toward that component at one end of the apparatus and toward the less volatile component at the other.

## Equipment

The vessel is a vertical column. Contact inside it is provided by trays, horizontal plates stacked up the height, or by packing, a filling that spreads liquid into films over a large surface. Vapour rises through the trays or the packing voids, liquid descends over them, and the exchange of the principle proceeds along the whole height.

A reboiler at the foot boils the liquid collected there and generates the rising vapour. A condenser at the top condenses the vapour arriving from the uppermost contact, and the condensate divides: part returns to the column as reflux, and part is withdrawn as the overhead product, the distillate. Liquid withdrawn from the bottom is the bottoms product. Feed enters at an intermediate height, chosen so the feed composition matches the streams it joins. The section above the feed point enriches the vapour in the more volatile component; the section below it strips that component from the descending liquid so it is not lost in the bottoms.

Trays and packing achieve the same contact by different means. A tray holds a pool of liquid through which vapour bubbles, and the pool is renewed from above as it overflows downward. Packing holds no pools: liquid spreads over the filling and vapour passes through the voids, and contact occurs across the wetted surface. The choice between them belongs to the duty; the model of the chapter treats both alike, as providers of contacts in sequence.

## Worked example

A two-component feed enters partway up the column and divides at the feed point: its vapour joins the vapour rising from below, and its liquid joins the liquid descending from above. Above the feed point, the rising vapour passes from contact to contact, and at each contact it gives up less volatile component to the descending liquid and takes up more volatile component from it. The vapour reaching the condenser is rich in the more volatile component, and the distillate shares that composition. The distillate is not the pure component: each contact exchanges only in part, and the enrichment at the top is the sum of partial exchanges.

Below the feed point, the descending liquid passes from contact to contact, and at each contact it gives up more volatile component to the rising vapour and takes up less volatile component from it. The liquid reaching the reboiler is depleted in the more volatile component, and the bottoms are enriched in the less volatile one, again short of purity. The two products are drawn toward opposite ends of the composition range by one internal traffic, maintained by heat supplied at the reboiler and removed at the condenser. The separation achieved rests on the number of effective contacts the traffic passes through and on the reflux supplied to sustain the descending stream.

## Limits

The model of this chapter idealises every contact as an equilibrium contact, in which vapour and liquid leave one another at the compositions equilibrium allows. Real trays and packing fall short of that ideal: contact time is finite and mixing is imperfect, so a real column needs more height than the ideal picture suggests for the same separation. The model also takes the volatility difference as a fixed property of the mixture. In real mixtures it shifts with composition and with operating pressure, and some mixtures form a constant-boiling combination at which vapour and liquid have the same composition; enrichment stops there, and simple distillation does not carry a separation past that point. The model counts compositions and contacts only. Energy consumed at the reboiler and condenser, pressure drop of the rising vapour, and components that react or decompose at the boiling temperature all stand outside it.

fact_base: A tutorial passage explains feedback control through a level loop on a process vessel. The passage covers the sensor, the controller, the final element and the sign of the feedback, in that order. No tuning numbers are given; the passage explains structure, not settings.
input:
Feedback control is a fundamental idea in process engineering, and a clear way to understand it is the level loop, in which the level of liquid in a process vessel is held at its desired value by adjusting a flow. The loop has several parts, worked through in turn: the sensor, the controller, the final element, and the sign of the feedback that ties the arrangement together.

The sensor measures the level in the vessel and converts the measurement into a signal passed to the rest of the system. The reading is the loop's only source of information about the level: everything the loop does is done in response to the reading rather than the level itself, so a faulty reading makes the rest of the loop act faithfully on incorrect information.

The controller receives the reading and compares it with the set point, the level the vessel is intended to maintain. The difference between set point and reading is the error, and the controller uses it to work out the correction required, producing an instruction whose size and direction depend on that error.

The final element puts the controller's instruction into practice, and in a level loop it is typically a valve on a line entering or leaving the vessel. When the valve moves, the flow changes; when the flow changes, the level changes; and the changed level is picked up by the sensor, closing the loop.

Finally, the sign of the feedback in a level loop is negative, and this is what makes the arrangement work as a regulator. If the level rises above the set point, the correction acts to bring it down again, and if it falls, the correction acts to raise it, so the loop continually opposes the disturbance that moved it. Were the sign positive instead, the loop would push the level ever further from the set point, either filling the vessel or emptying it altogether.
target:
A level loop holds the level in a process vessel at its set point by acting on a stream entering or leaving the vessel. The loop has four parts, taken in order: the sensor, the controller, the final element, and the sign of the feedback that joins them.

The sensor measures the level and reports it to the controller as a signal. Level is the height of liquid in the vessel, and the reading is the loop's only knowledge of it: every later part acts on the reading, not on the level itself, so a faulty reading drives correct hardware to a wrong action.

The controller compares the reading with the set point and decides the correction. Set point is the level the vessel is to hold. The comparison gives an error, the difference between set point and reading, and the controller turns the error into an instruction whose size and direction follow from it.

The final element carries out the instruction, and in a level loop it is a valve on an inlet or outlet line. The valve changes the flow, the flow changes the level, and the sensor reads the changed level. Measurement, decision and action follow one another continuously while the vessel runs, and the loop is closed.

The sign of the feedback is negative. A rise in level above the set point produces a correction that lowers the level, and a fall produces a correction that raises it, so the loop opposes the disturbance that moved it. Feedback of the opposite sign would drive the level away from the set point and empty or fill the vessel. Negative sign is what makes the arrangement a regulator rather than an amplifier of error.

fact_base: A review passage on adsorbents for gas drying, in four parts: scope, established results, disagreements, and gaps. The review covers 147 papers from the last 9 years. The disagreements part names the quantity on which reports conflict; the gaps part names the measurement nobody reports.
input:
## Scope

This review surveys the published literature on adsorbents used for the drying of gases, taking in 147 papers that have appeared over the last 9 years. The field it covers is the removal of water vapour from gas streams by passing the gas over a solid material that takes up the water preferentially, holding it on and within the solid until the material is regenerated and the water is driven off again. The gases concerned are those of ordinary industrial practice, including air supplied to instruments and processes, natural gas being prepared for transport and sale, and a variety of process gases whose moisture content must be brought down to a low level in order to protect downstream equipment, to prevent the formation of solids within pipelines, or to meet a specification attached to the gas as sold. The adsorbents within the scope of the review are the families of materials that are used for this purpose in practice and studied for it in the literature: silica gel, activated alumina, and the zeolite molecular sieves, together with newer materials that individual papers propose as candidates for the same duty. The review is concerned with performance in service as much as with capacity in the laboratory, and it therefore includes papers on regeneration, on the ageing of beds in cyclic operation, and on the behaviour of adsorbents in the presence of the contaminants that real gas streams carry, alongside the much larger number of papers that report uptake measurements on fresh material under controlled conditions. Papers concerned solely with the synthesis of new materials, without any measurement of water uptake, fall outside the scope, as do papers dealing with the drying of liquids or of solids, and papers in which adsorption is used to remove some component other than water.

## Established results

Across so large a body of work, a number of findings recur so consistently that they may fairly be regarded as established. It is established, in the first place, that the quantity of water an adsorbent takes up at equilibrium rises steeply as the partial pressure of water vapour in the gas increases from low values, and that the shape of this rise differs characteristically between the material families: the zeolite molecular sieves take up a large share of their capacity at very low partial pressures, which is what fits them for drying a gas to very low moisture contents, whereas silica gel takes up relatively little at low partial pressures and reaches its capacity only as the gas approaches saturation, which fits it instead for removing the bulk of the water from a wet gas. It is established, secondly, that capacity falls as temperature rises, so that a bed dries best when it is kept cool, and that regeneration is correspondingly carried out by heating the bed, by reducing the pressure over it, or by sweeping it with a dry purge gas, the water being expelled as the conditions that favoured uptake are reversed. It is established, thirdly, that the rate at which water is taken up is governed not by the equilibrium capacity but by transport: by the movement of vapour through the gas film around each particle, and by diffusion within the particle toward the surfaces on which uptake occurs, so that particle size and gas velocity influence the length of bed that a given duty requires even where they do not influence the amount the material can ultimately hold. It is established, finally, that contaminants in the gas stream degrade performance: heavy hydrocarbons, oils and other strongly held species occupy capacity and foul surfaces, and beds in real service lose working capacity over their lives even where the fresh material, as characterised in the laboratory, appears entirely satisfactory. These findings are supported by the great majority of the 147 papers taken together, and no serious body of work within the review contradicts any of them.

## Disagreements

The literature is considerably less harmonious when it turns to the quantitative comparison of the material families, and the quantity on which reports principally conflict is the equilibrium water uptake of the zeolite molecular sieves at low partial pressures of water vapour, the very region of operation on which their reputation rests. Some groups report capacities in this region that are markedly higher than those reported by other groups for materials that are nominally of the same type, and the discrepancy between the highest and lowest reported values is large enough to reverse the ranking of materials that a designer would draw from the literature taken at face value. The disagreement does not appear to be a simple matter of error on one side or the other. The conflicting reports differ systematically in the conditions under which the measurements were made: in the pretreatment and activation of the samples before measurement, in the temperature at which uptake was recorded, in the manner in which the partial pressure was established and held, and in whether the uptake was measured by following the weight of the sample or by following the moisture content of the gas passing over it. Each of these choices is defensible in itself, and some of them are known to shift the measured uptake, but because the choices vary from group to group in combination rather than one at a time, the literature does not at present allow the discrepancy to be assigned to any single cause. There is a secondary disagreement, less sharply drawn, concerning the working capacity that should be expected of silica gel in bulk drying service, where reports differ over how much of the equilibrium capacity remains available once the dynamics of a real bed, with its incomplete regeneration and its ageing, are taken into account. Until the measurement conventions in this field converge, or until a round of measurements is made on shared samples under shared conditions, quantitative rankings drawn from different groups' reports will continue to carry an uncertainty that the individual papers, each internally consistent, do not disclose.

## Gaps

The most striking gap in the literature is a measurement that, on the evidence of the 147 papers surveyed, nobody reports: the water uptake that an adsorbent retains after extended regeneration cycling under a realistic humid feed. Papers report the capacity of fresh material in abundance, and a smaller number report capacity after some ageing or after exposure to a named contaminant, but a systematic record of how the drying capacity of a bed declines, cycle by cycle, over the long sequence of adsorption and regeneration steps that constitutes its working life, is essentially absent. The omission matters because the economics of gas drying turn on precisely that decline: the interval at which a bed must be changed, the energy consumed in regenerating it throughout its life, and the moisture excursions experienced by the downstream plant as the bed ages are all governed by the cycling behaviour that the literature does not measure. A second gap lies in the reporting of the conditions under which uptake was measured: pretreatment of the sample, in particular, is described loosely or not at all in a substantial minority of papers, which renders the disagreements described in the preceding section needlessly difficult to resolve after the fact. A third gap concerns mixtures: almost all measurements are made with water vapour in a clean carrier gas, whereas the industrial duty involves water in the presence of hydrocarbons and other adsorbable species whose competitive uptake shapes the performance of the bed, and measurements under such mixed conditions, over cycling, on the materials in ordinary use, would do more to advance the practical design of gas drying than further refinements of single-component capacity on fresh samples.
target:
## Scope

This review covers adsorbents for gas drying in 147 papers from the last 9 years. Gas drying is the removal of water vapour from a gas stream by a solid that takes up the water and holds it until regeneration drives it off. The gases in scope are those of ordinary practice: air for instruments and processes, natural gas prepared for transport and sale, and process gases whose moisture must be brought low to protect downstream equipment, to prevent solids forming in pipelines, or to meet a sale specification. The adsorbents in scope are the families used and studied for the duty: silica gel, activated alumina and the zeolite molecular sieves, with newer materials that papers propose as candidates for the same duty. Performance in service is in scope alongside capacity in the laboratory, so papers on regeneration, on bed ageing in cyclic operation and on behaviour in the presence of carried contaminants stand beside the larger number that report uptake on fresh material under controlled conditions. Papers on synthesis without a water-uptake measurement are outside the scope, as are papers on drying liquids or solids and papers on removing a component other than water. The review treats the established families as the centre of the field and the candidate materials as its margin, because service experience, supply and regeneration practice attach to the established families, and a candidate is of interest chiefly as a possible replacement for one of them on a named duty. Duties are compared on the moisture content to be reached and on the continuity of the service, since a bed that dries deeply but regenerates slowly answers a different need from a bed that dries moderately in a rapid cycle.

## Established results

Four findings recur across the literature and stand as established. Equilibrium water uptake rises steeply with the partial pressure of water vapour, and the shape of the rise differs by family: zeolite molecular sieves take up a large share of their capacity at very low partial pressures, which fits them for drying to very low moisture contents, while silica gel takes up little at low partial pressures and reaches capacity only as the gas approaches saturation, which fits it for bulk water removal. Capacity falls as temperature rises, so a bed dries best cool, and regeneration is carried out by heating the bed, by lowering the pressure over it, or by sweeping it with dry purge gas, reversing the conditions that favoured uptake. Uptake rate is governed by transport, not by equilibrium capacity: by vapour movement through the gas film around each particle and by diffusion within the particle, so particle size and gas velocity set the bed length a duty requires without changing what the material can ultimately hold. Contaminants degrade performance: heavy hydrocarbons, oils and other strongly held species occupy capacity and foul surfaces, and beds in real service lose working capacity over their lives even where fresh material characterises well in the laboratory. The great majority of the 147 papers support these findings, and no serious body of work in the review contradicts them. The established findings also fix the vocabulary of the field. Capacity without a stated partial pressure and temperature is not a comparable quantity, and working capacity, the share of equilibrium capacity a real cycle can use between regenerations, is the figure by which beds are actually sized. Reports that keep the two apart can be set side by side; reports that merge them cannot, and much of the apparent scatter in the literature is a scatter of definitions before it is a scatter of materials.

## Disagreements

Reports conflict on one named quantity: the equilibrium water uptake of zeolite molecular sieves at low partial pressures of water vapour, the region on which their reputation rests. Some groups report uptakes in this region markedly higher than other groups report for materials nominally of the same type, and the spread between the highest and lowest values is large enough to reverse the ranking of materials a designer would draw from the literature at face value. The disagreement is not simple error on one side. The conflicting reports differ systematically in measurement conditions: in sample pretreatment and activation before measurement, in the temperature of the measurement, in the way the partial pressure was established and held, and in whether uptake was followed by sample weight or by the moisture content of the gas passing over the sample. Each choice is defensible, and some are known to shift the measured uptake, but the choices vary between groups in combination rather than one at a time, so the literature does not allow the discrepancy to be assigned to a single cause. A secondary disagreement concerns the working capacity of silica gel in bulk drying: reports differ on how much of the equilibrium capacity survives the dynamics of a real bed, with its incomplete regeneration and ageing. Until measurement conventions converge, or shared samples are measured under shared conditions, rankings drawn across groups carry an uncertainty that the individual papers, each internally consistent, do not disclose. The disagreement also has a geography of method: groups that measure gravimetrically tend to report the higher uptakes, and groups that measure by the gas phase tend to report the lower, which suggests that part of the gap is carried by the measurement chain rather than by the samples. Neither chain is self-evidently the truer one, since each converts its raw observation into an uptake through its own assumptions about dead volume, buoyancy and the dryness of the reference state.

## Gaps

On the evidence of the 147 papers surveyed, the measurement nobody reports is the water uptake an adsorbent retains after extended regeneration cycling under a realistic humid feed. Fresh-material capacity is reported in abundance, and capacity after some ageing or after exposure to a named contaminant appears in a smaller number of papers, but a systematic record of drying capacity declining cycle by cycle over a bed's working life is essentially absent. The omission matters because the economics of gas drying turn on that decline: the bed change interval, the energy spent regenerating the bed over its life, and the moisture excursions passed downstream as the bed ages are all governed by cycling behaviour the literature does not measure. A second gap is the reporting of measurement conditions: sample pretreatment is described loosely or not at all in a substantial minority of papers, which leaves the disagreements above needlessly hard to resolve after the fact. A third gap concerns mixtures: nearly all measurements use water vapour in a clean carrier gas, while the industrial duty is water alongside hydrocarbons and other adsorbable species whose competitive uptake shapes bed performance. Mixed-feed measurements, over cycling, on the materials in ordinary use would advance practical design further than further refinement of single-component capacity on fresh samples. The gaps are connected. Cycling measurements on mixed feeds, reported with pretreatment stated in full, would at one stroke supply the ageing record the economics require, test the established findings under service conditions, and give the disagreement over low-pressure uptake a set of shared samples on which methods could be compared directly. The literature has the instruments for such work; what it has not yet produced is the work itself, and the absence is the more notable because every party to the disagreement would benefit from its removal.

fact_base: A tutorial passage explains the Nusselt number to second-year students. Definition in words: the Nusselt number is the ratio of convective to conductive heat transfer at a surface. The passage must state what a value near 1 means and what a large value means, without inventing numerical examples.
input: When students begin to study heat transfer, one of the most important dimensionless quantities they will encounter is the Nusselt number, and it plays a crucial role in helping us understand how effectively heat is transferred at a surface. In essence, the Nusselt number can be thought of as a comparison between two different ways in which heat can move at a surface: on the one hand, convection, which is the transfer of heat into a moving fluid, and on the other hand, conduction, which is the transfer of heat through a stagnant layer of fluid. More precisely, the Nusselt number is defined as the ratio of convective to conductive heat transfer at a surface, and this seemingly simple ratio actually tells us a great deal about which process is dominating in any given situation. When the Nusselt number is close to 1, this means that the two mechanisms are roughly comparable in size, and heat is essentially being transferred in much the same way as it would be if the fluid were barely moving at all, with conduction doing most of the work; a Nusselt number of exactly 1 would correspond to transfer by conduction alone. However, when the Nusselt number takes on a large value, this indicates that convection has become much stronger than conduction, and the movement of the fluid is now enhancing the transfer of heat very significantly compared with the purely conductive baseline. Overall, by keeping this interpretation firmly in mind, students can use the Nusselt number not merely as a number to be calculated, but as a meaningful indicator of the underlying heat transfer behaviour in a wide range of different situations.
target: The Nusselt number is the ratio of convective to conductive heat transfer at a surface. Convection is heat transfer from a surface into a moving fluid. Conduction is heat transfer from the same surface through a stagnant layer of that fluid. The conductive rate is the rate the surface would show with the fluid at rest, and it is the fixed side of the comparison; the convective rate is the rate with the fluid in motion. A value near 1 means the two rates are nearly equal. Convection then adds little to what conduction alone would give, and the surface transfers heat almost as it would into still fluid; a value of 1 is the limiting case of transfer by conduction alone. A large value means the convective rate stands far above the conductive rate. Movement of the fluid then sets the transfer, and the conductive part is small by comparison. Between the two readings, the meaning moves with the ratio itself: the further the value stands above unity, the larger the share of the transfer that convection carries, and the less the result depends on the stagnant-layer rate. The number is a ratio of two rates of the same kind, so it carries no unit. Second-year work meets the number wherever a surface meets a moving fluid, and the reading is always the same comparison, stated before any calculation: near unity, conduction sets the rate; large, convection sets it.

fact_base: Goal: compute the Reynolds number for water in a pipe and state the flow regime. The Reynolds number Re (dimensionless) is computed from density rho (kg m-3), mean velocity v (m s-1), pipe diameter D (m) and dynamic viscosity mu (Pa s) by Re = rho v D / mu. Water at 293 K: rho = 998 kg m-3, mu = 1.00 x 10-3 Pa s. Pipe diameter D = 0.08 m; mean velocity v = 1.5 m s-1. Worked result: Re = 119800 (computed as 998 x 1.5 x 0.08 / 0.001). Flow is laminar below Re = 2300 and turbulent above Re = 4000; between the two values the regime is transitional and is not assigned by the number alone.
input: In this worked example, we are going to calculate the Reynolds number for water flowing inside a pipe, and then we will use the result to determine what the flow regime actually is. The Reynolds number, which is a dimensionless quantity denoted by Re, is computed from the density rho (kg m-3), the mean velocity v (m s-1), the pipe diameter D (m) and the dynamic viscosity mu (Pa s), using the relationship Re = rho v D / mu. For water at a temperature of 293 K, the density rho is equal to 998 and the dynamic viscosity mu is equal to 1.00 x 10-3, in the units that have just been stated. In this particular case, we will take the pipe diameter D to be 0.08 and the mean velocity v to be 1.5, again in the units stated above. Substituting all of these values into the equation gives us Re = 998 x 1.5 x 0.08 / 0.001, and when we work through this calculation step by step, the numerator works out to 119.76, so dividing by 0.001 gives a final Reynolds number of Re = 119800. It is worth noting that the units cancel out completely in this calculation, which is exactly what we would expect for a dimensionless quantity: the density, velocity and diameter terms combine in the numerator, and the viscosity term in the denominator removes what they leave. Now, in order to interpret this result, it is important to keep in mind the standard thresholds: the flow is laminar when the Reynolds number is below 2300, it is turbulent when the Reynolds number is above 4000, and between 2300 and 4000 the flow is in a transitional regime, which cannot really be assigned from the number alone. Since our calculated value of 119800 stands far above the upper threshold of 4000, we can conclude that the flow in this pipe is turbulent, well outside the transitional band and firmly in the range that the thresholds assign to turbulent flow.
target: The Reynolds number for water in the pipe is 119800, and the flow is turbulent. The Reynolds number Re (dimensionless) is computed from the density rho (kg m-3), the mean velocity v (m s-1), the pipe diameter D (m) and the dynamic viscosity mu (Pa s) by Re = rho v D / mu. Water at 293 K has rho = 998 and mu = 1.00 x 10-3, in the units of that roster. Take the pipe diameter as D = 0.08 and the mean velocity as v = 1.5, in the same units. Substitution of these values in Re = rho v D / mu gives Re = 998 x 1.5 x 0.08 / 0.001. The numerator collects the density, velocity and diameter terms (the product of the density, velocity and diameter terms, 119.76 in the combined units of the three quantities), and division by the viscosity (0.001 Pa s) removes the units. Thus Re = 119800, and the Reynolds number is dimensionless because the units in the numerator and the denominator cancel. The regime is read from the thresholds. Flow is laminar below Re = 2300 and turbulent above Re = 4000; between 2300 and 4000 the regime is transitional and is not assigned by the number alone. The computed value stands above the upper threshold (4000) by a wide margin, in the range the thresholds assign to turbulent flow. No part of the transitional range is involved. The check on the result is the threshold comparison itself, and the comparison is not close: the value sits far into the turbulent range, so the assignment does not depend on any fine reading of the thresholds, and a small error in any of the input quantities would leave the regime unchanged.

fact_base: A tutorial passage explains absolute and relative error through a temperature measurement. Worked figures: reading 180 units, tolerance 0.5% of reading, so the absolute error is 0.9 units. The passage distinguishes error from uncertainty and does not merge the two terms.
input: When we make a measurement of any kind, it is very important to understand that the value we read off an instrument is never going to be perfectly exact, and this is where the closely related but subtly different concepts of error and uncertainty come into play. In this passage, we are going to explore the ideas of absolute error and relative error by looking at a simple temperature measurement. The absolute error is essentially the size of the difference between the measured value and the true value, and it is expressed in the same units as the measurement itself. The relative error, on the other hand, expresses that same difference as a fraction or percentage of the reading, which can often be more informative. Let us consider a concrete example: suppose we have a temperature reading of 180 units, and suppose the tolerance on that reading is 0.5% of the reading itself. Working through the calculation, 0.5% of 180 units gives us an absolute error of 0.9 units, which tells us the scale of the discrepancy in the units we are actually working with. It is worth emphasising that error and uncertainty are not really the same thing, even though people often use the words interchangeably: error refers to a difference in a particular measurement, whereas uncertainty describes the doubt or spread that surrounds a result more generally, and carefully distinguishing between these two ideas is an important part of reporting measurements in a clear and rigorous way. In short, the relative error here is 0.5%, the absolute error is 0.9 units, and stating the tolerance as 0.5% of the reading is what connects the two statements.
target: Absolute error is the size of the difference between a reading and the value the reading stands for, stated in the units of the reading. Relative error is the same difference stated as a fraction of the reading, usually as a percentage. A temperature measurement shows the two forms on one set of figures. The reading is 180 units and the tolerance is 0.5% of the reading. The absolute error is thus 0.5% of 180 units, which is 0.9 units. The relative error is the tolerance itself, 0.5%, and it carries no unit. The two statements answer different questions. The absolute error (0.9 units) gives the size of the discrepancy in the units of the measurement, and the relative error (0.5%) gives that size against the size of the reading. Error and uncertainty are separate terms and are not merged here. Error belongs to a single reading: it is the difference between that reading and the value it stands for, and it can in principle be stated as one number. Uncertainty belongs to the result: it states the range within which the value is held to lie, and it reflects what is not known about the measurement rather than a counted difference. A report that gives an error where an uncertainty is meant overstates what the measurement establishes, and a report that gives an uncertainty as an error does the same in the other direction.

fact_base: A defect-reduction project on a filling line cut the reject rate from 5.4% to 2.5% over one quarter. At 96k units per year the change avoids about 2784 rejected units per year. The quarter included a planned shutdown; rates are not adjusted for it.
input: In this case study, we will take a closer look at a highly successful defect-reduction project that was carried out on a filling line, and we will examine the impressive results that were achieved over the course of one quarter. At the beginning of the period in question, the reject rate on the line stood at 5.4%, which meant that a fairly substantial proportion of the units being produced were not meeting the required quality standards. However, thanks to the efforts of the project team, this figure was brought down considerably, and by the end of the quarter the reject rate had fallen to just 2.5%. To put the change plainly, the line went from 5.4% rejects to 2.5% rejects in the space of a single quarter, a fall from 5.4% to 2.5% that was recorded across the whole line. In order to put these figures into some kind of perspective, it is helpful to consider the production volumes involved: at a rate of 96k units per year, this reduction in the reject rate means that the change avoids approximately 2784 rejected units per year, that is, 2784 units counted on the full 96k units produced in a year, which represents a meaningful saving in materials, time and rework. It should be noted, however, that the quarter in question also included a planned shutdown of the line, and the rates that are reported here have not been adjusted to take that shutdown into account, so a degree of caution is advisable when interpreting the figures. Overall, the project demonstrates the significant value that focused improvement work can deliver on a production line.
target: A defect-reduction project on a filling line cut the reject rate from 5.4% to 2.5% over one quarter. At 96k units per year, the change avoids about 2784 rejected units per year. The saving stands in rejected units not produced: each avoided reject is a unit that does not consume material, filling time and rework, and the count of 2784 units is stated on the full annual volume of 96k units. The rates carry one qualification in the same terms as the result. The quarter included a planned shutdown, and the rates are not adjusted for it. The reject rate before the change (5.4%) and the reject rate after it (2.5%) are both quarter averages over a period that contained stopped time, so the comparison is between two quarters as run, not between two quarters at equal running hours. No adjustment has been made, and none is implied by the figures as reported. The result as stated is narrow: on this filling line, over this quarter, the reject rate went from 5.4% to 2.5%, and at the stated annual volume that change corresponds to that many fewer rejected units per year. The figures say nothing about whether the lower rate holds in a quarter with no shutdown, and nothing about the cost of the work that produced the change, which is not reported here. What the project establishes is the movement in the rate on this line over this quarter; any wider claim would need the following quarters to hold the rate at its new level, on running conditions that match those of the quarter reported.

fact_base: Goal: compute the half-life of a first-order reaction and the fraction remaining after 60 min. For a first-order reaction the rate constant k (min-1) fixes the half-life t1/2 (min) by t1/2 = ln(2) / k, and the fraction remaining after time t (min) is exp(-k t). Measured rate constant: k = 0.046 min-1 at 323 K, from concentration measurements every 5 min over 90 min. Worked results: t1/2 = 15.1 min; the fraction remaining after 60 min is 0.06 (dimensionless), both computed from the stated relations. The relations hold for a first-order reaction only; a reaction of another order follows a different decay law.
input: In this worked example, our goal is to calculate the half-life of a first-order reaction, and also to work out what fraction of the reactant remains after a period of 60 min has elapsed. For a first-order reaction, the rate constant k (in units of min-1) determines the half-life t1/2 (in min) through the simple relationship t1/2 = ln(2) / k, and the fraction of the reactant that remains after a time t (in min) is given by exp(-k t). In the case we are considering here, the measured rate constant is k = 0.046 min-1 at a temperature of 323 K, and this value was obtained from concentration measurements that were taken every 5 min over a total period of 90 min. Substituting the value of k into the half-life formula, we find that the half-life is 15.1 min, which means that the amount of reactant falls to half of its value every 15.1 min. Moving on to the second part of the problem, we can substitute k = 0.046 min-1 and t = 60 min into the decay expression, and this gives us a fraction remaining after 60 min of 0.06, which means that only a small proportion of the original material is still present at that point. The fraction remaining after 60 min is 0.06 because the interval spans several half-lives: with a half-life of 15.1 min, successive halvings reduce the amount step by step until a fraction of 0.06 is left. It is important to bear in mind that these particular relationships are valid for a first-order reaction only; a reaction of a different order would follow a different decay law, and the same formulas would not apply to it.
target: The half-life of the reaction is 15.1 min, and the fraction remaining after 60 min is 0.06. For a first-order reaction the rate constant k (min-1) fixes the half-life t1/2 (min) by t1/2 = ln(2) / k, and the fraction remaining after time t (min) is exp(-k t). The measured rate constant is k = 0.046 min-1 at 323 K, from concentration measurements every 5 min over 90 min. Substitution in the half-life relation with k = 0.046 min-1 gives the half-life as 15.1 min. Substitution in exp(-k t) with the same rate constant and t = 60 min gives the fraction remaining after 60 min as 0.06 (dimensionless). The two results read together state the decay plainly: the amount halves every 15.1 min, so an interval of 60 min contains several successive halvings, and the fraction left at the end of it (0.06) is correspondingly small. The relations hold for a first-order reaction only. A reaction of another order follows a different decay law, and neither the half-life relation nor the exponential fraction applies to it; the half-life of such a reaction is not fixed by the rate constant alone in this way, and it changes as the reaction proceeds. Both results come from the one measured rate constant, and each can be checked against the other before either is used.

subtype: worked example with equation: available NPSH
fact_base: A pump draws water from an open tank at atmospheric pressure, 101.3 kPa. Vapour pressure at the pumping temperature is 2.3 kPa, the static lift is 3.6 m and suction-line friction loss is 1 m. Available net positive suction head $NPSH_a$ is 5.5 m. The pump's required NPSH at the duty flow comes from the vendor curve and must be exceeded with margin.
input:
In this example, we are going to work through the calculation of the available net positive suction head, usually abbreviated to $NPSH_a$, for a pump that is drawing water up from an open tank at 101.3 kPa. The pump draws water from the open tank at atmospheric pressure, which is 101.3 kPa, and the vapour pressure of the water at the pumping temperature is 2.3 kPa. In addition, the static lift that the pump has to overcome is 3.6 m, and the friction loss in the suction line is 1 m. The available net positive suction head is calculated using the following relationship, in which $P_{atm}$ is the atmospheric pressure, $P_v$ is the vapour pressure, $\rho$ is the density, $g$ is the acceleration due to gravity, $h_{lift}$ is the static lift and $h_f$ is the friction loss:

$$NPSH_a = \frac{P_{atm} - P_v}{\rho g} - h_{lift} - h_f$$

When all of the values are substituted into this equation, the available net positive suction head $NPSH_a$ comes out at 5.5 m, and it is this available head of 5.5 m that has to be used in the comparison. It is very important to remember that this available value has to be compared against the pump's required NPSH at the duty flow, which is taken from the vendor curve, and the available value must exceed the required value with a suitable margin in order to avoid problems during operation.
target:
The available net positive suction head $NPSH_a$ for the pump is 5.5 m. The pump draws water from an open tank, and $NPSH_a$ (m) is obtained from the atmospheric pressure $P_{atm}$ (kPa), the vapour pressure at the pumping temperature $P_v$ (kPa), the density $\rho$, the acceleration due to gravity $g$, the static lift $h_{lift}$ (m) and the suction-line friction loss $h_f$ (m) by

$$NPSH_a = \frac{P_{atm} - P_v}{\rho g} - h_{lift} - h_f$$

The pressure term converts the pressure margin above vapour pressure into a head of liquid; the lift and the friction loss are then subtracted from that head. The tank is open, so $P_{atm}$ is 101.3 kPa. Substitution of $P_{atm}$ = 101.3 kPa, $P_v$ = 2.3 kPa, $h_{lift}$ = 3.6 m and $h_f$ = 1 m gives $NPSH_a$ = 5.5 m. The figure is an available head at the stated conditions, and its use is a comparison. The pump's required NPSH at the duty flow comes from the vendor curve, and $NPSH_a$ must exceed that required value with margin; the available head establishes nothing on its own until the required value from the vendor curve is set against it. Each term in the equation is a head, so the result is read directly against the required head, with no conversion standing between the two sides of the comparison, and the margin is the difference between the two heads at the duty flow.

fact_base: A centrifugal pump moves water between two vessels at grade. At the duty point the flow is 101 m3 h-1 against a head of 20 m, with pump efficiency 65%. Shaft power at the duty point is 8.5 kW. The motor is rated 15% above this value. Cavitation was not observed in the acceptance test, which ran for 4 h at the duty point only.
input: This passage presents the results of a duty assessment for a centrifugal pump that is used to move water between two vessels that are located at grade. At the all-important duty point, the pump delivers a flow of 101 m3 h-1 against a head of 20 m, and it operates with a pump efficiency of 65%. Based on these figures, the shaft power at the duty point works out at 8.5 kW, which is the power that has to be delivered to the pump shaft in order to sustain the duty. The motor that drives the pump is rated 15% above this value, which provides a certain amount of headroom above the calculated requirement at the duty point. During the acceptance test, which was run for a period of 4 h at the duty point only, no cavitation was observed at any stage, which is an encouraging sign. It is worth pointing out, however, that the test covered only the single duty point and only for that limited duration, so the results that are reported here relate specifically to that operating condition and should be interpreted in that light. The two vessels are located at grade, so the duty is stated for a transfer between vessels at the same level, and all of the figures that have been presented relate to that arrangement. Taken together, the assessment gives a clear picture of what the pump is being asked to do at its intended operating point, and of the power that has to be supplied to the shaft in order to sustain that duty on a continuous basis.
target: A centrifugal pump moving water between two vessels at grade delivers 101 m3 h-1 against a head of 20 m at the duty point, with pump efficiency 65%. Shaft power at the duty point is 8.5 kW. The motor is rated 15% above this value, so the installed rating carries a margin over the shaft power the duty requires; the margin is a rating allowance and states nothing about operation at other flows. Cavitation was not observed in the acceptance test, which ran for 4 h at the duty point only. The test result is a detection statement at one operating point: over the test at the duty flow and the duty head, no cavitation was detected. Operation away from the duty point was not tested, and longer running at the duty point was not tested either. The duty figures themselves form one consistent set at one point on the pump's range; they do not describe the pump at part load or at higher flow, where the head, the efficiency and the shaft power all take other values that are not reported here. The duty point is a single point on the operating range, chosen for the transfer between the two vessels at grade. Away from that point the pump delivers other flows against other heads, and the efficiency and the shaft power move with the operating point; the values reported here are the values at the duty point and are not a description of the pump in general. For design use, the set is read as one point with its test scope attached, and any extension of the result beyond that point requires test evidence that the acceptance run does not provide.

subtype: worked example with equation: Ergun pressure drop
fact_base: Gas flows through a packed bed of 1 mm particles. The void fraction $\varepsilon$ is 0.4, the superficial velocity $u$ is 0.45 m s-1 and the bed length is 3 m. The Ergun equation gives a pressure gradient of 10.8 kPa m-1, or 32.5 kPa over the bed. Particle diameter $d_p$ is 1 mm; gas density is 1.2 kg m-3 and viscosity is 1.8 x 10-5 Pa s.
input:
In this worked example, we will calculate the pressure drop that occurs when a gas flows through a packed bed, using the well-known Ergun equation. The bed in question is made up of particles that are 1 mm in diameter, and the gas flows through it with a void fraction $\varepsilon$ of 0.4 and a superficial velocity $u$ of 0.45 m s-1, over a bed length of 3 m. The Ergun equation, which is given below, combines a viscous term and an inertial term, and in the equation $\Delta P$ is the pressure drop, $L$ is the bed length, $\mu$ is the viscosity, $d_p$ is the particle diameter, $\rho$ is the gas density and $u$ is the superficial velocity:

$$\frac{\Delta P}{L} = \frac{150 \mu (1-\varepsilon)^2}{\varepsilon^3 d_p^2} u + \frac{1.75 (1-\varepsilon)}{\varepsilon^3 d_p} \rho u^2$$

For this particular bed, the particle diameter $d_p$ is 1 mm, the gas density is 1.2 kg m-3 and the viscosity is 1.8 x 10-5 Pa s. When all of these values are substituted into the Ergun equation, it gives a pressure gradient of 10.8 kPa m-1, which corresponds to a total pressure drop of 32.5 kPa over the bed. This is quite a substantial pressure drop, and it shows how important it is to take the resistance of the packing properly into account when a packed bed is being designed. The bed is treated as uniform from end to end, with the same voidage and the same particle size throughout its length, and the gas is treated as passing through the bed once, at the stated rate, under the stated conditions.
target:
The Ergun equation gives a pressure gradient of 10.8 kPa m-1 for the bed, or 32.5 kPa over the bed. Gas flows through a packed bed of 1 mm particles with void fraction $\varepsilon$ = 0.4 at a superficial velocity $u$ = 0.45 m s-1, and the bed length is 3 m. The pressure drop $\Delta P$ (Pa) over the bed length $L$ (m) is obtained from the viscosity $\mu$ (Pa s), the void fraction $\varepsilon$ (dimensionless), the particle diameter $d_p$ (m), the gas density $\rho$ and the superficial velocity $u$ by

$$\frac{\Delta P}{L} = \frac{150 \mu (1-\varepsilon)^2}{\varepsilon^3 d_p^2} u + \frac{1.75 (1-\varepsilon)}{\varepsilon^3 d_p} \rho u^2$$

The first term is the viscous contribution and the second is the inertial contribution; the equation adds the two and states the gradient directly. Substitution uses the particle diameter $d_p$ = 1 mm, the gas density of 1.2 kg m-3 and the viscosity of 1.8 x 10-5 Pa s, with the void fraction and the superficial velocity as stated above. The gradient that results is uniform over the bed in this calculation, so the pressure drop grows in proportion to the length of bed the gas traverses. At a low superficial velocity the viscous term carries most of the gradient; as the velocity rises, the inertial term grows with the square of the velocity and takes the larger share, and the stated gradient is the sum of the two at the stated velocity. The result is a design figure for this packing: it is the resistance that the machine supplying the gas must overcome across this item, stated before any allowance for distributors, supports or entrance and exit losses, none of which are inside the equation. Both figures rest on the stated bed: a change in the particle diameter, the void fraction or the superficial velocity changes the gradient, and the values reported here hold for this packing and this gas rate only.

fact_base: Excerpt content: the absorber wall thickness is 68 mm after the corrosion allowance is added. The excerpt compares two gasket materials on temperature limit only and prefers the higher-rated one. The excerpt ends mid-argument; it neither summarises the report nor previews the next section.
input: With regard to the wall thickness of the absorber, it is worth noting that once the corrosion allowance has been duly added, the thickness in question comes to some 68 mm, and this is the figure that should be carried forward. Turning now to the gasket materials that are currently under consideration, a comparison has been carried out between the two candidate materials, focusing specifically and exclusively on the temperature limit, since this is the aspect that matters most in this context. On this basis, it would appear that the second of the two materials is to be preferred, because its temperature rating is higher and it therefore offers a greater degree of headroom against the excursions that the absorber may experience in service, whereas the first material sits somewhat closer to its limit, and in addition to this the question of how the joint behaves around the lean solvent pump also has to be borne in mind when the behaviour of the two materials is weighed against one another, because the margin that is available at the higher rating is precisely what is relied upon when
target: The wall thickness of the absorber is 68 mm after the corrosion allowance is added, and the allowance is inside that figure rather than additional to it. For the gasket, two materials are compared on temperature limit only. Neither is assessed here on any other property, and the comparison gives no ranking on sealing, on life or on cost. On temperature limit the second material is preferred. Its rating stands higher, so the excursion the absorber can impose on the joint stays inside the rated range with room to spare, where the first material runs closer to its limit under the same excursion. The preference is narrow in scope: it decides the gasket on the one property the service presses hardest, and it leaves the remaining properties of both materials unexamined.
