fact_base: Adsorption of a dye from water on activated carbon was measured in batch tests at 298 K. The fitted Langmuir capacity was 218 mg of dye per gram of adsorbent at pH 7. At an adsorbent dose of 0.8 g L-1, removal after 120 min was 87% of the initial dye concentration of 50 mg L-1. The Langmuir fit is reported for pH 7 only; capacity at other pH values was not measured.
input: This study set out to investigate the adsorption of a dye from water onto activated carbon, and a series of batch tests was carried out at a temperature of 298 K in order to explore the behaviour of the system. The experimental data were fitted to the Langmuir model, and the fitted Langmuir capacity was found to be 218 mg of dye per gram of adsorbent at pH 7, which represents the maximum capacity according to that particular model. In a further set of experiments, an adsorbent dose of 0.8 g L-1 was used, and after a contact time of 120 min the removal had reached 87% of the initial dye concentration, which was 50 mg L-1 at the start of the test. In that test, removal after 120 min reached 87% of the initial dye concentration of 50 mg L-1 at the adsorbent dose of 0.8 g L-1. The fitted capacity of 218 mg of dye per gram of adsorbent at pH 7 is the value that the Langmuir model approaches under those conditions. These results show that the activated carbon is quite effective at removing the dye under the conditions that were studied, and they provide a useful starting point for thinking about how the material might perform in a treatment process, where the contact between the water and the carbon would be arranged in a rather different way from a batch test and where the water itself would bring other substances with it. It should be noted, however, that the Langmuir fit is reported for pH 7 only, and the capacity at other pH values was not measured in this work, so the findings should be interpreted within that particular scope.
target: Adsorption of a dye from water on activated carbon was measured in batch tests at 298 K. The fitted Langmuir capacity was 218 mg of dye per gram of adsorbent at pH 7. At an adsorbent dose of 0.8 g L-1, removal after 120 min was 87% of the initial dye concentration of 50 mg L-1. The capacity figure and the removal figure describe different quantities. The Langmuir capacity is a fitted parameter of the isotherm at pH 7: it states the loading the fitted model approaches, and it comes from the fit rather than from a single measurement. The removal figure (87% after 120 min at a dose of 0.8 g L-1) is a measured outcome at one dose, one contact time and one initial concentration of 50 mg L-1. A change in any of those conditions changes the removal, and that percentage does not transfer to other doses or other starting concentrations. Scope is stated with the results: the Langmuir fit is reported for pH 7 only, and capacity at other pH values was not measured. Whether the same capacity holds away from that pH is therefore open, and the value of 218 mg per gram holds at that pH, not as a property of the carbon across pH. The two figures also have different standing as evidence. A fitted capacity depends on the model chosen for the fit and on the range of concentrations the fit was made over, neither of which is carried by the number itself; a measured removal depends on the arrangement of the test and on nothing else. A reader who takes the capacity as a measured loading, or the removal as a property of the carbon rather than of the test, reads both figures as more than they are.

fact_base: 214 pumps run at the plant. Maintenance records for 12 months show 1056 h of unplanned downtime; bearing failures account for 48% of the downtime hours. A sensor set for all 214 pumps is quoted at $460k installed, plus $58k per year. In a vendor trial on a comparable unit, the sensors cut downtime by 19%; the figure is a vendor figure and was not measured at this plant. A pilot on 24 pumps costs $30k over three months. Spare-part lead times are unchanged by the sensors. The memo recommends the three-month pilot; the reliability engineering group owns the pilot and reports before the March capital review; the decision on full installation is held until the pilot results are reported.
input: This memo looks at whether condition-monitoring sensors should be installed on the pumps at the plant, and it draws on the maintenance records that are available for the last 12 months. There are 214 pumps running at the plant, and over that period the records show a total of 1056 h of unplanned downtime, which is a very significant amount of lost production time. Looking more closely at the breakdown of that downtime, bearing failures account for 48% of the downtime hours, which makes them by far the largest single contributor. A full sensor set for all 214 pumps has been quoted at $460k installed, plus an additional $58k per year on an ongoing basis. In a trial carried out by the vendor on a comparable unit, the sensors were able to cut downtime by 19%, although it should be stressed that this figure is a vendor figure and it was not actually measured at this plant. As a more cautious first step, a pilot installation on 24 pumps would cost $30k over three months. It is also worth noting that spare-part lead times are completely unchanged by the sensors, so that aspect of downtime would not be improved. Taking all of this into account, the memo recommends going ahead with the three-month pilot; the reliability engineering group will own the pilot and will report before the March capital review, and the decision on full installation will be held until those pilot results have been reported.
target: Recommendation: run the three-month pilot on 24 pumps at $30k, and hold the decision on full installation until the pilot results are reported. The reliability engineering group owns the pilot and reports before the March capital review. The plant runs 214 pumps. Maintenance records for 12 months show 1056 h of unplanned downtime, and bearing failures account for 48% of the downtime hours; the bearing share is the part of the downtime that bearing monitoring addresses. A sensor set for all 214 pumps is quoted at $460k installed, plus $58k per year. Against that cost stands one effectiveness figure: in a vendor trial on a comparable unit, the sensors cut downtime by 19%. That percentage is a vendor figure and was not measured at this plant, so it sizes the possible benefit but does not establish it here. The pilot converts that vendor figure into a plant figure, against a full-installation commitment at the quoted installed price plus the quoted annual charge. Spare-part lead times are unchanged by the sensors, and downtime waiting on parts is outside what the pilot can improve. The pilot therefore tests the bearing-failure share of the downtime hours, under this plant's operating conditions, and its report to the March capital review is the evidence on which the full-installation decision rests. What the pilot measures is detection in service: whether the sensors flag the bearing deterioration that precedes failure, on these pumps, in time for a planned intervention to replace an unplanned stop. That is the quantity the full-installation decision turns on, and it is the one quantity the vendor trial, run elsewhere, cannot supply for this plant.

fact_base: Pervaporation is a membrane separation in which a liquid feed contacts one side of a membrane and vacuum on the other side draws the permeating component through as vapour. Flux is the mass permeating per unit membrane area per hour (kg m-2 h-1). The separation factor is the water-to-alcohol ratio in the permeate divided by the same ratio in the feed (dimensionless). Feed: 85 wt% ethanol in water, at 60 °C. One feed composition was tested; no test ran beyond 500 h. Polymer membrane: flux 2.4 kg m-2 h-1, separation factor 180, flux fell 10% over 500 h. Zeolite membrane: flux 1 kg m-2 h-1, separation factor 560, flux unchanged over 500 h within measurement error. Flux, selectivity and stability are seldom reported together for the same membrane.
input: Pervaporation is a membrane separation in which a liquid feed contacts one side of a membrane and vacuum on the other side draws the permeating component through as vapour. Flux is the mass permeating per unit membrane area per hour (kg m-2 h-1). The separation factor is the water-to-alcohol ratio in the permeate divided by the same ratio in the feed (dimensionless). Both membranes were tested on one feed, 85 wt% ethanol in water at 60 °C; one feed composition was tested, and no test ran beyond 500 h. The polymer membrane gave a flux of 2.4 kg m-2 h-1 with a separation factor of 180, and its flux fell 10% over 500 h. The zeolite membrane gave a flux of 1 kg m-2 h-1 with a separation factor of 560, and its flux was unchanged over 500 h within measurement error. The two membranes divide the performance figures between them. The polymer membrane passes more mass per unit area and per hour; the zeolite membrane separates more sharply, with a permeate far richer in water, relative to alcohol, than the feed. Stability divides them in the same direction as selectivity: the polymer membrane loses flux over the test period, and the zeolite membrane holds its flux within measurement error. No ranking of the two membranes follows from these figures alone, because a duty sets the flux and the separation factor it requires, and neither requirement is stated here. Flux, selectivity and stability are seldom reported together for the same membrane; here all three stand on the one feed composition, and behaviour at any other composition was not measured.

fact_base: A continuous stirred-tank reactor runs a neutralisation that is first order in the limiting reactant. The rate constant is 0.139 min-1 at the operating temperature and the mean residence time is 37 min. Steady-state conversion for an ideal CSTR is 83.7%. The estimate assumes perfect mixing and constant density; tracer tests on the actual vessel have not been run.
input: In this worked example, we will explore how to estimate the steady-state conversion for a continuous stirred-tank reactor, often abbreviated as a CSTR, that is being used to carry out a neutralisation reaction. It is important to note that the reaction in question is first order in the limiting reactant, which means that the rate depends linearly on the concentration of that particular reactant, and this assumption forms the basis of the calculation that follows. The rate constant for the reaction, at the operating temperature of the system, is given as 0.139 min-1, and the mean residence time of material within the reactor is 37 min, so both of the key parameters needed for the ideal-reactor calculation are available. When these values are brought together in the standard design relation for an ideal CSTR, the steady-state conversion comes out at 83.7%, which represents the fraction of the limiting reactant that is converted under the assumed conditions. However, it is worth keeping in mind that this estimate rests on two important idealisations, namely perfect mixing throughout the vessel and constant density of the reacting mixture as the reaction proceeds. In a real vessel, mixing may not be perfectly uniform, and these assumptions should therefore be treated with a degree of caution. Furthermore, tracer tests, which would help to characterise the actual flow behaviour inside the vessel, have not been run on the actual vessel, so the idealised picture has not yet been checked against experimental evidence from the real system. The figure of 83.7% should therefore be read as the conversion predicted by the idealised model rather than as a measured outcome for the vessel itself.
target: A continuous stirred-tank reactor (CSTR) runs a neutralisation that is first order in the limiting reactant. The rate constant at the operating temperature is 0.139 min-1 and the mean residence time is 37 min. For an ideal CSTR at steady state, these values give a conversion of the limiting reactant of 83.7%. Conversion here is the fraction of the limiting reactant converted in a single pass at steady state, and the result follows from the first-order rate law combined with the residence time in the standard CSTR design relation. Two idealisations carry the estimate. Perfect mixing is assumed, so the composition everywhere in the vessel equals the outlet composition, and density is taken as constant through the reaction. A real vessel departs from both: mixing is never complete, and a density change would alter the residence time at a fixed volumetric flow. The direction of the combined error is not fixed by the calculation itself. Tracer tests on the actual vessel have not been run. A tracer test would measure the residence-time distribution of the real vessel and show how far it departs from the perfectly mixed case, so the 83.7% figure stands as an ideal-reactor estimate, uncorrected for the flow behaviour of the equipment in which the neutralisation would actually be carried out. The residence time enters the result directly: at fixed rate constant, a longer residence time raises conversion, and a shorter one lowers it, in the proportion the design relation sets.

subtype: worked example with equation: Antoine vapour pressure
fact_base: The vapour pressure of ethanol at 60 °C is estimated from the Antoine equation with constants $A$ = 8.20417, $B$ = 1642.89 and $C$ = 230.3 (pressure in mmHg, temperature in °C). The estimate is 46.8 kPa. The constants are valid only over their fitted temperature range; the source databank value governs design.
input:
In this example, we are going to estimate the vapour pressure of ethanol at a temperature of 60 °C by making use of the well-known Antoine equation, which is a widely used correlation that relates vapour pressure to temperature through three substance-specific constants. The Antoine equation is written in the following form:

$$\log_{10} P = A - \frac{B}{T + C}$$

Here, the constants for ethanol are given as $A$ = 8.20417, $B$ = 1642.89 and $C$ = 230.3, and it should be noted that in this correlation the pressure is expressed in mmHg while the temperature is expressed in °C, so care needs to be taken with the units throughout the calculation. When the temperature of 60 °C is substituted into the equation together with these constants, and the resulting pressure is converted into kilopascals, the estimated vapour pressure of ethanol at 60 °C comes out at 46.8 kPa, and the 46.8 kPa value is the figure carried forward from the calculation. This value provides a useful and convenient estimate for design-related purposes; however, it is important to remember that the Antoine constants are only valid over the temperature range over which they were originally fitted, and they should not be extrapolated beyond that range. For actual design work, therefore, the value held in the source databank should always be the value that governs, rather than the output of this correlation alone.
target:
The vapour pressure of ethanol at 60 °C is estimated from the Antoine equation, in which $P$ denotes the vapour pressure (mmHg), $T$ denotes the temperature (°C), and $A$, $B$ and $C$ denote the fitted constants for the substance:

$$\log_{10} P = A - \frac{B}{T + C}$$

For ethanol, $A$ is 8.20417, $B$ is 1642.89 and $C$ is 230.3. Substitution of $T$ = 60 °C gives the pressure in mmHg, and conversion to SI units gives an estimated vapour pressure of 46.8 kPa. The estimate is a correlation result, not a measurement. The three constants were fitted over a limited temperature range, and the equation is valid only within that range; outside it, the same constants can return pressures with no experimental support. The check on the figure is therefore its source: the source databank value for ethanol at 60 °C governs design, and the Antoine estimate serves where a rapid value is needed and the databank value has confirmed the correlation at nearby conditions. Within its fitted range, the correlation reproduces the databank behaviour closely enough for screening calculations, which is the use made of the 46.8 kPa figure here. The constants belong to ethanol alone, and the same form of equation with constants fitted to another substance would describe that substance, not this one; the correlation is empirical throughout, and no term in it carries a theoretical value that could be transferred between substances or corrected from first principles.

fact_base: Excerpt content: the analogy between the transfer processes is stated, then qualified by the case where it fails. The excerpt works one short numerical check with numbers given inside the excerpt itself. The excerpt assumes the chapter's earlier definitions and adds none.
input: In this passage, the Chilton-Colburn analogy provides a remarkably useful link between mass transfer and fluid friction, and it suggests that the mass-transfer factor and the friction factor are connected in a simple and elegant way for a given flow system. Under the analogy, the value of $j_D$ is expected to track the friction behaviour captured by $f$, which means that mass-transfer performance can, in principle, be estimated from friction data that may be much easier to obtain. A short numerical check helps to illustrate the point: for a representative case in which $f$ takes the value 0.010, half of that value is 0.0050, whereas a measured value of $j_D$ for the same system comes out at 0.0042, so the two figures are close to one another without being identical. Nevertheless, it is important to recognise that the analogy has its limits, and it tends to break down in situations where form drag makes a significant contribution to the overall friction, as can happen with rough surfaces or complex geometries, because pressure drag of that kind has no direct counterpart in the mass-transfer process itself.
target: Under the Chilton-Colburn analogy, $j_D$ follows the friction behaviour recorded by $f$, and mass transfer can be estimated from friction data for the same system. A short check shows both the reach and the limit of that estimate. At $f$ = 0.010, the analogy gives 0.0050, against a measured $j_D$ of 0.0042 for the same system: close, and not equal. The qualification is structural. Friction collects skin friction and form drag in a single factor; mass transfer has no counterpart to form drag. Where form drag is small beside skin friction, the analogy tracks the measurement, as the check shows. Where form drag dominates, on rough surfaces or in geometries that separate the flow, $f$ rises with no matching rise in $j_D$, and an estimate taken from friction alone overstates the transfer rate. The analogy also presumes that the same surface does both jobs, transfer and friction, over the same flow field. A surface treatment that changes roughness without changing transfer area, or a geometry that shelters part of the transfer surface from the flow that generates the friction, breaks that shared basis as well, and the estimate inherits the break without signalling it.
