fact_base: Excerpt content: a budget overrun of 7 weeks is reported with its cause; the excerpt proposes one mitigation and its owner. The excerpt does not open or close the memo and does not restate its subject line.
input: The budget position has, unfortunately, deteriorated further during the current period, and it is now necessary to report an overrun that currently stands at 7 weeks against the planned position. The principal cause of this overrun lies in the EPC packages, where prices that were eventually settled with vendors came in materially above the tender allowances that had been carried in the estimate, and this effect has worked its way through the forecast in a progressive manner. A number of smaller estimating gaps have also contributed at the margins, although the settled package prices remain the dominant driver by a considerable distance. In terms of mitigation, it is proposed that further scope changes should be frozen for the time being, so that no additional commitments are entered into while the forecast is being rebuilt, and it is suggested that this freeze should remain in place until a revised and fully reconciled forecast can be presented. Responsibility for the mitigation is assigned to the project board, which would decide when the freeze can be lifted and for approving any exceptions that may be brought forward in the meantime. The position is therefore a serious one, and the 7 weeks in question will not be recovered by optimism alone; they will have to be managed through the controls that are now being put in place, together with a clearer line of sight over the packages that have still to be settled, where further movement of a similar kind cannot at this stage be ruled out.
target: The overrun now stands at 7 weeks. Its cause sits in the EPC packages: prices settled with vendors came in above the tender allowances carried in the estimate, and the difference has moved the forecast as each package has closed. Smaller estimating gaps add to the total but do not drive it; the settled package prices do. One mitigation is proposed. Scope changes are frozen from this point, so no new commitments enter the forecast while it is rebuilt, and the freeze holds until the project board has seen a revised forecast that reconciles the settled prices against the remaining allowances. The project board owns the mitigation: it lifts the freeze, and it approves any exception requested while the freeze is in place. Without the freeze, the rebuilt forecast would be overtaken by new commitments before the board could act on it, and the 7 weeks would grow by the same route that produced them. The freeze also protects the packages still to be settled. Their prices will move the forecast again when they close, and a forecast rebuilt once, against a fixed scope, can absorb that movement as a single identified change instead of as a drift. What the freeze cannot do is recover time already lost: the overrun is in the settled prices, not in future behaviour, and the board's decision is about containing the remainder of the programme, not about revisiting commitments that are already priced and placed.

fact_base: A shell-and-tube exchanger heats crude oil in a refinery preheat train. Duty is 1062 kW. Hot stream: 150 °C in, 110 °C out. Cold stream: 25 °C in, 40 °C out. The log-mean temperature difference is 97 K and the installed area is 43.1 m2, giving an overall coefficient of 254 W m-2 K-1. Fouling was assessed from a single 90-day run; no cleaning cycle has been completed.
input: This passage reports the performance of a shell-and-tube heat exchanger that is used to heat crude oil as part of a refinery preheat train, an application in which reliable heat recovery plays an important role in overall energy efficiency. The duty handled by the exchanger is 1062 kW, which is a substantial rate of heat transfer. On the hot side of the unit, the stream enters at a temperature of 150 °C and leaves at 110 °C, while on the cold side the crude stream enters at 25 °C and is heated to an outlet temperature of 40 °C. Based on these terminal temperatures, the log-mean temperature difference for the exchanger works out at 97 K, and this value, taken together with the installed heat-transfer area of 43.1 m2, leads to an overall heat-transfer coefficient of 254 W m-2 K-1. It is worth noting, however, that the assessment of fouling in the unit was based on a single 90-day run, which is a relatively limited body of evidence, and no cleaning cycle has been completed as yet, so the longer-term fouling behaviour of the exchanger under service conditions remains to be established in a fuller manner. The reported coefficient should accordingly be treated as a description of the exchanger as it was found during that particular run, rather than as a guaranteed figure for the unit in a cleaned condition or for its behaviour over a much longer period of operation in the preheat train.
target: A shell-and-tube exchanger in a refinery preheat train heats crude oil at a duty of 1062 kW. The hot stream enters at 150 °C and leaves at 110 °C; the crude enters at 25 °C and leaves at 40 °C. Terminal temperatures give a log-mean temperature difference of 97 K. With the installed area of 43.1 m2, the duty corresponds to an overall coefficient of 254 W m-2 K-1. The coefficient is a clean-condition figure in one respect and a service figure in another. It is computed from measured temperatures and the installed area, so it describes the exchanger as run; it is not corrected for the fouling layer that the run itself deposited. Fouling was assessed from a single 90-day run. No cleaning cycle has been completed, so the run gives one fouling state, at one crude throughput history, with no cleaned baseline measured in the same campaign. The value therefore characterises the exchanger over that run only. A coefficient intended for design margin, or for predicting performance after cleaning, needs the cleaned condition and a second fouling interval, neither of which the present evidence supplies. Terminal temperatures alone cannot separate the two resistances that the single coefficient combines, the film resistance on each side and the fouling resistance between them. Any cleaning decision taken from the present figure would be taken blind: the figure says how far performance sits from the temperature driving force, and it does not say how much of that distance a cleaning cycle would recover. A repeat run after cleaning, at matched throughput, is the measurement that would divide the coefficient into its parts.

subtype: worked example with equation: Ergun pressure drop
fact_base: Gas flows through a packed bed of 1 mm particles. The void fraction $\varepsilon$ is 0.5, the superficial velocity $u$ is 0.13 m s-1 and the bed length is 3 m. The Ergun equation gives a pressure gradient of 0.8 kPa m-1, or 2.5 kPa over the bed. Particle diameter $d_p$ is 1 mm; gas density is 1.2 kg m-3 and viscosity is 1.8 x 10-5 Pa s.
input:
In this worked example, we will calculate the pressure drop that arises when a gas flows through a packed bed, using the well-established Ergun equation, which is the standard correlation for this type of system. The packed bed in question is made up of particles of 1 mm in diameter, and the gas passes through the bed under conditions that are specified in detail below. The Ergun equation itself is written as follows:

$$\frac{\Delta P}{L} = \frac{150 \mu (1-\varepsilon)^2}{\varepsilon^3 d_p^2} u + \frac{1.75 (1-\varepsilon)}{\varepsilon^3 d_p} \rho u^2$$

In this system, the void fraction of the bed, denoted by $\varepsilon$, is 0.5, the superficial velocity of the gas, denoted by $u$, is 0.13 m s-1, and the total length of the bed is 3 m. In addition, the particle diameter $d_p$ is 1 mm, the density of the gas is 1.2 kg m-3, and its viscosity is 1.8 x 10-5 Pa s. When all of these values are substituted into the Ergun equation, the resulting pressure gradient is found to be 0.8 kPa m-1, which corresponds to a total pressure drop of 2.5 kPa over the full length of the bed. This result gives a clear indication of the resistance that the bed presents to the flowing gas under the stated conditions. In other words, at the stated superficial velocity of 0.13 m s-1, the bed presents a total resistance of 2.5 kPa across its 3 m length, and this is the pressure duty that any blower or compressor serving the bed would need to overcome under the stated operating conditions, before any allowance is made for the distributors, supports and pipework that surround the bed itself.
target:
Gas flows through a packed bed of particles with diameter $d_p$ of 1 mm. The pressure gradient is calculated from the Ergun equation, in which $\Delta P$ denotes the pressure drop (Pa), $L$ denotes the bed length (m), $\mu$ denotes the gas viscosity (Pa s), $\varepsilon$ denotes the bed void fraction, $\rho$ denotes the gas density (kg m-3) and $u$ denotes the superficial velocity (m s-1):

$$\frac{\Delta P}{L} = \frac{150 \mu (1-\varepsilon)^2}{\varepsilon^3 d_p^2} u + \frac{1.75 (1-\varepsilon)}{\varepsilon^3 d_p} \rho u^2$$

At a void fraction $\varepsilon$ of 0.5, a superficial velocity $u$ of 0.13 m s-1, a gas density of 1.2 kg m-3 and a viscosity of 1.8 x 10-5 Pa s, the equation gives a pressure gradient of 0.8 kPa m-1. Over the bed length of 3 m, the pressure drop is 2.5 kPa. The two terms of the equation separate the loss by mechanism: the first term collects viscous loss at the particle surface and the second collects inertial loss. At the stated velocity the gradient is the sum the design must carry, and the split matters where the velocity changes, because the inertial term grows with the square of $u$ while the viscous term grows only in proportion to $u$. A blower sized on the 2.5 kPa figure at 0.13 m s-1 therefore has no margin built into the number for operation above that velocity. The void fraction carries a sensitivity of the same kind. Both terms of the equation rise steeply as the bed is packed tighter, so a small error in the void fraction used for design passes into the gradient amplified, and a bed that settles in service toward a lower void fraction will show a pressure drop above the calculated figure even at the design velocity. The stated gradient is therefore a property of the bed as packed and described, not of the particles alone.

subtype: worked example with equation: friction loss
fact_base: Water at 293 K flows in a horizontal pipe. The density $\rho$ is 998 kg m-3. Mean velocity $v$ is 1.6 m s-1, pipe diameter $D$ is 0.1 m, pipe length $L$ is 84 m and the Darcy friction factor $f$ is 0.02. The friction pressure drop is 21.5 kPa.
input:
This worked example is concerned with the calculation of the friction pressure drop that occurs when water flows through a horizontal pipe, which is a very common situation in process engineering practice. The water is at a temperature of 293 K and has a density, denoted by $\rho$, of 998 kg m-3. The flow conditions and the pipe dimensions are as follows: the mean velocity of the water, denoted by $v$, is 1.6 m s-1, the pipe diameter, denoted by $D$, is 0.1 m, the pipe length, denoted by $L$, is 84 m and the Darcy friction factor, denoted by $f$, is 0.02. The relationship that connects these quantities to the friction pressure drop is the Darcy-Weisbach relation, which is written in the following form:

$$\Delta P = f \frac{L}{D} \frac{\rho v^2}{2}$$

When the numerical values that have been listed above are substituted into this equation in a careful and systematic manner, the friction pressure drop for the pipe is found to be 21.5 kPa. This figure represents the pressure energy that is lost purely as a result of friction between the moving water and the pipe wall over the full length of the run, and because the pipe is horizontal, there is no additional contribution from a change in elevation to be taken into account in this particular calculation. The example also illustrates a more general point about pipe-flow calculations of this kind, namely that the friction loss accumulates steadily along the entire length of the run, so that long pipelines of modest diameter can generate surprisingly large pressure duties even at velocities (in m s-1) that appear, at first sight, to be quite moderate and unremarkable.
target:
Water at 293 K flows in a horizontal pipe, and the friction pressure drop is calculated from the Darcy-Weisbach relation, in which $\Delta P$ denotes the pressure drop (Pa), $f$ denotes the Darcy friction factor, $L$ denotes the pipe length (m), $D$ denotes the pipe diameter (m), $\rho$ denotes the density and $v$ denotes the mean velocity (m s-1):

$$\Delta P = f \frac{L}{D} \frac{\rho v^2}{2}$$

The density $\rho$ is 998 kg m-3, the mean velocity $v$ is 1.6 m s-1, the diameter $D$ is 0.1 m, the length $L$ is 84 m and the friction factor $f$ is 0.02. Substitution gives a friction pressure drop of 21.5 kPa. Because the pipe is horizontal, no elevation term enters: the result is the whole pressure loss over the run, and it is the figure a pump or a gravity head must supply to hold the stated velocity in this pipe. The velocity carries the largest sensitivity in the result. The pressure drop varies with the square of $v$, so a modest rise in throughput costs disproportionately more pressure, while the friction factor enters only in direct proportion. The calculation takes $f$ as given; in an application the factor would itself be read from the flow regime and the pipe roughness, and an error there passes into $\Delta P$ unchanged in proportion. Length and diameter enter as a ratio, and the ratio is what the designer trades: a larger diameter at the same velocity lowers the loss in direct proportion to the ratio change, before the further benefit of the lower velocity that a larger bore brings at fixed volumetric flow is counted. The worked figure is therefore best read as one point on that trade-off, fixed by the stated geometry, rather than as a property of water flow in general.

fact_base: A food plant uses 2074 MWh of electricity per year in refrigeration. A heat-recovery retrofit is projected by the equipment vendor to save 12% of that use, a derived saving of 249 MWh per year at the vendor figure. Capital cost is $409k. At an electricity price of $0.12 per kWh, the derived annual saving is $30k and the derived simple payback is 13.6 years. The saving figure is a vendor projection and was not measured at this plant; refrigeration load in the summer peak month was not modelled. The recommendation is a metered trial on one of the three refrigeration lines before any capital decision. The plant engineer owns the trial.
input: This executive summary looks at a possible heat-recovery retrofit at a food plant and at whether the project should move forward at this stage. The plant currently uses 2074 MWh of electricity per year in refrigeration, which is a substantial part of the overall picture being considered here. According to the equipment vendor, the retrofit is projected to save 12% of that electricity use, which works out to a derived saving of 249 MWh per year at the vendor figure. The capital cost of the retrofit is $409k. Using an electricity price of $0.12 per kWh, the derived annual saving is $30k, and the derived simple payback therefore comes out at 13.6 years, and a 13.6-year payback is a long period over which to recover the investment. It is very important to emphasise that the saving figure is a vendor projection and was not measured at this plant, so it carries a significant degree of uncertainty. In addition, the refrigeration load in the summer peak month was not modelled, which means that the period of highest demand is not properly represented in the figures as they currently stand. Against this background, the recommendation of this summary is that a metered trial should be carried out on one of the three refrigeration lines before any capital decision is taken, and the plant engineer will own the trial and will be responsible for reporting its results.
target: The recommendation is a metered trial on one of the three refrigeration lines before any capital decision; the plant engineer owns the trial. The plant uses 2074 MWh of electricity per year in refrigeration. The vendor projects that a heat-recovery retrofit would save 12% of that use, a derived saving of 249 MWh per year at the vendor figure, at a capital cost of $409k. At an electricity price of $0.12 per kWh, the derived annual saving is $30k and the derived simple payback is 13.6 years. The payback rests on an unmeasured figure. The saving is a vendor projection and was not measured at this plant, and the refrigeration load in the summer peak month was not modelled, so the highest-load period is absent from the evidence behind the projection. A payback of 13.6 years computed from a projection of that standing does not support a capital decision in either direction. The trial replaces the projection with a measurement on one line, at the cost of metering rather than of the retrofit, and its result scales to the full refrigeration load with the peak-month gap stated. The capital decision should wait for the trial figure. The trial also fixes the second weakness in the case. Metering one line through the peak month measures the load shape that the projection omitted, so the scaled saving that follows the trial rests on the plant's own refrigeration behaviour across the full load range, rather than on an annual average applied to a peak that was never examined.

fact_base: Adsorption of a dye from water on a zeolite 13X sample was measured in batch tests at 298 K. The fitted Langmuir capacity was 195 mg of dye per gram of adsorbent at pH 6. At an adsorbent dose of 1.2 g L-1, removal after 120 min was 88% of the initial dye concentration of 50 mg L-1. The Langmuir fit is reported for pH 6 only; capacity at other pH values was not measured.
input: This passage presents the results of a series of batch adsorption tests in which the adsorption of a dye from water onto a sample of zeolite 13X was measured under controlled laboratory conditions at a temperature of 298 K. The equilibrium data that were obtained from these tests were fitted to the Langmuir model, and the fitted Langmuir capacity of the adsorbent was found to be 195 mg of dye per gram of adsorbent, a value that was obtained at pH 6. In a separate practical test of the material, an adsorbent dose of 1.2 g L-1 was used, and under these conditions the removal achieved after a contact time of 120 min was 88% of the initial dye concentration, which had been set at 50 mg L-1 at the start of the experiment. It should be noted that the Langmuir fit is reported for pH 6 only, which is an important limitation of the work as presented, and the capacity of the zeolite at other pH values was not measured during this study, so no conclusions can be drawn about its performance across a wider pH range on the basis of these experiments alone.
target: Adsorption of a dye from water on zeolite 13X was measured in batch tests at 298 K. The Langmuir fit at pH 6 gives a capacity of 195 mg of dye per gram of adsorbent. Capacity here is the fitted monolayer capacity of the Langmuir model, the saturation value of the fitted isotherm rather than a loading measured at any single concentration. At an adsorbent dose of 1.2 g L-1, removal after 120 min was 88% of the initial dye concentration of 50 mg L-1. The two figures describe different quantities. The removal percentage belongs to one dose, one initial concentration and one contact time; it falls as the initial concentration rises toward the capacity limit, and it is not a property of the zeolite alone. The Langmuir fit is reported for pH 6 only. Capacity at other pH values was not measured, and dye adsorption on a zeolite surface is pH-sensitive through both the dye speciation and the surface charge, so the capacity figure carries no support outside that condition. Within that condition, the fit and the removal test agree in showing a high-capacity material at the tested concentration. The batch test also fixes the contact time at which removal is quoted, and removal continues to change while contact lasts; a shorter contact would report a lower removal for the same material and dose, and the comparison of adsorbents on removal percentage alone, without matched dose, concentration and contact time, ranks the experiments rather than the materials.

subtype: worked example with equation: Antoine vapour pressure
fact_base: The vapour pressure of benzene at 78 °C is estimated from the Antoine equation with constants $A$ = 6.90565, $B$ = 1211.033 and $C$ = 220.79 (pressure in mmHg, temperature in °C). The estimate is 94.9 kPa. The constants are valid only over their fitted temperature range; the source databank value governs design.
input:
In this example, the vapour pressure of benzene at a temperature of 78 °C is going to be estimated by means of the Antoine equation, a well-known empirical correlation that is widely used for exactly this kind of calculation. The Antoine equation takes the following general form:

$$\log_{10} P = A - \frac{B}{T + C}$$

For benzene, the constants that are used in the correlation are $A$ = 6.90565, $B$ = 1211.033 and $C$ = 220.79, and it is important to be careful about the units here, because the pressure in this correlation is expressed in mmHg and the temperature is expressed in °C. When the temperature of 78 °C is inserted into the equation along with these three constants, and the resulting pressure is converted from mmHg into kilopascals, the estimated vapour pressure of benzene is found to be 94.9 kPa. While this estimate is very useful for practical purposes, it should be remembered that the Antoine constants are valid only over the temperature range over which they were fitted in the first place. For design calculations, the value that is held in the source databank is the value that governs, and the correlation result should be treated as supporting evidence rather than as the primary source.
target:
The vapour pressure of benzene at 78 °C is estimated from the Antoine equation, in which $P$ denotes the vapour pressure (mmHg), $T$ denotes the temperature (°C), and $A$, $B$ and $C$ denote the fitted constants for the substance:

$$\log_{10} P = A - \frac{B}{T + C}$$

For benzene, $A$ is 6.90565, $B$ is 1211.033 and $C$ is 220.79. Substitution of $T$ = 78 °C gives the pressure in mmHg, and conversion to SI units gives an estimated vapour pressure of 94.9 kPa. The figure is a correlation estimate at a temperature close to the normal boiling region of benzene, where vapour pressure changes rapidly with temperature and a small error in $T$ moves $P$ by more than the same error would at lower temperatures. The constants are valid only over their fitted temperature range. The source databank value governs design; the Antoine result is a check on it and a means of interpolating between databank points inside the fitted range, not a replacement for the databank at any temperature. The conversion at the end of the calculation deserves the same care as the substitution at its start. The correlation returns its native unit, and a figure carried into a design document in the wrong unit is wrong by a fixed factor at every later use, however carefully the substitution itself was performed. Stating the estimate in SI units, as here, removes that step from the chain of later calculations that will draw on the value.

fact_base: A review passage on membrane separations for solvent recovery, in four parts: scope, established results, disagreements, and gaps. The review covers 104 papers from the last 11 years. The disagreements part names the quantity on which reports conflict; the gaps part names the measurement nobody reports.
input:
Scope

This review sets out to provide a comprehensive overview of the rapidly evolving field of membrane separations for solvent recovery, drawing together a substantial body of literature that has appeared in recent years. In total, the review covers 104 papers that have been published over the last 11 years, and this body of work reflects the growing importance that is attached to solvent recovery in the process industries, where solvents are used in large quantities and where their recovery can contribute to reduced raw-material costs, lower waste volumes and improved environmental performance. The scope of the review is centred on membrane processes that are used to recover organic solvents either from process streams or from waste streams, and it encompasses pervaporation, organic solvent nanofiltration and vapour permeation, all of which have attracted considerable attention. Polymeric membranes feature prominently throughout the literature, although inorganic and mixed-matrix membranes are also considered where they have been applied to solvent duties. The review is organised so as to move from the scope of the field, through the results that are now well established, to the areas where different research groups continue to report conflicting findings, and finally to the gaps that remain in the evidence base, which are important for readers who wish to understand where further work is most needed.

Established results

A number of findings have now been reported consistently by many different groups, and these can be regarded as established features of the field. It is well established, for example, that membrane performance in solvent duties is characterised by a trade-off between flux and selectivity, so that membranes which allow a solvent to pass very rapidly will tend to discriminate less sharply between the components of a mixture, whereas tighter membranes achieve higher selectivity at the cost of lower throughput. Swelling of polymeric membranes in aggressive solvents is another firmly established effect, and it is widely recognised that a membrane which swells strongly will generally lose selectivity, because the swollen polymer network offers less resistance to the passage of the components that are meant to be retained. Crosslinking of the polymer is established as an effective response to this problem, and many studies have shown that crosslinked membranes retain their separation performance in solvents that would cause an uncrosslinked membrane of the same polymer to fail. It has also become clear that the overwhelming majority of the published work has been carried out at a small laboratory scale, with flat sheet samples or small modules and with synthetic feeds of known composition, and that demonstrations at pilot scale remain comparatively rare. The solvents that have been studied most frequently are the common process solvents, such as methanol, ethanol, acetone and toluene, and the behaviour of membranes in these systems is correspondingly better understood than their behaviour in less common or more aggressive solvent environments. Taken together, these established results provide a reasonably secure foundation on which the rest of the discussion in this review is built.

Disagreements

Despite the areas of agreement described above, there remain significant disagreements within the literature, and the most important of these concerns the selectivity that is reported for the same solvent pair when it is separated by nominally similar membranes. Different groups have reported selectivity values that differ by a wide margin for what appears to be the same separation, and these discrepancies cannot always be explained by differences in the membranes themselves. Part of the explanation lies in the feed conditions that have been used, which vary considerably from one study to another: the composition of the feed, its temperature and the way in which the permeate side of the membrane is operated all influence the selectivity that is measured, and they are not always reported in sufficient detail to allow a strict comparison to be made. There is also disagreement about the stability of membrane performance over extended operation, with some groups reporting that flux and selectivity are maintained over long periods, while others observe a steady decline that they attribute to compaction, fouling or gradual chemical attack by the solvent. Because the duration of the tests and the way in which performance is recorded differ so much between studies, it is difficult at present to determine whether these conflicting accounts reflect genuinely different membrane behaviour or simply different measurement and reporting practices adopted in different laboratories.

Gaps

Alongside the disagreements, the literature also contains a number of notable gaps, and perhaps the most striking of these is that the performance of membranes measured on real process streams over extended runs is the measurement that nobody reports. Almost all of the available data have been obtained with clean, synthetic feeds in which every component is known and in which the impurities, trace contaminants and variability of an actual plant stream are entirely absent, and this leaves a significant question mark over how the membranes that perform so well in the laboratory would behave when they are exposed to the feeds that they would actually encounter in service. Extended operation is similarly under-reported, and the great majority of studies are terminated long before the kind of operating lifetime that an industrial installation would require has been demonstrated. Until measurements of this kind begin to appear in the literature on a regular basis, the translation of laboratory results into reliable industrial solvent-recovery processes will continue to rest on a comparatively narrow evidence base, and this is arguably the most important limitation that future research in the field will need to address.
target:
Scope

Membrane separations for solvent recovery are reviewed from 104 papers published over the last 11 years. The processes covered are pervaporation, organic solvent nanofiltration and vapour permeation applied to organic solvents in process and waste streams. Polymeric membranes dominate the literature; inorganic and mixed-matrix membranes are covered where they have been run on solvent duties. The review is confined to recovery of the solvent as the product. Separations in which the membrane merely treats an aqueous effluent fall outside it, and the solvent set considered is the organic solvent set of the source papers, which is weighted toward common process solvents and away from the aggressive solvents of greatest industrial interest. The papers divide by duty as well as by process. Recovery from reaction and extraction streams, recovery from cleaning and wash streams, and recovery for reuse within the same process each impose a different separation target, and a membrane result gained on one duty transfers to another only where the retained component and the purity demanded of the recovered solvent match. The review keeps those duties apart where the source papers allow it, because a selectivity reported without its duty reads as a property of the membrane when it is partly a property of the task.

Established results

Flux and selectivity trade against each other in every membrane class reported. A membrane that passes solvent rapidly discriminates weakly between components; a tighter membrane raises selectivity and lowers throughput. The trade-off is the organising fact of the field, and claims of progress are read against it. Swelling is the mechanism behind most selectivity loss in polymeric membranes. A strongly swelling solvent opens the polymer network, the retained component passes more freely, and selectivity falls toward the value of an open film. Crosslinking answers swelling directly: crosslinked membranes of a given polymer hold their separation performance in solvents that destroy the uncrosslinked material, and the result repeats across polymer families. Reported work is overwhelmingly laboratory work. Flat sheets and small modules, synthetic feeds of fixed composition, and short runs form the standard experiment, and pilot demonstrations are rare enough to be individually notable. The solvents studied most are methanol, ethanol, acetone and toluene; membrane behaviour in those systems is mapped in detail, and behaviour in harsher solvents is known mainly by extrapolation from them. Reporting practice compounds the scale problem. Conditions that decide performance, feed composition in full, temperature, and the state of the permeate side, are reported unevenly, and a result stated without them cannot be reproduced or placed on the trade-off with confidence. Reviews of the field inherit that unevenness: the established results above are the results that survive it, stated at the level the underlying reporting supports, and finer claims about individual membrane classes are read in the source papers rather than asserted here.

Disagreements

Reports conflict on the selectivity measured for the same solvent pair through nominally similar membranes, and the conflict survives the obvious explanations. Part of it is feed condition. Feed composition, temperature and permeate-side operation all move the measured selectivity, and all three vary between laboratories, often without enough reporting detail to reconstruct the comparison. Part of it is the membrane sample itself, where preparation history differs between groups. Stability over extended operation attracts the same disagreement in a second form. Some groups report flux and selectivity held over long runs; others report a steady decline assigned to compaction, fouling or chemical attack by the solvent. Run durations and recording practice differ so widely that the two accounts cannot yet be separated into membrane behaviour and measurement practice. The disagreement is therefore a reporting disagreement as much as a materials disagreement: the field has no shared test protocol against which a selectivity or a stability claim can be checked from one laboratory to another. A protocol would not need to be burdensome to be effective. A shared feed pair at a stated composition and temperature, a stated permeate condition, and performance recorded at the start and at the end of a run of stated length would align the measurements that now drift apart, and would let a later laboratory place its membrane on the same axes as the earlier work it claims to improve on.

Gaps

Performance measured on real process streams over extended runs is the measurement nobody reports. The evidence base rests on clean synthetic feeds of known composition. Real streams carry trace impurities, off-specification excursions and composition drift, and each of these acts on a membrane in service; none of them appears in the standard experiment. Extended operation is missing on the same pattern. Runs end far short of an industrial service life, so the slow processes that decide a membrane's value in a plant, ageing, cumulative fouling and gradual chemical attack, are observed only in their opening stages. The gap is specific and closable: membranes with published laboratory performance run on plant streams, with performance recorded over periods that reach into service life. Until such measurements exist, design from the published record extrapolates twice, from synthetic feed to real feed and from short run to long run, and the size of either extrapolation error is unknown. A second missing measurement sits inside the first. Recovery processes are bought on cost per unit of solvent recovered, and the literature reports separation performance almost without the energy and membrane-replacement terms that set that cost. A membrane of moderate selectivity and long life can outrank a sharper membrane that a solvent stream destroys, and the published record, which ranks on selectivity and flux alone, cannot make that judgement. Reporting the duty a membrane actually performed, on the stream it actually treated, for as long as it actually lasted, would convert the review literature from a catalogue of materials into an engineering basis for choosing between them. The same gap hides the fouling record of real streams. Laboratory feeds are filtered, characterised and stable; plant streams are none of these, and a membrane that meets its laboratory figure on a clean feed may spend its service life below it on a stream that carries the solids, oils and degradation products of the process itself. No strand of the reviewed literature follows that difference through, and it remains the largest single unknown between the published record and an installed recovery unit.

fact_base: Carbon dioxide and hydrogen react over a copper-zinc oxide catalyst to give formaldehyde. Space-time yield is the mass of product per unit catalyst volume per hour (kg L-1 h-1). Test conditions: 280 °C, 40 bar, feed ratio H2/CO2 = 3, one feed composition. Washcoated monolith catalyst: space-time yield 0.93 kg L-1 h-1, pressure drop 0.27 bar, activity loss 6% after 100 h. Extruded pellet catalyst: space-time yield 0.41 kg L-1 h-1, pressure drop 1.03 bar, activity loss 16% after 100 h. No sulfur-bearing feed was tested. Yield and pressure drop are seldom reported for the same catalyst charge.
input: This abstract reports a comparison of two catalyst forms for the reaction of carbon dioxide and hydrogen over a copper-zinc oxide catalyst to give formaldehyde, which is a reaction of considerable interest in the context of carbon utilisation. In order to make the comparison meaningful, it is helpful to define the space-time yield, which is the mass of product obtained per unit catalyst volume per hour, expressed here in kg L-1 h-1. The tests that are reported were carried out under a single set of conditions, namely a temperature of 280 °C, a pressure of 40 bar and a feed ratio H2/CO2 = 3, with one feed composition being used throughout. The washcoated monolith catalyst achieved a space-time yield of 0.93 kg L-1 h-1, with a pressure drop of 0.27 bar and an activity loss of 6% after 100 h on stream. The extruded pellet catalyst, by comparison, achieved a space-time yield of 0.41 kg L-1 h-1, with a pressure drop of 1.03 bar and an activity loss of 16% after 100 h. It should also be noted that no sulfur-bearing feed was tested in this work, so the sensitivity of either catalyst to sulfur remains unknown. Finally, it is worth observing that yield and pressure drop are seldom reported together for the same catalyst charge, which makes comparisons of this kind less common than might be expected. The comparison is also unusual in that both forms were examined on the same charge basis and under the same conditions, which removes a number of the ambiguities that normally complicate comparisons drawn from separate studies reported in different parts of the literature at different times.
target: Carbon dioxide and hydrogen react over a copper-zinc oxide catalyst to give formaldehyde. Two catalyst forms are compared on space-time yield, the mass of product per unit catalyst volume per hour (kg L-1 h-1), at 280 °C and 40 bar with a feed ratio H2/CO2 = 3 and one feed composition. The washcoated monolith gives a space-time yield of 0.93 kg L-1 h-1, a pressure drop of 0.27 bar and an activity loss of 6% after 100 h. The extruded pellet gives 0.41 kg L-1 h-1, a pressure drop of 1.03 bar and an activity loss of 16% after 100 h. On all three measures the monolith stands ahead at these conditions: yield is higher by a factor above two, pressure drop is lower by a factor near four, and activity over the same period is better retained. The comparison is a single-condition comparison. One feed composition was tested, at one temperature and one pressure, so the ranking carries no support at other conversions or space velocities, where the pellet form's higher catalyst inventory per volume could close the yield gap. No sulfur-bearing feed was tested; the sensitivity of either form to sulfur poisoning is unmeasured, and sulfur tolerance is the property most likely to reorder the ranking in service. Yield and pressure drop are seldom reported for the same catalyst charge, which is what gives the paired figures here their weight: the monolith's yield advantage is not bought with pressure drop. The pressure-drop contrast has a plant consequence of its own. A monolith bed of the same duty imposes a smaller load on the feed compression than a pellet bed, and the difference recurs for every hour on stream, whereas the yield difference is set by the reaction conditions of the hour in question. Reactor selection between the two forms therefore turns on which of the two advantages the plant values more at its own conditions, a judgement the single-condition data inform but do not settle.

fact_base: A defect-reduction project on a moulding cell cut the reject rate from 4.6% to 3.1% over one quarter. At 138k units per year the change avoids about 2070 rejected units per year. The quarter included a planned shutdown; rates are not adjusted for it.
input: In today's fast-paced manufacturing environment, improving product quality remains a crucial priority, and defect reduction plays a pivotal role in enhancing overall operational efficiency. This report delves into a recent defect-reduction project undertaken on a moulding cell and showcases the results that were achieved over the course of one quarter. At the beginning of the quarter, the reject rate stood at 4.6%, which meant that a significant share of the units produced by the cell were being rejected. By the end of the quarter, thanks to the efforts of the project team, this figure had been brought down to 3.1%, representing a reduction of 1.5 percentage points and highlighting the effectiveness of the measures that were implemented. When this improvement is viewed in the context of the cell's annual production volume of 138k units per year, its impact becomes even more tangible: the reduction of 1.5 percentage points corresponds to approximately 2070 fewer rejected units each year (138k x 0.015), underscoring meaningful savings in materials, rework, and disposal efforts. It is important to note, however, that the quarter in question also included a planned shutdown, and the reported rates have not been adjusted for this shutdown, so a degree of caution is warranted when interpreting the results. Overall, the project delivered a robust improvement in quality performance, cutting the reject rate from 4.6% to 3.1% and avoiding about 2070 rejected units per year at the stated volume of 138k units per year.
target: A defect-reduction project on a moulding cell reduced the reject rate from 4.6% to 3.1% over one quarter. The reject rate is the share of produced units that are rejected, so the change is a reduction of 1.5 percentage points in that share, measured on the same cell before and after the project. At the stated volume of 138k units per year, a reduction of 1.5 percentage points corresponds to about 2070 fewer rejected units per year (138k x 0.015). The annual figure is a projection from the quarterly rates: it holds the rates and the volume fixed, and it inherits the uncertainty of both. The quarter included a planned shutdown, and the reported rates are not adjusted for the shutdown. The comparison therefore mixes production in normal running with production around a stopped period, and the reported figures do not separate a project effect from any shutdown effect on the rates. The size of a shutdown effect is not stated. Within that limit, the recorded outcome stands as follows: a reject rate of 3.1% against 4.6% before the project, and an implied avoidance of about 2070 rejected units per year at a volume of 138k units per year.

fact_base: A tutorial passage explains phase equilibrium for a partially miscible liquid pair. The passage states the equilibrium condition in words (equality of chemical potential across phases) before any equation is named. No numerical data are introduced; the passage is conceptual.
input: Phase equilibrium is a fascinating and truly foundational concept in the world of chemical engineering, and it plays a crucial role in understanding how mixtures behave. In this passage, we will delve into the intriguing case of a partially miscible liquid pair, exploring what happens when two liquids are mixed together but refuse to dissolve completely in one another. When such a pair is brought together, the liquids dissolve in each other only to a limited extent, and over a certain range of overall compositions the mixture does not form a single, uniform liquid. Instead, it separates into two distinct liquid phases, each of which is essentially a saturated solution: one phase is rich in the first liquid and contains as much of the second liquid as it can hold, while the other phase is rich in the second liquid and contains as much of the first as it can hold. Interestingly, within this range, the compositions of the two phases remain fixed at a given temperature and pressure, and changing the overall composition merely changes the relative amounts of the two phases rather than what each phase actually contains. Outside this range, the mixture exists as a single phase, because one liquid is perfectly capable of dissolving the whole of the other. The condition that governs this equilibrium is expressed in terms of chemical potential, which can be thought of as a measure of the tendency of a component to leave a phase. A component will move between the phases as long as its chemical potential differs between them, and this movement continues until the chemical potential of each component is exactly the same in both phases. Only later is this condition written down as an equation, but the underlying idea is simple: equilibrium is the state in which no component has any tendency to move. It is worth noting that equilibrium is not a static state at the molecular level, since molecules continue to cross the boundary between the phases in both directions; the crossings simply balance, so nothing changes overall, highlighting the dynamic nature of the balance that nature achieves.
target:
Two liquids that dissolve in each other only to a limited extent form a partially miscible pair. Mixed in suitable proportions at fixed temperature and pressure, such a pair does not give a single homogeneous liquid. The mixture separates instead into two liquid phases, each a saturated solution of one component in the other. One phase is rich in the first component and holds as much of the second as it can dissolve; the other phase is rich in the second component and holds as much of the first as it can dissolve. Between the two solubility limits, the composition of each phase is fixed by the temperature and pressure, and a change in the overall composition of the mixture changes only the amounts of the two phases, not what either phase contains. Outside those limits the mixture is a single phase, because one liquid can dissolve the whole of the other.

Equilibrium between the phases is stated in terms of chemical potential. The chemical potential of a component in a phase is its partial molar Gibbs energy in that phase, and it measures the tendency of the component to leave the phase. A component passes from one phase to the other while its chemical potential differs between the phases, and the transfer lowers the total Gibbs energy of the mixture. Transfer stops when the chemical potential of each component is the same in both phases. That equality, holding for every component, is the condition of phase equilibrium for the pair. The condition is commonly written as an equation that sets the chemical potential of each component in one phase equal to its chemical potential in the other phase, and the equality of fugacities used in applied work is the same condition in another form. At equilibrium the phases are not static: molecules of each component cross the interface in both directions at equal rates, so the compositions stay constant while exchange continues. A change of temperature displaces the compositions until the equalities hold again at the new state.

fact_base: A food plant uses 2089 MWh of electricity per year in refrigeration. A heat-recovery retrofit is projected by the equipment vendor to save 12% of that use, a derived saving of 251 MWh per year at the vendor figure. Capital cost is $368k. At an electricity price of $0.11 per kWh, the derived annual saving is $28k and the derived simple payback is 13.1 years. The saving figure is a vendor projection and was not measured at this plant; refrigeration load in the summer peak month was not modelled. The recommendation is a metered trial on one of the three refrigeration lines before any capital decision. The plant engineer owns the trial.
input: This executive summary delves into an exciting opportunity to enhance energy efficiency at the food plant through a proposed heat-recovery retrofit, and it presents a comprehensive overview of the projected benefits, costs, and recommended next steps. The plant currently uses a substantial 2089 MWh of electricity per year in refrigeration, making refrigeration a key focus area for improvement. According to the equipment vendor, the retrofit is projected to save 12% of that electricity use, which corresponds to a derived saving of 251 MWh per year at the vendor figure. The capital cost of the retrofit is $368k, and at an electricity price of $0.11 per kWh, the derived annual saving works out to $28k, giving a derived simple payback of 13.1 years. It is important to note that the saving figure is a vendor projection and was not measured at this plant, and refrigeration load in the summer peak month was not modelled, so the projections should be treated with a degree of caution. In light of these considerations, it is recommended that a metered trial be carried out on one of the three refrigeration lines before any capital decision is taken, in order to validate the projected savings under real operating conditions. The plant engineer will own the trial and will be responsible for reporting its findings.
target: The recommendation is a metered trial of the heat-recovery retrofit on one of the three refrigeration lines, before any capital decision. The plant engineer owns the trial. The plant uses 2089 MWh of electricity per year in refrigeration. The equipment vendor projects a saving of 12% of that use, a derived saving of 251 MWh per year at the vendor figure. Against a capital cost of $368k, the derived annual saving is $28k at an electricity price of $0.11 per kWh, and the derived simple payback is 13.1 years. The trade-off is therefore a long payback resting on an unverified figure: the saving is a vendor projection and was not measured at this plant, and refrigeration load in the summer peak month was not modelled. A metered trial on one line replaces the projection with a measurement at this plant, on one of the three lines whose combined use the retrofit would address. The capital decision should wait for the trial result, since the payback is long enough that a shortfall in the measured saving would change the decision. The trial is a measurement exercise on one line, run ahead of the capital commitment, and its result is the evidence the capital decision currently lacks. The trial also tests the retrofit against the plant's own refrigeration load pattern, which the vendor projection does not use. Until the trial reports, every figure in this summary is the vendor's figure or a derivation from it, and the saving at this plant is unknown.

subtype: worked example with equation: Ergun pressure drop
fact_base: Gas flows through a packed bed of 1 mm particles. The void fraction $\varepsilon$ is 0.6, the superficial velocity $u$ is 0.35 m s-1 and the bed length is 1 m. The Ergun equation gives a pressure gradient of 1.2 kPa m-1, or 1.2 kPa over the bed. Particle diameter $d_p$ is 1 mm; gas density is 1.2 kg m-3 and viscosity is 1.8 x 10-5 Pa s.
input:
In this worked example, we will explore how the pressure drop across a packed bed can be estimated using the well-known Ergun equation, which serves as a valuable tool for engineers designing gas-solid contacting equipment. Let us consider a scenario in which gas flows through a packed bed made up of particles of 1 mm in diameter. The void fraction of the bed, denoted by $\varepsilon$, is 0.6, the superficial velocity $u$ of the gas is 0.35 m s-1, and the length of the bed is 1 m. The Ergun equation, which combines a viscous contribution and an inertial contribution that varies with $\rho u^2$, is written as follows:

$$\frac{\Delta P}{L} = \frac{150 \mu (1-\varepsilon)^2}{\varepsilon^3 d_p^2} u + \frac{1.75 (1-\varepsilon)}{\varepsilon^3 d_p} \rho u^2$$

In this equation, $\mu$ represents the viscosity of the gas, which is 1.8 x 10-5 Pa s, $\rho$ represents its density, which is 1.2 kg m-3, $d_p$ is the particle diameter of 1 mm, and $\Delta P$ is the pressure drop over the bed length $L$. When all of these values are carefully substituted into the equation, the Ergun equation gives a pressure gradient of 1.2 kPa m-1, which, over a bed length of 1 m, corresponds to a total pressure drop of 1.2 kPa over the bed. It is worth noting that this result depends on the bed being uniformly packed and on the gas properties remaining constant along the bed, highlighting the importance of checking these assumptions in practice.
target:
The worked example estimates the pressure drop of a gas flowing through a packed bed from the Ergun equation:

$$\frac{\Delta P}{L} = \frac{150 \mu (1-\varepsilon)^2}{\varepsilon^3 d_p^2} u + \frac{1.75 (1-\varepsilon)}{\varepsilon^3 d_p} \rho u^2$$

The bed holds particles of diameter $d_p$ 1 mm. The void fraction $\varepsilon$ is 0.6, the superficial velocity $u$ is 0.35 m s-1, and the bed length $L$ is 1 m. The gas density $\rho$ is 1.2 kg m-3 and the gas viscosity $\mu$ is 1.8 x 10-5 Pa s. In the Ergun equation, the term in $\mu$ is the viscous contribution and the term in $\rho u^2$ is the inertial contribution; $\Delta P$ denotes the pressure drop over the length $L$. Substitution of the stated values gives a pressure gradient of 1.2 kPa m-1. Over a bed length of 1 m, the pressure drop is therefore 1.2 kPa, numerically equal to the gradient because the length is 1 m. The result holds for a uniformly packed bed with the stated void fraction throughout, and for gas properties that stay at the stated values along the bed. A bed that packs unevenly, or a gas whose density changes as the pressure falls, moves the pressure drop away from the computed value, and the equation gives no indication of either departure. The superficial velocity is the velocity the gas would have if the bed were empty; the particles raise the velocity in the voids, and the equation works with the superficial value throughout. Particle diameter enters the denominator of each term, so a bed of finer particles at the same flow holds a steeper gradient, and the stated diameter is the input to which the result is most sensitive.

fact_base: Project proposal for a rooftop solar installation, in four sections: case, costs, schedule, and decision requested. Capital cost is $1041k with a 7-year appraisal horizon. The schedule section gives a start one quarter after approval; no contractor is named. The decision requested is approval to proceed to detailed design, not to construction.
input:
This proposal sets out an exciting opportunity for the organisation to take a bold step towards a more sustainable future by installing a rooftop solar installation on its building, and it seeks approval to proceed to the detailed design stage, at an estimated capital cost of $1041k. In today's rapidly evolving energy landscape, organisations are increasingly looking for ways to reduce their exposure to volatile electricity prices, cut their carbon emissions, and make better use of the assets they already own. A rooftop installation speaks to all of these priorities at once: it generates electricity exactly where that electricity is consumed, it turns a large and currently unproductive roof surface into a productive asset, and it does so using a mature and well-understood technology that has been deployed successfully in countless comparable settings. This document presents the case for the installation, an overview of the costs involved, the proposed schedule, and the decision that is being requested at this stage, so that decision makers can consider the proposal in a structured and transparent way.

## Case

The case for a rooftop solar installation rests on a combination of financial, environmental, and strategic considerations that reinforce one another. From a financial perspective, every unit of electricity generated on the roof is a unit that does not have to be purchased from the grid, and because the generation takes place behind the meter, the saving is made at the full retail price of electricity rather than at a wholesale export price. This is a particularly attractive feature at a time when electricity prices have shown themselves to be volatile and difficult to forecast, and when budgets benefit from costs that are predictable over the long term. Once installed, a solar array has no fuel cost, and its output can be forecast with a high degree of confidence from one year to the next, which makes it a stabilising element in the organisation's energy budget. From an environmental perspective, generating electricity from sunlight displaces electricity that would otherwise be drawn from the grid, and thereby reduces the emissions associated with the organisation's activities, supporting the organisation's wider sustainability commitments and demonstrating visible leadership to staff, customers, and the wider community. The roof itself is, at present, an underutilised asset: it is a large, unshaded surface that is already owned, already maintained, and already connected to the building's electrical infrastructure. Using it for generation avoids the cost and complexity of acquiring land, and it avoids the visual and planning impacts that a ground-mounted installation might attract. There are also strategic benefits to consider. An organisation that generates a meaningful share of its own electricity is less exposed to future changes in the energy market, better positioned for future requirements around carbon reporting and building performance, and able to point to a tangible, visible investment when it describes its environmental performance to others. Taken together, these considerations make a compelling case for examining the installation seriously, and the purpose of the detailed design stage is precisely to test this case rigorously against the specific characteristics of the building, so that the eventual decision about construction can be taken on the basis of firm information rather than estimates and assumptions.

## Costs

The capital cost of the installation is estimated at $1041k, appraised over a 7-year appraisal horizon. This headline figure is an estimate at proposal stage, and it is important to be transparent about what it is intended to cover and about the level of confidence that attaches to it. The estimate covers the full scope of the works: the solar panels themselves and the mounting system that secures them to the roof; the inverters that convert the generated electricity into a form the building can use; the electrical works needed to connect the installation to the building's distribution system and to the grid; any protection, metering, and monitoring equipment the connection requires; the design work, surveys, and approvals that precede construction; and the management of the project through to commissioning and handover. At this stage, no contractor has been appointed and no tendered prices have been obtained, so the estimate is built up from budget information and comparable experience rather than from competitive quotations, and it should be treated as an indicative figure with a corresponding margin of uncertainty. The detailed design stage exists largely to close this gap: it will produce a defined scope, a completed structural assessment, agreed connection arrangements, and a design against which contractors can price competitively, so that the construction decision can be taken against tendered prices rather than estimates. The appraisal over the 7-year horizon weighs the capital cost against the value of the electricity the installation is expected to generate over that period, together with the running costs of operating and maintaining the installation, which include inspection, cleaning, monitoring, insurance, and the maintenance of the electrical equipment. Because the benefits depend on electricity prices and on the amount of generation the roof actually delivers, both of which carry uncertainty, the appraisal should be read as a framework for decision-making rather than as a guarantee of a particular financial outcome, and the detailed design stage will revisit it with firmer inputs before any construction commitment is made.

## Schedule

The proposed schedule begins one quarter after approval is given, and it is organised as a sequence of stages in which each stage prepares the ground for the next. The first stage is the detailed design itself, during which the layout of the array is fixed, the structural capacity of the roof is confirmed by survey and calculation, the electrical design is completed, and the connection arrangements are agreed with the network operator. Running alongside the design, the necessary consents and approvals are pursued, so that no avoidable delay is introduced between the design finishing and the works being ready to start. Once the design is complete and the construction decision has been taken, procurement follows, with the equipment ordered and a contractor appointed through a competitive process. The installation works then proceed on the roof and in the electrical rooms, sequenced so that the building can remain in normal use while the work is carried out, with the noisier and more disruptive activities arranged to minimise their impact on the building's occupants. The final stages are testing, commissioning, and handover, during which the installation is proved to operate as designed, the monitoring is brought into service, and the documentation and training needed by those who will look after the installation are handed over. The main risks to the schedule are the time taken to agree the grid connection, the findings of the structural survey, and the weather during the roof works, and the detailed design stage will firm up the programme in the light of the first two of these, so that the construction decision can be taken with a realistic programme in front of it.

## Decision requested

The decision requested at this stage is approval to proceed to detailed design, and it is important to be clear about what that approval does and does not commit the organisation to. Approval commits the organisation to the design stage described above: the surveys, the design work, the connection application, and the preparation of a tender-ready scope. It does not commit the organisation to construction, and no construction contract will be placed on the basis of this approval. The construction decision will return to this forum once the detailed design is complete, supported by tendered prices, a firmed capital cost against the $1041k estimate, a refreshed appraisal over the 7-year horizon, and a realistic programme, so that the merits of building the installation can be judged on firm information. If the detailed design shows that the installation is materially less attractive than the proposal stage suggests, the project can be stopped at that point, having incurred only the cost of the design work, and the organisation will still hold a completed design and survey record that would inform any future proposal for the roof. Decision makers are therefore asked to approve progression to detailed design, with a start one quarter after approval, on the understanding that construction remains a separate and subsequent decision.
target:
Approval is requested to proceed to detailed design for a rooftop solar installation, at an estimated capital cost of $1041k appraised over a 7-year horizon. The approval covers design work only. Construction is not requested, and it would return for a separate decision against tendered prices once the design is complete. Work would start one quarter after approval.

## Case

A rooftop installation generates electricity at the point where the building consumes it. Electricity generated on the roof displaces electricity bought from the grid, and the displacement is valued at the retail price the organisation pays, not at a wholesale export price. The array has no fuel cost, and its output in any year can be forecast within narrow limits, so the saving it produces is one of the more predictable lines in an energy budget that is otherwise exposed to price movements the organisation does not control. Generation on site also reduces the emissions attributable to the organisation's electricity use, because grid electricity carries the emissions of the generation mix behind it. The roof is already owned and maintained, and it is at present unproductive; using it avoids the land cost of a ground-mounted installation and keeps the generating asset on the building it serves. None of this establishes that this installation, on this roof, is a sound investment. Output depends on the roof's orientation, shading, and usable area; cost depends on the roof's structure and on the connection the network operator will accept. Those are properties of the specific building, and they are established by survey and design, not by the general case for solar generation. The case for the design stage is narrower than the case for the installation: the general argument is strong enough to justify spending on design, and the design converts the general argument into figures that can be judged. Generation above the building's own demand is exported at a price below the price the organisation pays for supply, so the array is sized against the building's demand and not against the largest array the roof could physically hold. That sizing question, and the connection capacity behind it, are design questions, and they are among the reasons the construction figures cannot be settled at proposal stage. The design tests that sizing against the surveyed roof and the agreed connection.

## Costs

The capital cost is estimated at $1041k, over a 7-year appraisal horizon. The estimate covers the panels and their mounting system, the inverters, the electrical works connecting the installation to the building's distribution system and to the grid, protection and metering equipment, surveys and design, and project management through to commissioning. It is an estimate at proposal stage. No contractor is named, no tender has been run, and no part of the figure is a quoted price; it is built from budget information and comparable installations, and it carries the uncertainty of that basis. The appraisal sets the capital cost against the value of the generation over the horizon and against the running costs of the installation, which are inspection, cleaning, monitoring, insurance, and maintenance of the electrical equipment. Both sides of that comparison move: the value of the generation moves with the electricity price, and the generation itself moves with the weather the roof actually receives. The appraisal is therefore a framework for the decision, not a forecast of a financial outcome. The detailed design narrows the largest uncertainties in sequence: the structural survey fixes what the roof can carry and what strengthening, if any, the mounting requires; the agreed connection fixes the electrical scope; and a defined design lets contractors price the same scope competitively, replacing the estimate with tendered prices. The construction decision should be taken on those prices, with the appraisal refreshed, rather than on the proposal-stage estimate. The design stage returns an itemised scope in place of the single estimate: array layout, mounting and any strengthening the survey requires, electrical works, and connection charges stated separately, so that the movement from estimate to tendered price can be seen item by item rather than as a single unexplained change. It also states the allowances the estimate carries for the items the survey has not yet reached, and identifies which of them the design retires.

## Schedule

Work starts one quarter after approval. The first stage is the detailed design: the array layout is fixed, the roof structure is surveyed and checked for the loads the installation imposes, the electrical design is completed, and the connection is applied for and agreed with the network operator. Consents run alongside the design rather than after it, so that the programme is not held at the point where the design finishes. Procurement follows a construction decision, not this approval: equipment is ordered and a contractor appointed competitively against the completed design. The installation works are sequenced so that the building stays in normal use, with roof works and electrical works planned around occupancy. Testing, commissioning, and handover close the programme; the installation is proved against the design, monitoring is brought into service, and operating documentation passes to those who will maintain it. Three risks act on the programme. The connection agreement is outside the project's control and can set the pace. The structural survey can return a roof that needs strengthening, which adds scope before anything is installed. Weather during the roof works can stop them. The design stage resolves the first two risks into known quantities; the programme presented with the construction decision will show their effect explicitly. The design stage is governed as a project in its own right, with progress reported against the survey, the design, and the connection application as its three workstreams. A design freeze closes the stage: after it, the scope offered to tenderers does not change, and any later change is priced as a change rather than absorbed into the works.

## Decision requested

The decision requested is approval to proceed to detailed design. The approval commits the organisation to surveys, design work, the connection application, and a tender-ready scope of works. It does not commit the organisation to construction, and no construction contract follows from it. The construction decision returns to this forum when the design is complete, with tendered prices in place of the estimate, the capital cost firmed against $1041k, the appraisal over the 7-year horizon refreshed, and a programme that reflects the survey and the connection terms. If the design shows the installation to be materially less attractive than the proposal suggests, the project stops at that point; the expenditure is then limited to the design stage, and the survey and design record remains available to any future proposal for the roof. Approval is therefore requested for the design stage, starting one quarter after approval, with construction held as a separate decision. The returning decision will be asked to compare like with like: the tendered price against the estimate on the same scope, the refreshed appraisal against the appraisal in this proposal, and the programme against the sequence set out above. Where any of the three has moved materially, the movement and its cause will be stated, so the forum can judge whether the proposal it approved in principle is the project it is now being asked to build.

fact_base: Excerpt content: two groups report conflicting selectivity values for the same material class; the excerpt weighs their test conditions. The excerpt reaches a limited preference and states the condition on which it rests.
input: The selectivity values that have been reported for the benchmark material by the two groups are, it must be said, remarkably difficult to reconcile with one another, and the size of the disagreement is considerably larger than the scatter that either group reports for its own repeated measurements, which raises important questions about what is really being measured. A closer examination reveals that the difference appears to track the test conditions rather than the material itself. One of the groups derives its values from pure-component isotherms, which are then combined by means of IAST in order to predict what the mixture selectivity ought to be, whereas the other group measures selectivity directly on mixtures, working from the composition of the adsorbed phase that is found in equilibrium with a gas phase of known composition. These two approaches will only deliver the same answer in cases where the adsorbed mixture behaves ideally, and the benchmark material would appear to be one of the cases in which that assumption comes under considerable strain, since the components involved differ markedly in the strength with which they interact with the surface and indeed with one another. It is also worth noting that, where the isotherm route is followed, the resulting prediction inevitably inherits any weaknesses in the fitting of the pure-component data at low pressure, which is a region in which the two groups did not measure with equal care. On balance, therefore, the mixture measurements are to be preferred for the benchmark material, although this preference is subject to an important condition, namely that it holds where the comparison is made at feed compositions and total pressures that are reasonably close to those of the intended separation, and it ceases to hold in situations where the mixture data were obtained far away from those conditions.
target: The selectivity values reported for the benchmark material by the two groups do not agree, and the disagreement is larger than the scatter each group reports for repeated measurements of its own. The difference follows the test conditions rather than the material. One group obtains its values from pure-component isotherms, combined through IAST into a predicted mixture selectivity; the other measures selectivity directly on mixtures, from the composition of the adsorbed phase in equilibrium with a gas phase of known composition. The two quantities coincide only where the adsorbed mixture behaves ideally. For the benchmark material that assumption is strained, because the components differ in how strongly they interact with the surface and with each other. The isotherm route also imports the fit of the pure-component data at low pressure, a region in which the two groups measured with different care, so part of the gap between the reported values is a gap in the underlying data rather than in the material. The mixture measurements are therefore preferred for the benchmark material, on one condition: the preference holds where the comparison is made at feed compositions and total pressures close to those of the intended separation, and it lapses where the mixture data were taken far from those conditions. Judged on that basis, the higher of the two reported values rests on the isotherm route and is set aside, and the lower value, measured on mixtures, is the value carried forward for this material class.
