fact_base: Project proposal for a rooftop solar installation, in four sections: case, costs, schedule, and decision requested. Capital cost is $785k with a 7-year appraisal horizon. The schedule section gives a start one quarter after approval; no contractor is named. The decision requested is approval to proceed to detailed design, not to construction.
input:
Organisations across every sector are increasingly recognising that the buildings they occupy represent a powerful and largely untapped opportunity in the journey towards lower energy costs and reduced carbon emissions, and the roof is perhaps the clearest example of this untapped potential. This proposal explores the opportunity presented by a rooftop solar installation for the organisation's building and seeks approval to move forward to the detailed design stage, which is the essential next step in turning an attractive concept into a well-defined and deliverable project. Rooftop solar is a proven, mature, and increasingly cost-effective technology, and generating electricity on site offers a wide range of benefits, from reduced exposure to rising and unpredictable grid prices, through to a visible demonstration of environmental responsibility that resonates with staff, customers, and stakeholders alike. In the pages that follow, the case for the installation is set out in full, the costs are presented transparently, a schedule for taking the project forward is described, and the specific decision that is being requested at this stage is clearly stated.

## Case

The case for installing solar generation on the roof is built on several mutually reinforcing strands. First and foremost, there is the financial strand: the building consumes electricity throughout the day, and electricity generated on the roof is consumed on site, offsetting purchases from the grid at the full price the organisation pays for its supply. In a market where prices have risen sharply and remain difficult to predict, the ability to generate a portion of the organisation's electricity at a cost that is fixed once the installation is built offers valuable protection and makes an important contribution to budget stability. Alongside the financial strand sits the environmental strand: every unit of solar electricity used in the building is a unit that does not need to be generated elsewhere, and this directly reduces the carbon emissions associated with the organisation's operations, supporting its broader sustainability ambitions and enhancing its reputation with the growing number of customers and partners who take environmental performance seriously. There is also a practical strand that is sometimes overlooked. The roof is an asset the organisation already owns, insures, and maintains, and at present it performs no function beyond sheltering the building. Putting it to work avoids the considerable cost and complexity of finding, acquiring, and preparing land for a ground-mounted alternative, and it places the generation directly at the point of use, minimising losses and connection complexity. Finally, there is a strategic strand: organisations that act early on on-site generation position themselves well for a future in which carbon reporting, building performance standards, and energy costs are all likely to move in directions that reward those who have already invested. It is important to acknowledge, however, that a strong general case is not the same thing as a proven case for this particular roof, and the detailed design stage is the mechanism by which the general case is tested against the realities of the building's orientation, shading, structure, and electrical infrastructure, ensuring that the eventual construction decision is grounded in evidence.

## Costs

The estimated capital cost of the rooftop solar installation is $785k, and the proposal is appraised over a 7-year appraisal horizon. This figure should be understood as a carefully prepared estimate at the proposal stage, assembled from budget pricing and experience of comparable installations, rather than as a fixed or guaranteed price. No contractor has yet been appointed, and it would be misleading to present the estimate as anything firmer than it is; one of the central purposes of the detailed design stage is to transform this indicative figure into a set of competitively tendered prices that can be relied upon. The estimate is comprehensive in its scope, embracing the solar panels and the mounting system by which they are fixed to the roof, the inverters and associated electrical equipment, the cabling and connection works that link the installation to the building's electrical distribution and to the wider grid, the protective devices and metering that a safe and compliant connection requires, the surveys, design work, and approvals that the project needs, and the costs of managing the project through installation, testing, and commissioning. The appraisal that accompanies the proposal balances this capital cost against the value of the electricity the installation is expected to produce across the 7-year horizon, net of the ongoing costs of running it, which include routine inspection, cleaning of the panels, monitoring of performance, insurance, and maintenance of the electrical equipment over time. Because the value of the output depends on future electricity prices, and the output itself depends on the weather and on the characteristics of the roof, the results of the appraisal are necessarily subject to uncertainty, and they are presented as a sound basis for deciding whether the project deserves to proceed to design, rather than as a precise prediction of the financial returns that will ultimately be achieved.

## Schedule

Subject to approval, the project will start one quarter after approval is given, and it will unfold through a logical sequence of stages, each building on the one before. The opening stage is the detailed design itself, in which the precise layout of the panels on the roof is determined, the load-bearing capacity of the roof structure is verified through survey and engineering assessment, the electrical design is developed in full, and the arrangements for connecting the installation to the grid are discussed and agreed with the relevant network operator. In parallel with this design work, the project will pursue whatever consents and approvals are required, so that momentum is maintained and the project is not delayed unnecessarily at a later point. Following the completion of the design, and subject to a separate and subsequent decision to proceed to construction, the project will move into procurement, with equipment ordered and an installation contractor selected through a competitive tendering process based on the completed design. The physical installation will then be carried out in a manner carefully planned to minimise disruption to the building and its occupants, with the works on the roof and the works to the electrical systems coordinated so that the building can continue to function normally throughout. The programme concludes with testing and commissioning, during which the installation is thoroughly checked and demonstrated to perform as intended, and with a formal handover of the documentation, monitoring arrangements, and maintenance information to the team who will be responsible for the installation in operation. The schedule is subject to a number of risks, most notably the time required to secure the grid connection, any strengthening work that the structural survey may identify as necessary, and the effect of poor weather on work at roof level, and the detailed design stage will clarify the programme in respect of these factors.

## Decision requested

The decision that is now requested is approval to proceed to detailed design, and it is essential that the scope of this decision is properly understood by everyone involved. Granting this approval authorises the design stage and the work that goes with it, including the surveys, the engineering design, the application for a grid connection, and the preparation of a complete and tender-ready definition of the works. It does not authorise construction, and it does not commit the organisation to building the installation; that commitment would only arise from a further decision, taken once the design is complete and firm prices are available. When the project returns for that decision, it will bring with it tendered prices to replace the current estimate of $785k, an updated appraisal across the 7-year horizon, and a clarified programme, allowing the construction decision to be taken on a firm and transparent basis. If, on the other hand, the detailed design reveals that the installation would be significantly less attractive than the proposal stage currently suggests, the project can be brought to a close at that point, with the organisation's exposure limited to the cost of the design work itself and with the benefit of a body of survey and design information that would remain valuable for any future consideration of the roof. Decision makers are therefore invited to approve the move to detailed design, commencing one quarter after approval, in the knowledge that the construction decision remains entirely separate and still to come.
target:
A rooftop solar installation is proposed for the building, and approval is requested to proceed to detailed design. The estimated capital cost is $785k, appraised over a 7-year horizon. The requested approval is for design only; construction is a separate decision, taken later against tendered prices. Work starts one quarter after approval.

## Case

Solar generation on the roof is used in the building that carries it. Each unit generated on site is a unit not bought from the grid, and its value is the retail price the organisation pays for electricity. Once built, the installation has no fuel cost, so the price of its output is fixed by the capital and running costs already committed, in a budget otherwise set by a market the organisation cannot influence. Output varies with the weather but is predictable in aggregate from year to year, and it is produced during the day, when the building is occupied and consuming. The environmental effect follows from the same displacement: grid electricity carries the emissions of the generation behind it, and electricity generated on the roof and used below it does not. The roof is the other half of the case. It is owned, insured, and maintained already, and it currently does nothing but shelter the building. Generation placed on it needs no land, and the point of generation is the point of use. These arguments establish that rooftop generation deserves examination; they do not establish the value of this installation. Output depends on how much of the roof is usable, how it faces, and what shades it. Cost depends on the structure beneath the covering and on the connection the network operator allows. Neither can be known from the general case. Detailed design exists to measure them, and the strength of the general case is the reason the measurement is worth paying for before the construction question is put. The match between generation and demand deserves emphasis, because it is what makes the value side of the case robust in a way the cost side is not: the building uses electricity through the working day, the array produces through the same hours, and the self-consumed share of the output is therefore high by construction rather than by assumption. The exported remainder earns less, and the design will state the split the roof and the load imply.

## Costs

The capital cost is estimated at $785k, with a 7-year appraisal horizon. The scope inside the estimate is the panels and the mounting system that fixes them to the roof, the inverters, the cabling and connection works to the building's distribution system and the grid, protection and metering equipment, surveys, design and approvals, and project management through installation, testing, and commissioning. The estimate is a proposal-stage figure. No contractor is named in it and no tender stands behind any part of it; it is assembled from budget pricing and comparable installations, and its uncertainty is the uncertainty of that basis. Against the capital cost, the appraisal sets the value of the expected generation over the horizon, less the running costs of inspection, panel cleaning, performance monitoring, insurance, and maintenance of the electrical equipment. The value side of the appraisal is uncertain for two distinct reasons: the generation depends on the roof and the weather, and its price depends on electricity prices over the horizon. The detailed design attacks the cost side and the generation side together — survey and design fix the scope and the expected output, and a tender converts the estimate into prices offered competitively for that fixed scope. The construction decision should rest on the tendered figure and on the refreshed appraisal, not on the proposal-stage numbers. Two features of the running costs are worth stating at this stage. The electrical components of the installation have shorter service lives than the panels and will need attention within the life of the project, and the cost of that attention belongs in the appraisal rather than in a later maintenance budget. The panels themselves carry no moving parts, and their upkeep is inspection and cleaning rather than repair.

## Schedule

The programme starts one quarter after approval. Detailed design is the first stage: the panel layout is settled, the roof structure is surveyed and assessed for the loads imposed on it, the electrical design is completed, and the grid connection is applied for and agreed with the network operator. Consents are pursued in parallel with the design, so that approval processes do not become the constraint once the design is finished. Procurement belongs after the construction decision: equipment is ordered and an installer appointed by competitive tender against the completed design. Installation is planned around the building in use; roof works and electrical works are coordinated so that normal occupation continues, and the disruptive elements are placed where they disturb least. Testing and commissioning follow, in which the installation is demonstrated against the design, and handover passes the documentation, the monitoring arrangements, and the maintenance requirements to the team that will operate it. The programme carries three named risks. The connection agreement is in the network operator's hands and may set the pace. The structural survey may require strengthening works that were not in the scope. Weather can halt roof works. The design stage converts the first two risks from possibilities into facts with prices and durations attached, and the programme offered with the construction decision will show them. Building users are told the programme before the roof works begin, and the noisy stages are placed where occupation is lightest; the obligation runs the other way as well, in that access the design assumes has to be kept available while the works proceed. The design stage also fixes the evidence the commissioning must produce, so that handover is a comparison against stated requirements and not a general inspection.

## Decision requested

Approval is requested to proceed to detailed design, and the scope of the approval should be read exactly. It authorises surveys, engineering design, the grid connection application, and a tender-ready definition of the works. It does not authorise construction, and no commitment to build arises from it. The construction decision returns to this forum with tendered prices in place of the estimate, the appraisal over the 7-year horizon refreshed on the designed scope, and a programme that reflects the survey findings and the connection terms. Taken then, the construction decision rests on firm prices and measured characteristics of the roof. If the design instead shows the installation to be materially worse than the proposal indicates, the project closes at design stage; the cost incurred is the design cost, and the survey and design record remains as an asset for any future proposal affecting the roof. The request is therefore for the design stage only, starting one quarter after approval, with construction expressly reserved for a later decision. Deferral is the remaining alternative, and its cost should be stated plainly: the roof, the prices, and the connection terms available now are not held open by delay, and a later proposal would start again from survey. Nothing in the design stage forecloses that choice, but the choice should be made knowing that the present figures lapse with it.

fact_base: Goal: compute the Reynolds number for water in a pipe and state the flow regime. The Reynolds number Re (dimensionless) is computed from density rho (kg m-3), mean velocity v (m s-1), pipe diameter D (m) and dynamic viscosity mu (Pa s) by Re = rho v D / mu. Water at 293 K: rho = 998 kg m-3, mu = 1.00 x 10-3 Pa s. Pipe diameter D = 0.025 m; mean velocity v = 2 m s-1. Worked result: Re = 49900 (computed as 998 x 2 x 0.025 / 0.001). Flow is laminar below Re = 2300 and turbulent above Re = 4000; between the two values the regime is transitional and is not assigned by the number alone.
input: The goal of this worked example is to calculate the Reynolds number for water flowing through a pipe and to determine, on the basis of that calculation, what the flow regime is. The Reynolds number, which is a dimensionless quantity denoted by Re, provides a highly useful way of characterising the flow, and it is computed from the density rho (in kg m-3), the mean velocity v (in m s-1), the pipe diameter D (in m), and the dynamic viscosity mu (in Pa s), using the relationship Re = rho v D / mu. For water at a temperature of 293 K, the density rho is equal to 998 kg m-3 and the dynamic viscosity mu is equal to 1.00 x 10-3 Pa s. In the present example, the pipe diameter D is 0.025 m and the mean velocity v is 2 m s-1. Substituting these values into the expression gives Re = 998 x 2 x 0.025 / 0.001, and carrying out the arithmetic (the numerator, 998 x 2 x 0.025, comes to 49.9, which is then divided by 0.001) yields a Reynolds number of Re = 49900. In order to interpret this result, it is important to recall the standard thresholds: the flow is laminar when the Reynolds number is below Re = 2300, it is turbulent when the Reynolds number is above Re = 4000, and between these two values the regime is transitional and cannot be assigned by the number alone. Since the computed value of 49900 stands well above the threshold of 4000, the flow in this case can confidently be described as turbulent, and the transitional range between 2300 and 4000 plays no part in the conclusion.
target: Compute the Reynolds number for water in a pipe, and state the flow regime. The Reynolds number Re (dimensionless) compares the inertial effect in the flow with the viscous effect, and it is computed from the density rho (kg m-3), the mean velocity v (m s-1), the pipe diameter D (m), and the dynamic viscosity mu (Pa s) by Re = rho v D / mu. The units cancel in the ratio, and the Reynolds number is dimensionless. For water at 293 K, rho is 998 kg m-3 and mu is 1.00 x 10-3 Pa s. Take D as 0.025 m and v as 2 m s-1. Substitution gives Re = 998 x 2 x 0.025 / 0.001. The numerator, 998 x 2 x 0.025, is 49.9, and division by 0.001 gives Re = 49900. Flow is laminar below Re = 2300 and turbulent above Re = 4000; between 2300 and 4000 the regime is transitional and is not assigned by the number alone. The computed value of 49900 stands far above 4000, outside the transitional range and clear of its upper boundary, so the flow is turbulent. The check on the result is the threshold comparison itself: the value stands well clear of the upper boundary, so no plausible rounding in the inputs moves the assignment. The same computation serves for any liquid in a circular pipe once the four inputs are stated, and the same thresholds carry the assignment. What changes from case to case is only the margin between the computed value and the boundaries, and it is the margin, rather than the value alone, that decides how much trust the assignment deserves.

fact_base: Goal: compute the Reynolds number for water in a pipe and state the flow regime. The Reynolds number Re (dimensionless) is computed from density rho (kg m-3), mean velocity v (m s-1), pipe diameter D (m) and dynamic viscosity mu (Pa s) by Re = rho v D / mu. Water at 293 K: rho = 998 kg m-3, mu = 1.00 x 10-3 Pa s. Pipe diameter D = 0.08 m; mean velocity v = 1.6 m s-1. Worked result: Re = 127700 (computed as 998 x 1.6 x 0.08 / 0.001). Flow is laminar below Re = 2300 and turbulent above Re = 4000; between the two values the regime is transitional and is not assigned by the number alone.
input: In this example, the aim is to work out the Reynolds number for water flowing in a pipe and then to use the value that is obtained to say something meaningful about the nature of the flow regime. The Reynolds number Re is a dimensionless number that is widely used in fluid mechanics because it captures, in a single quantity, the balance between inertial and viscous effects, and it is calculated from the density rho (in kg m-3), the mean velocity v (in m s-1), the pipe diameter D (in m), and the dynamic viscosity mu (in Pa s), by means of the formula Re = rho v D / mu. The data for this example are as follows: the water is at a temperature of 293 K, at which its density rho is 998 kg m-3 and its dynamic viscosity mu is 1.00 x 10-3 Pa s; the pipe diameter D is 0.08 m; and the mean velocity v of the water is 1.6 m s-1. Putting all of these values into the formula gives Re = 998 x 1.6 x 0.08 / 0.001, and evaluating this step by step (the product in the numerator, 998 x 1.6 x 0.08, is 127.7, and dividing by 0.001) gives a final Reynolds number of Re = 127700. To interpret the result, the value is compared with the usual dividing lines: flow is laminar if the Reynolds number is below Re = 2300, and it is turbulent if the Reynolds number is above Re = 4000, whereas between the two values, in the range from 2300 to 4000, the regime is described as transitional and cannot be assigned from the number alone. The value obtained here, 127700, is enormously larger than 4000, so the conclusion is clear and unambiguous: the flow is turbulent.
target: Water flows in a pipe of diameter D 0.08 m at a mean velocity v of 1.6 m s-1. The task is the Reynolds number of the flow and the flow regime it assigns. The Reynolds number Re (dimensionless) is computed from the density rho (kg m-3), the mean velocity v (m s-1), the pipe diameter D (m), and the dynamic viscosity mu (Pa s) by Re = rho v D / mu. The units of the four quantities cancel in the combination, leaving a pure number, and the number is read against fixed thresholds rather than against the data of the case in hand. A large value of Re marks a flow in which inertial effects dominate viscous effects; a small value marks the opposite balance, which is why a single number can carry the regime assignment. Water at 293 K has rho 998 kg m-3 and mu 1.00 x 10-3 Pa s. Substitution of the stated values gives Re = 998 x 1.6 x 0.08 / 0.001. The numerator collects to 127.7 (998 x 1.6 x 0.08), and division by 0.001 gives Re = 127700. The result is checked against the regime thresholds. Flow is laminar below Re = 2300 and turbulent above Re = 4000; between 2300 and 4000 the regime is transitional and is not assigned by the number alone. The computed value, 127700, exceeds the upper threshold by a wide margin, and the assignment is not a borderline judgement against 4000: the flow is turbulent. The transitional range matters to the method rather than to this case, since a value falling inside that range would have to be reported as transitional, with the regime settled by observation of the flow and not by the Reynolds number. The diameter enters the number directly, so at a stated velocity the wider pipe is always the more turbulent case.

fact_base: A shell-and-tube exchanger heats cooling water in a refinery preheat train. Duty is 687 kW. Hot stream: 150 °C in, 110 °C out. Cold stream: 25 °C in, 50 °C out. The log-mean temperature difference is 92.3 K and the installed area is 25.7 m2, giving an overall coefficient of 290 W m-2 K-1. Fouling was assessed from a single 90-day run; no cleaning cycle has been completed.
input: A shell-and-tube heat exchanger installed in a refinery preheat train was used to heat cooling water, and its performance was assessed in order to establish how effectively it was transferring heat under the conditions studied. The duty of the exchanger was found to be 687 kW, which represents the total rate at which heat was being transferred from the hot stream to the cold stream. The hot stream entered the exchanger at a temperature of 150 °C and left at 110 °C, so it was cooled through a temperature change of 40 K as it gave up its heat. The cold stream, the cooling water being heated, entered at a much lower temperature of 25 °C and left at 50 °C, so it was warmed through a temperature change of 25 K. Because the two streams pass through the exchanger in opposite directions, the temperature difference that drives the heat transfer varies along the length of the unit, and it is therefore characterised by the log-mean temperature difference, which in this case was 92.3 K; the terminal differences at the two ends of the exchanger, obtained from the inlet and outlet temperatures, are 100 K and 85 K respectively. The installed heat transfer area of the exchanger is 25.7 m2, and bringing the duty, the area, and the log-mean temperature difference together gives an overall heat transfer coefficient of 290 W m-2 K-1. It is important to note that fouling of the heat transfer surfaces was assessed on the basis of a single 90-day run, and no cleaning cycle has yet been completed, so the picture of fouling behaviour that is available remains limited at this stage.
target: A shell-and-tube exchanger in a refinery preheat train heats cooling water at a duty of 687 kW. The hot stream enters at 150 °C and leaves at 110 °C, a fall of 40 K. The cold stream enters at 25 °C and leaves at 50 °C, a rise of 25 K. The terminal temperature differences are 100 K at the end where the hot stream enters and 85 K at the end where it leaves, and the log-mean temperature difference computed from them is 92.3 K. The installed area is 25.7 m2. Duty divided by area and by the log-mean temperature difference gives the overall coefficient: 290 W m-2 K-1 for the exchanger as it ran. The coefficient bundles the two film resistances and the wall resistance into a single figure, and the run does not separate them. The duty is the rate at which heat passed from the hot stream to the cold stream during the run, and the streams run countercurrently, so each end of the exchanger pairs the entering stream of one side with the leaving stream of the other. The coefficient is a property of the run, not of the exchanger in any state. Fouling was assessed from a single 90-day run, and no cleaning cycle has been completed, so the surfaces during the run carried whatever deposit the run had laid down, and the coefficient is the fouled value over that period. What the coefficient becomes after cleaning, and how quickly it falls again, are not established by a single run with no cleaning in it. The reported figures therefore fix the performance in the state in which the exchanger was measured, with the fouling condition of the run behind them. The figures are also internally consistent: the duty, the area, and the temperature difference return the stated coefficient, and no figure in the set depends on a measurement outside the run.

fact_base: Excerpt content: the absorber wall thickness is 20 mm after the corrosion allowance is added. The excerpt compares two gasket materials on temperature limit only and prefers the higher-rated one. The excerpt ends mid-argument; it neither summarises the report nor previews the next section.
input: Turning to the absorber itself, the wall thickness adopted for the absorber is 20 mm, a figure that is arrived at once the corrosion allowance has been added on top of the thickness that is required by the pressure considerations alone. The allowance is applied in full on the process side of the wall, which is the side that is exposed to the circulating solvent, since it is there that the wastage of the metal is expected to take place over the life of the vessel. As far as the gasket materials for the flanged joints of the absorber are concerned, the two candidate materials have been compared with one another purely on the basis of their temperature limits, and it is on that basis that a preference emerges. Other considerations, such as the behaviour of the materials under the bolting loads and their general availability, have deliberately been set to one side for the purposes of this particular comparison, because it is the temperature limit that separates the two materials by a margin that is significant in the context of this service. The material with the higher temperature rating is the one that is preferred, since its limit sits comfortably further above the temperatures that the joint will experience in service, and this additional margin is obtained without the need for any change to the flange facing or to the bolting that is used.
target: The wall thickness adopted for the absorber is 20 mm, after the corrosion allowance is added to the thickness the pressure duty requires. The allowance is carried in full on the process side, the side wetted by the solvent the lean solvent pump keeps in circulation, because that is the surface from which metal is lost in service. For the gasket at the absorber flanges, the comparison of the two candidate materials is made on temperature limit only. Seating behaviour, resistance to the solvent, and availability are excluded from this comparison, not because they do not matter, but because the temperature limit is the property on which the two materials differ by a margin that bears on the duty. The higher-rated material is preferred. Its limit stands further above the highest temperature the joint can reach, including the excursions that follow a loss of circulation, and the margin is gained without any change to the flange facing or the bolting. The lower-rated material stays within its limit in normal operation, but with a margin that an excursion consumes, and the same comparison, on the same basis, remains open at the discharge flange of the lean solvent pump.

fact_base: Liquid-liquid extraction recovers acetone from an aqueous stream into an organic solvent. The distribution coefficient (organic over aqueous) is 1.33 at 25 °C and the design uses 8 countercurrent stages. Predicted recovery is 89% of the acetone in the feed. The prediction assumes equilibrium stages and negligible mutual solubility; neither has been checked on the actual solvents.
input: Liquid-liquid extraction is an attractive and widely used separation technique, and in the present work it was applied to the recovery of acetone from an aqueous stream by contacting the stream with an organic solvent into which the acetone preferentially dissolves. The performance of any such extraction is governed to a considerable extent by the distribution coefficient, which expresses the ratio in which the solute divides itself between the two liquid phases at equilibrium, and for the system studied here the distribution coefficient of acetone, defined as the concentration in the organic phase over the concentration in the aqueous phase, has a value of 1.33 at a temperature of 25 °C. Building on this foundation, the design of the extraction unit makes use of 8 countercurrent stages, an arrangement in which the two liquid streams flow in opposite directions through the cascade so that the driving force for transfer is maintained from stage to stage. On the basis of the design calculations, the predicted recovery of acetone is 89% of the acetone that is present in the feed, which represents a substantial degree of removal. It is important to appreciate, however, that this prediction rests on certain assumptions that underpin the calculation, most notably the assumption that every stage behaves as an equilibrium stage and the assumption that the mutual solubility of the two solvents is negligible. Neither of these assumptions has yet been checked against the actual solvents that would be used, and so the figure of 89% should be regarded as a prediction whose reliability remains to be confirmed rather than as an established performance figure.
target: Liquid-liquid extraction recovers acetone from an aqueous stream into an organic solvent. The distribution coefficient, the concentration of acetone in the organic phase over its concentration in the aqueous phase at equilibrium, is 1.33 at 25 °C. The design uses 8 countercurrent stages, in which the two phases pass in opposite directions and each phase leaves against the freshest portion of the other. Predicted recovery is 89% of the acetone in the feed. Recovery is stated on the acetone in the feed: it is the share of the feed's acetone that leaves in the organic phase. The distribution coefficient is a property of the two solvents and the solute at the stated temperature, and the stage count is where the design spends it, stage by stage against the incoming feed. A measured recovery on the actual solvents would test both assumptions together, since each moves the result away from the prediction in a different part of the cascade. The prediction carries its assumptions inside it. It assumes that each stage reaches equilibrium, so the streams leaving a stage stand in the ratio the distribution coefficient fixes, and it assumes that the mutual solubility of the two solvents is negligible, so neither phase gains or loses volume to the other as the acetone moves. Neither assumption has been checked on the actual solvents. The direction of the exposure is known for the first assumption: a stage that falls short of equilibrium transfers less acetone than the calculation credits to it, so recovery in operation falls below 89% for the same stage count, by an amount the prediction does not state. The second assumption, if it fails, changes the phase flows themselves, and with them the stage-to-stage balance on which the predicted recovery rests. The predicted recovery is therefore a design figure, conditional on equilibrium stages and negligible mutual solubility, and it awaits a check on the actual solvents before it can be read as expected performance.

fact_base: Excerpt content: a seal replacement takes about 83 min with the unit isolated; the excerpt gives the isolation steps only. The excerpt warns once about stored pressure and does not repeat the warning.
input:
For the seal replacement to be carried out safely, the duty pump
must first be isolated from the process, as follows. The standby
pump is started and allowed to settle, so that it can be confirmed
that it has taken over the flow without disturbance. The duty pump
is then stopped, and the shaft allowed to come fully to rest. Its
discharge isolation valve is closed, followed by the suction
isolation valve, so that the pump is separated from the process on
both sides. Where a seal flush is fitted, its connection is also
closed at the root valve. The pump motor is isolated at its
starter, and a personal lock and tag are applied under the PTW,
and the control room is informed that the duty pump is out of
service and the standby pump is the running machine.

The casing vent and casing drain are opened so that the casing
contents can run down into the closed drain system, and the seal
housing vent is opened as well, both vents being left open while
draining takes place. Where only a single closed valve stands
between the duty pump and a live header, the isolation is best
regarded as incomplete until a second barrier is in place.

Care is needed here because stored pressure may remain trapped in
the seal housing even after the casing itself has been vented and
drained. The seal housing is therefore proved, by its test point,
to be at atmospheric pressure, and the casing pressure gauge is
confirmed to read zero, before any seal housing joint is disturbed.

The isolation is recorded on the PTW, with the closed valves, the
locked starter and the open vents listed in the order in which they
were made. With the duty pump isolated, locked and proved in this
condition, the seal replacement that follows takes about 83 min.

fact_base: Goal: compute the diffusive flux of oxygen through a stagnant water film. The diffusive flux J (mol m-2 s-1) is computed from the diffusivity D (m2 s-1) and the concentration gradient dC/dx, where C is concentration (mol m-3) and x is position (m). Fick's first law: J = -D dC/dx; the negative sign states that diffusion runs from high concentration to low concentration. Oxygen in water: D = 1.6 x 10-9 m2 s-1. Concentration falls by 0.4 mol m-3 across a film 0.8 mm thick, so dC/dx = -500 mol m-4. Worked result: J = 8.00x 10-7 mol m-2 s-1. The law as stated covers a stagnant medium; a moving medium adds convection, which the equation does not include.
input:
In this worked example, we will work through the calculation of
the diffusive flux of oxygen through a stagnant water film, a
quantity that plays a central role in a wide range of mass-transfer
problems. The diffusive flux, denoted J and expressed in
mol m-2 s-1, represents the amount of oxygen that crosses a unit
area of the film per unit time, and it is determined by two
quantities working together: the diffusivity D, which is measured
in m2 s-1, and the concentration gradient dC/dx, in which C stands
for the concentration in mol m-3 and x stands for position in m.
The connection between them is given by Fick's first law, which
takes the form J = -D dC/dx. It is worth pausing on the negative
sign, because it carries the physical meaning of the law: diffusion
always runs from a region of high concentration towards a region of
low concentration, so the flux points in the direction opposite to
the gradient, from the side where the concentration is higher
towards the side where it is lower.

Turning now to the numbers for the present case, the diffusivity
of oxygen in water is D = 1.6 x 10-9 m2 s-1. The concentration is
found to fall by 0.4 mol m-3 across a film that is 0.8 mm thick, so
that the gradient is simply the fall divided by the film thickness,
with the sign of the fall retained: dC/dx = -500 mol m-4, the
concentration decreasing as x increases on the way from the
oxygen-rich side to the oxygen-poor side.

Substituting into J = -D dC/dx, we obtain J = -(1.6 x 10-9) x
(-500), which evaluates to J = 8.00 x 10-7 mol m-2 s-1. The flux
through the film is therefore J = 8.00 x 10-7 mol m-2 s-1. The
outcome is reassuringly consistent with the sign convention
discussed above: a negative gradient, with the concentration
falling as position increases, produces a positive flux in the
direction of increasing x, towards the lower concentration. It should finally
be borne in mind that Fick's first law in the form used here
applies to a stagnant medium; if the medium were moving, convection
would contribute to the transport as well, and that contribution is
not included in the equation as it stands.
target:
The goal is to compute the diffusive flux of oxygen through a
stagnant water film. The flux is 8.00 x 10-7 mol m-2 s-1.

The diffusive flux J (mol m-2 s-1) is the amount of oxygen crossing
unit area of the film per unit time, and it is computed from the
diffusivity D (m2 s-1) and the concentration gradient dC/dx, where
C denotes the concentration (mol m-3) and x denotes position (m).
Fick's first law states the relation as J = -D dC/dx. The negative
sign states that diffusion runs from high concentration to low
concentration: the flux is directed opposite to the gradient, from
the side where the concentration is higher towards the side where
it is lower.

For oxygen in water, D = 1.6 x 10-9 m2 s-1. The concentration falls
by 0.4 mol m-3 across a film 0.8 mm thick, so the gradient is the
fall divided by the film thickness and carries the sign of the
fall: dC/dx = -500 mol m-4, concentration decreasing as x increases
in the direction from the oxygen-rich side to the oxygen-poor side.

The gradient, not the concentration itself, drives the flux. Two
films with the same concentrations at their faces but different
thicknesses carry different fluxes, because their gradients differ;
two films with the same gradient carry the same flux, whatever the
absolute concentrations at the faces. The flux is therefore fixed
once the diffusivity and the gradient are fixed, and every
statement about the size of the flux is a statement about those two
quantities.

Substitution in J = -D dC/dx gives J = -(1.6 x 10-9) x (-500), and
J = 8.00 x 10-7 mol m-2 s-1. The result has the sign the law
predicts: a negative gradient, concentration falling with position,
gives a positive flux in the direction of increasing x, towards the
lower concentration. Fick's first law as stated holds for a
stagnant medium; a moving medium adds convection, which the
equation does not include.

fact_base: A tutorial passage explains the Prandtl number to second-year students. Definition in words: the Prandtl number is the ratio of momentum diffusivity to thermal diffusivity. The passage must state what a value near 1 means and what a large value means, without inventing numerical examples.
input:
When a fluid flows over a surface, two spreading processes are at
work at the same time, both arising from the same underlying
molecular mechanism. Momentum spreads outwards from the surface
into the fluid, and heat spreads outwards as well, but the two
processes do not in general proceed at the same rate, and their
relative speed is captured by a dimensionless quantity known as the
Prandtl number. The Prandtl number is defined
as the ratio of the momentum diffusivity to the thermal diffusivity.
To unpack the two terms, momentum diffusivity can be understood as
a measure of how rapidly a difference in velocity spreads through
the fluid and is evened out, while thermal diffusivity similarly
measures how rapidly a difference in temperature spreads through
the fluid and is evened out. Since both diffusivities are
properties of one and the same fluid in one and the same state,
forming their ratio provides a compact way of ordering the two
spreading processes against one another: the number indicates which
process runs ahead, and by how much, independently of the size of
the equipment or the speed of the flow.

In the case where the value is near 1, the two diffusivities are
nearly equal to one another. Momentum and heat consequently spread
at comparable rates, and the velocity boundary layer and the
temperature boundary layer grow to nearly the same thickness. At
any given distance from the surface, the fluid has been set in
motion over roughly the same depth to which it has been heated or
cooled, and neither field can be said to run ahead of the other.

In the contrasting case of a large value, the momentum diffusivity
far exceeds the thermal diffusivity. Momentum spreads readily
whereas heat spreads only slowly, and the velocity boundary layer
grows to a thickness much greater than that of the temperature
boundary layer. Differences in temperature remain confined within
a thin layer against the surface, in fluid that is still moving
well below the free-stream velocity, while differences in velocity
reach much farther out into the flow. Heat transfer at the surface
is then governed by conduction across the thin temperature layer,
and the temperature field near the surface responds only slowly to
any change imposed on it, long after the velocity field has
adjusted itself.
target:

mechanism, at rates that depend on the fluid, and the Prandtl
number compares the two rates. The Prandtl number is defined as
the ratio of momentum diffusivity to thermal diffusivity. Momentum
diffusivity measures how fast a difference in velocity spreads
through the fluid and is evened out. Thermal diffusivity measures
how fast a difference in temperature spreads through the fluid and
is evened out. Both diffusivities are properties of the same fluid
in the same state, and their ratio orders the two spreading
processes against each other: the number reports which process runs

reach much farther out. Conduction across the thin temperature
layer then governs the heat transfer at the surface, and the

fact_base: Goal: compute the Reynolds number for water in a pipe and state the flow regime. The Reynolds number Re (dimensionless) is computed from density rho (kg m-3), mean velocity v (m s-1), pipe diameter D (m) and dynamic viscosity mu (Pa s) by Re = rho v D / mu. Water at 293 K: rho = 998 kg m-3, mu = 1.00 x 10-3 Pa s. Pipe diameter D = 0.05 m; mean velocity v = 2.3 m s-1. Worked result: Re = 114800 (computed as 998 x 2.3 x 0.05 / 0.001). Flow is laminar below Re = 2300 and turbulent above Re = 4000; between the two values the regime is transitional and is not assigned by the number alone.
input:
This worked example is concerned with the Reynolds number for
water flowing in a pipe, the aim being to calculate its value and
then to establish the flow regime. The Reynolds number, denoted Re
and dimensionless, is calculated from the density rho (kg m-3),
the mean velocity v (m s-1), the pipe diameter D (m) and the
dynamic viscosity mu (Pa s), combined in the relation
Re = rho v D / mu. Each quantity enters the relation in the unit
stated alongside it, and the units cancel in the quotient, which
is why the Reynolds number itself carries no unit. For water at
293 K, the property values are rho = 998 kg m-3 and mu = 1.00 x
10-3 Pa s. The pipe has a diameter D = 0.05 m, and the water moves
through it at a mean velocity v = 2.3 m s-1.

When the values are substituted, the result is Re = 998 x 2.3 x
0.05 / 0.001 = 114800. The flow regime is then determined by
setting the computed value against the standard thresholds: the
flow is laminar below Re = 2300 and turbulent above Re = 4000,
while between the two values the regime is transitional and cannot
be assigned on the basis of the number alone. The computed value
stands far above the upper threshold, comfortably within the
turbulent range and well clear of the transitional band. Given
that the value is not close to either threshold, no plausible error
in the inputs could alter the conclusion: the flow in the pipe is
turbulent, with Re = 114800.

fact_base: Excerpt content: a strainer cleaning takes about 65 min with the unit isolated; the excerpt gives the isolation steps only. The excerpt warns once about stored pressure and does not repeat the warning.
input:
Before the strainer cleaning can begin, the duty has to be
transferred in an orderly fashion. The transfer begins by starting
the standby pump, and once it is delivering steadily, the duty
pump can be stopped. The strainer outlet valve is then closed, followed by the
strainer inlet valve, so that the strainer body is separated from
the line on both sides. Because the strainer serves the suction of
the duty pump, its starter is locked under the PTW, so that the
pump cannot be started against a blanked suction path, and the
control room is informed which pump is now the running machine.

The strainer vent and drain are opened so that the body can drain
into the closed drain, and the vent is left open while draining is
in progress, with time allowed for the element to drip dry.

A point calling for care is that stored pressure can remain held
in the strainer body, trapped behind a fouled element, even after
the body has been vented. The body is therefore proved to be at
atmospheric pressure by its test point, and the drain checked to
have stopped running, before the cover is slackened.

The isolation is then recorded on the PTW in the order in which it
was made. With the strainer isolated, drained and proved in this
condition, the cleaning and refitting that follow take about
65 min.

Transfer the duty to the standby pump before the strainer is
touched. Start it, prove that it is delivering steadily, and stop
the duty pump.
Close the strainer outlet valve, and then the strainer inlet valve,
so that the strainer body is separated from the line on both sides.
Lock the duty pump starter under the PTW, since the strainer serves
the suction of the duty pump and the pump must not be started
against a blanked suction path. Tell the control room which pump is
now the running machine.

Open the strainer vent and the strainer drain, and drain the body
to the closed drain. Leave the vent open while the body drains, and
allow time for the element to drip dry into the body.

Stored pressure can be held in the strainer body behind a fouled
element after the body has been vented. Prove the body at
atmospheric pressure at the test point, and check that the drain
has stopped running, before the cover is slackened.

Record the isolation on the PTW in the order in which it was made.

the cleaning and refitting that follow take about 65 min.

fact_base: Staffing review for a quality laboratory: 12 full-time staff, overtime at 7% of paid hours last year. Replacing half the overtime with one additional hire costs $87k per year fully loaded. Overtime is concentrated in two seasonal peaks; a hire is paid for the full year.
input:
This review examines the staffing position of the quality
laboratory, with particular attention to the balance between
overtime working and permanent headcount. The laboratory currently
employs 12 full-time staff, and over the course of last year
overtime working amounted to 7% of paid hours, a level that has
prompted the question of whether an additional permanent
appointment would represent a better use of resources. The option
under consideration is to replace half of the overtime with one
additional hire. Half of the overtime corresponds to 3.5% of paid
hours, and the hire who would absorb that work would cost $87k per
year fully loaded, a figure bundling the salary and the associated
employer costs, charged in every month of the year.

A closer look at the pattern of the work, however, reveals a
significant complication. The overtime is not spread evenly across
the calendar but is concentrated in two seasonal peaks, when
submissions arrive faster than they can be cleared, while between
the peaks the existing staff carry the workload within ordinary
hours. An additional hire, by contrast, is paid for the full year.
The laboratory would in effect be paying $87k during the off-peak
months, when the additional capacity is not required, to remove
overtime that arises only in the peak months. The comparison is
therefore between a fixed cost spread across the whole year and a
variable cost incurred in only part of it, and on the figures
available the variable arrangement remains the smaller commitment.

Taking all of this into consideration, the recommendation is that
laboratory management should hold staffing at its present level,
continue to cover the two peaks with overtime, and revisit the
question only if the peaks should lengthen or merge, since a
longer peak would change the balance on which the present figures
rest. The hire is not dismissed on its merits as additional
capacity; it is set aside because its cost runs for the full year
whereas the need it would answer runs for only part of it.
target:

question only if the peaks lengthen or merge, or if the workload
between the peaks grows beyond what ordinary hours can carry,
because either change alters the balance the figures rest on. The hire is not rejected
on its merits as capacity; it is rejected because its cost runs for
the full year while the need it answers runs for part of it.

fact_base: Goal: compute the Reynolds number for water in a pipe and state the flow regime. The Reynolds number Re (dimensionless) is computed from density rho (kg m-3), mean velocity v (m s-1), pipe diameter D (m) and dynamic viscosity mu (Pa s) by Re = rho v D / mu. input:
In the present worked example, the task is to determine the
Reynolds number for water flowing through a pipe and, on the basis
of the value obtained, to identify the flow regime. The water, at
293 K, flows in a pipe of diameter 0.05 m at a mean velocity of
1.8 m s-1. The Reynolds number, denoted Re and dimensionless, is
computed from the density rho (kg m-3), the mean velocity v
(m s-1), the pipe diameter D (m) and the dynamic viscosity mu
(Pa s), which are combined in the relation Re = rho v D / mu. For
water at the temperature in question, the property values are
rho = 998 kg m-3 together with mu = 1.00 x 10-3 Pa s, these being
properties of the liquid in the pipe, while the diameter and the
velocity are properties of the flow within it.

Carrying out the substitution, Re = 998 x 1.8 x 0.05 / 0.001 =
89800. Assigning the regime then amounts to a comparison against
the recognised thresholds, which are statements about the number
rather than about the pipe itself: the flow is laminar below
Re = 2300 and turbulent above Re = 4000. Between the two values the
regime is transitional, and in that band the number alone does not
settle the assignment, since the behaviour of the flow also depends
on the disturbances that the stream carries into the pipe. None of
that uncertainty arises in the present instance. At 89800, the
value stands far above the upper threshold, squarely in the
turbulent range with the transitional band far below it, and the
conclusion follows directly: the flow is turbulent, with
Re = 89800, and no borderline judgement has to be defended.

subtype: worked example with equation: available NPSH
fact_base: A pump draws condensate from an open tank at atmospheric pressure, 101.3 kPa. Vapour pressure at the pumping temperature is 7.4 kPa, the static lift is 3.7 m and suction-line friction loss is 0.8 m. Available net positive suction head $NPSH_a$ is 5.1 m. The pump's required NPSH at the duty flow comes from the vendor curve and must be exceeded with margin.
input:
This worked example walks through the determination of the
available net positive suction head for a pump drawing condensate
from an open tank, the quantity that decides whether the pump can
draw at its duty flow without cavitation. Because the tank is open,
the pressure at the surface of the liquid is the atmospheric
pressure $P_{atm}$, 101.3 kPa. Set against this is the vapour
pressure $P_v$ of the condensate at the pumping temperature,
7.4 kPa. Two further quantities complete the picture: the static
lift $h_{lift}$, 3.7 m, and the friction loss $h_f$ in the suction
line, 0.8 m. The available net positive suction head is computed
from these quantities by the relation

$$NPSH_a = \frac{P_{atm} - P_v}{\rho g} - h_{lift} - h_f$$

in which $\rho$ stands for the density of the condensate and $g$
for gravitational acceleration. The first term represents the
pressure head standing above vapour pressure at the tank surface,
expressed as a height of the liquid itself, while the static lift
and the friction loss are subtracted because both are heads the
liquid must supply before it reaches the pump inlet. Substituting
the values gives the result $NPSH_a$ = 5.1 m.

It remains to be emphasised that the computed head, 5.1 m, is a
margin to be tested rather than a result to be filed away. The
pump's required NPSH at the duty flow comes from the vendor curve,
and the available head of 5.1 m must be shown to exceed that
required value with a proper margin; should it fall short, the
pump will cavitate at the duty flow.

fact_base: A textbook chapter section on process control, in four parts: principle, equipment, a worked example, and limits. The worked example uses only the numbers given in the principle part; no new data appear later in the chapter. The limits part states where the simple model fails, in plain terms, without new equations.
input:
## Principle

Process control rests on a simple idea: a process can be held at a desired value by feedback. The story begins with the controlled variable — a level, a temperature, a pressure, a flow — which is measured continuously. The measurement is compared with the set point, the value that the variable is required to hold. The difference between the set point and the measurement is known as the error, and it is the error that serves as the input to the controller. Working from the error, the controller computes an output, and the output moves a final element, which changes a manipulated variable — a stream, a duty, or some similar quantity — that acts back on the process itself. The loop is closed: every change in the controlled variable finds its way back, through the measurement, to the controller.

Crucially, the feedback employed in control is negative in sign. When the controlled variable rises, the controller produces an action that opposes the rise, driving the manipulated variable in the direction that brings the controlled variable back towards the set point. The loop therefore corrects disturbances it was never told about. A change in the feed, a change in the ambient conditions, a surface that gradually fouls — any influence that pushes the controlled variable away from its set point generates an error, and the error generates the correction. No model of the disturbance is required; the measurement simply reports its combined effect.

The simplest form of controller action is proportional action, under which the change in the output is proportional to the error, the constant of proportionality being the controller gain. Proportional action on its own, however, leaves an offset once a disturbance has settled, because a changed manipulated variable can only be held by a changed output, and a changed output can only be produced by an error that continues to stand. Integral action addresses this shortcoming by continuing to move the output for as long as any error persists, thereby removing the offset. Derivative action responds to the rate at which the error is changing, and anticipates where the error is heading. Underpinning all of this is a deliberately simple working model: the process is treated as though it responds in proportion to a change in its input, with a lag and a dead time for its dynamics. The sections that follow build the loop up from that model before turning to where the model breaks down.

## Equipment

A control loop is assembled from a measuring element, a transmitter, a controller and a final element, connected in that order around the process. The measuring element senses the controlled variable: a level element is displaced or loaded by the liquid, a resistance thermometer changes resistance with temperature, and a pressure element deforms under the pressure applied to it. The transmitter converts the response of the measuring element into a standard signal that can be carried over a distance, and it is the signal, rather than the variable itself, that the remainder of the loop handles.

The controller receives the signal, forms the error against the set point, and computes the output. In a modern plant, the controller is one function among many in a distributed control system, and its settings — the gain, the integral time and the derivative time — are entered as part of the system's configuration rather than being dialled in on the instrument itself. The set point is supplied by the operator, or from a higher-level calculation supervising the loop.

The final element converts the controller output into the actual change in the manipulated variable. It usually takes the form of a control valve: an actuator moves the valve stem, while a positioner compares the actual stem position with the position demanded by the output and drives the actuator until the two agree, so that the stem follows the output in spite of friction and the forces exerted on the plug by the process. An important design consideration is that the valve is specified to fail in the safe direction should its power supply be lost: a valve that must be shut to protect the process fails closed, whereas a valve that must stand open to protect the process fails open. The choice is made loop by loop, from the consequences of the valve sitting in its failed position while the process is unattended.

## Worked example

Consider a tank fed by a stream whose flow the operator does not control, with liquid drawn off through a control valve in the outlet line. The level in the tank plays the role of the controlled variable, the outflow that of the manipulated variable, and a level controller holds the level at its set point by moving the valve as required. Initially the tank runs steadily: inflow and outflow are equal, the level stands at the set point, the error is zero, and the valve sits part-open at the opening the steady outflow requires.

Now suppose the feed rate rises, and stays higher. Inflow now exceeds outflow, and the level begins to climb. The measurement climbs with the level, the error changes as the measurement moves above the set point, and the controller responds by opening the valve further. As the valve opens, the outflow rises. The level continues to climb while inflow still exceeds outflow, although the climb slows as the outflow approaches the new inflow, until outflow and inflow come back into balance with the valve at a wider opening and the level at a standstill.

The standstill, however, does not occur at the set point. Under proportional action alone, the wider valve opening is held by a larger controller output, and that larger output can only be produced by an error that continues to stand, so the level settles above the set point and remains there: exactly the offset the principle section predicts, in precisely the predicted form. If the same loop is fitted with integral action, the picture changes: the output continues to creep while the offset persists, the valve opens further still, the level is brought back to the set point, and the error is driven to zero, after which the output holds its new value with no error left to sustain it. The example thus bears out the principle in both forms: proportional action holds the new balance at the price of an offset, while integral action removes the offset by removing the error on which it stands.

## Limits

The model underlying the principle section is a simplification, and its shortcomings mark the limits of what a single loop can achieve. The model treats the process as though it responds in proportion to its input. Real processes are under no such obligation: the gain of a heat exchanger changes with throughput, the gain of a tank level changes with the cross-section of the tank wherever the section is not uniform, and a valve passes a flow that depends on the pressure drop across it as well as on its opening. A controller tuned at one operating point has been tuned for one particular gain, and its performance deteriorates as the process moves away from that point — sluggish at one extreme of the range, oscillatory at the other.

The model also allows for dead time, but treats the response as beginning cleanly once the dead time has elapsed. Where dead time makes up a large part of the overall response — a long pipe run between the valve and the measurement, or a composition obtained by an analyser through a sample line — the controller is condemned to act on information that is already old. Corrections arrive late, overshoot, and are corrected late in their turn; the loop oscillates however carefully it has been tuned, and the genuine remedy is to relocate the measurement or accept a slower loop, rather than to raise the gain.

Saturation imposes a harder limit still. A valve fully open can pass no more, and a valve fully shut can pass no less; once the travel of the final element is exhausted, the loop is effectively open and the variable uncontrolled, regardless of what the controller computes. The remaining limit is set by the measurement. Noise on the signal is passed to the controller as though it were genuine movement of the variable, and derivative action is particularly prone to amplifying it, so the quality of the measurement caps the tightness of control the loop can usefully employ.

Finally, loops do not operate in isolation. The level loop of the worked example shares its tank with every other loop that moves the same streams, and each loop's correction becomes the next loop's disturbance. A treatment confined to single loops can state this limit plainly but cannot remove it: interacting loops must be detuned against one another, or the control problem reformulated with the interaction inside it.

Feedback control, as presented in this chapter, is the correction of a measured variable by an error-driven loop built from a measuring element, a controller and a final element. Its great strength is that the disturbance itself never needs to be known. Set against that strength are its limits: the linearity the model assumes, the dead time the loop cannot remove, the travel of its final element, and the quality of its measurement.

fact_base: A flat firebrick wall has thickness 150 mm and thermal conductivity $k$ of 1.1 W m-1 K-1. The temperature difference $\Delta T$ across the wall is 382 K, giving a heat flux $q$ of 2801 W m-2. The calculation is steady and one-dimensional; film resistances are excluded.
input:
In this example we consider the conduction of heat through a flat
firebrick wall, with the object of determining the heat flux by
means of Fourier's law, which relates the flux to the properties
of the wall and to the temperature difference maintained across it.
The wall in question is flat, it has a thickness of 150 mm, and its
thermal conductivity $k$ is 1.1 W m-1 K-1. Firebrick is a
refractory material, which is to say that it is capable of
withstanding furnace temperatures that few structural materials
could tolerate, and its conductivity is low, so that a wall built
from it serves the double purpose of containing the furnace and
limiting the heat that escapes through it. The temperature
difference $\Delta T$ across the wall is 382 K, and the thickness,
converted into metres, is $\Delta x$ = 0.15 m.

For the case of steady one-dimensional conduction, the flux is
computed by the relation

$$q = k \frac{\Delta T}{\Delta x}$$

in which $q$ denotes the heat flux, $k$ the thermal conductivity,
$\Delta T$ the temperature difference and $\Delta x$ the wall
thickness. The description steady indicates that the temperatures
do not change with time, while one-dimensional indicates that the
temperature varies only through the thickness, uniformly over the
face of the wall, so that a single gradient is sufficient to
describe the whole wall. Substituting the values, $q$ = 1.1 x 382 /
0.15 = 2801 W m-2.

Two points of caution complete the example. The calculation
excludes the film resistances at the two faces of the wall, and
since a surface film adds its own resistance in series with the
wall, the flux through the real construction, with the films
included, would be lower than 2801 W m-2. The value obtained,
2801 W m-2, is thus the flux through the wall alone, and it should
be read as an upper figure for the assembly of which the wall forms
a part.

Fourier's law gives the flux from the wall properties and the
temperature difference across the wall. The heat flux $q$ is
2801 W m-2.

conductivity $k$ is 1.1 W m-1 K-1. Firebrick is a refractory
material: it withstands furnace temperatures that few structural
materials tolerate, and its conductivity is low, so a wall of it
both contains the furnace and limits the heat lost through it. The
temperature difference $\Delta T$ across the wall is 382 K. The
thickness, expressed in metres, is $\Delta x$ = 0.15 m.

For steady one-dimensional conduction, the flux is computed by

$$q = k \frac{\Delta T}{\Delta x}$$

where $q$ denotes the heat flux, $k$ the thermal conductivity,
$\Delta T$ the temperature difference and $\Delta x$ the wall
thickness. Steady means that the temperatures do not change with
time; one-dimensional means that the temperature varies only
through the thickness, uniformly over the face of the wall, so that
a single gradient describes the whole wall. Heat flows through the
wall from the hot face towards the cold face, in the direction of
falling temperature. The flux is a rate per unit area: a larger
wall passes more heat in total at the same flux, because the
gradient through it and the material of it are unchanged.
Substitution gives $q$ = 1.1 x 382 / 0.15 = 2801 W m-2.

The calculation excludes the film resistances at the two faces of
the wall. A surface film adds its own resistance in series with the
wall, so the flux through the real construction, films included, is
lower than 2801 W m-2. The stated value is therefore the flux
through the wall alone, and it stands as an upper figure for the
assembly of which the wall forms a part.

fact_base: Project proposal for a water recycling plant, in four sections: case, costs, schedule, and decision requested. Capital cost is $400k with a 7-year appraisal horizon. The schedule section gives a start one quarter after approval; no contractor is named. The decision requested is approval to proceed to detailed design, not to construction.
input:
## Case

This proposal sets out the case for a water recycling plant and seeks support for taking the project forward. By way of background, the site currently takes the whole of its process water from the municipal supply and returns the whole of its effluent to the municipal sewer. An important consequence of this arrangement is that the site's water costs are effectively set twice over: a charge is incurred on the water that is drawn in, and a further charge is incurred on the water that is sent out, and both of these charges fall on water that passes through the process just once before being discarded. Alongside the question of cost, the arrangement also determines the site's exposure. Because the process holds no water supply of its own, any interruption or restriction affecting the municipal supply would reach production directly and without any buffer, while the terms of the discharge consent govern the stream of effluent leaving the site, a stream which the site has no practical ability to hold back.

It is against this background that the recycling proposal has been developed. A water recycling plant would treat the effluent on site and return the treated water to the process for reuse. The intake from the municipal supply would fall, the discharge to the municipal sewer would fall by the same recovered stream, and the process would gain a supply that sits under the site's own control. It is worth emphasising that the recovered water is not a by-product in search of a use: it would displace purchased water at precisely the point where the site already uses water, and it would relieve the discharge at precisely the point where the consent binds most tightly. The case for the plant is therefore a case about cost and security taken together — on the one hand the ongoing running cost of a single-use water system, and on the other hand the operational risk of depending on a supply and a discharge that both lie outside the site's control.

It should also be recognised that a proposal of this kind cannot by itself settle the questions on which a construction decision would have to rest. The treatment duty has to be fixed on the measured quality of the actual effluent, the treatment process has to be selected against that duty, and the plant has to be priced from vendor quotations rather than estimated from comparable installations elsewhere. All of that work belongs to detailed design, the stage at which a case of this kind is converted into a price. The scope that the design has to settle covers the whole path of the water: collection of the effluent as it leaves the process, equalisation so that the treatment stage sees a steady load rather than the swings of the producing process, the treatment stage itself, storage of the treated water, and return of that water to the points of use at the quality that each use requires. Which of those elements turns out to be large and which turns out to be small depends on the effluent and on the uses, and it is that dependence which leads this proposal to fix the scope by function and to leave the sizing of it to the design stage.

## Costs

Turning to the financial side of the proposal, the estimated capital cost of the water recycling plant is $400k. This figure is an estimate prepared at proposal stage, built up from the expected scope of the treatment plant and its installation, and it will in due course be replaced, during detailed design, by firm prices for the selected process and its equipment. The appraisal of the plant runs over a 7-year horizon, and the comparison that it makes is between two complete positions over that period: on one side, the cost of building and operating the recycling plant, and on the other side, the cost of continuing to take all process water from the municipal supply and to discharge all effluent to the municipal sewer.

A word is in order about the standing of the capital figure itself. An estimate made at proposal stage, before the process has been selected and before any vendor has priced the equipment, is a planning figure with a wide tolerance around it, and it is used in this proposal for one purpose only, namely to size the commitment that a construction decision would involve, so that the sequence of decisions is proportioned to the sum at stake. It is not a price and it is not a budget, and to treat it as either would be to overstate what is currently known. The appraisal has been constructed so as to absorb its replacement: when the firm price arrives from detailed design, the appraisal is simply rerun on that price, with no change required to its structure.

The operating costs of the plant, by contrast, are not yet fixed, and this proposal does not attempt to state them as figures. Energy for treatment and pumping, treatment consumables, maintenance of the treatment equipment and the labour of operating the plant all belong to the operating account, and each of them depends on the process that detailed design selects and on the duty that the measured quality of the effluent imposes. The savings side of the appraisal is open in much the same way: the value of the recovered water depends on the volume recovered and on the intake and discharge charges that it displaces, and the volume recovered is itself one of the results of the design. What can be stated at this stage is the structure of the appraisal and the term over which it runs. The appraisal period is 7 years from the start of operation, the capital figure under appraisal is the $400k estimated here and, in due course, the firm price that replaces it, and the decision that the appraisal exists to support is the construction decision rather than the decision sought in this proposal.

## Schedule

In terms of timing, work would start one quarter after approval. The first stage is detailed design itself, which comprises characterisation of the effluent by means of a sampling programme — the treatment duty has to rest on the effluent as it actually is, rather than on the effluent as it might be assumed to be — together with selection of the treatment process against the measured duty and pricing of the plant from vendor quotations for the selected process. Detailed design concludes with a firm capital price and a completed appraisal, and with the construction case stated on the basis of both.

Procurement, construction and commissioning then follow the design in that order. No contractor is named in this proposal, and none should be inferred from it: the construction contractor is to be appointed by competitive tender on the completed design, so that all of the tenders are priced against one and the same fixed scope. Commissioning returns the plant to the operating organisation with the quality of its treated water demonstrated against the duty that the design set. It should be noted that each stage following approval depends on the stage before it: procurement cannot be priced before the design has fixed the scope, and construction cannot be tendered before procurement has established the market. The schedule is therefore best understood as a sequence with one fixed point at its head — the start, one quarter after approval — and with the construction decision standing between detailed design and everything that is to follow it.

## Decision requested

It remains to state the decision that this proposal requests. The decision requested is approval to proceed to detailed design for the water recycling plant. In the event of approval, the project team would proceed to detailed design, encompassing the effluent sampling programme, the selection of the treatment process and the firm pricing of the plant. Approval on this basis would commit the organisation to that design work and to nothing beyond it: it would not authorise construction, it would not commit the $400k of capital, and it would not select a contractor.

The construction decision would come back to the same point of decision once detailed design is complete, supported at that stage by the firm price and the completed appraisal in place of the estimate and the structure set out in this document. Should it turn out that the firm price or the appraisal does not support construction, the project would end at the design stage, leaving the site with its effluent characterised and its treatment options priced, information that retains its value either way. The request is accordingly a deliberately narrow one: to approve the stage that turns a proposal into a priced and appraised project, reserving the larger commitment until the evidence on which it should rest actually exists.

A heat-recovery retrofit is projected by the equipment vendor to save 17% of that use, a derived saving of 365 MWh per year at the vendor figure. Capital cost is $455k.
