With these figures established, attention can now be turned to the wall thickness of the absorber, which is a value that several of the subsequent design decisions will ultimately rest upon. Once the corrosion allowance has been added, the absorber wall thickness comes to 21 mm, and it is this figure, rather than the pressure-only thickness, that will govern the quantity of material to be ordered. It should be noted that the corrosion allowance does not contribute to the strength of the wall in any structural sense; rather, it represents a sacrificial provision, put in place in anticipation of the gradual loss of metal that will occur over the operating life of the absorber, so that the wall which remains at the end of that life is still sufficient for the duty imposed upon it. The 21 mm figure therefore embodies an assumption about the corrosiveness of the service, and it follows that any change in that assumption would feed directly through into the thickness itself.

The gasket selection, by way of contrast, has been approached from a considerably narrower standpoint. The two candidate gasket materials have been compared on the basis of temperature limit only, and on this basis the higher-rated of the two materials emerges as the preferred option. It is important to appreciate, however, what such a preference actually amounts to: it is, in essence, a ranking of ratings rather than a demonstration of performance under service conditions. A temperature limit indicates the boundary up to which a material is rated to operate, but it says nothing about how that material behaves as the boundary is approached. Nor does it take any account of the environment in which the gasket will actually function, an environment characterised in part by the $\Delta P$ developed across the absorber and by the suction conditions, expressed in terms of NPSH, that are encountered at the lean solvent pump. Neither of these considerations is touched upon by a comparison that has been conducted purely in terms of temperature limit, and the extent to which the preferred material will perform satisfactorily in practice therefore remains, at this stage, an open question, pending the point at which the actual service temperature at the joint is brought into the comparison alongside the rating itself.

The allowance is sacrificial metal: it is there to be corroded away over the life of the absorber, and the wall remaining at the end of that life is the wall the pressure duty is checked against. The 21 mm figure thus rests on the corrosion assumption behind the allowance, and a change to that assumption changes the thickness by the same amount, with no further calculation in the chain to catch the error.

The gasket comparison is narrower in scope. Two gasket materials are compared on temperature limit only, and the higher-rated material is preferred. A temperature limit is a rating boundary: it states the temperature the material is certified to withstand. It states nothing about the material's behaviour below that boundary, and nothing about the duty the gasket will see in service, where the $\Delta P$ across the absorber and the NPSH at the lean solvent pump are set by the process and not by the gasket. The comparison also omits the service temperature at the joint itself, and it leaves the gasket's other duties untouched: the material must seal at the joint and stay sealed as conditions at the joint change, and a comparison made on temperature limit alone cannot rank the two materials on either count, since neither was examined. The margin between the rating and the temperature the gasket will actually reach is the quantity on which the preference depends, and that margin is not stated anywhere in the comparison. As it stands, the preference for the higher-rated material is a preference between two ratings, formed before the condition that would test the rating has been fixed, and the argument remains open at the point where that condition has to enter it.

fact_base: Pervaporation is a membrane separation in which a liquid feed contacts one side of a membrane and vacuum on the other side draws the permeating component through as vapour. Flux is the mass permeating per unit membrane area per hour (kg m-2 h-1). The separation factor is the water-to-alcohol ratio in the permeate divided by the same ratio in the feed (dimensionless). Feed: 85 wt% n-butanol in water, at 60 °C. One feed composition was tested; no test ran beyond 500 h. Polymer membrane: flux 1.8 kg m-2 h-1, separation factor 240, flux fell 14% over 500 h. Zeolite membrane: flux 1.1 kg m-2 h-1, separation factor 320, flux unchanged over 500 h within measurement error. Flux, selectivity and stability are seldom reported together for the same membrane.
input:
Pervaporation is a membrane separation process in which a liquid feed is brought into contact with one side of a membrane, while a vacuum applied on the other side draws the permeating component through the membrane in the form of a vapour. In order to characterise the performance of the membranes examined in this work, two key indicators are employed throughout. The first of these is the flux, which is defined as the mass of material permeating per unit membrane area per hour (kg m-2 h-1). The second is the separation factor, defined as the water-to-alcohol ratio in the permeate divided by the same ratio in the feed, a quantity which is, accordingly, dimensionless in nature. The experiments were conducted using a feed comprising 85 wt% n-butanol in water at a temperature of 60 °C, and the tests themselves were run for 500 h. It should be noted that only one feed composition was investigated, which inevitably places some limits on the extent to which the findings can be generalised.

As far as the results are concerned, the polymer membrane delivered a flux of 1.8 kg m-2 h-1 in combination with a separation factor of 240, although it is worth mentioning that its flux declined by 14% over the course of 500 h, suggesting a gradual deterioration in performance with time. The zeolite membrane, on the other hand, exhibited a somewhat lower flux of 1.1 kg m-2 h-1, albeit alongside a higher separation factor of 320, and its flux remained essentially unchanged over 500 h, within the bounds of measurement error. Taken together, these results point to an inherent trade-off between throughput and selectivity, with the question of long-term stability adding a further dimension to the comparison. This is particularly significant in light of the fact that flux, selectivity and stability are seldom reported together for one and the same membrane, which makes a combined assessment of this kind a valuable contribution to the field.
target:
Pervaporation is a membrane separation in which a liquid feed contacts one side of a membrane and vacuum on the other side draws the permeating component through as vapour. Performance is stated in two quantities. Flux is the mass permeating per unit membrane area per hour (kg m-2 h-1). The separation factor is the water-to-alcohol ratio in the permeate divided by the same ratio in the feed, and is dimensionless. Both membranes were tested on a feed of 85 wt% n-butanol in water at 60 °C, and each test ran for 500 h.

The polymer membrane gave a flux of 1.8 kg m-2 h-1 and a separation factor of 240, and its flux fell 14% over the 500 h. The zeolite membrane gave a flux of 1.1 kg m-2 h-1 and a separation factor of 320, and its flux was unchanged over the 500 h within measurement error. The polymer membrane therefore leads on flux and trails on separation factor, and it is the only one of the two whose performance moved during the test: the flux advantage that is its reason for selection is the quantity that decayed. The zeolite membrane holds its initial flux at the cost of the lower throughput. A choice between the two rests on whether the duty can accept the lower flux in exchange for the higher separation factor and the stable operation, and that exchange is unfavourable wherever the flux decline continues past the tested duration. Only one feed composition was tested, so the comparison is established at that composition; flux, selectivity and stability are seldom reported together for the same membrane, and the stability contrast recorded here is available only because both membranes were held on test for the full duration.

input: The pump that has been selected for this particular duty is a centrifugal unit, and its role is to move caustic solution between two vessels that are both situated at grade. At the specified duty point, the pump delivers a flow of 48 m3 h-1 against a head of 28 m, and it operates at this point with an efficiency of 71%, which can be regarded as a perfectly respectable figure for a service of this kind. The shaft power that is absorbed at the duty point amounts to some 5.2 kW, and the motor that drives the pump has been rated 15% above this value, so that a comfortable degree of margin is available to accommodate the kinds of variation that inevitably arise in normal operation. It is, moreover, reassuring to note that no evidence of cavitation was observed at any stage during the acceptance test, although it is only fair to point out that the test in question was run for a period of 4 h and, furthermore, that it was carried out at the duty point only. As a consequence, the behaviour of the pump under conditions that depart from the duty point has yet to be demonstrated, and some caution is therefore appropriate when it comes to extrapolating the test results to other operating regimes that the pump may encounter in service.
target: A centrifugal pump moves caustic solution between two vessels at grade. At the duty point the flow is 48 m3 h-1 against a head of 28 m, with a pump efficiency of 71%. Shaft power at the duty point is 5.2 kW, and the motor is rated 15% above this value. Cavitation was not observed in the acceptance test. The acceptance test ran for 4 h and at the duty point only, so its result is a statement about that operating point: the pump ran there without cavitation, at the flow and head the service specifies. The test states nothing about higher flows, where the suction condition tightens, or about sustained operation away from the point at which the efficiency is quoted. The margin the installation carries for duties above the specified point is the difference between the motor rating and the shaft power at the duty point, and any increase in the required flow or head moves the duty point and raises the shaft power against that fixed margin. The figures also fix what the pump costs to run at the specified duty, since the energy drawn in service follows from the shaft power and the hours spent at the point. A service that lives at its duty point is fully described by them. A service that moves around its duty point is described by them only at the point itself, and the acceptance test, confined as it is to that point, cannot be stretched to cover the rest of the operating range.

fact_base: Energy assessment of a dairy plant, in four sections: current use, refrigeration, steam, and recommendation. Electricity use is 1603 MWh per year; refrigeration takes the largest share. A heat-recovery retrofit is projected to save 18% of electricity use, a derived saving of 289 MWh per year, at a capital cost of $268k. At $0.12 per kWh the derived annual saving is $34625 and the derived simple payback is 7.7 years. Steam figures are from one winter month and are flagged as seasonal in the recommendation.
input:
This document presents the findings of an energy assessment that has been carried out at a dairy plant, and its purpose is to build a picture of where energy is used across the site and where the most promising opportunities for improvement may lie. The assessment looks at the plant's energy position from a number of angles, taking in the current pattern of use, the refrigeration load, the steam position, and a set of recommendations that emerge from the analysis. Readers will find that the various threads are drawn together at the end of the document, where a particular measure is identified as offering the most attractive combination of saving and deliverability.

## Current use
In terms of the overall picture, electricity is the dominant energy stream at the plant, and the total electricity use amounts to some 1603 MWh per year, a figure that has been compiled from the plant's billing records over a full twelve-month period. Electricity is consumed right across the site, in production activities, in refrigeration, and in the various site services that support day-to-day operations, and it is an important feature of the profile that consumption does not simply fall away when production stops, since refrigeration and standby loads continue to draw power through idle periods. The baseline figure of 1603 MWh per year is used throughout the assessment as the reference against which potential savings are gauged, and it provides a stable foundation for the analysis. As a general observation, it can be said that measures directed at small or intermittent loads are only ever capable of recovering a limited slice of a total of this size, which is why the assessment focuses its attention primarily on the larger and more continuous loads, where the scope for meaningful savings is correspondingly greater.

## Refrigeration
Turning now to refrigeration, it is this load that accounts for the largest share of the plant's electricity consumption, and it deserves to be examined in some detail. Refrigeration at a dairy plant is essentially a continuous activity: incoming product has to be cooled down, cooled product has to be held at temperature in cold storage, and the refrigeration plant must run more or less around the clock in order to hold those temperatures steady against heat that finds its way in through the building fabric, through doorways that are opened for the movement of product and people, and from the product itself as it is brought down to its storage temperature. One consequence of this continuous character is that refrigeration looms even larger in the plant's consumption during nights, weekends and shutdown periods, when most other loads are switched off. From an energy-saving point of view, this is a significant observation, because a refrigeration plant is continuously rejecting heat at the very same time as other parts of the plant are consuming energy in order to generate heat. The opportunity that arises from this juxtaposition is explored further in the recommendations, but it is already clear at this stage that the sheer size and the unremitting continuity of the refrigeration load make it the single most important load in the plant's energy profile, and the natural starting point for any serious attempt to reduce consumption.

## Steam
The steam position is somewhat less clear-cut than the electricity position, and a degree of caution is needed in interpreting the available figures. Steam is used at the plant for a variety of heating duties, including heating product, maintaining process temperatures, and cleaning, and the figures that were available to the assessment team were drawn from one winter month. It has to be recognised that a winter month cannot be regarded as a representative sample of steam demand across the year as a whole: heating loads are inevitably at their heaviest when ambient temperatures are at their lowest and when incoming materials arrive at their coldest, so figures from such a month will tend to overstate the demand that would be seen in an average month, and it would not be sound to scale them up to an annual figure in any simple way. The assessment has therefore used the steam figures in a more limited fashion, principally to identify the main steam users and to understand the broad shape of demand through the production day. It is also worth bearing in mind that any interaction between heat recovery and duties that are currently served by steam would show itself in the steam balance rather than in the electricity figures, and the assessment has not attempted to quantify effects of that kind.

## Recommendation
Drawing the threads of the analysis together, the assessment's principal recommendation is that the plant should proceed with a heat-recovery retrofit. The retrofit is projected to deliver a saving of 18% of the plant's electricity use, and in absolute terms that 18% corresponds to a saving of 289 MWh per year. The capital cost of the retrofit is estimated at $268k, which is a significant commitment, but when the saving is valued at $0.12 per kWh it is worth some $34625 per year, and on that basis the simple payback on the $268k capital cost works out at 7.7 years. It is acknowledged that a payback of 7.7 years is not a short one, and that the calculation is a simple one which does not take account of maintenance costs or of possible movements in the electricity price; it is also the case that the outcome depends on the recovered heat being used throughout the year, although the continuous nature of the refrigeration load gives good grounds for confidence on that score. The projected saving of 289 MWh per year, valued at $34625 per year, is regarded as a robust central estimate, and the recommendation is accordingly that management approve the retrofit, subject to consumption being metered after installation so that the savings actually achieved can be monitored against those projected.
target:
The assessment recommends the heat-recovery retrofit. The retrofit is projected to save 289 MWh of electricity per year, which is 18% of the plant's current use, at a capital cost of $268k. At current prices the saving is worth $34625 a year, and the simple payback on the capital cost is 7.7 years. Refrigeration is the load the case rests on, and it is the largest single use of electricity at the plant. The steam evidence is thinner than the electricity evidence, and the assessment says so where it matters.

## Current use
Electricity use at the plant is 1603 MWh per year, taken from billing records over a full year. Electricity is the stream the assessment can state with confidence, and it is the stream against which savings are measured. Use is spread across production, refrigeration and site services, and it does not fall to zero when production stops: refrigeration and standby loads run through idle periods, and a share of the annual total is therefore independent of output. This pattern governs what a saving measure can reach. A measure acting on a small or intermittent load can only ever recover that load's share of the total, while a measure acting on a continuous load recovers value in every week of the year. The assessment accordingly concentrates on the largest loads and on measures that act across them. The billed total is taken as recorded; it is not re-measured, and the uncertainty in the assessment sits in the projected savings rather than in the baseline they are measured against. Every figure that follows is stated against this baseline, and the recommendation at the end returns to it.

## Refrigeration
Refrigeration takes the largest share of electricity use at the plant. The load is continuous in character. Product arrives warm and is cooled; cooled product is then held at temperature in cold storage; and the refrigeration plant runs throughout to hold those temperatures against heat entering through the building fabric, through doors opened for the movement of product and people, and from the product itself while it is being brought down to temperature. Because the load never fully stops, refrigeration accounts for a larger share of annual consumption than of peak demand, and it dominates consumption during nights, weekends and shutdowns, when most other loads are off. This is the load on which the retrofit case rests. A refrigeration plant rejects heat continuously, and it rejects that heat at the same time as other parts of the plant are consuming energy to produce heat. Heat recovery takes part of the rejected heat and returns it to a duty the plant currently serves from a purchased stream. The match is structural rather than incidental: the source runs all year, and a use for recovered heat that also runs all year is what converts a rejection stream into a saving. The projected saving is stated against electricity use as a whole rather than against the refrigeration load alone, because the retrofit's effect is measured at the meter; but it is the size and continuity of the refrigeration load that make a saving of that order available at all.

## Steam
Steam serves the heating duties of the plant: heating product, holding process temperatures, and cleaning. The steam figures available to the assessment are drawn from one winter month, and they are the weakest figures in it. A winter month is not a representative sample of steam demand. Heating loads are at their heaviest when ambient temperatures are at their lowest and when incoming product and water arrive coldest, so a steam figure from that month overstates the demand of an average month and cannot be carried across the year by simple scaling. The assessment uses the steam figures only for what they can support: the identification of the principal steam users and the shape of demand across a production day. No saving is computed from them. Where heat recovery touches a duty currently served by steam, the effect falls on the steam balance; it is not counted in the electricity saving on which the recommendation is based, and it is treated here as unquantified. A steam record covering a full year would be required before the steam side of the case could be stated to the same standard as the electricity side, and obtaining that record is a measurement task, not a modelling one.

## Recommendation
Plant management is recommended to approve the heat-recovery retrofit at a capital cost of $268k. The retrofit is projected to save 18% of electricity use, which is a saving of 289 MWh per year against current use of 1603 MWh per year. At $0.12 per kWh the saving is worth $34625 per year, and the simple payback on the capital cost is 7.7 years. The payback is stated before maintenance costs and before any movement in the electricity price, and it lengthens if the recovered heat displaces less electricity than projected. The condition on which the projection rests is continuity of use: the recovered heat must be taken up throughout the year, and the refrigeration load, which runs in every week, is what provides that take-up. The steam figures play no part in the saving figure, and because they come from a single winter month and are seasonal, the recommendation does not depend on them; a decision taken on the electricity figures alone is a decision taken on the sound part of the evidence. Approval should carry one condition: electricity use after installation is to be metered on the same basis as the baseline, so that the saving projected here can be checked against the saving the plant actually records.

At $0.12 per kWh the derived annual saving is $56582 and the derived simple payback is 6.8 years. Steam figures are from one winter month and are flagged as seasonal in the recommendation.
input:
This energy assessment has been prepared in order to develop a comprehensive understanding of the way in which energy is used across a dairy plant, and to identify, from among the various opportunities that present themselves, the measure that offers the most compelling case for investment. The document is organised so as to move from the general to the particular: it begins with the current pattern of energy use across the site as a whole, goes on to examine the refrigeration load and the steam position in turn, and only then draws the threads together in a set of recommendations. It is in that final part of the document that the assessment's central proposal is set out, together with the figures on which it rests, and readers who are pressed for time may wish to turn to those pages first, although the reasoning that supports the proposal is developed in the sections that precede it.

## Current use
Electricity is the principal energy stream at the plant, and total electricity use amounts to 3368 MWh per year, a figure that has been assembled from the plant's billing records covering a full twelve months. The pattern that lies behind that total is a mixed one. On the one hand, there are the loads that are tied to production, which start and stop with the working day and fall away in the plant's quieter periods; on the other hand, there are loads, refrigeration foremost among them, together with standby and site services, which pay no attention to the production schedule at all and continue to draw power through nights, weekends and shutdowns. The total of 3368 MWh per year is used throughout this assessment as the baseline against which any potential saving is assessed, and it is worth emphasising that it is a full-year figure, since production itself varies over the course of the year and an average month, scaled up, would not provide a sound basis for comparison. It follows from the mixed character of the load that measures which operate only while production is running are inherently capable of less, over the course of a year, than measures which act upon the loads that run continuously, and this consideration has shaped the assessment's priorities from the outset, directing attention towards the largest loads and towards those which are present in every week of the year.

## Refrigeration
Refrigeration is the largest single consumer of electricity at the plant, and understanding its character is essential to understanding the plant's energy position as a whole. The load arises in the first instance from the product itself: incoming product arrives above its storage temperature and has to be cooled down, and once it has been cooled it has to be held at temperature in cold storage for as long as it remains on site. Holding product at temperature is not a passive state but a continuous duty, because heat is constantly finding its way into the cold spaces, through the fabric of the building, through doorways each time product or people pass through them, and in the air that is exchanged at every opening. The refrigeration plant works against that ingress without pause, and it also serves chilled duties within the process itself. During the plant's idle periods, when production loads have stopped, the holding duty remains, and it is this duty, accumulated hour by hour across the whole year, that makes refrigeration the dominant load. There is a further point of considerable significance. Refrigeration is, in essence, the removal of heat, and the heat that is removed, together with the energy consumed in removing it, is rejected at the condensers. At the very same time, other parts of the plant are purchasing energy in order to produce heat for process and cleaning duties. The plant is therefore paying, simultaneously and continuously, to take heat out in one place and to put heat in in another, and it is this juxtaposition that the assessment's principal recommendation seeks to address.

## Steam
The steam position at the plant is a good deal less firmly established than the electricity position, and the figures that relate to it need to be handled with a certain amount of care. Steam is used for the plant's heating duties, which include bringing product up to process temperatures, providing hot water for cleaning operations, and holding temperatures where the process requires them to be held. The figures that were made available to the assessment were drawn from a single winter month, and it is important to appreciate the limitations that attach to figures of that provenance. In a winter month, ambient temperatures are at their lowest, so losses from the building and from ventilation are at their greatest; incoming product and water arrive at their coldest, so the heating duty attaching to each unit of throughput is at its highest; and even the water used for cleaning has further to be heated. All of these effects operate in the same direction, and the combined result is that a winter month's steam consumption is bound to overstate the consumption of an average month, to an extent that cannot be quantified from one month of data alone. The figures have accordingly been used in a restrained way, to identify the principal steam users and to give a sense of the shape of demand through a production day, and no attempt has been made to annualise them or to build savings calculations upon them. It should also be noted that, insofar as heat recovery might displace steam in any particular duty, that effect, while real enough, has not been quantified in this assessment and forms no part of the case that is set out below.

## Recommendation
In the light of the analysis set out above, the assessment recommends that the plant should proceed with a heat-recovery retrofit, and the figures on which that recommendation rests are as follows. The capital cost of the retrofit is estimated at $382k. The retrofit is projected to save 14% of the plant's electricity use, and, in absolute terms, that 14% equates to a saving of 472 MWh per year. When that saving is valued at $0.12 per kWh, it is worth $56582 per year, and the simple payback on the capital cost of $382k is therefore 6.8 years. A payback of 6.8 years is not, it must be said, a particularly rapid return, and the calculation is a simple one, which takes no account of maintenance costs or of possible future movements in the electricity price; moreover, the projected saving of 472 MWh per year, worth $56582 per year, is dependent upon the recovered heat being taken up throughout the year, although the continuous character of the refrigeration load, which is present in every week of the year, provides a sound physical basis for expecting that it will be. The recommendation is accordingly that management approve the retrofit, and it is further recommended that electricity consumption be metered following installation, on the same basis as the baseline, so that the savings that are actually achieved can be monitored against the annual saving that has been projected.

Ambient temperatures are at their lowest, so fabric and ventilation losses are at their largest; incoming product and water arrive at their coldest, so the heating duty per unit of throughput is at its largest; and cleaning water is heated from a colder start. Every one of those effects inflates a winter figure relative to an average month, and they all act in the same direction. A winter month's steam consumption therefore cannot be annualised: multiplied up, it would overstate the year's steam demand by an amount the assessment cannot bound from a single month of data. The figures are used for the limited purposes they can serve. They identify the principal steam users, they show the shape of demand across a production day, and they establish that steam is a material stream in the plant's energy position. They quantify nothing beyond the month they were measured in, and no saving in this assessment is computed from them. If heat recovery displaces steam in any duty, that displacement is a real effect and an unquantified one; it is additional to the electricity saving on which the recommendation is based, and it is not counted in it. A full year of steam records, kept on the same basis as the electricity records, is what a quantified steam case would require.

## Recommendation
Plant management is recommended to approve the heat-recovery retrofit at a capital cost of $382k. The retrofit is projected to save 14% of electricity use, a saving of 472 MWh per year against current use of 3368 MWh per year. At $0.12 per kWh, that saving is worth $56582 per year, giving a simple payback of 6.8 years on the capital cost. The figures are stated on the electricity side of the plant's energy position only. The payback takes no account of maintenance costs on the installed equipment and no account of movement in the electricity price in either direction; it lengthens if the recovered heat is taken up for fewer hours than projected, and the take-up is the assumption the outcome depends on. The physical basis for expecting the take-up is the refrigeration load: it runs in every week of the year, so the heat is there to be recovered in every week of the year, and a use matched to it is supplied on the same schedule. The steam position does not enter the case. The steam figures come from one winter month and are seasonal, and the recommendation has been constructed so that nothing in it needs them: the saving is an electricity saving, computed from billed electricity and a stated price. Approval should carry two conditions, both of them cheap. Electricity use after installation is to be metered on the same basis as the baseline, so that the projected saving can be checked against the recorded saving. And steam use is to be recorded for a full year, so that the steam side of the plant's position, at present the unquantified side, can be stated on evidence if the case is revisited.

fact_base: A centrifugal pump moves water between two vessels at grade. At the duty point the flow is 26 m3 h-1 against a head of 64 m, with pump efficiency 80%. Shaft power at the duty point is 5.7 kW. The motor is rated 15% above this value. Cavitation was not observed in the acceptance test, which ran for 4 h at the duty point only.
input: In this section, the performance of the centrifugal pump that has been installed to transfer water between two vessels located at grade is described in some detail. Operating at its designated duty point, the pump provides a flow of 26 m3 h-1 against a total head of 64 m, and the efficiency achieved at this point is 80%, which represents a strong performance for a machine of this type. The shaft power absorbed by the pump at the duty point has been determined as 5.7 kW, and in order to ensure reliable operation under a range of conditions, the driving motor has been rated 15% above this figure, thereby providing a useful safety margin. During the course of the acceptance testing, no cavitation whatsoever was detected, which is an encouraging outcome; nevertheless, it is important to keep in mind that the acceptance test was conducted over a period of 4 h and exclusively at the duty point itself. This means that, while the pump has clearly demonstrated its ability to meet the specified duty under the tested conditions, its behaviour across the wider operating envelope, including part-load and overload conditions, remains to be established, and further testing may well be advisable in due course in order to confirm performance under those circumstances as well. None of this detracts from the fact that the specified duty itself has been met and demonstrated in a satisfactory manner, and the figures that have been obtained provide a firm and useful reference point against which the results of any future testing programme can be compared in the months and years ahead.
target: A centrifugal pump moves water between two vessels at grade. At the duty point the flow is 26 m3 h-1 against a head of 64 m, with a pump efficiency of 80%. Shaft power at the duty point is 5.7 kW, and the motor is rated 15% above this value. No cavitation was detected in the acceptance test, which ran for 4 h at the duty point only. The result therefore covers one operating point. At that point the pump delivered the specified flow and head without cavitation, and the efficiency and shaft power are the values the energy consumption of the service follows from. Away from that point the record is empty: neither the flow at which cavitation begins nor the efficiency at part load has been measured, and the acceptance test cannot be read as evidence for either. For the point it ran at, the test record is complete: flow, head, efficiency, shaft power and the absence of cavitation are all stated there. The gap in the record is not a defect of the test but a boundary on its use, and the boundary lies exactly at the edge of the duty point. What the test does fix is the duty against which the motor was sized. The rating stands above the shaft power at the specified point by that margin, so a duty revised upward consumes the margin first, and a duty revised beyond it exceeds the motor. The pump is demonstrated at the specified duty and untested elsewhere, and any future change to the required flow or head is a change to the one point for which evidence exists. Any statement about the pump's behaviour elsewhere in its range will need its own test, run at the condition it describes.

fact_base: A viscous liquid of viscosity $\mu$ = 0.05 Pa s flows laminarly through a tube of radius $R$ = 6 mm and length $L$ = 21 m. At a pressure drop $\Delta P$ of 20 kPa the volumetric flow $Q$ is 34.9 L h-1. The Hagen-Poiseuille equation assumes laminar, fully developed flow of a Newtonian liquid.
input:
In this worked example, we will determine the volumetric flow rate of a viscous liquid flowing laminarly through a tube, making use of the well-known Hagen-Poiseuille equation. The liquid in question has a viscosity $\mu$ of 0.05 Pa s, and it flows through a tube having a radius $R$ of 6 mm and a length $L$ of 21 m. The pressure drop $\Delta P$ that drives the flow amounts to 20 kPa. The Hagen-Poiseuille equation, which relates the volumetric flow $Q$ to precisely these quantities, is written as follows:

$$Q = \frac{\pi R^4 \Delta P}{8 \mu L}$$

It is important to note that this elegant equation rests upon a number of underlying assumptions: it assumes that the flow is laminar in character, that it is fully developed along the length of the tube, and that the liquid in question behaves as a Newtonian fluid. When the values set out above are substituted into the equation, the volumetric flow $Q$ comes out at 34.9 L h-1. This result should, of course, be interpreted in the light of the assumptions that have just been mentioned, since any departure from the laminar regime, or any non-Newtonian behaviour on the part of the liquid, would mean that the relationship embodied in the equation no longer provides a dependable description of the flow, and an alternative approach would then have to be sought.
target:
The task is to determine the volumetric flow of a viscous liquid in laminar flow through a tube. The liquid has a viscosity $\mu$ of 0.05 Pa s; the tube has a radius $R$ of 6 mm and a length $L$ of 21 m; the pressure drop $\Delta P$ along the tube is 20 kPa. The flow is taken as laminar and fully developed, and the liquid as Newtonian. Under those conditions the Hagen-Poiseuille equation holds for the flow and gives the volumetric flow $Q$ from the radius, the pressure drop, the viscosity and the length by

$$Q = \frac{\pi R^4 \Delta P}{8 \mu L}$$

Substitution of the stated values in the equation gives $Q$ as 34.9 L h-1. The check on the result is the regime: the value is the flow that the stated pressure drop maintains while the flow stays laminar and fully developed in a Newtonian liquid. A flow outside the laminar regime is outside the equation, and the equation states no value for it; the result therefore stands or falls with the regime, not with the arithmetic, which the stated values fix completely. The stated values are also the whole of the data the example uses — the geometry of the tube, the property of the liquid and the driving pressure drop — and no other quantity is needed by the relation or admitted into the result.

fact_base: A single-stage compressor raises air from 1 bar to 4 bar. Inlet temperature is 293 K. For isentropic compression with a heat-capacity ratio of 1.4, the discharge temperature is 435 K. The isentropic estimate excludes mechanical losses; the installed machine's measured discharge temperature is higher.
input:
A single-stage compressor raises air from 1 bar to 4 bar, and the discharge temperature is required. The inlet temperature is 293 K. The compression is treated as isentropic, with a heat-capacity ratio of 1.4, and on that basis the discharge temperature is 435 K.

Isentropic compression is compression with no heat transfer between the gas and its surroundings and no irreversibility within the gas. The discharge temperature from the isentropic relation is therefore the temperature the pressure rise alone fixes, given the inlet temperature and the heat-capacity ratio. The calculation takes the two pressures, the inlet temperature and the ratio as its whole input: no property of the machine enters it, and no measured quantity is used. The heat-capacity ratio is likewise taken as a single stated value for the gas across the compression, which is the form in which the relation uses it.

The isentropic estimate excludes mechanical losses. The installed machine's measured discharge temperature is higher than 435 K. The two figures answer different questions. The estimate states the discharge temperature of a compression carried out without loss; the measurement states the discharge temperature the machine reaches, with the losses the estimate excludes present in it. The estimate is the figure the pressure rise requires, and the measurement is the check against it: the gap between them is the size of everything the idealisation leaves out, stated in the unit the design works in. For design use, the figure to carry forward is the measured one; the estimate's role is to show what part of that figure the pressure rise by itself accounts for.

fact_base: Adsorption of a dye from water on a metal-organic framework was measured in batch tests at 298 K. The fitted Langmuir capacity was 239 mg of dye per gram of adsorbent at pH 6. At an adsorbent dose of 0.8 g L-1, removal after 120 min was 87% of the initial dye concentration of 50 mg L-1. The Langmuir fit is reported for pH 6 only; capacity at other pH values was not measured.
input: The adsorption of a dye from water onto a metal-organic framework was investigated by means of a series of batch tests carried out at 298 K. The experimental data were fitted to the Langmuir model, and the fitted Langmuir capacity was found to be 239 mg of dye per gram of adsorbent at pH 6, which represents a substantial uptake. In a further set of experiments, an adsorbent dose of 0.8 g L-1 succeeded in removing, after a contact time of 120 min, some 87% of the initial dye concentration of 50 mg L-1. These results are certainly encouraging as far as the removal of the dye is concerned. It should nevertheless be borne in mind that the Langmuir fit has been reported for pH 6 only, and that the capacity of the material at other pH values was not measured during the course of this work, so that any statements about performance under conditions of different acidity would, at this stage, be speculative. Further investigations would accordingly be needed before the behaviour of the adsorbent across the wider pH range could be characterised with confidence, and the conclusions of the present work should be read with that reservation firmly in mind.
target: Adsorption of a dye from water on a metal-organic framework was measured in batch tests at 298 K. The fitted Langmuir capacity was 239 mg of dye per gram of adsorbent at pH 6. At an adsorbent dose of 0.8 g L-1, removal after 120 min was 87% of the initial dye concentration of 50 mg L-1. The capacity figure and the removal figure describe different things: the capacity is a property of the fitted isotherm at the stated pH, and the removal is the outcome at one dose, one contact time and one initial concentration. A higher dose or a longer contact time would change the removal without changing the capacity, and the two figures cannot be substituted for each other. Both figures were obtained in the setting the batch test fixes: a closed vessel, a stated temperature, and contact between the adsorbent and the solution for the stated time. Nothing in the results addresses flow through a bed, regeneration of the material after use, or competition from other solutes present in a real effluent, and the figures should not be read across to those settings. The Langmuir fit is reported for pH 6 only; capacity at other pH values was not measured. The results therefore establish the material's performance at the stated pH and under the stated test conditions, and they are silent on the pH dependence that a treatment application would need.

fact_base: Goal: compute the diffusive flux of oxygen through a stagnant water film. The diffusive flux J (mol m-2 s-1) is computed from the diffusivity D (m2 s-1) and the concentration gradient dC/dx, where C is concentration (mol m-3) and x is position (m). Fick's first law: J = -D dC/dx; the negative sign states that diffusion runs from high concentration to low concentration. Oxygen in water: D = 2.1 x 10-9 m2 s-1. Concentration falls by 0.4 mol m-3 across a film 0.5 mm thick, so dC/dx = -800 mol m-4. Worked result: J = 1.68x 10-6 mol m-2 s-1. The law as stated covers a stagnant medium; a moving medium adds convection, which the equation does not include.
input: Welcome to this tutorial, in which we are going to work through a complete example of how to compute the diffusive flux of oxygen through a stagnant water film, step by step. Let us begin by getting clear about the quantities that are involved. The diffusive flux, denoted J (mol m-2 s-1), is computed from the diffusivity D (m2 s-1) together with the concentration gradient dC/dx, where C is the concentration (mol m-3) and x is the position (m). The governing relationship is Fick's first law, which takes the form J = -D dC/dx, and it is worth pausing to appreciate the negative sign, which tells us something physically meaningful: diffusion always runs from regions of high concentration towards regions of low concentration. For oxygen in water, the diffusivity D takes the value 2.1 x 10-9 m2 s-1. In our example, the concentration falls by 0.4 mol m-3 across a film which is 0.5 mm thick, and so the concentration gradient works out as dC/dx = -800 mol m-4. It is also worth noting how the sign of the gradient and the sign of the flux are connected to one another, because this is a point on which students frequently stumble when they first meet the law in this form. Putting all of this together and carrying out the multiplication, the worked result is J = 1.68 x 10-6 mol m-2 s-1. One final point deserves emphasis: the law in the form stated here covers a stagnant medium only, and if the medium were moving, convection would enter the picture as well, something which the equation as written does not include.
target: The goal is to compute the diffusive flux of oxygen through a stagnant water film. The result is J = 1.68 x 10-6 mol m-2 s-1, and the steps below show where it comes from. The diffusive flux J (mol m-2 s-1) is computed from the diffusivity D (m2 s-1) and the concentration gradient dC/dx, where C is concentration (mol m-3) and x is position (m). Fick's first law, J = -D dC/dx, relates the three; the negative sign states that diffusion runs from high concentration to low concentration. For oxygen in water, D = 2.1 x 10-9 m2 s-1. The concentration falls by 0.4 mol m-3 across a film 0.5 mm thick, so the gradient is dC/dx = -800 mol m-4: the fall is divided by the film thickness, and the sign records that concentration decreases as x increases. The gradient is the steepest quantity in the example: the concentration change itself is modest, but it is compressed into a film half a millimetre thick, and division by that thickness is what produces a gradient of this size. The flux inherits that size through the diffusivity, which for a solute in a liquid is small, and the two effects — a large gradient and a small diffusivity — are the whole content of the multiplication. Substitution of the diffusivity and the gradient in Fick's first law gives the flux stated at the head of this example, and the sign of the gradient carries through to the direction of the flux. The result is a flux per unit area of film, and the total transfer across any area of film follows from it by multiplication by that area. Fick's first law holds for a stagnant medium; a moving medium adds convection, which the equation does not include, so the computed flux is the diffusive contribution alone.

fact_base: A tutorial passage explains absolute and relative error through a flow measurement. Worked figures: reading 359 units, tolerance 0.5% of reading, so the absolute error is 1.79 units. The passage distinguishes error from uncertainty and does not merge the two terms.
input: Have you ever wondered how far out a measurement that you read off an instrument might actually be? In this short tutorial, we are going to explore the ideas of absolute error and relative error, and we will do so through a simple flow measurement that makes the distinction nice and concrete. Suppose your flowmeter gives you a reading of 359 units. Every instrument comes with a tolerance, and in this case the tolerance is 0.5% of the reading. What that means in practice is that the absolute error attached to your measurement is 1.79 units: in other words, the true value could sit above or below the figure shown on the display by up to that amount. The relative error, by contrast, expresses the very same tolerance as a fraction of the reading you have taken, which is precisely why it ends up being quoted as a percentage. It is very tempting to use the word uncertainty in exactly the same breath, but it is important to be careful here, because error and uncertainty are not the same thing at all. The error is the difference between the reading and the true value, whereas the uncertainty is the range within which the true value can reasonably be expected to lie, and muddling the two of them up is a surprisingly common source of confusion in practice.
target:
Absolute error and relative error describe the same instrument tolerance in different units, and a flow measurement shows the distinction. A reading of 359 units carries a tolerance of 0.5% of reading. The absolute error is 1.79 units: the difference between the reading and the true value, expressed in the units of the measurement itself. The relative error is that difference divided by the reading, and is dimensionless; stated as a percentage, it is the tolerance in the form in which instrument specifications usually quote it. The two forms convert into each other through the reading, and neither contains information the other lacks.

Error and uncertainty are separate terms and are not interchangeable. Error belongs to a single measurement: it is the difference between the measured value and the true value, and because the true value is not known exactly, the error of a given reading is bounded by the tolerance rather than known outright. Uncertainty belongs to the result as reported: it is the interval, assembled from the tolerance and from every other contribution the measurement carries, within which the true value is asserted to lie. A report that states an error where an uncertainty is meant overstates what the instrument establishes, and a report that merges the two terms leaves the reader unable to tell what has been bounded and what has merely been estimated.

fact_base: A defect-reduction project on a packing line cut the reject rate from 3.8% to 2.3% over one quarter. At 304k units per year the change avoids about 4560 rejected units per year. The quarter included a planned shutdown; rates are not adjusted for it.
input: A defect-reduction project that has recently been carried out on a packing line has delivered a meaningful improvement in the line's quality performance over the course of one quarter. The reject rate, which previously stood at 3.8%, has been brought down to 2.3%, corresponding to a reduction of 1.5 percentage points. When this improvement is set against the line's output of 304k units per year, it can be seen that the change avoids approximately 4560 rejected units each year, which represents a considerable saving in wasted product and in rework. It is worth noting, in the interests of balance, that the quarter in question did include a planned shutdown of the line, and that the rates reported here have not been adjusted in order to take that shutdown into account. This caveat does not detract from the progress that has been achieved; it does, however, mean that the full picture will only become clear once a further quarter of operation, unaffected by any shutdown, has been completed, at which point the figures can be compared on a truly like-for-like basis and the improvement confirmed as a lasting one. The project team is to be commended for the progress that has been recorded here, and the position will be reviewed once again when the figures for the further quarter are available for consideration.
target: The packing line cut its reject rate from 3.8% to 2.3% over one quarter, a reduction of 1.5 percentage points. At 304k units per year, the change avoids about 4560 rejected units per year. The figures are the project's own comparison: the rate recorded before the project and the rate recorded after it, on the same line, with the avoided units computed at the current annual volume. The avoided units follow from the rate difference at that volume, and they are the whole of the benefit the project is credited with; effects on cost, on rework labour and on output are outside this comparison and are not claimed here. One qualification stands on the rates themselves. The quarter in which the new rate was recorded included a planned shutdown, and the rates are not adjusted for it. A shutdown quarter is not a typical quarter: the line stops and restarts, and the running periods either side of the stop carry a different mix of work from a full quarter's running. The recorded reduction is therefore the reduction of that quarter, and a further quarter without a shutdown is the evidence that would show whether the new rate holds in ordinary operation. Until that evidence exists, the avoided-units figure carries the same qualification as the rate difference it is computed from. The project is therefore credited with a real but provisionally evidenced improvement, and the credit stands to be confirmed or revised by the rates of the quarter that follows.

fact_base: The rate constant k (s-1) of a first-order liquid-phase reaction was measured at two temperatures. At 300 K, k = 0.071 s-1. At 340 K, k = 2.683 s-1, computed from the Arrhenius relation with activation energy 77 kJ mol-1 as a derived value. Each temperature was measured in triplicate; the relative standard deviation of k was 4%. Above 340 K the solvent evaporated during sampling, so no rate constant is reported above 340 K.
input: In this study, the rate constant of a first-order liquid-phase reaction was investigated at two temperatures in order to gain a better understanding of how the reaction rate responds to temperature. It is worth noting that the reaction is first order, which means that a single rate constant k, expressed in s-1, describes the rate at any given temperature. At 300 K, the rate constant k was measured as 0.071 s-1, whereas at 340 K, k was found to be 2.683 s-1, representing a substantial increase over the range studied. Importantly, the value at 340 K was not measured directly; instead, it was computed from the Arrhenius relation using an activation energy of 77 kJ mol-1, and it is therefore reported as a derived value. The activation energy of 77 kJ mol-1 plays a key role in this computation and underpins the derived figure. Each temperature was measured in triplicate in order to ensure reliability, and the relative standard deviation of k was 4%, highlighting the consistency and reproducibility of the measurements. Overall, between 300 K and 340 K, k rises from 0.071 s-1 to 2.683 s-1. It should also be noted that no rate constant is reported above 340 K, because above 340 K the solvent evaporated during sampling, which made it impossible to collect samples without significant solvent loss. The relative standard deviation of 4% was obtained from the triplicate measurements spanning 300 K to the upper end of the range. In summary, the reported results comprise a measured rate constant at 300 K, a derived rate constant at 340 K, and a relative standard deviation of 4%, painting a comprehensive picture of the reaction kinetics across the accessible temperature range.
target: Rate constants for a first-order liquid-phase reaction were measured at two temperatures, 300 K and 340 K. The reaction is first order, so at a fixed temperature a single rate constant k, with units of s-1, sets the rate. At 300 K, k was 0.071 s-1. At 340 K, k was 2.683 s-1. The upper value was not measured directly; it was computed from the Arrhenius relation with an activation energy of 77 kJ mol-1, and it is reported here as a derived value. The activation energy of 77 kJ mol-1 enters the reported results only through that computation. Each temperature was measured in triplicate. The relative standard deviation of k was 4%. The triplicate measurements at the two temperatures carry that relative standard deviation of 4% in k. Between 300 K and 340 K, k rises from 0.071 s-1 to 2.683 s-1. The two temperatures are the only temperatures at which k is reported. No rate constant is reported above 340 K. Above 340 K the solvent evaporated during sampling, and sampling loss set the upper end of the range. A value at any higher temperature would require sampling that the solvent loss prevents. The reported results are accordingly a measured rate constant at 300 K, a derived rate constant at 340 K, and a relative standard deviation of 4%, with no value above the upper temperature because the solvent evaporated during sampling.

fact_base: Goal: compute the half-life of a first-order reaction and the fraction remaining after 60 min. For a first-order reaction the rate constant k (min-1) fixes the half-life t1/2 (min) by t1/2 = ln(2) / k, and the fraction remaining after time t (min) is exp(-k t). Measured rate constant: k = 0.012 min-1 at 323 K, from concentration measurements every 5 min over 90 min. Worked results: t1/2 = 57.8 min; the fraction remaining after 60 min is 0.49 (dimensionless), both computed from the stated relations. The relations hold for a first-order reaction only; a reaction of another order follows a different decay law.
input:
Let's work through a classic first-order kinetics problem step by step. The goal here is to compute the half-life of a first-order reaction and to determine the fraction remaining after 60 min. The answers, which we will derive below, are a half-life of 57.8 min and a fraction remaining of 0.49 after 60 min.

First, it is important to note the two key relationships. For a first-order reaction, the rate constant k (min-1) fixes the half-life t1/2 (min) through the relation t1/2 = ln(2) / k, while the fraction remaining after a time t (min) is given by exp(-k t). It is worth emphasising that these relations hold for a first-order reaction only, since a reaction of another order follows a completely different decay law. The half-life is the time that the concentration takes to fall to one half of its starting value, and the fraction remaining is simply the concentration at time t divided by the starting concentration.

In this example, the measured rate constant is k = 0.012 min-1 at 323 K, obtained from concentration measurements taken every 5 min over a period of 90 min. It is interesting to note that these measurements cover a period of 90 min, which is longer than the half-life that the calculation will return, so the data set extends beyond one half-life.

Substituting into the half-life relation, we obtain t1/2 = ln(2) / 0.012, and since ln(2) = 0.693, this gives t1/2 = 0.693 / 0.012 = 57.8 min. Next, for the fraction remaining after 60 min, the exponent is -k t = -(0.012)(60) = -0.72, so the fraction remaining works out to exp(-0.72) = 0.49.

Finally, a quick sanity check confirms the result: because 60 min is slightly longer than the half-life of 57.8 min, the fraction remaining of 0.49 sits just below one half, exactly as one would expect just past one half-life. In summary, both results rest on the single measured rate constant, k = 0.012 min-1 at 323 K.
target:

Both relations hold for a first-order reaction only; a reaction of another order follows a different decay law. The half-life is the time the concentration takes to fall to one half of its starting value, and the fraction remaining is the concentration at time t divided by the starting concentration.

The rate constant comes from concentration measurements taken every 5 min over 90 min. The measurements cover 90 min, longer than the half-life the calculation returns, so the data set extends past one half-life.

Substitution in the half-life relation gives t1/2 = ln(2) / 0.012. With ln(2) = 0.693, t1/2 = 0.693 / 0.012 = 57.8 min. For the fraction remaining after 60 min, the exponent is -k t = -(0.012)(60) = -0.72, and exp(-0.72) = 0.49.

The check is internal: 60 min is slightly longer than the half-life of 57.8 min, so the fraction remaining, 0.49, sits just below one half, as it should just past one half-life. Both results rest on the single measured rate constant, k = 0.012 min-1 at 323 K. The example closes on its own data: the measured rate constant, the two relations, and the comparison between the time asked for and the half-life.

fact_base: Excerpt content: the analogy between the transfer processes is stated, then qualified by the case where it fails. The excerpt works one short numerical check with numbers given inside the excerpt itself. The excerpt assumes the chapter's earlier definitions and adds none.
input:
The Chilton-Colburn analogy provides an elegant and widely used link between momentum transfer and mass transfer, setting the mass-transfer factor $j_D$ equal to one half of the friction factor, in the form $j_D$ = $f/2$, for the same geometry and the same flow conditions. In other words, the analogy effectively allows a friction measurement to stand in for a mass-transfer coefficient, so that one transport quantity can be read directly from the other, which is a considerable practical convenience. A brief numerical check illustrates the arithmetic involved: at $f$ = 0.046, the analogy gives $j_D$ = 0.046 / 2 = 0.023. It should be noted that no measurement enters into this step, and the value of 0.023 is simply the friction result restated in mass-transfer form.

However, it is important to recognise that the analogy holds only where the resistance to momentum transfer and the resistance to mass transfer are located in the same place. It breaks down where part of the friction arises from form drag, since a rough surface, or a body that sheds a wake, expends momentum on pressure forces that have no direct counterpart in mass transfer. In such cases, the measured $f$ overstates the portion of the resistance that the analogy is able to use, and $j_D$ consequently falls below $f/2$, with the shortfall growing as the share of form drag in $f$ increases.
target:
The Chilton-Colburn analogy sets the mass-transfer factor $j_D$ equal to half the friction factor, $j_D$ = $f/2$, for the same geometry and flow. Stated in that form, the analogy lets a friction measurement stand in for a mass-transfer coefficient: one transport quantity is read from the other. A short check shows the arithmetic the analogy asks for. At $f$ = 0.046, the analogy gives $j_D$ = 0.046 / 2 = 0.023. No measurement enters that step; the value 0.023 is the friction result restated in mass-transfer form.

The analogy holds where the resistance to momentum transfer and the resistance to mass transfer sit in the same place. It fails where part of the friction comes from form drag. A rough surface, or a body that sheds a wake, spends momentum on pressure forces that have no counterpart in mass transfer, and the measured $f$ then overstates the part of the resistance the analogy can use. In that case $j_D$ falls below $f/2$, and the shortfall grows with the share of form drag in $f$. For such surfaces the measured $f$ cannot be halved into a mass-transfer factor, because part of $f$ was never a transfer resistance at all.
