fact_base: A contract packaging firm runs 2 plants; revenue is $76 million per year. Evidence base: order records for 12 months, 11368 orders. On-time delivery over the last two quarters was 88%, against a target of 95%. Overtime cost was $1.7 million last year, up 19% on the year before. The order backlog stands at 3.7 weeks, against 1.6 weeks a year ago. Plant 2 accounts for 60% of late orders. A scheduling system for all plants is quoted at $275k; Plant 2 alone is $137k. An internal estimate (not a vendor figure) puts the overtime reduction at Plant 2 at 15-20% in the first year. The recommendation under consideration: install at Plant 2 first, hold the other plants until Plant 2 results are reported. The operations director owns the scheduling programme.
input:
This executive summary provides an overview of delivery performance at a contract packaging firm that operates 2 plants and generates revenue of $76 million per year. The analysis is based on a comprehensive review of order records covering a period of 12 months and encompassing no fewer than 11368 orders, providing a robust evidence base for the findings that follow.

Over the last two quarters, on-time delivery stood at 88%, falling short of the target of 95%. Overtime cost reached $1.7 million last year, an increase of 19% compared with the year before, while the order backlog currently stands at 3.7 weeks, compared with just 1.6 weeks a year ago, highlighting a deteriorating operational picture. A closer look at the data reveals that Plant 2 accounts for 60% of all late orders, suggesting that the delivery challenge is concentrated rather than spread evenly across the business.

A scheduling system for all plants has been quoted at $275k, while Plant 2 alone would cost $137k. The figure for the first stage is $137k, the quoted cost for Plant 2 alone. That $137k tests the programme where 60% of late orders arise. An internal estimate, rather than a vendor figure, suggests that the overtime reduction at Plant 2 could be in the region of 15-20% in the first year. Against this backdrop, the recommendation under consideration is to install the system at Plant 2 first and to hold the other plants until the results from Plant 2 have been reported. The operations director owns the scheduling programme and would oversee the rollout.
target:
The recommendation under consideration is to install the scheduling system at Plant 2 first, at $137k, and to hold the other plants until Plant 2 results are reported. The operations director owns the scheduling programme. The evidence base is order records for 12 months, 11368 orders at a contract packaging firm that runs 2 plants and has revenue of $76 million per year.

On-time delivery over the last two quarters was 88%, against a target of 95%. Overtime cost was $1.7 million last year, up 19% on the year before, and the order backlog stands at 3.7 weeks, against 1.6 weeks a year ago. Plant 2 accounts for 60% of late orders, so the late-order problem sits mainly at one plant rather than across both. An internal estimate, not a vendor figure, puts the overtime reduction at Plant 2 at 15-20% in the first year.

The backlog and the overtime bill are the costs the programme has to move first. The staged route sets the two quoted figures against each other in one comparison: $137k for Plant 2 alone against $275k for all plants. Spending the $137k first tests the programme where 60% of late orders arise, and the all-plant decision waits on measured results from Plant 2.

subtype: worked example with equation: first-order decay
fact_base: A drug in solution decomposes by first-order kinetics with rate constant $k$ = 0.043 min-1. After 74 min the fraction remaining $C / C_0$ is 0.042. The rate constant was measured at one temperature; no activation energy is available.
input:
In this example, we consider a drug in solution that decomposes according to first-order kinetics, and the objective is to determine the fraction of the drug that remains after a specified period of time. It is well established that, for a first-order process, the rate of decomposition at any given moment is directly proportional to the concentration that is still present, which means that equal time intervals remove equal fractions of the remaining drug rather than equal amounts.

The relationship between the fraction remaining and time is captured by the integrated rate law,

$$\ln\frac{C}{C_0} = -k t$$

where $C/C_0$ represents the fraction of the drug remaining at time $t$, $k$ is the rate constant (min-1), and $t$ is the time (min). It is important to note that the fraction $C/C_0$ is dimensionless, since it is simply the concentration at time $t$ divided by the starting concentration.

In the present case, the rate constant is $k$ = 0.043 min-1. Substituting $k$ = 0.043 min-1 and $t$ = 74 min into the relation, the exponent becomes $-k t$ = -(0.043)(74) = -3.182, and the fraction remaining is therefore exp(-3.182) = 0.042. In other words, after 74 min, a fraction of 0.042 of the drug remains in solution.

After 74 min, the fraction remaining $C/C_0$ has fallen to 0.042 of the starting concentration, and the integrated law returns that same figure of 0.042 whenever the stated values of $k$ and $t$ are used. It should nevertheless be emphasised that the rate constant was measured at one temperature only, and no activation energy is available. As a result, the findings hold at the measured temperature only, and without an activation energy it is not possible to compute the rate constant at another temperature or to state the fraction remaining after 74 min under any other conditions.
target:
A drug in solution decomposes by first-order kinetics. The rate constant is $k$ = 0.043 min-1, and after 74 min the fraction remaining $C/C_0$ is 0.042.

For a first-order process, the rate of decomposition at any moment is proportional to the concentration still present, so equal time intervals remove equal fractions of what remains, not equal amounts. The integrated rate law collects that behaviour into one relation between the fraction remaining, the rate constant and the time:

$$\ln\frac{C}{C_0} = -k t$$

where $C/C_0$ is the fraction of the drug remaining at time $t$, $k$ is the rate constant (min-1), and $t$ is the time (min). The fraction $C/C_0$ is dimensionless: it is the concentration at time $t$ divided by the starting concentration.

Substitution of $k$ = 0.043 min-1 and $t$ = 74 min gives the exponent $-k t$ = -(0.043)(74) = -3.182. The fraction remaining is exp(-3.182) = 0.042. After 74 min, 0.042 of the drug remains in solution.

The relation also fixes what the result does not say. It gives a fraction, not an amount: the concentration remaining in absolute terms follows only when the fraction is combined with the starting concentration of the experiment. The starting concentration is not among the quantities reported here, so the outcome is stated as a fraction throughout.

The rate constant was measured at one temperature, and no activation energy is available. The result therefore holds at the measured temperature only: with no activation energy, the rate constant at another temperature cannot be computed from the value reported here, and the fraction remaining after 74 min at any other temperature is not given by 0.042.

fact_base: A tutorial passage explains absolute and relative error through a temperature measurement. Worked figures: reading 195 units, tolerance 0.5% of reading, so the absolute error is 0.97 units. The passage distinguishes error from uncertainty and does not merge the two terms.
input:
It is important to understand that the terms error and uncertainty are frequently confused in measurement practice, yet they describe different properties of a measurement and should never be used interchangeably. The error of a measurement is defined as the difference between the measured value and the true value. The absolute error is the magnitude of that difference, expressed in the same units as the measurement itself, whereas the relative error is the absolute error divided by the reading, producing a dimensionless ratio often expressed as a percentage.

To illustrate these concepts, consider a temperature measurement in which the reading is 195 units and the tolerance is 0.5% of the reading. The absolute error amounts to 0.5% of 195, which corresponds to 0.97 units. Expressed in relative terms, the very same error is 0.5%: the absolute form, 0.97 units, carries the unit of the reading, while the relative form, 0.5%, does not.

Uncertainty, by contrast, is not simply another name for error. Error is associated with a single measurement and represents one specific difference, complete with a sign, between the measured value and the true value. Uncertainty, on the other hand, describes the spread of values that repeated measurement or imperfect knowledge leaves open around a result, and is a range rather than a single signed difference. Consequently, a measurement may well exhibit a small error together with a large uncertainty, or a large error within a small stated uncertainty, and reporting one of these quantities says nothing about the other. The worked figures pin down the error terms for the example: a reading of 195 units, a tolerance of 0.5% of the reading, and an absolute error of 0.97 units.
target:
Error and uncertainty describe different properties of a measurement, and the two terms are not interchangeable. The error of a measurement is the difference between the measured value and the true value. The absolute error is the size of that difference, stated in the units of the measurement itself. The relative error is the absolute error divided by the reading, a dimensionless ratio that is often stated as a percentage.

A temperature measurement makes the distinction concrete. The reading is 195 units and the tolerance is 0.5% of the reading. The absolute error is 0.5% of 195, which is 0.97 units. The same error stated relatively is 0.5%: the absolute form, 0.97 units, carries the unit of the reading, and the relative form, 0.5%, does not.

Uncertainty is not a second name for error. Error belongs to a single measurement: it is one difference, with a sign, between the measured value and the true value. Uncertainty describes the spread of values that repeated measurement or imperfect knowledge leaves open around a result; it is a range, not a single signed difference. A measurement can therefore carry a small error and a large uncertainty, or a large error inside a small stated uncertainty, and reporting one quantity says nothing about the other. The worked figures fix the error terms for the example at hand: a reading of 195 units, a tolerance of 0.5% of the reading, and an absolute error of 0.97 units.

fact_base: Goal: compute the Reynolds number for water in a pipe and state the flow regime. The Reynolds number Re (dimensionless) is computed from density rho (kg m-3), mean velocity v (m s-1), pipe diameter D (m) and dynamic viscosity mu (Pa s) by Re = rho v D / mu. Water at 293 K: rho = 998 kg m-3, mu = 1.00 x 10-3 Pa s. Pipe diameter D = 0.025 m; mean velocity v = 1.1 m s-1. Worked result: Re = 27400 (computed as 998 x 1.1 x 0.025 / 0.001). Flow is laminar below Re = 2300 and turbulent above Re = 4000; between the two values the regime is transitional and is not assigned by the number alone.
input:
Let's calculate the Reynolds number for water flowing through a pipe and determine the flow regime. By working through the numbers step by step, we will arrive at a Reynolds number of 27400, which, as we shall see, corresponds to turbulent flow.

The Reynolds number Re is a dimensionless quantity that is computed from the density rho (kg m-3), the mean velocity v (m s-1), the pipe diameter D (m) and the dynamic viscosity mu (Pa s), using the relation Re = rho v D / mu. The Reynolds number provides a comparison between the inertial effects in the flow and the viscous effects, with larger values indicating that inertia plays the dominant role. Each of the symbols relates either to the fluid or to the pipe: rho and mu are properties of the water, v is the mean velocity across the pipe section, and D is the pipe diameter.

For water at a temperature of 293 K, the density is rho = 998 kg m-3 and the dynamic viscosity is mu = 1.00 x 10-3 Pa s. Both properties are the values for water at 293 K, and they are used at that temperature throughout the calculation. The pipe diameter is given as D = 0.025 m, and the mean velocity is v = 1.1 m s-1.

Substituting these values into the relation gives Re = 998 x 1.1 x 0.025 / 0.001 = 27400. The units cancel out completely during this substitution, since the kilograms, metres and seconds in the numerator and denominator divide out, leaving Re with no unit at all.

The flow regime is then read from the standard thresholds. Flow is classified as laminar below Re = 2300 and as turbulent above Re = 4000, while between 2300 and 4000 the regime is described as transitional and cannot be assigned on the basis of the number alone. The computed value of 27400 lies far above the upper threshold, deep within the turbulent range, and no part of the transitional interval is involved. This comparison serves as a useful check on the result, since 27400 exceeds the turbulent threshold of 4000 by a very wide margin, so the classification as turbulent does not depend on a value near a boundary.
target:
Goal: compute the Reynolds number for water flowing in a pipe, and state the flow regime. The result is Re = 27400, and the flow is turbulent.

The Reynolds number Re (dimensionless) is computed from the density rho (kg m-3), the mean velocity v (m s-1), the pipe diameter D (m) and the dynamic viscosity mu (Pa s) by Re = rho v D / mu. The Reynolds number compares the inertial effect in the flow with the viscous effect: a large value marks a flow in which inertia dominates, and a small value a flow in which viscosity dominates. Each symbol belongs to the water or to the pipe: rho and mu are properties of the water, v is the mean velocity across the pipe section, and D is the pipe diameter.

For water at 293 K, rho = 998 kg m-3 and mu = 1.00 x 10-3 Pa s. The pipe diameter is D = 0.025 m and the mean velocity is v = 1.1 m s-1. Both fluid properties are the values at 293 K, and the computation uses them at that temperature throughout.

Substitution gives Re = 998 x 1.1 x 0.025 / 0.001 = 27400. The units cancel in the substitution: the units in the numerator and the denominator divide out, and Re carries no unit.

The regime is read from the thresholds. Flow is laminar below Re = 2300 and turbulent above Re = 4000; between 2300 and 4000 the regime is transitional and is not assigned by the number alone. The computed value, 27400, stands above 4000, in the turbulent range, and no part of the transitional interval is involved. The check on the result is the threshold comparison itself: a value below the lower threshold would be laminar, a value between the thresholds would stay unassigned, and the value obtained, 27400, is turbulent.

subtype: worked example with equation: Arrhenius ratio
fact_base: Rate constants for a food spoilage study were measured at two temperatures. With activation energy $E_a$ of 47 kJ mol-1, raising the temperature from 300 K to 320 K multiplies the rate constant $k$ by 3.25. The estimate holds the pre-exponential factor $A$ constant over the interval.
input:
Rate constants for a food spoilage study were measured at two temperatures, and the temperature dependence of the process is described by the well-known Arrhenius relation,

$$k = A \exp\left(-\frac{E_a}{R T}\right)$$

in which $A$ denotes the pre-exponential factor, $E_a$ is the activation energy, $R$ is the gas constant, and $T$ is the absolute temperature. The activation energy, which can be thought of as the energy barrier that the spoilage process must overcome, has a value of $E_a$ = 47 kJ mol-1 for the process under consideration.

When the temperature is raised from 300 K to 320 K, the rate constant $k$ is multiplied by a factor of 3.25. This is an increase in temperature of some 20 K, and across this interval the spoilage rate constant at 320 K is fully 3.25 times its value at 300 K, underlining the strong sensitivity of the process to temperature. Expressed as a ratio between the two temperatures, the factor is 3.25, the figure the study reports for the interval.

It is important to note that this estimate rests on the assumption that the pre-exponential factor $A$ remains constant over the interval in question. The factor of 3.25 therefore arises entirely from the exponential term, evaluated using $E_a$ = 47 kJ mol-1 at the two temperatures of 300 K and 320 K, and any variation in $A$ across the same interval has not been taken into account. It should also be emphasised that the two temperatures effectively bound the claim being made here: the factor of 3.25 is specifically the ratio between 320 K and 300 K, and no rate constant at any third temperature is either reported or implied by the relation in the form in which it has been used.
target:
Rate constants for a food spoilage study were measured at two temperatures. The study tracked a spoilage process through its rate constant at each of the two temperatures, and the outcome is reported as a ratio between the two values rather than as two separate constants. The rate constant $k$ follows the Arrhenius relation

$$k = A \exp\left(-\frac{E_a}{R T}\right)$$

where $A$ is the pre-exponential factor, $E_a$ is the activation energy, $R$ is the gas constant and $T$ is the absolute temperature. The activation energy is the energy term in the exponent of the relation: it sets how strongly the rate constant responds to a change in temperature. For the spoilage process studied, $E_a$ is 47 kJ mol-1.

Raising the temperature from 300 K to 320 K multiplies the rate constant $k$ by 3.25. The rise is 20 K, and over that interval the factor on $k$ is 3.25: the rate constant at 320 K is 3.25 times the value at 300 K.

The estimate holds the pre-exponential factor $A$ constant over the interval. The factor of 3.25 therefore comes from the exponential term alone, evaluated with $E_a$ = 47 kJ mol-1 at the two temperatures, 300 K and 320 K. A change in $A$ over the same interval is not included, and the stated factor rests on that constancy. Within the interval, the relation with $A$ held constant is the whole basis of the factor; outside the interval, the same relation would need the same constancy over a wider range, which the study does not test. The two temperatures bound the claim: the factor 3.25 is the ratio between 320 K and 300 K, and no rate constant at a third temperature is reported or implied by the relation as used here.

fact_base: Inventory policy for a spare motor: mean demand 1668 units per week, standard deviation 238 units per week, replenishment lead time 4 weeks. Safety stock for a 95% cycle service level is 785 units. Demand is treated as normal and independent between weeks; seasonal peaks are excluded.
input:
This case considers the inventory policy for a spare motor and the question of how much safety stock should be held to protect availability. The bottom-line recommendation is that safety stock for the spare motor should be set at 785 units, a figure designed to deliver a 95% cycle service level given mean demand of 1668 units per week, a standard deviation of 238 units per week, and a replenishment lead time of 4 weeks.

Safety stock fulfils a specific and important function within the policy: because demand during the lead time fluctuates around its mean, the stock is held to absorb that fluctuation and prevent a stockout before the next replenishment delivery arrives. The three inputs together determine the scale of the fluctuation that the stock is required to absorb. Demand averages some 1668 units per week, the week-to-week standard deviation stands at 238 units, and a replenishment order takes 4 weeks to arrive. The service level, in turn, determines how much of that fluctuation the stock is expected to cover: a 95% cycle service level consciously accepts that a stockout will occur in the remaining cycles, rather than holding stock for the largest demand the distribution could generate.

The reorder point can be derived from exactly the same set of inputs. Mean demand over the 4-week lead time amounts to 1668 x 4 = 6672 units, and once safety stock is added, the reorder point becomes 6672 + 785 = 7065 units.

The policy proceeds on the basis that demand is normally distributed and independent from week to week. Seasonal peaks are excluded from the demand figures, which means that the 785 units have not been sized with seasonal peaks in mind, and any peak falling within a lead time will draw on stock the calculation did not set aside for it. Within these parameters, the figure is fully determined by the inputs as stated: mean demand of 1668 units per week, a standard deviation of 238 units, a lead time of 4 weeks, and a 95% cycle service level together give a safety stock of 785 units.
target:
Set safety stock for the spare motor at 785 units. The figure delivers a 95% cycle service level on the stated demand: mean demand of 1668 units per week, a standard deviation of 238 units per week, and a replenishment lead time of 4 weeks.

Safety stock covers one exposure: demand during the lead time varies around its mean, and the stock absorbs that variation so a replenishment cycle does not run out before the next delivery arrives. The three inputs fix the variation the stock must absorb. Demand averages 1668 units per week, the week-to-week standard deviation is 238 units, and a replenishment order takes 4 weeks to arrive. The service level sets the share of that variation the stock covers: at a 95% cycle service level, the remaining cycles are accepted as stockouts rather than covered by stock sized for the largest demand the distribution could produce.

The reorder point follows from the same inputs. Mean demand over the 4-week lead time is 1668 x 4 = 6672 units, and with the safety stock added, the reorder point is 6672 + 785 = 7065 units.

The policy treats demand as normal and independent between weeks. Seasonal peaks are excluded from the demand figures, so the 785 units are not sized for seasonal peaks, and a peak inside a lead time draws on stock the calculation did not provide for it. Within those terms the figure is fixed by the inputs as stated: mean demand of 1668 units per week, a standard deviation of 238 units, a lead time of 4 weeks, and a 95% cycle service level give a safety stock of 785 units.

fact_base: Pervaporation is a membrane separation in which a liquid feed contacts one side of a membrane and vacuum on the other side draws the permeating component through as vapour. Flux is the mass permeating per unit membrane area per hour (kg m-2 h-1). The separation factor is the water-to-alcohol ratio in the permeate divided by the same ratio in the feed (dimensionless). Feed: 85 wt% isopropanol in water, at 60 °C. One feed composition was tested; no test ran beyond 500 h. Polymer membrane: flux 1.8 kg m-2 h-1, separation factor 180, flux fell 9% over 500 h. Zeolite membrane: flux 1.2 kg m-2 h-1, separation factor 320, flux unchanged over 500 h within measurement error. Flux, selectivity and stability are seldom reported together for the same membrane.
input:
Pervaporation is a membrane separation technique in which a liquid feed is brought into contact with one side of a membrane, while a vacuum applied on the other side draws the permeating component through the membrane in the form of vapour. In the present study, a polymer membrane and a zeolite membrane are compared in terms of flux, separation factor and stability for a single feed consisting of 85 wt% isopropanol in water at 60 °C. For clarity, flux is defined as the mass permeating per unit membrane area per hour (kg m-2 h-1), while the separation factor is defined as the water-to-alcohol ratio in the permeate divided by the corresponding ratio in the feed, and is a dimensionless quantity.

The polymer membrane delivered a flux of 1.8 kg m-2 h-1 together with a separation factor of 180, whereas the zeolite membrane delivered a lower flux of 1.2 kg m-2 h-1 but a higher separation factor of 320. In terms of stability, however, the picture is reversed: the flux of the polymer membrane fell by 9% over 500 h, while the flux of the zeolite membrane remained unchanged over 500 h within the limits of measurement error. Taken together, these findings indicate that the polymer membrane leads in terms of flux, while the zeolite membrane leads in terms of separation factor and long-term stability over the duration of the test. It is important to note that no test was conducted beyond 500 h and that one feed composition was investigated, so the comparison is limited to 85 wt% isopropanol at 60 °C and to a maximum of 500 h of operation, the conditions under which flux, selectivity and stability were reported together for the same membrane.
target:
Pervaporation separates a liquid mixture through a membrane: the feed contacts one side of the membrane, and vacuum on the other side draws the permeating component through as vapour. This study compares a polymer membrane and a zeolite membrane on flux, separation factor and stability for one feed, 85 wt% isopropanol in water at 60 °C. The comparison was made because flux, selectivity and stability are seldom reported together for the same membrane. Flux is the mass permeating per unit membrane area per hour (kg m-2 h-1); the separation factor is the water-to-alcohol ratio in the permeate divided by the same ratio in the feed, and is dimensionless.

The polymer membrane gave a flux of 1.8 kg m-2 h-1 and a separation factor of 180. The zeolite membrane gave a flux of 1.2 kg m-2 h-1 and a separation factor of 320. On stability the order reverses: the polymer flux fell 9% over 500 h, and the zeolite flux was unchanged over 500 h within measurement error. The polymer membrane leads on flux, and the zeolite membrane leads on separation factor and on stability over the test duration. No test ran beyond 500 h, and one feed composition was tested: the comparison is limited to 85 wt% isopropanol at 60 °C and to 500 h of operation, the conditions under which flux, selectivity and stability were reported together for the same membrane.

fact_base: Excerpt content: the reboiler wall thickness is 52 mm after the corrosion allowance is added. The excerpt compares two gasket materials on temperature limit only and prefers the higher-rated one. The excerpt ends mid-argument; it neither summarises the report nor previews the next section.
input:
The reboiler wall thickness is 52 mm, obtained once the corrosion allowance has been added to the pressure-retaining thickness. The figure represents the two components together: the allowance is not a separate plate or a later addition, and the combined figure of 52 mm is carried on the fabrication drawing. Over the service life, the allowance is consumed as the wall thins, so the thickness at any later inspection is the original 52 mm less the loss the allowance was intended to absorb. The allowance plays no part in increasing the pressure the shell can carry at the end of life, since the check at that stage is performed on the thinned wall, and the figure of 52 mm belongs to the as-new condition. The reboiler stands in the solvent circuit served by the lean solvent pump, and its flanged joints form part of that circuit.

Two candidate gasket materials are assessed against one another purely in terms of temperature limit. Other criteria, including pressure class, seating stress and resistance to the solvent, do not form the grounds of the comparison, because the two materials could not be separated on those grounds in the data available to this section. On temperature limit, by contrast, the two materials separate clearly. One material is rated for continuous service above the highest temperature the reboiler reaches in service, whereas the other reaches its rating limit within the temperatures the reboiler experiences. The higher-rated material is accordingly preferred, albeit on that single ground alone.

The preference is a limited one: it says nothing about which material seals better at low temperature, nothing about relative cost, and nothing about availability, none of which this section addresses. What it indicates is that, at a joint operating at elevated temperature, the lower-rated material works close to the boundary of its limit while the higher-rated material retains a margin, and the gasket at the edge of its temperature limit is the one most likely to relax and weep in service. The lower-rated material is not excluded from the unit as a whole: it remains a candidate at joints whose temperatures stay below its limit, and the comparison is at its sharpest at the reboiler flanges, where the joint temperature comes closest to the lower rating.
target:
