fact_base: A shell-and-tube exchanger heats crude oil in a refinery preheat train. Duty is 1726 kW. Hot stream: 180 °C in, 130 °C out. Cold stream: 30 °C in, 50 °C out. The log-mean temperature difference is 114.3 K and the installed area is 49.6 m2, giving an overall coefficient of 304 W m-2 K-1. Fouling was assessed from a single 90-day run; no cleaning cycle has been completed.
input:
A shell-and-tube heat exchanger in a refinery preheat train heats crude oil by means of a hot process stream. The duty of the exchanger is 1726 kW. The hot stream enters at 180 °C and leaves at 130 °C, while the crude oil enters at 30 °C and leaves at 50 °C. The log-mean temperature difference for the exchanger works out at 114.3 K, and the installed area is 49.6 m2, which together give an overall heat transfer coefficient of 304 W m-2 K-1.

This coefficient is the value the installed area and the log-mean temperature difference return when combined with the stated duty: at a duty of 1726 kW, with an area of 49.6 m2 and a driving force of 114.3 K, the overall coefficient is 304 W m-2 K-1. The two streams undergo quite different changes in temperature, amounting to 50 K on the hot side, from 180 °C down to 130 °C, and 20 K on the cold side, from 30 °C up to 50 °C, and the log-mean difference of 114.3 K represents the driving force against which the area has been sized. The reported performance amounts to a single operating point: one duty, one pair of inlet and outlet temperatures for each stream, and one installed area.

Fouling was assessed on the basis of a single 90-day run, and no cleaning cycle has yet been completed. The coefficient of 304 W m-2 K-1 therefore rests upon a single 90-day fouling history, and neither performance following cleaning nor fouling behaviour over a longer period is covered by the figures reported here.
target:
A shell-and-tube exchanger in a refinery preheat train heats crude oil against a hot stream. The duty is 1726 kW. The hot stream enters at 180 °C and leaves at 130 °C; the crude oil enters at 30 °C and leaves at 50 °C. The log-mean temperature difference is 114.3 K and the installed area is 49.6 m2, giving an overall coefficient of 304 W m-2 K-1.

The coefficient is the value the installed area and the log-mean difference return at the stated duty: at 1726 kW, an area of 49.6 m2 and a driving force of 114.3 K give an overall coefficient of 304 W m-2 K-1. The reported performance is a single operating point: one duty, one pair of inlet and outlet temperatures for each stream, and one area. The two streams change temperature by different amounts: 50 K on the hot side, from 180 °C to 130 °C, and 20 K on the cold side, from 30 °C to 50 °C, and the log-mean difference of 114.3 K is the driving force the area is sized against.

Fouling was assessed from a single 90-day run, and no cleaning cycle has been completed. The coefficient of 304 W m-2 K-1 therefore rests on one 90-day fouling history: performance after cleaning, and fouling over a longer run, are not covered by the reported figures.

fact_base: A textbook chapter section on process control, in four parts: principle, equipment, a worked example, and limits. The worked example uses only the numbers given in the principle part; no new data appear later in the chapter. The limits part states where the simple model fails, in plain terms, without new equations.
input:
## Principle

In this chapter we will explore the principle of feedback control by looking at a common and instructive example, the control of liquid level in a tank. The arrangement is a simple one to describe. Liquid flows into the tank, and liquid flows out of it, and the task of the control loop is to hold the level of liquid in the tank at a desired value, which is known as the set point, even though the flows entering and leaving the tank may change over time.

The loop is made up of a number of elements that work together. A measuring device observes the level and produces a signal that represents it. A controller compares that signal with the set point and works out how the outflow needs to be adjusted. A valve on the outlet line then makes the adjustment. If the level rises above the set point, the controller opens the valve further so that more liquid leaves the tank, and if the level falls, the controller closes the valve so that less liquid leaves. The action is therefore always in the direction that opposes the change in level, and it is this opposition that makes the control a feedback arrangement.

The controller considered in this chapter is a proportional controller, which means that the change it makes to the outflow is proportional to the departure of the level from the set point. In the example used throughout this chapter, the numbers are as follows. The inflow to the tank is normally 10 cubic metres per hour, and at the set point the outflow matches it, so the level is steady. The controller is arranged so that the outflow changes by 5 cubic metres per hour for every metre by which the level departs from the set point. Suppose now that the inflow undergoes a step change, rising by 2 cubic metres per hour so that the inflow goes from 10 cubic metres per hour to a new value of 12 cubic metres per hour, and stays there.

An important consequence follows from the proportional action, and it is one that students often find surprising. The outflow can only change if the level changes, because it is the departure of the level from the set point that drives the controller. A sustained increase in the inflow therefore cannot be balanced at the original level. The level has to move to a new position, and to stay there, so that the valve is held open by exactly the extra amount that the new inflow requires. The permanent departure of the level from the set point that results is known as offset, and it is an inherent feature of proportional control rather than a defect of any particular controller.

## Equipment

The equipment of the loop consists of three main elements, together with the tank itself. The first element is the level transmitter, which is the sensor of the loop. Its job is to measure the level in the tank and to turn that measurement into a signal that can be transmitted to the controller. Different designs of transmitter sense the level in different ways, for example by the pressure at the base of the tank or by a float that rides on the surface of the liquid, but in every case the output of the device is a signal that stands for the level.

The second element is the controller itself. The controller receives the signal from the transmitter, compares it with the set point that the operator has chosen, and calculates the adjustment that is needed. In a modern plant the controller is usually an electronic or digital device, and the comparison and calculation happen inside it continuously.

The third element is the control valve on the outlet line, which is the final element of the loop. The valve is operated by an actuator that responds to the signal from the controller, opening or closing the valve so that the outflow changes. The valve is the only part of the loop that touches the process directly. It is also, in many ways, the least ideal part of the arrangement, because real valves have friction, they respond with a small delay, and the relationship between the signal they receive and the flow they pass is not perfectly regular. These imperfections matter for the limits discussed later in the chapter, but they do not change the principle.

## Worked example

We can now work through the example that was set up in the principle section, and the numbers used are exactly the numbers that were given there, with no new data introduced. The inflow steps up from 10 cubic metres per hour to 12 cubic metres per hour, which is an increase of 2 cubic metres per hour, and the question is to find where the level finally settles.

Immediately after the step, the outflow is still at its old value, because the level has not yet moved and the controller has had nothing to respond to. More liquid is therefore entering the tank than is leaving it, and the level begins to rise. As the level rises above the set point, the controller responds by opening the outlet valve, and the outflow increases. The level continues to rise, and the outflow continues to increase, until the two come back into balance.

The level settles when the outflow has increased by the same amount as the inflow, that is, by 2 cubic metres per hour. Since the outflow changes by 5 cubic metres per hour for every metre of departure from the set point, the departure that produces the required increase is given by 2 / 5 = 0.4 m. The level therefore settles at a new steady position that is above the set point, and the size of the offset in this example is 0.4 m.

The result can be checked by working backwards. At a departure of that size, the outflow has increased by exactly the amount of the inflow step, so inflow and outflow are once again equal, and there is no reason for the level to move any further. The offset is not a temporary feature of the adjustment; it is the permanent price that proportional control charges for balancing a sustained change in load, and it would only disappear if the controller were given an additional action that the simple proportional law does not contain.

## Limits

The account given in this chapter rests on a deliberately simple model, and it is important to be clear about the places where the simple model stops being an adequate description of a real loop. The first limitation is the offset itself, which has already been discussed. Proportional control balances a sustained change in inflow only by accepting a permanent departure from the set point, and for services in which the level has to be held close to its set point, that behaviour is not acceptable. Controllers used in practice therefore contain a further action that removes the offset over time, and that action brings its own complications, which the simple model does not describe at all.

A second limitation concerns the valve. The model treats the valve as though the outflow it passes were an exact and immediate function of the controller signal. Real valves depart from this in several ways: the flow they pass depends on the pressure drop across them as well as on their opening, the actuator takes time to move, and friction in the mechanism means that the valve does not always respond to a small change in signal. Each of these effects makes the real loop slower and less exact than the model suggests, and none of them is represented in the calculation of the worked example.

A third limitation is that the model says nothing about measurement. The transmitter is treated as though it reported the level instantly and exactly. Real measurements carry noise, and they lag behind the quantity being measured. A controller that responds to noise wastes valve movement, and a measurement lag can make a loop oscillate that the simple model predicts to be settled. Closely related to this is the question of disturbance size. A much larger disturbance than the modest step of the worked example can drive the valve to the end of its travel, at which point the controller loses its grip on the level altogether, and the proportional law no longer describes what happens.

Finally, the tank itself has been treated in the simplest possible way, as a vessel whose outflow is set entirely by the valve. In many real installations the outflow also depends on the level, because the level provides the head that drives the flow, and a tank of that kind is partly self-regulating: a rise in level increases the outflow even if the valve does not move. That behaviour changes the size of the offset and the speed of the response. The model of this chapter is therefore a starting point. It gives the structure of feedback, the meaning of offset, and the form of the calculation, and it holds for the ideal loop it describes; the loops of an operating plant require the further effects named here to be added to it.
target:
## Principle

Feedback control holds a process variable at a set point by acting against the changes that disturb it. The example used throughout this chapter is the level of liquid in a tank. Liquid enters the tank and leaves it, and the level is the balance between the two flows at every instant. A level loop measures the level, compares it with the set point, and moves a valve on the outlet line so that the outflow opposes any change: level above the set point opens the valve further, and level below it closes the valve down. The action is called feedback because the measurement of the controlled variable is fed back into the action taken on it.

The controller in this chapter is proportional. A proportional controller changes the outflow in proportion to the error, the departure of the level from the set point, and it makes no other response. The data of the chapter are fixed here and are the only data the worked example uses. The inflow is normally 10 cubic metres per hour, matched at the set point by the outflow, so the level is steady. The controller changes the outflow by 5 cubic metres per hour for each metre of departure from the set point. The load change examined is a step in the inflow from 10 cubic metres per hour to a sustained 12 cubic metres per hour, an increase of 2 cubic metres per hour.

Offset follows from the proportional law, and it is the central result of the chapter. The outflow can change only when the level departs from the set point, because the departure is what the controller responds to. A sustained rise in inflow therefore cannot be balanced at the original level. The level moves to a new position and stays there, holding the valve open by the extra amount the new inflow requires. The permanent departure is called offset. Offset is inherent in proportional control; it is not a fault in a particular controller, and no adjustment of a purely proportional controller removes it while the law itself is kept.

## Equipment

The loop has three elements besides the tank: a transmitter, a controller, and a valve. Each element has one function, and the loop is the chain of the three.

The transmitter is the sensor. It measures the level and converts the measurement into a signal that can be sent to the controller. Transmitters sense level in different ways, by the pressure at the base of the tank, by a float on the surface, or by other means; the choice affects the measurement, and the limits section returns to it, but every design delivers the same thing to the loop, a signal that stands for the level.

The controller receives the signal, compares it with the set point, and computes the valve movement the error requires. The controller measures nothing and moves nothing. It is the decision element of the loop, and in a proportional loop its whole decision rule is the one proportion stated in the principle: outflow change against level departure.

The valve is the final element, the only part of the loop that acts on the process itself. An actuator drives it in response to the controller signal, and the outflow changes as it moves. The valve is also the least ideal element in the chain. Friction in its mechanism, the time its actuator takes to move, and the dependence of its flow on the pressure drop across it all separate the real valve from the valve of the principle, which passes exactly the flow its signal demands. The separation matters for practice; it does not change the structure of the loop.

## Worked example

The inflow steps from 10 cubic metres per hour to 12 cubic metres per hour, an increase of 2 cubic metres per hour, and the level's final position is required. The data are those of the principle section; no new data enter the calculation.

At the instant of the step the outflow is still at its former value, because the level has not moved and the controller has had no error to answer. Inflow exceeds outflow, and the level rises. The rise creates the error, the controller opens the valve against it, and the outflow grows as the level grows. Movement stops where the two flows are equal again.

Balance requires the outflow to grow by the amount of the step, 2 cubic metres per hour. The controller gives 5 cubic metres per hour of outflow change for each metre of departure, so the departure that yields the required change is 2 / 5 = 0.4 m. The level settles 0.4 m above the set point.

The check is the balance itself. At that departure the outflow has risen by exactly the inflow step, inflow and outflow are equal, and no further movement is driven. The offset is permanent under the proportional law: it is the position at which the loop can hold the new load, and it persists for as long as the load persists.

## Limits

The model of this chapter is an ideal loop, and its limits are the points where a real loop departs from the ideal. The limits are stated here in plain terms, because each of them is a place where a prediction from the model would mislead a reader who took it to the plant.

Offset is the first limit, and it is structural. Proportional control holds a new load only at a new level. Services that must hold level close to the set point need a controller with a further action that removes offset over time. That action exists in practice and is standard, but it is outside this model, and it brings behaviour, including the risk of oscillation, that the proportional calculation does not predict.

The valve is the second limit. The model gives the valve an exact, immediate response to its signal. A real valve passes a flow that depends on the pressure drop across it as well as on its opening; its actuator takes time to travel; friction can hold it still against a small change of signal and then release it in a jump. The loop that results is slower and less exact than the model, and under a large disturbance the valve reaches the end of its travel. At full travel the controller has no action left, the proportional law has nothing to act through, and the level is uncontrolled until the disturbance retreats.

Measurement is the third limit. The model takes the transmitter signal as the level itself, delivered instantly and without error. A real measurement lags the level and carries noise. Lag adds delay to a loop whose stability depends on prompt action, and noise invites the controller to chase fluctuations that are not level changes at all, wearing the valve in the process.

The tank is the fourth limit. The model sets the outflow by the valve alone. In many installations the outflow also rises with the level, because the level supplies the head that drives flow through a fixed restriction, and such a tank is partly self-regulating: its level moves less for a given load change, and the offset is smaller than the chapter's calculation gives. The chapter's model is the limiting case in which none of that self-regulation exists.

The chapter's content is the structure of the feedback loop, the proportional law and the offset it forces, the three elements that carry the loop, and the calculation that turns a load step into a settling position. The limits named here mark where that content stops: at offset, at the real valve, at the real measurement, and at the real tank.

fact_base: Staffing review for a dispatch office: 8 full-time staff, overtime at 22% of paid hours last year. Replacing half the overtime with one additional hire costs $84k per year fully loaded. Overtime is concentrated in two seasonal peaks; a hire is paid for the full year.
input:
It is important to note that staffing decisions in a modern dispatch office are rarely straightforward, and the question of overtime working deserves a careful and thorough examination. Last year, the office's team of 8 full-time staff relied on overtime for a substantial 22% of all paid hours, a figure that raises wider questions about continuity of cover and about how the office copes at its busiest times.

One option that has been considered in some detail is the addition of a single full-time hire. Such a hire would replace half of the existing overtime, which corresponds to 11% of paid hours, and would cost $84k per year on a fully loaded basis. This option has a number of features that are worth weighing carefully, including the fact that the cover it provides is permanent rather than arranged week by week, and the fact that the post would be present throughout the year rather than only when overtime is currently worked.

However, it is equally worth noting that the overtime is not spread evenly across the year. Instead, it is concentrated in two seasonal peaks, while a new hire would be paid for the full year, at the full $84k annual cost, including the quieter months between the peaks. In other words, the $84k buys cover that is most valuable at the peaks and less valuable between them, and the 11% of paid hours that would be removed is removed mainly at those peaks rather than evenly across the year.

Overall, then, the decision is a balanced one. It will depend on how much weight is placed on having reliable cover at the two seasonal peaks, set against a cost that runs for the full year, and different readers may reasonably weigh those considerations differently.
target:
The dispatch office should add one full-time dispatcher. The hire replaces half of the overtime worked last year, overtime equal to 11% of paid hours, and costs $84k per year fully loaded.

The office operates with 8 full-time staff, and overtime reached 22% of paid hours last year. Cover is the ground for the recommendation. At the times when the office is busiest, work is currently covered by overtime, which depends on the same staff working longer hours. A post held for the full year does not depend on that willingness, and the cover it gives at busy times is part of the establishment rather than an arrangement renewed week by week. The post also gives the roster a margin that overtime cannot give: cover that is present before it is needed, and that does not have to be found again each week.

The limit on the case is timing. Overtime is concentrated in two seasonal peaks, and a hire is paid for the full year, so the $84k is spent in the quiet months as well as at the peaks. The trade-off is one line: overtime equal to 11% of paid hours is removed, and the cost is $84k per year. No reduction in overtime outside the peaks is claimed, because little overtime is worked there.

Dispatch office management is asked to approve the hire on the peak evidence alone. Whether a post paid for the full year is justified between peaks, as cover for leave and sickness, is a separate question, and it is not part of this case.

subtype: worked example with equation: Fourier conduction
fact_base: A flat carbon steel wall has thickness 150 mm and thermal conductivity $k$ of 45 W m-1 K-1. The temperature difference $\Delta T$ across the wall is 131 K, giving a heat flux $q$ of 39300 W m-2. The calculation is steady and one-dimensional; film resistances are excluded.
input:
A flat wall made of carbon steel has a thickness of 150 mm. The thermal conductivity $k$ of the steel is 45 W m-1 K-1, and a temperature difference $\Delta T$ of 131 K is maintained across the wall. It is required to determine the heat flux through the wall, on the basis that the conduction is steady and one-dimensional in character.

The relevant relation is Fourier's law, which for one-dimensional conduction through a flat wall takes the form

$$q = k \frac{\Delta T}{\Delta x}$$

where the symbols have the following meanings: $q$ denotes the heat flux (W m-2), $k$ the thermal conductivity of the material (W m-1 K-1), $\Delta T$ the temperature difference across the wall (K), and $\Delta x$ the thickness of the wall (m).

Before any substitution can be made, the thickness must be expressed in metres: $\Delta x$ = 0.15 m. The substitution is then $q$ = 45 x 131 / 0.15, with $k$ = 45 W m-1 K-1 and $\Delta T$ = 131 K, and this gives $q$ = 39300 W m-2.

It is worth noting that the units work out consistently, since W m-1 K-1 combined with K and divided by m yields W m-2, which is the correct unit for a heat flux. The result, 39300 W m-2, should nevertheless be interpreted with a degree of care, because it takes no account whatsoever of the film resistances at the surfaces of the wall; it is the flux due to conduction through the steel under the stated steady, one-dimensional conditions, and under those conditions alone.
target:
Calculate the steady heat flux through a flat carbon steel wall. The wall is 150 mm thick, its thermal conductivity $k$ is 45 W m-1 K-1, and the temperature difference $\Delta T$ across the wall is 131 K. The calculation is steady and one-dimensional: temperatures do not change with time, and heat crosses the wall along its thickness, with no flow along the faces. Both conditions are assumptions of the calculation, and they are stated before the relation that uses them.

Heat flux is the rate of heat transfer per unit area of wall. A flux result has a practical advantage over a total rate: it belongs to the wall construction rather than to any particular wall, and the rate for a wall of known area follows from it by multiplication by that area. Fourier's law gives the heat flux $q$ for conduction through a flat wall as

$$q = k \frac{\Delta T}{\Delta x}$$

where $q$ is the heat flux (W m-2), $k$ is the thermal conductivity of the wall material (W m-1 K-1), $\Delta T$ is the temperature difference across the wall (K), and $\Delta x$ is the wall thickness (m).

The thickness $\Delta x$ is 0.15 m. Substitution of $k$ = 45 W m-1 K-1 and $\Delta T$ = 131 K gives $q$ = 45 x 131 / 0.15, and thus $q$ = 39300 W m-2.

The units close the check: W m-1 K-1 multiplied by K and divided by m leaves W m-2, the unit of a heat flux, and no other unit enters the calculation at any step. Film resistances at the wall faces are not included in the result. The value 39300 W m-2 is the conduction flux through the steel alone, for the steady state and the single direction of flow assumed at the start.

fact_base: A continuous stirred-tank reactor runs an esterification that is first order in the limiting reactant. The rate constant is 0.09 min-1 at the operating temperature and the mean residence time is 68 min. Steady-state conversion for an ideal CSTR is 86%. The estimate assumes perfect mixing and constant density; tracer tests on the actual vessel have not been run.
input:
In this worked example, we will examine a continuous stirred-tank reactor, often abbreviated to CSTR, which is being used to carry out an esterification reaction. The reaction is first order in the limiting reactant, which means that its rate is directly proportional to the concentration of that reactant. At the operating temperature of the reactor, the rate constant has a value of 0.09 min-1, and the mean residence time of material inside the vessel is 68 min.

The key quantity of interest here is the conversion that the reactor achieves at steady state. The conversion depends on the combined effect of the rate constant and the residence time, and it is helpful to consider their product, which is 0.09 x 68 = 6.12 and which is dimensionless. When this product appears in the standard design relation for an ideal CSTR, the steady-state conversion comes out at 86%, a result that reflects the fact that a product of 6.12 represents a residence time that is long compared with the characteristic time of the reaction.

It should be noted, however, that this result of 86% rests on certain idealising assumptions. In particular, it assumes perfect mixing throughout the vessel and it also assumes that the density of the reacting mixture remains constant. In practice, real vessels may depart from these assumptions to a greater or lesser extent, and if the departure is large the actual conversion could fall below 86% even at a residence time of 68 min.

Finally, it is worth emphasising that the estimate has not been verified experimentally for the actual vessel in question. Tracer tests, which would provide valuable information about how closely the vessel approaches the ideal of perfect mixing, have not been carried out. The figure of 86% should therefore be understood as the ideal-reactor prediction, based on a rate constant of 0.09 min-1 and a residence time of 68 min, rather than as a measured conversion.
target:
A continuous stirred-tank reactor running an esterification that is first order in the limiting reactant reaches a steady-state conversion of 86%. The rate constant at the operating temperature is 0.09 min-1, and the mean residence time in the vessel is 68 min.

Conversion in an ideal continuous stirred-tank reactor is fixed by the product of the rate constant and the residence time. The product here is 0.09 x 68 = 6.12 (dimensionless). At a product of 6.12, the reactant spends several times the characteristic reaction time inside the vessel, and the conversion corresponding to that product is 86%. What matters is the pairing of the two quantities, and the product is the record of that pairing. The rate constant and the residence time enter only through their product: a reactor with twice the residence time and half the rate constant would give the same conversion, and a change in either quantity alone moves the conversion only as far as it moves the product.

The value of 86% rests on two assumptions, and both are stated with it. The first is perfect mixing: the contents are at the outlet composition throughout, so the whole volume reacts at the outlet concentration of the limiting reactant. The second is constant density: the volumetric flow leaving the vessel equals the flow entering it, and the residence time of 68 min is the vessel volume divided by that flow.

The estimate is unchecked against the actual vessel. Tracer tests, which would show how closely the vessel approaches perfect mixing, have not been run on it. The conversion of 86% is the ideal-reactor value for a rate constant of 0.09 min-1 and a residence time of 68 min, and it stands as that value until tracer evidence replaces the mixing assumption with a measured residence-time distribution.

fact_base: Goal: compute the diffusive flux of oxygen through a stagnant water film. The diffusive flux J (mol m-2 s-1) is computed from the diffusivity D (m2 s-1) and the concentration gradient dC/dx, where C is concentration (mol m-3) and x is position (m). Fick's first law: J = -D dC/dx; the negative sign states that diffusion runs from high concentration to low concentration. Oxygen in water: D = 2.1 x 10-9 m2 s-1. Concentration falls by 0.25 mol m-3 across a film 0.5 mm thick, so dC/dx = -500 mol m-4. Worked result: J = 1.05x 10-6 mol m-2 s-1. The law as stated covers a stagnant medium; a moving medium adds convection, which the equation does not include.
input:
The goal of this worked example is to compute the diffusive flux of oxygen through a stagnant film of water. We begin by introducing the quantities that are involved. The diffusive flux, denoted by J and measured in mol m-2 s-1, is computed from the diffusivity D, which has units of m2 s-1, together with the concentration gradient dC/dx, where C stands for concentration in mol m-3 and x stands for position in m.

The relationship between these quantities is given by Fick's first law, which takes the form J = -D dC/dx. The negative sign in this expression is significant, because it tells us that diffusion takes place in the direction that runs from a region of high concentration towards a region of low concentration, in other words, down the concentration gradient.

For the particular case of oxygen dissolved in water, the diffusivity has the value D = 2.1 x 10-9 m2 s-1. The concentration of oxygen decreases by 0.25 mol m-3 across a film that is 0.5 mm in thickness, which means that the concentration gradient can be written as dC/dx = -500 mol m-4.

Substituting these values into the equation gives J = -(2.1 x 10-9) x (-500), and evaluating this expression leads to a diffusive flux of J = 1.05 x 10-6 mol m-2 s-1. The positive value of the result is consistent with the direction of the coordinate, while the transport itself proceeds from the higher concentration towards the lower one. The flux of 1.05 x 10-6 mol m-2 s-1 is the final result of the example.

It should be noted, in closing, that Fick's first law in the form used here applies to a stagnant medium. If the medium is moving, convection contributes to the transport as well, and that contribution is not represented in the equation used above.
target:
The goal is to compute the diffusive flux of oxygen through a stagnant water film. The result is a flux of 1.05 x 10-6 mol m-2 s-1, directed from the higher concentration toward the lower.

The diffusive flux J (mol m-2 s-1) is computed from the diffusivity D (m2 s-1) and the concentration gradient dC/dx, where C is concentration (mol m-3) and x is position (m). Fick's first law states the flux as J = -D dC/dx; the negative sign states that diffusion runs from high concentration to low concentration.

The gradient is the slope of the concentration profile across the film, and the thickness of the film is the only length the calculation needs. The area of the film does not enter the result, because a flux is a rate per unit area: the same gradient in a wider film gives the same flux and a larger total rate, and nothing in the example asks for that rate.

For oxygen in water, D = 2.1 x 10-9 m2 s-1. The concentration falls by 0.25 mol m-3 across a film 0.5 mm thick, so the gradient is dC/dx = -500 mol m-4, the fall in concentration divided by the thickness over which it falls.

Substitution gives J = -(2.1 x 10-9) x (-500) = 1.05 x 10-6 mol m-2 s-1. The sign is the check on the result: two negative quantities, the sign in the law and the gradient of a falling concentration, give a positive flux along the direction in which concentration falls, and a flux in the opposite sense would contradict the statement of the law.

Fick's first law as stated here holds for a stagnant medium. A moving medium adds convection to the transport, and the equation does not include that contribution.

fact_base: A shell-and-tube exchanger heats crude oil in a refinery preheat train. Duty is 469 kW. Hot stream: 150 °C in, 110 °C out. Cold stream: 30 °C in, 50 °C out. The log-mean temperature difference is 89.6 K and the installed area is 39.9 m2, giving an overall coefficient of 131 W m-2 K-1. Fouling was assessed from a single 90-day run; no cleaning cycle has been completed.
input:
This passage describes a shell-and-tube heat exchanger that is installed in a refinery preheat train, where its role is to heat crude oil before the oil passes to the downstream processing units. The exchanger delivers a duty of 469 kW. On the hot side, the heating stream enters the exchanger at a temperature of 150 °C and leaves it at a temperature of 110 °C. On the cold side, the crude oil enters at 30 °C and is heated to an outlet temperature of 50 °C.

It may also be noted that the hot stream cools by 40 K across the exchanger, while the crude oil stream warms by 20 K. The temperature differences at the two ends of the exchanger can be worked out from these figures. At the hot end the difference is 100 K, obtained from 150 - 50, and at the cold end it is 80 K, obtained from 110 - 30. Combining these two differences gives a log-mean temperature difference of 89.6 K for the exchanger. The installed heat-transfer area is 39.9 m2, and the overall heat-transfer coefficient that corresponds to the stated duty is 131 W m-2 K-1.

With regard to fouling, it should be noted that the assessment of fouling is based on a single run lasting 90 days. No cleaning cycle has yet been completed for this exchanger, which means that the behaviour of the coefficient of 131 W m-2 K-1 over longer periods of operation remains uncertain.
target:
A shell-and-tube exchanger in a refinery crude-oil preheat train delivers a duty of 469 kW. The hot stream enters at 150 °C and leaves at 110 °C; the crude oil enters at 30 °C and leaves at 50 °C.

Terminal temperature differences are 100 K at the end where the hot stream enters (150 - 50) and 80 K at the other end (110 - 30), and the log-mean temperature difference taken from them is 89.6 K. The hot stream cools by 40 K across the exchanger and the crude oil warms by 20 K. Installed area is 39.9 m2. The overall coefficient that carries the stated duty over that area at that temperature difference is 131 W m-2 K-1.

The duty is a joint property of the two streams: the heat that leaves the hot stream enters the oil, and the overall coefficient states how much installed area that transfer requires at the temperature difference the streams provide. A larger area would carry the same duty at a smaller temperature difference, and a smaller area would demand a larger one; area and temperature difference are the two sides of the same design balance.

Fouling in the exchanger was assessed from a single 90-day run, and no cleaning cycle has been completed. The coefficient of 131 W m-2 K-1 is therefore the value for the state reached within that run. How the coefficient changes over a full operating cycle, and what cleaning restores, are both unknown on the present evidence.

fact_base: Design report for an amine absorber, in four sections: basis, sizing, materials, and risks. Design throughput is 33 t per day and the removal or separation duty is 96% of the key component. Materials are 316L stainless steel for wetted parts; the basis section states this once. The risks section names fouling and turndown as open items; neither is resolved in the report.
input:
## Basis

This report presents the design of an amine absorber that is to be installed for the treatment of a gas stream. In an amine absorption unit of this kind, the gas is brought into contact with an amine solvent inside a column, and the solvent selectively absorbs the key component from the gas, so that the treated gas leaving the top of the column is substantially freed of that component. The design throughput of the unit is 33 t per day, and the separation duty that the design is required to achieve is the removal of 96% of the key component present in the incoming gas. The materials basis for the design is that all wetted parts, that is, all parts that come into contact with the process fluids, are to be manufactured in 316L stainless steel.

The basis of the design also includes a number of broader assumptions that should be recorded here. The unit is intended for continuous operation, and the design is developed around a steady treating duty rather than around intermittent or batch operation. The solvent circulates between the absorber and its regeneration equipment, and the absorber itself is designed as one part of that circulating system, although the design of the regeneration equipment as such is not the subject of this report. The treated gas specification is expressed in terms of the removal duty stated above, and the design is judged against that duty. Layout, tie-ins, foundations and structures lie outside the scope of the present document.

## Sizing

The sizing of the absorber is governed by two largely separate considerations, namely the diameter of the column and its height, and it is helpful to treat them in turn. The diameter is set by the gas traffic through the column. As the gas rate rises, the gas velocity in the column rises with it, and there is a limiting velocity at which the rising gas begins to hold back the liquid that is trying to flow down, a condition generally known as flooding. The diameter is therefore chosen so that the design gas rate corresponds to a velocity that sits comfortably below the flooding velocity, with a margin that allows the unit to absorb the ordinary fluctuations of operation without approaching the limit. A column that is too narrow will flood and lose its separation; a column that is wider than necessary wastes capital and can, paradoxically, create its own problems of liquid distribution at low rates.

The height of the column is set by the contact that the separation requires. The removal duty is demanding, and the gas and the solvent must be given enough contact, over enough transfer surface, for the key component to pass from the gas into the liquid to the extent that the duty specifies. Height is provided by the internals of the column, which may take the form of trays or of packing, and the choice between these alternatives is one of the main decisions of the design. Trays are robust and tolerant of fouling and of uneven operation, while packing offers a large surface in a given volume and a low pressure drop, at the price of a greater sensitivity to the quality of liquid distribution. In either case, the height must also accommodate the entry and exit arrangements for the gas and the liquid, and the disengagement space in which droplets of solvent are separated from the treated gas before the gas leaves the column.

It is worth adding that the sizing cannot be separated from the solvent circulation, which interacts with both the diameter, through the liquid load, and the height, through the driving force maintained along the column. The design therefore treats circulation, diameter, and height as a single package of decisions.

## Materials

The materials section of the design is concerned mainly with the environment that the wetted parts of the absorber will experience in service, and with whether the specified material is a suitable response to that environment. The environment inside an amine absorber is a demanding one. The solvent is corrosive in its own right, and its corrosiveness increases where it has absorbed the key component and where the temperature is highest. Degradation products form in the solvent over time as it circulates and is regenerated, and some of these products are themselves aggressive towards metals. The result is that the corrosion risk is not uniform over the unit: it concentrates in the regions where the loaded solvent is hottest and where velocities are high enough to strip away protective surface films.

Against that environment, the design specifies a stainless steel grade for the wetted parts, as recorded in the basis. The reasoning is that a stainless grade resists the general corrosive attack of the amine environment far better than an ordinary carbon steel would, and in particular that it avoids the rapid and localised attack that amine systems can inflict on less resistant materials. The specification applies to the column shell where it is wetted, to the internals, and to the wetted parts of the associated nozzles and fittings within the battery limit of this design.

Attention is also given in the design to the details that often decide whether a material specification succeeds in practice. Welds and heat-affected zones are treated as part of the wetted surface, not as exceptions to it. Crevices, in which loaded solvent can stagnate and concentrate, are avoided in the arrangement of the internals wherever the geometry allows. Where dissimilar metals would otherwise meet in the wetted zone, the design keeps them apart or accepts the junction only where the galvanic consequences have been considered. None of these points changes the headline specification, but each of them protects it.

## Risks

Two risks are recorded in this report as open items, and it is important to be clear that neither of them is resolved by the design as it stands. The first is fouling. Fouling is the deposition of material on the internal surfaces of the column, and in an amine unit it can arise from degradation products in the solvent, from contaminants carried in with the feed gas, or from corrosion products generated within the system itself. Its consequences would be felt in the sizing first of all: deposits narrow the passages through the internals, raise the pressure drop, disturb the distribution of liquid, and so erode both the capacity and the separation that the sizing was developed to deliver. The difficulty is that the design cannot presently quantify the risk, because the fouling tendency of the actual feed gas and of the actual solvent over a long campaign is not characterised. Until operating evidence or test evidence exists, fouling remains an open item, and the margins in the sizing should be read with that openness in mind.

The second open item is turndown. The design is developed at the design throughput, but the unit will not always be asked to run at that rate, and its behaviour at reduced rates raises questions that the design point does not answer. At low gas rates the internals may distribute the liquid less evenly, and at low liquid rates parts of the packing or the trays may run partially dry, so that the contact on which the removal duty depends is no longer achieved even though the column is tall enough. The solvent circulation, too, has practical minima below which pumps, level control, and distribution devices cease to behave as the design intends. How far the unit can be turned down while still meeting its removal duty is therefore not established by this report. It is recorded here as an open item, to be settled by the combination of vendor information, operating experience on comparable units, and the detailed design work that follows this report.
target:
## Basis

The unit is an amine absorber treating a gas stream. Gas passes up the column against a down-flowing amine solvent, and the solvent absorbs the key component from the gas, so the treated gas leaves the column substantially freed of that component. Design throughput is 33 t per day. The separation duty is removal of 96% of the key component in the incoming gas. Wetted parts are 316L stainless steel; that specification is stated here once and governs the materials section.

The absorber is one part of a circulating solvent system. Solvent leaves the absorber loaded with the absorbed component, is regenerated elsewhere in the system, and returns lean. Regeneration equipment is outside this report, but the absorber is designed as part of that loop, and its sizing assumes a lean solvent of the quality the loop is intended to deliver. Operation is continuous and the design is developed at a steady treating duty. The treated-gas requirement is the removal duty stated above, and the design stands or falls against it. Layout, tie-ins, foundations and structures are outside the report; its subject is the absorber, the reasoning that fixes its size, and the specification that follows from that reasoning.

## Sizing

Column diameter and column height are set by different limits, and the design treats them separately before combining them.

Diameter is set by gas traffic. Rising gas holds back the down-flowing liquid, and at the flooding velocity the column ceases to separate at all. The diameter is chosen so the design gas rate runs at a velocity held below flooding with a working margin, wide enough to absorb ordinary operating fluctuation and no wider: an oversized column spends capital to no purpose and distributes liquid poorly at low rates, which is the turndown problem recorded in the risks section.

Height is set by the contact the duty requires. The key component must pass from gas to solvent to the extent of the stated removal, and the internals must provide the transfer surface and the contact time that transfer needs. The choice of internals is the main open decision inside the sizing. Trays tolerate fouling and maldistribution and forgive uneven operation. Packing gives more surface per volume and a lower pressure drop, and pays for it with a stricter demand on liquid distribution. Either choice must also accommodate gas and liquid entry arrangements and a disengagement space in which entrained solvent droplets leave the treated gas.

Pressure drop is checked alongside both decisions, because the gas has to be moved through the column at the design rate within the pressure the upstream system can supply, and an internals choice that wins on contact can still fail on pressure drop.

Solvent circulation binds the two decisions together. The circulation rate fixes how much key component each pass of solvent carries, loads the internals with liquid, and maintains the driving force along the column. Diameter, height and circulation are therefore settled as one package. A change to any one of them reopens the other two.

## Materials

The material question is set by the environment the wetted parts meet. Amine solvent is corrosive; loaded solvent, carrying the absorbed component, is more corrosive than lean; and the attack is strongest where the loaded solvent is hottest and where flow strips the protective film from the surface. Degradation products formed in the circulating solvent add to the attack over time. Corrosion risk in this unit is therefore not uniform. It concentrates in defined regions, and the specification answers the concentrated risk, not an average one.

The grade named in the basis is specified for wetted parts on that evidence. A stainless grade resists the general attack of the amine environment and, more importantly, the rapid localised attack that amine systems inflict on plainer materials in exactly the hot, loaded regions identified above. The specification covers the wetted shell, the internals, and the wetted parts of nozzles and fittings within this design's battery limit.

The specification is protected in the details. Welds and heat-affected zones count as wetted surface, with no exception for their different structure. Crevices in which loaded solvent can stagnate and concentrate are avoided in the arrangement of the internals wherever geometry allows. Junctions of dissimilar metals in the wetted zone are kept apart, or accepted only where the galvanic consequence has been examined. The headline specification is one line in the basis; these provisions are what make it hold in the built unit. Inspection access belongs to the same protection: the regions where the risk concentrates are the regions an inspection has to be able to reach, and an arrangement that cannot be inspected cannot be said to be covered by the specification at all.

## Risks

Two risks are open items in this report. Neither is resolved here, and the design is not represented as resolving them.

Fouling is the first. Deposits form on internal surfaces from solvent degradation products, from contaminants entering with the feed gas, and from corrosion products generated inside the system. The consequences land on the sizing: deposits narrow the flow passages, raise pressure drop, and disturb liquid distribution, so capacity and separation both fall away from the values the sizing delivers on clean internals. The risk cannot be quantified in this report. The fouling tendency of the actual feed gas and the actual solvent over a long campaign is uncharacterised, and no test or operating evidence on these streams exists yet. Fouling stays open until such evidence exists, and the sizing margins are to be read as margins against an unquantified risk.

Turndown is the second. The design is developed at the design throughput, and behaviour at reduced rates is not established by designing at that point. At low gas and liquid rates the internals distribute liquid less evenly, packing and tray surfaces can run partially dry, and the contact the removal duty depends on is lost inside a column tall enough to provide it. Solvent circulation has its own practical minima, set by pumping, by level control and by the distribution devices. How far the unit turns down and still meets its removal duty is therefore an open question, to be settled by vendor information, by operating experience on comparable units, and by the detailed design that follows this report.

fact_base: A centrifugal pump moves water between two vessels at grade. At the duty point the flow is 70 m3 h-1 against a head of 32 m, with pump efficiency 74%. Shaft power at the duty point is 8.2 kW. The motor is rated 15% above this value. Cavitation was not observed in the acceptance test, which ran for 4 h at the duty point only.
input:
A centrifugal pump is used to move water between two vessels that are located at grade, that is to say, at ground level, so that no static lift between the two vessels enters into the duty that the pump is required to meet. At the duty point of the pump, which is the point at which it is intended to operate, the flow rate delivered is 70 m3 h-1, and this flow is delivered against a head of 32 m. The efficiency of the pump at this operating point is 74%.

The shaft power that is required at the duty point is 8.2 kW. In line with normal practice, the motor that drives the pump is rated somewhat higher than this figure, in fact 15% above the shaft power at the duty point, so that the motor is not obliged to run continuously at the very limit of its rating when the pump is at its duty point.

During the acceptance test that was carried out on the pump, no cavitation was observed. It is important to note, however, that the acceptance test ran for a duration of 4 h and that it covered the duty point only. The absence of cavitation is therefore established for the conditions of that test, and it should not automatically be assumed to extend to other conditions, such as different flows or suction arrangements, that were not part of the test programme.
target:
A centrifugal pump moves water between two vessels at grade. At the duty point the flow is 70 m3 h-1 against a head of 32 m, with a pump efficiency of 74%.

The duty point is the operating point the pump is selected for, and the three figures belong together: the flow and the head state what the pump delivers, and the efficiency states what that delivery costs in power. Shaft power at the duty point is 8.2 kW. The motor is rated 15% above this value. That margin is part of the specification, not a reserve discovered afterwards: the drive is sized so that continuous operation at the duty point sits inside its rating, with the rating held above the shaft requirement at the one point where the pump is required to run.

Efficiency enters the result directly. At a fixed flow and head, the hydraulic power is fixed, and the shaft power is that hydraulic power divided by the efficiency; a pump of lower efficiency at the same duty point would draw more shaft power to deliver the same flow against the same head.

Cavitation was not observed in the acceptance test, and the test record is the whole of the evidence on the point. The test ran for 4 h and covered the duty point only. The result is a detection statement at one operating point: no cavitation over that test at the duty point. Running at other flows, or with a lower suction level than the test arrangement provided, is outside the evidence, and the test says nothing about it.

fact_base: Excerpt content: two groups report conflicting lifetime values for the same material class; the excerpt weighs their test conditions. The excerpt reaches a limited preference and states the condition on which it rests.
input:
The picture that emerges from the reported lifetimes is, on closer inspection, a somewhat confusing one, because the two groups that have studied the benchmark material report lifetime values that differ from one another by a margin that is too large to be explained away as ordinary scatter. Both groups were working with materials of the same class, and both describe careful measurement programmes, so the discrepancy cannot simply be attributed to carelessness on one side or the other, and it deserves to be examined in terms of the conditions under which the measurements were actually made.

The conditions, it turns out, were far from identical. In one programme, the material was exposed continuously to a feed that carried moisture, and its lifetime was recorded as the time over which its performance declined under that exposure. In the other programme, the feed was dry, and the material was taken through repeated cycles of use and regeneration, so that the reported lifetime reflects survival under cycling rather than under continuous exposure to a challenging feed. These are, in effect, measurements of two different kinds of endurance, and it is perhaps not surprising that they lead to different numbers.

On balance, and with some hesitation, the values obtained under the moist feed appear to be the more relevant guide for the benchmark material where the intended service involves a feed that carries moisture, since those values were earned under conditions that resemble that service more closely. The preference is, however, a limited and a conditional one, and it rests on that resemblance.
target:
Lifetime is the quantity on which the two groups disagree most sharply. Both report on the same class of material, and both report on the benchmark material directly, yet the lifetime values stand far enough apart that neither can be absorbed into the scatter of the other. The disagreement survives the obvious explanations: the measurement programmes are both described in detail, and neither group reports conditions that would make its own value an outlier on its own terms.

The test conditions differ in the feed and in the duty cycle, and the difference is enough to account for the gap. One group held the material under continuous exposure to a feed carrying moisture, and lifetime in that programme is endurance against a wet feed. The other group worked with a dry feed and took the material through repeated cycles of use and regeneration, so lifetime there is endurance against cycling. The two programmes measure different failure routes, and a value from one cannot be used to correct a value from the other.

A limited preference follows. Where the intended service carries moisture in the feed, the values from the moist-feed programme are the better guide for the benchmark material, because they were earned against the failure route that service imposes. The preference rests on that condition and reaches no further: for dry, cycling duty the other programme is the relevant one, and neither set of values displaces it there.
