fact_base: Inventory policy for a resin grade: mean demand 1020 units per week, standard deviation 287 units per week, replenishment lead time 7 weeks. Safety stock for a 95% cycle service level is 1253 units. Demand is treated as normal and independent between weeks; seasonal peaks are excluded.
input:
This passage sets out the inventory policy that is proposed for a particular resin grade held in stock. Demand for this grade occurs at a mean rate of 1020 units per week, although there is appreciable variation around that mean, with a standard deviation of 287 units per week. When stock is replenished, the replenishment lead time is 7 weeks, which is a relatively long period during which demand must be met from the stock that is on hand.

Over a lead time of 7 weeks, the expected demand is 1020 x 7 = 7140 units. Because actual demand fluctuates, however, ordering only when stock falls to the expected lead-time demand would lead to stock being exhausted in roughly half of all replenishment cycles. A safety stock is therefore held in addition, and the safety stock that corresponds to a 95% cycle service level is 1253 units. Adding the two components together, the reorder point becomes 7140 + 1253 = 7766 units: when the stock position falls to 7766 units, a replenishment order is placed.

It should be noted that the policy rests on the assumptions that demand is normally distributed and that the demands in successive weeks are independent of one another. Seasonal peaks in demand are excluded from the analysis, and those figures should consequently be understood as applying to demand outside those peaks. A safety stock of 1253 units is, in summary, the quantity that the policy requires.
target:
Materials planning should hold a safety stock of 1253 units of the resin grade, with the reorder point set at 7766 units.

Demand for the grade averages 1020 units per week, with a standard deviation of 287 units per week, and replenishment has a lead time of 7 weeks. Average demand over the lead time is 1020 x 7 = 7140 units. The reorder point is that average plus the safety stock, 7140 + 1253 = 7766 units. The safety stock is the part of the policy that carries the service level: it is the buffer that holds the cycle service level at 95% against the week-to-week spread in demand during the 7 weeks in which an order is outstanding. The average component of the reorder point covers expected use; the safety stock covers the variation around it, and the two parts should not be merged when the policy is reviewed.

The reorder point is a trigger on the stock position, which counts stock on hand together with stock already on order. When the position falls to the reorder point, an order is placed, and the stock on hand at that moment has to carry demand until the order arrives. Setting the trigger on the position rather than on the shelf alone prevents a second order being placed while an earlier one is still outstanding, and it keeps the safety stock intact as a reserve against variation rather than as working stock.

The figures rest on two stated assumptions. Demand is treated as normal, and demand in one week is treated as independent of demand in the next. Seasonal peaks are excluded from the demand figures altogether. The policy is therefore a policy for ordinary demand: in a peak, the stock of 1253 units is consumed faster than the variation model supposes, and that service level is not delivered by this stock level under peak conditions.

subtype: worked example with equation: Fourier conduction
fact_base: A flat firebrick wall has thickness 20 mm and thermal conductivity $k$ of 1.1 W m-1 K-1. The temperature difference $\Delta T$ across the wall is 212 K, giving a heat flux $q$ of 11660 W m-2. The calculation is steady and one-dimensional; film resistances are excluded.
input:
Consider a flat wall constructed from firebrick, with a thickness of 20 mm. The thermal conductivity $k$ of the firebrick is 1.1 W m-1 K-1, and the temperature difference $\Delta T$ that is maintained across the wall is 212 K. The task is to estimate the heat flux passing through the wall, on the understanding that the conduction is both steady and one-dimensional.

The method used here is the standard one for steady conduction through a plane wall, and the governing relation is Fourier's law for a flat wall, which may be written in the form

$$q = k \frac{\Delta T}{\Delta x}$$

where $q$ stands for the heat flux (W m-2), $k$ for the thermal conductivity (W m-1 K-1), $\Delta T$ for the temperature difference (K), and $\Delta x$ for the thickness of the wall (m).

Since the thickness is given in millimetres, it must first be converted: $\Delta x$ = 0.02 m. Substitution then gives $q$ = 1.1 x 212 / 0.02, from which $q$ = 11660 W m-2.

A quick check of the units confirms that they are consistent, because W m-1 K-1 multiplied by K and divided by m produces W m-2. It should be borne in mind, however, that the figure of 11660 W m-2 represents conduction through the brick alone, since the film resistances at the faces of the wall have not been included in the calculation.
target:
A flat firebrick wall is 20 mm thick, its thermal conductivity $k$ is 1.1 W m-1 K-1, and the temperature difference $\Delta T$ across the wall is 212 K. The steady, one-dimensional heat flux $q$ through the wall is required. Steadiness means that the temperatures at the faces do not change with time; one-dimensional conduction means that heat crosses along the thickness and not along the faces. A flux result also separates the wall from its setting: the same construction returns the same flux wherever it is built, and the total rate of heat loss through any particular wall of this construction follows from the flux once the area of that wall is known.

Fourier's law gives the heat flux $q$ for a flat wall as

$$q = k \frac{\Delta T}{\Delta x}$$

where $q$ is the heat flux (W m-2), $k$ is the thermal conductivity of the wall material (W m-1 K-1), $\Delta T$ is the temperature difference across the wall (K), and $\Delta x$ is the wall thickness (m).

The thickness $\Delta x$ is 0.02 m. Substitution gives $q$ = 1.1 x 212 / 0.02, and thus $q$ = 11660 W m-2.

The unit check is short: W m-1 K-1 multiplied by K and divided by m leaves W m-2, the unit the result has to carry. Film resistances at the faces are not included in the calculation. The flux of 11660 W m-2 is therefore the conduction flux through the brick alone, on the two assumptions named at the start, and a wall calculation that needs the surface films as well must add them to this result rather than use it as it stands.

fact_base: Goal: compute the Reynolds number for water in a pipe and state the flow regime. The Reynolds number Re (dimensionless) is computed from density rho (kg m-3), mean velocity v (m s-1), pipe diameter D (m) and dynamic viscosity mu (Pa s) by Re = rho v D / mu. Water at 293 K: rho = 998 kg m-3, mu = 1.00 x 10-3 Pa s. Pipe diameter D = 0.025 m; mean velocity v = 0.8 m s-1. Worked result: Re = 20000 (computed as 998 x 0.8 x 0.025 / 0.001). Flow is laminar below Re = 2300 and turbulent above Re = 4000; between the two values the regime is transitional and is not assigned by the number alone.
input:
In this example, the goal is to compute the Reynolds number for water flowing inside a pipe, and then to use the computed value in order to state the flow regime that applies. The Reynolds number, which is denoted by Re and which is a dimensionless quantity, is computed from the density rho, measured in kg m-3, the mean velocity v, measured in m s-1, the pipe diameter D, measured in m, and the dynamic viscosity mu, measured in Pa s, by means of the relation Re = rho v D / mu.

For water at a temperature of 293 K, the density is rho = 998 kg m-3 and the dynamic viscosity is mu = 1.00 x 10-3 Pa s. The pipe in question has a diameter of D = 0.025 m, and the mean velocity of the water flowing through it is v = 0.8 m s-1.

Substituting the values into the relation gives Re = 998 x 0.8 x 0.025 / 0.001, and the worked result of this calculation is Re = 20000. A Reynolds number of 20000 is not a marginal case, as the interpretation will show. It remains to interpret this number in terms of the flow regime. Flow is generally regarded as laminar when the Reynolds number is below Re = 2300, and as turbulent when it is above Re = 4000. Between these two values, the regime is described as transitional, and in that range the regime is not assigned by the number alone.

Since the value obtained here, 20000, is considerably above the threshold value of 4000, the flow in the pipe is turbulent.
target:
The goal is to compute the Reynolds number for water in a pipe and to state the flow regime. The result is Re = 20000, and the flow is turbulent.

The Reynolds number Re (dimensionless) is computed from the density rho (kg m-3), the mean velocity v (m s-1), the pipe diameter D (m) and the dynamic viscosity mu (Pa s) by Re = rho v D / mu. For water at 293 K, rho = 998 kg m-3 and mu = 1.00 x 10-3 Pa s. The pipe diameter D is 0.025 m and the mean velocity v is 0.8 m s-1.

The number compares the inertia of the moving fluid with the viscous forces that resist the motion. A large value means that inertia dominates and the flow breaks up into turbulence; a small value means that viscosity holds the flow orderly and layered. The thresholds used below mark the band in which neither influence is in full control, and in that band the observed regime depends on disturbances and on the state of the pipe as well as on the number itself.

Substitution gives Re = 998 x 0.8 x 0.025 / 0.001 = 20000. A Reynolds number carries no unit, and the absence of a unit in the result is the first check on the substitution: density, velocity and diameter in the numerator and viscosity in the denominator cancel to a pure number.

Flow is laminar below Re = 2300 and turbulent above Re = 4000; between the two values the regime is transitional and is not assigned by the number alone. The computed value of 20000 lies above 4000, outside the transitional band and well into the turbulent range, so the regime follows from the number without any further condition.

fact_base: Inventory policy for a packaging film: mean demand 2399 units per week, standard deviation 596 units per week, replenishment lead time 4 weeks. Safety stock for a 95% cycle service level is 1967 units. Demand is treated as normal and independent between weeks; seasonal peaks are excluded.
input:
Inventory management plays a crucial role in ensuring that production can continue smoothly without unnecessary interruptions, and safety stock is one of the key tools that planners utilise in order to achieve this goal. In the case of the packaging film considered here, demand averages 2399 units per week, although it is important to note that weekly demand is by no means constant, exhibiting a standard deviation of 596 units per week. The replenishment lead time is 4 weeks, which means that, on average, demand over the lead time amounts to 9596 units, while the standard deviation of demand over the lead-time period is 1192 units, reflecting the accumulation of variability across the independent weeks.

Against this background, the safety stock for the packaging film has been set at 1967 units, corresponding to a 95% cycle service level. This means that the policy is designed to provide a high level of protection against stockouts during the replenishment cycle. It should be noted that the underlying calculations rest on certain assumptions, including the assumptions that demand follows a normal distribution and that demand in each week is independent of demand in other weeks. Furthermore, seasonal peaks have been excluded from the analysis, which may potentially affect the adequacy of the 1967 units during peak periods, highlighting the importance of reviewing the policy on an ongoing basis.
target:
Safety stock for the packaging film is 1967 units, held against demand variation over a replenishment lead time of 4 weeks. The cycle service level is 95%: the probability that one replenishment cycle ends without a stockout.

Demand averages 2399 units per week, with a standard deviation of 596 units per week. Mean demand over the lead time is 9596 units, and the standard deviation of demand over the lead time is 1192 units. Weekly demand is treated as independent between weeks, and the lead-time spread follows from that treatment: the standard deviation grows with the square root of the lead time, not in proportion to it, and demand is treated as normal, so the stock is read from the normal distribution at that level.

Two limits stand on the figure. Seasonal peaks are excluded from the demand record, so the 1967 units carry no allowance for them, and a peak that falls inside a replenishment cycle is met from stock sized for ordinary weeks. Independence between weeks is an assumption of the calculation, not a property measured in the record: correlated weekly demand would widen the lead-time spread, and the stock the stated level requires would rise with it.

fact_base: A tutorial passage explains absolute and relative error through a flow measurement. Worked figures: reading 117 units, tolerance 2% of reading, so the absolute error is 2.34 units. The passage distinguishes error from uncertainty and does not merge the two terms.
input:
When it comes to flow measurement, it is essential to understand the concepts of error and uncertainty, as these terms are frequently encountered in engineering practice and are, unfortunately, often used interchangeably, even though they refer to quite different ideas. In this passage, we will explore the distinction between absolute error and relative error, using a straightforward worked example based on a flow measurement.

Let us consider a flow reading of 117 units, where the instrument tolerance is specified as 2% of reading. This means that the absolute error — that is, the error expressed in the same units as the measurement itself — is 2.34 units. In other words, the reading of 117 units may differ from the true value of the flow by up to 2.34 units. The relative error, by contrast, expresses the error as a proportion of the reading, which in this case is 2%. It is worth noting that the absolute error depends on the magnitude of the reading, whereas the relative error provides a more portable way of characterising instrument performance across different readings and operating conditions.

Turning now to uncertainty, it is important to emphasise that uncertainty is not simply another word for error. Error refers to the difference between a measured value and the true value, whereas uncertainty refers to the range of values within which the true value is believed to lie. Because the true value is generally not known, the actual error in a given reading cannot usually be determined, highlighting the importance of specifying uncertainty when reporting measurement results in a rigorous and transparent manner.
target:
Error is the difference between a measured value and the true value of the quantity measured. A flow reading of 117 units with a tolerance of 2% of reading carries an absolute error of 2.34 units. The absolute error is the error stated in the units of the measurement itself, and it is tied to the reading at which it is evaluated: at a larger reading, the same percentage tolerance gives a larger absolute error. Converting a tolerance stated as a percentage into units requires the reading itself, and the worked figures perform exactly that conversion.

The relative error states the same error as a fraction of the reading. The tolerance here is given in relative form, as 2% of reading, and the 2.34 units are that percentage applied to the 117 units. The two forms answer different questions. The absolute error states how far the reading may lie from the true flow, in the units the operator reads. The relative error states the same departure against the size of the reading, and the relative form is the one that transfers between readings: a tolerance stated as a percentage of reading holds at any reading within the instrument's range, while the absolute error changes in proportion to the reading.

Uncertainty is not error under another name. Error is a single difference, between one reading and the true value, and it has a sign: the reading lies above the true value or below it. The true value is not known in practice, and the error of a particular reading is therefore not known either; what the tolerance states is the band within which the error is expected to lie. Uncertainty describes that band. It characterises the spread of values that could reasonably be assigned to the quantity, given the instrument and the procedure by which the reading was taken. A reading can accordingly be reported with an uncertainty while its error remains unknown. Merging the two terms hides the distinction: error belongs to a reading, and uncertainty belongs to the state of knowledge about the quantity the reading reports.

fact_base: Staffing review for a dispatch office: 4 full-time staff, overtime at 16% of paid hours last year. Replacing half the overtime with one additional hire costs $70k per year fully loaded. Overtime is concentrated in two seasonal peaks; a hire is paid for the full year.
input:
Staffing decisions can have a significant impact on both service quality and operating costs, and the dispatch office considered here provides a useful illustration of the trade-offs involved. The office currently employs 4 full-time staff, and over the course of last year, overtime accounted for 16% of paid hours, which is a substantial proportion by any standard. In response to this situation, consideration has been given to replacing half of the overtime — equivalent to 8% of paid hours — with one additional hire. The fully loaded cost of such a hire would be $70k per year.

However, it is important to note that the overtime in question is not spread evenly throughout the year. Instead, it is concentrated in two seasonal peaks, which means that demand for additional hours is particularly intense during certain periods and considerably lower at other times. A new hire, by contrast, would be paid for the full year, regardless of whether the peaks are in progress or not. This creates a potential mismatch between the pattern of costs and the pattern of demand, underscoring the complexity of the decision. Ultimately, decision-makers will need to weigh the $70k annual cost of the additional hire against the overtime expenditure it would displace, taking into account the seasonal profile described above, in order to arrive at a balanced and sustainable outcome.
target:
Replacing half of the dispatch office's overtime with one additional hire costs $70k per year, fully loaded. The office has 4 full-time staff. Overtime ran at 16% of paid hours last year, so the swap removes overtime equal to 8% of paid hours and replaces it with a salaried post paid across the whole year.

The case turns on the shape of the overtime, not its total. The overtime is concentrated in two seasonal peaks, and that share is an average over the year: the rate inside the peaks stands above the average, and the rate outside them stands below it. Within the peaks, the hire absorbs work that overtime would otherwise cover. Across the rest of the year, the post is an addition to the existing staff, paid at its full-year cost whether or not peak work is present, with no overtime saving set against it in those months. A post bought for the peaks is therefore paid for at the year's length, while the overtime it displaces is bought only in the weeks that generate it.

The comparison as stated is incomplete in one respect: the cost of the hire is given and the cost of the overtime it replaces is not, so the net effect on the pay bill cannot be computed from these figures. What the figures establish is the commitment the office takes on, a fixed yearly cost set against overtime that arises only in two seasonal peaks. A decision on the swap needs the overtime cost for the peak periods, stated at the same yearly scale as the $70k.

fact_base: A shell-and-tube exchanger heats propylene glycol in a refinery preheat train. Duty is 660 kW. Hot stream: 180 °C in, 130 °C out. Cold stream: 35 °C in, 55 °C out. The log-mean temperature difference is 109.3 K and the installed area is 54.8 m2, giving an overall coefficient of 110 W m-2 K-1. Fouling was assessed from a single 90-day run; no cleaning cycle has been completed.
input:
Heat exchangers play a vital role in a wide range of industrial processes, and the shell-and-tube design is among the most widely used configurations. This passage reports the performance of a shell-and-tube exchanger that heats propylene glycol as part of a refinery preheat train. The duty of the exchanger was measured at 660 kW. The hot stream entered at 180 °C and left at 130 °C, representing a temperature change of 50 K, while the cold stream entered at 35 °C and left at 55 °C, corresponding to a rise of 20 K. At the two ends of the exchanger, the temperature differences between the streams were 125 K and 95 K respectively, resulting in a log-mean temperature difference of 109.3 K. With an installed area of 54.8 m2, the overall heat transfer coefficient was calculated to be 110 W m-2 K-1.

It is worth noting that fouling was assessed on the basis of a single 90-day run. As no cleaning cycle has yet been completed, the extent to which performance may change over longer periods of operation remains uncertain, and further monitoring will be required in order to fully characterise the long-term behaviour of the exchanger, highlighting the importance of continued data collection.
target:
Duty in the shell-and-tube exchanger is 660 kW, heating propylene glycol in a refinery preheat train. The propylene glycol is the cold stream, heated through the tube walls against the hot stream. The hot stream enters at 180 °C and leaves at 130 °C, a fall of 50 K. The cold stream enters at 35 °C and leaves at 55 °C, a rise of 20 K. The temperature difference between the streams is 125 K at the end where the hot stream enters and 95 K at the end where it leaves, and the log-mean temperature difference is 109.3 K. Installed area is 54.8 m2, and the overall coefficient at the stated conditions is 110 W m-2 K-1.

The coefficient is a single value for the exchanger as tested. It folds the two film resistances and the wall resistance into one number, together with whatever fouling the surfaces carried during the run, and it is separable from the area only as a product: the test fixes the duty, the temperatures, and the area, and the coefficient is what those figures return. Fouling was assessed from a single 90-day run, and no cleaning cycle has been completed. The run therefore states the coefficient for the exchanger in its tested state over the run. How the coefficient moves as fouling builds across a longer campaign, and what cleaning restores, are both outside the record, and a figure carried into design for a longer run needs a fouling allowance this test does not supply.

fact_base: Goal: compute the diffusive flux of oxygen through a stagnant water film. The diffusive flux J (mol m-2 s-1) is computed from the diffusivity D (m2 s-1) and the concentration gradient dC/dx, where C is concentration (mol m-3) and x is position (m). Fick's first law: J = -D dC/dx; the negative sign states that diffusion runs from high concentration to low concentration. Oxygen in water: D = 1.6 x 10-9 m2 s-1. Concentration falls by 0.2 mol m-3 across a film 0.4 mm thick, so dC/dx = -500 mol m-4. Worked result: J = 8.00x 10-7 mol m-2 s-1. The law as stated covers a stagnant medium; a moving medium adds convection, which the equation does not include.
input:
Diffusion is one of the most fundamental transport processes in chemical engineering, and Fick's first law provides a simple yet powerful framework for quantifying it. In this worked example, we will calculate the diffusive flux of oxygen through a stagnant water film, step by step.

Fick's first law states that J = -D dC/dx, where J is the diffusive flux (mol m-2 s-1), D is the diffusivity (m2 s-1), and dC/dx is the concentration gradient, with C representing concentration (mol m-3) and x representing position (m). The negative sign in the equation indicates that diffusion takes place from regions of high concentration to regions of low concentration, which is consistent with our physical intuition.

For oxygen in water, the diffusivity is D = 1.6 x 10-9 m2 s-1. The concentration falls by 0.2 mol m-3 across a film that is 0.4 mm thick, which means that the concentration gradient is dC/dx = -500 mol m-4. Substituting these values into Fick's first law, we obtain a flux of J = 8.00 x 10-7 mol m-2 s-1. It is worth noting that the flux is positive, even though the gradient is negative, because of the negative sign in the equation itself. The resulting flux, 8.00 x 10-7 mol m-2 s-1, is relatively small, reflecting the low diffusivity of 1.6 x 10-9 m2 s-1.

Finally, it should be emphasised that Fick's first law in the form used here applies to a stagnant medium. If the medium were moving, convection would also contribute to the transport, and this additional contribution is not included in the equation, highlighting the importance of recognising the limits of the model.
target:
Compute the diffusive flux of oxygen through a stagnant water film. The flux is 8.00 x 10-7 mol m-2 s-1, directed from the side of higher concentration toward the side of lower concentration.

Fick's first law gives the flux: J = -D dC/dx. In this relation the flux J (mol m-2 s-1) is computed from the diffusivity D (m2 s-1) and the concentration gradient dC/dx, where C is concentration (mol m-3) and x is position (m). The negative sign states that diffusion runs from high concentration to low concentration.

For oxygen in water, D = 1.6 x 10-9 m2 s-1. The concentration falls by 0.2 mol m-3 across a film 0.4 mm thick, so the gradient is dC/dx = -500 mol m-4, the sign recording that concentration decreases as x increases. Substitution in Fick's first law gives J = 8.00 x 10-7 mol m-2 s-1. The sign checks: a negative gradient in a law that carries a negative sign returns a positive flux, in the direction of decreasing concentration. The magnitude is set by the diffusivity: at 1.6 x 10-9 m2 s-1, transport through the film is slow, and the flux stays small.

Fick's first law as stated holds for a stagnant medium. A moving medium adds convection, which the equation does not include, and the total flux in a moving medium is the diffusive flux and the convective transport together, not the diffusive term alone.

fact_base: A textbook chapter section on heat exchangers, in four parts: principle, equipment, a worked example, and limits. The worked example uses only the numbers given in the principle part; no new data appear later in the chapter. The limits part states where the simple model fails, in plain terms, without new equations.
input:
## Principle

Heat exchangers are widely used in the process industries to transfer heat from a hot stream to a cold stream through a wall that keeps the two streams separate; the streams do not mix, and only heat crosses the wall. The rate at which heat is transferred is known as the duty, $Q$. Each stream obeys its own energy balance: apart from losses to the surroundings, the heat given up by the hot stream equals the heat taken up by the cold stream, and each side's share is determined by its mass flow, its specific heat capacity, and its temperature change.

At any point along the exchanger, the local rate of heat transfer is governed by the temperature difference between the streams there and by the overall heat transfer coefficient, $U$, which combines the film and wall resistances into a single quantity. However, the temperature difference is not constant along the exchanger: each stream changes temperature as it gives up or takes up heat, so the difference takes one value where the hot stream enters and another where it leaves, and sizing with a single temperature difference requires an appropriate average of a varying quantity. For a constant coefficient and constant specific heat capacities, that average is the log-mean temperature difference, $\Delta T_{lm}$, which is defined as follows:

$$\Delta T_{lm} = (\Delta T_1 - \Delta T_2) / \ln(\Delta T_1 / \Delta T_2)$$

Here $\Delta T_1$ is the difference between the stream temperatures at the end where the hot stream enters, and $\Delta T_2$ is the difference at the end where it leaves. The sizing relation for the exchanger can then be written as

$$Q = U A \Delta T_{lm}$$

where $A$ is the heat transfer area. This relation captures the essential trade-offs of exchanger design: for a specified duty, the area required falls as the coefficient or the log-mean difference increases, and rises in direct proportion to the duty.

The direction of flow also plays an important role, entering through the terminal differences. In countercurrent flow, the streams enter at opposite ends and the temperature difference is maintained more evenly along the length; the cold stream can even leave hotter than the hot stream leaves. In cocurrent flow, both streams enter at the same end and the difference decreases from its largest value there; the cold stream cannot leave hotter than the hot stream leaves. In both arrangements the log-mean difference is formed from the terminal differences in the same way; the terminal differences themselves, and hence the required area, are what differ.

## Equipment

Shell-and-tube exchangers carry one stream through a bundle of tubes while the other flows across the outside of the tubes, inside a shell. Baffles inside the shell support the tubes and direct the shell-side stream across the bundle, raising the shell-side coefficient at the cost of pressure drop. The tube-side stream may make several passes through the bundle, and the shell-side stream may likewise make more than one pass; passes increase the velocity, and hence the coefficient, in a given shell, although they complicate the temperature pattern the log-mean difference summarises. The construction is robust, covers the widest range of pressure and temperature of the common types, and the tube side can be opened for mechanical cleaning.

Plate exchangers pass the streams through narrow channels between corrugated plates, sealed by gaskets. The narrow channels give high coefficients in a compact unit, and the pack opens for cleaning, suiting duties that foul and need frequent access. Nevertheless, the gaskets impose clear limits: pressures and temperatures beyond the gasket material's range cannot be accommodated, and the narrow channels are less tolerant of solids than a tube.

A double-pipe exchanger, one pipe inside another, is the simplest construction and is used for small duties. Air-cooled exchangers pass one stream through finned tubes and use fans to drive air across the fins; they are larger than a water-cooled unit of the same duty and are chosen where cooling water is scarce or restricted. The choice among types turns on the pressures and temperatures to be contained, the fouling behaviour of the streams, the access needed for cleaning, and the space available. The sizing relation of the Principle section applies to each type once its coefficient and area are stated.

## Worked example

Let us consider an exchanger to be sized for a specified duty, with the terminal temperatures of both streams specified and the overall coefficient taken from experience with the same pair of fluids in the same type of exchanger. The task is to find the area required.

The first step is to determine the terminal differences: at the end where the hot stream enters, from the hot stream's inlet temperature and the cold stream's temperature there, and at the end where it leaves, from the two temperatures there. The log-mean temperature difference then follows from the two terminal differences by the relation in the Principle section. The area follows from rearranging the sizing relation: $A$ is obtained from $Q = U A \Delta T_{lm}$ with the duty in the numerator and the coefficient and the log-mean difference together in the denominator.

There are two useful ways of checking the result. The first is a units check: the coefficient carries units of power per unit area per unit temperature difference, so dividing the duty by the coefficient and the log-mean difference gives a result in units of area, as required. The second is a limiting case: as the two terminal differences approach equality, the log-mean difference approaches their common value, and the relation returns the area that a constant difference of that value would require, which is the result it must give when the difference does not vary. A further sense check follows from the relation's form: at a fixed coefficient and fixed terminal temperatures, a larger specified duty should return a proportionally larger area, and an area that moved in the opposite direction would indicate an error.

## Limits

It is important to recognise that the sizing relation treats its quantities as constants, and its limits are the limits of that treatment. The coefficient is taken as a single value for the whole exchanger. In practice it varies with temperature along the length and falls as fouling builds on the surfaces. An area calculated from a clean coefficient is therefore an area for the exchanger in its cleaned state, rather than as it will run after months in service. Designers allow for this with a fouling allowance in the coefficient, although such an allowance is not a prediction of how fast fouling will grow.

The log-mean difference is the correct average only for a constant coefficient and constant specific heat capacities. Where a stream's specific heat capacity varies strongly with temperature, the temperature profiles take shapes the log mean does not properly average, and it is better to treat the exchanger in sections, each with its own mean difference. A stream that condenses or boils holds its temperature while it changes phase, and the terminal-difference construction can accommodate that case; even so, the coefficient on that side varies along the length, and the single-coefficient treatment weakens as it does.

Finally, arrangements with several passes do not follow the pure countercurrent pattern, and the log-mean difference must then be multiplied by a correction factor depending on the arrangement and terminal temperatures. As the cold stream's outlet temperature approaches the hot stream's outlet temperature, this factor falls steeply, and an arrangement whose factor has fallen a long way ought really to be changed rather than sized. Other effects, including maldistribution, bypassing, and heat loss to the surroundings, lie outside the relation altogether. The relation also sizes only for the stated terminal conditions: behaviour at other flows and temperatures must be found by a rating calculation, with the area fixed and the outlet temperatures unknown, and this is not a matter of reading the sizing relation backwards.

fact_base: A tutorial passage explains representative sampling of a powder blend. The passage covers where samples are taken, how many increments form one sample, and why a single grab sample misleads. No numerical limits are quoted; regulatory limits belong to the site's permit, not to the passage.
input:
Sampling is a critical step in the quality assessment of powder blends, because the results of any subsequent analysis can only ever be as reliable as the sample on which the analysis is performed. Unfortunately, powder blends are prone to segregation, which means that the composition of the blend may vary considerably from one part of a lot to another. This happens because particles of different sizes and densities tend to separate during handling and storage: finer particles tend to settle downwards, while coarser particles often migrate towards the top and the sides of a container, and vibration during transport can make the situation even worse.

In order to address this challenge, it is standard practice to take a series of small increments from a wide variety of locations within the lot, including different depths and, where applicable, different containers, or from across the full width of a moving stream at various points in time. These increments are then combined together to form a single composite sample, which is the sample that is ultimately analysed. The idea behind this approach is that each region of the lot should contribute to the final sample in proportion to its share of the lot as a whole.

By contrast, a single grab sample taken from one convenient location can be highly misleading. Such a sample may accurately reflect the material at the point where it was taken, but it tells us little or nothing about the rest of the lot, and it may badly misrepresent the blend's overall composition. It is also worth noting that questions of acceptance — whether the blend meets the limits set out in the site's permit — are separate from the sampling process itself, which is concerned with establishing what the blend actually contains.
target:
A powder blend is sampled to establish what the lot contains, and the sample serves that purpose only if the blend's composition can be read from it. Blends segregate. Particles differ in size and density, and handling sorts them: fines settle toward the bottom and centre of a container, coarse particles roll toward the walls and the upper layers, and vibration in transport drives the sorting further. A sample drawn from one place in the lot reports that place, not the lot.

Increments are therefore drawn from many places: across the surface and at depth, from several containers where the lot is packed in more than one, and, where the blend is moving, from the full cross-section of the stream at intervals along the run. Each increment is small. The increments are combined into one composite sample, and the composite is the sample that analysis reports. Their number and placing are set so that every region of the lot contributes to the composite in proportion to its share of the lot; an increment pattern that favours the accessible surface rebuilds the bias the pattern exists to remove.

A single grab sample misleads because it confuses a location with the lot. Taken from the top of a container, it overstates the coarse fraction; taken after transport, it reports the sorting the journey imposed. Its result is accurate for the material in the scoop and silent about everything outside it. Whether the blend passes is a separate question, judged against limits held in the site's permit: sampling establishes what the blend contains, and the permit states what it must contain.

fact_base: A contract packaging firm runs 2 plants; revenue is $60 million per year. Evidence base: order records for 12 months, 15726 orders. On-time delivery over the last two quarters was 91%, against a target of 95%. Overtime cost was $2.5 million last year, up 29% on the year before. The order backlog stands at 3.8 weeks, against 1.7 weeks a year ago. Plant 2 accounts for 59% of late orders. A scheduling system for all plants is quoted at $334k; Plant 2 alone is $129k. An internal estimate (not a vendor figure) puts the overtime reduction at Plant 2 at 15-20% in the first year. The recommendation under consideration: install at Plant 2 first, hold the other plants until Plant 2 results are reported. The operations director owns the scheduling programme.
input:
This executive summary reviews the delivery performance of a contract packaging firm that operates 2 plants and generates revenue of $60 million per year. The analysis is based on order records for 12 months, covering a total of 15726 orders, and focuses in particular on the last two quarters, during which on-time delivery was 91%, compared with a target of 95%.

A number of concerning trends can be identified. Overtime cost reached $2.5 million last year, which represents an increase of 29% compared with the year before, while the order backlog has grown to 3.8 weeks, up from just 1.7 weeks a year ago. It is also notable that Plant 2 is responsible for 59% of late orders, suggesting that Plant 2 is where the problem is concentrated rather than evenly spread across the business. A scheduling system covering all plants has been quoted at $334k, while Plant 2 alone would cost $129k. According to an internal estimate, which it should be stressed is not a vendor figure, installing the system at Plant 2 could reduce overtime at Plant 2 by 15-20% in the first year.

In light of these findings, the recommendation under consideration is to install the system at Plant 2 first, at $129k, while holding the other plants until results from Plant 2 are reported, rather than committing the full $334k at once. The scheduling programme is owned by the operations director, who will oversee Plant 2's implementation and the wider programme going forward.
target:
Install the scheduling system at Plant 2 first, and hold the other plants until Plant 2 results are reported. On-time delivery is 91% against a target of 95%, on order records for 12 months covering 15726 orders. The firm is a contract packaging business running 2 plants with revenue of $60 million per year, and the shortfall is concentrated in one place: Plant 2 accounts for 59% of late orders.

The supporting figures move together. Overtime cost was $2.5 million last year, up 29% on the year before. The order backlog stands at 3.8 weeks, against 1.7 weeks a year ago; the backlog has more than doubled in a year. A scheduling system for all plants is quoted at $334k, and Plant 2 alone is $129k. An internal estimate, not a vendor figure, puts the overtime reduction at Plant 2 at 15-20% in the first year.

The sequencing is the substance of the recommendation. Plant 2 carries the majority of late orders, so the system is tested where the failure is, at $129k of the $334k full cost, before the remaining plant is committed. The operations director owns the scheduling programme. The weakest figure in the set is the internal estimate of the overtime reduction, and the Plant 2 installation is the test of it: Plant 2's results, reported before any wider installation, decide the second step.

fact_base: An amine absorption unit was tested at pilot scale on gas from a cement kiln. Over 60 days at 11 t of carbon dioxide per day, the unit captured 83% of the carbon dioxide in the treated gas. Steam demand was 3.7 gigajoules per tonne of carbon dioxide captured; solvent loss was 1.8 kg per tonne captured. Beyond 60 days, the effect of kiln dust on the solvent is untested.
input:
Carbon capture is widely recognised as an important technology for reducing industrial emissions, and amine absorption is one of the most established approaches available. This passage reports a pilot-scale test of an amine absorption unit treating gas from a cement kiln. The test was conducted over 60 days, at a rate of 11 t of carbon dioxide per day, and a range of performance indicators was recorded throughout the period.

The results were as follows. The unit captured 83% of the carbon dioxide in the treated gas. Steam demand was 3.7 gigajoules per tonne of carbon dioxide captured, while solvent loss amounted to 1.8 kg per tonne captured. These figures provide a useful initial picture of the unit's performance under the conditions studied, and they form a basis for comparing the process with alternative configurations in future work. Steam demand is particularly significant because, in amine-based capture, the solvent must be regenerated by heating, and the energy required for regeneration typically represents a major component of the overall operating cost of the process. Solvent loss, meanwhile, represents an ongoing make-up requirement that must be factored into any assessment of the process economics.

It should nevertheless be noted that certain questions remain open. In particular, the effect of kiln dust on the solvent beyond 60 days is untested, and it is possible that longer-term operation could reveal effects that were not apparent during the test period. Further work over an extended timeframe would therefore be valuable in order to fully characterise the long-term behaviour of the solvent, highlighting the need for continued monitoring as the technology is developed further.
target:
An amine absorption unit was tested at pilot scale on gas from a cement kiln. The test ran over 60 days at 11 t of carbon dioxide per day, and capture, steam demand, and solvent loss were recorded across the run. The treated gas is the gas passed through the unit during the run, and capture is stated against the carbon dioxide that gas carried. The question the test answers is what the unit captures on this gas, and at what consumption of steam and solvent; what kiln dust does to the solvent over a longer exposure stands outside the test, and the closing states the results inside that boundary.

The unit captured 83% of the carbon dioxide in the treated gas. Steam demand was 3.7 gigajoules per tonne of carbon dioxide captured. Solvent loss was 1.8 kg per tonne captured. The denominators are part of the results: steam and solvent are charged against each tonne captured, not each tonne treated, so both consumption figures move if the capture rate moves, and they are comparable with another unit's figures only where the capture rates and the basis agree. On the stated basis, steam is the energy term of the process and solvent loss is the make-up term, and the two figures together price the capture the first figure reports. The capture figure is a mean over the whole run, and the consumption figures are means on the same basis; the test does not report their variation within the run, and no trend across the run is stated.

The claim the test supports is correspondingly narrow: capture at the stated rate, at the stated steam and solvent consumption, on cement-kiln gas over the run's length. Kiln dust reaches the solvent with the gas, and its effect on the solvent beyond 60 days is untested.

subtype: worked example with equation: Fourier conduction
fact_base: A flat stainless steel wall has thickness 12 mm and thermal conductivity $k$ of 16 W m-1 K-1. The temperature difference $\Delta T$ across the wall is 129 K, giving a heat flux $q$ of 172000 W m-2. The calculation is steady and one-dimensional; film resistances are excluded.
input:
Heat conduction through solid walls is a fundamental topic in heat transfer, and Fourier's law provides the foundation for analysing it quantitatively. In this worked example, we will calculate the heat flux $q$ (W m-2) through a flat stainless steel wall, using the thermal conductivity $k$ (W m-1 K-1), the temperature difference $\Delta T$ across the wall, and the wall thickness $\Delta x$. Fourier's law is expressed as:

$$q = k \frac{\Delta T}{\Delta x}$$

The wall in question is 12 mm thick, and the thermal conductivity of the stainless steel is $k$ = 16 W m-1 K-1. The temperature difference across the wall, $\Delta T$, is 129 K. Before substituting, the thickness must be converted into metres, giving $\Delta x$ = 0.012 m. Substituting the values, we obtain $q$ = 172000 W m-2.

This is a large flux, and it arises because the temperature difference of 129 K is concentrated across a thickness of only 0.012 m, corresponding to a temperature gradient of 10750 K m-1. It should be noted that the calculation assumes steady, one-dimensional conduction, and that film resistances have been excluded, which means that the result represents the conduction through the solid wall itself rather than the overall transfer between fluids on either side. Recognising these assumptions is important when applying the result in practice, as real situations may involve additional resistances that reduce the flux below the calculated value. The units also check out: W m-1 K-1, multiplied by K and divided by m, gives W m-2, as it should for a heat flux.
target:
The heat flux $q$ (W m-2) through a flat stainless steel wall is calculated from the thermal conductivity $k$ (W m-1 K-1), the temperature difference $\Delta T$ (K) across the wall, and the wall thickness $\Delta x$ (m), by Fourier's law:

$$q = k \frac{\Delta T}{\Delta x}$$

The wall is 12 mm thick, with thermal conductivity $k$ of 16 W m-1 K-1, and the temperature difference $\Delta T$ across the wall is 129 K. In metres the thickness is $\Delta x$ = 0.012 m, and substitution gives $q$ = 172000 W m-2.

The size of the flux is a gradient effect. The difference of 129 K falls across 0.012 m, a gradient of 10750 K m-1, and the conductivity multiplies that gradient into the flux. The calculation is steady and one-dimensional: the temperature varies only in the direction through the wall, and the flux is stated per unit area, so the extent of the wall does not enter. Heat flows from the hotter face toward the colder face, and the sign of the result follows the direction chosen for $\Delta x$.

Film resistances are excluded. The stated difference is the drop across the solid alone; a wall bounded by fluids carries part of its total temperature drop in the films on its faces, leaving a smaller drop across the solid and a smaller flux than the figure calculated here. The result is therefore the flux the wall itself conducts under the stated difference, and it is checked by its units: W m-1 K-1 multiplied by K and divided by m returns W m-2, the unit of the flux the example set out to find.

fact_base: The rate constant k (s-1) of a first-order liquid-phase reaction was measured at two temperatures. At 300 K, k = 0.029 s-1. At 340 K, k = 2.331 s-1, computed from the Arrhenius relation with activation energy 93 kJ mol-1 as a derived value. Each temperature was measured in triplicate; the relative standard deviation of k was 4%. Above 340 K the solvent evaporated during sampling, so no rate constant is reported above 340 K.
input:
Reaction kinetics is a cornerstone of chemical engineering, and the temperature dependence of reaction rates is one of the most important aspects of the subject. This passage reports measurements of the rate constant k (s-1) of a first-order liquid-phase reaction at two temperatures. Measurements at each temperature were carried out in triplicate, and the relative standard deviation of k was found to be 4%, indicating good reproducibility. The reaction was studied in the liquid phase, and the measurements were performed in a manner designed to ensure that the samples analysed were representative of the reacting mixture at each of the temperatures investigated.

At 300 K, the rate constant was measured as k = 0.029 s-1. At 340 K, the value of k was 2.331 s-1. It should be noted that this value is a derived value rather than a directly measured one, having been computed from the Arrhenius relation using an activation energy of 93 kJ mol-1.

The increase in temperature of 40 K therefore corresponds to an increase in the rate constant from 0.029 s-1 to 2.331 s-1, demonstrating the strong sensitivity of the reaction rate to temperature. This behaviour is consistent with the well-known exponential dependence embodied in the Arrhenius relation.

Unfortunately, no rate constant is reported above 340 K. This is because, above 340 K, the solvent evaporated during sampling, which made it impossible to obtain reliable samples under those conditions. Further work would be needed to extend the measurements beyond this limit, perhaps by adopting a modified sampling technique, highlighting the practical challenges that can arise in experimental kinetics and the care needed when interpreting values that have been derived rather than measured directly.
target:
The rate constant k (s-1) of a first-order liquid-phase reaction was measured at two temperatures. A first-order reaction has a rate proportional to the concentration of the single reactant it consumes, and k is the constant of that proportionality: the larger k, the larger the fraction of reactant consumed in each second at a given concentration. Each temperature was measured in triplicate, and the relative standard deviation of k was 4%. The measurements were made on the reacting liquid itself, at the temperature of the reaction, and the constant reported for each temperature is the value the triplicate measurements returned.

At 300 K, k = 0.029 s-1. At 340 K, k = 2.331 s-1. The second value is derived, not measured: it is computed from the Arrhenius relation with an activation energy of 93 kJ mol-1, and it is stated as a derived value wherever it is used.

The interval between the temperatures is 40 K, and across it the constant rises from the measured 0.029 s-1 to the derived 2.331 s-1. The pair of values is therefore a statement about temperature sensitivity anchored at its measured end. The derived end carries the scatter of the measurements and, in addition, whatever error the activation energy holds; the standard deviation quoted belongs to the measurements and does not extend to the derivation.

No rate constant is reported above 340 K. Above that temperature the solvent evaporated during sampling, and a sample that loses solvent while it is collected no longer carries the composition of the reacting liquid. The limit sits in the sampling step, not in the reaction: the reported range ends at 340 K because measurement failed there, not because the kinetics changed. The same point governs any use of the pair outside the interval: an extrapolation carries the derivation further from its measured anchor, and the sampling limit that closed the range stands in the way of checking it.

fact_base: An amine absorption unit was tested at pilot scale on gas from a cement kiln. Over 60 days at 14 t of carbon dioxide per day, the unit captured 87% of the carbon dioxide in the treated gas. Steam demand was 3.9 gigajoules per tonne of carbon dioxide captured; solvent loss was 2.1 kg per tonne captured. Beyond 60 days, the effect of kiln dust on the solvent is untested.
input:
Pilot-scale testing plays an essential role in the development of carbon capture processes, providing data under realistic conditions before any commitment to larger installations. This passage reports a test of an amine absorption unit operated on gas from a cement kiln. The test extended over 60 days, processing 14 t of carbon dioxide per day.

During the test, the unit captured 87% of the carbon dioxide in the treated gas. Steam demand was 3.9 gigajoules per tonne of carbon dioxide captured, and solvent loss was 2.1 kg per tonne captured. These results indicate that the unit was able to sustain a high capture rate over the test period while consuming steam and solvent at the rates stated, offering encouragement for the further development of the process.

Nevertheless, some caution is warranted when interpreting the findings. Beyond 60 days, the effect of kiln dust on the solvent is untested, and it remains possible that dust accumulating in the solvent over a longer period could alter its performance in ways that the present test could not reveal. Additional long-term testing would be beneficial in order to address this uncertainty and to build a more complete understanding of solvent behaviour over extended operation.
target:
Capture reached 87% of the carbon dioxide in the treated gas in a pilot amine absorption unit run on gas from a cement kiln. The unit treated cement-kiln gas throughout. The run lasted 60 days at 14 t of carbon dioxide per day. Steam demand was 3.9 gigajoules per tonne of carbon dioxide captured, and solvent loss was 2.1 kg per tonne captured.

Steam and solvent are both stated per tonne captured, and both figures are reported as measured, on the run as a whole. The basis matters for comparison: a unit capturing a smaller share of the gas can show a lower steam figure per tonne treated while using more steam per tonne actually captured, and the per-tonne-captured basis is the one that prices the product of the unit. On that basis the run's two consumption figures stand together, each stated for a tonne of carbon dioxide taken out of the kiln gas.

The claim closes at the run's edge. Beyond 60 days, the effect of kiln dust on the solvent is untested. Dust enters with the gas throughout the run, and the exposure within the run showed in the reported figures only as far as they go; solvent condition after longer exposure, and any rise in solvent loss that follows from it, are outside what this test states.

fact_base: A gravity settler removes sand from a process stream. Design overflow rate is 0.53 m h-1 at a throughput of 284 m3 h-1, giving a plan area of 536 m2. The overflow-rate basis is a vendor rule for this solid; no settling test on the actual slurry has been run.
input: It is important to note that gravity settlers play a crucial role in the removal of sand from process streams, and this passage delves into the key design considerations. The design is based on the overflow rate, which can be defined as the volumetric throughput divided by the plan area of the settler. With a throughput of 284 m3 h-1 and a design overflow rate of 0.53 m h-1, the required plan area works out to 536 m2. This parameter is particularly significant because, in an ideal settler, a particle is removed when its settling velocity exceeds the upward velocity of the liquid, and the overflow rate represents that upward velocity over the whole plan area, providing a convenient basis for sizing. The units themselves underscore the comparison: a throughput in m3 h-1 divided by an area in m2 returns a velocity in m h-1, the same unit as a settling velocity. It is worth noting that the design figure of 0.53 m h-1 is a vendor rule for sand, and the rule is specific to this solid; a finer or lighter solid would typically take a lower rate. Importantly, this figure was not measured on the stream to be treated, and no settling test on the actual slurry has been run, so the sizing stands on the vendor basis and carries the limitations associated with that basis. Factors such as particle size distribution, solids concentration and inlet distribution can each influence the removal achieved in practice, and the vendor figure does not account for any of them. The plan area of 536 m2 is the area required by the rule at the stated throughput; the length and width are not fixed by the sizing and will follow from the available plot and the inlet arrangement. Overall, a settling test on the actual slurry is the measurement that would replace the vendor rule with a site-specific value, and the area should be regarded as provisional until such a test has been carried out.

subtype: worked example with equation: Raoult partial pressure
fact_base: An ideal liquid mixture holds hexane in heptane at a liquid mole fraction $x$ of 0.34 for the volatile component. Its pure-component vapour pressure $P^*$ at the mixture temperature is 5.9 kPa, so the partial pressure $p$ is 2 kPa by Raoult's law. Raoult's law assumes an ideal solution; activity coefficients for the real mixture are not applied.
input:
In this worked example, we will calculate the partial pressure $p$ of hexane over a liquid mixture of hexane in heptane, making use of the well-known Raoult's law. The liquid mole fraction $x$ of hexane, which is the volatile component in this system, is 0.34, and the pure-component vapour pressure $P^*$ of hexane at the mixture temperature is 5.9 kPa.

It is worth recalling that the partial pressure of a component in the vapour above a liquid mixture can be understood as the pressure that the component alone would exert if it occupied the vapour volume at the mixture temperature, and the overall vapour pressure is obtained by summing the partial pressures of all of the components. Raoult's law provides a simple and elegant relationship for an ideal solution, stating that the partial pressure of a component is equal to its liquid mole fraction multiplied by its pure-component vapour pressure at the same temperature, as follows:

$$p = x P^*$$

Substituting $x$ = 0.34 and $P^*$ = 5.9 kPa into this expression gives $p$ = 2 kPa. This result can be sanity-checked against the limiting case: as $x$ approaches one, the law naturally returns $P^*$ itself, which is the vapour pressure of pure hexane, and at $x$ = 0.34 the partial pressure sits proportionally below $P^*$, exactly as one would expect. It is important to note that Raoult's law fundamentally assumes an ideal solution, in which the interactions between unlike molecules are essentially the same as those between like molecules, and the calculation presented here is carried out on that basis. Activity coefficients for the real mixture are not applied, and no correction for any departure from ideal-solution behaviour has been included. Overall, the value of 2 kPa should therefore be interpreted as the ideal-solution partial pressure of hexane over the mixture at the stated composition and temperature, bearing in mind that a real-mixture value would require the activity coefficient that this calculation omits.
target:

The partial pressure of a component in the vapour over a liquid mixture is the pressure that component alone would exert if it occupied the vapour volume at the mixture temperature; for the mixture as a whole, the vapour pressure is the sum of the partial pressures of the components. The mole fraction $x$ is the amount of hexane in the liquid divided by the total amount of liquid, the amounts taken in moles, and it fixes the share of hexane molecules among the molecules the vapour is in equilibrium with. Raoult's law gives the partial pressure of a component over an ideal solution: the liquid mole fraction of the component multiplied by its pure-component vapour pressure at the same temperature.

$$p = x P^*$$

Substitution of $x$ = 0.34 and $P^*$ = 5.9 kPa in Raoult's law gives $p$ = 2 kPa. The check on the result is the limiting case: as $x$ rises toward one, the law returns $P^*$ itself, the vapour pressure of pure hexane, and at $x$ = 0.34 the partial pressure stands below $P^*$ in the proportion the mole fraction fixes. Raoult's law holds for an ideal solution, in which the interactions between unlike molecules match the interactions between like molecules, and it is applied here on that basis. Activity coefficients for the real mixture are not applied, and no correction for departure from ideal-solution behaviour enters the calculation. The value of 2 kPa is therefore the ideal-solution partial pressure of hexane over the mixture at the stated composition and temperature, and a real-mixture value would require the activity coefficient that this calculation omits.

fact_base: Inventory policy for a spare motor: mean demand 873 units per week, standard deviation 127 units per week, replenishment lead time 9 weeks. Safety stock for a 95% cycle service level is 629 units. Demand is treated as normal and independent between weeks; seasonal peaks are excluded.
input:
The spare motor holding is set by a safety stock of 629 units. Safety stock is the stock held against demand variation during replenishment: demand for the motor averages 873 units per week with a standard deviation of 127 units per week, replenishment takes 9 weeks, and the 629 units cover the variation expected over that lead time at a 95% cycle service level. A cycle service level of 95% states the share of replenishment cycles that end without a stockout while the replacement order is in transit; the remaining cycles carry the stockout risk that the policy accepts.

The calculation treats demand as normal and independent between weeks. Under that treatment the variation over the lead time grows more slowly than the lead time itself, because a high week and a low week offset each other inside the 9 weeks, and the safety stock is sized on the combined variation rather than on nine repetitions of the worst week. Independence is the condition the figure rests on: a cause that raises demand for several weeks in succession breaks the offsetting, and the cover the 629 units provide falls below the stated service level.

Seasonal peaks are excluded from the policy. Demand in a peak period sits outside the distribution the safety stock was sized on, and the holding does not claim cover for it; a peak is met by ordering ahead of the season, not by raising the year-round safety stock. The policy is therefore a statement about ordinary weeks: 873 units per week on average, variation of 127 units per week, 9 weeks to replenish, and 629 units held to keep stockouts to the accepted share of cycles.

fact_base: Cost review of a cross-dock transfer: 861 km per trip at $1.09 per km, 893 trips per year. Annual transport cost is $838k. Costs are carrier invoices for the last 12 months; empty running is included in the trip count.
input:
This cost review examines the annual transport cost associated with a cross-dock transfer operation, drawing on the available invoicing data in order to establish the overall expenditure. In total, the annual transport cost comes to $838k, a figure that is built up from a small number of key components. The transfer itself runs 861 km per trip, at a cost of $1.09 per km, and a total of 893 trips are made per year. Distance emerges as the principal driver of the figure: the rate of $1.09 per km is the carrier's charged rate, and the annual cost moves in direct proportion to both the trip count and the distance travelled per trip, so that a change in either one feeds straight through into the total, with no fixed element in the stated basis to absorb it.

The evidence base for this review consists of the carrier invoices for the last 12 months, which means that the rate and the trip count are invoiced values rather than estimates, and the annual figure is essentially a record of what the transfer actually cost over that period under the operation as it was run. Importantly, the trip count includes empty running: a trip is counted whenever the vehicle travels the route, loaded or not, so the $838k represents the cost of the entire movement pattern that the cross-dock requires, and not merely the loaded legs. It follows that any comparison with an alternative arrangement needs to be made on exactly the same basis, with empty running included in the count, otherwise the comparison will understate the present cost.

Finally, the figure carries the limitations of its base period: twelve months of invoices fix the rate and the trip count at the values that period happened to produce, and a rate revision by the carrier, or a change in the number of trips that the operation demands, would move the annual cost away from $838k in direct proportion. Within those limits, however, the cost statement is complete: 861 km per trip, $1.09 per km, 893 trips per year, and $838k per year, all grounded in invoiced evidence.

fact_base: Design report for a distillation column, in four sections: basis, sizing, materials, and risks. Design throughput is 41 t per day and the removal or separation duty is 88% of the key component. Materials are 316L stainless steel for wetted parts; the basis section states this once. The risks section names fouling and turndown as open items; neither is resolved in the report.
input:
## Basis

This report presents the design of a distillation column that separates a key component from a liquid feed by means of fractionation. The design throughput is 41 t per day of feed. The separation duty is the recovery of 88% of the key component at the specified product points: in other words, the column is sized to take that share of the key component overhead while the remainder leaves with the bottoms, and every sizing figure in this report traces back to those two statements. It is important that the duty be stated in this form, as a recovery of a named component, because a design that does not state its duty in that way cannot readily be checked, and stating it here allows the sizing section to be audited against it.

The wetted parts of the column are specified in 316L stainless steel. The grade is fixed here, in the basis, and the materials section will work from it without restating it; corrosion, fabrication and inspection are all assessed against that single specification. No alternative material is carried in the design.

The basis is a steady-state, continuous design. Feed rate, feed condition and product specifications are held at their design values throughout the sizing exercise; departures from those values in actual operation are treated later, in the risks section, rather than by adjusting the basis itself. Physical properties are taken for the design feed composition over the temperature and pressure range that the column internals will see, and the equilibrium data behind the stage calculation belong to the same property set, which ensures that the material balance, the stage count and the hydraulics all rest on one consistent description of the mixture. Utilities are assumed to be available at the battery limit at their normal supply conditions; the reboiler and condenser are sized as part of the column system, and their detailed design follows the same basis. Design margins are not buried in the basis figures: where a margin is applied, it is applied openly in the sizing step that needs it, so that the margin can be located and challenged.

## Sizing

The sizing proceeds in the order in which the calculation depends on itself. The material balance comes first: at 41 t per day of feed and a recovery of 88% of the key component overhead, the distillate and bottoms rates are fixed, and with them the internal liquid and vapour traffic in each section of the column once a reflux condition is chosen. The stage requirement then follows from the equilibrium relation for the mixture and the operating lines that the balance defines; the count obtained in this way is a count of theoretical stages, and it is converted into actual contacting stages through a stage efficiency that reflects the contacting device selected. It should be noted that efficiency is an empirical quantity, and the value adopted belongs to the device and the system, not to the calculation method.

Diameter is set by hydraulics. The column must be able to pass the largest vapour and liquid traffic in each section without flooding, and the diameter is chosen so that the design traffic stands below the flooding limit with the margin that the design practice for the selected internals requires. Diameter and stage count together fix the height: the contacting height from the number of actual stages and their spacing, plus disengaging space above the top stage, feed entry space, and a bottom sump that holds enough liquid for stable level control and pump suction. Pressure drop is calculated stage by stage over the same traffic, because the pressure at the base sets the boiling temperatures that the reboiler must reach and feeds back into the property set. The condenser and reboiler duties come out of the balance around the column at the chosen reflux: the condenser removes the heat that the rising vapour carries in, and the reboiler returns it, and the two duties together close the energy balance on which the sizing stands. A sizing that does not close its own material and energy balances has not been properly checked, and the closure is an integral part of the result.

## Materials

The specification fixed in the basis governs every wetted part: the shell, the internals, the nozzles and the wetted faces of attached equipment are all assessed as one material system. The assessment essentially turns on three key questions. The first question is corrosion: the feed and its products contact the metal over the full temperature range of the column, including the hot base, and the grade is required to resist the mixture as fed, not a cleaned-up version of it; where the feed carries trace components that are known to attack stainless steels, the assessment addresses those components by name rather than the bulk composition. The second question is fabrication: the grade must weld with standard procedures, form to the shell and internals geometry, and accept the surface finish that the contacting devices need in order to seat and seal. The third question is inspection and repair: the material must allow the welds to be examined and local damage to be made good over the life of the unit without resorting to exotic procedures.

Non-wetted parts are separated from this assessment. Supports, external attachments and bolting follow their own specifications and are not upgraded to the wetted grade where the process does not touch them; conversely, no wetted part is value-engineered down to a lesser material, because the corrosion question has already been settled for the grade that the basis fixes. Gaskets and seals are the remaining wetted items that are not metal, and they are selected for compatibility with the same feed over the same temperature range, with the same trace components taken into consideration. A materials section that settles the shell and forgets the gaskets has not, in the end, settled the wetted system as a whole.

## Risks

Two risks are named here as open items, and it should be emphasised that neither of them is resolved in this report.

Fouling is the first. Deposition on the contacting surfaces and in the reboiler degrades a distillation column slowly, and on both of its duties at once: heat transfer falls, so the reboiler delivers less boil-up at the same steam condition, and open area falls, so pressure drop rises and the flooding limit is approached at unchanged throughput. The design as sized carries clean-surface hydraulics, and the fouling tendency of the feed has not been established either by test or by operating history on a comparable service. Until it is, the margin between design traffic and flooding should be read as partly spoken for, and the operating plan should include the pressure-drop trend as the fouling indicator, since pressure drop is the measurement that announces fouling before the separation duty visibly fails.

Turndown is the second risk. The column is sized at its design throughput, and its behaviour well below that rate is not established by the sizing calculation. At low liquid rates, the contacting devices distribute liquid less evenly, and at low vapour rates some devices weep, passing liquid downward without the contact that the stage count assumes; either effect spends separation that the design counted on, so the duty of 88% recovery is not guaranteed at deep turndown by anything in this report. The control range of the reflux and level loops over the same span is likewise untested. Turndown is therefore recorded here as an open item for operating trials, and the report closes with both items still open: fouling untested, turndown untested, and the design valid at the basis on which it was sized.
