Feed rate, feed condition and product specifications are held at their design values throughout the sizing; departures from those values in operation are treated in the risks section, not by adjusting the basis. Physical properties are taken for the design feed composition over the temperature and pressure range the column internals will see, and the equilibrium data behind the stage calculation belong to the same property set, so that the material balance, the stage count and the hydraulics all rest on one consistent description of the mixture. Utilities are assumed available at the battery limit at their normal supply conditions; the reboiler and condenser are sized as part of the column system, and their detailed design follows the same basis. Design margins are not buried in the basis figures: where a margin is applied, it is applied openly in the sizing step that needs it, so that the margin can be found and challenged.

## Sizing

Sizing proceeds in the order the calculation depends on itself. The material balance comes first: at 41 t per day of feed and a recovery of 88% of the key component overhead, the distillate and bottoms rates are fixed, and with them the internal liquid and vapour traffic in each section of the column once a reflux condition is chosen. The stage requirement follows from the equilibrium relation for the mixture and the operating lines the balance defines; the count obtained is a count of theoretical stages, and it is converted to actual contacting stages through a stage efficiency that reflects the contacting device selected. Efficiency is an empirical quantity, and the value adopted belongs to the device and the system, not to the calculation method.

Diameter is set by hydraulics. The column must pass the largest vapour and liquid traffic in each section without flooding, and the diameter is chosen so that the design traffic stands below the flooding limit with the margin the design practice for the selected internals requires. Diameter and stage count together fix the height: the contacting height from the number of actual stages and their spacing, plus disengaging space above the top stage, feed entry space, and a bottom sump that holds enough liquid for stable level control and pump suction. Pressure drop is calculated stage by stage over the same traffic, because the pressure at the base sets the boiling temperatures the reboiler must reach and feeds back into the property set. Condenser and reboiler duties come out of the balance around the column at the chosen reflux: the condenser removes the heat the rising vapour carries in, and the reboiler returns it, and the two duties close the energy balance the sizing stands on. A sizing that does not close its own material and energy balances has not been checked, and the closure is part of the result.

## Materials

The specification fixed in the basis governs every wetted part: shell, internals, nozzles and the wetted faces of attached equipment are assessed as one material system. The assessment turns on three questions. The first is corrosion: the feed and its products contact the metal over the full temperature range of the column, including the hot base, and the grade is required to resist the mixture as fed, not a cleaned-up version of it; where the feed carries trace components known to attack stainless steels, the assessment addresses those components by name rather than the bulk composition. The second question is fabrication: the grade must weld with standard procedures, form to the shell and internals geometry, and accept the surface finish the contacting devices need to seat and seal. The third is inspection and repair: the material must allow the welds to be examined and local damage to be made good over the life of the unit without exotic procedures.

Non-wetted parts are separated from this assessment. Supports, external attachments and bolting follow their own specifications and are not upgraded to the wetted grade where the process does not touch them; conversely, no wetted part is value-engineered down to a lesser material, because the corrosion question has already been settled for the grade the basis fixes. Gaskets and seals are the remaining wetted items that are not metal, and they are selected for compatibility with the same feed over the same temperature range, with the same trace components considered. A materials section that settles the shell and forgets the gaskets has not settled the wetted system.

## Risks

Two risks are named as open items, and neither is resolved in this report.

Fouling is the first. Deposition on the contacting surfaces and in the reboiler degrades a distillation column slowly and on both of its duties at once: heat transfer falls, so the reboiler delivers less boil-up at the same steam condition, and open area falls, so pressure drop rises and the flooding limit approaches at unchanged throughput. The design as sized carries clean-surface hydraulics, and the feed's fouling tendency has not been established by test or by operating history on a comparable service. Until it is, the margin between design traffic and flooding should be read as partly spoken for, and the operating plan should include the pressure-drop trend as the fouling indicator, since pressure drop is the measurement that announces fouling before the separation duty visibly fails.

Turndown is the second. The column is sized at its design throughput, and its behaviour well below that rate is not established by the sizing calculation. At low liquid rates the contacting devices distribute liquid less evenly, and at low vapour rates some devices weep, passing liquid downward without the contact the stage count assumes; either effect spends separation the design counted on, so the duty of 88% recovery is not guaranteed at deep turndown by anything in this report. The control range of the reflux and level loops over the same span is likewise untested. Turndown is recorded here as an open item for operating trials, and the report closes with both items open: fouling untested, turndown untested, and the design valid at the basis on which it was sized.

fact_base: A food plant uses 1827 MWh of electricity per year in refrigeration. A heat-recovery retrofit is projected by the equipment vendor to save 16% of that use, a derived saving of 292 MWh per year at the vendor figure. Capital cost is $401k. At an electricity price of $0.13 per kWh, the derived annual saving is $38k and the derived simple payback is 10.6 years. The saving figure is a vendor projection and was not measured at this plant; refrigeration load in the summer peak month was not modelled. The recommendation is a metered trial on one of the three refrigeration lines before any capital decision. The plant engineer owns the trial.
input:
This executive summary looks at a possible heat-recovery retrofit at a food plant and at whether the project should move forward at this stage. The plant currently uses 1827 MWh of electricity per year in refrigeration, which is a substantial part of the overall picture being considered here. According to the equipment vendor, the retrofit is projected to save 16% of that electricity use, which works out to a derived saving of 292 MWh per year at the vendor figure. The capital cost of the retrofit is $401k. Using an electricity price of $0.13 per kWh, the derived annual saving is $38k, and the derived simple payback period is 10.6 years.

It is important to note, however, that the saving figure is a vendor projection and has not been measured at this plant, and, furthermore, the refrigeration load in the summer peak month was not modelled, which introduces an additional element of uncertainty into the analysis. On the basis of these considerations, the recommendation is that a metered trial should be carried out on one of the three refrigeration lines before any capital decision is taken, so that the projected saving can be tested against an actual measurement on the plant's own load. The plant engineer owns the trial.
target:
Run a metered trial on one of the three refrigeration lines before any capital decision on the heat-recovery retrofit; the plant engineer owns the trial. The recommendation rests on the size of the claim and the standing of the figure behind it. The food plant uses 1827 MWh of electricity per year in refrigeration, and the equipment vendor projects that the retrofit would save 16% of that use, a derived saving of 292 MWh per year at the vendor figure. Capital cost is $401k. At an electricity price of $0.13 per kWh, the derived annual saving is $38k and the derived simple payback is 10.6 years.

The trial is metered, so the saving it returns is a measured value on one line's refrigeration load over the trial period, set against the same line's present use.

The saving figure is a vendor projection and was not measured at this plant, and refrigeration load in the summer peak month was not modelled. The payback stands or falls with the projected saving: a measured saving below the projection lengthens the payback in proportion, and the trial exists to replace the projection with a measurement on the plant's own load before capital is committed.

fact_base: A vapour-compression unit serves an ice rink, evaporating at 0 °C and condensing at 45 °C. The Carnot coefficient of performance between these temperatures is 6.07; the installed unit achieves 2.5. The achieved value is from the manufacturer's test at full load; part-load performance is not stated.
input:
In this worked example, we consider a vapour-compression refrigeration unit that serves an ice rink, evaporating at 0 °C and condensing at 45 °C, and we examine its coefficient of performance, which can be defined as the refrigeration effect divided by the work input. It is instructive to begin with the theoretical ceiling: the Carnot coefficient of performance between these temperatures is 6.07, a value that is set by the two temperatures alone and is obtained from the evaporating temperature, expressed in absolute temperature, divided by the difference between the condensing and evaporating temperatures. No refrigerator operating between 45 °C and 0 °C can exceed this value, regardless of how it is designed.

Against this benchmark, the installed unit achieves a coefficient of performance of 2.5, based on the manufacturer's test at full load. This stands comfortably below the Carnot ceiling, as of course it must: the gap between 2.5 and 6.07 essentially reflects the combined irreversibilities of the real machine, including compression away from the isentropic path, throttling instead of expansion work, and heat transfer across finite temperature differences in both exchangers. The comparison also provides a useful sanity check on the figures: an achieved coefficient above the Carnot value would indicate that something was wrong with the measurement, while a value far below it would suggest a machine fault rather than a limitation of the cycle itself. A value of 2.5 against a ceiling of 6.07 is broadly in line with what one would expect from a real vapour-compression machine working between these temperatures.

It is important to note, finally, that the achieved value is the manufacturer's test value at full load, and that part-load performance is not stated; the figure should therefore be understood as carrying that scope, since at reduced load the balance between fixed losses and refrigeration effect shifts, and the full-load coefficient does not necessarily describe the unit across its operating year on the rink.

No cycle rejecting heat at 45 °C and absorbing it at 0 °C can exceed 6.07, whatever its design.

fact_base: A review passage on catalysts for carbon dioxide hydrogenation, in four parts: scope, established results, disagreements, and gaps. The review covers 109 papers from the last 12 years. The disagreements part names the quantity on which reports conflict; the gaps part names the measurement nobody reports.
input:
## Scope

This review covers the literature on catalysts for carbon dioxide hydrogenation, that is, the reaction of carbon dioxide with hydrogen over a solid catalyst to give reduced carbon products, with methanol chief among them in the literature reviewed. The evidence base consists of 109 papers published over the last 12 years. A paper is included in the review if it reports a catalyst tested for this reaction with measured activity or selectivity, presented in a form that allows the test conditions to be recovered; papers that report a catalyst for the reverse reaction, or for the hydrogenation of carbon monoxide alone, fall outside the scope, because the water formed from carbon dioxide changes both the catalyst surface and the equilibrium position, meaning that results from the carbon monoxide reaction do not transfer without that correction.

It is worth emphasising that the scope is set by the reaction, rather than by the catalyst family. Copper-based catalysts dominate the base, just as they dominate the field, but oxide catalysts, noble-metal catalysts and carbide systems are all included on the same terms, so that the established results presented below reflect what the whole literature supports, and not merely what its largest family supports. Test conditions are treated as part of the evidence wherever they are reported: temperature, pressure, feed composition and space velocity are recorded alongside each result, because the disagreements section turns on them. Where a paper omits a condition that is needed for comparison, the result is carried as reported and flagged as incomparable, rather than being silently aligned with the others. The review is a reading of published measurements: it does not re-measure any catalyst, and its claims stand at the scope that the published record supports.

## Established results

Copper dispersed on zinc oxide, usually with alumina as a structural component, is the established catalyst system for methanol formation from carbon dioxide and hydrogen, and the published record supports it at a depth that no rival system currently matches. The working picture that the literature converges on has the reaction proceeding at the interface between the copper surface and the oxide: the oxide and the interface adsorb and activate carbon dioxide, the copper supplies dissociated hydrogen, and zinc species that migrate onto the copper under reaction conditions are implicated in the active site by several independent lines of evidence. The preparation method also matters, at a level the record establishes beyond dispute: catalysts prepared by co-precipitation, with the copper and zinc intimately mixed before reduction, outperform impregnated preparations of the same nominal composition, and the difference is attributed to the dispersion and interface area that the preparation creates.

Water represents the second established result. The reaction produces water, water competes for the very sites that the reaction needs, and exposure to water sinters copper; consequently, rates fall and selectivity shifts as the water partial pressure rises, and every durable result in the record is reported against that constraint. Temperature divides the products: methanol formation is favoured at lower temperatures, where equilibrium allows it but kinetics are slow, whereas the reverse water-gas shift reaction, which gives carbon monoxide, takes a growing share as the temperature rises. Promoters modify this picture at the margins rather than overturning it: zirconia as a support or promoter is repeatedly associated with improved stability and methanol selectivity, and alkali and other additives shift activity in directions that depend on loading. Overall, supports, promoters and preparation are the established levers, while the reaction network and the water constraint form the established frame within which they operate.

## Disagreements

Reports conflict on methanol selectivity at a given conversion, and, along with it, on the ranking of catalyst formulations that the selectivity figures imply. One group reports a formulation as a clear advance on the copper-zinc oxide benchmark, while another group, testing a closely similar formulation, finds it at or below the benchmark. The conflict is identified here as a conflict about selectivity at matched conversion, because that is the quantity on which the claims are made and the quantity that the record does not settle.

On weighing the two sides, the review concludes that the conflict follows the test conditions more than it follows the catalysts themselves. Selectivity to methanol falls as conversion rises along any one catalyst, because the product distribution shifts as products accumulate and water builds up; two reports at different conversions are therefore not measuring the same point, and a formulation compared against a benchmark at unmatched conversion can be made to look either better or worse purely by the choice of operating point. Feed composition also differs across the conflicting reports, in particular the share of carbon monoxide in the feed, which changes both the water formed and the surface state; space velocity differs as well, which moves conversion independently of the catalyst; and several reports state selectivity on a carbon basis that excludes carbon monoxide while others include it, so that the same experiment would print two different selectivity figures under the two conventions. Where the conditions are brought closest together — comparable conversion, comparable feed, and the same selectivity convention — the disagreement narrows to the size of the claimed advances, and the ranking of the leading formulations is not established by the present record. The limited preference the review reaches is for reports that state selectivity at a stated conversion on a stated basis: their claims can be checked, whereas the unchecked remainder cannot.

## Gaps

The measurement that nobody reports is catalyst stability, measured in a way that allows comparison. Papers report activity and selectivity from short tests, commonly at the start of operation; long runs are rare, and where a catalyst is held on stream, the report seldom gives the rate of deactivation as a measured quantity with the conditions of the run — the water partial pressure above all — stated beside it. Deactivation is the property that decides whether a catalyst survives contact with the water that this reaction necessarily makes, and it is the property that the record leaves unmeasured in comparable form. As a result, a formulation can lead the literature on activity and selectivity while its standing on the property that governs its working life remains unknown, and the present record provides no basis for ranking catalysts on lifetime at all.

This gap propagates through the rest of the review. Because deactivation is not reported on a common basis, the established results rest disproportionately on initial performance; the disagreements cannot be closed by appeal to long-run behaviour; and a reader who needs to choose a catalyst for sustained operation finds the literature richest exactly where the decision needs it least. Secondary gaps follow the same pattern: carbon balances are not always closed in print, so selectivity figures cannot always be audited, and the state of the catalyst after reaction is characterised less often than the state before it. The review closes on the primary gap: until deactivation under stated conditions is measured and reported as routinely as initial activity, comparisons in this field will continue to compare beginnings.

fact_base: Pricing case for a SaaS tier: price $374 per unit, variable cost $187 per unit, fixed costs $282k per year. Break-even volume is 1508 units per year; current volume is 801 units per year. Volume figures are last year's actuals; the effect of the price on volume is not estimated.
input:
This pricing case examines the break-even position of a SaaS tier. The tier is priced at $374 per unit, with a variable cost of $187 per unit and fixed costs of $282k per year. On this basis, the break-even volume works out to 1508 units per year. Current volume, however, is 801 units per year, which means that the tier is currently selling well below the volume it needs in order to break even. Each unit sold contributes the difference between the price and the variable cost toward covering the fixed costs, and at 801 units that contribution covers only part of the $282k, leaving the tier short of break-even by the contribution on the missing volume.

It is worth noting that the volume figures used here are last year's actuals, so the comparison effectively describes where the tier stood over the course of that year at the stated price and costs. One important quantity is, however, missing from the case: the effect of the price on volume has not been estimated. As a result, the break-even figure answers a fixed-price question, namely what volume the present price and cost structure requires, and it does not show what a different price would do, because the volume response that a price change would produce is precisely the quantity that has not been estimated.

The tier is priced at $374 per unit with a variable cost of $187 per unit and fixed costs of $282k per year, which puts break-even at 1508 units per year; current volume is 801 units per year. The gap between the two volumes is the finding: each unit sold contributes the difference between price and variable cost toward the fixed costs, and at 801 units that contribution covers only part of the $282k, leaving the tier short of break-even by the contribution on the missing volume.

It does not show what a different price would do, because the volume response that a price change would produce is the very quantity that has not been estimated.

fact_base: Pervaporation is a membrane separation in which a liquid feed contacts one side of a membrane and vacuum on the other side draws the permeating component through as vapour. Flux is the mass permeating per unit membrane area per hour (kg m-2 h-1). The separation factor is the water-to-alcohol ratio in the permeate divided by the same ratio in the feed (dimensionless). Feed: 85 wt% n-butanol in water, at 60 °C. One feed composition was tested; no test ran beyond 500 h. Polymer membrane: flux 1.8 kg m-2 h-1, separation factor 120, flux fell 8% over 500 h. Zeolite membrane: flux 1.3 kg m-2 h-1, separation factor 420, flux unchanged over 500 h within measurement error. Flux, selectivity and stability are seldom reported together for the same membrane.
input:
Pervaporation is a membrane separation process in which a liquid feed contacts one side of a membrane while a vacuum applied on the other side draws the permeating component through as a vapour. In this study, two membranes are compared using a feed of 85 wt% n-butanol in water at 60 °C, with the comparison focusing on flux and the separation factor. Flux is defined as the mass permeating per unit membrane area per hour (kg m-2 h-1), while the separation factor is defined as the water-to-alcohol ratio in the permeate divided by the same ratio in the feed, and is dimensionless.

The polymer membrane delivers a flux of 1.8 kg m-2 h-1 and a separation factor of 120. Its flux fell by 8% over 500 h, indicating that the higher throughput is not fully sustained over the test duration. The zeolite membrane, by contrast, delivers a lower flux of 1.3 kg m-2 h-1 but a considerably higher separation factor of 420, and its flux remained unchanged over 500 h within measurement error. Overall, the comparison reveals a clear trade-off: the polymer membrane leads on flux, the zeolite membrane leads on selectivity, and only the zeolite holds its flux across the period tested, so the preferred option will ultimately depend on the duty for which the membrane is intended.

It is important to note that only one feed composition was tested, and that no test ran beyond 500 h. It should also be noted that flux, selectivity and stability are seldom reported together for the same membrane; in this study, the three are reported together, albeit at one composition and over one duration.
target:

Two membranes are compared on an 85 wt% n-butanol feed in water at 60 °C, on flux and on the separation factor. Flux is the mass permeating per unit membrane area per hour (kg m-2 h-1); the separation factor is the water-to-alcohol ratio in the permeate divided by the same ratio in the feed, and is dimensionless.

The polymer membrane passes more mass and separates less sharply: flux 1.8 kg m-2 h-1, separation factor 120. Its flux fell 8% over 500 h, so the higher throughput is not held over the test duration. The zeolite membrane gives flux 1.3 kg m-2 h-1 and a separation factor of 420, and its flux was unchanged over 500 h within measurement error. The contrast is therefore two-sided: the polymer leads on flux by a wide margin and loses on selectivity by a wider one, and only the zeolite holds its flux across the period tested. The stability comparison rests on the flux record alone: unchanged within measurement error is a statement about flux over the duration, not a statement that the separation factor held its value across the same period. Which property governs the choice depends on the duty the membrane is bought for, and the comparison supplies both figures rather than a ranking.

One feed composition was tested, and no test ran beyond 500 h. Flux, selectivity and stability are seldom reported together for the same membrane; the three are reported together here, at one composition and over one duration.

fact_base: A tutorial passage explains the pump affinity laws for a centrifugal pump at varying speed. The passage states the three proportionalities in words: flow with speed, head with speed squared, power with speed cubed. A worked check is included: doubling speed multiplies power by 8. No other numbers are introduced.
input:
In this tutorial passage, we will explore the affinity laws for a centrifugal pump, which are a set of useful relationships that describe how flow, head and power vary with the speed of the pump. By the end of the passage, you will be able to state all three relationships and apply them to a simple worked check: when the speed of a pump doubles, its flow doubles, its head rises fourfold, and its power rises eightfold.

The first relationship concerns flow: the flow through a centrifugal pump varies in direct proportion to its speed, so if you double the speed, the impeller passes twice the volume in the same time and the flow doubles accordingly. The second relationship concerns head, which varies with the square of the speed: the impeller throws the liquid out faster in proportion to the speed, and the energy imparted to each unit of liquid grows with the square of that velocity, meaning that doubling the speed multiplies the head by four. The third relationship concerns power, which varies with the cube of the speed; interestingly, this is not really a separate rule, but rather follows from the two relationships before it, because power is the product of flow and head, the flow carries one factor of speed and the head carries two, and the product therefore carries three. Doubling the speed thus multiplies the power by 8, which serves as a helpful worked check that the three laws are consistent with one another.

Finally, it is important to keep the conditions of the laws in mind when applying them: they compare one pump at two speeds, moving the same liquid, at corresponding points of its characteristic, and they are not a comparison between different pumps, nor do they say anything about whether the system the pump feeds will accept the higher flow. Used within those conditions, the three proportionalities allow a known duty point to be moved to a new speed without the need for a new test.

The laws compare one pump at two speeds, moving the same liquid, at corresponding points of its characteristic; they are not a comparison between different pumps, and they say nothing about whether the system the pump feeds will accept the higher flow. Used inside those conditions, the three proportionalities let you move a known duty point to a new speed without a new test.

fact_base: Performance of a natural-draft tower at a chemical site was logged over one summer month. Mean wet-bulb temperature was 23 °C, the approach was 3 K and the range was 10 K. Performance outside the logged month, in particular at winter wet-bulb temperatures, was not measured.
input:
Performance of a natural-draft cooling tower at a chemical site was logged over one summer month. The mean wet-bulb temperature of the air over the month was 23 °C. The tower's approach was 3 K and its range was 10 K. The approach is the difference between the temperature of the water leaving the tower and the wet-bulb temperature of the air entering it; it states how closely the tower brings the water to the limit the air condition sets. The range is the difference between the temperature of the water entering the tower and the temperature of the water leaving it; it states the cooling the tower achieved across the logged month.

The two figures describe different things and are not interchangeable. The range depends on the heat load placed on the tower as much as on the tower itself, while the approach depends on the tower and on the wet-bulb temperature it worked against. An approach of 3 K at a mean wet-bulb temperature of 23 °C is the tighter statement of the pair: it fixes the leaving-water condition the tower reached under the air conditions of that month, and it is the figure a comparison with another period has to be made on.

The record carries the limit of its period. Performance was logged over one summer month, and performance outside the logged month was not measured. In particular, performance at winter wet-bulb temperatures is absent from the record: the tower's behaviour under the lower wet-bulb temperatures of winter, when both the approach it can hold and the load placed on it differ from the summer values, is not established by this log and is not claimed here.

The approach is the difference between the temperature of the water leaving the tower and the wet-bulb temperature of the air entering it; it states how closely the tower brings the water to the limit the air condition sets. fact_base: Pricing case for a catering contract: price $52 per unit, variable cost $25 per unit, fixed costs $327k per year. Break-even volume is 12111 units per year; current volume is 1484 units per year. Volume figures are last year's actuals; the effect of the price on volume is not estimated.
input: In today's highly competitive catering landscape, it is important to note that pricing decisions play a pivotal role in determining whether a contract is ultimately sustainable over the long term. This catering contract is currently priced at $52 per unit, while the variable cost associated with delivering each unit stands at $25 per unit. When these figures are brought together, it can be seen that each unit sold contributes $27 toward the contract's fixed costs, which amount to a substantial $327k per year. Based on these numbers, the break-even volume for the contract works out to 12111 units per year. However, the current volume being achieved is just 1484 units per year, which means that there is a considerable gap of 10627 units per year between the volume that is required and the volume that is actually being delivered. It is worth noting that the volume figures used here are last year's actuals, and that the effect of the price on volume has not been estimated, which inevitably adds a layer of uncertainty to any forward-looking assessment. Overall, a range of options could potentially be explored going forward, including revisiting the price, seeking to grow the volume, or some combination of the two, and each unit delivered continues to add $27 of contribution in the meantime. Further analysis may well be needed in order to determine the most appropriate path forward for all of the stakeholders involved. A decision will in due course need to be taken once the available options have been fully worked through and their implications for the contract and its customer have been properly understood.
target: The catering contract does not cover its fixed costs at the current price and volume. The price is $52 per unit and the variable cost is $25 per unit, so each unit contributes $27 toward fixed costs of $327k per year. Break-even volume is 12111 units per year. Current volume is 1484 units per year, and the shortfall against break-even is 10627 units per year. The contract was priced as a continuing service and has been delivered at the volume the customer currently takes. Its terms rest on a throughput the operation has not reached, and the question the renewal has to answer is whether the price, the committed volume, or both change before the next period begins. The volume figures are last year's actuals, and they are the whole of the evidence behind the comparison. The effect of the price on volume is not estimated, so the response of volume to a higher price is unknown, and an increase in price cannot be entered in the case as a certain remedy for the shortfall. At the current volume, the contribution earned carries only a small part of the fixed costs, and the gap is structural rather than marginal: it is set by the distance between the volume priced for and the volume delivered, and it does not close by minor adjustment to either figure on its own. Contract management should reprice the contract or secure a committed volume as a condition of renewal, and the renewal should not proceed on the present terms. Until one of those changes is agreed, each unit delivered adds $27 of contribution against a fixed-cost base that the present volume cannot support.

subtype: worked example with equation: log-mean difference
fact_base: A countercurrent exchanger cools a process stream from 160 °C to 120 °C with water entering at 40 °C and leaving at 75 °C. The terminal differences are 85 K and 80 K, and the log-mean temperature difference $\Delta T_{lm}$ is 82.5 K. The log-mean value assumes constant overall coefficient and no phase change.
input:
In this example, we are going to work through the calculation of the log-mean temperature difference for a countercurrent heat exchanger, which is a really important concept in heat transfer. The exchanger in question cools a process stream from 160 °C all the way down to 120 °C, using water that enters at 40 °C and leaves at 75 °C. In a countercurrent arrangement, the temperature differences at the two ends of the exchanger are not the same, and here they work out to 85 K at the hot end and 80 K at the cold end. Because these differences are not equal, a simple arithmetic average is not strictly appropriate, and the log-mean temperature difference is used instead, since it properly reflects the way the driving force varies along the length of the exchanger. It is calculated using the well-known formula shown below:

$$\Delta T_{lm} = \frac{\Delta T_1 - \Delta T_2}{\ln(\Delta T_1 / \Delta T_2)}$$

When the values of 85 K and 80 K are substituted into this formula, the log-mean temperature difference comes out to 82.5 K. It is worth noting that this result rests on certain assumptions, namely that the overall heat transfer coefficient remains constant along the exchanger and that no phase change takes place in either stream, so the value of 82.5 K should be applied with those conditions in mind.
target:
Calculate the log-mean temperature difference for a countercurrent exchanger that cools a process stream from 160 °C to 120 °C with water entering at 40 °C and leaving at 75 °C. The temperature difference between the two streams is not constant along the exchanger, so the driving force for heat transfer is represented by a mean taken over the length. The terminal differences, formed from the temperatures at the two ends, are 85 K at the end where the process stream enters and 80 K at the end where it leaves. Where the two terminal differences differ, the mean is the log-mean temperature difference $\Delta T_{lm}$, defined by

$$\Delta T_{lm} = \frac{\Delta T_1 - \Delta T_2}{\ln(\Delta T_1 / \Delta T_2)}$$

in which the symbols in the numerator and the denominator are the two terminal differences. Substitution of 85 K and 80 K gives $\Delta T_{lm}$ = 82.5 K. The check is the arithmetic mean of the same two differences, 82.5 K: the log mean lies close to the arithmetic mean because the terminal differences are close to each other, and it falls between them, as a mean must. The value assumes a constant overall coefficient along the exchanger and no phase change in either stream; a stream that condenses or boils develops a different temperature profile and takes a different treatment.

fact_base: Adsorption of a dye from water on a metal-organic framework was measured in batch tests at 298 K. The fitted Langmuir capacity was 205 mg of dye per gram of adsorbent at pH 5. At an adsorbent dose of 0.6 g L-1, removal after 120 min was 82% of the initial dye concentration of 50 mg L-1. The Langmuir fit is reported for pH 5 only; capacity at other pH values was not measured.
input: In this study, the adsorption of a dye from water onto a metal-organic framework was investigated in a series of batch tests, which were carried out at 298 K. The results were analysed using the Langmuir model, and the fitted Langmuir capacity was found to be 205 mg of dye per gram of adsorbent at pH 5, which highlights the considerable capacity of the material under the conditions studied. In further experiments, an adsorbent dose of 0.6 g L-1 was used, and it was observed that removal after 120 min reached 82% of the initial dye concentration of 50 mg L-1, meaning that the concentration was brought down to a residual level of 9 mg L-1. It is important to note, however, that the Langmuir fit is reported for pH 5 only, and the capacity at other pH values was not measured, so care should be taken when generalising these findings beyond the conditions that were actually examined. The performance of the adsorbent may well vary across the wider range of conditions that could be encountered in practice, and the figures obtained here relate specifically to the tested condition at pH 5, where the solution chemistry, the dose, and the contact time all came together in the particular combination that was examined during the course of this work. The batch method that was used allowed each test to be run under closely controlled conditions, with the adsorbent brought into contact with the dye solution and the two then separated once the contact period had elapsed, after which the remaining dye in the solution was measured in order to establish how much had been taken up by the material during the test.
target: Adsorption of a dye from water on a metal-organic framework was measured in batch tests at 298 K. The fitted Langmuir capacity at pH 5 was 205 mg of dye per gram of adsorbent. At an adsorbent dose of 0.6 g L-1, removal after 120 min was 82% of the initial dye concentration of 50 mg L-1, leaving a residual concentration of 9 mg L-1. The capacity is a fitted parameter of the Langmuir model applied to the batch data, and it states the loading the model reaches as concentration rises; it is not a loading measured at a single concentration. The removal figure belongs to its own conditions as a bundle: dose, contact time, and initial concentration stand together, and a change in any of them takes the result outside the measured set. Both results were obtained at the tested pH, and the Langmuir fit is reported for that pH only. Capacity at other pH values was not measured, so neither figure extends beyond pH 5. Dye uptake on an adsorbent of this kind is set in part by the charge state of the surface and of the dye, both of which move with pH, and an unmeasured pH is an unmeasured capacity. The passage therefore supports comparison with other materials tested at pH 5 under the same dose and contact time, and it supports no claim about performance in a stream whose pH differs from the tested value. The batch arrangement behind the figures matters to their use: the adsorbent and the solution are brought together for the stated contact period and then separated, and the measurement is of the solution that remains. A continuous stream, a mixed feed, or an adsorbent already carrying a loading from earlier use sits outside the arrangement tested, and the figures transfer to such a case only as an estimate whose error is unmeasured.

fact_base: A shell-and-tube exchanger heats cooling water in a refinery preheat train. Duty is 1287 kW. Hot stream: 150 °C in, 110 °C out. Cold stream: 35 °C in, 60 °C out. The log-mean temperature difference is 82.3 K and the installed area is 52.8 m2, giving an overall coefficient of 296 W m-2 K-1. Fouling was assessed from a single 90-day run; no cleaning cycle has been completed.
input: This passage presents the results of a performance assessment carried out on a shell-and-tube heat exchanger that heats cooling water as part of a refinery preheat train. The exchanger was found to have a duty of 1287 kW under the conditions examined. On the hot side, the stream enters the exchanger at 150 °C and leaves at 110 °C, while on the cold side, the cooling water enters at 35 °C and leaves at 60 °C. Taking these terminal temperatures into account, the log-mean temperature difference for the unit works out to 82.3 K. The exchanger has an installed area of 52.8 m2, and when the duty, the area, and the log-mean temperature difference are combined, the overall heat transfer coefficient comes out to 296 W m-2 K-1, which reflects the performance of the unit as assessed. It is important to note that the fouling of the exchanger was assessed on the basis of a single 90-day run, and that no cleaning cycle has been completed as yet. Because of this, the picture of how fouling develops over the 90 days and beyond remains incomplete at this stage, and the coefficient reported here should be understood in that context when it is used for further comparison or design purposes. The temperatures recorded during the run were nevertheless consistent, and the exchanger continued to deliver its heating duty to the preheat train throughout the period that was covered by the assessment, with the cooling water leaving the unit at its intended outlet condition on the cold side.
target: A shell-and-tube exchanger in a refinery preheat train heats cooling water at a duty of 1287 kW. The hot stream enters at 150 °C and leaves at 110 °C; the cooling water enters at 35 °C and leaves at 60 °C. The log-mean temperature difference across the unit is 82.3 K and the installed area is 52.8 m2, giving an overall coefficient of 296 W m-2 K-1. The coefficient is the duty divided by the product of the area and the log-mean temperature difference, and it describes the exchanger in the state in which it was assessed: it bundles the wall, the two films, and the fouling present during the run into a single figure. Fouling was assessed from a single 90-day run, and no cleaning cycle has been completed. The coefficient therefore carries the fouling accumulated over 90 days and no more. It is not a clean-surface value, and the rate at which fouling builds beyond the assessed period is unmeasured, because the run ended before any cleaning could show what the surface recovers to. A design calculation that enters the assessed coefficient as the clean coefficient imports the fouled state into the new design without stating it, and a comparison against a freshly cleaned unit has to make the same allowance in the opposite direction. The duty and the terminal temperatures stand as measured for the run; the coefficient is the derived quantity, and its scope is the run it was derived from. The preheat duty is also the context for the figure: the exchanger sits in a train in which the hot stream gives up heat it would otherwise lose, and the coefficient is the quantity a later revamp calculation will reach for first, which is why its scope has to travel with it wherever it is quoted.

fact_base: Excerpt content: a staffing gap of 7 weeks is reported with its cause; the excerpt proposes one mitigation and its owner. The excerpt does not open or close the memo and does not restate its subject line.
input: Turning to the resourcing position, it should be noted that a staffing gap of 7 weeks has now opened up within the delivery team. This gap has arisen because members of staff have moved on from the project before their replacements have been able to start, which has unfortunately left a period during which key roles are not covered. The work that is affected sits within the EPC workstream, and the gap is expected to have an impact on the pace at which deliverables can be progressed during the affected period, since the tasks that the departing staff were responsible for cannot simply be picked up by others who are already fully committed to their own work. In order to address this issue, it is proposed that agency cover be approved in order to bridge the gap until the permanent replacements are in place, and it is further proposed that the project manager should own the delivery of this mitigation, including arranging the cover and reassigning the affected work in the meantime. It is hoped that this approach will help to minimise the disruption that might otherwise be caused, although it should be acknowledged that the effectiveness of agency cover will depend to a considerable extent on how quickly suitable individuals can be identified and brought on board, and on how much handover can be achieved in the circumstances. The full extent of the gap is 7 weeks, and the matter is raised here so that it can be considered alongside the other resourcing pressures that the team is currently facing, with a view to reaching a position that protects the programme as far as reasonably possible.
target: A staffing gap of 7 weeks stands in the delivery team. Staff have left the project before their replacements start, and the roles they held are uncovered for that period. The uncovered work sits inside the EPC scope, and it does not redistribute itself: the remaining staff are committed to their own deliverables, and the tasks attached to the vacant roles wait for cover or for the replacements. Deliverables that depend on those tasks move with them. The mitigation proposed is agency cover for the gap, approved by the project board, with the project manager owning its delivery: engaging the cover, settling the incoming staff into the vacant roles, and reassigning the affected work until the cover is in place. Agency cover shortens the gap only where the vacant roles can be filled from the agency market at the specialisms the project needs, and cover engaged late shortens it by less than its full length. The 7 weeks therefore remains the planning figure until cover is actually in post, and any programme commitment made in the meantime should be read against the uncovered figure rather than against the mitigated one. The board is asked to treat the gap as a schedule risk on that basis: a period in which named work has no owner, with a mitigation whose effect is real only once the people are in place. The cause is structural rather than personal: recruitment runs behind departure on this project, and a leaver's notice period ends before a successor can be selected, cleared, and started. Until that sequence shortens, any departure in a scarce specialism opens a gap of the same kind, and the cover proposed here treats the present instance rather than the pattern. The board may therefore want the recruitment position itself reported alongside the gap, so that the next gap is forecast rather than discovered.

subtype: worked example with equation: Stokes settling
fact_base: Sand grains of diameter $d_p$ = 50 micrometres and density 1400 kg m-3 settle in water at 293 K. Stokes' law gives a terminal velocity $v_t$ of 0.55 mm s-1. The estimate requires creeping flow; the particle Reynolds number must be checked before the value is used.
input:
In this example, we are going to estimate how fast sand grains settle through water. The grains in question have a diameter $d_p$ of 50 micrometres and a density of 1400 kg m-3, and they are settling in water at 293 K. For small particles moving slowly through a fluid, the terminal settling velocity can be estimated using Stokes' law, which is given by the following equation:

$$v_t = \frac{g d_p^2 (\rho_p - \rho)}{18 \mu}$$

Here, $v_t$ denotes the terminal velocity, $g$ is the acceleration due to gravity, $d_p$ is the particle diameter, $\rho_p$ is the particle density, $\rho$ is the fluid density, and $\mu$ is the fluid viscosity. When the values for the sand grains are worked through, Stokes' law gives a terminal velocity $v_t$ of 0.55 mm s-1. The result is a slow settling rate, as would be expected for grains of this size in a liquid of this kind. It is important to note, however, that this estimate is only valid for creeping flow, and the particle Reynolds number must be checked before the value is used, because if the flow around the particle is not in the creeping regime, the equation will not give a reliable answer and the true settling velocity may differ from the one calculated. The calculation is a standard one for settling problems of this type and is widely used for a first estimate.
target:
Estimate the terminal settling velocity of sand grains of diameter $d_p$ = 50 micrometres and density 1400 kg m-3 in water at 293 K. A grain falling through the water accelerates until the drag on it balances its immersed weight, and it then continues at the terminal velocity $v_t$. For a small particle in creeping flow, Stokes' law gives that velocity as

$$v_t = \frac{g d_p^2 (\rho_p - \rho)}{18 \mu}$$

where $g$ denotes the acceleration due to gravity, $\rho_p$ the density of the grain, $\rho$ the density of the water, and $\mu$ the viscosity of the water. Substitution of the grain diameter and the two densities gives $v_t$ = 0.55 mm s-1. The velocity depends on the square of the diameter, so it is the grain size, more than any other input, that fixes the result. Stokes' law holds for creeping flow only. The check on the result is the particle Reynolds number formed from the computed velocity and the grain diameter: the computed velocity is usable only where that check places the flow around the grain in the creeping regime. Outside the regime, drag rises above the Stokes relation and the grain settles more slowly than the equation states, so the error is in the direction of overstating the settling rate. The estimate also sets the scale for any separator sized from it: a settling vessel designed around the computed velocity assumes that grains reach the bottom within the residence the vessel provides, and a velocity overstated by the use of the equation outside its regime passes directly into a vessel that is too small for the duty it has to perform.

fact_base: A single-stage compressor raises natural gas from 1 bar to 4 bar. Inlet temperature is 303 K. For isentropic compression with a heat-capacity ratio of 1.4, the discharge temperature is 450 K. The isentropic estimate excludes mechanical losses; the installed machine's measured discharge temperature is higher.
input: In this worked example, we are going to look at what happens to the temperature of natural gas when it is compressed in a single-stage compressor. The compressor raises the natural gas from a pressure of 1 bar up to a pressure of 4 bar, and the gas enters the machine at an inlet temperature of 303 K. If the compression is assumed to be isentropic, which is to say that it takes place without any irreversibility, the discharge temperature can be estimated from the inlet temperature and the pressure ratio of 4 using the standard isentropic relation, taking the heat-capacity ratio of the gas to be 1.4. When the inlet temperature of 303 K and the other values are worked through in this relation, the calculation gives a discharge temperature of 450 K. It is important to note, however, that this isentropic estimate excludes mechanical losses, which are inevitably present in any real machine. As a result, the measured discharge temperature of the installed machine is higher than the estimated figure, and the value of 450 K should therefore be treated as an idealised result rather than as a prediction of the temperature that will actually be observed in practice. Examples of this kind are commonly used when a compressor is being specified, since the discharge temperature has a bearing on the materials that are selected for the machine and on the cooling that may need to be provided downstream of it.
target: A single-stage compressor raises natural gas from 1 bar to 4 bar from an inlet temperature of 303 K; calculate the discharge temperature on an isentropic basis. The isentropic relation connects the discharge temperature to the inlet temperature through the pressure ratio and the heat-capacity ratio of the gas. With a pressure ratio of 4 and a heat-capacity ratio of 1.4, substitution of the inlet temperature of 303 K gives a discharge temperature of 450 K. The isentropic basis is an idealisation: the compression is treated as reversible, and mechanical losses are excluded from the estimate. The installed machine's measured discharge temperature is higher than 450 K, as it must be once those losses enter as heat in the gas. The isentropic value is therefore the floor for the discharge temperature of the real machine and not its expected value, and the difference between the two temperatures is the thermal signature of everything the estimate leaves out. A design that has to bound the discharge temperature from above cannot take the isentropic figure as the bound; it takes the measured behaviour of the installed machine, with the isentropic value marking how much of the rise the compression alone accounts for. The relation also shows where the estimate is sensitive: the pressure ratio enters through an exponent set by the heat-capacity ratio, so the result moves with the ratio rather than with either pressure on its own, and a machine raising the gas through a larger ratio in a single stage would return a discharge temperature well above the present figure, which is the reason staging enters real designs.

subtype: worked example with equation: radiative exchange
fact_base: A furnace wall at 800 K faces surroundings at 300 K. Its emissivity $\varepsilon$ is 0.95. Net radiative heat flux $q$ is 21.6 kW m-2, with the Stefan-Boltzmann constant $\sigma$ = 5.67 x 10-8 W m-2 K-4. The estimate treats both surfaces as large and parallel; view factors for the real geometry are not included.
input:
In this example, we consider the heat that is transferred by radiation from a hot furnace wall to its surroundings. The furnace wall is at a temperature of 800 K, while the surroundings are at a much lower temperature of 300 K. The emissivity $\varepsilon$ of the wall surface is 0.95. The net radiative heat flux can be calculated from the Stefan-Boltzmann law, which is expressed by the equation below:

$$q = \varepsilon \sigma (T_1^4 - T_2^4)$$

In this equation, $q$ represents the net radiative heat flux, $\varepsilon$ is the emissivity, $\sigma$ is the Stefan-Boltzmann constant, which has a value of 5.67 x 10-8 W m-2 K-4, and $T_1$ and $T_2$ are the absolute temperatures of the wall and the surroundings respectively. When the numbers are put into the equation, the net radiative heat flux $q$ comes out to 21.6 kW m-2. It should be noted that this estimate treats both surfaces as large and parallel, and that view factors for the real geometry are not included, so the result is an idealisation of the actual arrangement and the exchange in a real furnace may be somewhat less than the calculated value suggests.
target:
Calculate the net radiative heat flux from a furnace wall at 800 K to surroundings at 300 K, where the emissivity $\varepsilon$ of the wall is 0.95. The net flux $q$ between two large parallel surfaces is given by

$$q = \varepsilon \sigma (T_1^4 - T_2^4)$$

where $\sigma$ denotes the Stefan-Boltzmann constant, 5.67 x 10-8 W m-2 K-4, and $T_1$ and $T_2$ denote the absolute temperatures of the wall and the surroundings. Substitution gives $q$ = 21.6 kW m-2. The fourth-power dependence makes the wall temperature the governing input: the surroundings, at their much lower absolute temperature, return only a small part of what the wall emits, and the net flux is close to the wall's own emission. The estimate treats both surfaces as large and parallel, and view factors for the real geometry are not included. A wall that faces the surroundings over only part of its boundary exchanges less than the computed flux, by the part the view factor removes, so the value is an upper figure for the real arrangement rather than a description of it. Radiation is also the mode that grows fastest as the wall temperature rises, because of the fourth power, and at furnace temperatures it dominates the exchange with the surroundings wherever the wall can see them. Conduction through the wall and convection at its surface carry their own shares of the total loss, and neither is part of the figure computed here.

fact_base: A centrifugal pump moves caustic solution between two vessels at grade. At the duty point the flow is 64 m3 h-1 against a head of 33 m, with pump efficiency 67%. Shaft power at the duty point is 8.6 kW. The motor is rated 15% above this value. Cavitation was not observed in the acceptance test, which ran for 4 h at the duty point only.
input: This passage describes the duty point of a centrifugal pump that is used to move caustic solution between two vessels that are located at grade. At the duty point, the pump delivers a flow of 64 m3 h-1 against a head of 33 m, and it operates with an efficiency of 67%. Under these conditions, the shaft power required at the duty point is 8.6 kW. In order to provide a suitable margin for the drive, the motor that powers the pump is rated 15% above this value. During the acceptance test that was carried out on the pump, no cavitation was observed, although it is important to note that this test ran for 4 h at the duty point only. This means that the absence of cavitation has been demonstrated at the tested condition, while behaviour at other flows and at other points on the operating curve has not been covered by the test at all. Some care is therefore needed when drawing broader conclusions about the performance of the pump across its full operating range, since a machine that runs quietly at its duty point may behave quite differently when it is asked to operate well away from that point, where the flow through the pump and the conditions at the suction side are no longer those that were examined during acceptance.
target: A centrifugal pump moves caustic solution between two vessels at grade. At the duty point the flow is 64 m3 h-1 against a head of 33 m, with pump efficiency 67%. Shaft power at the duty point is 8.6 kW, and the motor is rated 15% above this value. The duty point is the condition the pump was selected for, and the figures belong to that condition as a set: flow, head, and efficiency are the values the pump delivers there, and the shaft power follows from them. Cavitation was not observed in the acceptance test. The test ran for 4 h at the duty point only, so the result is a detection statement for that condition and no other: no cavitation at the duty point over the duration of the test. Behaviour at other flows is untested. Away from the duty point the suction conditions change with flow, and the absence of cavitation at the tested point does not extend along the pump curve in either direction; a statement about cavitation at higher or lower flow needs a test at that flow. The margin on the motor belongs to the same discipline: the drive is sized above the duty-point shaft power so that the machine can deliver the duty without running at its limit, and the margin is stated against the duty point because that is the condition the selection was made for. None of the figures describes the pump at part load or at overload, and an enquiry about either condition starts from the pump curve and the system the pump works against, not from the duty-point set.

fact_base: A tutorial passage explains the pump affinity laws for a centrifugal pump at varying speed. The passage states the three proportionalities in words: flow with speed, head with speed squared, power with speed cubed. A worked check is included: doubling speed multiplies power by 8. No other numbers are introduced.
input: In this passage, we are going to explore the pump affinity laws, which are a set of really useful relationships that describe how the performance of a centrifugal pump changes when its speed is changed. There are three proportionalities that lie at the heart of these laws. First, the flow delivered by the pump is proportional to the speed, which means that if the speed goes up, the flow goes up in direct proportion. Second, the head produced by the pump is proportional to the speed squared, so a change in speed has a stronger effect on the head than it does on the flow. Third, the power taken by the pump is proportional to the speed cubed, which means that the power responds even more strongly to a change in speed than either the flow or the head. A simple worked check helps to bring this to life: if the speed is doubled, the speed cubed term means that the power is multiplied by 8. This shows just how sensitive the power consumption of a centrifugal pump is to the speed at which it is run, and why even modest changes in speed can have a noticeable effect on power.
target: The pump affinity laws give the performance of a centrifugal pump at a speed other than the speed at which it was measured. The laws are three proportionalities. Flow is proportional to speed. Head is proportional to the speed squared. Power is proportional to the speed cubed. Each law rescales the same pump: the flow, head, and power at the new speed come from the values at the measured speed and the ratio of the two speeds, with no other quantity entering. The worked check is the power law at a doubling of speed: the speed ratio cubed multiplies the power by 8. The laws are used wherever a measured pump is run at a changed speed, and their use is a substitution, not a new test: a performance measured at the original speed is carried to the new speed by the ratios, and the carried values stand in for a measurement at that speed. The proportionalities do not act independently in a running system, because the three quantities they rescale are the coordinates of a single operating point; applying the flow law and leaving the head at its measured value describes a point the pump does not pass through. Power is the quantity most exposed to a speed change, head next, and flow least, and that ordering is the practical content of the laws: a modest change in speed buys a modest change in flow at a disproportionate change in power. Any estimate of a speed change that applies one proportionality without the other two misstates the operating point.
