fact_base: A viscous liquid of viscosity $\mu$ = 0.001 Pa s flows laminarly through a tube of radius $R$ = 10 mm and length $L$ = 31 m. At a pressure drop $\Delta P$ of 11 kPa the volumetric flow $Q$ is 5016.4 L h-1. The Hagen-Poiseuille equation assumes laminar, fully developed flow of a Newtonian liquid.
input:
In this example, we are going to calculate the volumetric flow rate of a viscous liquid that is flowing through a long tube. The liquid has a viscosity $\mu$ of 0.001 Pa s, and it flows in a laminar fashion through a tube that has a radius $R$ of 10 mm and a length $L$ of 31 m. The flow is driven by a pressure drop $\Delta P$ of 11 kPa along the tube. For laminar flow of this kind, the relationship between the flow rate and the pressure drop is given by the Hagen-Poiseuille equation, which is shown below:

$$Q = \frac{\pi R^4 \Delta P}{8 \mu L}$$

Here, $Q$ is the volumetric flow, and the other symbols represent the quantities that have already been introduced above. When the values are substituted into this equation, the volumetric flow $Q$ comes out to 5016.4 L h-1. It is important to bear in mind that the Hagen-Poiseuille equation assumes laminar, fully developed flow of a Newtonian liquid, so it should only be applied where those conditions are actually met, and the result will not be reliable if the flow is turbulent or if the liquid does not behave in a Newtonian manner, as some liquids with suspended material in them may not.
target:
Calculate the volumetric flow of a viscous liquid of viscosity $\mu$ = 0.001 Pa s through a tube of radius $R$ = 10 mm and length $L$ = 31 m at a pressure drop $\Delta P$ of 11 kPa. For laminar, fully developed flow of a Newtonian liquid, the Hagen-Poiseuille equation gives the flow $Q$ directly from the tube geometry, the viscosity, and the pressure drop:

$$Q = \frac{\pi R^4 \Delta P}{8 \mu L}$$

Substitution of the stated values gives $Q$ = 5016.4 L h-1. The radius enters at the fourth power, so the result rests on $R$ more heavily than on any other input: a small error in the radius carries into the flow at four times its relative size, and the flow is correspondingly less sensitive to the pressure drop and the length, which enter at the first power. Fully developed flow is part of the result, not a detail: near the tube entrance the velocity profile is still forming and the pressure gradient is steeper than the equation gives, so the equation describes the tube away from its entrance. The value holds for laminar flow of a Newtonian liquid, and those are the conditions under which the computed flow stands. The entrance length in a tube in this service is short against the stated length, so the fully developed part of the flow governs the pressure drop as a whole.

fact_base: A tutorial passage explains the pump affinity laws for a centrifugal pump at varying speed. The passage states the three proportionalities in words: flow with speed, head with speed squared, power with speed cubed. A worked check is included: doubling speed multiplies power by 8. No other numbers are introduced.
input:
When it comes to running a centrifugal pump, one of the most crucial concepts to grasp is how the pump's performance responds when its rotational speed is changed. The affinity laws provide a powerful and elegant framework for describing exactly this behaviour, and they are widely regarded as essential knowledge for anyone who works with pumping systems on a day-to-day basis.

At their core, the affinity laws describe three simple proportionalities that link performance to speed. The volumetric flow rate is directly proportional to the speed, which means that when the speed goes up, the flow rises in step with it. The head, meanwhile, is proportional to the square of the speed, reflecting the way the energy imparted to the liquid builds as the impeller turns faster. The power, in turn, is proportional to the cube of the speed, underscoring just how steeply the energy demand can climb with even modest speed increases.

A worked check helps to bring the point home. If the speed of the pump is doubled, the power requirement does not simply double alongside the flow; instead, it increases by a factor of 8, climbing to 8 times its original value. It is important to note that all three quantities shift together, so a speed adjustment is never only about flow. The whole operating point moves at once, with significant implications for motor sizing, energy consumption, and the wider system as a whole.
target:
Doubling the speed of a centrifugal pump multiplies the power it draws by 8. The affinity laws state the full set of proportions behind that result, and the power proportion is the one to check before any speed increase is made on an installed pump.

The affinity laws describe one pump at varying rotational speed, with the impeller unchanged and the same liquid handled throughout. Flow varies in direct proportion to speed, so a pump at twice the speed delivers twice the flow. Head varies with the square of the speed. Power varies with the cube of the speed, and rises fastest of the three quantities as speed increases.

The proportions compare duties of a single machine, and they do not rate a different pump. A speed change also fixes all three quantities at once: a change chosen to gain flow raises the head and the power in their stated proportions at the same time.

The worked check tests the power proportion alone. Doubling the speed makes the speed ratio two, and the power ratio is the cube of the speed ratio. Cubing two returns the factor of 8 stated at the start, and the check closes there: the power at the doubled speed stands at eight times the power at the original speed, and the motor and drive sized for the original duty must carry the increase.

fact_base: A viscous liquid of viscosity $\mu$ = 0.001 Pa s flows laminarly through a tube of radius $R$ = 6 mm and length $L$ = 34 m. At a pressure drop $\Delta P$ of 24 kPa the volumetric flow $Q$ is 1293.3 L h-1. The Hagen-Poiseuille equation assumes laminar, fully developed flow of a Newtonian liquid.
input:
In this worked example, we will determine the volumetric flow rate of a viscous liquid flowing through a long tube, making use of the well-known Hagen-Poiseuille equation. The liquid in question has a viscosity $\mu$ of 0.001 Pa s, and it flows through a tube with a radius $R$ of 6 mm and a length $L$ of 34 m, with a pressure drop $\Delta P$ of 24 kPa driving the flow along the tube.

It is worth noting that the Hagen-Poiseuille equation rests on a set of underlying assumptions that should always be kept in mind. The flow is assumed to be laminar, meaning that the liquid moves in smooth, orderly layers, and fully developed, meaning that the velocity profile no longer changes along the length of the tube. The liquid is also assumed to be Newtonian, so that its viscosity remains constant regardless of the shear conditions. Subject to these assumptions, the volumetric flow $Q$ is given by the following relationship:

$$Q = \frac{\pi R^4 \Delta P}{8 \mu L}$$

Substituting the values stated above into this equation, the volumetric flow $Q$ works out to 1293.3 L h-1. Interestingly, the radius appears raised to the fourth power in the equation, which highlights the remarkable sensitivity of the flow to the tube radius: even a relatively small error in the measured radius can translate into a considerably larger error in the calculated flow. Finally, it should be borne in mind that where the flow near the entrance of the tube is not yet fully developed, the actual pressure drop for a given flow will be higher than the equation suggests, so the equation tends to overstate the flow in situations where entrance effects occupy a substantial portion of the tube.
target:
Calculate the volumetric flow $Q$ of a viscous liquid through a tube of radius $R$ = 6 mm and length $L$ = 34 m, where the liquid has viscosity $\mu$ = 0.001 Pa s and the pressure drop $\Delta P$ along the tube is 24 kPa.

The flow is laminar and fully developed, and the liquid is Newtonian. Laminar flow moves in layers without mixing across the stream; fully developed flow has a velocity profile that no longer changes along the tube. Under these conditions the Hagen-Poiseuille equation gives the volumetric flow as

$$Q = \frac{\pi R^4 \Delta P}{8 \mu L}$$

Substitution of the stated values gives $Q$ = 1293.3 L h-1.

The radius stands at the fourth power in the equation, and the result inherits that sensitivity: a small error in the measured radius returns a larger error in the flow, in the same direction. The stated flow is therefore only as reliable as the radius it was calculated from.

The quantities in the equation divide into two groups. The pressure drop and the flow are the operating quantities: one is imposed and the other is returned. The radius, the length, and the viscosity are fixed by the tube that was built and the liquid that was chosen. The equation also fixes how the result moves when a fixed quantity changes: the flow rises in direct proportion to the pressure drop and falls in direct proportion to the viscosity and to the length, so doubling the tube length at the same pressure drop halves the flow. A change in the radius passes into the result four times over, through the fourth power already noted.

The closing check is the entrance condition. Near the tube entrance the flow is not yet fully developed, and over that length the pressure drop at a given flow is higher than the equation gives. Where entrance effects occupy a substantial part of the tube, the actual flow at the stated pressure drop falls below the calculated value; the equation overstates it.

fact_base: Energy assessment of a paper mill, in four sections: current use, refrigeration, steam, and recommendation. Electricity use is 1727 MWh per year; refrigeration takes the largest share. A heat-recovery retrofit is projected to save 20% of electricity use, a derived saving of 345 MWh per year, at a capital cost of $883k. At $0.12 per kWh the derived annual saving is $41448 and the derived simple payback is 21.3 years. Steam figures are from one winter month and are flagged as seasonal in the recommendation.
input:
## Current use

In today's highly competitive industrial environment, understanding exactly how energy is used across a site is absolutely essential, and this assessment takes a comprehensive look at the energy picture at the paper mill in order to build a detailed picture of current consumption and to identify where meaningful savings might be achieved. The mill currently uses 1727 MWh of electricity per year, which represents a substantial quantity of energy by any measure. Of the various loads on the site, refrigeration stands out as taking the largest share of this electricity use, and it therefore deserves particular attention as the assessment unfolds. Alongside electricity, the mill also makes extensive use of steam, and both of these energy streams are considered in what follows, with a particular opportunity around heat recovery emerging as a central theme of the assessment. Energy touches every part of what the mill does, from the preparation of the stock through the forming and pressing of the sheet to the drying that finishes it, and the cost of that energy forms a significant part of the overall cost of production, so even relatively modest percentage improvements can be well worth pursuing in financial terms.

## Refrigeration

Refrigeration is, as noted above, the single largest consumer of electricity at the mill, and it plays a pivotal role in the site's day-to-day operations. The refrigeration plant runs compressors that remove heat from the areas and processes that require cooling, and that heat is ultimately rejected at the condensers, where it is simply given up and lost under current arrangements. This arrangement is interesting because it means that, at one and the same time, the site is spending heavily on electricity in order to throw heat away. The refrigeration load also has the advantage, from an energy-recovery standpoint, of running steadily throughout the year, since the cooling duty does not disappear with the changing seasons, and the chillers serve production areas whose cooling needs persist in summer and winter alike. It is precisely this combination of a large, steady cooling load and a continuous stream of rejected heat that makes the refrigeration plant such an attractive starting point when considering heat recovery on the site, and it forms the basis of the proposal that is developed later in this assessment. Sites of this kind typically spend a great deal on heating water and other process fluids at the very same time as their refrigeration plant is discarding heat, and it is this overlap, this simultaneous discarding and purchasing of heat, that heat recovery seeks to exploit by bringing the two sides together in a single, integrated arrangement.

## Steam

Steam is the mill's other major energy stream, and it is raised in boilers in order to supply the heat that the paper-making process demands, most notably for drying the sheet as it passes through the machine, as well as for heating process water and meeting a range of other heating duties around the site. The drying stage is particularly steam-hungry, since water has to be driven out of the sheet in large quantities, and the steam raised for it has to be available whenever the machine is running. It is important to note, however, that the steam figures available for this assessment are drawn from one winter month only, and this has significant implications for how confidently they can be used. Winter is the period when steam demand is at its most intense: incoming water is at its coldest, and heating requirements across the site are at their peak. Figures captured in such a month therefore risk overstating what steam demand looks like across a typical year as a whole, and they should be treated as seasonal rather than representative. This caveat is flagged here and carried forward into the recommendation, where it has a bearing on the decision that is ultimately reached.

## Recommendation

Bringing all of the strands together, the assessment has examined a possible heat-recovery retrofit in which heat rejected by the refrigeration plant would be captured and put to useful work elsewhere on the site. The retrofit is projected to save 20% of the mill's electricity use of 1727 MWh per year, which works out at a saving of 345 MWh per year. Using an electricity price of $0.12 per kWh, this translates into a financial saving of $41448 per year. Set against these savings, however, the capital cost of the retrofit comes in at $883k, and dividing the one by the other gives a simple payback period of 21.3 years, which is a very long time indeed. On top of this, it should not be forgotten that the steam side of the picture rests on figures from a single winter month, with all of the seasonal uncertainty that that entails. Taking everything into account, the prudent course of action would appear to be to hold back from committing the capital at this stage, and instead to gather a fuller picture of steam and refrigeration loads across an entire year before returning to the appraisal with firmer numbers on which to base a final decision. In the meantime, the opportunity itself is not in question, and nothing in this recommendation should be read as a judgement against heat recovery in principle, which remains an attractive prospect for the site in due course.
target:
## Current use

The mill uses 1727 MWh of electricity per year, and refrigeration takes the largest share of that use. A heat-recovery retrofit on the refrigeration plant is the measure under assessment: it is projected to cut electricity use, but at a capital cost that the projected saving repays only over a long period, and the steam figures behind the assessment rest on one winter month. The recommendation is stated in full at the end of this assessment; the sections before it give the use figures, the refrigeration position, and the limit on the steam data.

Electricity is metered for the whole site, and the annual total is firm. The internal split between loads is less firm, because not every load is separately metered; the refrigeration share is the largest by the plant's own running records, and no figure in this assessment depends on the exact split. Electricity use follows production: the mill's drives, pumps, and refrigeration plant run when the machines run, and the annual total moves with the tonnage the mill makes. Steam is the second energy stream. Steam serves the drying of the sheet on the paper machine and the heating of process water, and its use is not metered as an annual total at all.

## Refrigeration

Refrigeration is the largest electricity load on the site, and it runs in every month of the year: the cooling duty follows production, not the weather. The refrigeration plant removes heat at its evaporators and rejects that heat at its condensers, where it is currently discharged and lost. A refrigeration plant of this kind is a heat source as well as a cooling source, and the rejected heat is steady because the load that produces it is steady.

The retrofit under assessment recovers heat at the condensers and delivers it to duties that are otherwise heated directly, preheating process water being the natural first duty on this site. A paper mill heats water in quantity: stock preparation, washing, and cleaning all draw hot water through the day, and each of those draws is a duty that recovered heat can serve in place of heat raised directly. The recovery does not change the cooling the plant provides; it changes the destination of heat the plant already moves. The limit on the scheme sits on the demand side: recovered heat has value only where a heated duty can take it at the time it is produced, and the assessment has not established that match hour by hour. Condenser heat is produced when the refrigeration plant runs, and hot water is drawn when production calls for it; the two patterns overlap on this site but have not been shown to coincide. The projected saving in the recommendation is therefore a projection from annual totals, not a metered result.

## Steam

Steam figures for the mill come from one winter month, and they are flagged here as seasonal. A winter month carries the year's coldest incoming water and its highest heating demand alongside the process load, so a winter month read as a typical month overstates steam use across the year. No annual steam figure is stated in this assessment, because none has been measured.

Steam serves the drying section, where it heats the cylinders over which the sheet passes and drives the water out of the sheet, and it serves process water heating across the mill. Both duties are production duties, and both run whenever the machine runs; the seasonal element sits in the incoming water temperature and in building heating, not in the process itself. That is what makes the winter figure treacherous: it mixes a steady process load, which a winter month represents fairly, with a seasonal load at its annual peak, and the two cannot be separated from one month's total.

The steam limit matters to the retrofit decision in one direction only. Heat recovery displaces heat that would otherwise be raised directly, and the value of the recovered heat depends on how much direct heating the site actually does over a year. A steam record built from a single winter month inflates that value. The electricity saving stands on metered data; the supporting steam picture does not, and the recommendation is written to keep the two apart.

## Recommendation

The retrofit is projected to save 20% of electricity use, a saving of 345 MWh per year on the metered base of 1727 MWh per year. At $0.12 per kWh the saving is $41448 per year, against a capital cost of $883k: a simple payback of 21.3 years. Mill management should not commit the capital on these figures. A payback of that length outruns the period over which either the tariff or the load can be forecast, and the case rests in part on steam data that one winter month cannot support.

The appraisal is a simple-payback appraisal, and its limits should be read with the figure. Simple payback charges the whole capital in the year it is spent and credits the saving at today's tariff in every year that follows; it allows nothing for the cost of the money, for maintenance of the new plant, or for the price of electricity moving in either direction. Those omissions do not rescue the case here. A case that fails on simple payback over a period of this length is not brought back by refinements that mostly charge it more, and the metering recommendation stands independently of them.

The next step belongs to the mill's energy manager: meter the steam system and the refrigeration load through a full year, and re-run the appraisal on the metered record. The metering should also resolve the question the annual totals leave open, whether recovered heat and heated demand coincide closely enough through the day for the projected saving to be collected in practice. Heat recovery at the condensers remains the candidate measure, and the refrigeration load that makes it attractive is not in question. What is missing is the annual evidence, and the decision should wait for it. If the metered record confirms the projection and the payback still stands where it stands now, the honest finding will be that the measure does not pay on energy savings at this site, and the assessment should be closed on that basis rather than carried forward on better hopes.

fact_base: A tutorial passage explains representative sampling of an effluent stream. The passage covers where samples are taken, how many increments form one sample, and why a single grab sample misleads. No numerical limits are quoted; regulatory limits belong to the site's permit, not to the passage.
input:
Sampling an effluent stream may sound like a simple, everyday task, but in practice it is absolutely essential to go about it in the right way, because the results obtained in the laboratory can only ever be as meaningful as the sample that was collected in the first place. A well-designed sampling procedure ensures that the sample genuinely represents the effluent as a whole, rather than merely capturing whatever happened to be passing at a particular moment.

First and foremost, the location at which samples are taken is of critical importance. Samples should be collected at a point where the effluent stream is thoroughly mixed and flowing steadily, such as at the outlet of a discharge pipe or just downstream of a weir, where the liquid has been turned over and its composition is uniform throughout. By contrast, dipping a container at the edge of a slow-moving channel, at the surface, or in a quiet corner where liquid sits almost still will only ever recover the liquid that happens to rest there, which may differ considerably from the effluent that the plant is actually discharging.

Equally important is the way in which increments are gathered and combined. Rather than relying on a single container filled at a single moment, a number of increments should be drawn at intervals spread across the whole of the discharge period under consideration, and these increments should then be combined, in proportion to the flow at the time each was drawn, to form one composite sample for analysis. This approach smooths out short-lived fluctuations and produces a sample that reflects the average composition of the discharge over the period as a whole.

The single grab sample, by comparison, is deeply misleading. The composition of an effluent stream changes continually throughout a shift as batches are emptied, vessels are washed down, and production rises and falls, so a sample captured at just one instant records whichever of those conditions happened to be passing at that moment. The result is then all too easily read as though it described the entire stream, painting a picture that is inaccurate and potentially costly in its consequences.
target:
A representative sample of an effluent stream is built, not taken. The sample that reaches the laboratory must stand for the whole discharge, and a composite sample assembled from increments drawn across the discharge period does this; a single grab sample does not.

Take the increments where the stream is mixed. The sampling point belongs where the flow is turbulent and the composition uniform across the stream: at the outlet of a discharge pipe, or downstream of a weir, where the liquid has just been turned over. A point at the bank of a slow channel, at the surface, or in a stagnant corner returns the liquid that happens to rest there, and that liquid is not the effluent the plant discharges.

Draw each increment at intervals spread over the period the sample has to cover, and combine the increments in proportion to the flow at the time each was drawn. The combined volume is the sample. Analysis then reports the composition of the discharge averaged over the period, weighted as the discharge itself was weighted.

The composite must also be handled as a sample in its own right. The combined increments are mixed before any portion is taken for analysis; a portion dipped from the top of an unmixed composite repeats the grab-sample error at a smaller scale, because the increments were drawn at different states of the stream and settle or separate while they stand. The record that travels with the sample states the period the sample covers and when each increment was drawn, so the laboratory result can be read against the discharge it claims to describe.

A grab sample fails on timing alone. Effluent composition changes through a shift as batches are emptied, vessels are washed down, and flows rise and fall. One container filled at one moment catches whichever of those states was passing, and the result is then read as if it described the whole stream. The analysis is not at fault; the sample was never the stream.

subtype: worked example with equation: Antoine vapour pressure
fact_base: The vapour pressure of acetone at 78 °C is estimated from the Antoine equation with constants $A$ = 7.11714, $B$ = 1210.595 and $C$ = 229.664 (pressure in mmHg, temperature in °C). The estimate is 202.9 kPa. The constants are valid only over their fitted temperature range; the source databank value governs design.
input:
The Antoine equation is a widely used empirical correlation that allows the vapour pressure of a pure substance to be estimated from its temperature, provided that a set of substance-specific constants is available. In this example, we will estimate the vapour pressure of acetone at a temperature of 78 °C. The Antoine constants for acetone are $A$ = 7.11714, $B$ = 1210.595 and $C$ = 229.664, and it should be noted that these constants are tied to a particular choice of units, with the pressure expressed in mmHg and the temperature expressed in °C.

The Antoine equation itself takes the following form:

$$\log_{10} P = A - \frac{B}{T + C}$$

Here, $P$ denotes the vapour pressure and $T$ denotes the temperature. Substituting the temperature of 78 °C together with the three constants into the equation and carrying out the calculation, the vapour pressure of acetone at 78 °C comes out at an estimated value of 202.9 kPa.

It is important to bear in mind that the Antoine constants are obtained by fitting experimental data over a limited temperature range, and they are strictly valid only over the range to which they were fitted, so the temperature of interest must fall within that range if the estimate is to be relied upon. Furthermore, the result is only ever an estimate produced by a correlation rather than a direct measurement, and wherever an accurate design value is required, the value held in the source databank should be regarded as the governing figure, with the Antoine estimate serving a supporting, confirmatory role.
target:
Estimate the vapour pressure of acetone at 78 °C from the Antoine equation. The constants for acetone are $A$ = 7.11714, $B$ = 1210.595 and $C$ = 229.664, with the pressure in mmHg and the temperature in °C.

$$\log_{10} P = A - \frac{B}{T + C}$$

where $P$ is the vapour pressure and $T$ is the temperature. The Antoine equation is an empirical correlation: the three constants are fitted to measured vapour pressures of the pure substance, and they hold only for the substance and the units they were fitted in. A constant set quoted for pressure in mmHg and temperature in °C returns the pressure in mmHg when the temperature is entered in °C, and the same constants entered with a temperature in kelvin would return a wrong value without any sign of error in the arithmetic.

Substitution of $T$ = 78 °C and the three constants gives the estimate: the vapour pressure of acetone at 78 °C is 202.9 kPa.

In practice the equation supplies a vapour pressure where a measured value is missing, for a pure component inside the fitted range. Its errors are errors of basis, not of arithmetic: the wrong constant set, or units that do not match the set used.

Two limits stand on the estimate. The constants hold only over the temperature range to which they were fitted, and the temperature must lie inside that fitted range for the estimate to stand; outside the range the correlation is an extrapolation and its error is uncontrolled. The estimate is also a correlation result, not a measurement. Where a design value is needed, the value in the source databank governs, and the Antoine estimate serves as the check on that value, not as its replacement.

subtype: worked example with equation: Ergun pressure drop
fact_base: Gas flows through a packed bed of 1 mm particles. The void fraction $\varepsilon$ is 0.6, the superficial velocity $u$ is 0.14 m s-1 and the bed length is 3 m. The Ergun equation gives a pressure gradient of 0.4 kPa m-1, or 1.1 kPa over the bed. Particle diameter $d_p$ is 1 mm; gas density is 1.2 kg m-3 and viscosity is 1.8 x 10-5 Pa s.
input:
When a gas flows through a packed bed, it experiences a resistance to its flow, and the resulting pressure drop is an important quantity that frequently needs to be estimated in practice. In the case considered here, the gas flows through a packed bed made up of particles with a diameter $d_p$ of 1 mm. The void fraction $\varepsilon$ of the bed, which is a measure of the proportion of the bed volume that is empty space available for the gas to flow through, is 0.6, while the superficial velocity $u$ of the gas is 0.14 m s-1 and the length of the bed is 3 m. In addition, the gas itself has a density $\rho$ of 1.2 kg m-3 and a viscosity $\mu$ of 1.8 x 10-5 Pa s.

The pressure drop can be estimated using the well-known Ergun equation, which expresses the pressure gradient as the sum of two contributions: a viscous term that dominates under conditions of slow, orderly flow, and an inertial term that becomes increasingly important as the velocity rises. The equation is written as follows:

$$\frac{\Delta P}{L} = \frac{150 \mu (1-\varepsilon)^2}{\varepsilon^3 d_p^2} u + \frac{1.75 (1-\varepsilon)}{\varepsilon^3 d_p} \rho u^2$$

Substituting the values given above into the Ergun equation, the pressure gradient is found to be 0.4 kPa m-1, which corresponds to an overall pressure drop of 1.1 kPa across the full 3 m length of the bed. It should be noted that this result depends strongly on the particle size and the void fraction adopted, and different values for these quantities would lead to a noticeably different estimate.
target:
Calculate the pressure drop $\Delta P$ for a gas flowing through a packed bed of length $L$ = 3 m. The bed is packed with particles of diameter $d_p$ = 1 mm and has void fraction $\varepsilon$ = 0.6; the gas flows at a superficial velocity $u$ of 0.14 m s-1, with density $\rho$ of 1.2 kg m-3 and viscosity $\mu$ of 1.8 x 10-5 Pa s.

The void fraction is the share of the bed volume that is void space; the superficial velocity is the velocity the gas would have in the empty vessel, before the packing is added. The Ergun equation gives the pressure gradient as the sum of a viscous term and an inertial term:

$$\frac{\Delta P}{L} = \frac{150 \mu (1-\varepsilon)^2}{\varepsilon^3 d_p^2} u + \frac{1.75 (1-\varepsilon)}{\varepsilon^3 d_p} \rho u^2$$

Substitution of the stated values gives a pressure gradient of 0.4 kPa m-1. Over the 3 m bed the pressure drop $\Delta P$ is 1.1 kPa.

The viscous term carries the velocity to the first power and the inertial term to the second, so the inertial share grows as the velocity rises. The result rests on the stated particle diameter and void fraction: the gradient responds strongly to both, and a bed packed to a different void fraction returns a different pressure drop at the same duty.

fact_base: Energy assessment of a dairy plant, in four sections: current use, refrigeration, steam, and recommendation. Electricity use is 3857 MWh per year; refrigeration takes the largest share. A heat-recovery retrofit is projected to save 11% of electricity use, a derived saving of 424 MWh per year, at a capital cost of $762k. At $0.12 per kWh the derived annual saving is $50912 and the derived simple payback is 15 years. Steam figures are from one winter month and are flagged as seasonal in the recommendation.
input:
## Current use

This assessment takes a detailed and comprehensive look at how energy is used at the dairy plant, with a view to understanding the current position and identifying where worthwhile savings could potentially be made. The plant currently uses 3857 MWh of electricity per year, which is a very considerable amount of energy indeed. Within that overall total, refrigeration emerges as the load taking the largest share of electricity, which is perhaps not surprising for a dairy, where milk has to be cooled promptly after it arrives and finished products have to be kept cold in store. Steam is the other major energy stream on the site, and it is used for duties such as pasteurisation and for producing the hot water that cleaning regimes depend upon. Both streams are considered in this assessment, and an opportunity around heat recovery features prominently as the analysis develops. Energy is woven into every stage of the dairy's work, from the intake of raw milk through processing and packaging to the cold storage of the finished product, so a careful look at where it goes is a worthwhile exercise in its own right.

## Refrigeration

Refrigeration is the largest single consumer of electricity at the plant, and it is a load that the dairy simply cannot do without. Raw milk must be cooled soon after collection and held cold, and the cold stores for finished product run continuously as well, so the refrigeration plant works hard each and every day of the year. The compressors remove heat from the cold rooms and the milk cooling duty, and that heat is then rejected at the condensers, where under present arrangements it is simply thrown away. It is worth pausing on this point, because it means the plant is simultaneously spending a great deal of electricity in order to dispose of heat, even while it buys in energy elsewhere on the site to produce heat for other purposes. The load is also a steady one across the year, since milk arrives and is processed in every season, and this steadiness makes the rejected heat a dependable stream to work with when heat recovery is being considered, rather than an intermittent one that appears and disappears with the weather.

## Steam

Steam serves a range of essential heating duties at the dairy, most notably the pasteurisation of milk and the production of hot water for the cleaning of vessels, pipework and plant, cleaning being a duty that a food site can never treat lightly. It is important to note, however, that the steam figures available for this assessment come from one winter month only, which places an important limitation on how far they can be generalised. Winter is the season in which incoming water is coldest and heating requirements are generally at their highest, so a single winter month is likely to give an inflated impression of the steam demand that prevails over the course of a full year. This seasonal caveat is flagged here and is taken into account again when the recommendation is reached, since a decision of this size deserves foundations that are as solid as they can reasonably be made.

## Recommendation

Pulling the threads together, this assessment has considered a heat-recovery retrofit in which the heat rejected by the refrigeration plant would be captured and reused elsewhere on the site, for example to preheat water that would otherwise be heated directly. The retrofit is projected to save 11% of the plant's electricity use of 3857 MWh per year, amounting to a saving of 424 MWh per year. At an electricity price of $0.12 per kWh, that saving is worth $50912 per year. Against this, the capital cost of the retrofit is $762k, which gives a simple payback period of 15 years, a lengthy period by any standard. On top of that, the steam side of the analysis rests on one winter month of figures, with all of the seasonal uncertainty that involves. All things considered, the sensible course would seem to be to put the capital commitment on hold for the time being, while steam and refrigeration loads are monitored over a complete year so that the appraisal can be revisited on the basis of much firmer evidence. The opportunity itself remains a genuine one, and a fresh look at the numbers once a full year of data is in hand may yet paint a different picture.
target:
## Current use

The plant uses 3857 MWh of electricity per year, and refrigeration takes the largest share of that use. A heat-recovery retrofit on the refrigeration plant is the measure under assessment: it is projected to cut electricity use, but the capital cost is repaid only over a long period, and the steam figures behind the assessment rest on one winter month. The sections below give the use position, the refrigeration position, and the limit on the steam data; the recommendation closes the assessment.

Electricity is metered for the whole site and the annual total is firm. The split between loads is not separately metered; the refrigeration share is the largest by the plant's running records, and no figure in this assessment turns on the exact split. Electricity use follows the milk intake: cooling, processing, and cold storage all run when milk is being handled, and milk arrives in every month. Steam is the second stream, serving pasteurisation and the hot water that cleaning depends on, and steam use has no annual metered total.

## Refrigeration

Refrigeration runs in every month of the year. Raw milk is cooled on arrival and held cold, finished product is held in cold store, and both duties follow the milk intake, which does not stop with the seasons. The plant removes heat at its evaporators and rejects the heat at its condensers, where it is currently discharged and lost. A refrigeration plant is a heat source as well as a cooling source, and here the rejected heat is steady because the load behind it is steady. The cold chain also cannot be traded against the recovery scheme: the cooling temperatures are set by the product, and any arrangement that recovered heat at the cost of cooling performance would fail on the dairy's first duty. The retrofit is assessed on heat that is rejected after the cooling has been done, and on no other basis.

The retrofit recovers heat at the condensers and delivers it to duties otherwise heated directly, the preheating of cleaning water being the first such duty on this site. A dairy heats water in quantity and on a daily rhythm set by its cleaning cycles, so the demand for heat and the production of rejected heat are at least driven by the same working day. Recovery does not change the cooling provided; it changes the destination of heat the plant already moves. Its limit sits on the demand side: recovered heat has value only where a heated duty can take it when it is produced, and that match has not been established hour by hour. The projected saving is therefore built on annual totals, not on a metered match.

## Steam

Steam figures for the plant come from one winter month and are flagged as seasonal. The month carries the year's coldest incoming water and its highest heating demand on top of the process load of pasteurisation and cleaning, so read as a typical month it overstates steam use across the year. No annual steam figure is stated, because none has been measured. The process part of the steam load, the heating of milk and of cleaning water, follows production and is steadier than the total suggests; the seasonal part rides on top of it in the water temperature and the building load, and one month's figure mixes the two inseparably.

The limit bears on the retrofit in one direction: recovered heat displaces direct heating, and its value depends on how much direct heating the site does over a full year. A winter-only record inflates that value. The electricity saving stands on metered data; the steam picture behind it does not, and the recommendation keeps the two apart.

## Recommendation

The retrofit is projected to save 11% of electricity use, a saving of 424 MWh per year on the metered base of 3857 MWh per year. At $0.12 per kWh the saving is $50912 per year, against a capital cost of $762k: a simple payback of 15 years. Site management should not commit the capital on these figures. The payback outruns the period over which the tariff and the load can be forecast, and part of the case rests on steam data that one winter month cannot support.

The appraisal is a simple-payback appraisal. It charges the capital in the year it is spent and credits the saving at today's tariff in every later year, with no allowance for the cost of the money or for maintaining the new plant. That roughness does not drive the result: a case that fails on simple payback at this length is not restored by refinements that mostly charge it more, and the metering recommendation stands independently of the appraisal method.

The next step belongs to the plant's engineering manager: meter the steam system and the refrigeration load through a full year, and re-run the appraisal on that record. The metering should be specified to answer the open question as well, whether the rejected heat and the site's demand for heat coincide closely enough through the working day for the projected saving to be collected. The candidate measure is unchanged, and the refrigeration load that makes it attractive is not in question. The missing piece is annual evidence, and the decision should wait for it.

fact_base: A review passage on adsorbents for gas drying, in four parts: scope, established results, disagreements, and gaps. The review covers 128 papers from the last 13 years. The disagreements part names the quantity on which reports conflict; the gaps part names the measurement nobody reports.
input:
## Scope

The field of gas drying is one that has attracted a great deal of research attention over the years, and adsorbents sit right at the heart of a wide range of drying processes across industry. Gas streams have to be dried for all sorts of reasons: water vapour left in a gas can condense in cold pipework, corrode equipment, form solid hydrates that block lines, or interfere with a downstream process that expects a dry feed, and in application after application, from natural gas leaving a wellhead to the instrument air that drives plant control systems, it is adsorbents that are called upon to remove that water. This review sets out to survey the literature on adsorbents for gas drying, taking in the three great families of materials that dominate the area in practice: silica gel, activated alumina, and zeolite molecular sieves. In total, the review covers 128 papers published over the last 13 years, which together provide a rich and varied picture of a field that continues to evolve. The review is organised into four parts, moving from the scope of the literature, through the results that can be regarded as firmly established, to the areas where different research groups disagree with one another, and finally to the gaps where further work is sorely needed.

## Established results

A number of findings have emerged again and again across the literature and can now be treated as firmly established. All three families of adsorbent are capable of drying gas streams effectively, and each has found its established place in industrial practice. Silica gel and activated alumina are widely used where the drying duty is moderate, while molecular sieves are the materials of choice where very dry gas is required, since they continue to take up water strongly even when the gas is already quite dry and even at elevated temperatures, conditions under which the other materials lose much of their capacity. It is also well established that these adsorbents are used in cycles: a bed takes up water until it approaches saturation, and it is then regenerated, typically by heating it or by passing a dry purge gas through it, so that it can be returned to service. In practice this cyclic character is commonly managed by arranging beds in pairs or in groups, so that while one bed is on stream drying the gas, another is being regenerated, and the two exchange roles on a regular switching cycle that keeps the drying duty continuous. The regeneration step is every bit as much a part of the process as the adsorption step, and the conditions under which it is carried out, the temperature reached, the purge used, and the completeness with which the bed is dried back, all have a bearing on the performance that follows. The broad pattern of behaviour, in other words, is not in doubt, and the literature speaks with a largely consistent voice on these fundamentals.

## Disagreements

Beneath that settled surface, however, there are important areas where the published reports do not agree with one another, and chief among these is the quantity of water uptake reported at low water vapour concentrations in the gas. Different groups, studying what are nominally very similar materials under apparently similar conditions, have published values that differ from one another by margins far larger than the uncertainties the individual studies themselves suggest. This is a frustrating state of affairs for anyone who wishes to design a dryer on the basis of the published data, because the low-concentration uptake is precisely the quantity that governs how dry the gas leaving the bed will ultimately be. A careful reading of the conflicting reports suggests that the divergence has a great deal to do with the way the measurements were made: some groups measured uptake directly by weighing the adsorbent, while others inferred it from breakthrough behaviour, and the activation and pretreatment of the samples before measurement also varied considerably from study to study, which can shift the results significantly. On top of this, the studies differ in the form of material tested, some working with fine powders and others with the formed pellets and beads that are actually loaded into industrial vessels, and in how long the sample was left in contact with the humid gas before the measurement was taken, a detail that matters greatly where uptake is slow to settle at low concentrations. The humidity of the test gas itself was generated and controlled in different ways, adding yet another layer of variation that is difficult to unpick after the event. Until these methodological questions are ironed out, the disagreement on this quantity is likely to persist.

## Gaps

Finally, there are striking gaps in the literature where measurements that ought to exist simply have not been reported at all. The most notable of these concerns what happens to an adsorbent over the long term in real cyclic service. Study after study reports the uptake of a fresh sample, carefully activated and measured under clean laboratory conditions, yet the measurement that nobody seems to report is how the capacity of the same material holds up after it has been put through repeated adsorption and regeneration cycles, one after another, as it would be in any real plant. Closely related to this is the near-absence of reporting on the regeneration side of the cycle: many studies are vague about the exact conditions used to dry their samples back between measurements, which makes it hard to know whether the material being measured in one laboratory is in the same state as the material measured in another. Alongside this, the effects of trace contaminants in industrial gas streams, which are largely absent from laboratory feeds, are seldom followed over time, even though in service it is often contamination rather than water itself that slowly degrades a bed. There is also a scale question that the literature largely steps around, in that nearly all measurements are made on small samples under carefully controlled conditions, while the behaviour of a full industrial bed, with its flow distribution and its temperature fronts, is inferred rather than observed. These gaps matter enormously, because a dryer is not bought for its first cycle but for years of cycling, and the literature, for all its richness, leaves the designer largely guessing on precisely the questions that service life depends upon.
target:
## Scope

This review covers adsorbents for gas drying: silica gel, activated alumina, and zeolite molecular sieves, the three material classes in industrial use for removing water vapour from gas streams. The duties behind the literature are consistent: water left in a gas condenses in cold pipework, corrodes steel, forms solid hydrates that block lines, and enters downstream processes that require a dry feed. Natural gas, instrument air, and process gas feeds are the recurring applications, and the adsorbent bed is the standard means of drying all three. The review draws on 128 papers from the last 13 years. It reports first what the literature establishes, then the quantity on which reports conflict, and finally the measurement the literature does not contain.

## Established results

The literature reports the outcome of a drying duty as the water content, or the dew point, of the treated gas, and reports the adsorbent side of the duty as an uptake: the mass of water the material takes up under stated conditions. Uptake is the quantity the sections below keep returning to, because it is the quantity from which bed size, cycle time, and the dryness reached are all worked out. Where a report gives the one without the conditions that produced it, the figure cannot be carried to another duty.

The three classes all dry gas, and their ordering by duty is settled. Silica gel and activated alumina carry the moderate duties. Molecular sieves carry the duties where very dry gas is required: a molecular sieve keeps taking up water at low water vapour concentrations, and at temperatures, where silica gel and activated alumina have lost most of their capacity. That behaviour is reported consistently enough, across enough independent groups, to be treated as established.

The mode of operation is likewise settled. An adsorbent bed takes up water until it approaches saturation and is then regenerated, by heating or by a dry purge gas, and returned to service. Industrial dryers arrange this as a switching cycle, with one bed drying the gas while another regenerates, so the duty is continuous although each bed alternates. Regeneration is part of the duty, not a pause in it: the temperature the bed is taken to, the purge it is swept with, and the dryness it is brought back to together set the state from which the next adsorption step starts. Drying on these materials is a cyclic process in every industrial application the review covers, and comparisons between materials are comparisons between cycles, not between single passes. Fresh-sample capacity is therefore a property of the first cycle only, a point the gaps section returns to.

## Disagreements

Reports conflict on the water uptake of these materials at low water vapour concentrations. Groups studying nominally similar materials under nominally similar conditions publish values that stand apart by more than the uncertainty any of the studies claims for itself. The conflict cannot be settled from the published values, because the values were not measured the same way. It matters because low-concentration uptake is the property that sets how dry the treated gas can be made: the contested quantity is the design quantity.

Weighing the conflicting reports against their test conditions points to method as the source. Some groups measured uptake directly, by weighing the adsorbent; others inferred uptake from breakthrough curves, a route that folds the dynamics of the test bed into the figure reported as capacity. Pretreatment differed as well: the activation of the sample before measurement, which sets the state the measurement starts from, was neither uniform nor always reported in full. The form of the sample differed, powder in some studies and formed pellets in others, and formed material presents its water with a longer path into each particle. Contact time differed too, and at low vapour concentrations uptake settles slowly, so a measurement closed early reports a value still on its way to equilibrium. The humidity of the test gas was generated by different means in different laboratories, with different control over the concentration that the whole measurement depends on. A disagreement produced by method is not evidence about the materials, and the review treats the low-concentration uptake of all three classes as unsettled until the measurements are made on a common basis.

A further share of the conflict sits in the materials themselves. A class name is not a material specification: silica gels, aluminas, and molecular sieves from different makers differ in binder, in forming, and in pore structure, and two samples carrying the same class name can be measurably different adsorbents. Reports that name the class and not the maker, or the maker and not the grade, leave the reader unable to tell a method difference from a material difference, and part of the published spread is likely to be exactly that confusion, recorded as if it were a property of the class.

## Gaps

The measurement nobody reports is the change in capacity over repeated cycles. The literature characterises fresh samples: activated, clean, measured once. A dryer in service adsorbs and is regenerated cycle after cycle, and its working capacity after many cycles is the figure a design actually spends. That figure is absent. Reports do not follow one sample through repeated regeneration under stated conditions and report the capacity it retains.

Two neighbouring absences compound the first. The regeneration conditions used between measurements are themselves often reported loosely, so the state of the material at the start of one group's measurement cannot be matched to the state in another's; and the trace contaminants present in industrial gas, absent from laboratory feeds, are not followed over time, although in service it is contamination as much as water that ages a bed. The published measurements are also made on small samples under controlled flow, and the step from sample behaviour to the behaviour of a full bed, with its flow distribution and moving temperature fronts, is taken by inference in every design the review covers.

The gap is structural, not incidental: a cycling study takes far longer than a fresh-sample study and produces a less quotable result. Its absence nonetheless fixes the scope of every claim the literature supports. What is established is how these adsorbents behave when new; how they behave in the service they are bought for is, on the published record, unmeasured.

fact_base: Carbon dioxide and hydrogen react over a copper-zinc oxide catalyst to give dimethyl ether. Space-time yield is the mass of product per unit catalyst volume per hour (kg L-1 h-1). Test conditions: 230 °C, 60 bar, feed ratio H2/CO2 = 3, one feed composition. Washcoated monolith catalyst: space-time yield 1.04 kg L-1 h-1, pressure drop 0.25 bar, activity loss 6% after 100 h. Extruded pellet catalyst: space-time yield 0.46 kg L-1 h-1, pressure drop 1.3 bar, activity loss 18% after 100 h. No sulfur-bearing feed was tested. Yield and pressure drop are seldom reported for the same catalyst charge.
input:
In recent years, the conversion of carbon dioxide into useful chemical products has attracted considerable attention, and the reaction of carbon dioxide with hydrogen over a copper-zinc oxide catalyst to produce dimethyl ether is an interesting route that has been the subject of ongoing investigation. In this study, two different forms of the catalyst, namely a washcoated monolith catalyst and an extruded pellet catalyst, were tested and compared under identical conditions in order to assess their relative performance. Space-time yield, which is a key performance indicator in this context, is defined as the mass of product obtained per unit catalyst volume per hour (kg L-1 h-1). The tests were carried out at 230 °C and 60 bar, with a feed ratio H2/CO2 = 3 and a single feed composition throughout.

Turning to the results, the washcoated monolith catalyst achieved a space-time yield of 1.04 kg L-1 h-1, with a pressure drop of 0.25 bar and an activity loss of 6% after 100 h on stream. The extruded pellet catalyst, by comparison, delivered a space-time yield of 0.46 kg L-1 h-1, with a pressure drop of 1.3 bar and an activity loss of 18% after 100 h. Overall, the monolith therefore appears to offer a considerably more favourable combination of performance characteristics, delivering the higher yield while at the same time imposing the lower pressure drop and retaining its activity noticeably better over the duration of the test. It is worth adding that no sulfur-bearing feed was tested in this work, and that yield and pressure drop are seldom reported together for the same catalyst charge in the wider literature.

Carbon dioxide and hydrogen react over a copper-zinc oxide catalyst to give dimethyl ether. Two forms of the catalyst, a washcoated monolith and an extruded pellet, are compared at one feed composition. Space-time yield is the mass of product per unit catalyst volume per hour (kg L-1 h-1).

Both catalysts were tested at 230 °C and 60 bar with a feed ratio H2/CO2 = 3. The washcoated monolith gave a space-time yield of 1.04 kg L-1 h-1, a pressure drop of 0.25 bar, and an activity loss of 6% after 100 h. The extruded pellet gave a space-time yield of 0.46 kg L-1 h-1, a pressure drop of 1.3 bar, and an activity loss of 18% after 100 h.

The monolith leads on all three measures at the tested conditions: the higher yield, the lower pressure drop, and the smaller activity loss over the same test duration. The comparison is a comparison of catalyst form at fixed chemistry and fixed conditions, and the margins are large enough that the ranking does not rest on any single measure.

Each measure answers a different design question, and the three are stated together because a catalyst is chosen on the three together. Space-time yield sets the catalyst volume a duty requires. Pressure drop sets the cost of passing the feed through that volume, paid as compression or as pumping. Activity loss sets how long the charge holds its initial performance before the yield figures above cease to describe it. A form that led on yield alone, at a heavy pressure drop or with a fast loss of activity, would present a genuine trade-off; at the tested conditions no trade-off arises, because the same form leads on all three.

The claim is limited to the tested scope. One feed composition was tested, and no sulfur-bearing feed was tested, so behaviour on sulfur-bearing feeds is outside the claim. Yield and pressure drop, reported here for the same catalyst charge, are seldom reported together in the literature, and the comparison with other catalysts is limited accordingly.

fact_base: Inventory policy for a packaging film: mean demand 1933 units per week, standard deviation 435 units per week, replenishment lead time 2 weeks. Safety stock for a 95% cycle service level is 1015 units. Demand is treated as normal and independent between weeks; seasonal peaks are excluded.
input: In order to maintain reliable availability of a packaging film while at the same time avoiding the excessive holding of stock, an appropriate safety stock level needs to be established for the item. Demand for the film averages 1933 units per week, although it fluctuates considerably from week to week, with a standard deviation of 435 units per week. The replenishment lead time for the film is 2 weeks, which means that any order placed takes some time to arrive, and it is during this window that the safety stock has to provide its protection. The policy adopted here targets a 95% cycle service level, which is to say that in 95% of replenishment cycles, demand should be met without running out of stock. Working through the calculation on this basis, the safety stock comes out at 1015 units. In arriving at this figure, demand has been treated as though it were normally distributed and independent from one week to the next, and it is worth pointing out that seasonal peaks in demand have been left out of the picture altogether, so the 1015 units should be read with that important qualification in mind.
target:
Set the safety stock for the packaging film at 1015 units. The figure is the planning team's to hold and review.

Safety stock covers the variation in demand over the replenishment lead time. Demand for the film averages 1933 units per week with a standard deviation of 435 units per week, and the lead time is 2 weeks. The policy target is a 95% cycle service level: in 95% of replenishment cycles, demand is met without a stockout. On the stated demand figures and that service target, the safety stock is 1015 units.

The level is a policy figure, not a forecast for any particular week. In most cycles the stock is untouched; it is drawn on in the cycles where demand over the lead time ran above its mean. A higher service target returns a higher stock on the same demand figures; the target is where the cost of holding film is set against the cost of a stockout, and that choice belongs to the business.

The figure rests on its basis, and the basis has a named limit: demand is treated as normal and independent between weeks, and seasonal peaks are excluded. A seasonal peak is exactly the week in which demand departs from that basis, and the stock set here is not sized for it. The level should be revisited when the demand pattern changes, not after a stockout has shown the change.

fact_base: A single-stage compressor raises air from 1 bar to 6 bar. Inlet temperature is 303 K. For isentropic compression with a heat-capacity ratio of 1.4, the discharge temperature is 506 K. The isentropic estimate excludes mechanical losses; the installed machine's measured discharge temperature is higher.
input:
In this worked example, we will estimate the discharge temperature of a single-stage compressor that is used to compress air. The compressor raises the air from a pressure of 1 bar up to a pressure of 6 bar, and the air enters the machine at an inlet temperature of 303 K. In order to carry out the estimate, the compression is treated as isentropic, which is an idealised process in which the compression is both reversible and adiabatic, and the heat-capacity ratio of air is taken as 1.4.

Under the isentropic assumption, the temperature of the gas rises as its pressure is increased, with the discharge temperature being determined by the inlet temperature together with the pressure ratio across the machine and the heat-capacity ratio of the gas. Carrying out the calculation with the values given above, the discharge temperature of the compressor is found to be 506 K.

It is important to appreciate, however, that this figure is obtained from an idealised estimate from which mechanical losses have been deliberately excluded. Real machines inevitably experience such losses, and as a consequence the discharge temperature that is actually measured on the installed machine is higher than the value estimated here. The isentropic figure should therefore be understood as an ideal benchmark against which the performance of the real machine can be compared, rather than as a prediction of the temperature that will be observed in practice.
target:
Calculate the discharge temperature of a single-stage compressor raising air from 1 bar to 6 bar, with an inlet temperature of 303 K. The compression is taken as isentropic and the heat-capacity ratio of air as 1.4.

Isentropic compression is reversible and adiabatic: no heat crosses the boundary and no loss is charged inside the machine. Those are the assumptions, and they stand before the result because the result depends on them. For an isentropic compression the discharge temperature is set by the inlet temperature, the pressure ratio, and the heat-capacity ratio; substitution of the stated values gives a discharge temperature of 506 K.

Along the compression the pressure and the temperature rise together, and the heat-capacity ratio controls the rise: at a fixed pressure ratio, a gas with the larger ratio returns the larger temperature rise. The inlet temperature sets the level the rise starts from, so the same machine discharges hotter on a hotter inlet at unchanged pressures.

The check on the estimate is the installed machine. The isentropic estimate excludes mechanical losses, and the measured discharge temperature of the installed machine is higher. The direction of the difference is the one the assumptions predict: losses the model omits appear in the real machine as additional temperature rise. The estimate is therefore the lower bound of the pair, and it is used as such: a measured temperature close to it speaks for the machine's condition, and a measured temperature well above it is the deviation that needs explaining, not the estimate.

fact_base: A gravity settler removes sand from a process stream. Design overflow rate is 0.69 m h-1 at a throughput of 141 m3 h-1, giving a plan area of 204 m2. The overflow-rate basis is a vendor rule for this solid; no settling test on the actual slurry has been run.
input:
A gravity settler is a widely used item of equipment whose purpose is to remove solid particles from a liquid stream by allowing them to settle out under the influence of gravity, and in the present case the settler is required to remove sand from a process stream. The sizing of such a unit is commonly approached through the design overflow rate, which is the throughput of liquid divided by the plan area of the settler, and which effectively represents the upward velocity of the liquid that the settling particles have to overcome. For this particular duty, the design overflow rate has been set at 0.69 m h-1, and the settler is required to handle a throughput of 141 m3 h-1. Dividing the throughput by the design overflow rate in order to obtain the required area, the plan area of the settler works out at 204 m2.

It is very important to appreciate the basis on which this sizing rests. The design overflow rate adopted here does not come from any experimental work carried out on the material in question; instead, it is a vendor rule that is customarily applied to this solid. Moreover, no settling test has actually been run on the real slurry that the settler will have to treat, which means that the settling behaviour of the sand in the actual process liquid has never been directly observed or measured. The resulting area should therefore be regarded as an estimate that is founded upon a general rule of thumb for this kind of solid, rather than as a figure that has been verified against the behaviour of the specific slurry concerned, and some caution is accordingly appropriate when the result is carried forward into subsequent design work.
target:
A gravity settler removes sand from a process stream. The liquid passes slowly enough through the vessel for the sand to fall to the bottom while the clarified liquid leaves over the top. Settler sizing turns on the overflow rate, the throughput divided by the plan area of the vessel: the overflow rate is the upward velocity of the liquid in the settler, and particles settle out against it where their own settling velocity exceeds it.

The design overflow rate for this duty is 0.69 m h-1 and the throughput is 141 m3 h-1. Division of the throughput by the overflow rate gives the plan area: 204 m2.

Two features of the sizing deserve stating. The plan area, not the vessel volume, is the dimension the calculation returns: depth is set by other considerations, by the room the settled sand needs and by the flow distribution the inlet can achieve, and a deeper vessel of the same area settles no more sand. The overflow rate is also the settler's operating limit, not only its design figure: throughput pushed above the design value raises the upward velocity in the same proportion, and the particles that settled at the design rate are the first to be carried over the top when the rate rises.

The limit on the result stands in its basis. The design overflow rate is a vendor rule for this solid, not a measured property of the slurry the settler will treat, and no settling test has been run on the actual slurry. A settling test would return the rate from the slurry's own behaviour in the process liquid; the vendor rule stands in for that measurement, on the strength of the vendor's experience with the solid in other liquids. The plan area is therefore a rule-based estimate. It is fit for layout and cost work at this stage, and the settler should not be committed to fabrication until a settling test on the actual slurry has either confirmed the rate or replaced it.

It is worth noting that the shortfall is by no means evenly spread, highlighting the extent to which one site dominates the problem: Plant 2 accounts for 59% of late orders across the business as a whole.

The wider context is equally important. The recommendation under consideration is therefore to install at Plant 2 first and hold the other plants until Plant 2 results are reported, with the operations director owning the scheduling programme. fact_base: Goal: compute the Reynolds number for water in a pipe and state the flow regime. The Reynolds number Re (dimensionless) is computed from density rho (kg m-3), mean velocity v (m s-1), pipe diameter D (m) and dynamic viscosity mu (Pa s) by Re = rho v D / mu. Water at 293 K: rho = 998 kg m-3, mu = 1.00 x 10-3 Pa s. Pipe diameter D = 0.05 m; mean velocity v = 0.7 m s-1. Worked result: Re = 34900 (computed as 998 x 0.7 x 0.05 / 0.001). Flow is laminar below Re = 2300 and turbulent above Re = 4000; between the two values the regime is transitional and is not assigned by the number alone.
input:
In this worked example, we are going to calculate the Reynolds number for water flowing in a pipe and then use the result to determine what the flow regime is. The Reynolds number, denoted Re, is a dimensionless quantity that is computed from the density rho (kg m-3), the mean velocity v (m s-1), the pipe diameter D (m) and the dynamic viscosity mu (Pa s), using the well-known relation Re = rho v D / mu. It is important to note that each of these quantities plays its own role in the calculation, with rho and mu being properties of the liquid at the temperature in question, v being the mean velocity, and D being the diameter of the pipe.

For water at 293 K, the values that we will use are rho = 998 kg m-3 and mu = 1.00 x 10-3 Pa s. The pipe diameter is given as D = 0.05 m and the mean velocity is v = 0.7 m s-1. Substituting all of these values into the relation therefore gives a Reynolds number of 34900.

In terms of interpreting the result, flow is laminar below Re = 2300 and turbulent above Re = 4000, while between the two values the regime is transitional and cannot be assigned by the number alone. Since the value that has been obtained here is considerably higher than the upper threshold, it can be concluded that the flow in the pipe is turbulent, highlighting the usefulness of the Reynolds number as a simple and effective criterion for classifying flow regimes.

The Reynolds number for water in the pipe is 34900, and the flow is turbulent. The Reynolds number Re (dimensionless) is computed from the density rho (kg m-3), the mean velocity v (m s-1), the pipe diameter D (m) and the dynamic viscosity mu (Pa s) by Re = rho v D / mu. Each quantity in the relation is a property of the flow as stated: rho and mu belong to the liquid at its temperature, v is the mean velocity over the pipe cross-section, and D is the pipe diameter.

Water at 293 K has rho = 998 kg m-3 and mu = 1.00 x 10-3 Pa s. The pipe diameter is D = 0.05 m and the mean velocity is v = 0.7 m s-1. Substitution of these values in Re = rho v D / mu gives the number stated at the head of the example, with the units cancelling between numerator and denominator, as they must for a dimensionless group.

Flow is laminar below Re = 2300 and turbulent above Re = 4000; between the two values the regime is transitional and is not assigned by the number alone. The computed value stands far above the upper threshold, so no part of the transitional band is involved and the assignment to turbulent flow does not rest on a marginal reading of the scale.

subtype: worked example with equation: radiative exchange
fact_base: A blackened plate at 600 K faces surroundings at 290 K. Its emissivity $\varepsilon$ is 0.9. Net radiative heat flux $q$ is 6.3 kW m-2, with the Stefan-Boltzmann constant $\sigma$ = 5.67 x 10-8 W m-2 K-4. The estimate treats both surfaces as large and parallel; view factors for the real geometry are not included.
input:
In this example we consider a blackened plate that is held at a temperature of 600 K and faces surroundings that are at a temperature of 290 K, with the emissivity of the plate being 0.9. The quantity that we wish to determine is the net radiative heat flux, denoted $q$, and the relevant relation is the Stefan-Boltzmann expression

$$q = \varepsilon \sigma (T_1^4 - T_2^4)$$

in which $T_1$ is the temperature of the plate, $T_2$ is the temperature of the surroundings, $\varepsilon$ is the emissivity, and $\sigma$ is the Stefan-Boltzmann constant, which has the value 5.67 x 10-8 W m-2 K-4. When the stated values are substituted into this expression, the net radiative heat flux is found to be 6.3 kW m-2, which represents the net rate at which energy is exchanged per unit area once the radiation received from the surroundings has been set against the radiation emitted by the plate itself.

It should be noted, however, that this estimate rests on the assumption that both surfaces are large and parallel to one another. View factors for the real geometry are not included in the calculation, so the result should be understood as applying to the idealised arrangement described by the equation rather than to any actual arrangement in which the plate is of finite size or the surroundings only partially enclose it.
target:
A blackened plate at temperature $T_1$ = 600 K faces surroundings at $T_2$ = 290 K. The emissivity $\varepsilon$ of the plate is 0.9. The net radiative heat flux $q$ from the plate is given by

$$q = \varepsilon \sigma (T_1^4 - T_2^4)$$

where $\sigma$ is the Stefan-Boltzmann constant. The flux is the difference of two fourth-power terms: the plate emits on its own temperature and receives on the temperature of the surroundings, and the emissivity scales the exchange below the blackbody value at the same temperatures. The net flux is the difference between the radiation the plate sends out and the radiation it receives back from the surroundings. Each side of the difference is set by the temperature of the surface it leaves, raised to the fourth power, so the hotter side dominates the balance and the exchange runs outward from the plate, from the hot surface toward the cold surroundings, at every point the two face each other. With $\sigma$ = 5.67 x 10-8 W m-2 K-4, substitution of the stated temperatures and emissivity gives $q$ = 6.3 kW m-2.

The estimate treats both surfaces as large and parallel. View factors for the real geometry are not included, so the value holds for the idealised arrangement the equation describes; a plate of finite size, or surroundings that enclose it only in part, exchange on view factors this estimate does not carry, and the flux for such a geometry is not the figure computed here.

fact_base: Inventory policy for a resin grade: mean demand 3027 units per week, standard deviation 874 units per week, replenishment lead time 2 weeks. Safety stock for a 95% cycle service level is 2039 units. Demand is treated as normal and independent between weeks; seasonal peaks are excluded.
input:
This passage sets out the inventory policy that has been adopted for a resin grade, focusing in particular on the level of safety stock that should be held. Mean demand is 3027 units per week, with a standard deviation of 874 units per week, and the replenishment lead time is 2 weeks. On this basis, the safety stock for a 95% cycle service level has been set at 2039 units, a figure that is designed to ensure that the business is well positioned to maintain continuity of supply in the face of the normal variability that is inevitably present in weekly demand patterns.

It is important to note the assumptions that underpin this policy. Demand is treated as normal, which means that the spread of weekly demand is summarised by the standard deviation and the safety stock scales accordingly, and demand is also treated as independent between weeks, so that the variation experienced over the lead time is the variation of unrelated weekly draws rather than of a sustained run in a single direction. Seasonal peaks, however, are excluded from the policy altogether, which means that the safety stock figure should not be regarded as providing cover for such periods: a seasonal peak that raises weekly demand above the mean for the duration of the lead time will steadily draw the safety stock down and may well exhaust it entirely, and any cover for those periods will need to be determined separately, on the basis of the peak itself, at the appropriate time.
