The figure is the stock held above mean lead-time demand so that demand over the lead time is met from stock at a 95% cycle service level, and a shortage is recorded against a cycle only when lead-time demand runs past the mean and the safety stock together. The figure is reviewed when the demand record changes materially, since both quantities it rests on are properties of that record rather than of the store that holds the stock.

The policy rests on two stated treatments of the demand data. Demand is treated as normal, so the spread of weekly demand is summarised by the standard deviation and the safety stock scales with it; and demand is treated as independent between weeks, so the variation over a two-week lead time is the variation of two unrelated draws rather than of a run in one direction. Seasonal peaks are excluded from the policy. The stock figure therefore covers ordinary week-to-week variation at the stated service level and does not cover a seasonal peak: a peak that lifts weekly demand above the mean for the length of the lead time draws the safety stock down and can exhaust it, and cover for such periods has to be set by a separate decision on the peak itself.

fact_base: Goal: compute the half-life of a first-order reaction and the fraction remaining after 60 min. For a first-order reaction the rate constant k (min-1) fixes the half-life t1/2 (min) by t1/2 = ln(2) / k, and the fraction remaining after time t (min) is exp(-k t). Measured rate constant: k = 0.046 min-1 at 323 K, from concentration measurements every 5 min over 90 min. Worked results: t1/2 = 15.1 min; the fraction remaining after 60 min is 0.06 (dimensionless), both computed from the stated relations. The relations hold for a first-order reaction only; a reaction of another order follows a different decay law.
input:
In this worked example, the aim is to compute the half-life of a first-order reaction and to determine the fraction of the reactant that remains after 60 min. For a first-order reaction, the rate constant k (min-1) fixes the half-life t1/2 (min) through the relation t1/2 = ln(2) / k, and the fraction remaining after a time t (min) is given by exp(-k t). It is worth emphasising that the half-life depends on the rate constant alone; the amount of material present at the start has no bearing on it, and the same fraction disappears in each successive half-life for as long as the reaction remains first order in character.

The measured rate constant is k = 0.046 min-1 at 323 K, obtained from concentration measurements taken every 5 min over 90 min. Substituting the measured value into the half-life relation gives the half-life as 15.1 min. Turning to the fraction remaining after 60 min, the exponent is -(0.046 x 60) = -2.76, so that exp(-2.76) = 0.06: the great majority of the reactant has been consumed, as one would expect after an interval amounting to four half-lives in round terms, since repeated halving over such a span leaves only a small residue behind. It should be noted, however, that these relations hold for a first-order reaction only; a reaction of another order follows a different decay law altogether, and the figures arrived at here do not carry over to such a case.

The half-life depends on k alone: the amount present at the start does not enter it, and the same fraction is lost in each successive half-life for as long as the reaction stays first order.

For the fraction remaining, the exponent is -k t with t at 60 min: -(0.046 x 60) = -2.76, and exp(-2.76) is the fraction stated above. Sixty minutes is four half-lives in round terms, and the check on the result is that repeated halving over that span leaves a residue of the size the exponential gives: the two routes agree because the half-life and the exponential are the same decay law stated in two forms. The relations hold for a first-order reaction only; a reaction of another order follows a different decay law, and neither figure carries over to one.

fact_base: Cost review of a cross-dock transfer: 579 km per trip at $1.98 per km, 890 trips per year. Annual transport cost is $1020k. Costs are carrier invoices for the last 12 months; empty running is included in the trip count.
input:
This cost review examines the annual transport cost associated with a cross-dock transfer operation. The route in question involves 579 km per trip, charged at a rate of $1.98 per km, and the operation runs a total of 890 trips per year. When these components are brought together, the annual transport cost comes to $1020k, making transport a significant element of the overall cost picture for the operation. The figures are drawn from carrier invoices for the last 12 months, so they reflect the charges that have actually been incurred over that period rather than any estimated or budgeted amounts.

It is important to note that empty running is included in the trip count, which means that the trips that have been counted are all of the trips that the carrier invoiced, whether they were loaded or running empty. The annual figure therefore represents the cost of running the transfer operation as a whole, and it should not be interpreted as the cost of the loaded movement on its own. Indeed, a cost per loaded kilometre calculated from these figures would come out higher than the headline rate might suggest, precisely because the empty trips add distance and cost without carrying any load. For this reason, any comparison with an alternative routing or an alternative carrier needs to be carried out on a like-for-like basis, with all trips counted, in order to ensure that the comparison is a fair one.

Empty running is included in the trip count: the trips counted are all the trips the carrier invoiced, loaded and empty alike. The annual cost is therefore the cost of the transfer operation as a whole, and not the cost of the loaded movement alone. A cost per loaded kilometre drawn from these figures would stand higher than the invoiced rate, because the empty trips add distance and charge while carrying no load, and the loaded kilometres over which the total is spread are fewer than the kilometres on which the total was incurred.

Any comparison of the transfer against an alternative routing or an alternative carrier has to be made on the same basis, with all trips counted. A comparison that counted loaded trips only would credit the alternative with an efficiency the present operation's figures do not claim, and the saving it appeared to show would be an artefact of the counting rather than a property of the alternative.

fact_base: Excerpt content: the analogy between the transfer processes is stated, then qualified by the case where it fails. The excerpt works one short numerical check with numbers given inside the excerpt itself. The excerpt assumes the chapter's earlier definitions and adds none.
input:
The Chilton-Colburn analogy draws a direct parallel between the transfer processes by setting the mass-transfer factor $j_D$ equal to half of the friction factor $f$, a relationship that can be written compactly as

$j_D$ = $f/2$

It is worth pausing on what this statement actually involves. It is an equality between two ratios that are formed from quite different processes, with $j_D$ being obtained from a measured mass-transfer rate and $f$ being obtained from a measured pressure loss. In those situations where the two happen to be formed from one and the same surface action, the equality provides an elegant summary of the measurements on both sides. That action is skin friction: the resistance at the surface is the drag of the fluid as it moves along the surface, and it is precisely the same surface motion that is responsible both for dragging on the flow and for carrying material to and from the surface itself.

A brief numerical check helps to fix the arithmetic involved. If we take a surface for which $f$ = 0.0064, the analogy immediately gives $j_D$ = 0.0064 / 2 = 0.0032, and a measured value of $j_D$ for that surface can be compared against this figure: agreement lends support to the analogy for the surface concerned, whereas any disagreement indicates a surface where the shared action does not account for the whole of the resistance.

There is, however, an important qualification, namely the case in which pressure forces acting on the body make their own contribution to the measured resistance. Flow across a bluff body is the standard example of this: a large part of the drag is form drag, arising from pressure acting on the projected area of the body, and there is no corresponding action transferring material at the surface. The value of $f$ that is formed from the total drag consequently exceeds the skin-friction component, while $j_D$ continues to respond to the surface action alone, with the result that the measured $j_D$ falls below $f/2$. The analogy should therefore be understood as a statement about surfaces whose resistance is skin friction; where form drag is present, applying it will overstate the transfer factor by the share of the drag that is supplied by pressure forces.

fact_base: A continuous stirred-tank reactor runs a neutralisation that is first order in the limiting reactant. The rate constant is 0.073 min-1 at the operating temperature and the mean residence time is 50 min. Steady-state conversion for an ideal CSTR is 78.5%. The estimate assumes perfect mixing and constant density; tracer tests on the actual vessel have not been run.
input:
A continuous stirred-tank reactor, or CSTR, is used to run a neutralisation reaction that is first order in the limiting reactant. For an ideal CSTR operating at steady state, the conversion that is achieved is governed by the product of the rate constant and the mean residence time, because the material balance on the limiting reactant is written over the whole vessel and the rate is evaluated at the outlet concentration, the contents of the vessel being uniform throughout as a consequence of the mixing.

In the present case, the rate constant is 0.073 min-1 at the operating temperature and the mean residence time is 50 min, which means that the product of the two quantities is 0.073 x 50 = 3.65, a dimensionless figure. The conversion is then obtained as this product divided by one plus the product, that is, 3.65 / 4.65 = 0.785, corresponding to a steady-state conversion of 78.5%. The reason the denominator takes this form is that the flowing stream continuously removes unreacted material from the vessel, so a CSTR converts less of its feed than a batch vessel that is held for the same length of time at the same rate constant.

It should be noted that this estimate rests on two important assumptions, namely perfect mixing and constant density. Perfect mixing is what permits the balance to be written in terms of a single outlet concentration, and a real vessel with stagnant zones or short-circuiting will tend to fall short of the ideal figure. Constant density, for its part, keeps the residence time as a property of the vessel and the flow alone. Tracer tests on the actual vessel have not been carried out, so neither assumption has yet been verified against the vessel's own behaviour, highlighting the fact that the conversion that has been calculated here is strictly the ideal-CSTR value for the stated conditions.

subtype: worked example with equation: Raoult partial pressure
fact_base: An ideal liquid mixture holds hexane in heptane at a liquid mole fraction $x$ of 0.29 for the volatile component. Its pure-component vapour pressure $P^*$ at the mixture temperature is 20.1 kPa, so the partial pressure $p$ is 5.8 kPa by Raoult's law. Raoult's law assumes an ideal solution; activity coefficients for the real mixture are not applied.
input:
Consider an ideal liquid mixture that consists of hexane held in heptane. The liquid mole fraction, denoted $x$, of hexane, which is the volatile component of the pair, is 0.29. The partial pressure of the hexane over the mixture, denoted $p$, can be obtained from Raoult's law, which states that the partial pressure of a component is equal to its liquid mole fraction multiplied by its pure-component vapour pressure:

$$p = x P^*$$

In this expression, $P^*$ represents the pure-component vapour pressure of hexane at the temperature of the mixture. At the temperature in question, this vapour pressure is 20.1 kPa, and applying the relation with the stated mole fraction therefore gives a partial pressure of 5.8 kPa for the hexane over the mixture.

It should be noted that Raoult's law is built on the assumption of an ideal solution, in which the molecules of each component escape from the liquid essentially as though the other component were not there, so that the partial pressure is simply the pure pressure scaled by the mole fraction. Activity coefficients for the real mixture have not been applied in arriving at this estimate, and a mixture in which the components interact unequally will depart from the behaviour described by the law, meaning that the partial pressure over such a mixture would not be the figure that has been calculated here.
target:
An ideal liquid mixture holds hexane in heptane. The liquid mole fraction $x$ of hexane, the volatile component, is 0.29. The partial pressure $p$ of hexane over the mixture is 5.8 kPa. Raoult's law gives the partial pressure of a component as its liquid mole fraction times its pure-component vapour pressure:

$$p = x P^*$$

where $P^*$ is the pure-component vapour pressure of hexane at the mixture temperature. At the stated temperature $P^*$ is 20.1 kPa, and the partial pressure stated above follows from the mole fraction and that pressure through the relation, with no further data entering the calculation.

The two quantities the relation joins are both fixed by the stated mixture at the stated temperature: the mole fraction by the make-up of the liquid, and the pure pressure by the temperature at which the mixture stands. Nothing about the vapour beyond the partial pressure itself is asserted; the total pressure over the mixture would require the second component's contribution as well, which this estimate does not compute.

Raoult's law assumes an ideal solution: each component's molecules leave the liquid as if the other component were absent, and the partial pressure is the pure pressure scaled by the mole fraction alone. Activity coefficients for the real mixture are not applied in this estimate. A mixture whose components interact unequally departs from the line the law draws, and the partial pressure over such a mixture is not the figure computed here.

fact_base: Excerpt content: a budget overrun of 4 weeks is reported with its cause; the excerpt proposes one mitigation and its owner. The excerpt does not open or close the memo and does not restate its subject line.
input:
It should be reported that a budget overrun of 4 weeks has now built up on the current package, the cause of which is the late completion of the EPC scope that feeds into the package: work which ought to have been closed out before the package got under way has instead continued to run alongside it, with the result that the package has effectively carried both its own costs and the costs of the unfinished work within the same accounts. It should also be noted that the overrun is by no means spread evenly across the package as a whole; it is concentrated in that part of the work which depends on the unfinished scope, while the remainder of the package continues to run at its planned rate.

The mitigation that is proposed in response to this position is that outstanding commitments on the package should be re-approved before they are placed, in order to ensure that no further cost is committed against the package until each commitment has been properly checked against the state of the scope that it serves. Responsibility for this mitigation sits with the project board, which will hold the re-approval process, and any work that cannot pass through that process will be held rather than being charged on in the expectation that the position will in due course correct itself.
target:
A budget overrun of 4 weeks has built up on the current package, and its cause is the late completion of the EPC scope feeding into it: work that was to have closed out before the package started has instead run alongside it, and the package has carried both its own cost and the cost of the unfinished work in the same accounts. The overrun is not spread evenly across the package; it sits in the part of the work that depends on the unfinished scope, and the remainder of the package is running at its planned rate. The position is reported as it stands, without allowance for recovery that has not yet been earned.

The mitigation proposed is that outstanding commitments on the package are re-approved before they are placed, so that no further cost is committed against the package until the commitment has been checked against the state of the scope it serves. Responsibility for the mitigation sits with the project board: the board holds the re-approval, and work that cannot pass it is held rather than charged on in the expectation that the position will correct itself.

fact_base: A shell-and-tube exchanger heats crude oil in a refinery preheat train. Duty is 1925 kW. Hot stream: 150 °C in, 110 °C out. Cold stream: 35 °C in, 55 °C out. The log-mean temperature difference is 84.6 K and the installed area is 55.7 m2, giving an overall coefficient of 408 W m-2 K-1. Fouling was assessed from a single 90-day run; no cleaning cycle has been completed.
input: It is important to note that shell-and-tube exchangers play a crucial role in refinery preheat trains, and the unit considered here, which heats crude oil, provides a useful illustration of how design data and operating data are brought together in practice. The exchanger in question handles a substantial thermal duty of 1925 kW. On the hot side of the unit, the stream enters at a temperature of 150 °C and leaves at 110 °C, while on the cold side the crude oil enters at 35 °C and is heated up to 55 °C. When all of these terminal temperatures are taken into account, it is possible to calculate the log-mean temperature difference, which comes out at 84.6 K, thereby providing a measure of the effective driving force for heat transfer across the unit as a whole. Furthermore, the installed heat-transfer area of the exchanger is 55.7 m2, and when this area is combined with the duty and with the log-mean temperature difference, an overall heat-transfer coefficient of 408 W m-2 K-1 is obtained, shedding light on the thermal performance of the unit in its installed condition. It should also be noted that the assessment of fouling was based on a single 90-day run, and, notably, no cleaning cycle has yet been completed, which means that the longer-term picture, including how performance develops over time and how the unit responds once cleaning has taken place, remains incomplete at this stage.
target: A shell-and-tube exchanger heats crude oil in a refinery preheat train. Duty is 1925 kW, with the hot stream cooled from 150 °C to 110 °C and the crude oil heated from 35 °C to 55 °C. The log-mean temperature difference for these terminal temperatures is 84.6 K. The log-mean temperature difference is the mean driving force for heat transfer along the exchanger: the local driving force varies from end to end as the streams approach each other in temperature, and the log-mean value is the single difference that, used with the installed area, reproduces the duty. Installed area is 55.7 m2, and area, duty and the log-mean temperature difference together give an overall coefficient of 408 W m-2 K-1. The overall coefficient states the installed performance directly, as the heat transferred per unit area per kelvin of mean driving force, with the wall and both films folded into the one figure. A coefficient stated on this basis can be compared directly with a later test of the same unit at the same terminal temperatures, and a lower value on retest is the signature of added resistance in the unit, since the area and the streams are unchanged. Fouling was assessed from a single 90-day run, and no cleaning cycle has been completed. The fouling state after cleaning, and the rate at which fouling returns once the unit is back in service, are not covered by the assessment, so the state of the unit over a longer campaign rests on a test that has not yet been made.

fact_base: Pervaporation is a membrane separation in which a liquid feed contacts one side of a membrane and vacuum on the other side draws the permeating component through as vapour. Flux is the mass permeating per unit membrane area per hour (kg m-2 h-1). The separation factor is the water-to-alcohol ratio in the permeate divided by the same ratio in the feed (dimensionless). Feed: 85 wt% isopropanol in water, at 60 °C. One feed composition was tested; no test ran beyond 500 h. Polymer membrane: flux 1.6 kg m-2 h-1, separation factor 180, flux fell 14% over 500 h. Zeolite membrane: flux 1.1 kg m-2 h-1, separation factor 320, flux unchanged over 500 h within measurement error. Flux, selectivity and stability are seldom reported together for the same membrane.
input:
Pervaporation separates a liquid mixture across a membrane under vacuum. The liquid feed contacts one side of the membrane, and vacuum on the other side draws the permeating component through as vapour. Two quantities describe performance, and both are stated per membrane as installed, on the feed as tested. Flux is the mass permeating per unit membrane area per hour (kg m-2 h-1). The separation factor is the water-to-alcohol ratio in the permeate divided by the same ratio in the feed, and is dimensionless.

A feed of 85 wt% isopropanol in water at 60 °C was tested on a polymer membrane and a zeolite membrane. One feed composition was tested, and no test ran beyond 500 h. The polymer membrane gave a flux of 1.6 kg m-2 h-1 with a separation factor of 180; its flux decreased 14% over 500 h. The zeolite membrane gave a flux of 1.1 kg m-2 h-1 with a separation factor of 320, and its flux was unchanged over 500 h within measurement error. Neither membrane leads on all three quantities. Rate favours the polymer membrane; selectivity and stability favour the zeolite membrane. Flux, selectivity and stability are seldom reported together for the same membrane, and this comparison is limited to the single feed composition and the duration tested.

The separation factor is the water-to-alcohol ratio in the permeate divided by the same ratio in the feed, and is dimensionless.

fact_base: An amine absorption unit was tested at pilot scale on gas from a cement kiln. Over 90 days at 13 t of carbon dioxide per day, the unit captured 92% of the carbon dioxide in the treated gas. Steam demand was 3.8 gigajoules per tonne of carbon dioxide captured; solvent loss was 1.8 kg per tonne captured. Beyond 90 days, the effect of kiln dust on the solvent is untested.
input: Amine absorption is widely regarded as a key technology for capturing carbon dioxide from industrial gas streams, and pilot-scale testing plays a vital role in building confidence before any move to full-scale deployment. In the work described here, an amine absorption unit was tested at pilot scale on gas from a cement kiln, a source whose gas composition and dust burden make it a demanding application for solvent-based capture. Over a period of 90 days, the unit treated gas at a rate of 13 t of carbon dioxide per day, and it is noteworthy that it captured 92% of the carbon dioxide in the treated gas, highlighting the effectiveness of the process under the conditions studied. In addition, the steam demand associated with the process was 3.8 gigajoules per tonne of carbon dioxide captured, while the solvent loss was 1.8 kg per tonne captured. Both figures are important considerations in their own right, because the energy required to regenerate the solvent and the rate at which solvent must be made up feed directly into the operating cost of any capture plant built on this basis. It should be noted, however, that beyond 90 days, the effect of kiln dust on the solvent remains untested, underscoring the need for further long-term investigation before the results are extrapolated to extended campaigns.
target: An amine absorption unit at pilot scale treated gas from a cement kiln. Over 90 days at 13 t of carbon dioxide per day, the unit captured 92% of the carbon dioxide in the treated gas. Kiln gas is the application as well as the test medium: capture and both demands were measured on the gas the process would actually treat, so the figures are not transferred from a cleaner or simpler stream. Steam demand was 3.8 gigajoules per tonne of carbon dioxide captured, and solvent loss was 1.8 kg per tonne captured. Steam demand is the regeneration energy per tonne of product and is the largest single energy input to an amine unit, so the figure sets the energy cost of the process as run. Solvent loss sets the make-up rate, a continuing cost per tonne captured for as long as the unit operates. The capture figure and both demands hold for the test as run, on kiln gas of the composition treated during the test. Beyond 90 days, the effect of kiln dust on the solvent is untested. Performance over longer campaigns, with dust accumulating in the solvent over time, is not established by this test, and neither is the solvent life that a commercial unit would plan against. A longer test, run with the dust burden present throughout, is the measurement that would settle both questions.

fact_base: Staffing review for a quality laboratory: 16 full-time staff, overtime at 11% of paid hours last year. Replacing half the overtime with one additional hire costs $72k per year fully loaded. Overtime is concentrated in two seasonal peaks; a hire is paid for the full year.
input: This staffing review takes a closer look at the position in the quality laboratory, where a team of 16 full-time staff is responsible for handling the workload that comes through the laboratory over the course of the year. It is worth noting that overtime working has become a significant feature of the overall picture, with overtime standing at 11% of paid hours last year, reflecting the considerable pressure that is placed on the laboratory at certain times of the year and the extent to which the team has come to rely on additional hours in order to keep up with the work that is expected of it. One option that has been considered in some detail is the possibility of replacing half of the overtime with one additional hire, and it has been estimated that this would cost $72k per year on a fully loaded basis, taking into account the salary together with the associated costs of employment. On the face of it, this appears to offer a straightforward way of reducing the dependence on overtime while adding permanent capacity to the team. However, it should also be borne in mind that the overtime in question is concentrated in two seasonal peaks, whereas an additional hire would be paid for the full year, including those quieter periods of the year when the extra capacity may well not be fully utilised. This complicates the comparison considerably and underscores the need to weigh the recurring, year-round cost of the hire against a pattern of demand that is anything but even across the year, as well as the practical question of whether the work that arises outside the peaks can actually absorb the additional hours that the hire would provide.
target: Overtime in the quality laboratory is 11% of paid hours (16 full-time staff, last year). One additional hire, replacing half the overtime, costs $72k per year fully loaded. The trade-off is stated in one sentence: the hire spreads its cost evenly across the year, while the overtime it replaces is concentrated in two seasonal peaks. Fully loaded means the salary together with the costs of employing the person, and the figure is a recurring annual cost, incurred in full in quiet periods as well as at peak. The review does not compare the two costs as annual totals alone, because the totals conceal the difference that decides the question: when each cost falls. The overtime cost, by contrast, arises only when the hours are worked, so it tracks the demand pattern that causes it. Laboratory management owns the decision, and the test to apply is whether work exists outside the peaks that can be scheduled into the hired hours. If the hired hours can be filled outside the peaks with work the laboratory needs done, the hire converts a peak-only cost into year-round capacity at the stated price. If they cannot, the hire pays for idle time for much of the year, and the overtime, concentrated as it is, remains the closer match to the demand pattern. The review therefore turns on the content of the off-peak hours, not on the headline cost: the same salary is good value against a full off-peak programme and poor value against an empty one, and the laboratory's own forward work list is the evidence on which the decision should rest. Until that list is examined, the figures support neither option, and the review records the position rather than a recommendation.

fact_base: A viscous liquid of viscosity $\mu$ = 0.05 Pa s flows laminarly through a tube of radius $R$ = 10 mm and length $L$ = 12 m. At a pressure drop $\Delta P$ of 7 kPa the volumetric flow $Q$ is 164.9 L h-1. The Hagen-Poiseuille equation assumes laminar, fully developed flow of a Newtonian liquid.
input:
In this worked example, we are going to look in some detail at how the Hagen-Poiseuille equation can be used to determine the volumetric flow rate of a viscous liquid flowing through a tube under laminar conditions. Let us consider a viscous liquid with a viscosity $\mu$ of 0.05 Pa s, which flows in a laminar manner through a tube having a radius $R$ of 10 mm and a length $L$ of 12 m. When a pressure drop $\Delta P$ of 7 kPa is applied along the tube, the volumetric flow $Q$ turns out to be 164.9 L h-1. The relationship between these quantities is captured by the Hagen-Poiseuille equation, which can be written in the following form:

$$Q = \frac{\pi R^4 \Delta P}{8 \mu L}$$

It is important to note that this equation rests on a number of important assumptions that should always be borne in mind when it is applied in practice. In particular, the flow is assumed to be laminar, meaning that the liquid moves in smooth layers without mixing across the tube; the flow is assumed to be fully developed, so that the velocity profile no longer changes along the length of the tube; and the liquid is assumed to behave as a Newtonian liquid, with a viscosity that does not depend on how fast it is sheared. It is also worth bearing in mind that the radius appears in the equation raised to the fourth power, which means that the flow is extremely sensitive to the size of the tube, and even a modest change in radius will have a very pronounced effect on the flow that the equation predicts. Where any of these conditions does not hold, the equation should be applied with considerable caution, if at all.
target:
Calculate the volumetric flow of a viscous liquid in laminar flow through a tube, from the following data: viscosity $\mu$ = 0.05 Pa s, tube radius $R$ = 10 mm, tube length $L$ = 12 m, and pressure drop $\Delta P$ = 7 kPa along the tube. The liquid is Newtonian, so its viscosity does not depend on the shear rate. The flow is taken as laminar, with the liquid moving in layers that do not mix across the tube, and as fully developed, with a velocity profile that no longer changes along the tube. The Hagen-Poiseuille equation applies to flow under these conditions and gives the volumetric flow $Q$ as

$$Q = \frac{\pi R^4 \Delta P}{8 \mu L}$$

where $Q$ is the volumetric flow, $R$ is the tube radius, $\Delta P$ is the pressure drop along the tube, $\mu$ is the viscosity and $L$ is the tube length. In the equation, the pressure drop drives the flow and the viscosity resists it, while the radius enters at the fourth power because a wider tube both presents more area to the flow and allows faster flow at every point of the profile. Substitution of the stated values gives $Q$ = 164.9 L h-1. The fourth power on $R$ makes the radius the quantity to measure with the greatest care: an error in $R$ produces an error in $Q$ about four times as large in proportion, a sensitivity no other input in the equation shares. The result holds only while the flow stays laminar and fully developed and the liquid stays Newtonian; outside those conditions the equation does not apply, and the pressure drop for a given flow rises faster than the equation predicts. Every symbol in the roster is a quantity that can be measured on the tube as installed, which is what makes the equation a calculation from measurements rather than a correlation fitted to them.

subtype: worked example with equation: available NPSH
fact_base: A pump draws water from an open tank at atmospheric pressure, 101.3 kPa. Vapour pressure at the pumping temperature is 19.9 kPa, the static lift is 2.7 m and suction-line friction loss is 0.3 m. Available net positive suction head $NPSH_a$ is 5.3 m. The pump's required NPSH at the duty flow comes from the vendor curve and must be exceeded with margin.
input:
Net positive suction head is a crucial consideration in the operation of any pump, and in this worked example we look at how the available net positive suction head, denoted $NPSH_a$, can be determined for a pump that draws water from an open tank. The surface of the water in the tank is exposed to the atmosphere, so the pressure acting on it is the atmospheric pressure of 101.3 kPa. The vapour pressure of the water at the pumping temperature is 19.9 kPa, and the difference between these two pressures, which is the pressure available above the vapour pressure, is 81.4 kPa, corresponding to a head of 8.3 m of water. In addition to this, the static lift that the pump has to overcome is 2.7 m, and the friction loss in the suction line is 0.3 m. The available net positive suction head is then given by the following equation:

$$NPSH_a = \frac{P_{atm} - P_v}{\rho g} - h_{lift} - h_f$$

Substituting the values discussed above into this equation gives an available net positive suction head $NPSH_a$ of 5.3 m. It should be noted that the required net positive suction head of the pump at the duty flow is not calculated here but is obtained from the vendor curve, and the available value must exceed the required value with margin for satisfactory operation.
target:
Determine the available net positive suction head $NPSH_a$ for a pump drawing water from an open tank. The tank surface is at atmospheric pressure, $P_{atm}$ = 101.3 kPa. The vapour pressure $P_v$ at the pumping temperature is 19.9 kPa, the static lift $h_{lift}$ is 2.7 m and the suction-line friction loss $h_f$ is 0.3 m. The available net positive suction head is the head at the pump inlet above the head corresponding to vapour pressure, after the lift and the suction losses are met. The pressure available above vapour pressure is the difference of the two pressures, 81.4 kPa, and division by the weight density $\rho g$ of the water converts that pressure to a head of 8.3 m. Stating the balance in metres of the liquid pumped puts every term in one form: the tank pressure drives the liquid up the suction line, gravity and friction take their share of the head, and what remains is the margin above vapour pressure at the pump inlet. The available net positive suction head is then

$$NPSH_a = \frac{P_{atm} - P_v}{\rho g} - h_{lift} - h_f$$

where every symbol is as defined in the set-up above. Thus $NPSH_a$ = 5.3 m, the pressure head less the lift and the friction loss. The pump's required net positive suction head at the duty flow is taken from the vendor curve, and the available value must exceed it with margin.

fact_base: Excerpt content: a staffing gap of 6 weeks is reported with its cause; the excerpt proposes one mitigation and its owner. The excerpt does not open or close the memo and does not restate its subject line.
input: Turning to the position on staffing, it should be noted that a gap of 6 weeks has now opened up in the programme, and this is beginning to cause a degree of concern in a number of quarters. The gap has arisen because the planners who were due to hand over the current package of work have finished and moved on earlier than the incoming resource could be mobilised, with the result that the planning function is currently operating below the level that the remaining packages require if they are to be taken forward in an orderly fashion. This matters a great deal because the planning work is what underpins the readiness of the packages that follow on behind it, and any slippage at this stage tends to be passed on, in one form or another, to the teams that are waiting on issued schedules and on coordinated access to the areas in which they need to work. It also interacts with the EPC programme, where the sequence of packages is tightly coupled, so that a delay in planning output can all too easily translate into idle time elsewhere in the programme, with resources standing by for work that has not yet been released to them. As a mitigation, it is proposed that the remaining planning work is re-sequenced so that the packages that sit on the critical path are staffed and issued first, with the less urgent packages following on as and when capacity returns to the team, and it is further suggested that the project board takes ownership of this re-plan, monitoring progress against it on a continuing basis until the gap has been closed and the planning function is once again operating at the strength the programme requires of it.
target: The staffing gap is 6 weeks. Contract planners finished the current package and left before their replacements could be mobilised, and the planning function is below the strength the remaining packages require. The effect falls on package readiness: schedules issue late, coordinated access is arranged late, and the teams waiting on both either start late or start without them. The gap sits in one function, but its consequences are distributed across every package that function serves, and they arrive at different times, which makes the total effect easy to underestimate from the position of any one package. The EPC sequence couples the packages tightly, so planning delay does not stay inside the planning function; it becomes idle time in construction, with resources standing by for work that has not been released. The mitigation is a re-plan of the remaining planning work. Packages on the critical path are staffed and issued first; the remaining packages follow as capacity returns to the team. The project board owns the re-plan and tracks delivery against it until staffing reaches the level the programme requires. The re-plan asks two things of the board: that the order of issue is held when later packages press for attention, and that slippage against the re-plan is reported as it occurs, not at the point where it reaches the critical path. Re-sequencing does not shorten the gap, and it does not recover the weeks already lost. It decides where the gap does its damage, keeping the critical path staffed at the expense of work that can wait, and it leaves the understaffed period with a defined end: the point at which replacement planners are in post and the full order of work resumes. The board's part in the re-plan is to hold that order against the claims of individual packages, each of which can make a local case for priority that the re-plan exists to overrule.

fact_base: The rate constant k (s-1) of a first-order liquid-phase reaction was measured at two temperatures. At 300 K, k = 0.017 s-1. At 340 K, k = 0.642 s-1, computed from the Arrhenius relation with activation energy 77 kJ mol-1 as a derived value. Each temperature was measured in triplicate; the relative standard deviation of k was 4%. Above 340 K the solvent evaporated during sampling, so no rate constant is reported above 340 K.
input: The rate constant k of a first-order liquid-phase reaction was measured at two temperatures in order to characterise the way in which the rate of the reaction responds to temperature. At 300 K, the rate constant k was found to be 0.017 s-1, whereas at 340 K it had increased very markedly to 0.642 s-1, which represents an increase by a factor of 37.8 across the interval studied. It should be noted that this second value was not measured directly but was computed from the Arrhenius relation using an activation energy of 77 kJ mol-1, and it is therefore presented as a derived value rather than as a direct experimental measurement. Each of the temperatures was measured in triplicate, and the relative standard deviation of k was 4%, which indicates a good level of repeatability in the underlying measurements. It should also be borne in mind, however, that above 340 K the solvent was found to evaporate during sampling, which meant that no rate constant is reported above that temperature, and the temperature range over which data are available is therefore limited accordingly. The distinction between the measured and the derived values is worth keeping in mind, since the derived value depends not only on the measurements made at the lower temperature but also on the extent to which the Arrhenius relation, with a single activation energy, faithfully describes the reaction over the whole interval.
target: The rate constant $k$ of a first-order liquid-phase reaction was measured at two temperatures. At 300 K, $k$ = 0.017 s-1. At 340 K, $k$ = 0.642 s-1, a factor of 37.8 above the lower-temperature value. The second value is derived, not measured: it was computed from the Arrhenius relation with an activation energy of 77 kJ mol-1, and it carries the assumptions of that relation with it. The relation treats the activation energy as constant over the interval, and the derived value is exact only to the extent that the reaction keeps the same mechanism, and the same energy barrier, across the whole range. Each temperature was measured in triplicate, and the relative standard deviation of $k$ was 4%. The spread therefore describes the repeatability of the measurement at each temperature; it does not extend to the derived value, whose uncertainty also includes whatever error the Arrhenius extrapolation contributes. Triplicate measurement at each temperature is what allows that spread to be stated at all: a single measurement would have given a value with no measure of its own scatter. The temperature range of the study is bounded by the solvent: above 340 K the solvent evaporated during sampling, and no rate constant is reported above that temperature. The two values as they stand show a strong temperature dependence over the interval measured, with the upper value resting on the Arrhenius computation rather than on a sampling measurement of the same standing as the lower one. A measured upper value, taken under sampling that prevents the evaporation, would put the derived figure to the test.

fact_base: A gravity settler removes activated sludge from a process stream. Design overflow rate is 0.57 m h-1 at a throughput of 271 m3 h-1, giving a plan area of 475 m2. The overflow-rate basis is a vendor rule for this solid; no settling test on the actual slurry has been run.
input: Gravity settlers are widely used for separating solids from process streams, and in the case considered here a gravity settler is to be used to remove activated sludge from a process stream. The sizing of the unit has been carried out on the basis of a design overflow rate of 0.57 m h-1, and at the design throughput of 271 m3 h-1 this gives rise to a required plan area of 475 m2. The overflow rate can be thought of as the upward velocity of the stream through the settler, and it is this quantity that has to be kept low enough for the sludge solids to be able to settle against the flow and be retained in the unit rather than carried over with the clarified stream. It is important to note, however, that the overflow-rate basis adopted for this design is a vendor rule for this particular solid, rather than a value that has been established by testing on the stream in question. Indeed, no settling test on the actual slurry has been run, which means that the extent to which the behaviour of the real slurry, with its own particle characteristics and its own response to the conditions in the feed, matches the behaviour that the vendor rule assumes remains unconfirmed at this stage. The area that has been derived from the rule should therefore be regarded as carrying this uncertainty with it, since any departure of the actual settling behaviour from the assumed basis would feed directly through into the performance of the settler as installed.
target: A gravity settler removes activated sludge from a process stream. The design overflow rate is 0.57 m h-1 at a throughput of 271 m3 h-1, giving a plan area of 475 m2. The overflow rate is the throughput per unit plan area, and it works as an upward velocity: sludge that settles faster than the overflow rate is retained, and sludge that settles more slowly is carried out with the clarified stream. Plan area is the horizontal area over which the stream rises through the settler, measured at the surface where the clarified stream leaves it, and the sludge blanket forms where the settling solids meet the rising stream. The plan area is therefore not a free choice once the rate is fixed; area is the throughput divided by the rate the solid is trusted to settle at, and every error in the rate appears in the area at the same proportion. In this design the rate is a vendor rule for this solid. No settling test on the actual slurry has been run. The rule was therefore set on other slurries of the same solid, not on the stream the settler will treat, whose particle condition and feed state govern the settling it will actually show. The stated area is exactly as reliable as that rule: if the actual slurry settles more slowly than the rule assumes, the settler is undersized in the same proportion, and the shortfall appears as solids in the clarified stream rather than as any change in the stated figures. The design is complete on its own terms, since rate, throughput and area agree with each other; what is missing is not arithmetic but evidence, and the missing evidence is a settling test on the slurry itself, run at the condition of the feed the settler will receive.

fact_base: Cost review of a returns flow: 900 km per trip at $1.74 per km, 309 trips per year. Annual transport cost is $484k. Costs are carrier invoices for the last 12 months; empty running is included in the trip count.
input: This cost review takes a detailed look at the transport costs associated with a returns flow, which is an area of the operation that has attracted increasing attention in recent times. Each trip within the flow covers some 900 km, and the cost of the movement works out at $1.74 per km, taking into account the charges raised by the carrier for the work involved. Over the course of a year, the flow accounts for a total of 309 trips, and when all of these elements are brought together, the annual transport cost of the flow comes to $484k in total. It is worth noting that the figures used in this review are drawn from the carrier invoices for the last 12 months, so they reflect the amounts that were actually charged for the work over that period rather than any quoted or estimated rates. It should also be borne in mind that empty running is included in the trip count, which means that the trips recorded include the movements made by vehicles travelling without a load as part of the overall pattern of the flow, and the annual figure should be read with that coverage in mind when it is compared with other flows or carried forward into future planning.
target: The returns flow costs $484k per year (900 km per trip at $1.74 per km, 309 trips per year). The figure is assembled from the carrier invoices for the last 12 months, so it states what was charged for the work over that period, at the rates actually applied, rather than a quoted rate carried forward. Empty running is included in the trip count. The annual figure is therefore the cost of the whole movement cycle, loaded and empty running together, and it should be compared only with figures assembled on the same coverage: a flow costed on loaded trips alone would understate the same operation. Read on that basis, the figure gives operations management a settled baseline for the flow as it currently runs. Any change to the flow, in routing, in trip pattern or in carrier, can be costed against the baseline, provided the costing keeps the same coverage of empty running and the same invoice basis. A change that removes empty running would show against this baseline as a reduction in trips at the stated cost per kilometre; a change that only moves work between carriers would show as a change in the rate. The two kinds of saving are different in kind, and the baseline as stated keeps them separate. The baseline also fixes the questions that any proposal for change has to answer: which trips disappear, which kilometres shorten, or which rate changes, each stated against the same trip count and the same coverage.

fact_base: Liquid-liquid extraction recovers acetone from an aqueous stream into an organic solvent. The distribution coefficient (organic over aqueous) is 0.91 at 25 °C and the design uses 8 countercurrent stages. Predicted recovery is 91% of the acetone in the feed. The prediction assumes equilibrium stages and negligible mutual solubility; neither has been checked on the actual solvents.
input: Liquid-liquid extraction is a well-established technique for recovering valuable or unwanted solutes from liquid streams, and in the present case it is to be used to recover acetone from an aqueous stream into an organic solvent. The distribution coefficient, which expresses the ratio between the concentration of the solute in the organic phase and its concentration in the aqueous phase, is 0.91 at 25 °C for this system, and the design that has been developed on this basis makes use of 8 countercurrent stages. On the basis of these figures, the predicted recovery is 91% of the acetone in the feed, which represents a substantial proportion of the material to be recovered. The practical consequence of a coefficient of this size is that the solvent has to do its work over a number of successive contacts rather than in a single equilibrium stage, which is why a multi-stage countercurrent arrangement has been adopted for the separation. It should be noted, however, that this prediction rests on a number of assumptions, in particular the assumption that every stage behaves as an equilibrium stage and the assumption that the mutual solubility of the two phases is negligible. Neither of these assumptions has been checked on the actual solvents that are to be used, and so the recovery figure should be understood as a prediction that is conditional on the behaviour of the real system, which may well depart from the idealised behaviour that has been assumed in arriving at it.
target: Liquid-liquid extraction recovers acetone from an aqueous stream into an organic solvent. The distribution coefficient, the concentration of acetone in the organic phase divided by its concentration in the aqueous phase at equilibrium, is 0.91 at 25 °C. A coefficient below unity means that at equilibrium the aqueous phase holds more acetone per unit volume than the organic phase takes up, so a single contact leaves most of the acetone behind; recovery is built up over stages instead. The design uses 8 countercurrent stages, in which the phases pass in opposite directions and the leanest solvent meets the most depleted aqueous stream. Countercurrent flow keeps a concentration difference alive along the whole cascade: at every stage the aqueous phase meets solvent that has taken up less acetone than the solvent it met at the stage before, so transfer continues even as the aqueous stream is depleted. Predicted recovery is 91% of the acetone in the feed. The prediction assumes equilibrium stages, with the phases leaving each stage in equilibrium at the stated coefficient, and negligible mutual solubility, with each phase keeping its own volume through the cascade. Neither assumption has been checked on the actual solvents. The recovery therefore stands as a design estimate: if the phases fall short of equilibrium on each stage, or dissolve into each other enough to move material between them, the recovery achieved will fall below the predicted figure, and the size of the shortfall is not known until the solvents are tested. The estimate is nevertheless the design basis as it stands, and the stage count of the design has been fixed from it.

fact_base: Excerpt content: a seal replacement takes about 33 min with the unit isolated; the excerpt gives the isolation steps only. The excerpt warns once about stored pressure and does not repeat the warning.
input: Before the seal on the duty pump is disturbed in any way, running duty should first of all be transferred to the standby pump, so that the duty pump can then be taken out of service in a properly controlled manner. Once the standby pump is carrying the load, the duty pump itself is stopped and is isolated under the PTW arrangements, with its suction and discharge valves closed and locked off so that it cannot be started again or pressurised inadvertently while the work is going on. It is absolutely essential at this point to bear in mind that the pump casing and the pipework connected to it may still contain stored pressure even after isolation has been completed, and this pressure must be released in a controlled way before any joint is broken or the seal housing is opened up. Once the pump has been isolated, drained and vented, the seal replacement itself takes about 33 min, and the work should be carried out carefully and methodically throughout, so that the faces of the new seal are not damaged in the course of fitting.
target: Transfer running duty to the standby pump, and confirm that the standby pump is carrying the flow. Stop the duty pump. Isolate the duty pump under PTW before any work on the seal begins: close the suction and discharge valves, fit locks and tags, and isolate the drive so that the pump cannot be started. Work through the steps in order; the order is the protection, since each step removes one route by which energy or flow can reach the pump. The casing and the connected pipework hold stored pressure after isolation. Release the stored pressure through the vent, and confirm on the local gauge that no pressure remains before a joint is broken. Drain the casing fully, and check that the casing no longer drips at the drain before the first joint is slackened; a casing that still drips is still releasing pressure or liquid, and the vent step is repeated. Keep the isolation in place for the whole of the work that follows: the seal replacement takes about 33 min with the unit isolated in this state, and the isolation is taken off only when the seal work is complete and the casing is closed again.

fact_base: Project proposal for a water recycling plant, in four sections: case, costs, schedule, and decision requested. Capital cost is $1326k with a 10-year appraisal horizon. The schedule section gives a start one quarter after approval; no contractor is named. The decision requested is approval to proceed to detailed design, not to construction.
input:
This proposal requests approval to proceed to the detailed design stage for a water recycling plant. The capital cost of the plant is $1326k, and the proposal has been appraised over a horizon of 10 years. It is important to note that the decision requested at this stage is approval of the design stage only; construction is not being requested, and no contractor has been named.

At present, the site takes its water from the mains supply and discharges its effluent to the sewer, and both of these streams flow in one direction only: water is purchased, used once, and then paid for again as it leaves the site. A recycling plant would effectively reverse part of that flow. Effluent that is currently discharged would be collected, treated, and returned to service as recycled water, and the site's purchases and discharges would both be reduced by the amount that the plant recovers. The case for the plant is essentially the case for that reversal, and the costs, the schedule, and the decision requested all follow from it.

## Case

Water enters the site as a purchased input and leaves it as a charged waste, and the site controls neither of the two prices involved. Mains water is bought at the supplier's tariff, while effluent is discharged under consent, at a cost that is set by the receiving authority and under conditions that the authority is able to tighten. A plant that recovers water from the effluent stream reduces both of these exposures at the same time: every unit of water that is recycled is a unit that does not have to be bought and a unit that does not have to be discharged.

The security of the supply represents the second ground. A site that draws the whole of its water from the mains is exposed to any interruption of that supply, whether that interruption is caused by a restriction in a dry period or by a failure in the network. A recycling plant holds part of the site's demand inside the site itself: the recovered stream continues while the store of treated water lasts, and the duties that it serves can be carried on at a reduced mains draw. The plant does not make the site independent of the mains, and the proposal does not claim that it does; it simply reduces the share of demand that an interruption would bring to a stop.

The third ground concerns the discharge itself. Effluent leaves the site under consent conditions that limit what may be discharged and in what quantity, and a consent is essentially a permission that can be reviewed. By reducing the discharged volume, the site reduces the load that the consent has to accommodate and gains headroom against a tighter consent in the future. That headroom has no line in the appraisal, and the proposal claims no money value for it; it is a ground of the case, rather than a ground of the costs.

Furthermore, the recycled water is not a substitute for mains water in every duty. It serves the duties whose quality requirements the treatment is able to meet: washdown, flushing, cooling make-up, and irrigation are the ordinary candidates on a site of this kind, while duties that involve contact with product or people remain on mains water. The plant is therefore an addition to the site's water system, not a replacement for the supply, and it is at the detailed design stage that the duties to be served are fixed and the treatment is matched to them.

## Costs

The capital cost of the plant is $1326k. This figure represents the cost of building the plant as the concept currently stands: the treatment units that clean the effluent, the storage that holds treated water against the pattern of demand, the pipework that collects the effluent and distributes the recycled water, the controls that run the plant and guard the quality of what it produces, and the installation and commissioning of the whole. It is a concept-stage figure. It is firm enough to be appraised, but it is not firm enough to build to, and converting it into a price that a contractor can actually be held to is part of what the detailed design is for.

Against the capital stand the savings that the plant is expected to make: mains water that is not bought, and effluent that is not discharged, in the quantities that the plant recovers. Between the two stand the operating costs involved in running the plant: the energy that the treatment consumes, the chemicals and media that it uses up, the maintenance of its equipment, the labour of operating it, and the monitoring that demonstrates that the recycled water meets the quality its duties require. Neither the savings nor the operating costs are stated as figures in this proposal. They are estimated in the appraisal that supports it, at the level that a concept can support, and they are the figures that the detailed design exists in order to firm up: quantities of water recovered, duty by duty, and the cost of recovering them.

The appraisal runs over a horizon of 10 years. Over the 10 years, the capital is weighed against the savings and the operating costs taken together, and no payback figure is presented as a finding of this proposal, because the figures that would carry it are concept-stage estimates. What the appraisal establishes is narrower in scope: at $1326k of capital, the scheme is worth the cost of being designed properly. The decision that commits the capital belongs to the later case, which will be built on designed quantities and tendered prices, and it is there that the saving figures will carry the weight that this proposal does not place on them.

## Schedule

Work will start one quarter after approval. The first stage is the detailed design itself: the duties to be served are fixed, the treatment is selected against the quality that those duties require, the plant is laid out on the site, and the capital cost is rebuilt from designed quantities. Procurement follows the design, because what is to be bought cannot be specified until the design has specified it; construction follows procurement, and commissioning follows construction, ending with the plant treating effluent and supplying recycled water under its controls.

No contractor is named in this proposal. The contractor will be chosen by tender against the detailed design, and naming one at this stage would either prejudge that tender or rest the schedule on a party that has not priced the work. The schedule therefore runs from the approval, rather than from a contractor's programme: one quarter after approval the design begins, and each later stage begins when the stage before it has delivered what it needs. A construction schedule, complete with dates, belongs to the construction case and will be built from the contractor's tendered programme; this proposal commits the project to the design stage and to the sequence, and to no dates beyond the start.

## Decision requested

Approval is requested to proceed to detailed design for the water recycling plant. The approval covers the design stage and nothing beyond it: it authorises the project team to fix the duties that the plant will serve, to design the treatment, storage, and distribution that the concept describes, and to rebuild the costs from designed quantities and tendered prices. It does not authorise construction, and it does not commit the capital.

The construction decision is a separate decision, which will be taken on the figures produced by the detailed design. When the design is complete, the case for construction will return with a capital cost that a contractor can be held to, savings stated duty by duty, and a schedule built from a tendered programme. If those figures do not support the plant, the project will stop at the design stage, having spent the design stage and no more. The decision that is requested now is therefore the smaller of the two decisions that the project will ask for, and it is the one that the present evidence supports: the concept is worth designing, and the design is what the remaining questions are waiting for.

subtype: worked example with equation: Ergun pressure drop
fact_base: Gas flows through a packed bed of 1 mm particles. The void fraction $\varepsilon$ is 0.4, the superficial velocity $u$ is 0.35 m s-1 and the bed length is 1 m. The Ergun equation gives a pressure gradient of 7.7 kPa m-1, or 7.7 kPa over the bed. Particle diameter $d_p$ is 1 mm; gas density is 1.2 kg m-3 and viscosity is 1.8 x 10-5 Pa s.
input:
In this worked example, we will consider the situation in which a gas flows through a packed bed of particles with a diameter $d_p$ = 1 mm. It is important to note that packed beds are widely utilised in reactors, absorbers and dryers, and the pressure drop across the bed plays a crucial role in determining the duty of the machine that moves the gas. The void fraction of the bed, denoted by $\varepsilon$, is 0.4, and the superficial velocity $u$ is 0.35 m s-1; the superficial velocity is the velocity that the gas would have in the empty column at the same volumetric flow rate. The length of the bed, $L$, is 1 m.

In order to estimate the pressure gradient, the Ergun equation relates the pressure gradient $\Delta P/L$ to the particle diameter, the void fraction, the superficial velocity, the viscosity of the gas $\mu$ and the density of the gas $\rho$, as shown below:

$$\frac{\Delta P}{L} = \frac{150 \mu (1-\varepsilon)^2}{\varepsilon^3 d_p^2} u + \frac{1.75 (1-\varepsilon)}{\varepsilon^3 d_p} \rho u^2$$

where $\mu$ is 1.8 x 10-5 Pa s and $\rho$ is 1.2 kg m-3. When the stated values are substituted into the equation, a pressure gradient of 7.7 kPa m-1 is obtained. It should be noted that both the viscous term and the inertial term are evaluated at a void fraction of 0.4, and that the gradient applies at a superficial velocity of 0.35 m s-1. Over the bed length of 1 m, a gradient of 7.7 kPa m-1 gives an overall pressure drop of 7.7 kPa. Furthermore, the gradient increases steeply as the void fraction decreases, because the void fraction enters both denominators cubed, and a smaller particle diameter also raises the gradient through both terms.

fact_base: Goal: compute the diffusive flux of oxygen through a stagnant water film. The diffusive flux J (mol m-2 s-1) is computed from the diffusivity D (m2 s-1) and the concentration gradient dC/dx, where C is concentration (mol m-3) and x is position (m). Fick's first law: J = -D dC/dx; the negative sign states that diffusion runs from high concentration to low concentration. Oxygen in water: D = 1.6 x 10-9 m2 s-1. Concentration falls by 0.4 mol m-3 across a film 0.8 mm thick, so dC/dx = -500 mol m-4. Worked result: J = 8.00x 10-7 mol m-2 s-1. The law as stated covers a stagnant medium; a moving medium adds convection, which the equation does not include.
input:
In this example, the goal is to calculate the diffusive flux of oxygen through a stagnant water film, and it will be shown that the resulting flux is 8.00 x 10-7 mol m-2 s-1. Fick's first law gives the flux as J = -D dC/dx, where J represents the diffusive flux (mol m-2 s-1), D represents the diffusivity (m2 s-1), C represents the concentration (mol m-3) and x represents the position (m). It is important to note that the negative sign in Fick's first law indicates that diffusion takes place from a region of high concentration to a region of low concentration.

For oxygen in water, the value of D is 1.6 x 10-9 m2 s-1. The concentration falls by 0.4 mol m-3 across a film that is 0.8 mm thick, so the concentration gradient dC/dx is -500 mol m-4; in other words, the gradient is the concentration change divided by the film thickness. When the diffusivity and the gradient are substituted into Fick's first law, the result obtained is J = 8.00 x 10-7 mol m-2 s-1. A useful check on the units confirms the form of the result: the diffusivity (m2 s-1), when multiplied by the concentration gradient (mol m-4), gives mol m-2 s-1, which is the unit of flux. Essentially, the flux describes how much oxygen crosses each square metre of film area in each second, driven by a concentration difference that is maintained across a film less than a millimetre thick. It should also be noted that Fick's first law, as it is stated here, applies to a stagnant medium; in a moving medium, convection would also be present, which the equation does not include.

fact_base: Capital appraisal for a bottling line: installed cost $717k, expected net saving $140k per year for 8 years. At a discount rate of 8% the present value of the savings is $805k and the net present value is $88k. Savings are vendor and utility estimates; no saving has yet been measured on a comparable installation.
input: This capital appraisal examines a proposed bottling line and returns a net present value of $88k. The installed cost of the line is $717k, and the expected net saving is estimated at $140k per year for 8 years. When these savings are discounted at 8%, they have a present value of $805k, which means that the present value of the savings exceeds the installed cost, with the excess representing a net present value of $88k. It is important to note that the appraisal is expressed in today's money, in the sense that the discounting converts each year's saving into the sum that, if it were held now, would be equivalent to it, and the net present value is what remains once the cost of the line itself has been charged against those converted savings. A positive figure indicates that the project returns more than the rate used to discount it. Furthermore, the case rests heavily on the saving figure: an annual saving that is held at $140k over the full term supports the result, whereas a saving that fell short of the estimate would pull the present value of $805k down towards the installed cost. It should also be noted that these savings are vendor and utility estimates, and no saving has yet been measured on a comparable installation, so the $88k margin is essentially an estimate built on estimates, which would be confirmed or lost during the first years of operation, when the actual saving can be compared with the $140k per year that the appraisal assumes.

fact_base: Excerpt content: the reboiler wall thickness is 72 mm after the corrosion allowance is added. The excerpt compares two gasket materials on temperature limit only and prefers the higher-rated one. The excerpt ends mid-argument; it neither summarises the report nor previews the next section.
input: The wall thickness of the reboiler, once the corrosion allowance has been added, is 72 mm. This figure represents the thickness that is required by the pressure calculation, together with the allowance for material that is lost to corrosion over the life of the vessel, and it is the thickness that will be carried on the fabrication drawings. The flanges that close the reboiler raise a separate question, namely the choice of gasket material, and the comparison that is made here is between two materials that are judged on the basis of temperature limit alone. On this criterion, the higher-rated material is preferred: the flange face is exposed to the full temperature of the vapour space, and a gasket whose limit sits close to the operating temperature has essentially no margin for the excursions that start-up and upset conditions can produce. subtype: worked example with equation: Stokes settling
fact_base: Catalyst fines of diameter $d_p$ = 100 micrometres and density 1400 kg m-3 settle in water at 293 K. Stokes' law gives a terminal velocity $v_t$ of 2.19 mm s-1. The estimate requires creeping flow; the particle Reynolds number must be checked before the value is used.
input:
In this worked example, we will consider catalyst fines that are settling in water at 293 K, and the quantity that is sought is the terminal velocity at which a single particle falls at a constant speed. The fines have a particle diameter $d_p$ of 100 micrometres and a density of 1400 kg m-3. A falling particle reaches its terminal velocity when the net gravitational force acting on it, that is, its weight less the buoyancy of the water that it displaces, is exactly balanced by the viscous drag on its surface; below that velocity it will accelerate, and above it the drag will exceed the net gravitational force and it will slow down.

For a sphere in creeping flow, Stokes' law can be utilised to give the terminal velocity $v_t$ in the following form:

$$v_t = \frac{g d_p^2 (\rho_p - \rho)}{18 \mu}$$

where $\rho_p$ denotes the particle density, $\rho$ denotes the fluid density, $\mu$ denotes the fluid viscosity and $g$ denotes the gravitational acceleration. When the particle diameter of 100 micrometres and the particle density of 1400 kg m-3 are substituted into the equation, a terminal velocity $v_t$ of 2.19 mm s-1 is obtained. This value represents a settling speed of the order of millimetres per second, which means that a particle takes minutes rather than seconds to cross a vessel of ordinary depth, and any separation process that relies on settling has to allow for that residence time. It is important to note that Stokes' law is based on the assumption of creeping flow around the particle, with the drag in the laminar form that the equation assumes. This estimate therefore requires that condition to be satisfied: the particle Reynolds number, which is formed from the terminal velocity and the particle diameter, must be checked before the value of 2.19 mm s-1 is used, and a Reynolds number outside the creeping-flow range would place the particle outside the conditions under which Stokes' law holds.

fact_base: Inventory policy for a spare motor: mean demand 3812 units per week, standard deviation 1006 units per week, replenishment lead time 5 weeks. Safety stock for a 95% cycle service level is 3712 units. Demand is treated as normal and independent between weeks; seasonal peaks are excluded.
input: Under this inventory policy for a spare motor, the safety stock is set at 1856 units, which gives a reorder point of 20916 units. Demand for the motor averages 3812 units per week, with a standard deviation of 1006 units per week, and replenishment takes 5 weeks. At a 95% cycle service level, the stock that is held against demand variation over the lead time is 1856 units; the reorder point is calculated by adding that cover to the demand that is expected during the 5 weeks of lead time, at 3812 units per week, so that an order placed at the reorder point will arrive, on average, just as the cover begins to be used. The cycle service level can be understood as the probability that a replenishment cycle ends without a stockout occurring, and the safety stock is essentially what converts that probability into units on the shelf. It is important to note that the policy treats demand as normal and independent between weeks, and seasonal peaks are excluded from the calculation. This means that a seasonal peak is effectively outside the protection that the policy provides: demand above the average in a peak week will draw on the safety stock faster than the policy assumes, and the 95% service level holds only for the demand pattern that the policy describes.

fact_base: Capital appraisal for a warehouse extension: installed cost $579k, expected net saving $128k per year for 10 years. At a discount rate of 8% the present value of the savings is $859k and the net present value is $280k. Savings are vendor and utility estimates; no saving has yet been measured on a comparable installation.
input: This capital appraisal considers a proposed warehouse extension and returns a net present value of $280k. The installed cost of the extension is $579k, and the expected net saving is estimated at $128k per year for 10 years. When the savings are discounted at 8%, they are found to have a present value of $859k, and the excess of that present value over the installed cost represents a net present value of $280k. A positive net present value indicates that the project returns more than the discount rate that was used to appraise it. It is important to note that the appraisal is expressed in today's money: the discounting process converts each year's saving into the sum that, if it were held now, would be equivalent to it, and the net figure is what remains after the cost of the extension has been charged against the converted savings. Over the 10 years, the saving is assumed to be held at $128k per year, and the result is sensitive to this assumption, in that a saving below the estimate would reduce the present value of $859k towards the installed cost and narrow the margin accordingly. Furthermore, the savings are vendor and utility estimates, and no saving has yet been measured on a comparable installation. The margin is therefore provisional in a specific sense: it depends on figures that have been supplied by the parties who would sell or supply the works, and it is the first years of operation, when metered savings can be compared with the estimate, that would confirm or remove it.

fact_base: A centrifugal pump moves caustic solution between two vessels at grade. At the duty point the flow is 61 m3 h-1 against a head of 63 m, with pump efficiency 75%. Shaft power at the duty point is 14 kW. The motor is rated 15% above this value. Cavitation was not observed in the acceptance test, which ran for 4 h at the duty point only.
input: At its duty point, the centrifugal pump in question moves caustic solution at 61 m3 h-1 against a head of 63 m, with an efficiency of 75% and a shaft power of 14 kW. The pump is responsible for transferring the solution between two vessels at grade, and the duty point can be understood as the operating point that the installation asks of the pump in normal service. It is important to note that the figures belong together: the flow of 61 m3 h-1, the head, the efficiency of 75% and the shaft power of 14 kW together represent the pump's response at that point, and none of them is stated for any other flow. The head represents the height of a column of the solution that the pressure rise produced by the pump would support, and the efficiency indicates the share of the shaft power that actually reaches the solution in the form of pressure and flow. The shaft power is the power that the motor must deliver to the pump shaft in order to sustain the duty point, before the motor's own losses are taken into account. The motor is rated 15% above the shaft power at the duty point, and a margin of this kind is held for the excursions of flow and head that ordinary service produces around the duty point; it is consumed by those excursions rather than being held against a change of duty. Cavitation was not observed during the acceptance test, which ran for 4 h at the duty point only. This means that the test covers a single operating point for a limited duration; cavitation at other flows, or over longer periods of running, was not examined, and the absence of cavitation in the test is a statement about the duty point and the test duration, rather than about the pump's behaviour across its full range.
