fact_base: A gravity settler removes calcium carbonate from a process stream. Design overflow rate is 0.92 m h-1 at a throughput of 308 m3 h-1, giving a plan area of 335 m2. The overflow-rate basis is a vendor rule for this solid; no settling test on the actual slurry has been run.
input: A gravity settler is used to remove calcium carbonate from a process stream, and it is sized on the basis of an overflow rate of 0.92 m h-1. At a throughput of 308 m3 h-1, this rate requires a plan area of 335 m2. The overflow rate can be understood as the throughput divided by the plan area, and it is the controlling figure for the settler: a particle that settles faster than the overflow rate will reach the bottom of the vessel before the flow carries it out, whereas a particle that settles more slowly will leave together with the clarified stream. The plan area of 335 m2 is therefore determined by the rate at which the process stream is allowed to rise through the vessel, rather than by the depth of the vessel, and at the stated throughput the area follows directly from the rate of 0.92 m h-1. Calcium carbonate is the solid that the basis names, and the design overflow rate is a vendor rule for this solid: it is the vendor's figure for the rate at which this material can be loaded, and it is drawn from the vendor's practice rather than from a test on the stream that is to be treated. It is important to note that no settling test on the actual slurry has been carried out. The size of the settler thus rests on a rule whose value for the actual slurry, with its own particle sizes and concentrations, remains unverified; a settling test would either confirm the rate of 0.92 m h-1 and the area of 335 m2 that it produces at 308 m3 h-1, or replace both of them with figures that have been measured on the material itself.

fact_base: An amine absorption unit was tested at pilot scale on gas from a cement kiln. Over 45 days at 11 t of carbon dioxide per day, the unit captured 85% of the carbon dioxide in the treated gas. input: An amine absorption unit was tested at pilot scale on gas from a cement kiln. Pilot scale places the unit somewhere between the laboratory and a full installation: the gas is the kiln's own gas, and the quantities involved are large enough to expose the solvent to the stream that it would treat in service. Over a period of 45 days at 11 t of carbon dioxide per day, the unit captured 85% of the carbon dioxide in the treated gas. The steam demand was 3.3 gigajoules per tonne of carbon dioxide captured, and the solvent loss was 1.4 kg per tonne captured. It is important to note that the three figures describe the same run: the capture of 85% was achieved at the stated steam demand and solvent loss over the 45 days, and the steam figure represents the price of the capture in energy terms, paid in the regeneration of the solvent that the absorption process requires. The solvent loss is stated per tonne captured, which means that it scales with the amount treated rather than with the size of the unit. Beyond 45 days, however, the effect of kiln dust on the solvent remains untested. The reported performance is therefore a 45-day performance; whether capture, steam demand and solvent loss would hold as the solvent ages in contact with kiln dust lies outside the test, and a longer run is the measurement that would be needed in order to settle it.

fact_base: A binary distillation separates benzene/toluene at a relative volatility of 1.82 that is taken as constant over the column. Specifications: distillate 98 mol% light component, bottoms 2 mol% light component. The Fenske minimum stage count is 13 theoretical stages including the reboiler. The actual design uses a reflux ratio of 1.3 times the minimum; the stage count at that reflux comes from a separate simulation.
input:
It is important to note that binary distillation plays a crucial role in the separation of benzene/toluene mixtures, and a comprehensive assessment of the separation typically begins by examining the minimum-stage limit. In this context, the relative volatility is 1.82, and it is generally assumed to remain constant over the column, which effectively means that a single, unified parameter can be utilized to describe the equilibrium behaviour at every stage. Furthermore, the specifications are clearly defined: the distillate is set at 98 mol% light component, while the bottoms are set at 2 mol% light component. The well-known Fenske equation serves as a valuable tool for determining the minimum number of theoretical stages that the stated separation requires at total reflux. At total reflux, no product is withdrawn, which means that the resulting count represents a lower bound, highlighting the fact that any column operating at finite reflux will inevitably require more stages than this minimum value.

When the stated specifications are combined with the constant relative volatility of 1.82, the Fenske minimum stage count is 13 theoretical stages, including the reboiler. This result is driven by the two product specifications and the volatility acting together. Both specifications are relatively tight, and the volatility can be described as moderate, underscoring why the minimum already stands at 13 stages even before any allowance is made for finite reflux. The reboiler is included in the total because it performs one stage of separation, and the condenser is not counted separately in cases where it returns the condensed distillate without any further separation step.

It is worth noting that the actual design does not operate at the minimum. The design reflux ratio is 1.3 times the minimum reflux ratio, and the stage count at that particular reflux level is obtained from a separate simulation. Ultimately, the Fenske count and the design count address different questions: the first bounds the separation, while the second sizes the column. The constant-volatility assumption also bounds the result in the same way. The Fenske minimum stage count of 13 is valid for a relative volatility of 1.82 held constant over the column; a volatility that varies with composition would change the count, and the simulation serves as the source for the design figure.

fact_base: A defect-reduction project on a packing line cut the reject rate from 3.4% to 1.9% over one quarter. At 322k units per year the change avoids about 4830 rejected units per year. The quarter included a planned shutdown; rates are not adjusted for it.
input:
It is important to note that the defect-reduction project on the packing line has delivered a meaningful improvement in quality performance over the course of one quarter. Specifically, the reject rate decreased from 3.4% to 1.9%, which represents a reduction of 1.5 percentage points. At the current volume of 322k units per year, this improvement avoids about 4830 rejected units per year, underscoring the tangible operational benefit of the project. The result is based on one quarter of production on the packing line, and it is worth noting that the quarter included a planned shutdown; the rates have not been adjusted for the shutdown.

In practical terms, a reject rate reflects the share of units that the line rejects, with the denominator being the production of the line over the period that is measured. The decrease of 1.5 percentage points therefore represents a change in the share itself, stated on the same denominator in both quarters of the comparison. The avoided units are stated at the current annual volume of 322k units, and any future change in volume would move the avoided count in proportion, while the measured rates themselves would stand as recorded. Expressed at the annual volume, the decrease corresponds to the stated figure of 4830 avoided units per year.

The shutdown caveat is also important to keep in mind, and it cuts into the finding in one direction only. Rates measured over a quarter that included a planned shutdown may not fully represent a full quarter of normal running, and no adjustment has been made in order to account for this. Overall, the headline finding for the quarter is the rate decrease from 3.4% to 1.9%; the annual figure essentially restates the same decrease at the annual volume and does not add any new measurement. Going forward, a full-year rate, measured over quarters without a planned shutdown, will be the figure that confirms whether the decrease truly holds over the longer term.

fact_base: Excerpt content: the analogy between the transfer processes is stated, then qualified by the case where it fails. The excerpt works one short numerical check with numbers given inside the excerpt itself. The excerpt assumes the chapter's earlier definitions and adds none.
input:
It is also worth noting that the Chilton-Colburn analogy extends essentially the same relation to mass transfer, with $j_D$ taking the place of the heat-transfer factor. Under this analogy, $j_D$ is equal to $f/2$, which means that the mass-transfer factor is exactly one half of the friction factor for the same flow. This relation is based on the assumption that the boundary layers for momentum and for the transferred component develop in essentially the same way, thereby allowing a single coefficient ratio to describe both processes in a unified manner.

A brief numerical check helps to illustrate the typical size of the numbers involved. For turbulent flow in a smooth pipe at a Reynolds number of 20000, the measured value of $f$ is 0.0064. Applying the analogy then gives $j_D = f/2 = 0.0032$. If a measured mass-transfer coefficient converts to a value of $j_D$ that is well away from 0.0032, this is generally taken, under the analogy, as an indication that one of its underlying conditions is not fully satisfied in the flow under consideration, and the check is used in precisely that direction: agreement supports the measurement, whereas disagreement directs the reader back to the conditions rather than to the arithmetic.

However, the qualification is arguably just as important as the relation itself. Friction in a pipe consists of two components: skin friction at the wall and form drag, which arises where the flow separates or changes direction. The boundary-layer argument that underpins the analogy covers skin friction only. In situations where form drag accounts for a large share of $f$, such as flow across a bank of tubes or through a packed bed, $f$ increases without any matching increase in the transfer rate, and $j_D$ correspondingly falls below $f/2$. As a result, the analogy then overstates the transfer factor, and the magnitude of the error grows in line with the form-drag share. Nevertheless, within its conditions — namely turbulent flow, dominant skin friction, and similar behaviour of the two boundary layers — the relation remains a compact and useful way to estimate a transfer factor from a friction measurement, as well as to check a measured transfer factor against the friction of the same flow.

The Chilton-Colburn analogy extends the same relation to mass transfer, with $j_D$ in the place of the heat-transfer factor. Under the analogy, $j_D$ equals $f/2$: the mass-transfer factor is one half of the friction factor for the same flow. The relation rests on the boundary layers for momentum and for the transferred component developing in the same way, so that one coefficient ratio describes both processes.

A short check shows the size of the numbers involved. For turbulent flow in a smooth pipe at a Reynolds number of 20000, the measured friction factor $f$ is 0.0064. The analogy then gives $j_D = f/2 = 0.0032$. A measured mass-transfer coefficient that converts to a $j_D$ well away from 0.0032 is, under the analogy, a sign that one of its conditions is not met in the flow at hand, and the check is used in that direction: agreement supports the measurement, and disagreement sends the reader back to the conditions rather than to the arithmetic.

The qualification matters as much as the relation. Friction in a pipe has two parts: skin friction at the wall and form drag where the flow separates or changes direction. The boundary-layer argument behind the analogy covers skin friction only. topic: tut:phase:a pure component at its boiling point
fact_base: A tutorial passage explains phase equilibrium for a pure component at its boiling point. The passage states the equilibrium condition in words (equality of chemical potential across phases) before any equation is named. No numerical data are introduced; the passage is conceptual.
input:
In order to understand phase equilibrium for a pure component at its boiling point, it is necessary to appreciate what the equilibrium condition means. A pure component at its boiling point maintains liquid and vapour in phase equilibrium when the chemical potential of the component is equal in the two phases. The chemical potential can be thought of as a measure of the driving force for a species to leave a phase; when the two values are equal, neither phase gains the component at the expense of the other, and transfer across the interface continues in both directions at equal rates. This condition is stated here in words because it serves as the definition that the rest of the discussion relies upon: boiling is essentially the visible sign of the equality, rather than its underlying cause.

Furthermore, at the boiling point, the temperature and the pressure of the pure component are not independent variables. Fixing the pressure fixes the boiling temperature, because the equality of chemical potential can only be satisfied at one temperature for that pressure. Increasing the pressure increases the temperature at which the two chemical potentials meet, which helps to explain why a change in pressure shifts the boiling point instead of breaking the equilibrium. Additionally, the vapour formed has the same composition as the liquid, since the component is pure; nothing in the condition acts to separate one part of the substance from another.

The equality also determines what any disturbance will do. Heat added at the boiling point converts liquid into vapour at constant temperature, and the chemical potentials remain equal while both phases are present. Only when one phase has disappeared can the temperature begin to move again. The quantitative form of the pressure dependence is provided by the Clapeyron equation, which relates the slope of the boiling curve to the enthalpy of vaporisation and the volume change on boiling. Importantly, this equation is a direct consequence of the equality described above, and it introduces no second condition.

The condition is stated here in words because it is the definition the rest of the discussion uses: boiling is the visible sign of the equality, not its cause.

At the boiling point the temperature and pressure of the pure component are not independent. fact_base: Excerpt content: the contingency allowance is set at 11% and the excerpt defends that figure against a lower alternative. The excerpt refers to the project's cost table by section name and does not repeat its figures.
input:
It should be emphasised that the contingency allowance for the upgrade project is currently set at 11%, and there are several important reasons why this figure should be maintained rather than reduced at this stage. Essentially, the figures presented in the cost table in the Costs section relate only to the defined scope of the project. The allowance, by contrast, is intended to cover an entirely different category of cost: namely, items that the project will certainly require but which cannot yet be defined with sufficient precision to be priced individually. Between the current estimate and FID, items progressively move from the second category into the first as the design work defines them more clearly, and the history of that movement, as reflected in the estimate's own revisions, provides the most reliable measure of the allowance that the project actually needs.

A lower allowance would effectively assume that the undefined scope is smaller than the current position genuinely supports. The undefined items are not optional extras that can simply be removed; rather, they represent work whose absence from the priced list merely reflects the present stage of design, and not any judgement that the work itself will not ultimately be carried out. Reducing the allowance does not reduce that work in any way. Instead, it simply converts an explicit provision into an overrun that will only emerge after approval has been given, at a point when the steering group will have far fewer options available for absorbing it.

The allowance is held against the undefined items as a class, and it is drawn upon only as items become defined and are priced into the base estimate. On this basis, 11% is the figure that the estimate supports at the present stage: it corresponds to the share of cost that remains undefined, and it naturally falls as definition proceeds, since each defined item transfers its cost from the allowance into the priced table. The steering group reviews the balance at every revision of the cost table, and the allowance that the project eventually carries into FID is the residue remaining after those transfers, rather than the figure that is being defended here.

fact_base: Cost review of a returns flow: 571 km per trip at $1.22 per km, 673 trips per year. Annual transport cost is $469k. Costs are carrier invoices for the last 12 months; empty running is included in the trip count.
input: Annual transport cost for the returns flow is $469k. The figure is built from 571 km per trip at $1.22 per km across 673 trips per year, and each element comes from the same base: carrier invoices for the last 12 months. The trip count includes empty running, so the cost covers the full movement the returns flow generates, loaded and empty together, and not loaded movement alone. On that basis the annual figure is complete for the flow as currently run. A change in the trip count or in the carrier rate moves the annual cost directly; the distance is set by the route, and no element of the total is estimated rather than invoiced. The 12-month base also fixes the pattern behind the total: the rate, the trip count and the distance are recent actual values, and each holds only while the route, the carrier and the returns volume hold. A renegotiated rate supersedes the rate per kilometre; a route change supersedes the distance; a sustained change in returns volume supersedes the trip count. Until one of those changes is made, the annual plan takes the returns flow cost as $469k, and a comparison against any alternative arrangement is made on the same invoice basis.

fact_base: A centrifugal pump moves water between two vessels at grade. At the duty point the flow is 54 m3 h-1 against a head of 43 m, with pump efficiency 73%. Shaft power at the duty point is 8.7 kW. The motor is rated 15% above this value. Cavitation was not observed in the acceptance test, which ran for 4 h at the duty point only.
input:
A centrifugal pump is used to move water between two vessels that are located at grade, and the duty point is essentially determined by the demand of the receiving vessel. At the duty point, the flow is 54 m3 h-1 against a head of 43 m, with a pump efficiency of 73%. The shaft power at the duty point is 8.7 kW. It is worth noting that the motor is rated 15% above the shaft power, which means that the installed rating provides a comfortable margin over the duty requirement rather than merely meeting it exactly.

The acceptance test was carried out at the duty point only, over a period of 4 h, and it is important to note that no cavitation was observed at any point during the test. This result, however, only covers the tested condition and nothing beyond it. Operation away from the duty point was not tested, and the suction behaviour at other flow rates therefore rests on the pump curve rather than on any direct test evidence. Within the tested condition, the pump can be said to meet the duty as specified; outside that condition, the duty figures should be regarded as specification values rather than as measured performance, and the margin in the motor rating is a margin against the specified power, not against a measured one.

fact_base: An amine absorption unit was tested at pilot scale on gas from a cement kiln. Over 45 days at 11 t of carbon dioxide per day, the unit captured 89% of the carbon dioxide in the treated gas. Steam demand was 3.1 gigajoules per tonne of carbon dioxide captured; solvent loss was 2.1 kg per tonne captured. Beyond 45 days, the effect of kiln dust on the solvent is untested.
input:
An amine absorption unit was tested at pilot scale using gas obtained from a cement kiln, and the unit successfully captured 89% of the carbon dioxide contained in the treated gas. The test was conducted over a period of 45 days at a rate of 11 t of carbon dioxide per day. The steam demand was 3.1 gigajoules per tonne of carbon dioxide captured, while the solvent loss amounted to 2.1 kg per tonne captured. It is important to note that the capture figure and the two consumption figures all describe the same 45-day run, and each figure is expressed per tonne captured in order to allow the run to be compared with other campaigns on a consistent basis.

The main limitation of the test is its duration. Beyond 45 days, the effect of kiln dust on the solvent remains untested, and the reported capture and consumption figures cannot simply be extended beyond the test period. The figures produced by the unit are pilot figures: they establish what the solvent and the unit were able to achieve on kiln gas over the test period and at the stated rate. Any scale-up exercise will use these figures as a starting point, with the dust question still open and unresolved.
target:

Steam demand was 3.1 gigajoules per tonne of carbon dioxide captured, and solvent loss was 2.1 kg per tonne captured. The capture figure and the two consumption figures describe the same 45-day run, and each is stated per tonne captured, so the run can be compared with other campaigns on the same basis.

Stated per tonne captured, the steam demand prices the separation in energy terms and the solvent loss prices it in material terms; the two figures together describe the running cost of the capture at the rate tested, before any allowance for the capital of the unit itself. The capture percentage, the steam demand and the solvent loss were all measured on the same gas over the same period, so the three figures belong to one another and are not to be combined with figures from other campaigns.

The figures are pilot figures: they fix what the solvent and the unit achieved on kiln gas over the test period, at the stated rate, and a scale-up starts from them with the dust question open.

fact_base: Capital appraisal for a bottling line: installed cost $1596k, expected net saving $447k per year for 12 years. At a discount rate of 10% the present value of the savings is $3046k and the net present value is $1450k. Savings are vendor and utility estimates; no saving has yet been measured on a comparable installation.
input:
A capital appraisal has been carried out for the proposed bottling line, and it is important to note that the appraisal gives a net present value of $1450k, which indicates that the project clears its appraisal hurdle on the basis of the stated estimates. The installed cost is $1596k, while the expected net saving is $447k per year for 12 years; at a discount rate of 10%, the present value of the savings works out at $3046k, exceeding the installed cost by the stated $1450k. It is worth emphasising that the evidence base here is the estimate set itself: the savings figures are vendor and utility estimates, and no saving has yet been measured on any comparable installation.

As a result, the positive net present value effectively rests on estimated savings rather than on measured performance. The decision that the appraisal supports is therefore conditional in one important respect. If the savings are verified on a comparable installation, the case will stand as computed; until that point, $1450k should be regarded as an estimate-based figure, and the savings line is clearly the figure that should be verified first, because the appraisal result follows it in full: any shortfall in the saving reduces the present value by the same proportion.

fact_base: Excerpt content: the analogy between the transfer processes is stated, then qualified by the case where it fails. The excerpt works one short numerical check with numbers given inside the excerpt itself. The excerpt assumes the chapter's earlier definitions and adds none.
input:
For heat transfer, the analogy essentially takes the same form, with the heat-transfer factor occupying the place of $j_D$. The Chilton-Colburn analogy sets the heat-transfer factor equal to $f/2$ for the same flow, based on the same underlying boundary-layer argument: namely, that the layer which resists the flow also resists the passage of heat. A short check using measured friction data illustrates how the analogy works in practice. At a Reynolds number of 45000 in a smooth tube, the measured value of $f$ is 0.0056, which means that $f/2$ comes out at 0.0028. A heat-transfer factor that is obtained from measured temperature differences should therefore lie close to that value wherever the conditions of the analogy are satisfied.

Radiation represents one important boundary of those conditions. The analogy is constructed around the convective exchange taking place at the wall; in situations where a substantial proportion of the heat is transferred by radiation, as happens with a hot surface facing cooler surroundings, the total transfer will exceed the convective part that the analogy is able to estimate. In such cases the friction factor effectively checks only the convective share, and a heat-transfer factor calculated from the total duty will stand above $f/2$, without this implying any failure of the measurements on either side.

subtype: worked example with equation: Antoine vapour pressure
fact_base: The vapour pressure of acetone at 78 °C is estimated from the Antoine equation with constants $A$ = 7.11714, $B$ = 1210.595 and $C$ = 229.664 (pressure in mmHg, temperature in °C). The estimate is 202.9 kPa. The constants are valid only over their fitted temperature range; the source databank value governs design.
input:
The task is to estimate the vapour pressure of acetone at 78 °C by making use of the Antoine equation. The Antoine constants for acetone, with the pressure $P$ expressed in mmHg and the temperature $T$ expressed in °C, are given as $A$ = 7.11714, $B$ = 1210.595 and $C$ = 229.664. The equation essentially relates the vapour pressure to the temperature by means of these three constants, as shown below:

$$\log_{10} P = A - \frac{B}{T + C}$$

In this expression, $P$ denotes the vapour pressure and $T$ denotes the temperature. The substitution process begins with the denominator: at $T$ = 78 °C, the sum $T + C$ evaluates to 307.664. The quotient $B / (T + C)$ therefore comes out at 3.935, and the right-hand side of the equation, calculated as $A$ minus the quotient, is 3.182. This means that the vapour pressure is 10 raised to the power 3.182, expressed in mmHg; when this value is converted into kilopascals, the resulting estimate is 202.9 kPa.

It is important to note that the validity of the result depends on the range of the constants. The Antoine constants are only valid over the temperature range to which they were fitted, and the estimate of 202.9 kPa can only be relied upon inside that range; the calculation itself does not test whether the temperature used actually lies inside it. For design purposes, the source databank value governs, and the Antoine estimate should be regarded as an independent check on that value rather than as a replacement for it. The worked value is therefore an estimate with a fully stated route: the constants, the substitution and the conversion are all set out openly, and any reader who holds a databank value for the same temperature can place the two side by side for comparison.

subtype: worked example with equation: radiative exchange
fact_base: A blackened plate at 600 K faces surroundings at 290 K. Its emissivity $\varepsilon$ is 0.95. Net radiative heat flux $q$ is 6.6 kW m-2, with the Stefan-Boltzmann constant $\sigma$ = 5.67 x 10-8 W m-2 K-4. The estimate treats both surfaces as large and parallel; view factors for the real geometry are not included.
input:
A blackened plate at 600 K is facing surroundings at 290 K, and the objective is to estimate the net radiative heat flux from the plate using the Stefan-Boltzmann relation. The plate temperature $T_1$, the surroundings temperature $T_2$, the emissivity $\varepsilon$ of the plate and the Stefan-Boltzmann constant $\sigma$ are connected by the following relation:

$$q = \varepsilon \sigma (T_1^4 - T_2^4)$$

In this relation, $q$ denotes the net radiative heat flux. The emissivity $\varepsilon$ has a value of 0.95, and $\sigma$ is 5.67 x 10-8 W m-2 K-4. Substituting the two temperatures into the relation gives the flux directly, since the relation does not contain any other property of the plate or of the surroundings. The resulting net radiative heat flux $q$ works out at 6.6 kW m-2. It is also worth observing that the fourth-power term for the surroundings amounts to just 5.46% of the plate term, which means that the net flux is quite close to the value the plate would radiate toward surroundings at zero temperature, and the result is predominantly determined by the plate temperature.

It should be noted that the estimate treats both surfaces as large and parallel. View factors for the actual geometry have not been included, so the value of 6.6 kW m-2 is only valid for the idealisation that has been stated: a plate that sees only the surroundings, with the full temperature difference acting across the gap. In a geometry where the plate sees other surfaces at other temperatures, the exchange is split into separate parts that the single relation does not cover, and each part then has its own temperature difference.

fact_base: Goal: compute the half-life of a first-order reaction and the fraction remaining after 60 min. For a first-order reaction the rate constant k (min-1) fixes the half-life t1/2 (min) by t1/2 = ln(2) / k, and the fraction remaining after time t (min) is exp(-k t). Measured rate constant: k = 0.012 min-1 at 323 K, from concentration measurements every 5 min over 90 min. Worked results: t1/2 = 57.8 min; the fraction remaining after 60 min is 0.49 (dimensionless), both computed from the stated relations. The relations hold for a first-order reaction only; a reaction of another order follows a different decay law.
input:
The half-life of a first-order reaction with rate constant k = 0.012 min-1 at 323 K is 57.8 min, and the fraction of reactant remaining after 60 min is 0.49. Both values come from the two relations that govern first-order decay, applied to a rate constant measured from concentration measurements taken every 5 min over 90 min. The goal is the pair of figures a first-order decay is usually summarised by: how long the reactant takes to fall to half its initial amount, and how much of it is left at a stated time.

For a first-order reaction, the rate constant k (min-1) fixes the half-life t1/2 (min) by t1/2 = ln(2) / k, and the fraction remaining after a time t (min) is exp(-k t). Substitution of the measured rate constant gives t1/2 = ln(2) / 0.012 = 57.8 min. The fraction remaining after 60 min thus follows as exp(-0.012 × 60) = 0.49.

The check is internal: 60 min stands close to the half-life of 57.8 min, and the fraction remaining, 0.49, stands close to one half, as the two figures require of each other. The relations hold for a first-order reaction only. A reaction of another order follows a different decay law, and neither figure carries over to it.

fact_base: Excerpt content: the analogy between the transfer processes is stated, then qualified by the case where it fails. The excerpt works one short numerical check with numbers given inside the excerpt itself. The excerpt assumes the chapter's earlier definitions and adds none.
input:
The position is somewhat more subtle than it first appears. According to the Chilton-Colburn analogy, the mass-transfer factor is simply equal to half of the friction factor, so that $j_D = f/2$, at least in situations where the drag is of the skin-friction kind. The reason the two quantities can be linked in this way is that both of them are concerned with transfer at the surface: the friction factor reflects the momentum that is transferred to the wall, while $j_D$ reflects the mass that is transferred to it, and the analogy in effect treats these as two views of one and the same process. A simple numerical check illustrates the point: if the friction factor has been measured as $f$ = 0.008, the analogy gives $j_D$ = 0.004, and a value measured independently that came out very different from this would fall outside what the analogy can account for.

The difficulty arises when the drag is not purely skin friction. Where a body experiences form drag, part of what is captured in the measured friction factor has to do with the separated flow and the wake, and this part has no equivalent in the transfer of mass at the surface. The friction factor is then larger than the skin-friction value that the analogy presumes, and the $j_D$ worked out from it is correspondingly overestimated. The moral is that the analogy can only be trusted where the drag really is skin friction, and it should be set aside for geometries in which form drag makes a significant contribution to the measured factor.
target:
For flow over a surface where the drag is skin friction, the Chilton-Colburn analogy sets the mass-transfer factor equal to half the friction factor, $j_D = f/2$. The statement is compact because the two factors rest on the same surface process: the friction factor measures the momentum carried to the wall, and $j_D$ measures the mass carried to it, and the analogy asserts that the two standings are one. Neither factor is adjusted to reach the other; the equality is the content of the analogy. A check fixes the arithmetic of the claim. At a measured $f$ of 0.008, the analogy returns $j_D$ = 0.004, and a mass-transfer measurement that lands far from that value is a measurement the analogy does not describe.

The limit of the statement is the drag itself. Where the drag on the body is form drag, the friction factor counts momentum transfer that has no counterpart in the mass flux at the surface: the flow separates, the wake carries the momentum away, and $f$ stands above the skin-friction value the analogy assumes. The $j_D$ taken from such an $f$ is correspondingly high, and the error is not in the arithmetic but in the reading of $f$. The distinction is in what the measured drag is made of, and it is made before the analogy is applied, not after. The analogy is therefore used where the drag is skin friction, and set aside where the geometry puts form drag into the measured factor.

fact_base: A flat firebrick wall of thickness 20 mm separates two process streams. Thermal conductivity of the wall is 1.1 W m-1 K-1 and the measured temperature difference across it is 276 K. Steady one-dimensional conduction gives a heat flux of 15180 W m-2. Surface (film) resistances are excluded from this estimate; including them lowers the flux.
input:
In this example, we consider a flat wall made of firebrick that has a thickness of 20 mm and separates two process streams from one another. The thermal conductivity of the firebrick wall is 1.1 W m-1 K-1, and careful measurement shows that the temperature difference across the wall is 276 K. When steady, one-dimensional conduction through the wall is assumed, the resulting heat flux works out to 15180 W m-2, which is a strikingly large value.

It is worth walking through how this number is obtained. The heat flux can be calculated by taking the thermal conductivity, multiplying it by the temperature difference, and dividing it by the wall thickness, which gives 1.1 × 276 / 0.02 = 15180 W m-2 once the thickness is expressed as 0.02 m. In other words, the whole result is determined by just four quantities, and nothing else about the two streams needs to be known. Because heat flux means the heat transferred per unit area per unit time, the large figure essentially reflects the combination of a large temperature difference and a thin wall, even though firebrick itself is a poor conductor of heat.

It should be noted, however, that surface (film) resistances have been left out of this estimate. If they were included, they would add resistance in series with the wall, and the actual flux would come out lower than 15180 W m-2. The quoted figure is therefore best understood as the wall-only value, and anyone wanting a design figure for the streams would need the film resistances as well.
target:
A flat firebrick wall of thickness 20 mm separates two process streams. The thermal conductivity of the wall is 1.1 W m-1 K-1, and the measured temperature difference across the wall is 276 K. Steady one-dimensional conduction through the wall gives a heat flux of 15180 W m-2.

The flux follows from the conductivity, the temperature difference and the thickness in one step: 1.1 × 276 / 0.02 = 15180 W m-2, with the thickness taken as 0.02 m. Four quantities fix the result, and no other property of the streams enters it. The wall temperature field is taken as settled, and the same flux passes every plane parallel to the faces. Heat flux is the heat transferred per unit area of wall per unit time, stated here in watts per square metre. The figure is large because the temperature difference is large and the wall is thin; the conductivity of firebrick is low, and the thinness and the temperature difference outweigh it in the product.

Surface (film) resistances are excluded from this estimate. Including them adds resistance in series with the wall and lowers the flux below 15180 W m-2; the figure is therefore the wall-only value, and a design figure for the streams requires the film resistances that this estimate omits. Used as it stands, the estimate bounds the duty from above.

fact_base: Goal: compute the Reynolds number for water in a pipe and state the flow regime. The Reynolds number Re (dimensionless) is computed from density rho (kg m-3), mean velocity v (m s-1), pipe diameter D (m) and dynamic viscosity mu (Pa s) by Re = rho v D / mu. Water at 293 K: rho = 998 kg m-3, mu = 1.00 x 10-3 Pa s. Pipe diameter D = 0.025 m; mean velocity v = 1.1 m s-1. Worked result: Re = 27400 (computed as 998 x 1.1 x 0.025 / 0.001). Flow is laminar below Re = 2300 and turbulent above Re = 4000; between the two values the regime is transitional and is not assigned by the number alone.
input:
In this worked example, we are going to determine the Reynolds number for water flowing through a pipe, and then use the result to say whether the flow is laminar or turbulent. The pipe has a diameter of 0.025 m, and the water flows with a mean velocity of 1.1 m s-1. It turns out that the Reynolds number is large enough that the flow is turbulent.

The Reynolds number, usually written as Re, is a dimensionless quantity that is calculated from four properties of the flow: the density rho, which is measured in kg m-3, the mean velocity v, measured in m s-1, the pipe diameter D, measured in m, and the dynamic viscosity mu, measured in Pa s. The relationship is Re = rho v D / mu. For water at a temperature of 293 K, the density rho is equal to 998 kg m-3, and the dynamic viscosity mu is 1.00 x 10-3 Pa s.

If we substitute the numbers into the relationship, we get Re = 998 x 1.1 x 0.025 / 0.001 = 27400. To interpret this, it is helpful to remember that flow is regarded as laminar when the Reynolds number is below Re = 2300, and as turbulent when it is above Re = 4000. For values in between, the regime is described as transitional, and the number by itself does not settle which regime applies. In the present case the calculated value of 27400 lies far above the upper of the two thresholds, so the flow can be classified as turbulent with some confidence.
target:
The Reynolds number for water flowing in a pipe of diameter 0.025 m at a mean velocity of 1.1 m s-1 is 27400, and the flow is turbulent.

The Reynolds number Re (dimensionless) is computed from the density rho (kg m-3), the mean velocity v (m s-1), the pipe diameter D (m) and the dynamic viscosity mu (Pa s) by Re = rho v D / mu. Water at 293 K has rho = 998 kg m-3 and mu = 1.00 x 10-3 Pa s. Each quantity is taken at the stated temperature.

Substitution of the values gives Re = 998 x 1.1 x 0.025 / 0.001 = 27400. Flow is laminar below Re = 2300 and turbulent above Re = 4000. Between the two values the regime is transitional and is not assigned by the number alone. The computed value stands above the upper threshold by a wide margin, and the regime is turbulent. The number compares the inertial effect of the flow with the viscous effect at the wall; a large value marks a flow in which viscosity no longer orders the motion across the whole section. The thresholds used here are the pipe-flow thresholds, and the assignment is made for the stated diameter and velocity only; a change in either moves the value and can move the regime across a threshold.

fact_base: 180 pumps run at the plant. Maintenance records for 12 months show 969 h of unplanned downtime; bearing failures account for 38% of the downtime hours. A sensor set for all 180 pumps is quoted at $443k installed, plus $63k per year. In a vendor trial on a comparable unit, the sensors cut downtime by 19%; the figure is a vendor figure and was not measured at this plant. A pilot on 22 pumps costs $38k over three months. Spare-part lead times are unchanged by the sensors. The memo recommends the three-month pilot; the reliability engineering group owns the pilot and reports before the March capital review; the decision on full installation is held until the pilot results are reported.
input:
The three-month pilot on 22 pumps should proceed, at a cost of $38k, and the decision on full installation should be held until the pilot results are reported. The pilot is owned by the reliability engineering group, which reports before the March capital review.

The base is the plant's own record. Across 180 pumps, maintenance records for 12 months show 969 h of unplanned downtime, and bearing failures account for 38% of the downtime hours. A sensor set for all 180 pumps is quoted at $443k installed, plus $63k per year: the full commitment is large against a benefit that has not been measured at this plant. In a vendor trial on a comparable unit, the sensors cut downtime by 19%; the figure is a vendor figure, and it is the only performance figure in the case.

The pilot buys the missing measurement. Run on 22 pumps over three months, it tests the sensors on the plant's own pumps, under the plant's own operating pattern, and returns a downtime figure the full decision can rest on. The trade stands in one sentence: $38k and one reporting cycle, against a commitment of $443k plus $63k per year taken on a vendor's number. Spare-part lead times are unchanged by the sensors, and the pilot does not disturb that position: a bearing failure detected early is still a bearing failure awaited on the same lead time, and no part of the case rests on spares.

The recommendation is therefore bounded. The pilot proceeds; full installation is neither approved nor refused, and it returns to the March capital review with the pilot results in hand.
