fact_base: Project proposal for a rooftop solar installation, in four sections: case, costs, schedule, and decision requested. Capital cost is $1236k with a 7-year appraisal horizon. The schedule section gives a start one quarter after approval; no contractor is named. The decision requested is approval to proceed to detailed design, not to construction.
input:
## Case
This proposal sets out the case for a rooftop solar installation, and explains why approval is being sought to take the project forward to the detailed design stage. The underlying idea is a straightforward and appealing one. The site in question has a large roof that is not currently used for any productive purpose, and the site also consumes electricity in the course of its normal operations. By placing solar generation on the roof, the site would be able to generate power on its own premises, at the point where that power is used, and on a surface that already exists and is currently doing nothing.

It is important to be clear, at the same time, about what stage the project has reached and what it has not. A number of the figures that would be needed to make a complete financial case for the installation are not yet available. Nobody has yet established exactly how much power an array on this roof would generate over the course of a year, what proportion of that output the site would be able to use itself, or on what terms any surplus might be exported. All of these are, in the nature of things, outputs of a design exercise, and until that exercise has been carried out, they can only be guessed at. For that reason, this proposal does not attempt to claim that the installation will definitely pay for itself, or to put a figure on the benefit it will deliver. What it does claim is that the combination of circumstances at the site — a large unused roof, and a demand for electricity on the same premises — makes the idea well worth taking to the next stage, and that the open questions are precisely the kind of questions that a detailed design is intended to answer.

## Costs
The capital cost of the installation is estimated at $1236k. The appraisal of the project is carried out over a horizon of 7 years.

The figure of $1236k is intended to represent the whole of the capital commitment: the solar array itself and the mounting system that holds it on the roof, the inverters and electrical connection equipment, the cabling and protection, and the installation and commissioning work required to bring the complete system into service. It is a single, all-in figure, and the appraisal is conducted on the basis of that figure rather than on a series of separate allowances that might later be added together. No savings have been netted off against it, and nothing has been held back.

Other elements of the financial picture are, for the reasons given above, not yet stated. The running costs of the installation, the value of the electricity it will generate, and the arrangements for exporting any surplus all depend on decisions and calculations that belong to the design stage: the layout that the design finally settles on, the yield that it calculates, and the connection that it agrees. Once those are known, a proper appraisal over the 7 years of the appraisal horizon can be put together; until then, any appraisal would rest on assumptions that this proposal is not in a position to support.

## Schedule
It is proposed that work would start one quarter after approval is given.

The work would proceed in a logical sequence. The first stage is detailed design, which covers the layout of the array, the checking of the roof structure, the electrical design, and the application for connection, and it is only when the design has been fixed that it makes sense to buy anything. Procurement follows, against the specification that the design produces. Installation comes after procurement, and connection and commissioning bring the sequence to a close. It should be noted that no contractor is named anywhere in this proposal. This is deliberate: the appointment of a contractor belongs to the procurement stage, and it ought to be made on the basis of the finished design rather than in advance of it.

The schedule is expressed in terms of a starting point and an order of stages, rather than as a programme of fixed dates. The dates of the later stages will depend to a considerable extent on what the design finds, and on the connection process, and neither of these can be pinned down in advance. What can be stated firmly is the order in which things will happen, and the point from which they will start to happen, namely one quarter after approval.

## Decision requested
The decision that is being requested is approval to proceed to detailed design. Nothing more than that is being asked for. In particular, this proposal does not request approval to construct the installation, and approving this proposal should not be taken as approving construction.

The detailed design will produce the information that a construction decision requires: a fixed layout, a calculated yield, the capital cost confirmed against the figure of $1236k quoted at this stage, and the terms on which connection will be granted. When that information is available, the case for or against construction can be made properly, on real figures instead of on the general fit between a roof and a demand for power, and it will be made in a separate proposal.

The commitment involved in approving this proposal is accordingly a limited one: it is the cost and the time of the design stage itself. If the design were to show that the roof could not carry the installation, or that the yield did not justify the capital cost, or that the connection terms were unacceptable, then the project could simply be stopped at that point, and the construction question would never have to be put at all. If, on the other hand, the design supports the case, the decision that follows will be a decision about a fully designed installation with a confirmed price attached to it. Either way, the decision being requested at this stage is the smaller and better-informed one, and it is the decision that the current state of the information supports.
target:
## Case
Approval is sought to take a rooftop solar installation to detailed design. The case is for the design stage, and it is made on the site's position rather than on a finished yield figure.

The site buys the electricity it uses, and its roof is a large surface that currently does no work. A rooftop installation puts generation on that surface, at the point where the power is consumed, without taking land or building volume from the operation the site exists for. The fit between the asset and the use is the substance of the case: the generation and the demand stand in the same place, under the same ownership, and the installation asks nothing of the site except the roof it already has.

What the case does not yet rest on is a settled account of value. The yield of the array, the share of the output the site would consume, and the terms on which any surplus would leave the site are all quantities that a design fixes, and none of them is stated here as a fact. The proposal therefore does not argue that the installation pays, because the figures that would carry that argument are not yet in hand. It argues the narrower point: that the site's position makes the installation worth designing, that the questions standing between the concept and a construction decision are design questions, and that they can only be answered by doing the design. The case is for finding out, made because the finding-out is small against the commitment it would inform, and because the site's circumstances give the answer a real chance of being favourable.

## Costs
The capital cost of the installation is $1236k. The appraisal horizon is 7 years.

The capital figure is the installed cost of the complete system: the array and its mounting, the inversion and connection equipment, the cabling and protection, and the installation work that puts them in place and brings the system into service. It is a single figure for the whole commitment, and it is the figure the appraisal runs on. No part of it is held back as a later addition, and no saving is netted against it at this stage.

Running costs, the value of the generated power, and the terms for any export are not stated in this proposal, because each of them depends on the design: on the layout the design settles, the yield it calculates, and the connection it agrees. An appraisal over the 7-year horizon can be assembled once the design returns those quantities, and it cannot be assembled honestly before. The costs section therefore fixes what is known, the capital commitment of $1236k and the horizon over which it is judged, and leaves the rest of the account open, marked as design output rather than filled with estimates.

## Schedule
Work starts one quarter after approval.

The sequence runs in the order the work requires. Detailed design comes first: the layout, the structural check of the roof, the electrical design, and the connection application all belong to it, and nothing is procured against a design that has not been fixed. Procurement follows the design, on the design's specification. Installation follows procurement, and connection and commissioning close the sequence. No contractor is named in this proposal, because the appointment belongs to the procurement stage and is made against the finished design.

The schedule is stated as a sequence and a start, not as a dated programme. Dates for the later stages depend on the design's findings and on the connection process, neither of which this proposal can settle in advance. What is fixed is the order, and the point from which the order runs: one quarter after approval, the design stage opens.

## Decision requested
The decision requested is approval to proceed to detailed design. Construction is not requested, and approval of this proposal does not approve it.

Detailed design returns the quantities the construction decision needs: a fixed layout, a calculated yield, the confirmed capital cost against the $1236k now stated, and the connection terms. With those in hand, the construction case can be made on figures rather than on the fit between a roof and a site's demand, and it will be made as a separate proposal to the same decision body.

The exposure accepted by approving this proposal is the design stage itself. If the design shows that the roof will not carry the array, that the yield does not support the capital cost, or that the connection terms fail the appraisal, the project stops at the design, and the construction question is never put. If the design sustains the case, the decision that follows is a decision on a designed installation at a confirmed cost. Either way, the decision requested now is the smaller one, and it is the one the present state of the figures supports.

fact_base: Staffing review for a dispatch office: 15 full-time staff, overtime at 21% of paid hours last year. Replacing half the overtime with one additional hire costs $89k per year fully loaded. Overtime is concentrated in two seasonal peaks; a hire is paid for the full year.
input:
This passage looks at the staffing position in a dispatch office and asks whether it would make sense to take on one additional member of staff in order to reduce the amount of overtime being worked. The office currently employs 15 people on a full-time basis, and over the course of last year overtime accounted for 21% of all paid hours, which is a substantial share by any standard.

At first glance, the arithmetic looks quite attractive. Taking on one more person on a fully loaded basis would cost $89k per year, and in return roughly half of the overtime that is currently worked would no longer be needed. Looked at purely in terms of the annual totals, that can appear to be a straightforward exchange of overtime hours for establishment capacity.

The picture becomes more complicated, however, once the timing of the overtime is taken into account. The overtime is not spread smoothly across the year; instead, it is concentrated in two distinct seasonal peaks, with much quieter periods in between. A new hire, by contrast, is paid for the whole year, in the quiet months just as much as in the busy ones. The $89k is therefore committed in every month, whereas the relief it provides is felt mainly in the peak weeks, when the office is genuinely stretched.

In the end, then, the question is not really whether the office can justify another salary across the year as a whole, but whether covering the peaks with a permanent member of staff is worth the price. Away from the peaks, the extra capacity has little to do, and it is the peak weeks alone that carry the case for the hire.
target:
One additional hire for the dispatch office costs $89k per year fully loaded and replaces half of the overtime the office works. The office employs 15 full-time staff, and overtime ran at 21% of paid hours last year.

Overtime in the dispatch office is not spread evenly across the year. It is concentrated in two seasonal peaks, and between the peaks the present establishment covers the work inside ordinary hours. A staffing change keyed to an annual total therefore misreads the problem the office has. The complication for the staffing case is that a hire is paid for the full year: the salary runs through the quiet months at the same level as through the peak weeks, while the overtime it replaces occurs in the peaks alone.

The hire buys peak cover. In the peak weeks, where the office is short, an additional member of staff in post removes overtime hours that would otherwise be worked, and the removal is worth most where the load is highest. Outside the peaks, the same salary buys capacity the dispatch work does not call on. The trade stands in one sentence: $89k per year, in every month of the year, against relief that arrives in the peak weeks only.

Judged on the year as a whole, the case is weak; judged on the peaks, it is the cost of covering them with establishment staff rather than with overtime. The review makes no claim beyond the peaks: the hire replaces half of the present overtime, and the half it replaces is peak overtime. Whether that cover is worth its price is a judgement on the peak service, not on the annual overtime bill.

fact_base: A vapour-compression unit serves an ice rink, evaporating at -25 °C and condensing at 35 °C. The Carnot coefficient of performance between these temperatures is 4.13; the installed unit achieves 2.03. The achieved value is from the manufacturer's test at full load; part-load performance is not stated.
input:
In this example we look at a vapour-compression refrigeration unit that serves an ice rink, and we compare the performance it actually achieves with the best performance that could in principle be achieved between the same temperatures. The unit operates with an evaporating temperature of -25 °C and a condensing temperature of 35 °C. Between these two temperatures, the Carnot coefficient of performance works out to 4.13, whereas the installed unit achieves a coefficient of performance of 2.03, so there is a considerable gap between the two figures.

The coefficient of performance, or COP, is essentially a measure of how much cooling effect is obtained for each unit of work that is supplied to the machine. The Carnot COP represents the theoretical upper limit for any refrigerator that works between a given pair of temperatures, which in this case are -25 °C on the cold side and 35 °C on the hot side, and no real machine can do better than this limit of 4.13. The installed unit's figure of 2.03 corresponds to about 0.49 of the Carnot value, which gives a simple way of expressing how close the real machine comes to the ideal.

It is important to bear in mind, however, that the achieved figure comes from the manufacturer's own test, carried out at full load. The performance of the unit at part load is not stated anywhere, and in practice an ice rink does not call for full-load operation all of the time. The comparison that has been made is therefore strictly a full-load comparison, and it should not be taken as a description of how the unit behaves across the whole range of loads that the rink places on it over a season.
target:
The installed vapour-compression unit at the ice rink achieves a coefficient of performance of 2.03, against a Carnot coefficient of performance of 4.13 between the same two temperatures. The unit evaporates at -25 °C and condenses at 35 °C, and the achieved figure is the manufacturer's test value at full load.

The coefficient of performance states the cooling duty delivered per unit of work supplied. The Carnot value is the ceiling for any refrigerator working between the two temperatures: no machine between an evaporating temperature of -25 °C and a condensing temperature of 35 °C exceeds 4.13, and a real machine stands below the ceiling by the losses its cycle carries. The installed unit, at 2.03, delivers 0.49 of the Carnot performance. The two coefficients share the same temperatures, and the comparison holds the duty fixed. That ratio is the finding of the comparison; it is computed from the two stated coefficients and from nothing else. The distance between the two values is the room the cycle leaves for improvement, and it is read against the ceiling rather than against another machine, because no second machine is stated.

What the figure does not state is how the unit performs away from the test point. The achieved value comes from the manufacturer's test at full load, and part-load performance is not stated. A season at an ice rink is not run at full load throughout, and the rink's energy use follows the part-load behaviour that the test figure leaves open. The comparison is therefore a full-load comparison. It ranks the installed unit against the ceiling for its duty, and it says nothing about the unit's standing across the load range the rink actually imposes. A part-load figure would be needed before the unit's seasonal performance can be stated.

fact_base: Design report for a spray dryer, in four sections: basis, sizing, materials, and risks. Design throughput is 34 t per day and the removal or separation duty is 97% of the key component. Materials are 316L stainless steel for wetted parts; the basis section states this once. The risks section names fouling and turndown as open items; neither is resolved in the report.
input:
## Basis
This report presents the design of a spray dryer and sets out the basis on which the design has been carried out. The design throughput of the dryer is 34 t per day. The duty that the dryer is required to perform is the removal of 97% of the key component from the feed. In other words, the feed comes in as a liquid in which the key component is present, and the product is required to leave as a dry powder from which the great majority of that component has been removed.

The feed itself is a pumpable liquid. It is atomised at the top of the drying chamber, so that it enters the hot air as a spray of fine droplets, and the droplets are dried as they travel through the chamber. The dried powder is collected partly from the chamber itself and partly from the separation stage that is fitted on the exhaust air leaving the chamber. It is important to appreciate that everything else in this report — the sizing of the equipment, the selection of materials, and the discussion of risks — is built on the basis described in this section: a stated throughput, a stated removal duty, a liquid feed going in, and a powder product coming out. If any of those things were different, the design would be different too.

As far as materials are concerned, all wetted parts of the dryer are to be made in 316L stainless steel. This statement is made here, in the basis, and it is not repeated elsewhere in the report; the materials section develops what follows from it.

Finally, the scope of the design should be understood. The design covers the dryer itself together with its own auxiliaries. What happens before the dryer — the preparation of the feed — and what happens after it — the handling of the powder — are outside the scope of this design.

It is also worth emphasising what kind of duty this is. Taking out nearly all of a component is considerably more demanding than taking out most of it, even at the same throughput, because the last part of the removal is where the air, the heat and the chamber volume are spent.

## Sizing
The sizing of the dryer is based on the throughput given in the basis, namely the 34 t per day of feed, together with the removal duty that the basis lays down. This section explains, in general terms, how the principal parts of the machine have been sized, proceeding from the atomiser outwards.

The atomiser that has been selected is a rotary atomiser. This choice has been made because the feed is a liquid from which a fine and even powder is required, and because a rotary atomiser is relatively tolerant of variations in the condition of the feed, which a pressure nozzle would tend to pass on to the spray. The rotating wheel breaks the feed up into droplets at the top end of the chamber, and in a very real sense everything that comes after the wheel is sized by reference to the droplets that it produces. The size of the droplets determines how long each droplet needs to spend in the hot air, and that drying time in turn determines the size of the chamber.

The chamber has accordingly been sized with two considerations in mind: the time that the droplets need in order to dry, and the path that the air takes as it passes through the chamber. The air comes in hot and meets the spray, giving up its heat in order to carry out the evaporation that the duty requires. The volume of the chamber is such as to hold the droplets in the air for the necessary length of time, while the shape of the chamber is intended to keep the wettest of the droplets away from the walls for as much of that time as the geometry will permit.

The air system — the heater, the fan and the separation stage — has been sized on the evaporation that has to be achieved. The heater must raise the whole of the air flow to the inlet condition, the fan must move that air through the chamber and through the separation stage, and the separation stage, which consists of cyclones with a polishing step on the exhaust, must recover the fine powder that the air carries out of the chamber. The exhaust air leaves the system carrying the removed component with it, and the separation stage is there to make sure that, as far as is reasonably possible, what leaves is vapour rather than product.

## Materials
All of the wetted parts of the dryer are made in the stainless steel grade that is stated in the basis section. By wetted parts is meant every surface that can come into contact with the feed, with the powder, with the wash liquor that is used to clean the machine, or with condensate from the exhaust. This includes the chamber and its roof, the atomiser and the pipe that feeds it, the ducting, the separation stage, and the outlets through which the powder leaves the machine.

The reason for the choice of grade is the range of contact that the wetted surfaces have to withstand. The feed is a liquid, and it will inevitably remain in the machine whenever the machine is stopped. The powder is the product, and its quality is affected by the surfaces it passes over. And the machine is washed down between campaigns, so that over the course of its life the wetted surfaces are exposed in turn to the product, the feed, the cleaning liquor and the air. The grade stated in the basis is able to resist this whole range of contact without relying on a coating that might fail or a lining that might lift, and it can be cleaned to a standard that the product requires.

Parts of the machine that do not come into contact with the process — the supporting steelwork, the cladding, the casing of the heater and the casing of the fan — are made of carbon steel with a protective coating, since what they have to withstand is weather and mechanical load rather than chemical contact. The dividing line between the two materials follows the wetted boundary throughout the machine, and any part that is wetted on one side, even if it is structural on the other, is treated as a wetted part.

Seals, gaskets and flexible connections have been selected to suit the same duties as the parts they connect, including the temperatures found in the air path. Joints in the powder path have been made flush and capable of being cleaned, and access has been provided so that the wetted surfaces can be inspected without the machine having to be dismantled.

## Risks
There are two significant risks that remain open at the conclusion of this design, and this section describes them honestly rather than attempting to design them away. They are fouling and turndown, and neither of them has been resolved by the work reported here.

Fouling means the gradual build-up of product in places where the product ought simply to pass through. In a spray dryer, the vulnerable places are well known. Deposits can form at the atomiser, where even a small build-up can throw the wheel out of balance and make the spray coarser. They can form on the walls of the chamber, where a layer of material insulates the wall, can scorch, and can eventually fall away into the product. And they can form in the separation stage, where the passages become progressively narrower. The design does what it can to reduce the exposure — the shape of the chamber is intended to keep the wettest spray away from the walls, and the access provided allows deposits to be found and cleaned off — but it would be misleading to describe this as a solution. This risk will only be closed when the machine has been run on the feed and the rate of fouling has been observed for real.

Turndown is the risk at the opposite end of the operating range. The dryer has been designed for its stated throughput, but a plant does not always call for the full rate. At reduced rates, the atomiser produces a different spray, the balance between the air and the feed changes, and the margins that the design relies on to keep wet powder away from the walls and out of the exhaust are used up in a different pattern. The lowest throughput at which the dryer will still perform its duty satisfactorily has not been established, and no figure for it is given in this report. The risk will be closed when turndown has either been tested or guaranteed on the basis of evidence; in the meantime, anyone operating the dryer below its design rate should be aware that they are operating outside the scope of what this report covers.

The sizing stands for the duty laid down in the basis. The risks stand alongside it, unresolved.
target:
## Basis
The design covers a spray dryer with a design throughput of 34 t per day. The duty of the dryer is the removal of 97% of the key component from the feed: the feed enters as a liquid carrying the key component, and the product leaves as a dry powder from which all but the remainder of that component has been taken.

The feed is a pumpable liquid. It is atomised at the top of the drying chamber, and the droplets dry in the hot air that shares the chamber with them. The powder is collected from the chamber and from the separation stage on the exhaust air. What the dryer is asked to do is fixed by the two figures above and by the form of the feed and the product: a stated rate, a stated removal, a liquid in and a powder out. The sizing, the materials and the risks in this report all hang on that statement, and nothing outside it is designed here.

Materials are 316L stainless steel for all wetted parts. The grade is stated here, once, and the materials section works from this statement without repeating it.

The boundary of the design is the dryer and its own auxiliaries. Feed preparation upstream of the dryer and powder handling downstream of it are outside the boundary. The design takes the feed as it is delivered to the dryer, and it delivers powder and exhaust air across the boundary in the other direction. Conditions at the interfaces are the conditions of the plant the dryer serves, and they are inputs to this design, not outputs of it.

The duty is a removal duty, and what that means for the rest of the design is stated plainly. A dryer asked to take out nearly all of a component is a different machine from one asked to take out most of it, even at the same throughput: the last of the removal is the expensive part, in air, in heat and in chamber, and the sizing that follows is a sizing for the stated removal, not for a lesser one that would be easier to reach.

## Sizing
The dryer is sized on the throughput of the basis, the 34 t per day of feed, and on the removal the basis states. Sizing proceeds from the atomiser outward.

The atomiser is a rotary atomiser, chosen because the feed is a liquid whose duty is a fine, even powder, and because the rotary form tolerates the variation in feed state that a pressure nozzle passes on to the spray. The wheel throws the feed into droplets at the top of the chamber, and everything downstream of the wheel is sized on the droplets it makes: their size sets the time each droplet needs in the air, and that time sets the chamber.

The chamber is sized on drying time and on the path the air takes through it. The air enters hot, meets the spray, and gives up its heat to the evaporation the duty requires; the chamber volume holds the droplets in the air for the time the drying takes, and the chamber shape keeps the wettest droplets off the walls for as much of that time as the geometry allows. The diameter is set by the air path and the spray pattern together, and the height by the fall the droplets need. Neither figure is a catalogue figure; both follow from the throughput and the removal, and both would change if either changed.

The air system is sized on the evaporation. The heater raises the full air flow to the inlet condition, the fan moves it through the chamber and the separation stage, and the separation stage, cyclones with a polishing step on the exhaust, returns the fines the air carries out of the chamber. The exhaust leaves with the removed component in it, and the separation stage is sized so that what leaves in the exhaust is vapour and as little powder as the stage can hold back.

## Materials
All wetted parts are built in the stainless steel grade stated in the basis. Wetted parts are every surface the feed, the powder, the wash liquor or the exhaust condensate can touch: the chamber and its roof, the atomiser and its feed pipe, the ducts, the separation stage, and the powder outlets.

The grade is chosen for the contact it has to survive. The feed is a liquid that will sit in the machine during every stoppage, the powder is the product and takes its standing from the surfaces it touches, and the machine is washed down between campaigns, so the wetted surfaces meet the product, the feed, the wash and the air in turn. The grade named in the basis resists that range of contact without a coating to fail or a lining to lift, and it can be cleaned to a standard the product can accept.

Structure that does not meet the process, the supporting steelwork, the cladding, the heater casing, the fan casing, is carbon steel, protected by coating, because its duty is weather and load rather than contact. The division between the two materials follows the wetted boundary everywhere, and where a part is wetted on one face and structural on the other, it is built as a wetted part.

Seals, gaskets and flexible connections are picked for the same contact as the parts they join, and for the temperatures of the air path they sit in. Joints in the powder path are made flush and cleanable, and the chamber is fitted with access that lets the wetted surfaces be inspected without dismantling the machine. A material that cannot be inspected cannot be kept, and inspection is part of the materials decision, not an afterthought to it.

## Risks
Two risks stand open at the end of this design: fouling, and turndown. Neither is resolved here, and this section states them as open items, with the condition on which each would close.

Fouling is the risk that the product builds up where it should pass through. A spray dryer fouls at the places where wet or sticky powder meets a surface: at the atomiser, where a deposit unbalances the wheel and coarsens the spray; on the chamber walls, where a layer insulates, scorches and falls into the product; and in the separation stage, where the passages narrow. The design reduces the exposure, in that the chamber shape keeps the wettest spray off the walls and the access the materials section provides lets deposits be found and removed, but reduction is not resolution. How fast this feed fouls this machine, and how often it must be cleaned, are questions the design cannot answer, because they rest on the behaviour of the actual feed over actual campaigns. The risk closes when the machine has run the feed and the fouling rate has been seen; until then it stands.

Turndown is the risk at the other end of the rate. The dryer is designed at its stated throughput, and a plant does not always ask for the full rate. Below it, the atomiser makes a different spray, the air-to-feed balance shifts, and the margin the design carries against wet powder reaching the wall or the exhaust is spent differently. The lowest rate at which the dryer still makes its duty has not been established, and the design does not state one. The risk closes when the turndown has been tested or guaranteed on evidence; until then, operation below the design rate is operation outside what this report covers.

Both risks are stated here rather than designed away, because a design report that hides its open items behind its sizing is worse than one that names them. The sizing stands for the duty of the basis. The risks stand beside it, open.

subtype: worked example with equation: Ergun pressure drop
fact_base: Gas flows through a packed bed of 1 mm particles. The void fraction $\varepsilon$ is 0.5, the superficial velocity $u$ is 0.45 m s-1 and the bed length is 2 m. The Ergun equation gives a pressure gradient of 4.1 kPa m-1, or 8.3 kPa over the bed. Particle diameter $d_p$ is 1 mm; gas density is 1.2 kg m-3 and viscosity is 1.8 x 10-5 Pa s.
input:
Gas is passed through a packed bed made up of particles that are 1 mm in size, and the pressure drop that the gas experiences as it flows through the bed is estimated by means of the Ergun equation. In the case considered here, the superficial velocity of the gas is 0.45 m s-1 and the bed is 2 m in length.

The Ergun equation, which is the standard relation for this purpose, expresses the pressure gradient in the bed in the form

$$\frac{\Delta P}{L} = \frac{150 \mu (1-\varepsilon)^2}{\varepsilon^3 d_p^2} u + \frac{1.75 (1-\varepsilon)}{\varepsilon^3 d_p} \rho u^2$$

In this equation, $\Delta P$ is the pressure drop (in kPa) over the length $L$ (in m) of the bed, $\mu$ is the viscosity of the gas (in Pa s), $\varepsilon$ is the void fraction of the bed, which is dimensionless, $d_p$ is the particle diameter (in m), $u$ is the superficial velocity (in m s-1), and $\rho$ is the density of the gas (in kg m-3). The equation is made up of two contributions: a first term, which represents the resistance due to viscosity, and a second term, which represents the resistance due to inertia.

For the particular bed considered here, the void fraction $\varepsilon$ is 0.5, the particle diameter $d_p$ is 1 mm, the superficial velocity $u$ is 0.45 m s-1, the density $\rho$ is 1.2 kg m-3, and the viscosity $\mu$ is 1.8 x 10-5 Pa s. Putting these values into the equation gives a pressure gradient of 4.1 kPa m-1, which corresponds to a total pressure drop of 8.3 kPa across the 2 m bed.
target:
Gas flows through a packed bed of 1 mm particles, at a superficial velocity of 0.45 m s-1, through a bed 2 m long. The Ergun equation gives the pressure gradient in the bed as

$$\frac{\Delta P}{L} = \frac{150 \mu (1-\varepsilon)^2}{\varepsilon^3 d_p^2} u + \frac{1.75 (1-\varepsilon)}{\varepsilon^3 d_p} \rho u^2$$

where $\Delta P$ (kPa) is the pressure drop over the bed length $L$ (m), $\mu$ (Pa s) is the gas viscosity, $\varepsilon$ (dimensionless) is the void fraction of the bed, $d_p$ (m) is the particle diameter, $u$ (m s-1) is the superficial velocity and $\rho$ (kg m-3) is the gas density.

The first term carries the viscous resistance and the second the inertial resistance. At the stated conditions, $\varepsilon$ = 0.5, $d_p$ = 1 mm, $u$ = 0.45 m s-1, $\rho$ = 1.2 kg m-3 and $\mu$ = 1.8 x 10-5 Pa s, the gradient is 4.1 kPa m-1, and the pressure drop over the 2 m bed is 8.3 kPa. The two terms divide the resistance by its source. The viscous term grows in direct proportion to the velocity, and the inertial term grows with the square of the velocity, so the balance between them shifts as the flow rises: at low velocity the viscous term governs the gradient, and at high velocity the inertial term takes over. The gradient is the transferable figure. A longer or shorter bed at the same conditions carries the same gradient, and its pressure drop follows from its length; the value over this bed is an instance, not the result.

fact_base: Pervaporation is a membrane separation in which a liquid feed contacts one side of a membrane and vacuum on the other side draws the permeating component through as vapour. Flux is the mass permeating per unit membrane area per hour (kg m-2 h-1). The separation factor is the water-to-alcohol ratio in the permeate divided by the same ratio in the feed (dimensionless). Feed: 85 wt% ethanol in water, at 60 °C. One feed composition was tested; no test ran beyond 500 h. Polymer membrane: flux 2.3 kg m-2 h-1, separation factor 120, flux fell 13% over 500 h. Zeolite membrane: flux 1.3 kg m-2 h-1, separation factor 560, flux unchanged over 500 h within measurement error. Flux, selectivity and stability are seldom reported together for the same membrane.
input:
In this study, two different membranes are compared for the separation of ethanol and water by pervaporation. Pervaporation is a membrane separation technique in which a liquid feed is placed in contact with one side of a membrane, while a vacuum applied on the other side draws the component that permeates through the membrane out as a vapour. The feed used in the experiments consisted of 85 wt% ethanol in water, and the tests were carried out at 60 °C. Only this single feed composition was investigated, and none of the tests was run for longer than 500 h.

Two quantities are used to describe the performance of the membranes. The flux is the mass of material that permeates through a unit area of membrane in one hour, expressed in kg m-2 h-1, and the separation factor is the ratio of water to alcohol in the permeate divided by the corresponding ratio in the feed, and is therefore dimensionless. The polymer membrane achieved a flux of 2.3 kg m-2 h-1 together with a separation factor of 120, although its flux fell by 13% over the course of 500 h. The zeolite membrane, by contrast, achieved a flux of 1.3 kg m-2 h-1 and a much higher separation factor of 560, and its flux remained unchanged over 500 h to within the error of the measurements.

Overall, the results show a familiar trade-off: the polymer membrane offers the higher throughput, while the zeolite membrane offers the better selectivity and the more stable performance. It is worth remarking that flux, selectivity and stability are rarely all reported together for one and the same membrane, which is part of what makes this comparison useful, although the findings are limited to the single composition and the durations that were actually tested.
target:
Two membranes were compared for the pervaporation of a feed of 85 wt% ethanol in water at 60 °C. Pervaporation is a membrane separation in which a liquid feed contacts one side of a membrane and vacuum on the other side draws the permeating component through as vapour. The polymer membrane gave the higher flux and the lower separation factor; the zeolite membrane gave the lower flux, the higher separation factor, and the stable flux. The comparison was made on one feed, over a bounded duration, so that flux, selectivity and stability rest on the same run for each membrane.

Flux is the mass permeating per unit membrane area per hour (kg m-2 h-1). The separation factor is the water-to-alcohol ratio in the permeate divided by the same ratio in the feed. The polymer membrane gave a flux of 2.3 kg m-2 h-1 and a separation factor of 120, and its flux fell 13% over 500 h. The zeolite membrane gave a flux of 1.3 kg m-2 h-1 and a separation factor of 560, with its flux unchanged over 500 h within measurement error.

The comparison is a trade between rate and selectivity, with stability standing on the zeolite side. One feed composition was tested, and no test ran beyond 500 h; flux, selectivity and stability are seldom reported together for the same membrane, and the standing of either membrane outside the tested composition and duration is not established by these results. Within those bounds, the choice between the membranes is a choice of what the separation is for.

fact_base: Performance of a mechanical-draft tower at a chemical site was logged over one summer month. Mean wet-bulb temperature was 27 °C, the approach was 6 K and the range was 5 K. Performance outside the logged month, in particular at winter wet-bulb temperatures, was not measured.
input:
The performance of a mechanical-draft cooling tower at a chemical site was recorded over a period of one summer month, and the results give a picture of how the tower behaved under summer conditions. During the month in question, the mean wet-bulb temperature was 27 °C, the approach was 6 K, and the range was 5 K. From these figures it is possible to work out the actual water temperatures involved: the approach means that the cold water left the tower at 33 °C, and the range means that the hot water entered it at 38 °C.

To understand these terms properly, it should be explained that the wet-bulb temperature represents the lowest temperature to which the water could theoretically be cooled, and the approach is the difference between the cold-water temperature and this limiting value. The range, on the other hand, is simply the drop in temperature that the water undergoes as it passes through the tower. Putting the figures together, the tower was taking in water at 38 °C and returning it at 33 °C, against a wet-bulb temperature of 27 °C.

It must be emphasised, however, that these measurements cover one summer month and nothing more. How the tower performs at other times of year was not measured, and this is a real limitation, because in winter the wet-bulb temperature is much lower and there is no guarantee that the tower would hold the same approach or the same range. The results should therefore be treated as a description of the tower's summer behaviour at this particular site, and not as a general statement about its performance throughout the year.
target:
Over one summer month at a chemical site, a mechanical-draft tower ran with a mean wet-bulb temperature of 27 °C, an approach of 6 K and a range of 5 K. The approach places the cold-water temperature at 33 °C, and the range places the hot-water temperature at 38 °C. The three figures are means and differences over the month, and they carry the month with them.

The wet-bulb temperature is the floor for the cold water: a tower cools toward the wet-bulb temperature and does not reach it, and the approach is the distance the cold water stands above that floor. The range is the fall in temperature the water makes across the tower, from the hot water entering to the cold water leaving. The approach is the figure the tower is judged by, because it measures the tower against the limit the air imposes rather than against its own inlet state. Read together, the figures fix the tower's working point for the logged month: water entered at 38 °C, left at 33 °C, and the wet bulb stood at 27 °C.

The record is a single summer month. Performance outside the logged month was not measured, and the gap stands where it matters most: at winter wet-bulb temperatures the floor falls, the approach a tower holds against a lower floor is a separate question, and neither the approach nor the range logged in summer can be carried into winter. A winter figure would have to be measured in winter, on the same tower. The figures describe the tower as it ran in one summer month at one chemical site, and the claim for them ends there. Nothing in the record speaks for the tower in any other month, and the record is not extended by argument.

fact_base: A defect-reduction project on a filling line cut the reject rate from 5.4% to 3.4% over one quarter. At 354k units per year the change avoids about 7080 rejected units per year. The quarter included a planned shutdown; rates are not adjusted for it.
input:
The filling-line defect-reduction project was associated with a decrease in the reject rate from 5.4% to 3.4% during one quarter. Based on production of 354k units per year, this change corresponds to approximately 7080 fewer rejected units per year. It is important to note that the quarterly comparison is not adjusted for a planned shutdown that occurred during the same quarter. As a result, the two rates describe performance across a period that included production and shutdown-related interruption, rather than a cleanly isolated operating interval. The annual figure should therefore be interpreted as an annualised representation of the observed rate change at the stated production level, rather than as a separately counted total of avoided rejects. The available information does not separate the influence of the shutdown from the influence of the project, and it does not provide an adjusted reject rate for a shutdown-free comparison. Within those limits, the reported outcome is still a reduction between the starting and ending reject rates for the quarter, together with an annual avoided-unit estimate tied directly to the specified volume and dependent on the lower rate and operating pattern being sustained.

The shutdown also limits attribution, because the comparison period was not a uniform production interval and no separate rate is supplied for the time away from the shutdown. The result is best read as the change observed across the project quarter. Its annual form follows from applying that change to annual production, not from observing a full year at the lower rate.
target:
A defect-reduction project on a filling line cut the reject rate from 5.4% to 3.4% over one quarter. At 354k units per year, the change avoids about 7080 rejected units per year.

The annual figure applies the recorded rate change to the stated annual volume. It is an annual equivalent of the quarterly result, not a count accumulated over a full year, and it depends on the reduced rate applying at that volume under comparable conditions. The quarter included a planned shutdown; the rates are not adjusted for it. No shutdown-free rate is reported, and the project effect cannot be separated from any effect of the shutdown period in the figures given. The supported result is the recorded reduction over the quarter and the corresponding annual quantity of avoided rejects at the stated volume, with the shutdown left inside the measurement period rather than removed by adjustment.

The shutdown limits attribution. It formed part of the measurement period, and no separate rate is given for production outside it. The annual figure should therefore be used with its basis attached: a quarterly observed reduction extended to the stated annual volume. It should not be presented as an adjusted steady-state rate or as a count of rejects avoided over a completed year.

fact_base: A contract packaging firm runs 2 plants; revenue is $104 million per year. Evidence base: order records for 12 months, 13383 orders. On-time delivery over the last two quarters was 87%, against a target of 95%. Overtime cost was $1.7 million last year, up 20% on the year before. The order backlog stands at 3.8 weeks, against 1.7 weeks a year ago. Plant 2 accounts for 68% of late orders. A scheduling system for all plants is quoted at $273k; Plant 2 alone is $138k. An internal estimate (not a vendor figure) puts the overtime reduction at Plant 2 at 15-20% in the first year. The recommendation under consideration: install at Plant 2 first, hold the other plants until Plant 2 results are reported. The operations director owns the scheduling programme.
input:
A contract packaging firm operating 2 plants, with revenue of $104 million per year, is considering a phased scheduling-system installation beginning at Plant 2 and then holding the remaining plants until results from Plant 2 are reported. The operations director owns the scheduling programme. The evidence base consists of order records for 12 months and 13383 orders. Over the last two quarters, on-time delivery was 87%, compared with a target of 95%. Overtime cost was $1.7 million last year, an increase of 20% on the year before, while the order backlog has risen to 3.8 weeks from 1.7 weeks a year ago. Plant 2 accounts for 68% of late orders, which is why it is the proposed starting point. A scheduling system for all plants is quoted at $273k, whereas Plant 2 alone is quoted at $138k. An internal estimate, rather than a vendor figure, suggests that overtime at Plant 2 could be reduced by 15-20% in the first year. Taken together, the figures point to a delivery problem concentrated mainly in one part of the operation, although the estimate of overtime benefit remains internal and has not yet been demonstrated in operation.

It is also relevant that the proposal is not simply to buy the system at a lower initial cost. The sequence matters because the firm can learn whether scheduling changes affect delivery performance and overtime in the plant where the problem is most visible before committing the same approach elsewhere. The backlog increase and the missed delivery target provide the operational context, while the concentration of late orders provides the reason for a staged approach. At the same time, the evidence does not establish that scheduling is the only cause of late delivery, nor does it quantify how much of the backlog would be cleared by the system. The quoted prices establish the difference in initial scope, but the internal overtime estimate remains the least secure part of the case. The recommendation therefore links expansion to reported results instead of treating the estimate as proof, and the named owner gives the programme a single point of accountability for reporting those results.

The order backlog stands at 3.8 weeks, against 1.7 weeks a year ago. Plant 2 accounts for 68% of late orders, so the delivery shortfall is concentrated rather than evenly spread across the firm.

A scheduling system for all plants is quoted at $273k; Plant 2 alone is $138k. The lower initial commitment tests the programme where late orders are concentrated. That estimate is a benefit to verify from reported results, not a saving already established.
