fact_base: The rate constant k (s-1) of a first-order liquid-phase reaction was measured at two temperatures. At 300 K, k = 0.085 s-1. At 340 K, k = 1.311 s-1, computed from the Arrhenius relation with activation energy 58 kJ mol-1 as a derived value. Each temperature was measured in triplicate; the relative standard deviation of k was 4%. Above 340 K the solvent evaporated during sampling, so no rate constant is reported above 340 K.
input:
In this work, the rate constant k (s-1) of a first-order liquid-phase reaction was measured at two different temperatures, in order to establish how the rate of reaction responds to temperature. At 300 K, the rate constant was found to be k = 0.085 s-1. At 340 K, by contrast, k = 1.311 s-1, this second value having been computed from the Arrhenius relation with an activation energy of 58 kJ mol-1 and being presented here as a derived value rather than as a direct measurement.

Each temperature was measured in triplicate, and the relative standard deviation of k was 4%, which gives a reasonable indication of the reproducibility of the measurements. It can be seen that the value at 340 K stands 15.4 times the value at 300 K, so that the rate constant increases very steeply indeed over what is a relatively modest interval of temperature, a behaviour that is consistent with the size of the activation energy involved. It is perhaps worth noting that, because the higher-temperature value is derived rather than measured, it depends jointly on the quality of the lower-temperature measurement and on the activation energy that has been adopted.

Above 340 K, difficulties were encountered because the solvent evaporated during sampling, so no rate constant is reported above 340 K. This is essentially a practical limitation of the experimental procedure, in that samples taken at higher temperatures lost solvent before they could be analysed, and any value extracted from them would have been unreliable.

Each temperature was measured in triplicate, and the relative standard deviation of k was 4%. The triplicate measurement fixes the precision of the measured value at the lower temperature, and the derived value at the higher temperature is computed from that measured base through the Arrhenius relation, so its reliability rests on the measured value and on the activation energy together. The value at 340 K stands 15.4 times the value at 300 K: across the interval the rate constant rises steeply, and the size of the rise is the size the activation energy produces over this temperature span for a reaction of this order. A change in either input, the measured rate constant or the activation energy, would move the derived value in proportion, and the reported figure should be read with that dependence in view.

Above 340 K the solvent evaporated during sampling, so no rate constant is reported above 340 K. The evaporation is a limit of the measurement, not a property of the reaction: samples taken at higher temperatures lost solvent before analysis, and a rate constant computed from them would describe the sampling failure rather than the kinetics. The reported results therefore cover the two stated temperatures and the interval between them, and the Arrhenius computation is not extended past the point where the measurement itself failed.

fact_base: A defect-reduction project on a filling line cut the reject rate from 5.5% to 2.4% over one quarter. At 217k units per year the change avoids about 6727 rejected units per year. The quarter included a planned shutdown; rates are not adjusted for it.
input:
This case describes a defect-reduction project that was carried out on a filling line, in which the reject rate was cut from 5.5% to 2.4% over the course of one quarter, corresponding to a reduction of 3.1 percentage points. At 217k units per year, it is estimated that the change avoids about 6727 rejected units per year, which gives a helpful sense of the scale of the improvement in practical terms.

It is worth explaining the relationship between these figures. The reject rate expresses the proportion of production that the line rejects, and the number of rejected units that are avoided over a year is obtained by applying the reduction in that rate to the annual volume of production. The two figures therefore describe one and the same improvement in two different ways: the rate is the more useful figure for comparing the performance of this line with the performance of other lines, since it does not depend on how much a line produces, whereas the count of avoided units is the more useful figure for assessing the value of the improvement, although it will naturally change if the production volume changes.

One caveat should be attached to these results. The quarter in question included a planned shutdown, and the rates are not adjusted for it, which means that the comparison is drawn across a period that was not entirely representative of normal production. The figures should accordingly be read as the rates that were actually recorded, with the avoided count derived from them at the stated volume.
target:

The reject rate is the share of production the line discards, so the avoided count follows from the rate reduction applied to the annual volume: the project changed the rate, and the count is that change expressed in units at the stated throughput. Both figures describe the same improvement on different scales. The rate states what the line now does with each unit it fills, independently of how many units pass through; the count states what the improvement is worth across a year of production at the current volume, and it would move with the volume even if the rate held steady. A reader comparing this line with another should compare rates, while a reader costing the improvement should work from the count and the volume it assumes.

The quarter included a planned shutdown, and the rates are not adjusted for it. Production during the quarter was therefore interrupted in a way the figures do not correct for, and the comparison between the rate before the project and the rate after it is a comparison across a quarter that was not a normal production period. The improvement is reported on that basis: the rates are the rates as recorded, the avoided count is derived from them at the stated annual volume, and neither figure has been restated to remove the shutdown.

fact_base: Project proposal for a water recycling plant, in four sections: case, costs, schedule, and decision requested. Capital cost is $2351k with a 7-year appraisal horizon. The schedule section gives a start one quarter after approval; no contractor is named. The decision requested is approval to proceed to detailed design, not to construction.
input:
## Case

This proposal concerns the construction of a water recycling plant for the site. At present, the site takes all of its water from an external supply and discharges all of its effluent after treatment. It is worth noting that a significant part of the site's water demand consists of uses that do not actually require fresh-water quality, such as washdown and utility make-up, and these uses currently draw on the incoming supply simply because no alternative source has been connected to them. The proposed recycling plant would take a suitable effluent stream after treatment, treat it further to the quality that those uses require, and return it to them, thereby meeting part of the site's demand from water that the site has already used once.

The case for the plant rests on the overall structure of the site's water flows. Every unit of water that is recycled is a unit that does not have to be purchased from the external supply, and it is also a unit that does not have to be discharged, so the plant has an effect at both ends of the site's water position at the same time. A site that recycles part of its flow is less exposed to interruption or restriction in the external supply, and also less exposed to any tightening of the conditions on its discharge, than a site that passes the whole of its demand through the boundary in both directions. Furthermore, the recycled flow is under the site's own control, and its availability follows the site's own operation rather than a supplier's network.

The scope of the proposal is the site's own uses. The plant would not supply water to third parties, and it would not replace the existing effluent treatment, since the residual stream that is not recycled would continue to that treatment and to discharge as at present. The plant should be seen as an addition between the treated effluent and the low-grade uses, and its sizing would follow those uses rather than the whole of the site's demand. Uses that need fresh-water quality would remain on the external supply.

The alternative to the plant is simply to continue with the present arrangement, under which the low-grade uses remain on purchased water and the treated effluent continues to be discharged in full. That arrangement works, although it does not give the site any reduction in its exposure on either side. Partial measures short of the plant, such as returning untreated or partly treated water to the least demanding uses, have been set aside on quality grounds, because the receiving uses still have quality requirements that have to be met.

It should also be emphasised that the boundary between the recycled supply and the fresh supply is an important feature of the proposal. The recycled supply would be carried in separate pipework, and the design would include arrangements for monitoring its quality and for diverting it back to treatment if it were found to be off specification, so that it could not reach a use for which it was not intended.

## Costs

The capital cost of the plant is $2351k. This figure covers the plant as a whole, including the treatment equipment, the storage, the pipework and tie-ins to the effluent stream and to the receiving uses, the installation, and the commissioning. No breakdown of the figure between these elements is provided at this stage, because such a breakdown is a product of the detailed design, and presenting one now would suggest a level of precision that the underlying design does not yet support.

The appraisal horizon is 7 years. Within that horizon, the operating costs of the plant are to be set against its savings. The operating costs are the running costs of the treatment itself, including energy, treatment chemicals, operating labour, maintenance of the plant and its instruments, and the cost of the residual discharge that remains. The savings are the purchased water that would no longer be bought for the uses the plant supplies, and the discharge charges that would no longer be paid on the recycled flow. Neither side of this running account is quantified in this proposal, because the quantities follow from the detailed design and from the operating pattern of the receiving uses, and both will be reported when the design is complete. The capital figure is therefore the cost figure on which this proposal asks for a decision, and the decision it supports is the decision to design, rather than the decision to build.

## Schedule

The schedule starts one quarter after approval. The first stage is the detailed design, which will confirm the effluent streams that the plant draws on, the quality that the receiving uses require, the treatment route, and the sizing of the plant against the demand pattern of the uses it will serve. The design stage will also fix the tie-in points, the storage between treatment and use, and the control arrangements.

Procurement and construction will follow the design, and they will be subject to a separate approval. It should be noted that no contractor is named in this proposal, and no construction commitment is sought at this stage. The construction schedule is itself an output of the design stage, because the duration of the build will follow from the plant that the design specifies and from the windows that the site can offer for tie-ins to live systems. The tie-ins represent the principal constraint on the schedule, since the effluent stream and the receiving uses are in service, and the connection points will have to be taken when the site can release them.

## Decision requested

The decision that is requested is approval to proceed to detailed design. It is not approval to construct, and nothing in this proposal commits the site to the build itself. The product of the design stage will be the material that the construction decision needs, namely a firmer capital cost in place of the proposal figure of $2351k, an operating account that is quantified on both sides, a construction schedule set against the site's tie-in windows, and the treatment route and sizing fixed in engineering detail.

Approving the design stage would buy that material at design cost while holding every later commitment open. Declining it would leave the site on its present arrangement. If the design stage returns figures that no longer support the case, the proposal will end at that point and the construction decision will never be reached, which is the reason for staging the decision in this way.

fact_base: Goal: compute the Reynolds number for water in a pipe and state the flow regime. The Reynolds number Re (dimensionless) is computed from density rho (kg m-3), mean velocity v (m s-1), pipe diameter D (m) and dynamic viscosity mu (Pa s) by Re = rho v D / mu. Water at 293 K: rho = 998 kg m-3, mu = 1.00 x 10-3 Pa s. Pipe diameter D = 0.025 m; mean velocity v = 1.2 m s-1. Worked result: Re = 29900 (computed as 998 x 1.2 x 0.025 / 0.001). Flow is laminar below Re = 2300 and turbulent above Re = 4000; between the two values the regime is transitional and is not assigned by the number alone.
input:
In this worked example, we will determine the Reynolds number for water flowing through a pipe and then use the result to identify the type of flow regime. The Reynolds number, Re, is a dimensionless quantity that is calculated from the density, the mean velocity, the pipe diameter and the dynamic viscosity using the equation Re = rho v D / mu, where rho is the density in kg m-3, v is the mean velocity in m s-1, D is the pipe diameter in m, and mu is the dynamic viscosity in Pa s.

For water at a temperature of 293 K, the density rho is 998 kg m-3 and the dynamic viscosity mu is 1.00 x 10-3 Pa s. The pipe diameter D is 0.025 m and the mean velocity v is 1.2 m s-1. Substituting these values into the equation gives Re = 998 x 1.2 x 0.025 / 0.001, which works out to a Reynolds number of 29900.

It is worth noting that the flow regime can be determined by comparing the Reynolds number against two well-established threshold values. The flow is considered to be laminar when Re is below 2300, and it is considered to be turbulent when Re is above 4000. Between these two values, the regime is transitional and cannot be assigned on the basis of the number alone. Since the calculated value of 29900 is significantly higher than the upper threshold, it can be concluded that the flow is fully turbulent. Importantly, the value does not lie anywhere near the transitional band between 2300 and 4000, so there is no ambiguity in this classification.
target:
The Reynolds number for water in a pipe is 29900, and the flow is turbulent.

The Reynolds number Re (dimensionless) is computed from the density rho (kg m-3), the mean velocity v (m s-1), the pipe diameter D (m) and the dynamic viscosity mu (Pa s) by Re = rho v D / mu. Each quantity stands in the unit stated with it. The units cancel in the ratio, which is why Re carries no unit, and the number compares flows across sizes and fluids on one scale.

Water at 293 K has rho = 998 kg m-3 and mu = 1.00 x 10-3 Pa s. The pipe diameter D is 0.025 m and the mean velocity v is 1.2 m s-1. Substitution of these values in Re = rho v D / mu gives Re = 998 x 1.2 x 0.025 / 0.001 = 29900.

The regime is read from the thresholds. Flow is laminar below Re = 2300 and turbulent above Re = 4000; between the two values the regime is transitional and is not assigned by the number alone. In the transitional band the flow state depends on the disturbance level in the pipe and on the history of the flow, and either state, or an alternation between the two, can occur in practice. Outside the band the number is decisive on its own. The computed value stands above the upper threshold by a wide margin, in the range the thresholds assign to turbulent flow. No part of the transitional range is involved: the assignment does not rest on a value near a boundary, and the check on the result is the threshold comparison itself. A value below the lower threshold would be laminar, a value between 2300 and 4000 would stay unassigned, and the value obtained is turbulent.

fact_base: A contract packaging firm runs 3 plants; revenue is $94 million per year. Evidence base: order records for 12 months, 13805 orders. On-time delivery over the last two quarters was 84%, against a target of 95%. Overtime cost was $2.1 million last year, up 26% on the year before. The order backlog stands at 3.6 weeks, against 2 weeks a year ago. Plant 2 accounts for 60% of late orders. A scheduling system for all plants is quoted at $264k; Plant 2 alone is $141k. An internal estimate (not a vendor figure) puts the overtime reduction at Plant 2 at 15-20% in the first year. The recommendation under consideration: install at Plant 2 first, hold the other plants until Plant 2 results are reported. The operations director owns the scheduling programme.
input:
This executive summary looks at delivery performance at a contract packaging firm and at whether a new scheduling system should be installed. The firm operates 3 plants and has revenue of $94 million per year. The evidence base for this summary is the firm's order records for 12 months, covering a total of 13805 orders.

Over the last two quarters, on-time delivery was 84%, which is well below the target of 95%. Overtime cost was $2.1 million last year, which represents an increase of 26% compared with the year before. The order backlog currently stands at 3.6 weeks, compared with 2 weeks a year ago, so the position has deteriorated on several measures at the same time.

It is worth noting that the problem is concentrated in one location: Plant 2 accounts for 60% of all late orders. A scheduling system covering all plants has been quoted at $264k, while Plant 2 alone would cost $141k. An internal estimate suggests that the overtime reduction at Plant 2 could be in the region of 15-20% in the first year, although it should be emphasised that this is an internal estimate rather than a vendor figure. The recommendation under consideration is therefore to install the system at Plant 2 first and to hold the other plants until the Plant 2 results are reported. The operations director owns the scheduling programme.

It should also be noted that the recommendation is a staged one rather than a partial one, in the sense that the other plants are not being removed from the programme; rather, their installation is deferred until evidence from the first installation is available, at which point a further decision can be taken in the light of that evidence.
target:
Install the scheduling system at Plant 2 first; the other plants are held until the Plant 2 results are reported. The operations director owns the scheduling programme.

The firm runs 3 plants with revenue of $94 million per year. The evidence base is order records for 12 months, covering 13805 orders. On-time delivery over the last two quarters was 84%, against a target of 95%. Overtime cost was $2.1 million last year, up 26% on the year before. The order backlog stands at 3.6 weeks, against 2 weeks a year ago.

Late delivery is concentrated: Plant 2 accounts for 60% of late orders. A scheduling system for all plants is quoted at $264k; Plant 2 alone is $141k. An internal estimate puts the overtime reduction at Plant 2 at 15-20% in the first year; the estimate is internal, not a vendor figure, and it is the only quantified benefit in the case. The sequence spends the smaller sum first and tests the benefit where late orders concentrate. The backlog and the overtime bill are the two figures the programme is expected to move, and both are at their weakest where the system would go in first. If the reported results hold, the case for the remaining plants rests on measured delivery and overtime figures from the firm's own operation rather than on the estimate alone, and the decision to extend is taken on that evidence.

The recommendation is staged rather than partial: the held plants are not descoped, and their installation follows on the reported result without a second case being built. What the staging buys is a decision point with evidence in hand. What it costs is time, since the held plants run on the present arrangements while the first installation is assessed, and the overtime and backlog figures for those plants are not expected to improve in the interval.

fact_base: A binary distillation separates ethanol/water at a relative volatility of 2.13 that is taken as constant over the column. Specifications: distillate 98 mol% light component, bottoms 2 mol% light component. The Fenske minimum stage count is 10.3 theoretical stages including the reboiler. The actual design uses a reflux ratio of 1.3 times the minimum; the stage count at that reflux comes from a separate simulation.
input:
In this passage, the minimum number of theoretical stages for a binary distillation separating an ethanol/water mixture is considered. The separation is characterised by a relative volatility of 2.13, which is assumed to remain constant over the entire column. The separation specifications are that the distillate should contain 98 mol% of the light component, while the bottoms should contain 2 mol% of the light component.

By applying the well-known Fenske equation, which gives the minimum stage count under conditions of total reflux, the minimum number of theoretical stages is found to be 10.3, and it should be noted that this count includes the reboiler. It is important to emphasise that this is a minimum value, corresponding to total reflux, and that an actual operating column will require more stages than this minimum of 10.3 stages, because product is withdrawn and the reflux has to be generated. In the actual design, a reflux ratio of 1.3 times the minimum reflux ratio is used, and the number of stages at this reflux ratio is obtained from a separate simulation rather than from the Fenske equation itself. It should also be borne in mind that the relative volatility has simply been assumed to be constant, which is an idealisation. Overall, the Fenske result provides a useful lower bound for the separation, while the detailed design figures come from the simulation study, and the two sets of results should be read together.
target:
Ethanol/water separates at a minimum of 10.3 theoretical stages. A binary distillation separates ethanol/water at a relative volatility of 2.13, taken as constant over the column. The specifications are a distillate of 98 mol% light component and a bottoms of 2 mol% light component.

The Fenske relation gives the minimum stage count for these specifications at total reflux, the condition under which no product is drawn and every stage works at its full separating power. The count is 10.3 theoretical stages, and the reboiler is included in the count. A stage count at total reflux is a lower bound: a column that draws product needs reflux to sustain the separation, and reflux returned to the column is vapour that must be raised again in the reboiler, so the operating column needs more stages than the minimum or more reflux than the minimum, and in practice some of both. The minimum also tightens as the specifications tighten: a purer distillate or a leaner bottoms raises the separation the stages must deliver, and the count follows from the ratio the two specifications set between the ends of the column.

The actual design uses a reflux ratio of 1.3 times the minimum. The stage count at that reflux comes from a separate simulation, not from the Fenske relation, and no operating stage count is stated here. The constant relative volatility is an idealisation of the same kind: the value is taken as one number over the whole column, and where the volatility in fact varies with composition the minimum count moves with it. The Fenske value stands as the bound against which the simulated design is read, and a simulated count below the bound would mark an error in the simulation, not a defect in the bound.

fact_base: 180 pumps run at the plant. Maintenance records for 12 months show 1375 h of unplanned downtime; bearing failures account for 38% of the downtime hours. A sensor set for all 180 pumps is quoted at $439k installed, plus $72k per year. In a vendor trial on a comparable unit, the sensors cut downtime by 22%; the figure is a vendor figure and was not measured at this plant. A pilot on 23 pumps costs $43k over three months. Spare-part lead times are unchanged by the sensors. The memo recommends the three-month pilot; the reliability engineering group owns the pilot and reports before the March capital review; the decision on full installation is held until the pilot results are reported.
input:
This memo recommends that a three-month pilot of condition sensors should be carried out before any decision is taken on installing sensors across the whole plant. The plant operates a total of 180 pumps. Maintenance records covering a period of 12 months show 1375 h of unplanned downtime, and it is notable that bearing failures account for 38% of the downtime hours.

A sensor set for all 180 pumps has been quoted at $439k installed, plus a further $72k per year. In a vendor trial carried out on a comparable unit, the sensors were reported to cut downtime by 22%; however, it should be emphasised that this is a vendor figure and that it was not measured at this plant. A pilot on 23 pumps would cost $43k over three months, and the 23 pumps would be drawn from the plant's own pump population. Spare-part lead times are unchanged by the sensors, so the pilot would test the detection benefit only.

The memo therefore recommends the three-month pilot. The reliability engineering group owns the pilot and will report before the March capital review, and the decision on full installation is held until the pilot results have been reported and can be considered by the review.

In addition, it should be borne in mind that the downtime record itself provides the baseline against which any improvement would be judged, and the pilot would allow that comparison to be made on a consistent basis, under the plant's own operating and maintenance conditions, rather than relying on results obtained elsewhere.
target:
A three-month pilot of condition sensors on 23 pumps is recommended. The decision on full installation is held until the pilot results are reported, and the reliability engineering group owns the pilot and reports before the March capital review.

The plant runs 180 pumps. Maintenance records for 12 months show 1375 h of unplanned downtime, and bearing failures account for 38% of the downtime hours. A sensor set for all 180 pumps is quoted at $439k installed, plus $72k per year. In a vendor trial on a comparable unit, the sensors cut downtime by 22%; the figure is a vendor figure and was not measured at this plant, and it carries the trial's conditions with it.

The pilot is sized to the failure mode that dominates the record. Bearing failure is the largest single share of downtime hours, and it is the mode the sensors detect. A pilot on 23 pumps at $43k over three months buys the plant's own downtime evidence at a small fraction of the full installed cost, on the pumps and under the maintenance regime the full decision concerns. Spare-part lead times are unchanged by the sensors, so any reduction the pilot shows comes from earlier warning, not from faster repair, and the two effects are not confounded in the pilot's figures. The capital review decides on full installation with the pilot's reported downtime in hand. The pilot reports downtime on the same basis as the maintenance record, so its result reads directly against the baseline the full case is built on.

subtype: worked example with equation: Fourier conduction
fact_base: A flat stainless steel wall has thickness 12 mm and thermal conductivity $k$ of 16 W m-1 K-1. The temperature difference $\Delta T$ across the wall is 403 K, giving a heat flux $q$ of 537333 W m-2. The calculation is steady and one-dimensional; film resistances are excluded.
input:
In this example, we will calculate the heat flux through a flat stainless steel wall. The wall has a thickness of 12 mm, and the thermal conductivity $k$ of the stainless steel is 16 W m-1 K-1. The temperature difference $\Delta T$ across the wall is 403 K.

The calculation is based on Fourier's law for steady, one-dimensional conduction through a plane wall, which can be written as follows:

$$q = k \frac{\Delta T}{\Delta x}$$

In this equation, $q$ represents the heat flux in W m-2, $k$ is the thermal conductivity in W m-1 K-1, $\Delta T$ is the temperature difference across the wall in K, and $\Delta x$ is the thickness of the wall in m. Converting the thickness into metres gives 0.012 m. Substituting the values into the equation, we obtain $q$ = 16 x 403 / 0.012, which gives a heat flux of 537333 W m-2.

It should be noted that this calculation assumes steady, one-dimensional conduction, and that film resistances have been excluded, so the result, 537333 W m-2, represents the conduction through the wall material only, and the actual heat flux in a real installation with surface films would be expected to be lower than this value.
target:
The heat flux through the stainless steel wall is 537333 W m-2.

A flat stainless steel wall of thickness 12 mm has a thermal conductivity $k$ of 16 W m-1 K-1. The temperature difference $\Delta T$ across the wall is 403 K. Fourier's law for steady one-dimensional conduction through a plane wall gives the heat flux $q$ as

$$q = k \frac{\Delta T}{\Delta x}$$

where $q$ is the heat flux (W m-2), $k$ is the thermal conductivity (W m-1 K-1), $\Delta T$ is the temperature difference across the wall (K) and $\Delta x$ is the wall thickness (m). The thickness in metres is 0.012 m. Substitution gives $q$ = 16 x 403 / 0.012 = 537333 W m-2.

The calculation is steady and one-dimensional: the temperature varies through the thickness only, and no term covers flow along the wall. The flux is proportional to the temperature difference and inversely proportional to the thickness, so the same wall at twice the thickness would pass half the flux at the same temperatures. Film resistances are excluded. The flux is conduction through the wall material alone, and a wall with surface films on either side passes less, by the resistance the films add in series with the wall. The value is therefore the ceiling for this wall at these temperatures, reached only where the surface temperatures are the fluid temperatures themselves.

fact_base: Cost review of a regional delivery route: 784 km per trip at $1.54 per km, 836 trips per year. Annual transport cost is $1009k. Costs are carrier invoices for the last 12 months; empty running is included in the trip count.
input:
This passage reviews the cost of a regional delivery route. The route covers 784 km per trip, and the cost is $1.54 per km, with a total of 836 trips per year. On this basis, the annual transport cost works out at $1009k. The costs are taken from carrier invoices for the last 12 months, so they represent the amounts actually invoiced rather than estimates.

It is worth noting that empty running is included in the trip count, which means that the annual figure of $1009k covers all of the trips that were made during the year, both loaded and empty. This is an important point to bear in mind when the figure is used, because it means that the cost cannot simply be attributed to loaded deliveries alone, and comparisons with other figures need to be made on a like-for-like basis.

Overall, the review establishes the annual cost of the route on a consistent basis, and this figure can be used as the starting point for considering any changes to the route or to the arrangements with the carrier in the future.

It should also be understood that the annual figure combines two rather different drivers, namely the distance covered on each trip and the number of trips that are made in the year, and the review does not attempt to separate the contribution of each of these drivers to the total that has been reported.
target:
Annual transport cost on the regional delivery route is $1009k. The figure is derived from the route's operating numbers: 784 km per trip, at $1.54 per km, over 836 trips per year. Costs are carrier invoices for the last 12 months, so the figure is invoiced cost, not an estimate built from rates alone.

Empty running is included in the trip count. The cost therefore stands against all invoiced trips, loaded and empty together, and no part of the $1009k is assigned to loaded running alone; a cost per loaded trip would need the loaded share of the count, which the invoices do not separate. The rate is likewise a blended figure: it averages the trips the route actually ran, at the distances they actually covered, and it moves if either the trip pattern or the carrier's pricing moves.

The review covers the transport leg only. It states what the route cost over the year on a consistent trip definition, which is the figure any change to the route, the vehicle or the carrier is costed against. Comparisons with earlier periods hold only where the trip count was kept on the same basis, empty running included; a period counted on loaded trips alone would show a lower cost for the same operation.

The figure is a cost of record for one route over one year. It does not separate the cost of distance from the cost of frequency: a route run less often at the same distance, or over a shorter distance at the same frequency, would present a different total through a different term, and the review does not rank the two levers against each other.

fact_base: A centrifugal pump moves water between two vessels at grade. At the duty point the flow is 95 m3 h-1 against a head of 36 m, with pump efficiency 70%. Shaft power at the duty point is 13.3 kW. The motor is rated 15% above this value. Cavitation was not observed in the acceptance test, which ran for 4 h at the duty point only.
input:
This passage describes the duty point of a centrifugal pump that moves water between two vessels at grade. At the duty point, the flow is 95 m3 h-1 against a head of 36 m, and the pump efficiency at this point is 70%. The shaft power at the duty point is 13.3 kW. The motor is rated 15% above this value, in order to provide a suitable margin.

It should be noted that the shaft power of 13.3 kW is the power that is required at the duty point itself, and operation away from the duty point would be expected to draw a different power, in line with the characteristics of the pump.

Cavitation was not observed during the acceptance test. However, it is important to bear in mind that the acceptance test ran for 4 h at the duty point only, so the absence of cavitation has only been demonstrated at that particular operating point and over that particular duration, and no conclusion can be drawn about other operating conditions or longer periods of operation.

The duty point, it should be added, is the operating point against which the pump was originally selected, being the combination of flow and head that the system was designed to deliver, and the figures that are quoted in this passage relate specifically to that point.
target:
At the duty point, the pump delivers 95 m3 h-1 of water against a head of 36 m, at an efficiency of 70%. Shaft power at the duty point is 13.3 kW.

The pump is a centrifugal unit moving water between two vessels at grade, so the head is the lift and loss the system imposes at the duty flow, with no static difference between the vessels to add. Efficiency at the duty point is the ratio of the hydraulic power in the delivered stream to the shaft power drawn, and the 13.3 kW figure is the power the motor must supply at that point. The motor is rated 15% above this value; the margin covers operation at the duty point, and it is not a rating for sustained running far from that point, where the power drawn follows the pump curve rather than the duty figure.

Cavitation was not observed in the acceptance test, which ran for 4 h at the duty point only. The test result is a detection statement at one operating point: no cavitation was detected there, in that run. Behaviour away from the duty point, at the ends of the curve, and over runs longer than the test, is outside what the test reports. The duty point is the operating point the selection was made against: it is the flow and head the system was designed to deliver, and the figures above describe the pump there, not across its range.

fact_base: Pricing case for a contract cleaning service: price $206 per unit, variable cost $131 per unit, fixed costs $113k per year. Break-even volume is 1507 units per year; current volume is 6992 units per year. Volume figures are last year's actuals; the effect of the price on volume is not estimated.
input:
This case considers the pricing of a contract cleaning service. The price is $206 per unit, the variable cost is $131 per unit, and the fixed costs are $113k per year. On the basis of these figures, the break-even volume can be calculated as 1507 units per year. The current volume is 6992 units per year, which is considerably higher than the break-even level.

It should be noted that the volume figures used here are last year's actuals. The effect of the price on volume has not been estimated, which is an important limitation of the analysis, because it means that the break-even volume is only valid at the current price, and it cannot be assumed that the same volume would be achieved if the price were to be changed.

Overall, the analysis shows that, at the current price and at last year's volumes, the service is operating above its break-even volume, although this conclusion depends on the volume being maintained at a similar level in the future.

The comparison is, in other words, a statement about the position under the present terms, taking the price, the variable cost and the fixed costs as they currently stand, and the volumes as they were in the year that has been reported.
target:
Break-even volume for the contract cleaning service is 1507 units per year, against a current volume of 6992 units per year.

The price is $206 per unit and the variable cost is $131 per unit, so each unit sold contributes the difference between the two toward fixed costs of $113k per year. The break-even volume is the fixed costs divided by that per-unit contribution: the volume at which the contribution covers the fixed costs exactly, with nothing over. Current volume stands well above it, so at last year's volumes the service covers its costs at the current price.

Volume figures are last year's actuals. The effect of the price on volume is not estimated, and the break-even volume inherits that limit: it is computed at the current price and the current variable cost, and it states the volume the service must hold, not the volume the price will attract. A price change moves both sides of the comparison at once, the contribution directly and the volume by an amount this case does not quantify, so the figure is a reference point for the present contract terms and not a forecast under new ones. The comparison is a statement about the present terms: price, variable cost and fixed costs as they stand, and volumes as they were.

fact_base: Excerpt content: two groups report conflicting pressure drop values for the same material class; the excerpt weighs their test conditions. The excerpt reaches a limited preference and states the condition on which it rests.
input:
The pressure drop values that have been reported for the benchmark material by the two groups differ considerably, and it is important to consider the reasons for this difference before any preference between the two sets of values can be established. It should be noted that the difference between the two sets is larger than the scatter that either group reports within its own runs, which suggests that the difference is a systematic one rather than a matter of measurement error.

On closer examination, it appears that the two groups did not in fact measure the material under the same conditions. One group carried out its measurements on a bed that had been packed for the test and was used in that state, whereas the other group carried out its measurements after the bed had been subjected to repeated adsorption and regeneration cycles, and it is the second group that reports the higher values. This is perhaps not surprising, because a bed that has been cycled is no longer the same as a freshly packed bed: the particles are worked against one another, fines are generated and migrate into the void spaces, and the passages available for the gas become narrower, so that a higher pressure drop is only to be expected.

It would therefore seem reasonable to prefer the values obtained on the cycled bed, provided that the duty under consideration does in fact involve cycling of the same kind. Where the bed is to be packed, used once and replaced, the fresh-bed values would be the more appropriate set, and on balance the preference depends on the condition of the bed in service rather than on any judgement about the quality of the measurements themselves.
target:
For the benchmark material, the two reported sets of pressure drop values stand apart by more than either group reports as scatter within its own runs, and the gap follows the test conditions rather than the material. One group measured on a bed packed for the test and used as packed. The other measured after the bed had been through repeated adsorption and regeneration, and its values are the higher of the two. A cycled bed is not the bed that was packed: cycling works the particles against each other, fines form and migrate into the voids, and the passages the gas sees are narrower than those of the fresh packing, so a higher pressure drop at the same duty is what the bed's state predicts, not an anomaly in either measurement.

Read on that basis, the two sets are not in conflict about the material. They describe the benchmark material in two states of the bed, and the apparent disagreement is a difference in what was actually put under test. The cycled values also carry a condition the fresh values do not: the fresh state can be reproduced at will, while the cycled state depends on the whole cycling history, and that history has to travel with the numbers wherever they are quoted.

The preference here is for the cycled-bed values, on one stated condition: that the duty under consideration cycles the bed in the same way. For a bed that is packed, used once and replaced, the fresh-bed values are the relevant set and the preference reverses. Neither set is set aside as a measurement failure, and the error lies in taking a design figure from the wrong state.

fact_base: An operating-manual chapter for a pressure relief valve, in four sections: start-up, normal operation, alarms, and shutdown. The alarms section lists two alarms and the operator action for each; no other alarms are introduced. The chapter addresses the operator directly and uses imperative verbs for actions.
input:
## Start-up

Before the pressure relief valve is placed in service, it is important to ensure that a number of checks have been carried out. In the first place, it should be confirmed from the valve tag and from the equipment record that the valve that has been fitted is the correct valve for this duty. The valve body, the inlet and outlet flange faces and the joint bolts should be inspected carefully for any signs of damage, corrosion or potential leakage paths. It should also be confirmed that no blind, blank or plug that may have been fitted for transport or testing purposes remains in either the inlet or the outlet.

The inlet isolation valve should then be opened fully and sealed in the open position, and the outlet isolation valve should be treated in the same way. It should be borne in mind that a relief valve that can be isolated by means of a partly open valve cannot be regarded as being in service. The discharge line should be walked from the valve outlet to its safe discharge point, in order to confirm that the line is unobstructed, that its drains are free, and that no valve in the discharge path is standing closed. It should also be confirmed that the pressure gauge on the protected equipment is in service.

The equipment should be brought up to pressure in accordance with its own start-up procedure. As the pressure rises, the valve inlet and outlet joints should be checked for leakage, and the valve should be listened to for simmer, which is the audible leakage past the seat that indicates that the valve is close to its set pressure or is passing. Once the equipment is at normal operating pressure and the valve is quiet, the valve should be recorded as being in service in the equipment log.

## Normal operation

During normal operation, the valve remains shut, and the operator's role is essentially one of ensuring that it remains able to act should it be required to do so. Both isolation valves should be kept fully open and sealed open at all times while the protected equipment is live. The valve should be included in the routine rounds, and it should be checked for leakage at the body and joints, listened to for simmer or chatter, checked for icing or deposits at the outlet, and its discharge line should be confirmed as being unobstructed with its drains free.

It is important to note that the set pressure should not be adjusted, that no gag, clamp or blank should be fitted in order to stop a passing valve, and that the inlet isolation valve should not be throttled in order to quieten a valve that is simmering. A valve that passes, that simmers persistently, or that shows damage or heavy corrosion should be regarded as defective; it should be reported, it should be recorded in the equipment log, and its removal and bench test should be planned for the next suitable opportunity.

## Alarms

There are two alarms that concern this valve. The first is the high-pressure alarm on the protected equipment, which warns that the pressure is approaching the valve's set pressure. If the valve lifts and the pressure steadies or falls, the equipment should be held at the reduced state and the shift supervisor should be informed. If the pressure continues to rise even though the valve has lifted, the equipment should be taken to the safe state that is given in its own procedure.

The second alarm is the discharge alarm, which indicates that the valve has lifted and is discharging, or that it has failed to reseat after lifting. The discharge should be confirmed at the valve and on the discharge line indication, the cause of the overpressure should be found and removed by the normal operating routes, and the discharge indication should be watched until the valve reseats and the discharge stops. A relief valve that can be isolated by a partly open valve is not in service, whatever the state of the rest of the line. In normal operation the valve stays shut and does nothing, and the operator's task is to keep it able to act. fact_base: The rate constant k (s-1) of a first-order liquid-phase reaction was measured at two temperatures. At 300 K, k = 0.015 s-1. At 340 K, k = 0.718 s-1, computed from the Arrhenius relation with activation energy 82 kJ mol-1 as a derived value. Each temperature was measured in triplicate; the relative standard deviation of k was 4%. Above 340 K the solvent evaporated during sampling, so no rate constant is reported above 340 K.
input:
In this work, the rate constant k of a first-order liquid-phase reaction was carefully measured at two different temperatures to characterise how the reaction responds to temperature. At 300 K, k was found to be 0.015 s-1, whereas at the higher temperature of 340 K, k rose substantially to 0.718 s-1. Over the 40 K interval between the measurements, the rate constant increased by a factor of 47.9, highlighting its strong temperature sensitivity.

The value at 340 K is a derived value. It was computed from the Arrhenius relation using an activation energy of 82 kJ mol-1, rather than being measured directly, and the value at 300 K serves as the measured anchor for that computation. Each temperature was measured in triplicate, and the relative standard deviation of k was 4%, which indicates that the reported constants are based on three readings at each temperature rather than on single readings. The 4% figure represents the spread of those triplicate readings around their mean at each temperature, and the derived constant at 340 K effectively carries the same relative spread through the computation, since the computation starts from the measured constant together with the stated activation energy.

Between the two temperatures, a rate constant at an intermediate temperature can also be obtained from the same Arrhenius relation with the same activation energy, although such a value would have the same status as the 340 K constant, namely computed rather than measured. The temperature dependence described is steep, and it is the dependence of the stated reaction in the stated solvent over the stated interval.

The dataset is bounded at the top by the solvent. Above 340 K, the solvent evaporated during sampling, so no rate constant is reported above 340 K. The two constants describe the reaction at 300 K and 340 K, with the upper one derived, and they do not extend beyond 340 K, as a value above that temperature would require a sampling method that keeps the solvent in place.

fact_base: Excerpt content: the staffing ramp is set at 18% and the excerpt defends that figure against a lower alternative. The excerpt refers to the project's cost table by section name and does not repeat its figures.
input:
It should be noted that the staffing ramp for the upgrade project has been set at 18%, and this figure is being maintained in response to the lower alternative that was put forward to the steering group. A ramp below 18% effectively prices the recruitment profile at its planned rate for the full build, in the sense that it assumes every post is filled on exactly the week the plan assumes, no post remains vacant while its work is due, and no allowance is made for the overlap that handover between outgoing and incoming staff typically requires. The costs section of this proposal is built on the profile that the ramp produces, and the cost table referred to there takes the ramped profile as its staffing basis. A lower ramp would therefore leave the cost table unchanged in form while, at the same time, removing the staff on which the table is costed.

The case for 18% essentially rests on the shape of the work rather than on its volume. The upgrade project involves running construction and commissioning against a plant that remains in production throughout, and the posts that the ramp adds early are the posts that keep the existing operation covered while the commissioning teams are being formed. Setting the ramp lower would concentrate recruitment into the commissioning window, where the project would be competing for the very same staff it is trying to release. By contrast, the 18% figure spreads that recruitment over the preceding period, albeit at the cost of carrying some posts for longer. The steering group is therefore asked to weigh the two profiles on that basis: the lower alternative is cheaper in total paid time only if recruitment lands exactly on plan, and it carries no margin whatsoever for the slippage that the ramp is there to absorb. FID is taken on the ramped profile, and a decision to set the ramp lower would amount to a decision to re-cut the staffing basis of the cost table, rather than a saving found inside the existing one. On the evidence of the profile, 18% represents the lowest figure that keeps recruitment, handover and cover together within a single coherent plan.

fact_base: A food plant uses 2220 MWh of electricity per year in refrigeration. A heat-recovery retrofit is projected by the equipment vendor to save 14% of that use, a derived saving of 311 MWh per year at the vendor figure. Capital cost is $370k. At an electricity price of $0.09 per kWh, the derived annual saving is $28k and the derived simple payback is 13.2 years. The saving figure is a vendor projection and was not measured at this plant; refrigeration load in the summer peak month was not modelled. The recommendation is a metered trial on one of the three refrigeration lines before any capital decision. The plant engineer owns the trial.
input:
This summary looks at a proposed heat-recovery retrofit at a food plant and at whether the project should move forward at this stage. The plant currently uses 2220 MWh of electricity per year in refrigeration, which represents a substantial part of the site's overall energy picture. According to the equipment vendor, the retrofit is projected to save 14% of that electricity use, which works out to a derived saving of 311 MWh per year at the vendor figure. The capital cost of the retrofit is $370k. Using an electricity price of $0.09 per kWh, the derived annual saving is $28k, and the derived simple payback is 13.2 years.

It is important to note that the saving figure is a vendor projection and was not measured at this plant, and that refrigeration load in the summer peak month was not modelled either. Against that background, the recommendation is that the plant first carries out a metered trial on one of its three refrigeration lines before any capital decision is taken, so that the projected saving can be checked against actual operating experience. The plant engineer owns the trial.
target:
Recommendation: the plant runs a metered trial of the heat-recovery retrofit on one of its three refrigeration lines before any capital decision. The plant engineer owns the trial.

The case rests on a vendor projection, not on a measurement. The plant uses 2220 MWh of electricity per year in refrigeration. The equipment vendor projects that the retrofit saves 14% of that use, a derived saving of 311 MWh per year at the vendor figure. Capital cost is $370k. At an electricity price of $0.09 per kWh, the derived annual saving is $28k and the derived simple payback is 13.2 years. A payback of that length, resting on an unmeasured saving, does not carry a capital decision on its own.

Two gaps stand in the evidence. The saving figure was not measured at this plant, and refrigeration load in the summer peak month was not modelled, so the projected saving has not been tested against the plant's highest-load conditions, which are the conditions under which refrigeration demand and the recovered heat are both at their most demanding. The metered trial closes the first gap on one line: it measures the saving where the retrofit would actually run, and it gives the plant a measured figure to set against the projected annual saving and the capital cost before the remaining lines are considered for the same treatment.

fact_base: Design report for a spray dryer, in four sections: basis, sizing, materials, and risks. Design throughput is 5 t per day and the removal or separation duty is 97% of the key component. Materials are 316L stainless steel for wetted parts; the basis section states this once. The risks section names fouling and turndown as open items; neither is resolved in the report.
input:
Basis

This report presents the design of a spray dryer that dries a liquid feed to a free-flowing solid by atomising the feed into a stream of heated gas. The design throughput is 5 t per day. The removal duty is set on the key component, namely the moisture carried in with the feed: the dryer removes 97% of that moisture, and the product leaves at the residual moisture implied by the duty. Operation is continuous, with the feed supplied as a liquid that can be pumped and atomised, and the dried solid is discharged from the bottom of the drying chamber while the exhaust gas leaves together with the evaporated moisture and the finest fraction of the solid.

The basis fixes the feed in the state in which it reaches the dryer battery limit: filtered, at its supply temperature, and at a solids content within the range that the atomiser is able to handle. Heat is supplied to the drying gas upstream of the chamber; the gas acts both as the drying medium and as the transport medium for the droplets and the dried particles. Wetted parts are 316L stainless steel; the materials section goes on to develop the selection from the service conditions. The basis states the duty at the design throughput, and no margin is carried on throughput itself: margins in this design are held in the gas flow and the heat input, where they can actually be used in operation, rather than in the rated capacity of the chamber.

The report sizes the chamber and the principal auxiliaries, records the materials selection for the wetted parts, and registers the risks that the design does not fully close. Two risks are identified as open items: fouling and turndown. Neither of these is resolved anywhere in this report.

Sizing

The chamber is sized on the basis of the drying time of the largest droplets produced by the atomiser. A droplet needs to give up its moisture before it reaches a wall or the chamber outlet; a droplet that arrives wet will stick, while a droplet that arrives dry travels onward with the gas. The chamber diameter is determined by the gas flow and by the need to keep the spray envelope clear of the walls, and the chamber height is determined by the falling path that the largest droplets require for their drying time at the design gas temperature. The sizing therefore proceeds from the droplet rather than from the throughput: at the design throughput of 5 t per day, the feed rate fixes the liquid loading on the gas, but the chamber geometry follows the droplet trajectory and the gas residence that it requires.

The atomiser is selected to deliver the droplet size distribution that the chamber sizing assumes. Atomiser duty and chamber sizing form a matched pair: a finer spray dries more quickly and can be accommodated in a smaller chamber, at the cost of additional energy at the atomiser and a finer product that the collection system must then be able to catch. The gas system is sized together with the chamber: the heater raises the drying gas to its inlet temperature, the fans move the gas through the chamber, the collection equipment and the exhaust path against their combined resistance, and the collection system separates the dried solid from the exhaust. Cyclones take the coarse fraction and a fabric filter takes the fines; the split between them follows the particle size distribution delivered by the atomiser and the chamber, and the product stream is the sum of the two collected fractions. Exhaust treatment beyond solids collection falls outside this design. Instruments on the sized system monitor the variables that the operator is able to act on: gas inlet and outlet temperatures, chamber pressure, feed rate and product moisture, each provided with its alarm in the operating instructions.

Materials

The wetted parts of the dryer operate in three distinct services, and the selection responds to each of them. The feed system and the atomiser see the liquid feed as supplied: a process liquor that is corrosive to lesser grades under the cleaning regime applied by the plant, and the wetted surfaces must additionally withstand the wash liquors used to clean them. The chamber and the product contact surfaces see hot, moist gas on one side and a hygroscopic solid on the other; condensation forms on these surfaces whenever the unit cools down, and the condensate is effectively feed liquor in a dilute and aggressive form. The exhaust path sees the same moist gas below its dew point at the cold end, which represents the most corrosive service in the unit.

Against those services, the selection provides a grade with resistance to the feed and wash liquors, to the condensate, and to the cleaning cycle applied between campaigns, together with a surface finish on product contact parts that releases deposits and can be cleaned to the standard required by the product. Welds in wetted service are finished flush for the same reason: a crevice or a rough weld retains liquor, dries it in place, and initiates the deposit that the cleaning cycle subsequently has to remove. Non-wetted structure is specified separately, on the basis of strength and temperature alone. Elastomers and gaskets in the wetted boundary are selected for the wash liquors as well as for the feed, since a gasket that survives the process but fails in cleaning still fails in service. The exhaust duct at the cold end is treated as wetted for selection purposes, because its service is governed by condensation rather than by the dry gas temperature upstream.

Risks

Fouling is the first open item. The deposit mechanism is understood in outline: droplets that reach a surface while still wet, or particles that settle where the gas slows down, dry in place and build up a layer that alters the gas flow, insulates the surface, and eventually sheds into the product. What the design does not establish is the rate: the deposit rate on this feed, in this chamber, at the design temperatures has not been measured, and the cleaning interval that the plant would need to hold is therefore not yet known. The design responds to fouling with access, finish and cleanability, and with instrumentation that reveals a deposit forming as a drift in temperatures and pressures; it does not answer the question of how often the unit must be stopped for cleaning. That question is carried forward as an open item, and it represents the largest single uncertainty in the operating cost of the unit.

Turndown is the second open item. Spray dryer turndown is not simply a feed valve movement: at reduced feed, the atomiser produces a different droplet spectrum, the gas-to-liquid ratio increases, the outlet temperature control behaves differently, and the product moisture responds to all three effects at the same time. The removal duty of 97% is stated at the design point. The depth of turndown at which the dryer still meets that duty, with the product inside its moisture specification, has not been established by testing on this feed, and the design does not claim a figure for it. Operation below the design point is therefore an open item as well: the plant can run the dryer down, but the report cannot state how far down the product remains within specification. Both items are identified for resolution in the next design stage, through test work on the actual feed; neither is resolved in this report.

fact_base: A tutorial passage explains the pump affinity laws for a centrifugal pump at varying speed. The passage states the three proportionalities in words: flow with speed, head with speed squared, power with speed cubed. A worked check is included: doubling speed multiplies power by 8. No other numbers are introduced.
input:
This passage explains the pump affinity laws, a set of relationships describing how the performance of a centrifugal pump changes when its speed is varied. The affinity laws relate the performance of a centrifugal pump at one speed to its performance at another speed, for the same pump and the same liquid, and they consist of three proportionalities. Firstly, flow varies in direct proportion to speed, so that at twice the speed the pump delivers twice the flow. Secondly, head varies with the square of speed, meaning that at twice the speed the head rises by a factor of 4. Thirdly, power varies with the cube of speed, so that at twice the speed the power rises by a factor of 8. A helpful worked check is provided by the power law: a speed ratio of 2, when cubed, gives the power ratio of 8, while the head factor of 4 is simply the same ratio squared. In other words, doubling the speed of a centrifugal pump multiplies its power draw by 8.

It is important to understand the conditions under which these proportionalities are valid. They describe the pump at corresponding points of its characteristic, where the flow pattern through the impeller is geometrically similar. They are statements about the pump rather than about the system it is connected to, since the duty point the pump actually reaches is determined by the intersection of the pump characteristic with the system resistance, and that intersection does not in general move in proportion to speed. A speed change also leaves efficiency approximately unchanged only near the corresponding point; at speeds far removed from the point at which the laws are anchored, the efficiency shifts and the proportionalities gradually lose accuracy. The laws are applied to the same impeller diameter throughout, as a change of diameter follows different relations, and a change of liquid density leaves flow and head unchanged while scaling power in direct proportion to density.

Used within those limits, the laws allow one measured characteristic to be converted into the characteristic at any other speed, and the cube law is the term that dominates the arithmetic: modest speed reductions deliver disproportionately large power savings, while modest speed increases are paid for at exactly the same rate in reverse.

Flow varies in direct proportion to speed: at twice the speed, the pump delivers twice the flow. Head varies with the square of speed: at twice the speed, the head rises by a factor of 4. Power varies with the cube of speed: at twice the speed, the power rises by a factor of 8. The worked check is the power law read directly: a speed ratio of 2, cubed, gives the power ratio of 8, and the head factor of 4 is the same ratio squared.

The three proportionalities describe the pump at corresponding points of its characteristic, where the flow pattern through the impeller is geometrically similar. They are statements about the pump, not about the system it is connected to: the duty point the pump actually reaches is set by the intersection of the pump characteristic with the system resistance, and that intersection does not in general move in proportion to speed. A speed change also leaves efficiency approximately unchanged only near the corresponding point; at speeds far from the point at which the laws are anchored, the efficiency shifts and the proportionalities lose accuracy. The laws are applied to the same impeller diameter throughout: a change of diameter follows different relations, and a change of liquid density leaves flow and head unchanged while scaling power in direct proportion to density.

Used inside those limits, the laws turn one measured characteristic into the characteristic at any other speed, and the cube law is the term that dominates the arithmetic: modest speed reductions return disproportionately large power savings, and modest speed increases are paid for at the same rate in reverse.

fact_base: Liquid-liquid extraction recovers acetone from an aqueous stream into an organic solvent. The distribution coefficient (organic over aqueous) is 1.93 at 25 °C and the design uses 8 countercurrent stages. Predicted recovery is 95% of the acetone in the feed. The prediction assumes equilibrium stages and negligible mutual solubility; neither has been checked on the actual solvents.
input:
Liquid-liquid extraction can be used to recover acetone from an aqueous stream into an organic solvent. The distribution coefficient of acetone, defined as the ratio between the organic and aqueous phases, is 1.93 at 25 °C, and the design is based on 8 countercurrent stages. On this basis, the predicted recovery is 95% of the acetone present in the feed.

The coefficient effectively determines the scale of the separation task: at a value of 1.93, each equilibrium contact transfers a majority of the acetone present toward the solvent phase, and the 8 countercurrent stages progressively compound that transfer along the column. The 95% recovery figure is the result of that staging under the two assumptions stated in the design. Firstly, the prediction assumes equilibrium stages, meaning that every stage is taken to reach the distribution described by the coefficient. Secondly, it assumes negligible mutual solubility, so that the aqueous and organic streams retain their identity from stage to stage and the coefficient measured for the pair remains applicable throughout. However, neither of these assumptions has been checked on the actual solvents. The equilibrium assumption may break down where contact time or dispersion in a real stage leaves the streams short of equilibrium, while the solubility assumption may break down where the actual solvent pair dissolves into each other sufficiently to shift the distribution. As a result, the 95% figure should be regarded as a prediction that rests on stated assumptions, with its two most important assumptions still untested on the solvents the design would actually run.

fact_base: A tutorial passage explains feedback control through a temperature loop on a process vessel. The passage covers the sensor, the controller, the final element and the sign of the feedback, in that order. No tuning numbers are given; the passage explains structure, not settings.
input:
Feedback control is widely used for regulating the temperature of a process vessel, and is based on a closed loop of four elements in signal order: the sensor, the controller, the final element, and the process itself, whose measured temperature is fed back to the sensor.

The sensor measures the vessel temperature and reports it to the controller as a signal proportional to the measured value. Measurement is the loop's only contact with the actual state of the vessel, so any error in the sensor's reading enters the loop as though it were a genuine change in temperature. The controller then compares the reported temperature with the set point and calculates an appropriate correction based on the difference, known as the error. The sign of the controller's response is established at this stage: for a heating duty, a temperature below the set point must call for more heat, whereas a temperature above it must call for less. The final element carries out the correction, adjusting the heating input to the vessel in response to the controller's signal; in a heated vessel, it is typically the valve or heater drive that determines the heat supply. The process then responds: the vessel temperature moves toward the set point, the sensor reports the new temperature, and the comparison begins again.

The feedback is negative when the correction opposes the error that produced it, as in the arrangement above. Negative feedback is what makes the loop a regulator, since a disturbance that pushes the temperature away from the set point generates its own counteracting correction. If the sign were reversed, the correction would reinforce the error instead, and each pass around the loop would drive the temperature further from the set point.

fact_base: Excerpt content: a calibration check takes about 86 min with the unit isolated; the excerpt gives the isolation steps only. The excerpt warns once about stored pressure and does not repeat the warning.
input:
The isolation for the calibration check is carried out with the unit stopped and the standby pump in service. The check takes about 86 min with the unit isolated, and the isolation must be proved before the instrument is disturbed. The order of the steps follows the order of the isolation itself: duty is transferred first, the machine is isolated second, and the isolated section is proved safe before any joint is broken.

The duty pump is stopped at the local panel and the run-down confirmed on the panel indication. The standby pump is then started, and discharge pressure must be confirmed as held by the running machine before any valve is moved; the standby pump carries the duty for the whole check, and no isolation step is taken until the changeover is complete and stable. The duty pump suction isolation valve is then closed, followed by the discharge isolation valve, and the locks and tags are fitted under the PTW. The padlock keys remain with the holder who fitted them.

Stored pressure remains in the casing and in the suction line even after the valves have been closed. The isolated section is drained and vented to the closed drain, and is treated as live until the vent runs clear and the local gauge reads zero. The isolation is proved at the gauge and again at the drain point before any joint is broken; a section that will not depressurise is reported to the shift supervisor and left locked, rather than forced.

Once isolation has been proved, the calibration check proceeds on the isolated instrument, free of flow and free of pressure. The 86 min covers the isolation, the check itself and the reinstatement. Reinstatement reverses the order of isolation: the section is refilled and vented, locks and tags are removed by the holder who fitted them, and the valves are reopened in the order given in the changeover procedure. The duty pump returns to service only when the instrument is back in circuit and reading, and the standby pump is stood down in the normal changeover once the duty pump is carrying the load again. If a check cannot be completed as written, it ends with the unit left isolated, the PTW still open, and the instrument state recorded in the shift log.

fact_base: Inventory policy for a spare motor: mean demand 3708 units per week, standard deviation 953 units per week, replenishment lead time 8 weeks. Safety stock for a 95% cycle service level is 4448 units. Demand is treated as normal and independent between weeks; seasonal peaks are excluded.
input:
Safety stock for the spare motor is 4448 units. The stock is held against variation in demand during the replenishment lead time, at a 95% cycle service level, and the figure follows from the demand and lead time stated below.

Demand for the spare motor averages 3708 units per week, with a standard deviation of 953 units per week. The replenishment lead time is 8 weeks. Safety stock is sized on the variation of demand over the whole lead time, not on the variation of a single week: weekly variations partly cancel across the lead time, and the stock covers the spread of total lead-time demand that remains. At a 95% cycle service level, lead-time demand is met from stock in all but a small minority of replenishment cycles, and the 4448 units are the quantity that the stated demand spread requires for that service level.

The policy treats demand as normal and independent between weeks. Independence is what allows the weekly variations to cancel in part; if demand in successive weeks moved together, the spread of lead-time demand would be wider than the policy assumes, and the same stock would deliver a lower service level than the one stated. Seasonal peaks are excluded from the policy. No additional stock is held for peak periods, and a seasonal peak that falls inside a replenishment lead time draws on the same safety stock as any other week. The policy therefore states a service level for ordinary demand variation across the year, and it leaves peak cover to be decided separately if operating experience shows the exclusion is not tenable.

fact_base: A vapour-compression unit serves a cold store, evaporating at 0 °C and condensing at 45 °C. The Carnot coefficient of performance between these temperatures is 6.07; the installed unit achieves 2.75. The achieved value is from the manufacturer's test at full load; part-load performance is not stated.
input:
A vapour-compression refrigeration unit serves a cold store, evaporating at 0 °C and condensing at 45 °C, which corresponds to a temperature lift across the machine of 45 K. Between these two temperatures, the Carnot coefficient of performance is 6.07. The installed unit, by comparison, achieves a coefficient of performance of 2.75, which is equivalent to 0.45 of the Carnot value.

The Carnot coefficient represents the theoretical ceiling for any vapour-compression machine operating between the same two temperatures. It is based on the assumption of fully reversible operation throughout: no pressure drop in the heat exchangers or lines, no superheat or subcooling penalty, and no losses in the compressor or its motor. The achieved value of 2.75 is taken from the manufacturer's test at full load, and the gap between 2.75 and 6.07 essentially represents the sum of the real losses that the Carnot figure excludes. Expressed as a ratio, the installed unit returns 0.45 of the ideal performance at its test condition, which is really the comparison that the two coefficients exist to make: the ideal value prices the temperature lift, whereas the achieved value prices the lift and the machine together.

It should be noted that the achieved coefficient is stated at full load only. Part-load performance is not stated by the manufacturer, and the coefficient at reduced duty cannot simply be inferred from the full-load figure, so a unit that spends its life operating at part load is not adequately described by 2.75.
