fact_base: A viscous liquid of viscosity $\mu$ = 0.05 Pa s flows laminarly through a tube of radius $R$ = 4 mm and length $L$ = 15 m. At a pressure drop $\Delta P$ of 5 kPa the volumetric flow $Q$ is 2.4 L h-1. The Hagen-Poiseuille equation assumes laminar, fully developed flow of a Newtonian liquid.
input:
A viscous liquid flows in a laminar regime through a horizontal tube, and the flow can be regarded as steady and fully developed. The liquid is Newtonian in character, with a viscosity $\mu$ = 0.05 Pa s. The tube has a radius $R$ = 4 mm and a length $L$ = 15 m. At a pressure drop $\Delta P$ of 5 kPa along the tube, the volumetric flow $Q$ works out to 2.4 L h-1.

For laminar, fully developed flow of a Newtonian liquid in a circular tube, the Hagen-Poiseuille equation provides a relationship between the flow and the pressure drop and the tube dimensions, as follows:

$$Q = \frac{\pi R^4 \Delta P}{8 \mu L}$$

where $Q$ denotes the volumetric flow (L h-1), $R$ the tube radius (m), $\Delta P$ the pressure drop (Pa), $\mu$ the viscosity (Pa s) and $L$ the tube length (m). The equation is essentially the integrated form of the balance between the pressure force acting on the liquid and the viscous shear at the wall, under the conditions stated.

Substitution can be used to check the stated flow. With $R$ = 0.004 m and $\Delta P$ = 5000 Pa, the fourth power of the radius emerges as the controlling term: the numerator collects the pressure drop and the tube area term, the denominator collects the viscosity and the length, and the equation returns $Q$ = 2.4 L h-1. The result highlights the feature of the relation that governs its use, namely that flow varies with the fourth power of the radius, so that a small change in tube bore outweighs a proportionally much larger change in pressure drop, viscosity or length. Halving the radius at the same pressure drop would reduce the flow far more than halving the pressure drop itself.

The equation is valid only within its underlying assumptions. It requires laminar flow, so it cannot be applied once the flow in the tube becomes turbulent; it requires a Newtonian liquid, so a liquid whose viscosity varies with shear rate falls outside its scope; and it requires fully developed flow, so entrance lengths where the velocity profile is still forming are not described by it. Within those limits, however, the equation gives the flow from the pressure drop directly, without the need for any empirical coefficient.

fact_base: Project proposal for a water recycling plant, in four sections: case, costs, schedule, and decision requested. Capital cost is $1116k with a 10-year appraisal horizon. The schedule section gives a start one quarter after approval; no contractor is named. The decision requested is approval to proceed to detailed design, not to construction.
input:
Case

This proposal requests approval to proceed to detailed design for a water recycling plant. It is important to clarify at the outset that the decision requested at this stage is design approval only: construction is not being requested, and no contractor is named anywhere in this proposal.

The plant would serve a site that currently takes its process water from the mains supply and discharges its used water after treatment. A recycling plant effectively closes part of that loop on the site itself: used water that currently leaves as discharge is treated to the standard the process requires and returned to service. The case for the plant essentially rests on the two flows it displaces. Every unit of water that is recycled is a unit not drawn from the mains and a unit not discharged, and the site's exposure to supply interruption and to discharge consent limits is reduced by the same movement. The case is stated at the level this proposal can support: the recycling route is technically standard, the treatment steps it requires are established practice, and the question the proposal needs to answer is not whether the water can be recycled but rather what the plant costs, how it is built into a working site, and what approval is being asked for now.

The proposal therefore places the decision in its proper position. Detailed design converts the concept into a priced, scheduled construction package; it is also the stage at which the remaining uncertainties in the scheme are priced rather than merely described. Approving detailed design commits the project to that design work and to nothing beyond it. The construction decision will follow on the detailed design, with its own case, its own costs and its own approval.

Costs

The capital cost is $1116k. This figure is a proposal-stage estimate for the complete plant: the treatment process itself, the civils and building work the plant requires, installation and tie-ins to the existing water and discharge systems, and commissioning. The appraisal horizon for the project is 10 years, and the capital figure is the cost on which the appraisal is run.

The estimate is stated at the accuracy that a proposal-stage figure carries. It is built up from the process design as it currently stands, from vendor indications for the principal equipment, and from the site's own rates for civils and installation; it is not a tender price, and no contractor has priced the work. Detailed design is the stage that firms up the figure: it fixes the equipment list, the tie-in points and the construction sequence, and it returns a cost on which the construction decision can be taken. Operating cost is carried in the appraisal qualitatively at this stage, as the plant's energy, chemical and labour demands depend on the equipment choices made in detailed design; the appraisal structure is set now so that those figures can enter it without rebuilding the case when they become known. The $1116k is held as the single capital figure of this proposal, and any change to it belongs to the detailed design report, stated together with its reasons.

Schedule

The project is scheduled to start one quarter after approval. The schedule is stated from that start point in sequence, because the dates that matter to the site are the order of the stages and the points at which the working site is affected, and both of these follow from the sequence rather than from a calendar fixed in advance of approval.

Detailed design comes first, and it ends at a defined point: a priced construction package and a construction schedule that the site can plan around. Procurement follows design, with the long-lead treatment equipment ordered against the specifications produced by the detailed design. Construction and installation follow procurement, and these are the stages that touch the operating site: tie-ins to the water and discharge systems are made in planned windows, and the existing systems continue running outside those windows. Commissioning closes the sequence: the plant is proved on the site's actual used water, at the site's actual demand, before being handed over as a working part of the water system. Each stage starts from the completed output of the stage before it, and the approval requested here covers the first stage only; later stages will return for their own approvals as their costs become firm.

Decision requested

The decision requested is approval to proceed to detailed design for the water recycling plant, on the capital basis of $1116k and the 10-year appraisal horizon stated in this proposal. The approval commits the project to the detailed design work: the process design completed to construction standard, the equipment list fixed and priced, the tie-ins engineered, and a construction cost and schedule returned for a separate construction decision. It does not commit the project to construction, and it authorises no construction spending whatsoever.

The design stage carries its own discipline. It reports against this proposal: the capital figure it returns is compared with the figure approved here, item by item, and a movement in either direction is explained by the design work that produced it. The stage does not expand the plant's scope on its own authority; a larger or smaller plant than the one proposed is a change of case, and it returns with the construction decision rather than inside it.

Two features of the ask are deliberate. The ask is made at the point where the remaining uncertainties are matters of price and programme, which detailed design exists to settle; seeking construction approval now would price those uncertainties as contingency instead of resolving them. And the ask names its own boundary: if detailed design returns a materially different capital figure, or a construction sequence that the site cannot accept, the construction case will come back as a new decision, rather than as an extension of this one. The steering decision is therefore a bounded one: approve the design stage, on the stated basis, and receive in return the priced package on which the full decision can properly be taken.

fact_base: A contract packaging firm runs 4 plants; revenue is $117 million per year. Evidence base: order records for 12 months, 11852 orders. On-time delivery over the last two quarters was 91%, against a target of 95%. Overtime cost was $2.4 million last year, up 18% on the year before. The order backlog stands at 3.8 weeks, against 1.9 weeks a year ago. Plant 2 accounts for 63% of late orders. A scheduling system for all plants is quoted at $339k; Plant 2 alone is $120k. An internal estimate (not a vendor figure) puts the overtime reduction at Plant 2 at 15-20% in the first year. The recommendation under consideration: install at Plant 2 first, hold the other plants until Plant 2 results are reported. The operations director owns the scheduling programme.

This executive summary provides an overview of delivery performance at a contract packaging firm that operates 4 plants and generates revenue of $117 million per year, and it considers a recommendation that has been put forward in response to ongoing challenges in meeting delivery commitments. The analysis draws on order records for 12 months, comprising 11852 orders in total.

Over the last two quarters, on-time delivery stood at 91%, which falls short of the target of 95% that the firm has set for itself. A closer look at the data reveals that Plant 2 accounts for 63% of all late orders, highlighting the extent to which the issue is concentrated in a single location. Meanwhile, overtime cost reached $2.4 million last year, up 18% on the year before, and the order backlog currently stands at 3.8 weeks, compared with 1.9 weeks a year ago, underscoring the growing pressure on the operation.

A scheduling system for all plants has been quoted at $339k, while Plant 2 alone would cost $120k. An internal estimate — it should be noted that this is not a vendor figure — suggests that the overtime reduction at Plant 2 could be in the region of 15% to 20% in the first year. Against this backdrop, the recommendation under consideration is to install the system at Plant 2 first and to hold the other plants until Plant 2 results are reported, thereby allowing the firm to validate the expected benefits before committing further. The operations director owns the scheduling programme and will oversee its implementation going forward.

fact_base: A tutorial passage explains the Sherwood number to second-year students. Definition in words: the Sherwood number is the ratio of convective to diffusive mass transfer at a surface. The passage must state what a value near 1 means and what a large value means, without inventing numerical examples.
input:
The Sherwood number is the ratio of convective to diffusive mass transfer at a surface. The number compares two routes by which a species reaches or leaves the surface: convection, which carries the species with the moving fluid, and diffusion, which moves the species through the fluid under a concentration difference. Both routes are stated for the same surface and the same driving difference, so the ratio is dimensionless.

A Sherwood number near 1 means the two routes proceed at comparable rates. Convection then adds little to what diffusion alone would deliver, and the transfer rate is set mainly by diffusion through the fluid at the surface. A large Sherwood number means convection is much faster than diffusion. The moving fluid then delivers the species to the surface faster than diffusion can carry it away, and the resistance to transfer sits in the thin layer at the surface where diffusion still governs the final step.

The Sherwood number is used where a transfer coefficient must be estimated for a surface in a flowing fluid. Its value depends on the flow at the surface and on the species being transferred, and it is read alongside the definition of the coefficient it supports: change the length or the diffusivity in that definition and the number changes with them, while the physical transfer rate stays the same.

fact_base: A textbook chapter section on distillation, in four parts: principle, equipment, a worked example, and limits. The worked example uses only the numbers given in the principle part; no new data appear later in the chapter. The limits part states where the simple model fails, in plain terms, without new equations.
input:
## Principle

Distillation is one of the most widely used separation techniques in the process industries, and it is fundamentally based on the differences in volatility between the components of a liquid mixture. When a liquid mixture is heated and partially vapourised, the vapour that is produced is richer in the more volatile component than the liquid from which it was generated, because the more volatile component has a greater tendency to escape into the vapour phase. However, it is important to understand that a single stage of boiling and condensation can only enrich the product to a limited extent, and it cannot deliver a pure product on its own. 

Inside the column, these repetitions take place through intimate contact between vapour rising up the column and liquid flowing back down it. As the vapour leaving a given stage encounters liquid returning from the stage above, an exchange of components takes place between the two phases: the more volatile component transfers into the vapour, while the less volatile component transfers into the liquid. The extent of separation achieved on each stage is governed by the relative volatility, which provides a convenient measure of the relative escaping tendencies of the two components under identical conditions. When the relative volatility is close to unity, each stage delivers very little enrichment and a large number of stages will be needed, whereas when it is well above unity, only a relatively small number of stages may be required.

It is also essential to appreciate the role played by reflux in making the enrichment process cumulative rather than merely repetitive. A portion of the condensed product is returned to the top of the column as liquid reflux, and this returning liquid progressively washes the rising vapour as it passes from stage to stage. Heat is supplied at the base of the column in order to boil the liquid and generate the upward flow of vapour, while heat is removed at the top in order to condense the vapour and provide the reflux. The net result is that the feed is separated into a distillate product that is rich in the more volatile component and a bottoms product that is rich in the less volatile component, with energy being consumed in order to bring this about.

## Equipment

The column itself takes the form of a vertical shell which is fitted with contacting devices distributed along its height. Trays are widely used for this purpose, holding up a layer of liquid through which the vapour is made to pass, with each tray effectively acting as a single contacting stage. Several tray designs are in common use: sieve trays are essentially perforated plates, valve trays incorporate movable caps which adjust the vapour opening in response to the flow, and bubble-cap trays force the vapour to pass up through risers which are covered by caps submerged in the liquid layer. 

The feed is introduced into the column at an intermediate height, at the stage whose composition most closely matches that of the feed itself. Above the feed point, the column serves to enrich the vapour towards the composition of the distillate, while below the feed point it serves to strip the more volatile component out of the descending liquid towards the composition of the bottoms. A reboiler located at the base of the column supplies the heat required for vaporisation, and a condenser located at the top liquefies the overhead vapour. A part of the resulting condensate is withdrawn as distillate product, while the remainder is returned to the column as reflux by way of a reflux drum. 

## Worked example

Let us consider, by way of illustration, a binary feed of composition $z$, where $z$ denotes the mole fraction of the more volatile component in the feed. The objective is for the column to deliver a distillate of composition $x_D$ together with a bottoms product of composition $x_B$, both compositions being expressed as mole fractions of the same component. An overall material balance establishes the relationship between the three flow rates concerned, since the feed rate must equal the sum of the distillate rate and the bottoms rate. A component balance provides a second, complementary relationship, in that the more volatile component entering with the feed must leave divided between the two product streams, in proportion to their respective flow rates and compositions. Taken together, these two balances fully determine the way in which the feed is split between distillate and bottoms once the two product compositions have been specified, and they demonstrate that the split is by no means a free choice: if a purer distillate is demanded at a fixed bottoms composition, a smaller proportion of the feed will report to the overhead product.

Within the column itself, a stepping construction can be used to count the number of stages required. The construction proceeds between the operating relation, which is imposed by the material balances on the liquid and vapour compositions between successive stages, and the equilibrium relation, which determines the vapour composition that can be produced by a liquid of any given composition. Stepping off between these two relations, from the distillate composition down to the bottoms composition, gives one equilibrium stage for each step taken. Where the two relations come close to one another, the steps become progressively smaller and the number of stages required grows without limit, so that the construction also reveals the point at which a specified separation ceases to be attainable at a given reflux. 

The result obtained can be checked by reference to the limiting case. As the relative volatility approaches unity, the equilibrium relation approaches the line of equal compositions, the steps become smaller and smaller, and the number of stages needed to achieve the specified products increases beyond anything that could be contemplated in a practical column. Conversely, as the relative volatility increases, the steps become wider and the separation can be accomplished with only a small number of stages. The example therefore illustrates something that the balances on their own cannot show, namely that purity has to be purchased with stages and with reflux, and that the price of both is ultimately set by the relative volatility of the particular pair of components being separated.

## Limits

It should be borne in mind that the simple model described above treats the relative volatility as though it were constant throughout the column. In a real mixture, however, the relative volatility varies with both composition and temperature, and it may approach unity at some particular composition even where it is comfortably different from unity elsewhere. Where the relative volatility actually reaches unity, the mixture is said to form an azeotrope, and no column operating at that pressure can carry the separation beyond the azeotropic composition, irrespective of the number of stages fitted or the amount of reflux employed.

The notion of the equilibrium stage is itself an idealisation. The streams leaving a real tray are not truly in equilibrium with each other, since the contact time available and the degree of mixing achieved are both finite, with the consequence that a real tray delivers only a fraction of the enrichment that an ideal stage would deliver, and the column requires more trays than the stepping construction predicts. 

Finally, practical operation imposes its own set of limits. If the vapour rises too rapidly it will entrain liquid and flood the column, while if it rises too slowly the liquid will weep through the trays and the quality of contact will be destroyed. The working range of the column lies between flooding and weeping, and the model has nothing to say about this range. In a similar way, the model says nothing about cost: it counts stages and reflux requirements, but the energy cost associated with both of these is left to be evaluated by a separate calculation.

## Principle

Distillation separates a liquid mixture by the difference in volatility of its components. When a liquid mixture is boiled, the vapour formed is richer in the more volatile component than the liquid from which it came, because the more volatile component escapes into the vapour more readily. A single boiling and condensation therefore enriches the volatile component but does not purify it. Distillation repeats the operation many times inside one apparatus, so that each repetition adds enrichment and the product can approach either component in a high state of purity.

The repetitions take place between vapour rising through the column and liquid flowing down. Vapour leaving a stage meets liquid returning from the stage above, and the two streams exchange components: the volatile component passes into the vapour, and the less volatile component passes into the liquid. A stage on which the leaving streams are in equilibrium sets the limit of what one contact can do, and the design counts stages in these equilibrium units. The separation that a stage achieves depends on the relative volatility, which compares the escaping tendency of the two components under the same conditions. Where the relative volatility stands close to unity, each stage enriches the vapour very little and the column needs many stages; where it stands well above unity, few stages suffice.

Reflux makes the enrichment cumulative. Part of the condensed product is returned to the top of the column as liquid, and this returning liquid washes the rising vapour stage by stage. Heat supplied at the base boils the liquid and drives the vapour upward; heat removed at the top condenses the vapour and provides the reflux. The column therefore separates the feed into a distillate rich in the volatile component and a bottoms product rich in the less volatile component, and it spends energy to do so.

## Equipment

The column is a vertical shell fitted with contacting devices along its height. Trays hold a layer of liquid through which the vapour passes, and each tray acts as one contacting stage. Sieve trays are perforated plates; valve trays carry movable caps that adjust the vapour opening to the flow; bubble-cap trays force the vapour through risers covered by caps submerged in the liquid. Packed columns replace trays with a bed of packing that spreads the liquid into films and gives a large area of contact in a continuous manner rather than in discrete stages.

The feed enters at an intermediate height, at the stage whose composition best matches the feed. Above the feed point the column enriches the vapour toward the distillate composition; below it the column strips the volatile component out of the descending liquid toward the bottoms composition. A reboiler at the base supplies the heat of vaporisation, and a condenser at the top liquefies the overhead vapour. Part of the condensate leaves as distillate and part returns as reflux from a reflux drum. Instruments measure temperatures along the column, and the temperature profile indicates where the composition changes most steeply.

## Worked example

Take a binary feed of composition $z$, where $z$ denotes the mole fraction of the volatile component in the feed. The column is to deliver a distillate of composition $x_D$ and a bottoms product of composition $x_B$, with both compositions stated as mole fractions of the same component. An overall balance fixes the relation among the three flow rates: the feed rate equals the sum of the distillate and bottoms rates. A component balance adds the second relation: the volatile component entering with the feed leaves divided between the two products, in proportion to their flow rates and compositions. The two balances together determine the split of the feed between distillate and bottoms once the two product compositions are specified, and they show that the split is not a free choice: demanding a purer distillate at a fixed bottoms composition sends a smaller share of the feed overhead.

Inside the column, the stepping construction counts the stages. Between the operating relation, which the balances impose on the liquid and vapour compositions between stages, and the equilibrium relation, which fixes the vapour composition that a liquid of given composition can produce, the construction steps from the distillate composition down to the bottoms composition. Each step is one equilibrium stage. Where the two relations approach each other, the steps become small and the stage count grows without limit; the construction therefore also shows where a specified separation stops being attainable at a given reflux. Raising the reflux moves the operating relation away from the equilibrium relation and reduces the stage count, at the price of vapourising and condensing more material for the same product rates.

The check on the result is the limiting case. As the relative volatility approaches unity, the equilibrium relation approaches the line of equal compositions, the steps shrink, and the stage count required for the specified products rises beyond any practical column. As the relative volatility grows, the steps widen and few stages accomplish the separation. The example therefore shows what the balances alone cannot: purity is bought with stages and with reflux, and the price of both is set by the relative volatility of the pair being separated.

## Limits

The simple model treats the relative volatility as constant along the column. In a real mixture the relative volatility changes with composition and with temperature, and it can approach unity at some composition even where it is comfortable elsewhere. Where the relative volatility reaches unity the mixture forms an azeotrope, and no column operating at that pressure can carry the separation past the azeotropic composition, whatever its stage count or reflux.

The equilibrium stage is also an idealisation. Streams leaving a real tray are not in equilibrium, because contact time and mixing are finite, so a real tray achieves only a fraction of the enrichment of an ideal stage and the column needs more trays than the stepping construction counts. The model further assumes that the molar flows of liquid and vapour stay constant along each section, which holds only where the components have similar heats of vaporisation and the heat losses are small.

Operation sets the remaining limits. Vapour rising too fast entrains liquid and floods the column; vapour rising too slowly lets liquid weep through the trays and destroys the contact. Between flooding and weeping stands the working range of the column, and the model says nothing about it. The model likewise prices nothing: it counts stages and reflux but leaves the energy cost of both to a separate calculation.

fact_base: A review passage on membrane separations for solvent recovery, in four parts: scope, established results, disagreements, and gaps. The review covers 140 papers from the last 11 years. The disagreements part names the quantity on which reports conflict; the gaps part names the measurement nobody reports.
input:
## Scope

This review sets out to survey the field of membrane separations for solvent recovery, drawing together a body of literature that has grown considerably in recent years. In total, the review covers 140 papers from the last 11 years, encompassing laboratory studies, pilot demonstrations and a smaller number of reports from industrial practice. The scope is deliberately restricted to membranes used for the recovery of organic solvents from process streams, and it includes both polymeric and ceramic membranes, as well as the hybrid configurations that have begun to appear in the literature. Studies concerned purely with aqueous separations fall outside the scope, as do patents and manufacturers' literature, which are not subject to the same scrutiny as the peer-reviewed work on which this review is based.

## Established results

There are several findings on which the literature is now in broad agreement, and these can be regarded as established. It is well established, firstly, that solvent-resistant membranes can maintain useful selectivity over extended periods in a number of the milder solvent environments, and that the catastrophic loss of performance that was once feared in organic media is not the general rule. Secondly, there is a consensus that the swelling of the membrane material by the solvent is the central phenomenon governing performance, since swelling alters both the transport of the solvent itself and the rejection of dissolved species, and it is now widely accepted that membrane screening carried out in one solvent cannot simply be read across to another. Thirdly, it has become clear that the economics of membrane solvent recovery are most favourable where the membrane unit displaces a thermal separation duty rather than competing with one that is already efficient, and that the strongest cases are those in which the recovered solvent has a high value or the stream would otherwise incur a disposal cost.

In addition to these general findings, the literature provides a reasonably consistent picture of the way in which performance responds to operating conditions. Increases in pressure are reported to raise solvent flux, although the benefit is frequently offset by compaction of the membrane structure, and increases in temperature are reported to reduce rejection in many polymeric systems as the material swells and the transport of solutes becomes easier. Cross-flow operation is consistently reported to mitigate the accumulation of rejected material at the membrane surface, and the practice of staging membrane units so that the retentate passes through successive units is well documented in the larger studies. On these points, at least, the reader can proceed with some confidence.

## Disagreements

Against this background, however, there remains one important quantity on which the published reports come into direct conflict with one another, and that quantity is the decline in solvent flux during extended operation. A substantial group of studies reports that flux settles, after an initial settling-in period, to a value that is then maintained more or less indefinitely, and these studies present the membrane as being essentially stable in service. Another substantial group, working with what appear to be comparable membranes and comparable solvents, reports a continuing and progressive decline in flux that shows no sign of levelling off within the duration of the experiments described. Both positions cannot be correct as general statements about the same class of materials, and yet each is supported by a body of careful work.

A variety of explanations have been put forward for this discrepancy. It has been suggested that the difference lies in the pretreatment of the feed, in the presence or absence of trace contaminants that adsorb on the membrane, in the cleaning regimes applied between runs, and in the simple matter of how long the experiments were allowed to run. Studies reporting stability have tended to be shorter than studies reporting decline, which raises the uncomfortable possibility that the stable picture is an artefact of duration. Equally, it has been argued that the declining picture reflects contaminants present in real process streams that are absent from the cleaner model mixtures used elsewhere, so that the disagreement may not be about the membrane at all, but rather about the stream to which it was exposed. At the present time, the literature does not contain the controlled, side-by-side comparison that would be needed in order to resolve the matter, and the reader is left to weigh the two bodies of evidence against each other.

## Gaps

Finally, there are significant gaps in the literature that deserve to be highlighted. The most striking of these concerns a measurement that, remarkably, nobody appears to report: the solvent flux of a membrane measured after repeated cleaning cycles at module scale. Individual studies report flux before and after a single cleaning, and a great many studies report flux on small membrane coupons that have never been cleaned at all, but the cumulative effect of cleaning on the performance of a full module, which is the form in which the technology would actually be deployed, is essentially absent from the record. This is a serious omission, because cleaning is one of the principal operating costs of a membrane plant, and a membrane that recovers its flux fully after each of many cleanings is a very different proposition from one that loses a little performance with every cycle.

Related gaps appear elsewhere in the record. Long-duration studies remain rare relative to the number of short screening studies, and reports of performance on genuine process streams, as opposed to synthetic mixtures prepared for the laboratory, are rarer still. Information about the condition of membranes after service, and about the mechanisms by which they eventually fail, is seldom provided. Until these gaps are filled, assessments of the technology for solvent recovery will continue to rest on a foundation that is narrower than the confidence of much of the writing in the field would suggest.

It is also worth noting, by way of context, that the literature surveyed here reflects what researchers have chosen to investigate and to publish, which is not necessarily the same thing as what industry has chosen to install. Duties that were taken into operation without any accompanying publication do not appear in the record, and neither do duties that were abandoned at an early stage, so that the picture presented by the literature may be systematically more favourable than the picture that would be given by a survey of operating plants, if such a survey could somehow be carried out.

None of this should be taken to diminish the value of the work that has been done. The field has established a great deal in a comparatively short period, and the techniques involved are now understood far better than they were. Nevertheless, the combination of a live disagreement about long-term behaviour and a set of gaps concentrated in exactly the areas that matter most for industrial deployment means that considerable caution is still called for, and it is hoped that this review will assist readers in directing that caution to the places where it is most needed.

## Scope

Work on aqueous separations stands outside the scope, as do patents and manufacturers' literature, which are not examined by the review process applied to the journal papers. Reports are laboratory studies in the main, with pilot demonstrations a minority and reports from industrial practice a small minority.

## Established results

Three results are established across the literature. Solvent-resistant membranes maintain useful selectivity over extended periods in the milder solvent environments, and the rapid destruction of performance in organic media that early work led readers to expect is not the general rule. Swelling of the membrane material by the solvent governs performance: swelling changes the transport of the solvent and the rejection of dissolved species together, and screening results obtained in one solvent do not transfer to another. The economics are strongest where the membrane unit displaces a thermal separation duty, and strongest of all where the recovered solvent has a high value or the stream would otherwise carry a disposal cost.

The response of performance to operating conditions is also consistent across reports. Raising the pressure raises solvent flux, with part of the gain lost to compaction of the membrane structure. Raising the temperature lowers rejection in many polymeric systems, as the material swells and solute transport becomes easier. Cross-flow operation reduces the accumulation of rejected material at the membrane surface, and staging units so that the retentate passes through successive units is documented in the larger studies. On these points the reports agree in direction, and differ mainly in magnitude.

## Disagreements

Reports conflict on one quantity: the decline in solvent flux during extended operation. One body of studies reports that flux falls during an initial period and then holds at a level value for the remaining duration of the work. Another body, on membranes and solvents that appear comparable, reports a flux that continues to decline throughout the run and shows no approach to a level value. The two accounts cannot both hold as general descriptions of the same materials in the same duty.

The candidate explanations are visible in the reports themselves. The studies differ in feed pretreatment, in the trace contaminants available to adsorb on the membrane, in the cleaning applied between runs, and in duration. The studies reporting stable flux are in general shorter than the studies reporting decline, which leaves open the possibility that the stable account is an artefact of duration: a run that ends during the level period of a slow decline reports stability. The studies reporting decline more often used real process streams, which leaves open the opposite possibility, that the decline belongs to the contaminants of a real stream and not to the membrane. No study in the set runs the same membrane on the same stream under both cleaning regimes for long enough to separate these explanations, and the disagreement is therefore a disagreement about confounded variables, stated in the literature as a disagreement about membranes. The limited preference the evidence supports is conditional: on clean, prepared feeds, flux after the initial period is stable in most reports; on unprepared process streams, a continuing decline is the safer planning assumption.

## Gaps

One measurement is absent from the whole set: the solvent flux of a full module after repeated cleaning cycles. Studies report flux before and after a single cleaning, and many report flux on small coupons that were never cleaned. The cumulative effect of cleaning on module performance is not reported, although cleaning is a principal operating cost of a membrane plant and the deployment question turns on it. A membrane that recovers its flux fully after each of many cleanings supports one design; a membrane that loses performance at every cycle supports another, with more membrane area, more frequent replacement, or a different process. The literature does not allow the reader to distinguish between the two.

The surrounding gaps are of the same kind. Long-duration studies are few beside the many short screening studies, and reports on genuine process streams are few beside reports on synthetic mixtures. The condition of membranes after service, and the failure mechanism that ended their service, are seldom described. The evidence base for solvent recovery by membranes is consequently narrower than the volume of publication suggests: it is deep on screening and on short-term behaviour, and thin on exactly the long-term, module-scale, cleaned-and-reused performance on which an industrial decision would rest.

The scope has a consequence the reader should hold in mind. Because the set is limited to examined journal work, it describes what researchers have chosen to study and publish, not what plants have chosen to install. Solvent recovery duties that reached operation without generating a publication are absent, and duties that failed early are absent with them. The established results below are therefore established for the systems studied, under the conditions reported, and the extension of any of them to an unstudied solvent or an unreported membrane is an inference the literature itself does not make.

A further point of agreement concerns reporting practice rather than performance. Most studies condition a new membrane before measurement and report the conditioning, most report the feed composition and the temperature, and most state whether the feed was a synthetic mixture or a process stream. This consistency of reporting is what makes the disagreements in the next section informative: where reports conflict on an outcome while agreeing on the description of what was done, the cause is more likely to sit in a variable that none of them reports than in sloppy description by one side.

The disagreement also has a practical edge. A designer who believes the stable account sizes the plant with little spare membrane area and a modest cleaning provision; a designer who believes the declining account installs spare area, provides for frequent cleaning, or rejects the membrane option at the outset. The two accounts therefore lead to different plants and different costs from the same evidence, and the conflict is not an academic one. It sits inside every estimate prepared from this literature, usually invisibly, because the estimator adopts one account by adopting one subset of the papers as representative.

The gaps share a common cause. Screening studies are quick and publishable; long studies tie up equipment and produce their result slowly; module studies require hardware that many laboratories do not own; cleaning studies produce wear that a laboratory may prefer not to inflict on a scarce membrane sample. The literature is shaped by these incentives, and the thin places in the record are thin for reasons that have nothing to do with their importance to a decision. Naming the cause matters because it indicates the remedy: the missing measurements will not appear as a by-product of more screening work, and a reader who needs them must either commission them or proceed without them, knowing which choice was made.

fact_base: Energy assessment of a brewery, in four sections: current use, refrigeration, steam, and recommendation. Electricity use is 3222 MWh per year; refrigeration takes the largest share. A heat-recovery retrofit is projected to save 15% of electricity use, a derived saving of 483 MWh per year, at a capital cost of $339k. At $0.12 per kWh the derived annual saving is $57996 and the derived simple payback is 5.8 years. Steam figures are from one winter month and are flagged as seasonal in the recommendation.
input:
## Current use

This energy assessment examines the current energy position of a brewery and identifies where the principal opportunities for improvement may lie. In terms of electricity, the brewery currently uses 3222 MWh per year, and it is clear from the breakdown of this consumption that refrigeration accounts for the largest share of the total. This is perhaps unsurprising, given the central role that cooling plays in the brewing process, but it does mean that any serious attempt to reduce electricity consumption at the site will need to focus primarily on the refrigeration systems and on the uses to which refrigeration is put.

## Refrigeration

Refrigeration at the brewery serves a number of important duties. It is required for the control of fermentation temperatures, since the heat that is generated during fermentation has to be removed in order to hold the product at the temperature the process demands, and it is required for the cold storage of finished product prior to dispatch. It is also relevant to note that cold rooms and cellars lose cold continuously to their surroundings, so that the refrigeration plant is required to run even when production is not actively taking place. Taken together, these duties explain why refrigeration dominates the electricity consumption of the site, and why the way in which waste heat is handled elsewhere in the brewery is of such importance to the overall energy picture.

## Steam

Steam is used at the brewery for a variety of heating duties, including the heating of brewing liquor and the cleaning of vessels and pipework. It is, however, important to note an important limitation of the figures that are available in this area: the steam figures presented in this assessment are drawn from one winter month, and they therefore reflect the demands of the site during the colder part of the year rather than providing a balanced picture across the year as a whole. This seasonal aspect needs to be borne in mind whenever the steam figures are used, and it will be returned to in the recommendation below.

## Recommendation

The principal recommendation arising from this assessment concerns a heat-recovery retrofit. It is projected that the retrofit will save 15% of electricity use, which equates to a derived saving of 483 MWh per year. The capital cost of the retrofit is $339k. At an electricity price of $0.12 per kWh, the derived annual saving works out at $57996, and the derived simple payback is 5.8 years. It is, however, essential to flag once again that the steam figures on which parts of this assessment rest are seasonal in nature, having been drawn from a single winter month, and for this reason the recommendation should be read with that qualification firmly in mind.

More broadly, it is worth reflecting on the fact that the pattern of consumption described above is by no means unusual for a brewery of this type. Brewing is an energy-intensive activity at both ends of the temperature scale: a great deal of heat is required in order to bring the brewing liquor and the wort to the temperatures that the process demands, and a great deal of cooling is subsequently required in order to bring the product back down again and to keep it cold thereafter. It is this combination of substantial heating duties and substantial cooling duties, existing side by side in the same process, that makes the question of heat recovery such a natural one to ask in the context of a brewery, since heat that is removed at one point in the process is, at least in principle, available to be used at another.

Looking ahead, it is clear that the refrigeration load will remain the dominant feature of the brewery's electricity consumption for the foreseeable future, since it is tied directly to the nature of the product and to the temperatures at which that product has to be held. Unless the scale of production changes materially, the proportions described in this assessment are unlikely to alter, and this stability in the pattern of consumption is itself relevant to the recommendation, because it means that a saving directed at the refrigeration-related loads is a saving directed at a load that will still be there, at a similar scale, for many years to come.

A final observation concerns the brewery's steam demand, which follows the rhythm of the brewing process itself. Because brewing takes place in batches, the demand for steam is not spread evenly across the working day but is instead concentrated into peaks associated with particular stages of the process, with quieter intervals in between. This pattern has practical implications for heat recovery, because heat that becomes available at a steady rate cannot always be absorbed by a demand that arrives in peaks, and some allowance for this mismatch may need to be made when the retrofit is designed in detail.
target:
## Current use

The brewery uses 3222 MWh of electricity per year. Refrigeration takes the largest share of that total. The assessment therefore concentrates on refrigeration and on the heat that refrigeration rejects, because the largest saving available to the site stands in the relationship between the two: heat recovered from the refrigeration system displaces heat that the steam system would otherwise raise, and the electricity saving credited to heat recovery depends on where the refrigeration load falls.

## Refrigeration

Refrigeration at the brewery covers fermentation cooling, wort cooling after the boil, and the cold storage of finished product. Fermentation cooling is a process load that follows the production schedule; cold storage is a standing load that continues whether or not production is running, because the stores lose cold to their surroundings continuously. The standing character of the storage load matters for heat recovery: a refrigeration plant that runs through the night and through shutdown periods rejects heat at times when the demand for recovered heat elsewhere in the brewery is at its lowest, and the value of the recovered heat depends on the coincidence of rejection and demand as much as on the quantity rejected.

## Steam

Steam serves the heating duties of the brewery: brewing liquor, the boil, and cleaning of vessels and pipework. The steam figures in this assessment come from one winter month. They describe the site under winter conditions, when space heating and the temperature of incoming water both raise steam demand, and they are not an average month. A steam balance built on these figures overstates the annual steam demand, and any saving calculated against that balance inherits the overstatement.

## Recommendation

A heat-recovery retrofit is projected to save 15% of electricity use, a derived saving of 483 MWh per year, at a capital cost of $339k. At $0.12 per kWh the derived annual saving is $57996 and the derived simple payback is 5.8 years. The recommendation is to proceed with the retrofit on these figures, with one qualification carried from the steam section: the steam figures are from one winter month and are seasonal, so the part of the case that rests on steam displacement should be re-examined against a full year of steam records before the design is fixed. The electricity saving and the payback stand on the electricity figures, which are annual; the seasonal qualification applies to the steam side of the assessment and does not change the payback as stated.

The structure of the electricity use also limits what an assessment can recommend. Because refrigeration dominates, measures aimed at the smaller electrical demands of the site, in lighting, in drives, and in office and ancillary loads, cannot move the annual total by more than a small amount even where they succeed completely. An assessment that distributes its recommendations evenly across all uses misrepresents the site: the refrigeration load is where the electricity is, and the refrigeration load is where the recoverable heat is, and the two facts together make heat recovery the natural centre of any programme for this brewery.

The rejected heat from refrigeration is not all equally available. Heat rejected at the condenser is at a temperature set by the condensing condition, and it can serve only those heating duties whose required temperature it can reach. Duties above that temperature still require steam, however much heat the refrigeration plant rejects. The retrofit case therefore depends on the brewery having enough demand at or below the rejection temperature, in the brewhouse, in cleaning, and in space and water heating, to absorb the recovered heat across the year rather than in a single season.

The steam section of an assessment is also where the brewery's operating pattern enters. Brewing is a batch process, and the steam demand of a batch process arrives in peaks at mashing, at the boil, and at cleaning, with quiet intervals between them. A heat-recovery system that delivers heat steadily meets a demand that arrives intermittently, and storage or a tolerance for wasting surplus heat at quiet times is part of the real design even where it is absent from the saving calculation. The annual figures in the recommendation are totals; they do not by themselves show how much of the recovered heat the brewery's daily pattern can actually absorb.

The qualification about the steam figures deserves its weight in the reading of this assessment. A single winter month is not a defective record of that month; it is an accurate record of the wrong period for annual conclusions. Steam raised in winter serves demands that shrink or vanish in summer, and the annual steam demand of the brewery is certainly lower than twelve times the winter figure. Any extension of the retrofit, beyond the electricity saving on which the recommendation rests, that is justified by steam displacement should wait for a full year of steam records, which the brewery can accumulate without capital spending and which would convert the weakest part of the present evidence into the strongest.

subtype: worked example with equation: Arrhenius ratio
fact_base: Rate constants for a catalyst ageing test were measured at two temperatures. With activation energy $E_a$ of 70 kJ mol-1, raising the temperature from 300 K to 330 K multiplies the rate constant $k$ by 12.82. The estimate holds the pre-exponential factor $A$ constant over the interval.
input:
In this worked example, we are going to look at how the rate constant for a catalyst ageing test responds when the temperature is increased, drawing on rate constants that were measured at two temperatures. The relationship in question is the well-known Arrhenius equation, which can be written as follows:

$$k = A \exp\left(-\frac{E_a}{R T}\right)$$

In this equation, $k$ represents the rate constant, $A$ represents the pre-exponential factor, $E_a$ represents the activation energy, $R$ is the gas constant, and $T$ is the absolute temperature. It is worth noting that the estimate presented here holds the pre-exponential factor $A$ constant over the temperature interval that is being considered, which is an important underlying assumption of the calculation.

With an activation energy $E_a$ of 70 kJ mol-1, raising the temperature from 300 K to 330 K can be shown to multiply the rate constant $k$ by 12.82, which really underlines just how sensitive the rate constant is to even a relatively modest change in temperature. In other words, the ageing of the catalyst proceeds considerably more rapidly at the higher temperature, and this has significant implications for how accelerated ageing tests of this kind should be interpreted and for how far their results can be extrapolated to lower operating temperatures in practice.

It should also be borne in mind that an accelerated test of this kind is only as meaningful as the assumption that the same ageing mechanism is operating at both temperatures, since the calculation can say nothing about a change of mechanism.
target:
Rate constants for a catalyst ageing test were measured at two temperatures. The Arrhenius equation relates the rate constant $k$ to the absolute temperature $T$,

$$k = A \exp\left(-\frac{E_a}{R T}\right)$$

where $A$ is the pre-exponential factor, $E_a$ is the activation energy, and $R$ is the gas constant. With $E_a$ of 70 kJ mol-1, raising the temperature from 300 K to 330 K multiplies $k$ by 12.82. The estimate holds $A$ constant over the interval.

The size of the multiplier is the point of the example. A temperature rise that is small next to the absolute temperature changes the rate constant by more than an order of magnitude, because the temperature stands inside an exponential and is multiplied by the activation energy. An ageing test run at the higher temperature therefore does not reproduce the lower-temperature behaviour at a faster rate in any simple proportion: it amplifies the activated process, and a process with a different activation energy would be amplified by a different factor. Extrapolation from the test temperature to an operating temperature inherits the full uncertainty of $E_a$, and the constant-$A$ assumption is part of that uncertainty. The measured pair of rate constants fixes the multiplier between the two measured temperatures; it does not by itself fix the rate constant at any third temperature.

For a catalyst ageing test the point of the calculation is comparative. Ageing is studied at an elevated temperature because the test must finish in a practical time, and the Arrhenius relation is the bridge between the test condition and the service condition. The bridge carries the full weight of the comparison: if the activation energy belongs to the ageing mechanism at the test temperature and the mechanism changes before the service temperature is reached, the extrapolated rate describes a process that is no longer the one under study.

fact_base: A tutorial passage explains absolute and relative error through a pressure measurement. Worked figures: reading 331 units, tolerance 2% of reading, so the absolute error is 6.62 units. The passage distinguishes error from uncertainty and does not merge the two terms.
input:
In this tutorial passage, we will explore the important distinction between absolute error and relative error, using a pressure measurement as our worked example. Suppose that we have a pressure reading of 331 units, and suppose that the tolerance associated with this reading is 2% of the reading itself. On this basis, the absolute error works out at 6.62 units, and it is this figure that tells us how far the reading might actually lie from the true value in the units of the measurement.

The absolute error is expressed in the same units as the measurement, which makes it directly interpretable: an absolute error of 6.62 units on a reading of 331 units means that the true value is expected to lie within that distance on either side of the reading. The relative error, by contrast, expresses the error as a proportion of the reading, and in this case it is simply the tolerance of 2% restated in relative form. Relative error is particularly useful when measurements of very different sizes need to be compared on a like-for-like basis.

It is also important to note that error should not be confused with uncertainty, even though the two terms are often used interchangeably in everyday language. Error refers to the difference between a reading and the true value, whereas uncertainty describes the range within which the true value is believed to lie. Keeping these two concepts clearly separate is essential for sound measurement practice.
target:
A pressure reading of 331 units with a tolerance of 2% of reading carries an absolute error of 6.62 units. The tutorial separates the two forms of the same statement: absolute error, stated in the units of the measurement, and relative error, stated as a fraction of the reading.

Absolute error is the difference between the reading and the true value, expressed in the units of the measurement itself. It answers the question the operator asks: how far, in units, might this reading lie from the value it reports? Relative error divides the absolute error by the reading, so the same instrument performance can be compared between a small reading and a large one. The conversion in this example is a single step: 2% of 331 units is 6.62 units, obtained by multiplying the reading by the tolerance fraction. The tolerance is quoted as a percentage of reading, not of full scale, and the basis matters: a percentage of full scale would give a different absolute error at the same reading, and a larger one wherever the reading sits below full scale.

Error is not uncertainty. Error is the difference between a reading and the true value; it has a sign in principle, even where the sign is unknown. Uncertainty is the range within which the true value is believed to lie, and it is the quantity a measurement report can actually state. A reading can therefore be reported with its uncertainty, but never with its error, because the true value that defines the error is the thing the measurement is trying to find.

fact_base: A tutorial passage explains representative sampling of a gas emission. The passage covers where samples are taken, how many increments form one sample, and why a single grab sample misleads. No numerical limits are quoted; regulatory limits belong to the site's permit, not to the passage.
input:
When it comes to characterising a gas emission, the question of how the sample is taken is just as important as the analysis that is subsequently performed on it, because a poorly taken sample can undermine even the most careful laboratory work. Representative sampling is concerned with ensuring that the material actually collected faithfully reflects the emission as a whole, across both the duct cross-section and the period over which the emission is being characterised.

Firstly, the location at which samples are taken matters a great deal. The sampling point needs to be positioned where the gas stream is as well mixed as possible, so that the concentration measured at that point is genuinely indicative of the stream as a whole rather than of a local pocket or a stratified layer. In practice, this means thinking carefully about the effects of bends, junctions and other disturbances, and about whether a single point can adequately represent a stream whose composition may vary across its width.

Secondly, a single sample is rarely built from a single act of collection. Instead, several increments are typically collected over the sampling period and combined to form one sample for analysis, so that short-term fluctuations in the emission are averaged out rather than captured by chance. Last but not least, it is worth emphasising why a single grab sample can be so misleading: an emission is not constant over time, and a grab sample freezes one moment, which may coincide with a peak, a lull, or a transient that bears little relation to the emission's typical behaviour.
target:
Representative sampling of a gas emission has one requirement: the material collected must stand for the emission as a whole, over the full cross-section of the duct and over the whole period the sample claims to cover. Every choice in the sampling procedure is judged against that requirement.

The sampling point is placed where the gas is well mixed. A stream leaving a bend or a junction can be stratified, with concentration varying across the duct, and a probe in such a stream measures the layer it sits in rather than the stream. A point measurement represents the emission only where the composition at the point matches the average composition across the section, so the location is chosen away from disturbances, and a traverse across the section is used where mixing cannot be assumed. The sampling rate and the probe arrangement are held steady during collection, because a varying draw distorts the share of the stream that reaches the sample.

One sample is built from several increments collected across the sampling period and combined before analysis. Each increment is a small portion of the gas taken at its moment; combined, the increments average the fluctuations of the emission over the period instead of reporting whichever moment a single collection happened to catch. The number of increments and their spacing follow the variability of the source: a steady emission needs fewer increments than one that swings with the process cycle.

A single grab sample misleads for exactly this reason. An emission varies over time as the process load changes, and a grab sample freezes one instant of that variation. The result is a true measurement of the instant and a false picture of the period: a peak reads as the typical level, a lull reads as compliance, and neither can be corrected afterwards, because the sample carries no record of the variation it missed.

fact_base: Cost review of a cross-dock transfer: 609 km per trip at $1.71 per km, 575 trips per year. Annual transport cost is $599k. Costs are carrier invoices for the last 12 months; empty running is included in the trip count.
input:
This cost review looks at a cross-dock transfer operation and sets out what it currently costs to run on an annual basis. The transfer involves 609 km per trip, and the carrier charges $1.71 per km, with a total of 575 trips being undertaken per year. When these figures are combined, the annual transport cost comes to $599k, which represents a significant line item in the logistics budget.

The figures presented here are drawn from carrier invoices for the last 12 months, so they reflect what was actually paid over that period rather than any estimate or projection. It is important to note that empty running is included in the trip count, which means that the cost per kilometre is effectively spread across both loaded and unloaded legs of the operation. This is a meaningful consideration, because it means the headline cost reflects the full operational reality of the transfer, including the return journeys that generate no revenue.

Understanding the structure of this cost is an important first step in any broader review of the transfer operation, since the annual figure is built up from a small number of clear components: the distance travelled on each trip, the rate charged per kilometre, and the total number of trips made across the year. Any change in one of these components would flow directly through to the annual total.

It is also worth bearing in mind that each of these components can move independently of the others, so that the annual figure may change from one year to the next for quite different reasons, whether because the carrier revises its rates, because the route itself changes, or because the volume of goods passing through the dock rises or falls.
target:
A cross-dock transfer costs $599k per year. The figure is built from three components: 609 km per trip, a carrier rate of $1.71 per km, and 575 trips per year.

The costs are carrier invoices for the last 12 months, not estimates. They are therefore a record of what the transfer cost at the trip rate and trip count of that period, and they will move with either quantity: the annual figure is the product of the three components, so a change in trip distance, in the per-kilometre rate, or in trip frequency changes the total in direct proportion. Empty running is included in the trip count. The rate is consequently spread over loaded and empty kilometres alike, and the cost of a loaded kilometre is higher than the rate suggests when the return leg runs empty. Any comparison of this transfer against an alternative routing or carrier must be made on the same basis, with empty running inside the trip count on both sides, or the comparison will understate the cost of whichever operation hides its empty legs. The review establishes the cost of the transfer as it is currently run; it does not price any alternative.

The three components also show where any future change in the cost will come from. The rate per kilometre is a carrier price and changes at renegotiation. The trip count follows the volume of goods moving through the dock and changes with the business itself. A review that reports only the annual total cannot distinguish a cost increase caused by a higher carrier rate from one caused by more trips, and the two call for different responses: the first is a purchasing question, the second a capacity question. The invoice base makes the distinction recoverable, because each invoice carries its own distance and its own rate.

fact_base: Energy assessment of a dairy plant, in four sections: current use, refrigeration, steam, and recommendation. Electricity use is 1059 MWh per year; refrigeration takes the largest share. A heat-recovery retrofit is projected to save 17% of electricity use, a derived saving of 180 MWh per year, at a capital cost of $877k. At $0.12 per kWh the derived annual saving is $21604 and the derived simple payback is 40.6 years. Steam figures are from one winter month and are flagged as seasonal in the recommendation.
input:
## Current use

This energy assessment presents the current energy position of a dairy plant and considers the scope for reducing its energy consumption. The plant uses 1059 MWh of electricity per year, and of the various demands placed on the electrical supply, refrigeration is responsible for the largest share. This pattern will be familiar to anyone acquainted with dairy operations, since milk and dairy products have to be kept cold from the moment the milk arrives at the site until the moment the finished product leaves it. Nevertheless, the dominance of refrigeration in the electricity total does mean that it is the natural focus of any assessment of this kind, and it is with refrigeration that the detailed discussion below begins.

In addition to refrigeration itself, the assessment also considers the steam system, which serves the heating duties of the plant, and it concludes with a recommendation concerning a heat-recovery retrofit that has been proposed for the site. Before turning to the detail, it should be said that the purpose of this assessment is to establish the current position on the basis of the records that are available, and to evaluate the proposed retrofit on the figures that those records support.

## Refrigeration

Refrigeration at the dairy plant serves a wide range of duties. Raw milk has to be cooled on arrival and held cold in storage before it is processed, and finished products such as yoghurt and cream have to be cooled after processing and held in cold stores until they are dispatched. Refrigeration is also involved in the cooling of process streams at various points in the production sequence. It is important to appreciate that several of these loads are effectively continuous: cold stores lose cold to their surroundings at all hours, and milk arrives at the site throughout the day, so that the refrigeration plant is called upon to operate for extended periods rather than only during the hours of production.

It follows from this that the refrigeration system is not merely the largest single consumer of electricity at the plant but also one of the most continuously operating systems on the site. The heat that the refrigeration plant rejects as it works is, in principle, available for recovery, and it is this rejected heat that the proposed retrofit is designed to capture. However, the value of capturing it depends on there being a demand for heat at the times when the refrigeration plant is rejecting it, and this question of timing is one that will recur in the recommendation.

## Steam

Steam is used at the dairy plant for the heating duties associated with processing, including the heating of product streams and the cleaning of equipment and pipework, which in a dairy is a substantial and recurring duty. It is, however, of the utmost importance to note a significant limitation affecting the steam figures used in this assessment: the steam figures are taken from one winter month, and they therefore reflect the operating conditions of the plant during the coldest part of the year rather than providing an even picture across all of the seasons. The recommendation that follows will accordingly flag the steam figures as seasonal, and any conclusions that rest upon them should be treated with appropriate caution.

Because cleaning is such a large part of the steam demand in a dairy, and because cleaning takes place at particular points in the production cycle, the steam demand of the plant is far from steady over the course of a day. This has a bearing on the heat-recovery question, since recovered heat can only displace steam that would otherwise have been raised at that moment, and steam that is demanded in short peaks cannot always be matched by heat that is rejected on a different pattern.

## Recommendation

The recommendation arising from this assessment concerns the proposed heat-recovery retrofit. The retrofit is projected to save 17% of the plant's electricity use, which corresponds to a derived saving of 180 MWh per year, and its capital cost is $877k. At an electricity price of $0.12 per kWh, the derived annual saving amounts to $21604, and the derived simple payback works out at 40.6 years. It is only fair to acknowledge that this is a very long payback period, and it means that the retrofit, considered purely as a means of saving electricity, repays its capital cost only over a timescale that extends far beyond the horizon over which such projects are normally assessed. As flagged above, the steam figures are seasonal, having been drawn from one winter month, and this qualification should be borne in mind in connection with any part of the case that depends on steam. The assessment therefore presents the retrofit figures as they stand, notes the length of the payback, and draws attention to the seasonal nature of the steam evidence on which parts of the assessment rest.

It is also worth observing that the general pattern described in this assessment, with refrigeration dominating the electricity consumption of the site, is one that is encountered again and again in the dairy industry, and indeed in food processing more generally, wherever a product has to be kept cold continuously from its arrival in raw form through to its departure as a finished article. The cold chain admits of no real interruption, and the electricity that it consumes is therefore one of the least discretionary items in the entire cost base of a plant of this kind. This is part of the reason why energy assessments of dairy plants so often return to the refrigeration system when they are looking for savings, since it is at one and the same time the largest load and the load that is most continuously present.

A related consideration is the extent to which the different energy systems of the plant interact with one another. Electricity and steam are sometimes discussed as though they were separate subjects, but in a plant of this kind they are closely connected: the refrigeration system consumes electricity and produces rejected heat, while the steam system consumes fuel in order to produce heat, and it is precisely at the junction between these two systems that the proposed retrofit is intended to operate. An improvement in one system can therefore have consequences in the other, and it is important that these consequences are thought through as a whole rather than evaluated in isolation, since a saving that appears in one account may be partly offset by an increase that appears in the other, and only a view of the plant as a complete system will reveal whether this is happening.
target:
## Current use

The dairy plant uses 1059 MWh of electricity per year, and refrigeration takes the largest share. The structure of the assessment follows from that single fact: the refrigeration section describes where the electricity goes, the steam section describes the heating system against which any recovered heat would be credited, and the recommendation evaluates a heat-recovery retrofit whose case rests on the relationship between the two systems.

## Refrigeration

Refrigeration at the plant covers the cooling of raw milk on arrival, its storage before processing, the cooling of products after processing, and the cold storage of finished products until dispatch. Two properties of this load govern its place in the assessment. The first is its size relative to the other electrical demands of the site: it exceeds each of them, so a given fractional saving in refrigeration is worth more than the same fraction anywhere else in the electricity account. The second is its continuity. Cold stores lose cold to their surroundings at all hours, and milk arrives across the day, so the refrigeration plant runs far beyond the hours of production. A continuous refrigeration load rejects heat continuously, including at night and at weekends, and that timing decides how much of the rejected heat can be used: recovered heat has value only where a heating demand exists at the moment of recovery, and a dairy's heating demands are concentrated in processing and cleaning periods rather than spread evenly across the week.

The refrigeration system is therefore both the largest consumer of electricity at the plant and the source of the heat the proposed retrofit would recover. Those two statements are not independent. The projected electricity saving from heat recovery arises because heat recovered from refrigeration displaces electric or steam heating elsewhere; the size of the refrigeration load sets the quantity of heat available, and its timing sets the share of that heat for which a demand exists.

## Steam

Steam serves the heating duties of the plant: the heating of product streams during processing and the cleaning of equipment and pipework, which in a dairy is a large and recurring duty. Steam demand is not steady. Cleaning takes place at set points in the production cycle, so demand arrives in peaks, and recovered heat can displace only the steam that would otherwise be raised at the moment the heat becomes available.

The steam figures in this assessment are from one winter month and are seasonal. They record the plant in the coldest part of the year, when incoming water is at its coldest and the heating component of processing is at its largest. A steam total built on a winter month overstates the annual steam demand, and a saving calculated by displacement against that total inherits the overstatement in the same proportion. The figures are used in this assessment because they are the records available; the qualification is stated here and carried into the recommendation, and it applies to every conclusion that rests on the steam side of the plant's energy balance.

## Recommendation

A heat-recovery retrofit is projected to save 17% of electricity use, a derived saving of 180 MWh per year, at a capital cost of $877k. At $0.12 per kWh the derived annual saving is $21604 and the derived simple payback is 40.6 years.

The payback is the finding of this assessment. That payback means that the retrofit, judged on the stated electricity saving alone, returns its capital cost over a period far longer than the working life over which such equipment is normally assessed, and the case for the retrofit cannot be made on the energy figures as they stand. The projected saving is a projection, not a measurement, and it is stated as such; the seasonal character of the steam figures, flagged in the steam section, qualifies the steam side of the assessment but does not rescue the payback, which is computed from the annual electricity figures. The recommendation is therefore that the retrofit not be approved on the present case. A case could be reopened on different evidence: a measured refrigeration load profile across a full year, steam records for a full year in place of the single winter month, or a capital cost materially below the figure quoted.
