On the evidence in this assessment, the electricity saving is real in direction and insufficient in size, and the plant's energy attention is better spent first on the refrigeration load itself, whose size is the reason both the electricity total and the rejected-heat quantity are what they are.

The electricity total also sets the scale against which every recommendation in this assessment must be judged. A measure that saves a small fraction of a small load is a small measure, whatever its percentage, and the percentages quoted for individual systems can mislead a reader who does not hold the total in mind. Refrigeration's share of the total is the reason the retrofit was evaluated at all: a heat-recovery project attached to a minor load could not have produced even the saving projected here. The share is equally the reason the assessment ends where it does, because the same dominance that makes refrigeration the obvious place to look for savings also means that the load itself, rather than the recovery of its rejected heat, is the quantity that most deserves the plant's attention.

Within the refrigeration load, the duties differ in how they can be changed. The cooling of incoming milk is fixed in quantity by the volume and temperature of the milk itself, and no efficiency measure alters the heat that must be removed from it; only the efficiency of the plant that removes it can change. Cold storage, by contrast, contains an element that better insulation, better door discipline, and better control of infiltration can genuinely reduce, because part of that load is heat leaking into a space that is then expensively held cold. An assessment that treats the refrigeration total as one number cannot separate the part of the load that is intrinsic to the product from the part that is an artefact of the building and its operation, and the separation matters, because the two parts respond to different measures and different spending.

The steam system has its own bearing on the retrofit question that the payback figure alone does not capture. Recovered heat from refrigeration is available at the times the refrigeration plant runs, which is to say broadly and continuously; steam demand at the plant is concentrated at cleaning and at processing peaks. The mismatch does not appear in an annual balance, where the totals can be set against each other as if they were simultaneous, but it appears in operation, where heat recovered at a moment of no demand is heat wasted. A design that took the annual totals at face value would overstate the displacement the retrofit can achieve, and the overstatement would grow with the size of the installation. This is a further reason, beyond the payback, for treating the projected saving as an upper bound on what the retrofit would deliver.

The assessment closes on the state of the evidence rather than on the state of the plant. The plant's energy position, as far as the records show it, is ordinary for its type: a refrigeration-dominated electricity demand, a seasonal and peaky steam demand, and a proposed retrofit whose projected saving is too small against its cost. What is not ordinary is how much of the case rested on how little record: a single winter month of steam data asked to support annual conclusions, and a projected saving asked to support a capital decision. The plant can put both right cheaply, by metering and by keeping the records it already generates for a full year before the question is asked again. The next assessment of this plant should be able to argue from a year of evidence, and this one is written so that its conclusions can be replaced by that argument, point by point, when the evidence exists.

fact_base: A defect-reduction project on a moulding cell cut the reject rate from 4.9% to 2.2% over one quarter. At 139k units per year the change avoids about 3753 rejected units per year. The quarter included a planned shutdown; rates are not adjusted for it.
input:
This operations case describes a defect-reduction project that was carried out on a moulding cell, and it reports the impact that the project has had on the reject rate over the course of one quarter. Before the project, the reject rate stood at 4.9%, but following the changes that were implemented, it was successfully reduced to 2.2%, which represents a substantial improvement in the performance of the cell.

In terms of volume, the cell produces 139k units per year, and at this level of output the change in the reject rate means that the operation avoids about 3753 rejected units per year, which would otherwise have been produced and subsequently scrapped. This gives a tangible sense of the scale of the benefit that the project has delivered in practice.

It is important to note, however, that the quarter in question included a planned shutdown, and the rates that are reported here are not adjusted for it. This is a relevant caveat, because the shutdown may have influenced the volumes and the production mix during the quarter, and so the reported improvement should be interpreted with this context in mind when it is compared with performance in other periods.

Going forward, it will be interesting to see whether the improved reject rate can be sustained in subsequent quarters, when the cell is operating under more normal conditions and without the disruption associated with the project itself, and the results of those quarters will provide a firmer basis on which to judge the lasting impact of the changes that have been made.
target:
A defect-reduction project on a moulding cell cut the reject rate from 4.9% to 2.2% over one quarter. At 139k units per year, the change avoids about 3753 rejected units per year.

The two figures describe the same result at different scales. The rate difference is the share of production no longer rejected; the unit figure is that difference applied to the annual volume of the cell, and it is the figure that connects the project to scrap handling, rework capacity, and material consumption. Both figures rest on the quarter's rates holding for a full year at the stated volume. The project changed the cell's reject performance within the quarter in which the changes were made; the annual unit figure is the quarter's rate difference carried forward, not a count of units observed over a year.

The quarter included a planned shutdown, and the rates are not adjusted for it. A shutdown changes the running hours and the mix of work the cell handled in the quarter, so the reported rates describe a quarter that was not a normal production period. The size of that effect is not separated in the reported figures, and the improvement is therefore stated as measured, with the shutdown named as part of the conditions under which it was measured.

The result is a rate, and it should be read as one. A reject rate compares rejected units with the units produced in the same period, so it is not distorted by the shutdown in the way a simple count of rejected units would be; a shorter running period produces fewer rejects and fewer good units together. The reported improvement is therefore a comparison between the cell as it ran in the project quarter and the cell as it ran in the period before the project, under production conditions that were not held constant, and it is stated without any adjustment for that difference.

fact_base: Excerpt content: a seal replacement takes about 72 min with the unit isolated; the excerpt gives the isolation steps only. The excerpt warns once about stored pressure and does not repeat the warning.
input:
With the PTW in place and the work area prepared, attention turns to the isolation of the duty pump so that the seal replacement can be carried out safely, the whole task taking about 72 min once the unit has been properly isolated. The first step is to stop the duty pump in the normal manner and to confirm that the standby pump has taken over the duty without interruption, since the process must continue to run throughout the work. The suction and discharge isolation valves are then closed in turn, and the pump is drained down to the safe drain point so that the casing is emptied of process fluid.

It is essential to appreciate that the pump casing and the connected pipework may still contain stored pressure even after the pump has been stopped and the valves have been closed, and for this reason the isolation is not considered to be complete until the pressure has been proven to be fully released at the vent point. Once this has been confirmed, the isolation valves are locked and tagged in accordance with the PTW arrangements, and the zero-energy state of the pump is verified before any tools are brought to the seal housing. Only at this point, with each of these steps completed and recorded, is the duty pump handed over in a safe condition for the seal itself to be removed.

The proving of the vent point deserves particular emphasis, since it is the step that converts the isolation from a matter of valve positions into a condition that has actually been demonstrated, and experienced technicians are well aware that a line which appears to be fully isolated can on occasion retain a surprising quantity of trapped energy. For this reason the step is never omitted, even where the same task has been performed many times before without incident.
target:
Isolation of the duty pump begins with the transfer of duty. The duty pump is stopped in the normal manner and the standby pump is confirmed running and carrying the flow, because the process continues throughout the seal replacement, which takes about 72 min with the unit isolated. The suction isolation valve is closed first, then the discharge isolation valve, so that the pump is separated from the system on both sides. The casing is drained to the safe drain point until it runs empty.

Stored pressure can remain in the casing and in the pipework between the closed valves after the pump has stopped, and the isolation is not complete until that pressure has been released and proved released at the vent point. The isolation valves are then locked and tagged under the PTW, the locks are recorded against the permit, and the zero-energy state is verified by a further check at the vent and drain before the pump is handed over. The handover is the end of the isolation: the pump stands stopped, drained, vented, and locked out, and the seal housing can be opened. No step in the sequence is shortened by the changeover having gone smoothly; a standby pump that starts cleanly says nothing about the state of the isolated machine.

The drain and the vent are proved separately, because each guards a different failure. A casing that drains freely can still hold pressure in a pocket above the liquid level if the vent is blocked, and a vent that blows clear says nothing about liquid trapped below a closed internal passage. Proving both is what converts the isolation from a valve position into a state that has been tested. The locks then preserve that state against the most likely disturbance, which is not malice but routine: another operator, on another task, restoring a valve that appears to have been left closed in error. The tag carries the permit reference so that the person who finds the lock can find the reason for it before anything is touched.

fact_base: Energy assessment of a dairy plant, in four sections: current use, refrigeration, steam, and recommendation. Electricity use is 3617 MWh per year; refrigeration takes the largest share. A heat-recovery retrofit is projected to save 20% of electricity use, a derived saving of 723 MWh per year, at a capital cost of $498k. At $0.12 per kWh the derived annual saving is $86808 and the derived simple payback is 5.7 years. Steam figures are from one winter month and are flagged as seasonal in the recommendation.
input:
## Current use

This energy assessment provides a comprehensive overview of energy use at a dairy plant, with a particular focus on electricity consumption and on the opportunities that may exist to improve the overall energy position of the site. Electricity use at the plant is 3617 MWh per year, and this annual figure forms the central reference point for the assessment as a whole. Within that total, refrigeration takes the largest share of electricity use, which means that refrigeration is not simply one load among many but is instead the dominant element in the site's electricity profile. This is an important point, because it helps to explain why the assessment gives particular attention to refrigeration and to the possibilities for recovering heat from the refrigeration system. At the same time, it is worth noting that an annual electricity total of this kind brings together a wide range of operating patterns across the year. Production schedules change, storage requirements vary, and the demands placed on the plant are not constant from week to week or from season to season. The annual figure is therefore best understood as an aggregate picture of electricity use rather than as a description of any single operating day. Nevertheless, it provides a clear and useful basis for the assessment, and the prominence of refrigeration within the total is a consistent theme that runs through the sections that follow.

## Refrigeration

Refrigeration occupies a central position in the energy profile of the dairy plant, both because it takes the largest share of electricity use and because it operates in support of activities that are fundamental to the functioning of the site. The refrigeration system has to maintain appropriate conditions for materials and products that depend on reliable cooling, and it has to do so in a dependable manner across the full range of operating circumstances that the plant experiences. Loads on the system arise from the products that are cooled and stored, from heat entering cooled spaces, from the operation of associated equipment, and from the general movement of people and materials around the site. For these reasons, refrigeration demand is not a single fixed quantity but a changing load that responds to production activity and to the way in which cooled spaces are used and managed. Good operational practice therefore has an important role to play. Careful attention to the use of cooled storage, prompt attention to maintenance needs, and disciplined management of the openings through which heat can enter cooled areas all contribute to keeping the refrigeration load as low as reasonably practicable. At the same time, refrigeration is also the source of the heat that the proposed retrofit seeks to recover. In the course of its operation, the refrigeration system rejects heat, and it is this rejected heat that creates the opportunity for heat recovery. Any heat-recovery arrangement nevertheless has to respect the primary purpose of the refrigeration system. Cooling performance cannot be compromised in the pursuit of recovered heat, and the recovery arrangement needs to work alongside the refrigeration duty rather than in competition with it. It is within this context that the retrofit proposal should be understood.

## Steam

Steam forms the other major element of the energy picture considered in this assessment, although the evidence available in relation to steam is considerably less complete than the evidence available in relation to electricity. The steam figures used in the assessment are from one winter month. This is an important qualification, because a single month cannot be expected to represent the pattern of steam use across a whole year, and a winter month in particular may reflect seasonal conditions that differ markedly from those experienced at other times. Steam use at the plant is associated with the heating duties that arise in the course of production and with the general services that support operation. As with refrigeration, the load is not constant, and it varies with the level and pattern of activity on the site. Distribution and standby losses also form part of the overall picture, since steam systems characteristically lose energy between the point at which steam is raised and the points at which it is used. Because the available figures rest on one winter month, the assessment treats the steam position with appropriate caution. The figures are used to indicate the presence and general character of steam demand rather than to support detailed annual conclusions. This seasonal limitation is flagged again in the recommendation, where it is important that decisions are not based on steam figures that may give a misleading impression of the year as a whole. The steam section should therefore be read as a qualified part of the assessment, in contrast to the electricity position, which rests on a full annual figure.

## Recommendation

The recommendation of this assessment is that the heat-recovery retrofit should be taken forward, on the basis of the electricity case set out in the preceding sections. The retrofit is projected to save 20% of electricity use, which corresponds to a derived saving of 723 MWh per year, at a capital cost of $498k. At an electricity price of $0.12 per kWh, the derived annual saving is $86,808, and the derived simple payback is 5.7 years. These figures indicate that the project offers a worthwhile financial return on the basis of the electricity savings alone, while also reducing the overall energy demand of the site. It is recommended that site management should now progress the retrofit to the next stage of development, including confirmation that the recovered heat can be used effectively within the plant and that the arrangement can be integrated with the refrigeration system without compromising cooling performance. It is also recommended that the steam figures should not be used as part of the financial case at this stage, because those figures are drawn from one winter month and are flagged as seasonal. Overall, the assessment supports a positive decision on the retrofit, founded on the measured annual electricity position and on the central role of refrigeration within it, with the steam position to be revisited when a fuller picture of steam use across the year is available. Taken as a whole, the assessment is intended to give decision-makers a balanced and evidence-based picture: a clear account of where electricity is used, a careful explanation of the role played by refrigeration, a suitably cautious treatment of the steam position, and a recommendation that follows from the strongest parts of the evidence. The structure of the document reflects that intention, and each section contributes to the overall conclusion that the proposed retrofit merits further development.
target:
## Current use

Electricity is the firmly based part of this assessment, and refrigeration dominates it. Electricity use at the dairy plant is 3617 MWh per year. Refrigeration takes the largest share of that total. The retrofit case in the recommendation rests on those two statements: an annual electricity figure that is measured, and a load structure in which the largest single use is the system whose rejected heat the retrofit would recover. The annual total aggregates a year of varying production and storage activity. It is not a description of any single day, and it should not be used as one. Its role is to fix the scale of electricity use and the share structure within it. On that role it is sufficient. Steam stands on weaker evidence, as the steam section sets out, and no part of the financial case in the recommendation is built on steam. The assessment therefore separates its conclusions by the quality of their bases. Conclusions about electricity and refrigeration rest on the annual figure. Conclusions about steam are held at the level the evidence supports, which is qualitative. That separation governs the recommendation: the retrofit is appraised on electricity alone, and the steam position is recorded as an open item rather than absorbed into the case as if it were measured. A further feature of the annual figure is that it conceals the timing of use. Electricity taken by refrigeration during production peaks and electricity taken to hold storage conditions overnight enter the same total, although they arise from different activities and respond to different controls. The assessment does not separate them, because the retrofit case does not require the separation: the case turns on the annual quantity and on refrigeration's share of it. Where a later design stage needs the load profile, metering at the refrigeration system will have to supply it.

## Refrigeration

Refrigeration takes the largest share of electricity use because cooling at the plant is continuous, load-bearing work. Cooled materials and products depend on the system holding its conditions through production, storage and movement across the site. The load itself is composite. Product entering cooled space brings heat with it. Cooled rooms gain heat through their fabric and through their doors. Fans, pumps and other associated equipment add their own heat to the spaces they serve. Production activity sets the overall level, and the pattern of the working day sets its variation. Operational discipline acts on several of these components at once: doors kept closed limit heat entry, maintained heat-exchange surfaces keep the plant working at its intended duty, and set-points held at their specified values prevent the system from cooling beyond the requirement. None of that changes the structural point. Refrigeration is the site's largest electricity use and the source of a continuous rejected-heat stream. The retrofit addresses the second of those facts. It would recover heat that the refrigeration system must reject in any case. The governing condition is that recovery stays subordinate to cooling. A heat-recovery arrangement that raised the refrigeration system's condensing burden or disturbed its control would trade the plant's primary duty for a secondary gain, and the assessment does not support such an arrangement. Recovery must take the heat the system rejects under its normal operation, at conditions the system already produces. The load structure also explains why refrigeration is treated as the assessment's centre rather than as one item in a list of uses. A saving applied to the largest share acts on the largest base. Measures addressed to smaller uses may still be worth taking, but they cannot carry a site-level case of this size, and the assessment accordingly spends its detail where the electricity is.

## Steam

Steam figures in this assessment are from one winter month, and they are flagged as seasonal in the recommendation. That single qualification controls everything that can be said about steam here. A winter month shows steam demand under winter conditions: heating duties at their seasonal level, distribution losses under the corresponding load, and production at whatever level that month carried. It does not show the annual pattern. Annualising one winter month would build the seasonal peak into every month of the year and would overstate the steam position by an amount that cannot be estimated from the month itself. The assessment therefore makes no annual claim for steam. Steam is recorded as a present and material energy use, associated with the heating duties of production and with site services, and its distribution and standby losses are noted as part of that use. No quantity is attached to any of those statements, because the evidence does not carry one. This is a deliberate asymmetry in the assessment. Electricity has an annual measured figure and is used quantitatively. Steam has a single seasonal month and is used qualitatively. When a full year of steam figures is available, the steam position can be restated on the same basis as electricity and the assessment can be extended. Until then, the seasonal flag is not a defect in the assessment; it is the assessment's accurate statement of what the steam evidence is. The same caution applies to comparisons with other sites. Steam use depends on the products made, the heating duties they impose and the season in which the figures were taken. A winter month from this plant cannot be set against an annual figure from another plant, or against this plant's own annual electricity figure, without misstating both. The figures are kept in their own frame: one month, in winter, at this site.

## Recommendation

Site management should take the heat-recovery retrofit forward on the electricity case. The retrofit is projected to save 20% of electricity use, a derived saving of 723 MWh per year, at a capital cost of $498k. At $0.12 per kWh, the derived annual saving is $86,808 and the derived simple payback is 5.7 years. The case is complete without steam: the projected saving is a share of a measured annual figure, the price is stated, and the payback follows from the two. Three conditions attach to the recommendation. The recovered heat must have a use on site that can accept it at the conditions the refrigeration system produces. The recovery arrangement must leave refrigeration performance and control undisturbed, for the reason given in the refrigeration section. Post-installation metering must record the electricity saving so that the projected figure is replaced by a measured one. The steam figures are excluded from the financial case. They are from one winter month, they are seasonal, and including them would weaken a case that does not need them. The decision requested is approval to develop the retrofit on the electricity basis stated, with the steam assessment to be revisited when a full year of steam figures exists. Development of the retrofit should also fix the measurement boundary before installation. The projected saving is a share of site electricity use, attributed to the refrigeration system. Unless the refrigeration load is metered separately, the saving will be visible only as a change in the site total, where production variation can mask it. A metered boundary at the refrigeration system converts the post-installation check from an argument about the site total into a direct reading of the load the retrofit acts on.

subtype: worked example with equation: Arrhenius ratio
fact_base: Rate constants for a polymer cure were measured at two temperatures. With activation energy $E_a$ of 81 kJ mol-1, raising the temperature from 300 K to 330 K multiplies the rate constant $k$ by 19.15. The estimate holds the pre-exponential factor $A$ constant over the interval.
input:
Temperature plays a particularly important role in determining how quickly a polymer cure proceeds, and even a relatively modest change in temperature can lead to a substantial change in the overall rate of reaction. In this particular example, rate constants for a polymer cure were measured at two temperatures, thereby providing a useful basis for examining how sensitive the curing process is to thermal conditions. The relationship between the rate constant and temperature is commonly described by the Arrhenius equation, which can be written as follows:

$$k = A \exp\left(-\frac{E_a}{R T}\right)$$ 

In this expression, $k$ represents the rate constant, $A$ represents the pre-exponential factor, $E_a$ represents the activation energy, $R$ represents the gas constant, and $T$ represents the absolute temperature. For the polymer cure considered here, the activation energy $E_a$ has a value of 81 kJ mol-1. When the temperature is raised from 300 K to 330 K, the rate constant $k$ is multiplied by 19.15, which clearly illustrates the strong temperature dependence associated with this process. It is nevertheless important to keep in mind that this estimate is based on an important simplifying assumption, namely that the pre-exponential factor $A$ remains constant over the temperature interval under consideration. Overall, the result highlights the fact that raising the temperature over this interval produces a much faster cure according to the measured Arrhenius behaviour, while also underscoring that the numerical ratio depends on the stated constant-$A$ assumption being maintained throughout the interval. Furthermore, the example serves as a useful reminder that an exponential relationship of this kind does not produce a merely proportional response to temperature. Because the temperature appears inside the exponential function, the practical effect of moving between the two stated temperatures is captured by the ratio rather than by a simple comparison of the individual rate constants in isolation. The presentation of the result in this form also helps to keep the underlying assumption visible, which is valuable when the ratio is later used to discuss curing behaviour over the same interval.
target:
Rate constants for a polymer cure were measured at two temperatures. The Arrhenius equation relates the rate constant $k$ to the absolute temperature $T$ through the pre-exponential factor $A$, the activation energy $E_a$, and the gas constant $R$:

$$k = A \exp\left(-\frac{E_a}{R T}\right)$$ 

For this cure, $E_a$ is 81 kJ mol-1. Raising the temperature from 300 K to 330 K multiplies $k$ by 19.15. The cure therefore proceeds much faster at the upper temperature, under the stated Arrhenius relation. The estimate holds $A$ constant over the interval. That assumption is part of the result: the ratio is the value obtained when the temperature changes and $A$ does not. No separate temperature dependence for $A$ is included, and the reported multiplier should be read with that condition attached. The measured activation energy sets the strength of the temperature effect, the two temperatures fix the interval, and the constant-$A$ condition fixes the form of the comparison. Within those bounds, the calculation gives a clear outcome: the same cure has a rate constant at the higher temperature that is larger by the stated factor, because the exponential term changes over the interval while the pre-exponential factor is held unchanged. The ratio form states the result without requiring either individual rate constant. It compares the same cure at the two temperatures, with the same activation energy and the same pre-exponential factor, so the comparison is internal to the stated system. The Arrhenius form also shows where the temperature acts: not as a separate multiplier added to the rate, but inside the exponential that sets the rate constant at each temperature. Reading the result in that order matters. The equation gives the structure, the activation energy gives the sensitivity, and the two temperatures give the evaluated change. The constant-$A$ condition then marks the boundary of the statement, because a temperature-dependent $A$ would belong to a different estimate and would not be represented by the ratio reported here.

fact_base: Cost review of a returns flow: 569 km per trip at $0.93 per km, 592 trips per year. Annual transport cost is $313k. Costs are carrier invoices for the last 12 months; empty running is included in the trip count.
input: This cost review takes a detailed look at the transport costs associated with a returns flow, with a particular focus on understanding the overall annual expenditure involved in moving returned goods through the operation. Based on the available figures, the returns flow involves a distance of 569 km per trip at a cost of $0.93 per km, and a total of 592 trips per year is carried out. When these elements are brought together, the annual transport cost is $313k. It is important to note that these costs are drawn from carrier invoices for the last 12 months, which provides a recent and relevant basis for the review. In addition, empty running is included in the trip count, meaning that the reported number of trips reflects not only the loaded movements but also the unloaded movements that form part of the overall returns operation. Overall, the review provides a clear picture of the current cost position for the returns flow, based on invoiced activity over the period considered. This framing is useful because it keeps the distance travelled, the rate charged and the frequency of travel together in a single annual figure, rather than treating each element in isolation. It also means that the review reflects the operation as it was actually invoiced during the period, including movements that did not themselves carry returned goods but were nevertheless part of the overall transport activity.
target: Annual transport cost for a returns flow is $313k. The flow runs 569 km per trip at $0.93 per km, with 592 trips per year. The cost base is carrier invoices for the last 12 months. Empty running is included in the trip count, so the annual figure covers loaded and unloaded movement together. The review therefore states the full invoiced cost of the returns operation over that period, on the trip definition used by the carriers. No part of the empty running is separated out, and the trip count should not be read as a count of loaded trips only. The three components of the figure are the distance per trip, the rate per kilometre, and the number of trips in the year. Each comes from the invoice record for the same period, which keeps the annual cost on one consistent basis. Any comparison with another period or another carrier needs the same trip definition, the same treatment of empty running, and the same invoice basis before the totals can be set against each other. The annual figure should therefore be read as an operating total, not as a price for the loaded leg alone. Its basis is activity-based: distance, rate and trip frequency are all taken from the same invoice period, and the unloaded portion of the work is inside the total rather than estimated separately.

subtype: worked example with equation: Arrhenius ratio
fact_base: Rate constants for a polymer cure were measured at two temperatures. With activation energy $E_a$ of 87 kJ mol-1, raising the temperature from 300 K to 330 K multiplies the rate constant $k$ by 23.83. The estimate holds the pre-exponential factor $A$ constant over the interval.
input:
It is widely recognised that temperature can exert a major influence on the rate at which a polymer cure takes place, and this example provides a helpful illustration of that effect in quantitative terms. Rate constants for a polymer cure were measured at two temperatures, and the temperature dependence is represented by the Arrhenius equation shown below:

$$k = A \exp\left(-\frac{E_a}{R T}\right)$$ 

Here, $k$ is the rate constant, $A$ is the pre-exponential factor, $E_a$ is the activation energy, $R$ is the gas constant, and $T$ is the absolute temperature. The activation energy $E_a$ for the polymer cure is 87 kJ mol-1. When the temperature is increased from 300 K to 330 K, the rate constant $k$ is multiplied by 23.83. This result clearly demonstrates the pronounced sensitivity of the cure rate to temperature. At the same time, it is important to note that the estimate rests on the assumption that the pre-exponential factor $A$ remains constant over the interval, and the stated ratio should therefore be understood within the context of that assumption. In addition, the example illustrates why temperature control can be such an important consideration in curing operations more generally. A change that may appear moderate when expressed simply as the difference between two temperatures can correspond to a very much larger change in reaction rate when the Arrhenius relationship is applied. For that reason, the ratio provides a compact and meaningful way of summarising the measured behaviour, although it should always be read together with the assumption on which it is based and with the specific temperature interval to which it applies.
target:
A polymer cure has rate constants measured at two temperatures. The Arrhenius equation gives the rate constant $k$ at absolute temperature $T$ from the pre-exponential factor $A$, the activation energy $E_a$, and the gas constant $R$:

$$k = A \exp\left(-\frac{E_a}{R T}\right)$$ 

The activation energy $E_a$ is 87 kJ mol-1. Raising the temperature from 300 K to 330 K multiplies $k$ by 23.83. The cure is therefore much faster at the upper temperature. The estimate holds $A$ constant over the interval, and the multiplier belongs to that condition. The activation energy fixes how strongly the exponential term responds to temperature; the two temperatures fix the interval over which the response is evaluated. With $A$ unchanged, the whole change in $k$ comes through the exponential term, and the reported ratio states the size of that change for this cure. The ratio is specific to the interval evaluated. It is not a general property of polymer cures, and it is not transferable to another interval without returning to the equation. Its content is narrower and stronger than a general statement about temperature: for this cure, with this activation energy and $A$ held constant, the exponential term changes enough over the interval to produce the stated multiplier. The result also separates the measured quantity from the modelled step. The rate constants were measured; the ratio between temperatures is the Arrhenius reading of those measurements under the constant-$A$ condition.

fact_base: A shell-and-tube exchanger heats cooling water in a refinery preheat train. Duty is 1780 kW. Hot stream: 180 °C in, 130 °C out. Cold stream: 35 °C in, 60 °C out. The log-mean temperature difference is 107 K and the installed area is 25.2 m2, giving an overall coefficient of 660 W m-2 K-1. Fouling was assessed from a single 90-day run; no cleaning cycle has been completed.
input: This results passage describes the performance of a shell-and-tube exchanger that heats cooling water in a refinery preheat train, bringing together the main thermal figures that characterise the unit. The duty of the exchanger is 1780 kW. The hot stream enters at 180 °C and leaves at 130 °C, while the cold stream, namely the cooling water, enters at 35 °C and leaves at 60 °C. The log-mean temperature difference for the exchanger is 107 K, and the installed area is 25.2 m2, giving an overall coefficient of 660 W m-2 K-1. Taken together, these figures provide a useful overall picture of the thermal performance achieved by the exchanger under the conditions considered. It is also worth noting the position in relation to fouling. Fouling was assessed from a single 90-day run, and no cleaning cycle has yet been completed. This means that the fouling position is based on a limited operating period and has not been followed through a full cycle in which the exchanger is cleaned and then returned to service. Overall, the reported values describe the exchanger as tested, while the fouling assessment remains limited by the fact that it rests on one run and on an operating history that does not yet include cleaning. The distinction between what has been measured and what remains untested is an important part of the picture. The thermal figures are presented as a coherent set, and they allow the reader to see how the exchanger is performing in terms of duty, temperature change and overall heat-transfer performance. The fouling position, by contrast, is necessarily more provisional, because the evidence comes from a restricted portion of the operating history and does not yet show the condition of the exchanger after a cleaning intervention has taken place.
target: A shell-and-tube exchanger in a refinery preheat train heats cooling water at a duty of 1780 kW. The hot stream enters at 180 °C and leaves at 130 °C; the cooling water enters at 35 °C and leaves at 60 °C. At a log-mean temperature difference of 107 K, the installed area of 25.2 m2 gives an overall coefficient of 660 W m-2 K-1. The coefficient is therefore the value consistent with the stated duty, area and temperature difference for this exchanger. Fouling was assessed from a single 90-day run. No cleaning cycle has been completed. The fouling position is thus the position observed over one run, before any cleaning has intervened. It does not describe the exchanger after cleaning, and it does not show how fouling develops across repeated cycles of operation and cleaning. The reported performance and the fouling assessment also rest on different spans of evidence. The duty, stream temperatures, area and coefficient belong to the stated exchanger condition. The fouling statement belongs to the run that was observed. Keeping those bases separate matters when the figures are used: the thermal values characterise the exchanger at the reported condition, while the fouling conclusion is limited to the single run and to a history with no completed cleaning cycle. The passage also separates the exchanger as a heat-transfer device from the exchanger as a fouling surface. As a heat-transfer device, it is described by the balance between the two streams and by the coefficient that reconciles duty with area and temperature difference. As a fouling surface, it is described only by what one run showed. Those are different kinds of statement. The first can be checked internally, because the reported quantities belong to one consistent thermal picture. The second cannot be extended beyond its run without new evidence, because fouling is a history-dependent condition and the history available here contains no cleaning event. The result is a complete thermal description with a deliberately narrow fouling conclusion attached to it.

fact_base: A continuous stirred-tank reactor runs an esterification that is first order in the limiting reactant. The rate constant is 0.1 min-1 at the operating temperature and the mean residence time is 50 min. Steady-state conversion for an ideal CSTR is 83.3%. The estimate assumes perfect mixing and constant density; tracer tests on the actual vessel have not been run.
input: This worked example considers a continuous stirred-tank reactor, often referred to as a CSTR, which runs an esterification reaction that is first order in the limiting reactant. The purpose of the example is to determine the steady-state conversion that would be expected under ideal conditions in a reactor of this type. The rate constant for the reaction is 0.1 min-1 at the operating temperature, and the mean residence time in the reactor is 50 min. On this basis, the steady-state conversion for an ideal CSTR is 83.3%. This result is obtained under a particular set of assumptions that should be kept clearly in mind when the figure is interpreted. In particular, the estimate assumes perfect mixing throughout the vessel and constant density across the reactor. It is also important to note that tracer tests on the actual vessel have not been run. As a result, the conversion figure should be understood as the value associated with ideal CSTR behaviour under the stated assumptions, rather than as a measured or fully verified description of the performance of the real vessel. Overall, the example provides a clear benchmark value for the conversion, while also highlighting the respects in which the real system may depart from the idealised picture on which the calculation is based. The example is therefore valuable in two related respects. It shows how the kinetic information and the residence time combine under the ideal CSTR model to produce a definite conversion figure, and it also makes clear that the figure depends on idealisations that are built into the model from the outset. Where those idealisations are accepted, the result follows in a straightforward manner. Where the behaviour of the actual vessel is in question, the missing tracer information becomes the central limitation, because without it there is no direct evidence about how closely the vessel approaches the perfectly mixed condition assumed in the calculation.
target: A continuous stirred-tank reactor (CSTR) runs an esterification that is first order in the limiting reactant. The rate constant is 0.1 min-1 at the operating temperature and the mean residence time is 50 min. For an ideal CSTR at steady state, these values give a conversion of 83.3%. The conversion is a property of the ideal reactor model applied to the stated kinetics. Perfect mixing is assumed, so the composition and temperature are uniform through the vessel and the exit stream carries the vessel composition. Constant density is also assumed, so the residence time and the reaction rate are used on a single volumetric basis. The two assumptions define the reactor that the result describes. The actual vessel has not been characterised by tracer tests. Its residence-time behaviour is therefore unmeasured, and any departure from perfect mixing in the real vessel sits outside the estimate. The reported conversion is the ideal-CSTR value for the stated rate constant and residence time. It is a benchmark for the real vessel, not a measurement of it, and the absence of tracer data marks the point at which the benchmark stops short of describing the installed reactor. The example also shows what the ideal model does with the kinetic statement. First-order behaviour in the limiting reactant means that the rate follows the concentration of that reactant, and the CSTR balance then sets the steady state at which reaction within the vessel matches the flow of reactant through it. The conversion is the outcome of that balance under perfect mixing. Nothing in the result depends on a measured outlet composition; it is calculated from the rate constant, the residence time and the model. That is the strength of the figure as a teaching and design benchmark, and also its boundary. It states exactly what an ideal vessel would do with the stated kinetics, and it leaves the real vessel to be established by the tracer evidence that has not yet been obtained.

fact_base: Adsorption of a dye from water on a metal-organic framework was measured in batch tests at 298 K. The fitted Langmuir capacity was 235 mg of dye per gram of adsorbent at pH 5. At an adsorbent dose of 0.6 g L-1, removal after 120 min was 83% of the initial dye concentration of 50 mg L-1. The Langmuir fit is reported for pH 5 only; capacity at other pH values was not measured.
input: This passage reports the results of batch adsorption tests in which the adsorption of a dye from water on a metal-organic framework was measured at 298 K. The experimental data were fitted using the Langmuir model, and the fitted Langmuir capacity was 235 mg of dye per gram of adsorbent at pH 5. In a further test carried out at an adsorbent dose of 0.6 g L-1, removal after 120 min was 83% of the initial dye concentration of 50 mg L-1. These results provide a useful indication of the capacity of the material and of the level of removal achieved under the particular conditions examined. However, it is important to note that the Langmuir fit is reported for pH 5 only, and capacity at other pH values was not measured. As a result, the reported capacity should be understood in the context of the conditions under which it was obtained, and it should not be assumed that the same capacity applies across a broader range of pH conditions than those actually investigated in the batch tests. The findings should consequently be read as a linked set of results that apply to the conditions of the tests themselves. The fitted capacity describes the adsorbent through the Langmuir representation, the removal result describes what was achieved at the stated dose over the stated contact period, and the pH limitation defines the boundary within which the capacity figure has actually been established by measurement.
target: Adsorption of a dye from water on a metal-organic framework was measured in batch tests at 298 K. The fitted Langmuir capacity was 235 mg of dye per gram of adsorbent at pH 5. At an adsorbent dose of 0.6 g L-1, removal after 120 min was 83% of the initial dye concentration of 50 mg L-1. The capacity and the removal figure describe different aspects of the same tests. The Langmuir capacity is the fitted saturation capacity of the adsorbent under the model. The removal value is the fraction of the initial dye taken up at the stated dose and contact time. Neither figure extends the pH range of the work. The Langmuir fit is reported for pH 5 only; capacity at other pH values was not measured. The results therefore hold at that pH, at the stated temperature, dose and contact time, and the capacity should not be carried to other pH values as if it had been measured there. Read together, the figures give a bounded picture of the material. The capacity comes from a model fit and carries the model's form with it. The removal figure comes from a direct batch outcome at the stated dose and time. The pH statement then prevents the most likely misreading of the pair of results, which would be to treat a capacity fitted at one pH as a property of the adsorbent at every pH. The passage keeps the property where the measurement put it.

fact_base: Capital appraisal for a solar array: installed cost $1100k, expected net saving $159k per year for 8 years. At a discount rate of 10% the present value of the savings is $848k and the net present value is $-252k. Savings are vendor and utility estimates; no saving has yet been measured on a comparable installation.
input: This capital appraisal considers a proposed solar array and brings together the key financial figures that are relevant to the investment decision. The installed cost of the solar array is $1100k, while the expected net saving is $159k per year for 8 years. Using a discount rate of 10%, the present value of the savings is calculated as $848k, which leads to a net present value of $-252k. Taken together, these figures indicate that, on the basis of the estimates used in the appraisal, the present value of the expected savings does not fully cover the installed cost over the period considered. It is also important to note that the savings are based on vendor and utility estimates, and that no saving has yet been measured on a comparable installation. Overall, the appraisal therefore rests on projected savings rather than on measured performance from an installation of this kind, and this point should be kept in mind when the figures are considered. The negative outcome is therefore not a marginal feature of the presentation but a central result of the appraisal as it stands. Even before any question is raised about the reliability of the savings estimates, the discounted value of those savings is already lower than the amount that would need to be committed at the outset, and the evidential position adds a further reason for caution because the savings themselves remain unmeasured.
target: On the stated estimates, the solar array should not proceed: its net present value is $-252k. The installed cost is $1100k and the expected net saving is $159k per year for 8 years. At a discount rate of 10%, the present value of the savings is $848k, which falls short of the installed cost. The shortfall is the decision figure: discounted savings do not repay the capital outlay within the appraisal. The savings are vendor and utility estimates. No saving has yet been measured on a comparable installation, so the appraisal carries estimate risk on its central input. A measured saving from a comparable installation would change the quality of the evidence, though not the arithmetic on the present figures. Until such a measurement exists, the case rests on projected performance, and the negative net present value stands as the appraisal result. The appraisal separates into two questions. The first is arithmetic: on the stated cost, saving, life and discount rate, the project returns less in present-value terms than it costs. The second is evidential: the saving is the figure with no measured installation behind it, so it is also the figure most exposed to revision. Both questions point the same way on the current record. The arithmetic gives a negative result even when the estimates are taken at face value, and the evidence base gives no measured performance with which to argue that the estimates are conservative.

fact_base: A gravity settler removes activated sludge from a process stream. Design overflow rate is 1.74 m h-1 at a throughput of 194 m3 h-1, giving a plan area of 111 m2. The overflow-rate basis is a vendor rule for this solid; no settling test on the actual slurry has been run.
input: This passage describes the sizing basis for a gravity settler that is used to remove activated sludge from a process stream. The design is based on an overflow rate of 1.74 m h-1 at a throughput of 194 m3 h-1, giving a plan area of 111 m2. In other words, the size of the settler follows directly from the combination of the throughput that has to be handled and the overflow rate that has been adopted for design purposes. It is nevertheless important to note the basis on which the overflow rate has been selected. The overflow-rate basis is a vendor rule for this solid, and no settling test on the actual slurry has been run. This means that the plan area, while it follows clearly from the stated design figures, ultimately rests on a general rule supplied for the solid rather than on settling behaviour measured directly for the slurry that the settler will treat in practice. Overall, the sizing is therefore best understood as a rule-based design figure, with the absence of an actual settling test representing an important limitation on the extent to which the design has been verified. The passage therefore separates the sizing calculation itself from the separate question of how firmly the governing design rate has been established for the material in question.
target: A gravity settler removing activated sludge from a process stream is sized on a design overflow rate of 1.74 m h-1. At a throughput of 194 m3 h-1, the overflow rate gives a plan area of 111 m2. The area follows directly from the throughput and the adopted overflow rate: the settler must present enough plan area for the flow to pass at or below that rate. The overflow-rate basis is a vendor rule for this solid. No settling test on the actual slurry has been run. The design therefore rests on a general rule for the solid, not on measured settling behaviour of the slurry to be treated. That distinction fixes the status of the plan area. The arithmetic of the sizing is complete on the stated figures, but the input that governs the answer has not been checked against the actual material. A settling test on the slurry would test the overflow rate itself; until it is run, the area is a rule-based design value. The settler sizing is consequently complete as a calculation and incomplete as a verification. The plan area is the answer to the stated throughput at the adopted rate. The open point is not the division that produces the area but the rate that the division takes as given, and that point can only be closed by settling behaviour measured on the slurry itself.

fact_base: Excerpt content: the analogy between the transfer processes is stated, then qualified by the case where it fails. The excerpt works one short numerical check with numbers given inside the excerpt itself. The excerpt assumes the chapter's earlier definitions and adds none.
input: The discussion now turns to the Chilton-Colburn analogy, which provides a particularly useful way of linking the behaviour of momentum transfer with the behaviour of mass transfer. According to the Chilton-Colburn analogy, the mass-transfer factor $j_D$ is related in a simple and elegant way to the friction factor $f$, and this relationship allows insights gained in one area of transfer processes to be carried across into another. By way of a short numerical check, if the friction factor $f$ is 0.0064, then the corresponding value obtained from $f/2$ is 0.0032, and this is the value that the analogy assigns to $j_D$ in this instance. This kind of comparison is valuable because it shows, in concrete terms, how the analogy can be used to move between a friction quantity and a mass-transfer quantity. At the same time, however, it is important to recognise that the analogy has its limits. The analogy rests on the idea that the underlying transfer mechanisms are sufficiently similar for the comparison to be meaningful. Where part of the friction arises from effects that have no real counterpart in the mass-transfer process, such as form drag or pronounced surface roughness, the simple relationship becomes less dependable. In such cases, the friction factor reflects additional resistance that is not matched by a corresponding enhancement of mass transfer, and the analogy should therefore be applied with a degree of caution rather than being treated as universally valid. It should also be borne in mind that the value produced by the analogy is only as meaningful as the comparison that lies behind it. The analogy does not remove the need to think carefully about the nature of the surface and the character of the flow, and it is precisely in those features that the difference between a dependable application and a questionable one is most often to be found.
target: The Chilton-Colburn analogy also carries across the transfer processes: it sets the mass-transfer factor $j_D$ against the friction factor $f$ and treats the two as measures of comparable boundary-layer behaviour. A short check shows the size of the link. For $f$ at 0.0064, $f/2$ gives 0.0032 as the value of $j_D$. The check is purely internal to the analogy. It takes the friction quantity as given and returns the mass-transfer quantity that the analogy pairs with it. The qualification follows from what the friction factor can contain. Friction in a real passage is not always boundary-layer friction of the kind the analogy assumes. Where form drag contributes to $f$, or where a rough surface raises friction by disturbing the flow mechanically, the added resistance has no mass-transfer counterpart. The surface then exacts more momentum transfer than the analogy expects for the mass transfer it delivers, and the pairing between $j_D$ and $f$ weakens. The analogy therefore holds where the friction is of the comparable kind and fails progressively where friction is produced by geometry or roughness rather than by the boundary-layer process that mass transfer shares. Its proper use in this chapter is as a comparison with a stated boundary, not as an identity to be applied to every surface and every flow arrangement that produces a friction factor. The excerpt's check therefore does two things at once. It fixes the arithmetic of the analogy on a stated friction factor, and it marks the physical assumption that the arithmetic carries with it. Where that assumption is met, the analogy gives the mass-transfer factor directly from the friction factor and saves a separate measurement. Where it is not met, the same calculation still produces a number, but the number no longer represents the pairing the analogy asserts. The distinction is not between using the analogy and rejecting it. It is between using it inside the conditions that make its quantities comparable and using it where the friction factor has been inflated by effects that mass transfer does not share.

fact_base: A tutorial passage explains the pump affinity laws for a centrifugal pump at varying speed. The passage states the three proportionalities in words: flow with speed, head with speed squared, power with speed cubed. A worked check is included: doubling speed multiplies power by 8. No other numbers are introduced.
input: This tutorial passage explains the pump affinity laws, which are a set of simple and highly useful relationships that describe how the performance of a centrifugal pump changes when its speed is varied. Understanding these relationships is valuable because they allow the behaviour of the pump at one speed to be related, in a straightforward way, to its expected behaviour at another speed. The affinity laws consist of three proportionalities. First, the flow varies in direct proportion to the speed: as the speed increases, the flow increases in line with it. Secondly, the head varies with the square of the speed, so a change in speed produces a more pronounced change in the head that the pump generates. Thirdly, the power varies with the cube of the speed, which means that the power requirement responds even more strongly to a change in speed than either the flow or the head. A simple worked check helps to make this point clear. If the speed is doubled, the power is multiplied by 8. This striking result follows directly from the third proportionality and illustrates why even moderate changes in pump speed can have such a significant effect on power demand. Overall, the three proportionalities together provide a compact summary of how flow, head and power each respond when the speed of a centrifugal pump is changed. It is also worth emphasising that the laws are most helpful when they are considered together rather than in isolation. A change of speed does not alter only one aspect of pump performance; it alters the flow, the head and the power at the same time, each in its own proportion. Keeping the three relationships together gives a much fuller picture of what a proposed speed change actually involves for the pump and for the equipment that drives it.
target: The pump affinity laws state how a centrifugal pump responds to a change of speed, and the outcome for power is the sharpest of the three: doubling the speed multiplies the power by 8. The laws are three proportionalities. Flow is proportional to speed. Head is proportional to the square of the speed. Power is proportional to the cube of the speed. Each law compares the same pump at two speeds, with the geometry unchanged, and each quantity takes its own exponent. Flow follows the speed directly, because the volume displaced per unit time scales with how fast the impeller turns. Head follows the square, because the velocity imparted to the liquid scales with speed and the head follows the square of that velocity. Power follows the cube, because it combines the flow scaling with the head scaling in a single product. The worked check is the cube law read at a doubling. Twice the speed gives twice the flow at four times the head, and the power, as the product of the two, rises by the full factor stated at the outset. The three proportionalities should be applied as a set. Using the flow law alone gives the new duty rate but not the new duty point pressure or the new load on the driver. The affinity laws describe the pump itself under a speed change; they state how its characteristic quantities move together when speed is the only variable altered. The exponents also explain why speed is such a strong control variable for a pump. A modest increase in speed buys flow at a moderate rate, head at a faster rate, and a power bill at the fastest rate of all. Conversely, a modest reduction in speed gives up flow slowly while shedding power quickly. That asymmetry is the practical content of the affinity laws, and it follows from the exponents alone, without any property of a particular pump beyond the laws themselves. The same pump, the same liquid and the same geometry are assumed throughout; the laws compare speeds, and only speeds.

fact_base: Excerpt content: two groups report conflicting lifetime values for the same material class; the excerpt weighs their test conditions. The excerpt reaches a limited preference and states the condition on which it rests.
input: Turning to the disagreements that appear in the literature, it is clear that the position in relation to lifetime is considerably less settled than might initially be expected. For the benchmark material, two groups report conflicting lifetime values, even though both are concerned with the same general class of material. At first glance, this might appear to suggest that one of the two sets of results must simply be wrong. However, a closer examination of the reports shows that the position is more nuanced than that, because the test conditions under which the values were obtained are by no means identical. Lifetime is a particularly condition-sensitive quantity, and the way in which a test is carried out can have a substantial bearing on the value that is ultimately reported. Differences in how the material is exposed, how the test is continued over time, and how the end of useful life is recognised can all contribute to divergent outcomes. When the two reports are weighed against each other, the more persuasive account is the one whose conditions correspond more closely to the service for which the material is being considered, and whose treatment of the end of life is clearer and more consistent. On that basis, a limited preference can be given to the values obtained under conditions closer to the intended application. Nevertheless, this preference should be understood as a conditional one. It rests on the closeness of the test conditions to the proposed service, and it does not resolve the disagreement for applications whose conditions differ from those that support the preference expressed here. The disagreement is best approached in that conditional spirit throughout.
target: For the benchmark material, the conflicting lifetime values reported by the two groups are best read through their test conditions. Lifetime is not a fixed property that a test simply reveals. It is the outcome of an exposure carried out in a particular way, continued for a particular course, and ended by a particular judgement about when useful life is over. Each of those choices enters the reported value. A group that exposes the material gently and ends the test at a strict endpoint reports a different quantity, in effect, from a group that exposes it hard and allows a looser endpoint, even where the material class is the same. The disagreement is therefore partly a disagreement about what was measured. Weighing the reports means weighing those choices. The account that carries more weight is the one whose exposure and endpoint correspond more closely to the service under consideration, and whose endpoint is stated clearly enough for the correspondence to be judged. On that basis a limited preference rests with the values measured under conditions closer to the intended application. The preference is limited in two ways. It depends on the closeness that supports it, so a different application with different service conditions could reverse the weighing. It also leaves the underlying spread in place: the preference selects the more relevant report for a stated use, and it does not convert either value into a general lifetime for the material class. A further point concerns the endpoint by which life is judged. Two tests can expose a material in closely similar ways and still report different lifetimes because one treats life as ended at an earlier stage of decline than the other. Unless the endpoints are brought into the comparison, the values appear to conflict about the material when they may conflict only about the definition of the end of life.
