fact_base: A centrifugal pump moves light diesel between two vessels at grade. At the duty point the flow is 94 m3 h-1 against a head of 52 m, with pump efficiency 82%. Shaft power at the duty point is 16.2 kW. The motor is rated 15% above this value. Cavitation was not observed in the acceptance test, which ran for 4 h at the duty point only.
input: A centrifugal pump is used to transfer light diesel between two vessels that are located at grade, and this passage provides an overview of the performance that was recorded for the pump at its duty point. At the duty point, the pump delivers a flow of 94 m3 h-1 against a head of 52 m, with a pump efficiency of 82%, and the shaft power at the duty point is 16.2 kW. It is important to note that the motor is rated 15% above this value, giving a derived rating of 18.63 kW (16.2 x 1.15), so the installed motor stands comfortably above the power that the duty point requires. Cavitation was not observed in the acceptance test, which ran for 4 h at the duty point only, and this result is generally taken as a reassuring indication for the installation as a whole. The figures should be understood as a complete description of how the pump behaves at the point where it is intended to operate, covering the flow it moves, the head it develops, the efficiency it achieves and the power it draws, together with the cavitation behaviour that was seen during testing. Each of these quantities has been determined at one and the same operating condition, namely the duty point at which the pump is intended to run in service, and the values are mutually consistent in the sense that they all describe that single condition rather than a spread of conditions drawn from across the pump's operating range. The acceptance test, furthermore, was carried out at that same point, and it is on the basis of this test, and on no wider programme of testing, that the statement about cavitation ultimately rests. Overall, the picture that emerges is of a pump whose duty-point performance has been measured and recorded in full, with the motor sized above the measured shaft power and no cavitation observed during the acceptance test at that point.
target:
A centrifugal pump moves light diesel between two vessels at grade. At the duty point the flow is 94 m3 h-1 against a head of 52 m, with pump efficiency 82%. Shaft power at the duty point is 16.2 kW. The motor is rated 15% above the shaft power, a derived rating of 18.63 kW (16.2 x 1.15). Cavitation was not observed in the acceptance test, which ran for 4 h at the duty point only.

The duty point is the operating condition the pump is required to meet, and every figure in this passage belongs to that condition. Flow, head, efficiency and shaft power are stated together because each describes the same point: the flow the pump delivers, the head it develops at that flow, the efficiency at which the delivery is made, and the power the shaft draws in making it. No figure describes any other condition, and the passage reports no measurement away from the duty point.

The cavitation result is a detection statement with a narrow scope. Within a test at one operating point, no cavitation appeared; the test says nothing about cavitation at other flows, other heads, or over longer running. The motor margin is likewise a statement about the duty point alone: the rating exceeds the shaft power measured there, and no allowance for off-duty operation is stated or implied.

The two vessels stand at grade, and the passage makes no statement about transfer between vessels at different levels. Efficiency is the pump's efficiency at the duty point; it is not a motor efficiency, and it is not an overall figure for the installation. Taken together, the reported quantities specify the machine the duty requires: a pump that delivers the stated flow against the stated head, driven at the stated shaft power, with a motor rated above that power and a cavitation record that covers the tested condition only.

fact_base: An amine absorption unit was tested at pilot scale on gas from a cement kiln. Over 45 days at 11 t of carbon dioxide per day, the unit captured 85% of the carbon dioxide in the treated gas. Steam demand was 3.8 gigajoules per tonne of carbon dioxide captured; solvent loss was 1.3 kg per tonne captured. Beyond 45 days, the effect of kiln dust on the solvent is untested.
input:
An amine absorption unit was tested at pilot scale on gas from a cement kiln. Over 45 days at 11 t of carbon dioxide per day, the unit captured 85% of the carbon dioxide in the treated gas. Steam demand was 3.8 gigajoules per tonne of carbon dioxide captured; solvent loss was 1.3 kg per tonne captured.

Amine absorption separates carbon dioxide from a gas stream by contact with an amine solvent, which takes up the carbon dioxide from the gas. The capture percentage takes the carbon dioxide in the treated gas as its whole: it is the part of that carbon dioxide which the solvent removed, and the part not captured leaves the unit with the treated gas. The capture figure is the share of the carbon dioxide in the treated gas that the solvent took up. Steam demand and solvent loss are stated on the same basis, per tonne of carbon dioxide captured, so the three results describe one run on one gas: capture states what the unit removed, steam demand states the heat the removal consumed, and solvent loss states the solvent the run consumed with it.

The test conditions bound every figure. The gas came from a cement kiln, the unit was a pilot unit rather than a full-scale plant, and the run held one treated rate for its whole length. No result describes a different gas, a larger unit, or a longer campaign.

Beyond 45 days, the effect of kiln dust on the solvent is untested. The figures therefore stand for 45 days of pilot operation on kiln gas, and the solvent's behaviour under longer exposure to kiln dust is not known.
target:
An amine absorption unit was tested at pilot scale on gas from a cement kiln. Over 45 days at 11 t of carbon dioxide per day, the unit captured 85% of the carbon dioxide in the treated gas. Steam demand was 3.8 gigajoules per tonne of carbon dioxide captured; solvent loss was 1.3 kg per tonne captured.

Amine absorption separates carbon dioxide from a gas stream by contact with an amine solvent, which takes up the carbon dioxide from the gas. The capture percentage takes the carbon dioxide in the treated gas as its whole: it is the part of that carbon dioxide which the solvent removed, and the part not captured leaves the unit with the treated gas. The capture figure is the share of the carbon dioxide in the treated gas that the solvent took up. Steam demand and solvent loss are stated on the same basis, per tonne of carbon dioxide captured, so the three results describe one run on one gas: capture states what the unit removed, steam demand states the heat the removal consumed, and solvent loss states the solvent the run consumed with it.

The test conditions bound every figure. The gas came from a cement kiln, the unit was a pilot unit rather than a full-scale plant, and the run held one treated rate for its whole length. No result describes a different gas, a larger unit, or a longer campaign.

Beyond 45 days, the effect of kiln dust on the solvent is untested. The figures therefore stand for 45 days of pilot operation on kiln gas, and the solvent's behaviour under longer exposure to kiln dust is not known.

subtype: worked example with equation: Antoine vapour pressure
fact_base: The vapour pressure of ethanol at 78 °C is estimated from the Antoine equation with constants $A$ = 8.20417, $B$ = 1642.89 and $C$ = 230.3 (pressure in mmHg, temperature in °C). The estimate is 100 kPa. The constants are valid only over their fitted temperature range; the source databank value governs design.
input:
This worked example is concerned with estimating the vapour pressure of ethanol at a temperature of 78 °C, and it does so by means of the Antoine equation, which is widely used for this kind of estimation. The Antoine equation, which relates the vapour pressure $P$ to the temperature $T$ through three fitted constants, $A$, $B$ and $C$, is written as follows:

$$\log_{10} P = A - \frac{B}{T + C}$$

For ethanol, the constants take the values $A$ = 8.20417, $B$ = 1642.89 and $C$ = 230.3, with the pressure expressed in mmHg and the temperature in °C, and substituting these constants together with $T$ = 78 into the equation gives an estimate of 100 kPa. It should nevertheless be kept in mind that the constants are valid only over their fitted temperature range, and that the source databank value is the value that governs design, so the figure obtained here should be regarded as an estimate rather than as a design value. It is worth emphasising that the exercise is an estimation exercise throughout: the equation does not measure anything, and the figure it produces is only ever as good as the fitted constants and the measurements from which those constants were originally obtained. The example therefore proceeds by identifying the applicable constants for the substance in question, confirming the temperature at which the estimate is required, and carrying out the substitution in a single step, after which the result is reported together with the caution that attaches to it.
target:
The vapour pressure of ethanol at 78 °C is estimated from the Antoine equation as 100 kPa. The Antoine equation relates vapour pressure $P$ to temperature $T$ through three fitted constants, $A$, $B$ and $C$:

$$\log_{10} P = A - \frac{B}{T + C}$$

For ethanol, $A$ = 8.20417, $B$ = 1642.89 and $C$ = 230.3, with pressure in mmHg and temperature in °C. Substitution of the constants and $T$ = 78 gives the estimate. The constants are valid only over their fitted temperature range; outside that range the equation has no standing, and at any temperature the source databank value governs design. The estimate therefore serves where an approximate vapour pressure is sufficient, and it does not displace the databank figure where a design value is required.

Vapour pressure is the pressure at which the liquid and its vapour stand in equilibrium at the stated temperature. It fixes the tendency of the liquid to evaporate, and it enters every calculation in which ethanol is boiled, condensed, or held under its own vapour. An estimate of it is therefore a working quantity, used where the calculation tolerates approximation.

The three constants are not properties of ethanol in the way a density is a property. They are coefficients fitted to measured vapour pressures over a stated temperature interval, and the equation reproduces the measurements only inside that interval. Outside it, the same constants can depart from the measured curve without warning, because nothing in the form of the equation constrains it beyond the fitted range. Within the range, the equation gives the pressure from the temperature alone, with no measurement on the sample in hand.

fact_base: A tutorial passage explains the Prandtl number to second-year students. Definition in words: the Prandtl number is the ratio of momentum diffusivity to thermal diffusivity. The passage must state what a value near 1 means and what a large value means, without inventing numerical examples.
input: The Prandtl number is an extremely useful dimensionless quantity that plays a central role in the study of heat transfer, and it can be understood as a comparison between two different ways in which a fluid spreads things out. On the one hand, momentum diffusivity describes how rapidly differences in velocity are smoothed out across a moving fluid, while on the other hand, thermal diffusivity describes how rapidly differences in temperature are smoothed out across the same fluid. The Prandtl number is, in essence, the ratio of momentum diffusivity to thermal diffusivity, and it therefore captures, in a single number, which of these two smoothing processes is the faster one for a given fluid. When the Prandtl number takes a value near 1, the two diffusivities are broadly comparable in size, which means that momentum and heat spread through the fluid at similar rates. When, by contrast, the Prandtl number is large, momentum diffusivity is much greater than thermal diffusivity, so velocity differences are ironed out over a much wider region than temperature differences, which remain confined to a comparatively thin layer. Where the Prandtl number falls below 1, the position is reversed: thermal diffusivity is then the greater of the two, and temperature differences are spread over a wider region than velocity differences.
target:
The Prandtl number is the ratio of momentum diffusivity to thermal diffusivity. Momentum diffusivity states how fast velocity differences even out across a fluid; thermal diffusivity states how fast temperature differences even out. The Prandtl number compares the two rates for one fluid, and its size states which process spreads farther.

A value near 1 means the two diffusivities are comparable. Momentum and heat then spread at similar rates, and the velocity and temperature fields adjust over similar distances from a surface. A large value means momentum diffuses much faster than heat. Velocity differences are smoothed across a thick layer, while temperature differences persist in a thinner layer near the surface, so the temperature field is the more confined of the two. A value below 1 reverses the comparison: heat diffuses faster than momentum, and the temperature field spreads beyond the velocity field.

The Prandtl number is a property comparison, not a flow measurement. It ranks two diffusivities of the fluid itself, and it states nothing about any particular flow until it is combined with the quantities that describe that flow.

The two diffusivities belong to the fluid, not to the flow. Geometry, speed and size enter a heat-transfer calculation through other quantities; the Prandtl number contributes only the comparison between the two rates at which the fluid itself smooths out differences. Read that way, the number is a statement about the fluid's internal behaviour, made before any apparatus is specified.

fact_base: Performance of a mechanical-draft tower at a chemical site was logged over one summer month. Mean wet-bulb temperature was 24 °C, the approach was 3 K and the range was 10 K. Performance outside the logged month, in particular at winter wet-bulb temperatures, was not measured.
input: The performance of a mechanical-draft tower at a chemical site was logged over the course of one summer month, and the results that were obtained during that period are summarised in this passage. The mean wet-bulb temperature over the month was 24 °C, the approach was 3 K and the range was 10 K, and from the wet-bulb temperature and the approach it follows that the cold water left the tower at a derived temperature of 27 °C. These figures together provide a valuable picture of how the tower performed under the warm conditions of the logged month, with the approach showing how closely the cold water approached the wet-bulb temperature and the range showing the temperature drop that the water underwent across the tower. It is, however, important to bear in mind that performance outside the logged month, and in particular at the lower wet-bulb temperatures that occur in winter, was not measured, so the recorded figures should not simply be assumed to hold throughout the year. Taken together, the wet-bulb temperature, the approach and the range may be regarded as a compact characterisation of the tower's behaviour during the period in question: the first of them describes the condition of the air with which the tower had to work, the second describes how nearly the tower was able to approach the limit which that condition imposed, and the third describes the amount of cooling that was actually achieved in the water as it passed through the tower. It is on this basis that the figures are offered as a record of the tower's summer performance.
target:
Performance of a mechanical-draft tower at a chemical site was logged over one summer month. Mean wet-bulb temperature was 24 °C, the approach was 3 K and the range was 10 K. The cold water therefore left the tower at 27 °C, a derived value (wet-bulb temperature plus approach).

A mechanical-draft tower moves its air with a fan, so the airflow does not depend on the height of the tower or on the wind. The wet-bulb temperature is the lowest temperature to which water can be cooled by evaporation into the air in its current state; it is a property of the air, not of the tower, and it sets the limit against which the approach is measured.

The approach is the difference between the cold-water temperature and the wet-bulb temperature; it states how closely the tower brought the water to the lowest temperature the air could accept. The range is the difference between the hot-water and cold-water temperatures; it states the cooling the water underwent in one pass through the tower. The range, by contrast with the approach, is a property of the duty: it states the cooling imposed on the water, whatever the air. Both figures are means over the logged month, and each belongs to that month's air conditions.

Performance outside the logged month was not measured. Winter wet-bulb temperatures in particular are untested, and the logged approach and range do not describe them: a lower wet-bulb temperature changes the limit the approach is measured against, and the tower's performance against that limit is unknown. A winter record would need winter air: the same tower, on colder and drier air, faces a lower wet-bulb temperature, and neither the approach it would hold nor the range it would show can be read off the summer figures. The figures stand as a one-month summer record for this tower at this site.

fact_base: A tutorial passage explains representative sampling of a gas emission. The passage covers where samples are taken, how many increments form one sample, and why a single grab sample misleads. No numerical limits are quoted; regulatory limits belong to the site's permit, not to the passage.
input: Representative sampling of a gas emission is a topic of considerable importance, because any measurement that is made on a gas stream can only ever be as good as the sample on which it is based. In order for a sample to be representative, it is essential that the samples are taken at a point where the emission stream is accessible and where the gas has had an opportunity to become thoroughly mixed, rather than at a point where the stream may still be stratified or disturbed. A sample, moreover, is not normally a single portion of gas collected on a single occasion; instead, it is built up from a number of increments that are collected at intervals over the period that the sample is intended to cover, and these increments are combined in order to form the one sample that is then analysed. A single grab sample, by contrast, captures the composition of the stream at one instant only, and it can therefore be seriously misleading, since the composition of a gas emission varies over time and a momentary sample may coincide with a peak, a dip, or a transient disturbance that the period as a whole does not resemble.
target:
Representative sampling of a gas emission rests on three choices: where samples are taken, how many increments form one sample, and over what period the increments are spread.

Samples are taken where the stream can be reached safely and where the gas is mixed. A stratified or disturbed stream gives different compositions at different points in the same cross-section, and a sample drawn from one point then describes that point rather than the emission. The sampling point is therefore chosen in a mixed region, and it is kept fixed, so that samples taken at different times differ because the emission differs, not because the sampling moved.

One sample is built from many increments, taken at intervals across the period the sample must represent and combined before analysis. A single grab sample holds the composition of one instant. Emissions vary over time, and an instant can fall on a peak, a dip, or a passing disturbance; the grab sample then reports that instant as if it were the period, and every quantity calculated from it inherits the error.

The increments are combined before analysis so that the laboratory receives the period, not a moment from it. Where increments cannot be combined, each is analysed and the results are averaged over the period; what matters is that no single instant stands for the whole. The sampling record states where the increments were taken and over what period, so that the result can be traced to the stream it claims to describe.

fact_base: A gravity settler removes activated sludge from a process stream. Design overflow rate is 1.67 m h-1 at a throughput of 233 m3 h-1, giving a plan area of 140 m2. The overflow-rate basis is a vendor rule for this solid; no settling test on the actual slurry has been run.
input: A gravity settler is used to remove activated sludge from a process stream, and the sizing of the unit is based on a design overflow rate of 1.67 m h-1 at a throughput of 233 m3 h-1, from which a plan area of 140 m2 is obtained for the settler. The relationship between these figures is a straightforward one, since dividing the throughput of 233 m3 h-1 by the overflow rate of 1.67 m h-1 gives the plan area of 140 m2 that the design adopts. It is worth noting, however, that the overflow-rate basis on which the whole sizing rests is a vendor rule for this solid, and that no settling test on the actual slurry has been run, so the design figures have not been confirmed against the behaviour of the material that the settler will in fact receive. The design procedure that has been followed is the conventional one for a unit of this kind: a permissible overflow rate is selected for the solid in question, the throughput that the unit is required to handle is established, and the plan area is then obtained directly from those two quantities, the intention being that a settler of that area will pass the required flow without exceeding the rate at which the solid can be expected to separate.
target:
A gravity settler removes activated sludge from a process stream. Design overflow rate is 1.67 m h-1 at a throughput of 233 m3 h-1, giving a plan area of 140 m2.

The overflow rate is the throughput divided by the plan area: the flow the settler accepts per unit of settling surface. The plan area follows from the two design figures (233 m3 h-1 divided by 1.67 m h-1 gives 140 m2), and it is the area the stated flow requires if the overflow rate is not to be exceeded. A larger throughput at the same area would raise the overflow rate above the design value, and the sizing holds only while the design rate is kept.

The overflow rate is the design handle on the settler. At the design rate, the upward velocity of the liquid in the settler is the rate at which a particle must settle to be removed, and the area is chosen so that the throughput does not drive that velocity higher. A larger throughput on the same area would raise the overflow rate beyond the design value, and the sizing would no longer rest on the vendor's rule.

The overflow-rate basis is a vendor rule for this solid. No settling test on the actual slurry has been run, so the rate the design assumes is the vendor's figure for the solid class, not a measured property of the slurry the settler will receive.

fact_base: Goal: compute the Reynolds number for water in a pipe and state the flow regime. The Reynolds number Re (dimensionless) is computed from density rho (kg m-3), mean velocity v (m s-1), pipe diameter D (m) and dynamic viscosity mu (Pa s) by Re = rho v D / mu. Water at 293 K: rho = 998 kg m-3, mu = 1.00 x 10-3 Pa s. Pipe diameter D = 0.05 m; mean velocity v = 0.7 m s-1. Worked result: Re = 34900 (computed as 998 x 0.7 x 0.05 / 0.001). Flow is laminar below Re = 2300 and turbulent above Re = 4000; between the two values the regime is transitional and is not assigned by the number alone.
input: In this worked example, the goal is to compute the Reynolds number for water flowing in a pipe and, having computed it, to state the flow regime that the result indicates. The Reynolds number Re (dimensionless) is computed from the density rho (kg m-3), the mean velocity v (m s-1), the pipe diameter D (m) and the dynamic viscosity mu (Pa s) by Re = rho v D / mu. For water at 293 K, the relevant values are rho = 998 kg m-3 and mu = 1.00 x 10-3 Pa s, while the pipe diameter is D = 0.05 m and the mean velocity is v = 0.7 m s-1. Substituting these values into the expression, that is, computing 998 x 0.7 x 0.05 / 0.001, gives a worked result of Re = 34900. In order to interpret this result, it is necessary to compare it with the usual thresholds: flow is laminar below Re = 2300 and turbulent above Re = 4000, while between the two values the regime is transitional and is not assigned by the number alone. The result that has been obtained, 34900, is therefore to be compared with these thresholds. Since 34900 lies well above the upper threshold, the flow in this case is turbulent. The example thus illustrates the general procedure by which a regime is assigned: the number is computed from the properties of the fluid and the geometry of the pipe, and the regime then follows from the position of the computed value in relation to the two thresholds, rather than from any direct observation of the flow itself.
target:
Compute the Reynolds number for water in a pipe and state the flow regime. The Reynolds number is 34900, and the flow is turbulent.

The Reynolds number Re (dimensionless) is computed from density rho (kg m-3), mean velocity v (m s-1), pipe diameter D (m) and dynamic viscosity mu (Pa s) by Re = rho v D / mu. Water at 293 K has rho = 998 kg m-3 and mu = 1.00 x 10-3 Pa s. Take the pipe diameter as D = 0.05 m and the mean velocity as v = 0.7 m s-1. Substitution of these values, 998 x 0.7 x 0.05 / 0.001, gives Re = 34900.

The regime follows from the thresholds. Flow is laminar below Re = 2300 and turbulent above Re = 4000; between the two values the regime is transitional and is not assigned by the number alone. The computed value stands above the upper threshold by a wide margin, so the assignment does not rest on the transitional range: at 34900 the flow is turbulent.

The check on the result is the threshold comparison itself. A value below the laminar limit would describe laminar flow, and a value between the limits would leave the regime unassigned; the value obtained stands in the turbulent range with room to spare, so no refinement of the input data at their stated precision would move the assignment. The viscosity is the input to which the result is most sensitive in kind: the Reynolds number varies inversely with it, and a different temperature, acting through the viscosity, would change the number, although at this margin it would not change the regime.

fact_base: A binary distillation separates propane/propylene at a relative volatility of 2.34 that is taken as constant over the column. Specifications: distillate 98 mol% light component, bottoms 2 mol% light component. The Fenske minimum stage count is 9.2 theoretical stages including the reboiler. The actual design uses a reflux ratio of 1.3 times the minimum; the stage count at that reflux comes from a separate simulation.
input: A binary distillation is used to separate a propane/propylene mixture, and the separation is characterised by a relative volatility of 2.34, which is taken as constant over the whole of the column. The specifications for the separation are that the distillate should contain 98 mol% of the light component while the bottoms should contain only 2 mol% of the light component. Applying the Fenske equation under these conditions gives a minimum stage count of 9.2 theoretical stages, including the reboiler, and this figure represents the lowest number of stages with which the specified separation could in principle be achieved. In the actual design, however, a reflux ratio of 1.3 times the minimum is used, and it should be noted that the stage count at that reflux does not come from the Fenske calculation but instead comes from a separate simulation, so the value of 9.2 stages should be understood as a limiting figure rather than as the design stage count. The minimum stage count is, in other words, a limiting result: it describes the separation as it would be performed under total reflux, and it is precisely because no actual column operates at total reflux that the figure is to be read as a bound upon the design rather than as a prediction of it.
target:
A binary distillation separates propane/propylene at a relative volatility of 2.34, taken as constant over the column. Specifications: distillate 98 mol% light component, bottoms 2 mol% light component. The Fenske minimum stage count is 9.2 theoretical stages including the reboiler.

The minimum stage count belongs to total reflux: it is the smallest number of stages that can make the specified split, and it is reached only in the limit where no product is withdrawn. The figure therefore bounds the design from below. It depends on the two specifications and on the relative volatility, and on nothing else; a tighter distillate specification or a lower relative volatility would raise it.

The relative volatility is the property the count turns on. It states how much more readily the light component vaporises than the heavy component in the same mixture, and a value well above unity is what makes the specified split attainable in few stages. Its constancy over the column is an assumption of the calculation; the count is exact only for the constant value stated.

The actual design uses a reflux ratio of 1.3 times the minimum. The stage count at that reflux comes from a separate simulation, not from the Fenske equation, and the design count will exceed 9.2 stages. Between the two bounds, minimum stages at total reflux and minimum reflux at an unlimited number of stages, the design chooses a working reflux and pays for it in stages.

fact_base: A flat firebrick wall of thickness 12 mm separates two process streams. Thermal conductivity of the wall is 1.1 W m-1 K-1 and the measured temperature difference across it is 318 K. Steady one-dimensional conduction gives a heat flux of 29150 W m-2. Surface (film) resistances are excluded from this estimate; including them lowers the flux.
input: This worked example considers a flat firebrick wall of thickness 12 mm that separates two process streams, and it sets out to determine the heat flux through the wall under steady conditions. The thermal conductivity of the wall is 1.1 W m-1 K-1 and the measured temperature difference across it is 318 K. For steady one-dimensional conduction, the heat flux is obtained by dividing the product of the conductivity and the temperature difference by the wall thickness, and since the thickness of 12 mm corresponds to 0.012 m, the calculation is 1.1 x 318 / 0.012, which gives a heat flux of 29150 W m-2. The figure of 29150 W m-2 is therefore best regarded as an upper estimate of the flux through the wall as installed. The example is a straightforward application of the conduction relation to a plane wall, and it depends upon the temperature difference being measured across the wall itself, upon the conductivity being the conductivity of the firebrick of which the wall is built, and upon the flow of heat being treated as one-dimensional, that is to say as passing straight through the wall from its hotter face to its colder one without spreading sideways within it. It should be noted that surface (film) resistances are excluded from this estimate, and that including them would lower the flux, so the value of 29150 W m-2 represents the conduction-only figure for the wall itself.
target:
A flat firebrick wall of thickness 12 mm separates two process streams. Thermal conductivity of the wall is 1.1 W m-1 K-1 and the measured temperature difference across it is 318 K. Steady one-dimensional conduction gives a heat flux of 29150 W m-2.

The thickness in metres is 0.012 m. The flux follows from the conductivity and the temperature difference divided by the thickness: 1.1 x 318 / 0.012 = 29150 W m-2. The result is large because the temperature difference is large and the wall, although a poor conductor, is thin; the flux is the product of those two stated quantities at the stated thickness, and it changes in direct proportion to the temperature difference.

Firebrick is chosen for its resistance to temperature rather than for its conductivity, and its conductivity is low. The flux is nevertheless large, because the temperature difference across a thin wall is large. The calculation treats the conductivity as constant across the wall, although conductivity is in fact a property that varies with temperature, and it treats the wall as uniform, with no cracks, joints or mortar lines offering a second path for the heat.

Surface (film) resistances are excluded from this estimate. Including them adds resistance in series with the wall and lowers the flux, so 29150 W m-2 is the conduction-only value for the 12 mm wall, not the flux the two streams would measure between them.

fact_base: Capital appraisal for a warehouse extension: installed cost $1575k, expected net saving $271k per year for 8 years. At a discount rate of 8% the present value of the savings is $1557k and the net present value is $-18k. Savings are vendor and utility estimates; no saving has yet been measured on a comparable installation.
input: This passage presents a capital appraisal for a warehouse extension, the purpose of which is to establish whether the expected savings from the project are sufficient to justify its installed cost. The installed cost of the extension is $1575k, and the expected net saving is $271k per year, which is expected to continue for 8 years. Discounting these savings at a discount rate of 8% gives a present value of the savings of $1557k, and when the installed cost is set against this figure, the net present value of the project works out at $-18k. It is important to appreciate that the savings figures used in this appraisal are vendor and utility estimates, and that no saving has yet been measured on a comparable installation, so the outcome of the appraisal rests on estimates that have not so far been confirmed in practice. The appraisal accordingly brings together the three elements that any such comparison requires: a capital figure that is incurred at the outset, a stream of savings that is expected to accrue evenly over the life of the project, and a rate at which those future savings are discounted in order to express them in present terms, and it is only when all three elements have been combined that the project can be said to have been appraised at all.
target:
The warehouse extension has a net present value of $-18k at a discount rate of 8%. The present value of the expected savings ($1557k) falls short of the installed cost ($1575k), so on the stated figures the savings do not repay the investment within the appraisal.

The appraisal rests on an expected net saving of $271k per year for 8 years. Discounted at that rate, those savings give the present value above; undiscounted, the same savings would exceed the installed cost, and the shortfall arises from discounting alone. The decision therefore turns on the discount rate and on the savings estimate, not on the arithmetic.

The appraisal is a comparison of two money figures at one point in time: what the extension costs to install, and what the savings are worth when each year's saving is reduced to its present value at the stated rate. A saving received later is worth less than the same saving received sooner, and discounting is the operation that expresses that difference; discounting, rather than the size of the savings, carries the result below zero. The finding is therefore marginal in size but not in sign.

The savings are vendor and utility estimates. No saving has yet been measured on a comparable installation, so the negative result carries the uncertainty of the estimates themselves: a measured saving below the estimate would deepen the shortfall, and the appraisal gives no measured figure against which the estimate can be checked.

fact_base: An amine absorption unit was tested at pilot scale on gas from a cement kiln. Over 60 days at 9 t of carbon dioxide per day, the unit captured 90% of the carbon dioxide in the treated gas. Steam demand was 3.6 gigajoules per tonne of carbon dioxide captured; solvent loss was 1.8 kg per tonne captured. Beyond 60 days, the effect of kiln dust on the solvent is untested.
input: An amine absorption unit was tested at pilot scale on gas from a cement kiln, and the results of the test are reported in this passage. Over a period of 60 days, during which the unit treated gas at a rate of 9 t of carbon dioxide per day, the unit succeeded in capturing 90% of the carbon dioxide in the treated gas. The steam demand associated with the capture was 3.6 gigajoules per tonne of carbon dioxide captured, while the solvent loss was 1.8 kg per tonne captured. These results are valuable as an indication of what the process can achieve under pilot conditions over a sustained period of 60 days, although it should be borne in mind that beyond 60 days the effect of kiln dust on the solvent remains untested, and so the longer-term behaviour of the solvent in this service is not yet known. The three results are reported together because they describe a single quantity of gas treated in a single run: the proportion of its carbon dioxide that the unit removed, the steam that the removal required, and the solvent that the run consumed, and none of the three figures can properly be detached from the conditions under which the others were obtained.
target:
An amine absorption unit was tested at pilot scale on gas from a cement kiln. Over 60 days at 9 t of carbon dioxide per day, the unit captured 90% of the carbon dioxide in the treated gas. Steam demand was 3.6 gigajoules per tonne of carbon dioxide captured; solvent loss was 1.8 kg per tonne captured.

Capture, steam demand and solvent loss are stated for the same run and the same gas. The capture figure is the share of the carbon dioxide in the treated gas that the unit removed; the steam and solvent figures are stated per tonne captured, so both scale with the quantity the capture figure counts.

The two consumption figures are the operating cost of the capture in physical terms: steam is the energy the separation consumes, and solvent loss is the material it consumes, and both are charged against the same tonne of captured carbon dioxide that the capture figure counts. A change in capture at the same total steam consumption would change the steam figure per tonne without any change in the unit's heat consumption in absolute terms, because the denominator of the figure is the captured quantity.Beyond 60 days, the effect of kiln dust on the solvent is untested. The results describe 60 days of pilot operation on kiln gas, and solvent behaviour over a longer exposure to kiln dust is not established by this test.

fact_base: Goal: compute the diffusive flux of oxygen through a stagnant water film. The diffusive flux J (mol m-2 s-1) is computed from the diffusivity D (m2 s-1) and the concentration gradient dC/dx, where C is concentration (mol m-3) and x is position (m). Fick's first law: J = -D dC/dx; the negative sign states that diffusion runs from high concentration to low concentration. Oxygen in water: D = 2.1 x 10-9 m2 s-1. Concentration falls by 0.2 mol m-3 across a film 0.4 mm thick, so dC/dx = -500 mol m-4. Worked result: J = 1.05x 10-6 mol m-2 s-1. The law as stated covers a stagnant medium; a moving medium adds convection, which the equation does not include.
input:
The goal is the diffusive flux of oxygen through a stagnant water film, and the result is 1.05 x 10-6 mol m-2 s-1. Fick's first law gives the flux from the diffusivity and the concentration gradient, and the steps below carry the stated values through that relation.

The diffusive flux J (mol m-2 s-1) is computed from the diffusivity D (m2 s-1) and the concentration gradient dC/dx, where C is concentration (mol m-3) and x is position (m). Fick's first law states the relation as J = -D dC/dx. The negative sign states that diffusion runs from high concentration to low concentration: where C decreases as x increases, the gradient is negative and the flux is positive in the direction of increasing x.

For oxygen in water, D = 2.1 x 10-9 m2 s-1. The concentration falls by 0.2 mol m-3 across a film 0.4 mm thick, so the gradient is dC/dx = -500 mol m-4, the fall divided by the film thickness with the sign of the direction of decrease.

Substitution gives J = -(2.1 x 10-9) x (-500) = 1.05 x 10-6 mol m-2 s-1. The flux is the product of a small diffusivity and a steep gradient; the steepness comes from the thinness of the film, and a film twice as thick at the same concentration fall would halve the gradient and the flux. The check on the result is the sign: a positive flux in the direction of decreasing concentration, as the setup requires.

Fick's first law as stated holds for a stagnant medium. A moving medium adds convection, which the equation does not include.

fact_base: Excerpt content: two groups report conflicting lifetime values for the same material class; the excerpt weighs their test conditions. The excerpt reaches a limited preference and states the condition on which it rests.
input:
It is worth noting that the lifetime values reported for the benchmark material differ quite substantially between the two groups, and this discrepancy arguably tells us more about the respective test conditions than about the material itself. The first group, for instance, measured lifetime on fresh beds under a dry feed and, perhaps unsurprisingly, reported the longer values, highlighting the stability of the material under favourable conditions. The second group, by contrast, worked with beds that had already been exposed to a humid feed, and its values are consistently lower right from the very first cycle onwards. When the two data sets are placed side by side, it becomes increasingly clear that they essentially describe two quite different ageing histories rather than two genuinely different materials, underscoring the importance of context when interpreting such results.

Another important factor in this comparison is the role of IAST. One group's lifetimes are based on breakthrough times predicted for mixtures, whereas the other group's lifetimes rest on direct mixture measurements, and this methodological difference should not be overlooked. Where the prediction and the measurement have actually been compared on the same bed, the prediction tends to run long, and the gap appears to widen as the feed humidity rises. This suggests that the dry-feed group's apparent advantage is, at least in part, an artefact of the route by which its numbers were obtained, with predicted lifetimes under relatively mild conditions being set against measured lifetimes obtained under noticeably harsher ones.

Overall, the measured values would seem to carry more weight, and a preference for the second group's figures as the basis for design therefore appears justified, albeit on one specific condition. That condition is that the design feed resembles the humid feed used in the measured tests. For a dry feed, the ranking is not really established by either data set, and the longer predicted lifetimes remain unconfirmed rather than wrong. What the comparison does ultimately settle is arguably narrower in scope: lifetime for the benchmark material is a function of feed humidity and ageing history, and a single lifetime value quoted without those conditions cannot simply be carried from one group's tests to the other's.
target:
The lifetime values reported for the benchmark material differ between the two groups by more than either group's internal scatter, and the difference tracks the test conditions each group chose rather than any property of the material itself. One group measured lifetime on fresh beds under a dry feed and reported the longer values. The other group measured on beds that had already seen humid feed, and its values sit lower from the first cycle onward. Read side by side, the two data sets describe two different ageing histories more than they describe two different materials.

IAST enters the comparison because one group's lifetimes rest on breakthrough times predicted for mixtures, while the other group's rest on direct mixture measurements. Where the prediction and the measurement have been compared on the same bed, the prediction runs long, and the gap widens as the feed humidity rises. The dry-feed group's advantage is therefore partly an artefact of the route by which its numbers were obtained: predicted lifetimes under mild conditions stand against measured lifetimes under harsher ones.

On the evidence available, the measured values carry more weight, and the preference goes to the second group's figures as the basis for design, on one condition. The condition is that the design feed resembles the humid feed of the measured tests. For a dry feed the ranking is not established by either data set, and the longer predicted lifetimes remain unconfirmed rather than wrong. What the comparison settles is narrower: lifetime for the benchmark material is a function of feed humidity and ageing history, and a single lifetime quoted without those conditions cannot be carried from one group's tests to the other's. Neither group is contradicted on its own ground; the conflict appears only when a value measured or predicted under one set of conditions is read as a property of the material, detached from the conditions that produced it.

fact_base: A vapour-compression unit serves a cold store, evaporating at 0 °C and condensing at 45 °C. The Carnot coefficient of performance between these temperatures is 6.07; the installed unit achieves 2.44. The achieved value is from the manufacturer's test at full load; part-load performance is not stated.
input:
In this example, we will examine the performance of a vapour-compression refrigeration unit serving a cold store, evaporating at 0 °C and condensing at 45 °C. The coefficient of performance, which is essentially the refrigeration effect divided by the work input, provides a convenient measure of how effectively the unit converts work into cooling. Between the two temperatures in question, the Carnot coefficient of performance is 6.07, and this value represents the theoretical maximum that no real cycle operating between 0 °C and 45 °C can exceed, regardless of how carefully it is designed or operated.

The installed unit, however, achieves a coefficient of performance of only 2.44, which is considerably lower than the Carnot value of 6.07. This gap arises because the ideal cycle does not account for a range of real-world losses, including pressure drops in the lines and heat exchangers, irreversibilities within the compressor, and heat transfer taking place across finite temperature differences in both the evaporator and the condenser. It is important to note that none of these individual contributions is separated out in the manufacturer's figure, which is simply a single overall test value for the complete unit.

Furthermore, the manufacturer's test was carried out at full load, so the stated value of 2.44 strictly applies to that particular operating condition. Part-load performance is not stated, and this is a significant limitation, because a cold store does not necessarily call for full load at all times. At part load, the balance between fixed losses and useful refrigeration shifts, and the coefficient of performance will move accordingly, in a direction that the available figure does not allow us to determine. Consequently, any seasonal energy estimate based on 2.44 will inevitably carry an unquantified degree of error, and the figure of 2.44 is really best suited to comparing units that have been tested in the same way, rather than to predicting actual running costs with any confidence. Any use of 2.44 outside the full-load condition should therefore be treated as provisional.
target:
A vapour-compression unit serving a cold store evaporates at 0 °C and condenses at 45 °C, and its coefficient of performance at full load is 2.44 against a Carnot value of 6.07 between the same temperatures. The coefficient of performance is the refrigeration effect divided by the work input. The Carnot value is the highest the ratio can reach for a cycle working between the two temperatures: it is fixed by the temperatures alone, and no machine exceeds it.

fact_base: Pricing case for a SaaS tier: price $206 per unit, variable cost $142 per unit, fixed costs $475k per year. Break-even volume is 7422 units per year; current volume is 7940 units per year. Volume figures are last year's actuals; the effect of the price on volume is not estimated.
input:
This pricing case examines a SaaS tier that is currently priced at $206 per unit, with a variable cost of $142 per unit and fixed costs of $475k per year. Each unit sold therefore contributes $64 towards covering the fixed costs and, ultimately, generating a profit. When the fixed costs of $475k are divided by this contribution of $64 per unit, the resulting break-even volume is 7422 units per year, which is the level of sales at which the tier exactly covers its costs and neither makes nor loses money.

Encouragingly, last year's actual volume was 7940 units, which is somewhat higher than the break-even level: the 7940 units achieved last year stand above the 7422-unit break-even level, with each unit carrying $64 of contribution. The difference between the two figures is 518 units, so the tier is currently operating above break-even, and the 518 units represent the whole of the safety margin, although it has to be said that the cushion is not especially large. A decline in volume of 518 units, for example, would bring the tier back to break-even, even before any changes in price or costs are taken into account, which highlights how sensitive the position is to relatively modest changes in demand.

It is also worth bearing in mind that all of these volume figures are based on last year's actuals, and may not necessarily be representative of future performance. More importantly, the effect of the price on volume has not been estimated, which means that the question of whether the $206 price should be changed cannot really be answered from these figures alone. A higher price would increase the contribution per unit above $64 and reduce the break-even volume below 7422 units, but what such a change would do to the current volume of 7940 units remains unknown, and could potentially offset the apparent gain.
target:

The figures are last year's actuals, and the case for changing the $206 price cannot be settled from them, because the effect of the price on volume is not estimated.

The price is $206 per unit and the variable cost is $142 per unit, so each unit contributes $64 toward the fixed costs of $475k per year. The fixed costs divided by the contribution per unit give the break-even volume of 7422 units per year: below that volume the tier loses money, and above it each further unit adds $64.

Last year's volume of 7940 units stands 518 units above break-even. The cushion is narrow. A decrease in volume of 518 units returns the tier to break-even before any change in price or costs, and the volume figures carry no allowance for a year weaker than last year. Volume is the exposed variable in the case: the price and both costs are set by the tier's own terms, while volume is set by customers and is the one figure in the calculation the tier does not control.

A higher price raises the contribution per unit above $64 and lowers the break-even volume below 7422 units. What a higher price does to the volume of 7940 units is not estimated, and that unknown decides whether the change pays: the arithmetic of break-even against the $475k of fixed costs is settled, and the demand response is the missing term.

fact_base: Adsorption of a dye from water on activated carbon was measured in batch tests at 298 K. The fitted Langmuir capacity was 257 mg of dye per gram of adsorbent at pH 7. At an adsorbent dose of 0.6 g L-1, removal after 120 min was 85% of the initial dye concentration of 50 mg L-1. The Langmuir fit is reported for pH 7 only; capacity at other pH values was not measured.
input:
In this study, the adsorption of a dye from water onto activated carbon was investigated in a series of batch tests carried out at 298 K. The experimental data were fitted to the Langmuir model, giving a fitted capacity of 257 mg of dye per gram of adsorbent at pH 7, which represents the maximum monolayer loading predicted by the model under these conditions. At an adsorbent dose of 0.6 g L-1, the removal achieved after 120 min was 85% of the initial dye concentration of 50 mg L-1, corresponding to a residual concentration of 7.5 mg L-1 remaining in solution.

It is important to understand that the capacity of 257 mg per gram is a parameter obtained from the fit rather than a directly measured loading. Essentially, it is the plateau that the Langmuir equation assigns to the isotherm at pH 7, and it therefore describes the carbon and dye combination at that specific pH value only. The capacity at other pH values was not measured, and the figure should not be assumed to transfer across pH, since the charge carried by the dye and by the carbon surface both vary with pH, and the fitted value inevitably absorbs the combined effect of these changes.

Similarly, the removal figure of 85% is tied to the particular conditions under which it was obtained. With a dose of 0.6 g L-1 and an initial concentration of 50 mg L-1, a total of 42.5 mg L-1 was removed over the course of 120 min, and a different dose or a different starting concentration would produce a different percentage removal without any change in the carbon itself. The 85% figure can therefore only really be used to rank this carbon against other carbons when the comparison is made at the same dose, the same initial concentration, and the same contact time.
target:

At an adsorbent dose of 0.6 g L-1, removal after 120 min was 85% of the initial dye concentration of 50 mg L-1, leaving 7.5 mg L-1 in solution.

The capacity figure is a fit parameter, not a measured loading: it is the plateau the Langmuir equation assigns to the isotherm at pH 7, and it describes the carbon-dye pair at that pH only. Capacity at other pH values was not measured, and the value does not transfer across pH, because the charge on the dye and on the carbon surface both move with pH and the fit absorbs their combined effect.

The fitted capacity also fixes the scale of the removal test. A capacity of 257 mg per gram is the loading the carbon carries at the plateau of the isotherm, well above the loading reached in a test that removes 85% of the dye in solution, and the two figures describe different regions of the same isotherm: the removal test works on its rising part, where sites are still free, and states nothing about the plateau the fit extrapolates.

The removal figure belongs to its conditions. A dose of 0.6 g L-1 against an initial concentration of 50 mg L-1 removed 42.5 mg L-1 in 120 min; a weaker solution or a larger dose changes the percentage without any change in the carbon. The 85% ranks this carbon against others only at the same dose, concentration, and contact time.

fact_base: Carbon dioxide and hydrogen react over a copper-zinc oxide catalyst to give formaldehyde. Space-time yield is the mass of product per unit catalyst volume per hour (kg L-1 h-1). Test conditions: 280 °C, 40 bar, feed ratio H2/CO2 = 3, one feed composition. Structured catalyst: space-time yield 0.98 kg L-1 h-1, pressure drop 0.24 bar, activity loss 7% after 100 h. Pellet catalyst: space-time yield 0.37 kg L-1 h-1, pressure drop 1.14 bar, activity loss 20% after 100 h. No sulfur-bearing feed was tested. Yield and pressure drop are seldom reported for the same catalyst charge.
input:
In this work, the reaction of carbon dioxide and hydrogen over a copper-zinc oxide catalyst to give formaldehyde was investigated, with the aim of comparing two different catalyst forms under identical conditions. The performance of each catalyst was characterised in terms of its space-time yield, which is defined as the mass of product obtained per unit catalyst volume per hour (kg L-1 h-1). All of the tests were carried out at 280 °C and 40 bar, using a feed ratio H2/CO2 of 3 and a single feed composition, so that the two catalysts could be compared on a consistent basis.

The structured catalyst achieved a space-time yield of 0.98 kg L-1 h-1, with a pressure drop of 0.24 bar and an activity loss of 7% after 100 h on stream. The pellet catalyst, by contrast, gave a considerably lower space-time yield of 0.37 kg L-1 h-1, together with a much higher pressure drop of 1.14 bar and an activity loss of 20% after 100 h. The structured form therefore outperformed the pellet form on all three of the measures reported here, delivering more product per unit volume while imposing a smaller pressure penalty and retaining more of its initial activity over the test period.

It should nevertheless be noted that no sulfur-bearing feed was tested, so the tolerance of either catalyst to sulfur remains unknown. In addition, yield and pressure drop are seldom reported for the same catalyst charge in the wider literature, which makes it difficult to place these results in a broader context. Within the conditions actually tested, however, the comparison clearly favours the structured catalyst, and any extrapolation beyond the single feed composition used here should be made with caution.
target:
Carbon dioxide and hydrogen react over a copper-zinc oxide catalyst to give formaldehyde, and two catalyst forms were compared at one feed composition, at 280 °C and 40 bar with a feed ratio H2/CO2 of 3. Performance is stated as space-time yield, the mass of product per unit catalyst volume per hour (kg L-1 h-1), with pressure drop and activity loss reported for the same charges.

The structured catalyst gave a space-time yield of 0.98 kg L-1 h-1, a pressure drop of 0.24 bar, and an activity loss of 7% after 100 h. The pellet catalyst gave a space-time yield of 0.37 kg L-1 h-1, a pressure drop of 1.14 bar, and an activity loss of 20% after 100 h. The structured form is higher on yield and lower on both penalties at the tested conditions; the comparison is between the two forms as charged, and yield and pressure drop are seldom reported for the same catalyst charge elsewhere, which limits the outside comparisons that can be drawn.

Space-time yield is the measure that sizes the reactor: at a fixed duty, the form with the higher yield needs the smaller catalyst volume, and the structured form's advantage on pressure drop compounds in the same direction, since the charge that produces more per unit volume also resists the flow less. The two advantages point the same way here, which is not guaranteed in general: a form can win on yield and lose on pressure drop, and a comparison that reports only one of the two leaves the trade-off invisible.

No sulfur-bearing feed was tested, so neither form's tolerance to sulfur is known, and a feed carrying sulfur would test a property this comparison does not reach. The preference for the structured catalyst is a preference at the tested conditions and at the single feed composition used; a second feed composition, richer or leaner, could move the pressure drop and the activity loss in different proportions for the two forms, and the ranking is not claimed beyond the conditions that produced it.

fact_base: Energy assessment of a brewery, in four sections: current use, refrigeration, steam, and recommendation. Electricity use is 4125 MWh per year; refrigeration takes the largest share. A heat-recovery retrofit is projected to save 16% of electricity use, a derived saving of 660 MWh per year, at a capital cost of $244k. At $0.12 per kWh the derived annual saving is $79200 and the derived simple payback is 3.1 years. Steam figures are from one winter month and are flagged as seasonal in the recommendation.
input:
This report presents the findings of an energy assessment that was carried out at the brewery, covering current energy use, the refrigeration system, the steam system, and a recommendation for action. The headline finding is that a heat-recovery retrofit applied to the refrigeration system is projected to save 16% of the brewery's electricity use, which corresponds to a derived saving of 660 MWh per year, worth $79,200 per year at the current price of $0.12 per kWh. Set against a capital cost of $244k, this gives a derived simple payback of 3.1 years. It should be noted at the outset that the steam figures used in this assessment are drawn from a single winter month and should therefore be regarded as seasonal in nature, whereas the electricity figures are based on a full year.

## Current use
Total electricity consumption at the brewery amounts to 4125 MWh per year, and refrigeration accounts for the largest share of this total; indeed, the refrigeration load is the load to which the projected saving of 16% applies. The remainder of the electricity is consumed by a variety of other users, including the brewhouse, the packaging operation, compressed air generation, lighting, and general site services, none of which individually comes close to the refrigeration load. The figure of 4125 MWh per year provides the baseline against which all of the savings discussed in this assessment are measured, and it is worth emphasising that this is a metered figure for a complete year rather than an estimate assembled from equipment nameplate ratings. Demand remains relatively steady throughout the year, since brewing continues in every month and both the cold store and the fermentation vessels require cooling on a continuous basis, with the main seasonal variation appearing on the steam side rather than in electricity consumption.

## Refrigeration
Refrigeration is comfortably the largest single consumer of electricity on the site, and it is also the source of the heat that the proposed retrofit would recover. The refrigeration plant rejects heat arising from the cold store, the fermentation vessels, and the packaged-product store, and at present this rejected heat is simply lost to the atmosphere. The proposed retrofit would recover heat from the refrigeration discharge and use it in duties for which the site currently generates heat separately. The projected saving of 660 MWh per year is a derived figure, obtained by applying the vendor's projected recovery to the refrigeration share of the total annual consumption of 4125 MWh, and it has not yet been demonstrated on an operating installation at this particular site. Its accuracy consequently depends on the refrigeration share and on the number of hours for which the plant operates under load, both of which vary over the course of the year.

## Steam
Steam is used in the brewhouse for a range of duties, of which wort boiling, cleaning, and pasteurisation account for the bulk of the consumption. The steam figures quoted in this assessment are taken from one winter month, which is the heaviest month of the year for steam demand, and they therefore overstate the annual average position by an amount that has not been corrected for in this report. Crucially, however, the recommendation does not depend on these steam figures, because the proposed retrofit acts on the refrigeration system and the associated saving is expressed in terms of electricity. Any interaction whereby recovered heat displaces steam generation is acknowledged to be real, but it has not been quantified here and has deliberately been excluded from the payback calculation rather than estimated.

## Recommendation
It is recommended that the brewery proceeds with the heat-recovery retrofit at a capital cost of $244k, with responsibility for delivery resting with the brewery engineering manager. The projected saving is 660 MWh per year, representing 16% of current electricity use, and at $0.12 per kWh this corresponds to a derived annual saving of $79,200, noting that 660 MWh is equivalent to 660,000 kWh. On this basis, the derived simple payback is 3.1 years. This payback is a simple one and makes no allowance for the maintenance of the additional equipment, for the time value of money, or for any future movement in the price of electricity, and it takes the vendor's projected saving at face value. It is further recommended that two checks are built into the delivery plan: firstly, that the refrigeration share of annual consumption is confirmed by sub-metering before any order is placed, and secondly, that the output of recovered heat is metered throughout the first year of operation so that the projected saving can be tested against a measured value.
target:

The recommendation is approval to proceed, with the brewery engineering manager as owner. The steam figures in this assessment rest on one winter month and are treated as seasonal throughout; the electricity figures are annual and metered.

## Current use
Electricity use is 4125 MWh per year, and refrigeration takes the largest share of it. The remaining use is spread across the brewhouse, packaging, compressed air, lighting, and site services, none of which approaches the refrigeration load. Annual use of 4125 MWh is the base against which every saving in this assessment is measured, and it is a metered figure for a full year rather than an estimate built up from nameplate ratings. Demand is steady through the year by the standards of food and drink sites: brewing continues in every month, the cold store and the fermentation vessels call for cooling in every month, and the seasonal swing sits in the steam system rather than in electricity. No single end use besides refrigeration offers a saving of the size the retrofit addresses, which is why the assessment concentrates on the refrigeration plant and treats the other loads as background. The split between continuous and variable use matters for what follows. Much of the brewery's electricity runs whether or not beer is being packaged on a given day: refrigeration holds temperature continuously, and the cold store does not switch off between production runs. A measure that acts on a continuous load accumulates its saving over every hour of the year, which is part of the case for acting on refrigeration rather than on a load that runs only during production.

## Refrigeration
Refrigeration is the largest electricity consumer on the site and the source of the recoverable heat. The plant rejects heat from the cold store, the fermentation vessels, and the packaged-product store, and that rejected heat is currently lost to air. The recovered heat has a use on the same site at the same time. A brewery washes vessels, heats water, and warms spaces through the year, and the refrigeration plant rejects heat through the year as well; the match between a continuous source and a continuous demand is what makes the recovery practical rather than occasional. Where the recovered heat cannot be used at the moment it is produced, it is lost as surely as it is lost today, and the projected saving already stands or falls on the coincidence of the two profiles.

## Steam
Steam serves the brewhouse: wort boiling, cleaning, and pasteurisation draw the bulk of it. The steam figures in this assessment come from one winter month, the heaviest steam month of the year, and they overstate the annual average by an amount this assessment does not correct. The recommendation does not depend on the steam figures: the retrofit acts on the refrigeration system and its saving is stated in electricity. Where recovered heat displaces steam raising, the interaction is real but unquantified here, and it is excluded from the payback rather than estimated.

## Recommendation
The recommendation is to proceed with the heat-recovery retrofit at a capital cost of $244k, with the brewery engineering manager owning delivery. The projected saving is 660 MWh per year, 16% of current electricity use; at $0.12 per kWh the derived annual saving is $79,200 (660 MWh is 660,000 kWh), and the derived simple payback is 3.1 years on the capital cost. The payback is a simple payback: it takes no account of maintenance on the added equipment, of the time value of money, or of movement in the electricity price, and it holds the projected saving at its vendor figure. Two checks belong in the delivery plan: the refrigeration share of annual use is confirmed against sub-metering before the order is placed, and the recovered-heat output is metered through the first year so the projected saving is tested against a measured one. On those conditions the case rests on the electricity figures alone, which are annual and metered, and not on the seasonal steam figures. The decision the figures support is a decision to build, taken on metered electricity data and a vendor projection that the delivery plan then verifies. If the verification fails, the metering installed under the second check shows by how much, and the shortfall is a measured one rather than a suspicion.

subtype: worked example with equation: Ergun pressure drop
fact_base: Gas flows through a packed bed of 1 mm particles. The void fraction $\varepsilon$ is 0.4, the superficial velocity $u$ is 0.27 m s-1 and the bed length is 2 m. The Ergun equation gives a pressure gradient of 5.5 kPa m-1, or 11.1 kPa over the bed. Particle diameter $d_p$ is 1 mm; gas density is 1.2 kg m-3 and viscosity is 1.8 x 10-5 Pa s.
input:
Gas flows through a packed bed made up of particles with a diameter $d_p$ of 1 mm. The void fraction $\varepsilon$ is 0.4, the superficial velocity $u$ is 0.27 m s-1, and the length of the bed $L$ is 2 m. In order to estimate the pressure drop $\Delta P$ across the bed, the Ergun equation can be used, which brings together the particle diameter, the void fraction, the viscosity $\mu$ and density $\rho$ of the gas, and the superficial velocity:

$$\frac{\Delta P}{L} = \frac{150 \mu (1-\varepsilon)^2}{\varepsilon^3 d_p^2} u + \frac{1.75 (1-\varepsilon)}{\varepsilon^3 d_p} \rho u^2$$

The right-hand side of the equation is made up of two terms. The first of these is the viscous contribution, which increases linearly with $u$, while the second is the inertial contribution, which increases with $u^2$. Taking $\mu$ = 1.8 x 10-5 Pa s and $\rho$ = 1.2 kg m-3, the equation gives a pressure gradient of 5.5 kPa m-1, which corresponds to 11.1 kPa over the 2 m bed.

It is worth noting that the gradient is the figure that matters for design purposes, since equipment such as a blower is sized using 5.5 kPa m-1 multiplied by whatever bed length is actually in service. The calculated value depends on the stated void fraction of 0.4, and a bed that is packed more tightly would produce a substantially steeper gradient, because $\varepsilon$ appears in the denominator of both terms. The equation also assumes that the particles are of a uniform size of 1 mm, and a wide distribution of particle sizes is not properly represented by the single value of $d_p$ used here. The distributor and the support beneath the bed add their own resistance in series with the bed's, and that resistance is outside the figure: the equation prices the packed section alone, and a design total adds the internals separately.

fact_base: Goal: compute the half-life of a first-order reaction and the fraction remaining after 60 min. For a first-order reaction the rate constant k (min-1) fixes the half-life t1/2 (min) by t1/2 = ln(2) / k, and the fraction remaining after time t (min) is exp(-k t). Measured rate constant: k = 0.012 min-1 at 323 K, from concentration measurements every 5 min over 90 min. Worked results: t1/2 = 57.8 min; the fraction remaining after 60 min is 0.49 (dimensionless), both computed from the stated relations. The relations hold for a first-order reaction only; a reaction of another order follows a different decay law.
input:
The goal is the half-life of a first-order reaction and the fraction of reactant remaining after 60 min, computed from a measured rate constant. The half-life is 57.8 min and the fraction remaining after 60 min is 0.49.

For a first-order reaction, the rate constant k (min-1) fixes the half-life t1/2 (min) by t1/2 = ln(2) / k. The fraction remaining after time t (min) is exp(-k t). The half-life is the time at which the fraction remaining is one half, read directly from the decay relation. Both relations rest on the same statement: the rate of reaction at any instant is proportional to the concentration still present, so equal fractions disappear in equal times and the decay has no memory of how long it has already run.

The measured rate constant is k = 0.012 min-1 at 323 K, from concentration measurements every 5 min over 90 min. The sampling interval is short against the half-life, so the decay curve is fixed by many points rather than by the endpoints alone.

Substitution in the half-life relation gives t1/2 = ln(2) / 0.012 = 57.8 min. Substitution in the decay relation at t = 60 min gives exp(-0.012 x 60) = exp(-0.72) = 0.49. The two results agree in the way they must: 60 min stands just past the half-life of 57.8 min, so the fraction remaining stands just below one half.

The relations hold for a first-order reaction only. A reaction of another order follows a different decay law, and its half-life is not fixed by the rate constant alone in the same way.
