fact_base: A review passage on catalysts for carbon dioxide hydrogenation, in four parts: scope, established results, disagreements, and gaps. The review covers 84 papers from the last 11 years. The disagreements part names the quantity on which reports conflict; the gaps part names the measurement nobody reports.
input:
## Scope
This review sets out to survey the published work on catalysts for carbon dioxide hydrogenation over the last 11 years, drawing together a total of 84 papers that report a catalyst tested for the conversion of carbon dioxide with hydrogen and that provide sufficient experimental detail for the underlying test conditions to be recovered. The reaction families that fall within the scope of the review are methanol synthesis, the reverse water-gas shift reaction, and methanation. Electrochemical and photochemical conversion, by contrast, fall outside the scope, as do reaction sequences in which hydrogenation represents just one step among several and the catalyst is not characterised in its own right.

The material classes covered by the review are copper-based catalysts, iron-based catalysts, noble-metal catalysts, and oxide catalysts. The overwhelming majority of the papers are laboratory-scale studies, carried out in fixed beds at pressures, temperatures, and feed compositions that were selected by the original authors rather than harmonised across the field. This lack of a common basis inevitably limits what any review can realistically do with the 84 papers: results can be placed side by side and claims can be compared, but catalysts cannot simply be re-ranked on a single scale, because no single scale runs consistently through the underlying reports. Where a paper reports a quantity on a basis that other papers do not share, the review records the basis alongside the quantity and leaves the comparison open, rather than forcing an alignment that the source material does not support.

## Established results
A number of findings recur across different groups and across different material classes, and it is these findings that this section treats as established. First and foremost, the preparation route appears to decide a great deal of what a catalyst actually does: for copper-based materials, the way in which the copper is distributed in the support at the start of the test emerges as the strongest single predictor of the activity that is reported at the end of it, and catalysts that begin with copper finely divided tend to hold their advantage over catalysts that begin with copper in larger grains. Promoters, meanwhile, seem to change selectivity considerably more than they change activity. Across both the copper and the iron classes, a promoted catalyst and its unpromoted counterpart will generally convert carbon dioxide at broadly comparable rates while sending the products in quite different proportions, and claims to the effect that a promoter raises activity itself generally do not survive a careful check of the conversion at which the comparison was actually made.

Stability is the second major established theme, and it is a somewhat less comfortable one. Every material class covered in the review loses performance on stream, whether through sintering, through oxidation-state drift, through fouling, or through some combination of these mechanisms that the original authors were unable to separate. Water that is formed by the reaction is implicated in a great deal of this loss: the various classes differ markedly in how much water they can tolerate, and this difference appears to be a property of the class as a whole rather than of any individual preparation. Supports, furthermore, are by no means inert in this respect. A support that succeeds in holding a catalyst's active phase in place under a dry feed may well fail to do so under a wet one, and several well-known results in the field are, on closer re-reading, results about supports just as much as they are results about active phases. The reverse water-gas shift reaction and methanol synthesis also divide the classes in a relatively settled way: iron-based materials are the default choice where the shift reaction is the objective, and copper-based materials where methanol is the objective, and this particular division is one of the few points on which the literature does not appear to argue with itself.

## Disagreements
The disagreements in the literature are concentrated, to a large extent, on one particular quantity: the methanol selectivity that is reported at a stated conversion. Different groups working with closely similar copper-based catalysts report selectivities that differ by margins which no straightforward reading of the test conditions can explain. Part of this conflict is essentially a matter of accounting. Selectivity is reported on different bases across the 84 papers, with some groups counting carbon monoxide as the product of a side reaction and others treating it as an intermediate and excluding it altogether, and the two conventions inevitably move the reported number without any change whatsoever in the underlying catalyst. Where the convention is explicitly stated, the conflict narrows considerably; where it is not, the numbers simply cannot be reconciled from the published record, and this review makes no attempt to reconcile them.

Beneath this first conflict there runs a second one: whether the oxidation state of copper under reaction conditions is the quantity that actually decides methanol selectivity, or whether it merely tracks it. The evidence that is offered on each side is drawn from characterisation that was carried out either before or after reaction rather than during it, and the two camps tend to read the same spectra in rather different ways. The review takes no position on this question beyond recording what would actually settle it, namely a measurement of the working catalyst, under feed, at the conditions of the test itself. Measurements of that kind are rare in the papers covered by this review, and their rarity is, in itself, something of a finding about the current state of the evidence base.

## Gaps
Arguably the most important gap is a measurement that nobody appears to report: catalyst performance over an extended period of time on stream under a feed that carries with it the impurities of an industrial carbon dioxide source. The papers covered in this review test with clean feeds, over durations that are convenient for a laboratory programme, and report activity and selectivity from the early, stable-looking portion of the run. An industrial plant, however, offers none of these conveniences. Its carbon dioxide arrives either from a capture unit or from a process stream, complete with traces of whatever the upstream process happens to carry, and its catalyst is expected to go on performing for far longer than any test reported in the 11 years covered here. Whether the rankings that have been established on clean feeds would survive a realistic feed is simply unknown, because the experiment has not been carried out in a form that the literature records.

The second gap is a reporting gap rather than an experimental one. Test conditions that are capable of deciding a result, including the exact feed composition, the pretreatment that was applied, and the convention lying behind a reported selectivity, are missing from a substantial share of the papers, and it is their absence that turns what might have been recoverable differences into permanent disagreements. The adoption of a common reporting basis, of the kind that other branches of catalysis have already adopted, would cost the field very little, and would transform the next review of this literature from an excavation into a comparison.

subtype: worked example with equation: Arrhenius ratio
fact_base: Rate constants for a food spoilage study were measured at two temperatures. With activation energy $E_a$ of 93 kJ mol-1, raising the temperature from 300 K to 340 K multiplies the rate constant $k$ by 80.37. The estimate holds the pre-exponential factor $A$ constant over the interval.
input:
In the context of the food spoilage study examined here, the rate constants were measured at two different temperatures, and it is worth noting that the results reveal a substantial temperature sensitivity that underscores the central role played by the activation energy. With an activation energy $E_a$ of 93 kJ mol-1, raising the temperature from 300 K to 340 K multiplies the rate constant $k$ by a factor of 80.37, a dramatic increase that highlights just how strongly the spoilage process responds to temperature over this interval. This behaviour is captured by the well-known Arrhenius equation,

$$k = A \exp\left(-\frac{E_a}{R T}\right)$$

in which $k$ represents the rate constant, $A$ represents the pre-exponential factor, $E_a$ represents the activation energy, $R$ represents the gas constant, and $T$ represents the absolute temperature. It should be noted that the estimate holds the pre-exponential factor $A$ constant over the interval from 300 K to 340 K, and this assumption plays a key role in the result, because it means that the entire change in the rate constant is attributed to the exponential term rather than to any variation in $A$ itself. Overall, the analysis shows that a moderate rise in temperature can be associated with a very large multiplication of the rate constant when the activation energy is as high as 93 kJ mol-1, and the ratio of 80.37 contributes to a deeper understanding of how the measured values at 300 K and 340 K are connected.

$$k = A \exp\left(-\frac{E_a}{R T}\right)$$

where $k$ denotes the rate constant, $A$ the pre-exponential factor, $E_a$ the activation energy, $R$ the gas constant, and $T$ the absolute temperature. The activation energy $E_a$ is 93 kJ mol-1. The estimate holds the pre-exponential factor $A$ constant over the interval from 300 K to 340 K, so the whole of the change is carried by the exponential term. Any drift in $A$ across the interval would move the ratio away from 80.37, and no such drift is included in the estimate. The size of the ratio is a consequence of the activation energy. The exponent in the Arrhenius equation varies with $E_a$ and with the change in reciprocal temperature between the two states, so a reaction with a lower activation energy would show a smaller multiplication over the same interval, and a reaction with a higher activation energy a larger one. The measured rate constants at 300 K and 340 K are the two ends of the comparison, and the stated $E_a$ of 93 kJ mol-1 connects them through the relation as written. For the spoilage study the ratio is the result that carries forward: the rate constant at the higher temperature is the rate constant at the lower multiplied by the stated factor, under the stated condition on $A$, and any use of the pair of values outside the measured interval rests on the same condition holding there.

For a first-order reaction the rate constant k (min-1) fixes the half-life t1/2 (min) by t1/2 = ln(2) / k, and the fraction remaining after time t (min) is exp(-k t). Measured rate constant: k = 0.069 min-1 at 323 K, from concentration measurements every 5 min over 90 min. Worked results: t1/2 = 10 min; the fraction remaining after 60 min is 0.02 (dimensionless), both computed from the stated relations. The relations hold for a first-order reaction only; a reaction of another order follows a different decay law.
input: In this worked example, the goal is to compute the half-life of a first-order reaction and, in addition, to determine the fraction of the reactant that remains after 60 min have elapsed. For a first-order reaction, the rate constant $k$ (min-1) fixes the half-life $t_{1/2}$ (min) by the relation $t_{1/2} = \ln(2)/k$, and the fraction remaining after a time $t$ (min) is given by $\exp(-k t)$. In the case considered here, the measured rate constant is $k$ = 0.069 min-1 at 323 K, a value obtained from concentration measurements that were taken every 5 min over a period of 90 min. When the relevant substitutions are carried out, the worked results are a half-life of 10 min and a fraction remaining after 60 min of 0.02 (dimensionless), both of which are computed from the relations stated above. It is important to note that these relations are valid only for a first-order reaction, and a reaction of another order would follow a different decay law, so the results obtained here cannot simply be transferred to reactions that do not exhibit first-order behaviour. The concentration measurements on which the value rests were taken at regular intervals across the stated period, and because the temperature was held at 323 K throughout the measurements, the value of $k$ obtained applies to that temperature and to no other. The half-life has the further convenient property that it does not depend on how much reactant is present at the start, and it is precisely this independence that marks the first-order case out from the behaviour shown by reactions of other orders, where the corresponding time changes with the starting concentration. Overall, the example demonstrates how a single measured rate constant, namely $k$ = 0.069 min-1, is sufficient to determine both the half-life of 10 min and the fraction remaining after the stated time interval.

The two results are consistent with each other: the decay relation returns the half value at a time equal to the half-life, and the stated results satisfy that check at 10 min. A reaction of another order follows a different decay law, and neither result carries over to such a reaction: the half-life would then depend on the starting concentration, and the fraction remaining would follow the decay law of that order instead. input: This executive summary presents an overview of a proposed heat-recovery retrofit at a food plant, where refrigeration operations currently consume a total of 2202 MWh of electricity per year. According to projections provided by the equipment vendor, the retrofit is expected to save 15% of that annual use, which corresponds to a derived saving of 330 MWh per year at the vendor figure. The capital cost of the project is $472k, and at an electricity price of $0.14 per kWh the derived annual saving amounts to $46k, which in turn leads to a derived simple payback period of 10.3 years. It is important to note, however, that the saving figure is a vendor projection and has not been measured at this plant, and it should also be noted that the refrigeration load in the summer peak month was not modelled as part of this assessment, which means that a degree of uncertainty inevitably remains around the projected figures. Put in trade-off terms, the derived annual saving of $46k stands against a capital cost of $472k, and the relationship between the two figures is what produces the derived simple payback of 10.3 years quoted above, on the assumptions that have been stated. In light of these considerations, it is recommended that a metered trial be carried out on one of the three refrigeration lines before any capital decision is taken, so that measured data can be obtained in order to inform the final investment decision. The plant engineer will be responsible for owning and overseeing the trial.

The trial replaces the projection with a measured saving on a single line. A measured figure at that scale either supports the vendor figure or shows the gap between the projection and the plant, and the capital decision is taken on the measured result rather than on the projection. The payback of 10.3 years is long enough that the difference between the projected saving and a measured saving decides the case, which is the reason the trial comes before the capital decision and not after it. The trial also fixes the scope of any later decision: a retrofit beyond the trialled line is a separate decision, taken on the trial result and on the load profile with the missing peak month supplied.

subtype: worked example with equation: Stokes settling
fact_base: Glass beads of diameter $d_p$ = 50 micrometres and density 2500 kg m-3 settle in water at 293 K. Stokes' law gives a terminal velocity $v_t$ of 2.05 mm s-1. The estimate requires creeping flow; the particle Reynolds number must be checked before the value is used.
input:
Glass beads with a diameter $d_p$ of 50 micrometres and a density of 2500 kg m-3 are considered as they settle in water at 293 K. In order to estimate the settling behaviour, Stokes' law can be applied, and the law gives the terminal velocity $v_t$ of the beads through the following relation:

$$v_t = \frac{g d_p^2 (\rho_p - \rho)}{18 \mu}$$

in which $g$ represents the acceleration due to gravity, $\rho_p$ represents the particle density, $\rho$ represents the fluid density, and $\mu$ represents the fluid viscosity. On the basis of this relation, the terminal velocity $v_t$ is found to be 2.05 mm s-1. The relation balances the weight of the bead, reduced by the buoyancy of the water it displaces, against the viscous drag that the water exerts on the bead as it moves, and the terminal velocity is the velocity at which those two effects come into balance and the bead ceases to accelerate. It should nevertheless be emphasised that the estimate obtained in this way requires creeping flow, and the particle Reynolds number must therefore be checked before the value of 2.05 mm s-1 is used in any subsequent analysis, since the validity of the approach as a whole depends on that condition being satisfied.

Glass beads of diameter $d_p$ = 50 micrometres and density 2500 kg m-3 settle in water at 293 K. Stokes' law gives the terminal velocity $v_t$ as

$$v_t = \frac{g d_p^2 (\rho_p - \rho)}{18 \mu}$$

where $g$ denotes the acceleration due to gravity, $\rho_p$ the particle density, $\rho$ the fluid density, and $\mu$ the fluid viscosity. With the stated diameter and density, the terminal velocity $v_t$ is 2.05 mm s-1. The estimate requires creeping flow. The particle Reynolds number must be checked before the value is used, because Stokes' law is limited to the creeping-flow regime: outside that regime the drag on the bead no longer follows the linear relation behind the equation, and the computed velocity overstates the settling rate the bead actually reaches. The relation balances the weight of the bead, reduced by the buoyancy of the water displaced, against the viscous drag on the moving bead; the terminal velocity is the velocity at which the two balance and the bead stops accelerating. The velocity varies with the square of the diameter, so the stated diameter carries more weight in the result than any other single quantity in the relation, and it varies in direct proportion to the density difference between bead and water. The value 2.05 mm s-1 therefore stands as an estimate conditional on the Reynolds-number check, and the check belongs with the result wherever the result is reported or carried into a settling calculation.

input:
An ideal liquid mixture containing hexane in heptane is considered, in which the liquid mole fraction $x$ of the volatile component is 0.29. The pure-component vapour pressure $P^*$ at the temperature of the mixture is 5.9 kPa, and the partial pressure $p$ of the volatile component can be obtained by means of Raoult's law, which states the relationship in the following form:

$$p = x P^*$$

On the basis of this relation, the partial pressure $p$ works out at 1.7 kPa. The partial pressure obtained in this way is the contribution made by the volatile component to the total pressure of the vapour that stands in equilibrium with the liquid mixture, and it is governed, under the stated law, by the proportion of that component in the liquid and by nothing else. It is important to note, however, that Raoult's law is based on the assumption of an ideal solution, and in the calculation presented here no activity coefficients have been applied in order to account for the behaviour of the real mixture, which means that the value of 1.7 kPa should be understood as the ideal-solution result for the stated composition rather than as a fully corrected value for the actual mixture under consideration.
target:
An ideal liquid mixture of hexane in heptane holds the volatile component at a liquid mole fraction $x$ of 0.29. Raoult's law gives the partial pressure $p$ of that component as

$$p = x P^*$$

where $P^*$ denotes the pure-component vapour pressure at the mixture temperature. With $P^*$ = 5.9 kPa, the partial pressure $p$ is 1.7 kPa. Raoult's law assumes an ideal solution, and the result is limited to that assumption. Activity coefficients for the real mixture are not applied, so any departure of the real mixture from ideal behaviour moves the partial pressure away from 1.7 kPa by the factor an activity coefficient would supply. The partial pressure is the contribution of the volatile component to the total pressure of the vapour in equilibrium with the mixture. Under the law as stated it is set by the proportion of the component in the liquid and by the pure-component vapour pressure at the mixture temperature, and the composition enters the result through the mole fraction alone, with no separate term for the identity of the second component beyond what the ideal-solution assumption already contains. The stated value is the ideal-solution value at the stated composition and at the temperature belonging to $P^*$, and it is quoted on that basis: a correction for the real mixture would change the figure, not refine it, and no such correction is included in the result as reported here.

fact_base: Design report for a distillation column, in four sections: basis, sizing, materials, and risks. Design throughput is 60 t per day and the removal or separation duty is 92% of the key component. Materials are 316L stainless steel for wetted parts; the basis section states this once. The risks section names fouling and turndown as open items; neither is resolved in the report.
input:
Basis

This design report sets out the design of a distillation column, and the basis on which the design rests is described in this opening section. The design throughput of the column is 60 t per day, and the separation duty that the column is required to achieve is the removal of 92% of the key component from the feed stream. The materials basis for the design is 316L stainless steel for all wetted parts, and this is stated here at the outset so that the materials discussion later in the report can build upon it. The feed to the column is received from the upstream equipment in the state in which that equipment delivers it, and the design treats the stated separation duty as the governing requirement against which the column is sized, in the sense that the sizing work described below is directed towards meeting that duty at the stated throughput while at the same time providing a column that can be fabricated, installed, and operated within the wider unit of which the column forms a part.

Sizing

The sizing of the column is concerned in large part with the diameter and the height of the vessel, and each of these dimensions is governed by a different set of considerations. The diameter is governed principally by the vapour traffic that the column is required to handle, since the rising vapour must be accommodated without excessive entrainment of liquid and without the column approaching a flooded condition at the design throughput. The height, by contrast, is governed by the number of separation stages that the duty demands and by the spacing that is provided between the internals that deliver those stages, together with the additional allowances that are made at the top and the bottom of the vessel for disengagement and for the liquid inventory that is held in the base. The selection of the internals themselves, whether trays or packing, is made with reference to the separation duty, the properties of the fluids being handled, and the pressure drop that can be accepted across the column, and the sizing is carried out on a consistent basis so that the diameter, the height, and the internals together deliver the stated removal of the key component. It is also the case that the traffic within the column is established by the reflux that is returned at the top and by the vapour that is raised at the base, so that the diameter is in effect sized for that internal traffic rather than for the feed rate in isolation, and the stage efficiency has a bearing on the height through the number of actual stages that the internals are required to provide.

Materials

The materials of construction are an important aspect of the design, and the grade that is specified in the basis section is adopted for all of the wetted parts of the column, including the shell, the internals, and the nozzles through which the process fluids enter and leave the vessel. The selection of a stainless grade for the wetted envelope reflects the corrosive character of the service and the need for the column to retain its integrity over the design life without the wall thickness being consumed by corrosion at an unacceptable rate. Attention is also given in the design to the joints between the parts, to the gaskets and bolting that those joints require, and to the compatibility of each of these items with the fluids and the temperatures that they will encounter, as well as to the practical questions of welding, fabrication, and inspection access, all of which have a bearing on whether the specified materials can be realised in the finished equipment.

Risks

Two items are identified in this report as open risks, namely fouling and turndown, and it should be clearly understood that neither of these items is resolved within the scope of the present report. Fouling is a concern because deposits that accumulate on the internal surfaces of the column can progressively reduce the effective capacity of the internals and increase the pressure drop across the column, and the rate at which such deposits might accumulate cannot be established with confidence from the information that is currently available, since the fouling history of the feed in comparable service is not sufficiently documented. Turndown is a concern because the column will be required to operate below its design throughput for parts of its working life, and the behaviour of the internals at reduced rates, in particular the risks of weeping, maldistribution, and a loss of separation efficiency, has not yet been examined across the full operating range that the unit may demand. Both items are therefore carried forward as open items, to be addressed through further work and through the operating data that will become available in due course, and they are recorded here so that they are not lost sight of as the design is developed further. Until such time as these two items can be closed out, the design must be regarded as conditional in respect of both its capacity and its operating range.

The duty is a removal duty on the key component, and the performance of the column is judged against that removal at the design throughput, not against a product purity that the basis does not state. The basis is stated at the design throughput, and the feed rate and the duty are the pair of figures against which every later section is checked: a change to either reopens the sizing, and a change to the specified grade reopens the materials section.

Sizing

Diameter and height are governed by different considerations. The diameter is governed by the vapour traffic the column must handle: the rising vapour is accommodated without excessive entrainment of liquid and without the column approaching a flooded condition at the design throughput, with margin held between the operating point and the flooding limit. The height is governed by the number of separation stages the duty demands and by the spacing between the internals that deliver those stages, with allowances at the top of the vessel for disengagement of liquid from the leaving vapour and at the base for the liquid inventory held there. The internals, trays or packing, are selected against the separation duty, the properties of the fluids handled, and the pressure drop that can be accepted across the column. Diameter, height and internals are sized on one consistent basis, so that the three together deliver the stated removal of the key component at the design throughput, and no dimension is carried from a standard size where the duty requires otherwise. The traffic inside the column is set by the reflux returned at the top and the vapour raised at the base, and the diameter sized for the design throughput is sized for that traffic and not for the feed rate alone. Stage efficiency enters the height through the number of actual stages the internals must provide for the separation the duty demands, and the spacing allowed between stages carries the maintenance and inspection access the internals require over the life of the column.

Materials

The grade specified in the basis is adopted for all wetted parts: the shell, the internals, and the nozzles through which the process fluids enter and leave. A stainless grade is specified for the wetted envelope because the service is corrosive and the column must retain its integrity over the design life without the wall being consumed by corrosion at a rate the design cannot absorb. The joints between parts are designed with the main envelope: the gaskets and bolting those joints require are selected for compatibility with the fluids and temperatures they will meet, and the welds, the fabrication sequence and the access for inspection are settled with the material selection rather than after it, since a grade that cannot be welded, formed or inspected in the finished geometry is not a usable specification however well it resists the service. The same discipline applies to the smaller wetted items: instrument connections and drain and vent nozzles take the specified grade as well, since a single weaker item in the wetted envelope sets the corrosion performance of the whole vessel. Non-wetted parts stand outside that requirement and follow the general standard for the unit.

Risks

Fouling and turndown are open items. Neither is resolved in this report. Fouling is a risk because deposits accumulating on the internal surfaces reduce the effective capacity of the internals and raise the pressure drop across the column over time, and the rate at which deposits would accumulate cannot be established from the information currently available: the fouling history of the feed in comparable service is not documented well enough to support a rate, and no allowance in the sizing rests on one. Turndown is a risk because the column will operate below its design throughput for parts of its working life, and the behaviour of the internals at reduced rates has not been examined across the operating range the unit may demand: weeping, maldistribution and loss of separation efficiency are the failure modes at low rates, and each would show first as a shortfall against the stated removal duty. Both items are carried forward as open items, for further work and for the operating data that will settle them, and they are recorded here so that the limits of the design as it stands are stated in the report itself. Until the two items are closed, the design is issued with its capacity and its operating range both conditional: the capacity conditional on the fouling behaviour of the actual feed, and the range conditional on the behaviour of the internals at reduced rates.

fact_base: The rate constant k (s-1) of a first-order liquid-phase reaction was measured at two temperatures. At 300 K, k = 0.015 s-1. At 340 K, k = 1.325 s-1, computed from the Arrhenius relation with activation energy 95 kJ mol-1 as a derived value. Each temperature was measured in triplicate; the relative standard deviation of k was 4%. Above 340 K the solvent evaporated during sampling, so no rate constant is reported above 340 K.
input: The rate constant $k$ (s-1) of a first-order liquid-phase reaction was measured at two temperatures, and the results that were obtained are presented in this passage. At a temperature of 300 K, the value of $k$ was 0.015 s-1, whereas at a temperature of 340 K the value of $k$ was 1.325 s-1, although it should be noted that this second value was computed from the Arrhenius relation with an activation energy of 95 kJ mol-1 and therefore represents a derived value rather than a directly measured one. Each of the temperatures was measured in triplicate, and the relative standard deviation of $k$ was 4%, which provides an indication of the reproducibility of the measurements that were carried out. It is also important to note that no rate constant is reported above 340 K, and the reason for this is that above 340 K the solvent was observed to evaporate during the sampling process, which meant that reliable measurements could no longer be obtained in that region. The relative standard deviation of 4% was established from the triplicate measurements carried out at 300 K and at 340 K, and it applies to the measurements at both of the temperatures that were studied in the course of this work. Taken together, the results show a very substantial increase in the rate constant between 300 K and 340 K, spanning the interval over which measurements could be made, although the upper end of that interval is represented by a value that was obtained by calculation rather than by direct measurement.
target: The rate constant $k$ (s-1) of a first-order liquid-phase reaction was measured at two temperatures. At 300 K, $k$ = 0.015 s-1. At 340 K, $k$ = 1.325 s-1, computed from the Arrhenius relation with an activation energy of 95 kJ mol-1 as a derived value. Each temperature was measured in triplicate, and the relative standard deviation of $k$ was 4%. No rate constant is reported above 340 K: above that temperature the solvent evaporated during sampling, so samples taken at higher temperatures did not hold the composition the measurement requires, and no value from them is quoted. The increase between the two temperatures is large, and its upper end is a derived end. The value at 340 K rests on the Arrhenius relation and the stated activation energy, not on a measurement of the same standing as the value at 300 K, and the pair of values should be read with that difference in standing kept in view. The triplicate measurements fix the scatter of $k$ at each temperature at the stated 4%, and that scatter bounds the precision with which either value can be quoted. A derived value is not a weaker value for being derived, but it is a different kind of value: it inherits the uncertainty of the activation energy and of the relation itself, on top of the scatter the triplicate measurements record, and it cannot be checked against a sample in the way the measured value can. That difference in kind is stated wherever the pair is used. The reported pair therefore covers the interval from 300 K to 340 K and no more. The limit at the top of the interval is set by the sampling failure, not by the reaction: the reaction continues above 340 K, but the method used here returns no rate constant there.

fact_base: A food plant uses 1885 MWh of electricity per year in refrigeration. A heat-recovery retrofit is projected by the equipment vendor to save 13% of that use, a derived saving of 245 MWh per year at the vendor figure. Capital cost is $351k. At an electricity price of $0.11 per kWh, the derived annual saving is $27k and the derived simple payback is 13 years. The saving figure is a vendor projection and was not measured at this plant; refrigeration load in the summer peak month was not modelled. The recommendation is a metered trial on one of the three refrigeration lines before any capital decision. The plant engineer owns the trial.
input: The recommendation is a metered trial of the heat-recovery retrofit on one of the three refrigeration lines before any capital decision. The plant engineer owns the trial. The food plant uses 1885 MWh of electricity per year in refrigeration, and the equipment vendor projects that the retrofit will save 13% of that use, a derived saving of 245 MWh per year at the vendor figure. Capital cost is $351k. At an electricity price of $0.11 per kWh, the derived annual saving is $27k and the derived simple payback is 13 years: the retrofit returns $27k per year against a capital cost of $351k. The saving figure is a vendor projection and was not measured at this plant, and refrigeration load in the summer peak month was not modelled, so the payback rests on a projected saving and on a load profile with the peak month missing. The trial replaces the projection with a measured saving on a single line, at the cost of the metering and the trial period rather than the cost of the retrofit. A measured saving either supports the vendor figure or shows the gap between the projection and this plant, and the capital decision is then taken on the measured result. The trial is metered, so the saving it reports is a measured saving on the line where the trial runs, set against the use of that line over the trial period. No capital is committed while the trial runs, and the plant is not asked to carry the retrofit on the strength of a projection in the meantime. The payback at the vendor figure is long, and a long payback is the case where the difference between a projected saving and a measured saving decides whether the capital should be committed at all.

fact_base: A defect-reduction project on a moulding cell cut the reject rate from 2.9% to 1.2% over one quarter. At 116k units per year the change avoids about 1972 rejected units per year. The quarter included a planned shutdown; rates are not adjusted for it.
input: A defect-reduction project that was carried out on a moulding cell succeeded in cutting the reject rate from 2.9% to 1.2% over the course of one quarter, which represents a considerable improvement in the performance of the cell. When the improvement is expressed on an annual basis, at a production volume of 116k units per year the change corresponds to avoiding approximately 1972 rejected units per year, which gives a sense of the scale of the benefit that the project has delivered. The improvement was achieved across the whole of the quarter in which the project ran, and the annualised figure that follows from it is intended to give the reader a clearer sense of what the reduction in the reject rate amounts to when it is viewed at the scale of a full year of production. It should be noted, however, that the quarter in question included a planned shutdown, and the rates that are reported here have not been adjusted in order to take that shutdown into account, so a degree of caution should be exercised when the figures are interpreted and when they are compared with the performance of other periods.
target: A defect-reduction project on a moulding cell cut the reject rate from 2.9% to 1.2% over one quarter. At 116k units per year, the change avoids about 1972 rejected units per year. The quarter included a planned shutdown, and the rates are not adjusted for it. The comparison is therefore a comparison of rates over the production that ran: the shutdown reduced the output of the quarter without entering the rate figures, and the avoided-units figure is the annual volume carried at the stated rates, not a count of rejects avoided inside the quarter itself. The result stands as a rate result. The reject rate after the project is less than half the rate before it, on the production the quarter contained, and the annual figure states what that rate difference is worth at the stated volume. The rate figures themselves are the durable part of the result: volumes change with the programme of work, but a reject rate is a property of the cell as it now runs, and the reduction in that property is what the project is responsible for. The avoided-units figure translates that property into units for planning purposes. A quarter without a shutdown would test whether the new rate holds at full output, and that test has not yet been run.

fact_base: Goal: compute the half-life of a first-order reaction and the fraction remaining after 60 min. For a first-order reaction the rate constant k (min-1) fixes the half-life t1/2 (min) by t1/2 = ln(2) / k, and the fraction remaining after time t (min) is exp(-k t). Measured rate constant: k = 0.069 min-1 at 323 K, from concentration measurements every 5 min over 90 min. Worked results: t1/2 = 10 min; the fraction remaining after 60 min is 0.02 (dimensionless), both computed from the stated relations. The relations hold for a first-order reaction only; a reaction of another order follows a different decay law.
input: In this worked example, the goal is to compute the half-life of a first-order reaction and to determine the fraction remaining after 60 min. For a first-order reaction, the rate constant $k$ (min-1) fixes the half-life $t_{1/2}$ (min) by $t_{1/2} = \ln(2)/k$, and the fraction remaining after time $t$ (min) is $\exp(-k t)$. The measured rate constant in this case is $k$ = 0.069 min-1 at 323 K, obtained from concentration measurements taken every 5 min over 90 min. The worked results are a half-life of 10 min and a fraction remaining after 60 min of 0.02 (dimensionless), both computed from the stated relations. In this particular case the measured value, namely $k$ = 0.069 min-1, is the single experimental input from which both of the requested quantities are obtained, and the care that was taken over its measurement, with readings spread across the full duration of the experiment, is what allows the two results to be stated with confidence. It is important to note that the relations hold for a first-order reaction only, and that a reaction of another order follows a different decay law, so the results should not be applied beyond the first-order case to which they properly belong.
target: Compute the half-life of a first-order reaction with rate constant $k$ = 0.069 min-1 at 323 K, and the fraction remaining after 60 min. For a first-order reaction, the rate constant $k$ (min-1) fixes the half-life $t_{1/2}$ (min) by $t_{1/2} = \ln(2)/k$, and the fraction remaining after time $t$ (min) is $\exp(-k t)$. The rate constant was obtained from concentration measurements taken every 5 min over 90 min. Substitution of $k$ = 0.069 min-1 in the half-life relation gives a half-life of 10 min. Substitution in the decay relation at $t$ = 60 min gives a fraction remaining of 0.02, dimensionless. The two results are consistent with each other: the decay relation returns the half value at a time equal to the half-life, and the stated results satisfy that check. The rate constant rests on measurements spread across the whole decay rather than on a pair of readings, so the half-life derived from it is a property of the fitted decay and not of any single interval between readings. The example is worked at the temperature of the measurement throughout. The relations hold for a first-order reaction only. A reaction of another order follows a different decay law, and neither result carries over: the half-life would depend on the starting concentration, and the fraction remaining would follow the decay law of that order instead.

fact_base: Excerpt content: two groups report conflicting selectivity values for the same material class; the excerpt weighs their test conditions. The excerpt reaches a limited preference and states the condition on which it rests.
input: The selectivity values reported for the benchmark material differ considerably between the two groups, and it is worth examining the conditions behind each value before either one is used. The first group obtains its selectivity from IAST, applying the theory to single-component isotherms that were measured with dry, pure gases. The second group, by contrast, measures mixture breakthrough curves directly and derives selectivity from the amounts retained when the bed is exposed to the mixture of interest. This methodological difference is significant, because single-component isotherms contain no information whatsoever about competition between species for adsorption sites, whereas a breakthrough measurement inherently captures that competition as it unfolds. Moreover, the feed used in the breakthrough experiments contains water vapour, which competes for the same sites and displaces a portion of the adsorbed phase that the dry isotherms would predict. IAST, furthermore, rests on the assumption of an ideal adsorbed phase, an assumption that becomes increasingly questionable when the adsorbed species interact with quite different strengths, as is the case for water and the target component here. Taken together, these considerations help to explain why the dry-basis estimate sits above the mixture measurement: the estimate includes no competing species, while the measurement is shaped by one. On balance, the mixture-based values appear preferable for design work involving feeds that carry moisture, since the measured selectivity already reflects the displacement effect that a dry estimate simply omits. It should be emphasised, however, that this preference is conditional in nature: it rests on the presence of moisture in the feed of interest. Where a feed is dried upstream of the bed, the competing species is removed, and the balance of the argument shifts toward the quality of the isotherm fit and the spreading-pressure integration. What remains unresolved is the magnitude of the displacement at lower moisture contents, a regime in which neither group reports measurements, leaving an important gap that future work will need to address.
target: Selectivity for the benchmark material is reported at two values that differ by more than the stated uncertainty of either, and the difference follows the method. One group estimates selectivity with IAST from single-component isotherms measured on dry gases. The other group measures mixture breakthrough curves and takes selectivity from the retained amounts at the feed composition. A single-component isotherm records the uptake of one gas at a time and carries no information on competition for sites. A breakthrough measurement records the competition directly, because both species are present and the retained amounts settle under the mixture. Water vapour in the second group's feed competes for the same sites and displaces part of the adsorbed phase that the dry isotherms predict. IAST assumes an ideal adsorbed phase, and the assumption is weakest where the adsorbed species differ in interaction strength, as water and the target component do. The direction of the disagreement follows from the feed states: an estimate built on dry, single-gas data stands above a measurement made with a competing species present. Mixture values are preferred for design on feeds that carry moisture, because the measured selectivity already contains the displacement that the dry estimate omits. The preference rests on the feed condition. A feed dried upstream of the bed removes the competing species, and for such a feed the comparison turns instead on the isotherm fit and the spreading-pressure integration behind the IAST estimate. Each reported value is a property of the material under one feed state, stated with that state, and the comparison is between two feed states as much as between two reports. The size of the displacement at low moisture contents remains open, because neither group reports a measurement in that range, and the behaviour between the dry and the humid feed is untested at its lower end.

fact_base: Carbon dioxide and hydrogen react over a copper-zinc oxide catalyst to give dimethyl ether. Space-time yield is the mass of product per unit catalyst volume per hour (kg L-1 h-1). Test conditions: 230 °C, 60 bar, feed ratio H2/CO2 = 3, one feed composition. Structured catalyst: space-time yield 0.93 kg L-1 h-1, pressure drop 0.2 bar, activity loss 8% after 100 h. Pellet catalyst: space-time yield 0.35 kg L-1 h-1, pressure drop 1.32 bar, activity loss 19% after 100 h. No sulfur-bearing feed was tested. Yield and pressure drop are seldom reported for the same catalyst charge.
input: In this study, the performance of a copper-zinc oxide catalyst for the conversion of carbon dioxide and hydrogen to dimethyl ether is investigated in two different physical forms, namely a structured form and a conventional pellet form. The experiments were carried out at a temperature of 230 °C and a pressure of 60 bar, using a feed ratio H2/CO2 = 3 and a single feed composition throughout. Performance was evaluated in terms of space-time yield, defined as the mass of product obtained per unit catalyst volume per hour, together with the pressure drop across the catalyst bed and the loss of activity over time. The structured catalyst achieved a space-time yield of 0.93 kg L-1 h-1 with a pressure drop of only 0.2 bar, whereas the pellet catalyst delivered a space-time yield of 0.35 kg L-1 h-1 at a considerably higher pressure drop of 1.32 bar. In terms of stability, the activity loss after 100 h on stream amounted to 8% for the structured catalyst, compared with 19% for the pellet catalyst. These results clearly demonstrate that, under the conditions examined, the structured form offers a substantially higher yield while simultaneously imposing a much lower pressure drop, and it also retains its activity more effectively over the duration of the test. It is important to note that both catalysts were evaluated at the single feed composition stated above, and no sulfur-bearing feed was tested during this work. Furthermore, it should be pointed out that yield and pressure drop are seldom reported together for the same catalyst charge in the literature, which makes direct comparisons of this kind relatively uncommon.
target: Carbon dioxide and hydrogen react over a copper-zinc oxide catalyst to give dimethyl ether, and the physical form of the catalyst sets the pressure drop that accompanies a given yield. A structured form and a pellet form of the catalyst are compared at 230 °C and 60 bar, with a feed ratio H2/CO2 = 3 and one feed composition. Space-time yield, pressure drop, and activity loss were recorded for each form under the conditions stated. Space-time yield (the mass of product per unit catalyst volume per hour) was 0.93 kg L-1 h-1 for the structured catalyst and 0.35 kg L-1 h-1 for the pellet catalyst. The yield is stated per unit catalyst volume, so the comparison between the forms is made on the volume each charge occupies rather than on its mass. Pressure drop was 0.2 bar for the structured catalyst and 1.32 bar for the pellet catalyst. Activity loss after 100 h was 8% for the structured catalyst and 19% for the pellet catalyst. At the stated conditions the structured form gives the higher yield at the lower pressure drop, and its activity falls more slowly over the test. The two advantages fall to the same form, and no trade-off between yield and pressure drop appears at these conditions: the pellet form's lower yield is not accompanied by a lower pressure drop, and on both measures the pellet form stands behind the structured form. The comparison is limited to the one feed composition tested, at the stated temperature and pressure, and no sulfur-bearing feed was tested. Yield and pressure drop are seldom reported for the same catalyst charge, and the paired values are stated together here so that the yield comparison and the pressure-drop comparison rest on the same test.

fact_base: A viscous liquid of viscosity $\mu$ = 0.001 Pa s flows laminarly through a tube of radius $R$ = 10 mm and length $L$ = 24 m. At a pressure drop $\Delta P$ of 7 kPa the volumetric flow $Q$ is 4123.3 L h-1. The Hagen-Poiseuille equation assumes laminar, fully developed flow of a Newtonian liquid.
input:
In this worked example, the volumetric flow rate of a viscous liquid through a tube is to be determined by means of the Hagen-Poiseuille equation. The liquid in question has a viscosity of $\mu = 0.001$ Pa s, and it flows laminarly through a tube having a radius of $R = 10$ mm and a length of $L = 24$ m. The pressure drop driving the flow amounts to $\Delta P = 7$ kPa. It is important to note that the Hagen-Poiseuille equation is valid only under a specific set of assumptions, namely laminar, fully developed flow of a Newtonian liquid, and these assumptions are taken to hold in the present case. The equation is given by

$$Q = \frac{\pi R^4 \Delta P}{8 \mu L}$$

Substituting the values stated above into this equation and evaluating the result, it is found that the volumetric flow comes out at $Q = 4123.3$ litres per hour. It should be emphasised that the flow depends on the fourth power of the tube radius, which means that the radius is by far the most sensitive of the quantities appearing in the equation. The calculation has been carried out with the data expressed in SI units, and the resulting flow, which the equation delivers in cubic metres per second, has simply been restated in litres per hour for convenience. Finally, it is worth bearing in mind that the result rests entirely on the idealisations built into the equation, including the fully developed velocity profile and the Newtonian behaviour of the liquid; entrance effects, which are neglected here, would act to reduce the flow below the calculated value at the same pressure drop.
target:
Calculate the volumetric flow of a viscous liquid through a tube from the Hagen-Poiseuille equation. The liquid has viscosity $\mu = 0.001$ Pa s and flows laminarly through a tube of radius $R = 10$ mm and length $L = 24$ m, at a pressure drop $\Delta P = 7$ kPa. The Hagen-Poiseuille equation applies to laminar, fully developed flow of a Newtonian liquid, and the flow is taken as fully developed over the tube length. The equation is

$$Q = \frac{\pi R^4 \Delta P}{8 \mu L}$$

where $Q$ denotes the volumetric flow. Substitution of the stated values gives $Q = 4123.3$ litres per hour. The substitution is made with the data in SI units, and the flow the equation returns in cubic metres per second is restated in litres per hour. The radius enters the equation at the fourth power, and the flow is therefore more sensitive to the radius than to any other quantity in the relation: a fractional error in $R$ carries into $Q$ at four times its size, while the pressure drop, the viscosity, and the length each carry at their own size. The result rests on the fully developed profile and on the Newtonian behaviour of the liquid. Entrance effects are not included in the equation, and at the stated pressure drop they would lower the flow below the value calculated.

fact_base: An operating-manual chapter for a centrifugal pump, in four sections: start-up, normal operation, alarms, and shutdown. The alarms section lists two alarms and the operator action for each; no other alarms are introduced. The chapter addresses the operator directly and uses imperative verbs for actions.
input:
## Start-up

Before the motor is started, it is essential to ensure that the pump casing and the suction line have been completely filled with liquid. The vent located at the top of the casing should be opened and left open until such time as liquid, free from air, emerges from it, after which it should be closed again. It should be noted that a pump which is started with air present in the casing will fail to develop pressure, and dry running will cause damage to the seals. The suction valve should be confirmed as fully open, and the discharge valve should be confirmed as closed. A check should be made that the coupling guard is in place and that nothing is resting against the rotating parts. The oil level in the bearing housing should be checked at the sight glass, and topped up with the specified oil in the event that the level is found to be low. Where access permits, the shaft should be turned by hand in order to confirm that it rotates freely. The motor should then be bumped and the direction of rotation checked against the arrow marked on the casing; if the rotation is found to be incorrect, the electrical connections must be corrected before any further steps are taken. The motor may then be started, and the discharge valve opened slowly until a flow has been established. The discharge pressure should be observed as the valve is opened, and it will be seen to rise to the duty value as the flow builds up. While the pressure is rising, the seals and casing joints should be checked for leakage, and attention should be paid to any noise emanating from the casing. If the discharge pressure fails to rise, the pump should be stopped immediately and the priming step repeated, since the most usual cause is air that has been left in the casing or in the suction line.

## Normal operation

The pump should be run at its duty point, and the operating conditions should be maintained as steady as possible. At each operating round, the suction pressure, the discharge pressure, and the flow should be read and the readings entered into the log. These readings constitute the record against which subsequent changes are judged, and a drift in any one of them represents the earliest indication that a fault is developing. It is of particular importance that the suction pressure be kept up, since a falling suction pressure brings the pump ever closer to cavitation, a phenomenon which erodes the impeller and significantly shortens its working life. The suction valve must never be throttled in order to control the flow; flow control is to be exercised at the discharge valve. The pump should not be run against a closed discharge valve for longer than the short period permitted at start-up, because the liquid contained within the casing becomes heated when no flow is passing through it. The bearing housing temperature should be checked, by means of the fitted instrument or by hand, at each round, and a housing which is hotter than its usual state should be reported. The seal leakage should also be checked: a small degree of leakage at a packed gland is perfectly normal, whereas a dry gland or a sudden increase in leakage is not. The motor cooling passages should be kept clear and the pump base kept free of spilled liquid. Any abnormal noise, vibration, or burnt smell from the motor should be reported immediately, and the pump should be taken out of service where the fault lies in the rotating parts.

## Alarms

Two alarms are fitted to the pump, and each of them calls for a specific response on the part of the operator. The low suction pressure alarm sounds when the suction pressure falls below its set point. A loss of suction pressure indicates a loss of supply or a loss of prime, and continued running under such conditions will cavitate and damage the impeller. When this alarm sounds, the pump must be stopped. The level in the suction vessel should be checked, the suction line and the strainer should be checked for blockage, and the supply should be restored. The pump must be primed once again before it is restarted, and the underlying cause of the loss should be identified before the pump is returned to service. The high bearing temperature alarm sounds when the bearing housing temperature rises above its set point. A hot bearing is indicative of a lubrication fault or of an overloaded bearing, and continued running will result in the destruction of the bearing. When this alarm sounds, the pump must be stopped and left stopped. The bearings should be allowed to cool. The oil level and the condition of the oil should be checked, and the fault should be reported. The pump must not be restarted until such time as the cause has been found and cleared.

## Shutdown

In order to shut the pump down, the discharge valve should be closed gradually so as to bring the flow down, and the motor should be stopped when the valve is nearly shut. The suction valve should be closed after the motor has stopped. Where a pump is to stand idle, it should be drained at the casing drain if the pumped liquid would otherwise set, corrode the internals, or freeze, and the drainings should be directed to the drain system appropriate to the liquid concerned. Where the pump is to return to service directly and the liquid is stable within the casing, it should be left full. Before any work is carried out on the pump, it must be isolated electrically and the starter tagged, and the isolation must be proven before the work is allowed to start. In summary, this chapter has covered the running of the pump from start to finish: the priming and starting procedure, the readings and checks which form part of normal operation, the two alarms together with the action that each of them calls for, and the shutdown procedure which leaves the pump stopped, isolated, and ready either for work or for its next start.
target:
## Start-up

Confirm that the suction vessel holds enough liquid for the start and that the suction line draws on a filled section of the vessel. Confirm that the pump casing and the suction line are filled with liquid before the motor is started. Open the vent at the top of the casing and leave it open until liquid, free of air, comes from it, then close the vent. A pump started with air in the casing does not develop pressure, and running dry damages the seals. Confirm that the suction valve is fully open and that the discharge valve is closed. Check that the coupling guard is in place and that nothing rests against the rotating parts. Check the oil level in the bearing housing at the sight glass and top up with the specified oil where the level is low. Turn the shaft by hand where access allows and confirm that it rotates freely. Bump the motor and check the direction of rotation against the arrow on the casing; correct the electrical connections before proceeding if the rotation is wrong. Start the motor and open the discharge valve slowly until flow is established. Watch the discharge pressure as the valve opens. The pressure rises to the duty value as the flow builds. Check the seals and the casing joints for leakage while the pressure rises, and listen for noise from the casing. Stop the pump at once if the discharge pressure does not rise, and return to the priming step: the usual cause is air left in the casing or in the suction line.

Run the pump at its duty point and keep the operating conditions steady. Read the suction pressure, the discharge pressure, and the flow at each operating round and enter the readings in the log. Take the readings at the same points on each round, so that one round can be compared directly with the rounds before it. The readings are the record against which later changes are judged, and a drift in any of them is the first sign of a fault developing. Keep the suction pressure up: a falling suction pressure brings the pump toward cavitation, which erodes the impeller and shortens its life. Never throttle the suction valve to control flow. Control the flow at the discharge valve. Do not run the pump against a closed discharge valve beyond the short period allowed at start-up, because the liquid in the casing heats when no flow passes. Check the bearing housing temperature by the fitted instrument or by hand at each round, and report a housing that is hotter than its usual state. Check the seal leakage: a small leakage at a packed gland is normal, and a dry gland or a sudden increase in leakage is not. Keep the motor cooling passages clear and the pump base free of spilled liquid. Report abnormal noise, vibration, or a burnt smell from the motor at once, and take the pump out of service where the fault is in the rotating parts.

## Alarms

Two alarms are fitted to the pump. The low suction pressure alarm sounds when the suction pressure falls below its set point. Loss of suction pressure means loss of supply or loss of prime, and continued running cavitates and damages the impeller. On this alarm, stop the pump. Check the level in the suction vessel, check the suction line and the strainer for blockage, and restore the supply. Prime the pump again before restarting it, and find the cause of the loss before the pump is returned to service. The high bearing temperature alarm sounds when the bearing housing temperature rises above its set point. A hot bearing points to a lubrication fault or to an overloaded bearing, and continued running destroys the bearing. On this alarm, stop the pump and leave it stopped. Allow the bearings to cool. Check the oil level and the condition of the oil, and report the fault. Do not restart the pump until the cause has been found and cleared.

## Shutdown

Close the discharge valve gradually to bring the flow down, and stop the motor when the valve is nearly shut. Close the suction valve after the motor has stopped. A pump that is to stand idle is drained at the casing drain where the pumped liquid would set, corrode the internals, or freeze, and the drainings go to the drain system for the liquid concerned. Leave the pump full where it returns to service directly and the liquid is stable in the casing. Isolate the pump electrically and tag the starter before any work is done on it, and prove the isolation before the work starts. Record the shutdown in the log, with the state the pump is left in and any fault found during the running. The chapter covers the running of the pump: priming and starting, the readings and checks of normal operation, the two alarms and the action each one calls for, and the shutdown that leaves the pump stopped, isolated, and ready for work or for its next start.

fact_base: An amine absorption unit was tested at pilot scale on gas from a cement kiln. Over 90 days at 11 t of carbon dioxide per day, the unit captured 92% of the carbon dioxide in the treated gas. Steam demand was 3.4 gigajoules per tonne of carbon dioxide captured; solvent loss was 1.6 kg per tonne captured. Beyond 90 days, the effect of kiln dust on the solvent is untested.
input: An amine absorption unit was tested at pilot scale using gas obtained from a cement kiln, the pilot unit being a test unit, smaller than a plant unit, run in order to obtain performance figures on the actual gas before any larger installation is considered. In an amine absorption unit of this kind, the solvent takes up carbon dioxide from the gas that is passed through it and gives the carbon dioxide up again on regeneration, and it is the heat required for that regeneration which the steam demand of the process represents. Over a test period of 90 days, during which the unit was operated at 11 t of carbon dioxide per day, the unit succeeded in capturing 92% of the carbon dioxide present in the treated gas, the treated gas being the kiln gas passed through the unit and the capture figure being the share of its carbon dioxide that the solvent took out over the course of the test. The steam demand was determined to be 3.4 GJ per tonne of carbon dioxide captured, a figure which states the heat taken by the process for each tonne captured and which represents the principal energy requirement of the operation. The solvent loss was found to be 1.6 kg per tonne captured, stating the solvent lost by the unit for each tonne captured, a continuing loss which has to be made up during running. Taken together, the three figures describe the test as it was run over the whole of the 90 days, on kiln gas carrying the dust load of a working kiln. It should be noted that the results are limited to the period of the test itself. Beyond 90 days, the effect of kiln dust on the solvent remains untested, and the capture, the steam demand, and the solvent loss must accordingly be regarded as established for the tested period only.
target: An amine absorption unit was tested at pilot scale on gas from a cement kiln. A pilot unit is a test unit, smaller than a plant unit, run to obtain performance figures on the actual gas. In an amine unit the solvent takes up carbon dioxide from the gas passed through it and gives the carbon dioxide up on regeneration, and the steam demand of the process is the heat of that regeneration. Over 90 days at 11 t of carbon dioxide per day, the unit captured 92% of the carbon dioxide in the treated gas. The treated gas is the kiln gas passed through the unit, and the capture figure is the share of its carbon dioxide that the solvent took out over the test. Steam demand was 3.4 GJ per tonne of carbon dioxide captured. Solvent loss was 1.6 kg per tonne captured. Steam demand states the heat the process takes for each tonne captured, and it is the larger operating figure of the two. Solvent loss states the solvent the unit loses for each tonne captured, and the loss is made up continuously during running. The capture figure is a share of the carbon dioxide in the treated gas, not a share of the gas itself, and its denominator is the carbon dioxide in the gas as it entered the unit. Both operating figures are stated per tonne of carbon dioxide captured, so each one scales with the amount captured rather than with the volume of gas treated. The three figures are period figures for the test as run over the 90 days, on kiln gas carrying the dust load of a working kiln. The results are limited to the period tested. Beyond 90 days, the effect of kiln dust on the solvent is untested, and the capture, the steam demand, and the solvent loss are established for the tested period only.

subtype: worked example with equation: friction loss
fact_base: Water at 293 K flows in a horizontal pipe. The density $\rho$ is 998 kg m-3. Mean velocity $v$ is 0.7 m s-1, pipe diameter $D$ is 0.08 m, pipe length $L$ is 114 m and the Darcy friction factor $f$ is 0.02. The friction pressure drop is 7 kPa.
input:
In this example, the friction pressure drop is to be calculated for water flowing in a horizontal pipe. The water is at a temperature of 293 K and has a density of $\rho = 998\ \mathrm{kg\,m^{-3}}$. The mean velocity of the flow is $v = 0.7\ \mathrm{m\,s^{-1}}$, the pipe diameter is $D = 0.08$ m, and the pipe length is $L = 114$ m, while the Darcy friction factor takes the value $f = 0.02$. Because the pipe is horizontal, there is no elevation contribution to consider, and the entire pressure drop can be attributed to friction. The relevant relation is the Darcy-Weisbach equation in the form

$$\Delta P = f \frac{L}{D} \frac{\rho v^2}{2}$$

First of all, the length-to-diameter ratio is evaluated as $L/D = 1425$, and the velocity head is found to be 244.5 Pa. Combining these quantities, the friction factor and the length ratio together correspond to a loss of 28.5 velocity heads, and the friction pressure drop accordingly comes out at 7 kPa. It is worth noting that the friction factor is an empirical input to this calculation rather than something derived within it, and the answer is directly proportional both to that factor and to the velocity head, so any uncertainty in the factor passes straight through to the final result.
target:
Calculate the friction pressure drop for water flowing in a horizontal pipe. The water is at 293 K, with density $\rho = 998\ \mathrm{kg\,m^{-3}}$, and flows at a mean velocity $v = 0.7\ \mathrm{m\,s^{-1}}$ in a pipe of diameter $D = 0.08$ m and length $L = 114$ m. The Darcy friction factor is $f = 0.02$. The pipe is horizontal, so no elevation term enters the balance and the whole of the pressure drop is friction loss. The friction drop is given by

$$\Delta P = f \frac{L}{D} \frac{\rho v^2}{2}$$

where $\Delta P$ denotes the pressure drop. The length-to-diameter ratio is $L/D = 1425$: the pipe is that many diameters long, and each diameter of length adds its share of friction at the stated factor. The velocity head, the kinetic energy of the flow per unit volume, is 244.5 Pa. The friction factor and the length ratio together give a loss of 28.5 velocity heads, and thus the friction pressure drop is 7 kPa. The friction factor enters the calculation as an empirical input, taken as stated at the stated velocity, and it is not derived inside the calculation. The result is proportional to the factor and to the velocity head jointly, so an error in the factor passes into the pressure drop at the same relative size, with the density held at its stated value.

fact_base: Excerpt content: two groups report conflicting lifetime values for the same material class; the excerpt weighs their test conditions. The excerpt reaches a limited preference and states the condition on which it rests.
input: The lifetime values reported for the benchmark material also differ substantially between the two groups, and once again it is important to consider the test conditions before either figure can be relied upon. The first group derives its lifetime from accelerated ageing tests, in which samples of the material are held at elevated temperature in a dry gas stream and the loss of capacity is tracked over time. The second group, in contrast, subjects the material to repeated adsorption and regeneration cycles, with regeneration carried out in a steam-bearing gas, and reports the lifetime observed under that cyclic regime. These protocols are far from equivalent, because dry thermal ageing captures only the degradation caused by temperature alone, whereas regeneration in the presence of steam introduces a hydrothermal stress that can attack the material through an entirely additional mechanism. Over many cycles, this repeated exposure may progressively weaken the structure of the material, so that the capacity fades faster than a dry ageing test would ever suggest. The shorter lifetime reported by the second group is therefore consistent with the harsher and more complex conditions of its protocol. For a process that operates cyclically with steam regeneration, the lifetime from the cyclic tests appears to be the more appropriate basis, since it is the only one of the two that includes the stress the material will actually experience in service. This preference is nevertheless conditional: it rests on the regeneration in service resembling the cyclic protocol, with steam present at regeneration. Where a unit instead runs steadily on a dry feed with no steam regeneration, the accelerated ageing result becomes the relevant basis, and the cyclic figure would understate the lifetime. What neither protocol establishes is the behaviour under milder regeneration conditions, where steam is present but the severity is lower, and the ranking of the two values in that regime remains an open question.
target: Lifetime for the benchmark material is reported at two values that disagree well beyond the scatter either group quotes, and the disagreement follows the ageing protocol. One group ages samples at elevated temperature in a dry gas stream and takes lifetime from the loss of capacity over time. The other group runs repeated adsorption and regeneration cycles, with regeneration in a steam-bearing gas, and takes lifetime from the capacity loss over the cycles. Dry thermal ageing exposes the material to temperature alone, held steady for the duration of the test. Cyclic regeneration adds a hydrothermal stress at every cycle, because steam reaches the material at regeneration temperature and attacks it through a route that a dry test never applies. Cycling also repeats the temperature change at every regeneration, and the repeated expansion and contraction loads the material in a way that a constant-temperature test does not reproduce. Each protocol measures the lifetime of the material under one exposure regime, and neither value transfers to the other regime without the exposure being restated. Capacity fade under the cyclic protocol is therefore faster, and the shorter lifetime from that group is consistent with the harsher exposure, accumulated once per cycle rather than applied once. The cyclic value is the preferred basis for a process that regenerates with steam, because it is the only value of the two that contains the stress the material meets in service. The preference rests on the regeneration condition. A unit that runs steadily on dry feed, with no steam at regeneration, does not apply that stress, and for such a unit the accelerated-ageing value is the relevant basis and the cyclic value understates the lifetime. Neither protocol covers regeneration with steam at lower severity. The material's behaviour in that regime is unreported by both groups, and the ordering of the two lifetimes there cannot be taken from either value.
