fact_base: Carbon dioxide and hydrogen react over a copper-zinc oxide catalyst to give methanol. Space-time yield is the mass of product per unit catalyst volume per hour (kg L-1 h-1). Test conditions: 250 °C, 50 bar, feed ratio H2/CO2 = 3, one feed composition. Structured catalyst: space-time yield 0.68 kg L-1 h-1, pressure drop 0.18 bar, activity loss 7% after 100 h. Pellet catalyst: space-time yield 0.38 kg L-1 h-1, pressure drop 1.48 bar, activity loss 14% after 100 h. No sulfur-bearing feed was tested. Yield and pressure drop are seldom reported for the same catalyst charge.
input: This study presents a comparison of two forms of a copper-zinc oxide catalyst, a structured form and a pellet form, for the reaction of carbon dioxide and hydrogen to methanol. All of the experiments were performed at 250 °C and 50 bar, with a feed ratio H2/CO2 = 3 and a single, fixed feed composition. The performance of each form was assessed in terms of space-time yield, which is defined as the mass of product produced per unit catalyst volume per hour, along with the pressure drop across the bed and the loss of activity with time on stream. The structured catalyst recorded a space-time yield of 0.68 kg L-1 h-1 and a pressure drop of 0.18 bar, while the pellet catalyst recorded a space-time yield of 0.38 kg L-1 h-1 together with a pressure drop of 1.48 bar. With regard to stability, the activity loss after 100 h was 7% in the case of the structured catalyst and 14% in the case of the pellet catalyst. Overall, the structured form can be seen to deliver a higher yield at a lower pressure drop under the conditions studied, and it also deactivates more slowly. It should nevertheless be noted that the comparison is restricted to the one feed composition employed here, and that no sulfur-bearing feed was tested. Yield and pressure drop are, moreover, seldom reported for the same catalyst charge, which limits the comparisons that can be drawn with other published work.
target: Carbon dioxide and hydrogen react over a copper-zinc oxide catalyst to give methanol. The catalyst was tested in a structured form and a pellet form at 250 °C and 50 bar, with a feed ratio H2/CO2 = 3 and one feed composition. Space-time yield (the mass of product per unit catalyst volume per hour) was 0.68 kg L-1 h-1 for the structured catalyst and 0.38 kg L-1 h-1 for the pellet catalyst. The yield is stated per unit catalyst volume, so the two forms are compared on the volume each charge occupies. Pressure drop was 0.18 bar for the structured catalyst and 1.48 bar for the pellet catalyst. Activity loss after 100 h was 7% for the structured catalyst and 14% for the pellet catalyst. At the stated conditions the structured form gives the higher yield at the lower pressure drop, and its activity falls more slowly over the test; the pellet form's lower yield is not accompanied by a lower pressure drop. The comparison is limited to the one feed composition tested, at the stated temperature and pressure throughout, and no sulfur-bearing feed was tested at any point. Yield and pressure drop are seldom reported for the same catalyst charge, and the paired values are stated together here so that both comparisons rest on the same test.

fact_base: A continuous stirred-tank reactor runs a neutralisation that is first order in the limiting reactant. The rate constant is 0.199 min-1 at the operating temperature and the mean residence time is 69 min. Steady-state conversion for an ideal CSTR is 93.2%. The estimate assumes perfect mixing and constant density; tracer tests on the actual vessel have not been run.
input:
In this worked example, the steady-state conversion is to be estimated for a neutralisation reaction carried out in a continuous stirred-tank reactor. The reaction is first order in the limiting reactant, which is to say that the rate at which the reactant is consumed is directly proportional to its concentration. The rate constant at the operating temperature is $k = 0.199\ \mathrm{min^{-1}}$, and the mean residence time of the material in the vessel is $\tau = 69$ min, the residence time being the volume of the vessel divided by the volumetric flow rate through it. The estimate is based on the standard ideal stirred-tank balance, and it rests on the assumptions of perfect mixing and constant density throughout the vessel. For an ideal stirred tank with a first-order reaction, the conversion is given by

$$X = \frac{k \tau}{1 + k \tau}$$

The product $k\tau$ is first evaluated as 13.7, and the denominator $1 + k\tau$ is correspondingly 14.7. Substituting these values into the expression above, the steady-state conversion is obtained as 93.2%. The purpose of carrying out the calculation in this way is to obtain, from the two quantities that characterise the system, namely the rate constant and the residence time, a single figure which describes the performance that the ideal vessel would deliver under the conditions in question, and against which the behaviour of real equipment can subsequently be compared. It should be borne in mind that this figure is the conversion predicted for the ideal vessel under the assumptions stated, and that those assumptions, perfect mixing and constant density, are idealisations which a real vessel will only approach. Tracer tests on the actual vessel have not been run, and the conversion that the actual vessel achieves is therefore not established by this estimate, and may differ from 93.2% in either direction.
target:
Calculate the steady-state conversion of a neutralisation run in a continuous stirred-tank reactor. The reaction is first order in the limiting reactant: the rate of consumption of the reactant is proportional to its concentration. The rate constant at the operating temperature is $k = 0.199\ \mathrm{min^{-1}}$ and the mean residence time is $\tau = 69$ min, where the residence time denotes the vessel volume divided by the volumetric flow rate. The residence time is a mean. Liquid spends a spread of times in the vessel, and the ideal balance works with the mean alone, because perfect mixing makes the contents uniform and the outlet stream a sample of the contents. The estimate assumes perfect mixing and constant density, and both assumptions are stated before the balance is used. The balance is written on the limiting reactant over the whole vessel at steady state, with the outlet concentration set equal to the concentration in the vessel, as perfect mixing requires. For an ideal stirred tank with a first-order reaction the conversion is

$$X = \frac{k \tau}{1 + k \tau}$$

where $X$ denotes the conversion. The product $k\tau$ is 13.7, and the denominator $1 + k\tau$ is 14.7; thus the conversion is 93.2%. The product $k\tau$ compares the residence time with the reaction time: a value well above unity places the conversion near its upper end, short of complete conversion, at the stated rate constant and residence time. The estimate holds for the ideal vessel. Tracer tests on the actual vessel have not been run, and the conversion of the actual vessel is not established by the estimate; departure from perfect mixing in the vessel would move the achieved conversion away from 93.2%, and the size of that departure is what the tracer tests would measure.

fact_base: Cost review of a regional delivery route: 862 km per trip at $1.5 per km, 832 trips per year. Annual transport cost is $1076k. Costs are carrier invoices for the last 12 months; empty running is included in the trip count.
input: This case presents a review of the transport cost of a regional delivery route, based on the carrier invoices received over the last 12 months. The review has been undertaken in order to establish what the route currently costs the business over a full year of operation, and the figures which follow are drawn entirely from the invoiced record for the period in question. Each trip on the route covers a distance of 862 km, and the invoiced cost of the transport amounts to $1.5 per km, which corresponds to a cost of $1293 for each trip that is undertaken. In total, the route is operated 832 times per year. When these figures are brought together, the annual transport cost of the route is found to be $1076k. It is important to note that the trip count on which this figure is based includes empty running, so that the annual cost represents the cost of all of the running performed on the route, both loaded and empty, taken together, and no part of it can be read as the cost of the loaded running alone. The figure is, in other words, an invoice total for the route exactly as it is currently operated, at the distance, the rate, and the number of trips stated above, and it should be understood on that basis when it is compared with the cost of any alternative arrangement, since an alternative costed on a different basis, for example with empty running treated separately, would not be directly comparable with it.
target: Annual transport cost for the regional delivery route is $1076k, on carrier invoices for the last 12 months. The route runs 832 trips per year. Each trip covers 862 km at an invoiced cost of $1.5 per km, a trip cost of $1293, and the annual figure is the trip cost carried over the year's trips at the stated rate and distance. The trip cost is the unit figure for the route: it prices one trip at the invoiced rate over the invoiced distance, before the frequency of the service is applied to it. The annual cost has three components, and it changes in proportion with any one of them: the distance run on each trip, the rate paid per kilometre, and the number of trips run in the year. A change in the route that lengthens the trip, a change in the invoiced rate, or a change in the service frequency each moves the annual total directly, and the total on its own does not show which component moved. The trip count includes empty running. The annual cost is therefore the cost of all running on the route, loaded and empty together, and no part of the figure is the cost of loaded running alone. The basis of the figure is the invoice record for the period: the distance, the rate, and the trip count are the invoiced quantities for that period, and the annual cost is their product, stated as a single total for the route as it was run. fact_base: Adsorption of a dye from water on activated carbon was measured in batch tests at 298 K. The fitted Langmuir capacity was 123 mg of dye per gram of adsorbent at pH 5. input: The adsorption of a dye from water onto activated carbon was investigated by means of batch tests carried out at 298 K. In a batch test of this kind, a fixed volume of the dye solution is brought into contact with a known mass of the adsorbent and the concentration remaining in the solution is followed over time. The capacity of the carbon was characterised by fitting the Langmuir relation to the measured data, and the fitted Langmuir capacity was found to be 123 mg of dye per gram of adsorbent at pH 5, this parameter representing the saturation capacity of the adsorbent under the conditions of the fit. In a further test, an adsorbent dose of 0.7 g L-1 was employed, and it was found that the removal achieved after 120 min amounted to 87% of the initial dye concentration of 50 mg L-1, which means that the concentration remaining in solution at that point was 6.5 mg L-1. The capacity and the removal describe different aspects of the performance of the carbon: the capacity is a property of the adsorbent as characterised by the fit, expressed per gram of the material, whereas the removal is the outcome obtained in a particular test at a particular dose and contact time. It should be noted that the Langmuir fit is reported for pH 5 only, and that the capacity at other pH values was not measured, so that the capacity figure quoted here cannot be assumed to apply at other values of pH.

fact_base: A vapour-compression unit serves a cold store, evaporating at 0 °C and condensing at 45 °C. The Carnot coefficient of performance between these temperatures is 6.07; the installed unit achieves 2.88. input: In this example, the Carnot coefficient of performance is to be determined for a vapour-compression refrigeration unit serving a cold store, and the performance of the installed unit is to be compared with it. The coefficient of performance of a refrigerator expresses the heat removed from the cold space for each unit of work that is supplied to the unit. The unit in question evaporates at 0 °C and condenses at 45 °C. The evaporating temperature is the temperature at which the unit takes up heat within the cold store, while the condensing temperature is the temperature at which it rejects heat. Since the Carnot coefficient depends on the absolute temperatures, the evaporating temperature is first expressed as 273.15 K, and the temperature lift between condensing and evaporating is 45 K. The Carnot coefficient of performance between these temperatures is accordingly calculated as 273.15 / 45 = 6.07. The installed unit, by comparison, achieves a coefficient of performance of 2.88 according to the manufacturer's test at full load, and this corresponds to 47% of the Carnot value. The achieved figure is, as it must be, below the Carnot figure, which represents the upper bound for any refrigerator operating between the temperatures in question. It should finally be noted that the part-load performance of the unit is not stated, so that the comparison which has been made here is a comparison at full load only.

subtype: worked example with equation: log-mean difference
fact_base: A countercurrent exchanger cools a process stream from 160 °C to 120 °C with water entering at 30 °C and leaving at 65 °C. The terminal differences are 95 K and 90 K, and the log-mean temperature difference $\Delta T_{lm}$ is 92.5 K. The log-mean value assumes constant overall coefficient and no phase change.
input:
Heat exchangers play a crucial role across the process industries, and a sound grasp of the temperature driving force is essential for effective thermal design. In the present example, a countercurrent exchanger is used to cool a process stream from 160 °C to 120 °C, with cooling water entering at 30 °C and leaving at 65 °C. It is important to note that, under countercurrent operation, the hottest process fluid meets the warmest water, which helps to maintain a more uniform driving force along the whole length of the unit.

At the hot end of the exchanger, the terminal temperature difference works out to 95 K, whereas at the cold end it comes to 90 K. Because these two values are not identical, a representative average is required, and this is precisely where the log-mean temperature difference comes into play. The log-mean temperature difference is widely regarded as the appropriate mean for this purpose, and it is defined by the following well-known expression:

$$\Delta T_{lm} = \frac{\Delta T_1 - \Delta T_2}{\ln(\Delta T_1 / \Delta T_2)}$$

where $\Delta T_1$ represents the terminal difference at the hot end, $\Delta T_2$ represents the terminal difference at the cold end, and $\Delta T_{lm}$ represents the log-mean temperature difference itself. Substituting the two terminal values into the expression gives $\Delta T_{lm}$ = 92.5 K, a value that lies comfortably between 90 K and 95 K, thereby confirming that the result is physically sensible.

Overall, the value of 92.5 K can subsequently be used together with the duty and the overall heat transfer coefficient in order to determine the required exchanger area. It should nevertheless be noted that the log-mean value rests on the assumptions of a constant overall coefficient and no phase change, so that in situations involving condensation, boiling, or strongly temperature-dependent coefficients, a more detailed sectional approach may well be required.
target:
A countercurrent exchanger cools a process stream from 160 °C to 120 °C with water that enters at 30 °C and leaves at 65 °C. Countercurrent flow pairs the entering hot stream with the leaving water, so the temperature difference stays nearly even along the unit, and the two terminal differences fix the driving force at the ends.

The terminal difference at the hot end, between the entering process stream and the leaving water, is 95 K. At the cold end, between the cooled stream and the entering water, the difference is 90 K. A single mean difference must therefore stand in for a driving force that varies from one end of the exchanger to the other, and it must do so in a way that keeps the duty calculation exact.

The log-mean temperature difference is the mean that meets that requirement when the overall coefficient is constant:

$$\Delta T_{lm} = \frac{\Delta T_1 - \Delta T_2}{\ln(\Delta T_1 / \Delta T_2)}$$

where $\Delta T_1$ denotes the terminal difference at the hot end, $\Delta T_2$ the terminal difference at the cold end, and $\Delta T_{lm}$ the log-mean temperature difference. Substitution of the two terminal differences gives $\Delta T_{lm}$ = 92.5 K.

The value 92.5 K lies between 90 K and 95 K, as a mean must, and it sits near the midpoint of the two ends because the ends are close. The sizing calculation that follows uses the value with the duty and the overall coefficient to give the required area.

The log-mean value holds for a constant overall coefficient and no phase change in either stream. A condensing or boiling stream, or a coefficient that varies strongly with temperature, breaks the single-mean picture, and the exchanger is then rated in sections, each section with its own temperature difference and its own share of the area.

fact_base: A textbook chapter section on heat exchangers, in four parts: principle, equipment, a worked example, and limits. The worked example uses only the numbers given in the principle part; no new data appear later in the chapter. The limits part states where the simple model fails, in plain terms, without new equations.
input:
## Principle

Heat exchangers are among the most widely used items of equipment in the whole of process engineering, and a clear understanding of how they work is essential for any engineer involved in thermal design. In essence, heat passes from a hot stream to a cold stream through the wall that separates them, and the rate at which this transfer takes place is governed by three key factors: the area of the wall, the overall heat transfer coefficient, and the temperature difference between the two streams. It is important to note that the temperature difference is by no means constant along the length of an exchanger. Each stream changes temperature as it gives up or takes in heat, which means that the local difference at one end generally differs from the local difference at the other end, thereby making it necessary either to build the duty up from local rates or to adopt a suitable mean difference for design purposes.

Furthermore, two flow arrangements bound the behaviour of the unit. In countercurrent flow, the streams move in opposite directions, so that the hot inlet faces the cold outlet and the temperature difference remains comparatively even from end to end; remarkably, a temperature cross is possible under this arrangement, meaning that the cold stream can leave hotter than the hot stream leaves. In cocurrent flow, by contrast, the streams enter at the same end, the inlet difference is the largest in the unit, and the difference decays progressively along the length as the two streams approach a common temperature which, as a matter of principle, they cannot pass.

An energy balance written on each stream ties the duty to the temperature change experienced by that stream, and the two balances must, of course, agree on one and the same duty. The log-mean temperature difference serves as the constant difference which, when multiplied by the area and the overall coefficient, returns the true duty, provided that the coefficient is constant and the temperature changes follow the balance. For its part, the overall coefficient conveniently bundles together the resistances of the two fluid films and the wall into a single figure, while the film on each side depends on how fast and how turbulently that side happens to flow.

## Equipment

The shell-and-tube exchanger, which is widely regarded as the workhorse of the industry, carries one stream inside a bundle of tubes and the other around the bundle inside a shell. Baffles fold the shell-side path back and forth across the tubes, raising the velocity and, with it, the film coefficient, and the tube side may make several passes through the shell. This robust and versatile type tolerates high pressure and high temperature, and the bundle can be withdrawn for cleaning, although these advantages come at the cost of a large and heavy unit.

The plate exchanger, meanwhile, stacks thin corrugated plates with gaskets between them, and the two streams occupy alternate channels. The passages are narrow and the flow in them becomes turbulent at modest rates, so the unit is pleasingly compact and the coefficient high; however, the gaskets limit the pressure and temperature that the stack can hold, and the pack opens up for cleaning, which makes it well suited to duties where fouling is frequent and mild.

The air-cooled exchanger rejects heat to air blown over finned tubes. The fins generously extend the air-side area, on the side where the film coefficient is poor, and the type removes the need for cooling water altogether, which is valuable where water is scarce or expensive, at the cost of a large plot area and a cold-stream outlet temperature that follows the weather. Last but not least, the double-pipe exchanger, consisting simply of one pipe inside another, serves small duties and high pressures with simple construction and little area per unit length.

Overall, the choice among the types turns on pressure, temperature, the fouling tendency of the streams, and the cleaning that the unit will need in service. No type escapes the wall and the two films; the types differ essentially in how the area is packed and how the unit is opened, cleaned, and repaired.

## Worked example

As an illustrative example, consider a hot liquid stream that is to be cooled by water in a countercurrent unit, for which the required area is to be determined. First of all, the duty is taken from the energy balance on the hot stream: the duty is the heat that the stream gives up between its inlet and outlet temperatures. The duty is then checked against the balance on the water side, where exactly the same duty appears as the heat the water takes in between its own inlet and outlet, since the two balances describe one single transfer and must therefore return the same figure, highlighting the internal consistency of the approach.

Next, the terminal differences are found from the four stream temperatures. At the hot end, the entering hot stream faces the leaving water, while at the cold end the cooled stream faces the entering water. The hot-end difference turns out to be the larger of the two here, because the water leaves warm while the hot stream enters at its hottest. The log-mean of the two terminal differences is then adopted as the driving force. The log-mean lies between the two terminal values, nearer to the smaller one where the ends differ widely, and it is precisely the difference that the rate equation requires.

The duty is divided by the product of the overall coefficient and the log-mean difference in order to obtain the area. The result is checked in two ways. The log-mean difference falls between the terminal differences, as any respectable mean must, and the area comes out larger than the area a cocurrent unit would need only if the cocurrent mean difference were the larger, which it is not: the cocurrent arrangement allows the difference to collapse along the length, its mean is smaller, and it consequently needs the larger area for the same duty. The calculation therefore sizes the countercurrent unit, and the comparison neatly shows what the flow arrangement is worth.

## Limits

It must be emphasised that the simple model rests on a constant overall coefficient, and the coefficient is constant only where the fluid properties and the flow regimes hold steady along the unit. A stream whose viscosity changes sharply with temperature, or a stream that boils or condenses over part of the area, moves the coefficient from section to section, and a single mean difference then misstates the local driving force, so that the unit has to be rated in sections instead.

Moreover, fouling introduces an additional resistance that grows steadily in service, so the coefficient used by the model on the first day is not the coefficient of a year later, and any area chosen with no fouling margin inevitably falls short before the first cleaning. Multipass and crossflow arrangements fall short of the true countercurrent difference, and their mean difference is the countercurrent log-mean reduced by a correction factor that depends on the arrangement and the temperature changes. In cocurrent flow, the outlet temperatures cannot cross, which effectively caps the heat recovery that the arrangement can achieve regardless of how much area is provided. In conclusion, the model is best regarded as a sizing estimate: it returns the area that a stated duty requires under stated assumptions, and it says nothing about whether the streams, once distributed through a real unit, will actually meet those assumptions.

fact_base: Staffing review for a dispatch office: 15 full-time staff, overtime at 10% of paid hours last year. Replacing half the overtime with one additional hire costs $65k per year fully loaded. Overtime is concentrated in two seasonal peaks; a hire is paid for the full year.
input:
This report presents the findings of a comprehensive staffing review carried out for the dispatch office, to determine whether the current resourcing arrangements remain appropriate. The office currently employs 15 full-time staff, and over the course of last year overtime accounted for 10% of paid hours, underlining the extent to which the office relies on additional hours to cope with its workload.

This overtime is by no means spread evenly across the year: it is heavily concentrated in two seasonal peaks, when demand on the dispatch function rises sharply. Against this background, one option that has been considered is that of replacing half the overtime with one additional hire. Such a hire would cost $65k per year fully loaded, and a hire, once made, is paid for the full year, whereas the overtime it would displace is concentrated in the two peaks and incurred only when the need arises.

Weighing these factors together, the balance of argument points towards retaining the current arrangement. A permanent hire would commit the office to a full year of cost to address a problem that is seasonal in nature, and outside the peaks the additional capacity would have little work to absorb it. In conclusion, it may be worth considering holding the staffing level as it stands and continuing to meet the seasonal peaks with overtime, with the position to be revisited in the event that the peaks lengthen or the underlying workload grows.
target:
Recommendation: the dispatch office holds its staffing at 15 full-time staff and meets the seasonal peaks with overtime. The office manager owns the decision and reviews it after the next peak season, on the paid-hours record for the year.

The office covers its year-round workload within the paid hours of the present staff. Overtime reached 10% of paid hours last year, and nearly all of it fell in two seasonal peaks. The question the review answers is whether a permanent hire is cheaper than the present arrangement, and the evidence is last year's paid-hours record for the office.

Replacing half the overtime with one additional hire costs $65k per year fully loaded. The hire is paid for the full year; the overtime it would displace is concentrated in the two peaks. Outside the peaks, the added capacity has no work waiting for it, and the office pays for hours it does not use.

The trade is therefore a full-year salary against a load that arrives twice a year. The case for hiring strengthens only if the peaks lengthen or the year-round workload grows, and neither change appears in last year's pattern. While the peaks stay short, overtime is the cheaper instrument, and the staffing level is held.

fact_base: Excerpt content: two groups report conflicting lifetime values for the same material class; the excerpt weighs their test conditions. The excerpt reaches a limited preference and states the condition on which it rests.
input:
It is worth noting that the two lifetime values reported in the literature are, in reality, less far apart than the very different conditions behind them might at first suggest. The first group holds the benchmark material under dry gas at a steady temperature and reports the time taken to reach a fixed loss of capacity, whereas the second group cycles the feed between dry and humid states and reports the time taken to reach exactly the same loss. Under the dry protocol, the material spends its entire life away from the condition that degrades it, and the reported lifetime is, unsurprisingly, correspondingly long. Under cycling conditions, by contrast, water reaches the pore structure on every single cycle, and the loss duly arrives considerably sooner.

The preference expressed here rests, ultimately, on the duty that the material would actually see in service. Where the feed is humid in service, the cycled values describe the life of the benchmark material more closely, and the dry values tend to overstate it. Where the feed is dried upstream and remains dry, the ranking is reversed, and the longer values are the ones that properly apply. It should be noted, however, that neither protocol fully reproduces a real plant feed, in which humidity and temperature move together and neither variable is held steady

fact_base: A review passage on adsorbents for gas drying, in four parts: scope, established results, disagreements, and gaps. The review covers 143 papers from the last 6 years. The disagreements part names the quantity on which reports conflict; the gaps part names the measurement nobody reports.
input:
## Scope

Gas drying, which involves the removal of water vapour from a gas stream before the stream is compressed, transported, or processed further, is a mature and widely practised operation, and the adsorbents that perform the work are silica gel, activated alumina, and the molecular sieves. The present review covers a total of 143 papers published over the last 6 years. The quantities that the papers report include the equilibrium uptake of water, the dew point of the dried gas, the regeneration conditions, and the life of the bed in service. Papers have been included where the feed carries water as the principal adsorbate, while mixed feeds with competing adsorbates are treated only where the water results can be separated out in a satisfactory manner.

## Established results

It is well established that water adsorbs on all three material classes in preference to the permanent gases, and the dried gas leaves the bed at a dew point that is set by the state of the bed at the end of the adsorption step. Equilibrium uptake rises steeply at low partial pressure in the case of the molecular sieves and rather more gradually in the case of silica gel, so that the sieves hold their capacity into the driest part of the duty and are duly chosen where the dew point specification is severe. Activated alumina, for its part, sits somewhere between the two in uptake behaviour and is widely used where the specification is moderate and the feed is rough.

Regeneration is accomplished by heating the bed, by reducing the pressure, or by a combination of the two, and the completeness of the regeneration effectively sets the working capacity of the next cycle. Working capacity falls as the feed temperature rises, because the equilibrium moves against adsorption, and it likewise falls as regeneration is shortened or cooled. The pressure drop across a bed of pellets and the heat released on adsorption are reported consistently enough across the literature that neither is a live dispute: the real disagreements, as will be seen, lie elsewhere.

## Disagreements

Reports are in conflict on the equilibrium water uptake at low partial pressure. For what is nominally the same material, one laboratory's isotherm lies well above another's in exactly the region that fixes the dew point, and the dried-gas performance that a designer would calculate from the two isotherms differs accordingly. It should be emphasised that the conflict does not resolve into a simple error. Pretreatment differs between laboratories, and a bed that is dried harder before the measurement starts from a different state; the measurement itself also differs, being gravimetric in one laboratory and by breakthrough in another, and the two routes weight the slow part of the uptake in quite different ways. Sample history, moreover, is reported too unevenly to allow the matter to be settled from the published record.

A smaller disagreement runs alongside the main one. Some reports treat the uptake at low partial pressure as a property of the material alone, while other reports show it moving with the binder and the forming route, which would make it a property of the manufactured pellet rather than of the crystal or gel. The distinction is by no means a trivial one for specification: a designer buying on the first view accepts any pellet of the named material, whereas on the second view the pellet itself must be specified.

## Gaps

The measurement that nobody reports is the uptake retained after many regeneration cycles. Papers routinely give the fresh capacity, and a smaller number give the capacity after a mere handful of cycles, but the bed in service is regenerated hundreds of times between change-outs, and its working capacity late in life is precisely the figure that a design actually consumes. Ageing under a real feed, with its trace contaminants arriving cycle after cycle, is reported hardly at all in the literature.

This gap is far from being a mere detail. A drying unit is sized on working capacity, and if that capacity decays over the course of the bed's life, the dew point specification is duly met when the bed is new and missed well before the bed is changed. Until such time as retained uptake over long cycling is measured and published, designs will continue to carry the decay as an allowance rather than as a datum, and the allowance differs from designer to designer because the literature gives it nothing solid to rest on.

The pressure drop across a bed of pellets and the heat released on adsorption are reported consistently enough across the literature that neither is a live dispute: the disagreements lie elsewhere.

The heat released on adsorption raises the temperature of the bed during the adsorption step and works against uptake until the heat is carried away, so beds are cycled with a cooling or purge stage where the duty allows. The temperature excursion of the bed is one of the quantities on which reports agree closely, because it follows from the isotherm and the heat capacity of the bed rather than from any contested measurement.

## Disagreements

Reports conflict on the equilibrium water uptake at low partial pressure. For nominally the same material, one laboratory's isotherm lies well above another's in exactly the region that fixes the dew point, and the dried-gas performance a designer would calculate from the two isotherms differs accordingly. The conflict does not resolve into a simple error. Pretreatment differs between laboratories, and a bed dried harder before the measurement starts from a different state; the measurement itself differs, gravimetric in one laboratory and by breakthrough in another, and the two routes weight the slow part of the uptake differently. Sample history is reported too unevenly to settle the matter from the published record. Until pretreatment and measurement route are reported as standard, the conflict will persist in the literature, because each new isotherm is measured from a different starting state and the differences are absorbed into the material's name.

A smaller disagreement runs alongside the main one. Some reports treat the uptake at low partial pressure as a property of the material alone, while others show it moving with the binder and the forming route, which would make it a property of the manufactured pellet rather than the crystal or gel. The distinction matters for specification: a designer buying on the first view accepts any pellet of the named material, and on the second view must specify the pellet.

## Gaps

The measurement nobody reports is the uptake retained after many regeneration cycles. Papers give the fresh capacity, and a smaller number give the capacity after a handful of cycles, but the bed in service is regenerated hundreds of times between change-outs, and its working capacity late in life is the figure a design actually consumes. Ageing under a real feed, with its trace contaminants arriving cycle after cycle, is reported hardly at all.

A second gap runs with the first: no standard ageing protocol exists. Without an agreed cycle of humidity, temperature, and contaminant exposure, the few retention figures that do exist cannot be compared between laboratories, and each stands alone. Operators bridge the gap with the bed life a vendor will guarantee, which transfers the missing measurement into a commercial term rather than closing it.

The gap is not a detail. A drying unit is sized on working capacity, and if that capacity decays over the bed's life, the dew point specification is met when the bed is new and missed before the bed is changed. Until retained uptake over long cycling is measured and published, designs carry the decay as an allowance rather than a datum, and the allowance differs from designer to designer because the literature gives it nothing to rest on.

fact_base: A single-stage compressor raises natural gas from 1 bar to 4 bar. Inlet temperature is 293 K. For isentropic compression with a heat-capacity ratio of 1.4, the discharge temperature is 435 K. The isentropic estimate excludes mechanical losses; the installed machine's measured discharge temperature is higher.
input:
In this worked example, we consider a single-stage compressor that raises natural gas from 1 bar to 4 bar, and the aim is to determine the discharge temperature of the machine. The inlet temperature of the gas is 293 K. It is important to note that the estimate presented here is an isentropic one: in other words, the compression is treated as reversible and adiabatic, with no heat exchanged with the surroundings, and the gas is treated as ideal, with a heat-capacity ratio of 1.4.

For the isentropic compression of an ideal gas, the temperature rises together with the pressure, and the discharge temperature can be expressed as the inlet temperature multiplied by a factor that is set by the pressure ratio and the heat-capacity ratio, the temperature climbing ever more steeply as the ratio of specific heats increases. Substituting the inlet temperature, the two pressures, and the heat-capacity ratio into this relationship gives a discharge temperature of 435 K.

It should be emphasised, however, that this figure represents a bound rather than a prediction of the behaviour of the installed machine. The isentropic estimate necessarily excludes mechanical losses, and any work that is spent against friction and irreversibility inside the machine reappears as heat in the gas itself, so that the measured discharge temperature of the installed machine is higher than the estimate. The result therefore serves two valuable purposes: it provides the lowest discharge temperature that the compression could possibly reach, and it furnishes a check on any measured value, which must lie above the estimate and is to be regarded as suspect if it does not.

fact_base: A vapour-compression unit serves an ice rink, evaporating at -10 °C and condensing at 40 °C. The Carnot coefficient of performance between these temperatures is 5.26; the installed unit achieves 2.4. The achieved value is from the manufacturer's test at full load; part-load performance is not stated.
input:
A vapour-compression refrigeration unit serves an ice rink, evaporating at −10 °C and condensing at 40 °C. It is instructive to begin with the ideal benchmark for such a duty. The Carnot coefficient of performance between these temperatures works out to 5.26, and it is important to appreciate that this value represents a ceiling: it holds for a fully reversible machine operating between the same two temperatures, and no real unit working between the same temperatures can ever be expected to reach it.

In practice, the installed unit achieves a coefficient of performance of just 2.4. This achieved value is taken from the manufacturer's test conducted at full load. It stands well below the ceiling because the real cycle inevitably spends the ideal margin: the compression is not reversible, the expansion takes place as a throttling rather than as a work-producing step, and each exchanger requires a finite temperature difference in order to pass its duty. It should also be noted that part-load performance is not stated, and the figure should not be extended to part-load operation.

Taken together, the two figures serve to fix the scale of the losses involved. At full load, the unit returns less than half of the refrigeration per unit of work that a reversible machine between the same temperatures would return, and any duty estimate for the rink at full load should accordingly be made with the measured figure rather than with the theoretical bound. What the bound additionally provides is a useful check: any claimed performance above it, for these temperatures, would be wrong on its face.

fact_base: Design report for a distillation column, in four sections: basis, sizing, materials, and risks. Design throughput is 7 t per day and the removal or separation duty is 95% of the key component. Materials are 316L stainless steel for wetted parts; the basis section states this once. The risks section names fouling and turndown as open items; neither is resolved in the report.
input:
## Basis

The column is intended to separate a liquid feed at a design throughput of 7 t per day, with a separation duty under which 95% of the key component is to be taken overhead. All wetted parts are specified in 316L stainless steel, a point which is stated here once and is not repeated in the sections that follow. The feed is taken as characterised at the battery limit: its composition and condition are those of the upstream unit under its normal operation, and the design does not make provision for feed cases lying beyond the normal range. The product specifications comprise the overhead purity implied by the duty, together with a bottoms stream that is fit to pass on to the next unit. Utilities are assumed to be available at the site conditions, and the column is designed for continuous operation at the stated throughput, with the question of turndown left open at this stage and carried forward into the risks section. The design pressure and temperature, it should be noted, follow the relief case of the upstream unit together with the heating medium of the reboiler, and the shell is rated for the coincident case rather than for the normal operating point.

## Sizing

The diameter of the column is set by the vapour load at the top of the column, where the vapour rate is at its highest and the allowable velocity fixes the cross-sectional area required. The internals are chosen with a liquid feed of this size in mind: trays offer a robust separation with a predictable pressure drop and tolerate the solids and fouling tendency of a plant stream, whereas packing would offer a lower pressure drop in a taller, narrower shell, and is accordingly set aside on fouling grounds rather than on separation grounds. The height follows from the number of contacting stages that the separation duty requires at the chosen reflux, together with the disengaging and sump allowances at the two ends. It is worth noting that the reflux is set by the duty: the specified removal fixes the split, and the reflux ratio is the operating variable that delivers it, so that the sizing and the energy balance amount to one single calculation rather than two separate ones. The reboiler and the condenser are sized along with the column, on the basis of the vapour and liquid rates that the balance returns.

## Materials

The stainless steel specified in the basis is used for the shell, for the internals, and for the wetted parts of the nozzles and instruments. The grade has been chosen with the corrosion duty of the feed and the products at the column temperatures in mind: the feed is aqueous in character and carries chlorides at levels which rule out carbon steel for wetted service, and the grade specified resists that attack over the design life with the usual corrosion allowance duly applied. Gaskets and bolting follow the same duty, with the gasket materials matched to the process fluid and to the flange temperatures rather than to the shell. Carbon steel is confined to the skirt, to the platforms, and to the external supports, where the process fluid cannot reach it. No lining or cladding is proposed: the solid grade represents the simpler construction at this diameter, and it conveniently leaves the internal surfaces available for inspection.

## Risks

Fouling constitutes the first open item. The feed carries the fouling tendency that is recorded in the basis, and the design does not settle how rapidly deposits will form on the trays and in the reboiler, nor what effect they will have on the pressure drop and on the separation over the course of a run. The choice of internals reduces the exposure but does not remove it altogether, and no cleaning interval can responsibly be stated until such time as fouling data on this particular feed exist.

Turndown constitutes the second open item. The column has been designed at the stated throughput, and its behaviour at reduced rates has not been established: trays weep and packing maldistributes as rates fall, and the reflux that delivers the duty at the design rate may well fail to deliver it at the lowest rate that the plant will ask for. Neither item is resolved in this report. Fouling is carried as an allowance in the pressure drop and in the reboiler margin, and turndown as an operating limit still to be confirmed, and both are set out here so that the design is read with its open items duly attached.

fact_base: A binary distillation separates benzene/toluene at a relative volatility of 1.7 that is taken as constant over the column. Specifications: distillate 98 mol% light component, bottoms 2 mol% light component. The Fenske minimum stage count is 14.7 theoretical stages including the reboiler. The actual design uses a reflux ratio of 1.3 times the minimum; the stage count at that reflux comes from a separate simulation.
input:
A binary distillation is employed to separate a mixture of benzene and toluene. The relative volatility for the system is 1.7, which is taken as constant over the whole of the column. The specifications for the separation are a distillate containing 98 mol% of the light component and bottoms containing 2 mol% of the light component, and it is these two compositions, taken together with the volatility, that fix the separation which the column is required to make.

The well-known Fenske equation provides the minimum number of theoretical stages for a stated split under conditions of total reflux. At total reflux, no product is withdrawn from the column, the operating lines collapse onto the diagonal, and each stage performs the maximum separation work that a stage is capable of performing; the count that the equation returns is therefore a floor which no operating column can actually attain. Substituting the distillate and bottoms compositions and the relative volatility into the Fenske equation gives a minimum of 14.7 theoretical stages, including the reboiler. The reboiler is properly counted in this total because it performs a stage of separation in its own right, vaporising a liquid whose composition differs from the bottoms product that it leaves behind.

The resulting count is a bound which serves two useful purposes. In the first place, it tells the designer the least staging that the split could ever require, and in the second place it provides a scale for the staging that a real design will need once the reflux becomes finite. The design reflux ratio is 1.3 times the minimum reflux ratio. It should be noted that the stage count at that reflux does not follow from the Fenske result, and cannot be obtained merely by scaling the minimum count; it comes instead from a separate simulation, and it is not stated here. Finally, the figure of 14.7 also rests squarely on the volatility with which it was supplied: the constant value of 1.7 is the design basis, and a volatility that varies over the column, as the temperature and composition change from stage to stage, would inevitably move the minimum count.

fact_base: A tutorial passage explains phase equilibrium for a partially miscible liquid pair. The passage states the equilibrium condition in words (equality of chemical potential across phases) before any equation is named. No numerical data are introduced; the passage is conceptual.
input:
Two liquids which mix only in part form two liquid phases over a certain range of overall composition, and the pair is said to be in equilibrium when a particular condition on the components is satisfied. This condition, which lies at the very heart of the subject, is stated here in words, before any equation is introduced: at equilibrium, the chemical potential of each component is the same in the two phases. So long as the chemical potential of a component differs between the phases, the component passes from the phase in which its potential is higher to the phase in which it is lower, and this transfer continues until the potentials become equal and the net passage duly stops.

The equality of chemical potential fixes what each phase contains. At a stated temperature and pressure, each phase takes on a definite composition, which is set by the pair and by its interactions, and neither composition moves as the overall composition of the mixture is changed. What does change, instead, is the amount of each phase. A mixture whose overall composition lies near one end of the range holds more of the phase that is rich in that component, and the proportions of the two phases follow from where the overall composition falls between the two phase compositions, which are the ends of the tie line joining them.

Temperature, for its part, moves the boundary of the range. For many pairs, the region of partial miscibility shrinks as the temperature rises, the two phase compositions approach each other ever more closely, and the phases eventually merge into one at a consolute temperature; a smaller class of pairs, by contrast, widens its region on heating. The equilibrium condition itself remains unchanged across that boundary, and it governs the single phase just as it governs the two, the equality being satisfied there by a uniform composition throughout.

fact_base: A gravity settler removes calcium carbonate from a process stream. Design overflow rate is 0.72 m h-1 at a throughput of 218 m3 h-1, giving a plan area of 303 m2. The overflow-rate basis is a vendor rule for this solid; no settling test on the actual slurry has been run.
input:
A gravity settler is employed in order to remove calcium carbonate from a process stream. The settler is sized on the basis of the overflow rate, which may be understood as the upward velocity of the clarified liquid at which a particle settling at that rate is only just carried over to the overflow. At a throughput of 218 m3 h-1 and with a design overflow rate of 0.72 m h-1, the required plan area works out to 303 m2: the area is simply the throughput divided by the overflow rate, and it is the area, rather than the depth, that fixes the separation, since a particle has the whole depth of the tank in which to settle, whereas it is only the plan area that sets the upward velocity which it must beat.

The overflow-rate basis relied upon here is a vendor rule for this particular solid. It should be noted that no settling test on the actual slurry has been carried out, and the area therefore stands on that limitation: a slurry whose particles are finer, or whose liquid is more viscous, than the vendor's reference material will settle more slowly, and at the same throughput the shortfall would manifest itself as solids carried over in the overflow. The vendor figure is, in essence, an estimate carried over from other slurries of the same solid, rather than a measurement performed on this one, and the settling test on the actual slurry represents the check that would replace it with a firm datum.

fact_base: A defect-reduction project on a packing line cut the reject rate from 3.2% to 2.1% over one quarter. At 326k units per year the change avoids about 3586 rejected units per year. The quarter included a planned shutdown; rates are not adjusted for it.
input: In today's competitive manufacturing environment, maintaining high product quality is crucial, and a recent defect-reduction project on the packing line has delivered noteworthy results in this regard. Over the course of one quarter, the project successfully reduced the reject rate from 3.2% to 2.1%, representing a reduction of 1.1 percentage points that underscores the effectiveness of the improvement work undertaken. It is important to note that the reject rate serves as a key indicator of line performance, expressing the proportion of packed units that are rejected, and the figures discussed here compare the quarterly rates for the same line before and after the changes were implemented. When this reduction of 1.1 percentage points is considered against the line's annual volume of 326k units per year, it translates into approximately 3586 fewer rejected units per year, highlighting the tangible operational benefit of the improvement. This figure should be understood as an annualised estimate rather than a count of units already saved, as it applies the measured quarterly improvement to a full year at the stated volume, and it would naturally be lower in a year with reduced throughput. It is also worth noting that the quarter in question included a planned shutdown of the line, and the rates have not been adjusted for this shutdown, meaning that the shutdown period forms part of the measurement window and its influence has not been separated out. Overall, the project demonstrates a reduction of 1.1 percentage points in the reject rate, worth about 3586 avoided rejected units annually at 326k units per year, subject to the caveat regarding the unadjusted shutdown.

At the line's volume of 326k units per year, a sustained reduction of 1.1 percentage points in the reject rate avoids about 3586 rejected units per year. The quarter over which the improvement was measured included a planned shutdown of the line. The two rates are not adjusted for the shutdown, and no adjustment is made in the figures stated here; the shutdown stands inside the measurement period, and its effect on the rates is not separated from the effect of the project. Whether the lower rate holds in later quarters is not established by one quarter of measurement. The result therefore rests on the quarterly rates as measured: a reduction of 1.1 percentage points, worth about 3586 avoided rejected units per year at 326k units per year.

The Carnot coefficient of performance between these temperatures is 4.13; the installed unit achieves 1.45. The achieved value is from the manufacturer's test at full load; part-load performance is not stated.
input: In the realm of refrigeration engineering, the performance of a vapour-compression system can be better understood by comparing it against the ideal Carnot benchmark, and this example explores that comparison for a unit serving an ice rink. The unit in question operates with an evaporating temperature of −25 °C and a condensing temperature of 35 °C, and it is worth noting that these two temperatures define the window within which the refrigeration cycle operates. The coefficient of performance, which serves as the key measure of efficiency for such systems, expresses the amount of heat removed relative to the work consumed. When the temperatures are converted to the absolute scale, the evaporating temperature becomes 248.15 K while the condensing temperature becomes 308.15 K, giving a temperature difference of 60 K across the cycle. Leveraging the Carnot relationship, which divides the evaporating temperature by this difference (248.15 / 60), the Carnot coefficient of performance is calculated as 4.13, representing the theoretical maximum that no real machine operating between the same temperatures can surpass. By contrast, the installed unit achieves a coefficient of performance of just 1.45, a figure obtained from the manufacturer's full-load test data, highlighting the gap between idealised performance and real-world operation. It is reassuring that 1.45 sits below the Carnot ceiling of 4.13, as any higher value would indicate an error somewhere in the data. Furthermore, it should be emphasised that part-load performance is not stated by the manufacturer, meaning that the comparison between the achieved value and the benchmark value of 4.13 is strictly valid only at full load and at the specified operating temperatures, underscoring the importance of understanding the conditions attached to published performance figures.
target: A vapour-compression unit serves an ice rink, evaporating at −25 °C and condensing at 35 °C. Calculate the Carnot coefficient of performance (COP) between the two temperatures, and set the installed unit against it. The COP of a refrigerator is the heat removed at the evaporator divided by the work input; it is a ratio of two energy flows and carries no unit. The refrigerant boils in the evaporator and takes up heat from the rink side at the evaporating temperature; it condenses and rejects heat at the condensing temperature. The unit therefore lifts heat across the interval between the two temperatures, and the size of that interval, with the lower temperature, fixes the best performance any refrigerator can reach between them. On the absolute scale, the evaporating temperature is 248.15 K and the condensing temperature is 308.15 K, a difference of 60 K. The Carnot COP is the evaporating temperature divided by the difference between the two absolute temperatures, 248.15 / 60 = 4.13. The Carnot COP is the COP of a reversible refrigerator between the same temperatures, and no real unit working between them exceeds it. The installed unit achieves a COP of 1.45, well below the Carnot limit of 4.13, and the comparison passes the check that the achieved value must fall under the reversible limit. The difference between the achieved COP and the Carnot COP is the cost of the irreversibilities in the real cycle, which the reversible cycle does not carry. The achieved figure is from the manufacturer's test of the unit at full load. Part-load performance is not stated, and no COP at part load is given here: the comparison between 1.45 and 4.13 holds at full load and at the stated temperatures, and at no other condition.

fact_base: Excerpt content: two groups report conflicting pressure drop values for the same material class; the excerpt weighs their test conditions. The excerpt reaches a limited preference and states the condition on which it rests.
input: It is worth pausing over the pressure drop disagreement, because the two sets of values cannot both be correct under the conditions each group describes, and the discrepancy between them is considerably larger than the scatter that either group reports within its own runs, which strongly suggests the source lies in measurement practice rather than in the material itself. One factor is what the measured section actually contains. One group measured the pressure drop across the bed alone, using tappings arranged so that the distributor and the support fall outside the measurement, whereas the other group measured across the entire vessel, so part of the drop it reports is spent in the fittings rather than in the bed, which helps explain why its values sit higher. Furthermore, the beds themselves were not packed in the same manner. A bed that is poured in a single charge tends to settle unevenly and can leave a channel along the wall, and gas through such a channel meets less resistance than gas through a settled bed of the same depth; notably, one group describes a settling step after filling, while the other provides no information about how the bed was packed, so packing differences may account for part of the gap. The samples of the material also differ: one group sieved a narrow cut, while the other used the material as received, fines included, and it is well established that fines lodge in the voids between the larger pieces and thereby raise the pressure drop across the bed. The gas handling introduces another complication, since one group held the inlet pressure steady while the other held the outlet, and for a compressible stream the mean pressure within the bed, and hence the gas density, is not equivalent under the two arrangements. On balance, the values measured across the bed alone are to be preferred, as they are the only values that genuinely isolate the benchmark material from the vessel surrounding it. This preference is, however, a limited one, and it rests on a specific condition: it holds for comparisons at matched flow and matched bed depth, and since the reported runs match closely on neither, the methods can explain the direction of the disagreement and its likely scale, but cannot definitively settle its size.
target: Nor can the two sets of values both describe flow through the benchmark material under the conditions each group reports; the gap between them is wider than the scatter either group shows in its own runs, which puts measurement practice, rather than the material, at the centre of the disagreement. The measured section contains the first difference. The samples differ too. The gas handling differs in a way that matters for a compressible stream: one group held the inlet pressure steady, the other held the outlet, and the mean pressure in the bed, and with it the gas density, is not the same under the two arrangements. On the methods as reported, the values taken across the bed alone are preferred, because they are the only values that isolate the benchmark material from the vessel around it. subtype: worked example with equation: available NPSH
fact_base: A pump draws light oil from an open tank at atmospheric pressure, 101.3 kPa. Vapour pressure at the pumping temperature is 19.9 kPa, the static lift is 1.6 m and suction-line friction loss is 0.4 m. Available net positive suction head $NPSH_a$ is 6.3 m. The pump's required NPSH at the duty flow comes from the vendor curve and must be exceeded with margin.
input:
When a pump draws liquid from an open tank, it is essential to verify that the suction conditions are adequate, and this is done by calculating the available net positive suction head, commonly denoted $NPSH_a$, at the pump inlet. The calculation brings together several quantities: the pressure acting on the liquid surface in the tank, $P_{atm}$, the vapour pressure of the liquid, $P_v$, at the pumping temperature, the liquid density $\rho$, the gravitational acceleration $g$, the static lift $h_{lift}$ between the liquid surface and the pump, and the friction loss $h_f$ in the suction line, combined in the following relationship:

$$NPSH_a = \frac{P_{atm} - P_v}{\rho g} - h_{lift} - h_f$$

In essence, the first term of the expression converts the margin of pressure above the vapour pressure into an equivalent head of the liquid itself, while the lift and the friction loss are subtracted because both are effectively consumed before the liquid reaches the inlet. In the present case, the tank is open to the atmosphere, so $P_{atm}$ corresponds to the atmospheric pressure of 101.3 kPa. The vapour pressure at the pumping temperature is 19.9 kPa, which means that the pressure margin available above the vapour pressure is 81.4 kPa. The static lift amounts to 1.6 m, and the friction loss in the suction line amounts to 0.4 m. Taking all of these values together, the available net positive suction head works out at 6.3 m. It is instructive to note that the pressure term on its own contributes 8.3 m of head, while the lift and the friction losses together remove 2.0 m. This matters because, if the available head were to fall to the level the pump requires, the pressure at the inlet would reach the vapour pressure and cavitation would occur, so the margin between the two values provides valuable protection. The required net positive suction head at the duty flow is obtained from the vendor curve, and the available value of 6.3 m must exceed it with an adequate margin. As the required value is not stated here, the comparison against the vendor curve remains the outstanding check, highlighting the importance of confirming the margin before the installation is finalised.
target:
A pump draws light oil from an open tank, and the available net positive suction head at the pump inlet is to be determined from the suction conditions. The available net positive suction head $NPSH_a$ (m) is calculated from the pressure at the liquid surface in the tank $P_{atm}$ (kPa), the vapour pressure of the oil $P_v$ (kPa) at the pumping temperature, the oil density $\rho$ (kg m⁻³), the gravitational acceleration $g$ (m s⁻²), the static lift $h_{lift}$ (m) between the liquid surface and the pump inlet, and the friction loss $h_f$ (m) in the suction line:

$$NPSH_a = \frac{P_{atm} - P_v}{\rho g} - h_{lift} - h_f$$

The first term converts the pressure margin above the vapour pressure into a head of the oil itself; the lift and the friction loss are then subtracted, because both are spent before the oil reaches the inlet. The tank is open to the atmosphere, so $P_{atm}$ is the atmospheric pressure, 101.3 kPa. The vapour pressure at the pumping temperature is 19.9 kPa, and the pressure margin above it is thus 81.4 kPa. The static lift is 1.6 m and the suction-line friction loss is 0.4 m. For the stated conditions the available net positive suction head is 6.3 m. The pressure term contributes 8.3 m of that head, and the lift and friction together remove 2.0 m. Where the available head falls to the head the pump requires, the pressure at the inlet reaches the vapour pressure and the pump cavitates; the margin between the two values is the protection against that condition. The pump's required net positive suction head at the duty flow is read from the vendor curve, and the available value of 6.3 m must exceed it with margin. The required value is not stated here, so the comparison with the vendor curve is the check that remains: the available head is fixed by the suction conditions stated above, and it is the required head from the curve that decides whether the margin is adequate.

fact_base: A contract packaging firm runs 2 plants; revenue is $77 million per year. Evidence base: order records for 12 months, 17816 orders. On-time delivery over the last two quarters was 86%, against a target of 95%. Overtime cost was $1.6 million last year, up 27% on the year before. The order backlog stands at 2.9 weeks, against 1.9 weeks a year ago. Plant 2 accounts for 68% of late orders. A scheduling system for all plants is quoted at $283k; Plant 2 alone is $122k. An internal estimate (not a vendor figure) puts the overtime reduction at Plant 2 at 15-20% in the first year. The recommendation under consideration: install at Plant 2 first, hold the other plants until Plant 2 results are reported. The operations director owns the scheduling programme.
input: This executive summary presents an overview of delivery performance at a contract packaging firm operating 2 plants with revenue of $77 million per year, drawing on a comprehensive evidence base of order records for 12 months encompassing 17816 orders. Over the last two quarters, on-time delivery performance stood at 86%, which falls short of the target of 95% by a gap of 9 percentage points, highlighting a significant performance challenge. A closer examination of the data reveals that Plant 2 accounts for 68% of late orders, underscoring its central role in the overall problem. Meanwhile, the order backlog currently stands at 2.9 weeks, compared with 1.9 weeks a year ago, indicating that the shortfall is growing rather than diminishing. Overtime cost amounted to $1.6 million last year, up 27% on the year before, reflecting the substantial expense the firm incurs in attempting to keep pace with demand. In terms of potential solutions, a scheduling system for all plants has been quoted at $283k, while Plant 2 alone has been quoted at $122k. An internal estimate, rather than a vendor figure, suggests that the overtime reduction at Plant 2 could be in the region of 15–20% in the first year. Against this background, the recommendation under consideration is to install the system at Plant 2 first and to hold the remaining plants until Plant 2 results are reported, a staged approach that would commit $122k to test the estimate where the problem is most concentrated, rather than $283k committed across the firm at once. The operations director owns the scheduling programme, and any wider installation would be a second decision, taken on the Plant 2 evidence when it is reported, as the estimate covers Plant 2 only and no saving is claimed for the other plants.

fact_base: A viscous liquid of viscosity $\mu$ = 0.05 Pa s flows laminarly through a tube of radius $R$ = 4 mm and length $L$ = 38 m. At a pressure drop $\Delta P$ of 8 kPa the volumetric flow $Q$ is 1.5 L h-1. The Hagen-Poiseuille equation assumes laminar, fully developed flow of a Newtonian liquid.
input:
The Hagen-Poiseuille equation is a widely used relationship that allows the volumetric flow of a viscous liquid through a tube to be determined from the pressure drop, the tube dimensions and the viscosity. In this example, we consider a liquid of viscosity $\mu$ = 0.05 Pa s flowing through a tube of radius $R$ = 4 mm and length $L$ = 38 m, under a pressure drop $\Delta P$ of 8 kPa, and we wish to determine the resulting flow $Q$. It is important to note that the equation is valid only under specific conditions, namely laminar, fully developed flow of a Newtonian liquid, and these conditions are assumed to be satisfied here. The equation itself is expressed as follows:

$$Q = \frac{\pi R^4 \Delta P}{8 \mu L}$$

Substituting the given values into the equation yields a volumetric flow $Q$ of 1.5 L h⁻¹. Each term plays a meaningful role: the pressure drop provides the driving force, while the viscosity and the tube length resist it, so the flow increases in direct proportion to the pressure drop and decreases in direct proportion to the viscosity and the length. The radius behaves differently, because it appears raised to the fourth power, which means the flow is influenced by the radius more strongly than by any other variable; even a small change in the radius, from fouling or manufacturing tolerances, will alter the flow by roughly four times that change in proportional terms. The resulting flow of 1.5 L h⁻¹ is relatively small, consistent with the long, narrow tube and the viscous liquid, and it should be remembered that the result holds only while the flow remains laminar and fully developed along the tube. If the flow were turbulent, or still developing near the inlet, the equation would understate the resistance, and the actual flow at the same pressure drop would be lower than the value calculated here.
target:

Find the flow of a liquid of viscosity $\mu$ = 0.05 Pa s in a tube of radius $R$ = 4 mm and length $L$ = 38 m at a pressure drop $\Delta P$ of 8 kPa. The equation is valid only for laminar, fully developed flow of a Newtonian liquid, and that state is assumed for the conditions stated; the assumption stands before the calculation because the result has no standing without it. With $Q$ denoting the volumetric flow, the equation is:

$$Q = \frac{\pi R^4 \Delta P}{8 \mu L}$$

Substitution of the stated values gives $Q$ = 1.5 L h⁻¹. Each term has a plain meaning: the pressure drop drives the flow, the viscosity and the length resist it, and the flow rises in direct proportion to the pressure drop and falls in direct proportion to the viscosity and the length. It enters as its fourth power, so the flow is governed by the radius more strongly than by any other quantity in the equation: a small change in the radius, from fouling or from a tolerance in manufacture, changes the flow by about four times that change in proportion. The result of 1.5 L h⁻¹ is small, which is consistent with a long, narrow tube and a viscous liquid, and it holds only while the flow stays laminar and fully developed along the length. Where the flow is turbulent, or still developing near the inlet, the equation understates the resistance, and the flow at the same pressure drop would be lower than the value calculated here.

fact_base: 180 pumps run at the plant. Maintenance records for 12 months show 1114 h of unplanned downtime; bearing failures account for 44% of the downtime hours. A sensor set for all 180 pumps is quoted at $424k installed, plus $76k per year. In a vendor trial on a comparable unit, the sensors cut downtime by 27%; the figure is a vendor figure and was not measured at this plant. A pilot on 15 pumps costs $43k over three months. Spare-part lead times are unchanged by the sensors. The memo recommends the three-month pilot; the reliability engineering group owns the pilot and reports before the March capital review; the decision on full installation is held until the pilot results are reported.
input: This memo recommends that the plant undertake a three-month pilot of the maintenance sensor set on 15 pumps, at a cost of $43k, before committing to any full installation. The reliability engineering group will own the pilot and will report its findings before the March capital review, and it is proposed that the decision on full installation be held until the pilot results have been reported and evaluated. By way of background, the plant operates 180 pumps in total. Maintenance records covering a period of 12 months reveal a total of 1114 h of unplanned downtime, with bearing failures accounting for a substantial 44% of the downtime hours, highlighting the scale of the problem that the sensors are intended to address. A sensor set covering all 180 pumps has been quoted at $424k installed, plus a further $76k per year. In a trial conducted by the vendor on a comparable unit, the sensors were reported to cut downtime by 27%; it should be noted, however, that this figure is a vendor figure and was not measured at this plant, so it cannot simply be assumed to represent the saving that would be achieved here. The pilot offers a means of obtaining the plant's own evidence, based on three months of sensor performance on its own pumps under its own operating conditions, for an outlay of $43k, as against a full commitment of $424k plus $76k per year. It is also worth noting that spare-part lead times are unaffected by the sensors, so no element of the case depends on faster repairs once a failure has occurred. Ultimately, the pilot needs to demonstrate whether downtime on the pilot pumps falls over the three months, and by how much, thereby enabling the March capital review to decide on full installation on the basis of measured results rather than the vendor's trial.

What the pilot has to show is whether downtime on the pilot pumps falls over the three months, and by how much; the March capital review then decides on full installation with that measurement in hand, rather than on the vendor's trial.

fact_base: The rate constant k (s-1) of a first-order liquid-phase reaction was measured at two temperatures. At 300 K, k = 0.02 s-1. At 340 K, k = 1.607 s-1, computed from the Arrhenius relation with activation energy 93 kJ mol-1 as a derived value. Each temperature was measured in triplicate; the relative standard deviation of k was 4%. Above 340 K the solvent evaporated during sampling, so no rate constant is reported above 340 K.
input: The rate constant $k$ of a first-order liquid-phase reaction was investigated at two temperatures in order to characterise the temperature dependence of the reaction. For a first-order reaction, the rate is proportional to the concentration of the reacting species, and the rate constant $k$, which has the unit s⁻¹, serves as the constant of proportionality in this relationship. At a temperature of 300 K, the rate constant was found to be $k$ = 0.02 s⁻¹. At the higher temperature of 340 K, the corresponding value of $k$ was 1.607 s⁻¹. It is important to note that this second value was not obtained by direct measurement; rather, it was computed from the Arrhenius relation using an activation energy of 93 kJ mol⁻¹, meaning that it reflects the form of that relation rather than the variability associated with an experimental measurement. Each of the temperatures was measured in triplicate, and the relative standard deviation of $k$ across the measurements was 4%. The two reported values are therefore not of equivalent standing: the value at 300 K is a measured mean accompanied by a stated spread, whereas the value at 340 K is derived from the measured behaviour via the Arrhenius relation and the stated activation energy, so that anyone making use of it is implicitly relying on that relation as well. Between the two temperatures, the rate constant increases by a large factor, which is consistent with the behaviour predicted by the Arrhenius relation for a positive activation energy over this interval, since the exponential term grows rapidly as the temperature rises, and an activation energy of 93 kJ mol⁻¹ produces a particularly steep increase. No rate constant is reported above 340 K, because above that temperature the solvent was observed to evaporate during sampling, which meant that the sampling procedure on which a measurement depends could not be carried out in the same manner as at the lower temperatures, and the series therefore stops at 340 K.
