fact_base: Pervaporation is a membrane separation in which a liquid feed contacts one side of a membrane and vacuum on the other side draws the permeating component through as vapour. Flux is the mass permeating per unit membrane area per hour (kg m-2 h-1). The separation factor is the water-to-alcohol ratio in the permeate divided by the same ratio in the feed (dimensionless). Feed: 85 wt% ethanol in water, at 60 °C. One feed composition was tested; no test ran beyond 500 h. Polymer membrane: flux 1.8 kg m-2 h-1, separation factor 180, flux fell 14% over 500 h. Zeolite membrane: flux 1.1 kg m-2 h-1, separation factor 320, flux unchanged over 500 h within measurement error. Flux, selectivity and stability are seldom reported together for the same membrane.
input: Pervaporation is a membrane separation technique in which a liquid feed is brought into contact with one side of a membrane, while a vacuum applied on the other side draws the permeating component through the membrane in the form of vapour. In this study, a polymer membrane and a zeolite membrane are compared using the same feed, and the comparison is notable in that it reports flux, separation factor and stability together, three characteristics that are seldom reported together for the same membrane. Flux is defined as the mass permeating per unit membrane area per hour (kg m⁻² h⁻¹), while the separation factor is defined as the water-to-alcohol ratio in the permeate divided by the same ratio in the feed, and is dimensionless. The feed used in the tests consisted of 85 wt% ethanol in water, at a temperature of 60 °C. The polymer membrane achieved a flux of 1.8 kg m⁻² h⁻¹ together with a separation factor of 180; however, its flux fell by 14% over the course of 500 h. In contrast, the zeolite membrane achieved a flux of 1.1 kg m⁻² h⁻¹ with a separation factor of 320, and its flux remained unchanged over 500 h within measurement error. Overall, the two membranes exhibit a clear trade-off between flux on the one hand and separation performance and stability on the other. The polymer membrane allows more mass to pass per unit area, so that a given duty at its flux would require less membrane area, but it separates less sharply and progressively loses flux as the test proceeds. The zeolite membrane, by comparison, allows less mass to pass but separates more sharply and maintains its flux over the duration tested, meaning that the permeate it produces stands further from the feed composition, albeit at the cost of more area for the same throughput. It should be noted that only one feed composition was tested, and that no test was run beyond 500 h; consequently, the comparison is valid at that composition and within that duration, and the behaviour of the membranes at other feed compositions, together with their stability over longer periods of service, remains outside the scope of these tests.

fact_base: Liquid-liquid extraction recovers acetic acid from an aqueous stream into an organic solvent. The distribution coefficient (organic over aqueous) is 0.92 at 25 °C and the design uses 7 countercurrent stages. Predicted recovery is 94% of the acetic acid in the feed. The prediction assumes equilibrium stages and negligible mutual solubility; neither has been checked on the actual solvents.
input: Liquid-liquid extraction is a well-established separation technique that can be used to recover acetic acid from an aqueous stream by transferring it into an organic solvent. The distribution coefficient of acetic acid between the two phases, defined as its concentration in the organic phase divided by its concentration in the aqueous phase, is 0.92 at a temperature of 25 °C. A coefficient below unity indicates that the acid preferentially remains in the aqueous phase at equilibrium in a single contact, meaning that the recovery achieved by the design is built up through staging rather than through the coefficient alone. In a countercurrent cascade, the aqueous stream and the solvent flow in opposite directions through the stages, so that the freshest solvent comes into contact with the most depleted aqueous stream, while the loaded solvent leaves in contact with the incoming feed, ensuring that each stage operates against the most favourable composition difference that the arrangement can offer. The design employs a total of 7 countercurrent stages. On this basis, the predicted recovery is 94% of the acetic acid present in the feed. It is important to note that this prediction rests on two key assumptions, namely that every stage reaches equilibrium and that the mutual solubility of the two phases is negligible. Neither of these assumptions has been verified using the actual solvents. Consequently, the predicted recovery of 94% should be regarded as a design figure with its conditions attached: it holds where the stages equilibrate and the phases remain effectively immiscible, and the recovery that would be obtained with the actual solvents will differ wherever either assumption fails to hold, by an amount that the stated data do not determine.

fact_base: A tutorial passage explains representative sampling of a powder blend. The passage covers where samples are taken, how many increments form one sample, and why a single grab sample misleads. No numerical limits are quoted; regulatory limits belong to the site's permit, not to the passage.
input: Obtaining a sample that represents a powder blend is more subtle than it first appears, because a blend is not uniform from place to place, and any approach that ignores this risks misleading results. Whenever a blend is moved, tipped or allowed to stand, the coarse and fine particles tend to separate: the fines sift downwards through the voids between the larger particles, while the coarse particles roll towards the outside of a heap or the wall of a container. As a result, material at the surface differs from material at depth, and material at the centre differs from material at the edge, even where the blend was uniform when made. Samples are therefore taken from points spread throughout the mass, at depth as well as at the surface. Where the equipment permits, increments may be taken from the moving stream during transfer or discharge, since a stream in motion presents every part of the batch in turn, ensuring that no region is left untested because of its position. Each taking, referred to as an increment, is small beside the batch, and a sample is formed by combining many increments and mixing them thoroughly before any portion is withdrawn for testing. A single grab sample, one scoop taken from one location, is particularly misleading, because it reports only the segregated state of the spot it was taken from; a result obtained this way can clear a batch that is off composition elsewhere, or condemn one that is actually sound. It should be noted that no numerical limits are stated here, since the limits governing a product are held in the site's permit and are applied at that level rather than in a general passage of this kind.

fact_base: Capital appraisal for a warehouse extension: installed cost $1489k, expected net saving $265k per year for 12 years. At a discount rate of 6% the present value of the savings is $2222k and the net present value is $733k. Savings are vendor and utility estimates; no saving has yet been measured on a comparable installation.
input: The warehouse extension has a net present value of $733k on the estimates the appraisal rests on. The installed cost is $1489k. The expected net saving is $265k per year for 12 years, and at a discount rate of 6% the present value of the savings is $2222k. The net present value is the present value of the savings less the installed cost, $2222k less $1489k, which gives the stated $733k. The appraisal discounts each year's saving at the same rate of 6% and adds the discounted savings over the 12 years before setting the total against the installed cost, which is treated as spent at the start. The appraisal period is the 12 years over which the savings are projected; nothing in the appraisal values the extension beyond that period. The savings are vendor and utility estimates. No saving has yet been measured on a comparable installation, so the figures that decide the appraisal, the annual saving of $265k and the present value of $2222k built from it, are estimates throughout, and the installed cost of $1489k is the only figure in the appraisal that is a price rather than a forecast. The net present value of $733k is therefore as firm as the savings estimates and no firmer: if the realised saving falls short of $265k per year, the present value falls with it, and the margin of $733k is the amount by which the estimates can deteriorate before the appraisal turns. A measured saving on a comparable installation is the evidence that would settle the question the appraisal leaves open.

fact_base: Excerpt content: two groups report conflicting pressure drop values for the same material class; the excerpt weighs their test conditions. The excerpt reaches a limited preference and states the condition on which it rests.
input: It is worth noting that the two groups report substantially different pressure drop values for what is, on the surface, the same class of material, and closer examination of their test conditions reveals differences that help to explain the discrepancy. The higher values came from beds of loose powder, where the bed producing the drop is finer and more closely packed than any formed body the process will contain; the lower values came from pellets of the benchmark material in a shallow layer, where the reported drop includes the resistance of the holder and its supports, which the authors do not separate from the bed. The two measurements are therefore not strictly measuring the same thing, and the conflict is in part a conflict of test pieces. Bed depth plays a role as well, since the powder beds were deep relative to their diameter, so distribution and wall effects enter the two results differently. Each group reports the uptake at which the drop was measured; the pellet group's loadings sit closer to the working loading of the separation, and its tests cover the range of gas rates the duty requires, where the powder tests ran below that range. IAST is common to both groups' calculations and explains none of the difference. On the match of form and loading, the pellet values would appear to be the better guide for design, although the preference is a limited one: it holds for the benchmark material as formed pellets, at loadings near the working loading. A change of form, a finer feed, or a duty at loadings outside the tested range removes that ground, and neither set of values then carries over without a fresh measurement on the material in the form the duty will use.

fact_base: A tutorial passage explains representative sampling of a gas emission. The passage covers where samples are taken, how many increments form one sample, and why a single grab sample misleads. No numerical limits are quoted; regulatory limits belong to the site's permit, not to the passage.
input:
Sampling a gas emission representatively is a more subtle exercise than it might first appear. This passage explains where samples should be taken, how increments combine to form one sample, and why a single grab sample can mislead; together these points let a sampling visit be planned and its results read with appropriate confidence.

The sampling position comes first. The sample should be taken at a sampling plane across the duct, at a section where the flow has settled: downstream of bends, fans, and junctions by a clear length of straight duct, and upstream of any point where gas enters or leaves. At that plane the probe should be moved across the section during the run, because gas composition and flow are rarely uniform across a duct: the centre runs faster than the edges, and where droplets or solids are carried, their distribution across the section is uneven as well. A probe fixed at the wall samples the edge of the stream, not the stream.

A sample is then built up from increments. An increment is a single portion of gas drawn at one position and one time; the sample sent for analysis is the combination of many increments taken across the plane and across the whole period the measurement covers. The sampling plan for the source sets how many increments are taken and how they are spaced, and the spacing follows the way the emission varies: closer together where the process cycles quickly, wider apart where it runs steadily. The analysed sample thus has the composition of the period, averaged in the proportions the period produced.

A single grab sample misleads because it freezes one moment of a moving quantity: an emission rises and falls with load, with batch steps, and with cleaning and start-up, and a grab taken at a quiet moment reports the quiet moment. The analysis of the bottle may be exact, yet the result is still wrong for the period the grab is taken to represent, because the gas in the bottle is the gas of one moment only. Increments spread across the period average that movement into the sample: the analysed gas matches the gas the whole period discharged, which is what a representative sample means.

subtype: worked example with equation: friction loss
fact_base: Water at 293 K flows in a horizontal pipe. The density $\rho$ is 998 kg m-3. Mean velocity $v$ is 2.1 m s-1, pipe diameter $D$ is 0.05 m, pipe length $L$ is 85 m and the Darcy friction factor $f$ is 0.02. The friction pressure drop is 74.8 kPa.
input:
In this example, water flows through a horizontal pipe, and the objective is to determine the pressure drop caused by friction. The data are as follows: the water is at 293 K, the density $\rho$ is 998 kg m-3, the mean velocity $v$ is 2.1 m s-1, the pipe diameter $D$ is 0.05 m, the pipe length $L$ is 85 m, and the Darcy friction factor $f$ is 0.02. Because the pipe is horizontal, there is no elevation change to take into account, and because the diameter is constant, the velocity does not change along the pipe. The friction factor is taken as constant at the stated value. Under these conditions, the friction pressure drop $\Delta P$ can be calculated from the Darcy–Weisbach equation:

$$\Delta P = f \frac{L}{D} \frac{\rho v^2}{2}$$

Substituting the stated values, the ratio $L/D$ is first found to be 1700, and the equation then gives $\Delta P$ as 74.8 kPa. The result is consistent with what the data suggest, in that the pipe is long relative to its diameter, so the velocity head is multiplied by a large length ratio before the friction factor is applied. The result is conditional on the stated friction factor, which is an input to the calculation rather than an output of it: a rougher pipe wall or a different flow regime would produce a different factor and a different pressure drop. Within the stated data, friction accounts for the whole of the pressure change along the pipe.

fact_base: Excerpt content: the schedule float is set at 10% and the excerpt defends that figure against a lower alternative. The excerpt refers to the project's cost table by section name and does not repeat its figures.
input: The float for the upgrade project currently stands at 10%, and there is a strong case for holding it at that level, which rests essentially on where the remaining uncertainty in the programme actually sits. The steering group has before it a proposal to trim the float, largely on the ground that the design is now settled. It is true that the design is settled in outline; however, the items that actually consume float are not, for the most part, design items at all. They are, rather, the interfaces with the running plant: tie-in windows that depend on operations, deliveries whose dates the project does not control, and ground conditions that only excavation can finally settle. A lower float would effectively price those items as if they were already known quantities. At 10%, by contrast, the programme is able to absorb a slipped tie-in or a late delivery without moving the completion date that the business has planned around; below that figure, the very first slip would move the date, and the resulting cost of the move would fall outside the programme. The figures underpinning this argument are set out in the cost table in the Costs section and are therefore not repeated here. The steering group is accordingly asked to hold the allowance at its present level until the tie-ins have been completed, the long-lead deliveries are on site, and the excavation has revealed what the ground actually contains.

fact_base: A textbook chapter section on process control, in four parts: principle, equipment, a worked example, and limits. The worked example uses only the numbers given in the principle part; no new data appear later in the chapter. The limits part states where the simple model fails, in plain terms, without new equations.
input:
Principle

The purpose of process control is to hold a chosen variable at a chosen value even while the process around it is continually changing. A control loop achieves this in three steps: a sensor measures the variable, a controller compares the measurement with the set point, and a final element acts on the process in order to close the gap between the two. The arrangement is a feedback loop because the action taken depends on the measured result of the actions taken earlier. The feedback is negative when the action opposes the error, so that a measurement above the set point drives the process downwards and a measurement below it drives it upwards. Negative feedback is the stabilising form, and it is negative feedback that is assumed throughout this chapter.

As a running example, take a storage tank whose level is held by a controller acting on the outlet valve. Under steady conditions the inflow is 40 cubic metres per hour and the outflow matches it exactly, so the level remains constant. The tank itself stores any imbalance: when inflow exceeds outflow the level rises, and when outflow exceeds inflow the level falls. The controller changes the outflow by means of the valve, and the response of the outflow to level is determined by the sizing of the valve together with the settings of the controller. In the arrangement used throughout this chapter, a rise of one metre in the level increases the outflow by 8 cubic metres per hour. This response rate is the link the worked example will use, and it is stated here because no new data will be introduced later in the chapter.

The controller forms its action from the error, the difference between the set point and the measurement. The simplest form of action is proportional: the valve movement is proportional to the present error, so a large error moves the valve a long way and a small error moves it only a little. Proportional action on its own leaves an offset in a loop of the tank kind: the valve reaches its new position only because the level has moved, and the level must remain moved to hold the valve there. Integral action removes the offset by accumulating the error over time and continuing to move the valve while any error remains, until the measurement returns to the set point. Derivative action responds to the rate of change of the measurement and anticipates where it is heading; it is used where the process responds slowly, although it is sensitive to noise in the measurement. The three actions are combined within a single controller, and the equipment section identifies the devices that carry them out.

Equipment

The sensor measures the controlled variable and converts the measurement into a signal the controller can use. The level in a tank may be measured by a float resting on the surface of the liquid, by the pressure at the base of the tank, which rises with the depth of liquid above it, or by the time a pulse takes to return from the surface. Each device measures the same variable by a different route, and the choice between them rests on the liquid, the vessel, and the accuracy the loop requires. The transmitter conditions the output of the sensor into the standard signal of the plant and conveys it to the controller; a measurement that arrives late or distorted degrades the loop before any control action has begun.

The controller receives the measurement, compares it with the set point, and computes the action from the error. Controllers may be housed in the control room or in the field at the equipment, and the computation is the combination of proportional, integral, and derivative action described in the principle section, with settings that determine how strongly the controller responds to a given error. These settings are the tuning of the loop: a strongly tuned loop corrects quickly but may oscillate, whereas a weakly tuned loop corrects slowly and allows errors to persist for longer.

The final element carries out the action. In most loops it is a control valve, moved by an actuator against a spring or by air pressure on a diaphragm, and the valve changes the flow the loop manipulates. The valve is the point at which the loop meets the process: its size determines the largest change the loop can impose, and its characteristic, the relation between valve movement and flow, forms part of the response rate stated in the principle section. Positioners, boosters, and hand stations complete the installation, and the loop as installed is the chain from sensor to valve, with the process closing the chain.

Worked example

Suppose the inflow to the tank steps from 40 to 44 cubic metres per hour, a rise of 4 cubic metres per hour, and suppose the controller is proportional only. The problem is to determine the level at which the tank settles. Before the level can settle, the outflow must rise by the amount of the step, since a settling level requires inflow and outflow to be equal again. The level settles where the response of the outflow supplies that rise: dividing the step, 4, by the response rate, 8, gives an offset of 0.5 metres. The level therefore settles 0.5 metres above the set point, and remains there while the higher inflow lasts. The result can be checked against the principle: proportional action moves the valve by an amount determined by the error, so a standing error is the price of the new valve position, and an offset of the size calculated is exactly what such a loop should show. If integral action is added, the offset is removed, because the controller continues to move the valve until the level returns to the set point; the settling level with integral action is the set point itself, reached more slowly.

Limits

The account given above is a local one. The response rate linking level to outflow has been treated as a constant, whereas in a real installation it varies: the flow through a valve depends on the pressure drop across it as well as on its opening, and the pressure drop changes as other parts of the plant are moved. The model therefore holds only near the operating point at which the rate was stated, and its predictions drift as the loop moves away from that point. Time delays are likewise absent from the model. A measurement taken at a distance from the tank, a long signal path, or a slow actuator inserts dead time between action and effect, and dead time limits the speed any loop can achieve, since a controller tuned as though the response were immediate will oscillate on a loop with delay. Capacity lags act in the same direction, because a large vessel changes its level slowly and the controller sees the result of its action late. Interaction between loops is a further limit: the outlet valve of one tank is the inflow disturbance of the next, and two loops tuned separately can drive each other. Noise in the measurement limits derivative action in particular, since a rate computed from a noisy signal is itself noisy. Despite these qualifications, the simple model remains the starting point for design and for diagnosis, because it identifies the quantities on which a loop's behaviour turns; its predictions should nevertheless be read as local, and a loop that behaves otherwise should be examined first for delay, for interaction, and for a response rate that has moved.

subtype: worked example with equation: Ergun pressure drop
fact_base: Gas flows through a packed bed of 1 mm particles. The void fraction $\varepsilon$ is 0.4, the superficial velocity $u$ is 0.41 m s-1 and the bed length is 4 m. The Ergun equation gives a pressure gradient of 9.5 kPa m-1, or 38.1 kPa over the bed. Particle diameter $d_p$ is 1 mm; gas density is 1.2 kg m-3 and viscosity is 1.8 x 10-5 Pa s.
input:
This worked example concerns the pressure drop when a gas flows through a packed bed. The bed holds particles of diameter $d_p$ 1 mm, the void fraction $\varepsilon$ is 0.4, the superficial velocity $u$ is 0.41 m s-1, and the bed length $L$ is 4 m. The gas density $\rho$ is 1.2 kg m-3 and the viscosity $\mu$ is 1.8 x 10-5 Pa s. The pressure gradient $\Delta P/L$ can be calculated from the Ergun equation, which gives the gradient in terms of the packing and the gas state:

$$\frac{\Delta P}{L} = \frac{150 \mu (1-\varepsilon)^2}{\varepsilon^3 d_p^2} u + \frac{1.75 (1-\varepsilon)}{\varepsilon^3 d_p} \rho u^2$$

The first term of the equation represents the viscous contribution to the loss and the second the inertial contribution, and at the stated velocity both terms contribute to the gradient. Substituting the stated values gives a pressure gradient of 9.5 kPa m-1, corresponding to a total drop of 38.1 kPa over the 4 m bed. The gradient is a property of the packing and the gas state together: the same bed at a higher velocity would return a steeper gradient, the inertial term increasing with the square of the velocity while the viscous term increases in proportion to it. The calculated drop rests on a uniform packing at the stated void fraction, with particles of a single size; channelling through the bed, or a spread of particle sizes around the stated diameter, could move the measured drop away from the calculated value in either direction.

Determine the pressure drop for gas flowing through a packed bed. The bed holds particles of diameter $d_p$ 1 mm, the void fraction $\varepsilon$ is 0.4, the superficial velocity $u$ is 0.41 m s-1, and the bed length $L$ is 4 m. The gas density $\rho$ is 1.2 kg m-3 and the viscosity $\mu$ is 1.8 x 10-5 Pa s. The Ergun equation gives the pressure gradient $\Delta P/L$ in terms of the packing and the gas state:

$$\frac{\Delta P}{L} = \frac{150 \mu (1-\varepsilon)^2}{\varepsilon^3 d_p^2} u + \frac{1.75 (1-\varepsilon)}{\varepsilon^3 d_p} \rho u^2$$

The first term of the Ergun equation carries the viscous loss and the second term the inertial loss; at the stated velocity both terms contribute to the gradient. Substitution of the stated values gives a pressure gradient of 9.5 kPa m-1, or 38.1 kPa over the 4 m bed. The gradient is a property of the packing and the gas state together: the same bed at a higher velocity returns a steeper gradient, with the inertial term growing as the square of the velocity while the viscous term grows in proportion to it. The calculated drop rests on a uniform packing at the stated void fraction, with the particles of one size; channelling through the bed, or a spread of particle sizes around the stated diameter, would move the measured drop away from the calculated value in either direction.

fact_base: Excerpt content: the analogy between the transfer processes is stated, then qualified by the case where it fails. The excerpt works one short numerical check with numbers given inside the excerpt itself. The excerpt assumes the chapter's earlier definitions and adds none.
input: When the transfer processes are considered together, the Chilton-Colburn analogy sets the heat- and mass-transfer factors equal to one another and equal to half the friction factor, in the form $j_D = f/2$, and within the range of conditions the chapter has set out, this equality can be regarded as reasonably serviceable. The point can be made more concrete by a short check on the chapter's own terms: at $f$ = 0.0072 the analogy returns a value of $j_D$ = 0.0036, and a measured factor lying close to that value supports the analogy for the case in hand. The qualification to all of this sits in $f$ itself. Where the measured pressure drop is produced by surface friction alone, $f$ is measuring the same surface process that transfers heat and mass, and the analogy may be expected to hold. Where part of the drop is attributable to form drag — flow normal to a tube bank being the standing example — that part of $f$ has no counterpart in the transfer factors, and $f/2$ will overstate both of them. The analogy therefore fails in a quite definite direction, predicting transfer factors that lie above the measured ones, and it is best confined to the smooth, fully turbulent cases from which it was drawn.

fact_base: A binary distillation separates ethanol/water at a relative volatility of 2.26 that is taken as constant over the column. Specifications: distillate 98 mol% light component, bottoms 2 mol% light component. The Fenske minimum stage count is 9.5 theoretical stages including the reboiler. The actual design uses a reflux ratio of 1.3 times the minimum; the stage count at that reflux comes from a separate simulation.
input:
This passage reports a minimum-stage assessment for a binary distillation separating ethanol and water, carried out at a relative volatility of 2.26, taken as constant over the column. The specifications are a distillate containing 98 mol% of the light component and a bottoms product containing 2 mol% of the light component. Application of the Fenske equation at total reflux gives a minimum stage count of 9.5 theoretical stages, the reboiler included in the count.

This figure is a lower bound on the stages a working column requires. It is calculated at total reflux, where all the condensed vapour returns to the column and no product is withdrawn, so the separation achieved per stage is at its most effective. A column that withdraws product works at a finite reflux and needs more stages for the same specifications; minimum stages and minimum reflux are the two ends of the same trade-off, and a design fixes both quantities away from their limits. For fixed specifications the count is set by the relative volatility: the larger the volatility, the fewer stages the separation requires, and as the volatility approaches unity the stated specifications could not be reached with any practical stage count.

The design reflux ratio is set at 1.3 times the minimum, and the stage count at that reflux comes from a separate simulation rather than from the Fenske relation. Some caution is in order: the minimum count rests on the assumption of a constant relative volatility, whereas the volatility of ethanol and water varies with composition along the column, so the figure of 9.5 stages is only as reliable as that approximation, and it is the simulated count at the design reflux that the design properly rests upon.

fact_base: Performance of a natural-draft tower at a chemical site was logged over one summer month. Mean wet-bulb temperature was 23 °C, the approach was 4 K and the range was 11 K. Performance outside the logged month, in particular at winter wet-bulb temperatures, was not measured.
input:
Over the course of one summer month, the performance of a natural-draft cooling tower at a chemical site was logged. The mean wet-bulb temperature over the month was 23 °C, the approach was 4 K, and the range was 11 K. The approach is the difference between the temperature of the cold water leaving the tower and the wet-bulb temperature of the entering air, whilst the range is the fall in the water temperature across the tower, from inlet to outlet. Together with the wet-bulb temperature, these figures fix the water temperatures of the test: the cold water left the tower at 27 °C and the hot water entered at 38 °C.

A natural-draft tower draws its air without a fan. The air inside the tower is warm and moist, and lighter than the air outside; the density difference raises a current that pulls fresh air in at the base and discharges the warmed air at the top. The driving force thus depends on the state of the entering air, and the wet-bulb temperature is the relevant measure of that state for evaporative cooling: the cold water cannot leave the tower below the wet-bulb temperature, and the approach records how closely the tower approached that limit. An approach of 4 K, sustained over a month of summer operation at the stated range, is therefore the measured performance of the tower at a summer wet-bulb temperature.

The log, however, covers one month only, and the figures are the performance for that month. Performance outside the logged month has not been measured; at winter wet-bulb temperatures in particular, the tower's approach is unknown, because the entering air is then colder and drier, the density difference driving the draft is altered, and no winter log exists to test it. The summer figures thus rate the tower for summer duty. A winter rating would require a winter log, recorded at winter wet-bulb temperatures with the approach and the range logged in the same manner, and until such a log exists the cold-weather performance of the tower stands as not measured.

fact_base: Energy assessment of a paper mill, in four sections: current use, refrigeration, steam, and recommendation. Electricity use is 1423 MWh per year; refrigeration takes the largest share. A heat-recovery retrofit is projected to save 15% of electricity use, a derived saving of 213 MWh per year, at a capital cost of $405k. At $0.12 per kWh the derived annual saving is $25614 and the derived simple payback is 15.8 years. Steam figures are from one winter month and are flagged as seasonal in the recommendation.
input:
Current use

Electricity use at the mill currently amounts to 1423 MWh per year. Of this total, refrigeration accounts for the largest share; the remainder is spread across the mill's various drives, pumps, fans, and auxiliary services, none of which approaches the refrigeration load in scale. This figure is a metered annual total, and it serves as the base against which every saving identified in this assessment is expressed: a measure that saves a given share of electricity is credited with that share of the 1423 MWh, and no other base is used at any point. Steam is accounted for separately, in the steam section below, because its figures are drawn from a different record and cover a considerably shorter period. The assessment covers the site as metered: electricity generated on site, where such generation occurs, enters the figures through the same meters, and no attempt has been made to separate purchased and generated electricity within the totals that are used here. The annual total itself is built up from monthly meter readings, and it consequently smooths the seasons out of the site's demand: a heavy winter month and a light summer month enter the average side by side, which is the appropriate basis for measures whose savings likewise run throughout the year. Measures whose effect is essentially seasonal are not credited on this base, and none is assessed here.

Refrigeration

Refrigeration represents the largest single use of electricity at the mill. The plant supplies chilled water and cold air both to the process and to the stores, and it operates throughout the year, which is an important part of the explanation for the size of its share of the annual total: a load that runs in every month of the year inevitably accumulates more energy than a heavier load that runs for only part of it. Refrigeration is also the point at which the heat leaves the system. A refrigeration plant works by moving heat from the cooled spaces to its condensers and rejecting it at that point, and at present that rejected heat is simply discharged without being used. The heat-recovery retrofit that is assessed here would take heat from the discharge side of the refrigeration plant and return it to duties that currently draw on other sources. The saving that is projected is a saving of electricity: the recovered heat displaces work that would otherwise be done elsewhere in the mill's systems, and the assessment accordingly credits the retrofit with 15% of electricity use, corresponding to a derived saving of 213 MWh per year. It should be noted that this projection is a calculation based on the rated duty of the plant and its running hours, rather than a measurement of any kind; it rests on the assumption that the recovered heat will in fact be taken up whenever the plant is running, and a duty that is unable to accept heat at the times when the plant rejects it would inevitably return a smaller saving. It is also relevant that the heat rejected by the plant is low-grade in character: it is warm rather than hot, and it is therefore suited to duties that require warmth rather than high temperature, such as the heating of water and of air and the preheating of streams on their way to hotter duties. The mill possesses duties of this kind in every season, although their size varies with the weather, and it is the match between rejection and demand, considered hour by hour, that the projection assumes and that the design stage will have to test.

Steam

Steam serves the drying section together with the mill's space and process heating requirements. The steam figures that appear in the mill's records are drawn from one winter month, and this limitation deserves to be stated plainly. Winter is the season in which steam demand is at its heaviest: the incoming water and air are at their coldest, the heating load reaches its highest level, and the drying section is working against the coldest feed of the year. A figure taken from such a month, if it were read as a yearly figure, would overstate steam use across the year as a whole, and any saving expressed as a share of that month would overstate the saving itself in exactly the same way. For this reason, the steam section of this assessment quotes no annual steam total and ranks no steam-side measure: the available data support a statement about the winter month and about nothing beyond it. It is not that steam measures are dismissed by this limitation; rather, they are deferred by it. The metering installation that produced the winter figure remains in place, and a run of monthly figures extending across a full year would place steam on much the same footing as electricity, at which point steam-side measures could be costed and ranked against the refrigeration retrofit on a single consistent basis. The same caution would apply to any attempt to read the winter figure as representing a peak: the month in question was an ordinary working month rather than an extreme one, and nothing in the existing record serves to separate the contribution of the weather to the demand from the contribution of the production rate. Until monthly figures are available, even the direction of a steam saving is difficult to state with confidence, since a measure that saves steam in the winter may save comparatively little in the summer, when the load that it serves is smaller.

Recommendation

It is recommended that the refrigeration heat-recovery retrofit be taken forward to detailed design, with the site energy manager as the designated owner. The capital cost of the scheme is $405k. At a price of $0.12 per kWh, the derived annual saving works out at $25614, giving a derived simple payback of 15.8 years: the mill would be spending $405k in order to gain $25614 in each year, and the trade-off, stated in a single sentence, is a large capital sum set against a relatively small annual return. This is a long payback, and it should be emphasised that the recommendation is for design work, and not for immediate construction; the design stage is precisely where the principal assumption underlying the projection will be tested, namely the assumption that duties genuinely exist which are able to take the recovered heat at the times when the refrigeration plant is rejecting it. Should that assumption turn out to fail in part, the saving would fall below 213 MWh per year and the payback would lengthen beyond the figure stated above, and any decision to proceed to construction should then be taken on the basis of the design-stage numbers, rather than on the projection as it is restated here. The electricity base upon which the decision rests is, by contrast, firm: 1423 MWh per year, fully metered. The steam side of the mill's energy use is not yet ready for the same kind of treatment. The steam figures are drawn from one winter month and are accordingly flagged as seasonal in nature: no steam measure is recommended in this assessment, and the appropriate next step in relation to steam is the assembly of a full year of monthly figures, after which steam measures can be ranked against the retrofit on the same consistent basis. Two conditions are attached to the design work that is recommended. The first is that the heat sinks be confirmed at the times when the refrigeration plant actually rejects its heat, across the seasons of the year and not merely in the season in which the assessment was carried out. The second is that the capital figure be re-priced at the conclusion of the design stage, so that the eventual decision on construction is taken on the basis of a current price and a tested saving, with the payback recomputed on both of those foundations.

fact_base: Excerpt content: two groups report conflicting pressure drop values for the same material class; the excerpt weighs their test conditions. The excerpt reaches a limited preference and states the condition on which it rests.
input: The disagreement over the benchmark material is, on closer inspection, narrower than the two sets of values might initially suggest. One of the groups tested the material as a loose powder, whereas the other tested formed pellets held in a shallow holder, and the second set of values includes the resistance of the holder itself, which the authors leave incorporated within the reported drop. The powder bed is also finer and considerably more closely packed than the formed body that the duty will actually contain, so that the two tests are in reality measuring different packings, rather than measuring one and the same packing at two different levels of care. The loadings stated by the pellet group lie closer to the working loading of the separation in question, and its gas rates have the additional merit of covering the range that the duty requires. IAST underlies the calculations of both groups and can therefore account for none of the difference that separates them. The pellet values are accordingly to be preferred, although on that condition alone: that is to say, formed material, loadings close to the working loading, and rates within the range that the duty requires. Outside those particular conditions, the preference lapses altogether, and a fresh measurement carried out on the material in its formed state is the only remedy that either group has to offer.

The conditions each group chose were reasonable for the question each was asking; the difficulty is that the design question is only one of them. The pellet group's stated loadings lie closer to the working loading of the separation, and its gas rates cover the range the duty needs. IAST underlies both groups' calculations and accounts for none of the difference. The pellet values are preferred, on that condition alone: formed material, loadings near the working loading, rates within the range the duty requires. Outside those conditions the preference lapses, and a fresh measurement on the material as formed is the only remedy either group offers.

fact_base: Excerpt content: the staffing ramp is set at 7% and the excerpt defends that figure against a lower alternative. The excerpt refers to the project's cost table by section name and does not repeat its figures.
input: The staffing ramp for the upgrade project has been set at 7%, and the figure represents a rate of build-up rather than anything in the nature of a contingency. Its purpose is to phase recruitment and induction so that each work front opens with its full complement in place: supervision first, then the trades in the order the fronts start. The steering group has been offered a lower ramp in terms of a saving on early payroll. The saving is genuine but small, and its figures stand in the cost table in the Costs section. It would be bought by concentrating the same recruitment into the weeks before the shutdown, when the project competes for the same trades with every other site in the region, and by removing any slack for the attrition the early months invariably bring: in a thinly staffed crew, each leaver is a front delayed. At 7%, by contrast, the build-up completes ahead of the first front and a margin against attrition is retained; below that rate the margin disappears, and the shutdown plan takes upon itself the risk the ramp was set to remove. The ramp is therefore held at its present level until the crews for the opening fronts are complete and fully inducted.

fact_base: Energy assessment of a brewery, in four sections: current use, refrigeration, steam, and recommendation. Electricity use is 3220 MWh per year; refrigeration takes the largest share. A heat-recovery retrofit is projected to save 18% of electricity use, a derived saving of 580 MWh per year, at a capital cost of $775k. At $0.12 per kWh the derived annual saving is $69552 and the derived simple payback is 11.1 years. Steam figures are from one winter month and are flagged as seasonal in the recommendation.
input:
## Current use

It is worth noting that total electricity use at the brewery currently stands at 3220 MWh per year, a figure that provides the essential backdrop for everything that follows in this assessment. Refrigeration accounts for the largest share of this consumption, underscoring its central importance to the site's overall energy profile, and it is examined in greater detail in the dedicated section below. The remaining electricity is consumed by a wide range of activities across the brewhouse, the cellar, packaging, and site services. Pumps are utilised to move wort, water, and beer between vessels, while motors drive mills, conveyors, and packaging machinery. Compressed air supports valves and packaging equipment, and lighting and ventilation operate across all production areas. It should be emphasised that none of these uses is metered separately in the material available to the assessment, which means that the precise split of the remaining consumption between them cannot be stated with confidence. The annual figure is a metered total for the site as a whole, and it serves as the baseline against which every potential saving discussed in this document is measured. Production volumes naturally fluctuate over the course of the year, and electricity use fluctuates alongside them; the annual total already captures this variation, since it aggregates a full twelve months of operation. Consequently, any saving expressed as a proportion of electricity use is a proportion of the metered annual total, rather than of a peak month or a design load. Specific electricity use per unit of production is not reported, as production figures were outside the material supplied. Comparisons with other breweries are likewise not attempted, for the simple reason that a meaningful comparison would require a shared basis, and no such shared basis is currently available. In essence, the current-use picture consists of a total and a ranking of uses, and it is this ranking that shapes the direction of the remainder of the assessment.

## Refrigeration

Refrigeration represents the largest single use of electricity at the brewery, playing a pivotal role in the site's energy story. The fermentation process generates heat that must be continuously removed in order to maintain the temperature of the fermenting wort, and finished beer is held cold in storage until the point of dispatch. Cooling therefore operates in every month of the year, not merely during warmer weather, which means the refrigeration plant is best characterised as a continuous load rather than an intermittent one. The plant removes heat at evaporators located in the fermenters, the cold stores, and the cellar, and rejects that heat at the condensers. Compressors raise the refrigerant to the pressure at which it condenses, and it is the compressor motors that account for the majority of the electricity consumed by the plant, with condenser fans and coolant pumps accounting for the remainder. The physical condition of the plant has a direct bearing on the load. Fouled condenser surfaces push the condensing temperature upwards, forcing the compressors to work against a higher pressure for the same duty, while low refrigerant charge and worn compressor valves produce a similar effect through extended running hours. Regular cleaning of the condensers, together with the prompt repair of leaks, is therefore an important part of holding the present load at its current level, before any retrofit is even considered. At present, the heat rejected at the condensers is simply discharged into the surrounding air. This rejected heat is precisely the stream that the proposed retrofit seeks to recover: it is available whenever the plant is running, and the plant runs throughout the year. The load does, of course, vary across the seasons: higher summer ambient temperatures raise the condensing pressure and the associated compressor work, whereas winter operation lowers both. The annual electricity total already reflects this seasonal movement, and no separate monthly breakdown of the refrigeration load is available at this time.

## Steam

Steam plays a crucial role in the brewhouse, where it is responsible for heating the mash, boiling the wort, and supplying hot water for cleaning purposes. Steam is raised in the site boiler and distributed to the brewhouse through insulated mains. Condensate is returned wherever the layout permits, and returned condensate reduces the amount of fuel the boiler must burn for a given steam output. It is important to appreciate that losses from leaking traps and uninsulated fittings show up in the steam figures just as surely as genuine process use does, and a single month's record has no way of separating the two. The steam figures used in this assessment are drawn from one winter month. That month is the only steam record available, and it should not be interpreted as an annual figure. Steam demand at a brewery is inherently seasonal in nature. Space heating adds to the process load during the winter, cold feed water increases the heat required for every hot liquor preparation, and production schedules themselves vary over the course of the year. A winter month therefore tends to show steam use at or near its highest level, and simply scaling the month's figures up to form an annual total would overstate steam use for the year as a whole. For this reason, the assessment deliberately does not annualise the steam figures. They are used for two purposes only: to indicate the size of the steam load relative to the site's energy use in the month recorded, and to identify where steam is consumed within the brewhouse. Any saving that depends on steam quantities is presented subject to the same limitation. A full year of steam metering, or monthly records spanning a year, would ultimately replace the single month and remove this limitation; until such records exist, however, conclusions regarding steam necessarily remain at the level of the one month that was measured.

## Recommendation

It is recommended that the brewery should approve the heat-recovery retrofit. The retrofit is projected to deliver a saving of 18% of electricity use, which translates into a derived saving of 580 MWh per year when set against the metered total. The capital cost associated with the retrofit is $775k. At a price of $0.12 per kWh, the derived annual saving works out at $69552. Comparing the derived annual saving of $69552 with the capital cost of $775k gives a derived simple payback of 11.1 years. It takes no account of maintenance costs, of possible changes in the electricity price, or of the time value of money, and it should therefore be read as a screening figure rather than as a full investment appraisal. The recommendation set out here covers the retrofit only. The steam figures underpinning the assessment are drawn from one winter month and are accordingly flagged as seasonal. No steam measure is recommended on the basis of a single month, and gathering a full year of steam records is the logical next step before any steam saving can be properly costed. Electricity metering by individual use is likewise absent, and installing submeters on the refrigeration plant would allow the saving to be verified after installation rather than merely inferred from the site total. Subject to that reading, the retrofit stands as the one measure that the present evidence genuinely supports.

Compressed air serves valves and packaging equipment, and lighting and ventilation run across all production areas. None of these uses is metered separately in the material available to the assessment, so the split of the remaining use between them is not stated. The annual figure is a metered total for the site, and it is the base against which every saving in the assessment is measured. Low refrigerant charge and worn compressor valves have the same effect through longer running hours. subtype: worked example with equation: log-mean difference
fact_base: A countercurrent exchanger cools a process stream from 160 °C to 120 °C with water entering at 40 °C and leaving at 75 °C. The terminal differences are 85 K and 80 K, and the log-mean temperature difference $\Delta T_{lm}$ is 82.5 K. The log-mean value assumes constant overall coefficient and no phase change.
input:
This example works through the calculation of the log-mean temperature difference for a countercurrent heat exchanger that cools a process stream from 160 °C to 120 °C, with cooling water entering at 40 °C and leaving at 75 °C.

The terminal temperature differences at the two ends are established first. At the end where the process stream enters, the terminal difference $\Delta T_1$ is 85 K, the difference between the entering process stream at 160 °C and the leaving water at 75 °C. At the opposite end, where the process stream leaves, the terminal difference $\Delta T_2$ is 80 K, the difference between the leaving process stream at 120 °C and the entering water at 40 °C. Countercurrent flow maintains a temperature difference between the streams at every point along the exchanger, and the two terminal differences are quite close, because the temperature changes of the two streams are broadly similar in magnitude.

$$\Delta T_{lm} = \frac{\Delta T_1 - \Delta T_2}{\ln(\Delta T_1 / \Delta T_2)}$$

In this relation, $\Delta T_{lm}$ denotes the log-mean temperature difference, while $\Delta T_1$ and $\Delta T_2$ denote the terminal differences at the two ends of the exchanger. Substituting the terminal differences into the relation gives $\Delta T_{lm}$ = 82.5 K. In practice, heat-exchanger rating uses the log-mean temperature difference as the mean driving force for the unit as a whole, rather than a local difference.

The log-mean temperature difference is valid for an exchanger in which the overall coefficient remains constant along the length and neither stream changes phase. If either stream changes phase, or if the coefficient varies with temperature, the calculation moves outside the conditions under which the relation holds, and the exchanger must instead be rated in sections. The value of 82.5 K lies between the terminal differences of 85 K and 80 K. A mean of the two end differences must lie between them, and the log-mean value sits close to the arithmetic mean because the two terminal differences are close to each other.

fact_base: A tutorial passage explains representative sampling of a gas emission. The passage covers where samples are taken, how many increments form one sample, and why a single grab sample misleads. No numerical limits are quoted; regulatory limits belong to the site's permit, not to the passage.
input:
Representative sampling of a gas emission rests on a single fundamental requirement: the sample sent for analysis must faithfully carry the composition of the gas in the duct at the time of sampling, rather than the composition of one point or one moment within it.

Samples are generally taken where the gas is well mixed: downstream of a bend, a fan, or a junction, where the fitting has churned the stream and the composition is close to uniform. In a long straight run, or just past an inlet where a second stream enters, strata of differing composition may lie side by side, and a probe there samples one stratum only. Where the duct is large, samples are drawn at several positions and combined, ensuring no part of the flow is left unrepresented.

A single sample is built up from several increments: small portions drawn over short periods, spread across the period the sample has to cover, whether a batch, a shift, or a full cycle of the generating process. Combined into the one sample sent for analysis, the increments ensure that a constituent arising during part of the cycle is present in proportion to its share of the cycle, rather than absent, or dominant, by accident of timing.

A single grab sample can be misleading for the same reason. It is just one portion taken at one moment, whereas the composition of an emission varies from moment to moment with load, feed, and operating state. The grab sample reports the moment faithfully but the emission wrongly: a peak can be read as the norm, or a lull as cleanliness. No numerical limits are quoted here; regulatory limits belong to the site's permit, not to a sampling method.

subtype: worked example with equation: Stokes settling
fact_base: Sand grains of diameter $d_p$ = 50 micrometres and density 1400 kg m-3 settle in water at 293 K. Stokes' law gives a terminal velocity $v_t$ of 0.55 mm s-1. The estimate requires creeping flow; the particle Reynolds number must be checked before the value is used.
input:
In this example, we will estimate the terminal settling velocity of sand grains having a diameter $d_p$ = 50 micrometres and a density of 1400 kg m-3, settling in water at 293 K.

When a particle falls through a liquid, it accelerates until the drag acting on it balances the net driving force, which is to say the weight of the particle less the buoyancy of the liquid it displaces. Once this balance is reached, the particle falls at a constant velocity, referred to as the terminal velocity $v_t$. For a small spherical particle in creeping flow, the drag takes the well-known Stokes form, and the force balance leads directly to the following expression for the terminal velocity:

$$v_t = \frac{g d_p^2 (\rho_p - \rho)}{18 \mu}$$

In this relation, $g$ denotes the acceleration due to gravity, $d_p$ the particle diameter, $\rho_p$ the particle density, $\rho$ the density of the liquid, and $\mu$ the liquid viscosity. The density difference $\rho_p - \rho$ is what actually drives the motion: a particle that is denser than the liquid will sink, whereas a particle having exactly the same density as the liquid would have no terminal velocity at all. Substituting the stated diameter, densities, and viscosity into the expression gives $v_t$ = 0.55 mm s-1 for the sand grains in water at 293 K.

It is worth noting that this is a slow velocity in absolute terms, which is entirely to be expected for grains of only 50 micrometres: the velocity decreases with the square of the diameter, so fine grains settle considerably more slowly than coarse ones, and the residence times provided in any settling device must be set with this in mind. Stokes' law applies to creeping flow around the particle, with the drag remaining in the viscous regime throughout. The estimate therefore comes with an important condition that must be checked before the value is used in practice: the particle Reynolds number, formed using the terminal velocity and the particle diameter, must lie within the creeping-flow range. If the particle Reynolds number falls outside that range, the drag no longer follows the Stokes form, and the value of 0.55 mm s-1 should not be used until the check has been properly carried out.

subtype: worked example with equation: first-order decay
fact_base: A peroxide initiator decomposes by first-order kinetics with rate constant $k$ = 0.174 min-1. After 54 min the fraction remaining $C / C_0$ is 0. The rate constant was measured at one temperature; no activation energy is available.
input:
A peroxide initiator decomposes according to first-order kinetics, with a rate constant $k$ = 0.174 min-1. We are interested in determining the fraction of the initiator that remains after 54 min.

For a first-order reaction, the rate of decomposition is proportional to the concentration that remains at any given time, and integrating the rate expression yields the fraction remaining directly as a function of time, as expressed by the following relation:

$$\ln\frac{C}{C_0} = -k t$$

In this relation, $C$ denotes the concentration at time $t$, $C_0$ denotes the concentration at the start, and $k$ denotes the rate constant. Substituting $k$ = 0.174 min-1 and $t$ = 54 min into the expression gives $C / C_0$ = 0, at the precision of the stated value: the exponent is sufficiently large that the fraction remaining drops below any figure that the stated precision could meaningfully carry. In practical terms, the initiator can be regarded as fully decomposed at 54 min.

It should be noted that the rate constant was measured at one temperature only, and no activation energy is available. The value of $k$ therefore applies strictly at the temperature at which the measurement was made, and no correction of the rate constant to another temperature can be carried out on the basis of the data provided. The result is also specific to first-order kinetics: a decomposition following another order would obey a different decay law, and the relation above would not carry over to such a case.

subtype: worked example with equation: log-mean difference
fact_base: A countercurrent exchanger cools a process stream from 200 °C to 150 °C with water entering at 40 °C and leaving at 65 °C. The terminal differences are 135 K and 110 K, and the log-mean temperature difference $\Delta T_{lm}$ is 122.1 K. The log-mean value assumes constant overall coefficient and no phase change.
input:
In this example, we will work through the calculation of the log-mean temperature difference for a countercurrent heat exchanger that cools a process stream from 200 °C to 150 °C, using cooling water that enters at 40 °C and leaves at 65 °C.

We establish the terminal temperature differences at the two ends of the exchanger. At the end where the process stream enters, the terminal difference, denoted $\Delta T_1$, is 135 K, reflecting the difference between the entering process stream at 200 °C and the leaving water at 65 °C. At the other end, where the process stream leaves, the terminal difference $\Delta T_2$ is 110 K, reflecting the difference between the leaving process stream at 150 °C and the entering water at 40 °C. In this case the process stream undergoes the larger temperature change of the two streams, and the terminal differences are correspondingly further apart than the closest approach occurring anywhere within the unit.

$$\Delta T_{lm} = \frac{\Delta T_1 - \Delta T_2}{\ln(\Delta T_1 / \Delta T_2)}$$

In this relation, $\Delta T_{lm}$ denotes the log-mean temperature difference, while $\Delta T_1$ and $\Delta T_2$ denote the terminal differences at the two ends of the exchanger. Substituting the terminal differences into the relation gives $\Delta T_{lm}$ = 122.1 K. It is worth noting that simply taking the arithmetic mean of the two terminal differences would overstate the driving force, since the local temperature difference does not vary in a linear fashion along the exchanger; the log-mean value weights the smaller differences in the correct manner. In practice, heat-exchanger rating uses the log-mean temperature difference as the mean driving force for the unit as a whole.

It should be emphasised that the log-mean temperature difference is valid for an exchanger in which the overall coefficient remains constant along the length and neither stream undergoes a phase change. If either stream changes phase, or if the coefficient varies with temperature, the calculation moves outside the conditions under which the relation holds, and the exchanger must instead be rated in sections, with each section having its own log-mean difference. Finally, the value of 122.1 K lies between the terminal differences of 135 K and 110 K, and somewhat nearer to the smaller of the two, exactly as a logarithmic mean of the end values must.

fact_base: Goal: compute the half-life of a first-order reaction and the fraction remaining after 60 min. For a first-order reaction the rate constant k (min-1) fixes the half-life t1/2 (min) by t1/2 = ln(2) / k, and the fraction remaining after time t (min) is exp(-k t). Measured rate constant: k = 0.012 min-1 at 323 K, from concentration measurements every 5 min over 90 min. Worked results: t1/2 = 57.8 min; the fraction remaining after 60 min is 0.49 (dimensionless), both computed from the stated relations. The relations hold for a first-order reaction only; a reaction of another order follows a different decay law.
input:
In this worked example, we will calculate the half-life of a first-order reaction, together with the fraction of reactant remaining after 60 min. As we shall see, for the measured rate constant considered here, the half-life $t_{1/2}$ works out at 57.8 min, while the fraction remaining after 60 min comes to 0.49, both values being obtained from the standard relations set out below.

For a first-order reaction, the rate constant $k$ determines the half-life through the relation $t_{1/2} = \ln(2) / k$, and the fraction remaining after a time $t$ is given by $\exp(-k t)$. The measured rate constant in this case is $k$ = 0.012 min-1 at 323 K, obtained from concentration measurements taken every 5 min over a period of 90 min.

To find the half-life, we substitute $k$ = 0.012 min-1 into the half-life relation, so that $t_{1/2} = \ln(2) / k$ gives $t_{1/2}$ = 57.8 min. To find the fraction remaining at $t$ = 60 min, we turn to the decay relation: $\exp(-k t)$ with $k$ = 0.012 min-1 and $t$ = 60 min yields 0.49. It is reassuring to observe that the fraction remaining at 60 min is slightly below one half, which is entirely consistent with the half-life of 57.8 min: at exactly one half-life the fraction would be one half, and 60 min lies just beyond that point. It should be emphasised that these relations hold for a first-order reaction only; a reaction of any other order would follow a different decay law, and neither the half-life relation nor the decay relation would carry over to it.

fact_base: Excerpt content: the schedule float is set at 6% and the excerpt defends that figure against a lower alternative. The excerpt refers to the project's cost table by section name and does not repeat its figures.
input:
The lower figure, however, leaves the upgrade project exposed in a way that the headline saving does not immediately reveal. The float has been set at 6% because the work it protects is not a single activity but a chain: each stage of the upgrade proceeds from the finish of the one before it, and a delay in an early stage is inherited by every later stage unless float stands in front of it. Adverse weather stops outdoor work without regard for the programme. Deliveries arrive late for reasons outside the project's control. Tie-ins to the operating plant wait for shutdown windows set by the plant, not by the project. A smaller float absorbs none of this; it simply transfers the overrun into the completion date, where it costs more.

The steering group asked whether the float could be reduced and the saving taken now. The saving is real but small against the cost of a late finish, and it is taken once, while the exposure runs for the whole construction period. The figures themselves are set out in the Costs section and are not repeated here. The float is accordingly held at 6% until the long-lead items are on site, and the case for releasing part of it is made again then, against the work actually remaining

subtype: worked example with equation: available NPSH
fact_base: A pump draws condensate from an open tank at atmospheric pressure, 101.3 kPa. Vapour pressure at the pumping temperature is 2.3 kPa, the static lift is 1.1 m and suction-line friction loss is 0.8 m. Available net positive suction head $NPSH_a$ is 8.2 m. The pump's required NPSH at the duty flow comes from the vendor curve and must be exceeded with margin.
input:
In this example, we will calculate the available net positive suction head for a pump that draws condensate from an open tank at atmospheric pressure, 101.3 kPa.

The available net positive suction head, denoted $NPSH_a$, is the margin by which the pressure at the pump suction exceeds the vapour pressure of the liquid, expressed in terms of head of the pumped liquid. The vapour pressure at the pumping temperature is 2.3 kPa. The static lift, the height the liquid is raised from the tank surface to the pump centreline, is 1.1 m, and the friction loss in the suction line is 0.8 m. Both the lift and the friction loss consume a portion of the available pressure margin, and both therefore have to be subtracted from it, as set out in the following relation:

$$NPSH_a = \frac{P_{atm} - P_v}{\rho g} - h_{lift} - h_f$$

In this relation, $P_{atm}$ denotes the pressure acting on the liquid surface in the tank, $P_v$ denotes the vapour pressure at the pumping temperature, $\rho$ denotes the liquid density, $g$ denotes the acceleration due to gravity, $h_{lift}$ denotes the static lift, and $h_f$ denotes the suction-line friction loss. The pressure terms are divided by $\rho g$ so that every term is expressed in metres of liquid, allowing the terms to be added and subtracted directly. Substituting the values gives $NPSH_a$ = 8.2 m.

This figure is a margin rather than a duty: 8.2 m is the head available above vaporisation under the stated conditions. Its proper use is as a comparison. The pump's required NPSH at the duty flow is obtained from the vendor curve, and the available head must exceed the required head by a suitable margin. A pump whose required NPSH comes close to 8.2 m at the duty flow would not be acceptable for this service, no matter how closely the two figures might appear to agree, because the vapour pressure, the lift, and the friction loss all shift with changing operating conditions.

subtype: worked example with equation: friction loss
fact_base: Water at 293 K flows in a horizontal pipe. The density $\rho$ is 998 kg m-3. Mean velocity $v$ is 1.2 m s-1, pipe diameter $D$ is 0.05 m, pipe length $L$ is 84 m and the Darcy friction factor $f$ is 0.02. The friction pressure drop is 24.1 kPa.
input:
In this example, we will calculate the friction pressure drop for water at 293 K flowing through a horizontal pipe.

The density $\rho$ of the water is 998 kg m-3, the mean velocity $v$ is 1.2 m s-1, the pipe diameter $D$ is 0.05 m, the pipe length $L$ is 84 m, and the Darcy friction factor $f$ is 0.02. For flow in a pipe of constant diameter, the friction loss is described by the well-known Darcy–Weisbach relation, which takes the following form:

$$\Delta P = f \frac{L}{D} \frac{\rho v^2}{2}$$

In this relation, $\Delta P$ denotes the friction pressure drop, $f$ denotes the Darcy friction factor, $L$ denotes the pipe length, $D$ denotes the pipe diameter, $\rho$ denotes the density, and $v$ denotes the mean velocity. It is worth noting that the velocity enters the expression as its square, which means that the friction loss rises steeply as the flow rate increases: even a relatively modest increase in velocity comes at the cost of a considerably larger increase in pressure drop. Substituting the stated values into the relation gives $\Delta P$ = 24.1 kPa.

Since the pipe is horizontal and of constant diameter, there is no elevation term and no change in velocity head to be accounted for in the balance between the two ends of the pipe. The friction pressure drop of 24.1 kPa therefore represents the entire pressure difference between the inlet and the outlet of the 84 m length, and it is precisely this drop that the supply pressure must be able to cover for this particular section of line.

Substitution of the stated values gives $\Delta P$ = 24.1 kPa.

The friction pressure drop of 24.1 kPa is therefore the whole pressure difference between the inlet and the outlet of the 84 m length, and it is the drop the supply pressure must cover for this section of line at the stated flow.

fact_base: A tutorial passage explains the Sherwood number to second-year students. Definition in words: the Sherwood number is the ratio of convective to diffusive mass transfer at a surface. The passage must state what a value near 1 means and what a large value means, without inventing numerical examples.
input:
The Sherwood number is the ratio of convective to diffusive mass transfer at a surface. The ratio compares the two routes by which a species can cross the fluid layer adjacent to a wall, a particle, or a drop: convection, which carries the species along with the moving fluid, and diffusion, which moves it through the fluid under the action of a concentration difference. Expressed through the quantities that set the two rates, the Sherwood number $Sh$ is the mass-transfer coefficient multiplied by a characteristic length and divided by the diffusivity of the species in the fluid. A larger coefficient, a larger length, or a smaller diffusivity each raises the number.

A value near 1 indicates that diffusion alone accounts for the transfer. Convection adds nothing measurable, and the transfer rate is simply the rate that diffusion would give across a stagnant layer of the stated length. This is the limiting case of a particle in still fluid, or of flow so slow that the fluid movement does not disturb the surface layer. Correlations are anchored at this limit: as the flow falls towards zero, the Sherwood number approaches the stagnant value, and a correlation that fails to approach it is wrong at low flow.

A large value, by contrast, indicates that convection is the dominant mechanism. The moving fluid continually replaces the layer at the surface with fluid having the bulk composition, so that the concentration difference is compressed into a thinner layer, and the transfer rate is governed by the flow: by the velocity, the geometry, and the physical properties that control the thickness of the layer. Increasing the flow raises both the Sherwood number and the transfer rate, albeit with diminishing effect, since the layer thins more slowly as it becomes thinner. It should be noted that diffusion has not disappeared at large values; it still carries the species across the final part of the layer, immediately adjacent to the surface itself. What a large value really expresses is that diffusion acting across the whole length would be far slower than the rate actually achieved. The number can therefore be read as a measure of how much the flow improves upon diffusion alone, and it is widely used to compare contacting arrangements on precisely that basis.

subtype: worked example with equation: Raoult partial pressure
fact_base: An ideal liquid mixture holds hexane in heptane at a liquid mole fraction $x$ of 0.54 for the volatile component. Its pure-component vapour pressure $P^*$ at the mixture temperature is 20.1 kPa, so the partial pressure $p$ is 10.9 kPa by Raoult's law. Raoult's law assumes an ideal solution; activity coefficients for the real mixture are not applied.
input:
In this example, we will calculate the partial pressure of hexane above an ideal liquid mixture of hexane in heptane at the mixture temperature.

The liquid mole fraction $x$ of hexane, which is the volatile component of the pair, is 0.54. The pure-component vapour pressure $P^*$ of hexane at the mixture temperature is 20.1 kPa. For an ideal solution, Raoult's law states that the partial pressure of a component over the liquid is equal to its mole fraction in the liquid multiplied by its pure-component vapour pressure at the same temperature, which can be written as follows:

$$p = x P^*$$

In this relation, $p$ denotes the partial pressure of hexane, $x$ denotes its liquid mole fraction, and $P^*$ denotes its pure-component vapour pressure. Substituting the values gives $p$ = 0.54 × 20.1 kPa = 10.9 kPa. As one would expect, the partial pressure comes out at a little over half of the pure-component vapour pressure: the mole fraction is itself a little over one half, and Raoult's law simply scales the vapour pressure by the mole fraction.

It should be emphasised that Raoult's law applies to an ideal solution, in which the interactions between unlike molecules correspond closely enough to those between like molecules for the mixture to follow the linear relation. Hexane in heptane comes close to this case, the two components being neighbouring hydrocarbons of similar size. The present calculation does not apply any activity coefficients. For the real mixture, an activity coefficient would be used to multiply the mole fraction and thereby correct the partial pressure for whatever departure from ideality is present; since no coefficient has been applied here, the value of 10.9 kPa stands as the ideal-solution value at the stated composition and temperature.

The partial pressure is a little over half the pure-component vapour pressure, as it must be: the mole fraction is a little over one half, and Raoult's law scales the vapour pressure by the mole fraction directly.

Hexane in heptane is close to that case, the two being neighbouring hydrocarbons of similar size. The calculation applies no activity coefficients.
