The stated value is a property of the liquid equilibrium at the mixture temperature: it does not depend on the volume of vapour standing over the liquid, only on the composition and the temperature.

fact_base: A vapour-compression unit serves a cold store, evaporating at -25 °C and condensing at 35 °C. The Carnot coefficient of performance between these temperatures is 4.13; the installed unit achieves 1.84. The achieved value is from the manufacturer's test at full load; part-load performance is not stated.
input: It is important to note that vapour-compression refrigeration plays a crucial role in modern cold storage, and the performance of such a system can be meaningfully evaluated by comparing its actual behaviour against the theoretical Carnot limit. In the case considered here, a vapour-compression unit serves a cold store, evaporating at −25 °C and condensing at 35 °C. When these temperatures are converted to absolute terms, the evaporating temperature is 248.15 K and the condensing temperature is 308.15 K, giving an overall temperature lift of 60 K. The Carnot coefficient of performance (COP) between these two temperatures is obtained by dividing the evaporating temperature by the lift, 248.15/60, which yields a value of 4.13. This value represents an idealised upper bound that no real machine operating between the same temperatures can exceed, underscoring the gap that inevitably separates practical equipment from the reversible ideal. The cycle itself proceeds through compression, condensation, throttling, and evaporation, and irreversibilities are distributed across each of these steps in ways that are difficult to isolate individually. In practice, the installed unit achieves a COP of 1.84, which corresponds to approximately 0.45 of the Carnot value. The difference between 1.84 and 4.13 can be attributed to a range of losses associated with the compressor, the throttling process, and the heat exchangers, each of which contributes to the overall shortfall in its own way. It should also be emphasised that the achieved figure comes from the manufacturer's test conducted at full load, and part-load performance is not stated, meaning that the behaviour of the unit under the varying conditions typically encountered in day-to-day operation remains somewhat uncertain. Overall, the comparison highlights that, between −25 °C and 35 °C, no refrigerator can exceed a COP of 4.13, while the tested unit reaches 1.84 at full load, highlighting the importance of interpreting test figures with appropriate care.
target: A vapour-compression unit serves the cold store, evaporating at −25 °C and condensing at 35 °C. The coefficient of performance (COP) of a refrigerator is the heat removed from the cold space divided by the work supplied. In kelvin, the evaporating temperature is 248.15 K and the condensing temperature is 308.15 K, a lift of 60 K. The Carnot COP between the two temperatures is the evaporating temperature divided by the lift, 248.15/60, and comes to 4.13. No refrigerator working between the same two temperatures can pass that value, because the Carnot cycle is reversible and every real cycle carries losses the reversible cycle does not. The unit runs four steps in a loop: the compressor raises the vapour pressure, the condenser rejects heat and condenses the vapour, the throttling valve drops the pressure, and the evaporator takes up heat from the store as the liquid boils. The installed unit achieves a COP of 1.84, which is 0.45 of the Carnot value. The distance between 1.84 and 4.13 is the sum of the losses in the compressor, the throttling valve, and the heat exchangers. Compression falls short of the isentropic ideal, the valve throws away the expansion work an expander would return, and each exchanger needs a temperature difference of its own to pass heat at all. The achieved figure is from the manufacturer's test at full load. Part-load performance is not stated, and the test gives no COP for the part-load conditions under which a cold store runs for much of the year. An annual energy estimate for the store built on the full-load figure carries the full-load condition with it. Between −25 °C and 35 °C, the Carnot limit is a COP of 4.13, and the tested unit reaches 1.84 at the single condition at which it was measured.

fact_base: A tutorial passage explains phase equilibrium for a partially miscible liquid pair. The passage states the equilibrium condition in words (equality of chemical potential across phases) before any equation is named. No numerical data are introduced; the passage is conceptual.
input: In this tutorial, we will explore the fascinating concept of phase equilibrium as it applies to a partially miscible liquid pair, and by the end you will have a solid understanding of what equilibrium means in this context, what remains fixed when the amounts change, and what shifts when the temperature changes. Partial miscibility is a situation in which two liquids dissolve in one another only up to a certain limit, beyond which the mixture can no longer remain as a single homogeneous phase. When that limit is exceeded, the mixture splits into two distinct liquid phases, one of which is rich in the first liquid while the other is rich in the second liquid, creating a layered system with a visible boundary. At the heart of the matter lies the equilibrium condition, which can be stated in words as the equality of chemical potential across the phases: for each component, the chemical potential in one phase must be equal to the chemical potential in the other phase. Chemical potential can be thought of as the driving force for the movement of matter, in much the same way that a temperature difference drives the flow of heat, and movement continues as long as a difference persists, coming to a halt only when equality is achieved. It is worth noting, however, that this analogy has its limits, since chemical potential depends on composition as well as temperature, meaning that a component can in some circumstances move against its own concentration difference. Provided the temperature and pressure are held fixed, the compositions of the two phases remain fixed as well, and adding more of one liquid simply changes the relative amounts of the two phases rather than their compositions, with the growing phase expanding at the expense of the other. When the temperature is changed, by contrast, the mutual solubility of the pair shifts, the compositions of the phases move accordingly, and at a sufficiently high or low temperature the two phases may merge back into a single phase once again. Ultimately, equilibrium at any temperature means exactly the same thing: the chemical potentials of each component are equal in every phase in which that component is present.
target: Phase equilibrium for a partially miscible liquid pair is the condition in which two liquid phases sit side by side and neither changes. By the end of this passage you can state the equilibrium condition in words, say what stays fixed when more of one liquid is added, and say what changes when the temperature changes. Two liquids are partially miscible when each dissolves in the other only up to a limit. Past that limit, the mixture separates into two liquid phases, one rich in the first liquid and the other rich in the second. The equilibrium condition is equality of chemical potential across the phases: for each component, the chemical potential in one phase equals the chemical potential in the other phase. A component moves between phases while its chemical potential differs between them, and the movement stops when the two values meet. Chemical potential plays the part for matter that temperature plays for heat: matter moves down a chemical-potential difference as heat moves down a temperature difference, and movement in either case stops at equality. The analogy stops there, because chemical potential depends on composition as well as temperature, and a component can move against its own concentration difference when the composition of the receiving phase pulls the other way. At fixed temperature and pressure, the compositions of the two phases are fixed. Adding more of one liquid changes the amounts of the two phases, not their compositions: the phase rich in that liquid grows at the expense of the other, and the overall composition fixes the proportions in which the phases stand. Temperature changes the picture itself. The mutual solubility of the pair shifts with temperature, the two phase compositions move, and at a high enough or low enough temperature the phases merge into one. A partially miscible pair is described by the compositions of its two phases at each temperature, and equilibrium at any temperature means the same thing: equality of chemical potential for each component across the phases present.

fact_base: Excerpt content: the staffing ramp is set at 6% and the excerpt defends that figure against a lower alternative. The excerpt refers to the project's cost table by section name and does not repeat its figures.
input: The staffing ramp for the upgrade project has been set at 6%, and it is important to note that this figure has been carefully considered and is defended here against the lower alternative that has been proposed in some quarters. Essentially, a lower ramp would spread the same overall hiring requirement over a longer build-up period, leaving the early work packages staffed below the level that the programme genuinely needs, and the resulting shortfall would not simply disappear; instead, it would tend to re-emerge in the form of overtime and bought-in cover, at rates that are, as the cost table in the Costs section already demonstrates, significantly higher than the cost of direct hiring. Furthermore, the ramp is closely aligned with the rate at which supervision can realistically absorb new starters, since crews grow through successive intakes, each of which requires induction, permits, and a supervisor who has the time to check work properly before it is signed off. A faster ramp, by contrast, would deliver names on the roster while quietly paying for them in rework, highlighting the fact that headcount alone is not the same as capacity. The 6% figure should therefore be understood as a capacity figure as much as a cost figure, representing the fastest rate at which the upgrade project can take people on without the supervision ratio thinning beyond the point that the steering group has accepted elsewhere. Maintaining a steady ramp also serves to protect the FID date, because a slower start would compress the later packages into the window before handover, where the same work costs more per unit and competes for the very same supervisors. The steering group is accordingly asked to note that the alternative is not a saving in any meaningful sense, but rather a transfer, from planned hiring into cover, rework, and late compression, underscoring the point that the transfer runs against the upgrade project on every line of the comparison that has been drawn.

The ramp also matches the rate at which supervision can absorb new starters. The new starters a slow start defers are also the ones who would have been trained on the early packages, so the later packages inherit both the compressed programme and the least experienced crews. Cover staff also arrive without the plant knowledge that direct hires build package by package, and the packages least able to absorb delay are the ones a slow start staffs last. The steering group is asked to note that the alternative is not a saving but a transfer, from planned hiring into cover, rework, and late compression, and that the transfer runs against the upgrade project on every line of the comparison.

fact_base: A food plant uses 1935 MWh of electricity per year in refrigeration. A heat-recovery retrofit is projected by the equipment vendor to save 17% of that use, a derived saving of 329 MWh per year at the vendor figure. Capital cost is $498k. At an electricity price of $0.11 per kWh, the derived annual saving is $36k and the derived simple payback is 13.8 years. The saving figure is a vendor projection and was not measured at this plant; refrigeration load in the summer peak month was not modelled. The recommendation is a metered trial on one of the three refrigeration lines before any capital decision. The plant engineer owns the trial.
input: This executive summary presents an appraisal of a proposed heat-recovery retrofit at the food plant, where refrigeration currently accounts for a substantial 1935 MWh of electricity consumption per year. According to projections provided by the equipment vendor, the retrofit is expected to save 17% of that use, which corresponds to a derived saving of 329 MWh per year at the vendor figure. The capital cost of the project is $498k, and at an electricity price of $0.11 per kWh, the derived annual saving works out at $36k, giving a derived simple payback of 13.8 years. It is important to note that this represents a considerable capital commitment of $498k set against an annual saving of just $36k, and a payback of 13.8 years is, by any measure, a long horizon over which to recover the investment. Crucially, the saving figure is a vendor projection that has not been measured at this plant, and refrigeration load in the summer peak month has not been modelled, meaning that the appraisal rests on assumptions that remain unverified in the conditions that matter most. In light of these considerations, it is recommended that a metered trial be carried out on one of the three refrigeration lines before any capital decision is taken, with the plant engineer owning the trial and reporting the measured results, so that the eventual decision can be based on evidence gathered at this plant rather than on projections alone, however favourable those projections may appear at first sight.
target: A metered trial on one of the three refrigeration lines should come before any capital decision on the heat-recovery retrofit; the plant engineer owns the trial. The plant uses 1935 MWh of electricity per year in refrigeration. The equipment vendor projects a saving of 17% of that use, a derived saving of 329 MWh per year at the vendor figure. Capital cost is $498k. At an electricity price of $0.11 per kWh, the derived annual saving is $36k, and the derived simple payback is 13.8 years. The trade-off is $498k of capital now against $36k of saving per year at the vendor's figure. The saving is a vendor projection and was not measured at this plant. Refrigeration load in the summer peak month was not modelled, and the peak month is where the retrofit case is strongest or weakest, because recovered heat follows the load that produces it. A payback of 13.8 years is long against the working life of the equipment the retrofit would be fitted to, and it lengthens further if the realised saving falls below the projection. The trial settles the point the appraisal cannot. Metering one line through a full load cycle gives a measured saving at this plant, on this refrigeration load, with the projection tested against the plant's own meters. The trial also prices the disruption honestly: one line carries the instrumentation and the operating changes, and the other lines run untouched as the comparison. The plant engineer's report should state the measured saving per unit of refrigeration load, so that the figure for the full retrofit can be rebuilt from it line by line. The capital decision waits for the trial result, and the result it waits for is a measured saving, not a revised projection.

fact_base: A review passage on adsorbents for gas drying, in four parts: scope, established results, disagreements, and gaps. The review covers 87 papers from the last 9 years. The disagreements part names the quantity on which reports conflict; the gaps part names the measurement nobody reports.
input:
Scope

This review provides a comprehensive overview of the current state of knowledge regarding adsorbents for gas drying, a process of considerable industrial importance in which water vapour is removed from a gas stream by means of a solid adsorbent that captures the water and is subsequently regenerated so that it can be used again. The review draws on 87 papers published over the course of the last 9 years. The adsorbents falling within the scope of the review are silica gel, activated alumina, and molecular sieves, which together represent the principal families in routine drying service. The gases considered include natural gas, air, hydrogen, and light hydrocarbon streams, in all of which water is removed for a variety of reasons, including the protection of equipment, compliance with product specifications, and the prevention of hydrate formation and corrosion in cold equipment. Studies concerned with liquid-phase drying, membrane separation, and absorption into liquid solvents are excluded from consideration. The evidence base comprises three main types of study: isotherm measurements of water uptake, breakthrough tests conducted on packed beds, and cyclic tests in which uptake is tracked across regeneration steps. It is important to emphasise that a paper is treated as evidence for a performance claim only where the gas, the temperature range, and the regeneration conditions are clearly stated, since drying performance is fundamentally a property of the adsorbent operating within its duty, rather than of the adsorbent in isolation. The review is structured around what the literature collectively establishes, where it disagrees, and what it leaves unmeasured.

Established results

It is widely recognised that water uptake at low partial pressure is the characteristic that most clearly separates the families. Molecular sieves exhibit a strong uptake of water at low partial pressure, a behaviour that can be attributed to their pore openings, which admit water while excluding much of what travels with it, and to their extensive internal surface, which retains water even against a dry stream. Silica gel and activated alumina, by contrast, take up considerably less under the same dry conditions, although their uptake increases substantially as the gas approaches saturation, at which point condensation within the wider pores begins to supplement adsorption on the surface. Across the range covered by the literature, this ordering is not reversed: where the driest outlets are required, molecular sieves retain a clear advantage, although that advantage progressively narrows as the outlet requirement is relaxed. Outlet dryness is consequently a matter of selecting between families before it becomes a question of bed sizing, and beds of gel or alumina are typically sized larger for the same dry duty rather than being expected to match the performance of a sieve at low partial pressure.

Regeneration can be accomplished by heating, by pressure release, or by means of a dry purge gas, and every family is regenerated by at least one of these routes in commercial practice. Heating a saturated bed drives off the accumulated water and restores the greater part of its uptake capacity. The extent of restoration depends both on the temperature achieved and on the completeness with which the bed is cooled before being returned to service. A bed that is returned to service while still warm will take up less water during the subsequent cycle, and a number of papers attribute early breakthrough to incomplete cooling rather than to any genuine deterioration of the adsorbent, underscoring the point that cooling should properly be regarded as an integral part of the regeneration step rather than as an idle interval, and that cycle designs which shorten the cooling step effectively trade capacity for cycle time.

Breakthrough behaviour, meanwhile, follows a broadly consistent pattern across all three families. A mass-transfer zone is established at the inlet of the bed and migrates through it, and the outlet remains dry until such time as the zone reaches the bed outlet. The length of this zone increases with gas velocity and particle size, and decreases as the affinity for water becomes stronger. Because adsorption releases heat, the bed warms as the zone passes through it, and this warming reduces the local uptake, with the result that a rapidly loaded bed will break through earlier than a prediction based on the cold isotherm would suggest. Studies that record bed temperature alongside outlet moisture show the two quantities moving in tandem, highlighting the risk that designs which neglect the temperature rise will systematically overstate the useful cycle time.

Binders, furthermore, act to dilute capacity. Molecular sieve crystals are formed into beads and pellets with the assistance of a binder, and since the binder itself adsorbs very little water, a formed adsorbent inevitably exhibits a lower uptake per unit mass than the crystal from which it is manufactured. Where papers report crystal and formed material side by side, the formed material is consistently found to be lower in uptake and slower in its approach to equilibrium. Mechanical degradation occurs through attrition in cycled beds and through dusting during handling, and the resulting dust increases the pressure drop across the bed while also posing a fouling risk to downstream equipment. The slower degradation mechanism is hydrothermal in nature: repeated regeneration in the presence of water vapour progressively reduces the uptake of alumina and silica gel, with the loss proceeding more rapidly at higher regeneration temperatures. Heavy hydrocarbons present in the feed introduce an additional fouling pathway, since they adsorb strongly, are only incompletely removed at regeneration temperatures selected for water, and can obstruct pores against water in subsequent cycles.

Disagreements

The literature is notably divided on the equilibrium water uptake of molecular sieves at low partial pressure. Although the quantity is nominally the same in each case, namely the uptake per unit mass at a stated low partial pressure and temperature, the values reported for comparable materials diverge by margins that are too substantial to be dismissed as experimental scatter. On closer inspection, the conflict appears to track the measurement route adopted. Gravimetric measurements, in which a sample is exposed to a stream of controlled humidity until its mass stabilises, tend to yield the higher values. Values derived from breakthrough curves, on the other hand, tend to emerge lower, and the derivation itself depends on the assumed shape of the mass-transfer zone, meaning that a portion of the discrepancy is embedded in the calculation rather than measured directly. Equilibration time constitutes a second source of disagreement. At low partial pressure the uptake process is slow, and a measurement terminated at a predetermined time may capture a point on the trajectory towards equilibrium rather than equilibrium itself. Papers differ considerably in whether a steady reading was awaited, and the shorter tests systematically report lower uptakes. Pretreatment represents a third source: a sample that has been regenerated more aggressively prior to testing begins from a drier state and consequently adsorbs more, so the reported uptake partly reflects the regeneration the sample happened to receive. Formed and crystal samples are also intermingled in the comparisons, and the binder fraction alone is sufficient to shift the reported values. The disagreement is therefore best understood as a disagreement about method before it is a disagreement about materials, and it cannot be resolved on the basis of the published values alone, since the papers do not report their conditions on a common basis, and no two of the conflicting reports simultaneously share the same route, equilibration criterion, and pretreatment.

Gaps

Perhaps the most striking omission in the literature is that the measurement nobody reports is the retained uptake after extended regeneration cycling: that is, the water uptake of a formed adsorbent measured once more after the material has been regenerated many times under the conditions of its own intended duty. The literature reports fresh uptake in abundance, and ageing studies report uptake following steaming, storage, or exposure to a contaminant, but the cycled measurement, performed on the material that would actually be purchased, under the regeneration regime that the unit would actually apply, is conspicuously absent. This gap is of practical significance, because the selection between families ultimately turns on service life just as much as on fresh capacity. A family exhibiting the higher fresh uptake but the faster cyclic loss may well prove more expensive over the lifetime of a charge than a family that starts lower and retains its uptake, and at present that comparison simply cannot be performed on the basis of measurements, leaving purchasers to price the associated risk from warranty terms instead. A second gap follows naturally from the first: no paper reports uptake and mechanical condition together following cycling, and so the balance between capacity loss and attrition loss within one and the same charge remains unquantified, meaning that a bed may be retired on account of dust while its uptake is still sound, or alternatively retained in service on account of its uptake while its dust burdens the downstream equipment. Until the cycled measurement becomes available on a common basis, comparisons between the families will continue to rest on fresh material, and every judgement regarding selection in this review must be read subject to that limitation.
target:
Scope

This review covers adsorbents for gas drying: the removal of water vapour from a gas stream by a solid that takes up the water and is regenerated for reuse. The review covers 87 papers from the last 9 years. The adsorbents in scope are silica gel, activated alumina, and molecular sieves, the families in routine drying service. The gases in scope are natural gas, air, hydrogen, and light hydrocarbon streams, where water is removed to protect equipment, to meet a product specification, or to prevent hydrate formation and corrosion in cold equipment. Papers on liquid-phase drying, on membranes, and on absorption into a liquid solvent fall outside the scope. The evidence admitted is of three kinds: isotherm measurements of water uptake, breakthrough tests on packed beds, and cyclic tests in which uptake is followed across regeneration. A paper counts as evidence for a performance claim only where its gas, its temperature range, and its regeneration conditions are stated, because drying performance is a property of the adsorbent and its duty together, never of the adsorbent alone. The review is organised by what the papers establish jointly, where they conflict, and what they leave unmeasured.

Established results

Water uptake at low partial pressure separates the families. Molecular sieves take up water strongly at low partial pressure, because their pore openings admit water and exclude much of what travels with it, and their internal surface holds water against a dry stream. Silica gel and activated alumina take up less under the same dry conditions and take up more as the gas approaches saturation, where condensation inside the wider pores adds to uptake on the surface. The ordering reverses nowhere in the range the papers cover: for the driest outlets the molecular sieves hold the advantage, and the advantage narrows as the outlet requirement relaxes. Outlet dryness is therefore a selection between families before it is a question of bed size, and beds of gel or alumina are sized larger for the same dry duty rather than expected to match the sieve at low partial pressure.

Regeneration is by heat, by pressure release, or by a dry purge, and every family is regenerated by at least one of the three in commercial units. Heating a saturated bed drives the water off and restores most of the uptake. The restored amount depends on the temperature the bed reaches and on how completely the bed is cooled before it returns to service. A bed returned warm takes up less water in the next cycle, and several papers trace early breakthrough to incomplete cooling rather than to any loss of adsorbent capacity. Cooling is thus part of the regeneration step, not a pause after it, and cycle designs that shorten cooling buy cycle time with capacity.

Breakthrough behaviour follows one pattern across the families. A mass-transfer zone forms at the bed inlet and travels through the bed, and the outlet stays dry until the zone reaches it. The zone lengthens with gas velocity and with particle size, and shortens as the affinity for water strengthens. Uptake releases heat, and the bed warms as the zone passes; the warming lowers the local uptake, so a fast-loaded bed breaks through earlier than its cold isotherm promises. Papers that measure bed temperature alongside outlet moisture report the two moving together, and designs that ignore the temperature rise overstate the useful cycle time.

Binders dilute capacity. Molecular sieve crystals are formed into beads and pellets with a binder, and the binder takes up little water, so a formed adsorbent takes up less per unit mass than the crystal it is made from. Papers that report crystal and formed material side by side put the formed material lower on uptake and slower on the approach to equilibrium. Mechanical degradation is by attrition in cycled beds and by dusting in handling; the dust raises the pressure drop across the bed and can foul the equipment downstream. The slow loss is hydrothermal: repeated regeneration in the presence of water vapour reduces the uptake of alumina and of silica gel over time, and the loss runs faster at higher regeneration temperatures. Heavy hydrocarbons in the feed add a second fouling route, because they adsorb strongly, are driven off incompletely at regeneration temperatures set for water, and block pores against water in later cycles.

Disagreements

Reports conflict on the equilibrium water uptake of molecular sieves at low partial pressure. The quantity is the same on paper, uptake per unit mass at a stated low partial pressure and temperature, and the values reported for comparable materials differ by margins too wide to read as scatter. The conflict tracks the measurement route. Gravimetric measurements, in which a sample takes up water from a stream of controlled humidity until its mass steadies, tend to report the higher values. Values inferred from breakthrough curves tend to come out lower, and the inference rests on the shape assumed for the mass-transfer zone, so part of the gap is built into the calculation rather than measured. Equilibration time is the second source of the conflict. At low partial pressure uptake is slow, and a measurement stopped at a fixed time records a point on the way to equilibrium in place of equilibrium itself. Papers differ in whether they waited for a steady reading, and the shorter tests read lower. Pretreatment is the third source: a sample regenerated harder before the test starts drier and takes up more, so the reported uptake partly records the regeneration the sample was given. Formed and crystal samples are also mixed in the comparisons, and the binder share alone moves the values. The disagreement is about method before it is about material. It cannot be settled from the published values, because the papers do not state their conditions on a common basis, and no two of the conflicting reports share route, equilibration rule, and pretreatment at once.

Gaps

The measurement nobody reports is the retained uptake after extended regeneration cycling: the water uptake of a formed adsorbent, measured again after the material has been regenerated many times under the conditions of its own duty. Papers report fresh uptake. Ageing studies report uptake after steaming, after storage, or after exposure to a contaminant. The cycled measurement, on the material that would actually be bought, under the regeneration the unit would actually apply, is missing. The gap matters because selection between the families turns on service life as much as on fresh capacity. A family with the higher fresh uptake and the faster cyclic loss can cost more over the life of a charge than a family that starts lower and holds its uptake, and at present that comparison cannot be made from measurements. Purchasers price the risk from warranty terms instead. A second gap follows from the first: no paper reports uptake and mechanical state together after cycling, so the balance between capacity loss and attrition loss in the same charge is unmeasured, and a bed can be retired for dust while its uptake is still sound, or held in service for its uptake while its dust loads the downstream equipment. Until the cycled measurement exists on a common basis, comparisons of the families rest on fresh material, and every judgement on selection in this review carries that limit.

fact_base: 180 pumps run at the plant. Maintenance records for 12 months show 1108 h of unplanned downtime; bearing failures account for 43% of the downtime hours. A sensor set for all 180 pumps is quoted at $426k installed, plus $61k per year. In a vendor trial on a comparable unit, the sensors cut downtime by 19%; the figure is a vendor figure and was not measured at this plant. A pilot on 24 pumps costs $45k over three months. Spare-part lead times are unchanged by the sensors. The memo recommends the three-month pilot; the reliability engineering group owns the pilot and reports before the March capital review; the decision on full installation is held until the pilot results are reported.
input: This memo recommends that a three-month pilot be undertaken on 24 pumps, at a cost of $45k, before any decision is taken regarding full installation of the proposed sensor package. The plant operates a total of 180 pumps, and maintenance records covering a period of 12 months reveal no fewer than 1108 h of unplanned downtime, of which bearing failures account for a substantial 43% of the downtime hours. A sensor set covering all 180 pumps has been quoted at $426k installed, together with a recurring charge of $61k per year, and it is worth noting that in a vendor trial conducted on a comparable unit, the sensors were reported to cut downtime by 19%, although this figure originates from the vendor and has not been measured at this plant. Set against the full commitment of $426k plus $61k per year, the pilot at $45k offers a considerably lower-cost means of establishing whether the technology delivers a comparable benefit under local conditions. It should also be borne in mind that spare-part lead times are entirely unchanged by the sensors, since the sensors serve to shorten detection times rather than supply times, and a bearing that has been identified as failing will still have to await the arrival of its spare. The reliability engineering group will own the pilot and will report its findings in advance of the March capital review, and it is recommended that the decision on full installation be held until those pilot results have been reported and can be properly evaluated.
target: The recommendation is the three-month pilot on 24 pumps at $45k, before any decision on full installation. The reliability engineering group owns the pilot and reports before the March capital review. The plant runs 180 pumps. Maintenance records for 12 months show 1108 h of unplanned downtime, and bearing failures account for 43% of the downtime hours. A sensor set for all 180 pumps is quoted at $426k installed, plus $61k per year. In a vendor trial on a comparable unit, the sensors cut downtime by 19%; the figure is the vendor's and was not measured at this plant. The choice is $426k plus $61k a year for the full set, against $45k for a pilot that measures the reduction on this plant's own pumps. Bearings carry the largest single share of the downtime, so detection aimed at bearings addresses the part of the problem the records actually show. Spare-part lead times are unchanged by the sensors: detection shortens, supply does not, and a bearing caught failing still waits for its spare. The pilot therefore tests one claim, the downtime reduction, and leaves the other limit where it stands. The pilot report sets the downtime on the fitted pumps against the maintenance records for the same machines, so the vendor figure is checked on the plant's own evidence before the full price is paid. The decision on full installation is held until the pilot results are reported.

fact_base: Excerpt content: two groups report conflicting selectivity values for the same material class; the excerpt weighs their test conditions. The excerpt reaches a limited preference and states the condition on which it rests.
input: When the results reported for the benchmark material are placed side by side, it becomes apparent that the two groups' selectivity values cannot both be an accurate description of the same solid operating under the same conditions, and the divergence between them appears to track the test conditions considerably more closely than it tracks the material itself. The higher values were obtained from equilibrium measurements performed on samples that had been activated under vacuum and held at each point until the reading had fully stabilised, whereas the lower values emerged from mixture breakthrough tests, in which selectivity is inferred from the separation actually achieved rather than measured at equilibrium, and in which a slow approach to equilibrium within the pores can easily masquerade as a weaker separation. The IAST predictions that have been offered in support of each position do little to arbitrate between them, since the single-component isotherms on which those predictions rest were themselves measured under the two different regimes. On the basis of the evidence as it currently stands, the benchmark material would appear to be preferred where the feed is dry and the contact time is long, these being the conditions under which the equilibrium values were obtained, while under short-contact conditions the preference remains unestablished, and the breakthrough results continue to stand, unrefuted, on their own ground.

subtype: worked example with equation: Antoine vapour pressure
fact_base: The vapour pressure of ethanol at 40 °C is estimated from the Antoine equation with constants $A$ = 8.20417, $B$ = 1642.89 and $C$ = 230.3 (pressure in mmHg, temperature in °C). The estimate is 17.8 kPa. The constants are valid only over their fitted temperature range; the source databank value governs design.
input:
In this worked example, the vapour pressure of ethanol at 40 °C is estimated by means of the Antoine equation, a widely used correlation that relates the vapour pressure of a pure liquid to temperature through three empirically fitted constants. The equation takes the following form:

$$\log_{10} P = A - \frac{B}{T + C}$$

where $P$ denotes the vapour pressure and $T$ denotes the temperature. For ethanol, the constants in question are $A$ = 8.20417, $B$ = 1642.89, and $C$ = 230.3, with the pressure expressed in mmHg and the temperature in °C, and each constant plays its own distinctive role within the correlation, with $A$ effectively setting the level of the curve, $B$ governing the strength of the temperature dependence, and $C$ shifting the temperature scale in such a way that the curve is able to follow the measured data. Substituting $T$ = 40 into the equation and evaluating the right-hand side yields a vapour pressure of 133.5 mmHg, which, when converted into kilopascals, gives a final estimate of 17.8 kPa. It is important to note that this estimate is only as reliable as the fit on which it is based, since the constants are valid solely over the temperature range to which they were originally fitted, and an evaluation performed outside that range will still return a number, albeit one that carries no real standing. For design purposes, it is the source databank value that governs, and the Antoine estimate should properly be regarded as a convenient check on that value rather than as a substitute for it. Overall, the vapour pressure of ethanol at the temperature considered here, on the basis of the constants set out above, comes to 17.8 kPa, a figure that illustrates the usefulness of the correlation for rapid estimation while simultaneously underscoring the need to respect the limits within which the fitted constants can legitimately be applied.

where $P$ denotes the vapour pressure and $T$ denotes the temperature. For ethanol, the constants are $A$ = 8.20417, $B$ = 1642.89, and $C$ = 230.3, with the pressure in mmHg and the temperature in °C. The constants divide the work between them: $A$ sets the level of the curve, $B$ carries the strength of the temperature dependence, and $C$ shifts the temperature scale so that the curve follows the measured pressures across the fitted range. The logarithm form is what makes the fit usable: vapour pressure climbs steeply with temperature, and the equation straightens that climb into a form three constants can hold. Substitution of $T$ = 40 into the equation gives a vapour pressure of 133.5 mmHg, and conversion to kilopascals gives 17.8 kPa. The estimate is a fit value, and it holds only where the fit holds. The constants are valid over their fitted temperature range, and the stated temperature must lie inside that range for the estimate to mean anything. Outside the range the equation still returns a number, and the number has no standing. The source databank value governs design. The Antoine estimate checks the databank value and does not replace it; where the two disagree by more than the scatter of the fit, the databank value stands and the estimate is set aside. A check of the direction is also available from the equation itself: the subtracted term shrinks as the temperature rises, so the calculated pressure rises with temperature, as a vapour pressure must. The vapour pressure of ethanol at the stated temperature, on the stated constants, is 17.8 kPa.

fact_base: Capital appraisal for a solar array: installed cost $1968k, expected net saving $478k per year for 12 years. At a discount rate of 10% the present value of the savings is $3257k and the net present value is $1289k. Savings are vendor and utility estimates; no saving has yet been measured on a comparable installation.
input: This capital appraisal examines the case for a solar array with an installed cost of $1968k and an expected net saving of $478k per year sustained over a period of 12 years. Discounting the anticipated savings at a discount rate of 10% produces a present value of the savings of $3257k, and once the installed cost has been deducted, the resulting net present value stands at $1289k. On a purely undiscounted basis, the cumulative savings would pass the installed cost at some point during the fifth year of operation, with the discounted surplus being accumulated over the remainder of the array's service life. It is important to note, however, that the entire case rests on the savings, and the savings in question are vendor and utility estimates; no saving has as yet been measured on a comparable installation, which means that the income side of the appraisal remains unmeasured across the whole of the period it purports to cover. The estimation risk is located principally in two places, namely the electrical output of the array itself and the price of the electricity that the output displaces, and any shortfall in either of these will erode the saving year after year, causing the net present value of $1289k to fall correspondingly, with no offsetting item available on the cost side once the installation has been completed. The positive figure should therefore be interpreted as a surplus that materialises only if the savings arrive broadly as estimated, rather than as a measured or guaranteed return on the investment.

input: This executive summary reviews delivery performance across the firm, which operates 2 plants and generates revenue of $99 million per year. The evidence base consists of order records for 12 months, encompassing a total of 16050 orders. Over the last two quarters, on-time delivery stood at 91%, against a target of 95%, while overtime cost reached $2 million last year, an increase of 19% on the year before. The order backlog currently stands at 3.6 weeks, compared with 1.6 weeks a year ago, meaning that the backlog has more than doubled even as delivery performance has remained stubbornly below target. fact_base: Pricing case for a SaaS tier: price $64 per unit, variable cost $42 per unit, fixed costs $210k per year. Break-even volume is 9545 units per year; current volume is 3983 units per year. Volume figures are last year's actuals; the effect of the price on volume is not estimated.
input: In this section, we take a closer look at the pricing economics of the new SaaS tier, and the picture that emerges is a challenging one. The tier is priced at $64 per unit, while the variable cost associated with each unit is $42 per unit, which means that every unit sold generates a contribution of $22 that can be applied toward the fixed costs of $210k per year. When these figures are combined, the break-even volume works out to 9545 units per year. However, the current volume is just 3983 units per year, which means the tier is operating at a shortfall of 5562 units relative to the break-even point, highlighting the scale of the gap that would need to be closed. It is important to note that the volume figures are last year's actuals, and that the effect of the price on volume has not been estimated at this stage, so any change in price would introduce an additional layer of uncertainty into the analysis, making it difficult to say with confidence how the position might evolve going forward.
target: The SaaS tier does not cover its costs at the current volume. Break-even volume is 9545 units per year, the volume at which the contribution from units sold equals the fixed costs. Last year's volume was 3983 units, a shortfall of 5562 units against break-even. The price is $64 per unit and the variable cost is $42 per unit. Each unit sold contributes $22, and the fixed costs are $210k per year. The contribution is what each unit pays toward the fixed costs after its own variable cost has been met, and the tier covers its costs only when the contributions of all the units sold add up to the fixed-cost figure. At the current volume the contribution covers less than half of the fixed costs; the tier runs at a loss for as long as volume stays at last year's level and the price and costs stay as stated. The gap closes if volume grows at the current price. A higher price or lower costs would also close it arithmetically, but the figures support only the first reading. The volume figures are last year's actuals, and the effect of the price on volume is not estimated. A higher price would change the contribution per unit, and nothing in the figures states what it would do to the volume; the break-even volume is the volume the current price requires, no more.

input: Closely related to the question of performance is the question of how long materials of this class can be expected to last in service, and here too the published picture is far from consistent. Two groups have reported lifetime values for the same material class that differ by a wide margin, and at first sight the results appear to contradict one another directly. A closer look at the test conditions, however, suggests that the two groups were not really measuring the same thing. The dry series also held the material at its working state for long stretches between regenerations, while the humid series returned it to regeneration before its uptake had settled, so the two series age the material on different clocks as well. The group reporting the longer lifetime cycled the material under a dry feed gas and regenerated it gently, under conditions that place relatively little stress on the structure. The group reporting the shorter lifetime, by contrast, used a humid feed and regenerated fully after every cycle, which is a considerably more demanding regime. There is also a difference in what each group chose to count as the end of life: one group recorded the number of cycles completed before the uptake had fallen by a noticeable margin, while the other reported the time on stream before the outlet purity could no longer be maintained. These are not interchangeable measures, and part of the apparent conflict dissolves once the definitions are placed side by side. fact_base: Adsorption of a dye from water on activated carbon was measured in batch tests at 298 K. The fitted Langmuir capacity was 207 mg of dye per gram of adsorbent at pH 6. At an adsorbent dose of 0.7 g L-1, removal after 120 min was 84% of the initial dye concentration of 50 mg L-1. The Langmuir fit is reported for pH 6 only; capacity at other pH values was not measured.
input: The adsorption of a dye from water onto activated carbon was investigated in a series of batch tests carried out at 298 K, and the results provide a useful picture of the performance that can be achieved. In each test a measured mass of carbon was brought into contact with a volume of dye solution and the mixture was agitated while samples were withdrawn over time, so that both the approach to equilibrium and the equilibrium state itself could be observed. The equilibrium data were fitted to the Langmuir model, and the fitted capacity came out at 207 mg of dye per gram of adsorbent at pH 6, which represents a substantial uptake for this class of adsorbent. The Langmuir equation described the equilibrium data closely across the range of concentrations studied, with no systematic departure at either end of the range. In the kinetic tests, an adsorbent dose of 0.7 g L-1 was used, and after 120 min the removal had reached 84% of the initial dye concentration of 50 mg L-1, leaving a residual concentration of 8 mg L-1 in solution. These results highlight the effectiveness of activated carbon for this application and suggest that the material is capable of treating dye-bearing water to a low residual level. It is important to note, however, that the Langmuir fit is reported for pH 6 only, and the capacity at other pH values was not measured, so the fitted capacity should not be extrapolated to more acidic or more alkaline conditions without further experimental work being undertaken to support such an extension of the results.
target: Adsorption of a dye from water on activated carbon was measured in batch tests at 298 K. In each test a measured mass of carbon was contacted with a volume of dye solution and the mixture was agitated while samples were withdrawn, so that the approach to equilibrium and the equilibrium state were both observed. The fitted Langmuir capacity at pH 6 is 207 mg of dye per gram of adsorbent. The Langmuir equation described the equilibrium data closely across the concentrations studied, with no systematic departure at either end of the range. At an adsorbent dose of 0.7 g L-1, removal after 120 min reached 84% of the initial dye concentration (50 mg L-1), leaving 8 mg L-1 in solution. The capacity is an equilibrium figure from the fit, and it states the uptake the carbon approaches as the residual concentration rises; the removal figure is a kinetic result at one dose and one contact time, and the two figures answer different questions. Read together, they show a carbon that takes up a large mass of dye at equilibrium and removes most of the dye from a dilute solution within the stated contact time at the stated dose. A higher dose would raise the removal at the same contact time and lower the uptake per gram; the pair of figures fixes one operating point, not a curve. The tests are batch tests: they state nothing about behaviour in a continuous column or about capacity after regeneration. The Langmuir fit is reported for pH 6 only. Capacity at other pH values was not measured. Dye uptake on carbon shifts with pH through the charge on the dye and on the surface, and the capacity figure is a figure for the stated pH; at a different pH the uptake would differ, by an amount these tests do not give.

fact_base: Liquid-liquid extraction recovers acetone from an aqueous stream into an organic solvent. The distribution coefficient (organic over aqueous) is 1.87 at 25 °C and the design uses 5 countercurrent stages. Predicted recovery is 93% of the acetone in the feed. The prediction assumes equilibrium stages and negligible mutual solubility; neither has been checked on the actual solvents.
input: Liquid-liquid extraction offers an effective route for recovering acetone from an aqueous stream by contacting it with an organic solvent, and the design considered here is based on a countercurrent cascade. The cascade is arranged so that the aqueous stream and the solvent pass one another through the stages, with the freshest solvent meeting the most depleted aqueous stream at the end of the cascade. The distribution coefficient for acetone between the organic and aqueous phases is 1.87 at 25 °C, which indicates a favourable partitioning of the acetone into the solvent phase. The design uses 5 countercurrent stages, and on this basis the predicted recovery is 93% of the acetone in the feed, representing a high level of separation for a relatively modest number of stages. It is important to note, however, that this prediction rests on two assumptions that should be borne in mind when interpreting the figure. The prediction assumes equilibrium stages throughout the cascade, and it also assumes negligible mutual solubility between the two phases. Neither of these assumptions has been checked on the actual solvents involved, so the predicted recovery should be treated as an estimate that remains to be confirmed in practice, rather than as a guaranteed level of performance for the unit as it will actually be built and operated in the plant.
target: Liquid-liquid extraction recovers acetone from an aqueous stream into an organic solvent. The distribution coefficient, organic over aqueous, is 1.87 at 25 °C. With 5 countercurrent stages, the predicted recovery is 93% of the acetone in the feed. A distribution coefficient above unity puts most of the acetone in the solvent at each contact, and countercurrent flow keeps the leanest solvent against the leanest aqueous stream, so the driving force is held along the cascade; the recovery figure is the result of the coefficient and the stage count together, not of either alone. The stages are counted as equilibrium stages: each stage is credited with the full separation the coefficient allows at the compositions the stage actually sees, and no allowance is made for incomplete contacting within a stage. The prediction assumes equilibrium stages. A real stage falls short of equilibrium by an amount that depends on the contacting device, and the recovery of the built unit would fall short of the prediction by the corresponding amount. The prediction also assumes negligible mutual solubility of the two phases. Solvent lost to the aqueous raffinate, or water carried into the extract, would move both the recovery and the downstream loads. Neither assumption has been checked on the actual solvents. The recovery figure is a prediction on stated assumptions, to be replaced by a measured recovery when the actual solvents have been run.

fact_base: 180 pumps run at the plant. Maintenance records for 12 months show 1035 h of unplanned downtime; bearing failures account for 39% of the downtime hours. A sensor set for all 180 pumps is quoted at $456k installed, plus $73k per year. In a vendor trial on a comparable unit, the sensors cut downtime by 24%; the figure is a vendor figure and was not measured at this plant. A pilot on 21 pumps costs $43k over three months. Spare-part lead times are unchanged by the sensors. The memo recommends the three-month pilot; the reliability engineering group owns the pilot and reports before the March capital review; the decision on full installation is held until the pilot results are reported.
input: This memo considers the case for fitting vibration and temperature sensors across the pump population in order to reduce unplanned downtime. The plant operates 180 pumps, and the maintenance records for the past 12 months show a total of 1035 h of unplanned downtime, which represents a significant burden on production. Bearing failures account for 39% of the downtime hours, making them the largest single contributor and a natural focus for any monitoring programme. The downtime is spread across the year rather than concentrated in a single incident, and it recurs in a pattern that planned intervention could in principle interrupt, which is what makes monitoring a plausible response to it. A sensor set covering all 180 pumps has been quoted at $456k installed, with a further $73k per year in ongoing costs. In a vendor trial carried out on a comparable unit, the sensors were reported to cut downtime by 24%, although it should be noted that this figure is a vendor figure and was not measured at this plant, so its transferability remains uncertain. A more cautious first step is also available: a pilot on 21 pumps would cost $43k over three months. It is also worth noting that spare-part lead times are unchanged by the sensors. On balance, this memo recommends proceeding with the three-month pilot in the first instance; the reliability engineering group would own the pilot and report before the March capital review, and the decision on full installation would be held until the pilot results have been reported and considered in full.
target: Run the three-month pilot before any decision on full installation. The reliability engineering group owns the pilot and reports before the March capital review; the decision on full installation is held until the pilot results are reported. The evidence base is the plant's maintenance records for 12 months across 180 pumps. The records show 1035 h of unplanned downtime, and bearing failures account for 39% of the downtime hours. Bearings are the failure the sensors address: a sensor set detects the vibration and temperature rise that precede a bearing failure, in time to plan the repair inside a scheduled stop rather than lose the pump in service. A sensor set for all 180 pumps is quoted at $456k installed, plus $73k per year. In a vendor trial on a comparable unit the sensors cut downtime by 24%; the figure is a vendor figure and was not measured at this plant. The pilot covers 21 pumps and costs $43k over three months. It measures the downtime reduction on this plant's pumps, under this plant's operating pattern, which is the figure the full-installation decision needs and the vendor trial cannot give. The pilot also tests the detection chain in service: whether the sensors raise alarms the maintenance crew can act on, whether the alarms arrive early enough to plan around, and whether false alarms stay rare enough to keep the alarms credible. Spare-part lead times are unchanged by the sensors: detection shortens the response, not the supply chain, and a detected failure still waits for its part. The decision the pilot informs is whether the measured reduction justifies the full installation cost, and that decision stands at the March capital review with the pilot results in front of it.

fact_base: Goal: compute the diffusive flux of oxygen through a stagnant water film. The diffusive flux J (mol m-2 s-1) is computed from the diffusivity D (m2 s-1) and the concentration gradient dC/dx, where C is concentration (mol m-3) and x is position (m). Fick's first law: J = -D dC/dx; the negative sign states that diffusion runs from high concentration to low concentration. Oxygen in water: D = 1.6 x 10-9 m2 s-1. Concentration falls by 0.4 mol m-3 across a film 0.5 mm thick, so dC/dx = -800 mol m-4. Worked result: J = 1.28x 10-6 mol m-2 s-1. The law as stated covers a stagnant medium; a moving medium adds convection, which the equation does not include.
input: In this worked example, we will calculate the diffusive flux of oxygen through a stagnant water film, which is a classic application of Fick's first law. The diffusive flux J (mol m-2 s-1) is computed from the diffusivity D (m2 s-1) and the concentration gradient dC/dx, where C is the concentration and x is the position within the film. Fick's first law states that J = -D dC/dx, and it is important to understand the negative sign: it tells us that diffusion always runs from high concentration to low concentration. For oxygen in water, the diffusivity D takes the value 1.6 x 10-9. The concentration falls by 0.4 mol m-3 across a film that is 0.5 mm thick, which means that the concentration gradient works out to dC/dx = -800 mol m-4. Substituting these values into Fick's first law gives J = -(1.6 x 10-9) x (-800), and evaluating this expression yields a flux of J = 1.28 x 10-6 mol m-2 s-1. This result shows that even though the diffusivity of oxygen in water is quite small, a thin film and a steep concentration gradient can still sustain a measurable flux. It should be noted, however, that the law as stated covers a stagnant medium only; if the medium were moving, convection would also contribute to the transport, and that contribution is not included in the equation used here, so the result applies strictly to the stagnant case considered.
target: Calculate the diffusive flux of oxygen through a stagnant water film. The diffusive flux $J$ (mol m-2 s-1) is computed from the diffusivity $D$ and the concentration gradient dC/dx, where C denotes concentration and x denotes position. Fick's first law gives J = -D dC/dx. Note that the negative sign states the direction of the flux: diffusion runs from high concentration to low concentration, against the sign of the gradient. For oxygen in water, the diffusivity is 1.6 × 10-9 m2 s-1. The concentration falls by 0.4 mol m-3 across a film 0.5 mm thick. Thus dC/dx = -800 mol m-4: the fall is a decrease, and the gradient carries the negative sign. Substitution into Fick's first law gives J = -(1.6 × 10-9) × (-800) = 1.28 x 10-6 mol m-2 s-1. The two negative signs cancel, and the flux is positive in the direction from the concentrated side to the dilute side, as the sign convention requires. The film is thin, and the gradient is steep for a fall of this size; the flux is set by the gradient, not by the fall alone. Fick's first law holds for a stagnant medium. A moving medium adds convection, which the equation does not include; the flux calculated here is the diffusive part only, and it is the whole flux only while the film stays stagnant.

fact_base: Performance of a mechanical-draft tower at a chemical site was logged over one summer month. Mean wet-bulb temperature was 27 °C, the approach was 5 K and the range was 5 K. Performance outside the logged month, in particular at winter wet-bulb temperatures, was not measured.
input: The performance of a mechanical-draft cooling tower at a chemical site was logged over the course of one summer month, and the data collected provide a useful indication of how the tower behaves under warm-weather conditions. Over the logging period, the mean wet-bulb temperature was 27 °C, which is broadly representative of the summer conditions at the site. The tower operated with an approach of 5 K and a range of 5 K during this period. The approach, which describes how closely the cooled water temperature approaches the wet-bulb temperature, and the range, which describes the drop in water temperature as the water passes through the tower, are the two figures that are conventionally used to characterise the performance of a cooling tower of this kind. Taken together, the figures suggest that the tower was performing in line with what might be expected for a unit of this type under the conditions experienced, and they provide a baseline against which future performance could be compared. It is important to bear in mind, however, that the performance was characterised over a single summer month only. Performance outside the logged month, and in particular at the much lower wet-bulb temperatures that occur in winter, was not measured, so it would be inappropriate to extrapolate these results to the winter period or to treat them as a complete characterisation of the tower's behaviour across the full range of conditions that it will experience throughout the year of operation at the site.
target: A mechanical-draft tower at a chemical site was logged over one summer month. The mean wet-bulb temperature over the month was 27 °C. The tower ran at an approach of 5 K and a range of 5 K. The approach is the difference between the cooled-water temperature and the wet-bulb temperature: it states how close the tower brings the water to the limit the air imposes. The range is the fall in water temperature across the tower: it states the cooling the water receives in one pass. Both figures are stated for the flows and the loading of the logged month, and they move if the plant moves the water flow or the heat load away from that month's values. Read together, the two figures characterise the tower for the logged month: the cooling it delivered and the margin it held against the air condition, on the water and air flows that the plant ran during that month. They are summer figures. Performance outside the logged month was not measured, and at winter wet-bulb temperatures in particular the tower's behaviour is unrecorded. A tower that holds its approach in summer may hold it more easily in winter, when the air is cooler and the same water flow meets a larger driving force, or it may be limited instead by water distribution or fan operation under different loads; the logged month cannot distinguish these cases, because the conditions that separate them did not occur while the instruments were running. The figures stand as a summer characterisation of the tower. A winter figure would need a winter logging period of the same kind, and the two together would still leave the shoulder seasons unmeasured.

fact_base: Capital appraisal for a warehouse extension: installed cost $790k, expected net saving $203k per year for 12 years. At a discount rate of 8% the present value of the savings is $1530k and the net present value is $740k. Savings are vendor and utility estimates; no saving has yet been measured on a comparable installation.
input: This appraisal examines the financial case for a proposed warehouse extension. The installed cost of the extension is $790k, and the expected net saving is $203k per year over a period of 12 years. Discounting the savings at a rate of 8% gives a present value of $1530k, and subtracting the installed cost leads to a net present value of $740k, which is comfortably positive. On a simple payback basis, the installed cost is recovered in 3.89 years, after which the savings continue to accrue for the remainder of the appraisal period. The mechanics of the calculation are straightforward: each year's saving is worth progressively less in present-value terms the further it lies in the future, and the discount rate captures that effect across the whole period under consideration. If the savings were to fall short of the estimates, the net present value would fall correspondingly, because a shortfall in any one year is repeated, in effect, across every year of the period. These figures suggest that the extension represents an attractive investment that would strengthen the logistics position of the operation. It is important to note, however, that the savings figures are vendor and utility estimates, and no saving has yet been measured on a comparable installation, so the appraisal should be read as an indication of the potential return rather than as a firm prediction of the outcome that will actually be achieved once the extension has been built and has entered service.
target: The warehouse extension has a net present value of $740k on the stated estimates. The installed cost is $790k. The expected net saving is $203k per year for 12 years, and at a discount rate of 8% the present value of the savings is $1530k. The net present value is the present value of the savings less the installed cost: it states what the stream of savings is worth today, over and above the cost of obtaining it, with each year's saving discounted for the wait until it arrives. The margin is wide. The savings could fall well short of the estimate before the present value of the savings came down to the installed cost and the appraisal turned negative. On a simple payback basis the installed cost is recovered in 3.89 years, inside the first part of the appraisal period, and the savings of the remaining years are then return rather than recovery. The payback figure takes no account of discounting and is the weaker of the two measures; it is stated because it shows how long the capital is exposed before it is recovered, which the present-value figure does not show directly. The savings are vendor and utility estimates. No saving has yet been measured on a comparable installation, and the appraisal inherits that uncertainty in full: the discounting arithmetic is exact, but its largest input is an estimate, and a measured saving from a comparable extension would replace the weakest figure in the case. The decision the figures support is to proceed on the estimates as stated, with the saving treated as unproven until the extension has operated. If the realised saving matches the estimate, the return is as appraised; if it falls short, the net present value falls with it, year by year, across the whole period.

fact_base: The rate constant k (s-1) of a first-order liquid-phase reaction was measured at two temperatures. At 300 K, k = 0.017 s-1. At 340 K, k = 0.275 s-1, computed from the Arrhenius relation with activation energy 59 kJ mol-1 as a derived value. Each temperature was measured in triplicate; the relative standard deviation of k was 4%. Above 340 K the solvent evaporated during sampling, so no rate constant is reported above 340 K.
input: The kinetics of a first-order liquid-phase reaction were investigated experimentally, and the rate constant k was determined at two temperatures. At 300 K, the rate constant was measured as k = 0.017 s-1, providing a baseline value for the reaction under the milder condition. At the higher temperature of 340 K, the rate constant rises to k = 0.275 s-1, a value that was computed from the Arrhenius relation using an activation energy of 59 kJ mol-1 rather than measured directly at that temperature. The increase over the 40 K interval is substantial, and it illustrates the strong sensitivity of the reaction rate to temperature that is characteristic of a process with a significant activation energy. A reaction whose rate constant responds in this way to a modest change in temperature places particular weight on the control of temperature in any equipment in which it is carried out, since small departures from the intended temperature produce large departures from the intended rate. In a first-order reaction the rate at any moment is proportional to the concentration of the reactant that remains, so the rate constant fixes the whole course of the conversion once the starting concentration is known, and a change in the constant translates directly into a change in the time the reaction needs. Each temperature was measured in triplicate in order to establish the reproducibility of the measurements, and the relative standard deviation of k was found to be 4%, indicating a good level of consistency across the replicate runs. It should be noted, however, that the investigation was limited to the range studied: above 340 K, the solvent evaporated during sampling, which made reliable measurement impossible, and so no rate constant is reported above that temperature.
target: The rate constant k of a first-order liquid-phase reaction was measured at two temperatures. At 300 K, k = 0.017 s-1. At 340 K, k = 0.275 s-1, computed from the Arrhenius relation with an activation energy of 59 kJ mol-1; the higher value is a derived value, stated with the relation it comes from, and not a second measurement of the same kind. Over the 40 K interval the rate constant rises by more than an order of magnitude. In a first-order reaction the rate is proportional to the concentration of reactant remaining, and the rate constant sets the time scale of the whole conversion: a constant larger by this factor shortens the time to a given conversion by the same factor, at the same starting concentration. Temperature is therefore the dominant operating variable for this reaction in the range studied, and control of the rate in a reactor would be exercised through temperature before any other variable. The same sensitivity cuts the other way: a reactor held below its intended temperature would run slow by a large factor, and the rate would be recovered by temperature correction rather than by longer residence or higher concentration. Each temperature was measured in triplicate, and the relative standard deviation of k was 4%. The spread is small against the change between the two temperatures: the temperature effect stands well clear of the measurement scatter, and the comparison between the two values does not rest on differences of the size of the replicates' disagreement. The Arrhenius derivation of the higher value rests on the activation energy holding constant across the interval, which the two temperatures alone cannot test. Above 340 K, the solvent evaporated during sampling, so no rate constant is reported above the upper temperature; evaporation during sampling changes the concentration of the sample while it is being taken, and a constant measured on such a sample would describe the sampling as much as the reaction.
