fact_base: An operating-manual chapter for a centrifugal pump, in four sections: start-up, normal operation, alarms, and shutdown. The alarms section lists two alarms and the operator action for each; no other alarms are introduced. The chapter addresses the operator directly and uses imperative verbs for actions.
input:
Start-up
Before the pump is started, it is essential that a number of preparatory checks are carried out carefully, because a centrifugal pump that is started in the wrong condition can be damaged very quickly. First and foremost, the casing must be completely filled with the liquid that is to be pumped, so that the pump is fully primed; a pump that is started dry will deliver no liquid at all, and the seal faces will run without the cooling and lubrication that the liquid would normally provide, potentially leading to rapid wear. The suction valve should be opened fully, and the discharge valve should be left closed or only partly open, in accordance with whatever the plant procedure for the particular service lays down. The bearing housing should be inspected to confirm that the lubricant is standing at its correct mark and appears clean, and it should also be confirmed that the coupling guard is securely in place and that no tools or loose items have been left near the coupling. Where the design permits, the shaft should be turned by hand to check that it rotates freely, and the suction line should be verified as open along its whole length, with no blind inadvertently left in place and the suction strainer clean. The motor can then be started and the pump allowed to come up to speed, after which the discharge valve is opened gradually while the discharge pressure is watched as it rises towards its normal running value. The seal or gland should be observed for any leakage beyond a slight weep, and the operator should listen carefully for any abnormal noise. If the discharge pressure fails to rise, the pump must be stopped and the cause investigated before any further attempt is made, since running without prime, or running for an extended period against a closed discharge valve, will heat the liquid trapped inside the casing. The start can only be regarded as complete once pressure, leakage, and running sound are all entirely normal and steady.

Normal operation
During normal operation, the pump should be held as closely as possible at its duty flow and head, and the operating point should be kept within the range for which the pump was originally selected. The discharge pressure and the flow should be watched regularly, and any drift in either of them, occurring while valve positions remain unchanged, should be treated as an indication that something somewhere in the pump or in the surrounding system has changed. The suction side deserves particular attention: a falling suction level, a strainer that is gradually blocking, or air being drawn in at a flange will typically manifest itself first as increased noise and vibration, accompanied by an unsteady discharge pressure. It is important to appreciate that cavitation causes real damage to the impeller, and that it is corrected at the suction side, by restoring the level, clearing the strainer, or eliminating the air leak, rather than by adjustment at the discharge valve. The bearing housing should be checked for excessive heat, using the fitted instrument or the back of the hand, and the lubricant level and condition should be verified at the rounds interval that has been established for the plant. The seal or gland should likewise be kept under observation: although a slight weep is perfectly normal for a packed gland, a growing leak, hot running, or a gland that stops weeping altogether should be reported and attended to. The pump should never be run for long periods against a closed or nearly closed discharge valve, because the trapped liquid will heat up and the seals and casing may be damaged as a consequence. A log should be maintained of pressures, temperatures, and any changes in sound or vibration, with the time of each change recorded alongside it, and any departure from normal running should be reported immediately, together with a record of the action that was taken in response, so that the following shift can read the state of the pump from the log rather than relying on memory.

Alarms
The pump is fitted with two alarms, each of which requires a specific response from the operator. No other alarm is raised on this pump.
Low discharge pressure. This alarm indicates that the pump has effectively stopped delivering against the system, which may have happened because prime has been lost, because the suction supply has failed, or because the discharge path is standing open to a level that the pump is unable to hold. The suction supply and the suction level should be checked first of all. If the supply can be restored and the pressure returns to normal, the pump may be kept running and the event should be recorded in the log. If, on the other hand, the pressure does not return, the pump should be stopped, the discharge valve closed, and the event reported; under no circumstances should the pump be restarted until the underlying cause has been identified and the pump has been fully primed again.
High bearing temperature. This alarm indicates that the bearing is running hotter than it should, which may be attributable to a loss or failure of the lubricant, to misalignment, or to a load that falls outside the range for which the pump was selected. The pump should be stopped immediately and the discharge valve closed. The bearing should then be allowed to cool down naturally, without any interference. Once the housing has cooled sufficiently to be handled, the lubricant level and its condition should be checked. The pump must not be restarted until the cause of the overheating has been found and properly corrected, and the alarm, the action taken, and the eventual finding should all be recorded in the log. Restarting a bearing that is still hot, without having established why it became hot, risks converting what was merely a warning into an outright failure of the bearing itself, and very often of the seal that sits behind it as well.

Shutdown
When the pump is to be shut down, it should be brought to a stop broadly in the reverse order of the start-up procedure. The discharge valve should be closed gradually until the flow has stopped completely, bearing in mind that a sudden closure can send a damaging pressure surge back through the discharge line. The motor should then be stopped, and the suction valve closed. As the shaft runs down, it should be watched and listened to carefully, and any rubbing or knocking that is noticed as it slows should be reported and recorded before the pump is left unattended. If the pump is going to stand idle for any length of time, the casing should be drained wherever there is a risk that the liquid left inside it might solidify, attack the casing material, or freeze during cold weather, and the drain should be left in whatever state the plant procedure directs. All pressure within the casing and the connected lines must be relieved before any cover is slackened. Where maintenance work is to be carried out on the pump, it must first be isolated from both the suction and the discharge lines, the motor must be locked so that it cannot be started, and the pump must be proved dead before work begins. The pump should then be handed over to the maintenance crew in precisely that condition, with its state duly recorded in the log. It should be remembered that a pump which has been left filled, pressurised, or free to start cannot be regarded as shut down, regardless of the position of its valves.

Start-up
Prepare the pump and the connected pipework before the motor is started. Fill the casing with the liquid to be pumped until the pump is fully primed. A centrifugal pump started dry delivers no liquid, and the seal faces run without the cooling and lubrication that the liquid provides. Open the suction valve fully. Set the discharge valve closed or partly open, as the plant procedure for the service directs. Inspect the bearing housing and confirm that the lubricant stands at its mark and is clean. Confirm that the coupling guard is in place and that no tools or loose material rest near the coupling. Turn the shaft by hand where the design allows hand turning, and confirm that it turns freely. Confirm that the suction line is open along its whole length, with no blind left in place and the suction strainer clean. Start the motor and let the pump come up to speed. Open the discharge valve gradually and watch the discharge pressure rise to its normal running value. Inspect the seal or gland for leakage beyond a slight weep, and listen for noise beyond the normal running sound. Where discharge pressure does not rise, stop the pump and find the cause before a further start; a pump run without prime, or run for long against a closed discharge valve, heats the liquid trapped in the casing. The start is complete when pressure, leakage, and running sound are all normal and steady, and the pump is left in that state. Keep the area around the pump clear while the start is in progress, and stay at the pump until it has settled into steady running; a fault at start-up shows in the first minutes, and the operator at the pump is the one placed to stop it.

Normal operation
Hold the pump at its duty flow and head, and keep the operating point inside the range the pump was selected for. Watch the discharge pressure and the flow, and treat a drift in either, at unchanged valve positions, as a sign that something in the pump or in the system around it has changed. Keep the suction side under watch: a falling suction level, a blocking strainer, or air drawn in at a flange shows first as noise and vibration, with the discharge pressure unsteady. Cavitation damages the impeller and is corrected at the suction side, by restoring the level, clearing the strainer, or stopping the air leak; it is not corrected at the discharge valve. Check the bearing housing for heat by the fitted instrument or by hand, and check the lubricant level and condition at the rounds interval set for the plant. Watch the seal or gland: a slight weep is normal for a packed gland, while a growing leak, hot running, or a gland that stops weeping altogether is reported and seen to. Do not run the pump for long against a closed or nearly closed discharge valve; the trapped liquid heats, and the seals and casing are damaged by the heat. Keep a log of pressures, temperatures, and every change in sound or vibration, with the time of the change noted against it. Report departures from normal running at once, and record what was done in response, so that the next shift reads the state of the pump from the log and not from memory. Where the pump runs in parallel with a second pump on the same service, watch the sharing of the flow between the two as well; a drift in one machine moves load onto the other, and the pair is read together rather than as two separate machines.

Alarms
Two alarms are fitted to this pump, and each alarm has its operator action. No other alarm is raised on the pump.
Low discharge pressure. The alarm means that the pump has stopped delivering against the system: prime has been lost, the suction supply has failed, or the discharge path stands open to a level the pump cannot hold. Check the suction supply and the suction level first. Where the supply is restored and the pressure returns, keep the pump running and log the event. Where the pressure does not return, stop the pump, close the discharge valve, and report the event; do not restart until the cause has been found and the pump has been primed again.
High bearing temperature. The alarm means that the bearing is running hot, from loss or failure of the lubricant, from misalignment, or from a load outside the range the pump was selected for. Stop the pump at once and close the discharge valve. Let the bearing cool without interference. When the housing can be handled, check the lubricant level and its condition. Do not restart the pump until the cause of the heating has been found and corrected, and record the alarm, the action taken, and the finding in the log. A hot bearing restarted without a finding converts a warning into a failure of the bearing, and commonly of the seal behind it. An alarm that returns after its cause has been corrected is treated as a new event and not as a nuisance: the finding from the earlier event is re-opened, and the pump is not returned to unattended running until the repeat has been explained.

Shutdown
Bring the pump to a stop in the reverse order of the start. Close the discharge valve gradually until the flow stops; a sudden closure sends a pressure surge back through the discharge line. Stop the motor. Close the suction valve. Watch the shaft run down and listen for rubbing or knocking as it slows; a noise on rundown is reported and recorded before the pump is left. Where the pump will stand idle, drain the casing if the liquid left in it could solidify, attack the casing, or freeze in cold weather, and leave the drain in the state the plant procedure directs. Relieve the pressure in the casing and in the connected lines before any cover is slackened. Where work is to be done on the pump, isolate it from the suction and discharge lines, lock the motor against starting, and prove the pump dead before the work begins. Hand the pump over to the maintenance crew in that state, with the state recorded in the log. A pump left filled, pressurised, or free to start is not shut down, whatever the position of its valves. Record the shutdown in the log with the reason for it, planned or unplanned, and the state in which the pump is left, so that the next start begins from a known state rather than from an inspection made under time pressure.

fact_base: Liquid-liquid extraction recovers acetic acid from an aqueous stream into an organic solvent. The distribution coefficient (organic over aqueous) is 1.02 at 25 °C and the design uses 8 countercurrent stages. Predicted recovery is 95% of the acetic acid in the feed. The prediction assumes equilibrium stages and negligible mutual solubility; neither has been checked on the actual solvents.
input: Liquid-liquid extraction is a widely used and highly effective separation technique, and in this particular case it is applied to the recovery of acetic acid from an aqueous stream into an organic solvent. The design is based on a cascade of 8 countercurrent stages, a configuration that is generally considered capable of delivering strong separation performance. A key parameter in this process is the distribution coefficient, which describes how the acetic acid divides itself between the two liquid phases at equilibrium; here, the coefficient takes a value of 1.02 at 25 °C, indicating a slight preference for the organic phase. On the basis of these figures, the predicted recovery is an impressive 95% of the acetic acid present in the feed, underscoring the potential of the staged countercurrent arrangement. It is important to note, however, that this prediction rests on certain idealisations: it assumes that every stage reaches equilibrium, and it assumes that mutual solubility between the two solvents is negligible. Interestingly, neither of these assumptions has yet been verified against the actual solvents in question, which means that the real-world performance of the extraction could differ from the predicted value, either favourably or unfavourably. Overall, the results paint a promising picture, while also highlighting the importance of experimental validation going forward. In practical terms, a distribution coefficient only slightly above unity means that each individual stage achieves a relatively modest enrichment, so the burden of the separation falls heavily on the number of stages provided, and the countercurrent arrangement is what allows those stages to be used to their full cumulative effect. Before the design can be regarded as firm, laboratory or pilot work on the real solvent pair would clearly be desirable.
target: Liquid-liquid extraction recovers acetic acid from an aqueous stream into an organic solvent in 8 countercurrent stages. The distribution coefficient is 1.02 at 25 °C; the coefficient is the ratio of the acetic acid concentration in the organic phase to that in the aqueous phase at equilibrium. Predicted recovery is 95% of the acetic acid in the feed. A coefficient close to unity gives a modest enrichment per stage, and the stage count carries the separation: each countercurrent stage brings the two streams toward equilibrium at the local compositions, the extract leaves richest in acetic acid, and the raffinate leaves the last stage at the lowest acetic acid content. The prediction assumes equilibrium stages, so every stage is credited with the full transfer that equilibrium at its compositions allows. The prediction also assumes negligible mutual solubility, so the solvent is treated as staying in the organic stream and the aqueous stream as leaving free of solvent. Neither assumption has been checked on the actual solvents. Mutual solubility, where it occurs, moves solvent into the raffinate and water into the extract, and a stage that falls short of equilibrium transfers less acetic acid than the prediction credits to it. Predicted recovery is a design figure under two unchecked assumptions, and the check on the actual solvents is the measurement that would move it. The stage count and the coefficient together set the design: with the coefficient near unity, recovery is bought with stages, and a solvent with a higher coefficient would reach the same recovery in fewer stages, or a higher recovery in the same cascade. The raffinate is the stream the recovery figure is read on, since the figure states what the raffinate no longer carries.

fact_base: Excerpt content: a budget overrun of 8 weeks is reported with its cause; the excerpt proposes one mitigation and its owner. The excerpt does not open or close the memo and does not restate its subject line.
input: The overrun on the current phase has now grown to 8 weeks, and the principal reason for this disappointing development is the late delivery of a number of long-lead equipment packages that were ordered as part of the EPC scope. These packages were due to arrive well before the installation fronts that depend on them were scheduled to begin, and their late arrival has meant that several fronts have been unable to start on time, with unfortunate knock-on effects right across the sequence of works. It is important to note that work which does not depend on the delayed packages has continued to progress broadly as planned, and every effort is being made to protect the overall completion date. In order to mitigate the impact of the delay, it is proposed that the installation works be resequenced, so that fronts for which all materials are already on site are brought forward, while the delayed fronts absorb the released labour resources as and when their packages finally arrive. Responsibility for delivering this resequencing rests with the EPC contractor, who will report progress against the revised sequence to the project board on a regular basis. While this mitigation cannot recover time on fronts that remain blocked by the outstanding deliveries, it is expected to limit the further growth of the overrun and to make the best possible use of the resources that are currently available on site, although the recovery it can offer is ultimately bounded by the arrival of the packages themselves and by the order in which the completed systems must be handed over for testing.

fact_base: A centrifugal pump moves caustic solution between two vessels at grade. At the duty point the flow is 24 m3 h-1 against a head of 64 m, with pump efficiency 81%. Shaft power at the duty point is 5.2 kW. The motor is rated 15% above this value. Cavitation was not observed in the acceptance test, which ran for 4 h at the duty point only.
input: A centrifugal pump plays a crucial role in transferring caustic solution between two vessels that are located at grade, and its performance at the selected duty point is summarised here. At this duty point, the pump delivers a flow of 24 m3 h-1 against a head of 64 m, operating at an efficiency of 81%, which together result in a shaft power requirement of 5.2 kW. In other words, the motor driving the pump must be capable of supplying this power at the shaft in order to sustain the required flow against the system head. To provide a comfortable margin, the motor is rated 15% above this value, ensuring that the drive is not operating at the very edge of its capability. Furthermore, cavitation is often a major concern in pumping applications, and it is therefore reassuring to note that no cavitation was observed during the acceptance test. It should be emphasised, however, that this test was conducted over a period of 4 h and covered the duty point only, meaning that behaviour at other operating points, such as higher flows or reduced suction heads, remains untested. Overall, these figures provide a clear and concise snapshot of the duty that the pump was selected to perform, highlighting the interplay between flow, head, efficiency, and power in a single operating point. Taken as a whole, the duty point therefore encapsulates the essential bargain of the selection: a specified flow, delivered against a specified head, at a stated efficiency and a corresponding shaft power, with a sensibly margined motor and an acceptance test that, while reassuring in its own terms, was confined to that single point on the characteristic curve.
target: A centrifugal pump moves caustic solution between two vessels at grade. At the duty point, the flow is 24 m3 h-1 against a head of 64 m, and the pump efficiency is 81%. Shaft power at the duty point is 5.2 kW. The duty point is the operating point the pump was selected for. The head is the lift the system imposes at that flow, read from the system curve where it crosses the pump curve, and the shaft power is the power the motor must deliver to the pump shaft to hold the point. Efficiency relates the shaft power to the hydraulic power imparted to the liquid; the balance of the shaft power leaves the pump as heat in the casing and the liquid. The motor is rated 15% above the duty shaft power, so the drive holds the duty point below its rating. Cavitation was not observed in the acceptance test, which ran for 4 h at the duty point only. The observation covers the duty point. Operation away from the duty point, at higher flow or at lower suction head, sits outside the tested condition, and cavitation there is neither confirmed nor excluded by the test. The duty figures describe one point on the pump's range; behaviour across the range, and the margin between the duty point and the ends of the curve, are separate matters from the duty-point selection itself. Caustic service adds a materials condition to the duty: the casing, the impeller, and the seal faces are chosen for the liquid, and their suitability is part of the selection that the duty point summarises, although it is not stated in the duty figures themselves.

fact_base: Goal: compute the half-life of a first-order reaction and the fraction remaining after 60 min. For a first-order reaction the rate constant k (min-1) fixes the half-life t1/2 (min) by t1/2 = ln(2) / k, and the fraction remaining after time t (min) is exp(-k t). Measured rate constant: k = 0.046 min-1 at 323 K, from concentration measurements every 5 min over 90 min. Worked results: t1/2 = 15.1 min; the fraction remaining after 60 min is 0.06 (dimensionless), both computed from the stated relations. The relations hold for a first-order reaction only; a reaction of another order follows a different decay law.
input: In this worked example, the goal is to compute the half-life of a first-order reaction and to determine the fraction of reactant that remains after 60 min have elapsed. The measured rate constant for the reaction is k = 0.046 min-1 at 323 K, a value that was obtained by taking concentration measurements every 5 min over a period of 90 min and analysing how the concentration declined with time. For a first-order reaction, the half-life, denoted t1/2, is conveniently given by the simple relation t1/2 = ln(2) / k, which shows that the half-life depends only on the rate constant and not on how much reactant was present at the start. Substituting the measured rate constant into this relation gives a half-life of 15.1 min. In a similar fashion, the fraction of reactant remaining after a given time can be calculated from the exponential decay relation, and substituting the rate constant together with the elapsed time of 60 min gives a remaining fraction of 0.06. This result makes intuitive sense, because the elapsed time corresponds to almost four successive half-lives, and repeated halving over that span naturally leaves only a small fraction of the original material behind. It is important to note that these relations are valid for a first-order reaction only; a reaction following a different order would obey an entirely different decay law, and neither formula could be applied to it. In practice, the half-life is an especially convenient way of picturing the pace of such a reaction, because it allows the progress of the decay to be followed in equal steps of time, each step removing half of whatever remained at its beginning. The temperature at which the rate constant was measured should always be kept in mind, since rate constants are temperature-dependent and the quoted half-life and remaining fraction are strictly applicable only at the temperature of the measurement itself.
target: Calculate the half-life of a first-order reaction from the rate constant, and the fraction of reactant remaining after 60 min. The rate constant is k = 0.046 min-1 at 323 K, obtained from concentration measurements taken every 5 min over 90 min. For a first-order reaction, the half-life, denoted t1/2, is determined by the rate constant alone, through t1/2 = ln(2) / k. Substitution of the rate constant gives a half-life of 15.1 min. The half-life does not depend on the starting concentration: each successive halving of the amount remaining takes the same time, and that constancy is the defining feature of first-order decay. The rate constant itself comes from the measurements: for a first-order reaction, the logarithm of the concentration falls on a straight line against time, and the slope of that line gives the constant. The fraction remaining after a time t is exp(-k t); substitution of the rate constant and of 60 min gives 0.06. The interval spans a little under four half-lives, and repeated halving over that span leaves a fraction close to the calculated value; the check by halving agrees with the exponential result. The fraction is dimensionless, a ratio of the amount remaining to the amount at the start. Both relations hold for a first-order reaction only. A reaction of another order follows a different decay law, and neither the half-life relation nor the exponential fraction applies to it. The rate constant is stated at the measurement temperature because the constant is a function of temperature, and the results carry that temperature with them. The measurement interval is short against the half-life, so the concentration record holds several points inside each halving, and the fitted constant rests on the shape of the whole record rather than on any pair of readings. The fraction remaining is the quantity a yield or a residence-time calculation consumes: it converts a time directly into the share of the charge that has not yet reacted.

subtype: worked example with equation: Antoine vapour pressure
fact_base: The vapour pressure of benzene at 78 °C is estimated from the Antoine equation with constants $A$ = 6.90565, $B$ = 1211.033 and $C$ = 220.79 (pressure in mmHg, temperature in °C). The estimate is 94.9 kPa. The constants are valid only over their fitted temperature range; the source databank value governs design.
input:
Estimating vapour pressures is a routine yet crucial task in chemical engineering, and the Antoine equation serves as one of the most widely used tools for this purpose. In this example, the goal is to estimate the vapour pressure of benzene at a temperature of 78 °C. The Antoine equation, which correlates vapour pressure with temperature through three fitted constants, takes the following form:

$$\log_{10} P = A - \frac{B}{T + C}$$

In this equation, $P$ represents the vapour pressure and $T$ represents the temperature, while $A$, $B$, and $C$ are substance-specific constants that are obtained by fitting experimental data. For benzene, the constants are given as $A$ = 6.90565, $B$ = 1211.033, and $C$ = 220.79, with the pressure expressed in mmHg and the temperature in degrees Celsius. Substituting the temperature into the equation and converting the resulting pressure into kilopascals yields an estimated vapour pressure of 94.9 kPa. It is important to note that these constants remain valid only within the temperature range over which they were fitted, and using them outside that range can lead to significant errors. For design purposes, the value held in the source databank is the one that governs, and the Antoine estimate is best regarded as a convenient approximation for interpolation and checking within its valid range, rather than as a substitute for authoritative data. It is also worth remembering that the constants are inseparable from the units in which they were fitted, so that constants borrowed from a source using a different pressure unit will silently return pressures in that unit, a pitfall that has caught out many practitioners over the years. Used with appropriate care, however, the equation remains an extremely handy means of interpolating vapour-pressure data between measured points, provided always that the temperature of interest lies comfortably inside the range covered by the original fit.
target:
The vapour pressure of benzene at 78 °C is estimated from the Antoine equation:

$$\log_{10} P = A - \frac{B}{T + C}$$

In the Antoine equation, $P$ is the vapour pressure, $T$ is the temperature, and $A$, $B$ and $C$ are constants fitted to measured vapour-pressure data for the substance. The constants for benzene are $A$ = 6.90565, $B$ = 1211.033 and $C$ = 220.79, with pressure in mmHg and temperature in °C. The equation gives the logarithm of the vapour pressure, so the pressure itself follows by raising ten to the calculated power. Substitution of the temperature gives the vapour pressure in mmHg, and conversion from mmHg to kilopascals gives the estimate of 94.9 kPa. The units of the constants fix the units of the calculation: constants fitted for mmHg return mmHg, and a calculation that needs kilopascals converts at the end. The constants are valid only over their fitted temperature range. Inside that range the equation interpolates the fitted data; outside it, the equation extrapolates a fitted curve beyond the measurements behind it, and the estimate loses its basis. The source databank value governs design. The Antoine estimate serves where a quick value inside the fitted range suffices, and as a check on a databank figure quoted without its provenance: a disagreement between the two is a reason to re-read the databank entry, not to average the values. The estimate is an interpolation device, and its proper use is bounded accordingly: a design calculation that needs a vapour pressure takes the databank value, while a calculation that needs values at several temperatures inside the fitted range may take them from the equation, each carrying the uncertainty of the fitted constants with it. The constants belong to the substance and to the unit set together, and the equation gives no warning when the sets are mixed.

input: This memo considers whether maintenance sensors should be installed across the plant's pump population, and what the evidence currently available actually supports. The plant runs 260 pumps in total, and maintenance records covering a period of 12 months show a substantial 1333 h of unplanned downtime, of which bearing failures alone account for 46% of the downtime hours. A sensor set covering all 260 pumps has been quoted at $441k installed, plus a further $66k per year in ongoing costs. In a trial conducted by the vendor on a comparable unit, the sensors were reported to cut downtime by 20%, although it is important to note that this figure is a vendor figure and has not been measured at this plant. Rather than committing the full $441k on the strength of a vendor figure, it is recommended that a three-month pilot be carried out first, covering 16 pumps at a cost of $43k. The pilot would be owned by the reliability engineering group, which would report its findings before the March capital review, and the decision on full installation would be held until those results are available. The pilot, at $43k, would replace the vendor's claim with a measurement made on the plant's own pumps.

fact_base: A tutorial passage explains phase equilibrium for a partially miscible liquid pair. The passage states the equilibrium condition in words (equality of chemical potential across phases) before any equation is named. No numerical data are introduced; the passage is conceptual.
input: Phase equilibrium is a foundational concept in separation processes, and it becomes particularly interesting when two liquids are only partially miscible with one another. When such a liquid pair is mixed together, it does not necessarily form a single homogeneous phase; instead, over a certain range of compositions, it separates into two distinct liquid phases, each containing both components but in different proportions. At the heart of this behaviour lies a single unifying condition: at equilibrium, the chemical potential of every component must be exactly the same in both phases. This elegant criterion explains why the distribution of each component between the phases settles at a particular point: any imbalance in chemical potential drives transfer of that component from one phase to the other, and transfer continues until the imbalance disappears. Once this condition is satisfied, the compositions of the two phases become fixed at a given temperature and pressure, regardless of the relative amounts of the phases present. Depending on the overall composition of the mixture, the system may contain both phases in varying proportions, or it may fall outside the two-phase region altogether and exist as a single, fully miscible phase. Furthermore, temperature exerts a strong influence on this behaviour, typically narrowing or widening the composition range over which separation occurs. Overall, the equality of chemical potential provides a powerful and general framework for understanding not only liquid-liquid equilibrium, but phase equilibrium in all of its many forms. It is also worth noting that the proportions of the two phases, as distinct from their compositions, are governed by the overall composition of the mixture as charged: the closer the overall composition lies to the composition of one of the phases, the greater the proportion of that phase in the mixture as a whole. What matters for the practitioner is that the existence of the two phases, their compositions, and their proportions are all fixed once the temperature, the pressure, and the overall charge have been specified, leaving the system no freedom to adopt any other state at equilibrium.
target: Two liquids that are only partly miscible form, over a range of overall compositions, two liquid phases in equilibrium. The equilibrium condition is stated in words first: at equilibrium, the chemical potential of each component is equal in the two phases. A component passes between the phases while its chemical potential differs on the two sides, and the transfer runs in the direction that lowers the difference. Transfer stops when the chemical potentials match, and the phase compositions then stop changing. The compositions of the two phases are fixed by the temperature and the pressure. At a stated temperature and pressure, each phase has its own composition, and the two compositions mark the ends of the range over which the pair separates. An overall composition between the two phase compositions gives both phases, in proportions set by where the overall composition falls between them: nearer one end, that phase is the larger share of the mixture. An overall composition outside the range gives a single phase, in which the pair is fully miscible at that composition. Equality of chemical potential is the condition behind the other phase equilibria as well; a vapour in equilibrium with a liquid meets the same condition, with the phases and the components changed. The condition is a statement about the phases at equilibrium, not about the path by which equilibrium is reached. A mixture reaches the condition by transfer between the phases, and the rate of that transfer, set by mixing and by the area between the phases, is a separate matter. Temperature moves the boundary compositions, and for many pairs the two phases grow more alike as temperature rises, until above a critical solution temperature the pair is miscible in all proportions.

fact_base: Carbon dioxide and hydrogen react over a copper-zinc oxide catalyst to give formaldehyde. Space-time yield is the mass of product per unit catalyst volume per hour (kg L-1 h-1). Test conditions: 250 °C, 50 bar, feed ratio H2/CO2 = 3, one feed composition. Structured catalyst: space-time yield 0.75 kg L-1 h-1, pressure drop 0.29 bar, activity loss 8% after 100 h. Pellet catalyst: space-time yield 0.46 kg L-1 h-1, pressure drop 1.5 bar, activity loss 18% after 100 h. No sulfur-bearing feed was tested. Yield and pressure drop are seldom reported for the same catalyst charge.
input: The conversion of carbon dioxide and hydrogen into formaldehyde over a copper-zinc oxide catalyst has attracted considerable attention, and this study compares two different catalyst forms under identical test conditions. The performance of each catalyst is assessed primarily in terms of the space-time yield, defined as the mass of product obtained per unit catalyst volume per hour (kg L-1 h-1), a metric that captures how productively the catalyst volume is being used. All of the tests were carried out at 250 °C and 50 bar, using a feed ratio H2/CO2 = 3 and a single feed composition, in order to ensure a fair and consistent comparison. The structured catalyst delivered a space-time yield of 0.75 kg L-1 h-1, together with a remarkably low pressure drop of 0.29 bar and an activity loss of just 8% after 100 h on stream. By contrast, the conventional pellet catalyst achieved a space-time yield of only 0.46, with a substantially higher pressure drop of 1.5 bar and a more pronounced activity loss of 18% after 100 h. Taken together, these results clearly demonstrate the advantages of the structured form under the conditions investigated. It should be noted, however, that no sulfur-containing feed was tested, and it is also worth bearing in mind that space-time yield and pressure drop are seldom reported together for the same catalyst charge, which can make comparisons of this kind difficult to find in the literature.
target: Carbon dioxide and hydrogen react over a copper-zinc oxide catalyst to give formaldehyde. Two catalyst forms, structured and pellet, are compared on one feed, with space-time yield as the comparison measure: the mass of product per unit catalyst volume per hour (kg L-1 h-1). The tests ran at 250 °C and 50 bar, at a feed ratio H2/CO2 = 3 and one feed composition. The structured catalyst gave a space-time yield of 0.75 kg L-1 h-1, a pressure drop of 0.29 bar, and an activity loss of 8% after 100 h. The pellet catalyst gave a space-time yield of 0.46, a pressure drop of 1.5 bar, and an activity loss of 18% after 100 h. The structured form leads on all three measures at the tested conditions: more product per unit catalyst volume, a smaller pressure drop across the charge, and a slower loss of activity over the test period. The comparison ranks the two charges as tested, at one temperature, one pressure, and one feed composition; it does not separate the effect of the form from the effect of the preparation, which the test design holds together. Pressure drop is a charge property as much as a catalyst property, and the gap between the forms is read with the charge geometry in view. No sulfur-bearing feed was tested, and behaviour on such a feed is unmeasured. Space-time yield and pressure drop are seldom reported for the same catalyst charge, so the paired figures here give a comparison the literature usually lacks.

fact_base: A gravity settler removes calcium carbonate from a process stream. Design overflow rate is 1.51 m h-1 at a throughput of 67 m3 h-1, giving a plan area of 44 m2. The overflow-rate basis is a vendor rule for this solid; no settling test on the actual slurry has been run.
input: It is worth noting that gravity settling represents a well-established and widely utilised unit operation for the separation of solid particles from liquid streams, and in the present case it is applied to the removal of calcium carbonate from a process stream. In a gravity settler, the incoming stream is distributed across the plan area of the vessel, the solid particles gradually settle downwards under the influence of gravity towards the base, and a clarified liquid stream is withdrawn over a weir at the top of the unit. The sizing of such a unit is fundamentally governed by the overflow rate, which can be defined as the volumetric throughput divided by the plan area of the settler. At a throughput of 67 m3 h-1 and a design overflow rate of 1.51 m h-1, the required plan area works out to 44 m2. The underlying principle here is that a particle will be successfully removed if its settling velocity exceeds the overflow rate, whereas a particle that settles more slowly will inevitably be carried out with the clarified liquid, which means that the overflow rate effectively acts as the dividing line between the particles that are captured and those that are not. It should nevertheless be emphasised that the design overflow rate adopted here is derived from a vendor rule for this particular solid, and, crucially, no settling test has actually been carried out on the real slurry, so the vendor value may or may not be representative of the actual material, whose particle size distribution and solids concentration could differ in various respects. This introduces a degree of uncertainty into the stated area, and the consequences of any error are not necessarily symmetric, since an undersized unit would pass solids onwards to downstream equipment while an oversized unit would mainly attract additional cost. Overall, the stated sizing should therefore be viewed as a preliminary, vendor-based estimate, and a settling test on a representative sample of the actual slurry would clearly be a valuable next step in order to place the design on a firmer footing going forward.
target: A gravity settler removes calcium carbonate from a process stream. Liquid enters the vessel, solids settle under gravity to the base, and clarified liquid leaves over a weir at the top. Sizing is set by the overflow rate, defined as the volumetric throughput divided by the plan area of the settler. A particle is removed when its settling velocity exceeds the overflow rate; a particle that settles more slowly leaves with the clarified liquid, and the overflow rate is the cut between the two outcomes. At a throughput of 67 m3 h-1 and a design overflow rate of 1.51 m h-1, the plan area is 44 m2. The design rate comes from a vendor rule for calcium carbonate. No settling test has been run on the actual slurry, and the vendor material may differ from the stream treated here in particle size distribution and solids concentration. The stated area therefore carries an unquantified error in either direction. The consequences are not symmetric. An undersized settler passes solids to the downstream equipment, where carryover appears as fouling or off-specification product; an oversized settler costs vessel volume and plot space but leaves the separation intact. A settling test on a representative sample of the actual slurry would replace the vendor rule with a measured rate for this solid in this liquid, and would also show how the rate varies with feed concentration. Any later change in throughput at a fixed area moves the operating overflow rate in direct proportion, and a rate pushed above the settling velocity of a larger share of the solids degrades the separation in proportion. Until the test is run, the stated area supports a preliminary vessel size and an order for the test itself; it is not a measured performance figure, and the design should be revisited once a measured settling rate for the actual slurry is available.

topic: tut:phase:a pure component at its boiling point
fact_base: A tutorial passage explains phase equilibrium for a pure component at its boiling point. The passage states the equilibrium condition in words (equality of chemical potential across phases) before any equation is named. No numerical data are introduced; the passage is conceptual.
input: Phase equilibrium is a truly fundamental concept in thermodynamics, and nowhere is it more richly illustrated than in the familiar phenomenon of boiling. When a pure liquid is heated at a constant pressure, its temperature rises steadily at first, but once boiling commences something remarkable happens: the temperature simply stops rising, and all of the heat that continues to be supplied is consumed in converting liquid into vapour instead. The condition that governs this behaviour is the equality of the chemical potential of the substance in the two phases, which is to say that the chemical potential of the liquid and the chemical potential of the vapour are exactly the same at equilibrium, and it is this equality, expressed in words, that defines the boiling point before any equation is brought into play. If the chemical potential in the liquid were higher, molecules would pass into the vapour; if it were lower, vapour would condense, and in either case the system would keep changing until the two values came into balance. Boiling, then, is not merely the appearance of bubbles, picturesque as that may be: it is the visible signature of two phases coexisting in equilibrium, with molecules crossing the interface continuously in both directions at equal rates. This is also why the temperature remains pinned throughout the process, because any heat added at the boiling point shifts the balance of amounts between the phases rather than raising the temperature of either one, and the equilibrium condition itself depends only on temperature and pressure, not on how much of each phase happens to be present.
target: A pure component boils at a fixed temperature when the surrounding pressure is held constant, and heat supplied during boiling changes the amounts of the two phases, not the temperature. The equilibrium condition is stated in words first: at equilibrium, the chemical potential of the component in the liquid equals its chemical potential in the vapour. Chemical potential measures the tendency of the component to leave the phase it is in. Where the liquid value stands higher, material passes into the vapour; where the vapour value stands higher, material condenses. Transfer stops, on balance, only where the two values are equal, although molecules continue to cross the interface in both directions at equal rates. The boiling point is the temperature at which the equality holds under the imposed pressure. A rise in pressure moves the boiling point upward, because the equality is restored at a higher temperature; a fall in pressure moves the boiling point down by the same mechanism. During boiling itself, neither temperature nor pressure changes while both phases remain present. Heat added in this state converts liquid to vapour at the equilibrium temperature, and heat removed condenses vapour, so the phase amounts absorb the energy change that would otherwise appear as a temperature change. The condition depends on temperature and pressure alone, and not on the relative amounts of liquid and vapour in the vessel. It holds for a pure component; a mixture, whose composition changes as boiling proceeds, does not boil at one fixed temperature.

fact_base: Goal: compute the Reynolds number for water in a pipe and state the flow regime. The Reynolds number Re (dimensionless) is computed from density rho (kg m-3), mean velocity v (m s-1), pipe diameter D (m) and dynamic viscosity mu (Pa s) by Re = rho v D / mu. Water at 293 K: rho = 998 kg m-3, mu = 1.00 x 10-3 Pa s. Pipe diameter D = 0.05 m; mean velocity v = 2 m s-1. Worked result: Re = 99800 (computed as 998 x 2 x 0.05 / 0.001). Flow is laminar below Re = 2300 and turbulent above Re = 4000; between the two values the regime is transitional and is not assigned by the number alone.
input: Calculate the Reynolds number for water in a pipe, and state the flow regime. The Reynolds number Re (dimensionless) denotes the ratio of inertial to viscous forces in the flow. Re is calculated from the density ρ, the mean velocity v, the pipe diameter D and the dynamic viscosity μ by Re = ρ v D / μ. For water at 293 K, ρ = 998 kg m-3 and μ = 1.00 x 10-3 Pa s. Take D = 0.05 m and v = 2 m s-1. Substitution gives Re = 998 x 2 x 0.05 / 0.001 = 99800. Flow is laminar below Re = 2300 and turbulent above Re = 4000; between the two values the regime is transitional and is not assigned by the number alone. The calculated value exceeds the turbulent threshold by a wide margin, and the flow is turbulent. The result rests on the tabulated water properties at 293 K: a colder stream, with a higher viscosity, would return a lower Reynolds number at the same velocity and diameter, and a value near either threshold would need the transitional range treated as the answer rather than a single regime name. At the stated conditions no such qualification applies, and the regime assignment is unambiguous.

fact_base: A tutorial passage explains representative sampling of an effluent stream. The passage covers where samples are taken, how many increments form one sample, and why a single grab sample misleads. No numerical limits are quoted; regulatory limits belong to the site's permit, not to the passage.
input: Representative sampling is an absolutely essential, yet frequently underestimated, aspect of effluent monitoring, because every downstream decision, from process control right through to regulatory compliance, ultimately rests on the quality of the sample that was actually taken. One of the most important considerations is where the sample is drawn from: ideally, the sampling point should be located at a position where the stream is thoroughly well mixed, for instance downstream of a turbulent section or a bend, and downstream of the last point at which anything is added to or removed from the stream, so that the liquid passing the probe is as homogeneous as possible. A probe thrust into a stagnant corner or a slowly moving layer near the wall will, by contrast, faithfully report the composition of that unrepresentative corner rather than the stream as a whole. Equally important is how the sample itself is built up: best practice is to collect a series of small increments at intervals spread across the period of interest and to combine them into a single composite sample, because the composition of an effluent stream is rarely constant over time. Perhaps the most pervasive pitfall of all is the single grab sample, which captures the stream at one arbitrary instant and can therefore be profoundly misleading: a grab taken during a washdown, a batch discharge or a production upset will dramatically overstate the average load, while one taken during a quiet period will understate it, and neither says anything reliable about the stream over the day as a whole. In short, the sampling point, the increment pattern and the compositing together determine whether the laboratory result describes the effluent itself or merely the moment and the corner at which someone happened to dip a bottle into it.
target: A sample result is used as the composition of the whole effluent stream, and the sampling procedure decides whether that substitution is justified. The sampling point stands where the stream is mixed: in a turbulent reach, downstream of the last addition or withdrawal, with the probe in the moving body of the liquid. A point in a stagnant corner or in a slow layer near the wall returns the composition of that corner, and a settled or stratified stream returns the composition of the layer the probe happens to reach. One sample is built from increments, small portions drawn at intervals across the period the sample is to represent and combined before analysis. Effluent composition varies with the production cycle, with washdowns, batch discharges and upsets passing as slugs, and the increments spread the sampling across that variation instead of concentrating it at one point in the cycle. A single grab sample takes the stream at one instant. Drawn during a discharge, the grab overstates the average load; drawn in a quiet interval, it understates the load; and in neither case does the result carry any information about the stream outside the moment of sampling. The defect is not in the analysis but in the sample: the laboratory measures the bottle it receives, accurately or not, and no accuracy in the measurement repairs a sample that never represented the stream. Where a permit limit applies, the limit is a property of the site permit; the sampling procedure is judged by whether the composite, as built, matches the stream over the period the permit examines. Increments, mixing at the point, and a probe in the moving liquid are the three elements that make it match. The increments are also preserved and handled as the analysis requires, since a composite that degrades or separates in the bottle between collection and analysis carries the same defect as a badly sited probe: the measured liquid is no longer the liquid that was sampled.

fact_base: A continuous stirred-tank reactor runs a neutralisation that is first order in the limiting reactant. The rate constant is 0.282 min-1 at the operating temperature and the mean residence time is 85 min. Steady-state conversion for an ideal CSTR is 96%. The estimate assumes perfect mixing and constant density; tracer tests on the actual vessel have not been run.
input: A continuous stirred-tank reactor, or CSTR, is used to carry out a neutralisation reaction that is first order in the limiting reactant, and the performance of the reactor under steady-state conditions can be estimated in a fairly straightforward manner from the kinetic and operating data available. The rate constant at the operating temperature is 0.282 min-1, and the mean residence time of the material in the vessel is 85 min, so that the product of the rate constant and the residence time comes to 23.97, a comfortably large value that already suggests a high degree of conversion. Applying the standard design relation for an ideal CSTR under these conditions gives a steady-state conversion of the limiting reactant of 96%, which is to say that only a small residual fraction of the limiting reactant leaves the reactor unreacted in the effluent stream. It is, however, important to appreciate that this estimate is built upon some significant idealising assumptions, most notably the assumptions of perfect mixing throughout the vessel contents and of constant density across the reactor, and in a real vessel there may well be dead zones, short-circuiting or incomplete dispersion that cause the actual behaviour to depart from the ideal picture. Compounding this uncertainty, tracer tests on the actual vessel, which would reveal the true residence time distribution, have not in fact been run, so the closeness of the real reactor to the ideal model remains unverified. The 96% conversion should consequently be interpreted as an ideal-model estimate representing something close to an upper bound on performance, rather than as a guaranteed operating result, and the true conversion achieved in practice may fall somewhat below this figure if the mixing in the actual vessel turns out to be imperfect.
target: Steady-state conversion for an ideal continuous stirred-tank reactor (CSTR) running a first-order neutralisation is 96% of the limiting reactant. The rate constant is 0.282 min-1 at the operating temperature and the mean residence time is 85 min; the product of rate constant and residence time is 23.97, and the ideal-CSTR conversion relation applied to that product gives the stated conversion. A product well above unity is what the conversion rests on: at a product near one, the same relation returns a conversion near one half, and the estimate would be far more sensitive to errors in either input. Two assumptions carry the result. Mixing is taken as perfect, so the whole vessel contents sit at the effluent composition and the reaction proceeds everywhere at the exit rate; density is taken as constant, so the residence time computed from volume and feed rate is the residence time the reacting material experiences. Neither assumption has been checked on the actual vessel. Tracer tests, which would return the residence time distribution and expose dead volume or short-circuiting, have not been run. Dead volume lowers the effective residence time below the stated value, short-circuiting lets part of the feed leave early, and each defect lowers the conversion below the ideal value. The 96% figure is therefore an ideal-model estimate and an upper bound for the stated kinetics, not a measured performance. It is adequate for comparing operating conditions on a common basis, and for sizing downstream equipment that must handle the unreacted remainder; a guarantee of effluent quality would need the tracer response of the actual vessel.

fact_base: Design report for a distillation column, in four sections: basis, sizing, materials, and risks. Design throughput is 58 t per day and the removal or separation duty is 98% of the key component. Materials are 316L stainless steel for wetted parts; the basis section states this once. The risks section names fouling and turndown as open items; neither is resolved in the report.
input:
## Basis
This report sets out the design of a distillation column intended to separate a key component from a process stream, and it documents the basis on which the sizing has been performed, the materials selected, and the principal risks that remain open at this stage. The design throughput is 58 t per day, and the separation duty specified for the column is the removal of 98% of the key component from the feed, a demanding target that drives much of what follows in this document. The feed is taken to enter the column as a saturated liquid at its boiling point, an assumption that simplifies the internal traffic calculations and is regarded as a reasonable starting point for a design at this level of definition, although it will of course need to be revisited if the upstream equipment delivers the feed in a different condition. Wetted parts throughout the column are specified in 316L stainless steel, a choice that is stated here in the basis and is not repeated elsewhere in the report. Design margins have been applied in the customary manner in order to accommodate the uncertainties inherent in a design developed from estimated physical properties, and the operating pressure has been selected with a view to keeping the temperatures within the column compatible with the available heating and cooling utilities on site.
## Sizing
The sizing of the column proceeds from the separation duty stated in the basis. The number of theoretical stages is estimated by standard shortcut methods in the first instance, and a tray efficiency is then applied in order to arrive at the number of actual trays that will be installed, since real trays do not achieve the full equilibrium separation that the theoretical picture assumes. The reflux ratio is chosen as a multiple of the minimum reflux ratio, and this choice involves an important trade-off, because a higher reflux ratio reduces the number of stages required but simultaneously increases the vapour and liquid traffic inside the column, the diameter that is needed to handle that traffic, and the duties imposed on the reboiler and the condenser at either end. The column diameter is set by the hydraulic capacity of the trays at the point of maximum vapour loading, with a prudent allowance below the flooding limit so that the column retains some tolerance for the inevitable fluctuations in feed rate and composition that arise in normal operation. The reboiler and condenser are sized from the internal traffic at the design reflux condition, and the resulting duties are passed to the utility systems for checking against the capacity actually available on site. The column height follows from the tray count and the tray spacing, together with the disengagement allowances required above the top tray and below the bottom tray for satisfactory operation. Nozzle sizes are selected from the line sizes of the connecting pipework, and the associated pressure drops are checked for consistency with the overall pressure balance of the system.
## Materials
The materials selection is governed principally by the corrosive character of the process fluid and by the temperatures and pressures encountered within the column. Wetted parts are executed in the stainless steel specified in the basis, which offers adequate resistance to the process environment across the full range of operating conditions envisaged, including the more aggressive conditions that can arise during start-up, shutdown and process upsets, when concentrations and temperatures may depart considerably from their normal values. Welds in wetted service are made with matching filler material and are subject to the inspection regime appropriate to pressure equipment, since a weld of inferior corrosion resistance would simply become the preferential site of attack and would defeat the purpose of the overall selection. Gaskets and other non-metallic components are chosen for compatibility with the process fluid at the design temperature, and bolting is selected to match the flange duty. External surfaces are protected against atmospheric corrosion by the site coating system, and insulation, where fitted, is provided with cladding arranged to shed water away from the shell. Materials for the column internals are matched to those of the shell in order to avoid galvanic couples in the presence of a conductive process liquid, and particular attention is paid to crevices at tray supports and attachment points, which are recognised sites for accelerated local attack in stagnant conditions.
## Risks
Two risks stand out as unresolved at the present stage of the design and are recorded here as open items rather than as matters that the design has settled. The first is fouling: the feed contains components with a tendency to deposit on trays and in the reboiler, and deposition would progressively degrade both the separation efficiency and the heat transfer, narrowing the operating window of the column over the course of a run. The rate of fouling cannot be predicted reliably from the data currently available, so the design neither credits a fouling allowance beyond normal margins nor proposes a cleaning regime, and the matter is left for resolution with operating experience and, if necessary, feed pretreatment. The second open item is turndown: the column is sized at the design throughput, and its behaviour at substantially reduced rates, where trays may weep and the separation deteriorate, has not been established. If the plant is expected to operate for extended periods well below the design rate, the tray selection and the control scheme will both need to be revisited, but no such requirement has been stated, and the report therefore leaves the turndown question open. Neither item is resolved in this report, and both should be carried forward into the next stage of design.
target:
## Basis
The column separates a key component from a liquid feed at a design throughput of 58 t per day, with a separation duty of 98% of the key component removed. Wetted parts are in 316L stainless steel; the material is specified here and not repeated in the sections that follow. The feed enters as a saturated liquid at its boiling point. The assumption fixes the internal traffic at its simplest distribution between the rectifying and stripping sections, and it holds only while the upstream equipment delivers the feed in that condition; a subcooled or partly vaporised feed changes the traffic and the stage requirement, and the design would be rechecked against the delivered condition. Operating pressure is chosen so that column temperatures suit the heating and cooling utilities available on site. Physical properties used in the sizing are estimated values, and the design margins stated in the sizing section absorb the uncertainty those estimates carry. The basis is a preliminary design basis: adequate for fixing the column size, the tray count and the exchanger duties, and not a substitute for sizing on measured property data. Feed composition is taken as the stated average composition across the operating campaign. The separation duty is set by the key component alone; the remaining components distribute between the two products as the equilibrium and the stage count dictate, and no specification is placed on them in this report. Where the feed composition moves away from the average, the product purities move with it, and the column as sized absorbs the movement through the reflux and boil-up adjustments available to the operator rather than through any change in the installed equipment.
## Sizing
Stage requirement is estimated first by shortcut methods, which return the minimum reflux ratio and the minimum stage count as the two bounds of the separation. The design reflux ratio is set as a multiple of the minimum. A ratio close to the minimum keeps the vapour traffic, the diameter and the reboiler and condenser duties small, at the cost of a tall column; a larger ratio buys fewer stages with larger traffic and larger duties. The multiple chosen is the compromise the design carries, stated so that the trade can be reopened if energy or capital costs move. A tray efficiency converts the theoretical stages into actual trays. The efficiency is an estimate for this system, and the tray count inherits its uncertainty; internals are therefore arranged so that trays can be added at the top and bottom of the column if commissioning shows the efficiency to be lower than assumed. Diameter is set by tray hydraulics at the section of maximum vapour loading, with the operating point held below the flooding limit by the stated margin, so that feed fluctuations within the normal band do not flood the column. Reboiler and condenser duties follow from the internal traffic at the design reflux condition and are passed to the utility systems for checking against site capacity. Height follows from tray count and tray spacing, with disengagement space above the top tray and a sump below the bottom tray. Nozzle sizes follow the connecting line sizes, and pressure drops are checked against the overall pressure balance. Control of the separation rests on the reflux flow and the reboiler duty, with the product draw rates held by level control in the reflux drum and the column base. The sizing leaves the control scheme workable across the normal operating band: the valves selected pass the design traffic with travel in reserve in both directions, and the column pressure is held by the condenser, so that a change in cooling duty does not disturb the stage temperatures beyond the band the separation tolerates.
## Materials
The stainless steel specified in the basis covers the shell, the trays and all wetted internals. Corrosion resistance, not strength, governs the selection: the process fluid attacks carbon steel at rates no corrosion allowance would accommodate, and the selected grade resists the fluid across the operating range, including the off-design conditions of start-up and upset, when concentrations and temperatures depart from their normal values. Welds in wetted service take matching filler and the inspection regime for pressure equipment, since a weld of lower resistance than the parent metal becomes the site of preferential attack. Gaskets are non-metallic and are selected for compatibility with the process fluid at the design temperature. Bolting matches the flange duty. Internals use the same grade as the shell, so that no galvanic couple forms between dissimilar metals in contact with a conductive liquid. Attachment points and tray supports are detailed to avoid crevices, which hold stagnant liquid and concentrate the attack. External surfaces take the site coating system, and insulation cladding is arranged to shed water clear of the shell, since corrosion under wet insulation proceeds out of sight.
## Risks
Fouling and turndown are open items. Neither is resolved in this report. Fouling: the feed carries components that deposit on trays and on reboiler surfaces, and deposition degrades separation efficiency and heat transfer as a run proceeds. No fouling rate can be predicted from the data available, so the design credits no fouling allowance beyond the stated margins and proposes no cleaning regime. The item closes with operating experience, or earlier if feed pretreatment is adopted. Turndown: the column is sized at the design throughput, and tray behaviour at substantially lower rates has not been established. Trays that weep at low liquid rates lose separation, and a column required to run for long periods well below the design rate would need a different tray selection and a revised control scheme. No turndown requirement has been stated, so the design carries none. Both items are carried into the next design stage as they stand: the fouling item with a request for feed deposit data, the turndown item with a request for a stated operating range. A third matter is recorded for completeness rather than as a risk of the same order: the sizing rests on estimated physical properties, and the stage count and duties will move if measured properties differ from the estimates. The margins stated in the sizing section are the allowance the design makes for that movement, and measured data, when available, replace the estimates without reopening the structure of the design.

subtype: worked example with equation: radiative exchange
fact_base: A blackened plate at 800 K faces surroundings at 300 K. Its emissivity $\varepsilon$ is 0.95. Net radiative heat flux $q$ is 21.6 kW m-2, with the Stefan-Boltzmann constant $\sigma$ = 5.67 x 10-8 W m-2 K-4. The estimate treats both surfaces as large and parallel; view factors for the real geometry are not included.
input:
Radiative heat transfer is a critically important mechanism whenever surfaces at elevated temperatures exchange energy with their surroundings, and the present example considers a blackened plate at 800 K facing surroundings at 300 K. The emissivity of the plate, denoted by the symbol $\varepsilon$, is 0.95, which reflects the fact that the blackened surface radiates almost as effectively as an ideal black body. The net radiative heat flux from the plate is calculated from the well-known Stefan-Boltzmann relation, in which $q$ is the net heat flux, $\sigma$ is the Stefan-Boltzmann constant with a value of 5.67 x 10-8 W m-2 K-4, $T_1$ is the plate temperature and $T_2$ is the surroundings temperature:

$$q = \varepsilon \sigma (T_1^4 - T_2^4)$$

Substituting the values into this expression yields a net radiative heat flux $q$ of 21.6 kW m-2, a substantial figure that clearly demonstrates the sheer dominance of the fourth-power temperature dependence, since the contribution associated with the surroundings at their much lower temperature is comparatively very small. It is nevertheless important to bear in mind the idealisations embedded in this estimate: the calculation treats both surfaces as large and parallel, so that each surface effectively sees only the other, whereas in any real geometry the view factors that describe what fraction of the radiation leaving one surface actually strikes the other have not been taken into account at all. The quoted flux should therefore be understood as an estimate for the simplified geometry assumed, and a treatment of the actual installation, with its genuine view factors and possibly intervening surfaces, could give a noticeably different result.
target:
A blackened plate at 800 K faces surroundings at 300 K, and the net radiative heat flux $q$ is calculated from the Stefan-Boltzmann relation. In the relation, $q$ is the net heat flux, $\varepsilon$ is the emissivity of the plate (0.95 for the blackened surface), $\sigma$ is the Stefan-Boltzmann constant (5.67 x 10-8 W m-2 K-4), $T_1$ is the plate temperature and $T_2$ is the surroundings temperature:

$$q = \varepsilon \sigma (T_1^4 - T_2^4)$$

The relation gives $q$ = 21.6 kW m-2. The fourth-power terms govern the result: the surroundings term, at the lower temperature, removes only a small share of the emitted flux, and the net flux stands close to the emission of the plate alone. An error in the plate temperature carries four times its relative size into the flux, which makes the temperature the quantity the estimate is most sensitive to; the emissivity enters only in direct proportion. The estimate treats both surfaces as large and parallel, so each surface sees only the other. View factors for the real geometry are not included, and in an installation where the plate also faces cooler structure, or where part of its radiation escapes the enclosure, the net flux falls below the stated value. The figure is a parallel-plate estimate, adequate for comparing surface treatments or plate temperatures on a common basis. Surface condition enters through the emissivity alone in this treatment, and a plate whose blackening degrades in service drifts towards a lower emissivity and a lower flux than the stated value, with no change in either temperature. A design duty for the actual geometry requires the view factors of that geometry, and the stated flux is not used for that purpose.
