subtype: worked example with equation: friction loss
fact_base: Water at 293 K flows in a horizontal pipe. The density $\rho$ is 998 kg m-3. Mean velocity $v$ is 1.2 m s-1, pipe diameter $D$ is 0.1 m, pipe length $L$ is 115 m and the Darcy friction factor $f$ is 0.02. The friction pressure drop is 16.5 kPa.
input:
The pressure drop arising from friction in a horizontal pipe is one of the most fundamental calculations in fluid mechanics, and it is evaluated here for water flowing under a representative set of conditions. Water at 293 K has a density $\rho$ of 998 kg m-3, and it flows through the pipe at a mean velocity $v$ of 1.2 m s-1. The pipe has a diameter $D$ of 0.1 m and a length $L$ of 115 m, and the Darcy friction factor $f$ for the conditions in question is 0.02. The friction pressure drop is calculated from the Darcy-Weisbach relation, in which $\Delta P$ is the friction pressure drop, $f$ is the Darcy friction factor, $L$ is the pipe length, $D$ is the pipe diameter, $\rho$ is the fluid density and $v$ is the mean velocity:

$$\Delta P = f \frac{L}{D} \frac{\rho v^2}{2}$$

Substitution of the stated values into this relation gives a friction pressure drop of 16.5 kPa, which is the pressure that a pump or other driving device must supply merely in order to overcome friction along this length of pipe, over and above any pressure required for elevation changes or for the process itself. Because the pipe is horizontal, no allowance for static head is required in this particular calculation, and because the velocity enters the relation as a square, it follows that even modest increases in the flow rate, and hence in the mean velocity, will produce disproportionately large increases in the friction loss, a point that is well worth bearing in mind when operating conditions are changed. The result is of course sensitive to the friction factor adopted, and the value used here should be understood as the value appropriate to the stated conditions rather than as a universal constant for water flowing in pipes.
target:
Calculate the friction pressure drop for water in a horizontal pipe. Water at 293 K (density $\rho$ = 998 kg m-3) flows at a mean velocity $v$ of 1.2 m s-1 in a pipe of diameter $D$ = 0.1 m and length $L$ = 115 m; the Darcy friction factor $f$ is 0.02. The pipe is horizontal, so no static-head term enters the calculation, and the density is constant along the length. The friction pressure drop is calculated from the Darcy-Weisbach relation

$$\Delta P = f \frac{L}{D} \frac{\rho v^2}{2}$$

where $\Delta P$ is the friction pressure drop, $f$ is the Darcy friction factor, $L$ is the pipe length, $D$ is the pipe diameter, $\rho$ is the density and $v$ is the mean velocity. The relation gives $\Delta P$ = 16.5 kPa. The velocity term governs the sensitivity of the result: $\Delta P$ varies with the square of $v$, so a rise in flow rate raises the friction loss in proportion to the square of that rise, and the pump duty set from the stated figure must be revisited if the operating flow changes. The friction factor carries the remaining uncertainty. The value used is the value at the stated conditions; a rougher pipe wall, or a lower Reynolds number in a colder stream, raises $f$ and raises the pressure drop in direct proportion. The result is the friction loss for the stated pipe and conditions alone, and fittings, valves and entrance and exit losses are not included in it. In a pump calculation, the friction loss stands alongside the static lift and the pressure difference between the suction and delivery vessels, and the three are added before the pump head is fixed; the stated figure supplies only the first of the three, and a pump selected on the friction figure alone would be undersized for any duty that also lifts the liquid or delivers it against pressure. The length dependence is linear, so the figure scales to a revised routing in direct proportion to the added length, provided the diameter and the velocity are unchanged.

fact_base: 214 pumps run at the plant. Maintenance records for 12 months show 1328 h of unplanned downtime; bearing failures account for 39% of the downtime hours. A sensor set for all 214 pumps is quoted at $450k installed, plus $59k per year. In a vendor trial on a comparable unit, the sensors cut downtime by 27%; the figure is a vendor figure and was not measured at this plant. A pilot on 22 pumps costs $36k over three months. Spare-part lead times are unchanged by the sensors. The memo recommends the three-month pilot; the reliability engineering group owns the pilot and reports before the March capital review; the decision on full installation is held until the pilot results are reported.
input: This memo considers whether the plant should invest in sensors for the early detection of bearing deterioration, and it recommends that, rather than proceeding immediately to a full installation, the plant should first undertake a three-month pilot so that the benefits can be demonstrated on our own equipment before a major commitment is made. The reliability engineering group would own the pilot and would report in good time for the March capital review, at which point the decision on full installation can properly be taken. There are 214 pumps running at the plant, and the maintenance records for the last 12 months show a total of 1328 h of unplanned downtime, a very considerable figure, of which bearing failures account for 39% of the downtime hours, making bearings by far the single largest identified contributor. A sensor set covering all 214 pumps has been quoted at $450k installed, plus a further $59k per year in ongoing costs, so the financial commitment involved in going straight to full installation is by no means trivial. In a vendor trial carried out on a comparable unit, the sensors succeeded in cutting downtime by 27%, which is an encouraging result, although it must be acknowledged that this figure comes from the vendor and was not measured here at this plant, on our own machines, under our own operating conditions. The proposed pilot would equip 22 pumps at a cost of $36k over three months, and it would show whether a downtime reduction of that order is achievable in our service before the larger sum is committed. It should also be noted that spare-part lead times are entirely unaffected by the sensors, so no benefit on that side should be anticipated. In summary, the recommendation is to proceed with the pilot and to hold the decision on full installation until the pilot results are reported.
target: The reliability engineering group recommends a three-month pilot of bearing sensors on 22 pumps, at $36k, before any decision on plant-wide installation. The group owns the pilot and reports before the March capital review; the decision on full installation is held until the pilot results are reported. The evidence base is the plant maintenance record for 12 months. The plant runs 214 pumps, and the record shows 1328 h of unplanned downtime, of which bearing failures account for 39% of the hours. Full installation is quoted at $450k installed for all 214 pumps, plus $59k per year. Against that cost stands one performance figure: in a vendor trial on a comparable unit, the sensors cut downtime by 27%. The figure is a vendor figure, measured on another plant's equipment, and it is not evidence for this plant. The trade-off the pilot resolves is the pilot cost spent now against the full installation price committed on an unverified figure. The pilot measures the downtime reduction in this service, on the bearings that produce the largest share of the downtime hours, and returns a plant figure in place of the vendor figure. One limit stands regardless of the outcome: spare-part lead times are unchanged by the sensors, and no benefit is claimed on that side. If the pilot returns a reduction well below the vendor figure, the full installation case is rebuilt on the pilot number or not brought forward at all.

fact_base: Liquid-liquid extraction recovers acetic acid from an aqueous stream into an organic solvent. The distribution coefficient (organic over aqueous) is 0.53 at 25 °C and the design uses 5 countercurrent stages. Predicted recovery is 93% of the acetic acid in the feed. The prediction assumes equilibrium stages and negligible mutual solubility; neither has been checked on the actual solvents.
input: Liquid-liquid extraction recovers acetic acid from an aqueous stream into an organic solvent, and the design predicts a recovery of 93% of the acetic acid in the feed. The solvent selection rests on the distribution coefficient, defined as the concentration of acetic acid in the organic phase divided by its concentration in the aqueous phase at equilibrium; the coefficient is 0.53 at 25 °C. A coefficient below unity means the aqueous phase holds the acid more strongly than the solvent takes it up, and recovery is reached by staging rather than by a single contact. The design uses 5 countercurrent stages, in which the solvent meets progressively weaker aqueous streams and leaves in contact with the feed. The prediction assumes equilibrium stages: each stage is taken to reach the equilibrium distribution, so the stage count in the calculation is the stage count in the column. The prediction also assumes negligible mutual solubility, with no solvent carried out in the raffinate and no water carried into the extract. Neither assumption has been checked on the actual solvents. A stage that falls short of equilibrium delivers less transfer than the calculation credits to it, and mutual solubility, where it occurs, removes solvent with the raffinate and dilutes the extract, and solvent lost to the raffinate must be recovered downstream or made up, at a cost the present design does not carry. The 93% figure is a design prediction on the stated assumptions, adequate for sizing the column and the solvent circulation; it is not a measured recovery, and a guarantee would need stage-efficiency and solubility data on the solvents as supplied.

subtype: worked example with equation: Ergun pressure drop
fact_base: Gas flows through a packed bed of 1 mm particles. The void fraction $\varepsilon$ is 0.6, the superficial velocity $u$ is 0.41 m s-1 and the bed length is 4 m. The Ergun equation gives a pressure gradient of 1.5 kPa m-1, or 5.9 kPa over the bed. Particle diameter $d_p$ is 1 mm; gas density is 1.2 kg m-3 and viscosity is 1.8 x 10-5 Pa s.
input:
The pressure drop of a gas flowing through a packed bed is a key design quantity for reactors, absorbers and dryers alike, and in this example it is evaluated for a bed of 1 mm particles. The void fraction of the bed, $\varepsilon$, is 0.6, the superficial velocity $u$ of the gas is 0.41 m s-1, and the length of the bed is 4 m. The pressure gradient through the bed is calculated from the celebrated Ergun equation, in which $\Delta P$ is the pressure drop over the bed length $L$, $\mu$ is the gas viscosity, $\varepsilon$ is the void fraction, $d_p$ is the particle diameter, $u$ is the superficial velocity and $\rho$ is the gas density:

$$\frac{\Delta P}{L} = \frac{150 \mu (1-\varepsilon)^2}{\varepsilon^3 d_p^2} u + \frac{1.75 (1-\varepsilon)}{\varepsilon^3 d_p} \rho u^2$$

The particle diameter $d_p$ is 1 mm, the gas density is 1.2 kg m-3 and the gas viscosity is 1.8 x 10-5 Pa s. The equation accordingly gives a pressure gradient of 1.5 kPa m-1, which corresponds to a total pressure drop of 5.9 kPa over the bed as a whole. The structure of the equation is itself instructive, since the first of its two terms captures the viscous resistance that dominates at low velocities, whereas the second term captures the inertial resistance that takes over at higher velocities, so the equation gracefully spans both regimes within a single expression. The result obtained should nevertheless be treated as an estimate, because the equation embodies empirical constants that were established for beds of roughly uniform particles, and real beds, with their distributions of particle size and shape and their inevitable wall effects, may depart from the prediction to a greater or lesser extent in practice.
target:
Calculate the pressure drop of a gas through a packed bed of 1 mm particles. The bed void fraction $\varepsilon$ is 0.6, the superficial velocity $u$ is 0.41 m s-1 and the bed length is 4 m. The pressure gradient is calculated from the Ergun equation

$$\frac{\Delta P}{L} = \frac{150 \mu (1-\varepsilon)^2}{\varepsilon^3 d_p^2} u + \frac{1.75 (1-\varepsilon)}{\varepsilon^3 d_p} \rho u^2$$

where $\Delta P$ is the pressure drop over the bed length $L$, $\mu$ is the gas viscosity, $\varepsilon$ is the void fraction, $d_p$ is the particle diameter, $u$ is the superficial velocity and $\rho$ is the gas density. The particle diameter $d_p$ is 1 mm, the gas density is 1.2 kg m-3 and the gas viscosity is 1.8 x 10-5 Pa s. The equation gives a pressure gradient of 1.5 kPa m-1, or 5.9 kPa over the bed. The two terms divide the resistance by regime: the first term is the viscous contribution, proportional to $u$, and the second is the inertial contribution, proportional to $u$ squared, so a rise in velocity moves the gradient from the first term's proportion towards the second's. The gradient is also sensitive to the void fraction, which enters both terms in combinations that grow sharply as the bed packs tighter: a bed packed tighter than the stated void fraction returns a materially higher gradient at the same velocity, and a gradient measured on the real bed is the check on the packing actually achieved. The constants of the equation were fitted on beds of near-uniform particles, and the stated values are an estimate for a bed of mixed sizes or shapes, or for a bed in which fines have migrated into the voids. Wall effects act in the opposite direction: near the vessel wall the void fraction stands higher and the gas preferentially follows that path, which lowers the measured gradient below the prediction in a narrow bed. Within those limits, the figure sets the blower duty for the bed at the stated conditions, and the duty is revisited if the charge is changed or the velocity is raised.

fact_base: Goal: compute the diffusive flux of oxygen through a stagnant water film. The diffusive flux J (mol m-2 s-1) is computed from the diffusivity D (m2 s-1) and the concentration gradient dC/dx, where C is concentration (mol m-3) and x is position (m). Fick's first law: J = -D dC/dx; the negative sign states that diffusion runs from high concentration to low concentration. Oxygen in water: D = 2.6 x 10-9 m2 s-1. Concentration falls by 0.25 mol m-3 across a film 0.8 mm thick, so dC/dx = -312 mol m-4. Worked result: J = 8.13x 10-7 mol m-2 s-1. The law as stated covers a stagnant medium; a moving medium adds convection, which the equation does not include.
input: When oxygen dissolves in water and has to cross a thin, stagnant layer of liquid, it is important to understand how quickly the molecules actually move through that layer. Fick's first law provides a powerful and widely used framework for describing this process. In essence, the law states that the diffusive flux $J$ (mol m-2 s-1) is proportional to the concentration gradient dC/dx, where $C$ represents the concentration (mol m-3) and $x$ represents the position (m), with the diffusivity $D$ (m2 s-1) acting as the proportionality constant. The relationship is written as $J$ = -$D$ dC/dx, and the negative sign is crucial, because it captures the fact that diffusion naturally proceeds from regions of high concentration towards regions of low concentration. In this particular example, we consider oxygen in water, for which $D$ = 2.6 x 10-9 m2 s-1, moving across a film 0.8 mm thick over which the concentration falls by 0.25 mol m-3. This gives a concentration gradient of dC/dx = -312 mol m-4. Putting these values into the equation gives a diffusive flux of $J$ = 8.13 x 10-7 mol m-2 s-1. Overall, this result highlights how even a very small diffusivity can still produce a finite, measurable flux when the concentration gradient is steep. It is worth noting, however, that Fick's first law as stated here applies to a stagnant medium; in a moving medium, convection also plays a role, and the equation does not include that contribution.
target: Calculate the diffusive flux of oxygen through a stagnant water film. The film is 0.8 mm thick, and the oxygen concentration falls by 0.25 mol m-3 across it. Fick's first law gives the diffusive flux $J$ (mol m-2 s-1) from the diffusivity $D$ (m2 s-1) and the concentration gradient dC/dx, where $C$ denotes concentration (mol m-3) and $x$ denotes position (m). The law is written $J$ = -$D$ dC/dx, and the negative sign states that diffusion runs from high concentration to low concentration. For oxygen in water the diffusivity $D$ is 2.6 x 10-9 m2 s-1. The gradient is taken as uniform across the film, and the concentration change over the film thickness thus gives dC/dx = -312 mol m-4. Substitution of the stated values gives $J$ = 8.13 x 10-7 mol m-2 s-1. The gradient is negative because concentration falls as $x$ increases, and the negative sign in the law cancels it; the flux runs in the positive $x$ direction. The flux is small because the diffusivity of a dissolved gas in water is small, and the steep gradient across the thin film is what produces the stated value. Fick's first law holds for a stagnant medium. A moving medium adds convection, which the equation does not include, and the flux from the law alone is then only the diffusive part of the transfer.

fact_base: Staffing review for a dispatch office: 15 full-time staff, overtime at 14% of paid hours last year. Replacing half the overtime with one additional hire costs $82k per year fully loaded. Overtime is concentrated in two seasonal peaks; a hire is paid for the full year.
input: A staffing review has been carried out for the dispatch office, and this passage summarises the current position and the option under consideration. The office currently operates with 15 full-time staff, and over the course of last year overtime accounted for 14% of paid hours, which represents a substantial and ongoing commitment. One option that has been identified is to replace half of the overtime with one additional hire, and it has been estimated that a hire would cost $82k per year on a fully loaded basis. It is important to note, however, that the overtime is not spread evenly across the year: it is concentrated in two seasonal peaks, whereas a hire is paid for the full year, including the quieter periods in between. This means that the $82k per year cost of the hire is fixed and continuous, while the overtime it would replace is intermittent. At the peaks themselves, it should also be appreciated that only half of the overtime working would be replaced, and the remainder would continue as before, so the peaks would still place considerable demands on the existing team. Overall, the decision is not simply a comparison of costs, and a range of operational factors, including the question of cover outside the peaks and the resilience of the office during busy periods, would also need to be taken into account before any change is made. The review therefore presents the option and the figures behind it, and leaves the decision to be taken once those wider considerations have been worked through.
target: Replace half of the dispatch office overtime with one additional hire. The office manager owns the change. The office ran 15 full-time staff last year, and overtime took 14% of paid hours (payroll record for the year). A hire costs $82k per year fully loaded and replaces half of that overtime. The trade-off stands in one sentence: the hire costs $82k in every week of the year, while the overtime it replaces falls in two seasonal peaks. Outside the peaks the hire is paid at the same rate and the replaced overtime does not arise. At the peaks the change is narrower than the headline suggests: half of the peak overtime is replaced by rostered hours, and the other half of the overtime working at the peaks is untouched. The evidence base is the payroll record for one year. That record shows the hours and their distribution, and the two peaks stand in it as the periods where overtime concentrates; it says nothing about a year in which the peaks move or grow, and a different peak pattern changes the balance of the trade-off. The cost side of the decision is fixed by the figures above. The cover side is not in the figures: outside the peaks the hire is present and rostered, where the present arrangement offers only the overtime that happens to be worked. Next step: the office manager sets the hire against the roster for the two peaks and reports the cover outside the peaks before the decision is taken.

fact_base: Design report for an amine absorber, in four sections: basis, sizing, materials, and risks. Design throughput is 15 t per day and the removal or separation duty is 93% of the key component. Materials are 316L stainless steel for wetted parts; the basis section states this once. The risks section names fouling and turndown as open items; neither is resolved in the report.
input:
Introduction

This report presents the design of an amine absorber and sets out the basis on which the design has been developed, the sizing of the column, the materials selected for construction, and the risks that remain open at this stage. The design throughput is 15 t per day, and the removal duty is 93% of the key component in the feed gas. Wetted parts are specified in 316L stainless steel, and this selection is stated here in the basis so that the later sections can build on it.

Basis

The basis of the design is the starting point for everything that follows, and it is important that it is stated clearly and completely. The throughput and the duty are treated as fixed design values, and the sizing, materials and risks sections all work from these values. Only the design case is carried through the report: no second operating case is developed, and operation away from the design point is considered only where the risks section takes it up. The feed gas is treated as arriving at the absorber in the condition the design assumes, and the solvent is treated as the treating agent that removes the key component from the gas as the two streams pass through the column in contact with each other.

Sizing

The sizing of the absorber proceeds from the basis in a logical sequence. The diameter of the column is governed by the gas traffic at the design throughput, and the vapour velocity inside the column has to be kept comfortably below the point at which the liquid is carried back up the column and the separation breaks down. The height of the column is governed by the separation that the duty demands: the gas and the solvent have to remain in contact for long enough, and over enough transfer surface, for the removal to reach the specified level. The solvent circulation rate is closely linked to both of these, because it determines how much of the key component the solvent can take up as it passes through the column, and it also affects the liquid traffic that the internals have to handle. The pressure drop across the column is checked as part of the sizing, since it has an effect on the duty of the equipment around the absorber. Each of these elements interacts with the others, and the sizing represents a balanced position across all of them rather than the optimisation of any single one. It will be appreciated that the sizing is therefore an exercise in balance, and that changing any one element in isolation would tend to disturb the others.

Materials

The materials selection covers the wetted parts of the absorber, which are the parts that come into contact with the solvent and the process streams: the column shell, the internals, and the solvent pipework. Amine treating service is widely recognised as a demanding environment for materials, because the solvent, the products formed as the solvent degrades in service, and the wet gas itself can all attack materials that would perform perfectly well in other duties. The grade named in the basis has been selected to answer these challenges across the whole wetted envelope, so that no wetted surface is left as a weak point in the system. The welding and fabrication of the wetted parts are expected to preserve the corrosion resistance of the parent material, and the selection assumes that the completed equipment is inspected before it enters service. Parts of the equipment that never come into contact with the process fall outside the selection and are not covered by it.

Risks

Two risks are named in this report, and it should be emphasised that neither of them is resolved here. The first is fouling. Material can be deposited inside the column from several directions: solids entering with the feed gas, products formed as the solvent degrades, and products of corrosion within the system. As deposits build up, they can raise the pressure drop, disturb the distribution of the liquid, and reduce the quality of the contact between the gas and the solvent, so that the removal performance falls away from the design level. The second risk is turndown. The design is developed at a single design point, and the behaviour of the column at rates well below that point is not established: the solvent circulation and the distribution of liquid over the internals both change as the rate falls, and the removal duty cannot simply be assumed to hold. Both items remain open, and they are recorded here so that they are carried forward rather than lost. It is also fair to say that both risks are of a kind that tends to become apparent only in operation, which is precisely why they deserve to be recorded prominently at this stage rather than discovered later.
target:
Basis

This report covers the design of an amine absorber. The design throughput is 15 t per day. The duty is removal of 93% of the key component from the feed gas. Wetted parts are specified in 316L stainless steel; the selection is stated here, and the materials section works from it. The basis fixes the throughput and the duty as design values, and every later section works from these two figures. The design case is the only case sized in the report. Operation away from the design point is not sized; it is taken up as an open item in the risks section. The solvent removes the key component from the gas as the two streams pass through the column in contact. No sensitivity case stands in the basis: the report designs at the stated point, and a design at another throughput or another duty is a separate design.

Sizing

The column diameter is set by the gas traffic at the design throughput. The vapour velocity is held below the flooding limit with a margin, because at flooding the liquid is held up and carried back by the gas and the separation fails. The column height is set by the separation the duty requires: gas and solvent stay in contact over the height, and the removal reaches the specified level only if the contact surface and the contact time suffice. The solvent circulation rate is set by the loading the solvent reaches between its lean and rich ends, and it also fixes the liquid traffic the internals handle. The pressure drop across the column is calculated at the design point and checked against the driving force available from the equipment around the absorber. Diameter, height and circulation are coupled: a change in one moves the others, and the sizing states the position reached for all three together. Liquid distribution is part of the sizing. The solvent enters at the top and is spread over the internals, and the gas enters at the base and rises through it; maldistribution in either stream wastes contact surface, and the separation then falls short of the duty at the same geometry. The sizing proceeds in the standard sequence for an absorber: the traffic fixes the diameter, the separation fixes the height, and the solvent rate is set between them so that the loading stays within what the solvent reaches in this service.

Materials

The materials selection covers the wetted parts of the absorber: the column shell, the internals, and the solvent pipework. These are the surfaces in contact with the solvent and the process streams. Amine service attacks materials by three routes that act together: the solvent itself, the products formed as the solvent degrades in service, and the wet gas. A material that serves in a dry or a solvent-free duty is not evidence of performance here. The grade named in the basis is placed on every wetted surface, so the envelope has no surface of lower resistance. Welding of the wetted parts is specified to preserve the corrosion resistance of the parent material at the joints, and the selection assumes inspection of the completed wetted envelope before the equipment enters service. Parts that never contact the process stand outside the selection. The selection extends to the small wetted items as well as to the shell. Nozzles, distributors and supports see the same solvent and the same gas as the column wall, and a lesser material in a small part sets the corrosion life of the whole envelope.

Risks

Fouling and turndown are open items. Neither is resolved in this report. Fouling is the deposition of material inside the column, and the deposit has three sources in this service: solids entering with the feed gas, products of solvent degradation, and corrosion products from the system itself. A deposit raises the pressure drop, disturbs the distribution of liquid over the internals, and degrades the contact between gas and solvent; removal performance falls as the deposit grows. Turndown is the operation of the column at rates below the design point, and the design does not establish behaviour there. Solvent circulation falls with the gas rate, liquid distribution over the internals weakens, and the removal duty met at the design point is not met by default at the lower rate. The design is silent on both items beyond naming them, and each needs its own treatment before the design is relied on away from the design point or over a long campaign. No fouling allowance stands in the sizing, because no fouling rate for this service is established; a margin added without a rate behind it would be a guess in the form of a number. No turndown ratio is stated either. The lowest rate at which the column still meets the duty is a measured or a calculated quantity, and neither stands in the design as issued.

subtype: worked example with equation: Fourier conduction
fact_base: A flat stainless steel wall has thickness 12 mm and thermal conductivity $k$ of 16 W m-1 K-1. The temperature difference $\Delta T$ across the wall is 411 K, giving a heat flux $q$ of 548000 W m-2. The calculation is steady and one-dimensional; film resistances are excluded.
input:
In this worked example, we consider the conduction of heat through a flat stainless steel wall, which is a classic and instructive application of Fourier's law. The heat flux $q$ (W m-2) through the wall is related to the thermal conductivity $k$ (W m-1 K-1), the temperature difference $\Delta T$ (K) across the wall, and the wall thickness $\Delta x$ (m) by the following equation:

$$q = k \frac{\Delta T}{\Delta x}$$

The wall is flat, which means that the area available for conduction is the same at every depth, unlike the situation in a pipe wall, where the area grows with radius. In this particular case, the wall is made of stainless steel with a thermal conductivity $k$ of 16 W m-1 K-1, the temperature difference $\Delta T$ across the wall is 411 K, and the wall thickness $\Delta x$ is 12 mm, or 0.012 m. Substituting these values into the equation gives a heat flux $q$ of 548000 W m-2. It is worth noting that this calculation is based on a number of simplifying assumptions: it is steady and one-dimensional, and film resistances at the surfaces of the wall are excluded from the analysis. Overall, the result demonstrates the very high heat flux that can arise when a large temperature difference is maintained across a relatively thin metal wall. The example has deliberately been kept as simple as possible so that the working of the law can be followed clearly from beginning to end.
target:
Calculate the heat flux through a flat stainless steel wall. The heat flux $q$ (W m-2) is given by Fourier's law from the thermal conductivity $k$ (W m-1 K-1), the temperature difference $\Delta T$ (K) across the wall, and the wall thickness $\Delta x$ (m):

$$q = k \frac{\Delta T}{\Delta x}$$

Fourier's law states that the flux is proportional to the temperature gradient across the wall: at the same conductivity, a gradient twice as steep gives a flux twice as large. For this wall the thermal conductivity $k$ is 16 W m-1 K-1 and the temperature difference $\Delta T$ is 411 K. The wall thickness $\Delta x$ is 12 mm, or 0.012 m. Substitution of the stated values thus gives a heat flux $q$ of 548000 W m-2. The calculation is steady and one-dimensional. Steady states that the face temperatures are fixed in time, so the flux is the same at every plane through the thickness; one-dimensional states that the temperature varies only through the thickness, with no variation along the faces. Film resistances at the wall surfaces are excluded, and the exclusion has a direction: surface films act in series with the wall, and with them included the same overall temperature difference gives a lower flux. The stated value is therefore the flux for the wall alone, and the flux is large because the gradient is large, a large temperature difference standing across a thin wall. The example is the flat-wall case, in which the area is constant through the thickness; the same law treats a pipe wall in the radial form its geometry requires.

fact_base: Pricing case for a SaaS tier: price $387 per unit, variable cost $209 per unit, fixed costs $304k per year. Break-even volume is 1708 units per year; current volume is 3081 units per year. Volume figures are last year's actuals; the effect of the price on volume is not estimated.
input: This pricing case examines a SaaS tier and asks whether the current price covers the costs of providing the tier. The analysis follows the standard break-even approach, which separates the costs that vary with the number of units sold from the costs that are incurred regardless of volume. The price is $387 per unit, and the variable cost is $209 per unit, which means that each unit sold contributes $178 towards the fixed costs. The fixed costs amount to $304k per year. Dividing the fixed costs by the contribution per unit gives a break-even volume of 1708 units per year. Encouragingly, the current volume, at 3081 units per year, is comfortably above this level, so the tier is covering its fixed costs at the present price, with a considerable cushion before the break-even point would be reached. It should be noted that the volume figures used here are last year's actuals, and they therefore describe the position as it was rather than as it necessarily will be. It is also important to bear in mind that the effect of the price on volume has not been estimated, so it cannot be assumed that the same volume would be achieved at a different price, and the break-even calculation would need to be revisited if the price were to change.
target: The SaaS tier covers its fixed costs at the current price and volume. The price is $387 per unit and the variable cost is $209 per unit, so each unit contributes $178 to fixed costs of $304k per year. Fixed costs divided by the contribution per unit give a break-even volume of 1708 units per year. Current volume is 3081 units per year (last year's actuals), above break-even by a wide margin. The finding rests on last year's volumes at last year's price. Break-even is the volume at which the contribution from the units sold exactly meets the fixed costs for the year. Below that volume the tier returns a loss; above it, each further unit sold adds its contribution to the surplus. The present position is therefore a statement about volume at the stated price, and the width of the margin above break-even is what protects the tier against a fall in volume. A fall in volume at the stated price erodes the surplus unit by unit at the contribution rate. The effect of the price on volume is not estimated, and the break-even figure is not valid at a different price: at a lower price the contribution per unit falls and the break-even volume rises, by an amount the case does not quantify. The case likewise does not estimate the volume at the current price beyond last year's actual, so the margin is a record of last year, not a forecast.

fact_base: Performance of a natural-draft tower at a chemical site was logged over one summer month. Mean wet-bulb temperature was 22 °C, the approach was 3 K and the range was 6 K. Performance outside the logged month, in particular at winter wet-bulb temperatures, was not measured.
input: The performance of a natural-draft cooling tower at a chemical site was logged over the course of one summer month, and this passage summarises the principal findings. During the logged period, the mean wet-bulb temperature was 22 °C, the approach was 3 K, and the range was 6 K. The approach, which is the difference between the temperature of the cooled water leaving the tower and the wet-bulb temperature of the air, is a particularly important indicator, because it shows how close the tower is operating to the theoretical limit set by the wet-bulb temperature. The range, which is the difference between the temperatures of the water entering and leaving the tower, reflects the heat load that the tower is handling. An approach of 3 K against a mean wet-bulb temperature of 22 °C indicates that the tower was operating close to the limit imposed by the air conditions during the period in question. A natural-draft tower relies on the buoyancy of the warmed air inside the tower to draw fresh air in at the base, rather than on a fan, and its performance is therefore closely tied to the state of the air and to the condition of the fill over which the water is distributed. Taken together, these figures provide a useful picture of the tower's performance under summer conditions. It is worth noting, however, that performance outside the logged month was not measured, and in particular no measurements are available at winter wet-bulb temperatures, so the figures should not be taken as representative of the whole year, and any judgement about how the tower behaves across the full range of seasons would have to rest on measurements that have not been taken.
target: Performance of a natural-draft cooling tower at a chemical site was logged over one summer month. The mean wet-bulb temperature over the month was 22 °C. The approach was 3 K and the range was 6 K. The approach is the difference between the cooled-water outlet temperature and the wet-bulb temperature; it states how close the tower runs to the limit the wet bulb sets, because no cooling tower cools water below the wet-bulb temperature of the entering air. The range is the difference between the hot-water inlet temperature and the cooled-water outlet temperature; it states the temperature fall the tower gives the circulating water under the heat load of the logged month. An approach of 3 K at a mean wet bulb of 22 °C places the cooled water close to the entering-air limit for that month, and the tower held that approach across the month as logged. A natural-draft tower moves air by buoyancy: air warmed inside the tower rises, and fresh air enters at the base without a fan. The approach therefore depends on the fill, on the distribution of water over the fill, and on the air state, and a change in any of these moves it. The range is set on the water side, by the heat load the process sends to the tower and the rate at which the water circulates. The two figures answer different questions, and neither substitutes for the other. The values are means and period figures for the month; the record as summarised does not state the variation within the month, and no daily or peak figure is given. The figures describe the logged month only. Performance outside the month was not measured, in particular at winter wet-bulb temperatures, and the approach and range at winter wet-bulb temperatures are not established by this record.

fact_base: A tutorial passage explains absolute and relative error through a pressure measurement. Worked figures: reading 230 units, tolerance 0.5% of reading, so the absolute error is 1.15 units. The passage distinguishes error from uncertainty and does not merge the two terms.
input: In this tutorial, we will explore two closely related ideas that are fundamental to making good measurements: absolute error and relative error. We will work through them using a pressure measurement as our example. Suppose that an instrument gives a reading of 230 units, and suppose that the instrument has a tolerance of 0.5% of reading. The absolute error is the size of the error expressed in the units of the measurement itself, and in this case it is worked out as 230 x 0.5 / 100, which gives an absolute error of 1.15 units. The relative error, by contrast, expresses the same error as a fraction or percentage of the reading, which makes it much easier to compare errors across instruments of different sizes. It is also very important to distinguish error from uncertainty. Although the two terms are often used interchangeably in everyday language, they do not mean the same thing: the error is the difference between a measured value and the true value, whereas the uncertainty is an expression of the doubt that remains about the result. Keeping these ideas separate will help you to interpret measurements correctly and to avoid overstating what an instrument can actually tell you. An absolute error of 1.15 units is a statement about the reading in hand, and it should be reported alongside the reading rather than left for the reader to reconstruct from a percentage. With practice, stating both forms becomes routine, and the distinction between them, and between error and uncertainty, stops needing to be thought about at all.
target: This tutorial explains absolute and relative error through a pressure measurement, and keeps error separate from uncertainty. Work through the example and you will be able to state the error on a reading in units and as a percentage of the reading. Take a reading of 230 units from an instrument with a tolerance of 0.5% of reading. The absolute error is the error stated in the units of the measurement. It is calculated as 230 x 0.5 / 100, which gives 1.15 units. The reading therefore stands within 1.15 units of the value it reports, at the stated tolerance. The relative error is the same error divided by the reading, stated as a fraction or a percentage; it carries no units, and it is the form that compares across instruments of different sizes. Error and uncertainty are different terms and are not merged here. Error is a difference: the measured value minus the true value, or the bound the tolerance places on that difference. Uncertainty is the doubt that remains about the result after the measurement is made. A reading with a small stated error can still carry a large uncertainty when the conditions of the measurement are poorly known, and the two statements answer different questions. Uncertainty gathers every source of doubt about the result, the tolerance of the instrument among them, and it is expressed as an interval around the result rather than as a single difference. The tolerance in this example is stated as a percentage of the reading, and the basis matters: a percentage of the reading grows with the reading, where a percentage of full scale would not. Which form of the error to report depends on the use made of the reading. State the absolute error where the reading is checked against a limit expressed in units, and the relative error where readings from instruments of different sizes are compared. Report the error with the reading itself; a reading reported without its error claims more than the instrument establishes.

subtype: worked example with equation: first-order decay
fact_base: A drug in solution decomposes by first-order kinetics with rate constant $k$ = 0.151 min-1. After 55 min the fraction remaining $C / C_0$ is 0. The rate constant was measured at one temperature; no activation energy is available.
input:
In this example, we consider a drug in solution that gradually decomposes over time, and we ask how much of the drug is left after a given period. Questions of this kind arise whenever a substance is stored or held in solution and its strength matters, because the amount remaining, rather than the amount originally present, is what determines whether the solution is still fit for its purpose. The decomposition follows first-order kinetics, which means that the rate at which the drug disappears is proportional to the amount that is still present. A direct consequence of this behaviour is that the concentration falls by the same fraction in each equal interval of time, which is the characteristic pattern of a first-order process and the reason the process can be described by a single rate constant. The concentration $C$ at time $t$ is related to the initial concentration $C_0$ and the rate constant $k$ by the integrated first-order rate law:

$$\ln\frac{C}{C_0} = -k t$$

The rate constant $k$ for this drug is 0.151 min-1. We are interested in the fraction of the drug that remains after 55 min. Substituting the values into the equation, the fraction remaining $C/C_0$ works out to be 0, which indicates that, for practical purposes, the decomposition is essentially complete by this time. The result is a statement about the fraction, rather than about the concentration itself, and because the initial concentration cancels in the ratio, the same fraction would be obtained whatever the starting concentration had been. It is worth noting that the rate constant was measured at one temperature only, and no activation energy is available, so the result cannot readily be extended to other temperatures, where the decomposition would proceed at a different, and here unknown, rate.
target:
Calculate the fraction of a drug remaining in solution after 55 min. The drug decomposes by first-order kinetics: the rate of decomposition is proportional to the concentration still present. The concentration therefore falls by the same fraction in each equal interval of time, and a single rate constant describes the whole course of the decomposition. The fraction is the quantity asked for, because it is independent of the starting concentration: the initial concentration cancels in the ratio, and the same fraction holds whatever concentration the solution started at. The concentration $C$ at time $t$, the initial concentration $C_0$, and the rate constant $k$ are related by the integrated first-order rate law:

$$\ln\frac{C}{C_0} = -k t$$

The rate constant $k$ is 0.151 min-1. Substitution of the stated time and rate constant gives the fraction remaining, $C/C_0$, as 0 at the precision of the stated value. The fraction falls exponentially, and at the stated time the exponential term has decayed below the precision at which the fraction is reported; the drug is fully decomposed at that precision. A reported fraction of zero is a rounding statement, not a claim that no molecule survives: it states that the fraction is smaller than the last place to which it is reported. The relation itself behaves as it must at the start of the interval, returning the fraction as one at zero time and falling monotonically from there. The result holds at the temperature of the measurement. The rate constant was measured at one temperature and no activation energy is available, so the fraction at any other temperature is not given by this calculation, and the decomposition there is slower or faster by an amount this example does not determine. A rate constant measured across a range of temperatures, with an activation energy fitted to it, is what a calculation at another temperature would need.

fact_base: A tutorial passage explains the Sherwood number to second-year students. Definition in words: the Sherwood number is the ratio of convective to diffusive mass transfer at a surface. The passage must state what a value near 1 means and what a large value means, without inventing numerical examples.
input: The Sherwood number is one of the most important dimensionless groups in the whole of mass transfer, and a proper understanding of it is essential for any student of the subject. In simple terms, the Sherwood number can be thought of as the ratio of convective to diffusive mass transfer at a surface. In other words, it compares the rate at which a species is carried to or away from a surface by the movement of the fluid as a whole with the rate at which the same species would move by molecular diffusion alone. A value near 1 tells us that the two mechanisms are of comparable importance, so that the movement of the fluid adds very little to what diffusion would achieve on its own. At the other extreme, a large value tells us that convection dominates the transfer, and diffusion plays only a minor role, confined to a thin layer of fluid immediately next to the surface. The Sherwood number therefore provides a compact and convenient way of capturing the balance between these two fundamental mechanisms, and it plays a central role in the correlations that are used to predict mass-transfer coefficients in practice. Because the number is dimensionless, it allows results obtained under one set of conditions to be compared with results obtained under quite different conditions, and this is a large part of its appeal. Anything that strengthens the movement of the fluid relative to the movement of molecules will tend to push the value upwards, while anything that stills the fluid will bring it back down towards the diffusive case. It is, in short, a measure of which mechanism is in charge at the surface, and it should be read in that spirit whenever it is met.
target: The Sherwood number is a dimensionless group in mass transfer. It is defined as the ratio of convective to diffusive mass transfer at a surface: the rate at which the fluid motion delivers a species to the surface, or removes it, divided by the rate at which molecular diffusion alone moves the same species over the same length. A value near 1 means the two rates are comparable. Convection then adds little to diffusion, and the transfer at the surface is set by the diffusive step, as in a nearly stagnant fluid. A large value means convection is the larger rate by far. Diffusion is then confined to a thin layer of fluid at the surface, across which the concentration changes, and the resistance to transfer sits in that layer. Between the two cases the balance shifts continuously: as the fluid motion strengthens, the diffusive layer thins and the convective share of the transfer grows. Both rates in the ratio refer to the same surface and to the same driving difference in concentration. The group compares mechanisms, not sizes, and it has no units; two surfaces of different size in the same flow regime share the reading of the group even where their transfer rates differ. Anything that strengthens the fluid motion relative to molecular movement raises the group, and anything that stills the fluid lowers it towards the diffusive case. The group is used in correlations for the mass-transfer coefficient, where its value is stated as a function of the flow and the fluid properties; the definition above is what every such correlation reports, a comparison of the two transfer rates at the surface. Read the group as a comparison before reading it as a number: it states which mechanism sets the pace at the surface, and the correlations built on it inherit that reading.

fact_base: Energy assessment of a dairy plant, in four sections: current use, refrigeration, steam, and recommendation. Electricity use is 2854 MWh per year; refrigeration takes the largest share. A heat-recovery retrofit is projected to save 19% of electricity use, a derived saving of 542 MWh per year, at a capital cost of $286k. At $0.12 per kWh the derived annual saving is $65071 and the derived simple payback is 4.4 years. Steam figures are from one winter month and are flagged as seasonal in the recommendation.
input:
This report presents an energy assessment of a dairy plant, covering the current use of energy at the site, the refrigeration system, the steam system, and a recommendation arising from the assessment. The assessment has been carried out on the basis of the records available at the site, and its findings are set out in the sections that follow, taken in turn.

Current use

Electricity is the principal energy stream covered by this assessment, and the site currently uses 2854 MWh of electricity per year. The assessment has examined how this electricity is used across the plant, and refrigeration accounts for the largest share of the total. The remainder is spread across the processing operations, the cleaning of the plant, and the general services that support production, and no single one of these approaches the refrigeration share. The pattern of use follows the pattern of production, and the refrigeration load is present whenever product is being handled or held at temperature, which at this site is effectively continuous. It is also worth observing that the demand for refrigeration does not switch off when production pauses, since product that has been made still has to be held at temperature, and this gives the site a substantial baseline of consumption that continues around the clock, in quiet periods as well as in busy ones.

Refrigeration

Refrigeration is the largest single use of electricity at the plant, and it is therefore the natural focus of the assessment. The refrigeration system holds the product and the cold stores at temperature, and in doing so it rejects heat at its condensers. This rejected heat is currently lost to the surroundings, even though the plant also has a substantial demand for heated water for processing and for cleaning. Recovering the heat that the refrigeration system rejects, and putting it to work where heated water is needed, is the opportunity that the assessment identifies. The heat is available whenever the refrigeration plant is running, which matches well with the continuous character of the site's demand for hot water, although the detailed matching of the two has not been examined at this stage. The opportunity is, in a sense, a matter of putting two existing features of the plant together: a system that is continuously rejecting heat, and a set of duties that are continuously asking for it. Schemes of this general kind are well established in the food industry, where large refrigeration plants and a constant demand for hot water are so often found side by side on the same site.

Steam

Steam serves the heating duties of the plant, including the heat treatment of the product and the cleaning of the equipment. It should be noted that the steam figures available to this assessment are drawn from one winter month only. Winter is a period of high heating demand, and a single winter month cannot be taken as representative of the year as a whole. For that reason, the steam figures are reported here as they stand for that month, and they have not been extended or annualised in any way. Any conclusion that depends on steam use over a full year would need figures from a longer period, and the recommendation below is framed with that limitation in mind. None of this means that the steam figures are of no use: they describe the month they cover, and they are the best information available for that month. It does mean, however, that they have to be handled with care, and that any attempt to build a picture of the whole year upon them would risk seriously misleading the reader.

Recommendation

It is recommended that a heat-recovery retrofit be installed on the refrigeration system, and the site engineering manager would own the retrofit. The retrofit is projected to save 19% of electricity use, which corresponds to a derived saving of 542 MWh per year. The capital cost of the retrofit is $286k. At an electricity price of $0.12 per kWh, the derived annual saving is $65071, and the derived simple payback on the investment is 4.4 years. Overall, the assessment considers this to be an attractive opportunity, since the largest use of electricity on the site is also the source of the recovered heat. It is nevertheless important to remember that the steam figures behind parts of the assessment are seasonal, being drawn from one winter month, and this flag should be kept in mind when the recommendation is considered. The payback quoted is a simple payback, and it takes no account of the timing of the savings beyond the year in which they arise, which is the conventional treatment at the assessment stage and is appropriate to a decision of this size.
target:
A heat-recovery retrofit on the refrigeration system is recommended. The site engineering manager owns the retrofit.

Current use

The site uses 2854 MWh of electricity per year. Refrigeration takes the largest share of that use. The remaining electricity serves the processing operations, the cleaning of the plant, and the general services that support production; no one of these approaches the refrigeration share. Use follows production, and the refrigeration load runs whenever product is handled or held at temperature, which at this site is effectively continuous. The assessment works from the electricity record for the year; it does not re-measure the individual loads, and the split of the remainder between the smaller uses is stated qualitatively because the record supports the ranking, not a finer division. The year's figure is a total, and the assessment takes it as the base for the recommendation. Loads that run with production rise and fall with the production rate; the holding load does not, and the holding load is what keeps the baseline of use high between campaigns and outside production hours. Electricity is also the stream on which a change shows soonest: it is metered for the site as a whole, and a change in it is visible in the record without a special measurement campaign.

Refrigeration

Refrigeration is the largest use because the plant holds product and cold stores at temperature without interruption. The system rejects heat at its condensers, and that heat is currently lost to the surroundings. The plant also heats water for processing and for cleaning, and the demand for heated water runs across the same hours as the refrigeration load. The retrofit recovers heat from the condenser side of the refrigeration system and delivers it to the water-heating duties. The source and the demand are both continuous, and the recovery does not depend on storage to bridge a gap between them. The detailed matching of the recovered heat to each water-heating duty is design work; the assessment establishes the size of the source and the existence of the demand, and the recommendation is sized on the electricity the refrigeration system uses. The retrofit is an exchanger and a circulating loop on the condenser side. The refrigeration system itself is unchanged and continues to do its own duty; the retrofit takes heat the condensers reject in any case. The condenser heat is low-grade heat, and its value depends on the temperature the water-heating duties accept: duties that take warm water absorb more of it than duties that need the highest temperatures. The assessment does not grade the duties, and the grading belongs to the design stage named in the recommendation.

Steam

Steam serves the heating duties of the plant, including the heat treatment of the product and the cleaning of the equipment. The steam figures available to the assessment come from one winter month. A winter month is a high-demand month for heating, and it does not represent the year. The figures are therefore reported as they stand for that month and are not extended to a yearly figure anywhere in this assessment. No part of the recommendation is sized on the steam figures, and a decision that turned on yearly steam use would need a longer record before it could be taken. The flag is a limit on the use of the figures, not a defect in them: for the month they describe, they are the record of what the plant used. A full year of steam figures, set beside the production record for the same year, is what an annual steam balance would need, and collecting that year is a matter of time rather than of new instrumentation.

Recommendation

Install the heat-recovery retrofit on the refrigeration system. The site engineering manager owns the retrofit. The retrofit is projected to save 19% of electricity use, a derived saving of 542 MWh per year. The capital cost is $286k. At $0.12 per kWh the derived annual saving is $65071, and the derived simple payback is 4.4 years. The payback rests on the electricity record for the year and on the projected saving; the saving is a projection, not a measured result, and the first year of operation is the test of it. The steam figures behind the wider assessment are seasonal, drawn from one winter month, and that flag stands on the recommendation as it does on the steam section. The projection is stated on electricity alone. Any effect of the retrofit on steam use stands outside the payback as calculated, in either direction, because the steam record does not support a yearly figure against which to state it. A reader who took the steam figures as yearly figures would misjudge the balance of the plant, and the flag is repeated at the decision point to prevent exactly that reading of them. Next step: the site engineering manager takes the retrofit to detailed design, where the matching of recovered heat to the water-heating duties is fixed.

subtype: worked example with equation: available NPSH
fact_base: A pump draws water from an open tank at atmospheric pressure, 101.3 kPa. Vapour pressure at the pumping temperature is 19.9 kPa, the static lift is 3.5 m and suction-line friction loss is 0.4 m. Available net positive suction head $NPSH_a$ is 4.4 m. The pump's required NPSH at the duty flow comes from the vendor curve and must be exceeded with margin.
input:
In this worked example, we determine the available net positive suction head for a pump that draws water from an open tank. The available net positive suction head $NPSH_a$ is calculated from the atmospheric pressure $P_{atm}$, the vapour pressure $P_v$, the density $\rho$ and gravitational acceleration $g$, the static lift $h_{lift}$, and the suction-line friction loss $h_f$, using the following equation:

$$NPSH_a = \frac{P_{atm} - P_v}{\rho g} - h_{lift} - h_f$$

The tank is open, so the pressure at the surface is atmospheric pressure, 101.3 kPa. The vapour pressure of the water at the pumping temperature is 19.9 kPa, the static lift is 3.5 m, and the friction loss in the suction line is 0.4 m. The difference between the atmospheric pressure and the vapour pressure is 101.3 - 19.9 = 81.4 kPa, and dividing this pressure difference by the specific weight of water, 9.79 kN per cubic metre, gives a pressure head of 81.4 / 9.79 = 8.3 m. Subtracting the static lift and the friction loss, in the form 8.3 - 3.5 - 0.4, then gives an available net positive suction head of 4.4 m. The example is a standard one in pump practice, because a pump that is starved at the suction will cavitate, with noise, vibration and damage to the impeller, and the available head is the first check on that risk. It is important to note that this available value of 4.4 m has to be compared with the pump's required net positive suction head at the duty flow, which is obtained from the vendor curve, and the available value must exceed the required value with a suitable margin if cavitation is to be avoided.
target:
Calculate the available net positive suction head for a pump drawing water from an open tank. The available net positive suction head $NPSH_a$ is determined from the atmospheric pressure $P_{atm}$, the vapour pressure $P_v$, the density $\rho$, the gravitational acceleration $g$, the static lift $h_{lift}$, and the suction-line friction loss $h_f$:

$$NPSH_a = \frac{P_{atm} - P_v}{\rho g} - h_{lift} - h_f$$

The tank is open, and the pressure at its surface is atmospheric pressure, 101.3 kPa. The vapour pressure at the pumping temperature is 19.9 kPa, the static lift is 3.5 m, and the suction-line friction loss is 0.4 m. The pressure margin above vapour pressure is 101.3 - 19.9 = 81.4 kPa. Division by the specific weight of water, 9.79 kN per cubic metre, thus gives a pressure head of 81.4 / 9.79 = 8.3 m. Subtraction of the static lift and the friction loss then gives $NPSH_a$ = 8.3 - 3.5 - 0.4 = 4.4 m. The available head is 4.4 m at the stated conditions. The check on the result is a comparison the example does not close: the pump's required net positive suction head at the duty flow comes from the vendor curve, and the available head must exceed the required head with margin. Until that comparison is made, the figure states what the suction side offers, not that the pump is safe from cavitation. Cavitation is the failure the comparison guards against: where the pressure at the impeller inlet falls to the vapour pressure of the liquid, vapour cavities form and then collapse as the pressure recovers, and the collapse erodes the impeller and shakes the pump. The margin in the comparison absorbs the differences between the stated conditions and the conditions on a given day: the level in the tank, the temperature of the water, which moves the vapour pressure, and the state of the suction line, which moves the friction loss. A figure calculated at one set of conditions is therefore read with the least favourable of those variations in mind.

fact_base: Capital appraisal for a warehouse extension: installed cost $784k, expected net saving $158k per year for 8 years. At a discount rate of 8% the present value of the savings is $908k and the net present value is $124k. Savings are vendor and utility estimates; no saving has yet been measured on a comparable installation.
input: This passage presents a capital appraisal for a proposed warehouse extension. The appraisal follows the standard discounted cash flow approach, in which the savings expected in future years are discounted back to their value at the present day, so that they can be compared fairly with a cost that is incurred at the outset. The extension itself is an enlargement of the existing warehouse, and the savings arise from the additional capacity it provides. The installed cost of the extension is $784k, and it is expected to generate a net saving of $158k per year over a period of 8 years. Discounting these savings at a discount rate of 8% gives a present value of the savings of $908k. Subtracting the installed cost from the present value of the savings gives a net present value of $124k, which is positive and therefore indicates that the extension is financially worthwhile on the figures presented. It should nevertheless be noted that the savings are estimates provided by the vendor and the utility, and no saving has yet been measured on a comparable installation, so a considerable degree of uncertainty attaches to the figures and the appraisal should be read with that in mind. The $124k is, in other words, the surplus of the estimated savings over the estimated cost once the timing of both has been taken into account, and it is on that basis that the proposal is put forward for consideration by those responsible for the decision.
target: The warehouse extension has a positive net present value of $124k at the stated figures. The installed cost is $784k, and the expected net saving is $158k per year for 8 years. At a discount rate of 8% the present value of the savings is $908k, and the net present value is the present value less the installed cost, $124k. Discounting converts each year's saving to its value at the decision date, so that money arriving later counts for less than money in hand; the net present value is what remains when the installed cost, paid at the start, is set against that discounted stream. A positive value at the stated discount rate means that the savings repay the cost with the required return to spare, on the estimates. The result does not rank the extension against other uses of the same capital, and it says nothing about the savings being achieved in practice. The installed cost is the firmer side of the comparison, a figure that a contract will fix before the saving begins. The result is most exposed to the yearly saving, which is an estimate throughout the life, and to the length of the life itself: a shorter life removes whole years of saving from the discounted stream, and the margin is the first casualty of either change. The finding is a comparison of two estimates. The savings are vendor and utility estimates, and no saving has yet been measured on a comparable installation. The margin is therefore the gap between the estimates as stated, not a measured return: a shortfall in the yearly saving falls directly on the net present value, and the appraisal gives no measured installation from which to bound that shortfall.

fact_base: The rate constant k (s-1) of a first-order liquid-phase reaction was measured at two temperatures. At 300 K, k = 0.084 s-1. At 340 K, k = 2.176 s-1, computed from the Arrhenius relation with activation energy 69 kJ mol-1 as a derived value. Each temperature was measured in triplicate; the relative standard deviation of k was 4%. Above 340 K the solvent evaporated during sampling, so no rate constant is reported above 340 K.
input: Rate constants for a first-order liquid-phase reaction were measured at two temperatures. The rate constant $k$ was 0.084 s-1 at 300 K and 2.176 s-1 at 340 K. Each temperature was measured in triplicate, and the relative standard deviation of $k$ was 4% at each temperature. The value at 340 K is a derived value, computed from the Arrhenius relation with an activation energy of 69 kJ mol-1. The measured value at 300 K is the anchor for that computation: the Arrhenius relation carries $k$ from the measured temperature to the higher temperature at the stated activation energy. Between 300 K and 340 K, $k$ increases by a factor of 25.9 over an interval of 40 K, a steep temperature dependence for a liquid-phase reaction. The scatter of the triplicate measurements is small against that change: a relative standard deviation of 4% leaves the increase between the two temperatures far outside the range that measurement noise could produce. No rate constant is reported above 340 K. Above 340 K the solvent evaporated during sampling, and samples drawn at higher temperatures no longer represented the reacting liquid, so measurements above that temperature were not used. The reported values therefore cover the full range in which sampling kept the liquid intact. Any rate constant quoted above 340 K for this system would rest on samples whose composition had already changed during collection. Within the measured range, the pair of values gives the temperature sensitivity of the reaction on a stated basis: one measured rate constant, one rate constant derived from it through the Arrhenius relation, and a precision of 4% attaching to the measurements at both temperatures. Sampling at each temperature followed the same procedure, so the two values are comparable on one basis, and the comparison between them does not mix two sampling methods.
