fact_base: 260 pumps run at the plant. Maintenance records for 12 months show 928 h of unplanned downtime; bearing failures account for 39% of the downtime hours. A sensor set for all 260 pumps is quoted at $439k installed, plus $58k per year. In a vendor trial on a comparable unit, the sensors cut downtime by 22%; the figure is a vendor figure and was not measured at this plant. A pilot on 20 pumps costs $37k over three months. Spare-part lead times are unchanged by the sensors. The memo recommends the three-month pilot; the reliability engineering group owns the pilot and reports before the March capital review; the decision on full installation is held until the pilot results are reported.
input: This memo provides a recommendation in relation to the proposed deployment of condition-monitoring sensors across the plant's pump fleet, with a view to reducing unplanned downtime and improving overall maintenance performance going forward. The plant currently operates 260 pumps, and a review of the maintenance records covering the last 12 months shows a total of 928 h of unplanned downtime, with bearing failures accounting for 39% of the downtime hours. A sensor set covering all 260 pumps has been quoted at $439k installed, together with a recurring cost of $58k per year. In a vendor trial carried out on a comparable unit, the sensors were able to cut downtime by 22%, although it should be noted that this figure is a vendor figure and was not measured at this plant. Rather than proceeding directly to a full installation, it is recommended that a pilot be conducted on 20 pumps at a cost of $37k over a period of three months. The reliability engineering group owns the pilot and will report before the March capital review, and the decision on full installation is held until the pilot results are reported. It is also worth noting that spare-part lead times are unchanged by the sensors, so this aspect of maintenance performance would not be expected to change as a result of the project. Overall, the pilot represents a measured, low-risk step that will generate plant-specific evidence in support of the subsequent investment decision, helping to ensure that any future commitment of capital is based on robust, locally validated data rather than on vendor claims alone. By taking this staged approach, the plant can leverage the available evidence while minimising exposure, and the findings of the pilot will inform the wider reliability strategy in due course.
target:
The reliability engineering group recommends a three-month pilot of condition sensors on 20 pumps, at a cost of $37k, before any decision on full installation. The group owns the pilot and reports before the March capital review; the decision on full installation is held until the pilot results are reported.

The plant runs 260 pumps. Maintenance records for 12 months show 928 h of unplanned downtime, and bearing failures account for 39% of the downtime hours. The downtime is concentrated in one failure mode, and bearing condition is what a sensor set monitors, so the proposed measure addresses the largest recorded source of lost hours directly. A sensor set for all 260 pumps is quoted at $439k installed, plus $58k per year. In a vendor trial on a comparable unit, the sensors cut downtime by 22%. That figure is a vendor figure and was not measured at this plant; no reduction measured on this plant's pumps exists yet. Spare-part lead times are unchanged by the sensors, so the case for installation rests on downtime alone and on nothing else the sensors might improve.

The pilot is the step that replaces the vendor figure with plant data. Twenty pumps under monitoring for three months give the reliability engineering group a measured reduction, or the absence of one, on the equipment the full installation would cover. The March capital review then decides on full installation with the pilot results in front of it, rather than on a trial run elsewhere. The pilot also bounds the exposure: the expenditure under test is the pilot cost, and the larger commitment is made only after the plant has its own downtime figures for monitored and unmonitored pumps working side by side.

fact_base: A continuous stirred-tank reactor runs a neutralisation that is first order in the limiting reactant. The rate constant is 0.241 min-1 at the operating temperature and the mean residence time is 28 min. Steady-state conversion for an ideal CSTR is 87.1%. The estimate assumes perfect mixing and constant density; tracer tests on the actual vessel have not been run.
input: In this worked example, we consider a continuous stirred-tank reactor in which a neutralisation reaction is carried out, with the reaction being first order in the limiting reactant. At the operating temperature of the reactor, the rate constant is 0.241 min-1, and the mean residence time of the material in the vessel is 28 min. By applying the well-known steady-state design equation for an ideal CSTR, the conversion of the limiting reactant can be estimated at 87.1%. It is important to note that this estimate rests on a number of underlying assumptions, most notably the assumption of perfect mixing throughout the vessel and the assumption of constant density. In practice, it should also be borne in mind that tracer tests on the actual vessel have not been run, which means that the true residence time distribution may well deviate from the ideal behaviour that has been assumed here. As a result, the conversion of 87.1% should be regarded as an idealised estimate rather than a guaranteed operating value. This type of calculation is widely used as a first estimate in reactor design, as it provides a rapid indication of the level of performance that can be expected before more detailed modelling is undertaken. Nevertheless, the simplicity of the approach should not be allowed to obscure the fact that real vessels rarely behave in a perfectly ideal fashion, and dead zones, bypassing, and other departures from ideal mixing can all have an impact on the conversion that is actually achieved in practice.
target: A continuous stirred-tank reactor runs a neutralisation that is first order in the limiting reactant. The rate constant is 0.241 min-1 at the operating temperature, and the mean residence time is 28 min. The worked example asks for the steady-state conversion of the limiting reactant in an ideal CSTR. For a first-order reaction in a perfectly mixed vessel, conversion is fixed by the rate constant and the residence time together: a longer residence time or a faster reaction converts more, and the two quantities enter as a product. On the stated values, the conversion is 87.1%. The estimate assumes perfect mixing and constant density. Perfect mixing is the assumption that carries the number. It makes the concentration uniform through the vessel and equal to the concentration in the outlet stream, so the whole vessel volume reacts at the outlet concentration, the lowest in the system. Constant density keeps the mean residence time a property of the vessel volume and the flow alone. Tracer tests on the actual vessel have not been run. The residence time distribution of the real vessel is therefore unmeasured: dead volume would shorten the effective residence time, and bypassing would let part of the feed leave unreacted, and either would put the conversion of the actual vessel below 87.1%. The neutralisation is fast enough, on these values, that conversion is high but not complete: the unconverted fraction leaves with the product stream and is set by the same two quantities. The figure is the ideal-CSTR conversion for the stated rate constant and residence time, and it is the reference value a tracer test on the vessel would be read against.

fact_base: Cost review of a returns flow: 285 km per trip at $2.07 per km, 889 trips per year. Annual transport cost is $524k. Costs are carrier invoices for the last 12 months; empty running is included in the trip count.
input: This cost review examines the transport costs associated with the returns flow over the course of the last 12 months, drawing on carrier invoices as its primary source of data. In total, the returns flow involves some 889 trips per year, with each trip covering 285 km per trip at a rate of $2.07 per km, giving rise to an annual transport cost of $524k. It is worth noting that the figures used in this review are taken directly from carrier invoices, which means that the cost presented here reflects the amounts actually charged rather than a modelled estimate. Furthermore, empty running is included in the trip count, so the trips that have been counted encompass both loaded journeys and empty journeys, and the cost of empty running is therefore embedded within the overall figure. This has important implications for interpretation, since it means that the contribution of empty running cannot readily be isolated from the total on the basis of the invoice data alone. Going forward, a range of potential opportunities could in principle be explored in order to reduce this cost, including the consolidation of trips, the optimisation of routes and distances, and the renegotiation of rates with carriers. However, any such initiative would need to be evaluated carefully against the established baseline. In summary, the annual transport cost of the returns flow currently stands at $524k, and this figure provides the reference point against which the impact of any future cost-reduction measures can be assessed in a consistent and transparent manner.
target:
Annual transport cost for the returns flow is $524k. The cost is built from 889 trips per year, at 285 km per trip and $2.07 per km. The figures are carrier invoices for the last 12 months, so the total is invoiced cost over a full year, not an estimate assembled from a rate card and a distance table. Empty running is included in the trip count. The trips the carrier charged for are the trips counted, loaded and empty together, so the cost of running empty is inside the total and cannot be separated from it on this evidence. A saving from reduced empty running would have to be measured from trip records, which this review does not use.

Three quantities set the cost: the number of trips, the distance per trip, and the rate per km. The invoices fix all three for the year reviewed. A lower annual cost follows from fewer trips, shorter trips, or a lower rate, and a change in any one of them changes the total in proportion, at the values stated. The returns flow itself sets the pattern behind the trip count: goods come back from customers in the quantities and at the times customers return them, and the collection pattern follows that flow rather than a schedule the carrier chooses. Consolidation of returns into fewer, fuller trips is the lever that acts on the trip count, and depot location is the lever that acts on distance. The review makes no judgement between those routes; it establishes the baseline. On the present trip pattern and the present rate, the returns flow costs $524k per year, and any proposal to reduce the cost can be read against that figure and against the three quantities that compose it.

subtype: worked example with equation: log-mean difference
fact_base: A countercurrent exchanger cools a process stream from 120 °C to 85 °C with water entering at 30 °C and leaving at 55 °C. The terminal differences are 65 K and 55 K, and the log-mean temperature difference $\Delta T_{lm}$ is 59.9 K. The log-mean value assumes constant overall coefficient and no phase change.
input:
In this example, we consider a countercurrent heat exchanger in which a process stream is cooled from 120 °C to 85 °C by means of cooling water, which enters the exchanger at 30 °C and leaves at 55 °C. In order to characterise the temperature driving force within the exchanger, it is necessary to evaluate the temperature differences at the two ends of the unit. At the end where the hot stream enters, the temperature difference is 120 − 55 = 65 K, whilst at the end where the hot stream leaves, the difference is 85 − 30 = 55 K. The appropriate mean temperature difference for this situation is the log-mean temperature difference, $\Delta T_{lm}$, which is related to the two terminal differences, $\Delta T_1$ and $\Delta T_2$, by the following well-known expression:

$$\Delta T_{lm} = \frac{\Delta T_1 - \Delta T_2}{\ln(\Delta T_1 / \Delta T_2)}$$

Substituting $\Delta T_1$ = 65 K and $\Delta T_2$ = 55 K into this expression, the log-mean temperature difference $\Delta T_{lm}$ is found to be 59.9 K. It is important to note that this log-mean value is based on the assumptions of a constant overall heat transfer coefficient and no phase change taking place in either of the streams; where these assumptions do not hold, the calculated value should be treated with appropriate caution.
target:
A countercurrent exchanger cools a process stream from 120 °C to 85 °C. Water enters at 30 °C and leaves at 55 °C. At the end where the hot stream enters, the temperature difference is 120 − 55 = 65 K; at the end where the hot stream leaves, the difference is 85 − 30 = 55 K. The log-mean temperature difference $\Delta T_{lm}$ follows from the two terminal differences $\Delta T_1$ and $\Delta T_2$:

$$\Delta T_{lm} = \frac{\Delta T_1 - \Delta T_2}{\ln(\Delta T_1 / \Delta T_2)}$$

With $\Delta T_1$ = 65 K and $\Delta T_2$ = 55 K, $\Delta T_{lm}$ is 59.9 K. The value lies between the two terminal differences and just below their arithmetic mean, as a log mean must when the two terminal differences are close to each other. The log mean is the mean difference that, used with a constant overall coefficient, gives the duty the exchanger actually transfers over its area. The log-mean value assumes a constant overall coefficient along the exchanger and no phase change in either stream; a coefficient that varies with temperature, or a stream that condenses or boils along the exchanger, takes the calculation outside the stated basis. Countercurrent flow is what keeps the difference at the cold end positive here: the water leaves against the entering hot stream, so the two terminal differences are the pair the equation takes.

fact_base: A defect-reduction project on a moulding cell cut the reject rate from 5.4% to 2.8% over one quarter. At 312k units per year the change avoids about 8112 rejected units per year. The quarter included a planned shutdown; rates are not adjusted for it.
input: A defect-reduction project has been carried out on a moulding cell with the aim of reducing the level of rejects produced by the cell, and the results obtained over the course of one quarter are summarised here. Over the quarter in question, the reject rate was cut from 5.4% to 2.8%, which corresponds to a reduction of 2.6 percentage points. When this improvement is considered in the context of the cell's annual production volume of 312k units per year, the change avoids about 8112 rejected units per year, representing a substantial improvement in the overall performance of the cell. It should, however, be borne in mind that the quarter in question included a planned shutdown, and the rates that are reported here are not adjusted for it, which means that the shutdown period forms part of the basis on which the rates have been calculated. Nevertheless, the reduction that has been achieved is considerable, and the project demonstrates the value of a systematic approach to defect reduction in terms of the number of units that are no longer produced as rejects. Going forward, it will be important to monitor the reject rate on an ongoing basis in order to ensure that the improvement that has been achieved is sustained over time and that the annualised benefit continues to be realised in practice across the full production year.
target: A defect-reduction project on a moulding cell cut the reject rate from 5.4% to 2.8% over one quarter, a reduction of 2.6 percentage points. The reject rate is rejected units over units produced in the same period, and both rates are the recorded rates for the cell. At 312k units per year, the change avoids about 8112 rejected units per year. The avoided-units figure applies the rate reduction from one quarter to a full year at the stated volume, so it is an annualised figure built from one quarter's rates, and it holds only while the volume and the reduced rate both hold. The quarter included a planned shutdown, and the rates are not adjusted for it. The shutdown sits inside the production base on which the rates were computed, and production lost to the shutdown is not separated from production lost to rejects. A reader comparing this quarter with a quarter that ran without a shutdown should treat the rate comparison as a comparison of recorded rates, not of rates on a like-for-like running time. The result the project claims is the rate reduction itself, measured on the cell over the quarter. The annual figure states what that reduction is worth in units at the cell's present volume; it is not a separate measurement, and it moves with the volume if the volume changes. The two figures together give the finding and its scale: the rate fell by more than half on the recorded basis, and at the present annual volume the fall corresponds to the stated number of units that no longer come off the cell as rejects.

fact_base: A flat stainless steel wall of thickness 20 mm separates two process streams. Thermal conductivity of the wall is 16 W m-1 K-1 and the measured temperature difference across it is 97 K. Steady one-dimensional conduction gives a heat flux of 77600 W m-2. Surface (film) resistances are excluded from this estimate; including them lowers the flux.
input: In this worked example, we consider a flat wall made of stainless steel, with a thickness of 20 mm, which separates two process streams from one another. The thermal conductivity of the wall material is 16 W m-1 K-1, and the temperature difference that has been measured across the wall is 97 K. Under conditions of steady, one-dimensional conduction, the heat flux through the wall can be calculated by dividing the product of the thermal conductivity and the temperature difference by the thickness of the wall. Expressing the thickness in metres as 0.02 m and carrying out this calculation gives a heat flux of 77600 W m-2. It is important to note that this estimate relates solely to conduction through the wall itself. Surface (film) resistances have been excluded from this estimate, and it should be understood that including them would have the effect of lowering the flux, since the films would introduce additional resistances in series with the resistance of the wall. Consequently, the value that has been obtained here should be regarded as an idealised figure based on the properties of the wall alone, and the flux that would be observed in practice, taking the surface films into account, would be somewhat lower than the figure calculated above. In addition, it should be appreciated that the calculation treats the wall as a homogeneous slab of material with a single, uniform thermal conductivity, and it takes no account of any variation in the properties of the material with temperature, nor of any imperfections in the contact between the wall and the streams on either side of it. The approach that has been followed here is deliberately simple in nature, and its purpose is to provide a clear estimate of the conductive flux through the wall under the stated conditions, on the basis of the properties and measurements that have been provided.
target:
A flat stainless steel wall of thickness 20 mm separates two process streams. The thermal conductivity of the wall is 16 W m-1 K-1, and the measured temperature difference across the wall is 97 K. Steady one-dimensional conduction through a flat wall gives the heat flux as the conductivity times the temperature difference, divided by the thickness. With the thickness expressed as 0.02 m, the flux is 77600 W m-2. The flux is heat per unit wall area, so the result carries no wall area with it: the total rate through any given wall follows from this figure multiplied by that wall's area. The estimate is for conduction through the metal alone. Surface (film) resistances are excluded from this estimate; including them lowers the flux, because the films add resistance in series with the wall and take part of the overall temperature difference that the two streams present. The stated flux is therefore the wall-only value at the measured difference across the wall itself, and it is an upper value for the flux the two streams would actually exchange through the wall and its films together.

One-dimensional conduction is the right model where the wall is flat and its area is large against its thickness, so that edge losses carry a negligible share of the heat and the temperature varies only through the thickness. Steady state means the temperature difference is read after the wall has settled. While conditions are changing, the wall stores or releases heat, and the flux entering one face differs from the flux leaving the other; the stated figure applies once that storage has ended. The dependence the result rests on is direct: the flux rises in proportion to the conductivity and to the temperature difference, and falls in inverse proportion to the thickness, so a wall twice as thick passes half the flux at the same measured difference. The result is a single number on a stated basis: conductivity and temperature difference measured on the wall, thickness as built, films excluded.

subtype: worked example with equation: Ergun pressure drop
fact_base: Gas flows through a packed bed of 1 mm particles. The void fraction $\varepsilon$ is 0.4, the superficial velocity $u$ is 0.22 m s-1 and the bed length is 1 m. The Ergun equation gives a pressure gradient of 4.3 kPa m-1, or 4.3 kPa over the bed. Particle diameter $d_p$ is 1 mm; gas density is 1.2 kg m-3 and viscosity is 1.8 x 10-5 Pa s.
input:
In this example, we consider the flow of a gas through a packed bed consisting of particles with a diameter $d_p$ of 1 mm. The void fraction $\varepsilon$ of the bed is 0.4, and the superficial velocity $u$ of the gas is 0.22 m s-1, with the bed having a length $L$ of 1 m. The pressure drop through a packed bed of this kind can be estimated by means of the Ergun equation, which is written in terms of the pressure gradient as follows:

$$\frac{\Delta P}{L} = \frac{150 \mu (1-\varepsilon)^2}{\varepsilon^3 d_p^2} u + \frac{1.75 (1-\varepsilon)}{\varepsilon^3 d_p} \rho u^2$$

Here, the first term on the right-hand side represents the contribution arising from viscous effects, whilst the second term represents the contribution arising from inertial effects. Applying this equation to the bed under consideration gives a pressure gradient $\Delta P / L$ of 4.3 kPa m-1, which corresponds to a pressure drop of 4.3 kPa over the 1 m bed. The density $\rho$ of the gas is 1.2 kg m-3, and its viscosity $\mu$ is $1.8 \times 10^{-5}$ Pa s. It should be noted that the superficial velocity is based on the cross-section of the empty vessel, and the actual velocity of the gas within the voids of the bed will therefore be higher than this value.
target:
Gas flows through a packed bed of particles of diameter $d_p$ = 1 mm. The void fraction $\varepsilon$ is 0.4 and the superficial velocity $u$ is 0.22 m s-1 over a bed length $L$ of 1 m. The Ergun equation gives the pressure gradient in the bed as the sum of a viscous term and an inertial term:

$$\frac{\Delta P}{L} = \frac{150 \mu (1-\varepsilon)^2}{\varepsilon^3 d_p^2} u + \frac{1.75 (1-\varepsilon)}{\varepsilon^3 d_p} \rho u^2$$

The first term carries the viscosity $\mu$ and falls as the particle size grows; the second carries the density $\rho$ and the square of the velocity. For this bed the gradient $\Delta P / L$ is 4.3 kPa m-1, or 4.3 kPa over the 1 m bed. The gas density $\rho$ is 1.2 kg m-3 and the viscosity $\mu$ is $1.8 \times 10^{-5}$ Pa s. The superficial velocity is the velocity the gas would have in the empty vessel at the same flow; the gas in the voids moves faster, through the fraction $\varepsilon$ of the cross-section. The gradient is built from the particle size, the void fraction, and the gas properties as stated, with the bed treated as uniform along its length. The equation is applied here as the standard relation for a packed bed of uniform particles; it carries no allowance for channelling or for a spread of particle sizes, and the gradient it gives is the bed-average gradient that the stated properties support.

fact_base: Energy assessment of a paper mill, in four sections: current use, refrigeration, steam, and recommendation. Electricity use is 2884 MWh per year; refrigeration takes the largest share. A heat-recovery retrofit is projected to save 22% of electricity use, a derived saving of 634 MWh per year, at a capital cost of $396k. At $0.12 per kWh the derived annual saving is $76138 and the derived simple payback is 5.2 years. Steam figures are from one winter month and are flagged as seasonal in the recommendation.
input:
Current use

The purpose of this section is to provide an overview of the current energy use at the paper mill, in order to establish a baseline against which potential improvements can be assessed. Electricity use at the mill currently stands at 2884 MWh per year. Of this total, refrigeration accounts for the largest share, representing the single biggest area of electricity consumption at the site. The remaining electricity is distributed across a wide range of drives and services, including stock preparation, refining, the paper machine drives, vacuum systems, compressed air, pumping, and lighting, as well as numerous smaller motors and items of auxiliary equipment. The electricity figures that are presented here are based on a full year of metering data, which means that the seasonal variations that occur within the year have already been taken into account in the totals. It is important to note that this assessment considers the mill in its current configuration, with its present product mix, machine schedule, and operating practices; any significant change in these areas would have an impact on both the overall electricity consumption and the way in which that consumption is distributed. Overall, the picture that emerges is one of a substantial electricity load that is heavily concentrated in refrigeration, which in turn suggests that measures targeting this area are likely to offer the most significant opportunities for improvement. It is also relevant to observe that the distribution of consumption is just as significant as the headline total itself. Where consumption is spread across a large number of small and disparate uses, it can be considerably more difficult to identify measures that are capable of delivering material savings, since no single intervention is able to address more than a small fraction of the total. In the present case, however, the concentration of consumption in one dominant area means that the assessment is able to focus its attention on the area where the greatest potential for improvement is understood to reside.

Refrigeration

Refrigeration represents the largest single use of electricity at the mill and therefore constitutes a key area of focus for this assessment. The refrigeration plant provides cooling for a number of important duties across the site, including chilled process water, cooling for air serving temperature-sensitive areas and equipment, and the removal of heat rejected by the process into its water circuits. Plant of this type typically operates for extended periods of time, with loads that vary in line with production, and the combined electricity consumption of its compressors, pumps, and heat-rejection equipment determines the overall cost of delivering the cooling duty. The efficiency with which the plant is operated and controlled has a direct bearing on the amount of electricity that a given duty requires; plant that runs at part load for extended periods, or that rejects heat at temperatures higher than necessary, will consume more electricity than the duty itself demands. Another important consideration is the heat that is rejected by the refrigeration plant at its condensers. This heat is currently discarded, but it has the potential to be recovered and put to use for heating duties elsewhere on the site, and it is this opportunity that the retrofit considered in the recommendation section seeks to exploit. A further point that deserves emphasis is that refrigeration plant of this kind is often operated for long periods at partial load, and the manner in which the plant responds to varying demand can have a substantial influence on the efficiency that is achieved in practice. Against this background, the opportunity to recover heat from the plant has attracted considerable interest, since it offers the prospect of deriving additional value from energy that is already being consumed by the site, rather than depending solely on reductions in the cooling duty itself.

Steam

Steam is used at the mill for a variety of heating duties, the most significant and continuous of which is the drying of the sheet on the paper machine. In addition to this, steam is used for process heating, space heating, and a range of smaller duties that are associated with production activities across the site. The steam figures that are available for the purposes of this assessment are drawn from one winter month. It should be borne in mind that a single winter month cannot be regarded as representative of the year as a whole, since steam demand is influenced by the heating season as well as by levels of production, and a winter month will tend to reflect the heating load at its highest. For this reason, no attempt has been made to annualise the steam figures, as doing so would risk presenting a misleading picture of the mill's annual steam consumption. The steam position is therefore reported here on the basis of one winter month only, and the scale of the annual steam load, together with any savings that might be available in this area, remains to be established once a full year of steam metering data has been collected. It is a common feature of assessments of this kind that the data available for different energy streams are not of equivalent quality or coverage, and the present assessment is no exception in this regard. Where the evidence base is incomplete, the appropriate response is to report the position transparently on the basis that is available, and to identify clearly the further information that would be required in order to place the relevant conclusions on a firmer footing.

Recommendation

It is recommended that the heat-recovery retrofit on the refrigeration plant be taken forward. The retrofit is projected to save 22% of electricity use, corresponding to a derived saving of 634 MWh per year when set against the current electricity use of 2884 MWh per year, at a capital cost of $396k. At an electricity price of $0.12 per kWh, the derived annual saving amounts to $76138, which gives a derived simple payback of 5.2 years. Site engineering will own the retrofit through the design and installation phases, and the savings that are achieved will be verified against metered electricity consumption following installation, using the same full-year basis as the current-use figures presented earlier in this assessment. In coming to this recommendation, account has been taken of the straightforward nature of the calculation that underlies the payback figure. The payback that is presented is a simple payback, and it does not seek to incorporate factors such as the time value of money, future movements in electricity prices, or the maintenance requirements of the new equipment. It is considered, however, that this level of analysis is entirely appropriate for the purpose of screening the proposal at this stage, and that the figures provide a sound basis on which the decision can be taken. It should be emphasised that this recommendation relates to the electricity side of the mill's energy use only. The steam figures underpinning this assessment are derived from one winter month and are accordingly flagged as seasonal in nature; no steam-side measure is therefore recommended at this stage, and it is suggested that a full year of steam metering be obtained before any steam-side proposal is developed, in order to ensure that any such measure is appropriately sized against demand across the whole year rather than against a single, unrepresentative month.
target:
Current use

Electricity use at the mill is 2884 MWh per year. Refrigeration takes the largest share of that use. The remainder is spread across the mill's drives and services: stock preparation, refining, the paper machine drives, vacuum systems, compressed air, pumping, and lighting, together with the smaller motors and auxiliaries that serve them. The electricity figures rest on a full year of metering, so the seasonal movement of load inside the year is already averaged into the total. The assessment takes the mill as it currently runs, at its present product mix, machine schedule, and operating practice; a change to any of those moves both the electricity total and the shares within it. What the current-use picture establishes is the scale of the electricity load and where the load sits. The total is large enough that a saving measured as a share of it is a large saving in absolute terms, and the concentration of use in refrigeration is what makes a single retrofit measure worth assessing in detail, rather than a programme of small measures spread thinly across many small loads. Steam is raised and used alongside electricity at the mill, and the steam position is treated in its own section below, on the basis stated there. The shares within the total matter as much as the total itself. A load spread evenly across many small uses leaves no single point of attack, whereas a load concentrated in one large use can be addressed by one measure, assessed once, with its saving read off the site meters. The mill load has the second shape. It also has a shape in time: production loads follow the machine schedule while service loads follow occupancy and season, and the year of metering contains both. Ranking the uses needs the total and the shares, and both stand on the year of metering, so the ranking does not wait on separating those shapes.

Refrigeration

Refrigeration is the largest single use of electricity at the mill. The refrigeration plant serves the cooling duties the process depends on: chilled process water, cooling for air that serves temperature-sensitive areas and equipment, and the removal of heat that the process itself rejects into its water circuits. Refrigeration plant of this kind runs for long hours at loads that follow production, and its compressors, pumps, and heat-rejection equipment together set the electricity the duty costs. The efficiency of the plant as installed and as controlled decides how much electricity a given cooling duty takes; a plant that runs at part load for much of its time, or that rejects its heat at a higher temperature than the sink requires, spends electricity that the duty itself does not demand. The heat the refrigeration plant rejects is the point of contact with the rest of the mill's energy system. Rejected heat leaves the plant at the condenser, and heat recovered there can serve heating duties elsewhere on site that are currently met from other energy. That recovery is the retrofit assessed in the recommendation: it acts on the largest load on the site, and it acts on heat the site already produces and currently throws away. Two features of the plant decide how much of the rejected heat a retrofit can use. The first is temperature: heat rejected above the temperature a receiving duty needs can pass into that duty directly, while heat rejected below it cannot serve without being upgraded. The second is timing: recovery serves a heating duty only when the refrigeration plant is rejecting heat at the hours the duty calls for it. A recovery scheme is therefore matched, duty by duty, against the site heating loads, and the match, not the raw quantity of rejected heat, sets the saving the scheme can deliver.

Steam

Steam serves the mill's heating duties, of which the drying of the sheet on the paper machine is the largest and the most continuous. Steam also serves process heating, space heating, and the smaller duties that follow production around the site. The steam figures available to this assessment are from one winter month. A single winter month does not stand for the year: steam demand follows the heating season as well as production, and a winter month carries the heating load at its heaviest while the rest of the year runs lighter. No annual steam figure is stated in this assessment, because annualising the winter month would build the year's steam position on the least representative month available. The steam side of the mill's energy use is therefore recorded here as a position in one winter month only, and the size of the annual steam load, and of any saving available against it, stays open until steam metering covers a full year. The position would be different if the winter month stood as one month among twelve. On its own it fixes the scale of steam use in the heaviest month and nothing more: it cannot show how far demand falls in the lighter months, how steam use tracks production across the year, or what a steam-side measure would save in a full year. Those are the quantities a steam-side proposal would need, and they are the reason the steam side of this assessment is left as a stated limit rather than built into figures the evidence does not support.

Recommendation

The heat-recovery retrofit on the refrigeration plant is recommended. The retrofit is projected to save 22% of electricity use, a derived saving of 634 MWh per year against the current use of 2884 MWh per year, at a capital cost of $396k. At $0.12 per kWh, the derived annual saving is $76138, and the derived simple payback is 5.2 years. Site engineering owns the retrofit through design and installation, and the saving is to be verified against metered electricity use after installation, on the same full-year basis as the current-use figures. The payback is a simple payback: it divides the capital cost by the annual saving and takes no account of the timing of cash flows within the period, of maintenance on the retrofit, or of movement in the electricity price after installation. It is stated as derived because each of its inputs is stated: the saving share, the current use, the price, and the capital cost. If the electricity price moves, the annual saving moves with it and the payback moves inversely; the saving in energy, which the retrofit physically delivers, does not move. The recommendation therefore rests on the energy saving first and on the money saving at the stated price second. The recommendation is made on the electricity side only. The steam figures behind this assessment are from one winter month and are flagged as seasonal; no steam-side measure is recommended on that basis, and a full year of steam metering should precede any steam-side proposal, so that a steam measure is sized against the year's demand and not against its heaviest month.

fact_base: Excerpt content: the compressor wall thickness is 43 mm after the corrosion allowance is added. The excerpt compares two gasket materials on temperature limit only and prefers the higher-rated one. The excerpt ends mid-argument; it neither summarises the report nor previews the next section.
input: …it can be seen that the wall thickness of the compressor casing amounts to 43 mm once the corrosion allowance has been added on top of the thickness required for pressure containment purposes. It is worth emphasising that this additional material is provided to accommodate corrosion over the casing lifetime, rather than being required by the design pressure. With regard to the selection of the gasket material, a comparison has been carried out between the two candidate materials, focusing on the temperature limit. On this basis, the higher-rated material is preferred for the joint in question, since the temperature at the flange face is the condition the gasket must withstand, and it is on this condition that the two materials are most clearly distinguished, whereas their other recorded properties are broadly comparable. fact_base: A binary distillation separates ethanol/water at a relative volatility of 1.61 that is taken as constant over the column. Specifications: distillate 98 mol% light component, bottoms 2 mol% light component. The Fenske minimum stage count is 16.3 theoretical stages including the reboiler. The actual design uses a reflux ratio of 1.3 times the minimum; the stage count at that reflux comes from a separate simulation.
input: In this example, we consider a binary distillation system separating a mixture of ethanol and water, in which the relative volatility of the light component, ethanol, is 1.61, a value that is taken as being constant throughout the column. The separation that is to be achieved is specified in terms of product compositions, namely 98 mol% light component in the distillate and 2 mol% light component in the bottoms. By applying the Fenske equation, which relates the minimum number of stages at total reflux to the compositions of the two products and the relative volatility, it is possible to determine the minimum stage requirement for the separation in question. On the basis of the stated values, the minimum stage count is found to be 16.3 theoretical stages, including the reboiler. It is important to note that this figure represents a limiting value rather than a practical design value, since total reflux corresponds to a condition under which no product is actually withdrawn from the column. The actual design that has been adopted makes use of a reflux ratio of 1.3 times the minimum reflux ratio. The number of stages that is required at this reflux ratio has been obtained from a separate simulation, and this figure is not presented here. Nevertheless, the Fenske result provides a useful point of reference, in that the number of stages in any workable design must necessarily be greater than 16.3 stages if the specified product compositions are to be achieved.
target: A binary distillation separates ethanol and water. The relative volatility of the light component, ethanol, is 1.61, taken as constant over the column. The specifications are 98 mol% light component in the distillate and 2 mol% light component in the bottoms. The Fenske equation gives the minimum number of stages at total reflux for a sharpness of separation set by those two specifications. On the stated values, the minimum stage count is 16.3 theoretical stages, including the reboiler. The reboiler is counted as a stage in the total, on the usual convention for a minimum-stage count. The count is a bound rather than a design figure. Total reflux is the condition at which the column separates with the fewest stages, and it is also the condition at which no product leaves the column; an operating column works at finite reflux and needs more stages than the minimum. The actual design uses a reflux ratio of 1.3 times the minimum. The stage count at that reflux comes from a separate simulation; it is not computed here, and the Fenske count does not by itself give it. What the Fenske result establishes is the floor under the design: whatever stage count the simulation returns at the design reflux, it must exceed 16.3 stages for the stated specifications, or the simulation and the Fenske bound disagree. Constant relative volatility is the assumption the count rests on, and the count is as good as that single value's representation of the mixture over the column's composition range.

fact_base: A tutorial passage explains representative sampling of a powder blend. The passage covers where samples are taken, how many increments form one sample, and why a single grab sample misleads. No numerical limits are quoted; regulatory limits belong to the site's permit, not to the passage.
input: When it comes to the analysis of a powder blend, it is important to note that the sampling step is arguably the most crucial stage of the whole procedure, because no amount of sophisticated laboratory analysis can compensate for a sample that does not faithfully represent the material from which it was drawn. A powder blend, despite appearances, is rarely the perfectly uniform mixture that one might assume: during handling, transport, and storage, the finer particles gradually percolate downwards through the gaps between the larger particles, while the coarser particles tend to migrate outwards towards the walls and upwards towards the surface, thereby creating composition differences from place to place within the container. In light of this, good practice is to collect a series of small portions, referred to as increments, from a variety of different locations, for instance near the top, around the middle, and near the bottom of the container, or, alternatively, at intervals across the stream as the blender discharges its contents. These increments are then combined together and mixed thoroughly in order to form a single composite sample, which is subsequently reduced down to the size needed for the assay by a technique, such as riffling, that does not separate the particles according to their size. By contrast, a single grab sample, scooped hastily from one convenient spot, can be deeply misleading, since it captures only the local composition at that one place and moment: material taken from the surface will over-represent the coarse fraction, material taken from near the bottom will over-represent the fines, and the resulting figure gives no indication whatsoever that anything is amiss, presenting a varying blend as though it were perfectly uniform. Ultimately, then, it is by sampling from several positions, combining the increments, and reducing the composite with care that the analyst obtains a portion that genuinely reflects the batch as a whole, ensuring that the assay result can be relied upon.
target:
A powder blend assay is trusted only as far as the sample represents the batch. Sampling of a powder blend therefore builds one sample from increments taken at several positions, so that the assay portion carries the composition of the blend as a whole.

A blend is not uniform throughout its container. Fine particles percolate downward through the voids between coarser particles during handling and storage, and coarse particles migrate toward the surface and the walls, so the composition at any one position differs from the composition elsewhere.

Increments are taken near the top, at mid-depth, and near the bottom of the container, or at intervals across the stream while the blender discharges. Each increment is small compared with the batch, and the increments are spread so that the combined sample covers every region of the container. The increments are combined and mixed, and the combined sample is reduced to the assay portion by a method that does not sort the particles, such as riffling.

A single grab sample misleads because it reports the composition at one position and one moment. A scoop from the surface overstates the coarse fraction; a scoop from the bottom overstates the fines. The result carries no sign of its own bias, and a blend that varies across the container is reported as uniform. Where the blend is sampled decides what the assay can show, and the analysis that follows cannot correct a biased portion. Sampling at several positions, combining the increments, and reducing the combined sample without segregation gives an assay portion from which the batch can be judged.

subtype: worked example with equation: Raoult partial pressure
fact_base: An ideal liquid mixture holds ethanol in water (idealised) at a liquid mole fraction $x$ of 0.25 for the volatile component. Its pure-component vapour pressure $P^*$ at the mixture temperature is 20.1 kPa, so the partial pressure $p$ is 5 kPa by Raoult's law. Raoult's law assumes an ideal solution; activity coefficients for the real mixture are not applied.
input:
In this example, we are asked to determine the partial pressure of ethanol above a liquid mixture consisting of ethanol in water, which we shall treat as idealised, where the liquid mole fraction of the ethanol, the volatile component in question, is given as 0.25.

To tackle this, we make use of Raoult's law, a fundamental relation in solution thermodynamics which expresses the partial pressure $p$ of a volatile component in an ideal solution in terms of its liquid mole fraction $x$ and the vapour pressure $P^*$ of the pure component at the temperature of the mixture, as follows:

$$p = x P^*$$

In essence, the law captures the idea that the tendency of the volatile component to escape into the vapour phase is reduced in direct proportion to its share of the liquid, so that the partial pressure is simply the pure-component vapour pressure, here 20.1 kPa at the mixture temperature, scaled by the mole fraction. Turning to the numbers at hand, the mole fraction $x$ of ethanol in the liquid is 0.25, and substituting this value, together with the pure-component vapour pressure of 20.1 kPa, into Raoult's law, we obtain $p$ = 5 kPa for the partial pressure of ethanol above the mixture.

It is worth noting, however, that Raoult's law rests upon the assumption of an ideal solution, and real mixtures of ethanol and water are well known to deviate from ideality; in a more rigorous treatment, activity coefficients would be introduced in order to capture these non-ideal interactions. No activity coefficients are applied here, and the partial pressure over the real mixture will accordingly depart from 5 kPa by whatever factor the activity coefficient turns out to impose.
target:
Calculate the partial pressure of ethanol over an idealised mixture of ethanol in water, at a liquid mole fraction of 0.25 for ethanol.

The partial pressure $p$ of a volatile component in the vapour over a liquid mixture is the pressure that component would exert if it occupied the vapour space alone. Raoult's law gives the partial pressure of a volatile component in an ideal solution from two quantities: its liquid mole fraction $x$, and its pure-component vapour pressure $P^*$ at the mixture temperature. The law states the two quantities as a product:

$$p = x P^*$$

The product form is the content of the ideal-solution assumption: each molecule of the volatile component escapes into the vapour as it would from the pure liquid, and the share that escapes is set by the fraction of the liquid the component forms. The vapour pressure $P^*$ is a property of the pure component at the stated temperature and does not depend on the composition of the mixture. For the mixture at hand, the liquid mole fraction $x$ of ethanol is 0.25 and the pure-component vapour pressure $P^*$ at the mixture temperature is 20.1 kPa. Substitution of the two values in Raoult's law gives $p$ = 5 kPa.

The check is the pure-liquid limit: where the liquid is the pure volatile component, Raoult's law returns the pure-component vapour pressure $P^*$ itself, 20.1 kPa, and the stated partial pressure is the fraction of that limit set by the mole fraction. Raoult's law holds for an ideal solution. The real mixture of ethanol in water is not ideal, and activity coefficients for the real mixture are not applied in the calculation; the partial pressure over the real mixture departs from 5 kPa by the factor the activity coefficient sets.

fact_base: Capital appraisal for a solar array: installed cost $633k, expected net saving $155k per year for 12 years. At a discount rate of 8% the present value of the savings is $1168k and the net present value is $535k. Savings are vendor and utility estimates; no saving has yet been measured on a comparable installation.
input: This appraisal examines the financial case for installing a solar array, drawing together the capital cost, the anticipated savings, and the time value of money in order to assess whether the project creates value. The installed cost of the array is put at $633k, payable at the outset. Against this outlay, the array is expected to deliver a net saving estimated at $155k per year, and this saving is projected to continue for a period of 12 years, corresponding to the appraisal horizon adopted here. In order to compare money arising at different times on a like-for-like basis, the stream of savings is discounted at a rate of 8%, which brings the total present value of the savings to $1168k. Set against the installed cost of $633k, this yields a net present value of $535k, a positive figure which indicates that, on the estimates adopted, the project more than recovers its cost in present-value terms. It should nevertheless be borne in mind that the savings figures underpinning the appraisal are vendor and utility estimates, and that no saving has yet been measured on a comparable installation; consequently, the net present value of $535k is only as reliable as those estimates themselves, and the position should be revisited once metered data from the first year of operation become available.
target:
The solar array should be approved on the stated figures: the appraisal gives a net present value of $535k against an installed cost of $633k. The expected net saving is $155k per year for 12 years. At a discount rate of 8%, the present value of the savings is $1168k; set against the installed cost of $633k, the net present value is $535k.

The discount rate is the rate the business applies to its other capital appraisals, so the array is judged on the same terms as the projects it competes with for funds. The savings are vendor and utility estimates, and no saving has yet been measured on a comparable installation. Every figure after the installed cost rests on those estimates: the annual saving, the period over which the saving is held level, and the generation behind both. The installed cost is the only figure in the appraisal fixed by quotation rather than estimated from performance. A shortfall in the saving reduces the present value in proportion, and the appraisal states no margin because the estimates carry no measured spread. Approval on these figures is approval of an estimate, recorded as such. The first year of metered operation sets the saving against which the remaining years are judged, and the appraisal is reopened if that figure falls short of the estimate.

fact_base: Excerpt content: a budget overrun of 8 weeks is reported with its cause; the excerpt proposes one mitigation and its owner. The excerpt does not open or close the memo and does not restate its subject line.
input: Members will wish to be aware that the position on programme has deteriorated further since the last update, and the overrun now stands at some 8 weeks against the programme reported to the project board. The root cause of the slippage has been traced to the main equipment package, where a series of difficulties in fabrication led to completion falling progressively behind the dates set out in the accepted programme, with the consequence that delivery to site ultimately missed the installation window which the package was intended to meet. Because a considerable amount of the follow-on work is dependent, directly or indirectly, on the package being in place, that work has effectively stood idle in sequence, and the 8-week overrun which is now reported represents the accumulated slippage at the current position rather than any allowance for further deterioration. By way of mitigation, it is proposed that the remaining installation work under the EPC contractor be resequenced, so that those areas which do not depend on the package are progressed first, whilst the installation of the package itself is compressed into a shorter window once delivery has taken place; the planning manager will own the resequencing and will report progress against it at each review. It should be noted that resequencing can be expected to recover only that part of the slip which idle sequencing has caused, and that the balance, which arises from the late delivery itself, can be recovered only insofar as the compressed window can be held. Acceptance of the resequencing rests with the project board, and until such time as the board accepts it, the programme continues to carry the overrun unmitigated, with the completion forecast remaining where the slippage places it.

The overrun is stated against the accepted programme, the same basis as the last report, and no other workstream reports a slip of its own.

The mitigation proposed is a resequencing of the remaining installation work under the EPC contractor: areas that do not depend on the package proceed first, and the package installation is compressed into a shorter window once delivery lands. The planning manager owns the resequencing and reports progress against it at each review. Resequencing recovers the part of the slip that idle sequencing caused; the part caused by the late delivery itself is recovered only if the compressed window holds.

fact_base: A review passage on catalysts for carbon dioxide hydrogenation, in four parts: scope, established results, disagreements, and gaps. The review covers 104 papers from the last 7 years. The disagreements part names the quantity on which reports conflict; the gaps part names the measurement nobody reports.
input:
Scope

The present review surveys a body of 104 papers dealing with catalysts for carbon dioxide hydrogenation that have appeared in the literature over the last 7 years. Carbon dioxide hydrogenation, for those approaching the topic for the first time, may be understood as the reaction of carbon dioxide with hydrogen over a solid catalyst, a reaction which yields a range of products including, among others, methanol, methane, and carbon monoxide. The papers encompassed by the set report, in varying degrees of detail, the preparation of catalysts, their testing in continuous reactors, and the distributions of products obtained under the conditions stated by the authors. The scope of the set is restricted to heterogeneous catalysts for which carbon dioxide figures as the reactant under study; papers concerned with electrochemical conversion and papers concerned with photochemical conversion consequently fall outside it, as do papers in which carbon dioxide appears merely as an impurity in the feed. Studies of the reverse water-gas shift reaction are included where that reaction forms part of a broader hydrogenation scheme, and excluded in those cases where carbon monoxide is the only intended product and no hydrogenation step ensues. The review is organised in four parts, addressing in turn the scope of the set, the results which the set may be said to support, the points on which the reports are in conflict, and the measurements which the set does not contain. It should be emphasised that conditions vary very considerably from paper to paper, in pressure, in temperature, and in feed proportions, and the review accordingly compares reports in terms of the quantities the papers themselves state, rather than attempting any reduction to a common basis which the underlying papers do not share.

Established results

Copper-based catalysts constitute by far the most extensively reported family where the formation of methanol is concerned. The standard preparation is one in which copper is carried on zinc oxide, with alumina additionally present as a structural component serving to keep the copper in a dispersed state. Activity is found to track the exposed copper surface, in the sense that preparations which succeed in dispersing the copper more finely also convert more carbon dioxide per unit mass of catalyst, a relationship which appears to hold both across different preparations and across different laboratories. The reverse water-gas shift reaction proceeds in parallel wherever carbon dioxide and hydrogen are brought into contact with the catalyst, and carbon monoxide is accordingly found in the product of every methanol catalyst in the set. The proportion of carbon monoxide rises with temperature, while methanol selectivity falls as temperature rises, reflecting the fact that the shift reaction is favoured at higher temperatures whereas methanol formation is favoured at lower ones. Water, which is a product of both reactions, acts to inhibit the methanol reaction: rates are observed to fall as water accumulates, and arrangements in which water is removed between stages achieve correspondingly higher conversions. Oxide supports, it emerges, are by no means inert carriers, since the boundary between the metal and the oxide is the site to which a large part of the activity is attributed, and substituting zirconium oxide for zinc oxide changes activity and selectivity alike for one and the same metal. Indium oxide catalysts deliver high methanol selectivity accompanied by little methane, and display a resistance to the loss of surface which afflicts copper at temperature, although their activity per unit mass falls below that of the copper preparations in most reports. Nickel-based catalysts, for their part, carry the reaction through to methane and convert carbon dioxide almost completely under conditions where the methanol catalysts produce mixtures, so that the set divides along the lines of the intended product. Promoters introduced in small amounts are found to alter selectivity to a greater extent than they alter activity. Deactivation in the tests reported is dominated by the growth of the metal particles together with the action of the water formed in the reaction, two effects which the set rarely manages to separate.

Disagreements

Considerable disagreement exists in the literature with respect to the selectivity to methanol at a stated conversion, in the case of copper-based catalysts operated under conditions which the respective reports describe as comparable. One and the same preparation is reported as exhibiting quite different selectivities by different groups, the discrepancy comfortably exceeding the spread reported within any single study. One school of reporting attributes the selectivity to the size of the copper particles, maintaining that smaller particles afford the higher selectivity and that preparations are therefore to be ranked by particle size alone. A second school attributes the selectivity to the boundary subsisting between the copper and the oxide, ranking preparations instead by the extent of that boundary, with particle size entering the picture only in so far as it modifies the boundary. Since the two rankings order the selfsame preparations differently, and since the papers themselves do not resolve the question of which quantity the selectivity in fact follows, the matter must be regarded as open. Disagreement extends, furthermore, to the action of water. In one body of reports the inhibition exerted by water is portrayed as kinetic and reversible, the rate recovering once the water is removed, whereas in another body of reports the loss is portrayed as permanent, the water being held responsible for changing the catalyst itself in the course of a run. The distinction is far from academic, inasmuch as the two accounts point towards quite different reactor arrangements, namely staged beds with intermediate water removal in the one case and a catalyst selected for its ability to withstand water in the other. Neither conflict can be resolved from the set as published, for the simple reason that the papers state their conditions in forms which do not carry across from one report to another: conversion is quoted at differing positions within the bed, and selectivity is in many instances not quoted at a stated conversion at all.

Gaps

Perhaps the most striking omission in the set is that no paper in it reports conversion after extended time on stream. The measurement which nobody reports is, in other words, the activity of the catalyst following operation of a duration sufficient for deactivation, rather than initial activity, to become the governing factor in performance: the tests in the set are terminated while the catalyst remains close to its initial state, and such deactivation as the established results describe is inferred on the basis of short runs and post-mortem examination rather than measured over the run itself. The omission extends also to the feed employed. The papers test clean feeds composed of carbon dioxide and hydrogen, and no paper reports performance over time on a feed bearing the impurities characteristic of a captured industrial stream, notwithstanding that a catalyst in actual service would inevitably encounter such a feed. Regeneration fares no better: a handful of papers mention in passing that a catalyst was regenerated, yet none reports the activity thereby recovered, the number of cycles the catalyst is capable of withstanding, or the selectivity obtaining after regeneration. Carbon balances, moreover, are incomplete in a substantial part of the set, with the result that the fate of such carbon as does not appear among the stated products cannot be verified from the papers. The set accordingly supports comparisons between fresh catalysts operating under clean conditions, but does not support the comparison upon which an industrial selection would properly rest, namely performance sustained over time, on a realistic feed, following regeneration.
target:

The review covers 104 papers on catalysts for carbon dioxide hydrogenation published in the last 7 years. Papers are grouped in the review by the catalyst family they report rather than by the preparation in full, because preparations recur across papers with variations in detail that the review does not track. Methanol is the product aim of the largest part of the set, methane of a smaller part, and carbon monoxide of the remainder, where the shift reaction is studied for its own sake or as the first stage of a longer chain. A paper is counted once, under the product its authors state as the aim, where a paper reports more than one product.

Established results

Copper-based catalysts are the most reported family for the formation of methanol. The standard preparation carries copper on zinc oxide, with alumina present as a structural component that holds the copper dispersed. Activity tracks the exposed copper surface: preparations that disperse the copper more finely convert more carbon dioxide per unit mass of catalyst, and the relation holds across preparations and across laboratories. The reverse water-gas shift reaction runs in parallel wherever carbon dioxide and hydrogen meet the catalyst, and carbon monoxide appears in the product of every methanol catalyst in the set. The share of carbon monoxide rises with temperature, and methanol selectivity falls as temperature rises, because the shift reaction is favoured at the higher temperature while methanol formation is favoured at the lower. Water is a product of both reactions and inhibits the methanol reaction: rates fall as water accumulates, and reactor arrangements that remove water between stages raise the conversion reached. Promoters added in small amounts change selectivity more than they change activity. Conversion rises with pressure, because methanol formation reduces the number of gas molecules as it proceeds while the shift reaction does not; pressure therefore acts on selectivity as well as on conversion, and the higher pressures in the set are reported with the higher methanol selectivities. Feeds richer in hydrogen raise conversion on all families in the set, and on the methanation catalysts a hydrogen-rich feed is the normal condition reported. The preparation most reported for the copper family is coprecipitation, and preparations made by other routes are usually reported against a coprecipitated standard, which gives the set a common reference even where conditions differ. Deactivation in the tests reported is dominated by growth of the metal particles and by the action of the water formed, and the two are rarely separated in the set.

Disagreements

Reports conflict on the selectivity to methanol at a stated conversion, for copper-based catalysts run under conditions the reports describe as comparable. The same preparation is reported with different selectivities by different groups, and the difference is larger than the spread within any one report. One line of reports assigns the selectivity to the size of the copper particles: smaller particles are said to give the higher selectivity, and preparations are then ranked by particle size alone. A second line assigns the selectivity to the boundary between copper and oxide, and ranks preparations by the extent of that boundary, with particle size entering only as it changes the boundary. The two rankings order the same preparations differently, and the papers do not settle which quantity the selectivity follows. Reports also conflict on the action of water. In one set of reports the inhibition by water is kinetic and reversible: remove the water and the rate returns. In another set the loss is permanent, and the water is held to change the catalyst itself over the course of a run. The conflict matters because the two accounts prescribe different reactor arrangements, staged beds with water removal in the first case and a catalyst chosen to withstand water in the second. Reports conflict further on the part played by alumina in the standard copper preparation. In one account the alumina is a structural component only, present to hold the copper dispersed and taking no part in the reaction. In another account the alumina is held to enter the working surface and to contribute to the adsorption of carbon dioxide, so that removing it changes the chemistry and not only the texture of the catalyst. The preparations compared in the two accounts differ in more than the alumina content, and the set does not contain a comparison in which alumina alone is varied. Neither conflict is resolved by the set as published, because the papers state their conditions in forms that do not carry across reports: conversion is quoted at different positions in the bed, and selectivity is not always quoted at a stated conversion at all.

Gaps

No paper in the set reports conversion after extended time on stream. The measurement nobody reports is the activity of the catalyst after operation long enough for deactivation, rather than initial activity, to govern the performance: tests in the set end while the catalyst is still near its initial state, and the deactivation that the established results describe is inferred from short runs and from examination after the event, not measured over the run itself. The gap extends to the feed. Papers test clean feeds of carbon dioxide and hydrogen, and no paper reports performance over time on a feed carrying the impurities of a captured industrial stream, although the catalyst in service would meet such a feed. Regeneration is treated the same way: a few papers state that a catalyst was regenerated, and none reports the activity recovered, the number of cycles the catalyst withstands, or the selectivity after regeneration. Carbon balances are incomplete in much of the set, so the fate of the carbon that does not appear in the stated products cannot be checked from the papers. Characterisation in the set is of the fresh catalyst and of the spent catalyst after the run; no paper reports a measurement of the working surface made during the run itself, so the state of the catalyst at the moment its activity is quoted is inferred rather than observed. Start-up and shut-down are likewise absent: no paper reports what repeated cycling between reaction conditions and rest does to activity or to selectivity, although a catalyst in service on an intermittent renewable hydrogen supply would be cycled as a matter of routine. The set therefore supports the comparison of fresh catalysts under clean conditions, and does not support the comparison on which an industrial choice would rest: performance held over time, on a real feed, after regeneration.

fact_base: A tutorial passage explains the pump affinity laws for a centrifugal pump at varying speed. The passage states the three proportionalities in words: flow with speed, head with speed squared, power with speed cubed. A worked check is included: doubling speed multiplies power by 8. No other numbers are introduced.
input:
When the speed of a centrifugal pump is changed, its flow, its head, and the power it draws all change along with it, and the relationships which govern these changes are collectively known as the affinity laws. In what follows, the three proportionalities comprising the laws are set out and a worked check is then presented, in which it is shown that doubling the speed has the striking consequence of multiplying the power by 8.

It should be borne in mind throughout that the affinity laws pertain to one particular pump, in an unchanged condition and handling one particular liquid. The first of the laws states that the flow is proportional to the speed, so that at twice the speed the pump may be expected to deliver twice the flow. According to the second law, the head is proportional to the square of the speed, whilst according to the third law, the power is proportional to the cube of the speed. It must be emphasised that the laws serve to compare points on the characteristic of one and the same pump, and that they tell us nothing whatsoever about a different pump; furthermore, they presuppose that the efficiency at the two speeds under consideration remains near enough unchanged, an assumption which is generally satisfied for speed changes of the magnitude effected in service by a variable-speed drive.

By way of a worked check, let it be supposed that the speed rises by a factor of 2. The flow then rises by the factor 2 itself. The head, for its part, rises by the factor 2 squared, which works out to 4. The power, meanwhile, rises by the factor 2 cubed, which works out to 8. The cube appearing in the power law is thus the term which effectively governs the loading of the motor: the power at the raised speed is fully 8 times the power at the original speed, and a motor which was selected with little margin at the original speed will find itself overloaded at the raised speed, notwithstanding that the flow has done no more than double.

The affinity laws apply to one pump, unchanged, handling the one liquid. The flow is proportional to the speed: at twice the speed, the pump delivers twice the flow. The head is proportional to the square of the speed. The power is proportional to the cube of the speed. The laws compare points on the characteristic of the one pump; they state nothing about a different pump, and they hold where the efficiency at the two speeds is near enough unchanged, which is the case for speed changes of the size a variable-speed drive makes in service.

The laws are used in both directions. Run forward, they give the duty a pump delivers when its speed is raised to meet a higher demand, before any drive is ordered or fitted. Run backward, they give the duty surrendered when the speed is cut, and the cube in the power law is what makes the cut worth making: on a duty where the flow is held down by throttling, a speed reduction removes the throttling loss and reduces the power by the cube of the speed ratio at the same time.
