fact_base: Project proposal for a rooftop solar installation, in four sections: case, costs, schedule, and decision requested. Capital cost is $1334k with a 15-year appraisal horizon. The schedule section gives a start one quarter after approval; no contractor is named. The decision requested is approval to proceed to detailed design, not to construction.
input:
Case

This proposal sets out the case for fitting a solar installation on the roof of the building, and seeks approval to proceed to the stage of detailed design. The building currently purchases the whole of its electricity, and generation on the roof would act to displace purchased electricity during those hours when the building is occupied and the array is generating. The roof represents, in effect, the one surface available on the site which is capable of accommodating an array without encroaching upon land, yard space, or parking, and it is at present entirely unused. The case for the installation rests substantially upon the match which exists between generation and use: the building is occupied throughout the daylight hours, with the welcome consequence that the greater part of the generation is consumed on site at the very moment it is produced, and only the surplus arising at weekends and during the brightest periods is exported. Since export is worth appreciably less than displaced purchase, the value of the installation stands or falls on self-consumption, and the case has accordingly been stated on that basis. It is to be noted that the case presupposes no change in the building's use or in the level of its demand: the array is sized against the demand which the building already exhibits, and any fall in demand would diminish both the self-consumed share and the value along with it. Detailed design constitutes the stage at which the output of the actual roof is properly established, by reference to its orientation, its shading, and the area which the structure permits to be covered, rather than by reference to the generic figures which a case at the present stage is obliged to employ.

Costs

The capital cost of the installation is $1334k. The appraisal has been carried out over a horizon of 15 years, and the costs and savings falling within that horizon are those of the installation itself: the maintenance of the array and of its mountings, cleaning in so far as the exposure of the roof renders cleaning necessary, insurance, and the replacement of the inverters, which falls inside the horizon and is treated as a cost of the project rather than as a cost of the building. Set against these costs are the savings: the purchased electricity displaced by generation consumed on site, valued at the tariff which the building pays, together with the more modest return obtained on exported surplus. The capital cost of $1334k is to be understood as a budget figure at this stage; it will be fixed by tender following detailed design, and the appraisal will be rerun on the tendered figure before any decision regarding construction is taken. The savings appearing in the appraisal are estimates derived from the expected output of the roof and from the tariff currently in force; no output has as yet been measured on the building, and the appraisal accordingly records the savings as estimates throughout. The sensitivity of the case is, in essence, the sensitivity of these two figures: a tender exceeding the budget figure and an output falling short of the estimate act upon the return in one and the same direction, and either of them alone suffices to narrow the margin which the case presents. For the avoidance of doubt, the capital figure embraces the design, the surveys, the array together with its mountings, the inverters, the connection, and the metering; it does not embrace renewal of the roof covering itself, which forms part of the building's own programme and would fall to be spent whether the installation proceeded or not, so that to charge it to the project would be to charge one and the same item of work to two budgets simultaneously. The savings, for their part, are valued year by year at the tariff in force at the date of the appraisal, held level throughout the horizon; a rise in the tariff would enhance the value of the purchase displaced and would thereby improve the return, whilst a fall would act in precisely the contrary direction, and the appraisal, it should be noted, takes credit for neither movement, the return being presented throughout at present prices.

Schedule

Work will commence one quarter after approval has been given. The first stage consists of the detailed design itself, with the structural survey of the roof and the application for the connection being progressed within it. Procurement follows on from the design: the array, the mountings, and the inverters will be ordered once the design has fixed their respective specifications, and it is the lead times attaching to those orders which determine the interval which must elapse before installation can begin. Installation is to be planned in such a manner as to keep the building in use throughout, the roof work being sequenced so that the building remains weather-tight at the conclusion of each stage of the mounting work, and the electrical connection being effected in a single planned interruption arranged in agreement with the occupants. Commissioning brings the sequence to a close: the generation meter is fitted, the export arrangement is registered, and the output is read against the estimate from the first period of operation onwards. No contractor is named in this proposal; appointment will follow the tender which the detailed design serves to prepare, and the schedule has accordingly been stated in terms of stages reckoned from approval rather than in terms of dates drawn from a contractor's programme.

Decision requested

The decision which is requested is approval to proceed to detailed design, and not to construction. Detailed design will settle the questions which the case, at this stage, cannot: whether the structure of the roof is capable of carrying the array and its mountings with the margin which the structure requires, what layout is left available by the roof's obstructions and shading, what the connection will cost and on what terms the export will be accepted, and what fixed price the tender will return. Each of these answers bears directly upon the figures which the appraisal presents. Construction represents a second and separate decision, to be taken when the design and the tender price are both in hand, and this proposal seeks no commitment whatsoever to it at the present time. Approval of detailed design commits the design fee and the costs of the surveys, and nothing beyond them. Should the design demonstrate that the roof cannot carry the array, or should the tender return a price at which the appraisal fails, the project comes to a halt at that point, with the design costs expended and the construction cost remaining uncommitted. The board is therefore asked to approve the design stage, on the basis of the appraisal as stated, with the decision on construction expressly reserved. The alternatives open to the board at this juncture are three in number: to approve the design stage, to defer a decision, or to decline the installation altogether. Deferral preserves every option and involves the expenditure of nothing, albeit at the cost of separating the installation from the roof works and of reopening the appraisal in due course at the prices of a later date. Declining brings the matter to a definitive close and leaves the building dependent, as at present, upon purchased electricity in its entirety. Approval, by contrast, is the sole alternative which generates the evidence — the survey report upon the structure, the layout which the roof proves capable of accepting, the offer of connection together with its terms, and the price returned by tender — upon which a properly informed decision as to construction can subsequently be founded, and it is accordingly the course which this proposal commends to the board.

The design stage delivers the evidence the second decision needs: the survey report on the structure, the layout the roof accepts, the connection offer with its terms, and the tender price. fact_base: Goal: compute the Reynolds number for water in a pipe and state the flow regime. The Reynolds number Re (dimensionless) is computed from density rho (kg m-3), mean velocity v (m s-1), pipe diameter D (m) and dynamic viscosity mu (Pa s) by Re = rho v D / mu. Water at 293 K: rho = 998 kg m-3, mu = 1.00 x 10-3 Pa s. Pipe diameter D = 0.08 m; mean velocity v = 0.6 m s-1. Worked result: Re = 47900 (computed as 998 x 0.6 x 0.08 / 0.001). Flow is laminar below Re = 2300 and turbulent above Re = 4000; between the two values the regime is transitional and is not assigned by the number alone.
input:
The task in this worked example is to compute the Reynolds number for water flowing in a pipe, and, having computed it, to state the regime in which the flow finds itself.

The Reynolds number, denoted Re and dimensionless, is computed from the density rho (kg m-3), the mean velocity v (m s-1), the pipe diameter D (m) and the dynamic viscosity mu (Pa s), in accordance with the relation Re = rho v D / mu. The significance of the number lies in the comparison it embodies between the inertial forces acting upon the flow and the viscous forces: where its value is large, inertia is dominant and the flow is prone to turbulence, whereas where its value is small, viscosity prevails and organises the flow into orderly layers.

For water at 293 K, the relevant properties are rho = 998 kg m-3 and mu = 1.00 x 10-3 Pa s. The pipe diameter D is given as 0.08 m and the mean velocity v as 0.6 m s-1. Substituting these values into the relation, we accordingly obtain Re = 998 x 0.6 x 0.08 / 0.001 = 47900.

As a general rule, flow is regarded as laminar below Re = 2300 and as turbulent above Re = 4000, whilst between these two values the regime is transitional in character and cannot be assigned on the basis of the number alone, since a flow lying within that band may behave in either fashion depending upon the disturbances to which it is subject. The value computed here, Re = 47900, lies comfortably above the 4000 threshold, and the flow in the pipe is therefore to be classified as turbulent. It is reassuring to observe that the magnitude of the result is in line with expectation: the diameter and the velocity are both of perfectly ordinary magnitude, whilst the viscosity of water is small, so that a Reynolds number running into the tens of thousands is precisely the order of result one would anticipate, and an answer in the mere hundreds would immediately suggest that an error had crept into the substitution.

The number compares the inertial forces acting on the flow with the viscous forces: where the value is large, inertia dominates and the flow is liable to turbulence; where it is small, viscosity orders the flow into layers.

Between the two values the regime is transitional and is not assigned by the number alone, since a flow in that band may run either way according to the disturbance it carries. The computed value, Re = 47900, stands far above the 4000 threshold, and the flow in the pipe is turbulent. The regime is not a label only: the friction relation and the heat-transfer relation used downstream of the calculation are different relations for laminar and for turbulent flow, so the regime statement is part of the result. The size of the value is the check on the arithmetic: the diameter and velocity are of ordinary magnitude while the viscosity of water is small, so a Reynolds number in the tens of thousands is the expected order, and a result in the hundreds would point to an error in the substitution.

fact_base: A binary distillation separates ethanol/water at a relative volatility of 1.95 that is taken as constant over the column. Specifications: distillate 98 mol% light component, bottoms 2 mol% light component. The Fenske minimum stage count is 11.7 theoretical stages including the reboiler. The actual design uses a reflux ratio of 1.3 times the minimum; the stage count at that reflux comes from a separate simulation.
input:
For a binary distillation separating ethanol from water, the Fenske equation yields a minimum stage count of 11.7 theoretical stages, the reboiler included. The calculation proceeds on a relative volatility of 1.95, taken as constant throughout the column. The specifications are a distillate containing 98 mol% of the light component and bottoms containing 2 mol% of the light component.

The Fenske equation relates the number of stages to the separation accomplished at the two ends of the column, set against the relative volatility: a sharper specification at either end increases the count, and a volatility lying closer to unity increases it quite steeply. The count which the equation delivers is, moreover, the number of stages at total reflux, under which no product is withdrawn and the separation accomplished at each stage attains its maximum. The figure is consequently a minimum in the strict sense: no column separating the stated mixture to the stated specifications can operate with fewer stages, whatever reflux it is given, and every column in practice operates with more. The calculation rests, in addition, on the treatment of the relative volatility as a single number, whereas over an actual column the volatility varies with composition and temperature, and the constant value of 1.95 is the figure with which the calculation is charged for the column as a whole.

The design as proposed does not operate at total reflux. It instead employs a reflux ratio of 1.3 times the minimum, and the stage count at that reflux is obtained from a separate simulation of the column. The Fenske count of 11.7 stages thus bounds the design from below: the simulated count must exceed it, and a simulated count at or below the minimum would betray an error in one of the two calculations. The minimum is reported with the specifications to which it pertains, since the count varies with the specifications and has no meaning apart from them.

fact_base: Goal: compute the diffusive flux of oxygen through a stagnant water film. The diffusive flux J (mol m-2 s-1) is computed from the diffusivity D (m2 s-1) and the concentration gradient dC/dx, where C is concentration (mol m-3) and x is position (m). Fick's first law: J = -D dC/dx; the negative sign states that diffusion runs from high concentration to low concentration. Oxygen in water: D = 2.6 x 10-9 m2 s-1. Concentration falls by 0.4 mol m-3 across a film 0.5 mm thick, so dC/dx = -800 mol m-4. Worked result: J = 2.08x 10-6 mol m-2 s-1. The law as stated covers a stagnant medium; a moving medium adds convection, which the equation does not include.
input:
The object of this example is to compute the diffusive flux of oxygen passing through a stagnant film of water.

The diffusive flux J (mol m-2 s-1) is computed from the diffusivity D (m2 s-1) together with the concentration gradient dC/dx, where C denotes concentration (mol m-3) and x denotes position (m). Fick's first law expresses the flux in the form J = -D dC/dx, the negative sign serving to indicate that the diffusion proceeds in the direction from high concentration towards low concentration.

For oxygen dissolved in water, the diffusivity takes the value D = 2.6 x 10-9 m2 s-1. The concentration is found to fall by 0.4 mol m-3 across a film of thickness 0.5 mm, from which it follows that the concentration gradient dC/dx amounts to -800 mol m-4. Substituting into Fick's first law, we accordingly arrive at a flux of J = 2.08 x 10-6 mol m-2 s-1.

The smallness of the flux will occasion no surprise when it is recalled how small is the diffusivity of a dissolved gas in water, and how the film, slender though it is, nevertheless sustains the entirety of the concentration fall; indeed, it is precisely this slowness of passage across a stagnant film which leads, in gas-liquid contacting, to the film being regarded as the seat of the resistance to transfer. It should finally be observed that the law in the form stated is applicable to a stagnant medium; a medium in motion introduces convection in addition, an effect which the equation as written does not embrace.

Compute the diffusive flux of oxygen through a stagnant water film.

The diffusive flux J (mol m-2 s-1) is computed from the diffusivity D (m2 s-1) and the concentration gradient dC/dx, where C is concentration (mol m-3) and x is position (m). Fick's first law states the flux as J = -D dC/dx; the negative sign states that diffusion runs from high concentration to low concentration.

For oxygen in water, D = 2.6 x 10-9 m2 s-1. The concentration falls by 0.4 mol m-3 across a film 0.5 mm thick, so the concentration gradient dC/dx is -800 mol m-4. The gradient is the average gradient across the film, the concentration fall being taken as spread evenly over the film thickness. Substitution in Fick's first law gives J = 2.08 x 10-6 mol m-2 s-1.

The flux is small because the diffusivity of a dissolved gas in water is small, and the film, though thin, holds the whole of the concentration fall. A dissolved gas crosses a stagnant film slowly, and in a contact between a gas and a liquid the film is the resistance to which the transfer rate is usually charged. At no gradient the law gives no flux, and the sign of the result follows the sign convention of the gradient as stated. Fick's first law as stated holds for a stagnant medium; a moving medium adds convection, which the equation does not include.

fact_base: Project proposal for a fleet electrification, in four sections: case, costs, schedule, and decision requested. Capital cost is $1016k with a 7-year appraisal horizon. The schedule section gives a start one quarter after approval; no contractor is named. The decision requested is approval to proceed to detailed design, not to construction.
input:
Case

This proposal sets out the case for electrifying the vehicle fleet, and seeks approval to proceed to the stage of detailed design. The fleet operates out of the depot upon daily rounds of deliveries and site calls, and each and every vehicle returns to the depot at night. It is this pattern which forms the foundation of the case: vehicles returning nightly to a single base may be charged at that base, from charging infrastructure installed once and thereafter used by the fleet as a whole, whilst the daily rounds are of a length comfortably within the range of the electric vehicles presently offered for this class of work. Replacement provides the occasion for the change. The vehicles comprising the fleet reach the end of their working lives in turn, and every replacement is a purchase which will in any event be made; electrification simply takes those purchases as and when they fall due and directs them towards electric vehicles, rather than withdrawing serviceable vehicles from use prematurely. The case does not invite the board to pass judgement upon electric vehicles in the abstract. It invites the board to consider whether the fleet's own particular duty, operated from its own depot, is the species of duty which electric vehicles are well suited to serve, the contention being that the return-to-base pattern in conjunction with the short daily rounds renders it so. What the fleet surrenders in the exchange is the flexibility attaching to a vehicle which may be despatched anywhere at a moment's notice upon a tank replenished in a matter of minutes; the detailed design stage will test the duty records against that loss before any question of purchase is entertained.

Costs

The capital cost amounts to $1016k. The appraisal has been conducted over a horizon of 7 years. The capital cost of $1016k embraces the difference in price between the electric vehicles and the diesel vehicles which they replace, the charging installation at the depot, and such electrical work as the depot supply necessitates in order to support the charging load. Within the horizon, the running costs of the electric fleet are set against those of the diesel fleet which it displaces: electricity as against diesel fuel, and the maintenance of vehicles possessing fewer wearing parts as against the maintenance of engines, gearboxes, and exhaust treatment systems. The savings appearing in the appraisal are estimates, and estimates only. No electric vehicle has as yet been operated upon the fleet's rounds, and the consumption figures underlying the savings are the manufacturers' figures for the class rather than measurements gathered from the fleet's own duty. The appraisal duly records them as estimates, and the first vehicles to enter service will furnish the measured figures against which the remainder of the programme will be judged. Any shortfall in the saving will bear upon the appraisal of every subsequent replacement, each of which is appraised upon an identical basis.

Schedule

Work will commence one quarter after approval has been granted. The first stage comprises the detailed design itself: the duty records of the fleet are to be examined vehicle by vehicle, the depot supply assessed, and the charging layout definitively fixed. Procurement follows upon the design, vehicles being ordered against the replacement dates which the fleet already carries, in such a way that no vehicle is purchased in advance of its predecessor falling due. The charging installation is to be constructed in advance of the arrival of the first electric vehicle, and extended thereafter as the fleet progressively turns over. No contractor is named in this proposal; the installer will be appointed by means of a tender once the design has fixed the installation in detail. The schedule is expressed in terms of stages reckoned from approval for the reason that it is the replacement dates, and not the project, which dictate the pace of the changeover: the fleet becomes electric at the rate at which its vehicles fall due, and at no greater rate.

Decision requested

The decision which is requested is approval to proceed to detailed design, and not to the purchase of vehicles. Detailed design will resolve the questions which the case is unable to resolve: which of the vehicles upon the market are capable of covering the fleet's longest rounds with the margin which winter operation demands, whether the depot supply is capable of bearing the charging load of the fleet in its entirety or stands in need of reinforcement, what the charging installation will cost when put out to tender, and what the vehicles themselves will cost at tender. Every one of these answers bears directly upon the appraisal. Purchase constitutes a second decision, to be taken replacement by replacement as each falls due, in the light of the design and of the tender prices then in hand. Approval of detailed design commits the design fee together with the costs of the surveys, and nothing whatsoever beyond them. Should the design demonstrate that the duty cannot in fact be covered, or that the supply cannot be reinforced at a cost which the appraisal is able to carry, the programme halts at that point, the fleet continuing upon diesel as and when its replacements fall due.

The proposal is to electrify the vehicle fleet and to proceed to detailed design. The fleet works from the depot on daily rounds of deliveries and site calls, and every vehicle returns to the depot at night. That pattern is the ground of the case: vehicles that return to one base each night are charged at that base, from charging installed once and used by the whole fleet, and the daily rounds are short enough to sit within the range of the electric vehicles offered for this class of work. The depot is also where the fleet is maintained, so charging, maintenance, and parking sit on the one site. Replacement is the occasion. The vehicles in the fleet reach the end of their working lives in turn, and each replacement is a purchase that will be made in any case; electrification takes those purchases as they fall due and directs them to electric vehicles, rather than retiring serviceable vehicles early. The case does not ask the board to judge electric vehicles in general. It asks whether the fleet's own duty, run from its own depot, is the duty electric vehicles serve well, and the case is that the return-to-base pattern and the short daily rounds make it so. What the fleet gives up is the flexibility of a vehicle that can be sent anywhere at any notice on a tank filled in minutes; the detailed design stage tests the duty records against that loss before any purchase is proposed. Charging is taken overnight, while the vehicles stand in the depot and the site's own demand is at its lowest, so the charging load does not add to the peak the site draws. The drivers' working pattern does not change: vehicles leave charged in the morning and return at night, and no round in the fleet's present duty depends on refuelling away from the depot, which is the condition that makes a single charging site sufficient.

Costs

The capital cost is $1016k. The appraisal is run over a horizon of 7 years. The capital cost of $1016k covers the difference in price between the electric vehicles and the diesel vehicles they replace, the charging installation at the depot, and the electrical work the depot supply requires to carry the charging load. Within the horizon, the running costs of the electric fleet are set against those of the diesel fleet it displaces: electricity against diesel fuel, and maintenance of vehicles with fewer wearing parts against maintenance of engines, gearboxes, and exhaust treatment. The savings in the appraisal are estimates. No electric vehicle has yet run the fleet's rounds, and the consumption figures behind the savings are the makers' figures for the class, not measurements on the fleet's own duty. The appraisal records them as estimates, and the first vehicles in service give the measured figures against which the rest of the programme is judged. A shortfall in the saving acts on the appraisal of every later replacement, since each is appraised on the same basis. The vehicles are appraised over the horizon as whole vehicles: no separate value is set on the battery, and no battery replacement is charged within the horizon, the makers' cover being taken to run with the vehicle for its life in the fleet. Costs that do not change between the two fleets are excluded from both sides of the appraisal: the drivers, the depot itself, and the staff who maintain the fleet serve either fleet alike, and charging them to one side only would distort the comparison the appraisal exists to make.

Schedule

Work starts one quarter after approval. The first stage is the detailed design: the duty records of the fleet are examined vehicle by vehicle, the depot supply is assessed, and the charging layout is fixed. Procurement follows the design, with vehicles ordered against the replacement dates the fleet already carries, so that no vehicle is bought before its predecessor falls due. The charging installation is built before the first electric vehicle arrives, and is extended as the fleet turns over. No contractor is named in the proposal; the installer is appointed by tender once the design fixes the installation. Progress is reported to the board at its regular meetings against the stages stated here. The schedule is stated in stages from approval because the replacement dates, not the project, set the pace of the changeover: the fleet is electric at the rate at which its vehicles fall due, and not faster.

Decision requested

The decision requested is approval to proceed to detailed design, not to the purchase of vehicles. Detailed design settles the questions the case cannot: which vehicles on the market cover the fleet's longest rounds with the margin winter running requires, whether the depot supply carries the charging load of the whole fleet or must be reinforced, what the charging installation costs at tender, and what the vehicles cost at tender. Each answer acts directly on the appraisal. Purchase is a second decision, taken replacement by replacement as each falls due, on the design and the tender prices then in hand. Approval of detailed design commits the design fee and the survey costs, and nothing beyond them. If the design shows the duty cannot be covered, or the supply cannot be reinforced at a cost the appraisal carries, the programme stops there, with the fleet continuing on diesel as its replacements fall due.

fact_base: Goal: compute the half-life of a first-order reaction and the fraction remaining after 60 min. For a first-order reaction the rate constant k (min-1) fixes the half-life t1/2 (min) by t1/2 = ln(2) / k, and the fraction remaining after time t (min) is exp(-k t). Measured rate constant: k = 0.069 min-1 at 323 K, from concentration measurements every 5 min over 90 min. Worked results: t1/2 = 10 min; the fraction remaining after 60 min is 0.02 (dimensionless), both computed from the stated relations. The relations hold for a first-order reaction only; a reaction of another order follows a different decay law.
input:
The task is to compute the half-life of a reaction which proceeds according to first-order kinetics, together with the fraction of the reactant which remains after 60 min has elapsed.

For a reaction of the first order, the rate constant k (min-1) determines the half-life t1/2 (min) through the relation t1/2 = ln(2) / k, whilst the fraction of reactant remaining after a time t (min) is given by exp(-k t). The half-life may be understood as the time taken for the amount present to fall to one half of the amount with which the interval began, and it is a characteristic feature of first-order behaviour that this time is the same at every stage of the decay, the rate being at all times proportional to the amount which remains.

The rate constant has been measured as k = 0.069 min-1 at 323 K, the value resting upon concentration measurements taken every 5 min over a period of 90 min. Substituting into the relations set out above, we accordingly obtain t1/2 = 10 min, whilst the fraction remaining after 60 min works out at 0.02.

It will be observed that the results hang together in the manner which the definition leads one to expect: following the elapse of one half-life the fraction remaining is one half, and each successive half-life halves the fraction yet again, so that the residue surviving at the stated time is a small one, exactly as the computed figure indicates. It must, however, be emphasised that these relations are peculiar to a reaction of the first order; a reaction obeying a different order follows a different law of decay, and neither the half-life nor the fraction remaining can be carried across to such a case.
target:
Compute the half-life of a first-order reaction, and the fraction of the reactant remaining after 60 min.

For a first-order reaction, the rate constant k (min-1) fixes the half-life t1/2 (min) by t1/2 = ln(2) / k, and the fraction remaining after a time t (min) is exp(-k t). The half-life is the time in which the amount falls to one half of the amount at the start of the interval. The half-life of a first-order reaction is the same at every point of the decay, because the rate is proportional to the amount present: each interval of one half-life removes the same fraction of what the interval began with, however much that is. The temperature is stated with the rate constant because the constant belongs to the reaction at that temperature and at no other.

The measured rate constant is k = 0.069 min-1 at 323 K, from concentration measurements every 5 min over 90 min. Substitution in the two relations gives t1/2 = 10 min, and the fraction remaining after 60 min is 0.02.

The measurement run covers many half-lives, so the decay is followed from the initial concentration down to a small residue, and the rate constant is fitted over the whole course of the reaction rather than over its opening alone. The results are consistent with the definition of the half-life: after one half-life the fraction remaining is one half, and each further half-life halves the fraction again, so the residue at the end of the stated time is small, as the computed fraction states. The relations hold for a first-order reaction only; a reaction of another order follows a different decay law, and neither the half-life nor the fraction remaining transfers to it.

fact_base: Liquid-liquid extraction recovers acetic acid from an aqueous stream into an organic solvent. The distribution coefficient (organic over aqueous) is 0.82 at 25 °C and the design uses 6 countercurrent stages. Predicted recovery is 99% of the acetic acid in the feed. The prediction assumes equilibrium stages and negligible mutual solubility; neither has been checked on the actual solvents.
input: Liquid–liquid extraction is widely recognised as a powerful and versatile separation technique, and in this particular case it is being leveraged to recover acetic acid from an aqueous stream by transferring it into an organic solvent phase. It is important to note that the distribution coefficient, which expresses the ratio between the concentration in the organic phase and the concentration in the aqueous phase, has a value of 0.82 at 25 °C, and this single parameter plays a crucial role in governing how the separation is expected to perform. The design that has been developed around this system makes use of 6 countercurrent stages, an arrangement in which the two phases move in opposite directions so that a favourable concentration driving force can be maintained throughout the cascade. On the basis of this configuration, the predicted recovery is an impressive 99% of the acetic acid present in the feed, a figure that, at first glance, appears to suggest a highly effective separation. It is, however, worth emphasising that this prediction ultimately rests on assumptions that should not be overlooked: the stages are assumed to behave as equilibrium stages, and the mutual solubility of the two solvents is assumed to be negligible. Crucially, neither of these assumptions has yet been checked against the actual solvents that would be used in practice, which means that the predicted recovery should be interpreted with a degree of caution, since real behaviour may deviate from the idealised picture in ways that are difficult to anticipate in advance.
target: Liquid–liquid extraction into an organic solvent recovers acetic acid from an aqueous stream, and the design prediction is a recovery of 99% of the acetic acid in the feed. The distribution coefficient, the concentration in the organic phase divided by the concentration in the aqueous phase, is 0.82 at 25 °C. The design uses 6 countercurrent stages, with the aqueous feed and the solvent passing in opposite directions through the cascade. Countercurrent flow keeps the driving force distributed along the cascade: the leanest solvent meets the most depleted aqueous phase, and the richest solvent meets the incoming feed. A prediction at this level rests on the staging model behind it. Each stage is treated as an equilibrium stage: the phases leaving a stage are taken to stand in the ratio the distribution coefficient states. The two liquids are treated as mutually insoluble, so each phase keeps its own volume from stage to stage. The coefficient is stated at one temperature, and the prediction inherits that temperature; a plant stream running warmer or colder carries a different distribution and a different recovery. Neither assumption has been checked on the actual solvents. Where the solvents dissolve in each other to a material degree, phase volumes change along the cascade and the staged calculation no longer describes the separation. Where a stage falls short of equilibrium, the same shortfall repeats at every stage and the achieved recovery sits below the prediction. The recovery figure is a property of the model as much as of the solvent pair, and it stands as a prediction until the coefficient and the mutual solubility are measured on the solvents in question.

fact_base: Goal: compute the diffusive flux of oxygen through a stagnant water film. The diffusive flux J (mol m-2 s-1) is computed from the diffusivity D (m2 s-1) and the concentration gradient dC/dx, where C is concentration (mol m-3) and x is position (m). Fick's first law: J = -D dC/dx; the negative sign states that diffusion runs from high concentration to low concentration. Oxygen in water: D = 2.1 x 10-9 m2 s-1. Concentration falls by 0.4 mol m-3 across a film 0.4 mm thick, so dC/dx = -1000 mol m-4. Worked result: J = 2.10x 10-6 mol m-2 s-1. The law as stated covers a stagnant medium; a moving medium adds convection, which the equation does not include.
input: The goal of this worked example is to compute the diffusive flux of oxygen through a stagnant water film, a quantity that is of considerable importance in a wide range of mass-transfer situations. The diffusive flux $J$ (mol m-2 s-1) expresses the amount of oxygen that crosses a unit area in a unit of time. The relationship that governs this behaviour is Fick's first law, $J = -D dC/dx$, in which $D$ (m2 s-1) is the diffusivity, $C$ (mol m-3) is the concentration, and $x$ (m) is the position measured across the film. It is worth pausing on the negative sign, because it carries the physical meaning of the law: diffusion always proceeds from regions of high concentration towards regions of low concentration. For oxygen dissolved in water, the diffusivity takes the value 2.1 x 10-9 m2 s-1. The concentration, for its part, falls by 0.4 mol m-3 across a film that is 0.4 mm thick, which means that the concentration gradient works out to -1000 mol m-4. Bringing these values together in Fick's first law gives a flux $J$ of 2.10 x 10-6 mol m-2 s-1. Note that the law in the form stated here applies to a stagnant medium; once the medium itself is moving, convection enters the picture as an additional contribution that this equation, on its own, does not include.
target: Calculate the diffusive flux of oxygen through a stagnant water film from the diffusivity of oxygen in water and the concentration gradient across the film. The diffusive flux $J$ (mol m-2 s-1) is the amount of oxygen crossing unit area per unit time. Fick's first law relates the flux to the concentration gradient: $J = -D dC/dx$, where $D$ (m2 s-1) denotes the diffusivity, $C$ (mol m-3) the concentration, and $x$ (m) the position across the film. The negative sign in Fick's first law states that diffusion runs from high concentration to low concentration. The diffusivity of oxygen in water is 2.1 x 10-9 m2 s-1. The concentration falls by 0.4 mol m-3 across a film 0.4 mm thick, so the concentration gradient is -1000 mol m-4. The film thickness enters the calculation only through the gradient: the same concentration fall spread over a thicker film gives a smaller gradient and a smaller flux in proportion. The gradient is taken as uniform across the film, which is the form in which the concentration fall is reported. Substitution of the diffusivity and the gradient in Fick's first law gives a flux $J$ of 2.10 x 10-6 mol m-2 s-1. The computed flux is positive in the direction of falling concentration, as the sign convention requires. Fick's first law holds for a stagnant medium; a moving medium adds convection, which the equation does not include.

subtype: worked example with equation: Antoine vapour pressure
fact_base: The vapour pressure of ethanol at 60 °C is estimated from the Antoine equation with constants $A$ = 8.20417, $B$ = 1642.89 and $C$ = 230.3 (pressure in mmHg, temperature in °C). The estimate is 46.8 kPa. The constants are valid only over their fitted temperature range; the source databank value governs design.
input:
Ethanol is a widely used solvent and fuel component, and knowing its vapour pressure at a given temperature is essential for a whole host of design and safety calculations. In this case, the vapour pressure of ethanol at 60 °C is estimated by means of the well-known Antoine equation, an empirical correlation that links the vapour pressure $P$ to the temperature $T$ through three substance-specific constants, denoted $A$, $B$ and $C$:

$$\log_{10} P = A - \frac{B}{T + C}$$

It should be noted that, in this formulation, $P$ is expressed in mmHg while $T$ is expressed in °C. For ethanol, the constants take the values $A$ = 8.20417, $B$ = 1642.89 and $C$ = 230.3, and inserting the temperature of interest alongside these constants leads to an estimated vapour pressure of 46.8 kPa. This is certainly a convenient result, but it comes with an important caveat that should never be forgotten: the constants are only valid over the temperature range over which they were originally fitted, and outside that range the correlation can behave in unexpected and potentially misleading ways. For this reason, wherever a design decision genuinely matters, it is the value held in the source databank that should govern, with the Antoine estimate serving as a useful preliminary figure rather than as a definitive answer that can simply be carried into detailed design work without further scrutiny or checking against measured data.
target:
The vapour pressure of ethanol at 60 °C is estimated from the Antoine equation, which relates the vapour pressure $P$ to the temperature $T$ through three fitted constants, $A$, $B$ and $C$:

$$\log_{10} P = A - \frac{B}{T + C}$$

In the Antoine equation, $P$ is in mmHg and $T$ is in °C. For ethanol, $A$ = 8.20417, $B$ = 1642.89 and $C$ = 230.3. The constant $B$ carries the temperature sensitivity of the vapour pressure: a larger $B$ gives a vapour pressure that climbs faster as temperature rises. The constant $C$ shifts the temperature scale and keeps the denominator finite across the fitted range. The constant $A$ sets the level from which the temperature correction is subtracted. Substitution of the temperature and the constants gives an estimated vapour pressure of 46.8 kPa. An estimate of this kind is used at the screening stage of a design, where the vapour pressure enters a boiling-point or a condenser-duty calculation and a databank search has not yet been run. The estimate is an interpolation device, not a measurement: the constants were fitted over a limited temperature range, and the Antoine equation with these constants is valid only over that fitted range. The fitted range is a property of the data behind the constants, not of the equation, and it is reported with the constants in the source. Outside the range the same constants can depart from the measured vapour pressure without warning in the equation itself. The source databank value governs design, and the Antoine estimate serves where a databank value is absent and the temperature lies inside the fitted range.

fact_base: Adsorption of a dye from water on a zeolite 13X sample was measured in batch tests at 298 K. The fitted Langmuir capacity was 179 mg of dye per gram of adsorbent at pH 7. At an adsorbent dose of 1.2 g L-1, removal after 120 min was 79% of the initial dye concentration of 50 mg L-1. The Langmuir fit is reported for pH 7 only; capacity at other pH values was not measured.
input: Batch adsorption tests were carried out in order to investigate the uptake of a dye from water using a sample of zeolite 13X, with all of the measurements performed at a temperature of 298 K. The data were fitted to the Langmuir model, and the fitted Langmuir capacity came out at 179 mg of dye per gram of adsorbent at pH 7, a value that reflects the levelling-off behaviour captured by the isotherm. In a further test, an adsorbent dose of 1.2 g L-1 was employed, and under these conditions the removal achieved after 120 min amounted to 79% of the initial dye concentration of 50 mg L-1. It is important to appreciate that these results, encouraging as they may appear, come with a significant limitation that is easy to overlook: the Langmuir fit has been reported for pH 7 only, and the capacity at other pH values was simply not measured, so there is no basis for assuming that a similar performance would be obtained if the solution were more acidic or more alkaline than the condition that was actually tested. The tests were, in other words, conducted under a single, well-defined set of conditions, and the results belong to those conditions and to no others.
target: Adsorption of a dye from water on zeolite 13X was measured in batch tests at 298 K. Batch tests hold the adsorbent and the solution together in a closed vessel, so the measured removal is a property of the test as run, at the stated dose and contact time. The fitted Langmuir capacity was 179 mg of dye per gram of adsorbent at pH 7. The Langmuir capacity is the uptake at which the fitted isotherm levels off, and it is reported here as a property of the fit. At an adsorbent dose of 1.2 g L-1, removal after 120 min was 79% of the initial dye concentration of 50 mg L-1. The initial concentration fixes the amount of dye available per unit volume of solution at the stated dose. The two figures describe different things: the capacity is a fitted property of the isotherm, while the removal is an outcome of the dose, the contact time and the starting concentration in one batch test. A higher dose or a longer contact time changes the removal without changing the fitted capacity. The Langmuir fit is reported for pH 7 only; capacity at other pH values was not measured. The capacity figure cannot be carried to a treatment duty at a different pH, where the fit offers no value.

fact_base: Capital appraisal for a solar array: installed cost $1596k, expected net saving $257k per year for 12 years. At a discount rate of 6% the present value of the savings is $2155k and the net present value is $559k. Savings are vendor and utility estimates; no saving has yet been measured on a comparable installation.
input: This capital appraisal examines a proposal to install a solar array, and it brings together the principal financial figures that decision-makers will need in order to judge whether the investment is worthwhile. The installed cost of the array comes to $1596k, which represents a substantial upfront commitment of capital. Set against this outlay, the array is expected to deliver a net saving of $257k per year, and this saving is projected to continue for 12 years. Because money received in the future is worth less than money held today, the appraisal applies a discount rate of 6% in order to express the future savings in present-day terms. On this basis, the present value of the savings works out at $2155k. Subtracting the installed cost from this figure gives a net present value of $559k, which is positive and therefore points, on the face of it, towards an attractive investment. It must nevertheless be stressed that the savings underpinning the entire calculation are vendor and utility estimates, and that no saving has yet been measured on a comparable installation, so the figures should be treated as projections rather than as established facts.
target: The solar array returns a net present value of $559k at a discount rate of 6%. The installed cost is $1596k. Expected net saving is $257k per year for 12 years, and the present value of the savings is $2155k, which exceeds the installed cost by the amount of the net present value. The array is appraised as a capital purchase set against a stream of avoided electricity purchases. The discount rate converts each year's saving to its present value before the savings are summed; the net present value is what remains after the installed cost is set against that sum. The appraisal horizon is the period over which the vendor and utility figures are projected, and no saving beyond that horizon is credited to the array. The case rests on the saving figure, and the saving figure is an estimate. The savings are vendor and utility estimates; no saving has yet been measured on a comparable installation. A shortfall in the annual saving passes directly into the net present value: the appraisal holds no measured performance to set against the estimate. The decision the appraisal supports is conditional on the saving being achieved at close to the estimated level, and a measured saving from a comparable array, once one exists, replaces the estimate as the basis of the case.

fact_base: Excerpt content: two groups report conflicting lifetime values for the same material class; the excerpt weighs their test conditions. The excerpt reaches a limited preference and states the condition on which it rests.
input: The picture that emerges from the two lifetime reports is, at first sight, a rather confusing one, because the two groups appear to contradict one another flatly about how long the benchmark material can be expected to last. A closer look, however, suggests that the disagreement may be more apparent than real, since the two groups did not in fact age the benchmark material under the same conditions at all. One of the groups cycled the benchmark material using a dry feed and regenerated it under relatively gentle conditions that the material is known to tolerate well, whereas the other group deliberately worked with a humid feed and a considerably more aggressive regeneration, and the shorter lifetime it reports is therefore, to a significant extent, a reflection of that harsher duty rather than a property of the material alone. It has to be remembered that, for this class of materials, lifetime is intimately bound up with the cycling duty: the humidity of the feed determines the water load that the pores are required to surrender at every regeneration, and the severity of the regeneration determines how much of the framework each individual cycle consumes. It follows that a lifetime measured under one duty can only really be transferred to another duty when the two duties correspond in precisely these respects. The preference that emerges is accordingly a limited one: for a dry feed combined with the milder style of regeneration, the value reported by the first group is the more trustworthy guide, because its test reproduces the loads that govern the loss of capacity, whereas for humid service it is the second group's figure, lower though it is, that the design should carry. Neither report, it should be said, actually provides a lifetime at a declared cycling count with the feed humidity and the regeneration severity both stated alongside it.
target: The conflict between the two lifetime reports is narrower than the reported values suggest, because the two groups did not age the benchmark material under the same conditions. The benchmark material is the same in both studies; the synthesis route and the activation are reported in the same terms, so the difference in outcome is not explained by the specimen. One group cycled the benchmark material under a dry feed and regenerated at a severity the material tolerates well; the other group worked with a humid feed and a harder regeneration, and its shorter lifetime is a record of that duty as much as of the material. Lifetime in this class of materials is a property of the cycling duty: the feed humidity sets the water load the pores must give up at each regeneration, and the regeneration severity sets how much of the framework each cycle costs. The two reports also agree on more than they dispute: the material class, the benchmark specimen, and the direction in which harsher duty shortens life are common ground between them. A lifetime measured under either duty transfers to a new duty only where the two duties match in those respects. On that basis the preference here is limited: for a dry feed with regeneration of the milder kind, the first group's value is the better guide, because its test reproduces the loads that govern the loss of capacity. The preference does not extend to humid service, where the second group's conditions are the closer match and its value, though lower, is the one the design should carry. What neither report supplies is a lifetime under a stated cycling count with the feed humidity and the regeneration severity both declared alongside it, and until such a report exists the comparison stays where the present section leaves it, on the match of conditions rather than on the standing of either group.

fact_base: A contract packaging firm runs 3 plants; revenue is $60 million per year. Evidence base: order records for 12 months, 15733 orders. On-time delivery over the last two quarters was 86%, against a target of 95%. Overtime cost was $1.7 million last year, up 22% on the year before. The order backlog stands at 3.2 weeks, against 2.1 weeks a year ago. Plant 2 accounts for 58% of late orders. A scheduling system for all plants is quoted at $351k; Plant 2 alone is $157k. An internal estimate (not a vendor figure) puts the overtime reduction at Plant 2 at 15-20% in the first year. The recommendation under consideration: install at Plant 2 first, hold the other plants until Plant 2 results are reported. The operations director owns the scheduling programme.
input: This summary reviews the delivery performance of a contract packaging firm that operates 3 plants and generates revenue of $60 million per year. The analysis draws on the firm's order records for 12 months, encompassing no fewer than 15733 orders, and the picture that emerges is a concerning one. Over the last two quarters, on-time delivery stood at 86%, which falls noticeably short of the target of 95% that the firm has set itself. At the same time, the order backlog has grown to 3.2 weeks, compared with 2.1 weeks a year ago, and the cost of overtime reached $1.7 million last year, an increase of 22% on the year before. A closer examination of the data reveals that the problem is far from evenly spread: Plant 2 accounts for 58% of all late orders, which strongly suggests that the difficulties are concentrated in one location rather than systemic. Against this background, a scheduling system covering all plants has been quoted at $351k, while Plant 2 alone would cost $157k. An internal estimate — not a vendor figure, and therefore to be treated with some caution — suggests that overtime at Plant 2 could be reduced by 15–20% in the first year. The recommendation under consideration is accordingly to install the system at Plant 2 first and to hold the other plants until Plant 2 results are reported, with the operations director owning the scheduling programme.
target: Install the scheduling system at Plant 2 first, and hold the other plants until Plant 2 results are reported; the operations director owns the scheduling programme. The firm is a contract packaging business, and delivery reliability is the term on which its contracts are renewed. The evidence base is order records for 12 months, covering 15733 orders across the firm's 3 plants, which take $60 million of revenue per year. On-time delivery over the last two quarters was 86%, against a target of 95%. The two-quarter figure is the current run rate, measured against the same target the contracts carry. The order backlog stands at 3.2 weeks, against 2.1 weeks a year ago, and overtime cost was $1.7 million last year, up 22% on the year before. Overtime is the mechanism by which the plants currently protect delivery dates, and its cost is the price of the present shortfall. Late orders concentrate at Plant 2, which accounts for 58% of them. A scheduling system for all plants is quoted at $351k; Plant 2 alone is $157k, so the staged installation commits the smaller sum against the plant that carries most of the lateness. An internal estimate, not a vendor figure, puts the overtime reduction at Plant 2 at 15–20% in the first year. The staged route also bounds the commitment: if the results fall short of the estimate, the remaining plants have not yet been committed.

fact_base: Excerpt content: the absorber wall thickness is 90 mm after the corrosion allowance is added. The excerpt compares two gasket materials on temperature limit only and prefers the higher-rated one. The excerpt ends mid-argument; it neither summarises the report nor previews the next section.
input: The thickness of the wall of the absorber, once the corrosion allowance has been added on top of the thickness required by the pressure calculation, works out at 90 mm, and it is worth appreciating that the margin contained in this figure is provided by the allowance rather than by the pressure calculation itself. The corrosion allowance is, of course, gradually consumed over the life of the vessel, which means that the thickness present at commissioning is not the thickness the pressure case sees late in the inspection interval. Turning to the gasket that seals the same joint, the two candidate materials have been compared on the basis of temperature limit alone. One of the two materials is rated to a significantly higher temperature than the other, and it is the higher-rated material that is preferred, because the joint is exposed to the full operating temperature of the absorber, so that a gasket operating right at the limit of its rating would be left with no margin to accommodate any excursion. It should be emphasised that temperature limit is the only ground on which the two materials are being compared here; sealing behaviour under pressure belongs to the flange calculation, where the $\Delta P$ across the joint appears as a load case rather than as a ground for selection. Circulation against which the absorber operates is established by the lean solvent pump, and its NPSH margin is derived from the suction condition at the operating level, a condition that neither the wall thickness nor the gasket selection has any bearing upon. An open interaction between the two choices remains, in that a gasket which creeps at temperature relaxes the bolt load that the wall thickness calculation takes for granted, and the rate of that relaxation at the operating temperature is the quantity the comparison still has to establish.
target: The wall thickness of the absorber comes to 90 mm once the corrosion allowance is added to the pressure thickness, and the margin that figure carries is set by the allowance rather than by the pressure calculation. The corrosion allowance is consumed over the life of the vessel, so the thickness at commissioning is not the thickness the pressure case sees at the end of the interval between inspections. The gasket choice in the same joint is governed by a different limit. Of the two gasket materials carried forward, one is rated to the higher temperature, and the higher-rated material is preferred: the joint sees the full operating temperature of the absorber, and a gasket at its temperature limit has no allowance left for an excursion. Temperature limit is the only ground on which the two materials are compared here; the sealing behaviour at pressure belongs to the flange calculation, where $\Delta P$ across the joint enters as a load case rather than as a selection ground. Circulation that the absorber works against is set by the lean solvent pump, and its NPSH margin is taken from the suction condition at the operating level, a condition the wall and gasket choices do not change. What remains open in this section is the interaction between the two choices: a gasket that creeps at temperature relaxes the bolt load that the wall thickness calculation assumes, and the relaxation rate at the rated temperature is the next quantity the comparison has to establish before either material is released.

fact_base: Pricing case for a SaaS tier: price $239 per unit, variable cost $166 per unit, fixed costs $248k per year. Break-even volume is 3397 units per year; current volume is 7966 units per year. Volume figures are last year's actuals; the effect of the price on volume is not estimated.
input: This pricing case considers a SaaS tier and asks, in essence, how much volume the tier needs to sell in order to cover its costs. The tier is priced at $239 per unit, while the variable cost associated with each unit comes to $166 per unit. In addition, the business carries fixed costs of $248k per year, which have to be met regardless of how many units are sold. Bringing these figures together, the break-even volume works out at 3397 units per year, the level of sales at which the total contribution from the units sold exactly matches the fixed costs. Encouragingly, the current volume stands at 7966 units per year, which is comfortably above the break-even level and suggests that the tier is operating with a reasonable margin of safety. Two caveats should nevertheless be kept in mind when interpreting these numbers. The volume figures are last year's actuals, and as such they describe how the tier actually performed in the past rather than how it is guaranteed to perform in the future. Furthermore, the effect of the price on volume has not been estimated, which means that the analysis is silent on the question of how demand would respond if the price were to be changed in either direction.
target: Break-even volume for the SaaS tier is 3397 units per year. The price is $239 per unit and the variable cost is $166 per unit, so each unit sold contributes the difference between the two toward the fixed costs of $248k per year; the break-even volume is the fixed costs divided by that contribution. The contribution is stated per unit and the fixed costs per year, which is why the break-even figure carries units of volume per year rather than revenue. Current volume is 7966 units per year, more than double the break-even volume. The tier covers its fixed costs at the current price with room to spare, and a fall in volume could be absorbed down to the break-even point before the tier moved into loss. Two qualifications bound that statement. The volume figures are last year's actuals: they describe the tier as it sold, at the price then charged, and not necessarily as it will sell. The effect of the price on volume is not estimated, so the appraisal cannot say whether a price change would raise or lower the contribution the tier earns. A price rise increases the contribution per unit and reduces the break-even volume arithmetically, but it may also reduce the volume itself, and the second effect is the one the figures do not measure. The break-even statement is a yearly statement: it sets the year's contribution against the year's fixed costs and says nothing about the timing of sales within the year.

fact_base: Carbon dioxide and hydrogen react over a copper-zinc oxide catalyst to give dimethyl ether. Space-time yield is the mass of product per unit catalyst volume per hour (kg L-1 h-1). Test conditions: 230 °C, 60 bar, feed ratio H2/CO2 = 3, one feed composition. Washcoated monolith catalyst: space-time yield 1.1 kg L-1 h-1, pressure drop 0.23 bar, activity loss 6% after 100 h. Extruded pellet catalyst: space-time yield 0.48 kg L-1 h-1, pressure drop 1.02 bar, activity loss 14% after 100 h. No sulfur-bearing feed was tested. Yield and pressure drop are seldom reported for the same catalyst charge.
input: The production of dimethyl ether from carbon dioxide and hydrogen over a copper–zinc oxide catalyst is a reaction of growing interest, and this study sets out to compare two different physical forms of the catalyst: a washcoated monolith and an extruded pellet. In order to ensure a fair comparison, both catalysts were tested under identical conditions, namely at a temperature of 230 °C and a pressure of 60 bar, with an H2/CO2 feed ratio of 3 and a single feed composition. The performance of each catalyst was assessed in terms of the space-time yield, which is defined as the mass of product obtained per unit catalyst volume per hour (kg L-1 h-1). The results show that the washcoated monolith achieved a space-time yield of 1.1 kg L-1 h-1, accompanied by a remarkably low pressure drop of just 0.23 bar and an activity loss of only 6% after 100 h of operation. The extruded pellet, by contrast, delivered a space-time yield of 0.48 kg L-1 h-1, together with a considerably higher pressure drop of 1.02 bar and an activity loss of 14% after 100 h. It is worth noting, however, that no sulfur-bearing feed was tested in this work, and it should also be borne in mind that yield and pressure drop are seldom reported for the same catalyst charge, which can make comparisons of this kind more difficult than they might otherwise appear.
target: Dimethyl ether synthesis from carbon dioxide and hydrogen was compared over a copper–zinc oxide catalyst in two forms, a washcoated monolith and an extruded pellet. The two forms carry the same catalyst and differ in the geometry in which the catalyst is presented to the feed: the washcoat presents the catalyst as a layer on a channelled support, and the pellet as a bed of formed particles. Both catalysts were tested at 230 °C and 60 bar with an H2/CO2 feed ratio of 3, at one feed composition. Space-time yield, the mass of product per unit catalyst volume per hour (kg L-1 h-1), was the comparison measure. The monolith gave a space-time yield of 1.1 kg L-1 h-1 with a pressure drop of 0.23 bar and an activity loss of 6% after 100 h. The pellet gave a space-time yield of 0.48 kg L-1 h-1 with a pressure drop of 1.02 bar and an activity loss of 14% after 100 h. The monolith couples the higher yield with the lower pressure drop and the slower activity loss on this feed, and the pressure drop difference between the two forms is a consequence of their geometries. The comparison is a single-feed comparison: no sulfur-bearing feed was tested, and the yield ranking under a sulfur-bearing feed is untested. Yield and pressure drop are also seldom reported for the same catalyst charge; a charge reported for yield alone leaves its pressure drop to be inferred from other work, and the paired figures here are the basis on which the two forms can be set against each other at all.

topic: tut:phase:a binary mixture at fixed pressure
fact_base: A tutorial passage explains phase equilibrium for a binary mixture at fixed pressure. The passage states the equilibrium condition in words (equality of chemical potential across phases) before any equation is named. No numerical data are introduced; the passage is conceptual.
input: It is important to note that phase equilibrium is a truly fundamental concept in the study of mixtures, serving as the cornerstone for understanding how different phases coexist and interact within a system. In essence, when a binary mixture is held at a fixed pressure, equilibrium is governed by an elegant and powerful condition: the chemical potential of each and every component must be equal across all of the phases in which that component is present, ensuring that the system rests in a stable and balanced state. This essentially means that no component can gain anything by moving from one phase to another, and it is this delicate balance that ultimately defines the equilibrium state of the mixture as a whole. Consider, for example, a liquid mixture in contact with its own vapour at a fixed pressure. Interestingly, the liquid and the vapour do not share the same composition; rather, the more volatile component is enriched in the vapour phase, highlighting the selective and preferential nature of the transfer process. Furthermore, temperature is not an independent quantity in this particular setting: at fixed pressure, once the liquid composition has been specified, the boiling temperature is determined, and the vapour composition follows accordingly, underscoring the tightly coupled and interdependent nature of these variables. When the chemical potentials are not equal, a driving force exists that moves material between the phases, and this transfer continues until the potentials become equal and the system settles into equilibrium, reflecting the deeper tendency of the mixture to seek its lowest-energy configuration.
target: Phase equilibrium in a binary mixture at fixed pressure rests on one condition: at equilibrium, the chemical potential of each component is the same in every phase in which that component is present. The condition is stated in words because it is the definition from which the working relations come. A mixture is at equilibrium when no component can lower the total Gibbs energy by passing from one phase to another, and equality of chemical potential states that condition for each component separately. Consider a liquid mixture in contact with its vapour at a fixed pressure. The liquid has a composition and the vapour has a composition, and the two compositions differ: the more volatile component is richer in the vapour than in the liquid. Temperature is not free once the pressure and one composition are set. At fixed pressure, a binary mixture in two phases has one remaining degree of freedom, so the temperature of the boiling mixture is fixed by its liquid composition; change the liquid composition and the boiling temperature changes with it, and the vapour composition changes as well. Equilibrium is a relation among temperature and the two compositions at the stated pressure, not a property of either phase alone. Away from equilibrium, the chemical potential of a component differs between the phases, and the difference drives transfer of that component from the phase where its chemical potential is higher to the phase where it is lower, until the potentials meet and net transfer stops. The same condition governs condensation; only the direction of transfer reverses.

fact_base: A tutorial passage explains feedback control through a flow loop on a process vessel. The passage covers the sensor, the controller, the final element and the sign of the feedback, in that order. No tuning numbers are given; the passage explains structure, not settings.
input: Feedback control is a cornerstone of modern process operations, and the humble flow loop provides a particularly clear and instructive illustration of how it works in practice. The purpose of a flow loop is to hold the flow in a line serving a process vessel at its desired set point by acting directly on the flow itself. At the heart of the loop sits the sensor, which measures the flow in the line and transmits the measured value to the controller on a continuous basis. It is worth noting that the loop acts on the reading rather than on the true flow, so any error in the sensor quietly propagates into every subsequent action. The controller then compares the measured value against the set point and calculates an appropriate correction based on the difference between them, which is known as the error. This output is passed to the final element, typically a control valve installed in the line, which adjusts its position in order to change the flow in the required direction. Crucially, the sign of the feedback is negative: a rise in flow above the set point drives the valve toward closed, while a fall below the set point drives it toward open, meaning that the correction always opposes the deviation that produced it. It is this negative character that confers stability on the loop as a structure, since each departure from the set point generates an action that works to reduce that very departure. The description here concerns structure rather than settings; how far the valve travels for a given error, and how quickly the loop responds, are matters of tuning, and no tuning values are given.
target: A flow loop holds the flow in a line serving a process vessel at its set point by acting on the flow itself. The sensor measures the flow in the line and sends the measured value to the controller. A flow sensor reads the rate continuously, and the reading, not the true flow, is what the loop acts on; a sensor error enters every action the loop takes. The controller compares the measured value with the set point and calculates the correction from the difference between them, the error. The controller output goes to the final element, a control valve in the line, which moves to change the flow in the direction the controller demands. The sign of the feedback is negative. A rise in flow above the set point drives the valve toward closed, and a fall in flow below the set point drives the valve toward open, so the correction opposes the deviation that produced it. Negative feedback is what makes the loop stable in structure: each departure from the set point generates an action that reduces the departure. The loop as described is structure only. How far the valve moves for a given error, and how fast the loop responds, are settings, and no settings are stated here. The vessel the line serves receives the result of the loop as a steady inflow; disturbances entering with the flow are corrected in the line itself, before they reach the vessel as a changed charge rate.

fact_base: A contract packaging firm runs 4 plants; revenue is $63 million per year. Evidence base: order records for 12 months, 11099 orders. On-time delivery over the last two quarters was 84%, against a target of 95%. Overtime cost was $2.6 million last year, up 25% on the year before. The order backlog stands at 3.9 weeks, against 1.8 weeks a year ago. Plant 2 accounts for 54% of late orders. A scheduling system for all plants is quoted at $339k; Plant 2 alone is $151k. An internal estimate (not a vendor figure) puts the overtime reduction at Plant 2 at 15-20% in the first year. The recommendation under consideration: install at Plant 2 first, hold the other plants until Plant 2 results are reported. The operations director owns the scheduling programme.
input: This executive summary presents a comprehensive overview of the delivery performance challenges currently facing the business, and sets out the recommendation that is presently under consideration for addressing them. That recommendation is to install the new scheduling system at Plant 2 first, while holding the other plants until Plant 2 results have been reported and reviewed in full. The scheduling programme is owned by the operations director, who will be responsible for its delivery. In terms of the underlying performance picture, on-time delivery over the last two quarters stood at 84%, which compares unfavourably with a target of 95%; these figures are drawn from a robust evidence base consisting of order records for 12 months covering no fewer than 11099 orders. By way of background, the business is a contract packaging firm operating 4 plants, generating revenue of $63 million per year. It is particularly notable that Plant 2 accounts for a disproportionate 54% of all late orders, which clearly indicates that the delivery shortfall is heavily concentrated at a single plant rather than being spread evenly across the wider business. Meanwhile, overtime cost reached $2.6 million last year, up a substantial 25% on the year before, and the order backlog currently stands at 3.9 weeks, compared with just 1.8 weeks a year ago, underscoring the scale of the deterioration. A scheduling system covering all plants has been quoted at $339k, whereas Plant 2 alone comes in at $151k, meaning that the first stage represents less than half of the full programme cost while testing the system precisely where late orders are concentrated. An internal estimate, rather than a vendor figure, suggests that the overtime reduction at Plant 2 could be in the region of 15–20% in the first year. Overall, the staged approach limits the initial commitment to the plant with the clearly measured problem, and allows the case for extending the system to the remaining plants to be built on actual reported results from Plant 2 rather than on estimates alone.

The operations director owns the scheduling programme. fact_base: Excerpt content: two groups report conflicting lifetime values for the same material class; the excerpt weighs their test conditions. The excerpt reaches a limited preference and states the condition on which it rests.
input: It is worth emphasising that the disagreement between the two groups is, on closer inspection, considerably narrower than the headline lifetime figures might initially suggest. Both groups tested the benchmark material, and both ultimately report lifetimes that fall away under precisely the same condition, namely extended exposure to a wet feed; the genuine conflict is over dry service, where one group's values appear to hold up robustly across repeated cycles while the other group's fall away surprisingly early. In essence, the difference sits in the test conditions rather than in the material itself. The first group cycled the benchmark material in a dry single gas and measured lifetime to a fixed loss of capacity, a protocol that never actually loads the structure with water at any point. The second group, by contrast, worked with a humid mixed gas, which is considerably closer to a real separation duty, and its shorter lifetimes may well carry damage attributable to the humidity swings themselves rather than to cycling alone, highlighting an important methodological distinction. Read on those terms, the two sets of results do not truly contradict each other; instead, they bound the benchmark material from two complementary sides. The preference expressed here is for the second group's values wherever the duty is a genuine separation with water present in the feed, precisely because its conditions include the very agent that limits lifetime in service. That preference rests firmly on this condition and reverses for a dry duty, where the first group's protocol represents the closer match and its longer lifetimes provide the better guide. IAST enters both accounts merely as the frame the groups used to compare uptakes, and neither set of lifetimes depends on it in any way.
