fact_base: A review passage on catalysts for carbon dioxide hydrogenation, in four parts: scope, established results, disagreements, and gaps. The review covers 82 papers from the last 12 years. The disagreements part names the quantity on which reports conflict; the gaps part names the measurement nobody reports.
input:
## Scope

This review sets out to survey the rapidly growing literature on catalysts for the hydrogenation of carbon dioxide, a reaction that continues to attract enormous interest as a potential route for converting a waste gas into valuable products. The evidence base for the review consists of 82 papers published over the last 12 years. In broad terms, the reaction involves the conversion of carbon dioxide and hydrogen over a solid catalyst, and the products that are reported across the literature include methanol, methane, carbon monoxide, and higher hydrocarbons. The scope of the review is confined to thermal catalysis, and photochemical and electrochemical approaches, interesting though they are, fall outside it.

The catalyst families that are covered include copper-based catalysts, iron-based catalysts, and catalysts based on noble metals, along with the various supports and promoters that are reported in combination with them. Throughout the review, each paper's reported conversion and selectivity are treated as that author's own statement, made under the conditions that the author reports; where a paper happens not to state a particular condition, the review simply records the omission rather than attempting to supply the missing condition from elsewhere.

## Established results

There is a broad consensus in the literature regarding the general division of the field according to product. Copper-based catalysts are widely regarded as the established system for methanol formation, and their behaviour serves as the benchmark against which newer materials are typically reported. Iron-based catalysts, by contrast, tend to favour the hydrocarbon side of the product spectrum, ranging from methane through to longer-chain products. Noble-metal catalysts are generally reported as highly active systems, although the products they give are strongly dependent on both the metal and the support that is employed.

There is also widespread agreement that water is formed during the reaction and that this water has an effect on the catalyst. Although the direction of the effect varies from one system to another, its existence is not really in question: water is an inevitable product of the hydrogenation, it is present wherever conversion reaches appreciable levels, and a catalyst's ability to tolerate water forms part of its reported character. Another important point of consensus is the trade-off that exists between conversion and selectivity. Conditions that succeed in raising the conversion of carbon dioxide almost invariably shift the product distribution as well, and no report in the set manages to escape this trade-off entirely; the reports differ in where they judge the balance should be struck, rather than in whether such a balance exists at all.

It is further agreed that promoters and supports can change both the activity and the selectivity of a catalyst, in some cases by more than a change in the principal metal itself. The support must therefore be regarded as an integral part of the catalyst as reported, and any result that is stated for a metal in isolation should be treated as incomplete.

## Disagreements

One of the most notable areas of disagreement in the literature concerns the selectivity to methanol at a given conversion. When the comparison is made at matched conversion, some reports assign the higher selectivity to copper-based catalysts in their standard forms, whilst other reports assign it to modified or supported forms that their authors present as superior alternatives. Unfortunately, the set of papers does not resolve this conflict, largely because the conditions under which the various selectivities were measured differ from report to report in ways that are not always fully documented. The pressure, the feed composition, and the space velocity can each exert a significant influence on the selectivity, so a report that omits one of these variables cannot be compared exactly with a report that states it.

The disagreement also extends to the underlying source of the observed differences. One group of reports attributes the higher selectivity primarily to the state of the metal surface, whereas another group attributes it to the support and to the interface that exists between the metal and the support. These two attributions point towards quite different remedies, and the literature as it stands does not decide between them. The quantity that remains in conflict, therefore, is the selectivity itself, and until reports begin to state selectivity at matched conversion under fully documented conditions, the ranking of catalysts for methanol formation will remain an open question.

## Gaps

Perhaps the most striking gap in the literature is that the measurement nobody reports is the activity of the catalyst after extended time on stream. The papers in the set overwhelmingly report initial performance, that is, conversion and selectivity measured early on in a run using a fresh catalyst. By contrast, the behaviour of a catalyst following prolonged exposure to the reaction mixture, with water present and the feed flowing continuously, is recorded almost nowhere. Deactivation is a topic that is mentioned very frequently, yet it is measured only rarely, and no common, standardised way of reporting it has yet become established.

This gap has serious implications for every other part of the review, because the established results effectively rank catalysts according to their fresh performance, whereas a real plant does not operate with fresh catalyst indefinitely. A catalyst that leads the field in terms of initial selectivity but then loses its activity rapidly is a very different proposition from a catalyst with somewhat lower initial performance that nevertheless retains its activity over the long term, and the literature in its current state cannot reliably distinguish between these two cases. A standard long-run measurement, carried out and reported with the same degree of care as the initial measurements, would go a long way towards closing this gap, and its absence must be regarded as the single largest weakness of the present evidence base.

fact_base: A tutorial passage explains the Nusselt number to second-year students. Definition in words: the Nusselt number is the ratio of convective to conductive heat transfer at a surface. The passage must state what a value near 1 means and what a large value means, without inventing numerical examples.
input:
The Nusselt number is a dimensionless quantity that plays a central role in the study of convective heat transfer, and it can be understood, in essence, as the ratio of convective to conductive heat transfer at a surface. In order to appreciate what this ratio really tells us, it is helpful to imagine the comparison being made for one and the same surface, subject to one and the same temperature difference, across one and the same layer of fluid: on the one hand there is the heat that is actually carried away from the surface when the fluid is moving, and on the other hand there is the heat that conduction alone would be able to carry across the layer if the fluid were perfectly still.

This ratio is typically built up from three ingredients, namely the surface heat transfer coefficient, which captures the strength of the convection, the thermal conductivity of the fluid, and a characteristic length associated with the surface, which together capture the strength of the conduction against which the convection is being compared. Because it is a ratio of two heat transfer rates, the Nusselt number carries no units, and its numerical value expresses the outcome of the comparison in a direct and intuitive way.

When the Nusselt number is near 1, this tells us that convection is adding almost nothing over and above conduction. At a value of 1, in other words, the moving fluid is transferring heat at essentially the same rate that pure conduction across the layer would deliver, almost as though the fluid were stagnant, and the dominant resistance to heat transfer resides within the fluid layer itself. When the Nusselt number is large, by contrast, the picture is completely reversed: convection is carrying heat away from the surface far more rapidly than conduction across the layer ever could, the temperature change is squeezed into a thin region of fluid immediately adjacent to the surface, and the resistance of the layer becomes comparatively small. It is worth noting that there is no single fixed threshold that separates these two regimes; rather, the number measures the enhancement over conduction, and its significance is judged by how far it rises above the conduction limit, underscoring the fundamental role that fluid motion plays in surface heat transfer.

The Nusselt number is defined as the ratio of convective to conductive heat transfer at a surface. The comparison is made for the same surface, the same temperature difference, and the same fluid layer. The numerator is the heat carried away from the surface with the fluid in motion. The denominator is the heat that conduction alone would carry across the layer if the fluid were still.

The number is formed from the surface heat transfer coefficient, the thermal conductivity of the fluid, and a characteristic length of the surface. The coefficient states the strength of the convection; the conductivity and the length state the strength of the conduction against which the convection is compared. The ratio is dimensionless, and its value states the outcome of the comparison directly.

A Nusselt number near 1 states that convection adds almost nothing to conduction. At a value of 1, the moving fluid transfers heat at the rate that pure conduction across the layer would give, as if the fluid were stagnant, and the resistance to heat transfer sits in the fluid layer itself. The surface is then, in thermal terms, insulated by its own fluid.

A large Nusselt number states the opposite condition. Convection carries heat away from the surface far faster than conduction across the layer could carry it. The temperature change is compressed into a thin region of fluid at the surface, and the resistance of the layer is small beside the transfer the motion sustains. No fixed value separates the two conditions; the number measures an enhancement over conduction, and its meaning is read from its distance above the conduction limit.

The Nusselt number therefore reports how much the motion of the fluid improves heat transfer at a surface over conduction alone. A value at the conduction limit and a large value are the two ends of one scale, and every reported value stands between them.

The affinity laws are a set of simple yet powerful relationships that allow us to predict how the performance of a centrifugal pump will change when its operating speed is varied. Taken together, the laws consist of three proportionalities that link the main performance quantities to the rotational speed. First of all, the flow delivered by the pump is directly proportional to the speed, so that any change in speed produces the same proportional change in flow. Secondly, the head developed by the pump is proportional to the square of the speed, meaning that the head responds much more strongly to a speed change than the flow does. Thirdly, and most dramatically, the power absorbed by the pump is proportional to the cube of the speed, making power by far the most sensitive of the three quantities.

A simple worked check helps to make these relationships concrete. Suppose that the speed of the pump is doubled. The flow will simply double, in line with the first proportionality. The head, however, will rise fourfold, because the square of a doubled speed is four times the original value. The power, following the cube law, will increase by a factor of 8, a striking illustration of how expensive additional flow becomes when it is obtained by raising the speed. Conversely, even a modest reduction in speed can deliver a disproportionately large saving in power. It should be remembered that these laws relate the operating points of one and the same pump handling one and the same fluid, and that they describe what the pump offers at the new speed rather than the duty point that the surrounding system will ultimately settle at.

The head is proportional to the square of the speed. The power is proportional to the cube of the speed.

A worked check fixes the meaning of the three laws at one speed change. Double the speed. The flow doubles, because the flow follows the speed directly. The head rises fourfold, because the head follows the square of the speed, and the square of a doubled quantity is four times the original. The power rises by the cube of the speed ratio: a doubled speed multiplies the power by 8.

The check states the practical weight of the laws. Flow is bought with power at a steep rate, because the power grows with the cube of the speed while the flow grows only in direct proportion. The relation runs in reverse with the same force: a small reduction in speed removes a much larger share of the power than of the flow. The laws relate the operating points of one pump on one fluid to each other. They state nothing about the system the pump serves, and a point fixed by the laws is the pump's offering at the new speed, not the duty the system will settle at.

fact_base: Goal: compute the half-life of a first-order reaction and the fraction remaining after 60 min. For a first-order reaction the rate constant k (min-1) fixes the half-life t1/2 (min) by t1/2 = ln(2) / k, and the fraction remaining after time t (min) is exp(-k t). Measured rate constant: k = 0.023 min-1 at 323 K, from concentration measurements every 5 min over 90 min. Worked results: t1/2 = 30.1 min; the fraction remaining after 60 min is 0.25 (dimensionless), both computed from the stated relations. The relations hold for a first-order reaction only; a reaction of another order follows a different decay law.
input:
The goal of this worked example is to calculate the half-life of a first-order reaction, together with the fraction of reactant that remains after 60 min. The measured rate constant for the reaction is k = 0.023 min-1 at 323 K, and it was obtained from concentration measurements taken every 5 min over a period of 90 min.

For a first-order reaction, the half-life t1/2 is connected to the rate constant by the well-known relationship t1/2 = ln(2)/k, while the fraction of reactant remaining after a time t is given by exp(-k t). It is important to bear in mind that these relationships are valid for a first-order reaction only, since a reaction of any other order would follow an entirely different decay law.

Substituting the measured value into the half-life relationship gives t1/2 = ln(2)/0.023, which evaluates to 30.1 min. In a similar way, the fraction remaining after 60 min is obtained from the decay relationship as exp(-0.023 × 60), which comes out at 0.25. As a final sanity check, it is reassuring to observe that the elapsed time of 60 min is very close to twice the half-life of 30.1 min, and since each half-life reduces the amount of reactant by half, two half-lives should leave behind one quarter of the original amount, which is exactly the value of 0.25 that the calculation produced.

Both relations hold for a first-order reaction only; a reaction of another order follows a different decay law. The half-life is the time in which the amount of reactant falls to one half of the amount present at the start of the interval. The half-life of a first-order reaction does not depend on the amount present: every interval of one half-life halves what remains. The fraction remaining is the amount still present at the stated time, divided by the amount at the start.

The half-life follows from the rate constant directly: t1/2 = ln(2)/0.023 = 30.1 min. The fraction remaining after 60 min follows from the decay relation: exp(-0.023 × 60) = 0.25.

The fraction is checked against the half-life. The elapsed time, 60 min, is close to twice the half-life of 30.1 min, and two half-lives reduce the reactant to one quarter of its initial amount. The computed fraction, 0.25, is the quarter the check requires. The fraction is dimensionless, as a ratio of two amounts in the same unit must be.

fact_base: Goal: compute the diffusive flux of oxygen through a stagnant water film. The diffusive flux J (mol m-2 s-1) is computed from the diffusivity D (m2 s-1) and the concentration gradient dC/dx, where C is concentration (mol m-3) and x is position (m). Fick's first law: J = -D dC/dx; the negative sign states that diffusion runs from high concentration to low concentration. Oxygen in water: D = 1.6 x 10-9 m2 s-1. Concentration falls by 0.25 mol m-3 across a film 0.4 mm thick, so dC/dx = -625 mol m-4. Worked result: J = 1.00x 10-6 mol m-2 s-1. The law as stated covers a stagnant medium; a moving medium adds convection, which the equation does not include.
input:
The purpose of this worked example is to calculate the diffusive flux of oxygen through a stagnant film of water, making use of Fick's first law. Fick's first law provides a relationship for the diffusive flux J (mol m-2 s-1) in terms of the diffusivity D (m2 s-1) and the concentration gradient dC/dx, where C denotes the concentration (mol m-3) and x denotes the position (m). In mathematical form, the law states that J = -D dC/dx. The negative sign in this expression is by no means a mere formality; it indicates that diffusion always proceeds from regions of high concentration towards regions of low concentration, so that the flux is positive in the direction in which the concentration falls.

For the particular case of oxygen dissolved in water, the diffusivity takes the value D = 1.6 × 10-9 m2 s-1. Across the film, whose thickness is 0.4 mm, the concentration falls by 0.25 mol m-3, which means that the concentration gradient works out to dC/dx = -625 mol m-4. Substituting these values into Fick's first law, the diffusive flux is found to be J = 1.00 × 10-6 mol m-2 s-1.

This is, as one would expect, a very small flux, reflecting the fact that the diffusivity of oxygen in water is itself very small, so that even a fairly steep concentration gradient can only sustain a modest flow of material by diffusion alone. It should, however, be clearly understood that Fick's first law in the form stated here applies to a stagnant medium; if the medium were moving, convection would also contribute to the transport, and that contribution is not included in the equation.

The law states J = -D dC/dx. The negative sign states that diffusion runs from high concentration to low concentration: the flux is positive in the direction in which the concentration falls. The gradient is the change in concentration over the distance across the film, taken with the sign of the direction in which the flux is reckoned, and the law is stated for that direction throughout.

For oxygen in water, D = 1.6 × 10-9 m2 s-1. The concentration falls by 0.25 mol m-3 across a film 0.4 mm thick, and the gradient is therefore dC/dx = -625 mol m-4. The flux follows from the law: J = 1.00 × 10-6 mol m-2 s-1.

The result is small because the diffusivity of oxygen in water is small; the gradient is steep, but the gradient acts through that small diffusivity. The check is the sign and the order of magnitude taken together. A positive flux in the direction of falling concentration is the direction the law requires; a negative result would indict the sign of the gradient, not the law. Fick's first law as stated holds for a stagnant medium. A moving medium adds convection, which the equation does not include.

fact_base: Cost review of a returns flow: 128 km per trip at $1.7 per km, 857 trips per year. Annual transport cost is $186k. Costs are carrier invoices for the last 12 months; empty running is included in the trip count.
input:
Moving returned goods back through the supply chain is easy to overlook, yet it accumulates a substantial cost over a year. This review sets out to establish, on a firm evidential footing, exactly what the plant's returns flow costs in carrier transport.

The review draws exclusively on the plant's own records. The costs in question are the carrier invoices for the last 12 months, and no estimates, allocations, or apportionments have been introduced at any stage. The pattern of operation is straightforward: the returns flow runs 128 km per trip, the carrier charges a rate of $1.7 per km, and over the year the flow made a total of 857 trips. It is particularly important to note that empty running is included in this trip count, which means the figure represents the full cost of the flow as operated, rather than merely the cost of the loaded journeys. Multiplying the distance by the rate gives a cost per trip of $217.6, and it is this per-trip figure, carried over the year's trips, that builds up into the annual total.

Bringing all of these elements together, the returns flow costs $186k a year in carrier transport. Because the annual figure is the product of the trip length, the rate per kilometre, and the number of trips, it moves in direct proportion to any change in those quantities, underpinned throughout by the invoice record. In summary, the review establishes the annual cost of the returns flow at $186k, on a fully recorded basis, with empty running firmly inside the trip count.
target:
The returns flow costs $186k a year in carrier transport. The figure is the full cost of the flow as operated: empty running is included in it, not added to it.

The annual cost is the product of three recorded quantities. The flow runs 128 km per trip, the carrier charges $1.7 per km, and the flow makes 857 trips per year. The cost per trip is $217.6, and the annual total is the per-trip cost carried over the year's trips. Each quantity in the product is a record, not an estimate: the costs are carrier invoices for the last 12 months, and the trip count is the count of trips actually run, loaded and empty together. No allocation or apportionment enters the figure; each invoice belongs to a trip the flow made.

The per-trip figure is the working number of the review. It prices a single return movement at the recorded distance and the recorded rate, and it is the figure against which a change in the flow is costed: a change in trip length reprices every trip, and a change in the trip count scales the annual total in direct proportion. The annual figure moves with exactly the quantities that compose it and with nothing else.

The review closes on the recorded position. The returns flow costs $186k a year, established from carrier invoices, with empty running inside the trip count.

fact_base: A textbook chapter section on heat exchangers, in four parts: principle, equipment, a worked example, and limits. The worked example uses only the numbers given in the principle part; no new data appear later in the chapter. The limits part states where the simple model fails, in plain terms, without new equations.
input:
## Principle

A heat exchanger transfers heat from a hot stream to a cold stream across a solid wall that keeps the streams apart. The hot stream emerges colder than it entered, and the cold stream emerges warmer, and the transfer can continue, in any part of the unit, only while a temperature difference exists between the streams there. The overall balance is closed by the streams themselves: the heat given up by the hot stream reappears as heat taken up by the cold stream, losses to the surroundings aside. On either side, the load is determined by the mass flow rate, the specific heat capacity, and the temperature change of that stream.

Heat leaving the hot stream crosses, in succession, the hot-side fluid film, the wall, and the cold-side fluid film, and fouling deposited on the surfaces adds a further layer to the path. These resistances act in series, and the overall coefficient gathers them into a single measure of how readily the unit, as built, passes heat. A clean unit of a given construction has its own coefficient, which declines as fouling builds up, a decline that forms part of the unit's behaviour in service.

Under the usual arrangement, the temperature difference is greatest where the entering hot stream first encounters the leaving cold stream, and least where the two streams part company. The average the sizing relation calls for is the log-mean temperature difference, constructed from the differences at the two ends. With the coefficient and the area, the log-mean completes the sizing relation: the load carried by the unit is the product of the three.

Countercurrent flow, in which the streams move against one another, maintains a serviceable temperature difference along the whole length, and even permits the cold stream to be heated beyond the hot stream's leaving temperature. Parallel flow, in which the streams enter together, spends its temperature difference early and can never bring the two outlet temperatures across one another. The narrowest gap between the streams, commonly termed the pinch, governs the economics of the choice, because the area rises steeply as the pinch narrows, the mean driving force falling whilst the load remains unchanged.

## Equipment

The shell-and-tube exchanger is the general-purpose form against which the others are usually judged. A bundle of tubes carries one stream, whilst a shell around the bundle carries the other stream across the tubes. Baffles hold the tubes in place and force the shell-side stream to cross the bundle repeatedly, rather than running along it, which keeps the shell-side coefficient up. Where the design calls for a higher velocity, the tube-side stream may make more than a single pass through the bundle. This form tolerates the highest pressures and temperatures of any common form, is understood by every fabricator, and opens for inspection; its tube side cleans readily whilst its shell side does not, which is why a dirty stream is put through the tubes whenever the choice is free.

The plate exchanger builds its surface from a pack of thin corrugated plates, gasketed around their edges, with the streams in alternate gaps. The corrugations promote turbulence even at low velocities, the coefficient is high, and the pack provides a great deal of area in a small volume. The pack unbolts for cleaning and for adding or removing plates. Its ceiling is firmly set by the gaskets, which bound the pressure and the temperature of the service.

The double-pipe exchanger, quite simply a pipe within a pipe, suits small duties, is easily extended, and is at home at high pressures. The air cooler employs air itself as the cold stream: fans drive air across finned tubes, the fins compensating for the poor film coefficient of a gas, and the form is chosen where cooling water is scarce or expensive. The selection among the forms turns on the duty, the pressures and temperatures, the fouling the streams bring, and the cleaning the service will demand over the unit's life.

## Worked example

This worked example rates an installed exchanger against a duty. The task, with its data, is as follows: a hot process stream is to be cooled by a cold utility stream between terminal temperatures the process has specified, and an existing unit of known area and construction is offered for the service. The question is whether the installed area can carry the load at the stated terminal temperatures.

The load is fixed first, by the balance on the hot stream, using its mass flow rate, its specific heat capacity, and the specified fall in temperature. The balance then predicts the cold stream's rise in temperature, which is checked for consistency against the terminal temperatures stated in the task; a task whose two sides disagree is corrected before any sizing is attempted, because no exchanger can satisfy a balance that does not close.

From the terminal temperatures follow the two end differences, paired for countercurrent flow: the entering hot stream against the leaving cold stream at one end, the leaving hot stream against the entering cold stream at the other. The log-mean temperature difference is computed as the difference of the two end differences divided by the natural logarithm of their ratio, and stands as the driving force of the rating. The coefficient is estimated for the installed construction and the fluids stated, with allowance for the fouling the service is expected to need. The required area is the load divided by the product of the coefficient and the log-mean difference.

The required area is set against the installed area. Where the installed area exceeds the requirement, the unit carries the duty, and the excess is the margin the rating reports. Where the installed area falls short, the unit cannot carry the duty at the stated terminal temperatures, and the shortfall, not any verdict on the unit, is the result, since the same unit may serve at a relaxed terminal temperature. The example closes with the pressure drop on each side, calculated for the installed unit and read against the process allowances, because an exchanger that passes on area but fails on pressure drop does not serve.

## Limits

The rating and sizing methods of this chapter share the assumptions of the simple model, and the model fails wherever those assumptions fail. A stream that condenses or boils inside the unit holds its temperature whilst its enthalpy changes, so the temperature profile along the unit is no longer the one from which the log-mean is built. The remedy is to divide the unit where the regime changes, and to treat each part on its own profile.

Properties that change strongly with temperature break a second assumption, the constant coefficient. The film resistances depend on viscosity and conductivity, and a unit whose streams change temperature widely has a coefficient that changes along its length. A single coefficient then averages what the design needed to follow, and the error falls on the area in proportion. Fouling breaks a third assumption, in service rather than on paper: the coefficient used in the calculation belongs to the surface the calculation imagines, whereas deposits move the real coefficient away from it from the first day of operation.

It says nothing about the pressure drop a design imposes, nothing about tube vibration under cross-flow, nothing about the expansion stresses between a hot bundle and a cooler shell, and nothing about the mechanical codes the vessel must meet. Each of those questions is answered by its own method, and a design is complete only when all are answered. What the simple model delivers is the area a duty requires, on a stated set of assumptions. Those assumptions are listed here so the delivery can be weighed: where they hold, the area is sound; where they fail, the area is the first figure to re-examine.

fact_base: A tutorial passage explains feedback control through a flow loop on a process vessel. The passage covers the sensor, the controller, the final element and the sign of the feedback, in that order. No tuning numbers are given; the passage explains structure, not settings.
input:
Maintaining a steady flow is a basic requirement of good process operation, and the feedback control loop is the standard mechanism by which this is achieved. What follows walks through a flow loop on a process vessel: the sensor, the controller, and the final element, and then the sign of the feedback.

The first element is the sensor, which measures the flow in the line that serves the vessel and converts it into a signal for the rest of the loop. This signal is the loop's only source of knowledge about the process, so everything the loop does is based upon it, and any error in the measurement is acted upon just as faithfully as a genuine change in flow.

The signal then passes to the controller, which compares the measured flow against the set point in order to determine the error, that is to say, the size and direction of the flow's departure from its desired value. On the basis of this comparison, the controller generates an output signal, which is a command instructing the final element what to do; it is not itself a flow, but an instruction whose size and sign reflect the detected error.

The final element physically changes the flow, and in a loop of this kind it is typically a control valve in the line. The valve moves in response to the controller's signal, the movement alters the flow, and the new flow is measured again by the sensor as the cycle continues.

Finally, the sign of the feedback is negative, and this is the key to its behaviour. If the measured flow rises above the set point, the controller closes the valve further to bring the flow back down; if the flow falls below the set point, the action is reversed. Every departure thus generates a response that opposes it. Were the sign positive instead, the loop would reinforce every departure, driving the flow ever further from the set point until some physical limit intervened.
target:
A flow loop on a process vessel holds the flow at the set point. The loop measures the flow, compares the measurement with the set point, and acts on the difference. Its parts stand in the order in which a change travels around the loop: the sensor, the controller, and the final element. The sensor measures the flow in the line serving the vessel and delivers a signal that stands for the measured value. The signal is the loop's only knowledge of the process. Every action the loop takes rests on the measurement, and an error in the measurement is acted on as faithfully as a true change in flow.

The controller receives the signal and compares the measured flow with the set point. The comparison gives the error: the amount by which the flow stands away from the set point, and the direction of the departure. The controller answers with an output signal, sized and signed by the error. The output is a command to the final element, not a flow; the command states what the final element is to do.

The final element is the device that changes the flow itself, in this loop a control valve in the line. The valve receives the controller's signal and moves, and the movement changes the flow through the line. The changed flow is measured again by the sensor.

The sign of the feedback is negative. When the measured flow rises above the set point, the controller's action moves the valve towards closed and brings the flow down; when the flow falls below the set point, the action reverses. Each departure produces a response that opposes the departure. With the sign reversed, the loop would reinforce every departure and drive the flow away from the set point until a limit of the equipment stopped it.

fact_base: Design report for a distillation column, in four sections: basis, sizing, materials, and risks. Design throughput is 54 t per day and the removal or separation duty is 90% of the key component. Materials are 316L stainless steel for wetted parts; the basis section states this once. The risks section names fouling and turndown as open items; neither is resolved in the report.
input:
## Basis

This report presents the design of a distillation column intended for a continuous separation duty. The design throughput of the column is 54 t per day. The separation duty that the column is required to achieve is the removal of 90% of the key component from the incoming feed, and it is against this demanding duty that the column has been sized. All wetted parts are specified in 316L stainless steel. This grade is stated here, in the basis of the design, and the materials section that follows builds upon this statement rather than restating the grade itself.

The basis, in essence, establishes what the column is required to do. The feed arrives as a continuous stream at the design throughput, and the products likewise leave on a continuous basis. It should be noted that the duty is expressed in terms of the key component alone; the distribution of the remaining components is not separately specified, but simply follows from whatever separation the column succeeds in achieving. The column itself stands between an upstream supply and a downstream destination, both of which fall outside the scope of this report. The conditions prevailing inside the column are determined by the separation itself, together with the heating and cooling services that are available to the reboiler and the condenser.

## Sizing

The sizing exercise establishes the two principal dimensions of the column, namely its diameter and its height. The diameter is governed by the vapour and liquid traffic flowing within the column. Clearly, the column must be capable of passing this traffic without flooding, and flooding represents the limiting condition for the diameter: below the flooding condition, the two phases are able to separate and to pass one another in an orderly fashion, whereas at flooding this separation breaks down and the column can no longer perform its duty. The diameter is therefore derived from the internal traffic, the physical properties of the streams, and the particular internal arrangement that has been chosen.

The height, on the other hand, is governed by the separation requirement. The duty calls for a certain number of equilibrium stages; the physical column delivers these stages through its internals, operating at an efficiency that falls below the ideal, and the overall height emerges as the product of the number of stages and the height occupied by each stage. Standing behind both dimensions is the question of reflux. A higher reflux reduces the number of stages that the duty requires, but at the same time it increases the traffic that the diameter must accommodate, so the sizing ultimately represents a careful balance between these two opposing effects, trading stages against traffic and height against diameter. The pressure drop, which builds up progressively from stage to stage along the column, is reported alongside the sizing as a property of the design taken as a whole.

## Materials

The wetted parts of the column adopt the stainless grade that is stated in the basis. This grade is a corrosion-resistant stainless steel, and it has been selected because the wetted surfaces remain in continuous contact with the process fluids at the operating temperatures of the column, and because the separation duty leaves no room whatsoever for corrosion products to find their way into the products. The materials section sets out the requirements that the grade must satisfy in service, including resistance to the fluids being handled, weldability in fabrication, and availability in the plate and section forms that the construction of the column demands.

Parts of the equipment that do not come into contact with the process fluids fall outside the wetted-parts requirement. Supports, external attachments, and insulation simply follow the ordinary practice of the plant for equipment of this size and service, and they attract no special requirement arising from the separation. Joints and seals on the wetted side are specified to exactly the same standard as the wetted parts themselves, on the grounds that a joint constitutes a wetted surface at precisely the point where any leakage would occur. The selection therefore closes on the statement made in the basis: a single grade, stated once, covering every surface that the process touches.

## Risks

Two significant risks remain open at the close of this report, namely fouling and turndown. Neither of these risks is resolved within the report, and each one is carried forward as an open item against the design.

Fouling refers to the gradual build-up of deposits on the internal surfaces of the column. As these deposits accumulate, they narrow the passages available to the traffic, they push the pressure drop upwards, and they degrade the intimate contact upon which the separation depends. The report does not set any fouling allowance, nor does it name any cleaning provision, for the simple reason that the fouling behaviour of the feed in this particular service has not yet been established. The risk is recorded so that the allowance can be settled once that behaviour is properly understood; until that time, the sizing stands without any allowance for the deposits that service may in due course lay down.

Turndown refers to operation at throughputs well below the design value. A column that has been sized for its design traffic distributes liquid over its internals at that traffic; at substantially lower rates, however, this distribution deteriorates, the stages begin to lose their contact, and the separation falls away from the required duty. The report does not establish the lowest throughput at which the column will still succeed in meeting its duty, and the operating range of the design is consequently left open at its lower end. In summary, the column as designed meets its duty at the design point, whilst its behaviour away from that point, under conditions of fouling and of turndown, remains the unresolved content of the design.
target:
## Basis

The report covers the design of a distillation column for a continuous separation. The design throughput is 54 t per day. The separation duty is the removal of 90% of the key component from the feed, and the column is sized against that duty. Wetted parts are 316L stainless steel. The grade is stated here, in the basis; the materials section works from this statement and does not restate the grade.

The basis fixes what the column is required to do. The feed arrives as a continuous stream at the design throughput, and the products leave continuously. The duty is stated on the key component alone; the distribution of the remaining components follows from the separation the column achieves and is not separately specified. The column stands between an upstream supply and a downstream destination, and both are outside the report. Conditions inside the column are set by the separation itself and by the heating and cooling services available to the reboiler and the condenser. The basis is the authority for the rest of the report. A later section that needs a condition the basis does not state returns to the basis for the condition; conditions are not introduced for the first time in the sizing or in the materials section.

## Sizing

Sizing fixes the diameter and the height of the column. The diameter is set by the vapour and liquid traffic inside the column. The column must pass its traffic without flooding, and flooding is the condition that limits the diameter: below the flooding condition the phases separate and pass each other; at flooding the separation fails and the column ceases to perform its duty. The diameter follows from the traffic, the properties of the streams, and the internal arrangement chosen.

The height is set by the separation. The duty requires a stated number of equilibrium stages; the physical column delivers those stages through its internals, at an efficiency below the ideal, and the height is the product of the stage count and the height each stage occupies. Reflux stands behind both dimensions. A higher reflux reduces the number of stages the duty requires and raises the traffic the diameter must pass. The sizing is the balance of the two effects: stages against traffic, height against diameter. Pressure drop accumulates from stage to stage along the column and is reported with the sizing, as a property of the design as a whole. The sizing is reported as a pair of dimensions with their grounds stated: the diameter from the traffic and its flooding limit, the height from the stage requirement and the stage efficiency. A change in the duty reopens both dimensions; a change in the internal arrangement reopens the diameter alone.

## Materials

Wetted parts take the stainless grade stated in the basis. The grade is a corrosion-resistant stainless steel, selected because the wetted surfaces stand in continuous contact with the process fluids at the column's operating temperatures, and because the separation duty leaves no room for corrosion products in the products. The materials section states the requirements the grade must meet in service: resistance to the fluids handled, weldability for fabrication, and availability in the plate and section forms the column requires.

Parts that do not touch the process fluids stand outside the wetted-parts requirement. Supports, external attachments, and insulation follow the ordinary practice of the plant for equipment of this size and service, and carry no special requirement from the separation. Joints and seals on the wetted side are specified to the same standard as the wetted parts themselves, since a joint is a wetted surface at the point where leakage would occur. The selection closes on the basis statement: one grade, stated once, covering every surface the process touches.

## Risks

Two risks stand open at the close of the report: fouling and turndown. Neither risk is resolved in the report, and each is carried forward as an open item against the design.

Fouling is the build-up of deposits on the internal surfaces of the column. Deposits narrow the passages the traffic uses, raise the pressure drop, and degrade the contact on which the separation depends. The report sets no fouling allowance and names no cleaning provision, because the fouling behaviour of the feed in this service is not established. The risk is stated so that the allowance can be settled when the behaviour is known; until then, the sizing stands without an allowance for the deposits that service may lay down.

Turndown is operation well below the design throughput. A column sized for its design traffic distributes liquid over its internals at that traffic; at much lower rates the distribution deteriorates, stages lose their contact, and the separation falls away from the duty. The report does not establish the lowest throughput at which the column still meets its duty, and the operating range of the design is therefore open at its lower end. The column as designed meets its duty at the design point. Its behaviour away from that point, under fouling and under turndown, is the unresolved content of the design.

subtype: worked example with equation: Stokes settling
fact_base: Catalyst fines of diameter $d_p$ = 100 micrometres and density 1400 kg m-3 settle in water at 293 K. Stokes' law gives a terminal velocity $v_t$ of 2.19 mm s-1. The estimate requires creeping flow; the particle Reynolds number must be checked before the value is used.
input:
When catalyst fines are suspended in water, they will gradually settle under gravity, and estimating how fast they settle is a key step in understanding the behaviour of the system as a whole. In this example, the catalyst fines have a particle diameter $d_p$ of 100 micrometres and a density of 1400 kg m-3, and they settle in water at 293 K. Stokes' law provides a convenient and widely used way of estimating the terminal velocity $v_t$ in cases of this kind, and it gives a value of 2.19 mm s-1 for these particles.

The terminal velocity is a central quantity in solid-liquid separation, and it plays a pivotal role in the sizing of settlers, clarifiers and related equipment, because the rate at which particles settle ultimately determines how large a vessel must be in order to achieve the separation that is required.

Stokes' law can be written as

$$v_t = \frac{g d_p^2 (\rho_p - \rho)}{18 \mu}$$

where $g$ represents the gravitational acceleration, $\rho_p$ represents the density of the particle, $\rho$ represents the density of water, and $\mu$ represents the viscosity of water. It is important to note that this estimate rests on an important assumption: Stokes' law requires creeping flow, which means that the particle Reynolds number must be checked before the value of 2.19 mm s-1 is used in any further calculation. If the flow does not fall within the creeping-flow regime, the estimate will not be reliable, underscoring the need to verify the underlying assumptions before applying the result.
target:
Catalyst fines settle in water at 293 K. The fines have a particle diameter $d_p$ of 100 micrometres and a density of 1400 kg m-3. Determine the terminal velocity $v_t$ from Stokes' law, and state the condition on which the result depends.

A particle settling in a liquid accelerates until the viscous drag on its surface balances the net weight of the particle, the difference between its weight and the buoyancy of the liquid it displaces. The particle then continues at a constant velocity, and that constant velocity is the terminal velocity. Stokes' law gives the terminal velocity for the limiting case in which the flow around the particle is creeping flow. A check on the particle Reynolds number is therefore part of the result: the number must lie in the creeping-flow range before the value from the relation is used.

For a spherical particle settling under gravity, the relation is

$$v_t = \frac{g d_p^2 (\rho_p - \rho)}{18 \mu}$$

where $g$ denotes the gravitational acceleration, $\rho_p$ the density of the particle, $\rho$ the density of water, and $\mu$ the viscosity of water. Substitution of the stated diameter, densities and viscosity gives $v_t$ = 2.19 mm s-1.

The stated velocity is an estimate, not a design value. Stokes' law applies only to creeping flow, and the particle Reynolds number formed from the terminal velocity and the particle diameter must be checked before 2.19 mm s-1 is used. If the check places the flow outside the creeping range, the drag relation changes and the estimate does not hold.

fact_base: A tutorial passage explains feedback control through a level loop on a process vessel. The passage covers the sensor, the controller, the final element and the sign of the feedback, in that order. No tuning numbers are given; the passage explains structure, not settings.
input:
Feedback control is one of the most fundamental concepts in process engineering, and a level loop on a process vessel shows how it works. A feedback loop continuously monitors a process variable, compares the measured value with the desired value, and takes corrective action whenever a difference appears, helping the process to remain stable over time.

The first element of the loop is the sensor, which measures the level of liquid inside the vessel and converts it into a signal for the next element. Many types of sensor can be used for this purpose, and the choice depends on the application, but its function within the loop is the same in every case.

The controller receives the signal from the sensor, compares the measured level with the desired level, and works out the difference between them, a quantity generally referred to as the error. Based on the size of this error, the controller generates an output signal indicating how the process is to be adjusted to restore the level.

The final element is the component that acts on the process. In a level loop it is typically a control valve on the line into the vessel or on the line out of it, and by opening or closing in response to the controller output, the valve alters the flow and hence the level.

Finally, the sign of the feedback deserves attention. The loop is arranged so that its action opposes the deviation it detects: a rise in level brings action that brings the level down, and a fall brings action that brings it up. This is negative feedback, the self-correcting property that makes the loop work.
target:
A level loop holds the level in a process vessel at the value the operation requires, without an operator touching a valve. The loop has four parts: the sensor, the controller, the final element, and the sign of the feedback.

The sensor measures the level in the vessel and turns the measurement into a signal. A float, a pressure tapping at the vessel base, or a guided radar probe can serve; the form of the sensor does not change the structure of the loop. What matters is that the signal reports the level as the level now stands, continuously and without intervention.

The controller receives the sensor signal and compares the measured level with the level the vessel is to hold. The difference between the two is the error, and the controller turns the error into an output signal whose size depends on how far the level stands from the value required.

The final element acts on the process. In a level loop the final element is a control valve on the line into the vessel or on the line out of it, and the valve moves as the controller output changes, altering the flow and with it the level.

The sign of the feedback closes the loop. The action is arranged so that a rise in level produces a change that brings the level back down, and a fall produces a change that brings the level back up: the feedback is negative, and the loop corrects the deviation it detects.

subtype: worked example with equation: Raoult partial pressure
fact_base: An ideal liquid mixture holds ethanol in water (idealised) at a liquid mole fraction $x$ of 0.58 for the volatile component. Its pure-component vapour pressure $P^*$ at the mixture temperature is 12.7 kPa, so the partial pressure $p$ is 7.4 kPa by Raoult's law. Raoult's law assumes an ideal solution; activity coefficients for the real mixture are not applied.
input:
In this worked example, we consider an ideal liquid mixture consisting of ethanol in water, treated in an idealised way, and we aim to determine the partial pressure of the volatile component above the mixture. The liquid mole fraction $x$ of the volatile component is given as 0.58, while the pure-component vapour pressure $P^*$ at the temperature of the mixture is 12.7 kPa, and these two values provide everything that is needed for the calculation.

The calculation is based on Raoult's law, which is applicable to ideal solutions and which states that the partial pressure $p$ of a component in the vapour is equal to the product of its mole fraction in the liquid and the vapour pressure of the pure component:

$$p = x P^*$$

If we substitute the values into this expression, we obtain $p$ = 0.58 × 12.7 kPa, which works out to give a partial pressure of 7.4 kPa. It is worth noting that this result is smaller than the pure-component value, which is to be expected, since the volatile component makes up only a fraction 0.58 of the liquid phase. It should also be borne in mind that Raoult's law assumes an ideal solution, and that activity coefficients, which would be needed in order to describe the behaviour of the real mixture more accurately, have not been applied in this treatment.
target:
An ideal liquid mixture of ethanol in water (idealised) is held at a fixed temperature. Calculate the partial pressure of the volatile component from Raoult's law. The liquid mole fraction $x$ of the volatile component is 0.58, and the pure-component vapour pressure $P^*$ at the mixture temperature is 12.7 kPa.

Raoult's law applies to an ideal solution, and the idealisation is stated before the relation is used: the mixture is treated as ideal, and activity coefficients for the real mixture are not applied. For an ideal solution the partial pressure $p$ of a component is the product of its liquid mole fraction and its pure-component vapour pressure:

$$p = x P^*$$

Substitution of the stated values gives $p$ = 0.58 × 12.7 kPa = 7.4 kPa. The partial pressure is smaller than the pure-component vapour pressure by the factor $x$: only the fraction 0.58 of the liquid is the volatile component, and Raoult's law assigns the vapour pressure in that proportion. The calculation needs two inputs, the composition of the liquid and the vapour pressure of the pure component at the temperature of the mixture, and it returns the partial pressure over that mixture. The result holds for the idealised mixture. Ethanol and water form a non-ideal mixture in practice, and a calculation on the real mixture would require activity coefficients, which the idealised treatment omits.
