fact_base: Goal: compute the half-life of a first-order reaction and the fraction remaining after 60 min. For a first-order reaction the rate constant k (min-1) fixes the half-life t1/2 (min) by t1/2 = ln(2) / k, and the fraction remaining after time t (min) is exp(-k t). Measured rate constant: k = 0.046 min-1 at 323 K, from concentration measurements every 5 min over 90 min. Worked results: t1/2 = 15.1 min; the fraction remaining after 60 min is 0.06 (dimensionless), both computed from the stated relations. The relations hold for a first-order reaction only; a reaction of another order follows a different decay law.
input:
The aim of this example is to calculate the half-life of a first-order reaction, together with the fraction of the reactant that remains after a period of 60 min. The reaction has a measured rate constant $k$ of 0.046 min-1 at a temperature of 323 K, and this value was obtained from concentration measurements that were recorded at intervals of every 5 min over a total period of 90 min.

For a reaction that is first order, the half-life, which is denoted by $t_{1/2}$, can be obtained from the rate constant by means of the relationship $t_{1/2} = \ln(2) / k$. Since $\ln(2)$ has the value 0.693, substitution of the rate constant of 0.046 min-1 into this relationship leads to a half-life of $t_{1/2}$ = 15.1 min.

The fraction of the reactant that remains after a given time $t$ is described by the expression $\exp(-k t)$, and in the case considered here the exponent takes the value -2.76 when the stated rate constant and the time are combined. It follows that the fraction remaining after 60 min is 0.06, which indicates that only a relatively small proportion of the original material is still present at that point. It is important to emphasise that these relationships are valid only for a reaction that follows first-order kinetics; a reaction of a different order would decay in accordance with a different law, and the same formulae could not be applied to it.
target:
Calculate the half-life of a first-order reaction from its rate constant, and the fraction of reactant remaining after 60 min. The rate constant $k$ is 0.046 min-1 at 323 K, measured from concentration readings taken every 5 min over 90 min.

For a first-order reaction, the rate constant fixes the half-life: $t_{1/2} = \ln(2) / k$, where $t_{1/2}$ denotes the time taken for the concentration to fall to half its initial value. The half-life is set by the rate constant alone and does not depend on the initial concentration, which is the feature that distinguishes first-order decay from the decay of other orders. With $\ln(2)$ = 0.693 and $k$ = 0.046 min-1, the relation gives $t_{1/2}$ = 15.1 min. The value is a property of the reaction at the stated temperature, and a different sample of the same reaction mixture gives the same half-life.

The fraction remaining after a time $t$ is $\exp(-k t)$, a dimensionless ratio of the concentration at that time to the concentration at the start. At $t$ = 60 min the exponent $-k t$ takes the value -2.76, and the fraction remaining is 0.06. The fraction falls quickly at first and then more slowly, because the amount decaying in each interval is proportional to the amount still present. A check by halving gives the same result: the interval spans close to four half-lives, and four successive halvings leave close to one part in sixteen of the initial amount. The relations used here hold for a first-order reaction only; a reaction of another order follows a different decay law, and the half-life and the fraction would not come from these expressions.

fact_base: Inventory policy for a spare motor: mean demand 1830 units per week, standard deviation 483 units per week, replenishment lead time 6 weeks. Safety stock for a 95% cycle service level is 1952 units. Demand is treated as normal and independent between weeks; seasonal peaks are excluded.
input:
Effective inventory management requires that adequate safety stock be held in order to protect the organisation against the uncertainties that are inherent in demand, and in the case of the spare motor that is considered here, the safety stock requirement has been determined to be 1952 units. This stock is held in order to cover the variation in demand that can arise during the replenishment lead time, and it is based on a cycle service level of 95%.

The demand for the spare motor is characterised by a mean demand of 1830 units per week and a standard deviation of 483 units per week, while the replenishment lead time is 6 weeks. On the basis of these figures, and taking into account the fact that the stock must cover the variability of demand accumulated over the entire lead time rather than the variability of any single week, the safety stock of 1952 units is the quantity that is required in order to achieve the desired 95% cycle service level.

A number of assumptions underpin this policy. In particular, demand is treated as being normally distributed and independent from one week to the next, an assumption that is of considerable importance because it allows the variations in individual weeks to offset one another to some degree over the course of the lead time. Furthermore, seasonal peaks in demand are excluded from the analysis, which means that no additional provision has been made for periods of unusually high demand, and any peak that happens to arise within a lead time must be accommodated from the safety stock that is available.
target:
Safety stock for the spare motor is 1952 units. The stock covers variation in demand during the replenishment lead time at a 95% cycle service level.

Demand for the spare motor averages 1830 units per week, with a standard deviation of 483 units per week, and the replenishment lead time is 6 weeks. The safety stock is sized on the spread of demand over the whole lead time: weekly demand varies around its mean, and the stock has to absorb the accumulated variation across the full lead time, not the variation of a single week. At a 95% cycle service level, demand during the lead time is met from stock in all but a small minority of replenishment cycles, and 1952 units is the holding that the stated demand spread requires for that level.

The policy treats demand as normal and independent between weeks. Independence is the assumption that lets weekly variations partly cancel over the lead time; if demand in successive weeks moved together, the spread of lead-time demand would be wider and the same stock would return a lower service level. Seasonal peaks are excluded. No separate stock is held for peak periods, and a peak that falls inside a lead time draws on the safety stock in the same way as any other demand, so the stated service level describes ordinary variation across the year and not peak cover.

The figure is reviewed when the demand pattern or the lead time changes.

fact_base: A tutorial passage explains phase equilibrium for a partially miscible liquid pair. The passage states the equilibrium condition in words (equality of chemical potential across phases) before any equation is named. No numerical data are introduced; the passage is conceptual.
input:
When two liquids are mixed together, it is often assumed that they will blend into a single uniform phase, but this is by no means always the case. Certain pairs of liquids dissolve in one another only to a limited extent, and when such a pair is mixed in proportions that fall within the range of limited miscibility, the result is not a single homogeneous liquid but a separation into two distinct liquid phases, each of which is rich in one of the two components and saturated with the other.

The condition that governs the equilibrium between the two phases can be stated in words, without reference to any equation: for each component of the pair, the chemical potential of that component must be the same in both phases. The chemical potential can be thought of as a measure of the tendency of a component to move from one phase to another, and if it is higher in one phase than in the other, the component will tend to transfer into the phase where its potential is lower, and this transfer will continue until the potentials have become equal and the driving force for further transfer has disappeared.

An important consequence of this condition is that the compositions of the two phases are not arbitrary. At a given temperature and pressure, the composition of each phase is fixed by the equilibrium itself, and it does not depend on the proportions in which the two liquids were originally combined. Changing the overall proportions changes the relative amounts of the two phases present, but it leaves the composition of each individual phase unchanged, provided the mixture as a whole remains within the range in which two phases coexist.
target:
Two liquids that dissolve in each other only to a limited extent form a partially miscible pair. Mixed in proportions inside the miscibility gap, such a pair does not give a single homogeneous liquid: it separates into two liquid phases, one rich in the first liquid and the other rich in the second, and the two phases stand in equilibrium with each other.

Equilibrium between the phases has a precise condition, stated here in words before any symbol is attached to it. For each component of the pair, the chemical potential of that component is the same in one phase as in the other, and no net transfer of the component between the phases takes place. If the chemical potential of a component stood higher in one phase than in the other, the component would move into the phase of lower potential until the difference disappeared.

The condition fixes the compositions of the two phases. At a given temperature and pressure, each phase holds a definite composition, set by the equilibrium and not by the proportions in which the liquids were mixed. Adding more of one liquid to the mixture changes the amounts of the two phases, and leaves the composition of each phase unchanged, as long as the overall mixture stays inside the gap. Outside the gap, the pair mixes completely and a single phase results.

fact_base: A contract packaging firm runs 3 plants; revenue is $103 million per year. Evidence base: order records for 12 months, 12292 orders. On-time delivery over the last two quarters was 88%, against a target of 95%. Overtime cost was $1.4 million last year, up 27% on the year before. The order backlog stands at 3.4 weeks, against 1.8 weeks a year ago. Plant 2 accounts for 62% of late orders. A scheduling system for all plants is quoted at $332k; Plant 2 alone is $127k. An internal estimate (not a vendor figure) puts the overtime reduction at Plant 2 at 15-20% in the first year. The recommendation under consideration: install at Plant 2 first, hold the other plants until Plant 2 results are reported. The operations director owns the scheduling programme.
input:
This executive summary presents an overview of the delivery performance of a contract packaging firm that operates 3 plants and generates revenue of $103 million per year. The analysis is based on a comprehensive review of the order records for a period of 12 months, encompassing a total of 12292 orders, and it paints a picture of a business whose delivery performance has been deteriorating in a number of important respects.

Over the last two quarters, on-time delivery has averaged 88%, which falls noticeably short of the target of 95% that the business has set for itself. The problem is heavily concentrated in one part of the business: Plant 2 is responsible for no less than 62% of all late orders. At the same time, the order backlog has grown to 3.4 weeks, compared with 1.8 weeks a year ago, and overtime costs have risen to $1.4 million last year, representing an increase of 27% on the year before.

In order to address this situation, the installation of a scheduling system is under consideration. A system covering all plants has been quoted at $332k, while the cost of installing the system at Plant 2 alone would be $127k. According to an internal estimate, which it should be emphasised is not a vendor figure, the installation at Plant 2 could be expected to reduce overtime at that plant by some 15-20% during the first year of operation.

Against this background, the recommendation that is currently under consideration is that the system should be installed at Plant 2 in the first instance, with the other plants held back until the results from Plant 2 have been reported and evaluated. The scheduling programme as a whole is owned by the operations director, who will be responsible for reporting the outcomes of the initial installation.
target:
Install the scheduling system at Plant 2 first, and hold the other plants until the Plant 2 results are reported. The operations director owns the scheduling programme. The firm runs 3 plants on revenue of $103 million per year, and delivery performance has fallen behind the level the order book requires: the question this summary answers is where the failure sits and what to fund first.

The evidence base is the order records for 12 months, covering 12292 orders. On-time delivery over the last two quarters was 88%, against a target of 95%. Plant 2 accounts for 62% of late orders, and the failure is concentrated there rather than spread across the firm. The backlog stands at 3.4 weeks, against 1.8 weeks a year ago, and overtime cost was $1.4 million last year, up 27% on the year before. The pattern holds across both quarters in the evidence base, and the concentration of late orders in one plant is a property of the records, not of the sampling.

A scheduling system for all plants is quoted at $332k, and Plant 2 alone is $127k. An internal estimate, not a vendor figure, puts the overtime reduction at Plant 2 at 15-20% in the first year. The staged install takes the reduction where the late orders sit, at the single-plant price, and defers the remaining spend until the result is in.

The hold on the other plants is part of the recommendation, not a deferral of it: the spend on the remaining plants is committed only when the first install has reported, and the overtime and backlog figures above are the measures on which that report will be judged. The programme is judged on reported results, and the report is the decision point for the remaining plants.

fact_base: A tutorial passage explains feedback control through a temperature loop on a process vessel. The passage covers the sensor, the controller, the final element and the sign of the feedback, in that order. No tuning numbers are given; the passage explains structure, not settings.
input:
Feedback control is used throughout the process industries to keep important variables at the values required, and a temperature loop on a process vessel illustrates the principles involved. The loop consists of several distinct elements, and its operation can be understood by following the signal from one element to the next.

The first element is the sensor, whose task is to measure the temperature of the vessel contents and convert the measurement into a signal the other elements can use. Thermocouples and resistance thermometers are commonly employed for this purpose, and what the loop requires of the instrument is an accurate and responsive measurement of the temperature as it stands.

The controller receives the signal from the sensor and compares the measured temperature with the desired value, establishing the difference between them, which is known as the error. On the basis of the error, the controller produces an output calling for the heating or cooling applied to the vessel to be increased or decreased, as circumstances require.

The final element carries out the adjustment to the process, and in a temperature loop it is normally a control valve in the line supplying the heating medium or the line supplying the cooling medium. As the valve responds to the controller output, the flow of the medium changes, and the temperature of the contents changes in consequence.

Of particular importance is the sign of the feedback, which in a correctly arranged loop is negative. If the temperature rises above the desired value, the loop responds in the direction that brings it down again, and if it falls below, the response raises it once more, so that every departure provokes a reaction that works against it.
target:
A temperature loop holds the temperature in a process vessel at the value the process requires, acting on the heating or cooling supply as the temperature moves. The loop has four parts: the sensor, the controller, the final element, and the sign of the feedback.

The sensor measures the temperature of the vessel contents and turns the measurement into a signal. A thermocouple or a resistance thermometer can serve; what the loop asks of the sensor is a faithful and prompt report of the temperature as it now stands.

The controller receives the sensor signal and compares the measured temperature with the set value, and the difference between them is the error. From the error the controller forms an output that calls for heating or cooling to be raised or lowered, in the direction the error requires and by an amount that grows with the error.

The final element acts on the process. In a temperature loop the final element is a control valve on the line that feeds the heating medium to the vessel, or on the line that feeds the cooling medium, and the valve changes the flow of that medium as the controller output changes. The temperature follows the flow.

The sign of the feedback is negative. A temperature above the set value calls out action that brings the temperature down, and a temperature below the set value calls out action that brings it up: the response works against the deviation, and the loop returns the temperature to the set value.

fact_base: A tutorial passage explains the Prandtl number to second-year students. Definition in words: the Prandtl number is the ratio of momentum diffusivity to thermal diffusivity. The passage must state what a value near 1 means and what a large value means, without inventing numerical examples.
input:
The Prandtl number is a dimensionless quantity that plays a central role in the study of heat transfer, and it is defined as the ratio of momentum diffusivity to thermal diffusivity. In other words, it provides a comparison between two fundamental transport processes that take place within a fluid: the rate at which momentum is spread through the fluid by viscous effects, and the rate at which heat is spread through the fluid by conduction.

The significance of the number can be appreciated by considering the values that it can take. When the Prandtl number has a value close to 1, the implication is that momentum and heat are transferred through the fluid at broadly comparable rates, so that neither process runs significantly ahead of the other, and the boundary layers associated with the velocity and with the temperature grow to roughly the same thickness.

When the Prandtl number is large, on the other hand, the situation is quite different: momentum is spread through the fluid much more rapidly than heat, and as a consequence the velocity boundary layer becomes considerably thicker than the thermal boundary layer, while the temperature variations are confined to a relatively thin region close to the surface of the wall.

It is also worth emphasising that the Prandtl number is a property of the fluid itself, determined entirely by the physical properties of the material, and that it does not depend on the dimensions of the equipment in which the fluid is flowing or on the speed at which the flow takes place.
target:
The Prandtl number is the ratio of momentum diffusivity to thermal diffusivity. Momentum diffusivity measures how fast momentum spreads through a fluid by viscous action; thermal diffusivity measures how fast heat spreads through the fluid by conduction. The Prandtl number compares the two rates of spreading, and its size states how the velocity field and the temperature field of a flow stand in relation to each other.

A value near 1 means that momentum and heat spread at comparable rates. Neither field outruns the other: a disturbance in the velocity reaches about as far, in the same time, as a disturbance in the temperature, and the velocity boundary layer and the thermal boundary layer grow to about the same thickness.

A large value means that momentum spreads much faster than heat. Momentum reaches well beyond the region that conduction has warmed or cooled, and the velocity boundary layer is much thicker than the thermal boundary layer. Heat transfer in such a fluid is confined to a thin layer near the wall, across which the temperature changes from the wall value to the value in the moving stream outside.

The number is a property of the fluid, formed from its properties alone, and it states nothing about the size of the apparatus or the speed of the flow: the same fluid at the same state has the same Prandtl number in a pipe of any diameter.

fact_base: A vapour-compression unit serves a cold store, evaporating at 0 °C and condensing at 45 °C. The Carnot coefficient of performance between these temperatures is 6.07; the installed unit achieves 2.38. The achieved value is from the manufacturer's test at full load; part-load performance is not stated.
input:
A vapour-compression refrigeration unit is used to serve a cold store, and the operating conditions of the unit are defined by an evaporating temperature of 0 °C and a condensing temperature of 45 °C. In order to assess the performance of the unit, it is helpful to compare it with the best performance that could in principle be achieved between the same two temperatures, which is given by the Carnot coefficient of performance.

The Carnot coefficient of performance represents an ideal upper limit that no real refrigerator operating between 0 °C and 45 °C can exceed, and between these temperatures its value is 6.07. The installed unit, by comparison, achieves a coefficient of performance of 2.38, which corresponds to 39.2% of the Carnot value and therefore falls considerably short of the ideal figure, as would be expected for a real machine with real losses.

It should be noted, however, that the achieved figure is taken from the manufacturer's test of the unit at full load, and the performance of the unit at part load is not stated, so the extent to which the coefficient of performance changes when the unit is operated away from its full-load condition remains an open question that the available information does not resolve.
target:
A vapour-compression unit serves a cold store. The unit evaporates at 0 °C and condenses at 45 °C. State the Carnot coefficient of performance between these temperatures, and compare the performance the installed unit achieves.

The Carnot coefficient of performance is the upper limit for a refrigerator working between the same two temperatures: no machine on the same duty exceeds it, and real machines fall short of it through the losses their cycles contain: pressure drops in the circuit, heat transfer across finite temperature differences, and the losses of the compressor among them. Between 0 °C and 45 °C the Carnot coefficient of performance is 6.07.

The installed unit achieves a coefficient of performance of 2.38, which is 39.2% of the Carnot value: the unit returns well under half the cooling per unit of work that the ideal machine would return between the same temperatures. The comparison is made at the stated temperatures only; a change in either temperature changes both the Carnot limit and the achieved value, and the two do not move by the same amount.

The achieved value comes from the manufacturer's test at full load. Part-load performance is not stated, and the figure describes the unit at its tested duty only; the coefficient of performance at reduced load is not given by the test and cannot be read from the full-load value.

fact_base: A tutorial passage explains phase equilibrium for a partially miscible liquid pair. The passage states the equilibrium condition in words (equality of chemical potential across phases) before any equation is named. No numerical data are introduced; the passage is conceptual.
input:
Partial miscibility is a term that is used to describe the behaviour of certain pairs of liquids that dissolve in one another only to a limited extent. When two such liquids are brought together in proportions that lie within the range of limited miscibility, they do not merge into a single uniform liquid phase. Instead, the mixture separates into two distinct liquid phases, one rich in the first liquid and holding the second only up to its solubility limit, the other rich in the second liquid on the same basis, and the two phases coexist in a state of equilibrium with one another.

The condition that governs this equilibrium can be expressed in words, without the need for any equation. For each component that is present in the system, the chemical potential of that component must have the same value in both of the phases. The chemical potential may be thought of as a driving force for the transfer of a component between the phases: if the chemical potential of a component is higher in one phase than it is in the other, that component tends to move from the first phase into the second, and the movement will go on until the difference between the two potentials has been eliminated. At equality there is no net tendency for transfer in either direction, and the system is at equilibrium. It should be noted that this condition must be satisfied for each component individually, and equality in the case of one component does not by itself guarantee equality in the case of the other.

A further consequence is that the compositions of the two phases are determined by the equilibrium itself. At any given temperature and pressure, each phase has a definite composition that does not depend on the proportions in which the liquids were mixed in the first place. If the proportions of the overall mixture are altered, the compositions of the individual phases remain the same, as long as the mixture remains within the two-phase range, and what changes instead is the relative amount of each phase that is present. Beyond the limits of that range, the liquids dissolve in one another completely, only a single phase is formed, and the considerations described here no longer apply.
target:
Partial miscibility is the behaviour of a pair of liquids that dissolve in one another only to a limited extent. Mixed in the proportions that fall inside the miscibility gap, such a pair does not form a single homogeneous liquid. It separates into two liquid phases, one phase rich in the first liquid and holding the second only up to its limit of solubility, the other phase rich in the second liquid on the same terms, and the two phases rest in contact in equilibrium with each other.

The condition for that equilibrium is stated here in words, as the passage uses no equation for it. For every component of the pair, the chemical potential of the component is equal in the two phases. Chemical potential is the quantity whose difference drives transfer: a component moves from the phase in which its chemical potential stands higher to the phase in which it stands lower, and the movement continues until the difference is gone. At equality there is no driving force in either direction, and no net transfer of the component takes place. The condition holds component by component: equality for one component does not settle the other, and both equalities stand together in the equilibrium state.

The equilibrium fixes what each phase contains. At a given temperature and pressure the composition of each phase is set by the condition itself, and not by the proportions in which the two liquids were poured together. A mixture made up with more of the first liquid than another holds the same two phase compositions as that other mixture, as long as both mixtures fall inside the gap; what changes is the amount of each phase present, the phase rich in the added liquid growing at the expense of the other. Outside the gap the pair dissolves completely, a single phase forms, and the question of equilibrium between phases does not arise. Inside the gap, the two-phase state with equal chemical potentials is the state the mixture reaches and the state it keeps.

fact_base: Staffing review for a maintenance crew: 18 full-time staff, overtime at 8% of paid hours last year. Replacing half the overtime with one additional hire costs $87k per year fully loaded. Overtime is concentrated in two seasonal peaks; a hire is paid for the full year.
input: It is important to note that decisions around staffing levels are rarely straightforward, and the maintenance crew's current situation is no exception. At present, the crew comprises 18 full-time staff, and over the course of last year overtime accounted for 8% of paid hours, a level that many would regard as significant. One option under consideration is to replace half of the overtime with one additional hire, thereby reducing the reliance on overtime working. However, it is worth noting that such a hire would cost $87k per year on a fully loaded basis, and this cost would be incurred throughout the year. By contrast, the overtime itself is heavily concentrated in two seasonal peaks, meaning that for much of the year demand is considerably lower. This creates a complex picture involving cost, coverage, and flexibility, and decision-makers will need to weigh these factors carefully. In summary, while the $87k hire may offer benefits in terms of peak coverage and reduced pressure on existing staff, a thorough and balanced assessment will be essential before any commitment is made, and further analysis of the seasonal pattern would undoubtedly be valuable in informing the final decision. It goes without saying that any change to the establishment would also have knock-on effects for training, supervision, and holiday cover, all of which would need to be carefully planned for well in advance of any change taking effect.
target: Replacing half the overtime with one additional hire costs $87k per year fully loaded, and on last year's paid-hours record the exchange is not justified on cost: the overtime is concentrated in two seasonal peaks, while a hire is paid for the full year. The maintenance crew has 18 full-time staff, and overtime ran at 8% of paid hours last year. The pattern of the overtime matters more than its size. Hours bought through a hire arrive evenly across the year, but the demand for them does not: the peaks need extra hands for short periods, and between peaks the crew covers its planned work within normal hours. A hire therefore relieves the peaks only by adding capacity that stands idle for much of the year, and the annual cost buys the idle time along with the peak cover. The trade-off is $87k per year, every year, against overtime that arises only in the peak windows. Maintenance management should establish how much of the peak overtime is movable before the establishment is increased. Planned work that can be rescheduled out of the peak windows reduces overtime without a permanent addition to cost; work fixed by the production calendar cannot move, and for that share a hire is the dependable cover. The recommendation is that maintenance management quantify the movable share of the overtime and bring the hire forward only for the share that cannot be moved.

fact_base: An amine absorption unit was tested at pilot scale on gas from a cement kiln. Over 90 days at 14 t of carbon dioxide per day, the unit captured 90% of the carbon dioxide in the treated gas. Steam demand was 3.5 gigajoules per tonne of carbon dioxide captured; solvent loss was 1.6 kg per tonne captured. Beyond 90 days, the effect of kiln dust on the solvent is untested.
input: In a development that will be of considerable interest to the cement industry, an amine absorption unit has been successfully tested at pilot scale on gas from a cement kiln, demonstrating the considerable potential of this approach for industrial carbon capture. Over the course of a 90-day campaign, the unit treated 14 t of carbon dioxide per day and captured an impressive 90% of the carbon dioxide in the treated gas. Steam demand was 3.5 gigajoules per tonne of carbon dioxide captured, while solvent loss stood at just 1.6 kg per tonne captured, figures that compare favourably with expectations for this technology at this scale. It is worth noting, however, that beyond 90 days the effect of kiln dust on the solvent remains untested, and this represents an important area for future investigation. Overall, these results highlight the promise of amine absorption for kiln gas and underscore the need for longer-term testing in order to fully understand solvent behaviour over extended periods of operation. Going forward, it will be interesting to see how the technology performs when it is deployed at larger scales and over the longer campaigns that commercial operation would inevitably demand in practice.
target: An amine absorption unit at pilot scale captured 90% of the carbon dioxide in gas from a cement kiln. The unit treated 14 t of carbon dioxide per day over a 90-day campaign. Steam demand was 3.5 gigajoules per tonne of carbon dioxide captured, and solvent loss was 1.6 kg per tonne captured. Both consumption figures are stated per tonne captured rather than per tonne treated, so they scale with the captured quantity and not with the gas throughput. The capture rate and the consumption figures together define the operating cost of the process at this scale: steam sets the energy demand of the regeneration step, and solvent loss sets the make-up rate that a longer campaign would have to sustain. Neither figure is a design value; both are measured performance over the campaign as run. The gas treated was kiln gas as produced, at the composition the kiln delivered during the campaign, so the capture rate is reported for that gas and not for a cleaned or conditioned feed. The campaign establishes performance for its own duration only. Beyond 90 days, the effect of kiln dust on the solvent is untested; dust carried over with the gas may raise solvent loss or degrade capture, and neither outcome is excluded by the present data. A longer run with dust exposure monitored is the step that would extend the tested period.

fact_base: A pump draws condensate from an open tank at atmospheric pressure, 101.3 kPa. Vapour pressure at the pumping temperature is 19.9 kPa, the static lift is 1.3 m and suction-line friction loss is 0.6 m. Available net positive suction head $NPSH_a$ is 6.4 m. The pump's required NPSH at the duty flow comes from the vendor curve and must be exceeded with margin.
input:
When a pump draws liquid from a tank, it is essential to ensure that the pressure at the pump inlet remains sufficiently high to prevent cavitation, and this is where the concept of available net positive suction head becomes particularly important. In this example, a pump draws condensate from an open tank. Because the tank is open, the pressure acting on the liquid surface is atmospheric pressure, namely 101.3 kPa. The vapour pressure of the condensate at the pumping temperature is 19.9 kPa. In addition, the static lift, in other words the vertical distance between the liquid surface and the pump, is 1.3 m, and the friction loss in the suction line amounts to 0.6 m. The available net positive suction head, denoted $NPSH_a$, is calculated using the following well-known relation:

$$NPSH_a = \frac{P_{atm} - P_v}{\rho g} - h_{lift} - h_f$$

In this equation, $P_{atm}$ represents the atmospheric pressure, $P_v$ represents the vapour pressure, $\rho$ represents the density of the liquid, $g$ represents the acceleration due to gravity, $h_{lift}$ represents the static lift, and $h_f$ represents the friction loss. By substituting the values given above into this equation and carrying out the calculation, the available net positive suction head is found to be 6.4 m. It is important to note that this value must be compared with the pump's required net positive suction head at the duty flow, which is obtained from the vendor curve, and the available value must exceed the required value with an adequate margin in order to ensure reliable and trouble-free operation of the pump.
target:
A pump draws condensate from an open tank, and the available net positive suction head decides whether the pump can operate at its duty flow without cavitation. The quantity is computed from the pressures and levels on the suction side. The tank is open, so the pressure on the liquid surface is atmospheric pressure, 101.3 kPa. The vapour pressure at the pumping temperature is 19.9 kPa. The static lift, the height from the liquid surface to the pump centreline, is 1.3 m, and the friction loss in the suction line is 0.6 m. Available net positive suction head is defined by

$$NPSH_a = \frac{P_{atm} - P_v}{\rho g} - h_{lift} - h_f$$

where $P_{atm}$ denotes the pressure on the liquid surface, $P_v$ the vapour pressure, $\rho$ the liquid density, $g$ the gravitational acceleration, $h_{lift}$ the static lift, and $h_f$ the friction loss in the suction line. The first term converts the excess of surface pressure over vapour pressure into a head of liquid. The lift and the friction loss are subtracted because both are spent before the liquid reaches the impeller eye. Substitution of the stated values into the relation gives an available net positive suction head of 6.4 m. The calculation is made at the stated tank level and temperature. A lower tank level raises the static lift and lowers the available head by the same amount; a higher pumping temperature raises the vapour pressure and lowers the pressure term. Either change eats into the margin, so the comparison is made at the least favourable level and temperature the installation can present. The result is a property of the installation, not of the pump. It is checked against the pump's required net positive suction head at the duty flow, which is read from the vendor curve. The available value must exceed the required value, and it must exceed it with margin, because suction conditions vary in service and the vendor value is a test-stand figure. The available head computed here is the figure that comparison starts from.

fact_base: Design report for an amine absorber, in four sections: basis, sizing, materials, and risks. Design throughput is 58 t per day and the removal or separation duty is 93% of the key component. Materials are 316L stainless steel for wetted parts; the basis section states this once. The risks section names fouling and turndown as open items; neither is resolved in the report.
input:
Basis

This report sets out the design of an amine absorber intended for gas treatment service, and it is hoped that the following sections will provide a comprehensive overview of the basis, the sizing, the materials selection, and the principal risks that have been identified to date. The absorber works by bringing the incoming gas into contact with a circulating amine solvent, which absorbs the key component from the gas stream. The design throughput is 58 t of gas per day, and the removal duty is 93% of the key component in the feed gas, figures which together define the overall duty that the unit is required to perform. The rich solvent leaves from the base of the absorber and passes onwards to regeneration, while the treated gas leaves from the top of the column. It should be noted that this report is concerned with the absorber itself; the regeneration equipment, although closely related, is dealt with elsewhere in the design package. Wetted parts are 316L stainless steel, and this grade is stated here, in the basis, so that the materials section can build upon it. The basis of design takes the feed gas at its stated throughput and composition as received, with no pretreatment within the absorber battery limits other than the inlet separation that is needed in order to protect the packing from liquid carryover. The operating pressure and temperature are those of the upstream unit which delivers the gas, and the absorber has been designed for the full range of conditions that that unit can present, including upset conditions, rather than for one nominal operating point alone. The design follows the applicable pressure equipment code for the vessel, together with the project specifications covering internals, nozzles, and instrumentation. Pressure relief is provided in accordance with the relief design for the unit, and the absorber is protected against overpressure arising from blocked outlets and from the connected regeneration system. Instrumentation includes level control on the sump, differential pressure measurement across the packed bed, temperature measurements at the gas inlet and outlet and in the liquid distributors, and sampling points on both the lean and the rich solvent lines, all of which will play an important role in the safe and effective operation of the unit.

Sizing

The absorber takes the form of a packed column, which was selected after careful consideration of the alternatives. The diameter is set by the vapour load at the base of the bed, where the gas flow is at its highest, and it has been chosen in such a way that the operating point sits comfortably clear of flooding at the design throughput, with the margin required by the project specification. Particular attention has been paid to the rich end of the column, because the rich solvent has the higher viscosity and also the greater tendency to foam, and it is by no means automatic that a diameter which proves adequate at the top of the bed will also prove adequate at the bottom. The packing is a structured packing, selected on account of its low pressure drop and its good liquid-spreading characteristics at the liquid rates in question. The design of the distributor forms an integral part of the sizing, since maldistribution can waste bed depth more rapidly than any other single defect. The bed depth is set by the transfer requirement associated with the stated removal duty, and has been worked out from the equilibrium behaviour of the solvent system together with the approach to equilibrium that the design is prepared to claim; a conservative approach has deliberately been adopted, so that the resulting depth reflects the uncertainty present in the underlying rate data. The pressure drop across the bed at the design point is low by design, and the margin between the operating pressure drop and the flooding pressure drop is reported alongside the hydraulic calculation. The sump has been sized so as to hold the inventory needed for the level control to ride through the disturbances produced by the upstream unit, and the nozzles have been sized in line with the velocity limits set out in the project specification for gas and liquid lines. The question of turndown is addressed in the risks section; the sizing itself is stated at the design throughput, with the distributor turndown range being stated by the vendor as part of the internals package.

Materials

As stated in the basis, the wetted parts are the stainless steel grade specified there, and this section explains the reasoning behind that choice. Amine service presents a number of corrosion challenges which need to be properly understood. The amine itself can be handled readily enough, but the degradation products and heat-stable salts which gradually accumulate in a working solvent are known to attack carbon steel and, at higher temperatures and concentrations, can attack stainless grades as well. The choice of a stainless grade for the wetted parts is therefore fundamentally a corrosion decision rather than a pressure decision. Within the wider circuit, the reboiler and the hot rich-solvent lines are the locations giving greatest cause for concern, while within the absorber itself it is the distributor and the packing support which see the richest and warmest liquid. The packing itself is supplied in the same grade family as the shell, so that the internals and the vessel will age together and no galvanic couple is set up between them. Gasket materials at the flanged joints have been selected on the basis of temperature limit and resistance to the amine, and the bolting has been specified for the flange class and the service temperature in question. External surfaces are coated in order to provide protection against the atmosphere. Corrosion monitoring is carried out by means of solvent analysis during operation: the solvent is sampled on a regular cycle and its degradation state, iron content, and heat-stable salt level are all tracked, since a rising trend in any of these provides the earliest indication that the circuit is corroding somewhere, long before a wall thickness measurement would show it. Finally, inspection access is provided at the sump and at the distributor level, so that the internals can be examined at turnaround without any need to cut the vessel.

Risks

There are two items which remain open at the close of this report, namely fouling and turndown, and it is important to be clear that neither of them is resolved here. Fouling is an open item because the feed gas, as received, carries with it whatever the upstream unit sends, and the rate at which deposits form on the packing and in the distributor in this particular service has not been established by the operating data currently available. Deposits have the effect of raising the pressure drop across the bed and disturbing the liquid distribution, so fouling tends to show itself first as a hydraulic symptom and only later as a loss of removal duty; by the time the duty actually falls, the bed is already badly distributed. The design incorporates those mitigations which do not depend on knowing the rate in question: a differential pressure measurement across the bed with an alarm on the trend, access for washing, and an inlet separator to keep liquid carryover out of the packing. What is missing at this stage is a defensible cleaning interval, and that can only really come from operating experience on this gas, or from a pilot run carried out on a slipstream of it. Turndown is an open item because the absorber has been sized at the design throughput, and the behaviour of the packed bed at low rates is governed by the liquid distributor, whose effective range is a vendor figure rather than a measured one for this particular combination of packing and solvent. At low liquid rates there is a risk that the packing will run partly dry, in which case the removal duty falls away faster than the throughput does. The operating range which the unit can honestly claim has therefore not yet been established, and the low-rate behaviour will need either vendor test data on the selected distributor, or acceptance testing during commissioning, before the range is published to operations. Both items will remain on the risk register until such time as the evidence described above actually exists.

The packing itself is supplied in the same grade family as the shell, so that the internals and the vessel age together and no galvanic couple is set up between them. Gasket materials at flanged joints are selected on temperature limit and on resistance to the amine; bolting is specified for the flange class and the service temperature. External surfaces are coated for atmospheric protection. Corrosion monitoring is by solvent analysis in operation: the solvent is sampled on a regular cycle and its degradation state, iron content, and heat-stable salt level are tracked, since a rising trend in any of these is the earliest indication that the circuit is corroding somewhere, long before a wall thickness measurement would show it. Inspection access is provided at the sump and at the distributor level so that the internals can be examined at turnaround without cutting the vessel. Welding consumables match the shell grade family, and weld procedures are qualified for the solvent service, since an undermatched or sensitised weld is the first place amine attack shows in a stainless circuit.

Risks

Two items are open at the close of this report: fouling and turndown. Neither is resolved here. Fouling is open because the feed gas as received carries whatever the upstream unit sends with it, and the rate at which deposits form on the packing and in the distributor in this service is not established by the available operating data. Deposits raise the pressure drop across the bed and disturb the liquid distribution, so fouling shows first as a hydraulic symptom and only later as a loss of removal duty; by the time the duty falls, the bed is already badly distributed. The design carries the mitigations that do not depend on knowing the rate: a differential pressure measurement across the bed with an alarm on the trend, access for washing, and an inlet separator to keep liquid carryover out of the packing. What is missing is a defensible cleaning interval, and that can only come from operating experience on this gas or from a pilot run on a slipstream of it. Turndown is open because the absorber is sized at the design throughput and the behaviour of the packed bed at low rates is governed by the liquid distributor, whose effective range is a vendor figure rather than a measured one for this combination of packing and solvent. At low liquid rates the packing can run partly dry, and the removal duty then falls away faster than the throughput does. The operating range the unit can honestly claim is therefore not yet established, and the low-rate behaviour needs either vendor test data on the selected distributor or acceptance testing during commissioning before the range is published to operations. Both items stay on the risk register until the stated evidence exists.

subtype: worked example with equation: friction loss
fact_base: Water at 293 K flows in a horizontal pipe. The density $\rho$ is 998 kg m-3. Mean velocity $v$ is 1.1 m s-1, pipe diameter $D$ is 0.08 m, pipe length $L$ is 20 m and the Darcy friction factor $f$ is 0.02. The friction pressure drop is 3 kPa.
input:
In this example we consider water flowing in a horizontal pipe at a temperature of 293 K, and we wish to determine the pressure drop that arises due to friction. The relevant data are as follows. The density of the water, $\rho$, is 998 kg m-3, the mean velocity $v$ is 1.1 m s-1, the pipe diameter $D$ is 0.08 m, the pipe length $L$ is 20 m, and the Darcy friction factor $f$ has a value of 0.02. Because the pipe is horizontal, there is no change in elevation to take into account, and the pressure drop is therefore due to friction alone. The friction pressure drop can be calculated by means of the following well-known equation:

$$\Delta P = f \frac{L}{D} \frac{\rho v^2}{2}$$

In this equation, $\Delta P$ represents the friction pressure drop, $f$ represents the Darcy friction factor, $L$ represents the pipe length, $D$ represents the pipe diameter, $\rho$ represents the density of the fluid, and $v$ represents the mean velocity. It may be noted that the length-to-diameter ratio works out at 250, and that the velocity head, in other words the kinetic energy per unit volume of the flowing stream, is 0.6 kPa for the values given. Substituting all of the values into the equation and performing the calculation, the friction pressure drop is found to be 3 kPa. This is the pressure that must be supplied in order to overcome friction over this particular length of pipe, and it is important to note that the loss increases rapidly if the velocity is increased, since it depends on the square of the velocity.
target:
Water at 293 K flows in a horizontal pipe, and the friction pressure drop is computed from the Darcy friction factor. The density $\rho$ is 998 kg m-3, the mean velocity $v$ is 1.1 m s-1, the pipe diameter $D$ is 0.08 m, the pipe length $L$ is 20 m, and the Darcy friction factor $f$ is 0.02. The friction factor is stated for the pipe as given; it is not computed here. For a horizontal pipe there is no elevation change and no velocity change along the line, so the friction loss is the whole pressure drop, and it is given by

$$\Delta P = f \frac{L}{D} \frac{\rho v^2}{2}$$

where $\Delta P$ is the friction pressure drop, $f$ is the Darcy friction factor, $L$ is the pipe length, $D$ is the pipe diameter, $\rho$ is the fluid density, and $v$ is the mean velocity. The length-to-diameter ratio is 250, and the second factor is the velocity head, the kinetic energy per unit volume of the stream, which for the stated values is 0.6 kPa. The pressure drop is the friction factor applied to the length ratio and to the velocity head together. Substitution of the stated values gives a friction pressure drop of 3 kPa. The result is the pressure the pump must supply against friction alone over this length of line. The check on the result is structural: the loss is proportional to the velocity head and to the number of pipe diameters traversed, so a longer line raises it in proportion to the length, and a faster stream raises it with the square of the velocity.

subtype: worked example with equation: available NPSH
fact_base: A pump draws light oil from an open tank at atmospheric pressure, 101.3 kPa. Vapour pressure at the pumping temperature is 7.4 kPa, the static lift is 2.8 m and suction-line friction loss is 0.5 m. Available net positive suction head $NPSH_a$ is 6.3 m. The pump's required NPSH at the duty flow comes from the vendor curve and must be exceeded with margin.
input:
When a pump is required to draw liquid from a tank, it is very important to check that the available net positive suction head is sufficient, since otherwise cavitation may occur and the pump may be damaged. In this example, a pump draws light oil from an open tank. As the tank is open, the pressure on the surface of the liquid is atmospheric pressure, which is 101.3 kPa. The vapour pressure of the oil at the pumping temperature is 7.4 kPa, the static lift is 2.8 m, and the friction loss in the suction line is 0.5 m. The available net positive suction head is calculated by means of the following relation:

$$NPSH_a = \frac{P_{atm} - P_v}{\rho g} - h_{lift} - h_f$$

Here, $P_{atm}$ represents the pressure on the liquid surface, $P_v$ represents the vapour pressure, $\rho$ represents the density of the liquid, $g$ represents the acceleration due to gravity, $h_{lift}$ represents the static lift, and $h_f$ represents the friction loss in the suction line. Substituting the values given above, the available net positive suction head is found to be 6.3 m. It is important to note that this value must be compared with the pump's required net positive suction head at the duty flow, which is obtained from the vendor curve, and the available value must exceed the required value with an adequate margin if reliable operation is to be achieved.
target:
A pump draws light oil from an open tank, and the available net positive suction head decides whether the pump can run at its duty flow without cavitation. The tank is open, so the pressure on the liquid surface is atmospheric pressure, 101.3 kPa. The vapour pressure at the pumping temperature is 7.4 kPa, the static lift is 2.8 m, and the friction loss in the suction line is 0.5 m. Available net positive suction head is

$$NPSH_a = \frac{P_{atm} - P_v}{\rho g} - h_{lift} - h_f$$

where $P_{atm}$ denotes the surface pressure, $P_v$ the vapour pressure, $\rho$ the liquid density, $g$ the gravitational acceleration, $h_{lift}$ the static lift, and $h_f$ the suction-line friction loss. The first term turns the excess of surface pressure over vapour pressure into a head of liquid; the lift and the friction loss are subtracted because both are spent before the liquid reaches the impeller. Substitution of the stated values gives an available net positive suction head of 6.3 m. The figure belongs to the installation, not to the pump. It is checked against the pump's required net positive suction head at the duty flow, taken from the vendor curve, and the available value must exceed the required value with margin. A falling tank level or a warmer suction stream reduces the available head and eats into that margin, so the check is made at the least favourable level and temperature the service presents.

fact_base: Carbon dioxide and hydrogen react over a copper-zinc oxide catalyst to give formaldehyde. Space-time yield is the mass of product per unit catalyst volume per hour (kg L-1 h-1). Test conditions: 280 °C, 40 bar, feed ratio H2/CO2 = 3, one feed composition. Washcoated monolith catalyst: space-time yield 0.64 kg L-1 h-1, pressure drop 0.19 bar, activity loss 7% after 100 h. Extruded pellet catalyst: space-time yield 0.34 kg L-1 h-1, pressure drop 1.03 bar, activity loss 13% after 100 h. No sulfur-bearing feed was tested. Yield and pressure drop are seldom reported for the same catalyst charge.
input: In this study, the conversion of carbon dioxide and hydrogen over a copper-zinc oxide catalyst to formaldehyde is investigated, with a particular focus on the important question of catalyst form. Two different forms of the catalyst were compared, namely a washcoated monolith and an extruded pellet, using one feed composition. The space-time yield, which is defined as the mass of product per unit catalyst volume per hour (kg L-1 h-1), was selected as the principal performance measure. The tests were carried out at 280 °C and 40 bar, with a hydrogen-to-carbon-dioxide feed ratio of 3. The results were striking. The monolith achieved a space-time yield of 0.64 kg L-1 h-1 together with a pressure drop of only 0.19 bar, and it lost 7% of its activity after 100 h on stream. The pellet, by contrast, achieved a space-time yield of 0.34 kg L-1 h-1 at a pressure drop of 1.03 bar, and it lost 13% of its activity after 100 h. It is clear from these results that the monolith outperforms the pellet across the board, delivering a higher yield while at the same time imposing a lower pressure drop and retaining its activity more effectively. It should be noted, however, that no sulfur-bearing feed was tested, and it is also worth bearing in mind that yield and pressure drop are seldom reported for the same catalyst charge in the literature, which makes direct comparisons of this kind particularly valuable. Taken together, the findings provide a sound basis for preferring the monolith in this service, and they point the way towards further work in which the behaviour of both forms can be examined over considerably longer periods on stream.

The pellet gave a space-time yield of 0.34 kg L-1 h-1 at a pressure drop of 1.03 bar, and lost 13% of its activity after 100 h. The monolith leads on all three reported measures at the tested conditions, and the yield advantage does not have to be bought with pressure drop. The activity losses set the expected service behaviour: the monolith also loses activity more slowly, so its advantage at the start of a run is not one that the pellet recovers later in the run. For catalyst selection at these conditions, the structured form is the one the data support, since a higher space-time yield is a smaller catalyst volume for the same duty and a lower pressure drop is a lower compression duty on the feed. The comparison is bounded in two ways. No sulfur-bearing feed was tested, so tolerance to sulfur is unknown for both forms. And yield and pressure drop are seldom reported for the same catalyst charge in the wider literature, so the paired comparison made here, on one charge and one feed, is the basis for the preference.

fact_base: A binary distillation separates ethanol/water at a relative volatility of 2.36 that is taken as constant over the column. Specifications: distillate 98 mol% light component, bottoms 2 mol% light component. The Fenske minimum stage count is 9.1 theoretical stages including the reboiler. The actual design uses a reflux ratio of 1.3 times the minimum; the stage count at that reflux comes from a separate simulation.
input: The Fenske equation is a widely used and extremely useful relation in distillation design, since it allows the minimum number of theoretical stages to be estimated in a straightforward manner. In the present case, a binary distillation separates ethanol and water, and the relative volatility has a value of 2.36, which is taken as constant over the column for the purposes of the calculation. The product specifications are a distillate containing 98 mol% light component and a bottoms containing 2 mol% light component, the light component in this mixture being ethanol. Applying the Fenske equation to these specifications, the minimum stage count is found to be 9.1 theoretical stages, a figure which includes the reboiler. It is important to appreciate that this minimum corresponds to operation at total reflux, which represents a limiting condition rather than a practical operating mode, since no product is actually withdrawn. In practice, the actual design operates at a reflux ratio of 1.3 times the minimum, which is a more realistic basis for a working column. The stage count at that reflux ratio is not obtained from the Fenske equation itself; instead, it comes from a separate simulation, and it is that simulation result which ultimately determines the column that will be built. The Fenske result nevertheless remains valuable, since it establishes the lower bound against which the design arrived at by simulation can be meaningfully compared and assessed. It also provides a useful check on the simulation itself, since any simulated design which appeared to require fewer stages than the Fenske minimum would immediately be revealed as being in error, and would need to be investigated before it could properly be relied upon.
target: A binary distillation separates ethanol and water, and the Fenske equation gives the minimum stage count at total reflux for the stated separation. The relative volatility is 2.36, taken as constant over the column. The specifications are a distillate of 98 mol% light component and a bottoms of 2 mol% light component; the light component is ethanol. The Fenske minimum stage count is 9.1 theoretical stages, and the count includes the reboiler, which performs one stage of separation and is counted on the same footing as a tray. Total reflux is the limiting condition behind the number. At total reflux no product is withdrawn, the operating lines coincide with the diagonal, and each stage then does the most separation work it can do, so the stage requirement for a given pair of product specifications is at its smallest. A column that actually produces distillate and bottoms therefore needs more stages than the minimum, and the minimum serves as the reference the real design is measured against: a design that came out below it would be wrong, and the distance above it is the staging the chosen reflux buys. The count rests on the relative volatility being constant over the column; where the volatility varies strongly with composition, a single-value count of this kind is an approximation to the true minimum. The actual design operates at a reflux ratio of 1.3 times the minimum. The stage count at that reflux does not come from the Fenske relation; it comes from a separate simulation, and it is the simulation count, not the minimum, that the column is built to. The two limits frame the design between them: the minimum stage count fixes the least staging the separation can ever use, the minimum reflux fixes the least reflux it can ever run at, and the simulation connects the chosen operating point to a stage count for construction.

fact_base: Project proposal for a rooftop solar installation, in four sections: case, costs, schedule, and decision requested. Capital cost is $1075k with a 10-year appraisal horizon. The schedule section gives a start one quarter after approval; no contractor is named. The decision requested is approval to proceed to detailed design, not to construction.
input:
Case
This proposal sets out the case for a rooftop solar installation and seeks approval to move forward to the detailed design stage. This is not a request for approval to construct the installation itself, and no commitment to build should be inferred from the approval that is being requested at this point. The fundamental idea is simple: photovoltaic modules on the roof generate electricity where it is used, and every unit generated displaces a unit the site would otherwise purchase from the grid. At present, the roof carries no plant and earns nothing; fitted with modules, that same area becomes a productive generation asset, without taking up land or floor space that operations depend on. Generation from the array peaks in the middle of the day, precisely when site demand for lighting, ventilation and process services is also at its daily height, so a large share of the output is consumed on site as it is produced rather than exported at a lower value. Purchased electricity, by contrast, represents a continuing operating cost whose price the site does not control. Generation behind the meter reduces the volume exposed to that price, and this reduction endures for the entire life of the installation. It should be emphasised that the case does not rest on the array supplying the whole site: the array offsets part of the purchased volume, while the grid remains the source for the balance and for all hours of darkness. What has not been established at this stage is the roof itself. The capacity of the structure to carry the modules and their mounting loads, the orientation and pitch of the available slopes, the shading cast by plant on and around the roof, and the remaining life of the roof covering all bear directly on whether the installation is sound, and none of these questions is settled by the information behind this proposal. The detailed design will settle each point in turn. The appraisal presented in the costs section therefore tests a pre-design capital figure against the horizon over which the installation would operate, and the decision requested simply asks for the design work that will turn an outline case into a fully priced and thoroughly checked proposal.

Costs
The capital cost of the proposed installation is $1075k. This figure covers the photovoltaic modules, the inverters, the mounting system and its fixings, the cabling and switchgear, the grid connection works, and the labour of installation. This is a pre-design figure. No supplier has yet priced a final layout, the inverter selection is not fixed, and the allowance for the grid connection rests on the connection route that the detailed design will confirm with the network operator; each of these items could move the outturn cost in either direction. Running costs over the life of the installation are small beside the capital figure and are confined to cleaning of the module surfaces, periodic inspection of the mounting and electrical connections, and the monitoring service that reports generation and faults. The modules have no fuel cost and no moving parts. Inverters, however, have a shorter service life than modules, and a replacement will fall inside the appraisal horizon on the lives stated by the manufacturers; the detailed design will fix the inverter count and rating, and the appraisal will then carry a replacement allowance at the appropriate point in the horizon. Two costs are excluded from the capital figure, because neither can be priced before the design work is done: structural strengthening of the roof, should the survey show that the existing structure cannot carry the array, and any loss of use of the areas below the roof while installation proceeds overhead. The appraisal horizon is 10 years. The benefit side of the appraisal is the generation predicted by the detailed design, valued as displaced purchases at the tariff the site pays, with module output degrading year by year at the rate the design adopts. Costs and benefits are compared over the same horizon, and the appraisal will be re-run on the firmed figures when the detailed design reports, before any request to construct is made.

Schedule
Work starts one quarter after approval. The first stage is the detailed design itself, encompassing the roof survey and structural check, the array layout, the electrical design, and the connection application to the network operator, whose terms can govern the overall programme if the connection works turn out to be extensive. Procurement follows the design; modules, inverters and mounting are standard items with order lead times that the design programme will state, and no order will be placed before the design is issued. Installation then follows procurement and is sequenced slope by slope, so that only part of the roof is under work at any given time, the building below stays weather-tight at the end of each stage, and operations under the roof can continue with agreed exclusions around the working area. Commissioning closes the sequence: protection settings and metering are agreed with the network operator, the installation is tested and energised, and generation is handed over to the site with its monitoring in place. No contractor is named at this stage. The installation contractor will be appointed after the detailed design, under the procurement route that the design documents set out, and it is the design programme, rather than this proposal, that will carry the dates for each stage measured from the start.

Decision requested
In conclusion, the decision requested is approval to proceed to detailed design, and nothing further. The design will return a surveyed layout with a generation prediction the site can rely on, a structural statement for the roof, connection terms agreed in principle with the network operator, and a capital cost firm enough to appraise the installation as an investment. Construction is a separate decision, to be taken on the basis of those deliverables by the same route as this one. Approval of the design stage commits the site to the design fee and to no other spend: if the structural statement is adverse, if the connection terms are onerous, or if the firmed cost destroys the case set out above, the project simply stops at that point and the work done remains as a record of why. The appraisal will then be re-run on the firmed figures, and a construction request will be put forward only if the case survives it.

Two costs are excluded from the capital figure because neither can be priced before the design work is done: structural strengthening of the roof, if the survey shows the existing structure cannot carry the array, and any loss of use of the areas below the roof while installation proceeds overhead. The appraisal horizon is 10 years. The benefit side of the appraisal is the generation predicted by the detailed design, valued as displaced purchases at the tariff the site pays, with module output degrading year by year at the rate the design adopts. Costs and benefits are compared over the same horizon, and the appraisal is re-run on the firmed figures when the detailed design reports, before any request to construct is made.

Schedule
Work starts one quarter after approval. The first stage is the detailed design itself: the roof survey and structural check, the array layout, the electrical design, and the connection application to the network operator, whose terms can govern the programme if the connection works are extensive. Procurement follows the design; modules, inverters and mounting are standard items with order lead times that the design programme states, and no order is placed before the design is issued. Installation follows procurement and is sequenced slope by slope, so that only part of the roof is under work at any time, the building below stays weather-tight at the end of each stage, and operations under the roof continue with agreed exclusions around the working area. Commissioning closes the sequence: protection settings and metering are agreed with the network operator, the installation is tested and energised, and generation is handed over to the site with its monitoring in place. No contractor is named at this stage. The installation contractor is appointed after the detailed design, under the procurement route the design documents set out, and the design programme, not this proposal, carries the dates for each stage measured from the start.

Decision requested
The decision requested is approval to proceed to detailed design, and nothing further. The design returns a surveyed layout with a generation prediction the site can rely on, a structural statement for the roof, connection terms agreed in principle with the network operator, and a capital cost firm enough to appraise the installation as an investment. Construction is a separate decision, taken on those deliverables by the same route as this one. Approval of the design stage commits the site to the design fee and to no other spend: if the structural statement is adverse, if the connection terms are onerous, or if the firmed cost destroys the case set out above, the project stops at that point and the work done remains a record of why. The appraisal is then re-run on the firmed figures, and a construction request is put forward only if the case survives it.

fact_base: Goal: compute the Reynolds number for water in a pipe and state the flow regime. The Reynolds number Re (dimensionless) is computed from density rho (kg m-3), mean velocity v (m s-1), pipe diameter D (m) and dynamic viscosity mu (Pa s) by Re = rho v D / mu. Water at 293 K: rho = 998 kg m-3, mu = 1.00 x 10-3 Pa s. Pipe diameter D = 0.08 m; mean velocity v = 0.8 m s-1. Worked result: Re = 63900 (computed as 998 x 0.8 x 0.08 / 0.001). Flow is laminar below Re = 2300 and turbulent above Re = 4000; between the two values the regime is transitional and is not assigned by the number alone.
input:
In this worked example, we will calculate the Reynolds number for water flowing through a pipe, and we will also state the flow regime that corresponds to the result. The calculation gives $Re$ = 63900, and the flow is turbulent.
The Reynolds number $Re$ is a dimensionless quantity, and it is calculated from the density $\rho$ (kg m-3), the mean velocity $v$ (m s-1), the pipe diameter $D$ (m) and the dynamic viscosity $\mu$ (Pa s) by means of the relation $Re = \rho v D / \mu$. It is important to note that each quantity is taken at the conditions in the pipe, and the four values together fix the number without any further data being required. For water at 293 K, we have $\rho$ = 998 kg m-3 and $\mu$ = 1.00 x 10-3 Pa s. If we take the pipe diameter $D$ as 0.08 m and the mean velocity $v$ as 0.8 m s-1, with the mean being taken over the pipe cross-section, substitution of the values gives $Re$ = 998 x 0.8 x 0.08 / 0.001 = 63900. Interestingly, the units cancel out completely in the substitution: kg m-3 x m s-1 x m, divided by Pa s, leaves a pure number, exactly as a dimensionless quantity requires, and this cancellation serves as a useful check that the data have been entered in a consistent set of units. As a general rule, flow is laminar below $Re$ = 2300 and turbulent above $Re$ = 4000. Between 2300 and 4000, however, the regime is transitional, and the number alone does not assign it; a value in that band is reported as transitional, with the regime settled, if it must be settled, by observation of the flow itself. Overall, the calculated value of 63900 stands well above the turbulent threshold of 4000, clear of the transitional band by a wide margin, and so the flow in the pipe is turbulent.

fact_base: Excerpt content: a seal replacement takes about 88 min with the unit isolated; the excerpt gives the isolation steps only. The excerpt warns once about stored pressure and does not repeat the warning.
input: Once production has been transferred over to the standby pump, the duty pump is stopped and its driver is isolated under the PTW. The suction and discharge valves on the duty pump are then closed and locked in position, and the blanks are fitted at the casing flanges so that the pump is fully separated from the line on both sides. The casing drain is opened to the closed drain system and the contents of the casing are allowed to run down; the vent at the seal housing is opened as the level falls, so that air can enter and the casing empties fully rather than holding a vacuum. It is important to be aware that stored pressure can remain trapped in the casing between the closed discharge valve and the non-return valve even after the rest of the pump has drained, and this pressure must be released through the vent line and proven gone, both at the casing gauge and by a further crack of the vent, before any joint on the seal housing is slackened. The seal housing drain is opened once the casing has been proven empty, and the housing is flushed through until the discharge at the drain runs clear. Overall, the whole isolation, drain and prove sequence takes about 88 min with the unit isolated, and the housing bolts are slackened in sequence only after the flush is complete and the last of the washings has drained away.

fact_base: A tutorial passage explains feedback control through a temperature loop on a process vessel. The passage covers the sensor, the controller, the final element and the sign of the feedback, in that order. No tuning numbers are given; the passage explains structure, not settings.
input: A temperature loop holds the vessel temperature at the set point by acting on the heating supply, and the loop is built from a sensor, a controller and a final element, closed by the sign of the feedback. The sensor measures the vessel temperature. A temperature element immersed in the vessel contents produces a signal that follows the temperature, and this signal is all the loop knows of the controlled variable: a sensor in a stagnant pocket reports the pocket, and the loop controls the pocket temperature, not the vessel temperature. The controller compares the temperature with the set point and forms the error, the difference between the two. From the sign and size of the error, the controller sets the direction and amount of the correction: a temperature below the set point calls for more heating, and one above it calls for less. The controller moves nothing in the process itself; its output is a signal, and the signal carries no power. The final element turns the signal into a change in the process. The final element is the control valve in the heating line: the valve opens or closes on the controller signal, the flow of heating medium changes, and the changed flow moves the vessel temperature. The sign of the feedback is negative. A rise in temperature above the set point produces a correction that reduces the heating, and a fall produces a correction that increases it, so the loop acts against the deviation that produced the correction. Connected with the opposite sign, the loop would act with the deviation and drive the temperature away from the set point, and no controller setting would make it control.
