fact_base: A binary distillation separates ethanol/water at a relative volatility of 1.5 that is taken as constant over the column. Specifications: distillate 98 mol% light component, bottoms 2 mol% light component. The Fenske minimum stage count is 19.2 theoretical stages including the reboiler. The actual design uses a reflux ratio of 1.3 times the minimum; the stage count at that reflux comes from a separate simulation.
input: The separation of ethanol from water by binary distillation is a well-established operation, and the Fenske equation provides a widely used shortcut method for estimating the minimum number of theoretical stages required for a specified separation. In this case, the relative volatility of the mixture is taken as 1.5, and it is assumed to remain constant throughout the column, which greatly simplifies the calculation. The product specifications are demanding: the distillate is required to contain 98 mol% of the light component, while the bottoms stream may contain no more than 2 mol% of the light component. Applying the Fenske equation to these specifications yields a minimum stage count of 19.2 theoretical stages, a figure that includes the reboiler. It is important to note that this value represents an idealised lower bound that corresponds to total reflux, and it cannot be achieved in a real, operating column. In practice, the actual design operates at a reflux ratio of 1.3 times the minimum reflux ratio, and the number of stages required at that reflux ratio cannot be obtained from the Fenske equation alone; instead, it is determined by means of a separate, more rigorous simulation. Overall, the Fenske result of 19.2 stages provides a useful benchmark against which the simulation result can be compared, ensuring that the final design is grounded in a sound theoretical minimum.
target: A binary distillation separates ethanol and water at a relative volatility of 1.5, taken as constant over the column. Specifications are 98 mol% light component in the distillate and 2 mol% light component in the bottoms. For these specifications the Fenske equation gives a minimum stage count of 19.2 theoretical stages, including the reboiler. The minimum stage count is the stage count at total reflux. It is a lower bound on any operating design, not a design value: a column at finite reflux needs more stages than the minimum, by an amount the Fenske equation does not fix. The constant relative volatility is part of the result as stated. A column in which the volatility changes appreciably from stage to stage is not described by the count, and the count is not transferred to such a column without a stage-by-stage calculation. The design reflux ratio is 1.3 times the minimum reflux ratio. The stage count at the design reflux therefore comes from a separate simulation at that reflux, not from the Fenske result. The simulation result is read against the floor of 19.2 stages. A simulated count below the floor would show an error in the simulation; the margin above the floor is the stage cost of running at finite reflux rather than at total reflux. The minimum also sets the terms on which the reflux choice is judged: a reflux ratio below the minimum has no stage count at any column height, so the operating point must stand above the minimum reflux before the stage question arises at all.

fact_base: Excerpt content: a seal replacement takes about 65 min with the unit isolated; the excerpt gives the isolation steps only. The excerpt warns once about stored pressure and does not repeat the warning.
input: Before any work is carried out on the seal, it is absolutely essential that the pump is isolated properly and safely, in line with the requirements of the PTW. The first step is to start the standby pump and to make sure that it is running satisfactorily and carrying the full flow, so that the process is not disturbed when the duty pump is taken out of service. The duty pump is then stopped, and its motor starter is locked out and tagged so that it cannot be restarted inadvertently. Both the suction and the discharge block valves are closed and fitted with locks. The casing is drained to the closed drain system, and the vent at the high point of the suction line is opened. It should be borne in mind that pressure may remain trapped in the section between the closed block valves even after the casing has been drained, and for this reason the vent must be cracked open slowly and carefully, with the operator standing well clear, until it runs free of liquid and the gauge shows no pressure. A seal replacement on the isolated pump takes about 65 min. Throughout the work, the drain and the vent are left open and all locks and tags remain in place.
target: Start the standby pump and prove it on flow and discharge pressure before the duty pump is taken out of service. Stop the duty pump, and lock out and tag its motor starter under the PTW. Close the suction block valve and the discharge block valve on the duty pump, and fit locks to both valve handwheels. Open the casing drain to the closed drain system, and open the vent at the high point of the suction line. Pressure can remain trapped between the two block valves after the casing has drained: crack the vent slowly, stand clear of the vent outlet, and leave the vent open until it runs liquid-free and the pump pressure gauge reads no pressure. Try the starter once, with the motor locked out, to prove that the pump cannot start. A seal replacement on the isolated pump takes about 65 min. Keep the drain and the vent open for the whole of the work, and keep every lock and tag in place while the seal housing is open and the pump stands drained and depressured.

fact_base: Excerpt content: the staffing ramp is set at 16% and the excerpt defends that figure against a lower alternative. The excerpt refers to the project's cost table by section name and does not repeat its figures.
input: The staffing ramp for the upgrade project has been set at 16%, and although a lower figure has been suggested during the review process, there are strong reasons for holding the ramp at 16% for the time being. A lower ramp is essentially based on the assumption that every post will be filled smoothly and promptly on the very day on which the previous holder leaves it, but in reality recruitment for specialist posts rarely runs in such an orderly fashion: offers are declined, notice periods overlap, and when posts are filled late, all of the packages that depend on them are held up as a consequence. The ramp is intended to cover the overlap between incoming and outgoing post holders, the periods during which posts stand empty, and the release of staff for training. Reducing the ramp would not in itself eliminate any of these gaps; it would simply transfer their cost into overtime working and into delays to dependent packages. It should also be noted that the cost table in the Costs section has been built on the 16% figure, so a change at this stage would mean reopening a large number of package estimates. It is therefore suggested that the steering group holds the figure until the actual fill rate for the first posts can be seen.
target: The staffing ramp for the upgrade project is set at 16%, and the figure is held against the lower allowance proposed in review. A lower ramp assumes that each post is filled on the day the previous holder leaves it. Recruitment for the project's specialist posts does not run to that pattern: offers are declined, notice periods overlap, and a post filled late holds up every package that depends on it. The 16% ramp covers the overlap between an incoming post holder and the outgoing holder, the weeks in which a post stands empty, and the cover for training release. Cutting the ramp removes none of these gaps. Their cost moves into overtime and into delay on the packages that wait for staff. The cost table in the Costs section is built on the 16% figure; a change now reopens every package estimate that rests on it. The steering group is asked to hold the ramp until recruitment for the first posts shows the actual fill rate, when the figure can be revisited on evidence rather than on an assumption of clean handover at every post.

fact_base: A gravity settler removes sand from a process stream. Design overflow rate is 1.74 m h-1 at a throughput of 303 m3 h-1, giving a plan area of 174 m2. The overflow-rate basis is a vendor rule for this solid; no settling test on the actual slurry has been run.
input: The settler under consideration is a gravity unit that has been designed to remove sand from a process stream, and its sizing is based on the widely used overflow-rate method. The throughput of the unit is 303 m3 h-1, and the design overflow rate that has been adopted is 1.74 m h-1, a value taken from a vendor rule developed for this particular solid. The required plan area is obtained by dividing the throughput by the overflow rate, so that 303 m3 h-1 divided by 1.74 m h-1 gives a plan area of 174 m2 for the settler. It is important to note, however, that the overflow-rate basis has an important limitation: no settling test has actually been carried out on the real slurry, which means that the design rate has not been validated against the behaviour of the material that the unit will really treat. As a result, the plan area of 174 m2 should be regarded as an estimate that rests entirely on the vendor rule, and factors such as the particle size distribution of the sand, the solids loading, and short-circuiting near the inlet could all cause the performance of the installed unit to differ appreciably from the design intention, whether for better or for worse. For these reasons, the sizing should be understood as a first estimate that will need to be revisited once test data on the actual slurry become available at some point in the future.
target: A gravity settler removes sand from a process stream. The design overflow rate is 1.74 m h-1 at a throughput of 303 m3 h-1. Plan area follows from the overflow-rate definition: the area is the throughput divided by the overflow rate. Thus 303 m3 h-1 divided by 1.74 m h-1 gives a plan area of 174 m2. The overflow rate is a vendor rule for this solid. No settling test on the actual slurry has been run, so the rate has not been checked against the slurry as fed, and the plan area of 174 m2 stands on the vendor rule alone. The rule takes no account of the sand grading as fed, of the solids loading, or of short-circuiting at the inlet, and each of these moves the rate a working settler achieves. Plan area is the sizing variable because the overflow rate is stated per unit of area: the liquid rises through the settler at the overflow rate, and a particle that settles faster than the liquid rises reaches the floor of the unit, while a particle that settles more slowly is carried out with the overflow. The stated basis therefore fixes the area arithmetically and leaves its adequacy untested. Any margin for the untested basis has to be added to the area as a separate decision; nothing in the overflow rate, the throughput, or the division between them supplies one. The design as stated also leaves the plan dimensions, the depth, and the inlet and outlet arrangements open, and each of these affects how closely the installed unit approaches the uniform upward flow that the overflow-rate definition assumes. The figure to carry forward is a settler of the computed area, sized by a rule that the feed material has not yet confirmed.

fact_base: Capital appraisal for a warehouse extension: installed cost $1432k, expected net saving $259k per year for 12 years. At a discount rate of 10% the present value of the savings is $1765k and the net present value is $333k. Savings are vendor and utility estimates; no saving has yet been measured on a comparable installation.
input: This appraisal considers a proposed warehouse extension with an installed cost of $1432k, which is expected to generate net savings of $259k per year over a period of 12 years. When these savings are discounted at a discount rate of 10%, the present value of the savings amounts to $1765k. Subtracting the installed cost of $1432k from this figure gives a net present value of $333k, which is positive and therefore indicates that the project is financially attractive on the stated assumptions. It is important to note, however, that the savings figures are based on estimates provided by vendors and by the utility, and that no saving has as yet actually been measured on a comparable installation. This means that the net present value of $333k should be treated with a degree of caution, because any shortfall in the savings that are actually achieved would reduce the net present value accordingly. Overall, the appraisal shows a positive result, but the result depends heavily on estimates that have not yet been confirmed in practice on any comparable warehouse extension project.
target: The warehouse extension has a net present value of $333k at a discount rate of 10%: the present value of the expected savings, $1765k over 12 years at $259k per year, exceeds the installed cost of $1432k by that margin. The savings are vendor and utility estimates. No saving has been measured on a comparable installation, so the $333k rests on unmeasured inputs, and a shortfall in the achieved savings reduces the net present value in proportion. The cost side is an installed cost of $1432k, quoted as a single figure for the completed extension; the savings side is an estimate repeated year by year over the appraisal period, and the appraisal is only as firm as the weaker of the two. The two sides also differ in kind: the cost is committed once, at construction, while the savings accrue only if the extension performs as the vendors and the utility expect, year after year. On the stated figures the extension clears its cost of capital with the margin shown. The decision the appraisal supports is to proceed on the estimates as they stand, with the first year's measured saving as the check on the annual saving that the result assumes throughout the appraisal period.

fact_base: Goal: compute the half-life of a first-order reaction and the fraction remaining after 60 min. For a first-order reaction the rate constant k (min-1) fixes the half-life t1/2 (min) by t1/2 = ln(2) / k, and the fraction remaining after time t (min) is exp(-k t). Measured rate constant: k = 0.023 min-1 at 323 K, from concentration measurements every 5 min over 90 min. Worked results: t1/2 = 30.1 min; the fraction remaining after 60 min is 0.25 (dimensionless), both computed from the stated relations. The relations hold for a first-order reaction only; a reaction of another order follows a different decay law.
input: In this example, the aim is to calculate the half-life of a first-order reaction and also to determine the fraction of the reactant that remains after 60 min. For a first-order reaction, the half-life t1/2 is related to the rate constant k by the expression t1/2 = ln(2) / k, and the fraction remaining after a time t is given by exp(-k t). The measured rate constant for the reaction is k = 0.023 min-1 at 323 K, and this value was obtained from concentration measurements that were taken every 5 min over a total period of 90 min. Substituting the value of k into the half-life expression gives t1/2 = ln(2) / 0.023 = 30.1 min. In a similar way, substituting into the decay expression gives the fraction remaining after 60 min as exp(-0.023 * 60) = 0.25, which is dimensionless. It is worth noting that this result is consistent with the half-life, because 60 min corresponds to approximately two half-lives, and after two half-lives one quarter of the material would be expected to remain, namely a fraction of 0.25. Finally, it should be remembered that these relations are valid only for a first-order reaction, and that a reaction of a different order would follow a completely different decay law.
target: Calculate the half-life of a first-order reaction with rate constant k = 0.023 min-1 at 323 K, and the fraction of reactant remaining after 60 min. For a first-order reaction the half-life t1/2 is fixed by k through t1/2 = ln(2) / k, and the fraction remaining after time t is exp(-k t). The rate constant comes from concentration measurements taken every 5 min over 90 min. Substitution in the half-life relation gives t1/2 = ln(2) / 0.023 = 30.1 min. Substitution in the decay relation gives the fraction remaining after 60 min as exp(-0.023 * 60) = 0.25, dimensionless. The two results check against each other: 60 min is close to two half-lives, and two halvings leave one quarter of the starting amount, in agreement with the computed 0.25. The half-life can also be read back against the measurements behind the rate constant: a concentration series that halves over each interval of the computed length confirms the first-order form, while a series that does not halve uniformly contradicts it and sends the analysis back to the order of the reaction. Both results are reported as computed from the stated relations, on the measured rate constant as it stands, with no correction or fitting step between the measurement and the reported values. Both relations hold for a first-order reaction only. A reaction of another order follows a different decay law, and neither the half-life nor the fraction remaining carries over to it.

subtype: worked example with equation: Antoine vapour pressure
fact_base: The vapour pressure of acetone at 60 °C is estimated from the Antoine equation with constants $A$ = 7.11714, $B$ = 1210.595 and $C$ = 229.664 (pressure in mmHg, temperature in °C). The estimate is 115.5 kPa. The constants are valid only over their fitted temperature range; the source databank value governs design.
input:
The vapour pressure of acetone at a temperature of 60 °C can be estimated by means of the Antoine equation, which is a widely used correlation that relates vapour pressure to temperature through three fitted constants. The equation takes the form

$$\log_{10} P = A - \frac{B}{T + C}$$

where $P$ is the vapour pressure, $T$ is the temperature in °C, and $A$, $B$ and $C$ are the Antoine constants for the substance concerned. For acetone, the constants are $A$ = 7.11714, $B$ = 1210.595 and $C$ = 229.664, with the pressure expressed in mmHg and the temperature in °C. Substituting the temperature of 60 °C into the equation leads to an estimated vapour pressure of 115.5 kPa. The Antoine correlation is one of the standard tools of physical property estimation, and it is routinely used in process calculations whenever a measured value is not immediately to hand, because it requires nothing more than the temperature and a set of constants that have been tabulated for a very large number of common substances. It is important to note that the Antoine constants are valid only over the temperature range over which they were fitted, and that a temperature of 60 °C falling outside that range would leave the estimate without the support of the underlying data. Furthermore, the value obtained from the correlation is only an estimate, and for design purposes the value given in the source databank should be regarded as the governing value in place of the correlation estimate of 115.5 kPa, because it is the databank value that ultimately controls the design.
target:
The vapour pressure of acetone at 60 °C is estimated from the Antoine equation

$$\log_{10} P = A - \frac{B}{T + C}$$

where $P$ is the vapour pressure, $T$ is the temperature in °C, and $A$, $B$ and $C$ are fitted constants. For acetone $A$ = 7.11714, $B$ = 1210.595 and $C$ = 229.664, with pressure in mmHg and temperature in °C. Substitution of $T$ = 60 °C in the Antoine equation gives an estimate of 115.5 kPa. The constants hold only over their fitted temperature range. The estimate stands only where 60 °C lies inside that range; outside the range the correlation is an extrapolation and the result carries no support from the fit. The three constants are not interchangeable. The subtracted term carries the temperature dependence of the vapour pressure, the constant added to the temperature inside that term shifts the curve along the temperature axis, and the leading constant sets the level of the curve as a whole; a change in any one of them changes the estimate at every temperature, not only at the temperature of interest. The estimate is also stated on a different pressure basis from the constants: the constants take the pressure in mmHg, and the reported estimate is in kPa, so the figure as reported stands on the SI basis on which a design calculation is made. The estimate is a correlation value rather than a measured one. The source databank value governs design, and where the estimate and the databank value differ, the databank value is used and the difference is charged to the correlation. Acetone is therefore assigned 115.5 kPa provisionally: the number is adequate for screening calculations that tolerate correlation error, and it is replaced by the databank value at the point where the design is fixed.

subtype: worked example with equation: Raoult partial pressure
fact_base: An ideal liquid mixture holds hexane in heptane at a liquid mole fraction $x$ of 0.43 for the volatile component. Its pure-component vapour pressure $P^*$ at the mixture temperature is 20.1 kPa, so the partial pressure $p$ is 8.6 kPa by Raoult's law. Raoult's law assumes an ideal solution; activity coefficients for the real mixture are not applied.
input:
Raoult's law provides a simple and convenient method for estimating the partial pressure of a component in an ideal liquid mixture, and it is applied here to a mixture of hexane in heptane. The law is expressed by the equation

$$p = x P^*$$

where $p$ is the partial pressure of the volatile component, $x$ is its mole fraction in the liquid, and $P^*$ is the vapour pressure of the pure component at the temperature of the mixture. In this case, the liquid mole fraction of the volatile component is $x$ = 0.43, and the pure-component vapour pressure at the mixture temperature is $P^*$ = 20.1 kPa. Multiplying the mole fraction of 0.43 by the pure-component vapour pressure of 20.1 kPa gives the partial pressure as $p$ = 8.6 kPa. The law is attractive in practice because it reduces the whole problem to two quantities that are either known from the composition of the mixture or readily available from standard tables of physical properties, and it is very widely used as a first estimate in vapour-liquid equilibrium calculations of all kinds. It is important to note that Raoult's law is based on the assumption of an ideal solution, in which the interactions between unlike molecules are the same as those between like molecules. For a real mixture, this assumption is not generally exact, and activity coefficients would be used to correct the result; in the present calculation, however, no activity coefficients have been applied, so the value of 8.6 kPa should be understood as the ideal-solution estimate for the mixture at $x$ = 0.43 only.
target:
An ideal liquid mixture of hexane in heptane holds the volatile component at a liquid mole fraction $x$ of 0.43. Its pure-component vapour pressure $P^*$ at the mixture temperature is 20.1 kPa. Raoult's law gives the partial pressure $p$ as

$$p = x P^*$$

where $p$ is the partial pressure, $x$ is the liquid mole fraction of the volatile component and $P^*$ is its pure-component vapour pressure at the mixture temperature. Substitution gives $p$ = 0.43 × 20.1 kPa = 8.6 kPa. Raoult's law holds for an ideal solution. The partial pressure is the share of the total pressure over the mixture that the volatile component accounts for, and it is the quantity that links the liquid composition to the composition of the vapour in equilibrium with the liquid: a higher partial pressure for hexane means a vapour richer in hexane, at the same total pressure. Heptane enters the calculation only through the mole fraction. Its own vapour pressure does not appear in the stated data, because the partial pressure of the volatile component is fixed by its own mole fraction and its own pure-component vapour pressure alone. Activity coefficients for the real mixture are not applied in this calculation, so 8.6 kPa is the ideal-solution value: the partial pressure of the real mixture departs from it by the activity coefficient of the volatile component, which multiplies the ideal value and which the stated data do not supply. A mixture in which unlike molecules attract each other more strongly than like molecules holds the volatile component back and gives a lower partial pressure; a mixture with weaker unlike attraction gives a higher one. The result is used as the ideal reference against which a corrected value would be compared, and not as the partial pressure of the actual hexane and heptane mixture at $x$ = 0.43 and the stated temperature.

fact_base: A binary distillation separates propane/propylene at a relative volatility of 1.82 that is taken as constant over the column. Specifications: distillate 98 mol% light component, bottoms 2 mol% light component. The Fenske minimum stage count is 13 theoretical stages including the reboiler. The actual design uses a reflux ratio of 1.3 times the minimum; the stage count at that reflux comes from a separate simulation.
input: The separation of propane from propylene by binary distillation is a particularly demanding separation, because the two components have very similar volatilities (a relative volatility of 1.82). In this case, the relative volatility is taken as 1.82, and it is assumed to remain constant over the whole height of the column. The product specifications require the distillate to contain 98 mol% of the light component, while the bottoms stream is allowed to contain only 2 mol% of the light component. Applying the Fenske equation to these specifications gives a minimum stage count of 13 theoretical stages, including the reboiler. It is important to note that this minimum corresponds to operation at total reflux, and that it represents a lower bound rather than an achievable design value. The actual design is based on a reflux ratio of 1.3 times the minimum reflux ratio, and the number of stages that is required at that reflux ratio cannot be obtained from the Fenske equation itself. Instead, it is determined by means of a separate simulation. The Fenske result of 13 stages therefore serves as a benchmark: the simulation result must lie above 13, and the difference between the two indicates how far the operating design stands from the theoretical minimum for this separation. The result is a preliminary sizing figure of the kind used at the earliest stage of a design study, before any rigorous calculation is attempted.
target: A binary distillation separates propane and propylene at a relative volatility of 1.82, taken as constant over the column. Specifications are 98 mol% light component in the distillate and 2 mol% light component in the bottoms. For these specifications the Fenske equation gives a minimum stage count of 13 theoretical stages, including the reboiler. The minimum stage count is the stage count at total reflux, and it bounds every operating design from below. A column at finite reflux needs more stages, by an amount the Fenske equation does not determine. The design reflux ratio is 1.3 times the minimum reflux ratio. The stage count at the design reflux comes from a separate simulation at that reflux. The simulation result is read against the floor of 13 stages: a count below the floor would show an error in the simulation, and the margin above the floor is the stage cost of finite reflux. The specifications are symmetric in form: the distillate is nearly pure light component and the bottoms nearly pure heavy component, so the separation is a sharp split at both ends of the column, and the stage count prices both ends together rather than either end alone. Nothing in the result depends on the feed rate or on the column diameter; the count is a property of the separation specification and the volatility alone. The Fenske count also fixes the scale of the separation duty. A minimum of 13 stages at a relative volatility of 1.82 marks a separation in which each stage gives little enrichment, so the operating count from the simulation is expected to stand well above the minimum rather than close to it.

fact_base: Pervaporation is a membrane separation in which a liquid feed contacts one side of a membrane and vacuum on the other side draws the permeating component through as vapour. Flux is the mass permeating per unit membrane area per hour (kg m-2 h-1). The separation factor is the water-to-alcohol ratio in the permeate divided by the same ratio in the feed (dimensionless). Feed: 85 wt% n-butanol in water, at 60 °C. One feed composition was tested; no test ran beyond 500 h. Polymer membrane: flux 1.8 kg m-2 h-1, separation factor 180, flux fell 8% over 500 h. Zeolite membrane: flux 1.3 kg m-2 h-1, separation factor 320, flux unchanged over 500 h within measurement error. Flux, selectivity and stability are seldom reported together for the same membrane.
input: Pervaporation is a membrane separation process in which a liquid feed is brought into contact with one side of a membrane, while a vacuum applied to the other side draws the permeating component through the membrane as a vapour. In this study, two membranes are compared for the separation of a feed containing 85 wt% n-butanol in water at 60 °C. The flux, which is defined as the mass permeating per unit membrane area per hour (kg m-2 h-1), and the separation factor, defined as the water-to-alcohol ratio in the permeate divided by the same ratio in the feed, are used as the measures of performance. The polymer membrane achieved a flux of 1.8 kg m-2 h-1 with a separation factor of 180, although its flux fell by 8% over 500 h of operation. The zeolite membrane, by contrast, gave a flux of 1.3 kg m-2 h-1 and a separation factor of 320, and its flux remained unchanged over 500 h within the limits of measurement error. It should be noted that only one feed composition was tested and that no test was run beyond 500 h. Flux, selectivity and stability are seldom reported together for the same membrane, and the comparison presented here brings the three properties together for the two membranes under the same feed conditions of 85 wt% n-butanol in water at 60 °C, while the stability of either membrane beyond 500 h remains entirely untested.
target: Pervaporation is a membrane separation in which a liquid feed contacts one side of a membrane and vacuum on the other side draws the permeating component through as vapour. Two membranes are compared on a feed of 85 wt% n-butanol in water at 60 °C. Flux is the mass permeating per unit membrane area per hour (kg m-2 h-1), and the separation factor is the water-to-alcohol ratio in the permeate divided by the same ratio in the feed (dimensionless). The polymer membrane gave a flux of 1.8 kg m-2 h-1 and a separation factor of 180; its flux fell 8% over 500 h. The zeolite membrane gave a flux of 1.3 kg m-2 h-1 and a separation factor of 320, with flux unchanged over 500 h within measurement error. The zeolite membrane is the more selective and the more stable of the two; the polymer membrane passes more mass per unit area per hour. The two membranes divide the performance between them: neither leads on every measure, and the choice between them turns on whether the duty is limited by throughput or by product purity and by the working life expected of the membrane. Flux, selectivity and stability are seldom reported together for one membrane, and the pair of results supplies all three on one feed. The comparison rests on one feed composition and on tests capped at 500 h: the ordering of the two membranes is established at 85 wt% and 60 °C, and stability beyond 500 h is not covered by either result.

subtype: worked example with equation: Stokes settling
fact_base: Catalyst fines of diameter $d_p$ = 50 micrometres and density 2500 kg m-3 settle in water at 293 K. Stokes' law gives a terminal velocity $v_t$ of 2.05 mm s-1. The estimate requires creeping flow; the particle Reynolds number must be checked before the value is used.
input:
Catalyst fines with a diameter of 50 micrometres and a density of 2500 kg m-3 are settling in water at a temperature of 293 K, and their terminal settling velocity can be estimated by means of Stokes' law, which is written as

$$v_t = \frac{g d_p^2 (\rho_p - \rho)}{18 \mu}$$

where $v_t$ is the terminal velocity, $g$ is the gravitational acceleration, $d_p$ is the particle diameter, $\rho_p$ is the density of the particles, $\rho$ is the density of the fluid, and $\mu$ is the viscosity of the fluid. Applying the law to the stated fines gives a terminal velocity of 2.05 mm s-1. The calculation is a standard one in the design of settling equipment, and it is typically performed at an early stage of a design, long before any detailed sizing is attempted. It is important to note, however, that Stokes' law is valid only under creeping-flow conditions, which means that the particle Reynolds number at 293 K must be checked carefully before the calculated value of 2.05 mm s-1 is used for any design purpose. If the Reynolds number turns out to lie outside the creeping-flow range, the estimate will not be reliable and a different drag relation will have to be used instead.
target:
Catalyst fines of diameter $d_p$ = 50 micrometres and density 2500 kg m-3 settle in water at 293 K. Stokes' law gives the terminal velocity $v_t$ as

$$v_t = \frac{g d_p^2 (\rho_p - \rho)}{18 \mu}$$

where $g$ is gravitational acceleration, $\rho_p$ is the particle density, $\rho$ is the fluid density and $\mu$ is the fluid viscosity. For the stated fines, Stokes' law gives $v_t$ = 2.05 mm s-1. The diameter enters the law squared, so the velocity is set largely by the size of the fines: a modest change in the assumed diameter moves the result far more than the same proportional change in the density difference between particle and fluid. The stated diameter and density are therefore the figures on which the estimate stands, and an error in either of them passes into the computed velocity undiminished. Stokes' law holds for creeping flow only. The estimate is therefore conditional: the particle Reynolds number must be checked before the value is used, and a Reynolds number outside the creeping-flow range invalidates the estimate rather than merely qualifying it. The check uses the computed velocity itself, with the fluid properties at 293 K. Inside the creeping-flow range, 2.05 mm s-1 is the settling velocity to carry into a separation calculation; outside it, the drag on the fines follows a different relation and the velocity is recomputed on that relation.

input:
Catalyst fines with a diameter of 50 micrometres and a density of 1400 kg m-3 are settling in water at a temperature of 293 K, and their terminal settling velocity can be estimated by means of Stokes' law, which is written as

Because the density of these fines is only moderately greater than that of the fluid in which they are settling, the driving force for settling is comparatively small, and the fines settle slowly. If the Reynolds number turns out to lie outside the creeping-flow range, the estimate will not be reliable and a different drag relation will have to be used instead of the Stokes relation, and the whole estimate will then need to be revisited in the light of whatever relation replaces it.
target:
Catalyst fines of diameter $d_p$ = 50 micrometres and density 1400 kg m-3 settle in water at 293 K. Stokes' law gives the terminal velocity $v_t$ as

$$v_t = \frac{g d_p^2 (\rho_p - \rho)}{18 \mu}$$

where $g$ is gravitational acceleration, $\rho_p$ is the particle density, $\rho$ is the fluid density and $\mu$ is the fluid viscosity. For the stated fines, Stokes' law gives $v_t$ = 0.55 mm s-1. The density difference between the fines and the water is small, and the settling velocity is correspondingly low: the fines stay suspended under disturbances that denser particles of the same size would settle through. A velocity of this order sets the terms for any vessel intended to remove the fines: the liquid must stay in the vessel long enough for a particle to fall through the depth of liquid above the outlet, and a shallow, quiet settling zone serves the separation better than a deep, disturbed one. The estimate also treats the fines as settling singly. A concentrated suspension settles as a body, and more slowly than its single particles; the stated data give no solids concentration against which that effect could be judged, so the single-particle value stands as the result. Stokes' law holds for creeping flow only. The estimate is therefore conditional: the particle Reynolds number must be checked before the value is used, and a Reynolds number outside the creeping-flow range invalidates the estimate rather than merely qualifying it. The check uses the computed velocity itself, with the fluid properties at 293 K. Inside the creeping-flow range, 0.55 mm s-1 is the settling velocity to carry into a separation calculation; outside it, the drag on the fines follows a different relation and the velocity is recomputed on that relation.

fact_base: Staffing review for a quality laboratory: 18 full-time staff, overtime at 10% of paid hours last year. Replacing half the overtime with one additional hire costs $56k per year fully loaded. Overtime is concentrated in two seasonal peaks; a hire is paid for the full year.
input: Staffing levels in the quality laboratory have been the subject of considerable discussion in recent months, and this review brings together the key figures that underpin the current debate. The laboratory currently employs 18 full-time staff, and over the course of last year overtime working amounted to 10% of paid hours, a level that reflects the sustained pressure placed on the team's capacity. One option that has been carefully considered is the replacement of half of that overtime, equivalent to 5% of paid hours, with one additional hire, at a fully loaded cost of $56k per year. It is important to note, however, that the overtime is not distributed evenly across the year; instead, it is heavily concentrated in two seasonal peaks, whereas a new hire would be paid for the full year, including the quieter periods when the additional capacity is simply not required. The $56k commitment is therefore a fixed one, while overtime spending flexes with demand from week to week. Overall, the choice involves a careful balancing of cost, flexibility, and cover at the peaks, and a fuller analysis of the peak workload pattern will be needed before a final view can be reached.
target: One additional hire, replacing half of the overtime in the quality laboratory, costs $56k per year fully loaded; the decision rests with laboratory management. The laboratory employs 18 full-time staff, and overtime was 10% of paid hours last year. Half of the overtime is 5% of paid hours. The trade-off is one of timing: the $56k is paid across the full year, while the overtime it displaces falls in two seasonal peaks. In the quieter months the hire adds capacity that the workload does not call for, and the post cannot be stood down when demand falls. Overtime, by contrast, is bought only in the weeks when the peaks arrive, and it can fall away altogether in a quiet year. The review sets a fixed annual salary cost against a variable overtime cost of the same stated size at the peaks, and the deciding evidence is the shape of the peak workload: how much of the peak overtime is concentrated enough, and predictable enough, to be covered by one person's contracted hours rather than bought week by week. The review draws on last year's paid-hours record for the overtime figure and on the fully loaded cost of the post for the hire figure; both are stated on the same annual basis so that the comparison is like for like. What the record does not show is absence cover or training time, and neither is priced in either figure.

fact_base: A single-stage compressor raises nitrogen from 2 bar to 9 bar. Inlet temperature is 313 K. For isentropic compression with a heat-capacity ratio of 1.4, the discharge temperature is 481 K. The isentropic estimate excludes mechanical losses; the installed machine's measured discharge temperature is higher.
input: In order to estimate the discharge conditions of a single-stage compressor handling nitrogen, it is possible to draw on the well-established isentropic relations that are widely used for this type of calculation. The discharge temperature is a quantity of considerable practical interest, since it bears on the selection of materials of construction, on the duty of any downstream cooling that may be required, and on the safe operating envelope of the machine as a whole. In the case under consideration, the compressor raises the nitrogen from an inlet pressure of 2 bar to a discharge pressure of 9 bar, and the inlet temperature is 313 K. If the compression is assumed to be isentropic, and a heat-capacity ratio of 1.4 is adopted for the gas, the calculation yields a discharge temperature of 481 K. It is worth emphasising, however, that this figure should be regarded as an idealised estimate: the isentropic treatment by its nature excludes mechanical losses, and the installed machine's measured discharge temperature is in fact higher than the calculated value. The estimate nevertheless provides a useful first indication of the temperature level that the discharge arrangement will need to accommodate in practice.
target: Calculate the discharge temperature of a single-stage compressor that raises nitrogen from 2 bar to 9 bar, given an inlet temperature of 313 K. The compression is taken as isentropic, and the heat-capacity ratio is taken as 1.4; both assumptions are stated here, before the relation that uses them. The nitrogen is treated as a gas with constant heat capacity over the interval, so a single ratio serves for the whole compression. No property of the machine enters the estimate: the relation connects the two states of the gas, and the path between them is the reversible adiabatic path, not the path the installed machine follows. For isentropic compression of a gas with a constant heat-capacity ratio, the discharge temperature follows from the inlet temperature and the pressure ratio alone: the temperature ratio equals the pressure ratio raised to a power set by the heat-capacity ratio. Substitution of the inlet temperature and the two pressures gives a discharge temperature of 481 K. The check on the result is the installed machine. Its measured discharge temperature is higher than the isentropic value. The isentropic estimate excludes mechanical losses, and the installed machine carries those losses; the estimate is the ideal reference state for the machine, not its expected operating temperature, and a design that must accommodate the discharge stream is set against the measured behaviour rather than against the ideal figure.

subtype: worked example with equation: Arrhenius ratio
fact_base: Rate constants for a catalyst ageing test were measured at two temperatures. With activation energy $E_a$ of 53 kJ mol-1, raising the temperature from 300 K to 330 K multiplies the rate constant $k$ by 6.9. The estimate holds the pre-exponential factor $A$ constant over the interval.
input:
The temperature dependence of reaction rates is very commonly described by means of the Arrhenius relation, which provides a convenient framework within which the effect of a change in temperature on the rate constant can be assessed. In the present case, rate constants for a catalyst ageing test were measured at two temperatures, and the relation takes the following form:

$$k = A \exp\left(-\frac{E_a}{R T}\right)$$

In this expression, $k$ is the rate constant, $A$ is the pre-exponential factor, $E_a$ is the activation energy, $R$ is the gas constant, and $T$ is the absolute temperature. Taking the activation energy $E_a$ to be 53 kJ mol-1, it can be shown that raising the temperature from 300 K to 330 K has the effect of multiplying the rate constant $k$ by a factor of 6.9, which illustrates just how sensitive the ageing process is to the temperature at which it is carried out. It should be noted that this estimate rests on the assumption that the pre-exponential factor $A$ remains constant over the temperature interval in question, and a different behaviour of $A$ would of course lead to a somewhat different ratio. The relation is therefore a natural starting point for comparing the rates at which the catalyst ages under different thermal conditions in service.
target:
Rate constants for a catalyst ageing test were measured at two temperatures. The temperature dependence of the rate constant $k$ is stated by the Arrhenius relation,

$$k = A \exp\left(-\frac{E_a}{R T}\right)$$

where $k$ denotes the rate constant, $A$ the pre-exponential factor, $E_a$ the activation energy, $R$ the gas constant and $T$ the absolute temperature. Forming the ratio of the rate constants at the two temperatures removes the pre-exponential factor from the expression and leaves a single exponential in the activation energy and the reciprocal temperatures. With $E_a$ = 53 kJ mol-1, raising $T$ from 300 K to 330 K multiplies $k$ by 6.9. The ratio is formed from the relation at the two temperatures: $A$ cancels in the division, and the ratio is set by $E_a$ and the two temperatures alone. The estimate holds $A$ constant over the interval. A pre-exponential factor that varied with temperature would enter the ratio alongside the exponential term, and the stated factor would not then follow from $E_a$ and the temperatures alone; the stated factor is the value under the constant-$A$ assumption, and it is reported on that basis. For the ageing test the factor converts a rate measured at the lower temperature into the corresponding rate at the higher one, on the stated assumption, and it is this conversion that the factor is used for.

fact_base: Adsorption of a dye from water on a metal-organic framework was measured in batch tests at 298 K. The fitted Langmuir capacity was 254 mg of dye per gram of adsorbent at pH 6. At an adsorbent dose of 1.1 g L-1, removal after 120 min was 93% of the initial dye concentration of 50 mg L-1. The Langmuir fit is reported for pH 6 only; capacity at other pH values was not measured.
input: The adsorption of a dye from water onto a metal-organic framework was investigated by means of batch tests carried out at 298 K, and the results obtained provide a useful picture of the performance of the material under the conditions studied. The measurements were made with the dye in water throughout, so the solvent is the same in every test reported here. When the data were fitted to the Langmuir model, the fitted capacity came out at 254 mg of dye per gram of adsorbent at pH 6, which represents the saturation capacity implied by the model for this particular system. In a further set of measurements, an adsorbent dose of 1.1 g L-1 was employed, and it was found that the removal achieved after 120 min corresponded to 93% of the initial dye concentration of 50 mg L-1, leaving a residual concentration of 3.5 mg L-1 in the treated water. It is important to bear in mind that the Langmuir fit is reported for pH 6 only, and that the capacity at other pH values was not measured, so the fitted figure should not be taken to apply beyond the conditions under which it was obtained.
target: Adsorption of a dye from water on a metal-organic framework was measured in batch tests at 298 K. The fitted Langmuir capacity was 254 mg of dye per gram of adsorbent at pH 6. The capacity is a fitted parameter of the Langmuir model at the stated pH: it is the saturation uptake the model assigns to the adsorbent under the test conditions, not a directly weighed loading. At an adsorbent dose of 1.1 g L-1, removal after 120 min was 93% of the initial dye concentration of 50 mg L-1, a residual concentration of 3.5 mg L-1. The removal figure is stated against the initial concentration at the stated dose and contact time. The two figures describe different things. The capacity is a property of the fitted isotherm at saturation; the removal is an outcome at one dose and one contact time, and it falls short of the capacity whenever the residual concentration keeps the surface short of saturation. A higher dose or a longer contact time would change the removal figure without changing the capacity, and the two figures must not be interchanged. The batch tests were made in water at the stated temperature, and the reported values belong to that medium and that temperature. The Langmuir fit is reported for pH 6 only; capacity at other pH values was not measured, and the capacity figure does not extend to them.

fact_base: Inventory policy for a packaging film: mean demand 2035 units per week, standard deviation 433 units per week, replenishment lead time 5 weeks. Safety stock for a 95% cycle service level is 1598 units. Demand is treated as normal and independent between weeks; seasonal peaks are excluded.
input: The inventory policy for a packaging film has been reviewed in order to establish an appropriate level of safety stock, and the analysis draws on the recent demand history for the product in question. Mean demand is 2035 units per week, with a standard deviation of 433 units per week, and the replenishment lead time is 5 weeks, so that demand over the lead time averages some 10175 units. On this basis, the safety stock required to support a 95% cycle service level works out at 1598 units, and the corresponding reorder point, at which a replenishment order should be placed, is 11773 units. In practice the stock position is counted against the reorder point at each replenishment review, and an order is placed when the position falls to that point, with the safety stock held back as the buffer against demand running above its average while the order is in transit. It should be noted that the calculation treats demand as being normally distributed and independent from one week to the next, and that seasonal peaks in demand have been excluded from the analysis, so the figures may need to be revisited if the demand pattern changes materially in the future. The policy will then be applied to the film grades covered by the review from the next replenishment cycle onward.
target: Safety stock for the packaging film is 1598 units, set for a 95% cycle service level. The figure rests on the demand record: mean demand of 2035 units per week and a standard deviation of 433 units per week, with a replenishment lead time of 5 weeks. Demand over the lead time averages 10175 units, and the reorder point is 11773 units, the lead-time demand plus the safety stock. The service level is the probability that demand in a replenishment cycle is met from stock; the safety stock is the buffer held against the variability of weekly demand over the lead time, not against its mean. The calculation treats demand as normal and independent between weeks, and seasonal peaks are excluded. The stated stock covers ordinary week-to-week variation at the stated service level; a seasonal peak falls outside the basis of the figure, and cover for a peak would have to be set separately. In operation, the safety stock is not a working balance: it is drawn on only where demand over the lead time runs above its mean, and it is restored by the incoming replenishment. Where weekly demand is correlated rather than independent — a promotion, a contract start, a seasonal build — the variability over the lead time is larger than the stated basis assumes, and the same service level would need a larger buffer. The figure stands as a policy for ordinary variation, to be reviewed when the demand pattern or the lead time changes.

fact_base: A tutorial passage explains the Sherwood number to second-year students. Definition in words: the Sherwood number is the ratio of convective to diffusive mass transfer at a surface. The passage must state what a value near 1 means and what a large value means, without inventing numerical examples.
input: The Sherwood number is a dimensionless group that plays a central role in the analysis of mass transfer, and it is helpful to develop a clear physical picture of what it represents before it is used in design calculations. In essence, the Sherwood number expresses the ratio of convective to diffusive mass transfer at a surface, bringing together in a single quantity the relative importance of the two mechanisms by which a species can be transported through the fluid adjacent to the surface. When the value is near 1, the implication is that convection contributes little beyond what diffusion alone would achieve, and the transfer process is essentially diffusion-controlled in character. When the value is large, by contrast, convection is the dominant mechanism, the fluid at the surface is continually renewed, and transfer proceeds much more rapidly than diffusion alone would allow. The group is encountered throughout the treatment of gas absorption, liquid extraction, and drying, and in each of these operations it performs the same service of separating the contribution of the flow from the contribution of molecular motion. A sound grasp of these two limiting cases provides the foundation on which the use of the group in correlations and in equipment sizing is built.
target: The Sherwood number compares two routes by which a species crosses the fluid at a surface: transport carried by the moving fluid, and transport by molecular diffusion. The Sherwood number is defined as the ratio of convective to diffusive mass transfer at a surface. A value near 1 means the two routes contribute on comparable terms: convection adds little to the transfer that diffusion alone would give, and the rate is set largely by the diffusive step across the fluid at the surface. A large value means convection dominates. The flow continually renews the fluid at the surface, the layer across which diffusion must act is kept thin, and the transfer rate stands well above the rate that diffusion alone would sustain. The number is dimensionless, and it carries neither the size of the equipment nor the identity of the species into the comparison; two arrangements handling different duties can be set side by side on the strength of the number alone. Read in this way, the group tells the engineer which mechanism an improvement must attack: where the value is large, the diffusive step is already short and further gain lies in the surface or the driving force; where the value is near unity, the flow pattern at the surface is the limiting element and is the place to work.

topic: tut:phase:a binary mixture at fixed pressure
fact_base: A tutorial passage explains phase equilibrium for a binary mixture at fixed pressure. The passage states the equilibrium condition in words (equality of chemical potential across phases) before any equation is named. No numerical data are introduced; the passage is conceptual.
input: The condition that governs phase equilibrium can be stated quite simply, although its consequences are far-reaching. For a binary mixture held at fixed pressure, equilibrium between the phases requires that the chemical potential of each component be identical in every phase in which the component is present. The chemical potential may be thought of as a measure of the escaping tendency of a component from a phase: if the value in one phase exceeds the value in the other, there is a net driving force for the component to migrate across the boundary, and migration continues, with the compositions of both phases adjusting as it proceeds, until the two values come into balance. Because the pressure is held constant throughout, the system accommodates itself by way of temperature and composition rather than by way of pressure, and at any given temperature the compositions that the liquid and the vapour adopt at equilibrium are determined by the condition itself. It follows that equilibrium is a simultaneous requirement, applying to all components at once, and that a departure from equality for any one component is sufficient to set the system in motion again. The statement is general: it does not depend on the identity of the components involved.
target: Phase equilibrium for a binary mixture at fixed pressure rests on a single condition, stated in words before any equation is named: at equilibrium, the chemical potential of each component is the same in every phase in which that component appears. Chemical potential measures the tendency of a component to leave a phase. Where its value in one phase stands above its value in another, the component passes from the phase with the higher value to the phase with the lower, and the composition of both phases changes as it moves. The transfer stops when the values meet, and it stops for every component at the same state, since the phases share one temperature and one pressure throughout. Pressure is held fixed, so the adjustment falls on temperature and on the compositions: at a chosen temperature, the equilibrium compositions of the liquid and the vapour are fixed by the condition, and neither phase can hold an arbitrary composition while the other keeps its own. Away from equilibrium, the condition gives the direction of change as well as the end state, because the sign of the difference in chemical potential between the phases sets the direction in which each component moves. A mixture is at equilibrium only when the condition holds for every component at once; equality for one component alongside inequality for the other is a state still in motion.

fact_base: Performance of a natural-draft tower at a chemical site was logged over one summer month. Mean wet-bulb temperature was 24 °C, the approach was 4 K and the range was 7 K. Performance outside the logged month, in particular at winter wet-bulb temperatures, was not measured.
input: The performance of a natural-draft cooling tower at a chemical site was monitored over the course of one summer month, and the principal results are summarised below. Natural-draft towers rely on the buoyancy of heated air rather than on fan power in order to draw the cooling air through the fill, and their performance is accordingly sensitive to the ambient conditions under which they operate. The logging exercise was undertaken in order to establish a baseline for the unit under normal summer operation, against which any future deterioration in performance might subsequently be assessed. Daily readings were gathered over the month as a whole and the values reported are the averages for the period, individual excursions on particular days having been absorbed into the monthly means. Over the period in question, the mean wet-bulb temperature was 24 °C, the approach was 4 K, and the range was 7 K. The approach represents the difference between the temperature of the cooled water leaving the tower and the wet-bulb temperature of the incoming air, from which it follows that the cold water left at approximately 28 °C, while the range, which represents the temperature fall of the water across the tower, implies a hot-water inlet temperature of some 35 °C. These results provide a useful indication of the tower's behaviour under the conditions that prevailed during the logging period, although it should be emphasised that performance outside the logged month was not measured. In particular, no data are available for winter wet-bulb temperatures, and the figures should therefore not be extrapolated to the colder part of the year without further supporting measurements being obtained.
target: Performance of a natural-draft cooling tower at a chemical site was logged over one summer month. The mean wet-bulb temperature over the month was 24 °C, the approach was 4 K and the range was 7 K. The approach is the difference between the cold-water temperature and the wet-bulb temperature, so the cold water left the tower at 28 °C; the range is the fall in water temperature across the tower, so the hot water entered at 35 °C. The three figures describe the tower as it ran in the logged month: the wet-bulb temperature is set by the weather and not by the tower, while the approach measures how closely the tower brought the cold water to that limit, and the range measures the heat taken out of each pass of the circulating water. A natural-draft tower has no fan, and its air flow is set by the density difference between the air inside the tower and the air outside it; the logged performance therefore belongs to the air temperatures and water loadings of the month in which it was recorded, and it does not transfer unchanged to other seasons. The record is a monthly mean in each case, and day-to-day variation within the month is not reported; a hot spell inside the month and a cool spell are averaged together in the figures as stated. The figures are also a statement about the circulating-water rate and the heat load of the month: the range is the joint outcome of the two, and the same tower on a different load would show a different range at the same wet-bulb temperature. Performance outside the logged month was not measured. Winter wet-bulb temperatures in particular lie outside the record, and the tower's behaviour at them — the approach it would hold and the range it would sustain — is not established by these figures.

fact_base: The rate constant k (s-1) of a first-order liquid-phase reaction was measured at two temperatures. At 300 K, k = 0.08 s-1. At 340 K, k = 4.206 s-1, computed from the Arrhenius relation with activation energy 84 kJ mol-1 as a derived value. Each temperature was measured in triplicate; the relative standard deviation of k was 4%. Above 340 K the solvent evaporated during sampling, so no rate constant is reported above 340 K.
input: The rate constant k of a first-order liquid-phase reaction was measured at two different temperatures in order to characterise the temperature sensitivity of the reaction. At 300 K, the value of k was found to be 0.08 s-1. At the higher temperature of 340 K, the value of k was 4.206 s-1, this figure having been computed from the Arrhenius relation using an activation energy of 84 kJ mol-1, and it is presented as a derived value rather than as a direct experimental measurement. Each temperature was investigated in triplicate, and the relative standard deviation of k was 4%, which gives an indication of the reproducibility of the measurements. It should be noted that no rate constant is reported above 340 K, because at temperatures above 340 K the solvent was found to evaporate during the sampling process, which meant that reliable measurements could no longer be obtained under those conditions. The results nevertheless provide a clear indication of the strong temperature dependence exhibited by this particular reaction system over the range studied. The investigation forms part of a wider programme of work on the reaction, in which the temperature dependence of the rate is required for the design of the reactor in which the reaction is to be carried out on a larger scale.
target: The rate constant k of a first-order liquid-phase reaction was measured at two temperatures, each measurement in triplicate. At 300 K, k = 0.08 s-1. At 340 K, k = 4.206 s-1. The 340 K value is a derived value: it was computed from the Arrhenius relation with an activation energy of 84 kJ mol-1, and it is reported as computed, not as a direct measurement. The relative standard deviation of k across the replicate measurements was 4%. No rate constant is reported above 340 K: above that temperature the solvent evaporated during sampling, so samples taken there did not hold the composition they were drawn at, and no value from them is stated. The two values as reported therefore rest on different footings: the lower-temperature value is a measurement with its stated spread, and the higher-temperature value is a calculation from the stated activation energy, carrying the standing of the relation and of the activation energy rather than of a further set of replicates. The activation energy is the same quantity that links the two temperatures in the Arrhenius relation, and the computed value inherits any error in it directly. A reader who needs the rate constant between the two temperatures obtains it from the same relation and the same activation energy, on the same footing as the computed value.

fact_base: A tutorial passage explains the Prandtl number to second-year students. Definition in words: the Prandtl number is the ratio of momentum diffusivity to thermal diffusivity. The passage must state what a value near 1 means and what a large value means, without inventing numerical examples.
input: The Prandtl number is a dimensionless group of considerable importance in the study of heat transfer, and a clear understanding of its physical meaning is an essential foundation for its subsequent use. The Prandtl number is defined as the ratio of momentum diffusivity to thermal diffusivity, that is to say, it compares the rate at which momentum is transported through a fluid by viscous action with the rate at which heat is transported through the same fluid by conduction. When the value of the group is near 1, the two diffusivities are of comparable magnitude, and disturbances of velocity and of temperature spread through the fluid at broadly similar rates. When the value is large, on the other hand, momentum diffuses much more effectively than heat, and the region of fluid whose temperature has been affected by contact with a surface remains confined to a thin layer close to that surface, even though the influence of the surface on the velocity extends much further into the fluid. The group depends only on the properties of the fluid and on its state, and it provides a convenient means of judging, for any given fluid, the relative thicknesses of the layers within which velocity and temperature adjustments take place. It is for this reason that the group appears in the correlations by which surface heat transfer is calculated in practice across a wide range of equipment.
target: The Prandtl number sets two diffusivities side by side for the same fluid: the diffusivity of momentum, and the diffusivity of heat. The Prandtl number is defined as the ratio of momentum diffusivity to thermal diffusivity. Momentum diffusivity measures how fast a disturbance of velocity spreads through the fluid by viscosity alone; thermal diffusivity measures how fast a disturbance of temperature spreads by conduction alone. A value near 1 means the two spread at comparable rates. The velocity field and the temperature field then develop together: a layer of fluid that has been set in motion by a surface has been heated or cooled by that surface to a comparable depth, and neither field runs ahead of the other. A large value means momentum spreads far more readily than heat. The velocity disturbance reaches well beyond the region the temperature disturbance has reached, so the layer of fluid affected by a heated or cooled surface, in temperature, is thin compared with the layer affected in velocity. Heat then crosses a thin layer by conduction while momentum is exchanged across a much thicker one, and the surface heat transfer is governed by conduction across that thin layer. The number is a property of the fluid and its state, not of the apparatus: it is formed from the fluid's own transport properties, and it changes as those properties change with temperature. Its use is to say, for a given fluid, whether a surface process is limited by the spreading of momentum or by the spreading of heat, and the two limiting readings of the number frame every case between them.

subtype: worked example with equation: Stokes settling
fact_base: Glass beads of diameter $d_p$ = 100 micrometres and density 2500 kg m-3 settle in water at 293 K. Stokes' law gives a terminal velocity $v_t$ of 8.19 mm s-1. The estimate requires creeping flow; the particle Reynolds number must be checked before the value is used.
input:
The settling of fine particles in a liquid is a situation that arises in a wide range of separation processes, and a reliable estimate of the rate at which the particles fall is needed before the size of a settling vessel can be fixed with any confidence. At the terminal velocity the particle falls at a constant rate, the driving force provided by gravity, net of buoyancy, being exactly balanced by the resistance offered by the liquid through which the particle moves. In the case considered here, glass beads of diameter $d_p$ = 100 micrometres and density 2500 kg m-3 were allowed to settle in water at 293 K, and the terminal velocity was estimated by means of Stokes' law, which takes the following form:

$$v_t = \frac{g d_p^2 (\rho_p - \rho)}{18 \mu}$$

In this expression, $v_t$ is the terminal velocity, $g$ is the acceleration due to gravity, $d_p$ is the particle diameter, $\rho_p$ is the density of the particle, $\rho$ is the density of the fluid, and $\mu$ is the viscosity of the fluid. On this basis, Stokes' law gives a terminal velocity $v_t$ of 8.19 mm s-1 for the beads in question. It is, however, important to appreciate that the estimate requires creeping flow, and that the particle Reynolds number must be checked before the value is used in any subsequent calculation; if the check is not satisfied, the Stokes result cannot be relied upon, and a more general drag treatment would be required instead.
target:
Glass beads settle in water at 293 K. The beads have diameter $d_p$ = 100 micrometres and density 2500 kg m-3. Calculate the terminal velocity $v_t$ from Stokes' law. The estimate requires creeping flow around the bead; the assumption stands here, before the relation that rests on it. At the terminal velocity the bead no longer accelerates: the net weight of the bead, its weight less the buoyancy of the water it displaces, is balanced by the viscous drag of the water on the moving bead. Stokes' law states that balance for creeping flow:

$$v_t = \frac{g d_p^2 (\rho_p - \rho)}{18 \mu}$$

where $v_t$ denotes the terminal velocity, $g$ the acceleration due to gravity, $d_p$ the bead diameter, $\rho_p$ the density of the bead, $\rho$ the density of the water and $\mu$ the viscosity of the water. Substitution of the bead diameter and density gives $v_t$ = 8.19 mm s-1. The velocity rises with the square of the diameter in the relation, so the settling rate is far more sensitive to bead size than to the density difference that drives it, and a spread of bead sizes in a feed becomes a spread of settling velocities in the suspension. The value is a Stokes-law value, and it stands only where the creeping-flow requirement holds. The particle Reynolds number must be checked before the value is used: where that check fails, the drag on the bead no longer follows the Stokes form, and the terminal velocity must be found from a drag relation that covers the actual flow regime.

fact_base: Design report for a distillation column, in four sections: basis, sizing, materials, and risks. Design throughput is 29 t per day and the removal or separation duty is 94% of the key component. Materials are 316L stainless steel for wetted parts; the basis section states this once. The risks section names fouling and turndown as open items; neither is resolved in the report.
input:
## Basis

This report sets out the design basis for a distillation column that is intended to separate a key component from a liquid feed stream. The design throughput of the column is 29 t per day, and the separation duty that the column is required to achieve corresponds to 94% of the key component. It has been specified that all wetted parts of the column are to be manufactured from 316L stainless steel, and this requirement is recorded here in the basis section for the avoidance of doubt. The composition of the feed is not fixed, since it depends on the operation of the upstream process units, and the design has therefore been developed on the basis of the least favourable composition that is expected to arise within the normal feed envelope, so that the required duty can be achieved under all anticipated conditions rather than under nominal conditions only. The feed is introduced to the column as a liquid at its boiling point, and no allowance has been made in the design for any flash vapour that might be present in the feed stream. The operating pressure of the column is determined by the condensation of the overhead vapour against the cooling medium that is available on the site, and represents a compromise between the ease with which the separation can be achieved and the duty that is imposed on the condenser. The products of the column are an overhead product enriched in the key component and a bottoms product depleted in it, and the two product qualities are complementary aspects of the single separation duty that has been specified. Heating is provided by steam in the reboiler, and cooling by the site cooling medium in the condenser and in the product coolers that are provided downstream of the column.

## Sizing

The sizing of the column has been carried out in a stepwise manner, beginning with the determination of the stage requirement and proceeding from there to the internal traffic and finally to the dimensions of the shell itself. The stage requirement has been estimated by means of a shortcut calculation based on the equilibrium behaviour of the key component relative to the remainder of the feed. This approach yields the minimum number of stages that would be required at total reflux, together with the minimum reflux ratio at which the specified separation could in principle be achieved, and the operating reflux ratio has then been selected at a level above the minimum, at the point where the additional cost of providing further stages ceases to be justified by the corresponding saving in energy consumption. The internal vapour and liquid traffic within the column follows from the reflux ratio and from the product rates, and it is by no means uniform along the height of the column, since the liquid rate changes at the point at which the feed is introduced. The diameter of the column has been determined by reference to flooding, the vapour velocity at the design throughput having been held below the flooding velocity by a suitable margin, and the height has been built up from the number of trays, the spacing between them, and the various disengaging and access allowances that are required at the top and at the bottom of the column. The pressure drop through the column has been estimated tray by tray and taken into account in establishing the conditions at the base of the column, where it influences the temperature at which the reboiler is required to operate.

## Materials

As recorded in the basis section of this report, the wetted parts of the column are to be manufactured from the stainless steel grade that is specified there, and this section of the report is concerned with the reasoning that supports that selection and with the associated requirements for fabrication. The grade in question has been selected on the basis of its resistance to corrosion by the feed and by both of the products, over the whole of the temperature range that is encountered within the column, from the condenser at the top to the reboiler at the base. The same grade has been adopted at those locations where the process fluids are at their most concentrated, notably in the reboiler circuit and in the bottoms line, since it is at these locations that the combination of concentration and temperature is at its most severe. A corrosion allowance has been included in the thickness of the pressure-containing parts, over and above the thickness that is required by the pressure design, and this allowance is intended to provide for metal loss over the life of the plant rather than to contribute to the strength of the equipment. Welding is to be carried out using qualified procedures and matching consumables, and welds in wetted service are to be subjected to examination over their full length. The materials of gaskets and bolting have been selected for compatibility with the fluids and temperatures at the joints concerned, and external parts of the column that are not wetted by the process, such as the support skirt and the access platforms, are to be manufactured from carbon steel protected by a suitable coating system. Thermal insulation is to be provided where heat losses from the column would otherwise be sufficient to disturb the operation of the unit.

## Risks

There are two significant items that remain open at the time this report is issued, and it should be clearly understood that neither of them is resolved by the contents of the report. The first of these items concerns the fouling of the column internals, and the second concerns the behaviour of the column under turndown conditions. So far as fouling is concerned, the feed to the column will inevitably bring with it whatever material the upstream units pass forward, and the reboiler, where temperatures are at their highest and where the least volatile constituents of the feed tend to accumulate, is the item of equipment that is most exposed to the formation of deposits. The consequences of fouling would include a progressive reduction in the heat transfer performance of the reboiler, with a corresponding increase in steam consumption, together with a possible deterioration in the hydraulic behaviour of the trays. Unfortunately, the rate at which fouling would be expected to develop on this particular feed is simply not known at the present time, and no measurements are available that would allow a reliable estimate to be made. The provisions that might be adopted in response, which include additional reboiler capacity, facilities for cleaning, and various on-line washing arrangements, remain under consideration, as does the question of where responsibility for the decision should rest. So far as turndown is concerned, the column has been sized for its design throughput, and its performance at substantially lower throughputs has not been established. At reduced vapour rates the liquid seal on the trays is progressively weakened and liquid may begin to weep through the tray perforations, with a consequent loss of separation efficiency. The extent to which the column can be turned down while continuing to meet its specified duty is therefore a matter that can only be settled by testing, and the operating range that is to be guaranteed, and the means by which it is to be demonstrated, remain open questions. It should also be noted that the two items are not independent of one another, since a fouled column may be expected to turn down less satisfactorily than a clean one.

The sizing proceeds in three steps: the stage requirement, the internal traffic, and the shell dimensions that the traffic sets. Where the fluids concentrate — in the reboiler, where the least volatile components accumulate, and in the bottoms line — the same grade is used, since concentration and temperature act together at exactly those points.
