The condenser duty and the reboiler duty are the energy account of the column: nearly all the heat supplied at the base leaves at the top, and the traffic inside the shell is the traffic that account sustains. A column run at higher reflux moves more material between the phases on every stage and pays for the movement in reboiler steam and condenser cooling in proportion. The equipment is therefore sized as a system — shell, trays or packing, reboiler, condenser, and drum together — and a change to any one item, a larger condenser or a different tray, moves the operating point of the rest.

Worked example
Take the feed of the Principle part, of composition $z$ in the more volatile component, and follow the stepping construction with the relations stated there. Start from the bottoms product. The bottoms liquid, of composition $x_B$, sits on the lowest stage; the equilibrium relation gives the vapour leaving that stage, richer in the volatile component than $x_B$ by the enrichment the equilibrium relation states at that composition. The stripping relation then gives the liquid descending onto the stage from the stage above, and the equilibrium relation applied again gives the vapour leaving that stage. Stage by stage the composition climbs: each crossing from liquid to vapour enriches, and each move along the stripping relation repositions the liquid for the next crossing.

At the feed stage the accounting changes to the rectifying relation, because the liquid traffic above the feed carries the reflux rather than the feed-augmented flow below it, and the stepping continues on the rectifying relation toward the top. The last crossing gives the vapour that the condenser takes, of composition $y_D$, and condensation without a change of composition gives the overhead product at that composition. The count of crossings is the stage count the separation requires under the simple model, and it is read off the construction directly: the stepping stops when the composition passes the overhead product composition, and the stage on which it passes is the last stage counted. The check on the construction is the overall balance of the Principle part: the overhead and bottoms amounts from the stepping must return the feed amount and the feed composition when combined, and a construction that does not close the balance has misapplied a relation at some stage, most often at the feed stage where the relation changes.

Limits
The simple model fails where its stage picture fails. The model takes each stage to reach equilibrium; a real tray leaves the vapour and liquid short of equilibrium, and the shortfall varies with traffic, froth behaviour, and entrainment, so the stage count of the model understates the trays a real column needs by a margin the model itself does not supply. The model also takes the equilibrium relation as fixed by the mixture alone; mixtures whose components interact strongly bend the relation, and a mixture that forms an azeotrope has a composition at which the vapour and the liquid are identical, where no stepping construction crosses and ordinary distillation cannot pass. Heat losses from the shell, pressure drop through the internals, and the variation of traffic where heats of mixing are large are all outside the model as stated. The model remains the working picture for what a column does and for the size of the separation a stated reflux can buy; its numbers are the starting point for a rating that puts the real behaviour back in.

fact_base: A defect-reduction project on a packing line cut the reject rate from 3.6% to 2.1% over one quarter. At 259k units per year the change avoids about 3885 rejected units per year. The quarter included a planned shutdown; rates are not adjusted for it.
input: Over the course of one quarter, a defect-reduction project on a packing line succeeded in cutting the reject rate from 3.6% to 2.1%, which represents a substantial improvement in the performance of the line. At a throughput of 259k units per year, this change avoids approximately 3885 rejected units per year, which is a considerable saving in wasted product and rework. It should be noted, however, that the quarter in question included a planned shutdown, and the rates have not been adjusted to allow for it, so the comparison effectively runs between a quarter containing a shutdown and the period that came before it, on the basis of the rates exactly as recorded. The reduction is nonetheless clearly visible in the recorded rates, and the avoided-units figure follows directly from those rates at the stated annual volume. The project concentrated on the causes that the line records had already separated out, namely misfeeds at the infeed, seal faults that presented themselves as weight rejects, and label faults at the printer. Each cause was addressed in turn, the countermeasures were fitted during planned stops, and the reject count was read from the same checkweigher record before and after, which means that the rate comparison rests on a single instrument and a single counting rule throughout. A later quarter without a shutdown will provide a comparison over a full running period, and the project will be judged once again on that quarter before the change is adopted as settled practice on the line.
target: A defect-reduction project on a packing line cut the reject rate from 3.6% to 2.1% over one quarter. At 259k units per year, the change avoids about 3885 rejected units per year. The quarter included a planned shutdown, and the rates are not adjusted for it; the comparison therefore runs between a quarter with a shutdown in it and the period before it, on the rates as recorded. The reduction stands in the recorded rates, and the avoided-units figure follows from the recorded rates at the stated annual volume. The project worked on the causes the line records had already separated out: misfeeds at the infeed, seal faults that showed as weight rejects, and label faults at the printer. Each cause was taken in turn, the countermeasure was fitted during planned stops, and the reject count was read from the same checkweigher record before and after, so the rate comparison rests on one instrument and one counting rule throughout. A rate read from a changed counting rule would not carry the comparison, and no change of rule was made during the quarter. The avoided units are units that pass the checkweigher instead of leaving the line as waste or rework, and their value to the plant is the product and packing they no longer consume. A later quarter without a shutdown gives the comparison on a full running period, and the project is judged again on that quarter before the change is treated as settled practice on the line.

fact_base: A shell-and-tube exchanger heats crude oil in a refinery preheat train. Duty is 632 kW. Hot stream: 180 °C in, 130 °C out. Cold stream: 30 °C in, 45 °C out. The log-mean temperature difference is 116.6 K and the installed area is 23.7 m2, giving an overall coefficient of 229 W m-2 K-1. Fouling was assessed from a single 90-day run; no cleaning cycle has been completed.
input:
A shell-and-tube exchanger is used to heat crude oil within a refinery preheat train. The duty of the unit is 632 kW. The hot stream enters the exchanger at 180 °C and leaves at 130 °C, while the crude stream enters at 30 °C and leaves at 45 °C. The log-mean temperature difference works out to 116.6 K and the installed area is 23.7 m2, which gives an overall coefficient of 229 W m-2 K-1. This coefficient essentially represents the value that the installed area delivers at the stated duty and the stated log-mean difference, and it is the figure against which a fouling allowance for the train would normally be set.

It should be noted that fouling was assessed on the basis of a single 90-day run, and no cleaning cycle has yet been completed. The coefficient of 229 W m-2 K-1 therefore describes the behaviour of the exchanger over one run from its starting state, and the rate at which fouling continues to build up beyond that run is simply not captured in the record. A second run following cleaning would reveal how much of the resistance the cleaning actually removes and how the coefficient recovers, but on the basis of the present record that recovery remains unmeasured.
target:
A shell-and-tube exchanger heats crude oil in a refinery preheat train. The duty is 632 kW. The hot stream enters at 180 °C and leaves at 130 °C; the crude enters at 30 °C and leaves at 45 °C. The log-mean temperature difference is 116.6 K and the installed area is 23.7 m2, giving an overall coefficient of 229 W m-2 K-1. The coefficient is the value the installed area delivers at the stated duty and the stated log-mean difference, and it is the figure a fouling allowance for the train is set against.

Fouling was assessed from a single 90-day run, and no cleaning cycle has been completed. The coefficient of 229 W m-2 K-1 therefore describes the exchanger over one run from its starting state, and the rate at which fouling builds beyond that run is not in the record. Crude preheat service lays down deposits on both sides of the surface, and the coefficient as reported is a combined figure: it carries the tube-side and shell-side films, the wall, and whatever fouling resistance the run had built by its end, with no separation of the parts. A separation would need a clean-surface reading at the start of the run on the same instrument set. A second run after cleaning would show how much of the resistance the cleaning removes and how the coefficient recovers; on the present record that recovery is unmeasured, and the train is operated on the single-run figure until a post-cleaning run replaces it.

fact_base: A single-stage compressor raises air from 1 bar to 6 bar. Inlet temperature is 313 K. For isentropic compression with a heat-capacity ratio of 1.4, the discharge temperature is 522 K. The isentropic estimate excludes mechanical losses; the installed machine's measured discharge temperature is higher.
input: It is important to note that compressors are widely utilised across industry, and that an accurate estimate of the discharge temperature is crucial for both safety and efficiency. In this worked example, we consider a single-stage compressor that raises air from 1 bar to 6 bar. The air enters the compressor at an inlet temperature of 313 K, and the overall pressure ratio across the machine is 6. If the compression is assumed to be isentropic — in other words, both reversible and adiabatic — and a heat-capacity ratio of 1.4 is adopted, the discharge temperature can be estimated using the well-known isentropic relation $T_2 = T_1 (P_2/P_1)^{(\gamma-1)/\gamma}$. Applying this relation to the stated values yields a discharge temperature of 522 K, representing a substantial increase of 209 K over the inlet temperature. However, it is worth noting that this isentropic estimate deliberately excludes mechanical losses, such as friction and other irreversibilities, which are inevitably present in any real machine. As a result, the measured discharge temperature of the installed machine is higher than the predicted value of 522 K. Overall, the isentropic calculation serves as a valuable benchmark that highlights the best performance achievable in principle, while also underscoring the impact that real-world losses have on actual compressor behaviour. The example is deliberately simplified so that the effect of the underlying assumptions can be seen clearly, and it forms a useful starting point for more detailed calculations that take the characteristics of a specific machine into account.
target:
A single-stage compressor raises air from 1 bar to 6 bar, with an inlet temperature of 313 K. Calculate the discharge temperature, taking the compression as isentropic and the heat-capacity ratio $\gamma$ as 1.4.

For isentropic compression of an ideal gas, the discharge temperature follows from the inlet temperature and the pressure ratio through $T_2 = T_1 (P_2/P_1)^{(\gamma-1)/\gamma}$, with each temperature absolute and each pressure taken at its own station. The stated pressures give a pressure ratio of 6. Substitution of the stated values in the relation gives a discharge temperature of 522 K, which exceeds the inlet temperature by 209 K. The exponent in the relation depends on $\gamma$ alone, so the temperature rise over a fixed pressure ratio grows as the heat-capacity ratio grows. The calculation uses no property of the machine beyond the two pressures and the inlet state.

The result holds for isentropic compression only. An isentropic path is reversible and adiabatic by definition, and the estimate therefore excludes mechanical losses. Friction, leakage and turbulence in an installed machine add work to the gas, and work added beyond the reversible requirement leaves in the gas as heat. The installed machine's measured discharge temperature is higher than 522 K. The isentropic figure is a lower bound on the discharge temperature at the stated pressure ratio, and a discharge-temperature limit for the machine cannot be set from the estimate without a margin for the losses the estimate omits. The gap between the measured temperature and the estimate measures the departure of the actual compression from the reversible path.

fact_base: A review passage on membrane separations for solvent recovery, in four parts: scope, established results, disagreements, and gaps. The review covers 148 papers from the last 6 years. The disagreements part names the quantity on which reports conflict; the gaps part names the measurement nobody reports.
input:
Scope

Membrane technology has attracted growing attention in recent years as an energy-efficient alternative to traditional separation methods, and solvent recovery is widely regarded as one of its most promising areas of application. This review examines the literature on membrane separations for solvent recovery, in which a membrane is used to pass the solvent of a liquid mixture while retaining dissolved material, allowing the solvent to be reused rather than distilled or discarded. The review covers a total of 148 papers published over the last 6 years, encompassing both polymeric and ceramic membranes, laboratory studies and pilot-scale work, and a wide range of solvent-bearing streams arising from reaction, extraction and washing operations. Gas separations are excluded, while aqueous separations are included only where the same membrane has also been studied with a solvent stream. It is important to note that performance in this field is generally assessed using two key parameters, namely the solvent flux and the rejection of dissolved material, and it is essential to consider these together, since a high flux is of little value if the membrane retains very little solute, and a very high rejection may be impractical if the flux is extremely low.

Established results

A number of findings are reported consistently throughout the literature and can be regarded as well established. Firstly, the solvent flux typically increases with the applied pressure difference and decreases as the viscosity of the mixture increases. Moreover, the same membrane can exhibit very different fluxes in different solvents, because the solvent interacts with the membrane material, causing it to swell and thereby altering its resistance to flow. Secondly, rejection is not a property of the membrane alone: a solute that is effectively retained in one solvent may pass through the same membrane in another, because swelling changes the relationship between the size of the solute and the size of the membrane pores. Thirdly, chemical stability is a crucial factor that limits the applicability of membrane materials, since membranes that perform well in mild solvents may soften, swell excessively or even dissolve in more aggressive solvents. Finally, concentration polarisation, in which retained material accumulates at the membrane surface, can significantly reduce flux during operation, and cross-flow operation is commonly employed to mitigate this effect. Cleaning is generally found to restore part of the flux lost during operation, although it is not reported to restore flux completely.

Disagreements

Despite the broad agreement described above, the literature contains an important area of disagreement, namely the behaviour of the flux during extended operation. Some studies report that the flux declines initially and then levels off, remaining essentially stable for the rest of the run, whereas other studies report a flux that continues to decline for as long as the run continues. Interestingly, the disagreement extends beyond the magnitude of the decline to its underlying cause, with different authors attributing the decline to compaction of the membrane under pressure, to fouling of the membrane surface, or to gradual ageing of the membrane material in the solvent. This distinction is significant in practice, because the appropriate remedy depends on the mechanism involved: fouling, for example, can potentially be managed by cleaning, whereas compaction is an inherent property of the membrane under load. Furthermore, because most experimental runs are considerably shorter than a typical service interval, the published data do not allow the disagreement to be resolved, as the runs end before the competing predictions would clearly diverge. Overall, the flux trajectory over extended operation remains an open question that short-duration studies cannot settle.

Gaps

A further issue is that certain measurements that would be highly valuable for plant design are simply not reported in the literature. In particular, nobody reports the performance of a membrane after repeated cleaning cycles: flux and rejection are measured for new membranes and, in some cases, after a single cleaning event, but not after the many fouling and cleaning cycles that a membrane would experience over its service life. This is a significant gap, because a membrane that survives one cleaning may nevertheless degrade progressively over many cycles, and purchasers ultimately need to know how a membrane performs across its whole working life rather than when it is new. In addition, there is no common test protocol across the literature, and different studies use different solutes, concentrations and run durations, which makes it difficult to compare membranes between studies on a like-for-like basis. Until these gaps are addressed and flux after repeated cleaning is routinely measured and reported on a shared basis, the selection of membranes for solvent recovery will inevitably continue to rest largely on clean-membrane performance and on a flux decline behaviour that the literature itself has not yet resolved.
target:
Scope

This review covers membrane separations for solvent recovery: processes in which a membrane passes the solvent of a liquid mixture and holds back dissolved material, so that the solvent can be returned to the process instead of being distilled or discarded. The reviewed set is 148 papers from the last 6 years. The papers cover polymeric and ceramic membranes, laboratory measurements and pilot operation, and solvent-bearing streams from reaction, extraction and washing steps. Gas separations fall outside the review, and aqueous separations are covered only where the same membrane is also reported on a solvent stream. Recovery is judged throughout on the two quantities every application must state together: the rate at which solvent passes the membrane, and the fraction of dissolved material the membrane holds back. A membrane that passes solvent quickly but holds back little solute has not performed the separation, and a membrane that holds back nearly everything but passes solvent slowly may need more area than the plant can house. The review therefore reads flux and rejection as a pair, and treats a report of either quantity alone as an incomplete account of the separation. Papers were included where the membrane, the solvent and the solute are all identified and where flux or rejection is measured rather than estimated. Papers that report a separation without identifying the membrane material fall outside the set, because a result obtained with an unnamed material can neither be repeated nor transferred to another plant's solvent stream.

Established results

Several results are reported consistently enough across the set to be treated as established. Solvent flux rises with the pressure difference across the membrane and falls as the mixture grows more viscous, and the same membrane gives different fluxes in different solvents: the solvent is not a passive carrier, because it swells the membrane material and sets the resistance the membrane presents. Rejection is decided jointly by the solute and the membrane in the solvent concerned: a solute well held back in one solvent can pass in another, because swelling opens the membrane structure and changes the size relation between solute and membrane pores. Chemical stability bounds the whole field of application. Membranes that perform well in mild solvents can soften, swell excessively or dissolve in aggressive ones, and a membrane is usable only in the solvent classes in which its material survives. Concentration polarisation — the build-up of held-back material at the membrane surface — limits flux in operation even where the clean membrane passes solvent freely, and cross-flow over the surface is the standard counter-measure. Cleaning restores part of the flux lost in service, and no report in the set treats a fouled membrane as recoverable in full by cleaning alone. A further established point concerns the reporting itself: flux stated without the pressure difference at which it was measured, and rejection stated without the feed composition, cannot be compared with any other report, and the stronger papers in the set state both conditions as a matter of course.

Disagreements

Reports conflict on the flux decline during extended operation: how much flux a membrane loses as operating time accumulates, and whether the decline stops. Part of the set reports an early decline that levels off, after which flux holds steady for the remainder of the run; another part reports a decline that continues for as long as the run lasts. The disagreement is not only about the size of the decline. The two camps attribute the same observation to different causes: compaction of the membrane under pressure, fouling of the surface by held-back material, and ageing of the membrane material in the solvent are each offered as the mechanism, and the remedy each mechanism implies is different. A decline caused by compaction is a property of the membrane under load; a decline caused by fouling is a property of the stream and can be managed by cleaning. Because most runs are far shorter than a service interval, the reports cannot be reconciled from the published data: each camp's runs end before the other's predicted behaviour would separate from its own. The conflict quantity is therefore the flux trajectory over extended operation, and short runs do not settle it.

Gaps

The measurement nobody reports is the state of the membrane after repeated cleaning cycles: flux and rejection measured after the membrane has been fouled and cleaned many times, over a period comparable with service. Papers report cleaning recovery after a single fouling event, and a membrane can survive one cleaning and still degrade over a service life of many cycles; whether rejection survives repeated cleaning is reported by none of the set. Plant design needs exactly that quantity, because a membrane is bought for its performance across its whole life, not for its performance when new. Also missing from the set is any common test protocol: membranes are compared across papers that use different solutes, different concentrations and different run lengths, so rankings between membranes rest on measurements that were never made on a common basis. Until flux after repeated cleaning is measured and reported on a shared basis, the choice between membranes for solvent recovery rests on clean-membrane performance and on a flux decline that the literature itself has not settled. Start-up behaviour is also largely unreported: the flux a membrane gives at its first contact with a solvent differs from its settled value as the material takes up solvent and compacts, and the time the settling takes is rarely stated, although a plant must be started on the unsettled membrane every time a new one is fitted.

fact_base: A tutorial passage explains representative sampling of a gas emission. The passage covers where samples are taken, how many increments form one sample, and why a single grab sample misleads. No numerical limits are quoted; regulatory limits belong to the site's permit, not to the passage.
input: Sampling is a crucial step in the characterisation of gas emissions, because the quality of any subsequent analysis depends entirely on how well the sample represents the stream from which it was taken. It is important to note that a gas emission is rarely uniform: its composition can vary both across the duct and over time, and these variations must be taken into account if meaningful results are to be obtained. Samples should therefore be taken at a location where the stream is thoroughly mixed, rather than immediately downstream of bends or junctions where the flow may be stratified into layers of differing composition. In larger ducts, it is also advisable to draw the sample across the whole cross-section instead of relying on a single point close to the wall, since the gas near the wall may not reflect the composition of the bulk flow. Furthermore, a single sample should normally be built up from a number of increments, with each increment consisting of a small portion of gas drawn at a different time and the increments subsequently combined. This approach ensures that fluctuations in the emission over the sampling period are properly captured, including fluctuations associated with cyclical features of the process itself. By contrast, a single grab sample, taken at one point and at one moment, can be highly misleading: it may coincide with a temporary lull or a temporary peak, and there is no way of knowing from the result alone which has occurred. Overall, careful attention to the sampling location, the sampling pattern and the number of increments is essential if the final result is to provide a reliable picture of the emission as a whole.
target:
Sample a gas emission so that the laboratory result describes the emission, not the moment and the point at which the sample happened to be taken. A representative sample has the composition the whole stream has over the sampling period, averaged in the same proportions. Every choice in the sampling plan defends that average, and a result obtained from an unrepresentative sample cannot be repaired by careful analysis afterwards.

Take the sample where the stream is mixed. Gas leaving a bend, a junction or a partial obstruction travels in layers that differ in composition, and a probe placed in one layer draws from that layer only. A sampling plane in a straight run, downstream of the disturbance, lets the layers merge before the probe. Where the duct is wide, draw across the section rather than at a single point near the wall: the wall layer moves slowly and can differ from the core of the stream, and a wall sample reads the wall layer as if it were the stream.

Build one sample from several increments. An increment is a small portion drawn at one time; increments taken at intervals across the period and combined give a sample that follows the stream as its composition drifts. A process that cycles — a batch discharge, a firing pattern, a cleaning step — changes the emission on its own period, and increments spread over the whole cycle capture the high and the low parts of it. Record the process state alongside each increment, so that a result can later be read against the operation that produced it.

A single grab sample has neither defence. A grab sample is drawn at one point at one moment, and it reports that point and that moment faithfully. Read as the emission, it misleads in whichever direction the moment was unrepresentative: a lull understates the emission, a peak overstates it, and nothing in the result shows which has happened. Sampling effort belongs in the plane, the traverse and the increments, because the analysis that follows can only measure the sample it receives.

fact_base: A tutorial passage explains the Sherwood number to second-year students. Definition in words: the Sherwood number is the ratio of convective to diffusive mass transfer at a surface. The passage must state what a value near 1 means and what a large value means, without inventing numerical examples.
input: Mass transfer at a surface underlies a wide range of operations, including absorption, drying and heterogeneous catalysis, and in each case the designer needs to know how rapidly material can be brought to the surface. The Sherwood number is a dimensionless quantity that plays a central role in the analysis of such processes. It can be defined as the ratio of convective to diffusive mass transfer at a surface, and it provides a convenient way of assessing which of these two mechanisms is dominant in a given situation. When the Sherwood number is near 1, this indicates that convection contributes very little, and the transfer of material to the surface takes place essentially by diffusion alone, as would be expected in a stagnant fluid. In contrast, a large Sherwood number indicates that convection is much more effective at delivering material to the surface, so that the overall transfer is greatly enhanced compared with the purely diffusive case. The remaining resistance is then concentrated in a thin region close to the surface, where diffusion continues to operate. It is important to note that the Sherwood number is a ratio rather than a rate, and a value of 1 accordingly represents the lower limit at which the two mechanisms contribute equally. Overall, the Sherwood number serves as a valuable tool for comparing mass transfer behaviour across different systems and for interpreting the predictions of mass transfer correlations.
target:
The Sherwood number is the ratio of convective to diffusive mass transfer at a surface. The number compares two rates of supply to the same surface: convection, which carries material to the surface through the moving fluid, and diffusion, which carries material across the concentration gradient at the surface itself. A Sherwood number near 1 states that convection adds nothing to the transfer: material reaches the surface at the rate diffusion alone provides, as it does next to a surface in a stagnant fluid. The transfer is then set by the diffusion coefficient and by the length over which the concentration falls.

A large Sherwood number states the opposite ordering. Convection supplies material to the neighbourhood of the surface far faster than diffusion can carry it onward, and the resistance to transfer sits in a thin layer at the surface where diffusion still acts. Stirring, a faster flow or a geometry that renews the fluid at the surface all raise the number, because each strengthens convection while the diffusive step at the surface is unchanged in kind. Because the number is a ratio of two rates for the same surface and the same driving difference, the driving difference cancels: the number characterises the flow and the geometry, not the concentration level at which the transfer happens.

The Sherwood number is read as a comparison, not as a rate. Two systems with the same Sherwood number transfer mass in the same proportion between the two mechanisms, even where their absolute rates differ widely. A value of 1 is the lower limit of the comparison: convection cannot remove the diffusive step at the surface, and every real transfer process keeps that step.

fact_base: An operating-manual chapter for a plate heat exchanger, in four sections: start-up, normal operation, alarms, and shutdown. The alarms section lists two alarms and the operator action for each; no other alarms are introduced. The chapter addresses the operator directly and uses imperative verbs for actions.
input:
Start-up

Before the plate heat exchanger is started up, it is essential to carry out a thorough check of the unit in order to ensure that everything is in order. The plate pack should be confirmed as properly closed, with the bolts tightened evenly in the correct sequence and all gaskets correctly seated in their grooves. The vents at the high points of both circuits should then be opened, and the cold circuit should be filled first and vented until liquid flows steadily from the vent, after which the hot circuit can be filled and vented in the same way. It is important to note that an exchanger started with air still trapped inside the pack will typically exhibit uneven flow distribution and misleading temperature readings, so venting should never be rushed. The whole unit should also be checked carefully for leaks while the circuits are full and still cold, as it is much easier to correct a gasket leak at this stage than after heating has begun. The flows should then be started at a low rate and increased gradually to the operating rate, and the hot circuit should be brought up to temperature slowly, in order to avoid thermal shock to the plates and gaskets. During this period, the inlet and outlet temperatures and the pressure drop across the pack should be monitored closely. Start-up can be regarded as complete when both flows have reached their operating rates, the outlet temperatures are stable and no leaks are present.

Normal operation

During normal operation, the flows should be maintained at the rates required by the duty, and the inlet and outlet temperatures and pressures should be read and recorded on every round. Keeping a proper record is extremely valuable, because fouling of the plates usually develops gradually and reveals itself as a slow drift in the readings: the outlet temperature of the heated stream falls below its earlier value at unchanged flows, while the pressure drop across the pack rises. Operators should also ensure that the strainers in both inlet lines are kept clean, since a blocked strainer can starve the exchanger and produce symptoms similar to fouling. Care should be taken not to run the exchanger with one circuit stopped while the other remains hot, as the stagnant fluid may boil locally or deposit solids on the plates. The pressures within both circuits should be kept within the rated limits of the plates and gaskets, and any weeping at a gasket should be reported as a defect rather than accepted as normal. Where the temperature of the heated stream must be controlled within a band, adjustments should be made to the hot-side flow and sufficient time allowed for the unit to settle before further adjustments are made, in order to avoid hunting.

Alarms

The unit is provided with alarms that warn the operator of abnormal conditions. A high differential pressure across the plate pack indicates that the flow passages have become obstructed, for example by fouling of the plates or by solids carried into the pack. In this event, the throughput should be reduced and the differential pressure observed: if it falls and remains stable, operation may continue at the reduced rate and the condition should be reported. However, if the differential pressure remains high, the exchanger should be taken out of service following the shutdown procedure and the plates should be cleaned before the unit is returned to duty, as forcing the exchanger to operate against a rising differential pressure can damage the gaskets and may lead to a leak between the two circuits.

A low flow alarm in either circuit indicates that the supply to that circuit has failed, which may be due to a stopped pump, a closed valve or a blocked strainer. The operator should check the running of the pump, the position of the valves and the condition of the strainer, in that order. The other circuit should not be left running hot against a circuit that is stagnant. If the flow cannot be restored promptly, the unit should be shut down following the shutdown procedure and the fault reported. The alarm can be regarded as cleared only when the flow has been re-established and the temperatures have returned to their normal operating values.

Shutdown

When the exchanger is to be shut down, the flows should be reduced gradually and the hot circuit should be stopped first, so that the pack can cool under flow in the cold circuit and no hot fluid is left standing in the plates. The cold flow should be continued until the outlet temperatures have fallen close to the cold inlet temperature, after which the cold circuit can also be stopped. The inlet and outlet valves of both circuits should then be closed, the vents opened and both circuits drained completely. It should be noted that an exchanger left standing full of process fluid will foul while it stands, and a circuit left full in freezing weather may be damaged by ice formation. Where the fluids concerned are known to foul or set when cold, the plates should be cleaned before any extended standstill and the unit left drained, vented and open to inspection. Finally, any gasket weeping, plate damage and the general condition of the pack found during draining should be reported, so that the next start-up can begin from a known state.
target:
Start-up

Confirm before start-up that the plate pack is closed, that the bolts are tightened evenly in the sequence the frame marking shows, and that every gasket sits in its groove. Open the vents at the high points of both circuits. Fill the cold circuit first and vent it until liquid flows steadily from the vent; then fill and vent the hot circuit in the same way. An exchanger started with air trapped in the pack gives uneven flow and false temperature readings, and the venting step is not complete until both circuits run free of air. Check the whole unit for leaks while the circuits are full and still cold: a gasket leak found at this stage is corrected by re-tightening or by replacing the gasket, and no leak is acceptable once heating begins. Start the flows at a low rate and raise them gradually to the operating rate. Bring the hot circuit up to temperature slowly: a sudden admission of hot fluid shocks the plates and the gaskets and can start a leak at a joint that was sound when cold. Watch the inlet and outlet temperatures and the pressure drop across the pack as the unit comes up to duty. Open each drain briefly before filling and confirm that it runs clear, so that debris left in the lines by maintenance is found at the drain and not in the plate pack. Start-up is complete when both flows are at their operating rates, the outlet temperatures are steady, and no joint leaks.

Normal operation

Hold the flows at the rates the duty requires and read the inlet and outlet temperatures and the pressures at the unit on every round. Record the readings: the record, not a single reading, shows the state of the exchanger, because fouling announces itself as a slow drift — the outlet temperature of the heated stream falls away from its earlier value at unchanged flows, and the pressure drop across the pack rises. Keep the strainers in both inlet lines clean: a blocked strainer starves the exchanger and mimics fouling at the pressure gauges. Do not run the exchanger with one circuit stopped while the other is hot: a stagnant circuit boils locally or deposits solids on the plates, and the damage is done before the temperatures show it. Keep both circuits within the pressure the plates and gaskets are rated for, and treat any weep at a gasket as a defect to be reported, not as a normal feature of the unit. Where the heated stream must stay within a temperature band, adjust the hot-side flow and re-read the outlet temperature after the adjustment has had time to settle; repeated adjustment before the unit settles produces hunting and teaches the record nothing. Compare each round's readings with the record of the rounds before it: a change that appears between one round and the next is an event and is reported at once, while a change that grows slowly over many rounds is fouling or a failing component, and the two conditions are handled differently.

Alarms

The unit raises two alarms. Each alarm names the condition it detects, and the operator action for each alarm is stated with it.

A high differential pressure across the plate pack means the flow passages are obstructed, by fouling on the plates or by solids carried into the pack. Reduce the throughput and watch the differential pressure: if it falls and holds, continue at the reduced rate and report the condition. If the differential pressure stays high, take the exchanger out of service under the shutdown procedure and clean the plates before the unit is returned to duty; an exchanger forced to run against a rising differential pressure damages its gaskets and can open a leak between the circuits.

A low flow in either circuit means the supply to that circuit has failed: a stopped pump, a closed valve or a blocked strainer. Check the running of the pump, the position of the valves and the state of the strainer, in that order. Do not leave the other circuit running hot against a stagnant one. If flow cannot be restored promptly, shut the unit down under the shutdown procedure and report the fault; the alarm is cleared only when flow is re-established and the temperatures have returned to their operating values.

Shutdown

Reduce the flows gradually and stop the hot circuit first, so that the pack cools under flow in the cold circuit and no part of the plates is left holding hot stagnant fluid. Continue the cold flow until the outlet temperatures have fallen close to the cold inlet temperature, then stop the cold circuit. Close the inlet and outlet valves of both circuits, open the vents, and drain both circuits completely. An exchanger left standing full of process fluid fouls while it stands, and a circuit left full in freezing weather can be damaged by the ice that forms in it. Where the fluids foul or set when cold, clean the plates before a long standstill and leave the unit drained, vented and open to inspection. Report any gasket weep, any damaged plate and the state of the pack found at draining, so that the next start-up begins from a known condition. Tag the isolated valves, and enter the shutdown in the unit log with the readings taken at the moment of stopping, so that the condition in which the exchanger was left stands on record for the crew that returns it to service.

fact_base: Goal: compute the half-life of a first-order reaction and the fraction remaining after 60 min. For a first-order reaction the rate constant k (min-1) fixes the half-life t1/2 (min) by t1/2 = ln(2) / k, and the fraction remaining after time t (min) is exp(-k t). Measured rate constant: k = 0.046 min-1 at 323 K, from concentration measurements every 5 min over 90 min. Worked results: t1/2 = 15.1 min; the fraction remaining after 60 min is 0.06 (dimensionless), both computed from the stated relations. The relations hold for a first-order reaction only; a reaction of another order follows a different decay law.
input: First-order reactions are extremely common in chemical kinetics, and the half-life is a particularly useful quantity because it provides an intuitive measure of how quickly a reaction proceeds. In this example, we are asked to determine the half-life of a first-order reaction with a rate constant of 0.046 min⁻¹ at 323 K, together with the fraction of reactant remaining after 60 min. The rate constant itself was obtained experimentally from concentration measurements taken every 5 min over a total period of 90 min. For a first-order reaction, the half-life is related to the rate constant by the well-known expression $t_{1/2} = \ln 2 / k$, while the fraction remaining after a time $t$ is given by $\exp(-k t)$. Substituting the measured value of the rate constant into the half-life expression gives $0.693 / 0.046 = 15.1$ min. Similarly, after 60 min the fraction remaining is $\exp(-0.046 \times 60)$, which works out to approximately 0.06. This result is consistent with the half-life, since 60 min corresponds to roughly four half-lives of 15.1 min each, and repeated halving rapidly reduces the remaining fraction. It is important to note, however, that these relations are valid only for a first-order reaction; a reaction of a different order would follow an entirely different decay law, highlighting the importance of establishing the reaction order before applying the formulas. The example also illustrates why the half-life is quoted so widely in practice when first-order behaviour has been established experimentally.
target:
Calculate the half-life of a first-order reaction whose rate constant $k$ is 0.046 min⁻¹ at 323 K, and calculate the fraction of reactant remaining after 60 min. The rate constant was obtained from concentration measurements taken every 5 min over 90 min.

For a first-order reaction, the half-life is fixed by the rate constant through $t_{1/2} = \ln 2 / k$, and the fraction remaining after a time $t$ is $\exp(-k t)$. The half-life of a first-order reaction does not depend on the starting concentration, because the rate falls in proportion to the concentration that remains: each equal time interval removes the same fraction of the reactant, not the same amount. Concentration measurements at regular intervals fix the rate constant because the logarithm of the concentration falls linearly with time for a first-order reaction. Substitution of the measured rate constant gives a half-life of $0.693 / 0.046 = 15.1$ min. The fraction remaining after 60 min is $\exp(-0.046 \times 60)$, which evaluates to 0.06. The stated half-life is a property of the reaction at the stated temperature: the rate constant, and with it the half-life, changes when the temperature changes, and the result is not carried to another temperature without a rate constant measured there.

The fraction can be checked against the half-life: 60 min spans about four half-lives of 15.1 min, and four successive halvings leave close to one sixteenth of the initial concentration, in agreement with the computed fraction. The relations hold for a first-order reaction only. A reaction of another order follows a different decay law, and neither the half-life nor the fraction remaining can be obtained from the stated relations for such a reaction.

fact_base: A binary distillation separates ethanol/water at a relative volatility of 2.27 that is taken as constant over the column. Specifications: distillate 98 mol% light component, bottoms 2 mol% light component. The Fenske minimum stage count is 9.5 theoretical stages including the reboiler. The actual design uses a reflux ratio of 1.3 times the minimum; the stage count at that reflux comes from a separate simulation.
input: Distillation is one of the most widely utilised separation techniques in the chemical industry, and the Fenske equation provides a rapid and convenient way of estimating the minimum number of stages required for a given separation. In the present case, a binary distillation separates an ethanol/water mixture at a relative volatility of 2.27, which is taken to remain constant over the height of the column. The separation specifications are demanding: the distillate is required to contain 98 mol% of the light component, while the bottoms contain only 2 mol%. Applying the Fenske equation to these specifications gives a minimum stage count of 9.5 theoretical stages, including the reboiler. It is important to note that this value represents an absolute lower bound that cannot be achieved in practice, since it corresponds to operation at total reflux. In the actual design, a reflux ratio of 1.3 times the minimum has been adopted in order to achieve a more realistic balance between capital and operating costs. The corresponding stage count at this reflux ratio does not come from the Fenske equation itself, but instead comes from a separate, more detailed simulation. Overall, the Fenske result serves as a valuable first estimate that helps to frame the subsequent design work.
target:
A binary distillation separates ethanol and water at a relative volatility of 2.27, taken as constant over the column. For a distillate containing 98 mol% of the light component and bottoms containing 2 mol%, the Fenske equation gives a minimum stage count of 9.5 theoretical stages, including the reboiler.

The Fenske count is a minimum: it holds at total reflux, where no product is withdrawn, and no column separating the stated products can use fewer stages at any reflux ratio. The stated specifications fix both ends of the column: nearly all of the light component leaves overhead, and the bottoms carry only a small residue of it. A constant relative volatility over the whole column is the assumption the count rests on; a volatility that changes with composition changes the minimum with it. A fractional minimum is a computed equivalent rather than a hardware count: the reboiler and the trays together must supply at least the separation the fraction represents. The minimum stage count and the minimum reflux ratio are the two ends of the design trade-off, since stages fall as reflux rises, and the Fenske result fixes the stage end of that trade-off. The design reflux ratio is 1.3 times the minimum reflux ratio. The stage count at that reflux does not follow from the Fenske result and comes from a separate simulation, which resolves the column stage by stage at the operating reflux.

fact_base: Excerpt content: a staffing gap of 7 weeks is reported with its cause; the excerpt proposes one mitigation and its owner. The excerpt does not open or close the memo and does not restate its subject line.

In order to mitigate this issue, it is proposed that the commissioning packages be resequenced, so that the systems that are unaffected by the turnaround are dealt with first and the systems that depend on the turnaround are moved to the end of the programme. The project board will take ownership of this mitigation, approving the revised programme and monitoring progress against it at each status meeting. While this approach does not eliminate the gap entirely, it helps to ensure that the exposed work is moved to a point at which the replacement engineers will be available, thereby reducing the overall risk to the completion date.

fact_base: Inventory policy for a resin grade: mean demand 256 units per week, standard deviation 54 units per week, replenishment lead time 3 weeks. Safety stock for a 95% cycle service level is 154 units. Demand is treated as normal and independent between weeks; seasonal peaks are excluded.
input: Effective inventory management is crucial for ensuring that production can continue without interruption while avoiding excessive holding costs. For the resin grade considered here, it has been decided that a safety stock of 154 units will be held in order to protect against variability in demand during the replenishment lead time. This figure is based on a mean demand of 256 units per week and a standard deviation of 54 units per week, together with a replenishment lead time of 3 weeks, and it corresponds to a 95% cycle service level. The calculation treats demand as normally distributed and independent between weeks, which allows the weekly variability to be combined over the lead time in a straightforward manner. It should be noted, however, that seasonal peaks are excluded from the analysis, meaning that the safety stock of 154 units may not be sufficient during periods of unusually high demand. The policy will also be reviewed periodically to ensure that it continues to reflect actual demand patterns. Overall, the chosen policy provides a robust buffer under normal operating conditions while keeping the amount of capital tied up in inventory at a reasonable level.
target:
Safety stock for the resin grade is set at 154 units. The figure is calculated for a mean demand of 256 units per week with a standard deviation of 54 units per week and a replenishment lead time of 3 weeks, at a 95% cycle service level.

Cycle service level is the probability that a replenishment cycle ends without a stockout, and the buffer is sized against that probability. The policy treats demand as normal and independent between weeks: the variability that matters is the variability of demand over the lead time, not the weekly figure alone, and independence between weeks is what allows the weekly variability to be combined over the lead time. The buffer is held in addition to the stock that covers mean demand over the lead time, because the two quantities answer different questions: cycle stock covers the expected level of demand, and safety stock covers the departure from it. Seasonal peaks are excluded from the calculation. Demand in a peak week can exceed the buffer the stated service level implies, and the 154 units are not sized to cover it. The stock is reviewed against the same basis: a change in mean demand, in variability, or in lead time changes the safety stock the service level requires, and the figure is recalculated rather than carried forward.

fact_base: Excerpt content: a seal replacement takes about 42 min with the unit isolated; the excerpt gives the isolation steps only. The excerpt warns once about stored pressure and does not repeat the warning.
input: Before the seal on the duty pump can be replaced, it is essential that the pump is properly isolated in order to ensure that the work can be carried out safely. First, the standby pump should be started and it should be confirmed that the discharge pressure is being maintained satisfactorily. The duty pump can then be stopped, and the suction and discharge valves should be closed and secured with the locks and tags required under the PTW. The casing drain should then be opened to the closed drain system, together with the vent at the high point of the casing. It is important to note that stored pressure may remain trapped inside the casing even after the isolation valves have been closed, so the casing should always be treated as pressurised until the vent demonstrates that no pressure remains. Once the casing has been fully drained, the isolation should be proved once again at the drain before the seal joint is broken. The seal replacement itself takes about 42 min with the unit isolated, and the isolation is only complete when all of these steps have been carried out in full.
target:
Prove the duty pump stopped and isolated before any casing bolt is loosened. Start the standby pump and confirm that discharge pressure holds with the standby pump running. Stop the duty pump. Close the suction and discharge valves on the duty pump, and fit the locks and tags the PTW requires. Open the casing drain to the closed drain system and open the vent at the casing high point. Treat the casing as pressurised until the vent proves otherwise: stored pressure can remain trapped in the casing after the valves are closed, and a vent that shows no flow and no pressure is the only acceptable proof that the casing is safe to open. Drain the casing fully, then prove the isolation a second time at the drain before breaking the seal joint. Record the isolation on the PTW before the joint is broken.

The seal replacement takes about 42 min with the unit isolated. Isolation is complete only when the drain and the vent stand open, the valves are locked and tagged, and the standby pump carries the duty without alarms.

fact_base: Adsorption of a dye from water on a metal-organic framework was measured in batch tests at 298 K. The fitted Langmuir capacity was 256 mg of dye per gram of adsorbent at pH 6. At an adsorbent dose of 1 g L-1, removal after 120 min was 83% of the initial dye concentration of 50 mg L-1. The Langmuir fit is reported for pH 6 only; capacity at other pH values was not measured.
input: Adsorption is widely regarded as an effective and versatile technique for removing dyes from wastewater, and metal-organic frameworks have attracted considerable attention as adsorbents due to their exceptionally high surface areas. In this study, the adsorption of a dye from water on a metal-organic framework was measured in a series of batch tests conducted at 298 K. Each test was carried out by contacting a known mass of adsorbent with the dye solution and measuring the concentration remaining in solution after the stated contact time. The experimental data were fitted to the Langmuir isotherm model, giving a fitted capacity of 256 mg of dye per gram of adsorbent at pH 6. Furthermore, at an adsorbent dose of 1 g L⁻¹, the removal after 120 min reached 83% of the initial dye concentration of 50 mg L⁻¹, corresponding to a residual concentration of just 8.5 mg L⁻¹. These results highlight the considerable potential of the framework as an adsorbent for dye removal, and the combination of a high capacity with rapid removal is particularly encouraging. It is important to note, however, that the Langmuir fit is reported for pH 6 only, and the capacity at other pH values was not measured. As a result, caution should be exercised when extrapolating the findings to other conditions, and further work would be required to fully characterise the performance of the material across a broader range of pH values.
target:
Adsorption of a dye from water on a metal-organic framework was measured in batch tests at 298 K. The fitted Langmuir capacity was 256 mg of dye per gram of adsorbent at pH 6. At an adsorbent dose of 1 g L⁻¹, removal after 120 min was 83% of the initial dye concentration of 50 mg L⁻¹, leaving a residual concentration of 8.5 mg L⁻¹.

The fitted capacity is an equilibrium property of the isotherm fit: it states the loading the surface approaches as the solution concentration rises, not the loading reached in the stated batch test. The batch removal and the isotherm capacity answer different questions. Removal reports what one dose achieved in one contact time, while capacity bounds what the solid can hold at equilibrium. The removal figure belongs to the stated dose and contact time together; a lower dose or a shorter contact time leaves more dye in solution. The residual concentration is the quantity a discharge limit would be set against, and it is fixed by the removal and the initial concentration together. Reporting the two results together fixes the conditions under which the removal was obtained and the equilibrium limit the removal is measured against. The Langmuir fit is reported for pH 6 only. Capacity at other pH values was not measured, and the stated capacity cannot be carried to a water of a different pH: adsorption of a dye on a framework depends on the charge state of both, and pH sets that state. The capacity and the removal were obtained in batch tests at one temperature, and the results state what the adsorbent achieved under those conditions.

fact_base: Liquid-liquid extraction recovers phenol from an aqueous stream into an organic solvent. The distribution coefficient (organic over aqueous) is 1.58 at 25 °C and the design uses 8 countercurrent stages. Predicted recovery is 93% of the phenol in the feed. The prediction assumes equilibrium stages and negligible mutual solubility; neither has been checked on the actual solvents.
input:
Liquid-liquid extraction, in chemical separations, serves as a widely utilised and highly effective technique for recovering valuable compounds from process streams. In this case, the technique is applied to the recovery of phenol from an aqueous stream, with the phenol being transferred into an organic solvent phase. A key parameter that plays a crucial role in governing the separation is the distribution coefficient, defined as the ratio between the concentration in the organic phase and the concentration in the aqueous phase. This coefficient has a value of 1.58 at a temperature of 25 °C, indicating that phenol preferentially partitions into the organic phase, thereby facilitating efficient recovery. The design of the extraction unit is based on the use of 8 countercurrent stages, which work together to maximise contact between the two phases, ensuring thorough transfer throughout the cascade. On this design, the predicted recovery is an impressive 93% of the phenol contained in the feed.

It is important to note that this prediction rests on simplifying assumptions not yet validated. Firstly, every stage is assumed to behave as a perfect equilibrium stage, and secondly, the mutual solubility of the two solvents is assumed to be negligible, which together allow the calculations to proceed in a straightforward manner. Neither assumption has been checked against the real solvents involved, highlighting a significant gap between the idealised model and the physical system. Should real stages fall short of equilibrium, or should the solvents prove appreciably mutually soluble, the recovery achieved with 8 stages could potentially fall below the predicted 93%. Furthermore, the distribution coefficient is only a single value at 25 °C, so operation at another temperature would shift the equilibrium and the recovery the unit can deliver.
target:
Liquid-liquid extraction recovers phenol from an aqueous stream into an organic solvent. The distribution coefficient, the ratio of the phenol concentration in the organic phase to that in the aqueous phase, is 1.58 at 25 °C. A coefficient above unity means phenol favours the organic phase at equilibrium, and a countercurrent cascade repeats the contact so that the transfer accumulates stage by stage. The design uses 8 countercurrent stages. Predicted recovery is 93% of the phenol in the feed.

The prediction rests on two assumptions. Each stage is treated as an equilibrium stage, with the leaving streams at their equilibrium compositions. Mutual solubility of the two solvents is neglected, with each phase treated as solvent and phenol only, so the phase flow rates stay constant along the cascade. Neither assumption has been checked on the actual solvents: no stage-efficiency measurement and no mutual-solubility data for the solvent pair in use stand behind the design. The recovery figure is a prediction under idealised contacting, not a measured performance. If the actual stages fall short of equilibrium, or if the two solvents dissolve appreciably in each other, the recovery at 8 stages falls below 93%. The distribution coefficient is a single value at 25 °C; operation at another temperature changes the equilibrium, and the recovery changes with it.

fact_base: A tutorial passage explains representative sampling of an effluent stream. The passage covers where samples are taken, how many increments form one sample, and why a single grab sample misleads. No numerical limits are quoted; regulatory limits belong to the site's permit, not to the passage.
input:
The sampling of effluent streams is a critically important activity whose significance is very often underestimated. The aim of representative sampling is to ensure that the sample reaching the laboratory reflects the composition of the stream over the period in question, rather than merely a snapshot at one moment in time. This passage covers where samples are taken, how increments form one sample, and why a single grab sample misleads.

First, samples should be taken where the stream is thoroughly mixed. A point downstream of a bend, a pump discharge, or a junction has a moving, turbulent flow in which suspended solids and immiscible liquids are distributed across the section, thereby ensuring a representative draw. By contrast, a tap on a straight, slow run, or a draw from a quiet corner of a tank, returns only the local liquid: the portion that has settled, floated, or stagnated. The point must be one the operator can reach and use safely in normal operation, since a point avoided in practice is a point where sampling lapses.

In addition, the sample should be built from a series of increments, an increment being a small portion taken at one moment. Increments spread across the discharge period, combined in proportion to the flow at the moment each was taken, form one composite sample that averages the variation of the stream. Where the flow varies strongly, increments weighted by flow are more meaningful than increments taken at fixed clock times, because most of the load passes in the high-flow part of the period.

Finally, a single grab sample misleads, because an effluent stream is by no means constant. Its composition follows the process: batches discharge, wash water follows production, and cleaning cycles send short, concentrated slugs through the line. A grab taken in a quiet interval reports a dilute stream; a grab taken inside a slug reports the slug alone. Neither reports the period, and any compliance decision or treatment adjustment built on either grab will rest on the wrong load.

fact_base: An operating-manual chapter for a plate heat exchanger, in four sections: start-up, normal operation, alarms, and shutdown. The alarms section lists two alarms and the operator action for each; no other alarms are introduced. The chapter addresses the operator directly and uses imperative verbs for actions.
input:
This chapter covers the operation of the plate heat exchanger in its entirety, from the first fill to the final drain at the end of the run. Throughout the chapter, you, the operator, are addressed directly: the actions are your actions, presented as instructions, and the checks are your checks, to be carried out at the plate pack itself and at the instruments serving it.

Start-up

Before any flow is admitted to the unit, you should confirm that the plate pack has been correctly tightened and that the frame is showing no signs of distortion, that the gaskets are properly seated along their full length, and that the connections to the unit have been made up and adequately supported. The vents on both circuits should be opened. You should then line up the valves so that each circuit can be filled without flow being sent backwards through equipment that stands idle. The cold circuit should be filled first, and filled slowly, with venting continued until such time as liquid runs clear of air at the vent; it should be appreciated that a plate exchanger which is filled too quickly will trap air in the upper channels, and that any air so trapped will leave a portion of the surface effectively dry once the unit is in service. The hot circuit should be filled in exactly the same manner. While the unit is still cold and at low pressure, the pack edge and every connection should be carefully examined for any signs of leakage, bearing in mind that a gasket which weeps when cold is most unlikely to seal any better when hot. The hot stream should then be admitted gradually, with the outlet temperatures being watched closely as they rise. Both flows should be brought up to their duty values in a series of steps, with checks being made between steps to ensure that the pressures are steady and that no connection has started to weep as the plates expand. The exchanger can be regarded as being properly in service once the outlet temperatures are holding steady at the operating point and the pack is completely dry along its edges.

Normal operation

During normal operation, the flows should be held at the values required by the process, and the unit should be read as a whole, taking in the inlet and outlet temperatures on both sides, the pressure drop across the pack, and the general state of the gaskets at the edges. Readings should be recorded at whatever interval is laid down by the plant logging routine, since it is the record, rather than any single reading, that reveals the condition of the unit. A pressure drop that is rising whilst the flow remains unchanged indicates either that the channels are becoming fouled or that a gasket has become displaced into a port. Similarly, a temperature approach that is falling at unchanged flows indicates that the surface is losing its effectiveness, whether through fouling, through maldistribution, or through air that has found its way in with one of the streams. On no account should an attempt be made to chase a temperature deviation by forcing a flow beyond the duty of the unit, because the plate pack is a pressure boundary just as much as it is a heat-transfer surface, and its limits continue to stand regardless of the demands that the process may place upon it. The strainers on the inlet lines should be kept in service and cleaned in accordance with the routine laid down by the plant; a plate channel is a narrow passage, and solids that pass the strainer will lodge in the channels and can only be removed by opening the pack. Where the fluids involved are hazardous in nature, any weepage at the pack edge should be treated as a leak that is to be reported immediately, rather than as a minor defect that can simply be wiped away and kept under observation.

Alarms

The unit is served by two alarms. The high-temperature alarm on the hot outlet requires that the hot stream be checked: you should confirm that the cold flow is standing at its duty value, since a hot outlet temperature that is rising whilst the cold flow is falling points to a flow fault rather than to a surface fault. If the cold flow is in fact correct, the hot inlet flow should be reduced in steps until the temperature has returned within its limit, and the reduction should be reported; the unit will then be delivering less duty than the process asks for, and that shortfall belongs on the record. The high differential-pressure alarm across the pack requires that the flow be reduced and that the pack be taken out of service for inspection at the next opportunity that the process permits: a pressure drop which has climbed as far as the alarm point is stating that the channels have become obstructed, and any attempt to drive the flow against the obstruction places both the gaskets and the plates at risk. Neither alarm should simply be silenced so that operation can continue at the same duty. An alarm which repeats itself after the appropriate action has been taken amounts to a defect report, and the unit should remain at the reduced condition until such time as the underlying cause has been found.

Shutdown

When shutting down, the hot stream should be stopped first, and the cold stream should be kept flowing whilst the unit cools down; in this way the cold flow carries the stored heat out of the pack and prevents a hot, stagnant charge from standing against the gaskets. Once the outlet temperatures have fallen as far as the cold inlet temperature, the cold flow can be stopped. The unit should then be isolated on both circuits, vented, and drained down completely on both sides, because liquid that is left standing in the channels will attack the gaskets and will dry out into deposits that the next start-up will simply inherit. If the pack is to be opened, the tie bolts should be released evenly, in small steps around the frame, so that the pressure plate travels squarely and no plate is sprung. A unit that is to stand idle should be left drained, vented, and isolated, with its state properly recorded, so that the next start-up can begin from a condition that is known.
target:
This chapter covers the operation of the plate heat exchanger from first fill to final drain. The chapter addresses the operator directly: the actions are the operator's actions, stated as instructions, and the checks are the operator's checks, made at the plate pack and at the instruments that serve it.

Start-up

Confirm before any flow is admitted that the plate pack is correctly tightened and that the frame shows no distortion, that the gaskets are seated along their full length, and that the connections to the unit are made up and supported. Open the vents on both circuits. Line up the valves so that each circuit can be filled without sending flow backwards through equipment that stands idle. Fill the cold circuit first, slowly, and vent until liquid runs clear of air at the vent; a plate exchanger filled quickly traps air in the upper channels, and the trapped air leaves part of the surface dry in service. Fill the hot circuit in the same way. Examine the pack edge and every connection for leakage while the unit is still cold and at low pressure; a gasket that weeps cold seals no better hot. Admit the hot stream gradually and watch the outlet temperatures as they rise. Bring both flows to their duty values in steps, checking between steps that the pressures are steady and that no connection has begun to weep as the plates expand. The exchanger is in service when the outlet temperatures hold steady at the operating point and the pack is dry along its edges.

Normal operation

Hold the flows at the values the process requires, and read the unit as a whole: the inlet and outlet temperatures on both sides, the pressure drop across the pack, and the state of the gaskets at the edges. Record the readings at the interval the plant logging routine sets; the record, not the single reading, shows the condition of the unit. A rising pressure drop at unchanged flow means that the channels are fouling or that a gasket has displaced into a port. A falling temperature approach at unchanged flows means that the surface is losing effectiveness to fouling, to maldistribution, or to air that has entered with one of the streams. Do not chase a temperature deviation by forcing a flow beyond the duty of the unit: the plate pack is a pressure boundary as well as a surface, and its limits stand regardless of what the process asks of it. Keep the strainers on the inlet lines in service and clean them on the routine the plant sets; a plate channel is narrow, and solids that pass the strainer lodge in the channels and are removed only by opening the pack. Where the fluids are hazardous, treat any weep at the pack edge as a leak to be reported at once, not as a defect to be wiped and watched.

Alarms

Two alarms serve the unit. The high-temperature alarm on the hot outlet calls for the hot stream to be checked first: confirm that the cold flow stands at its duty value, because a hot outlet temperature rising on a falling cold flow is a flow fault and not a surface fault. If the cold flow is correct, reduce the hot inlet flow in steps until the temperature returns inside its limit, and report the reduction; the unit is then giving less duty than the process asks, and the shortfall belongs on the record. The high differential-pressure alarm across the pack calls for the flow to be reduced and the pack to be taken out of service for inspection at the next opportunity the process allows: a pressure drop that has risen to the alarm point states that the channels are obstructed, and driving the flow against the obstruction risks the gaskets and the plates. Do not silence either alarm and continue at the same duty. An alarm that repeats after its action has been taken is a defect report, and the unit stays at the reduced condition until the cause is found.

Shutdown

Shut the hot stream down first and keep the cold stream flowing while the unit cools; the cold flow carries the stored heat out of the pack and prevents a hot, stagnant charge from standing against the gaskets. When the outlet temperatures have fallen to the cold inlet temperature, stop the cold flow. Isolate the unit on both circuits, vent it, and drain both sides completely; liquid left standing in the channels attacks the gaskets and dries into deposits that the next start-up inherits. If the pack is to be opened, release the tie bolts evenly, in small steps around the frame, so that the pressure plate travels squarely and no plate is sprung. A unit that is to stand idle stays drained, vented, and isolated, with its state recorded, so that the next start-up begins from a known condition.

fact_base: Goal: compute the half-life of a first-order reaction and the fraction remaining after 60 min. For a first-order reaction the rate constant k (min-1) fixes the half-life t1/2 (min) by t1/2 = ln(2) / k, and the fraction remaining after time t (min) is exp(-k t). Measured rate constant: k = 0.046 min-1 at 323 K, from concentration measurements every 5 min over 90 min. Worked results: t1/2 = 15.1 min; the fraction remaining after 60 min is 0.06 (dimensionless), both computed from the stated relations. The relations hold for a first-order reaction only; a reaction of another order follows a different decay law.
input:
In this worked example, the goal is to compute the half-life of a first-order reaction and the fraction of reactant remaining after 60 min has elapsed. The measured rate constant is k = 0.046 min-1 at 323 K, obtained from concentration measurements taken every 5 min over 90 min.

For a first-order reaction, the rate constant k fixes the half-life t1/2 through the relation t1/2 = ln(2) / k, whilst the fraction remaining after time t can be expressed as exp(-k t). It is important to emphasise that these relations are valid for a first-order reaction only, since a reaction of any other order would follow an entirely different decay law, meaning that neither relation could simply be transferred across.

Substituting k = 0.046 min-1 into the half-life relation gives t1/2 = ln(2) / 0.046 = 15.1 min. The half-life can be understood as the time taken for the concentration to drop to exactly one half of its value at the start of the interval, and it is worth noting that t1/2 does not depend on the starting concentration, so every interval of 15.1 min halves whatever amount remains at its start. Substituting t = 60 min into the decay relation gives the fraction remaining as exp(-0.046 x 60) = 0.06. Reassuringly, the two results are fully consistent, because 60 min spans several half-lives of 15.1 min, and repeated halving over such a span naturally leaves only a very small fraction of the reactant, which is precisely what the value 0.06 indicates. Overall, the half-life of 15.1 min effectively sets the timescale of the reaction at 323 K, meaning that measurements intended to follow the decay need to be spaced well inside a single half-life, just as the stated readings every 5 min over 90 min indeed are.

The two relations hold for a first-order reaction only; a reaction of another order follows a different decay law, and neither relation transfers to it.

Substitution of k = 0.046 min-1 gives t1/2 = ln(2) / 0.046 = 15.1 min. The half-life is the time in which the concentration falls to one half of its value at the start of the interval, and t1/2 does not depend on the starting concentration: every interval of 15.1 min halves the amount that remains at its start. Substitution of t = 60 min gives the fraction remaining as exp(-0.046 x 60) = 0.06.
