Fixed costs are $108k per year, and the break-even volume is the fixed costs divided by the contribution per unit: the volume at which the contribution from the units sold exactly covers the fixed costs of the year. Volume above that level contributes at the rate of the contribution on each further unit sold, and volume below it leaves part of the fixed costs uncovered by the trading of the year.

Two limits bound the finding, and both stand on the volume side of the case. The volume figures are last year's actuals, so the margin above break-even is a statement about last year's trading and not a forecast of the year ahead; a contract priced on these figures carries last year's volume as an assumption built into the price. The effect of the price on volume is not estimated. The calculation holds the volume fixed at the level actually delivered and varies nothing else, so the calculation cannot say what volume a different price would bring. A price rise that cost volume could move the contract towards break-even even as the contribution per unit rose. What the figures establish is narrower than a pricing recommendation: at the present price and at last year's volume, the contract covers its fixed costs with volume to spare, and the size of that spare volume is the measure of the case.

fact_base: Adsorption of a dye from water on a metal-organic framework was measured in batch tests at 298 K. The fitted Langmuir capacity was 136 mg of dye per gram of adsorbent at pH 5. At an adsorbent dose of 0.6 g L-1, removal after 120 min was 87% of the initial dye concentration of 50 mg L-1. The Langmuir fit is reported for pH 5 only; capacity at other pH values was not measured.
input: It is worth noting that the adsorption of a dye from water onto a metal-organic framework was investigated in a series of batch tests carried out at 298 K. In each test, a known mass of the adsorbent was brought into contact with the dye solution, and the uptake was determined from the change in the solution concentration over the contact period. The equilibrium data were fitted using the Langmuir isotherm model, and the fitted capacity at pH 5 was found to be 136 mg of dye per gram of adsorbent. It should be emphasised that this capacity is the fitted Langmuir parameter, representing the dye loading that the fit assigns to the adsorbent as the equilibrium concentration increases, expressed on a per-gram basis. When an adsorbent dose of 0.6 g L-1 was used with an initial dye concentration of 50 mg L-1, the removal after 120 min reached 87%, which corresponds to a removed concentration of 43.5 mg L-1 and a residual concentration of 6.5 mg L-1. Importantly, the removal is expressed relative to the initial concentration, and the 87% figure is a removal fraction under the stated dose and contact time rather than a capacity. Furthermore, the dose and the contact time together define the conditions attached to the removal figure, so a different dose or a shorter contact time would be expected to give a different removal under the same test arrangement. Finally, the Langmuir fit is reported for pH 5 only; capacity at other pH values was not measured, which means that the fitted capacity of 136 mg per gram is established at pH 5 and cannot be assumed to apply at any other pH.
target: Adsorption of a dye from water on a metal-organic framework was measured in batch tests at 298 K. Each test contacted a known mass of adsorbent with the dye solution, and uptake was obtained from the change in solution concentration over the contact period. Equilibrium data were fitted with the Langmuir isotherm, and the fitted capacity at pH 5 was 136 mg of dye per gram of adsorbent. Capacity here is the fitted Langmuir parameter: the dye loading the fit assigns to the adsorbent as the equilibrium concentration rises, stated per gram of adsorbent. At an adsorbent dose of 0.6 g L-1 and an initial dye concentration of 50 mg L-1, removal after 120 min was 87%, corresponding to a removed concentration of 43.5 mg L-1 and a residual concentration of 6.5 mg L-1. In a batch test the adsorbent and the solution are brought together once and left in contact, so the measured uptake belongs to the starting concentration and the contact period of the test rather than to a flowing stream. Removal is stated against the initial concentration, and the 87% figure is a removal fraction at the stated dose and contact time, not a capacity. The dose and the contact time fix the conditions of the removal figure; a different dose or a shorter contact time gives a different removal under the same test arrangement. The Langmuir fit is reported for pH 5 only. Capacity at other pH values was not measured, and the fitted capacity of 136 mg per gram is established at pH 5 and at no other pH. A capacity quoted for this adsorbent without its pH is incomplete, because the fit behind the figure was made at one pH only.

fact_base: A defect-reduction project on a moulding cell cut the reject rate from 4.3% to 2.9% over one quarter. At 120k units per year the change avoids about 1680 rejected units per year. The quarter included a planned shutdown; rates are not adjusted for it.
input: A defect-reduction project carried out on a moulding cell succeeded in cutting the reject rate from 4.3% to 2.9% over the course of one quarter, which represents a reduction of 1.4 percentage points. The reject rate is the share of moulded units that are rejected at inspection, so the reduction should be understood as a fall in that share rather than a fall in production volume. At a volume of 120k units per year, the lower rate avoids approximately 1680 rejected units per year. It is worth noting that the avoided figure is obtained by multiplying the annual volume by the rate reduction, and it therefore holds only for as long as the improved rate is maintained; a return to the earlier rate would bring the rejected count back with it. The quarter in question included a planned shutdown, and the rates have not been adjusted to account for it. Output lost to the shutdown therefore sits inside the quarter's figures on exactly the same basis as the running production, and the comparison between the two rates is a comparison of unadjusted rates over a quarter that was not a full production quarter. Overall, the reduction is established for that one quarter, and reject performance over a longer period, or in a quarter without a planned shutdown, was not reported.
target: A defect-reduction project on a moulding cell cut the reject rate from 4.3% to 2.9% over one quarter, a reduction of 1.4 percentage points. The reject rate is the share of moulded units rejected at inspection, so the reduction is a fall in that share and not a fall in production volume. A rejected unit is a unit scrapped at inspection or set aside for rework, and the rate counts those units against all the units moulded in the period, good and rejected together. At 120k units per year, the lower rate avoids about 1680 rejected units per year. The avoided figure is the annual volume multiplied by the rate reduction, and it holds only for as long as the improved rate holds; a return to the earlier rate returns the rejected count with it. On the figures given, the project has changed the rate at which the cell produces rejects; whether the change came from the moulding conditions, the tooling or the inspection standard is not stated, and the annual saving figure inherits the basis of the quarter it was measured in.

fact_base: Performance of a mechanical-draft tower at a chemical site was logged over one summer month. Mean wet-bulb temperature was 23 °C, the approach was 7 K and the range was 8 K. Performance outside the logged month, in particular at winter wet-bulb temperatures, was not measured.
input: The performance of a mechanical-draft cooling tower at a chemical site was logged over the course of one summer month. The mean wet-bulb temperature recorded over the month was 23 °C. The approach was 7 K, which means that the cold water left the tower at 30 °C, and the range was 8 K, which means that the water entered the tower at 38 °C. It should be noted that the approach is defined as the difference between the leaving cold-water temperature and the wet-bulb temperature, while the range is the fall in water temperature across the tower, so the two figures together place the tower's water temperatures against the air condition prevailing during the logged month. A wet-bulb temperature, it may be explained, is the temperature that the air reaches when water is evaporated into it to saturation, and it sets the lowest temperature to which the tower is able to cool its water. The two water temperatures are the temperatures that the tower actually received and delivered during the month, and they are the figures that a user of the log would take for the duty that the tower performed over that period. A mechanical-draft tower moves air by means of a fan, and its performance follows the wet-bulb temperature of the entering air. It is important to emphasise, however, that performance outside the logged month was not measured. In particular, performance at winter wet-bulb temperatures is not established by this log, and the summer approach and range cannot simply be carried over and assumed to apply to winter operation.

Performance at winter wet-bulb temperatures in particular is not established by this log, and the summer approach and range are not transferable to winter operation. Any judgement about the tower in another season needs measurements taken in that season.

fact_base: A shell-and-tube exchanger heats propylene glycol in a refinery preheat train. Duty is 732 kW. Hot stream: 180 °C in, 130 °C out. Cold stream: 35 °C in, 50 °C out. The log-mean temperature difference is 111.6 K and the installed area is 24.8 m2, giving an overall coefficient of 265 W m-2 K-1. Fouling was assessed from a single 90-day run; no cleaning cycle has been completed.
input: A shell-and-tube exchanger located in a refinery preheat train is used to heat propylene glycol. It may be noted that the propylene glycol is being heated as part of the preheat duty of the train, and that the exchanger is one item within that train rather than a standalone unit. The duty of the exchanger is 732 kW. The hot stream enters at 180 °C and leaves at 130 °C, while the cold stream enters at 35 °C and leaves at 50 °C. For these terminal temperatures, the log-mean temperature difference works out at 111.6 K. With an installed area of 24.8 m2, the overall coefficient is 265 W m-2 K-1. The terminal temperatures fix the temperature programme of the unit: the hot stream gives up the stated duty across its stated fall in temperature, and the cold stream takes up the same duty across its corresponding rise. It is worth noting that the coefficient is stated on the basis of the installed area: it is the duty divided by the product of the area and the log-mean temperature difference, and it conveniently covers the resistance of both films and the wall in a single figure. The coefficient should be understood as an as-found figure for the run reported, and it will be expected to move as fouling builds up on the surfaces over time. Fouling was assessed on the basis of a single 90-day run. No cleaning cycle has yet been completed, and the assessment therefore covers one run from the start of service; fouling behaviour over repeated runs separated by cleaning is not covered by the assessment.

fact_base: A contract packaging firm runs 4 plants; revenue is $82 million per year. Evidence base: order records for 12 months, 11220 orders. On-time delivery over the last two quarters was 87%, against a target of 95%. Overtime cost was $2.2 million last year, up 16% on the year before. The order backlog stands at 4.1 weeks, against 1.9 weeks a year ago. Plant 2 accounts for 52% of late orders. A scheduling system for all plants is quoted at $346k; Plant 2 alone is $148k. An internal estimate (not a vendor figure) puts the overtime reduction at Plant 2 at 15-20% in the first year. The recommendation under consideration: install at Plant 2 first, hold the other plants until Plant 2 results are reported. The operations director owns the scheduling programme.
input: This summary reviews delivery performance at a contract packaging firm that runs 4 plants and generates revenue of $82 million per year. Drawing on order records for 12 months, covering 11220 orders, on-time delivery over the last two quarters stood at 87%, which falls short of the target of 95%. Late delivery is heavily concentrated: Plant 2 accounts for no less than 52% of late orders, more than the other plants combined. Overtime cost was $2.2 million last year, up 16% on the year before, while the order backlog now stands at 4.1 weeks, compared with 1.9 weeks a year ago. A scheduling system covering all plants is quoted at $346k, with Plant 2 alone quoted at $148k. An internal estimate, which it should be stressed is not a vendor figure, puts the overtime reduction at Plant 2 at 15–20% in the first year. Against this background, the recommendation under consideration is to install the system at Plant 2 first and to hold the other plants until Plant 2 results are reported; the operations director owns the scheduling programme. The trade-off at Plant 2 is the $148k installation against the internally estimated overtime saving. Holding the remaining plants costs no installation spend in the meantime, and it means that the wider decision will depend on measured Plant 2 performance rather than on the estimate alone.

The concentration matters for the remedy: a scheduling failure spread evenly across the firm would call for a firm-wide remedy, whereas a failure concentrated at a single plant can be treated at that plant first and judged there before any wider spend is committed. The trade-off at Plant 2 is the $148k installation against an overtime saving that an internal estimate, not a vendor figure, puts at 15–20% of Plant 2 overtime in the first year. Holding the remaining plants costs no installation spend in the meantime, and it makes the wider decision depend on measured Plant 2 performance rather than on the estimate. The decision supported by the summary is a staged one, with the second stage conditional on reported results from the first.

fact_base: A continuous stirred-tank reactor runs an esterification that is first order in the limiting reactant. The rate constant is 0.021 min-1 at the operating temperature and the mean residence time is 35 min. Steady-state conversion for an ideal CSTR is 42.4%. The estimate assumes perfect mixing and constant density; tracer tests on the actual vessel have not been run.
input: This worked example sets out to calculate the steady-state conversion of the limiting reactant in an esterification reaction carried out in a continuous stirred-tank reactor. The reaction is first order in the limiting reactant, which means that the rate is proportional to the concentration of that reactant, and the rate constant at the operating temperature is 0.021 min-1. The mean residence time in the vessel is 35 min; the mean residence time, it should be explained, is the vessel volume divided by the volumetric flow rate, and it represents the average time that a fluid element spends in the vessel. Multiplying the rate constant by the mean residence time gives a product of 0.735. The conversion is the fraction of the limiting reactant that is converted at the outlet, stated against the feed concentration of that reactant. Because the rate falls as the reactant is consumed, the conversion is set by the balance between the reaction taking place in the vessel and the flow passing through it, and not by the inlet concentration acting on its own. For a first-order reaction at steady state in an ideal CSTR (continuous stirred-tank reactor), the conversion is given by this product divided by one plus this product, since the whole contents of the vessel sit at the exit concentration and the rate is everywhere the exit rate. Substituting the numbers gives a conversion of 42.4%. It is important to note that the estimate rests on the assumptions of perfect mixing and constant density. Perfect mixing is the key assumption carrying the result: the exit-rate form holds only while the contents remain uniform. Tracer tests on the actual vessel have not been run, so mixing in the vessel remains unchecked, and any dead volume or bypassing would move the conversion away from 42.4% while leaving the stated rate constant and residence time unchanged. The resulting figure is also bounded by construction: it sits below complete conversion, as a finite residence time at a finite rate necessarily requires.

subtype: worked example with equation: friction loss
fact_base: Water at 293 K flows in a horizontal pipe. The density $\rho$ is 998 kg m-3. Mean velocity $v$ is 1.5 m s-1, pipe diameter $D$ is 0.08 m, pipe length $L$ is 83 m and the Darcy friction factor $f$ is 0.02. The friction pressure drop is 23.3 kPa.
input:
Water at a temperature of 293 K flows through a horizontal pipe, and the friction pressure drop is calculated by means of the Darcy–Weisbach relation, which is written as follows:

$$\Delta P = f \frac{L}{D} \frac{\rho v^2}{2}$$

In this relation, $\Delta P$ denotes the friction pressure drop, $f$ the Darcy friction factor, $L$ the pipe length, $D$ the pipe diameter, $\rho$ the density of the water and $v$ the mean velocity. Because the pipe is horizontal, the relation carries no elevation term, and the whole of the calculated drop is attributable to friction. The density $\rho$ is 998 kg m-3, the mean velocity $v$ is 1.5 m s-1, the diameter $D$ is 0.08 m, the length $L$ is 83 m and the friction factor $f$ is 0.02. It should be noted that the friction factor is taken as given for the pipe and the flow condition; the calculation does not attempt to derive it from a roughness value or from a Reynolds number. The length-to-diameter ratio works out at 1037.5, and the dynamic pressure, defined as the density times the square of the velocity, halved, is 1122.75 Pa. Multiplying the friction factor, the length-to-diameter ratio and the dynamic pressure together gives 23297 Pa. The friction pressure drop is therefore 23.3 kPa. Finally, it is worth observing that the drop grows with the square of the velocity and in proportion to the length, so the long pipe run, rather than the velocity, is the larger contributor at the stated values.

Each symbol in the relation is a property of the flow or of the pipe, and the relation combines them into the pressure that the supply head must provide to hold the stated flow. The pipe is horizontal, so the relation carries no elevation term, and the whole of the calculated drop is friction. fact_base: An operating-manual chapter for a pressure relief valve, in four sections: start-up, normal operation, alarms, and shutdown. The alarms section lists two alarms and the operator action for each; no other alarms are introduced. The chapter addresses the operator directly and uses imperative verbs for actions.
input:
Start-up

It is essential, before start-up, to confirm that the relief valve installed is the valve that has been specified for the duty. The nameplate should be read and the stamped set pressure checked against the set pressure given on the equipment data sheet; if any mismatch is found, work must stop and the mismatch must be reported, and the valve must not be put into service until the matter has been fully resolved. It should also be confirmed that the inspection tag is in date and that no test report for the valve is outstanding. Any transport gag or shipping restraint that was fitted for transit must be removed, and it must be confirmed that the restraint is completely clear of the spring and stem before the system is pressurised. The discharge line should be walked from the valve outlet through to its termination so that it can be confirmed that the path is open along its whole length: no blind flange left in place, no closed valve in the discharge path that is not locked open, and no temporary cap or plug remaining at the outlet. The inlet isolation valve, where one is fitted, must be confirmed fully open and locked or sealed in the open position, and the same check applies to any outlet isolation valve. Drains and vents on the inlet and discharge lines should be checked closed, and any tell-tale drain between the valve and its discharge header should be confirmed open to a safe place so that leakage past the seat shows there first. The valve body, bonnet and flange joints should be inspected for damage, corrosion and loose bolting, and the lever or cap confirmed to be in its normal position. The system pressure should then be raised slowly and in stages, holding at each stage so that the flange joints and the bonnet joint can be checked for leakage. The inlet pressure gauge should be watched as the pressure rises and the reading compared with the reading expected for the start-up stage, and any reading that does not follow the pressurising source should be investigated. As the pressure approaches normal operating pressure, the valve should be listened at for simmer or leakage past the seat. Finally, the start-up should be recorded in the shift log, including the valve identification, the checks completed and any defect found, with the defect reported through the maintenance system before the system is left in service.

Normal operation

The relief valve must be kept in service and available at all times while the protected system is pressurised. The valve must never be gagged, the lever must never be wired down, the discharge must never be blocked, and the set screw must never be adjusted; set-pressure adjustment is workshop work carried out under a test procedure, and it is never an acceptable field correction for a valve that lifts early or leaks. The valve should be made part of the normal operator round. On each round, the valve and its joints should be looked at for signs of leakage, corrosion, mechanical damage and loose bolting. Listening should be carried out for discharge noise, simmer or chatter carried through the discharge line. The discharge line downstream of the valve should be felt with the back of the hand where access is safe: a line that is warm when the valve has not lifted is an indication of leakage past the seat. The inlet pressure gauge should be read on the round and the reading entered in the round log, so that a slow rise in operating pressure towards the set pressure becomes visible in the record before it develops into an alarm. The area around the valve should be kept clear so that the nameplate, the lever and the discharge outlet remain accessible and visible. The discharge termination must be kept unobstructed: no stored material should be placed against it, no scaffold tied to it, and no temporary equipment hung from the discharge line. Leakage past the seat, damage, corrosion or a missing or out-of-date inspection tag should be reported through the maintenance system on the round on which it is found. Where a block valve arrangement allows the relief valve to be isolated, the isolation state should be treated as a controlled condition: the operating relief path must be open whenever the system is pressurised, and any change of isolation state must be made under the site permit procedure and recorded in the shift log, together with the time of the change and the name of the operator making it.

Alarms

Two alarms are fitted for this valve, and no others. The high inlet pressure alarm sounds when the pressure in the protected system rises above its alarm setting. When this alarm sounds, the pressure reading should first be checked against the local inlet gauge so that it can be confirmed that the rise is real. The pressure should then be reduced at its source: the heat input or the feed to the system should be cut by the normal operating procedure for the equipment being protected, and the manual vent to a safe location should be opened if the pressure continues to rise. The shift supervisor should be informed and the system kept under observation. It should be expected that the relief valve will lift if the pressure reaches the set pressure; a lift on a confirmed pressure rise is simply the valve doing its duty and is not by itself a defect. Personnel should stay clear of the discharge termination while the valve is lifting or may lift. The discharge alarm sounds when flow through the discharge line shows that the relief valve has lifted. When this alarm sounds, the operator should go to the valve and confirm the lift from the discharge indication, and should then find the cause of the overpressure in the protected system and remove it by the normal operating procedure. The lift should be recorded in the shift log, together with the pressure reached and the cause found. The valve should be watched to make sure that it reseats as the pressure falls, and after it has reseated it should be checked for continued leakage past the seat by means of the tell-tale drain and by listening at the discharge line. A valve that does not reseat, or that continues to leak after reseating, should be reported through the maintenance system, and the system pressure should be kept under observation until the defect has been dealt with. It should also be noted that a valve that has lifted is reported for inspection at the next opportunity, even when it reseats cleanly.

Shutdown

The relief valve should be taken out of service only when the protected system is depressurised, or when an alternative relief path is in service and has been recorded. The system pressure should be reduced in a controlled manner by the normal shutdown procedure, venting to a safe location, and it should be confirmed on the inlet gauge that the pressure has fallen and is stable before any isolation is made. The inlet isolation valve should be closed, and then the outlet isolation valve where one is fitted, and both valves should be locked and tagged under the site isolation procedure. The inlet line and the valve body should be drained through the drain connection to a safe place, and the discharge side should be vented so that no trapped pressure remains between the isolation valves. A check for trapped pressure should always be made before any flange is broken: the joint should be slackened slowly and work stopped at the first sign of pressure or discharge. The isolation should be recorded in the shift log and on the isolation register, together with the state of each valve in the line-up. Where the relief valve is removed for bench testing or overhaul, blind flanges should be fitted to the open inlet and discharge connections, the removed valve should be tagged with its identification and set pressure, and the removal should be recorded so that the protected system is not returned to service without a relief valve in place or an approved alternative. On return from test, the valve should be refitted with new gaskets, the test certificate should be confirmed to match the nameplate set pressure, and the line-up should be restored by means of the start-up checks set out in this chapter before the system is pressurised again.

On this alarm, first check the pressure reading against the local inlet gauge to confirm that the rise is real. Reduce the pressure at its source: cut the heat input or the feed to the system by the normal operating procedure for the equipment being protected, and open the manual vent to a safe location if the pressure continues to rise. Inform the shift supervisor and keep the system under observation. Expect the relief valve to lift if the pressure reaches the set pressure; a lift on a confirmed pressure rise is the valve doing its duty and is not by itself a defect. Stay clear of the discharge termination while the valve is lifting or may lift. The discharge alarm sounds when flow through the discharge line shows that the relief valve has lifted. On this alarm, go to the valve and confirm the lift from the discharge indication, then find the cause of the overpressure in the protected system and remove it by the normal operating procedure. Record the lift in the shift log with the pressure reached and the cause found. Watch for the valve to reseat as the pressure falls, and after it reseats check for continued leakage past the seat by the tell-tale drain and by listening at the discharge line. Report a valve that does not reseat, or that continues to leak after reseating, through the maintenance system and keep the system pressure under observation until the defect is dealt with. A valve that has lifted is reported for inspection at the next opportunity even when it reseats cleanly.

Shutdown

Take the relief valve out of service only when the protected system is depressurised or when an alternative relief path is in service and recorded. Reduce the system pressure in a controlled manner by the normal shutdown procedure, venting to a safe location, and confirm on the inlet gauge that the pressure has fallen and is stable before any isolation is made. Close the inlet isolation valve and then the outlet isolation valve where fitted, and lock and tag both valves under the site isolation procedure. Drain the inlet line and the valve body through the drain connection to a safe place, and vent the discharge side so that no trapped pressure remains between the isolation valves. Check for trapped pressure before breaking any flange: slacken the joint slowly and stop at the first sign of pressure or discharge. Record the isolation in the shift log and on the isolation register, with the state of each valve in the line-up. Where the relief valve is removed for bench testing or overhaul, fit blind flanges to the open inlet and discharge connections, tag the removed valve with its identification and set pressure, and record the removal so that the protected system is not returned to service without a relief valve in place or an approved alternative. On return from test, refit the valve with new gaskets, confirm the test certificate matches the nameplate set pressure, and restore the line-up by the start-up checks in this chapter before the system is pressurised again.

fact_base: A vapour-compression unit serves a cold store, evaporating at 0 °C and condensing at 45 °C. The Carnot coefficient of performance between these temperatures is 6.07; the installed unit achieves 2.64. The achieved value is from the manufacturer's test at full load; part-load performance is not stated.
input: A vapour-compression unit serves a cold store, evaporating at 0 °C and condensing at 45 °C. The coefficient of performance (COP) is the heat removed at the evaporator divided by the work input to the compressor. Between the evaporating and condensing temperatures stated, the Carnot coefficient of performance is 6.07; the Carnot value is the reversible limit for a refrigerator working between those two temperatures. The two temperatures are the temperature of the cold space being cooled and the temperature at which heat is rejected, and the limit is fixed by those temperatures alone. A unit working between different temperatures has a different limit, and its achieved performance is judged against the limit belonging to its own temperatures. The installed unit achieves a coefficient of performance of 2.64, which is 43.5% of the Carnot value. The shortfall is the irreversibility of the real machine and cycle: compression and expansion losses, pressure drops in the refrigerant lines and heat transfer across finite temperature differences in the evaporator and the condenser each move the achieved value below the reversible limit. The achieved value is from the manufacturer's test at full load. Part-load performance is not stated, and the value of 2.64 is established at full load and at a condensing temperature of 45 °C only.

fact_base: A centrifugal pump moves caustic solution between two vessels at grade. At the duty point the flow is 44 m3 h-1 against a head of 51 m, with pump efficiency 81%. Shaft power at the duty point is 7.5 kW. The motor is rated 15% above this value. Cavitation was not observed in the acceptance test, which ran for 4 h at the duty point only.
input: A centrifugal pump is used to move caustic solution between two vessels that stand at grade. The duty point is the flow and head at which the pump is required to run in normal service. The head, it should be explained, is the height of a column of the pumped liquid that the pressure rise at the pump is able to support, stated for the liquid being pumped; with the two vessels standing at grade, the head is not spent on a large static lift between them. Taken together, the figures that follow describe the pump at the one operating point that the process asks of it. At the duty point, the flow is 44 m3 h-1 against a head of 51 m, and the pump efficiency is 81%. The shaft power at the duty point is 7.5 kW; it should be understood that the shaft power is the hydraulic power imparted to the liquid divided by the pump efficiency, so the efficiency is already contained within the stated figure and must not be applied a second time. The motor is rated 15% above the shaft power, which corresponds to a rated output of 8.6 kW, and this margin is intended to cover motor loading at the duty point with headroom for the fall in efficiency and the rise in absorbed power that wear and off-duty operation can bring. The shaft power is the power that the motor must deliver to the pump shaft at that particular duty, after the pump's own inefficiency has taken its share of the power imparted to the liquid. Cavitation was not observed during the acceptance test. However, the acceptance test ran for 4 h at the duty point only. The absence of cavitation is therefore established at the duty point over a run of that length; cavitation at flows away from the duty point, at lower suction levels or at other liquid temperatures was not tested, and the test makes no statement whatsoever about them.

fact_base: Energy assessment of a brewery, in four sections: current use, refrigeration, steam, and recommendation. Electricity use is 1689 MWh per year; refrigeration takes the largest share. A heat-recovery retrofit is projected to save 11% of electricity use, a derived saving of 186 MWh per year, at a capital cost of $274k. At $0.12 per kWh the derived annual saving is $22295 and the derived simple payback is 12.3 years. Steam figures are from one winter month and are flagged as seasonal in the recommendation.
input:
Current use

Electricity use at the brewery amounts to 1689 MWh per year. The site load is divided between the brewhouse, the cellar and cold store, the packaging lines and the utility plant, and the metered total represents the sum of those uses over the course of the year. Refrigeration accounts for the largest share of the total, and the refrigeration section below deals with that share in greater detail. Steam is raised on site for the brewhouse and for cleaning purposes, and its figures rest on a considerably shorter measurement period than the electricity figures; the steam section sets out the basis, and the recommendation draws out the consequence for the saving case. It should be emphasised that no part of the assessment rests on nameplate ratings: the electricity figure is metered consumption, and the projected saving is stated against that metered figure.

Refrigeration

Refrigeration is the largest single use of electricity on the site. The load is continuous in character: fermentation vessels are held at controlled temperatures, finished beer is held cold, and glycol is circulated to the vessel jackets and to the cold store, so the compressors run through the day and the night rather than simply following the brewing programme. Because the load runs continuously, a saving in the refrigeration system is repeated in every operating hour of the year, and refrigeration is where a heat-recovery retrofit finds both its heat source and much of its recovered duty. Heat rejected at the condensers is available at a temperature that is well suited to preheating water for the brewhouse and for cleaning, duties that would otherwise be met from steam. The assessment treats the refrigeration plant as the point of recovery and the hot-water demand of the brewhouse as the point of use, and the projected saving is an electricity saving at the refrigeration plant together with the steam saving that follows from the displaced water heating; the steam part of the benefit is the part that is qualified in the recommendation. Compressor condition, suction and discharge pressures and glycol temperatures were all reviewed as part of the assessment, and no defect was found that would change the saving case: the projected saving is a recovery opportunity on plant that is working as intended, rather than a repair saving on plant that is not.

Steam

Steam serves the brewhouse vessels, the cleaning-in-place station and space heating, and it represents the second energy stream considered in the assessment. The steam figures are drawn from one winter month. Winter is the season of highest steam demand on this site: space heating is at its peak, incoming water is at its coldest, and the brewhouse works against the largest temperature lift of the year. A saving rate that is measured or estimated on a winter month therefore reads high when set against the year as a whole, and steam savings stated from that month would overstate the annual figure if they were carried across the year without correction. The assessment does not correct the steam figures to an annual basis, because no second measured month exists against which to correct them; the figures are presented as winter-month figures and are used in the recommendation only with that qualification firmly attached. The electricity figures are not affected by the same qualification, since they rest on a full year of metering.

Recommendation

A heat-recovery retrofit on the refrigeration plant is projected to save 11% of electricity use, which corresponds to a derived saving of 186 MWh per year, at a capital cost of $274k. At $0.12 per kWh, the derived annual saving works out at $22295, and the derived simple payback is 12.3 years. The payback is long when set against the life usually asked of refrigeration plant work, and it is stated on the electricity saving alone. It is important to note that the steam figures in this assessment are taken from one winter month and are flagged as seasonal: any steam saving added to the case would be stated on a winter basis and would tend to flatter the payback, so no steam saving has been counted in the figures above. The recommendation is that a decision on the retrofit be taken on the electricity case as stated, with the payback of 12.3 years clearly in view, and that the steam benefit be treated as unquantified until steam metering has covered a summer month as well as a winter one.

subtype: worked example with equation: Fourier conduction
fact_base: A flat stainless steel wall has thickness 150 mm and thermal conductivity $k$ of 16 W m-1 K-1. The temperature difference $\Delta T$ across the wall is 214 K, giving a heat flux $q$ of 22827 W m-2. The calculation is steady and one-dimensional; film resistances are excluded.
input:
A flat stainless steel wall separates two fluids, and the steady heat conduction through the wall is calculated by means of Fourier's law, which takes the following form:

$$q = k \frac{\Delta T}{\Delta x}$$

In this expression, $q$ denotes the heat flux through the wall, $k$ the thermal conductivity of the wall material, $\Delta T$ the temperature difference across the wall and $\Delta x$ the wall thickness. Fourier's law states the flux as proportional to the temperature gradient across the wall, with the conductivity appearing as the constant of the material. The gradient here is the stated temperature difference divided by the stated thickness, which is the form that the law takes for a flat wall of uniform thickness with a linear temperature profile through it. The wall thickness is 150 mm, or 0.15 m, and the thermal conductivity of the stainless steel is 16 W m-1 K-1. The temperature difference across the wall is 214 K. Substituting these values into the relation gives a heat flux $q$ of 22827 W m-2. It should be noted that the calculation is steady and one-dimensional: the temperature is taken to vary only across the thickness, and no heat is assumed to leave through the edges of the wall. Film resistances at the two faces of the wall are excluded from the calculation. If film resistances were included, the same overall temperature difference would give a lower flux than 22827 W m-2, since the films would add resistance in series with the wall.

fact_base: A defect-reduction project on a moulding cell cut the reject rate from 3.9% to 2.3% over one quarter. At 94k units per year the change avoids about 1504 rejected units per year. The quarter included a planned shutdown; rates are not adjusted for it.
input: In the context of an ongoing effort to improve performance on a moulding cell, it is worth noting that a defect-reduction project reportedly delivered a meaningful improvement over the course of one quarter, with the reject rate moving from 3.9% to 2.3%. When this improvement is considered against a production level of 94k units per year, the change is said to avoid about 1504 rejected units per year, which can be viewed as a substantial operational benefit. At the same time, however, it should also be kept in mind that the quarter in question included a planned shutdown, and the rates have not been adjusted for that shutdown. In other words, the figures are presented on an as-run basis rather than on a normalised basis that attempts to remove the influence of the shutdown period. This is important because the annual avoided count is derived by applying the improvement to the stated yearly volume, rather than by drawing on a separate measurement from another period. Overall, the passage presents a lower reject rate and a corresponding reduction in rejected units, while also acknowledging, albeit in a somewhat qualified way, that the comparison period contained a planned shutdown and that no adjustment has been made for it in the reported rates.

The annual avoided count uses the stated production volume as its basis; the count is not a separate measurement from another period. The quarter included a planned shutdown. Rates are not adjusted for the shutdown, so the reported change is the change in the recorded reject rate for the quarter as run. The result keeps two statements apart. The rate moved between the stated start and end values during the quarter, and the annual avoided count follows when the improvement is applied to the stated yearly volume. No adjustment removes the shutdown, estimates a shutdown-free rate, or restates the quarter on a different operating basis. That limit belongs with the headline figures because the shutdown formed part of the quarter in which the lower rate was recorded. A reject rate compares rejected units with production over the same period, and the two rates here are read on that common basis. The unadjusted form does not claim that operating conditions in the quarter matched any other quarter. The project result is a lower reject rate for the moulding cell and the corresponding avoided-reject count at the stated volume, with the shutdown left inside the comparison period and the basis stated beside the figures.

fact_base: A continuous stirred-tank reactor runs a neutralisation that is first order in the limiting reactant. The rate constant is 0.025 min-1 at the operating temperature and the mean residence time is 90 min. Steady-state conversion for an ideal CSTR is 69.2%. The estimate assumes perfect mixing and constant density; tracer tests on the actual vessel have not been run.
input: To estimate what happens in this case, it is helpful to consider a continuous stirred-tank reactor carrying out a neutralisation that is first order in the limiting reactant. Under the idealised assumptions that are typically invoked for this kind of calculation, namely perfect mixing and constant density, the rate constant is given as 0.025 per minute at the operating temperature, while the mean residence time is 90 min. If these values are brought together in the standard ideal-reactor relationship, the product of the rate constant and the mean residence time is 2.25, and the relevant denominator becomes 3.25 once the unit term in the relation is included. The arithmetic can be stated plainly: 2.25 is the product, and 3.25 is the denominator. On that basis, the steady-state conversion for an ideal continuous stirred-tank reactor is estimated at 69.2%. It is important to note, however, that this figure should not be read as a fully validated prediction for the actual vessel. In particular, tracer tests on the actual vessel have not been run, which means that the perfect-mixing assumption has not been checked directly against the vessel's real residence-time behaviour. The constant-density assumption is likewise part of the estimate rather than something established separately here. Overall, the value of 69.2% is best understood as the ideal-model result obtained from the stated rate constant and residence time under the stated assumptions.
target: Calculate the steady-state conversion for a neutralisation in a continuous stirred-tank reactor. The reaction is first order in the limiting reactant. Assume perfect mixing and constant density before the relation is used. The rate constant is 0.025 per minute at the operating temperature, and the mean residence time is 90 min. For an ideal continuous stirred-tank reactor, the product of the rate constant and the mean residence time is 2.25. Thus the conversion is obtained from 2.25 divided by 3.25, where 3.25 is the same product increased by the unit term in the ideal-reactor relation. The relation gives a steady-state conversion of 69.2%. Perfect mixing makes the composition in the reactor uniform in the ideal model, and constant density keeps the residence-time basis fixed through the calculation. The closing check is a limit on the estimate, not a second result. Tracer tests on the actual vessel have not been run, so the perfect-mixing part of the ideal model has not been checked against the vessel's residence-time behaviour. Constant density is also an assumption of the estimate, stated with the model rather than measured in the passage. The calculation is a steady-state calculation. It does not describe start-up, a change in feed rate, or a vessel whose contents are still moving toward the stated operating point. Those cases would require a different statement of the problem, because the relation used here is tied to the steady state and to the residence time at that state. The number 69.2% is therefore the conversion for the stated ideal continuous stirred-tank reactor under the stated assumptions. It is not a tracer-verified conversion for the actual vessel, and it does not remove the gap left by the missing tracer tests.

fact_base: Excerpt content: the schedule float is set at 14% and the excerpt defends that figure against a lower alternative. The excerpt refers to the project's cost table by section name and does not repeat its figures.
input: It is important to note that the proposed schedule float of 14% for the upgrade project has been the subject of some discussion, particularly in relation to the possibility that a lower alternative might be adopted instead. While a reduced figure could appear attractive at first sight, it would nevertheless leave the programme with considerably less room to respond when an approval, a delivery, or an interface between different packages takes longer than the planned sequence allows. The steering group is therefore not being asked to view the float simply as spare time that happens to sit at the end of the programme. Rather, the float should be understood as a mechanism for protecting the order of the work, in the sense that a delay arising in one package can be absorbed before it is passed on to the next package and effectively converted into a change in the completion position. This is especially relevant where dependencies cannot be run in parallel and where a late input can hold up more than the package that formally owns that input. It should also be emphasised that reducing the float would not, in itself, remove those dependencies. The figure of 14% should accordingly be read alongside the cost position for the upgrade project, with reference to the cost table in the Costs section, whose figures are not repeated here.

A smaller allowance would be defensible only if the sequence had fewer hard dependencies or if the steering group accepted a weaker completion position as the price of the reduction. Neither change is made in the excerpt. The defence is therefore narrow: the percentage is retained because the dependencies remain, and because the cost discussion is kept in the Costs section rather than mixed into the schedule allowance. For the steering group, the choice is between retaining 14% as the programme allowance and accepting that a smaller allowance transfers ordinary slippage directly to the end date.

subtype: worked example with equation: available NPSH
fact_base: A pump draws water from an open tank at atmospheric pressure, 101.3 kPa. Vapour pressure at the pumping temperature is 7.4 kPa, the static lift is 1 m and suction-line friction loss is 0.6 m. Available net positive suction head $NPSH_a$ is 8 m. The pump's required NPSH at the duty flow comes from the vendor curve and must be exceeded with margin.
input:
In this example, a pump is drawing water from an open tank, and the aim is to determine the available net positive suction head, usually written as $NPSH_a$, from the conditions on the suction side. The relevant quantities include atmospheric pressure $P_{atm}$, vapour pressure $P_v$, liquid density $\rho$, gravitational acceleration $g$, the static lift $h_{lift}$, and the suction-line friction loss $h_f$. The tank is at atmospheric pressure, 101.3 kPa, while the vapour pressure at the pumping temperature is 7.4 kPa. In addition, the static lift is 1 m and the suction-line friction loss is 0.6 m. Bringing these quantities together in the usual relation gives the following expression:

$$NPSH_a = \frac{P_{atm} - P_v}{\rho g} - h_{lift} - h_f$$

Here, $NPSH_a$ denotes available net positive suction head, $P_{atm}$ denotes atmospheric pressure, $P_v$ denotes vapour pressure, $\rho$ denotes liquid density, $g$ denotes gravitational acceleration, $h_{lift}$ denotes static lift, and $h_f$ denotes suction-line friction loss. When the stated values are substituted into the relation, the available net positive suction head is 8 m. It is worth emphasising that this available value is not, by itself, the end of the check. The pump's required NPSH at the duty flow has to be obtained from the vendor curve, and the available NPSH must exceed that required value with margin. No numerical vendor value or numerical margin is provided in the information given here.
target:
For an open tank supplying a pump with water, available net positive suction head $NPSH_a$ is determined from atmospheric pressure $P_{atm}$, vapour pressure $P_v$, liquid density $\rho$, gravitational acceleration $g$, static lift $h_{lift}$, and suction-line friction loss $h_f$. Atmospheric pressure is 101.3 kPa and vapour pressure at the pumping temperature is 7.4 kPa; static lift is 1 m and suction-line friction loss is 0.6 m. The available net positive suction head is calculated from the pressure margin over vapour pressure, with the lift and friction terms subtracted:

$$NPSH_a = \frac{P_{atm} - P_v}{\rho g} - h_{lift} - h_f$$

In the display, $NPSH_a$ denotes available net positive suction head, $P_{atm}$ denotes atmospheric pressure, $P_v$ denotes vapour pressure, $\rho$ denotes liquid density, $g$ denotes gravitational acceleration, $h_{lift}$ denotes static lift, and $h_f$ denotes suction-line friction loss. Substitution of the stated pressures and losses gives $NPSH_a$ of 8 m. The pressure term is a difference, not the atmospheric pressure alone: a higher $P_v$ reduces the pressure margin before the lift and friction terms are applied. The two subtracted head terms have different sources. Static lift $h_{lift}$ comes from the elevation the liquid must gain before the pump, and friction loss $h_f$ comes from flow through the suction line. The result is checked against the pump's required NPSH at the duty flow. Required NPSH is obtained from the vendor curve, and $NPSH_a$ must exceed the required value with margin. The passage states the available value and the comparison rule; it does not state a vendor value or a numerical margin.

fact_base: 180 pumps run at the plant. Maintenance records for 12 months show 1297 h of unplanned downtime; bearing failures account for 52% of the downtime hours. A sensor set for all 180 pumps is quoted at $432k installed, plus $78k per year. In a vendor trial on a comparable unit, the sensors cut downtime by 20%; the figure is a vendor figure and was not measured at this plant. A pilot on 14 pumps costs $45k over three months. Spare-part lead times are unchanged by the sensors. The memo recommends the three-month pilot; the reliability engineering group owns the pilot and reports before the March capital review; the decision on full installation is held until the pilot results are reported.
input: It is recommended that a three-month pilot should be carried out on 14 pumps at a cost of $45k, with the reliability engineering group taking ownership of the pilot and reporting back before the March capital review. Importantly, the decision on full installation should be held until those pilot results have been reported and considered. The background to this recommendation is that the plant operates 180 pumps, and maintenance records covering a period of 12 months show a total of 1297 h of unplanned downtime. Of those downtime hours, bearing failures account for 52%, which suggests that a substantial share of the problem is concentrated in one failure category. Against that background, a sensor set covering all 180 pumps has been quoted at $432k installed, plus a further $78k per year. By comparison, the proposed pilot involves a much smaller initial commitment of $45k, as opposed to the full installation figure of $432k installed plus $78k per year. In a vendor trial carried out on a comparable unit, the sensors were reported to cut downtime by 20%, although it should be noted that this is a vendor figure and was not measured at this plant. It should also be noted that spare-part lead times are unchanged by the sensors. Overall, the pilot is presented as the appropriate next step before any wider commitment covering all 180 pumps is made. The pilot is limited in scope, but the question it answers is the full-installation question, and that is why its results are tied to the March capital review.

fact_base: A tutorial passage explains the pump affinity laws for a centrifugal pump at varying speed. The passage states the three proportionalities in words: flow with speed, head with speed squared, power with speed cubed. A worked check is included: doubling speed multiplies power by 8. input: In this tutorial passage, the aim is to explain the pump affinity laws, which describe how flow, head, and power respond when the speed of a centrifugal pump is varied. Broadly speaking, the passage presents three proportional relationships. First, flow is proportional to speed. Second, head is proportional to the square of speed. Third, and most dramatically, power is proportional to the cube of speed. These relationships can be thought of as a compact way of summarising what happens to the main performance variables when one operating variable, namely speed, is changed for a centrifugal pump. Flow, in this context, is the delivered volume rate, and it follows speed in direct proportion. Head behaves differently, because it is linked to speed through a squared relationship rather than a simple linear one. Power behaves differently again, because it is linked to speed through a cubed relationship, which means that its response is stronger than the responses of both flow and head. To make this clearer, the passage includes a worked check based on the power relationship. In that check, doubling the speed is shown to multiply the power by 8. The example is useful because it highlights the practical implication of the cubic relationship: even a change that is described simply as a doubling of speed corresponds to a much larger change in power. The multiplier 8 is therefore not an incidental detail; it is the numerical signature of the cubic law in the passage.
target: This tutorial explains how flow, head, and power change when the speed of a centrifugal pump changes. The outcome is stated at the start: flow is proportional to speed, head is proportional to speed squared, and power is proportional to speed cubed. A worked check is included at the close: doubling speed multiplies power by 8. The three proportionalities describe one speed change on one centrifugal pump. Flow is the delivered volume rate in the comparison. When speed changes, the affinity law for flow applies the same proportional change to flow, with no separate correction introduced in the passage. Head is treated through its own proportionality. The square in the head law means that head does not follow the flow law: the relation is stronger than direct proportion because the speed term is squared before the comparison is read. Power has the strongest of the three relations. The cube in the power law is the reason the worked check gives a large multiplier from a doubling of speed. Read together, the laws separate three questions that are often merged. A speed change asks how much flow changes, how much head changes, and how much power changes; the affinity laws answer with direct proportion for flow, a squared proportion for head, and a cubed proportion for power. The worked check uses the power law only. Doubling speed multiplies power by 8, and the check confirms the cubic form of the power relation.

fact_base: A review passage on adsorbents for gas drying, in four parts: scope, established results, disagreements, and gaps. The review covers 50 papers from the last 9 years. The disagreements part names the quantity on which reports conflict; the gaps part names the measurement nobody reports.
input:
Scope
This review brings together 50 papers from the last 9 years that deal, in one way or another, with adsorbents for gas drying. In broad terms, the subject is the removal of water vapour from a gas stream by adsorption, and the focus throughout is on the adsorbent properties that determine whether a given material can dry a gas effectively and, just as importantly, whether it can continue to do so after it has been regenerated. The papers are considered against a shared set of questions. What water uptake is reported, and at what water partial pressure and temperature was it obtained? How is the adsorbent regenerated? What level of performance is reported once regeneration has taken place? And which of the quantities in a paper are measured directly, as opposed to being inferred from a breakthrough curve or from some form of model fitting? The scope is deliberately limited to adsorbent performance for drying. It does not attempt to cover full process design, vessel sizing, or economics in any systematic way, except where those topics are used by a paper to explain an adsorbent result. Materials are therefore discussed as adsorbents rather than as items in a catalogue. A material enters the discussion through its reported uptake, its regeneration behaviour, its stability, and the conditions under which those properties were measured. This framing is important because gas drying is often decided at the dry end of the bed. A large uptake under humid conditions does not, on its own, establish the property that is needed when the gas is already dry, and a good first cycle does not, on its own, establish what will happen after repeated regeneration.

Established results
Despite differences in emphasis, the established results are broadly consistent about the structure of the problem. An adsorbent intended for gas drying has to take up water strongly at low water partial pressure, it has to release that water under regeneration conditions that a real process can plausibly supply, and it has to retain a useful level of uptake after the regeneration step has been repeated. For that reason, equilibrium uptake at low partial pressure emerges as a central property, because the last section of a drying bed is working against gas that has already been substantially dried. At the same time, mass transfer cannot be separated from capacity. A material may possess adequate equilibrium capacity and still perform poorly in an actual bed if water moves too slowly into the adsorbent during loading, or if regeneration leaves part of the bed in a state that is not fully usable in the next cycle. The literature therefore tends to treat capacity, kinetics, and regeneration as connected aspects of performance rather than as wholly independent scores. Another established point is that reported uptake is always tied to conditions. Water uptake depends on partial pressure and temperature, but it can also depend on the state of the adsorbent before the measurement begins. Activation, earlier regeneration, and sample history can all shift the value that is recorded. Comparisons between papers are consequently reliable only where the measurement basis is sufficiently similar to support them. Breakthrough results require similar caution. A breakthrough curve is a result for a bed, not a pure property of a material, because it combines equilibrium behaviour, kinetics, flow distribution, bed geometry, and the threshold chosen to define breakthrough. The review accordingly treats breakthrough evidence as evidence about an adsorbent in a specified bed, not as a direct replacement for an isotherm. Finally, regeneration is not treated as a mere after-step. Heating, purge, pressure change, and time under regeneration conditions all influence how much of the initial uptake is available in the following cycle, so a drying material has to be judged by repeatable uptake as well as by the uptake it displays when fresh.

Disagreements
The disagreements in the literature are focused on one particular quantity: reports conflict on equilibrium water uptake at low partial pressure. It is important to be clear about the nature of this disagreement. The papers do not, for the most part, disagree that low-pressure uptake is important for deep drying. What they disagree about is the value that should be assigned to that uptake for comparable materials, and therefore about the ordering that results when numbers from different papers are placed next to one another. Several recurring sources of disagreement can be identified. Some papers report uptake on a dry adsorbent basis, whereas others do not state the basis with the same degree of care. Some measurements are made after a severe regeneration step and others after a milder one, so the starting state of the adsorbent is not the same before the isotherm is measured. Equilibration time is not always reported in a form that allows the reader to judge whether the low-pressure points represent true equilibrium values or only slow approaches towards equilibrium. Data reduction introduces further variation, because a value read directly from an isotherm, a value obtained from a model fit, and a value inferred from a breakthrough experiment are not strictly interchangeable, even when similar language is used to describe them. Temperature control at low partial pressure adds another layer of difficulty, since small errors in the water content of the feed gas can become large relative errors at the dry end of the measurement. For these reasons, the review does not attempt to average the conflicting values into a single representative figure. Doing so would tend to conceal the reasons for the dispute and could create a misleading impression that the quantity had been settled. The disagreement is therefore presented as a problem of measurement basis that attaches to a clearly named quantity: equilibrium water uptake at low partial pressure is reported inconsistently across the literature, and any ranking that is built on those reports inherits that inconsistency.

Gaps
The most significant gap identified by the review is the measurement that nobody reports: retained uptake after extended regeneration cycling. Many papers report an initial uptake value, and many also report uptake after one regeneration or after only a small number of cycles. What is missing is a measurement of the uptake that remains after extended cycling under clearly stated regeneration conditions, reported on the same basis as the initial uptake. In the absence of that measurement, the literature is much better equipped to compare fresh materials than to compare materials in working use. That limitation matters because a gas-drying adsorbent is, in practice, used by cycling it repeatedly. If a review cannot say how much uptake is retained after extended regeneration cycling, then the durability aspect of adsorbent selection cannot be settled from the published record alone. Several related gaps follow from the same general reporting pattern. Regeneration conditions are frequently described only loosely, cycle histories are often incomplete, and the low-pressure portion of an isotherm is sometimes represented mainly by a fitted curve rather than by measured points. These omissions also feed back into the disagreements discussed above, because where the starting state and cycle history of a sample are not reported, a dispute about uptake cannot be attributed to the material alone with any confidence. Overall, the published record is strongest where it deals with the equilibrium behaviour of fresh adsorbents and weakest where it deals with repeated use over time. The review therefore ends not with a definitive ranking, but with a reporting requirement for future work: papers should report low-pressure uptake together with its measurement basis, and should also report retained uptake after extended regeneration cycling together with the regeneration conditions, so that capacity and durability can eventually be compared on a common evidentiary footing.

fact_base: Liquid-liquid extraction recovers acetic acid from an aqueous stream into an organic solvent. The distribution coefficient (organic over aqueous) is 2.67 at 25 °C and the design uses 8 countercurrent stages. Predicted recovery is 88% of the acetic acid in the feed. The prediction assumes equilibrium stages and negligible mutual solubility; neither has been checked on the actual solvents.
input: In this case, liquid-liquid extraction is used in order to recover acetic acid from an aqueous stream into an organic solvent. The key equilibrium parameter is the distribution coefficient, defined on an organic-over-aqueous basis, which is given as 2.67 at 25 °C. The design is based on 8 countercurrent stages, and the predicted recovery is 88% of the acetic acid present in the feed. At a general level, the distribution coefficient describes how the acetic acid divides between the two phases at equilibrium, while the countercurrent stage arrangement provides a series of contacting steps in which the phases move in opposite directions. It is important to note, however, that the recovery figure is a prediction rather than a measured result. More specifically, the prediction rests on two important assumptions: it assumes equilibrium stages, and it also assumes negligible mutual solubility between the phases. Neither of these assumptions has been checked on the actual solvents that would be used. This means that the reported recovery of 88% should be understood as the outcome of the stated model, using 8 countercurrent stages and a distribution coefficient of 2.67 at 25 °C, rather than as a verified performance figure for the real solvent system. Overall, the result is promising in model terms, but it remains subject to the two stated assumptions that have not been tested on the actual solvents.
target: Liquid-liquid extraction recovers acetic acid from an aqueous stream into an organic solvent. The distribution coefficient, stated as organic over aqueous, is 2.67 at 25 °C. The design uses 8 countercurrent stages. Predicted recovery is 88% of the acetic acid in the feed. The distribution coefficient fixes the equilibrium split used in the prediction: at equilibrium, the organic phase carries acetic acid at the stated ratio to the aqueous phase. Countercurrent staging applies that equilibrium relation stage by stage in the design model, with the two phases moving in opposite directions through the stage sequence. The recovery figure is a prediction from that model, not a measured separation on the actual solvents. The prediction assumes equilibrium stages. The prediction also assumes negligible mutual solubility. Neither assumption has been checked on the actual solvents. Those two unchecked assumptions bound the result. If a stage does not reach equilibrium, the equilibrium-stage model overstates the separation obtained from that stage; if mutual solubility is not negligible, the phase flows and compositions used in the prediction depart from the model basis. The stage count and the equilibrium relation play different roles in the prediction. The coefficient describes the equilibrium split for a contacting stage; the stage sequence describes how many times that split is applied in the design model. Reading the recovery without that separation invites a mistake: the coefficient alone does not give recovery, and the stage count alone does not give recovery either. The predicted value comes from the two together, under the assumptions named. The passage states the predicted recovery and the assumptions together: 88% is the recovery predicted for 8 countercurrent stages at a distribution coefficient of 2.67 at 25 °C, under equilibrium stages and negligible mutual solubility, with neither assumption checked on the actual solvents.

subtype: worked example with equation: Ergun pressure drop
fact_base: Gas flows through a packed bed of 1 mm particles. The void fraction $\varepsilon$ is 0.5, the superficial velocity $u$ is 0.46 m s-1 and the bed length is 4 m. The Ergun equation gives a pressure gradient of 4.3 kPa m-1, or 17 kPa over the bed. Particle diameter $d_p$ is 1 mm; gas density is 1.2 kg m-3 and viscosity is 1.8 x 10-5 Pa s.
input:
In this worked example, gas is flowing through a packed bed, and the pressure drop is estimated by means of the Ergun equation. The equation connects the pressure gradient $\Delta P / L$ with a number of bed and gas properties, including the void fraction $\varepsilon$, the particle diameter $d_p$, the superficial velocity $u$, the gas density $\rho$, and the gas viscosity $\mu$. For the case considered here, the particles have a diameter $d_p$ of 1 mm, the void fraction $\varepsilon$ is 0.5, the superficial velocity $u$ is 0.46 m s-1, and the bed length $L$ is 4 m. The gas density $\rho$ is 1.2 kg m-3, while the gas viscosity $\mu$ is 1.8 × 10-5 Pa s. The Ergun equation can be written as follows:

$$\frac{\Delta P}{L} = \frac{150 \mu (1-\varepsilon)^2}{\varepsilon^3 d_p^2} u + \frac{1.75 (1-\varepsilon)}{\varepsilon^3 d_p} \rho u^2$$

In the display, $\Delta P$ denotes pressure drop, $L$ denotes bed length, $\mu$ denotes gas viscosity, $\varepsilon$ denotes void fraction, $d_p$ denotes particle diameter, $u$ denotes superficial velocity, and $\rho$ denotes gas density. Using the stated values, the Ergun equation gives a pressure gradient of 4.3 kPa m-1, which corresponds to a total pressure drop of 17 kPa over the bed. It is worth noting that the equation contains two contributions: a viscous contribution that depends directly on $u$, and an inertial contribution that depends on $u^2$ and on the gas density. Overall, the example shows how the bed properties and gas properties are combined in the Ergun relation in order to obtain the pressure gradient and, from it, the pressure drop across the full bed length.

Gas density $\rho$ is 1.2 kg m-3 and gas viscosity $\mu$ is 1.8 × 10-5 Pa s. The Ergun equation is:

$$\frac{\Delta P}{L} = \frac{150 \mu (1-\varepsilon)^2}{\varepsilon^3 d_p^2} u + \frac{1.75 (1-\varepsilon)}{\varepsilon^3 d_p} \rho u^2$$

In the display, $\Delta P$ denotes pressure drop, $L$ denotes bed length, $\mu$ denotes gas viscosity, $\varepsilon$ denotes void fraction, $d_p$ denotes particle diameter, $u$ denotes superficial velocity, and $\rho$ denotes gas density. The first term carries the viscosity and varies directly with $u$; the second term carries the density and varies with $u^2$. No separate bed measurement is reported. The result is bounded by the stated bed and gas properties: particle diameter, void fraction, superficial velocity, density, and viscosity are inputs to the relation, and a change in any of them changes the calculated gradient. The two terms also explain why the gradient is sensitive to particle size through the bed structure as well as through the flow area available in the voids. The worked example states the calculated pressure gradient and the corresponding pressure drop over the bed for the stated gas and bed.

fact_base: A tutorial passage explains the pump affinity laws for a centrifugal pump at varying speed. The passage states the three proportionalities in words: flow with speed, head with speed squared, power with speed cubed. A worked check is included: doubling speed multiplies power by 8. No other numbers are introduced.
input: This explainer is concerned with the pump affinity laws, which are used to describe what happens to flow, head, and power when the speed of a centrifugal pump is changed. The central message is that the three quantities do not all respond in the same way. Flow is proportional to speed, head is proportional to speed squared, and power is proportional to speed cubed. In other words, each quantity has its own relationship with speed, and those relationships become progressively stronger as one moves from flow, through head, to power. Flow is the most straightforward case, because it simply follows speed in direct proportion. Head is somewhat less straightforward, because it depends on the square of the speed, which means that it responds more strongly than flow when the speed is altered. Power is the most sensitive of the three, because it depends on the cube of the speed, which means that it responds more strongly still. This point is illustrated by the worked check that is included in the passage. When the speed is doubled, the power is multiplied by 8. That result can seem surprising at first, but it follows directly from the cubic relationship between power and speed. More generally, the affinity laws provide a useful way of thinking about speed changes in centrifugal pumps, because they show that a single change in speed does not produce a single common change across all performance variables. Instead, flow, head, and power each follow the particular proportionality that applies to them, and the worked check on power is included to make the strength of the cubic relationship especially clear. The value 8 is the check's result, and it belongs to power rather than to flow or head.
target: Speed is the variable in this explainer, and the outcome is stated before the detail. For a centrifugal pump at varying speed, flow follows speed in direct proportion, head follows the square of speed, and power follows the cube of speed. The worked check is plain: doubling speed multiplies power by 8. Each law is read as a comparison between operating points of the pump at different speeds. The flow law is the simplest of the three. A proportional rise in speed gives the same proportional rise in flow, and a proportional fall in speed gives the same proportional fall in flow; the law is a statement of proportion, not a statement that flow is fixed by speed under every condition outside the comparison. The head law is stronger. Because head follows speed squared, the head comparison turns on the square of the speed change, so head moves by a larger proportion than flow for the same change in speed. The power law is stronger again. Because power follows speed cubed, the power comparison turns on the cube of the speed change. That cubic dependence is the point of the worked check. Doubling is a single change in speed, stated in words; applying the cube gives the stated power multiplier. The three laws should not be interchanged. Flow, head, and power are different quantities, and the affinity laws assign a different speed dependence to each: direct proportion for flow, the square for head, and the cube for power. A reader who applies the flow proportion to power understates the power change, and a reader who applies the power proportion to flow overstates the flow change. The explainer closes on the worked check because the check separates the laws in one case: doubling speed multiplies power by 8, while the flow and head changes are read from their own proportionalities, not from the power result.
