The saving figure is a vendor projection and was not measured at this plant; refrigeration load in the summer peak month was not modelled. The recommendation is a metered trial on one of the three refrigeration lines before any capital decision. The plant engineer owns the trial.
input: It is recommended that the capital decision should be held at this stage and that a metered trial should instead be run on one of the three refrigeration lines, with the plant engineer taking ownership of the trial. The background is that a food plant currently uses 2167 MWh of electricity per year in refrigeration. A heat-recovery retrofit has been proposed, and the equipment vendor projects that it would save 14% of that annual use. This corresponds to a derived saving of 303 MWh per year at the vendor figure. The capital cost of the retrofit is $491k. Using an electricity price of $0.11 per kWh, the derived annual saving is $33k, and the derived simple payback is 14.9 years. The derived figures are 303 MWh per year, $33k per year, and a payback of 14.9 years on the stated capital cost. In simple terms, the trade-off can be summarised as $491k of capital set against $33k of derived annual saving. It is important to note, however, that the saving is a vendor projection and has not been measured at this plant. A further limitation is that refrigeration load in the summer peak month was not modelled, so the annual figures should not be taken as a complete picture of performance under peak conditions. Overall, a metered trial on one line is presented as a prudent intermediate step, because it would provide measured evidence from the plant itself before any final capital commitment is made.
target: Hold the capital decision and run a metered trial on one of the three refrigeration lines. The plant engineer owns the trial. A food plant uses 2167 MWh of electricity per year in refrigeration, and that annual use is the evidence base for the figures that follow. A heat-recovery retrofit is projected by the equipment vendor to save 14% of that use, a derived saving of 303 MWh per year at the vendor figure. Capital cost is $491k. At an electricity price of $0.11 per kWh, the derived annual saving is $33k and the derived simple payback is 14.9 years. The trade-off is $491k of capital against $33k of derived annual saving, with the saving projected by the vendor and not measured at this plant. The derived labels matter. The 303 MWh saving is derived from the vendor percentage applied to the stated annual use; the $33k annual saving is derived from the electricity price; and the 14.9-year payback is derived from the capital cost and the annual saving. Refrigeration load in the summer peak month was not modelled. The annual figures therefore do not settle the retrofit's value in the peak month, and the passage makes no peak-month claim. The other figures are arithmetic on stated values: a percentage applied to annual use, a price applied to saved energy, and a payback formed from cost and saving. fact_base: Excerpt content: two groups report conflicting lifetime values for the same material class; the excerpt weighs their test conditions. The excerpt reaches a limited preference and states the condition on which it rests.
input: The lifetime values reported for the benchmark material by the two groups do not agree with one another, and the disagreement is considerably larger than the uncertainty either group attaches to its own results, which strongly suggests that the difference cannot simply be attributed to ordinary measurement scatter. The first group aged specimens in a flowing gas stream, with lifetime defined as the time to reach a predetermined loss of capacity. The second group aged specimens in static vessels, and although the same endpoint was adopted, it was reached later in every test. The test conditions differ in several respects that may be relevant: the flowing configuration continually sweeps degradation products away from the specimen surface, whereas the static configuration allows them to accumulate; the specimen geometries, and therefore the diffusion paths, are different; and the humidity of the ageing gas was carefully controlled in one programme and left uncontrolled in the other. Both groups made use of IAST in converting their mixture data, so it seems unlikely that the conversion is responsible for the discrepancy. On balance, the flowing-gas values would appear to be the more suitable basis for design, given that the intended duty involves a flowing stream; however, this preference is conditional on the degradation products being volatile enough to leave the surface under flow, and it would cease to apply where the stream is stagnant or where the products condense.
target: Lifetime values for the benchmark material differ between the two groups by more than the uncertainty either group states, and the difference is too regular to be measurement scatter. One group aged specimens in a flowing gas stream and took lifetime as the time to a fixed loss of capacity. The other group aged specimens in static vessels and reached the same loss later in every test. The conditions differ in three respects that bear on the comparison. Flow removes degradation products from the surface, and the static tests retain them. Specimen form sets the diffusion path, and the two forms are not alike. Humidity of the ageing gas was controlled by one group and left uncontrolled by the other. Both groups used IAST to convert mixture data, and the conversion does not account for the disagreement. The flowing-gas values are preferred for design, because the intended duty is a flowing stream and its surface is swept clean in the same way. The preference rests on one condition: the degradation products must be volatile enough to leave the surface under flow. Where the stream is stagnant, or the products condense on the surface, the preference lapses and the static values govern.

fact_base: Inventory policy for a spare motor: mean demand 526 units per week, standard deviation 129 units per week, replenishment lead time 8 weeks. Safety stock for a 95% cycle service level is 602 units. Demand is treated as normal and independent between weeks; seasonal peaks are excluded.
input: The inventory policy adopted for the spare motor provides for a safety stock of 602 units, a level that has been set so as to deliver a 95% cycle service level across the full replenishment lead time. The underlying demand pattern is characterised by a mean demand of 526 units per week, with a standard deviation of weekly demand amounting to 129 units, and the replenishment lead time is 8 weeks. For the purposes of the calculation, weekly demand is treated as following a normal distribution, and demand arising in any given week is treated as statistically independent of the demand arising in any other week. It should be emphasised that the safety stock exists to absorb the variability that accumulates over the lead time, rather than the average demand itself, which is covered by the replenishment quantity. It is also important to note that seasonal peaks have been excluded from the demand history on which the calculation is based, so the 602 units cannot be relied upon to sustain the service level through a lead time falling in a peak season. The buffer will be maintained at this level for as long as the demand record and the lead time remain unchanged; should either the lead time lengthen or the spread of weekly demand widen, the required stock will be recalculated accordingly.
target: Safety stock for the spare motor is 602 units, which gives a 95% cycle service level over the replenishment lead time. Mean demand is 526 units per week, and the standard deviation of weekly demand is 129 units. The replenishment lead time is 8 weeks. Weekly demand is treated as normal, and demand in one week is treated as independent of demand in any other week. The stock covers the variation in demand that accumulates over the lead time under that pattern; it is not sized for the average demand itself, which the replenishment quantity covers. Seasonal peaks are excluded from the demand record behind the calculation. The 602 units therefore do not cover a lead time that falls in a peak season, and a policy that must hold service through the peaks needs a separate seasonal allowance. The buffer is held at the stated level while the demand record and the lead time stand. A longer lead time, or a wider spread in weekly demand, raises the stock that the same service level requires, and the figure is recalculated when either changes. Stock drawn below the safety level is cover consumed by variation, and it is restored by the next replenishment rather than treated as available for planned issues.

fact_base: A continuous stirred-tank reactor runs a neutralisation that is first order in the limiting reactant. The rate constant is 0.041 min-1 at the operating temperature and the mean residence time is 23 min. Steady-state conversion for an ideal CSTR is 48.5%. The estimate assumes perfect mixing and constant density; tracer tests on the actual vessel have not been run.
input: In this example, consideration is given to a continuous stirred-tank reactor in which a neutralisation reaction is carried out, the reaction being first order with respect to the limiting reactant. The rate constant at the operating temperature has a value of 0.041 min-1, and the mean residence time within the vessel is 23 min. When the standard ideal-CSTR design relation is applied at steady state, the conversion of the limiting reactant is obtained as 48.5%. The result follows from a steady-state material balance written over the limiting reactant: under steady conditions, the amount of reactant entering with the feed must be accounted for by the amount leaving with the product stream together with the amount consumed by reaction throughout the vessel volume. Since the ideal vessel is assumed to be perfectly mixed, the concentration at every point in the vessel is identical to the outlet concentration, so the reaction rate throughout the volume is governed by that single concentration. It follows that the conversion is determined by the balance between the rate constant and the residence time, increasing steadily as the residence time is extended and approaching complete conversion in the limit; at a residence time of 23 min, the stated rate constant leads to the conversion quoted above. By way of comparison, a plug-flow vessel of the same volume would be expected to achieve a somewhat higher conversion, because the concentration declines progressively along the flow path. It should be noted that the estimate rests on two underlying assumptions, namely perfect mixing and constant density, the latter ensuring that the residence time can be treated as a fixed ratio of volume to volumetric flow rate. No tracer tests have yet been carried out on the actual vessel, so its residence-time distribution remains uncharacterised; phenomena such as dead volume or bypassing, if they occur, would tend to depress the conversion actually achieved below 48.5%.
target: A continuous stirred-tank reactor (CSTR) runs a neutralisation that is first order in the limiting reactant. The rate constant is 0.041 min-1 at the operating temperature, and the mean residence time is 23 min. The steady-state conversion of the limiting reactant is 48.5% for an ideal CSTR. The conversion comes from the steady-state balance on the limiting reactant. At steady state, the reactant that enters with the feed is balanced by the reactant that leaves with the product and the reactant consumed by reaction in the vessel volume. Because an ideal CSTR is perfectly mixed, the concentration everywhere in the vessel is the outlet concentration, and the reaction rate in the whole volume is set by that concentration. The conversion therefore depends on the product of the rate constant and the residence time measured against that product plus one: as the residence time grows, the conversion rises towards complete conversion, and at 23 min the stated rate gives the stated figure. A plug-flow vessel of equal volume would give a higher conversion for the same feed, because its concentration falls along the flow path and the rate is higher over most of the volume. The estimate assumes perfect mixing and constant density. Constant density makes the residence time a fixed ratio of vessel volume to volumetric flow, and perfect mixing is the assumption that sets the rate. Tracer tests on the actual vessel have not been run. The residence-time distribution of the actual vessel is therefore unmeasured: dead volume would shorten the effective residence time, and bypassing would pass part of the feed through almost unreacted. Either fault would bring the actual conversion below 48.5%. The figure is the conversion of the ideal vessel at the stated conditions, and its application to the actual vessel rests on mixing behaviour that has not been verified.

fact_base: Liquid-liquid extraction recovers acetic acid from an aqueous stream into an organic solvent. The distribution coefficient (organic over aqueous) is 1.71 at 25 °C and the design uses 4 countercurrent stages. Predicted recovery is 95% of the acetic acid in the feed. The prediction assumes equilibrium stages and negligible mutual solubility; neither has been checked on the actual solvents.
input: In the process under consideration, liquid-liquid extraction is employed to recover acetic acid from an aqueous stream by transferring it into an organic solvent. The distribution coefficient of the acetic acid, defined as the ratio of its concentration in the organic phase to its concentration in the aqueous phase, is 1.71 at 25 °C, and the design is based on 4 countercurrent stages. On this basis, the predicted recovery is 95% of the acetic acid present in the feed. Because the distribution coefficient is greater than unity, the solvent is favoured as the receiving phase, and the countercurrent arrangement ensures that the freshest solvent comes into contact with the most thoroughly depleted raffinate, so that a useful driving force is maintained throughout the cascade rather than being exhausted at the feed end. Each successive stage recovers a further portion of the acid remaining in the aqueous phase, and the combined effect of the stages is to reduce the acid content of the raffinate to the stated residual fraction. The prediction is, however, subject to two significant assumptions. In the first place, the stages are assumed to be equilibrium stages, meaning that the two phases leaving any stage are taken to be in full equilibrium with one another at the stated distribution coefficient. In the second place, mutual solubility between the phases is assumed to be negligible, so that the flow rate of each phase can be treated as constant from stage to stage. Neither of these assumptions has yet been verified for the actual solvents concerned. If the stage efficiency falls short of the equilibrium ideal, or if appreciable mutual solubility occurs, the recovery actually achieved would be expected to fall below 95%, and experimental confirmation on the real solvent system would be required before the figure could be relied upon.
target: Liquid-liquid extraction recovers acetic acid from an aqueous feed into an organic solvent. The distribution coefficient of acetic acid, taken as the concentration in the organic phase over the concentration in the aqueous phase, is 1.71 at 25 °C. The design uses 4 countercurrent stages. The predicted recovery is 95% of the acetic acid in the feed. A distribution coefficient above unity favours the solvent, and countercurrent contact lets the leanest solvent meet the most depleted raffinate, so the driving force is held along the whole cascade rather than spent at the feed end. Each added stage recovers part of what the earlier stages left, and the stages together bring the raffinate down to the stated fraction of the feed content. The extract leaves loaded with the recovered acid, and the raffinate leaves carrying the fraction the cascade did not take. The solvent rate is the remaining design handle, and it is set high enough that the aqueous phase is nowhere close to saturation against the solvent it meets at any stage, which keeps the stated coefficient in force along the whole cascade rather than only at the feed end where the concentrations are highest. The prediction assumes equilibrium stages: the two phases leaving each stage are taken to be in equilibrium with each other, at the distribution coefficient stated. The prediction also assumes negligible mutual solubility, so the flow of each phase is treated as unchanged from stage to stage and the solvent is treated as free of feed components other than the transferred acid. Neither assumption has been checked on the actual solvents. Stage efficiency below the equilibrium value would lower the recovery at the stated stage count, and mutual solubility would change both phase flows and the effective distribution. The 95% is therefore the recovery of the ideal cascade on the actual feed only if the two assumptions hold closely enough on the solvents in use; a test on the actual solvents settles both points and has not been reported.

fact_base: Goal: compute the diffusive flux of oxygen through a stagnant water film. The diffusive flux J (mol m-2 s-1) is computed from the diffusivity D (m2 s-1) and the concentration gradient dC/dx, where C is concentration (mol m-3) and x is position (m). Fick's first law: J = -D dC/dx; the negative sign states that diffusion runs from high concentration to low concentration. Oxygen in water: D = 2.6 x 10-9 m2 s-1. Concentration falls by 0.25 mol m-3 across a film 0.4 mm thick, so dC/dx = -625 mol m-4. Worked result: J = 1.63x 10-6 mol m-2 s-1. The law as stated covers a stagnant medium; a moving medium adds convection, which the equation does not include.
input: The objective of this worked example is to determine the diffusive flux of oxygen passing through a stagnant film of water. The relevant relation is Fick's first law, $J = -D dC/dx$, in which $J$ denotes the diffusive flux (mol m-2 s-1), $D$ denotes the diffusivity (m2 s-1), $C$ denotes the concentration (mol m-3) and $x$ denotes the position (m) measured across the film. It is worth drawing attention to the negative sign appearing in the law, which expresses the fact that diffusion takes place in the direction running from a region of high concentration towards a region of low concentration. For the particular case of oxygen dissolved in water, the diffusivity $D$ has the value 2.6 x 10-9 m2 s-1. Across a film having a thickness of 0.4 mm, the concentration is found to fall by 0.25 mol m-3, from which it follows that the concentration gradient $dC/dx$ amounts to -625 mol m-4. Substituting the diffusivity and the gradient into Fick's first law, the diffusive flux $J$ is obtained as 1.63 x 10-6 mol m-2 s-1. The negative gradient and the negative sign in the law combine to give a positive flux in the direction of decreasing concentration, exactly as the physical picture requires. It should nevertheless be borne in mind that the form of Fick's first law employed here is applicable to a stagnant medium only; where the medium is in motion, convective transport is superimposed on the diffusive transport, and that contribution is not accounted for by the equation in the form used above.
target: Calculate the diffusive flux of oxygen through a stagnant water film. Fick's first law gives the diffusive flux $J$ from the diffusivity $D$ and the concentration gradient $dC/dx$: $J = -D dC/dx$, where $J$ denotes the diffusive flux (mol m-2 s-1), $D$ denotes the diffusivity (m2 s-1), $C$ denotes the concentration (mol m-3) and $x$ denotes the position (m). Note that the negative sign in Fick's first law states that diffusion runs from high concentration to low concentration. For oxygen in water, $D$ is 2.6 x 10-9 m2 s-1. The concentration falls by 0.25 mol m-3 across a film 0.4 mm thick. Thus the concentration gradient $dC/dx$ is -625 mol m-4. Substitution of the diffusivity and the gradient in Fick's first law gives a diffusive flux $J$ of 1.63 x 10-6 mol m-2 s-1. The sign works out as stated: the gradient is negative in the direction of falling concentration, and the flux comes out positive in that same direction. The magnitude is set by the gradient across a very thin film; the same concentration difference spread over a thicker film would give a smaller gradient and a correspondingly smaller flux. The film is treated as a plane layer of uniform thickness, and the concentration profile across it is taken as a straight line, which is the profile the stated gradient describes. The calculation is then a single substitution once the gradient has been formed from the concentration fall and the film thickness. Fick's first law as stated holds for a stagnant medium. A moving medium adds convection to the transport, and the equation does not include the convective part.

fact_base: A tutorial passage explains the Prandtl number to second-year students. Definition in words: the Prandtl number is the ratio of momentum diffusivity to thermal diffusivity. The passage must state what a value near 1 means and what a large value means, without inventing numerical examples.
input: The Prandtl number is defined as the ratio of momentum diffusivity to thermal diffusivity. Momentum diffusivity states how rapidly velocity differences are smoothed out within a fluid. Thermal diffusivity states how rapidly temperature differences are smoothed out within the same fluid. The Prandtl number sets the two rates side by side, and it is a property of the fluid and its state, not of the flow around it: the flow geometry decides how thick the boundary layers grow, and the Prandtl number decides how the two thicknesses compare once they have grown. Where a fluid flows over a surface, a velocity boundary layer and a thermal boundary layer form together. The velocity boundary layer is the region in which the velocity rises from its surface value to the free-stream value. The thermal boundary layer is the corresponding region for temperature. A Prandtl number near 1 means the two diffusivities are nearly equal. Velocity and temperature then adjust over comparable distances from the surface, and the two boundary layers are of similar thickness. A large Prandtl number means momentum diffusivity is much larger than thermal diffusivity. Momentum spreads readily through the fluid, while heat spreads slowly by comparison, so the temperature change between the surface and the free stream is compressed into a thin layer next to the surface, and the thermal boundary layer is much thinner than the velocity boundary layer. The comparison is used wherever a heat transfer coefficient is built up from the flow field, because it states where the resistance to heat transfer sits: in a thin layer that the velocity field has already crossed many times over, or in a layer that fills the whole region in which the velocity is still adjusting.

fact_base: Excerpt content: a strainer cleaning takes about 63 min with the unit isolated; the excerpt gives the isolation steps only. The excerpt warns once about stored pressure and does not repeat the warning.
input: The cleaning of a strainer occupies about 63 min when the unit has been isolated, and the procedure set out below is concerned exclusively with the steps by which that isolation is achieved before the housing is opened. In the first instance, the duty is transferred to the standby pump, and it is confirmed that the standby pump is running satisfactorily and carrying the full flow. The duty pump is then stopped, its discharge valve is closed, and the pump is secured against inadvertent restarting by the application of the lock and tag under the PTW arrangements. Attention is next turned to the strainer itself: the suction isolation valve and the discharge isolation valve are both closed, so that the housing is positively cut off from the line on either side of it, it being appreciated that isolation on one side alone would leave the housing connected to the plant through the other. The housing vent is opened to the closed drain and the contents are drained away until the flow ceases. It must be understood that stored pressure may remain trapped within the housing notwithstanding the closure of both isolation valves, and the vent indication is relied upon as the evidence that this pressure has been released; a housing that continues to register pressure is to be regarded as not isolated. After an interval, the vent is checked a second time, since a renewed build-up of pressure would indicate a passing valve and require the isolation to be remade. Where a spade is called for, it is fitted at the flange and entered on the isolation register, after which the isolation is complete.
target: A strainer cleaning takes about 63 min with the unit isolated, and the steps that follow isolate the strainer before the housing is opened. Transfer the duty to the standby pump and confirm that the standby pump is running and carrying the flow. Stop the duty pump, close its discharge valve, and prove the pump against restart by applying the lock and tag under the PTW. Close the suction isolation valve and the discharge isolation valve at the strainer, so that the housing is cut off from the line on both sides. A strainer isolated on one side only is still connected to the plant through the other side, and the pair of valves is what makes the isolation. Open the housing vent to the closed drain and drain the contents until the flow stops. Stored pressure can remain trapped in the housing after both lines are isolated, and the vent reading is the proof that the pressure has been released; a housing that still shows pressure is not isolated, whatever the valve positions say. Leave the housing vented for a pause, then check the vent again: pressure that builds up again in the interval points to a passing isolation valve, and the isolation is remade before any further step. Where the line specification calls for a spade, fit the spade at the strainer flange and record it on the isolation register. The isolation is complete when the duty pump is locked out, both isolation valves are closed and tagged, the housing is drained, and the vent has twice shown no pressure.

fact_base: A binary distillation separates ethanol/water at a relative volatility of 1.53 that is taken as constant over the column. Specifications: distillate 98 mol% light component, bottoms 2 mol% light component. The Fenske minimum stage count is 18.3 theoretical stages including the reboiler. The actual design uses a reflux ratio of 1.3 times the minimum; the stage count at that reflux comes from a separate simulation.
input: The separation under consideration is a binary distillation of ethanol and water, for which the relative volatility has a value of 1.53 and is taken, for the purposes of the calculation, to remain constant throughout the column. The product specifications call for a distillate containing 98 mol% of the light component and bottoms containing 2 mol% of the light component. Application of the Fenske relation yields a minimum stage count of 18.3 theoretical stages, the reboiler being included in the count. It should be appreciated that the Fenske figure corresponds to operation at total reflux, under which no product is withdrawn and the entire internal traffic is available for the separation; the figure accordingly represents a lower bound on the number of stages that any real column will require in order to achieve the specified split, since a column operated at a finite reflux ratio will invariably need additional stages. The assumption of constant relative volatility is what permits the minimum count to be evaluated directly from the end compositions and the volatility. In the actual design, a reflux ratio of 1.3 times the minimum value has been adopted. The number of stages required at this operating reflux cannot be obtained from the Fenske relation itself, which furnishes the count only in the total-reflux limit, and it has instead been obtained from a separate simulation of the column.
target: A binary distillation separates ethanol and water at a relative volatility of 1.53, taken as constant over the column. The specifications are a distillate of 98 mol% light component and bottoms of 2 mol% light component. The Fenske minimum stage count is 18.3 theoretical stages, including the reboiler. The Fenske count is the stage count at total reflux, where no product is withdrawn and the whole separation is driven by the internal traffic. It is a lower bound on the stages that any operating column needs for the stated split. A column run at finite reflux needs more stages than the minimum, because part of the traffic that total reflux spends on separation is withdrawn as product. The constant relative volatility is the assumption that lets the count be computed from the two end compositions and the volatility alone. The actual design uses a reflux ratio of 1.3 times the minimum. At that reflux the stage count comes from a separate simulation, not from the Fenske relation: the relation gives the count only at total reflux, and the minimum reflux only at an infinite count, so neither operating quantity follows from it. The two design quantities are therefore fixed by different routes. The minimum count also disciplines the simulation: a simulated stage count below the Fenske minimum for the same split would contradict the total-reflux bound and would point to an error in the simulation rather than to a discovery about the column.

fact_base: Excerpt content: a staffing gap of 3 weeks is reported with its cause; the excerpt proposes one mitigation and its owner. The excerpt does not open or close the memo and does not restate its subject line.
input: Attention is drawn to the fact that the staffing gap affecting the checking programme has now reached 3 weeks. The gap arose as a consequence of the departure, at short notice, of the contract checker who had been engaged for the package, coupled with the circumstance that the clearance of the replacement had still not been completed at the point when the work was due to recommence. As a result, the affected packages are being held in sequence rather than being issued without a check, and the slippage is confined to the checking stage itself; the downstream procurement and construction dates remain unchanged at the present time, and no other stage is experiencing a shortage of staff. Responsibility for recovery rests with the project board, under whose direction the outstanding checking load is being redistributed across the home-office teams, with the board reviewing the recovered position at each of its regular meetings until such time as the programme has been restored to the planned dates. The redistribution entails no additional cost beyond the hours that have already been authorised, and the issue standard is in no way diluted: no package will be issued without the full check having been carried out and recorded as usual.
target: The staffing gap now stands at 3 weeks on the checking programme. The gap opened when the contract checker engaged for the package left at short notice and the replacement's clearance had still not completed when the work was due to restart. The affected packages are being held in sequence rather than issued unchecked, and the slippage falls on the checking stage alone; the procurement and construction dates downstream of the check are unchanged at this point, and no other stage is short of staff. Recovery is assigned to the project board: the outstanding checking load is redistributed across the home-office teams, and the board reviews the recovered position at each of its regular meetings until the programme is back on the planned dates. The redistribution adds no cost beyond the hours already authorised, and it does not change the issue standard. No package leaves without the full check, the record of the check is filed with the package as before, and the gap is closed by spreading the work rather than by shortening the check on any package, wherever that package sits in the queue.

fact_base: Liquid-liquid extraction recovers acetic acid from an aqueous stream into an organic solvent. The distribution coefficient (organic over aqueous) is 1.83 at 25 °C and the design uses 7 countercurrent stages. Predicted recovery is 94% of the acetic acid in the feed. The prediction assumes equilibrium stages and negligible mutual solubility; neither has been checked on the actual solvents.
input: In this process, liquid-liquid extraction is used to recover acetic acid from an aqueous stream by transferring it into an organic solvent. The distribution coefficient of the acetic acid, expressed as the ratio of the concentration in the organic phase to that in the aqueous phase, is 1.83 at 25 °C, and the design provides for 7 countercurrent stages. The predicted recovery amounts to 94% of the acetic acid contained in the feed. The benefit of the countercurrent arrangement is that the aqueous phase, as it becomes progressively depleted in acid while passing through the cascade, is ultimately brought into contact with fresh solvent that retains a full capacity to take up acid even at the low concentrations involved, so that the driving force for transfer is maintained along the length of the cascade. The seven stages divide the overall separation into a series of steps, each of which brings the phases part of the way towards the final result at the stated distribution coefficient. Two assumptions underlie the prediction and should be clearly recognised. The stages are assumed to be equilibrium stages, so that the phases leaving each stage are taken to have reached equilibrium with one another. Mutual solubility between the two phases is also assumed to be negligible, so that neither phase flow is significantly altered by dissolution of the other phase. Neither assumption has been checked against the actual solvents to be used. Should the stages fall short of equilibrium, or should mutual solubility prove appreciable, the recovery achieved in practice would be lower than 94%, and confirmation by experiment on the real solvents would be needed.
target: Liquid-liquid extraction recovers acetic acid from an aqueous feed into an organic solvent. The distribution coefficient of acetic acid, taken as the concentration in the organic phase over the concentration in the aqueous phase, is 1.83 at 25 °C. The design uses 7 countercurrent stages. The predicted recovery is 94% of the acetic acid in the feed. The cascade works against the fall in driving force that a single contact would suffer: the aqueous phase gives up acid as it passes along the stages, and countercurrent flow brings it at the end against fresh solvent, which can still take up acid at the low concentration the raffinate has reached. Seven stages divide the separation into steps small enough that the stated recovery is reached at the stated distribution coefficient. The solvent leaves the cascade loaded with the recovered acid and is separated from it before reuse, and the raffinate leaves with the acid the cascade did not take. The solvent rate is the remaining design handle: it is set so that the aqueous phase is nowhere close to saturation against the solvent it meets, which keeps the coefficient the design uses valid along the whole cascade. The prediction assumes equilibrium stages: the two phases leaving each stage are taken to be in equilibrium with each other. The prediction also assumes negligible mutual solubility, so neither phase flow is changed by the other dissolving in it, and the solvent enters each stage carrying nothing but what the contact itself transfers. Neither assumption has been checked on the actual solvents. A stage that falls short of equilibrium delivers less transfer than the prediction credits to it, and mutual solubility alters both phase flows and the concentrations on which the coefficient is based. The 94% is therefore the prediction for the ideal cascade, and the recovery on the actual solvents stands or falls with the two assumptions it rests on.

fact_base: A defect-reduction project on a filling line cut the reject rate from 3.1% to 1.6% over one quarter. At 195k units per year the change avoids about 2925 rejected units per year. The quarter included a planned shutdown; rates are not adjusted for it.
input: A defect-reduction project carried out on a filling line succeeded in cutting the reject rate from 3.1% to 1.6% over the course of one quarter. When the improvement is applied to the line's throughput of 195k units per year, it is found that the reduction avoids approximately 2925 rejected units per year. Each avoided reject represents a filled unit that passes inspection in the normal way rather than being diverted to rework or scrap, and it is important that the reject rate has been measured on an identical inspection basis both before and after the change, so that the comparison is a valid one. fact_base: Excerpt content: the analogy between the transfer processes is stated, then qualified by the case where it fails. The excerpt works one short numerical check with numbers given inside the excerpt itself. The excerpt assumes the chapter's earlier definitions and adds none.
input: The analogy between the transfer processes may be stated, in the form employed by the Chilton-Colburn analogy, as follows: provided the resistance at a surface is of the same character for momentum transfer as it is for mass transfer, the behaviour of the one process is tied to the behaviour of the other, the relationship being expressed by $j_D$ = $f$/2 under those conditions in which the friction is generated within the same surface layer in which the transfer itself takes place. A brief numerical check shows the content of the statement. Taking $f$ = 0.0064, the analogy yields $j_D$ = 0.0032, exactly one half of the friction value; any measured transfer rate departing from this figure departs from the analogy rather than from the arithmetic. The analogy is, however, subject to an important qualification, which follows from the origin of the friction. Skin friction is generated in the layer immediately adjacent to the surface, and since transfer across that layer is governed by the same layer, the connection between the two factors rests on a physical basis. By contrast, where the drag takes the form of form drag, as in flow across a tube bank, the measured friction incorporates a pressure force acting on the body as a whole, for which there is no counterpart in the transfer process, and the analogy no longer holds.

A short check shows what the statement amounts to in numbers. For $f$ = 0.0064, the analogy gives $j_D$ = 0.0032, exactly half the friction value, and a measured transfer rate that departs from the figure departs from the analogy rather than from the arithmetic. The qualification follows from where the friction comes from. Skin friction is generated in the layer at the surface, and transfer across that layer is governed by the same layer, so the tie between the factors has a physical basis. Where the drag on the surface is form drag, as in flow across a tube bank, the measured friction collects a pressure force exerted on the body as a whole. That force has no counterpart in the transfer process, the two factors separate, and the analogy fails.

fact_base: Project proposal for a rooftop solar installation, in four sections: case, costs, schedule, and decision requested. Capital cost is $1673k with a 15-year appraisal horizon. The schedule section gives a start one quarter after approval; no contractor is named. The decision requested is approval to proceed to detailed design, not to construction.
input:
This proposal sets out an exciting opportunity to install a rooftop solar array, a project that would allow the site to generate its own clean electricity, reduce its exposure to energy prices, and take a meaningful step on its wider sustainability journey. The headline figures are a capital cost of $1673k, appraised over a 15-year horizon, and the ask at this stage is approval to proceed to detailed design, so that the project can move forward with confidence while the remaining questions are worked through in a structured way.

Case
The roof is currently unused, and the site buys all of its electricity for daytime operation. A rooftop array generates during the hours when the site load is present, so the case rests primarily on self-consumption: generated energy displaces purchased energy at the point of use, and no export income is assumed in the appraisal, which keeps the case prudent. Export is treated as incidental, because export prices are set outside the project, and a case built on them would rest on a term the project does not control. The roof is the one surface on the site that can hold generation without taking land from operations, parking, or storage, and generation on the roof avoids the cable runs and ground works of a ground-mounted array on a site with no spare ground, making it a natural fit overall.
It is worth noting that the condition of the roof covering and the load capacity of the structure are not yet fully established at proposal stage, and the case is written on the basis that detailed design confirms both before any installation is committed. A roof that needs early replacement would change the sequence, because panels fixed over a covering near the end of its life would be lifted and refitted at the first re-roofing; the survey at detailed design will state the remaining life of the covering and the installation will be planned against it. Access for installation and for later maintenance is also part of the case: a system that cannot be reached safely for cleaning, inspection, and repair will lose output over its life, and the access route is designed with the array rather than after it, ensuring that the installation remains maintainable throughout its life.

Generation and load fall in the same hours on most days the site operates, and this match is, in many ways, the load-bearing assumption behind the whole case. A site whose load peaked outside daylight hours would export most of what the array generates, and the same installation would return a quite different result on the same capital. The daytime pattern at this site is measured rather than assumed, and detailed design will test the layout against the metered profile, including the low-load days when generation can exceed the load and the surplus passes to export at the incidental value the appraisal allows it.

Costs
The capital cost is $1673k. This figure covers the modules, the inverters, the mounting system, cabling and switchgear, metering, access and scaffolding for the installation works, and the design and approval costs of the stages that follow this decision. No contractor is named at this stage, and the figure is a proposal-stage estimate built from the surveyed roof area and current supply prices; detailed design will replace it with priced items against a fixed layout, and the construction decision will be taken on the detailed figure, not on this one. The appraisal horizon is the period over which the installation is expected to generate without major component replacement beyond the inverter reserve carried in operating costs.
Operating costs are the costs of keeping the array in service: periodic cleaning where soiling is found to reduce output, inspection of fixings and cabling, monitoring of generation against expectation, and a reserve for inverter replacement within the horizon. Generation displaces purchases, and the saving in any year is the displaced energy valued at the tariff the site would otherwise pay; the appraisal states the saving on that basis and does not capitalise export. The result is sensitive to two terms that detailed design can narrow but not entirely remove: the share of generation the site consumes as it is generated, and the tariff path over the horizon. A lower self-consumption share sends more energy to export at a lower value, and the appraisal is therefore stated on the consumption pattern measured at the site rather than on a generic profile, which gives a more robust basis for the decision.

It should also be noted that the estimate is a proposal-stage figure and is labelled as such wherever it is used. Prices for modules and inverters move between proposal and procurement, and the construction proposal will restate the capital on the prices then current rather than defending this figure. Work the survey may bring forward — renewal of the roof covering, strengthening of the structure — is not inside the capital figure: if detailed design finds such work necessary, it will be priced and reported as enabling work with its own justification, because a roof renewal serves the building whether or not the array proceeds.

Schedule
Work starts one quarter after approval. The first stage is detailed design: the structural survey, the roof condition survey, the electrical design, and the layout are completed and the grid connection application is submitted on the designed capacity. Procurement follows design freeze, because module and inverter selection fixes the mounting design and the cable routes; ordering before freeze would buy equipment against a layout that may still change, creating avoidable risk. Installation is phased so that roof sections are taken in turn and the site stays in operation, with each phase closed, tested, and connected before the next begins. Commissioning covers protection settings, metering, and monitoring, and handover includes the operating instructions, the maintenance schedule, and the as-built records, ensuring a smooth transition into operation.
The schedule risk sits in two places. The grid connection terms can set conditions that change the electrical design, and a late answer would extend the design stage. Weather governs roof work, and the installation phases carry float for lost days rather than a compressed programme that assumes continuous access. Neither risk is priced as a contingency line in the capital figure; both will be reported at the construction decision with the design-stage findings, so that decision-makers have a complete picture.

Approvals run inside the design stage rather than after it. The connection application, the structural sign-off, and the roof warranty position are each settled on the designed layout, and each can return conditions; the programme holds the installation start until the conditions are known, because starting installation against unsettled conditions risks a built array that cannot be connected, or a covering warranty voided by the fixings. The float for lost weather days sits in the installation phases, where the weather acts, rather than in the design stage, where it does not, ensuring the programme remains realistic.

Decision requested
The decision requested is approval to proceed to detailed design. The capital projects team owns the detailed design stage and will report back with the survey findings, the fixed layout, the grid connection terms, and a priced construction proposal. No construction commitment is made by this approval, and no contractor is appointed under it. If the surveys return findings that change the case — a roof covering at the end of its life, a structure that cannot carry the array without strengthening, or connection terms that restrict export below the incidental level assumed — the construction proposal will state the change and the case will be reappraised before a construction decision is asked, ensuring that every step is taken on a sound footing.

fact_base: The rate constant k (s-1) of a first-order liquid-phase reaction was measured at two temperatures. At 300 K, k = 0.076 s-1. At 340 K, k = 6.712 s-1, computed from the Arrhenius relation with activation energy 95 kJ mol-1 as a derived value. Each temperature was measured in triplicate; the relative standard deviation of k was 4%. Above 340 K the solvent evaporated during sampling, so no rate constant is reported above 340 K.
input:
The temperature dependence of the rate constant $k$ was investigated for a first-order liquid-phase reaction, with measurements carried out at 300 K and at 340 K in order to characterise how the reaction responds to temperature. At 300 K, the rate constant was found to be $k$ = 0.076 s⁻¹. At 340 K, the corresponding value was $k$ = 6.712 s⁻¹; it is important to note that the value at 340 K was not measured directly but was computed from the Arrhenius relation using an activation energy of 95 kJ mol⁻¹, and it is therefore reported as a derived value. Each temperature was measured in triplicate, and the relative standard deviation of $k$ was 4% at each temperature, indicating good reproducibility overall.
The spread of the triplicate measurements is small compared with the change between the two temperatures: the derived value at 340 K stands far outside the scatter around the measured value at 300 K, highlighting a strong temperature dependence over the measured range, which is fixed by the pair of values and the activation energy that connects them. The derived value rests on the Arrhenius relation holding across the range; a direct measurement at 340 K would test it, and the sampling limitation described below prevented that check from being carried out.
Above 340 K, the solvent evaporated during sampling, so no rate constant is reported above 340 K. The reported range therefore ends at 340 K for that reason: a sample that loses solvent while it is being taken no longer has the composition at which the rate constant is stated, and a value measured on it would describe the sampling rather than the reaction itself. No value outside the measured range is stated.

fact_base: Excerpt content: two groups report conflicting lifetime values for the same material class; the excerpt weighs their test conditions. The excerpt reaches a limited preference and states the condition on which it rests.
input:
the two lifetime values reported for the benchmark material differ by more than either group's stated repeatability, and the difference sits in the test conditions rather than in the material. One group ages its samples under continuous flow and reports the time at which uptake has fallen to a stated fraction of the fresh value, while the other ages under repeated cycling and reports the cycle count at which the same fraction is reached. A lifetime stated in hours and a lifetime stated in cycles are not two measurements of one quantity until the duty is matched, and the flow group's figure can only be converted to the cycling group's basis on an assumed cycle length that neither group states.
IAST enters the comparison because both groups correct their working capacities with it, and the correction is larger for the group whose feed carries the heavier contaminant load. On matched duty — the same contaminant load, the same regeneration, and the end of life taken at the same retained fraction — the cycling group's value is the one this review rests on, because its samples met the contaminant in the form the application carries. The preference holds only on that condition: on a continuous duty with the lighter contaminant load, the flow group's value is the applicable one, and the lifetime in service will be set by the duty the application imposes.

fact_base: Goal: compute the diffusive flux of oxygen through a stagnant water film. The diffusive flux J (mol m-2 s-1) is computed from the diffusivity D (m2 s-1) and the concentration gradient dC/dx, where C is concentration (mol m-3) and x is position (m). Fick's first law: J = -D dC/dx; the negative sign states that diffusion runs from high concentration to low concentration. Oxygen in water: D = 2.1 x 10-9 m2 s-1. Concentration falls by 0.2 mol m-3 across a film 0.4 mm thick, so dC/dx = -500 mol m-4. Worked result: J = 1.05x 10-6 mol m-2 s-1. The law as stated covers a stagnant medium; a moving medium adds convection, which the equation does not include.
input:
This worked example calculates the diffusive flux of oxygen through a stagnant water film, illustrating how Fick's first law is applied in practice. The flux $J$ (mol m⁻² s⁻¹) is computed from the diffusivity $D$ (m² s⁻¹) and the concentration gradient $dC/dx$, where $C$ denotes the concentration (mol m⁻³) and $x$ denotes the position (m). Fick's first law, $J = -D dC/dx$, gives the flux from the gradient; the negative sign is important because it states that diffusion runs from high concentration to low concentration. The film is taken as uniform in thickness, and the gradient is taken as constant across it throughout the calculation.
For oxygen in water, $D$ = 2.1 × 10⁻⁹ m² s⁻¹. The concentration falls by 0.2 mol m⁻³ across a film 0.4 mm thick, and so the concentration gradient works out as $dC/dx$ = −500 mol m⁻⁴. Substituting these values into Fick's first law gives $J$ = 1.05 × 10⁻⁶ mol m⁻² s⁻¹. The check is the sign: the gradient is negative in the direction of falling concentration, the negative sign in the law returns a positive flux in the direction of $x$, and the flux runs from the concentrated side of the film to the dilute side, exactly as the law requires.
It is worth noting that Fick's first law as stated holds for a stagnant medium. A moving medium adds convection, which the equation does not include, and a flux computed from the law alone would omit the convective part wherever the water moves, which should be borne in mind when the result is applied.

fact_base: Excerpt content: two groups report conflicting lifetime values for the same material class; the excerpt weighs their test conditions. The excerpt reaches a limited preference and states the condition on which it rests.
input:
the lifetime figures reported for the benchmark material conflict, largely because the two groups end the test at different points in the material's decline. One group reports the service time at which capacity first falls below the level its separation needs, while the other reports the time at which half the fresh capacity remains. The second endpoint is naturally reached later in the life of the same sample, and a material that fails the first group's test early can still post the longer figure under the second group's endpoint. The reported order of the two materials in each study therefore follows the endpoint as much as the material, and the studies broadly agree once each figure is read against its own endpoint.
The conditions differ in a second way as well. One group regenerates fully between exposures, so that each measurement starts from the same state; the other regenerates on the application's schedule, and incomplete regeneration accumulates across the test. IAST is used by both groups to correct the mixed-gas capacities, and the correction does not account for the accumulated state, so the second group's later figures carry a decline that the correction leaves in the capacity rather than in the model. On the application's duty — regeneration on the application's schedule, and the end of life set by the capacity the separation needs — the second group's value is the one this review rests on, because its test reproduces the accumulation the application imposes. The preference rests on that match of duty: on a duty with full regeneration between exposures, the first group's value would be the applicable one, and neither figure transfers cleanly across the two duties

fact_base: Inventory policy for a packaging film: mean demand 332 units per week, standard deviation 43 units per week, replenishment lead time 9 weeks. Safety stock for a 95% cycle service level is 213 units. Demand is treated as normal and independent between weeks; seasonal peaks are excluded.
input:
This case sets the safety stock for the packaging film at 213 units. Mean demand is 332 units per week, the standard deviation of weekly demand is 43 units per week, and the replenishment lead time is 9 weeks. The stock is sized for a 95% cycle service level: in a cycle in which demand runs above its mean, the safety stock covers the excess up to that level, while the balance of the replenishment quantity covers mean demand over the lead time, ensuring that service is maintained in the large majority of cycles.
Demand is treated as normal and independent between weeks. Independence is the key assumption that carries the sizing: the lead-time spread is built up from the weekly spread on the basis that a high week is not followed by high weeks more often than chance gives, and a demand pattern with runs of high weeks would need a larger stock for the same service level. It is worth noting that seasonal peaks are excluded from the policy. Demand in a peak period is not drawn from the distribution the stock is sized on, and a service failure inside a peak is a failure of the exclusion, not of the stock: the peak is covered by the separate seasonal build, or it is accepted as a period the policy does not serve. Outside the peaks, the 213 units stand against the ordinary variation of weekly demand over the lead time, and the policy will be reviewed on the recorded demand, not on the assumed distribution, when the record is long enough to test it properly.

fact_base: A countercurrent exchanger cools a process stream from 120 °C to 85 °C with water entering at 40 °C and leaving at 75 °C. The terminal differences are 45 K and 45 K, and the log-mean temperature difference $\Delta T_{lm}$ is 45 K. The log-mean value assumes constant overall coefficient and no phase change.
input:
A countercurrent exchanger cools a process stream from 120 °C to 85 °C using water that enters at 40 °C and leaves at 75 °C. The terminal differences are taken at the two ends of the exchanger: $\Delta T_1$ at the end where the hot stream enters, and $\Delta T_2$ at the end where it leaves. where $\Delta T_{lm}$ denotes the log-mean temperature difference. The terminal differences work out at 45 K and 45 K. A difference in °C and a difference in K have the same size, so the values carry into the equation unchanged. fact_base: A tutorial passage explains absolute and relative error through a pressure measurement. Worked figures: reading 248 units, tolerance 0.5% of reading, so the absolute error is 1.24 units. The passage distinguishes error from uncertainty and does not merge the two terms.
input:
A pressure reading of 248 units carries a tolerance of 0.5% of reading, which means that the absolute error is 1.24 units. The two error figures state different things: the relative error, 0.5%, scales with the reading, while the absolute error, 1.24 units, is the relative error evaluated at this particular reading. A passage that reports only the percentage leaves the reader to compute the quantity that enters a balance or a specification check, whereas a passage that reports only the absolute figure hides how the error grows with the reading, so it is important to be clear about both.
Error, here, denotes the band within which the reading may depart from the value it reports, as the tolerance states it. Error is not the same thing as uncertainty. Uncertainty belongs to the result of a measurement procedure and combines the various contributions the procedure carries — the instrument, its calibration state, and the reading conditions — into one overall statement about the result. The two terms answer different questions, and a passage should not merge them: the error figure bounds the departure of this reading under its tolerance, and the uncertainty figure would state what the procedure delivers, which is a different quantity obtained by a different route.
Worked at a second reading, the distinction becomes mechanical. Take a reading twice the size on the same tolerance: the relative error is unchanged, and the absolute error doubles with it. The absolute error is thus a property of the reading and the tolerance together, not of the instrument alone, and a specification written as an absolute band at one reading does not hold at another reading on the same instrument. Stating the tolerance as a percentage of reading, and the absolute error at the reading in use, keeps both facts available: the rule that generates the band, and the band at the point where the measurement is actually used.

fact_base: Cost review of a returns flow: 275 km per trip at $1.53 per km, 621 trips per year. Annual transport cost is $261k. Costs are carrier invoices for the last 12 months; empty running is included in the trip count.
input:
The returns flow costs $261k a year in transport overall. This figure is built up from carrier invoices for the last 12 months: 275 km per trip at $1.53 per km, over 621 trips per year. It is important to note that empty running is included in the trip count, and the cost per trip is the invoiced cost of the whole movement, loaded and empty together; a review that priced only the loaded leg would understate the flow's cost by the empty return it also pays for, giving a misleading picture.
The evidence base is the invoice record rather than a tariff estimate: each trip in the count was actually run and invoiced, and the rate is the average the invoices give. The figure is therefore a record of what the flow cost over the period, at the volumes the period carried. A change in return volume changes the trip count and the cost with it, while the rate per km moves only when the carrier terms change; the two drivers are essentially separate, and the review holds them separate so that a cost movement can be assigned to volume or to rate. The $261k stands as the annual cost of the returns flow on the invoiced basis, for comparison against any change that alters the trip count, the distance, or the rate.

fact_base: The vapour pressure of ethanol at 78 °C is estimated from the Antoine equation with constants $A$ = 8.20417, $B$ = 1642.89 and $C$ = 230.3 (pressure in mmHg, temperature in °C). The estimate is 100 kPa. The constants are valid only over their fitted temperature range; the source databank value governs design.
input:
The vapour pressure of ethanol at 78 °C can be estimated from the Antoine equation. The constants for ethanol are $A$ = 8.20417, $B$ = 1642.89 and $C$ = 230.3, with pressure in mmHg and temperature in °C:
$$\log_{10} P = A - \frac{B}{T + C}$$
where $P$ denotes the vapour pressure and $T$ denotes the temperature. Substituting the temperature and the constants gives an estimate of 100 kPa, after the pressure from the equation is converted from the mmHg basis of the constants to kPa. The estimate is stated at the one temperature: the equation returns a pressure at the temperature substituted, and no value at another temperature is claimed from this calculation. The calculation is essentially a single substitution: one temperature, the three constants as listed, and one conversion at the end.
It is worth noting that the constants are valid only over their fitted temperature range. Outside that range the equation extrapolates a fit beyond the data it was fitted to, and the result is not an estimate of the same standing. The source databank value governs design: where a databank value exists at the design temperature, the databank value is used and the Antoine estimate serves as a useful check on it, rather than as a substitute for it. Within the fitted range, agreement between the estimate and the databank value tests the constants and the substitution together.

fact_base: Performance of a mechanical-draft tower at a chemical site was logged over one summer month. Mean wet-bulb temperature was 24 °C, the approach was 5 K and the range was 11 K. Performance outside the logged month, in particular at winter wet-bulb temperatures, was not measured.
input:
The performance of a mechanical-draft tower at a chemical site was logged over one summer month. The mean wet-bulb temperature over the month was 24 °C, the approach was 5 K, and the range was 11 K. The approach is the difference between the cold-water temperature leaving the tower and the wet-bulb temperature of the entering air, while the range is the fall in the water temperature across the tower. The two figures describe different ends of the duty: the range states how much heat the water gives up per pass, and the approach states how closely the cooled water approaches the limit the entering air sets, which together give a fuller picture of the tower's behaviour.
A mechanical-draft tower moves its air with a fan, and the air rate is set by the fan rather than by the wind; the logged performance is therefore the tower's performance at the fan duty and the water rate of the logged month. The wet-bulb temperature is the term the tower cannot design away: at a higher wet-bulb temperature the same approach leaves the cold water warmer, and the process that takes the water receives it at that temperature. The logged month fixes all three figures together — 24 °C wet-bulb, the approach, and the range — as one operating state, and the state is reported as a set rather than as three independent results.
It is important to note that performance outside the logged month was not measured. At winter wet-bulb temperatures, in particular, no measurement stands: the tower's approach and range in winter are not inferred from the summer log, because the air state, the water rate, and the heat load all move with the season and the log carries none of them. The reported performance is the performance of the logged month, and a winter figure would need a winter log on the same definitions.

fact_base: A tutorial passage explains phase equilibrium for a partially miscible liquid pair. The passage states the equilibrium condition in words (equality of chemical potential across phases) before any equation is named. No numerical data are introduced; the passage is conceptual.
input:
Phase equilibrium for a partially miscible liquid pair is set by the condition that no component can lower the total Gibbs energy of the system by moving between the liquid phases. The condition is stated in words before any equation is named: at fixed temperature and pressure, the chemical potential of each component is equal in the two liquid phases. Equality of chemical potential is the equilibrium condition, and equality for every component is required at the same time.

Partial miscibility means that the mixture separates into two liquid layers over part of the composition range. Each layer is rich in one of the liquids and holds the other as the minor part, and the compositions of the layers are fixed by the equilibrium condition rather than by the overall charge. A change in the overall composition inside the separation range changes the amounts of the two layers, while the composition of each layer stays at its equilibrium value at that temperature. Outside the separation range the mixture is a single liquid, and no equilibrium between layers arises.

Temperature acts on the boundary of the separation range. Where miscibility increases with temperature, heating closes the two-layer region and the layers merge into one liquid; where miscibility decreases with temperature, heating widens the region and a single liquid can split on warming. The equilibrium condition itself does not change: equality of chemical potential across the phases defines the state in either case, and the layer compositions follow from that equality together with the material balance on each component.

A settling or decanting step can be specified from the equilibrium layer compositions, because those compositions fix what each drawn stream can contain. Departures in practice come from incomplete settling, entrainment of one layer in the other, and temperature drift during separation, none of which alters the equilibrium condition itself.

fact_base: A binary distillation separates propane/propylene at a relative volatility of 1.81 that is taken as constant over the column. Specifications: distillate 98 mol% light component, bottoms 2 mol% light component. The Fenske minimum stage count is 13.1 theoretical stages including the reboiler. The actual design uses a reflux ratio of 1.3 times the minimum; the stage count at that reflux comes from a separate simulation.
input: In the case of the binary distillation that separates propane/propylene, the relative volatility is taken as 1.81, and this value is treated as though it remained constant over the column, which is a simplifying assumption that underpins the whole calculation. The specifications that have been set for the separation are quite demanding: the distillate is required to contain 98 mol% light component, whereas the bottoms is allowed to contain only 2 mol% light component, so a high degree of separation is being asked for at both ends of the column at the same time. When the well-known Fenske equation is applied under total reflux conditions, the minimum stage count that emerges from the calculation is 13.1 theoretical stages including the reboiler, and this figure is generally regarded as representing the absolute lower bound on the number of stages that any column performing this separation could possibly operate with. It is important to note, however, that the actual design does not operate at total reflux at all; instead, it works at a reflux ratio of 1.3 times the minimum, and the stage count that corresponds to that reflux is not obtained from the Fenske equation, but rather comes from a separate simulation that has been carried out for the design. Overall, the Fenske result should be understood as a benchmark figure, while the simulated stage count represents the design figure that is associated with the chosen operating reflux, and the two should not be confused with one another.
target:
Fenske minimum stages for the propane/propylene separation are determined from the product specifications at a relative volatility of 1.81, taken as constant over the column. The distillate specification is 98 mol% light component, and the bottoms specification is 2 mol% light component. At total reflux, the Fenske equation gives 13.1 theoretical stages including the reboiler as the minimum stage count.

Total reflux is the limiting operating condition behind the bound. At total reflux no product is withdrawn, the operating lines coincide with the diagonal, and each stage performs the largest separation the equilibrium relation allows, so no column separating the stated products can use fewer stages. The reboiler is counted in the total because the reboiler performs one equilibrium contact of the same kind as a tray. The actual design stands apart from the bound. Design reflux is a reflux ratio of 1.3 times the minimum, and the stage count at that reflux comes from a separate simulation. Finite reflux needs more stages than the total-reflux minimum, and the simulation, not the Fenske equation, fixes how many more for this column. The bound also disciplines the simulation. A simulated stage count below the Fenske minimum would indicate an error in the simulation set-up or in the specifications it was given, because no simulation of the same separation can fall below the total-reflux bound.

fact_base: A textbook chapter section on heat exchangers, in four parts: principle, equipment, a worked example, and limits. The worked example uses only the numbers given in the principle part; no new data appear later in the chapter. The limits part states where the simple model fails, in plain terms, without new equations.
input:
Principle

At the heart of every heat exchanger lies a deceptively simple idea: heat is transferred from a hot stream to a cold stream through a separating wall, and the two streams themselves never actually mix with one another. The duty of the exchanger, denoted $Q$, is the rate at which heat crosses that wall, and it can be obtained from an energy balance written on either stream: for each stream, the duty is equal to the mass flow multiplied by the heat capacity and by the change in temperature experienced by that stream, and, provided no heat is lost to the surroundings, the balance on the hot stream and the balance on the cold stream will give exactly the same duty.

Temperature does not remain constant along the exchanger. The hot stream cools as it gives up its heat and the cold stream warms as it receives heat, and consequently the temperature difference between the streams, which is the driving force for the heat transfer, varies from point to point along the length. The overall heat transfer coefficient, denoted $U$, is a quantity that conveniently gathers all of the resistances in the path into a single figure: convection in the hot stream, conduction through the wall, and convection in the cold stream, all referred to a stated area basis. The sizing relation then states that the duty is the product of the overall coefficient, the heat transfer area, denoted $A$, and a mean temperature difference, and where the coefficient is constant along the exchanger, the mean that makes this relation exact is the log-mean temperature difference, denoted $\Delta T_{lm}$, which is formed from the temperature differences at the two ends of the exchanger.

The flow arrangement plays a major role in how the driving force behaves. In counter-current flow the streams enter at opposite ends, the temperature difference remains comparatively even along the length, and the cold stream can actually leave hotter than the hot stream leaves. In co-current flow, by contrast, the streams enter at the same end, the difference is at its largest at the inlet and falls along the length, and no such crossing of the outlet temperatures is possible. At each end of the exchanger, the difference between the hot and cold temperatures is referred to as a terminal difference, and the smaller terminal difference is the tight end of the unit.

Equipment

The shell-and-tube exchanger is the standard industrial form, and it is the form against which the alternatives are usually measured. In this configuration, one stream flows inside a bundle of tubes while the other stream flows across the bundle inside a surrounding shell. Baffles are provided to support the tubes and to direct the shell-side stream repeatedly across the bundle, Tube sheets fix the ends of the tubes, and channels at each end distribute the tube-side stream among the tubes. The differential thermal expansion that arises between the shell and the tubes is accommodated by means of a floating head or an expansion joint, depending on the severity of the temperature difference between the streams.

Other forms exist to serve other duties. A plate exchanger clamps corrugated plates with gaskets between them: the resulting unit is compact, it can readily be opened for cleaning, and the gaskets inevitably bound the pressure and temperature that it can serve. An air-cooled exchanger passes the hot stream through finned tubes while fans move air across the fins, and it is typically chosen where cooling water is scarce where water is too warm for the duty. The selection among the forms turns on pressure, temperature, fouling tendency, access for cleaning, and the corrosiveness of the streams, with the stream that attacks the metal being placed on the side that can be built in the resistant material or cleaned most readily.

Worked example

The task is to size an exchanger for a stated duty, using only the quantities that have been given in the principle part. The duty is taken from the balance on the hot stream: the mass flow of the hot stream, its heat capacity, and its temperature change are the given quantities, and their product is the duty. The terminal differences are then obtained from the terminal temperatures: the hot stream enters at its inlet temperature and leaves at its outlet temperature, the cold stream enters cold and leaves warm, and the difference between the hot and cold temperatures at each end of the exchanger gives the terminal difference at that end. From the two terminal differences, the log-mean temperature difference is calculated. The overall coefficient is taken as the value given for the service in the principle part. Finally, the area is obtained by dividing the duty by the product of the overall coefficient and the log-mean temperature difference.

The example closes with two checks on the same data. Repeating the terminal-difference step for the other flow arrangement, with no change in any terminal temperature, shows the counter-current arrangement holding the larger mean difference and therefore needing the smaller area. Overall, the example demonstrates that a sizing of this kind rests on the duty, the coefficient, and the mean temperature difference, with the flow arrangement entering through the terminal differences alone.

Limits

The simple model set out in the principle part holds where the overall coefficient is steady along the exchanger and the streams remain in a single phase. Where a stream boils or condenses, however, the mechanism of heat transfer changes along the length, the coefficient varies with position, and a single mean temperature difference no longer adequately describes the local rates; in such cases the exchanger is rated in sections, each with its own coefficient and its own temperature difference.

Service introduces further limits that the clean calculation does not take into account. Deposits foul the surfaces and add resistance, so a coefficient that has been measured or computed for clean surfaces will overstate the duty after a period of time on stream; design practice allows for fouling by adding a fouling resistance to the clean resistances. Alongside these thermal considerations stand mechanical limits: pressure containment, differential expansion, and flow-induced vibration all bound the design independently of the sizing relation.

In summary, the chapter has set out the sizing of a heat exchanger from an energy balance, a mean temperature difference, and an overall coefficient; the equipment forms in which that sizing is realised; and the conditions under which the simple model stops describing the unit.
