The hot stream cools as it gives up heat and the cold stream warms as it receives heat, so the temperature difference between the streams, which is the driving force for heat transfer, varies from point to point. The overall heat transfer coefficient, denoted $U$, gathers the resistances in the path into one quantity: convection in the hot stream, conduction through the wall, and convection in the cold stream, all referred to a stated area basis. The sizing relation of the chapter states that the duty is the product of the overall coefficient, the heat transfer area, denoted $A$, and a mean temperature difference. Where the coefficient is constant along the exchanger, the mean that makes the relation exact is the log-mean temperature difference, denoted $\Delta T_{lm}$, which is formed from the temperature differences at the two ends of the exchanger.

Flow arrangement sets how the driving force varies. In counter-current flow the streams enter at opposite ends, the temperature difference is comparatively even along the length, and the cold stream can leave hotter than the hot stream leaves. In co-current flow the streams enter at the same end, the difference is largest at the inlet and falls along the length, and no such crossing of outlet temperatures is possible. At each end of the exchanger the difference between the hot and cold temperatures is a terminal difference. The smaller terminal difference is the tight end of the unit: at fixed duty and coefficient, the area grows steeply as the tight end is made tighter, and the tight end therefore prices the design.

Equipment

The shell-and-tube exchanger is the standard industrial form. One stream flows inside a bundle of tubes and the other flows across the bundle inside a shell. Baffles support the tubes and direct the shell-side stream across the bundle, which raises the shell-side coefficient and lengthens the path. Differential thermal expansion between shell and tubes is taken up by a floating head or by an expansion joint, according to the severity of the temperature difference between the streams.

Other forms serve other duties. A plate exchanger clamps corrugated plates with gaskets between them: the unit is compact, it opens for cleaning, and the gaskets bound the pressure and temperature it can serve. An air-cooled exchanger passes the hot stream through finned tubes while fans move air across the fins, and it is chosen where cooling water is scarce or where water temperatures are too warm for the duty. Selection among the forms turns on pressure, temperature, fouling tendency, access for cleaning, and the corrosiveness of the streams: the stream that attacks the metal is placed on the side that can be built in the resistant material or cleaned most readily.

Worked example

Size an exchanger for a stated duty, using only the quantities given in the principle part. Take the duty from the balance on the hot stream: the mass flow of the hot stream, its heat capacity, and its temperature change are the given quantities, and their product is the duty. Obtain the terminal differences from the terminal temperatures: the hot stream enters at its inlet temperature and leaves at its outlet temperature, the cold stream enters cold and leaves warm, and the difference between the hot and cold temperatures at each end of the exchanger gives the terminal difference at that end. Calculate the log-mean temperature difference from the two terminal differences. Take the overall coefficient as the value given for the service in the principle part. Obtain the area by dividing the duty by the product of the overall coefficient and the log-mean temperature difference.

The example closes with two checks on the same data. Repeating the terminal-difference step for the other flow arrangement, with no change in any terminal temperature, shows the counter-current arrangement holding the larger mean difference and therefore needing the smaller area. The area is the result of the example, and the example shows that a sizing rests on the duty, the coefficient, and the mean temperature difference, with the flow arrangement entering through the terminal differences alone.

Limits

The simple model of the principle part holds where the overall coefficient is steady along the exchanger and the streams stay in one phase. Where a stream boils or condenses, the mechanism of heat transfer changes along the length, the coefficient varies with position, and a single mean temperature difference no longer describes the local rates; the exchanger is then rated in sections, each with its own coefficient and its own temperature difference.

Service adds limits the clean calculation does not carry. Deposits foul the surfaces and add resistance, so a coefficient measured or computed for clean surfaces overstates the duty after time on stream; design practice allows for fouling by adding a fouling resistance to the clean resistances. Mechanical limits stand beside the thermal ones: pressure containment, differential expansion, and flow-induced vibration bound the design independently of the sizing relation.

The chapter has set out the sizing of a heat exchanger from an energy balance, a mean temperature difference, and an overall coefficient; the equipment forms in which that sizing is realised; and the conditions under which the simple model stops describing the unit.

fact_base: Cost review of a regional delivery route: 755 km per trip at $1.45 per km, 327 trips per year. Annual transport cost is $358k. Costs are carrier invoices for the last 12 months; empty running is included in the trip count.
input: This review examines the cost of the regional delivery route, drawing on carrier invoices for the last 12 months as its evidence base. The route is not a short one: each trip covers 755 km, and the carrier charges $1.45 per km, so the cost of a single trip is already considerable before any question of frequency is even considered. Frequency, however, is very much part of the picture, because the route runs 327 trips per year, and once that frequency is taken into account the annual transport cost builds up to $358k, which is a substantial commitment within the wider distribution budget. It is important to note that the trip count should not be understood as counting only those journeys in which the vehicle is carrying goods for delivery: empty running is included in the trip count, which means that the return legs and other unloaded movements are fully reflected in the figure as well. It is also worth emphasising that the annual figure has not been assembled from estimates or from standard rates applied in the abstract; it is grounded in what was actually charged, as recorded on carrier invoices for the last 12 months. In overall terms, therefore, the annual transport cost of $358k for the regional delivery route, arising from 755 km per trip at $1.45 per km over 327 trips per year with empty running included in the count, represents the complete invoiced cost of running the route over the period, and it forms the baseline against which the cost of any alternative arrangement would have to be measured.
target:
The regional delivery route costs $358k per year. The evidence base is carrier invoices for the last 12 months, and the cost is stated on that basis. Each trip covers 755 km at $1.45 per km, and the route runs 327 trips per year. Empty running is included in the trip count, so the annual figure covers loaded and empty legs together.

Two quantities set the cost. Distance and rate fix the charge per trip, because 755 km at $1.45 per km is billed on every trip whether the vehicle carries a load or returns empty. Trip count then scales the per-trip charge to the year. A rate change and a trip-count change are different levers: a lower rate reduces the cost of every kilometre on every trip, while fewer trips remove whole trips at the full per-trip charge, and neither saving implies the other. Service level enters through the same count, since a route that must run whether or not a full load is ready commits the empty legs that the count includes.

Comparisons with later periods hold only on the same basis. The $358k total rests on carrier invoices for the last 12 months, with 327 trips per year and empty running inside the count. A later invoice total stated on a different trip definition, or with empty running stripped out, would differ from the present figure even if rates and distances had not moved, and the difference would be an artefact of the basis rather than a change in the cost of the route itself. Route planning reads the figure the same way. Consolidating deliveries acts on trip count, renegotiating the carrier contract acts on the rate, and backloading acts on the empty share inside the count that is already charged.

fact_base: Inventory policy for a spare motor: mean demand 1400 units per week, standard deviation 306 units per week, replenishment lead time 8 weeks. Safety stock for a 95% cycle service level is 1428 units. Demand is treated as normal and independent between weeks; seasonal peaks are excluded.
input: This inventory policy concerns a spare motor, and it sets out the basis on which safety stock is to be held for the item. Mean demand is 1400 units per week, with a standard deviation of 306 units per week, and the replenishment lead time is 8 weeks, which is a considerable interval over which demand has to be covered before fresh stock can arrive. On the basis of these figures, the safety stock for a 95% cycle service level is 1428 units, a substantial holding that reflects both the scale of weekly demand and the length of the replenishment cycle. It is important to note the assumptions on which the policy rests. Demand is treated as normal and independent between weeks, and seasonal peaks are excluded, which means that the policy is calibrated to the ordinary run of demand rather than to the exceptional demand that can arise at particular times of the year. In other words, the safety stock is designed to absorb the normal week-to-week fluctuation in demand over the lead time at the chosen service level, and it should not be expected to provide the same degree of protection during seasonal peaks, when demand is likely to be systematically higher than the average on which the calculation has been based. Overall, the policy provides a clearly defined stockholding rule for the spare motor under the stated conditions.
target:
Safety stock for the spare motor is 1428 units, set for a 95% cycle service level. Mean demand is 1400 units per week, the standard deviation of demand is 306 units per week, and the replenishment lead time is 8 weeks. Demand is treated as normal and independent between weeks, and seasonal peaks are excluded from the policy.

Safety stock covers demand variability over the replenishment interval. Demand in a single week varies around its mean, and the lead time stretches that variability over the whole wait for replenishment, so the stock held above mean lead-time demand is what absorbs a run of heavy weeks without emptying the store. The service level fixes how much of that variability the stock is sized to absorb: the policy accepts stock-outs in the share of cycles that falls beyond the stated level, and that acceptance is part of the figure, not a defect in it.

The assumptions bound the result. Independence between weeks means a heavy week carries no information about the week that follows, and the normal treatment sets the shape of the demand spread that the stock is sized against. Seasonal peaks stand outside the policy: demand in a peak season is not drawn from the stated distribution, and stock sized on the stated mean and spread will run short in a peak season more often than the service level suggests. The policy therefore holds for ordinary demand over the stated lead time, and it is reopened when the lead time, the demand mean, or the demand spread changes materially.

subtype: worked example with equation: first-order decay
fact_base: A dye in effluent decomposes by first-order kinetics with rate constant $k$ = 0.156 min-1. After 38 min the fraction remaining $C / C_0$ is 0.003. The rate constant was measured at one temperature; no activation energy is available.
input:
In this example we consider a dye in effluent that decomposes by first-order kinetics, with a rate constant $k$ = 0.156 min-1, and we are interested in finding out what fraction of the dye remains after 38 min have elapsed. For a first-order process of this kind, the relationship between the concentration and time is given by the well-known integrated rate equation

$$\ln\frac{C}{C_0} = -k t$$

where $C$ denotes the concentration at time $t$, $C_0$ denotes the starting concentration, $k$ denotes the rate constant, and $t$ denotes the elapsed time. When the values are substituted into this equation, the fraction remaining, $C / C_0$, works out to be 0.003, which is a very small number indeed. In other words, by the that time, the decomposition has proceeded almost to completion, and only a tiny proportion of the original dye is still present in the effluent. It is important to note, however, that the rate constant was measured at one temperature, and no activation energy is available, so it would not be appropriate to apply this result at a different temperature, since the rate constant itself would be expected to change. Overall, the example shows how the integrated first-order relation can be used to estimate the extent of decomposition over a given period of time.
target:
Calculate the fraction of dye remaining in an effluent stream after 38 min. The dye decomposes by first-order kinetics with rate constant $k$ = 0.156 min-1, measured at one temperature. For first-order decay, the concentration ratio follows

$$\ln\frac{C}{C_0} = -k t$$

where $C$ denotes the concentration at time $t$, $C_0$ denotes the starting concentration, $k$ denotes the rate constant, and $t$ denotes the elapsed time. Substitution of the stated rate constant and the stated time into the relation gives the fraction remaining, $C / C_0$, as 0.003.

The fraction means the decomposition is nearly complete at the stated time under the stated kinetics: almost all of the dye present at the start has decomposed. The check is the limiting behaviour of the relation, in which the fraction falls continuously as time increases and approaches zero at long times. The example also shows the shape of the process: equal additions of time remove equal fractions of the dye that remains, so the concentration falls steeply at first, while the amount present is large, and then more slowly as the remaining amount shrinks. The rate of decomposition at any moment is proportional to the amount of dye still present, which is the content of the first-order assumption in running terms.

The result is tied to the temperature of the measurement. The rate constant was measured at one temperature and no activation energy is available, so the relation cannot be carried to another temperature, and the stated fraction is valid at the measured temperature under the first-order model.

fact_base: A flat stainless steel wall of thickness 150 mm separates two process streams. Thermal conductivity of the wall is 16 W m-1 K-1 and the measured temperature difference across it is 309 K. Steady one-dimensional conduction gives a heat flux of 32960 W m-2. Surface (film) resistances are excluded from this estimate; including them lowers the flux.
input: In this worked example, attention is turned to a flat stainless steel wall of thickness 150 mm that separates two process streams from one another. The thermal conductivity of the wall is 16 W m-1 K-1, and the measured temperature difference across it is 309 K, which is a very substantial driving force for heat transfer. Under conditions of steady one-dimensional conduction, the heat flux through the wall can be estimated by means of Fourier's law, and when the relevant values are inserted into that relationship, the resulting heat flux is 32960 W m-2, a strikingly high figure that reflects the combination of a large temperature difference and a highly conductive metallic wall. It is important to note, however, that this estimate comes with an important qualification: surface (film) resistances are excluded from this estimate, and including them lowers the flux, since the fluid films on either side of the wall would themselves offer resistance to the flow of heat and would absorb part of the temperature difference. In other words, the figure that has been obtained here should be understood as the flux attributable to the wall alone, under the full measured temperature difference, and the actual flux in the real configuration, with the films present, would be somewhat lower. Overall, the example serves to illustrate the application of Fourier's law to a simple conduction problem and the importance of being aware of what has been left out of the calculation.
target:
Calculate the heat flux through a flat stainless steel wall of thickness 150 mm. The thermal conductivity of the wall is 16 W m-1 K-1, and the measured temperature difference across the wall is 309 K. The wall separates two process streams, the flow is steady, and conduction is one-dimensional, normal to the wall face.

Under steady one-dimensional conduction, Fourier's law gives a flux proportional to the conductivity and to the temperature difference, and inversely proportional to the thickness. Substitution of the stated conductivity, temperature difference and thickness gives a heat flux of 32960 W m-2. The flux is the same at every plane inside the wall: at steady state no energy accumulates in the metal, so the rate at which heat enters any slice of the wall equals the rate at which it leaves.

The temperature falls linearly across the wall under the stated conditions, because the flux is uniform and the conductivity is constant: equal slices of the wall thickness carry equal shares of the temperature difference. The direction of the flux is from the hotter face to the colder face, and its size is set by the wall alone once the temperature difference across the metal itself is the stated difference.

The estimate carries one stated omission. Surface (film) resistances are excluded from the estimate, and including them lowers the flux, because the films add resistance in series with the wall and take part of the overall temperature difference themselves. The stated flux is therefore the wall-only value: it is the flux the metal alone would pass under the full measured difference, and a design figure for the real wall, bounded by the two process streams, sits below it by the amount the film resistances remove.

fact_base: A viscous liquid of viscosity $\mu$ = 0.05 Pa s flows laminarly through a tube of radius $R$ = 10 mm and length $L$ = 16 m. At a pressure drop $\Delta P$ of 24 kPa the volumetric flow $Q$ is 424.1 L h-1. The Hagen-Poiseuille equation assumes laminar, fully developed flow of a Newtonian liquid.
input:
In this example, we look at the flow of a viscous liquid through a tube and seek to determine the volumetric flow rate that results from a given pressure drop. The liquid in question is Newtonian, with a viscosity $\mu$ of 0.05 Pa s, and it flows laminarly through a tube of radius $R$ = 10 mm and length $L$ = 16 m. At a pressure drop $\Delta P$ of 24 kPa, the Hagen-Poiseuille equation can be used to work out the flow, since that equation relates the volumetric flow to the pressure drop and to the geometry of the tube in a compact and elegant way:

$$Q = \frac{\pi R^4 \Delta P}{8 \mu L}$$

where $Q$ denotes the volumetric flow, $R$ denotes the tube radius, $\Delta P$ denotes the pressure drop over the tube, $\mu$ denotes the viscosity, and $L$ denotes the tube length. Substituting the stated values into the equation gives the volumetric flow $Q$ as 424.1 L h-1. It is worth noting that this result depends quite sensitively on the radius of the tube, because the radius appears raised to the fourth power in the equation, so even a modest change in the radius would lead to a much larger change in the predicted flow. It should also be kept in mind that the Hagen-Poiseuille equation assumes laminar, fully developed flow of a Newtonian liquid, and its predictions should therefore be applied with appropriate caution outside that regime. Overall, the example illustrates how a single compact equation can capture the relationship between pressure drop and flow in laminar tube flow.
target:
Calculate the volumetric flow of a viscous liquid through a tube. The liquid is Newtonian, the flow is laminar and fully developed, and these assumptions are stated before the relation that rests on them. The viscosity $\mu$ is 0.05 Pa s, the tube radius $R$ is 10 mm, the tube length $L$ is 16 m, and the pressure drop $\Delta P$ is 24 kPa. For laminar, fully developed flow of a Newtonian liquid, the Hagen-Poiseuille equation gives the volumetric flow $Q$ as

$$Q = \frac{\pi R^4 \Delta P}{8 \mu L}$$

where $Q$ denotes the volumetric flow, $R$ denotes the tube radius, $\Delta P$ denotes the pressure drop over the tube, $\mu$ denotes the viscosity, and $L$ denotes the tube length. Substitution of the stated values gives $Q$ as 424.1 L h-1.

The velocity profile behind the relation is parabolic: the liquid at the wall is at rest, the velocity is greatest at the centre of the tube, and the stated flow is the average of that profile over the cross-section. Pressure falls steadily along the tube, and the fall per unit length is uniform where the flow is fully developed, which is why a single pressure drop over the whole length describes the tube.

The result is dominated by the radius. Flow varies with the fourth power of the radius, so a small error in the radius, or a deposit that narrows the bore, changes the flow far more than a comparable error in length or pressure drop; the stated flow is only as firm as the stated radius. Validity is bounded by the assumptions: the Hagen-Poiseuille equation holds for laminar, fully developed flow of a Newtonian liquid, and flow that is still developing at the tube inlet, or a liquid whose viscosity changes with shear, falls outside the relation and outside the stated result.

fact_base: Excerpt content: a supplier delay of 4 weeks is reported with its cause; the excerpt proposes one mitigation and its owner. The excerpt does not open or close the memo and does not restate its subject line.
input: It should be noted that the position with regard to the delayed package has deteriorated, in that the package now stands 4 weeks behind the date to which the supplier originally committed, and the underlying cause of this slippage lies with the supplier itself: fabrication capacity at the supplier's works was committed elsewhere first, and the package was rescheduled behind other work that was already in the shop. The consequences of this delay are not confined to the package, because the equipment contained in the package is erected before the piping tie-ins that follow on from it, and those tie-ins in turn release the loop checks and the pre-commissioning activities that sit behind them, so a slip at this particular point tends to move every dependent activity in the sequence. Against that background, the mitigation that is being proposed is essentially one of resequencing: installation fronts that do not depend on the delayed package would be brought forward, and the crews released by the slip would be held on those fronts rather than being stood down. The project board owns the mitigation and will settle the resequenced order, and the EPC schedule is being reissued on the same basis. What resequencing cannot do, however, is recover the erection window itself, and the balance of the delay that remains after mitigation is still under discussion with the supplier, whose revised date the board has not yet accepted
target:
The delayed package now stands 4 weeks behind the supplier's committed date, and the cause sits with the supplier: fabrication capacity was committed elsewhere first, and the package was rescheduled behind work already in the shop. The delay lands on the installation sequence at its most constrained point. The equipment in the package is erected before the piping tie-ins that follow it, and the tie-ins release the loop checks and the pre-commissioning work behind them, so a slip at the package moves every activity that hangs from it.

The mitigation proposed is resequencing. Installation fronts that do not depend on the delayed package are brought forward, and the crews released by the slip are held on those fronts rather than stood down. The project board owns the mitigation and settles the resequenced order. The EPC schedule is reissued on the same basis, with the package carried at the supplier's revised date and the brought-forward fronts in their new order. Resequencing recovers crew time and protects the later fronts; it does not recover the erection window itself, and the balance of the delay that survives mitigation is still under discussion with the supplier, whose revised date the board has not yet accepted

fact_base: A continuous stirred-tank reactor runs a hydrolysis that is first order in the limiting reactant. The rate constant is 0.144 min-1 at the operating temperature and the mean residence time is 23 min. Steady-state conversion for an ideal CSTR is 76.8%. The estimate assumes perfect mixing and constant density; tracer tests on the actual vessel have not been run.
input: This example considers a continuous stirred-tank reactor running a hydrolysis that is first order in the limiting reactant. The rate constant is 0.144 min-1 at the operating temperature, and the mean residence time is 23 min, and on the basis of these figures the steady-state conversion for an ideal CSTR works out at 76.8%. It is helpful to be clear about what lies behind that figure. In an ideal continuous stirred-tank reactor, the contents are assumed to be perfectly mixed, which means that the composition is uniform throughout the vessel and identical to the composition of the stream leaving it, and consequently the reaction proceeds everywhere in the vessel at the rate corresponding to the outlet concentration. Since the reaction is first order, that rate is the lowest rate anywhere in the system, because the reactant concentration is at its lowest at the outlet, and it is this rate that, combined with the residence time, determines the conversion that the balance over the vessel produces. The estimate does, however, rest on assumptions that deserve to be noted. It assumes perfect mixing and constant density, and while constant density is a relatively mild assumption in this context, perfect mixing is a stronger one, and it has not in fact been verified on the actual vessel, because tracer tests on the actual vessel have not been run. In a real vessel, bypassing or stagnant regions could allow part of the feed to pass through with considerably less reaction than the ideal calculation suggests. Overall, then, the figure of the ideal-vessel conversion should be read as the conversion that the stated kinetics and residence time would deliver under ideal conditions, rather than as a guaranteed prediction of the performance of the actual equipment.
target:
Steady-state conversion for the hydrolysis in an ideal continuous stirred-tank reactor is 76.8%. The reaction is first order in the limiting reactant, the rate constant is 0.144 min-1 at the operating temperature, and the mean residence time is 23 min.

An ideal continuous stirred-tank reactor is perfectly mixed, so the composition everywhere in the vessel equals the outlet composition, and the reaction proceeds throughout the vessel at the rate set by that outlet composition. The conversion then follows from a steady-state balance over the whole vessel: the rate at which the limiting reactant leaves in the outlet stream, together with the rate at which it is consumed by reaction, balances the rate at which it enters. Because the reaction is first order, the rate falls as the reactant is consumed, and the rate that governs the balance is the lowest in the system, the rate at the outlet concentration. Residence time sets how long the reacting mixture is exposed to that rate, and the stated conversion is the joint result of the two stated quantities under the ideal-mixing assumption.

The estimate assumes perfect mixing and constant density. Constant density fixes the residence time at its stated value, since the volumetric flow through the vessel then matches the flow the residence time was computed from. Perfect mixing is the stronger assumption, and it is unverified on the actual vessel: tracer tests have not been run, so the residence-time distribution is not measured. Bypassing or stagnant zones in a real vessel would let part of the feed leave with less reaction than the ideal figure states. The conversion is therefore the ideal-vessel result for the stated rate constant and residence time, and a measured conversion on the actual vessel stands as a separate quantity until the mixing assumption is tested.

fact_base: A binary distillation separates benzene/toluene at a relative volatility of 1.9 that is taken as constant over the column. Specifications: distillate 98 mol% light component, bottoms 2 mol% light component. The Fenske minimum stage count is 12.1 theoretical stages including the reboiler. The actual design uses a reflux ratio of 1.3 times the minimum; the stage count at that reflux comes from a separate simulation.
input: In the case of the binary distillation that separates benzene/toluene, the separation is specified in terms of a distillate containing 98 mol% light component and a bottoms containing just 2 mol% light component, so the column is being asked to achieve a considerable degree of separation between the two ends. The relative volatility is taken as 1.9, and this value is treated as remaining constant over the column, which is a convenient simplifying assumption on which the calculation depends. When the well-known Fenske equation is applied under total reflux conditions, the minimum stage count that is obtained is 12.1 theoretical stages including the reboiler, and this figure is best understood as the absolute lower bound on the number of stages that a column performing this separation could ever require. It is important to appreciate that total reflux is a limiting condition rather than an operating one: nothing is actually withdrawn as product, and each stage achieves the greatest separation that the equilibrium relationship allows. It should also be noted that the actual design does not operate anywhere near this limiting condition. The actual design uses a reflux ratio of 1.3 times the minimum, and the stage count at that reflux does not come from the Fenske equation at all, but instead comes from a separate simulation that has been performed for the design. Overall, the value of the Fenske calculation lies in the benchmark that it provides: it establishes the floor beneath the design, against which the simulated stage count associated with the chosen reflux can meaningfully be compared, and the two figures should not be confused with one another.
target:
The benzene/toluene column is specified at both ends: the distillate carries 98 mol% light component and the bottoms carries 2 mol% light component. At a relative volatility of 1.9, taken as constant over the column, the Fenske equation gives a minimum of 12.1 theoretical stages including the reboiler.

The Fenske minimum is a total-reflux bound. At total reflux, all condensed overhead returns to the column and all vaporised bottoms returns with it, no product leaves, and each contact performs the largest separation the equilibrium relation permits between the two streams that cross there. Stepping the composition ratio stage by stage at the constant volatility then counts the fewest contacts that can carry the distillate specification into the bottoms specification. The reboiler is counted among the stages because the reboiler is an equilibrium contact of the same kind: liquid partially vaporises there, and the vapour leaving it is richer in the light component than the liquid that remains.

Constant volatility is the assumption that makes the stepping exact. Benzene/toluene behaviour is close to ideal over much of the column, which is why a single volatility is serviceable here, but a volatility that drifted with composition or temperature would change the count obtained from the same specifications, and the bound would move with it.

The design does not run at the bound. The actual design uses a reflux ratio of 1.3 times the minimum, and the stage count at that reflux comes from a separate simulation. The Fenske count is therefore a screening figure: it fixes the floor under the design, it exposes any simulated count that falls below the floor as an error in the simulation or its specifications, and it leaves the working stage count itself to the simulation that the design rests on.

fact_base: A tutorial passage explains feedback control through a temperature loop on a process vessel. The passage covers the sensor, the controller, the final element and the sign of the feedback, in that order. No tuning numbers are given; the passage explains structure, not settings.
input:
Feedback control is a fundamental idea in process control, and the temperature loop on a process vessel is a classic example. In essence, the loop holds the vessel temperature close to its set point by adjusting the heat supply in response to the temperature actually measured, and it is helpful to follow the signal around the loop in order, from the sensor, through the controller, to the final element, before turning to the sign of the feedback.

The sensor measures the vessel contents temperature and converts it into a signal the controller can use. The position of the sensor determines what the loop actually controls: a sensor in the contents reports the contents temperature, whereas a sensor in a pocket reports the pocket temperature, which follows the contents with a lag.

The controller compares the measured temperature with the set point, and the difference is known as the deviation. From the deviation, the controller calculates a correction. A positive deviation and a negative deviation call for corrections in opposite directions, and the size of the correction follows the size of the deviation under the control law in use.

The final element receives the controller output and changes the heat supply to the vessel. In many cases the final element is a valve, together with its actuator, on the heating-medium line, while in other cases the heat is supplied by an electric heater and the final element varies the heater power. The loop acts only through the final element, so at its limit the loop has no authority over the temperature.

The feedback in the loop is negative, which means that the action of the controller opposes the deviation: when the temperature rises above the set point the heat supply is reduced, and when it falls below, the heat supply is increased. This opposing action returns the temperature towards the set point after a disturbance. Positive feedback, by contrast, would drive the temperature further from the set point, and it is not used for holding a temperature.
target:
Feedback control holds the temperature of a process vessel at its set point by acting on the heat supply in response to the measured temperature. The loop is followed in signal order: sensor, controller, final element, and the sign of the feedback.

The sensor measures the vessel temperature and converts the measurement into a signal the controller can use. Sensor position fixes what the loop controls. A sensor in the vessel contents reports the contents temperature; a sensor in a pocket reports the pocket temperature, which follows the contents temperature with a lag.

The controller compares the measured temperature with the set point. The difference between the two values is the deviation, and the controller calculates a correction from the deviation. A positive deviation and a negative deviation call for corrections in opposite directions, and the size of the correction follows the size of the deviation under the control law in use.

The final element receives the controller output and changes the heat supply to the vessel. Where the heating medium enters through a valve, the final element is that valve and its actuator; where an electric heater supplies the heat, the final element varies the heater power. The loop acts only through the final element, and a final element at its limit ends the loop's authority over the temperature.

The feedback is negative when the controller action opposes the deviation. A temperature above the set point reduces the heat supply, and a temperature below the set point increases it. Negative feedback returns the temperature toward the set point after a disturbance. Positive feedback would drive the temperature further from the set point and is not used for temperature holding.

fact_base: A tutorial passage explains the pump affinity laws for a centrifugal pump at varying speed. The passage states the three proportionalities in words: flow with speed, head with speed squared, power with speed cubed. A worked check is included: doubling speed multiplies power by 8. No other numbers are introduced.
input:
The pump affinity laws give the performance of a centrifugal pump at a changed speed from its performance at a known speed, for the same pump handling the same liquid. The laws are three proportionalities. Flow is proportional to speed: at double the speed, the pump delivers double the flow. Head is proportional to the square of the speed. Power is proportional to the cube of the speed. The three proportionalities hold together, so a speed change large enough to matter for flow has a larger effect on the head and a larger effect again on the power.

A worked check shows the size of the power term. Doubling the speed multiplies the power by 8. A drive and a motor selected for the duty at the original speed have no margin for a doubled speed, and a speed increase made for flow or for head is checked first against the power the drive can deliver.

The affinity laws are similarity relations. The affinity laws hold at the same relative position on the pump characteristic, and efficiency is taken as unchanged between the two speeds. A calculation that carries a duty point to a new speed states the new flow, head and power at the corresponding point, not at the same system resistance; the operating point settles where the pump characteristic meets the system curve.

fact_base: A food plant uses 2443 MWh of electricity per year in refrigeration. A heat-recovery retrofit is projected by the equipment vendor to save 13% of that use, a derived saving of 318 MWh per year at the vendor figure. Capital cost is $428k. At an electricity price of $0.13 per kWh, the derived annual saving is $41k and the derived simple payback is 10.4 years. The saving figure is a vendor projection and was not measured at this plant; refrigeration load in the summer peak month was not modelled. The recommendation is a metered trial on one of the three refrigeration lines before any capital decision. The plant engineer owns the trial.
input: It is recommended that a metered trial of the heat-recovery retrofit be carried out on one of the three refrigeration lines before any capital decision is taken, and the plant engineer will own the trial. To provide some context, refrigeration at the food plant currently uses some 2443 MWh of electricity per year, and the case for the retrofit rests essentially on a projection provided by the equipment vendor rather than on anything that has been measured at the plant itself. According to the vendor, the retrofit is projected to save 13% of that electricity use, which corresponds to a derived saving of 318 MWh per year at the vendor figure. At an electricity price of $0.13 per kWh, this works out to a derived annual saving of $41k, which can be set against a capital cost of $428k to give a derived simple payback of 10.4 years. It is important to emphasise that the saving figure has not been measured at this plant, and that refrigeration load in the summer peak month was not modelled, so the payback should really be read as a figure that holds at the vendor projection and outside the peak month. A metered trial on a single line would replace the projection with a measured saving for that line, and the capital decision could then be taken on the basis of the trial result together with a modelled peak month, which would represent a considerably firmer footing for a decision of this size.

fact_base: A tutorial passage explains the Nusselt number to second-year students. Definition in words: the Nusselt number is the ratio of convective to conductive heat transfer at a surface. The passage must state what a value near 1 means and what a large value means, without inventing numerical examples.
input:
The Nusselt number is a dimensionless quantity that is widely used in heat transfer, and it can be understood as the ratio of convective to conductive heat transfer at a surface. In other words, the comparison is made at one and the same surface and under the same temperature difference: the numerator of the ratio is the heat that is actually carried away from the surface by the moving fluid, while the denominator is the heat that conduction alone would carry across a stagnant layer of the fluid under exactly the same conditions. Because the Nusselt number is a ratio of two heat transfer rates expressed in the same units, it has no units of its own.

A value near 1 means that convection is adding very little to conduction, so the fluid at the surface is transferring heat at roughly the rate that a stagnant layer would transfer it, and the heat transfer at the surface is, in effect, limited by conduction. A large value, on the other hand, means that the motion of the fluid carries heat away much more rapidly than conduction across the layer would do, so the resistance at the surface becomes small in comparison with the conduction reference. Overall, the Nusselt number expresses the strength of surface convection measured against a fixed conduction reference, and comparisons between different cases are always comparisons against that same reference. It should be noted that the number does not by itself state the heat flux, since the flux also depends on the temperature difference and on the conduction reference for the particular geometry being considered.

fact_base: A single-stage compressor raises nitrogen from 2 bar to 9 bar. Inlet temperature is 313 K. For isentropic compression with a heat-capacity ratio of 1.4, the discharge temperature is 481 K. The isentropic estimate excludes mechanical losses; the installed machine's measured discharge temperature is higher.
input: Consider a single-stage compressor that raises nitrogen from 2 bar to 9 bar, with an inlet temperature of 313 K. For isentropic compression with a heat-capacity ratio of 1.4, the discharge temperature works out to 481 K. The calculation follows the standard isentropic relation, in which the discharge temperature is obtained from the inlet temperature and the pressure ratio through the heat-capacity ratio, and substituting the values given above leads directly to the stated result. The relation depends only on the inlet temperature, the pressure ratio and the heat-capacity ratio, all of which are given in the statement of the example. It is important to note that the isentropic estimate is an idealised figure: it excludes mechanical losses altogether, and the measured discharge temperature of the installed machine is, in practice, higher than the estimate. The isentropic value should therefore be regarded as the reference figure for the stated pressure rise, against which the actual performance of the machine can be compared, rather than as a prediction of the temperature that will be measured in service. Engineers generally treat the isentropic discharge temperature as a benchmark figure: it is the temperature that a perfect machine would deliver for the same duty, and any real machine will deliver something higher.

Substitution of the stated values gives a discharge temperature of 481 K. The discharge temperature rises with the pressure ratio because the work of compression enters the gas as internal energy, and the heat-capacity ratio fixes how much of that work appears as a temperature rise. The calculation treats the compression as a single stage throughout, with the stated inlet temperature at the stage inlet and the stated pressures at the stage boundaries.

The result is the isentropic estimate for the stated pressure rise. Isentropic compression is reversible and adiabatic, and the estimate excludes mechanical losses. The estimate is stated for nitrogen at the stated inlet condition.

subtype: worked example with equation: Fourier conduction
fact_base: A flat stainless steel wall has thickness 12 mm and thermal conductivity $k$ of 16 W m-1 K-1. The temperature difference $\Delta T$ across the wall is 207 K, giving a heat flux $q$ of 276000 W m-2. The calculation is steady and one-dimensional; film resistances are excluded.
input:
Fourier's law is the basic relation for conduction, and for steady, one-dimensional conduction through a flat wall it relates the heat flux $q$ to the temperature difference $\Delta T$ across the wall. In the present example, the wall is made of stainless steel and has a thickness of 12 mm, with a thermal conductivity $k$ of 16 W m-1 K-1, and the temperature difference $\Delta T$ across the wall is 207 K. Taking $\Delta x$ to denote the wall thickness, Fourier's law can be written as follows:

$$q = k \frac{\Delta T}{\Delta x}$$

where $q$ is the heat flux, $k$ is the thermal conductivity, $\Delta T$ is the temperature difference across the wall and $\Delta x$ is the wall thickness. Substituting the values given above, with the thickness expressed in metres, gives $q = 16 \times 207 / 0.012$, so that the heat flux comes out at 276000 W m-2. It should be noted that the calculation is steady and one-dimensional, and that film resistances have been excluded, so the figure obtained is the flux through the wall alone under the stated temperature difference; if film resistances were included, the same overall temperature difference would produce a lower flux, because the films would add resistance in series with the wall.

With $\Delta x$ denoting the wall thickness, Fourier's law gives

$$q = k \frac{\Delta T}{\Delta x}$$

where $q$ is the heat flux, $k$ is the thermal conductivity, $\Delta T$ is the temperature difference across the wall and $\Delta x$ is the wall thickness. Substitution of the stated values, with the thickness in metres, gives $q = 16 \times 207 / 0.012$, and the heat flux is 276000 W m-2. The heat flux is the rate of heat transfer per unit area of wall, and its direction is from the hot face to the cold face. The calculation is steady and one-dimensional, and film resistances are excluded; with film resistances included, the same overall temperature difference would give a lower flux, because each film adds resistance in series with the wall. The flux is large because the wall is thin: the same temperature difference across a thicker wall gives a flux reduced in inverse proportion to the thickness, as the relation shows. Fourier's law applies to conduction through the material of the wall, and the stated conditions fix the regime in which the relation is used here.

fact_base: Project proposal for a fleet electrification, in four sections: case, costs, schedule, and decision requested. Capital cost is $1453k with a 7-year appraisal horizon. The schedule section gives a start one quarter after approval; no contractor is named. The decision requested is approval to proceed to detailed design, not to construction.
input:
Case

This proposal concerns the company's vehicle fleet, which carries all of the company's delivery and service work and which currently runs entirely on diesel bought at retail prices. Fuel represents the largest single running cost, and it is a cost whose price is set entirely outside the company's control. At the same time, maintenance costs tend to rise as the fleet ages, and the oldest vehicles are the ones that spend the most time off the road. It is important to appreciate that replacement is already due for part of the fleet on age grounds alone, which means that the real choice is not between spending money and not spending money. The choice is between diesel replacements and electric replacements at a renewal point that will be reached in either case.

Electric vehicles are well suited to the greater part of the work the fleet carries out. Most routes are planned in advance, return to the depot each night, and sit comfortably within the range of the vehicles now available on the market. Overnight parking at the depot provides a long and predictable window for charging, and charging at the depot avoids any dependence on public charging infrastructure away from base. A minority of duties, however, do not suit early replacement: long routes with no fixed pattern, duties involving heavy payloads carried over distance, and work that depends on rapid turnaround away from base. Those vehicles will remain diesel at this stage and will be reconsidered when their own replacements fall due.

Drivers and depot staff have been consulted about the shape of the proposed change. The concerns they raised centred on range on the longest days, charging discipline at the depot, and cover arrangements when a vehicle is held for repair. Each of these concerns is addressed by the phasing set out in the schedule section below: replacement begins with the duties that suit electric operation best, and diesel cover is retained while the electric fleet settles into service.

It is also worth emphasising that the depot sits at the centre of the whole proposal. Every vehicle returns there, every charge is taken there, and the electrical capacity of the site therefore sets the pace of the entire change. A fleet that had to charge away from base would carry a rather different cost structure and a different risk profile. The proposal is accordingly built on depot charging throughout, and those duties that cannot return to the depot at night are among the ones held back for later replacement.

Costs

The capital cost of the proposal is $1453k. This capital covers the electric vehicles themselves together with the charging installation at the depot, including the chargers, the electrical works that the chargers require, and the civil works for the charging bays. Vehicle purchase accounts for the larger part of the capital. The depot works are the element most exposed to what the detailed design eventually finds, both in the ground and in the capacity of the existing electrical intake.

Running costs will change in structure rather than simply in size. Electricity replaces diesel as the energy cost, and overnight charging draws power at the hours when the depot is otherwise idle. Maintenance on the electric vehicles is expected to fall, because the drivetrain contains fewer wearing parts and because braking energy recovery reduces brake wear. Tyres, bodywork and damage costs remain unchanged in kind. Set against these changes are costs that diesel operation does not carry at all: charger maintenance, charge-management services, and the eventual battery replacement on those vehicles that are kept longest in service.

The appraisal horizon is 7 years. Residual values at the end of that horizon are uncertain for both fleets, and the appraisal treats them cautiously rather than resting the case on a favourable residual assumption. Battery life is the largest open cost item. The appraisal makes no battery-replacement allowance within the horizon and instead records the exposure as a risk to be carried into the detailed design stage, where vehicle selection and warranty terms will be able to price it. Two price exposures effectively change places under the proposal: diesel price exposure, which the company cannot realistically hedge at its scale, is replaced by electricity price exposure on overnight charging, which is contracted and broadly predictable over the appraisal period. Insurance, driver training and depot supervision costs are carried as unchanged in kind, and the balance between the lower energy and maintenance costs on the one hand and the new charging costs on the other is settled at the design stage, when both sides carry firm prices. Driver and depot staff training is carried within existing operating budgets and does not form part of the capital cost.

Schedule

Work will start one quarter after approval. The first stage is the detailed design, during which the depot's electrical capacity is assessed, charger positions are fixed against the parking layout, and vehicle selection is matched duty by duty against the work that each vehicle actually does. The design also settles the phasing of the programme, so that the vehicles replaced first are those whose duties suit electric operation and whose diesel predecessors are due for renewal.

Procurement follows on from the design. Vehicles are ordered against the design's selection, and the depot works are let as a separate package, so that installation can proceed while the vehicles are being built. The depot works are completed before the first vehicles arrive. Chargers are installed and commissioned on empty bays, and the charge-management system is set up and tested before it is required to carry the fleet.

Introduction is phased. Drivers receive instruction on the vehicles and on the charging routine before their own vehicles are changed, and the depot routine changes with the first group rather than after the last one. Diesel vehicles released by each phase are withdrawn at that phase, and the retained diesel cover shrinks as the electric fleet grows. The exposed dependency in the schedule is the depot electrical works: a connection upgrade, if the design shows that one is required, sits on the critical path and is commissioned before vehicle deliveries are accepted.

Two risks sit on the schedule. The first is the connection upgrade, whose timing rests with the network operator; the design stage opens that discussion before any vehicle order depends on the outcome. The second is vehicle supply against the phased plan: because orders are placed phase by phase, a delay in one phase moves that phase's withdrawals without holding up the vehicles that have already been converted. Instruction capacity is a third constraint, and training is therefore scheduled alongside the first phase rather than ahead of it.

Decision requested

Approval is requested to proceed to detailed design. Construction is not being requested at this stage, and no vehicle orders will be placed under this approval. The purpose of the design stage is to convert the estimates contained in this proposal into firm prices: depot works priced against a surveyed site, vehicles priced against named duties, and the battery exposure priced through warranty terms rather than left as an open allowance.

The design will return to the same decision body with a fixed capital price for the depot works and the charging installation, a vehicle-by-vehicle replacement list showing the duty each vehicle serves, and a phased schedule with its dependencies priced. The construction decision will then be taken on the basis of those products, not on the basis of this proposal.

If the design stage is declined, the renewal will simply proceed as like-for-like diesel replacement, vehicle by vehicle, without a priced electric alternative ever having been developed. Approving the design stage commits the design cost only. Both the construction decision and the vehicle orders remain open until the design reports. When the construction decision does come, it will be taken against three tests: the depot works at a fixed price, a vehicle list that matches vehicles to duties without spare capacity the duties do not use, and a schedule whose critical path no longer rests on an unpriced connection upgrade.

input: with the standby pump on line and the duty pump stopped, the isolation for the seal replacement is applied at the duty pump as follows. The suction valve and the discharge valve at the duty pump are closed, and both valves are locked and tagged in the closed position under the PTW. The motor of the duty pump is also electrically isolated and locked off, so that the pump cannot be started while the isolation is in place. The casing drain is then opened to the closed drain header and is left open. It should be noted that stored pressure can remain trapped in the casing even after the valves have been closed, and for this reason the drain must be proved clear and the pressure proved off before any casing bolt is slackened. The casing is vented through the vent connection until the vent runs dry, after which the vent is closed again and a check is made that no pressure builds up again while the drain is still open. The replacement itself takes about 39 min with the unit isolated, and the isolation is maintained for the whole of that period: neither valve is reopened in the meantime, and the standby pump carries the duty on its own. The isolation is recorded on the PTW, together with the valve positions as they have been left, and the pump is handed over drained, vented and proved, with the first casing bolt

The Reynolds number Re (dimensionless) is computed from density rho (kg m-3), mean velocity v (m s-1), pipe diameter D (m) and dynamic viscosity mu (Pa s) by Re = rho v D / mu. Water at 293 K: rho = 998 kg m-3, mu = 1.00 x 10-3 Pa s. Pipe diameter D = 0.025 m; mean velocity v = 1.4 m s-1. Worked result: Re = 34900 (computed as 998 x 1.4 x 0.025 / 0.001). Flow is laminar below Re = 2300 and turbulent above Re = 4000; between the two values the regime is transitional and is not assigned by the number alone.

The Reynolds number $Re$ is dimensionless. $Re$ compares the inertial effect in a flowing liquid with the viscous effect, and $Re$ is calculated from density $\rho$ (kg m-3), mean velocity $v$ (m s-1), pipe diameter $D$ (m) and dynamic viscosity $\mu$ (Pa s) by $Re = \rho v D / \mu$. Density and velocity set the inertial side of the comparison, viscosity sets the viscous side, and the diameter sets the length scale of the flow. A change in any one quantity moves the result in the direction the relation gives: a larger diameter or a higher velocity raises $Re$, and a higher viscosity lowers it.

For water at 293 K, $\rho$ is 998 kg m-3 and $\mu$ is 1.00 x 10-3 Pa s. The pipe diameter $D$ is 0.025 m and the mean velocity $v$ is 1.4 m s-1. Substitution gives $Re$ = 998 x 1.4 x 0.025 / 0.001 = 34900.

Flow is laminar below $Re$ = 2300 and turbulent above $Re$ = 4000; between the two values the regime is transitional and is not assigned by the number alone. The calculated value, 34900, stands above the upper threshold, and the flow is turbulent. The check is the threshold comparison itself: the result does not fall in the transitional band, so the regime follows from the number without a further condition. The result rests on the stated properties of water at 293 K, and a different temperature would enter the calculation through the density and the viscosity.

fact_base: A tutorial passage explains representative sampling of an effluent stream. The passage covers where samples are taken, how many increments form one sample, and why a single grab sample misleads. No numerical limits are quoted; regulatory limits belong to the site's permit, not to the passage.
input:
A representative sample of an effluent stream is a portion of the stream that carries the composition of the whole over the period the sample stands for. The composition of an effluent changes with the operations that feed the stream, and the sampling arrangement is designed around that variation.

Samples are taken at a point where the stream is well mixed and where the full flow passes, so that the portion drawn off genuinely has the composition of the stream at that moment. A point downstream of a junction or a weir, where the flow is turbulent and thoroughly blended, gives a mixed sample, whereas a point in a quiet side leg gives the composition of that leg, not of the stream.

A single sample is formed from a number of increments that are taken over the discharge period. Each increment is small and is drawn at intervals throughout the period, and the increments are then combined and mixed before the sample is analysed. In this way, the combined sample averages out the variation that any single moment would otherwise freeze into the result.

A single grab sample, by contrast, can be seriously misleading, because it presents the composition at one particular moment as though that moment stood for the whole period. A discharge that varies over the course of a shift will produce a grab result that depends largely on when the bottle happened to be filled, and two grab samples taken from the same stream can differ appreciably without there having been any change in the underlying discharge. It should be noted that no numerical limits are stated here: the limits that apply to the effluent are set out in the site's permit.

fact_base: Performance of a natural-draft tower at a chemical site was logged over one summer month. Mean wet-bulb temperature was 27 °C, the approach was 6 K and the range was 11 K. Performance outside the logged month, in particular at winter wet-bulb temperatures, was not measured.
input:
The performance of the natural-draft tower at the chemical site was logged over the course of one summer month. The approach is defined as the difference between the temperature of the cooled water leaving the tower and the wet-bulb temperature of the air entering it, while the range is the fall in the temperature of the water across the tower, from the hot water entering to the cooled water leaving. Over the month that was logged, the mean wet-bulb temperature was 27 °C, the approach was 6 K and the range was 11 K.

A natural-draft tower relies on buoyancy alone to move its air, and the wet-bulb temperature of the ambient air effectively sets the limit towards which the water can be cooled. The approach therefore indicates how close the tower managed to bring the water to that limit over the month in question, while the range indicates the amount of cooling that the water actually received over the same period. Both figures are monthly means over the logged operation, which means that they describe the tower as it actually ran, at the loads and water rates of that particular month, rather than a rating at some fixed duty. It should also be noted that the cooled water left the tower at the stated approach above the mean wet-bulb temperature throughout the period covered by the logging.

Performance outside the logged month was not measured. In particular, performance at winter wet-bulb temperatures was not measured at all, and the values obtained from the summer logging should not be taken to state what approach or range the tower will hold during the winter.

The range is the fall in water temperature across the tower, from the hot water entering to the cooled water leaving. Over the logged month, the mean wet-bulb temperature was 27 °C, the approach was 6 K and the range was 11 K.

The approach states how close the tower brought the water to that limit over the month, and the range states the cooling the water received in the same period. The cooled water left the tower at the stated approach above the mean wet-bulb temperature. Both values are monthly means over the logged operation: the values describe the tower as it ran, at the loads and water rates of that month, and not a rating at a fixed duty.

The two means are read together: a tower that cools through the stated range while holding the stated approach at the logged wet-bulb temperature performed as logged across the whole month, through its hotter and cooler days alike. The logging covers the tower's own operation only; the duty the tower serves sits outside the record. Performance outside the logged month was not measured. In particular, performance at winter wet-bulb temperatures was not measured, and the logged values do not state what approach or range the tower holds in winter.

fact_base: A tutorial passage explains feedback control through a temperature loop on a process vessel. The passage covers the sensor, the controller, the final element and the sign of the feedback, in that order. No tuning numbers are given; the passage explains structure, not settings.
input: Feedback control is best understood as a continuous conversation between a process and the equipment that watches over it, and a temperature loop on a process vessel offers a particularly clear window into that conversation. At the start of the loop stands the sensor, whose task is to observe the temperature of the material inside the vessel and to turn that observation into a signal that can travel onward. Without that signal, nothing else in the loop has anything to respond to, because the loop can only act on what it knows. The signal then reaches the controller, which compares the measured temperature with the desired temperature and considers not merely whether the two differ, but also the direction in which they differ. This comparison is the quiet decision point of the whole arrangement. Once the controller has formed its response, the instruction passes to the final element, the part of the loop that actually touches the process by changing the flow of heating or cooling medium that serves the vessel. It is at this point that information becomes action. Finally, the sign of the feedback completes the picture: the action taken is arranged to oppose the original deviation, so that a vessel growing hotter receives less heating effect, not more, and a vessel growing cooler receives more. The loop therefore works against its own error, repeatedly and patiently, which is precisely what makes it feedback rather than a one-way command passed down a chain. Each element, in other words, earns its place by what it hands to the next, and the chain is only as strong as the signal that travels along it from measurement to action.
target: A temperature loop on a process vessel has four parts in a fixed order: sensor, controller, final element, and the sign of the feedback. The sensor measures the temperature of the vessel contents and transmits the measurement as a signal. Measurement is the only information the loop holds; an unmeasured change in temperature produces no response until the sensor registers it. The controller receives the measurement and compares it with the set point, the desired temperature for the vessel contents. Comparison gives both the size of the error and its direction, and the controller sets its output from the two. The final element receives the controller output and changes the manipulated stream, the heating or cooling flow that serves the vessel. Action on the process occurs only at the final element; the sensor and the controller handle information alone. The sign of the feedback is negative. A temperature above the set point moves the final element to reduce the heating effect or increase the cooling effect, and a temperature below the set point moves the final element in the opposite direction. Each action opposes the deviation that produced it. The loop repeats the sequence continuously: measurement, comparison, action, and a further measurement of the changed temperature. The passage states structure only. No tuning values are given, and no response strength or speed follows from the structure alone. The order of the parts matters because each part depends on the part before it. A controller with no measurement has no error to answer, and a final element with no controller output has no instruction to follow. The sign completes the loop only when the action is arranged against the deviation; the same hardware joined with the opposite sign would drive the temperature away from the set point instead of toward it.

fact_base: Excerpt content: a budget overrun of 6 weeks is reported with its cause; the excerpt proposes one mitigation and its owner. The excerpt does not open or close the memo and does not restate its subject line.
input: What the current position shows, when all of the moving parts are considered together, is a completion date that has slipped and a plan that has not yet absorbed the slip. The overrun stands at 6 weeks, and it did not arise from a general loss of momentum across the whole project. Fabrication and delivery of the main equipment package finished late, and every activity that depended on that package moved with it. Work planned against delivered equipment waited, while the work that could proceed without the package was, in practice, too small to absorb the crews released by the delay. The EPC forecast now carries the overrun in the completion date itself rather than in float, because the float on the affected chain has already been used. Against that background, the proposal placed before the project board is a single mitigation: the remaining installation work is resequenced around the delayed package, so that activities with no dependence on the package move forward and the installation crews take those activities in place of the waiting work. It should be said plainly that resequencing does not recover the full overrun, since part of the delay sits in activities that cannot begin before the package arrives, and no rearrangement of later work can remove that part. What the mitigation does is limit further loss, at the cost of managerial attention and a tighter set of interfaces between activities, because resequenced work starts with less slack than the original plan allowed. The sequence, once changed, is also the basis on which progress is reported, so that the waiting work is shown as waiting and not as slow work. The board, as owner of the mitigation, reviews the resequenced plan at each status meeting and holds the sequence unless a further delay changes the order in which the activities depend on one another.
