subtype: worked example with equation: available NPSH
fact_base: A pump draws water from an open tank at atmospheric pressure, 101.3 kPa. Vapour pressure at the pumping temperature is 19.9 kPa, the static lift is 1.3 m and suction-line friction loss is 0.5 m. Available net positive suction head $NPSH_a$ is 6.5 m. The pump's required NPSH at the duty flow comes from the vendor curve and must be exceeded with margin.
input:
When a pump draws liquid from an open tank, the question that quietly governs whether the machine will run without cavitation is how much head remains at the suction side once every loss along the way has taken its share. Available net positive suction head, $NPSH_a$, expresses exactly that remaining margin as a head. Consider a pump drawing water from an open tank whose surface stands open to the atmosphere. The pressure at that surface, $P_{atm}$, is 101.3 kPa, while the vapour pressure of the water at the pumping temperature, $P_v$, is 19.9 kPa. Between the tank surface and the pump, the liquid must be lifted through a static lift, $h_{lift}$, of 1.3 m, and it loses a further share of its head to friction in the suction line, $h_f$, of 0.5 m. The relationship that gathers these quantities together is written as

$$NPSH_a = \frac{P_{atm} - P_v}{\rho g} - h_{lift} - h_f$$

where $\rho$ denotes the density of the water and $g$ denotes gravitational acceleration. When the stated values are placed into the relationship, the available net positive suction head comes out at 6.5 m. The structure of the calculation is worth pausing over: the pressure difference between the atmosphere and the vapour pressure is first converted into a head of water, and the lift and the friction loss are then subtracted from that head, because both of them consume part of it before the liquid reaches the impeller. The number on its own, however, is not the end of the matter. The pump's required NPSH at the duty flow is obtained from the vendor curve, and the available head must exceed that required value with margin; a merely equal value would leave nothing in hand for the difference between the conditions of the curve and the conditions of actual service.
target:
Available net positive suction head, $NPSH_a$, is the margin between the pressure available at the pump suction and the vapour pressure of the liquid, stated as a head. Determine $NPSH_a$ for a pump drawing water from an open tank. The tank surface is open to the atmosphere, and the pressure at the surface, $P_{atm}$, is 101.3 kPa. The vapour pressure of the water at the pumping temperature, $P_v$, is 19.9 kPa. The static lift from the tank surface to the pump, $h_{lift}$, is 1.3 m, and the friction loss in the suction line, $h_f$, is 0.5 m. The relation is

$$NPSH_a = \frac{P_{atm} - P_v}{\rho g} - h_{lift} - h_f$$

where $\rho$ denotes the density of the water and $g$ denotes gravitational acceleration. Substitution of the stated pressures and losses gives $NPSH_a$ = 6.5 m. The pressure term converts the excess of atmospheric pressure over vapour pressure into a head of water. The lift and the friction loss are subtracted from that head because both are consumed before the liquid reaches the impeller. An open tank fixes the surface pressure at atmospheric pressure; a closed or pressurised tank would change the first term of the relation and with it the result. The check on the result is a comparison rather than a second calculation. The pump's required NPSH at the duty flow is obtained from the vendor curve, and $NPSH_a$ must exceed the required value with margin. Equality with the required value leaves no allowance for the difference between curve conditions and service conditions. The stated result is valid at the stated lift and suction-line loss; a higher lift or a restricted suction line lowers $NPSH_a$ by the added loss. The result also shows the place of each term. The vapour pressure sets the floor of the pressure term: a warmer liquid with a higher vapour pressure leaves a smaller excess over that floor, and the available head falls before any loss in the line is counted.

subtype: worked example with equation: log-mean difference
fact_base: A countercurrent exchanger cools a process stream from 200 °C to 150 °C with water entering at 40 °C and leaving at 75 °C. The terminal differences are 125 K and 110 K, and the log-mean temperature difference $\Delta T_{lm}$ is 117.3 K. The log-mean value assumes constant overall coefficient and no phase change.
input:
In a countercurrent heat exchanger, the temperature difference that drives heat from one stream to the other is not the same at the two ends of the unit, and a single representative value is needed before the exchanger can be sized. The log-mean temperature difference, $\Delta T_{lm}$, is precisely that representative value. Consider an exchanger in which a process stream is cooled from 200 °C to 150 °C while the cooling water that serves it enters at 40 °C and leaves at 75 °C. Because the flow is countercurrent, the ends of the exchanger pair the streams in a particular way: at one end, the entering process stream faces the leaving water, and at the other end, the leaving process stream faces the entering water. Working through those pairings, the terminal differences come out at 125 K at the hot end and 110 K at the cold end. The log-mean temperature difference is then defined by the relation

$$\Delta T_{lm} = \frac{\Delta T_1 - \Delta T_2}{\ln(\Delta T_1 / \Delta T_2)}$$

where $\Delta T_1$ and $\Delta T_2$ denote the terminal differences at the hot and cold ends. Placing the two terminal differences into this relation gives a log-mean temperature difference of 117.3 K. It is worth noticing where that value sits: between the two terminal differences, and closer to the smaller of them, which is exactly where a logarithmic mean of two unequal quantities is expected to fall. The value rests on the assumptions that accompany it, namely that the overall coefficient stays constant along the exchanger and that neither stream changes phase; under those conditions, the log-mean value is the driving force the sizing calculation requires. The countercurrent pairing is what gives those two differences their meaning, since each one is read across the same end of the unit rather than along a single stream.
target:
A countercurrent exchanger cools a process stream with water, and the log-mean temperature difference $\Delta T_{lm}$ is the mean driving force used in the sizing relation. Calculate $\Delta T_{lm}$ from the terminal temperatures. The process stream cools from 200 °C to 150 °C, and the water enters at 40 °C and leaves at 75 °C. Countercurrent flow pairs the entering process stream with the leaving water at the hot end, and the leaving process stream with the entering water at the cold end. The terminal differences are 125 K at the hot end and 110 K at the cold end. The log-mean temperature difference is defined by

$$\Delta T_{lm} = \frac{\Delta T_1 - \Delta T_2}{\ln(\Delta T_1 / \Delta T_2)}$$

where $\Delta T_1$ and $\Delta T_2$ denote the terminal differences at the hot and cold ends. Substitution of the two terminal differences gives $\Delta T_{lm}$ = 117.3 K. The value lies between the two terminal differences and nearer the smaller one; a logarithmic mean of two unequal positive quantities has that position, and the position is the check on the calculation. An arithmetic mean of the same two differences would sit higher and would overstate the driving force over most of the exchanger length. The result assumes a constant overall coefficient along the exchanger and no phase change in either stream. The log-mean construction is limited to those conditions: a stream that changes phase holds its temperature over part of the length, and the driving force in that part is not described by the terminal differences in the same way. The two terminal differences are not interchangeable in the construction. Each belongs to its own end of the exchanger, and pairing the streams wrongly would produce differences that describe an arrangement the unit does not have. Countercurrent flow keeps the difference between the streams more nearly even along the length than the alternative arrangement, and the log-mean value summarises that profile for the sizing relation.

fact_base: Carbon dioxide and hydrogen react over a copper-zinc oxide catalyst to give methanol. Space-time yield is the mass of product per unit catalyst volume per hour (kg L-1 h-1). Test conditions: 250 °C, 50 bar, feed ratio H2/CO2 = 3, one feed composition. Washcoated monolith catalyst: space-time yield 0.88 kg L-1 h-1, pressure drop 0.24 bar, activity loss 9% after 100 h. Extruded pellet catalyst: space-time yield 0.32 kg L-1 h-1, pressure drop 1.57 bar, activity loss 18% after 100 h. No sulfur-bearing feed was tested. Yield and pressure drop are seldom reported for the same catalyst charge.
input: The conversion of carbon dioxide and hydrogen into methanol over a copper-zinc oxide catalyst is a reaction of considerable practical interest, and the form in which the catalyst is deployed can matter as much as the chemistry itself. This study sets the two forms side by side on one feed composition. Space-time yield, in this context, is the mass of product formed per unit catalyst volume per hour. The tests themselves were carried out at 250 °C and 50 bar with feed ratio H2/CO2 = 3. The washcoated monolith gave a space-time yield of 0.88 kg L-1 h-1, a pressure drop of 0.24 bar, and an activity loss of 9% after 100 h. The extruded pellet, by contrast, gave 0.32 kg L-1 h-1, a pressure drop of 1.57 bar, and an activity loss of 18% after 100 h. Read together, the figures paint a consistent picture: under the conditions tested, the monolith produced more methanol per unit volume, imposed a smaller resistance on the flowing gas, and gave up a smaller share of its activity over the test period than the pellet form did. That picture, however, comes with boundaries that should be kept firmly in view. No sulfur-bearing feed was tested at any point, and it is also the case that yield and pressure drop are seldom reported for the same catalyst charge, which makes comparisons of this kind harder to assemble than they might appear.
target: Carbon dioxide and hydrogen react over a copper-zinc oxide catalyst to give methanol, and two catalyst forms are compared on one feed composition. Space-time yield is the mass of product per unit catalyst volume per hour. The tests ran at 250 °C and 50 bar with feed ratio H2/CO2 = 3. The washcoated monolith gave a space-time yield of 0.88 kg L-1 h-1, a pressure drop of 0.24 bar, and an activity loss of 9% after 100 h. The extruded pellet gave 0.32 kg L-1 h-1, a pressure drop of 1.57 bar, and an activity loss of 18% after 100 h. The monolith has the higher yield, the lower pressure drop, and the smaller activity loss under the stated conditions. The ranking is a ranking of the two forms as charged and tested; it is not a ranking of the catalyst material in other forms or on other feeds. Pressure drop is stated for the catalyst charge as tested, and the activity losses are stated at the end of the same test period for both forms. The comparison is limited to the stated feed composition, temperature, and pressure. No sulfur-bearing feed was tested. Yield and pressure drop are seldom reported for the same catalyst charge, and the comparison inherits that limit. The three measures describe the same charges under the same conditions, and all three favour the same form. No measure in the set runs against the ranking the other two give.

fact_base: An operating-manual chapter for a plate heat exchanger, in four sections: start-up, normal operation, alarms, and shutdown. The alarms section lists two alarms and the operator action for each; no other alarms are introduced. The chapter addresses the operator directly and uses imperative verbs for actions.
input:
Start-up
Before you bring the exchanger into service, walk the unit and satisfy yourself that the plate pack is correctly assembled, that the frame is closed up evenly, and that every connection to the exchanger is made and tight. Check that the gaskets are seated along the plates and that no gasket material is displaced or trapped where it does not belong. Set the vents and drains as the lineup requires, with the vents open for filling and the drains closed. Fill the cold side first, slowly, and let the air leave through the vent until a steady stream of liquid appears; then close the vent. Fill the hot side in the same patient way. Rushing the fill traps air in the pack, and trapped air shows itself later as poor heat transfer and misleading temperatures. With both sides full, look carefully along the plate pack edges and around every connection for leakage, and deal with any leak you find before heat is applied. Start the cold-side flow and establish it steadily, then bring in the hot-side flow gradually. Sudden flow changes slam the pack and stress the gaskets, so make every change in small steps and watch the temperatures and pressures respond between steps. As the outlet temperatures move toward their normal values, confirm that the flows are steady, that no new leakage has appeared, and that the instruments read consistently with one another. Only when the exchanger is full, vented, tight, and steady should you regard the start-up as complete and hand the unit over to normal operation. Take the transport covers and blanks off before you fill, and make sure nothing has been left inside a connection. Prove each vent and drain clear as you fill by the discharge you see from it. Fill each side on its own where the fluids differ, and let the pressure build with the flow rather than ahead of it, pausing as you go so that any leak has time to declare itself; a joint that looks dry early on can still weep once the unit is warm and flowing properly.
Normal operation
During normal operation, your task is to keep the exchanger inside its normal pattern of temperatures, flows, and pressure drops, and to notice departures from that pattern early. Read the inlet and outlet temperatures on both sides, the flow on each side, and the pressure drop across the unit, and compare each reading with the pattern the exchanger has shown when clean and correctly lined up. Heat transfer that falls away while the pressure drop climbs is the familiar signature of fouling building on the plates. A pressure drop that rises suddenly points instead to a blockage or a wrongly set valve rather than to gradual fouling. Make changes to flow or temperature gradually, in small steps, because the plate pack and its gaskets answer sudden changes with stress they were not meant to carry. Keep the vents and drains closed and guarded while the unit is pressurised, and never loosen any part of the frame or any connection while pressure is on the exchanger. If leakage appears at the plate pack edge or at a connection, reduce the load on the unit and report the leak; do not attempt to correct leakage on a pressurised exchanger by tightening. Keep the area around the unit clear so that leaks are visible and access for inspection is not blocked. Record the readings at the routine rounds, because the trend across rounds, rather than any single reading, is what reveals fouling and drift. Read the readings as a set, because a change on one side shows up as a temperature change on the other. Judge the pressure drop at a steady flow, not while the flow is moving, and compare like with like between rounds, at the same flows where the duty allows. A gentle drift in the outlet temperatures at unchanged flows is heat transfer quietly going away, and that trend, not a single bad reading, is what justifies planning a cleaning opening.
Alarms
Two alarms are provided on this unit, and no others. The first is the high temperature alarm. When the high temperature alarm sounds, reduce the hot-side flow to cut the heat input, and check the cold-side flow and the position of the temperature control valve. If the temperature continues to rise after those actions, shut the hot side down and follow the shutdown procedure; do not hold a rising temperature by repeated small adjustments. The second is the low flow alarm. When the low flow alarm sounds, check that the pump on the affected side is running and that the valves in that line are open as the lineup requires. While the flow stays low, reduce the heat input to match the reduced flow. If the flow cannot be restored, shut the unit down in the normal order and report the cause before any restart. In both cases, acknowledge the alarm only after you have taken the stated action, and record the alarm, the action, and the result in the log. Whatever the alarm, act first and investigate in the order given; an alarm acknowledged and then left alone is worse than one left sounding, because the log then claims a response that never happened. If an alarm comes back after it has cleared, treat it as a new event and act again, and pass repeated alarms on in the record so that the next operator can see the pattern. Alarms are not to be silenced, bridged, or taken out of service to keep the unit running.
Shutdown
When you shut the exchanger down, reverse the order in which you started it. Reduce the hot-side flow first and let the heat input fall away, keeping the cold side flowing while the unit cools, because a hot, stagnant exchanger fouls and stresses its gaskets. When the temperatures have fallen toward the cold-side temperature, stop the hot-side flow completely, then stop the cold-side flow. Close the isolation valves on both sides. Open the vents and let the pressure fall to nothing before you open any drain, and confirm that the pressure has gone before you touch any connection. Drain both sides fully, and leave the unit drained and vented if it is to stand idle. Apply the locks and tags that the site practice requires for any later work on the unit. Report any leakage, damaged gasket, or distorted plate you noticed during the shutdown, and record the state in which the unit was left, so that the next start-up begins from a known condition. Once the unit is drained, look into the open connections for deposits, pieces of damaged gasket, and standing product, and put what you find in the shutdown record. If the pack is opened, support it as the frame comes off and keep the plates in their order. Store gaskets flat and out of heat and sunlight, and cover the open connections against dirt and weather, so that the unit you leave is one the next start-up can trust.
target:
Start-up
Inspect the exchanger before filling. Confirm that the plate pack is assembled correctly, the frame is closed evenly, the gaskets are seated, and every connection is made and tight. Set the vents open for filling and the drains closed. Fill the cold side slowly and vent the air until liquid flows steadily from the vent, then close the vent. Fill the hot side in the same way. A fast fill traps air in the pack; trapped air lowers heat transfer and falsifies the temperature readings. Check the plate pack edges and every connection for leakage with both sides full, and clear any leak before heat is applied. Establish the cold-side flow first and hold it steady. Bring the hot-side flow in gradually, in small steps, and watch the temperatures and pressures between steps; sudden changes stress the pack and the gaskets. The start-up is complete when the exchanger is full, vented, tight, and steady at its normal lineup, with the instruments in agreement. Remove the covers and blanks fitted for transport or storage before filling, and confirm that no tool, rag, or loose material has been left in any connection. Check that the drain and vent connections are clear by opening each briefly during filling and watching for a free discharge. Where the two sides carry different fluids, fill and vent each side separately and keep the sides separate throughout; a partly filled side reads as a false temperature pattern on the other side. Bring the pressure up with the flow, not ahead of it, and hold at each stage long enough for a leak to show. A joint that is dry at low flow may still weep when the flow and temperature reach their working pattern, and the start-up is not finished until the unit has been seen dry at that pattern.
Normal operation
Hold the exchanger at its normal pattern of temperatures, flows, and pressure drops, and read departures from that pattern early. Read the inlet and outlet temperatures on both sides, the flow on each side, and the pressure drop across the unit at the routine rounds, and record the readings. The trend across rounds carries the information; a single reading does not. Falling heat transfer with a rising pressure drop is fouling on the plates. A sudden rise in pressure drop is a blockage or a wrongly set valve, not gradual fouling, and it is investigated as such. Make every change of flow or temperature gradually. Keep the vents and drains closed while the unit is pressurised. Never loosen the frame or any connection under pressure. A leak at the plate pack edge or at a connection is reported and the load on the unit is reduced; leakage is not corrected by tightening a pressurised exchanger. Keep access around the unit clear, so leaks stay visible and inspection is not blocked. Keep the two sides in balance as the process requires; a change made on one side appears as a temperature change on the other, and the readings are always read as a set. Watch the pressure drop at steady flow rather than during changes, because a changing flow moves the pressure drop for reasons that have nothing to do with the state of the plates. Where the duty allows, note the outlet temperatures at the same flows each round, so that rounds can be compared directly. A slow drift in outlet temperature at unchanged flows is heat transfer being lost, and it is planned for cleaning on the evidence of the trend, not on the evidence of a single poor reading. Do not wait for the duty to fail before acting on a clear trend, and do not open the unit on a weak one.
Alarms
Two alarms are provided, and no others. High temperature: reduce the hot-side flow to cut the heat input, and check the cold-side flow and the position of the temperature control valve. If the temperature continues to rise, shut the hot side down and follow the shutdown section; a rising temperature is not held by repeated small adjustments. Low flow: check that the pump on the affected side is running and that the valves in that line are open as the lineup requires. Reduce the heat input to match the reduced flow while the flow stays low. If the flow cannot be restored, shut the unit down in the normal order and report the cause before any restart. Acknowledge each alarm after the stated action has been taken, and record the alarm, the action, and the result in the log. Treat every alarm as an instruction to act first and to investigate in the order stated. An alarm that is acknowledged and left is worse than an alarm left sounding, because the record then shows a response that did not happen. If an alarm returns after the stated action has been taken and the condition has cleared, treat the return as a new event and repeat the stated action rather than assuming the first event is still running. Report repeated alarms at the end of the round, with the times taken from the log, so that a pattern of returns is visible to the next operator. No alarm is to be suppressed, bridged, or left out of service to keep the unit running.
Shutdown
Reduce the hot-side flow first and let the heat input fall away. Keep the cold side flowing while the unit cools; a hot, stagnant exchanger fouls and stresses its gaskets. When the temperatures have fallen toward the cold-side temperature, stop the hot-side flow, then stop the cold-side flow. Close the isolation valves on both sides. Open the vents and confirm that the pressure has fallen to nothing before any drain is opened or any connection is touched. Drain both sides fully. Leave the unit drained and vented if it is to stand idle, and apply the locks and tags the site practice requires for later work. Report any leakage, damaged gasket, or distorted plate found during the shutdown, and record the state in which the unit was left. The next start-up begins from the recorded state. After draining, look into the open connections for deposits, damaged gasket material, and product left standing in the pack, and report what is found with the shutdown record. If the unit is to be opened, support the plate pack as the frame is released and keep the plates in their order, because the order is part of the assembly. Keep gaskets flat and away from heat and sunlight while the unit stands open. Cover open connections against dirt and weather. A unit left drained, vented, clean inside its connections, and recorded as such can stand without attention; a unit left wet, sealed, and unrecorded cannot be trusted at the next start-up and is inspected as an unknown unit.

fact_base: A single-stage compressor raises natural gas from 2 bar to 9 bar. Inlet temperature is 293 K. For isentropic compression with a heat-capacity ratio of 1.4, the discharge temperature is 450 K. The isentropic estimate excludes mechanical losses; the installed machine's measured discharge temperature is higher.
input: Compressing a gas in a single stage is, among other things, an exercise in watching temperature follow pressure upward. Consider a single-stage compressor handling natural gas, which it raises from 2 bar to 9 bar. The gas arrives at an inlet temperature of 293 K, and for the isentropic compression of that gas, with a heat-capacity ratio of 1.4, the discharge temperature works out at 450 K. That figure deserves a moment of attention, because it is an idealised one. The isentropic estimate is built on a compression with no mechanical losses, and a real machine is never quite so tidy: friction and the other imperfections of actual hardware add their share of heat to the gas as it passes through. It is for precisely this reason that the installed machine's measured discharge temperature is higher than the estimate. The estimate should therefore be read as the tidy limiting case against which the messier reality of the installed compressor is compared, and the gap between the two is, in effect, the thermal signature of everything the idealisation left out. None of this makes the estimate useless; it makes it a baseline, valuable exactly because it states what the compression alone would produce before the machinery adds its own contribution. Used in that spirit, the figure earns its keep: it tells the engineer what the compression itself demands, cleanly separated from what the hardware happens to add, and any discussion of the machine's condition can then begin from the size of the gap rather than from the raw discharge reading alone. That separation is the real service the idealised number performs.
target: A single-stage compressor raises natural gas from 2 bar to 9 bar, and the discharge temperature under isentropic compression is the quantity calculated here. The inlet temperature is 293 K and the heat-capacity ratio is 1.4. The isentropic estimate gives a discharge temperature of 450 K. Compression work raises the gas temperature as the pressure rises; the size of the rise is set by the pressure change and the heat-capacity ratio, and no other property of the gas enters the estimate. The estimate is limited to isentropic compression. Mechanical losses are not included in it, and the installed machine's measured discharge temperature is higher than the estimate. The difference between the measured temperature and the estimate is the part of the heating that the idealised compression does not carry. The estimate is used as the baseline for the installed machine: a measured discharge temperature at the estimate would leave the losses unaccounted for, and a measured temperature below the estimate would contradict the stated exclusion. The result is valid for the stated inlet temperature, pressures, and heat-capacity ratio. The estimate can be read in the other direction as well. A discharge temperature is the temperature the gas must reach when the stated pressure rise is produced with no loss counted; the work put into the gas appears as internal energy, and the temperature is where that work is visible. Intercooling, leakage past the moving parts, and heat exchange with the surroundings are all outside the stated case, and the case does not need them: it fixes the ideal temperature for the stated rise so that the installed machine can be compared against a case with nothing in it but compression. A machine whose measured temperature approaches the estimate is a machine whose losses are small against the work of compression; the comparison, not the estimate alone, carries that information.

fact_base: The rate constant k (s-1) of a first-order liquid-phase reaction was measured at two temperatures. At 300 K, k = 0.037 s-1. At 340 K, k = 2.581 s-1, computed from the Arrhenius relation with activation energy 90 kJ mol-1 as a derived value. Each temperature was measured in triplicate; the relative standard deviation of k was 4%. Above 340 K the solvent evaporated during sampling, so no rate constant is reported above 340 K.
input: The rate constant $k$ of a first-order liquid-phase reaction was measured at two temperatures, and the two values state the temperature dependence over the measured range. A first-order rate constant carries the unit s-1 because the rate of reaction is proportional to the concentration of the reactant; the constant itself is the proportionality factor at the stated temperature. At 300 K, $k$ was 0.037 s-1. At 340 K, $k$ was 2.581 s-1, computed from the Arrhenius relation with an activation energy of 90 kJ mol-1 as a derived value. The Arrhenius relation connects the rate constant to temperature through the activation energy, and the value at the higher temperature is reported on that basis rather than as a direct reading. Each temperature was measured in triplicate, and the relative standard deviation of $k$ was 4%. The triplicate measurements attach the same repeatability statement to each reported value; the spread is part of each result and not a separate finding. Above 340 K the solvent evaporated during sampling, so no rate constant is reported above 340 K. The measured range therefore ends at the higher temperature for a sampling reason: the sample changed while it was being taken, and a rate constant taken from a changed sample would not describe the reaction mixture. The two reported values, their common spread, and the stated end of the range are the complete result. The Arrhenius statement is the form in which the higher value is carried, and it is labelled as computed. The lower value stands as measured. Between them, the two values describe a reaction that runs faster at the higher temperature, and the description is confined to the interval the measurements cover. No value is carried beyond the upper temperature by the relation, because the sampling failure, not the relation, sets the end of the reported range.

fact_base: Pricing case for a SaaS tier: price $138 per unit, variable cost $68 per unit, fixed costs $145k per year. Break-even volume is 2071 units per year; current volume is 3238 units per year. Volume figures are last year's actuals; the effect of the price on volume is not estimated.
input: The question hanging over this particular SaaS tier is a simple one to state, even if the numbers deserve a careful read: at its current price, does the tier sell enough units to cover its costs? The tier is priced at $138 per unit, and each unit carries a variable cost of $68 per unit, which leaves a contribution of $70 per unit toward the fixed costs, a derived figure obtained by setting the two side by side. Those fixed costs stand at $145k per year. When the fixed costs are measured against the contribution, the break-even volume works out at 2071 units per year. The current volume, meanwhile, is 3238 units per year, which is to say that the tier, at its present volumes, sells comfortably more than the break-even requirement. Two cautions belong with that comfortable picture. The volume figures are last year's actuals, so the comparison is anchored in a year that has already happened rather than in a forecast. And the effect of the price on volume is not estimated anywhere in the case, so the comparison holds the present price and the present volume side by side without asking how a different price might move the volume itself.
target: The SaaS tier clears its break-even volume at last year's actual volume. The price is $138 per unit and the variable cost is $68 per unit, giving a contribution of $70 per unit, a derived figure. Fixed costs are $145k per year. Against that contribution, the break-even volume is 2071 units per year, and the current volume is 3238 units per year. The volume figures are last year's actuals, and the finding is stated on that base: the tier sold more units than the break-even volume requires in the year measured. The comparison takes the price and the volume as they stand together in the case. The effect of the price on volume is not estimated, and the break-even position under a price change is outside the case. The margin between the current volume and the break-even volume is the whole finding; it is a statement about the year measured, at the stated price and costs. Break-even volume is the volume at which the contribution from the units sold exactly covers the fixed costs for the year; below it the tier loses money on the stated costs, and above it the tier covers them. The case states no target volume and no price change, and the finding does not recommend either. What the case supports is a position statement for the year measured: the tier, as priced and as sold in that year, stood above the volume its cost structure requires.

Nothing in the comparison turns on $\Delta P$ across the joint, and nothing in it changes the NPSH position of the lean solvent pump, which sits outside the argument being made here. There is a practical edge to the narrowness of the comparison as well. The joint faces the temperature duty of the compressor discharge, and the gasket is the component that meets that duty directly; a lower-rated material would leave the joint as the weakest element in a wall that has just been thickened against corrosion, which is not a position the design can sensibly defend. fact_base: Staffing review for a maintenance crew: 16 full-time staff, overtime at 7% of paid hours last year. Replacing half the overtime with one additional hire costs $63k per year fully loaded. Overtime is concentrated in two seasonal peaks; a hire is paid for the full year.
input: The staffing question for the maintenance crew is, at bottom, a question about the shape of the year rather than about the size of the crew in the abstract. The crew currently numbers 16 full-time staff, and overtime ran at 7% of paid hours last year. One way of softening that overtime is to replace half of it with one additional hire, and the cost of doing so is $63k per year fully loaded. Set against that cost is an awkward pattern in the overtime itself: it is concentrated in two seasonal peaks, which means the hours the new hire would replace are not spread evenly across the calendar. A hire, however, is paid for the full year, in the quiet months just as in the peak months. The trade-off is therefore built into the structure of the case: the benefit of the hire arrives in the peak periods, where the cover is needed, while the cost of the hire runs continuously through the periods where it is not. Any judgement on the proposal has to weigh a full-year cost against a peak-season benefit, and the figures as stated offer no way around that weighing. Seen in that light, the proposal is neither plainly cheap nor plainly dear; it is a proposal whose cost and whose benefit arrive on different calendars, and it stands or falls on how much the peak cover is worth to the operation that has to staff those peaks.
target: The maintenance crew has 16 full-time staff, and overtime ran at 7% of paid hours last year. Replacing half the overtime with one additional hire costs $63k per year fully loaded. The trade-off is in the pattern of the overtime: the overtime is concentrated in two seasonal peaks, and a hire is paid for the full year. The hire's cost therefore runs through the quiet periods at the same rate as through the peaks, while the overtime it replaces falls only in the peaks. The case for the hire rests on cover in the peak periods; the case against rests on a cost that does not follow the pattern of the work. No figure for the cost of the overtime being replaced is stated, and the comparison is carried on the hire's cost and the overtime share alone. At the stated figures, the decision turns on whether peak cover is worth a full-year cost at the stated rate. Fully loaded cost is the whole cost of the hire: the wage and every employment cost that travels with it, stated for the full year. The overtime share is stated for the year that has passed, and the pattern within that year is the part of the evidence that decides the case. Peaks concentrate the overtime into short periods, and cover bought for a peak is cover that must be present in that period and is paid for outside it. The crew size enters the case only as the base the overtime share is measured against; the share itself, and the cost of replacing half of it, are the operative figures.

fact_base: A single-stage compressor raises nitrogen from 1 bar to 4 bar. Inlet temperature is 293 K. For isentropic compression with a heat-capacity ratio of 1.4, the discharge temperature is 435 K. The isentropic estimate excludes mechanical losses; the installed machine's measured discharge temperature is higher.
input: A single-stage machine compressing nitrogen offers a compact illustration of the same temperature story told by every isentropic estimate. The compressor raises nitrogen from 1 bar to 4 bar, and the gas enters at an inlet temperature of 293 K. For isentropic compression with a heat-capacity ratio of 1.4, the discharge temperature is 435 K. That discharge figure, like every isentropic figure, is an idealisation: the estimate deliberately leaves mechanical losses out of account, and the moving parts of a real machine return those losses to the gas as heat. It is therefore no surprise that the installed machine's measured discharge temperature is higher than the estimate. The estimate marks the floor that the compression alone would set, and the installed machine runs above that floor by exactly the amount its own imperfections contribute, which is why the two numbers belong together in any honest account of the machine. That is the real function of such an estimate in practice. It separates, cleanly and in advance, the temperature the gas must reach simply by being compressed from the further temperature the machinery of a particular installation adds on top, and it does so before a single measurement on the installed unit is taken. Discussions of condition, of fouling, of wear, and of performance all become sharper once that separation has been made, because each of them can then be attached to the gap where it belongs instead of being spread loosely over the whole discharge figure.

The inlet temperature is 293 K and the heat-capacity ratio is 1.4. The estimate gives a discharge temperature of 435 K. The temperature rise follows the pressure rise in the compression; the estimate holds the compression isentropic, and no property of the machine enters it. Nothing in it depends on the size of the compressor, the speed at which it runs, or the condition of its parts; those enter only through the losses the estimate excludes. The discharge temperature is therefore the reference temperature for the stated rise in pressure. Plant readings are compared with it in that spirit: the measured temperature is the temperature of a real compression, and the estimate is the temperature of the same compression with the machine taken out of the account. The gap between them belongs to the machine, and it is reported with the measured temperature wherever the comparison is used.

fact_base: Pervaporation is a membrane separation in which a liquid feed contacts one side of a membrane and vacuum on the other side draws the permeating component through as vapour. Flux is the mass permeating per unit membrane area per hour (kg m-2 h-1). The separation factor is the water-to-alcohol ratio in the permeate divided by the same ratio in the feed (dimensionless). Feed: 85 wt% isopropanol in water, at 60 °C. One feed composition was tested; no test ran beyond 500 h. Polymer membrane: flux 1.9 kg m-2 h-1, separation factor 120, flux fell 14% over 500 h. Zeolite membrane: flux 1 kg m-2 h-1, separation factor 560, flux unchanged over 500 h within measurement error. Flux, selectivity and stability are seldom reported together for the same membrane.
input: It is important to note that pervaporation is a membrane separation process in which a liquid feed is brought into contact with one side of a membrane, while a vacuum applied on the other side draws the permeating component through the membrane, where it emerges as a vapour. In this context, flux can be understood as the mass of material permeating per unit membrane area per hour, and the separation factor can be understood as the water-to-alcohol ratio in the permeate divided by the very same ratio in the feed. In the present comparison, two membrane types — a polymer membrane and a zeolite membrane — were evaluated using a single feed consisting of 85 wt% isopropanol in water at 60 °C. The polymer membrane delivered a flux of 1.9 kg m⁻² h⁻¹ together with a separation factor of 120, whereas the zeolite membrane delivered a flux of 1 kg m⁻² h⁻¹ together with a separation factor of 560. Furthermore, the stability behaviour differed considerably between the two options: over the course of 500 h, the flux of the polymer membrane fell by 14%, while the flux of the zeolite membrane remained essentially unchanged over 500 h, at least within measurement error. Taken together, these results highlight an interesting trade-off between throughput, selectivity, and long-term stability. It is also worth emphasising that flux, selectivity, and stability are seldom reported together for the same membrane, which makes direct comparisons of this kind relatively uncommon. Finally, it should be noted that only a single feed composition was tested and that no test was extended beyond the durations described above.
target: Pervaporation separates a liquid feed across a membrane under vacuum: the feed contacts one side of the membrane and the permeating component leaves the other side as vapour. Flux is defined as the mass permeating per unit membrane area per hour. The separation factor is defined as the water-to-alcohol ratio in the permeate divided by the same ratio in the feed. Two membranes, one polymer and one zeolite, were compared on a single feed of 85 wt% isopropanol in water at 60 °C, and each membrane was tested on the same feed, so feed composition and temperature are held fixed across the comparison. The polymer membrane gave a flux of 1.9 kg m⁻² h⁻¹ and a separation factor of 120; the zeolite membrane gave a flux of 1 kg m⁻² h⁻¹ and a separation factor of 560. The polymer membrane passes more mass per unit area per hour, and the zeolite membrane enriches the permeate more strongly in water. The zeolite membrane is the more selective membrane and the polymer membrane the faster one, and a choice between the two turns on whether throughput or enrichment governs the duty. Stability separates the pair further: over 500 h the polymer flux fell 14%, while the zeolite flux was unchanged within measurement error. Flux, selectivity and stability are seldom reported together for the same membrane, and the comparison is limited to one feed composition, with no test run beyond 500 h.

fact_base: Inventory policy for a packaging film: mean demand 3994 units per week, standard deviation 925 units per week, replenishment lead time 6 weeks. Safety stock for a 95% cycle service level is 3739 units. Demand is treated as normal and independent between weeks; seasonal peaks are excluded.
input: Safety stock plays a crucial role in ensuring that service levels are maintained in the face of variable demand, and it is therefore important to set the level in a careful and systematic manner. For the packaging film considered here, the relevant parameters are as follows: mean demand amounts to 3994 units per week, the standard deviation of weekly demand is 925 units per week, and the replenishment lead time is 6 weeks. On the basis of these parameters, and targeting a 95% cycle service level, the safety stock is set at 3739 units. In other words, holding 3739 units of safety stock is intended to ensure that demand fluctuations arising during the lead time can be accommodated in the great majority of replenishment cycles. It should be noted that this calculation rests on a number of important assumptions: demand is treated as normally distributed, demand from week to week is treated as independent, and seasonal peaks are excluded from the analysis. As a result, if a seasonal peak were to occur within a lead time, the safety stock might prove insufficient, and stockouts could occur despite the buffer that has been put in place. Overall, the figure provides a useful and practical basis for the inventory policy, provided that the underlying assumptions continue to hold for the film in question.
target: Set the safety stock for the packaging film at 3739 units. Mean demand is 3994 units per week, with a standard deviation of 925 units per week, and the replenishment lead time is 6 weeks. At a 95% cycle service level, the safety stock of 3739 units covers demand variation over the lead time at the stated service level. Cycle service level denotes the share of replenishment cycles that close without a stockout. The calculation treats demand as normal and as independent between weeks. Demand in one week carries no information about demand in the next week under the independence assumption, so variation builds across the lead time instead of cancelling. Seasonal peaks are excluded from the demand record, so the figure does not cover a seasonal peak that falls inside a lead time. A week of demand above the mean draws on the safety stock first; the stock is sized to the spread of weekly demand, not to the mean. The mean demand sets the cycle stock; the safety stock stands on top of the cycle stock and is untouched in an average week. If the lead time lengthens or the weekly spread widens, the same service level requires a larger stock, and the policy figure has to be recomputed from the new values.

fact_base: A single-stage compressor raises nitrogen from 1 bar to 4 bar. Inlet temperature is 303 K. For isentropic compression with a heat-capacity ratio of 1.4, the discharge temperature is 450 K. The isentropic estimate excludes mechanical losses; the installed machine's measured discharge temperature is higher.
input: In this example, we consider a single-stage compressor that is used to raise nitrogen from 1 bar to 4 bar, with an inlet temperature of 303 K. The objective is to estimate the discharge temperature of the machine. Compressors of this type are widely used in a wide range of industrial applications, and understanding their behaviour is an important part of process engineering practice. To do this, it is helpful to begin by making a simplifying assumption, namely that the compression process can be treated as isentropic, which essentially means that it is both reversible and adiabatic, and that mechanical losses can be neglected for the purposes of the estimate. Before turning to the calculation itself, it is useful to reflect briefly on what the isentropic assumption actually entails, since the validity of the final number depends to a large extent on the validity of this assumption. As the gas is compressed, work is done on it, and this work manifests itself as an increase in the internal energy and hence in the temperature of the gas. For nitrogen, the heat-capacity ratio is taken as 1.4. Using the well-known isentropic temperature relation for an ideal gas, together with the inlet temperature of 303 K, the pressure ratio obtained from 4 bar and 1 bar, and the heat-capacity ratio of 1.4, the discharge temperature can be calculated, and the result of the calculation is a discharge temperature of 450 K. It is worth noting, however, that this figure should be interpreted with some care. Because the isentropic estimate deliberately excludes mechanical losses, and because such losses inevitably generate additional heat in a real machine, the measured discharge temperature of the installed compressor is in practice higher than 450 K. The value of 450 K should therefore be regarded as an idealised reference value rather than as an exact prediction of the actual operating temperature. Nevertheless, despite this limitation, the isentropic estimate remains a valuable starting point for design work and for comparing the performance of different machines.
target: Calculate the isentropic discharge temperature for a single-stage compressor raising nitrogen from 1 bar to 4 bar. The inlet temperature is 303 K. The compression is taken as isentropic, and that assumption is stated before the relation that uses it: an isentropic compression is reversible and adiabatic, and mechanical losses are excluded from the estimate. The heat-capacity ratio for nitrogen is 1.4. For an ideal gas compressed isentropically, the discharge temperature is determined by the inlet temperature, the pressure ratio, and the heat-capacity ratio. The temperature rise is the direct result of the work input. Compression reduces the volume of the gas, and the work done on the gas raises its internal energy; with no heat removed during the stroke, the internal energy rise appears in full as a temperature rise. The pressure ratio fixes the strength of the compression: the discharge pressure is four times the inlet pressure, and a larger ratio at the same inlet temperature gives a higher discharge temperature. The heat-capacity ratio carries the gas property the relation needs, namely how the temperature of nitrogen responds when its volume changes without heat transfer. Substitution of the inlet temperature of 303 K, the pressure ratio formed from 4 bar over 1 bar, and the heat-capacity ratio of 1.4 into the isentropic temperature relation gives a discharge temperature of 450 K. The check on the result is its direction against the installed machine: the estimate excludes mechanical losses, and losses add heat to the gas, so the measured discharge temperature of the installed machine is higher than 450 K. The figure of 450 K is a lower reference value for the duty, valid for the isentropic idealization at the stated inlet state and pressure ratio, and not a prediction of the installed machine's discharge temperature.

fact_base: A viscous liquid of viscosity $\mu$ = 0.05 Pa s flows laminarly through a tube of radius $R$ = 10 mm and length $L$ = 11 m. At a pressure drop $\Delta P$ of 3 kPa the volumetric flow $Q$ is 77.1 L h-1. The Hagen-Poiseuille equation assumes laminar, fully developed flow of a Newtonian liquid.
input:
In this worked example, we are going to determine the volumetric flow rate of a viscous liquid flowing through a tube, and in order to do this we will make use of the well-known Hagen–Poiseuille equation. It is important to bear in mind that this equation is based on a number of assumptions, in particular that the flow is laminar and fully developed and that the liquid in question is Newtonian in its behaviour. The equation itself relates the volumetric flow $Q$ to various quantities, including the radius of the tube $R$, the length of the tube $L$, the pressure drop $\Delta P$ that occurs along the tube, and the viscosity $\mu$ of the liquid, and it can be written as follows:
$$Q = \frac{\pi R^4 \Delta P}{8 \mu L}$$
Turning now to the data that we have been given, the viscosity $\mu$ of the liquid is 0.05 Pa s, the radius $R$ of the tube is 10 mm, the length $L$ of the tube is 11 m, and the pressure drop $\Delta P$ is 3 kPa. It is interesting to observe that the radius appears in the equation raised to the fourth power, which means that the flow is extremely sensitive to the value that is used for the radius. Substituting all of these values into the equation, that is to say $\mu$ = 0.05 Pa s, $R$ = 10 mm, $L$ = 11 m and $\Delta P$ = 3 kPa, the volumetric flow $Q$ works out at 77.1 litres per hour. This figure of 77.1 litres per hour represents the flow that would be expected under the conditions that have been specified, although it should of course be remembered that it depends on the flow remaining laminar in character.
target:
Calculate the volumetric flow of a viscous liquid through a tube from the Hagen–Poiseuille equation. The Hagen–Poiseuille equation is valid for laminar, fully developed flow of a Newtonian liquid, and the assumption of laminar flow is stated here, before the equation is used. For a tube of radius $R$ and length $L$, the equation relates the volumetric flow $Q$ to the pressure drop $\Delta P$ and the viscosity $\mu$ of the liquid:
$$Q = \frac{\pi R^4 \Delta P}{8 \mu L}$$
The liquid has a viscosity $\mu$ of 0.05 Pa s. The tube radius $R$ is 10 mm, the tube length $L$ is 11 m, and the pressure drop $\Delta P$ along the tube is 3 kPa. Each symbol in the display stands for the quantity named in the set-up: the equation takes the tube geometry and the liquid property as its inputs and gives the flow as its output. The radius carries the strongest dependence in the equation, because $Q$ varies with the fourth power of $R$; a small error in the radius therefore outweighs a comparable error in the pressure drop, the viscosity, or the length. Substitution of $\mu$ = 0.05 Pa s, $R$ = 10 mm, $L$ = 11 m and $\Delta P$ = 3 kPa into the Hagen–Poiseuille equation gives a volumetric flow $Q$ of 77.1 litres per hour. The flow of 77.1 litres per hour is the value taken from the calculation for the stated liquid and tube. The result is valid at the stated pressure drop while the flow stays laminar and fully developed; a change of regime out of laminar flow removes the ground of the equation, and the same substitution would no longer give the flow.

subtype: worked example with equation: first-order decay
fact_base: A dye in effluent decomposes by first-order kinetics with rate constant $k$ = 0.098 min-1. After 30 min the fraction remaining $C / C_0$ is 0.053. The rate constant was measured at one temperature; no activation energy is available.
input:
It is well known that many decomposition reactions follow what is known as first-order kinetics, and the decomposition of the dye in the effluent that is considered here is a good example of this type of behaviour. In a first-order process, the rate at which the decomposition proceeds is directly proportional to the amount of the substance that is still present, which means that the decomposition is rapid at first and becomes progressively slower as time goes on. The rate constant $k$ for the dye has been found to be 0.098 per minute, and the question that we wish to answer is: what fraction of the dye will still remain after a period of 30 min has elapsed? The relationship between the fraction remaining and the time is given by the standard first-order decay law, in which $C$ represents the concentration at time $t$ and $C_0$ represents the initial concentration, and the law can be written in the following form:
$$\ln\frac{C}{C_0} = -k t$$
If we now substitute the values that we have been given, namely $k$ = 0.098 per minute and a time of 30 min, into this equation, we obtain a value for the fraction remaining $C/C_0$ of 0.053. This means that, after 30 min, only a relatively small proportion of the original dye, corresponding to the fraction 0.053, will still be present in the effluent. It should, however, be pointed out that this result is based on the rate constant that was measured at one particular temperature, and since no activation energy is available, it is not possible to say how the result would change if the temperature were different.
target:
A dye in effluent decomposes by first-order kinetics. First-order kinetics means that the rate of decomposition at any moment is proportional to the concentration of dye still present: the more dye remains, the faster it decomposes, and the rate falls as the concentration falls. Determine the fraction of the dye remaining after 30 min. The rate constant $k$ for the decomposition is 0.098 per minute. The rate constant was measured at one temperature, and the value is used here at that temperature. The first-order decay law relates the fraction remaining to the rate constant and the time: where $C$ denotes the concentration at time $t$ and $C_0$ denotes the concentration at the start, the law is written
$$\ln\frac{C}{C_0} = -k t$$
Substitution of $k$ = 0.098 per minute and a time of 30 min into the decay law gives the fraction remaining $C/C_0$ as 0.053. The calculation is a single substitution, because the law gives the fraction remaining directly once the rate constant and the time are fixed; no second relation and no iteration is needed. The result also fixes the shape of what follows: the decomposition continues at the same fractional rate; each further equal interval removes the same share of what is left, and the amount remaining is set by the accumulated time in the exponent rather than by the size of the residue at any one moment. The result can be checked against the limiting behaviour of the law: at the start the fraction remaining is the whole amount, and as time increases the fraction falls steadily towards zero without reaching it, so a small residue after half an hour is the behaviour the law leads one to expect. The fraction remaining, 0.053, is the share of the original dye still present at 30 min. The figure is valid at the temperature at which the rate constant was measured. No activation energy is available, so the rate constant cannot be corrected to another temperature, and the fraction at any other temperature is outside the reach of the stated data.

fact_base: Pricing case for a contract cleaning service: price $271 per unit, variable cost $129 per unit, fixed costs $144k per year. Break-even volume is 1014 units per year; current volume is 3551 units per year. Volume figures are last year's actuals; the effect of the price on volume is not estimated.
input: Break-even volume for the contract cleaning service is 1014 units per year, against a current volume of 3551 units per year. The service is priced at $271 per unit, with a variable cost of $129 per unit; each unit sold contributes the difference between price and variable cost toward fixed costs of $144k per year. The contribution per unit is the amount each unit leaves toward fixed costs after its variable cost is paid. The break-even volume is the annual volume at which that contribution covers the fixed costs in full; below it, the contribution falls short of fixed costs, and above it, the contribution exceeds them. Current volume stands well above the break-even volume, and the service covers its fixed costs at last year's volume. Both volume figures are last year's actuals. The calculation holds price and costs at their stated values, and the effect of the price on volume is not estimated: a price change would move volume by an amount the case does not quantify, and the break-even volume would have to be recomputed at the new price. The margin between current and break-even volume is a statement about last year's prices, costs and volumes, not a forecast for the coming year.

fact_base: Excerpt content: a strainer cleaning takes about 89 min with the unit isolated; the excerpt gives the isolation steps only. The excerpt warns once about stored pressure and does not repeat the warning.
input: Before the strainer can be opened up for cleaning, it is first of all necessary to take it out of service in a safe and orderly manner, and this is achieved by transferring the duty to the other pump and then isolating the strainer from the line. The standby pump should be started and allowed to settle down on the line, and once it is running steadily the duty pump can be stopped, at which point the strainer on the duty pump line is effectively out of service. The strainer is then isolated by means of its own valves: the discharge valve is closed first and the suction valve is closed second, and care should be taken to ensure that each valve is driven fully home against its stop. It is good practice to fit a lock and a tag at both of the valves and also at the duty pump starter, so that the pump cannot inadvertently be restarted against a closed line. All of this work is carried out under the PTW, and each isolation point is recorded as it is made. The body of the strainer should next be drained through its drain valve into the closed drain, and the drain is left open while the state of the body is checked. It must be remembered that the strainer body will still hold stored pressure even after the suction and discharge valves have been closed, and for this reason the vent at the top of the body is cracked open before any attempt is made to loosen a cover bolt, so that the trapped pressure can be released in a controlled manner to a safe place. The isolation can then be proved at the vent and at the drain together, and a gauge fitted at the body provides a useful second indication once the vent has stopped blowing. Taken as a whole, the cleaning takes about 89 min with the unit isolated, and the cover bolts are slackened in sequence, opposite bolts together, once the body has drained clear
target: Transfer the strainer duty before any joint is broken. Start the standby pump and let it settle on the line, then stop the duty pump; the strainer on the duty pump line is out of service once the standby pump runs steadily. Isolate the strainer at its own valves. Close the discharge valve first and the suction valve second, and drive each valve fully against its stop. Fit a lock and a tag at both valves and at the duty pump starter, so the pump cannot be restarted against a closed line. The work proceeds under the PTW, and the isolation is recorded point by point as each point is made. Drain the strainer body through its drain valve to the closed drain, and leave the drain open while the pressure state of the body is proved. The strainer body holds stored pressure after the suction and discharge valves are closed, and the vent at the top of the body is cracked open before any cover bolt is loosened, so the trapped pressure is released to a safe place in a controlled way. Prove the isolation at the vent and at the drain together: with both open and no flow from either, the body stands clear of the line pressure and the isolation holds. A gauge fitted at the body gives a second indication, and the gauge is read only after the vent has stopped blowing. Fit a blank at the suction flange where the procedure calls for a positive break, and leave the drain and vent open until the cover is off. The full cleaning takes about 89 min with the unit isolated, of which the isolation steps form the first part; the cover bolts are slackened in sequence, opposite bolts together, and the cover is eased off its face only after the last bolt is out and the body has drained clear

fact_base: Excerpt content: the analogy between the transfer processes is stated, then qualified by the case where it fails. The excerpt works one short numerical check with numbers given inside the excerpt itself. The excerpt assumes the chapter's earlier definitions and adds none.
input: It is a familiar observation in the study of transport processes that momentum, heat, and mass transfer are closely analogous to one another, since all three are brought about by essentially the same fluid motion within the fluid layer. This idea is taken a good deal further by the Chilton-Colburn analogy, which expresses the analogy in the form of a definite working relationship between the mass-transfer factor $j_D$ and the friction factor $f$, namely the relationship $j_D = f/2$, which holds good in those cases where the friction at the surface is due to skin friction alone. The practical value of this result is considerable, because it means that the mass-transfer factor can be obtained directly from a friction measurement, without the need for a separate mass-transfer experiment. By way of a short numerical illustration, if the friction factor $f$ has the value 0.0064, then the analogy gives the mass-transfer factor $j_D$ as 0.0032, so that the one quantity is read off from the other in a very straightforward way. It must be emphasised, however, that the analogy breaks down in cases where the pressure drop is produced by form drag rather than by skin friction. In the flow across a tube bank, for example, the fluid separates from the surface of each tube, and a part of the pressure drop is expended in maintaining the wake behind the tube; this contribution to the friction factor has no counterpart in mass transfer, and the value of the mass-transfer factor deduced from the friction factor will consequently be too high
target: The three transfer processes are treated together because the same fluid motion moves momentum, heat and mass through a fluid layer, and the comparison is more than a resemblance of form. The Chilton-Colburn analogy turns the comparison into a working relation between the mass-transfer factor $j_D$ and the friction factor $f$: where the friction on a surface comes from skin friction alone, the analogy sets the two equal in the form $j_D = f/2$. A friction measurement then yields the mass-transfer factor directly, with no separate mass-transfer experiment. A short check shows the size of the step the analogy takes: for a friction factor $f$ of 0.0064, the relation gives a mass-transfer factor $j_D$ of 0.0032, read off the friction factor with no further data. The check is short because the analogy leaves nothing else to determine: one measured factor supplies the other in full. The analogy fails where the pressure drop is produced by form drag rather than by skin friction. In flow across a tube bank the fluid separates from the surface of each tube, and part of the pressure drop pays for the wake behind the tube; that part of the friction factor has no counterpart in mass transfer, because the separated wake does not transfer mass in the way the attached layer does. The friction factor then counts drag the analogy cannot use, and a mass-transfer factor taken from it comes out too high, by the share of the pressure drop that the wake accounts for

fact_base: Design report for a spray dryer, in four sections: basis, sizing, materials, and risks. Design throughput is 9 t per day and the removal or separation duty is 93% of the key component. Materials are 316L stainless steel for wetted parts; the basis section states this once. The risks section names fouling and turndown as open items; neither is resolved in the report.
input:
## Basis
This report sets out the design of a spray dryer that dries a liquid feed to produce a powder product. The design throughput of the unit is 9 t per day of feed. The separation duty that is required is the removal of 93% of the key component from the feed, and the dried product is specified on the basis of this removal, in the sense that the product which leaves the dryer contains the balance of the key component that has not been removed. All wetted parts are manufactured in 316L stainless steel, and it is appropriate to state the grade once, at this point; the materials section of the report proceeds on the basis of this statement. The feed is a liquid which is capable of being pumped and atomised, and the design assumes that the feed is delivered to the battery limit of the dryer at the rate that has been stated. Operation is continuous at the design throughput, and the dryer is sized for that rate rather than for some form of campaign average. The drying gas is heated before it is admitted to the chamber, and the exhaust gas leaves the chamber together with the component that has been removed. The basis therefore establishes the duty and the rate, while matters such as the geometry of the chamber, the type of atomiser and the gas rate are dealt with in the sizing section.
## Sizing
The sizing starts from the two figures established in the basis, namely the design throughput of 9 t per day and the removal duty of 93% of the key component. The evaporation load follows directly from the duty, since the key component that is removed from the feed leaves the unit in the exhaust gas, and the gas rate is chosen in such a way as to carry this load while at the same time maintaining the outlet condition that is required by the product specification. The chamber itself is sized on the basis of the drying time of the droplets. The process of atomisation determines the size of the droplets, and the size of the droplets determines the length of time that each droplet requires in the hot gas in order to dry to the product condition; the volume of the chamber provides the droplets with this time at the design gas rate, with the margin being held in the height of the chamber rather than in a higher temperature of the gas. The atomiser is selected with reference to the feed as delivered: the feed is pumped to the atomiser at the design rate, and the atomiser must be capable of maintaining its droplet size over the operating range of the dryer. Product recovery forms an integral part of the sizing, in that the dried powder leaves the chamber together with the exhaust gas and is separated from the gas in the recovery step, which is sized for the full solids load at the design throughput. The heater is sized on the gas rate and on the temperature rise that the gas requires before it enters the chamber, and the pressure drop through the chamber, the recovery step and the connecting ducting determines the duty of the fan. The sizing concludes with a check of the whole train at the design rate.
## Materials
All wetted parts are manufactured in the stainless steel grade that has been named in the basis. The chamber, the body of the atomiser, the feed pipework and pump, the product outlet and the recovery equipment are all in contact with the feed, with the wet product or with the exhaust gas, and the grade applies to each and every one of them. The feed represents the most aggressive stream in the train: it wets the atomiser and the feed line on a continuous basis, and deposits derived from it find their way onto the wall of the chamber. The atomiser is subject to the hardest service, because the feed passes through it at considerable speed and any erosion that takes place there will alter the droplet size on which the sizing is based; for this reason the atomiser parts that are in the feed stream are treated as wearing parts and are designed to be replaceable. Product contact surfaces are finished smooth, in order that powder should not lodge in crevices and in order that cleaning should reach every surface with which the product comes into contact. Surfaces that are exposed only to dry gas are nevertheless held to the same grade in cases where condensate from the exhaust can form, because the exhaust gas carries the removed component and condensate derived from it cannot be regarded as clean water. Gaskets and seals are selected for the feed and for the cleaning fluids, and no gasket material is transferred from a different service without a suitable check being carried out.
## Risks
Two items remain open in the design at the present stage, namely fouling and turndown, and neither is resolved in this report. Fouling manifests itself at two places within the unit. In the first place, deposits build up on the wall of the chamber wherever droplets reach the wall before they have dried, and a fouled wall tends to shed lumps into the product as well as altering the flow of gas within the chamber; in the second place, deposits also build up at the atomiser, where even a small change in the atomising surface will alter the droplet size and, with it, the drying performance that the chamber was sized to deliver. The design provides cleaning access at the chamber and at the atomiser, and the cleaning interval is left to operating experience, since the deposit rate of the feed as delivered is not known at the design stage. Turndown constitutes the second open item. At rates below the design throughput, the atomiser has to maintain its droplet size on a reduced flow of feed, and it is by no means the case that all atomisers maintain droplet size as the flow is reduced; the gas rate falls together with the feed, the drying time of the droplets in the chamber becomes longer, and the product condition is maintained by the outlet temperature control operating over a narrower range. Both items are recorded in this report for attention at the next design stage.
