fact_base: Design report for a distillation column, in four sections: basis, sizing, materials, and risks. Design throughput is 32 t per day and the removal or separation duty is 90% of the key component. Materials are 316L stainless steel for wetted parts; the basis section states this once. The risks section names fouling and turndown as open items; neither is resolved in the report.
input:
## Basis
This report is concerned with the design of a distillation column, the purpose of which is to separate a liquid feed into two products, namely an overhead product and a bottoms product. The design throughput of the column is 32 t per day of feed. The separation duty that is called for is 90% of the key component present in the feed, taken overhead, so that the overhead product contains that share of the key component, while the bottoms contains the balance, together with the heavier components of the feed. All wetted parts are manufactured in 316L stainless steel, and the grade is stated once, at this point; the materials section of the report proceeds on the basis of this statement. The column operates continuously at the design throughput. The feed is introduced at the feed stage, vapour rises up the column against liquid flowing downwards, and the separation is effected by repeated contact between the two phases on the stages that are situated between the feed stage and the ends of the column. A condenser at the top of the column returns a part of the overhead vapour in the form of reflux and sends the remainder to product, and a reboiler at the bottom returns a part of the bottoms in the form of vapour and sends the remainder to product. The basis thus establishes the rate and the duty, and such matters as the number of stages, the reflux rate, the diameter of the column and the pressure level at which the separation is carried out are dealt with in the sizing section.
## Sizing
The sizing of the column takes as its starting point the design throughput of 32 t per day and the separation duty of 90% of the key component taken overhead. The number of stages is determined by the separation that the duty requires. Each stage brings the vapour and the liquid into contact with one another and moves the key component in the direction of the overhead product; the stages above the feed serve to enrich the vapour in the key component, and the stages below the feed serve to strip the key component out of the liquid that is running down to the bottoms. The count of stages is built up from the equilibrium behaviour of the mixture, stage by stage, and the feed stage is located at the position where the composition of the feed corresponds to the composition of the liquid on the stage, so that the introduction of the feed does not disturb the traffic in either section of the column. The reflux rate is fixed in conjunction with the stage count: a higher rate of reflux sharpens the separation that is achieved on each stage and reduces the number of stages that the duty requires, although this is at the price of a larger traffic of vapour and liquid within the column and a larger duty at the condenser and at the reboiler. The diameter of the column is determined by the traffic of vapour. The vapour that rises through the column and the liquid that runs down it share the cross-section of the column, and the diameter is selected in such a way that the vapour rate at the busiest section remains below the rate at which liquid begins to be carried upwards with the vapour and the stages cease to perform their separation. The condenser and the reboiler are sized on the basis of the traffic that results from the choice of reflux: the condenser deals with the whole of the overhead vapour, condensing both the part that is returned as reflux and the part that is sent to product, and the reboiler raises from the bottoms liquid the vapour that the column requires. The pressure drop is summed stage by stage through the column and is checked against the pressure level at which the column works, because the pressure determines the temperatures at which the two products condense and boil. The sizing concludes with a check of the column operating at the design rate.
## Materials
All wetted parts are manufactured in the stainless steel grade that has been named in the basis. The shell of the column, the stages together with their fittings, the feed inlet, the overhead line to the condenser, the condenser itself, the reflux return, the bottoms outlet and the reboiler are all in contact with the feed, with the products or with the liquids in the column, and the grade applies to each and every one of them. The liquids in the column represent the aggressive streams from the point of view of material selection: the feed wets the feed stage and the section below it on a continuous basis, the reflux wets the top section, and the bottoms liquid stands hot in the sump and in the reboiler, where a weakness in the material will show itself first in the form of attack at the heated surface. The fittings of the stages are subject to a second kind of service, in that they are handled at every shutdown and are removed and replaced during cleaning and inspection, and their material must therefore be able to withstand that handling as well as the process liquid. Small parts, such as downcomer bolts and stage fasteners, are held to the grade of the parts that they join, since a fastener manufactured in a weaker material may well fail in a crevice into which the inspection cannot see. Surfaces that are in product contact are finished in such a way that deposits can be cleaned off at a shutdown and do not lodge underneath the stages. Gaskets at the joints of the shell and at the connections of the condenser and the reboiler are selected for the liquids in the column and for the cleaning fluids that are used at shutdown.
## Risks
There are two items which remain open in the design, namely fouling and turndown, and it has to be said that neither of these items is resolved in this report. Fouling has a direct effect on the separation itself. Deposits are formed on the stages at the points where the feed enters and where any heavy material in the feed is able to settle, and a stage that has become fouled no longer brings the vapour and the liquid into contact in the manner that the sizing assumes: the liquid channels across the deposit, the vapour finds the open paths, and the stage delivers a smaller separation than its design value. Fouling also has the effect of narrowing the downcomers, with the result that the traffic of liquid for which the diameter was set cannot pass, and the column floods at a rate below its design rate. The design provides access for cleaning at the feed section and at the bottom of the column, and records the fouling rate of the feed as the quantity that is required at the next stage; until such time as that rate is known, no cleaning interval is stated. Turndown is the second of the open items. At rates below the design throughput, the rate of vapour falls, and the stages depend upon the vapour in order to hold the liquid up and to bring about the contact that the separation requires; at a sufficiently low rate of vapour the liquid weeps through the stages instead of flowing across them, and the separation deteriorates more rapidly than the rate itself. The reflux control maintains the compositions of the products over a part of the range, but the lower end of the range is determined by the behaviour of the stages and not by the controls. Both items are accordingly recorded for attention at the next design stage.
target:
## Basis
The design covers a distillation column that separates a liquid feed into an overhead product and a bottoms product. The design throughput is 32 t per day of feed. The separation duty is 90% of the key component in the feed, taken overhead: the overhead product carries that share of the key component, and the bottoms carries the balance together with the heavier components of the feed. Wetted parts are 316L stainless steel, and the basis states the grade once, here; the materials section works from this statement. The column works continuously at the design throughput. Feed enters the column at the feed stage, vapour rises against liquid flowing down, and the separation is made by repeated contact between the two phases on the stages between the feed stage and the ends of the column. A condenser at the top returns part of the overhead vapour as reflux and sends the rest to product; a reboiler at the bottom returns part of the bottoms as vapour and sends the rest to product. The basis fixes the rate and the duty. The number of stages, the reflux rate, the column diameter and the pressure level of the separation are set in the sizing section, and the basis does not prejudge them. The two products are drawn continuously, and the column inventories are held by level control at the sump and at the reflux return.
## Sizing
Sizing starts from the design throughput of 32 t per day and the separation duty of 90% of the key component taken overhead. The stage count is set by the separation the duty demands. Each stage brings vapour and liquid into contact and moves the key component towards the overhead product; the stages above the feed enrich the vapour in the key component, and the stages below the feed strip the key component out of the liquid running to the bottoms. The count is built up from the equilibrium behaviour of the mixture stage by stage, and the feed stage is placed where the feed composition matches the liquid on the stage, so the feed enters without disturbing the traffic in either section. The reflux rate is set with the stage count: a higher reflux rate sharpens the separation on each stage and lowers the stage count the duty needs, at the price of a larger vapour and liquid traffic in the column and a larger duty at the condenser and the reboiler. The sizing takes the pair of values, stage count and reflux, that meets the duty with the column in steady operation and holds a working margin above the minimum reflux the separation allows. The column diameter is set by the vapour traffic. The vapour rising through the column and the liquid running down share the cross-section, and the diameter is chosen so the vapour rate at the busiest section stays below the rate at which liquid is carried up with the vapour and the stages lose their separation. The section above the feed normally sets the diameter, because the reflux adds to its liquid traffic. Stage spacing is set by the need to separate the phases between stages and to give access for inspection and cleaning. The condenser and reboiler are sized on the traffic the reflux choice creates: the condenser takes the full overhead vapour, condenses the part returned as reflux and the part sent to product, and the reboiler raises the vapour the column needs from the bottoms liquid. Pressure drop is summed stage by stage through the column and checked against the pressure level the basis works at, because the pressure fixes the temperatures at which the two products condense and boil. The sizing closes with a check of the column at the design rate: feed in at the feed stage, overhead and bottoms out at the stated duty, stage traffic steady in both sections.
## Materials
Wetted parts are the stainless steel grade named in the basis. The column shell, the stages and their fittings, the feed inlet, the overhead line to the condenser, the condenser itself, the reflux return, the bottoms outlet and the reboiler all stand in contact with the feed, the products or the column liquids, and the grade is applied to each of them. The liquids in the column are the aggressive streams for material selection: the feed wets the feed stage and the section below it continuously, the reflux wets the top section, and the bottoms liquid stands hot in the sump and in the reboiler, where a material weakness shows first as attack at the heated surface. Stage fittings take a second kind of service: they are handled at every shutdown, removed and replaced during cleaning and inspection, and their material has to stand that handling as well as the process liquid. Small parts, downcomer bolts and stage fasteners are held to the grade of the parts they join, because a fastener of a weaker material fails in a crevice the inspection cannot see into. Surfaces in product contact are finished so that deposits can be cleaned off at a shutdown and do not lodge under the stages. Gaskets at the shell joints and at the condenser and reboiler connections are selected for the column liquids and for the cleaning fluids used at shutdown. The materials section adds no second statement of the grade: a part listed as wetted is governed by the basis statement.
## Risks
Fouling and turndown stand as open items in the design, and neither is resolved in this report. Fouling acts on the separation directly. Deposits form on the stages where the feed enters and where any heavy material in the feed can settle, and a fouled stage no longer contacts vapour and liquid as the sizing assumes: liquid channels across the deposit, vapour finds the open paths, and the stage delivers less separation than its design value. Fouling also narrows the downcomers, so the liquid traffic the diameter was set for cannot pass, and the column floods below its design rate. The design leaves access for cleaning at the feed section and the bottom of the column and records the fouling rate of the feed as the quantity the next stage needs; until that rate is known, no cleaning interval is stated and no spare capacity is claimed against fouling. Turndown is the second open item. Below the design throughput the vapour rate falls, and the stages depend on the vapour to hold the liquid up and to make the contact the separation needs; at a low enough vapour rate the liquid weeps through the stages instead of flowing across them, and the separation falls away faster than the rate does. The reflux control holds the product compositions over part of the range, but the lower end of the range is set by the stage behaviour, not by the controls. The report records the turndown item for the next design stage: it closes when the stage behaviour at reduced vapour rate is confirmed for the stage type selected, and the fouling item closes when a deposit rate for the feed is available from operation or test.

fact_base: Excerpt content: a strainer cleaning takes about 88 min with the unit isolated; the excerpt gives the isolation steps only. The excerpt warns once about stored pressure and does not repeat the warning.
input: The first step in the cleaning of the strainer is to transfer the pumping duty from the one machine to the other, so that the strainer can be taken out of service without interrupting the operation of the line as a whole. The standby pump is accordingly started and allowed to run steadily on the line, after which the duty pump is stopped and allowed to run down. Attention is then turned to the strainer served by the duty pump, which is isolated at the strainer itself by closing the suction valve and the discharge valve in turn, each valve being seated fully. A tag is hung on each valve, and the duty pump starter is locked in the off position, so that the line cannot be re-pressured while the strainer is open. Each isolation point is entered in the register as it is made, and the whole of the work is carried out under the PTW. The drain valve at the bottom of the strainer body is then opened and the body is drained into the closed drain header. It is important to appreciate that the body retains stored pressure even after both of the line valves have been shut, and the vent cock on the body cover is therefore opened a little at a time, until the pressure has blown down, before any cover bolt is touched. The isolation is checked by the combination of an open drain, an open vent, and the absence of any continuing flow at either point, and the body gauge, where one is fitted, provides a further indication. In all, cleaning the element takes about 88 min with the unit isolated, and the cover bolts are cracked in a cross sequence once the proving is complete
target: With the standby pump on the line and running steadily, stop the duty pump and let it run down. The strainer served by the duty pump is then isolated for cleaning, and the isolation is made at the strainer itself. Close the suction valve and the discharge valve in turn, and seat each valve fully. Hang a tag on each valve and lock the duty pump starter in the off position, so the line cannot be re-pressured while the strainer is open. Every isolation point is entered in the register as it is made, and the work runs under the PTW from the first valve movement. The register entry names each point in the order it was made, so the state of the isolation can be read back at the handover without returning to the line. Open the drain valve at the bottom of the strainer body and drain the body to the closed drain header. The body retains stored pressure after both line valves are shut, and the vent cock on the body cover is opened a quarter turn at a time until the pressure has blown down, before a single cover bolt is touched. Check the isolation before the cover is disturbed: open drain, open vent, and no continuing flow at either point together prove the body is separated from the line. Where the gauge connection is fitted, read the body gauge as a confirming indication, after the vent has finished blowing. Leave the drain open throughout the proving, and fit the suction blank once the body is empty. Cleaning the element takes about 88 min in total with the unit isolated; with the proving complete, the cover bolts are cracked in a cross sequence and the cover is lifted clear of its studs only when the body has stopped dripping at the drain

subtype: worked example with equation: Raoult partial pressure
fact_base: An ideal liquid mixture holds hexane in heptane at a liquid mole fraction $x$ of 0.65 for the volatile component. Its pure-component vapour pressure $P^*$ at the mixture temperature is 20.1 kPa, so the partial pressure $p$ is 13.1 kPa by Raoult's law. Raoult's law assumes an ideal solution; activity coefficients for the real mixture are not applied.
input:
Raoult's law is a very useful relationship which enables the partial pressure of a component above a liquid mixture to be estimated from the composition of the liquid, provided that the mixture in question can be regarded as an ideal solution. The essential idea behind the law is that the partial pressure of the component — that is to say, the contribution that the component makes to the total pressure of the vapour — is simply the fraction of the component in the liquid multiplied by the vapour pressure that the pure component would exert at the same temperature. In the present case we are concerned with hexane in heptane, where the liquid mole fraction $x$ of the volatile component is 0.65 and the pure-component vapour pressure $P^*$ at the temperature of the mixture is 20.1 kPa. Raoult's law, which relates the partial pressure $p$ to these two quantities, can be written in the following compact form:
$$p = x P^*$$
Substituting the values that have been given, namely $x$ = 0.65 and $P^*$ = 20.1 kPa, into this expression, we obtain a partial pressure $p$ of 13.1 kPa. It will be observed that this value is less than the vapour pressure of the pure component, which is exactly what one would expect, since the component accounts for only a part of the liquid. The answer of 13.1 kPa should, however, be treated as an idealised value, because Raoult's law is based on the assumption of an ideal solution, and activity coefficients for the real mixture have not been applied in arriving at it.
target:
Raoult's law gives the partial pressure of a component over an ideal liquid mixture from its liquid mole fraction and its pure-component vapour pressure. The partial pressure is the share of the total pressure the component contributes in the vapour, and for an ideal solution it is the component's fraction in the liquid, applied to the pressure the pure component would exert at the same temperature. The law is valid for an ideal solution, and that assumption is stated before the relation is used. For hexane in heptane at a liquid mole fraction $x$ of 0.65 for the volatile component, with a pure-component vapour pressure $P^*$ of 20.1 kPa at the mixture temperature, Raoult's law relates the partial pressure $p$ to the mole fraction and the pure-component pressure:
$$p = x P^*$$
Substitution of $x$ = 0.65 and $P^*$ = 20.1 kPa into Raoult's law gives a partial pressure $p$ of 13.1 kPa. The two quantities the law multiplies are both stated for the mixture as it stands: the mole fraction describes the liquid, and the pure-component pressure is taken at the temperature of that liquid; no temperature correction enters the substitution. The result sits where the relation places it: the partial pressure falls below the pure-component vapour pressure because the mole fraction is below unity, and the reduction is in direct proportion to the mole fraction, so the partial pressure of 13.1 kPa is the pure-component pressure scaled by the share of the component in the liquid. The calculation rests on the ideal-solution assumption throughout. Activity coefficients for the real mixture are not applied, and no activity data for the pair is carried into the result; a real mixture whose components interact unevenly would depart from the value the law gives, in either direction. The partial pressure is therefore the ideal-solution value for hexane in heptane at the stated composition and temperature, and it is reported on that footing.

fact_base: Goal: compute the half-life of a first-order reaction and the fraction remaining after 60 min. For a first-order reaction the rate constant k (min-1) fixes the half-life t1/2 (min) by t1/2 = ln(2) / k, and the fraction remaining after time t (min) is exp(-k t). Measured rate constant: k = 0.069 min-1 at 323 K, from concentration measurements every 5 min over 90 min. Worked results: t1/2 = 10 min; the fraction remaining after 60 min is 0.02 (dimensionless), both computed from the stated relations. The relations hold for a first-order reaction only; a reaction of another order follows a different decay law.
input: This worked example determines the half-life of a first-order reaction and the fraction of reactant remaining after 60 min, starting from a measured rate constant. The rate constant $k$ was measured as 0.069 min-1 at 323 K, from concentration measurements taken every 5 min over 90 min. For a first-order reaction, the rate constant $k$ (min-1) is connected to the half-life $t_{1/2}$ (min) by the relation $t_{1/2} = \ln(2)/k$, and the fraction remaining after a time $t$ (min) is given by $\exp(-k t)$. The half-life $t_{1/2}$ can be understood as the time needed for the concentration to drop to one half of its initial value, while the fraction remaining expresses the concentration at time $t$ as a proportion of the initial concentration. Substituting $k$ = 0.069 min-1 into the half-life relation gives $t_{1/2}$ = 10 min. Substituting the same value of $k$ = 0.069 min-1, together with $t$ = 60 min, into the decay relation gives a fraction remaining of 0.02. This can be cross-checked very simply: 60 min is equivalent to six half-lives of 10 min each, and halving the concentration six times over leaves only a small residue, broadly consistent with a remaining fraction of 0.02. It is worth emphasising that the half-life of 10 min and the fraction remaining of 0.02 are tied to the temperature at which the rate constant was measured, since a different temperature would produce a different rate constant and hence different results. Finally, it should be noted that both of these relations hold only for a first-order reaction; a reaction of any other order follows a completely different decay law, and the approach used here would not be applicable to it.
target: Calculate the half-life of a first-order reaction and the fraction of reactant remaining after 60 min: the half-life is 10 min and the fraction remaining is 0.02. Concentration measurements every 5 min over 90 min at 323 K gave the rate constant $k$ = 0.069 min-1. For a first-order reaction, the rate constant $k$ (min-1) fixes the half-life $t_{1/2}$ (min) by $t_{1/2} = \ln(2)/k$, and the fraction remaining after time $t$ (min) is $\exp(-k t)$. The half-life $t_{1/2}$ is the time at which the concentration has fallen to one half of its initial value, and the fraction remaining is the concentration at time $t$ divided by the initial concentration. The initial concentration appears in neither relation, which is why the half-life of a first-order reaction does not depend on the starting concentration. Substitution of $k$ = 0.069 min-1 in the half-life relation gives $t_{1/2}$ = 10 min. Substitution of $k$ = 0.069 min-1 and $t$ = 60 min in the decay relation gives the fraction remaining as 0.02. A check against the half-life gives the same picture: 60 min spans six half-lives of 10 min, and six successive halvings of the concentration leave a fraction close to 0.02. Both results belong to the stated temperature, because the measured rate constant belongs to that temperature; a rate constant measured at another temperature would return a different half-life. The two relations hold for a first-order reaction only; a reaction of another order follows a different decay law, and neither relation describes its decay.

fact_base: A defect-reduction project on a packing line cut the reject rate from 4% to 1.7% over one quarter. At 137k units per year the change avoids about 3151 rejected units per year. The quarter included a planned shutdown; rates are not adjusted for it.
input: Over the course of one quarter, a defect-reduction project on a packing line successfully reduced the reject rate from 4% to 1.7%, which represents a reduction of some 2.3 percentage points. This is a meaningful improvement in the performance of the line, because the reject rate captures the proportion of packed units that fail to meet the required standard and have to be removed from the output. Based on an annual volume of 137k units per year, it is estimated that this change will avoid approximately 3151 rejected units per year, which is a substantial saving in terms of wasted product, wasted packaging and wasted effort across the operation as a whole. The avoided figure is obtained by applying the difference between the two reject rates to the annual volume, so it rests on the assumption that the improved rate achieved during the quarter can be sustained across the full year and across the full mix of products handled by the line. It should also be noted that the quarter in question included a planned shutdown, and the reported rates have not been adjusted in any way to account for it, so the comparison should be read with that in mind. Overall, the results demonstrate a clear improvement in line performance over the period, although the figures should be understood as applying to the conditions under which they were measured, including the shutdown that formed part of the quarter. Further monitoring over subsequent quarters will show whether the improvement is maintained once the line has returned to its normal pattern of operation.
target: The packing line reject rate fell from 4% to 1.7% over one quarter, a reduction of 2.3 percentage points. At the stated volume of 137k units per year, the reduction avoids about 3151 rejected units per year. The reject rate is the count of rejected units divided by the units packed over the same period, so the two rates compare the line with itself on one counting basis. A rejected unit is a packed unit removed from the output as defective, and the avoided count is the number of such units the lower rate removes from a year of production at the stated volume. The avoided count is derived from the two rates and the annual volume: the earlier rate applied to the volume gives the rejections the year would have carried, the later rate gives the rejections it now carries, and the difference is the saving. The saving is stated per year because the volume is stated per year; the rates themselves were measured over one quarter. Carrying a quarter's rates across a full year assumes the product mix and the running pattern of the quarter stand for the year, and the figure inherits that assumption. The quarter included a planned shutdown, and the rates are not adjusted for it. The comparison therefore stands as measured: no allowance has been added for the shutdown, and any reader who needs rates on a running-time basis must restate them before use. The claim is limited to the two rates, the stated volume and the period in which the rates were measured. The two rates and the volume are reported together, so that the avoided count can be recomputed from them by any reader of the case.

fact_base: A tutorial passage explains the pump affinity laws for a centrifugal pump at varying speed. The passage states the three proportionalities in words: flow with speed, head with speed squared, power with speed cubed. A worked check is included: doubling speed multiplies power by 8. No other numbers are introduced.
input: The pump affinity laws are a very useful set of relationships that describe how the performance of a centrifugal pump changes when its operating speed is changed. In essence, there are three simple proportionalities that together capture the behaviour of the pump. Firstly, the flow delivered by the pump varies in direct proportion to the speed, so that if the speed is doubled, the flow is doubled as well. Secondly, the head developed by the pump varies with the square of the speed, which means that the head responds much more strongly to a change in speed than the flow does. Thirdly, the power absorbed by the pump varies with the cube of the speed, making the power the most sensitive of the three quantities to any change in operating speed. These relationships can be illustrated with a simple worked check: doubling the speed multiplies the flow by 2, the head by 4 and the power by 8. This dramatic increase in power is one of the key reasons why speed is adjusted so carefully in practice, since a relatively modest increase in speed, and hence in flow, can lead to a disproportionately large increase in the power that has to be supplied. It is important to remember that the affinity laws are statements about ratios between two operating speeds of the same pump, rather than absolute predictions, and that they rest on the assumption that the efficiency of the pump does not change significantly between the two speeds in question. The laws are at their most reliable when they are applied over a moderate range of speeds around the point at which the performance of the pump is actually known.
target: The pump affinity laws relate the duty of a centrifugal pump at one speed to the duty of the same pump at another speed. Flow varies in direct proportion to speed: at twice the speed the pump delivers twice the flow, through the same impeller and against the same system. Head varies with the square of the speed, so the head responds more strongly to a speed change than the flow does. Power varies with the cube of the speed, and responds most strongly of the three quantities. Each law takes the same form: the quantity at the new speed is its value at the known speed, multiplied by the ratio of the speeds raised to the power the law assigns to that quantity. Flow counts as a volume rate, head as the energy the pump adds to each unit weight of liquid, and power as the shaft power the driver must supply at the duty point. A worked check fixes the pattern of the three laws together. Doubling the speed multiplies the flow by 2, the head by 4 and the power by 8. The check shows why speed is set with care: a rise in speed buys flow at the first power and pays for power at the third, so the power consequence of a speed change is settled before the speed is raised. The laws state ratios, not absolute duties. An absolute duty at a new speed is calculated from a measured or rated duty at a known speed, and no affinity law supplies the starting duty itself. The proportionalities presume the same pump, the same liquid and a system that is unchanged between the two speeds, with efficiency taken as unchanged as well; where efficiency shifts between speeds, the power proportion is the first of the three to depart from the stated ratio.

fact_base: Carbon dioxide and hydrogen react over a copper-zinc oxide catalyst to give dimethyl ether. Space-time yield is the mass of product per unit catalyst volume per hour (kg L-1 h-1). Test conditions: 280 °C, 40 bar, feed ratio H2/CO2 = 3, one feed composition. Structured catalyst: space-time yield 0.9 kg L-1 h-1, pressure drop 0.1 bar, activity loss 5% after 100 h. Pellet catalyst: space-time yield 0.47 kg L-1 h-1, pressure drop 1.28 bar, activity loss 18% after 100 h. No sulfur-bearing feed was tested. Yield and pressure drop are seldom reported for the same catalyst charge.
input: In this study, dimethyl ether was produced from carbon dioxide and hydrogen over a copper-zinc oxide catalyst, and two different catalyst forms, namely a structured form and a conventional pellet form, were compared with one another under a single set of test conditions. The tests were carried out at 280 °C and 40 bar, with a feed ratio H2/CO2 = 3 and one feed composition throughout. The space-time yield, which is defined as the mass of product obtained per unit catalyst volume per hour (kg L-1 h-1), was used as the principal measure of performance. The structured catalyst achieved a space-time yield of 0.9 kg L-1 h-1, together with a pressure drop of only 0.1 bar and an activity loss of 5% after 100 h on stream. In contrast, the pellet catalyst gave a considerably lower space-time yield of 0.47 kg L-1 h-1, a much higher pressure drop of 1.28 bar, and a substantially larger activity loss of 18% after 100 h. Overall, the results show that the structured form outperforms the pellet form on all three of the measures reported here. It should be noted, however, that the comparison is based on a single feed composition, that no sulfur-bearing feed was tested, and that yield and pressure drop are seldom reported for the same catalyst charge, which makes wider comparisons with the existing literature rather difficult.
target: Dimethyl ether was prepared from carbon dioxide and hydrogen over a copper-zinc oxide catalyst in two forms, a structured form and a pellet form, and the two forms were compared under one set of test conditions at one feed composition. The test conditions were a temperature of 280 °C and a pressure of 40 bar, with a feed ratio H2/CO2 = 3. Space-time yield is the mass of product per unit catalyst volume per hour (kg L-1 h-1), and the comparison rests on the space-time yield, the pressure drop and the activity loss measured over the test duration. The structured catalyst gave a space-time yield of 0.9 kg L-1 h-1, a pressure drop of 0.1 bar and an activity loss of 5% after 100 h. The pellet catalyst gave a space-time yield of 0.47 kg L-1 h-1, a pressure drop of 1.28 bar and an activity loss of 18% after 100 h. At the stated conditions the structured form has the higher space-time yield, the lower pressure drop and the smaller activity loss, and the three measures rank the two forms in the same order. Activity loss is stated at the end of the stated duration for both forms, so the stability comparison is drawn at a common time on stream. The comparison is limited to the one feed composition tested and to the stated conditions. No sulfur-bearing feed was tested, and yield and pressure drop are seldom reported for the same catalyst charge, which limits the comparison that can be drawn with other catalysts.

topic: tut:phase:a pure component at its boiling point
fact_base: A tutorial passage explains phase equilibrium for a pure component at its boiling point. The passage states the equilibrium condition in words (equality of chemical potential across phases) before any equation is named. No numerical data are introduced; the passage is conceptual.
input: When a pure component is held at its boiling point, its liquid and vapour phases are able to coexist alongside one another in a state of phase equilibrium. The condition that has to be satisfied for this equilibrium to hold is that the chemical potential of the component is exactly the same in the liquid phase as it is in the vapour phase. In other words, the component has no tendency to move preferentially in either direction between the two phases, and although individual molecules are constantly passing back and forth across the interface, there is no net transfer of material from one phase to the other. This is an important idea because it explains why boiling takes place at a constant temperature: as long as both phases are present together, any heat that is added to the system is used to convert liquid into vapour rather than to raise the temperature, and the temperature stays fixed at the boiling point for the pressure that has been imposed. The boiling point itself is therefore not an arbitrary property of the component, but the temperature at which the equilibrium between the two phases is established at that pressure. If the temperature were raised above the boiling point at the same pressure, the equality of chemical potential could no longer be maintained with both phases present, and the liquid would disappear entirely, leaving only the vapour as the stable phase.
target: A pure component at its boiling point holds its liquid and vapour phases in equilibrium with each other. The equilibrium condition is stated in words as an equality: the chemical potential of the component in the liquid phase equals the chemical potential of the component in the vapour phase. Chemical potential is the quantity whose equality across a phase boundary marks the absence of any net driving force for transfer, so under the stated condition the component passes between the phases in both directions at equal rates and neither phase grows at the expense of the other. Boiling is the visible form of the condition. Heat added to the mixture at fixed pressure converts liquid into vapour while both phases remain present, and the temperature stays at the boiling point during the conversion because the added heat is taken up by the change of phase rather than by a rise in temperature. The boiling point is in this way fixed by the pressure: for a pure component, each pressure carries the one temperature at which the equality holds with both phases present. A temperature above the boiling point at the same pressure leaves the vapour as the only stable phase, and a temperature below it leaves the liquid; coexistence belongs to the boiling point alone. The condition is stated for a pure component, whose single chemical potential in each phase is enough to fix the equilibrium.

fact_base: A shell-and-tube exchanger heats cooling water in a refinery preheat train. Duty is 852 kW. Hot stream: 150 °C in, 110 °C out. Cold stream: 30 °C in, 50 °C out. The log-mean temperature difference is 89.6 K and the installed area is 83.8 m2, giving an overall coefficient of 113 W m-2 K-1. Fouling was assessed from a single 90-day run; no cleaning cycle has been completed.
input: A shell-and-tube exchanger installed in a refinery preheat train was used to heat cooling water, and the exchanger was found to operate at a duty of 852 kW. The hot stream entered the exchanger at 150 °C and left at 110 °C, while the cooling water entered at 30 °C and left at 50 °C. Based on these terminal temperatures, the log-mean temperature difference was calculated to be 89.6 K, and the installed area of the exchanger was 83.8 m2, which together give an overall heat transfer coefficient of 113 W m-2 K-1. This coefficient represents the combined performance of the exchanger as installed, bringing together the resistances of the two fluid films and the tube wall into a single figure referred to the installed area, while the log-mean temperature difference represents the mean driving force for heat transfer along the length of the unit. It is worth noting that the fouling of the exchanger was assessed on the basis of a single 90-day run, and that no cleaning cycle has yet been completed, which means that there is currently no information available about how much of the coefficient might be recovered if the exchanger were to be cleaned. The figures quoted here are therefore the figures for the exchanger in its current, as-found condition, and they should be used on that basis until such time as a cleaning cycle has been completed and the unit has been tested again.
target: A shell-and-tube exchanger in a refinery preheat train heats cooling water at a duty of 852 kW. The hot stream enters at 150 °C and leaves at 110 °C; the cooling water enters at 30 °C and leaves at 50 °C. The log-mean temperature difference calculated from the four terminal temperatures is 89.6 K, and the installed area is 83.8 m2. The overall coefficient obtained from the duty, the area and the log-mean temperature difference is 113 W m-2 K-1. The log-mean temperature difference is the mean driving force for the exchanger: the terminal differences at the two ends differ, and the log-mean value is the constant difference that returns the stated duty when it is applied over the installed area. The overall coefficient gathers the resistances of the hot-side film, the tube wall and the cold-side film into one figure referred to the installed area, so the coefficient describes the exchanger as built and as run, not any single surface within it. The two results are consistent as stated: the duty is the product of the coefficient, the area and the log-mean temperature difference, and the reported figures satisfy that product within the precision at which they are reported. The duty is the heat the hot stream gives up across the exchanger, and the terminal temperatures fix both ends of the exchange: the approach at the cold end and the approach at the hot end stand behind the single mean figure that the log-mean value reports. Fouling was assessed from a single 90-day run; no cleaning cycle has been completed, and the recovery of the coefficient after cleaning is not on record.

fact_base: A tutorial passage explains the Nusselt number to second-year students. Definition in words: the Nusselt number is the ratio of convective to conductive heat transfer at a surface. The passage must state what a value near 1 means and what a large value means, without inventing numerical examples.
input: The Nusselt number is a dimensionless quantity that is widely used in the study of convective heat transfer, and it can be understood as a comparison between two different mechanisms by which heat can be transferred at a surface. More specifically, the Nusselt number is defined as the ratio of convective heat transfer to conductive heat transfer at the surface in question. If the Nusselt number has a value near 1, this tells us that the two mechanisms are contributing roughly equally, and that the movement of the fluid is adding very little to the rate at which heat is transferred beyond what conduction through the fluid layer next to the surface would achieve on its own. On the other hand, if the Nusselt number is large, this indicates that convection is the dominant mechanism, and that the moving fluid is removing heat from the surface far more effectively than conduction alone would be able to do. The Nusselt number is therefore best thought of as a measure of how much the flow enhances the transfer of heat at the surface, expressed relative to the purely conductive case, which acts as the natural reference point for the comparison. It applies to the conditions actually prevailing at the surface, and it is in terms of those conditions that any particular value of the number has to be interpreted by the reader.
target: The Nusselt number compares two routes by which heat leaves a surface into a fluid: convection into the moving fluid, and conduction across the fluid layer that rests on the surface. The Nusselt number is defined as the ratio of convective to conductive heat transfer at the surface, and the conductive transfer is the reference against which the convective transfer is measured. A value near 1 means the two transfers are of the same size. Under that condition the moving fluid removes heat at about the rate at which conduction across the surface layer alone would remove it, and the motion of the fluid adds little to the transfer. A large value means convective transfer dominates the comparison: the moving fluid removes heat many times faster than conduction across the layer would, and the surface is held close to the temperature of the fluid by the flow. Both readings are taken at the surface and for the conditions at the surface, since the ratio compares the two mechanisms under one set of conditions rather than reporting a property of the fluid alone. The denominator of the ratio sets the floor of the scale. Conduction across the layer is the transfer that would remain if the fluid were still, so the number states how far the actual transfer stands above that floor for the same surface and the same driving temperature difference. Read in this way, the number ranks a surface condition by the standing of convection against its own reference, and the ranking is the whole content of the value.

fact_base: Design report for an amine absorber, in four sections: basis, sizing, materials, and risks. Design throughput is 10 t per day and the removal or separation duty is 98% of the key component. Materials are 316L stainless steel for wetted parts; the basis section states this once. The risks section names fouling and turndown as open items; neither is resolved in the report.
input:
Basis

This report presents the design of an amine absorber which has been developed in order to remove the key component from a gas stream by means of absorption into an amine solution. The design throughput of the unit is 10 t per day, and the removal duty that the design is required to achieve is 98% of the key component present in the feed gas. The feed gas has been taken exactly as it is received at the battery limit, with the composition and the state declared by the upstream unit, and the absorber has been designed for continuous operation at the duty stated above. The solvent is an aqueous amine solution which is circulated between the absorber and a regeneration step that falls outside the scope of the present report. The scope of the design itself covers the column shell, the packing together with its supports, the liquid distributors, the sump, and the nozzles located at the battery limit. All wetted parts are fabricated in 316L stainless steel, which is stated here once, as the material basis on which the whole of this report rests. The design pressure and the design temperature correspond to the highest pressure and temperature that the column can be expected to meet in service, each of them carrying the margin that is required by the applicable code, and the relief case is determined by the blocked outlet of the gas stream. The solvent circulation rate, the lean loading and the rich loading are design variables which are fixed by the sizing, within the working limits stated by the solvent supplier for the solution that is in use. It should be noted that no credit has been taken in the basis for operating experience gained on other units, and that no performance figure beyond the stated removal duty is claimed for the column as it has been designed.

Sizing

The diameter of the column is established by the gas rate at the design throughput and by the phenomenon of flooding within the packing. The diameter has been selected in such a way that the design gas rate stands below the flooding rate by the margin that the packing correlation requires if stable operation is to be achieved, with the liquid rate held at its design value within the same check. The height of packing is established by the transfer calculation corresponding to the stated removal duty: the number of transfer units is derived from the separation that the duty demands, and the height of a transfer unit is derived from the performance of the packing at the design gas and liquid rates, so that the height overall is a consequence of the duty rather than a round figure that has been chosen in advance. The liquid is distributed by means of a distributor which is rated for the design liquid rate across the whole of the column section, and a redistributor is provided wherever the packed height is divided into more than one bed. The sump is sized to hold the solvent inventory that the circulation loop requires for stable level control, and the gas outlet is fitted with a demister in order to keep the carry-over of solvent into the treated gas within the limit that the downstream unit is able to accept. The sizes of the nozzles follow the usual velocity practice for the service at each of the connections. It is important to emphasise that the sizing is stated for the design case only; operation at rates that differ from the design case has not been sized here, and is instead carried forward as an open item into the risks section.

Materials

All wetted parts are manufactured in the stainless steel grade that is named in the basis, and this grade is used for the shell, for the packing, for the distributors, for the internals of the sump and for the wetted necks of the nozzles. The selection has been made on the basis of the corrosion behaviour that is characteristic of amine service: it is the rich solution, loaded with the component that has been absorbed, that acts as the corrodent within the column, and its attack is at its strongest in those locations where the solution is at its hottest and where its velocity is at its highest. The degradation products of the amine themselves add to the corrosivity of the circulating solution, and this forms part of the reasoning behind the selection of a stainless grade for the wetted parts, rather than carbon steel. Welds that are exposed to the wetted service are made with a filler of matching composition, and crevices have been kept out of the wetted design wherever a crevice would tend to hold rich solution against a surface. Parts that are not wetted, which include the skirt and the external attachments, are made of carbon steel with a protective coating that is suitable for the atmosphere of the site. The gaskets at the wetted joints have been selected for their resistance to the amine solution at the design temperature. Access for inspection is provided at the sump and at each bed, so that the wetted surfaces on which the corrosion argument depends can be examined during service outages.

Risks

There are two significant open items that are addressed in this section, namely fouling and turndown, and it should be clearly understood that neither of these items is resolved in this report. Fouling in amine service arises from the degradation solids that are present in the circulating solution and from carry-over that enters the column together with the feed gas; the first effect that it produces in the absorber is a rise in the pressure drop across the packing, which is followed by maldistribution of the liquid and by a fall in the removal that the column is able to achieve. No fouling rate has been included in the design, because no rate obtained from a comparable duty is available to this report, and the provision that is made for monitoring is a trended measurement of the pressure drop across the packed beds, which is read against the clean condition that will be recorded at commissioning. What is missing at this stage is a fouling allowance: until such time as a rate has been established, neither the cleaning interval nor the margin in the packed height can properly be settled. Turndown remains open for a corresponding reason. At gas rates below the design case, the distribution of the liquid and the wetting of the packing both fall away, and the removal duty is placed at risk before any limit in the packing itself is actually reached; the lowest gas rate at which the stated duty still holds has not yet been established, either by testing or by vendor evidence, for the packing that has been selected. Both of these items are therefore carried forward into detailed design as open items, with the design as stated standing on the design case alone.

subtype: worked example with equation: Antoine vapour pressure
fact_base: The vapour pressure of acetone at 78 °C is estimated from the Antoine equation with constants $A$ = 7.11714, $B$ = 1210.595 and $C$ = 229.664 (pressure in mmHg, temperature in °C). The estimate is 202.9 kPa. The constants are valid only over their fitted temperature range; the source databank value governs design.
input:
The vapour pressure of acetone at 78 °C can be estimated by means of the Antoine equation, which is a well-known correlation that relates the vapour pressure of a pure substance to its temperature through a set of three empirical constants. The Antoine equation expresses the base-ten logarithm of the vapour pressure $P$ in terms of the temperature $T$ and the constants $A$, $B$ and $C$, as follows:
$$\log_{10} P = A - \frac{B}{T + C}$$
where the pressure $P$ is expressed in mmHg and the temperature $T$ is expressed in °C. For acetone, the constants take the values $A$ = 7.11714, $B$ = 1210.595 and $C$ = 229.664. Substituting the temperature of interest, together with these constants, into the equation, and converting the resulting pressure into kilopascals, gives an estimated vapour pressure of 202.9 kPa. It is important to appreciate that a value obtained in this way is only an estimate, because the Antoine constants are obtained by fitting the equation to experimental data over a limited range of temperatures, and they are valid only over the temperature range to which they were fitted. Outside that range the correlation cannot be relied upon, and for design purposes it is the value given in the source databank that governs, rather than the value produced by the correlation. The estimate should accordingly be treated as exactly that, namely an estimate, whenever it is carried into any subsequent calculation or comparison.
target:
The vapour pressure of acetone at 78 °C is estimated from the Antoine equation. Vapour pressure is the pressure at which the liquid and its vapour stand in equilibrium at the stated temperature, and the Antoine equation is the fitted relation used here to obtain that pressure from the temperature. The equation relates the vapour pressure $P$ to the temperature $T$ through three fitted constants, $A$, $B$ and $C$:
$$\log_{10} P = A - \frac{B}{T + C}$$
where $P$ is the vapour pressure in mmHg and $T$ is the temperature in °C. For acetone, the constants are $A$ = 7.11714, $B$ = 1210.595 and $C$ = 229.664. The substitution runs in the order the equation is written: the third constant is added to the temperature to form the denominator, the second constant is divided by that denominator, and the quotient is taken from the first constant to give the base-ten logarithm of the pressure. The result of the substitution, expressed in kilopascals, is the estimate of 202.9 kPa. An estimate from fitted constants carries the standing of the fit. The Antoine equation is fitted to measured vapour pressures over a stated temperature range and is valid only over that range; a temperature outside the range returns a number from the equation, but the number has no measured support behind it. Within the range, the estimate serves for calculation and for checking, and the source databank value governs design where the two differ. The estimate is a calculation from the temperature rather than a measurement, and its standing is that of the fitted relation from which it comes.

fact_base: A tutorial passage explains representative sampling of a gas emission. The passage covers where samples are taken, how many increments form one sample, and why a single grab sample misleads. No numerical limits are quoted; regulatory limits belong to the site's permit, not to the passage.
input: Representative sampling of a gas emission is concerned with obtaining a sample whose composition genuinely reflects the composition of the emission as a whole, and there are several aspects of the sampling procedure that have to be got right if this goal is to be achieved. The first of these aspects is the location at which samples are taken: the sample should be drawn from a point in the duct or stack where the gas is thoroughly mixed and where the stream is representative of the whole flow, rather than from a stagnant corner or from a position immediately downstream of a disturbance, where the composition may be quite untypical. The second aspect is the way in which the sample itself is built up: rather than relying on a single portion of gas, a proper sample is formed from a number of separate increments, each of them taken at a different time and combined together, so that the final sample averages over the fluctuations that occur in the emission. This brings us to the reason why a single grab sample can be so misleading: the composition of an emission is not constant, but varies with the state of the process, with the load on the plant and with time, and a grab sample captures nothing more than the state of the emission at one particular instant. Any limits that the sampling is intended to check against are a separate matter, since regulatory limits of that kind belong to the permit held by the site and not to the sampling method itself.
target: Representative sampling of a gas emission takes a portion of the gas whose composition stands for the composition of the whole emission over the period the sample is meant to cover. Where samples are taken decides much of the result. The sampling point is placed where the gas in the duct is mixed across the section and the stream at the point is the stream as a whole, not at a stagnant edge and not in the disturbed flow behind a bend or an obstruction, where the local composition can differ from the mean. How the sample is formed matters as much as where it is taken. One sample is built from several increments, each increment drawn at a different time across the sampling period and the increments combined, so the sample carries the average of the emission over that period rather than the state of the emission at a single moment. A single grab sample misleads for that reason. The composition of an emission varies with the state of the process that produces it, with load and with time, and a portion drawn at one instant freezes one state of a moving quantity: the same duct sampled at another moment returns another composition, and neither portion alone is the emission. The increments are the correction, since their spread across the period is what makes the combined sample representative. Numerical limits play no part in the method: the limits against which a result is judged belong to the permit held by the site, and the passage states none.

fact_base: A vapour-compression unit serves a process chiller, evaporating at 0 °C and condensing at 45 °C. The Carnot coefficient of performance between these temperatures is 6.07; the installed unit achieves 2.3. The achieved value is from the manufacturer's test at full load; part-load performance is not stated.
input: It is important to note that the performance of a vapour-compression unit serving a process chiller can be looked at from several complementary angles, and each angle contributes something to a fuller understanding of the machine. On the temperature side, the unit evaporates at 0 °C and condenses at 45 °C, which sets the thermal stage on which everything else plays out. Against this background, the Carnot coefficient of performance between these temperatures is 6.07, representing the idealised benchmark that no real refrigerator operating between the same temperatures can exceed. The installed unit, by contrast, achieves 2.3, a figure that comes from the manufacturer's test at full load and therefore reflects the machine as actually built and tested rather than as ideally conceived. It is also worth bearing in mind that part-load performance is not stated, so the picture that emerges is essentially a full-load picture, and any broader generalisation about how the unit behaves across its whole operating envelope would go beyond what the available information can support. This distinction between the ideal and the achieved is, in many ways, the central theme of practical refrigeration engineering. Taken together, these points suggest a machine whose tested performance sits well below the reversible benchmark, with the part-load region remaining, for the moment, uncharacterised.
target: The installed unit achieves a coefficient of performance of 2.3 at full load. Between the same temperatures, the Carnot coefficient of performance is 6.07. The machine is a vapour-compression unit serving a process chiller, evaporating at 0 °C and condensing at 45 °C. A coefficient of performance states the refrigeration effect obtained for each unit of work supplied, so the two values are compared on the same basis. The Carnot value is the reversible limit for refrigeration between those temperatures, and the achieved value comes from the manufacturer's test at full load. Part-load performance is not stated. The achieved coefficient of performance is therefore a full-load figure, and it carries no information about operation at reduced load, where a process chiller may spend much of its running time. No part-load test result stands behind any extension of the figure. The distance between the two values is the aggregate effect of the irreversibilities in the real machine, and the brief assigns no share of that distance to the compressor, the expansion device, or the heat exchangers. Any comparison with another unit is sound only at the tested condition: same duty point, same temperature levels, and a measured rather than estimated achieved value. Stated at its tested scope, the result is a full-load coefficient of performance below the reversible limit, with part-load behaviour unstated.

subtype: worked example with equation: available NPSH
fact_base: A pump draws water from an open tank at atmospheric pressure, 101.3 kPa. Vapour pressure at the pumping temperature is 7.4 kPa, the static lift is 2.5 m and suction-line friction loss is 1.2 m. Available net positive suction head $NPSH_a$ is 5.9 m. The pump's required NPSH at the duty flow comes from the vendor curve and must be exceeded with margin.
input:
When a pump draws water from an open tank, one of the most practically significant questions that arises is whether the liquid will reach the pump inlet without cavitating, and it is precisely this question that the concept of available net positive suction head is designed to answer. In the present case, the atmospheric pressure acting on the surface of the tank is 101.3 kPa, while the vapour pressure of the water at the pumping temperature is 7.4 kPa. The static lift that the liquid has to make is 2.5 m, and the friction loss in the suction line amounts to 1.2 m. In broad terms, the pressure difference between the atmosphere and the vapour pressure is what pushes the liquid towards the pump, while the lift and the friction loss work in the opposite direction, and the balance of these effects is what the calculation captures. Bringing these quantities together, the available net positive suction head, $NPSH_a$, can be expressed in terms of the atmospheric pressure, $P_{atm}$, the vapour pressure, $P_v$, the density, $\rho$, the acceleration due to gravity, $g$, the static lift, $h_{lift}$, and the friction loss, $h_f$, as follows:
$$NPSH_a = \frac{P_{atm} - P_v}{\rho g} - h_{lift} - h_f$$
Working through this relationship with the values given above leads to an available net positive suction head of 5.9 m. It should, however, be borne in mind that this available figure is only one half of the story, because the pump's required net positive suction head at the duty flow comes from the vendor curve, and the available value must exceed the required value with margin before the installation can be regarded as satisfactory from a cavitation standpoint.
target:
Available net positive suction head, $NPSH_a$, is calculated from the pressure at the surface of an open tank, the vapour pressure of the water at the pumping temperature, the static lift, and the friction loss in the suction line. The tank is open, so the surface pressure is the atmospheric pressure. The atmospheric pressure is 101.3 kPa and the vapour pressure is 7.4 kPa; the static lift, $h_{lift}$, is 2.5 m and the suction-line friction loss, $h_f$, is 1.2 m. For water of density $\rho$ under gravity $g$, the relation is
$$NPSH_a = \frac{P_{atm} - P_v}{\rho g} - h_{lift} - h_f$$
where $P_{atm}$ denotes the atmospheric pressure and $P_v$ denotes the vapour pressure. Substitution of the stated values gives an available net positive suction head of 5.9 m. The pressure term is the head that the atmosphere can support above the vapour pressure of the liquid at its pumping temperature. Each term in the relation is a head in metres, so the terms can be added and subtracted directly. Static lift and friction loss consume part of that head before the liquid reaches the pump inlet, and the remainder is the head available against cavitation at the duty flow. The pump's required net positive suction head at the duty flow comes from the vendor curve, and the available value must exceed the required value with margin. The comparison is therefore between a calculated available head and a vendor figure for the actual machine, and the brief states no numerical margin. A margin stated without the vendor value would be unsupported, so the worked result closes at the available head and the condition it must satisfy.

fact_base: A single-stage compressor raises natural gas from 1 bar to 4 bar. Inlet temperature is 293 K. For isentropic compression with a heat-capacity ratio of 1.4, the discharge temperature is 435 K. The isentropic estimate excludes mechanical losses; the installed machine's measured discharge temperature is higher.
input: In this example we consider a single-stage compressor that raises natural gas from 1 bar to 4 bar, a duty that is representative of a wide range of gas-handling applications. The inlet temperature of the gas is 293 K. If the compression is imagined to take place isentropically, with a heat-capacity ratio of 1.4, the discharge temperature that emerges from the calculation is 435 K. It is, however, essential to appreciate what this figure does and does not represent. The isentropic estimate excludes mechanical losses, which means that it paints a somewhat idealised picture of the machine, and the installed machine's measured discharge temperature is higher than the calculated value. In other words, the number that comes out of the isentropic calculation should be read as a benchmark arrived at under deliberately simplified assumptions, rather than as a faithful prediction of what a thermometer at the discharge of the real machine would actually register. The gap between the two temperatures is where all of the real-world imperfections of the machine reside, even though the calculation itself does not attempt to itemise them or to assign a share of the difference to any particular source of loss. There is also a broader methodological point worth making here, namely that idealised calculations of this type are valuable precisely because they strip away the complications of the real machine and expose the part of the behaviour that depends only on the stated pressures, the inlet temperature, and the properties of the gas, leaving everything else to be accounted for by measurement.
target: A single-stage compressor raises natural gas from 1 bar to 4 bar. A single stage takes the whole pressure rise in one machine, with no intercooling between stages. From an inlet temperature of 293 K, isentropic compression with a heat-capacity ratio of 1.4 gives a discharge temperature of 435 K. The heat-capacity ratio is the ratio of the specific heat at constant pressure to the specific heat at constant volume, and it fixes how strongly the temperature responds to the pressure change in the isentropic relation. The isentropic estimate excludes mechanical losses. Isentropic compression is compression without heat transfer and without irreversibility, so no allowance stands in the estimate for friction in the bearings, leakage past the seals, or irreversibility in the gas path. Each of those effects, where it acts, converts work into internal energy of the gas and raises the discharge temperature above the isentropic value. The installed machine's measured discharge temperature is higher, and the isentropic value is therefore a reference calculated for an idealised machine rather than a prediction of the installed discharge temperature. The brief quantifies none of the loss effects, and the difference between the calculated and measured temperatures cannot be divided among them from the stated data. The discharge temperature is the quantity that downstream cooling and the machine's own materials limits are set against, so the distinction between the calculated reference and the measured value is the operative point of the example. At the stated scope, the result is an isentropic discharge temperature for the specified pressure rise, with the installed machine running hotter for reasons the estimate does not attempt to cost.

fact_base: A continuous stirred-tank reactor runs a hydrolysis that is first order in the limiting reactant. The rate constant is 0.156 min-1 at the operating temperature and the mean residence time is 36 min. Steady-state conversion for an ideal CSTR is 84.9%. The estimate assumes perfect mixing and constant density; tracer tests on the actual vessel have not been run.
input: Steady-state conversion for an ideal continuous stirred-tank reactor (CSTR) running a hydrolysis that is first order in the limiting reactant is 84.9%. The rate constant at the operating temperature is 0.156 min-1, and the mean residence time in the vessel is 36 min. Conversion states the fraction of the limiting reactant that has reacted by the outlet, and a first-order reaction is one whose rate is proportional to the concentration of that reactant. Perfect mixing is assumed, so the composition and temperature are uniform through the vessel and the outlet stream has the vessel composition. Constant density is also assumed, so the mean residence time is set by the vessel volume and the volumetric flow alone. The estimate assumes perfect mixing and constant density; tracer tests on the actual vessel have not been run. The conversion figure therefore rests on the ideal-mixing assumption without an independent measurement of how long material actually spends in the vessel. A real vessel with short-circuiting or stagnant regions would hold a distribution of residence times rather than the single mean value, and its conversion would differ from the ideal figure in a direction the stated data do not fix. At its stated scope, the result is the conversion of the ideal reactor under the two named assumptions, not a measured performance of the installed vessel.
