topic: tut:phase:a pure component at its boiling point
fact_base: A tutorial passage explains phase equilibrium for a pure component at its boiling point. The passage states the equilibrium condition in words (equality of chemical potential across phases) before any equation is named. No numerical data are introduced; the passage is conceptual.
input: It is widely understood that boiling is one of those everyday phenomena that appear simple on the surface while resting on a surprisingly subtle foundation, and a closer look at what is happening at the molecular level repays the effort. When a pure component sits at its boiling point, the liquid and the vapour are in a state of phase equilibrium, which means that neither phase is growing at the expense of the other. The condition that defines this state can be put into words as the equality of the chemical potential of the component across the phases: the chemical potential in the liquid is exactly the same as the chemical potential in the vapour. The chemical potential can be thought of as a measure of how strongly the molecules of the component tend to escape from the phase they currently occupy. If the chemical potential in the liquid were higher than in the vapour, molecules would stream out of the liquid and the vapour would grow; if it were lower, the traffic would run the other way and the vapour would condense back into liquid. Only when the two are equal does the net traffic fall to zero, even though molecules continue to cross the interface in both directions at matching rates. At the boiling point, this delicate balance is maintained while vapour bubbles form throughout the body of the liquid, and heat that is supplied at constant pressure goes into converting liquid into vapour rather than into raising the temperature, which consequently stays fixed until one of the phases has disappeared altogether. It is also worth noting that, for a pure component, the boiling point is set by the pressure, since only one temperature at that pressure can make the two chemical potentials come out equal.
target: Phase equilibrium for a pure component at its boiling point is the state in which the liquid and vapour phases coexist and neither phase grows at the expense of the other. The equilibrium condition is stated in words as the equality of the chemical potential of the component across the phases: the chemical potential in the liquid equals the chemical potential in the vapour. The chemical potential measures the tendency of the component to leave the phase it is in. Where the chemical potential in the liquid stands higher than in the vapour, molecules pass from liquid to vapour and the vapour phase grows; where it stands lower, vapour condenses and the liquid phase grows. Transfer continues until the two values meet, and at equality the net transfer stops, although molecules continue to cross the surface in both directions at equal rates. At the boiling point this balance holds while bubbles of vapour form throughout the liquid, not only at its surface. Heat supplied at constant pressure then changes the amounts of the two phases rather than the temperature: liquid becomes vapour at a fixed temperature until one phase is gone. The same condition governs condensation, read in the reverse direction, and evaporation from an open surface, where the vapour above the liquid is continually removed and equilibrium is approached but not held. The boiling point itself is fixed by the pressure for a pure component, because only one temperature at that pressure makes the two chemical potentials equal. A pure component has a single boiling point at a given pressure precisely because the equality can be met at only one temperature there. Equilibrium is therefore a condition on the state of the two phases, stated without any measured data, and every boiling, condensation, or flash calculation for a pure component starts from it.

fact_base: Adsorption of a dye from water on a metal-organic framework was measured in batch tests at 298 K. The fitted Langmuir capacity was 125 mg of dye per gram of adsorbent at pH 5. At an adsorbent dose of 0.9 g L-1, removal after 120 min was 81% of the initial dye concentration of 50 mg L-1. The Langmuir fit is reported for pH 5 only; capacity at other pH values was not measured.
input: In a series of batch tests carried out at 298 K, the adsorption of a dye from water onto a metal-organic framework was investigated in some detail. The fitted Langmuir capacity came out at 125 mg of dye per gram of adsorbent at pH 5, which gives a sense of the uptake that the material can ultimately accommodate under the conditions studied. When the adsorbent was dosed at 0.9 g L-1, the removal after 120 min reached 81% of the initial dye concentration of 50 mg L-1, a result that speaks to the practical effectiveness of the material over the timescale of the test. Batch tests hold the liquid and the adsorbent together in a closed vessel, so the measured removal reflects the change in the liquid concentration over the contact time. It should nevertheless be kept in mind that the Langmuir fit is reported for pH 5 only, and that capacity at other pH values was not measured, so the figures that have been obtained should be understood as belonging specifically to the conditions under which the tests were performed rather than as properties that can be carried over without qualification to different conditions.
target: Adsorption of a dye from water on a metal-organic framework removed 81% of the initial dye concentration after 120 min in batch tests at 298 K. The initial dye concentration was 50 mg L-1 and the adsorbent dose was 0.9 g L-1. Batch tests hold the liquid and adsorbent together in a closed vessel, so the measured removal is the change in the liquid concentration over the contact time. The fitted Langmuir capacity was 125 mg of dye per gram of adsorbent at pH 5. Removal is stated against the initial concentration, so the percentage and the starting value together fix what the tests achieved. The Langmuir capacity is a fitted quantity: it is the plateau of the fitted isotherm, obtained from the batch data, and it is reported for pH 5 only. Capacity at other pH values was not measured. The result therefore describes uptake under the tested conditions — the stated temperature, dose, contact time, and starting concentration — and the closing limit is part of the result: an adsorbent compared at another pH would need its own fit before any ranking could be made. Within the tested scope, the framework took up the stated fraction of the dye and the fitted capacity stands as the single capacity figure the tests support for this adsorbent and this dye.

subtype: worked example with equation: radiative exchange
fact_base: An oxidised steel panel at 1000 K faces surroundings at 350 K. Its emissivity $\varepsilon$ is 0.9. Net radiative heat flux $q$ is 50.3 kW m-2, with the Stefan-Boltzmann constant $\sigma$ = 5.67 x 10-8 W m-2 K-4. The estimate treats both surfaces as large and parallel; view factors for the real geometry are not included.
input:
Radiative heat transfer between surfaces at different temperatures is governed by a relationship in which the temperatures enter through their fourth powers, which makes the hotter surface by far the dominant partner in the exchange. In the case considered here, an oxidised steel panel sits at 1000 K while the surroundings it faces are at 350 K. The emissivity of the panel, $\varepsilon$, is 0.9, reflecting the fact that an oxidised surface radiates much more effectively than a bright polished one would. The Stefan-Boltzmann constant, $\sigma$, takes the value 5.67 x 10-8 W m-2 K-4. Radiative exchange needs no medium between the surfaces, and the net flux is the difference between what the panel emits and what it absorbs from the surroundings. Putting these quantities into the standard relation for the net radiative heat flux, $q$, gives
$$q = \varepsilon \sigma (T_1^4 - T_2^4)$$
and working through the numbers leads to a net radiative heat flux of 50.3 kW m-2. It is worth emphasising, however, that this estimate treats both surfaces as large and parallel, whereas the view factors for the real geometry are not included, so the figure is best regarded as belonging to the idealised arrangement rather than to any particular installation with its own geometry. The strong temperature dependence is the reason a panel at such a temperature dominates the exchange so completely, and it is also why modest errors in the panel temperature would matter far more than comparable errors in the temperature of the surroundings.
target:
An oxidised steel panel at 1000 K faces surroundings at 350 K. Its emissivity, $\varepsilon$, is 0.9. Emissivity scales the emission of the real surface against that of a perfect emitter at the same temperature, which is why the value enters the relation as a simple multiplier. Radiative exchange needs no medium between the surfaces, and the net flux is the difference between what the panel emits and what it absorbs from the surroundings. With the Stefan-Boltzmann constant, $\sigma$, equal to 5.67 x 10-8 W m-2 K-4, the net radiative heat flux, $q$, for large parallel surfaces is
$$q = \varepsilon \sigma (T_1^4 - T_2^4)$$
where $q$ is the net radiative heat flux, $\varepsilon$ is the emissivity of the panel, and $\sigma$ is the Stefan-Boltzmann constant; the temperatures are the panel temperature and the surroundings temperature. Substitution gives a net radiative heat flux of 50.3 kW m-2. The fourth-power dependence makes the panel temperature the dominant term: the surroundings return only a small share of the emitted flux, and the net value is close to the gross emission of the panel. The estimate treats both surfaces as large and parallel. View factors for the real geometry are not included, so the figure belongs to the idealised arrangement and not to a panel facing surroundings of limited extent or at an angle. The panel radiates to the surroundings across the space between them, and the stated flux is the net rate per unit area at the panel surface. At its stated scope, the result is the net flux between large parallel surfaces at the two stated temperatures, with geometry effects outside the estimate.

subtype: worked example with equation: Antoine vapour pressure
fact_base: The vapour pressure of ethanol at 60 °C is estimated from the Antoine equation with constants $A$ = 8.20417, $B$ = 1642.89 and $C$ = 230.3 (pressure in mmHg, temperature in °C). The estimate is 46.8 kPa. The constants are valid only over their fitted temperature range; the source databank value governs design.
input:
The Antoine equation is a widely used empirical correlation that allows the vapour pressure of a pure substance to be estimated from its temperature, provided that a set of fitted constants is available for the substance in question. Here the substance is ethanol and the temperature of interest is 60 °C. The constants that go with the correlation are $A$ = 8.20417, $B$ = 1642.89 and $C$ = 230.3, with the pressure expressed in mmHg and the temperature in °C. In its usual form, the equation, which connects the vapour pressure, $P$, with the temperature, $T$, is written as
$$\log_{10} P = A - \frac{B}{T + C}$$
Carrying out the substitution with the values given above produces an estimate of 46.8 kPa for the vapour pressure. A number of qualifications nevertheless attach to this kind of estimate. The constants are valid only over their fitted temperature range, so the correlation should not be pushed beyond the range of the data from which it was derived. Furthermore, where a design figure is required, the source databank value governs design, and the Antoine estimate is best thought of as a convenient approximation that sits alongside the databank value rather than as a substitute for it. Taken together, these considerations mean that the estimate is a useful and readily obtained figure, as long as it is used within the bounds that its fitted constants impose. It is also helpful to remember that correlations of this kind earn their keep by being quick to evaluate and easy to embed in larger calculations, which is precisely why they remain in everyday use even though more fundamental treatments of vapour pressure exist.
target:
The vapour pressure of ethanol at 60 °C is estimated from the Antoine equation. The constants are $A$ = 8.20417, $B$ = 1642.89 and $C$ = 230.3, with pressure in mmHg and temperature in °C. The Antoine equation relates the vapour pressure, $P$, to the temperature, $T$, through the three fitted constants:
$$\log_{10} P = A - \frac{B}{T + C}$$
where $P$ denotes the vapour pressure and $T$ denotes the temperature. Substitution of the stated temperature gives an estimate of 46.8 kPa. The constants are empirical: they summarise measured vapour-pressure data over the temperature range to which they were fitted, and the relation is an interpolation device rather than a physical law. The form of the relation, a logarithm of pressure against a shifted reciprocal temperature, is chosen because vapour pressure rises steeply with temperature and the shift brings the curve close to a straight line over the fitted range. Each constant is tied to the units named with it, and the same numerical set cannot be carried into another unit system without refitting. The constants are valid only over their fitted temperature range. Outside that range the relation extrapolates a fitted curve beyond its evidence, and the error is not bounded by anything in the fit itself. The source databank value governs design, so the Antoine estimate serves as a check or a first value, and any design figure comes from the databank. The three constants belong to ethanol alone and to the stated unit system; another substance, or another set of units, requires its own fitted set. The estimate is therefore only as portable as its constants. At its stated scope, the result is an estimated vapour pressure at the stated temperature from the named constants, with the databank value standing as the governing figure wherever the two differ.

fact_base: A food plant uses 2198 MWh of electricity per year in refrigeration. A heat-recovery retrofit is projected by the equipment vendor to save 12% of that use, a derived saving of 264 MWh per year at the vendor figure. Capital cost is $415k. At an electricity price of $0.09 per kWh, the derived annual saving is $24k and the derived simple payback is 17.3 years. The saving figure is a vendor projection and was not measured at this plant; refrigeration load in the summer peak month was not modelled. The recommendation is a metered trial on one of the three refrigeration lines before any capital decision. The plant engineer owns the trial.
input: The recommendation is a metered trial on one of the three refrigeration lines before any capital decision. The plant engineer owns the trial. The trade-off is $415k of capital against a derived $24k per year: a payback of 17.3 years at the vendor figure. The saving figure is a vendor projection and was not measured at this plant. Refrigeration load in the summer peak month was not modelled, so the annual figures rest on the vendor's projection spread over a year whose peak month is unexamined. The trial exists to replace the projection with a measurement on one line under the plant's own operating pattern. Metering one line bounds the cost of finding out: the retrofit is neither approved on a projection nor rejected without evidence, and the capital decision waits for the trial result. At its stated scope, the position is a trial first, owned by the plant engineer, with the capital decision held until measured savings replace the vendor figure.

fact_base: A centrifugal pump moves water between two vessels at grade. At the duty point the flow is 47 m3 h-1 against a head of 18 m, with pump efficiency 69%. Shaft power at the duty point is 3.3 kW. The motor is rated 15% above this value. Cavitation was not observed in the acceptance test, which ran for 4 h at the duty point only.
input: The performance of a centrifugal pump moving water between two vessels at grade was characterised at its duty point, and the picture that emerges is as follows. At the duty point in question, the flow delivered by the pump is 47 m3 h-1 against a head of 18 m, and the pump efficiency at this operating point is 69%. The shaft power required at the duty point works out at 3.3 kW. The motor that drives the pump is rated 15% above this value, which builds a measure of headroom into the installation over and above the power that the duty itself demands. As far as cavitation is concerned, it is reassuring to note that cavitation was not observed in the acceptance test; that test, however, ran for 4 h at the duty point only, so the observation is tied to that particular set of conditions and to that duration, and it would be imprudent to read it as a guarantee covering the whole of the pump's operating range or extended periods of running. More broadly, a duty point of this kind is the anchor for the whole installation, because the motor selection, the acceptance test, and the day-to-day operation of the pump all refer back to the same specified condition.
target: A centrifugal pump moves water between two vessels at grade. The two vessels at grade stand at the same elevation, so the head is developed against the system resistance rather than against a lift between levels. At the duty point the flow is 47 m3 h-1 against a head of 18 m, with pump efficiency of 69%. Shaft power at the duty point is 3.3 kW. The motor is rated 15% above this value, so the motor carries a stated margin over the shaft power at the duty point and no more than that margin can be inferred. Cavitation was not observed in the acceptance test, which ran for 4 h at the duty point only. The duty point is the operating point at which the pump was tested and rated: the flow, head, efficiency, and shaft power all belong to that single point. Away from the duty point the pump follows its own characteristic, and none of the stated values describes operation at another flow. The cavitation statement is a detection statement with the same boundary: no cavitation was detected during a test of the stated duration at the stated point, and the test says nothing about longer runs or other operating points. At its tested scope, the result is a rated duty point with its shaft power and motor margin, and a cavitation observation bounded by the acceptance test.

fact_base: A food plant uses 2552 MWh of electricity per year in refrigeration. A heat-recovery retrofit is projected by the equipment vendor to save 11% of that use, a derived saving of 281 MWh per year at the vendor figure. Capital cost is $426k. At an electricity price of $0.11 per kWh, the derived annual saving is $31k and the derived simple payback is 13.7 years. input: This summary brings together the background, the figures, and the thinking behind a proposed heat-recovery retrofit at a food plant, where refrigeration accounts for a substantial share of the site's electricity consumption. The plant in question uses 2552 MWh of electricity per year in refrigeration, so even a modest percentage improvement translates into a meaningful quantity of energy. The equipment vendor projects that the retrofit would save 11% of that use, which works out at a derived saving of 281 MWh per year at the vendor figure. Set against this, the capital cost is $426k, and at an electricity price of $0.11 per kWh the derived annual saving is $31k, giving a derived simple payback of 13.7 years. Viewed in the round, $426k is a considerable sum to commit against $31k a year, and the payback stretches well into the longer term. It is important to appreciate that the saving figure is a vendor projection and was not measured at this plant, and that refrigeration load in the summer peak month was not modelled, so there are genuine uncertainties wrapped around the headline numbers. Against that background, the recommendation is a metered trial on one of the three refrigeration lines before any capital decision, so that measured performance can replace projection; the plant engineer owns the trial and will report what the metering shows. The metering exercise is deliberately modest in scope, since a single line can be instrumented without disturbing production on the rest of the site, and its results can be read directly against the projection.
target: The recommendation is a metered trial on one of the three refrigeration lines before any capital decision, and the plant engineer owns the trial. A food plant uses 2552 MWh of electricity per year in refrigeration. A heat-recovery retrofit is projected by the equipment vendor to save 11% of that use, a derived saving of 281 MWh per year at the vendor figure. Capital cost is $426k. At an electricity price of $0.11 per kWh, the derived annual saving is $31k and the derived simple payback is 13.7 years. The trade-off is $426k of capital committed now against a derived $31k per year, and it is unfavourable at the vendor figure without a measured saving behind it. A simple payback divides the capital by the annual saving and so takes no account of the timing of the savings, of maintenance, or of any change in the electricity price over the payback period. Those omissions are part of the figure's meaning and are carried with it wherever it is quoted. The saving figure is a vendor projection and was not measured at this plant; refrigeration load in the summer peak month was not modelled. The trial replaces the projection with a measurement on one line, taken under the plant's own load pattern, before capital is committed to the retrofit as a whole. Metering a single line bounds the cost of the check and leaves the other lines untouched until the measured figure is known. If the measured saving falls below the projection, the payback extends beyond the stated value and the case for extending the retrofit weakens accordingly. The decision the summary supports is the trial, not the retrofit.

fact_base: Adsorption of a dye from water on a metal-organic framework was measured in batch tests at 298 K. The fitted Langmuir capacity was 193 mg of dye per gram of adsorbent at pH 5. At an adsorbent dose of 0.7 g L-1, removal after 120 min was 85% of the initial dye concentration of 50 mg L-1. The Langmuir fit is reported for pH 5 only; capacity at other pH values was not measured.
input: The uptake of a dye from water by a metal-organic framework was examined in batch tests at 298 K, and the results can be summarised as follows. The fitted Langmuir capacity was 193 mg of dye per gram of adsorbent at pH 5, indicating the level of uptake that the fitted isotherm approaches at its plateau. With an adsorbent dose of 0.7 g L-1, the removal after 120 min reached 85% of the initial dye concentration of 50 mg L-1, showing that a substantial proportion of the dye was taken up within the duration of the test. Batch tests bring a fixed mass of adsorbent into contact with the dye solution in a closed vessel, and the removal is read from the change in the liquid concentration over the contact time. A qualification should nevertheless be attached to the capacity figure: the Langmuir fit is reported for pH 5 only, and capacity at other pH values was not measured, so the result belongs to the conditions studied and should not be assumed to hold more generally. The two headline figures therefore complement one another, the capacity describing the material's fitted ceiling and the removal describing what was actually achieved in the test as run.
target: Adsorption of a dye from water on a metal-organic framework reached 85% removal of the initial dye concentration after 120 min in batch tests at 298 K, at an adsorbent dose of 0.7 g L-1 and an initial dye concentration of 50 mg L-1. The fitted Langmuir capacity was 193 mg of dye per gram of adsorbent at pH 5. Batch tests bring a fixed mass of adsorbent into contact with the dye solution in a closed vessel, and the removal is read from the fall in the liquid concentration over the contact time. The capacity is a fitted plateau value from the isotherm fitted to the batch data, and the fit is reported for pH 5 only. Capacity at other pH values was not measured, so no capacity figure exists for any other condition of acidity. Removal and capacity answer different questions: the removal states what the tested dose achieved against the stated starting concentration in the stated time, and the capacity states the fitted ceiling on uptake per gram of adsorbent. The two figures are reported together because a capacity without the achieved removal, or a removal without the fitted capacity, would each describe only part of the test outcome. Both stand on the same batch tests, at the stated temperature. A comparison against another adsorbent is supported only at the tested pH and under the tested conditions; beyond them, the pair of figures does not travel.

fact_base: Staffing review for a quality laboratory: 15 full-time staff, overtime at 6% of paid hours last year. Replacing half the overtime with one additional hire costs $82k per year fully loaded. Overtime is concentrated in two seasonal peaks; a hire is paid for the full year.
input: It is important to note that overtime working in the quality laboratory amounted to 6% of total paid hours over the course of last year. The laboratory currently employs a team of 15 full-time staff members, and it should be emphasised that this overtime is by no means distributed evenly throughout the year; instead, it is heavily concentrated in two distinct seasonal peaks. One option that has been considered in some detail is to replace half of the overtime with one additional hire, an option that would cost $82k per year on a fully loaded basis, with the half in question corresponding to 3% of paid hours. However, it is worth bearing in mind that a new hire would be paid for the full year, including the quieter months that fall between the two peaks, when no overtime arises at all, whereas the overtime cost itself is incurred only during the peak periods themselves. It should also be noted that the remaining half of the overtime would still remain in place under this option, so the peaks would continue to be worked partly on overtime even after the hire was made. Overall, the comparison is essentially between a fixed commitment of $82k per year and a flexible, variable cost that arises only when demand peaks, and the decision ultimately hinges on how intense those peaks are, how far behind the laboratory falls during them, and what the resulting delays mean for the wider work that depends on laboratory results.
target: Overtime in the quality laboratory ran at 6% of paid hours last year, on a staff of 15 full-time employees. The overtime is concentrated in two seasonal peaks; outside the peaks, the laboratory's paid hours are covered by the existing staff and no overtime arises. Replacing half the overtime with one additional hire costs $82k per year fully loaded, and the half replaced amounts to 3% of paid hours. A hire is paid for the full year, including the months between the peaks, so the salary is a fixed cost set against a demand that arises in two parts of the year only. The remaining half of the overtime stays in place under this option, because the hire replaces only half of it, and the peaks would still be worked partly on overtime. The case for the hire rests on the intensity of the peaks: how far the laboratory falls behind during them, and what the delay costs the work that waits on laboratory results. Peak intensity also decides whether one hire is enough, since a hire adds fixed capacity in every peak week. Those effects are not costed in the figures stated here. On the stated figures, the laboratory is comparing a year-round salary commitment of $82k with a peak-only cost, and the annual overtime share frames that comparison without settling it.

fact_base: A contract packaging firm runs 4 plants; revenue is $118 million per year. Evidence base: order records for 12 months, 13536 orders. On-time delivery over the last two quarters was 91%, against a target of 95%. Overtime cost was $2.2 million last year, up 24% on the year before. The order backlog stands at 3.8 weeks, against 1.9 weeks a year ago. Plant 2 accounts for 63% of late orders. A scheduling system for all plants is quoted at $260k; Plant 2 alone is $112k. An internal estimate (not a vendor figure) puts the overtime reduction at Plant 2 at 15-20% in the first year. input: In recent quarters, the contract packaging firm, which operates 4 plants and generates revenue of $118 million per year, has experienced a noticeable deterioration in its delivery performance. Based on an analysis of order records covering a period of 12 months and encompassing a total of 13536 orders, on-time delivery over the last two quarters stood at 91%, which falls short of the target of 95%. It is worth noting that Plant 2 accounts for a disproportionate 63% of all late orders across the business. At the same time, overtime cost reached $2.2 million last year, representing an increase of 24% compared with the year before, while the order backlog has grown to some 3.8 weeks, compared with just 1.9 weeks a year ago. A scheduling system covering all plants has been quoted at $260k, whereas Plant 2 alone would cost $112k. An internal estimate — and it should be stressed that this is an internal estimate rather than a vendor figure — suggests that overtime at Plant 2 could potentially be reduced by 15–20% in the first year. The recommendation under consideration is therefore to install the system at Plant 2 first and to hold the other plants until the Plant 2 results are reported, with the operations director owning the scheduling programme, so that the initial commitment is limited to $112k and the plant responsible for 63% of late orders is addressed first; the wider rollout then rests on the Plant 2 evidence.

fact_base: Excerpt content: the schedule float is set at 7% and the excerpt defends that figure against a lower alternative. The excerpt refers to the project's cost table by section name and does not repeat its figures.
input: the argument in favour of retaining the float at 7% is essentially based on where the delay risk actually sits within the remaining programme of work. Much of what remains is interface work: tie-ins to plant that stays in service, deliveries whose dates the upgrade project does not control, and weather exposure on the outdoor scope. A delay in any one of these areas would arrive at the critical path with no allowance of its own, and the float within the programme is effectively the only provision available to absorb it. The lower alternative treats the float as a contingency for the project's own tasks, and on that reading a smaller figure would suffice, since the task estimates already contain their own allowances for overrun. The steering group, however, does not accept that reading. Float held at 7% is intended to cover the gaps between tasks: the handover that waits for a permit, the delivery that slips beyond its window, the tie-in that cannot begin until a shutdown commences. None of these gaps sits within any task estimate, and none would be removed by estimating the tasks more carefully. The Costs section sets out the cost of the programme on this basis; the float is fundamentally a time allowance, and its cost effect runs through the overall duration of the programme rather than through any single line of the table. Reducing the figure to the lower alternative would not, in itself, remove the delays; it would instead transfer them onto the completion date that the steering group has reported, and until FID those reported dates remain the basis on which the upgrade project is judged, so that a float consumed by the first interface delay would leave the completion date exposed to the risks it was intended to absorb, a position which the steering group is not prepared to

subtype: worked example with equation: Fourier conduction
fact_base: A flat stainless steel wall has thickness 12 mm and thermal conductivity $k$ of 16 W m-1 K-1. The temperature difference $\Delta T$ across the wall is 367 K, giving a heat flux $q$ of 489333 W m-2. The calculation is steady and one-dimensional; film resistances are excluded.
input:
In this example, we consider a flat stainless steel wall that separates two fluids, and the objective is to determine the heat flux passing through the wall for the temperature difference that exists across it. The calculation is based on a number of important assumptions: it is steady in nature and one-dimensional, and film resistances are excluded from the analysis, which means that the temperature difference $\Delta T$ should be understood as the difference across the wall material alone. Fourier's law allows the heat flux to be calculated from the thermal conductivity and the temperature gradient, as follows:

$$q = k \frac{\Delta T}{\Delta x}$$\n\nwhere $q$ denotes the heat flux, $k$ denotes the thermal conductivity of the wall, $\Delta T$ denotes the temperature difference across the wall, and $\Delta x$ denotes the wall thickness. In the present case, the wall thickness is 12 mm, which is equivalent to 0.012 m, the value of $\Delta T$ is 367 K, and for stainless steel the thermal conductivity $k$ has a value of 16 W m-1 K-1. Substituting these values into the expression gives $q$ = 16 × 367 / 0.012 = 489333 W m-2. It is worth noting that this value is a wall-only figure: because film resistances have been excluded, it represents the flux at the stated temperature difference across the wall itself, and if surface films were included against the same overall temperature difference, a lower flux would be obtained. The result is therefore valid for the steady, one-dimensional conditions that have been stated.
target:

The calculation is steady and one-dimensional, and film resistances are excluded, so the temperature difference $\Delta T$ is the difference across the wall material alone. Fourier's law gives the heat flux from the thermal conductivity and the temperature gradient:

$$q = k \frac{\Delta T}{\Delta x}$$\n\nwhere $q$ is the heat flux, $k$ the thermal conductivity of the wall, $\Delta T$ the temperature difference across the wall and $\Delta x$ the wall thickness. The wall thickness is 12 mm, or 0.012 m, $\Delta T$ is 367 K, and for stainless steel $k$ is 16 W m-1 K-1. Substitution gives $q$ = 16 × 367 / 0.012 = 489333 W m-2. The value is a wall-only figure: because film resistances are excluded, it is the flux at the stated temperature difference across the wall itself, and surface films set against the same overall temperature difference would return a lower flux. The temperature gradient is the temperature difference divided by the thickness, and the flux rises in proportion to the conductivity and to the gradient. A thicker wall at the same temperature difference returns a smaller flux, and a larger temperature difference at the same thickness returns a larger one. Fourier's law holds for the steady, one-dimensional conditions stated, and the result stands at those conditions, on the stated thickness and the stated difference.

fact_base: Staffing review for a dispatch office: 11 full-time staff, overtime at 6% of paid hours last year. Replacing half the overtime with one additional hire costs $69k per year fully loaded. Overtime is concentrated in two seasonal peaks; a hire is paid for the full year.
input: This staffing review examines the position in a dispatch office which employs 11 full-time members of staff and which recorded overtime amounting to 6% of paid hours over the course of last year. It is important to appreciate that this overtime is not spread evenly across the year as a whole; rather, it is concentrated in two distinct seasonal peaks, and between those peaks the office's paid hours are perfectly adequately covered by the existing staff, with no overtime arising at all. One option that has been put forward is to replace half of the overtime with one additional hire, which would cost $69k per year on a fully loaded basis, the half in question being equivalent to 3% of paid hours. However, any such hire would be paid for the full year, which means that the salary would continue to run through the quieter months as well as through the peaks, whereas the overtime that it replaces is purchased only in the weeks in which peak demand actually arises. The remaining half of the overtime would, of course, still remain in place under this option, and the peaks would continue to be worked partly on overtime. Overall, the comparison that the review presents is essentially between a fixed annual salary commitment and a variable cost that follows the pattern of demand across the year, together with the additional consideration that a hire would provide extra capacity in ordinary weeks, absorbing absence, leave and training without recourse to overtime, a benefit which the stated figure of $69k does not itself price. The decision ultimately rests on the height and duration of the two seasonal peaks, rather than on the annual percentage share of overtime in total paid hours.

That margin has a value the stated figures do not price, and it is not part of the comparison as costed. On the stated figures, the $69k buys out half of a peak-concentrated overtime bill at the price of a year-round commitment, and the case turns on the height and length of the two peaks rather than on the annual share of overtime in paid hours.

fact_base: A binary distillation separates benzene/toluene at a relative volatility of 2.15 that is taken as constant over the column. Specifications: distillate 98 mol% light component, bottoms 2 mol% light component. The Fenske minimum stage count is 10.2 theoretical stages including the reboiler. The actual design uses a reflux ratio of 1.3 times the minimum; the stage count at that reflux comes from a separate simulation.
input: The Fenske equation has been used in order to estimate the minimum number of stages required for the benzene/toluene separation under consideration, and it gives a minimum stage count of 10.2 theoretical stages, a figure which includes the reboiler. The specifications on which this calculation is based are a distillate containing 98 mol% of the light component and a bottoms stream containing 2 mol% of the light component, together with a relative volatility of 2.15, which has been taken as remaining constant over the whole of the column. It is important to note that the Fenske equation applies under conditions of total reflux, where each stage achieves its greatest possible separation and where the number of stages needed for any given separation is consequently at its minimum. This means that the count which is obtained in this way should properly be understood as a lower bound on the stages that an operating column would require, since no column that is working at a finite reflux ratio could achieve the stated separation in that number of stages. The reboiler is included within the figure because the reboiler itself performs one stage of separation. The assumption that the relative volatility remains constant over the column is also a significant one, because it is precisely this assumption that allows the separation to be expressed as a single stage count; if the relative volatility were instead to vary with composition along the column, a different count would be obtained from exactly the same specifications. The actual design, by contrast, operates at a reflux ratio of 1.3 times the minimum value, and the stage count that corresponds to that reflux has been obtained from a separate simulation rather than from the Fenske relation itself, and no stage count at the operating reflux is stated here. Between total reflux and the operating point, stages and reflux effectively trade against each other, and it is the simulation that resolves this trade-off for the stated duty. Overall, the figure of 10.2 stages stands as the reference value for the separation, representing the minimum that the stated compositions demand under the assumption of a constant relative volatility.
target: The Fenske equation gives a minimum stage count of 10.2 theoretical stages, including the reboiler, for the benzene/toluene separation at the stated specifications. The specifications are a distillate of 98 mol% light component and a bottoms of 2 mol% light component, and the relative volatility is 2.15, taken as constant over the column. The Fenske equation applies at total reflux, where each stage achieves its greatest separation and the stage count for a given separation is at its minimum. A count obtained at total reflux is a lower bound on the stages an operating column requires, and no column working at a finite reflux ratio separates the stated duty in that number of stages. The reboiler is counted in the figure because the reboiler performs one stage of separation, and the condenser practice assumed in the count is part of the basis on which the figure stands. Constancy of the relative volatility over the column is the assumption that lets the separation be stated as a single count: the equation works on the end compositions and the one relative volatility, and a relative volatility that varied with composition along the column would return a different count from the same specifications. No stage count at the operating reflux is stated here. Between total reflux and the operating point, stages and reflux trade against each other, and the simulation resolves that trade-off for the stated duty on its own basis. The 10.2 stages stand as the reference figure for the separation: the minimum the stated compositions demand, at the constant relative volatility, against which the operating design from the simulation is read.

subtype: worked example with equation: Raoult partial pressure
fact_base: An ideal liquid mixture holds ethanol in water (idealised) at a liquid mole fraction $x$ of 0.3 for the volatile component. Its pure-component vapour pressure $P^*$ at the mixture temperature is 20.1 kPa, so the partial pressure $p$ is 6 kPa by Raoult's law. Raoult's law assumes an ideal solution; activity coefficients for the real mixture are not applied.
input:
Raoult's law provides a means of calculating the partial pressure of a component in an ideal liquid mixture from its liquid mole fraction and its pure-component vapour pressure at the temperature of the mixture, in accordance with the following relationship:

$$p = x P^*$$\n\nwhere $p$ represents the partial pressure of the volatile component, $x$ represents its liquid mole fraction, and $P^*$ represents its pure-component vapour pressure at the mixture temperature. It is important to note that Raoult's law is based on the assumption of an ideal solution, and this assumption is stated here at the outset: no activity coefficients for the real mixture have been applied in this calculation. The mixture under consideration consists of ethanol in water, treated in an idealised manner, at a liquid mole fraction $x$ of 0.3 for the volatile component, while the value of $P^*$ at the mixture temperature is 20.1 kPa. Substituting these values into the relationship gives $p$ = 0.3 × 20.1 = 6.03 kPa, and the partial pressure is accordingly stated as 6 kPa. The partial pressure in question is the contribution made by the single component to the total pressure above the liquid, and it increases in direct proportion to the mole fraction, so that a richer liquid would yield a proportionally larger partial pressure at the same temperature. It should be emphasised, however, that the figure of 6 kPa which has been obtained is strictly an ideal-solution value: it applies to the mixture as idealised, at the mole fraction stated and at the temperature to which the pure-component vapour pressure relates, whereas a treatment of the real mixture would involve the application of activity coefficients and would produce a different partial pressure, and no activity-coefficient value has been stated or used in the present calculation.

Raoult's law assumes an ideal solution, and the assumption is stated before the relation is used: activity coefficients for the real mixture are not applied. fact_base: Goal: compute the Reynolds number for water in a pipe and state the flow regime. The Reynolds number Re (dimensionless) is computed from density rho (kg m-3), mean velocity v (m s-1), pipe diameter D (m) and dynamic viscosity mu (Pa s) by Re = rho v D / mu. Water at 293 K: rho = 998 kg m-3, mu = 1.00 x 10-3 Pa s. Pipe diameter D = 0.08 m; mean velocity v = 1.7 m s-1. Worked result: Re = 135700 (computed as 998 x 1.7 x 0.08 / 0.001). Flow is laminar below Re = 2300 and turbulent above Re = 4000; between the two values the regime is transitional and is not assigned by the number alone.
input: The task here is to calculate the Reynolds number for water flowing in a pipe and to state the flow regime that corresponds to it. The calculation gives a Reynolds number of 135700, which means that the flow is turbulent. The Reynolds number Re is computed from the density $\rho$, the mean velocity $v$, the pipe diameter $D$ and the dynamic viscosity $\mu$ by means of the relationship Re = $\rho v D / \mu$, and it is worth noting that the units cancel in the ratio, so that Re is a dimensionless quantity. For water at 293 K, the density $\rho$ has a value of 998 kg m-3 and the dynamic viscosity $\mu$ has a value of $1.00 \times 10^{-3}$ Pa s. The pipe diameter $D$ is 0.08 m, and the mean velocity $v$ is 1.7 m s-1. Substituting all of these values into the relationship gives Re = 998 × 1.7 × 0.08 / 0.001 = 135700. In general terms, flow is regarded as laminar below Re = 2300 and as turbulent above Re = 4000, while between these two values the regime is transitional in character and cannot be assigned on the basis of the number alone. The value that has been computed here, 135700, clearly lies above the turbulent threshold of 4000, and it is on the basis of this comparison that the flow of water in the pipe, at the stated diameter and velocity, is stated to be turbulent.

Because the number is proportional to the velocity and to the diameter, a faster flow or a wider pipe at the same properties returns a larger value, and a more viscous liquid returns a smaller one. Flow is laminar below Re = 2300 and turbulent above Re = 4000; between the two values the regime is transitional and is not assigned by the number alone. The computed value of 135700 lies above the turbulent threshold of 4000, and the regime statement rests on that comparison: at the stated diameter and velocity, the water in the pipe is in turbulent flow.

fact_base: Pricing case for a SaaS tier: price $321 per unit, variable cost $171 per unit, fixed costs $88k per year. Break-even volume is 587 units per year; current volume is 5971 units per year. Volume figures are last year's actuals; the effect of the price on volume is not estimated.
input: This pricing case examines the break-even position of a SaaS tier and establishes that the tier in question breaks even at 587 units per year, when set against a current volume of 5971 units per year. The price of the tier is $321 per unit, while the variable cost is $171 per unit, which means that each unit sold makes a contribution of $150 towards the fixed costs of $88k per year. Once sales reach 587 units, the accumulated contribution is sufficient to cover the fixed costs in their entirety, and beyond that particular volume each additional unit that is sold adds its $150 of contribution to the overall result for the year. The fixed costs stand regardless of whether the tier sells anything at all, whereas the variable cost follows the volume unit by unit, so the arithmetic of the case turns on the point at which the two behaviours meet. Below the break-even volume, the contribution for the year falls short of the fixed costs, while above it, the excess contribution represents the margin that the tier earns. The volume figures used here are last year's actuals. Current volume stands well above the break-even point, at roughly ten times the volume that the fixed costs require, and the distance between the two volumes represents the fall that the tier could sustain before the fixed costs would go uncovered at the stated price and costs. It should, however, be emphasised that the case holds the price fixed: the effect of the price on volume has not been estimated, and the break-even figure that has been calculated belongs specifically to the stated price. A lower price would reduce the contribution per unit, increase the volume needed in order to cover the fixed costs, and move the volume itself by an amount which the case does not attempt to quantify. Overall, on the figures as stated, the tier covers its fixed costs many times over at its current volume, and the genuinely open question is the one that the figures do not reach, namely what a change in price would do to the volume on which the entire calculation depends.

fact_base: Pervaporation is a membrane separation in which a liquid feed contacts one side of a membrane and vacuum on the other side draws the permeating component through as vapour. Flux is the mass permeating per unit membrane area per hour (kg m-2 h-1). The separation factor is the water-to-alcohol ratio in the permeate divided by the same ratio in the feed (dimensionless). Feed: 85 wt% n-butanol in water, at 60 °C. One feed composition was tested; no test ran beyond 500 h. Polymer membrane: flux 1.6 kg m-2 h-1, separation factor 180, flux fell 7% over 500 h. Zeolite membrane: flux 1.3 kg m-2 h-1, separation factor 320, flux unchanged over 500 h within measurement error. Flux, selectivity and stability are seldom reported together for the same membrane.
input: Pervaporation is a membrane separation technique in which a liquid feed is placed in contact with one side of a membrane, while a vacuum applied on the other side draws the component that permeates through the membrane as a vapour. In this work, flux is defined as the mass permeating per unit membrane area per hour (kg m-2 h-1), and the separation factor is defined as the water-to-alcohol ratio in the permeate divided by the same ratio in the feed. A polymer membrane and a zeolite membrane were both tested using a feed consisting of 85 wt% n-butanol in water at a temperature of 60 °C. The polymer membrane was found to give a flux of 1.6 kg m-2 h-1 together with a separation factor of 180, although its flux fell by 7% over the course of 500 h. The zeolite membrane, by contrast, gave a flux of 1.3 kg m-2 h-1 with a separation factor of 320, and its flux remained unchanged over 500 h, within the limits of measurement error. It can therefore be seen that the zeolite membrane is the more selective of the two membranes, whilst the polymer membrane is the more permeable, and the stability results separate them still further, since the zeolite membrane maintained its flux throughout the duration of the test whereas the polymer membrane did not. It should be noted that this comparison is based on a single feed composition, and that no test was run beyond 500 h; flux, selectivity and stability are seldom reported together for one and the same membrane, and the comparison that has been presented here applies to the feed and the duration that were actually tested.
target: Pervaporation separates a liquid feed across a membrane, with the feed on one side and vacuum on the other drawing the permeating component through as vapour. The ranking rests on one feed composition, as tested, and no test ran beyond 500 h; flux, selectivity and stability are seldom reported together for the same membrane, and the comparison is stated for the tested feed, at the tested temperature, and for the tested duration alone.

fact_base: Pervaporation is a membrane separation in which a liquid feed contacts one side of a membrane and vacuum on the other side draws the permeating component through as vapour. Flux is the mass permeating per unit membrane area per hour (kg m-2 h-1). The separation factor is the water-to-alcohol ratio in the permeate divided by the same ratio in the feed (dimensionless). Feed: 85 wt% isopropanol in water, at 60 °C. One feed composition was tested; no test ran beyond 500 h. Polymer membrane: flux 2.1 kg m-2 h-1, separation factor 120, flux fell 10% over 500 h. Zeolite membrane: flux 0.9 kg m-2 h-1, separation factor 420, flux unchanged over 500 h within measurement error. Flux, selectivity and stability are seldom reported together for the same membrane.
input: In this study, flux, selectivity and stability are compared for two different membranes applied to the pervaporation separation of isopropanol from water. Pervaporation is a membrane separation process in which a liquid feed is brought into contact with one side of a membrane, whilst a vacuum maintained on the other side draws the component that permeates through the membrane in the form of a vapour. Flux is defined as the mass that permeates per unit membrane area per hour (kg m-2 h-1), and the separation factor is defined as the water-to-alcohol ratio in the permeate divided by the same ratio in the feed, which expresses how strongly the membrane enriches the permeate in water relative to the feed. A polymer membrane and a zeolite membrane were both tested using a feed consisting of 85 wt% isopropanol in water at a temperature of 60 °C. The polymer membrane was found to give a flux of 2.1 kg m-2 h-1 together with a separation factor of 120, although its flux fell by 10% over the course of 500 h. The zeolite membrane, on the other hand, gave a flux of 0.9 kg m-2 h-1 and a separation factor of 420, and its flux remained unchanged over 500 h, within the limits of measurement error. The two membranes thus divide the three measures between them: the polymer membrane permeates at the faster rate but is considerably less selective, while the zeolite membrane permeates more slowly, enriches the permeate far more strongly, and succeeded in maintaining its flux over the full duration of the test where the polymer membrane lost flux. A duty that is governed by permeate purity therefore reads rather differently from a duty that is governed by throughput, and the difference in stability is relevant to both readings, since a flux that declines during the course of a run is not the flux on which the membrane was originally selected. It should be noted that only one feed composition was tested in this work, and that no test was run beyond 500 h. Flux, selectivity and stability are seldom reported together for one and the same membrane, and the comparison is complete on those three measures for the feed tested, without extending to other compositions or longer runs.
target: Flux, selectivity and stability are compared for two membranes in the pervaporation separation of isopropanol from water. Pervaporation is a membrane separation in which a liquid feed contacts one side of a membrane and vacuum on the other side draws the permeating component through as vapour. Flux is the mass permeating per unit membrane area per hour (kg m-2 h-1). The separation factor is the water-to-alcohol ratio in the permeate divided by the same ratio in the feed, and it states how strongly the membrane enriches the permeate in water relative to the feed. A polymer membrane and a zeolite membrane were tested on a feed of 85 wt% isopropanol in water at 60 °C. The polymer membrane gave a flux of 2.1 kg m-2 h-1 and a separation factor of 120, and its flux fell 10% over 500 h. The zeolite membrane gave a flux of 0.9 kg m-2 h-1 and a separation factor of 420, and its flux was unchanged over 500 h within measurement error. The two membranes divide the three measures between them. The polymer membrane permeates faster and is the less selective; the zeolite membrane permeates more slowly, enriches the permeate far more strongly, and held its flux over the full test duration where the polymer membrane lost flux. A duty that is set by permeate purity therefore reads differently from a duty set by throughput, and the stability difference bears on both readings, because a flux that declines over the run is not the flux the membrane was selected on. One feed composition was tested, and no test ran beyond 500 h. Flux, selectivity and stability are seldom reported together for the same membrane; the comparison is complete on those three measures for the tested feed, and it does not extend to other compositions or to longer runs.

fact_base: Design report for an amine absorber, in four sections: basis, sizing, materials, and risks. Design throughput is 34 t per day and the removal or separation duty is 90% of the key component. Materials are 316L stainless steel for wetted parts; the basis section states this once. The risks section names fouling and turndown as open items; neither is resolved in the report.
input:
Basis
The absorber has the function of removing the key component from the feed gas by means of absorption into a circulating amine solvent. The design throughput for the unit is 34 t per day of feed gas, and the removal duty is 90% of the key component that is present in the feed, measured between the feed gas as it enters and the treated gas as it leaves the absorber. The solvent circulates continuously between the absorber and its regeneration step: lean solvent enters at the top of the column, rich solvent leaves from the bottom carrying with it the component that has been absorbed, and the treated gas leaves from the overhead. It should be noted that the basis holds the duty on the absorber itself; the regeneration step is sized in order to return the solvent at the lean loading which the absorber basis assumes, and the performance that is stated in this report is therefore conditional upon that return condition actually being met in operation. The wetted parts are manufactured in 316L stainless steel, and the basis states this grade once, at this point; the materials section of the report works from the statement that has been made here. The feed composition and the operating pressure and temperature are taken as given for the purposes of the design, and the report does not revisit them. Performance is stated in terms of the removal of the key component only; any other components that are absorbed alongside it form part of the solvent duty but do not form part of the removal figure that has been stated.
Sizing
The column has been sized on the basis of the gas and liquid traffic that is established by the basis, together with the degree of contact that is needed in order to achieve the removal that has been stated. The diameter is determined by the gas rate, taken together with the liquid rate that the solvent circulation imposes at the removal duty, and it has been checked against flooding in order to ensure that the operating point sits below the flood point with the margin which good practice in amine service requires on account of the foaming tendency of the solvent. The packed or trayed height is determined by the mass-transfer requirement: the separation is expressed in terms of transfer units or stages, the height of a unit or of a stage is taken from the performance of the packing or trays in amine service, and the two are then combined in order to arrive at the contact height that the shell is required to contain. The solvent circulation is set by the removal duty and by the loading which the solvent is permitted to pick up between its lean and its rich states; a higher circulation makes the contact requirement easier to satisfy but increases the regeneration duty, and the sizing adopts the balance which the basis figures imply. An allowance has been made within the height for distribution, for redistribution and for the disengaging spaces at the two ends of the column, and the nozzles have been sized on the same traffic as the shell itself. It should be emphasised that the sizing is a design-point sizing: it establishes the vessel at the throughput and duty which have been stated, and it does not, by itself, establish the performance of the unit away from that point.
Materials
The wetted parts of the absorber are manufactured in the stainless steel that is named in the basis, and this choice is governed by the nature of amine service. Amine solvents are corrosive in proportion to their loading and to their temperature, and the degradation products which accumulate in a circulating solvent tend to add to the attack, so that the rich end of the circuit, where the loading and the temperature are at their highest in combination, represents the most exposed part of the whole system. The grade that is named in the basis is resistant to that service in circumstances where carbon steel would corrode at a rate that would shorten inspection intervals and would contaminate the solvent with corrosion products. The internals are specified in the same grade as the shell in those places where they are wetted, whilst non-wetted parts, supports and external attachments follow ordinary pressure-vessel practice appropriate to the design conditions. Welding and fabrication follow the vessel code that applies to the grade, with the solution-annealed condition being preserved in those places where forming or welding would otherwise sensitise the material. The materials statement that is made here covers the absorber and its internals; the solvent circuit beyond the column, the regeneration equipment and the interconnecting lines are all covered by their own statements elsewhere in the design, and nothing in this section should be taken as extending the grade of the absorber to those items.
Risks
There are two items which stand open at the close of the design, and it should be clearly stated that neither of them is resolved within this report. The first of these is the fouling of the internals. The feed gas carries solids and heavy ends into the column, the degradation of the solvent contributes solids of its own, and the deposits which form on the packing or on the trays act to reduce the contact which the sizing assumes and to raise the pressure drop across the column. The design states the duty on the basis of clean internals; the rate at which performance will fall away as fouling builds up, and the cleaning interval at which the service will eventually settle, are operating questions which the design figures are not able to answer, and the item accordingly stays open until it is closed by operating data or by a fouling allowance that is agreed with the solvent supplier. The second open item is turndown. The sizing is a design-point sizing, and at reduced levels of throughput the distribution of liquid over the packing or the trays deteriorates and the efficiency of contact falls, so that removal at low rates is not established by the design-point figures. The extent to which the absorber can be turned down while still meeting the removal that has been stated is not determined in this report, and the operating range of the unit is therefore stated at the design point only, with the turndown item being held open for the operating envelope study which follows the design.

The excerpt compares two gasket materials on temperature limit only and prefers the higher-rated one. The excerpt ends mid-argument; it neither summarises the report nor previews the next section.

Turning to the question of the gasket materials, it can be observed that the two candidate materials have been compared primarily and indeed exclusively on the basis of their temperature limits, and on balance it would appear that the material with the higher temperature rating is generally to be preferred. fact_base: A tutorial passage explains feedback control through a temperature loop on a process vessel. The passage covers the sensor, the controller, the final element and the sign of the feedback, in that order. No tuning numbers are given; the passage explains structure, not settings.
input: In this passage, we will explore how feedback control works by looking at a temperature loop on a process vessel, and it is hoped that by the end of it you will have a good overall understanding of the main ideas involved. Essentially, the starting point is the sensor, which is typically a temperature-sensing element placed in the vessel that basically measures the temperature on an ongoing basis and converts what it finds into a signal. This signal is then passed along to the controller, which compares the measured temperature against the desired set point and works out, in a fairly sophisticated way, how far apart the two values are and what sort of corrective action might be appropriate. The controller then sends its output onward to the final element, which is often a control valve on the heating medium line, and this valve actually does the physical work of changing the flow of heating medium so that more or less heat is delivered to the vessel. Finally, and perhaps most importantly, there is the question of the sign of the feedback, which is something that is absolutely fundamental to whether the whole arrangement works at all: the action taken has to oppose the change that triggered it, so that if the temperature rises too high the heating is reduced, and if it falls too low the heating is increased, thereby keeping everything nicely stable overall.
target: A temperature loop on a process vessel holds the vessel temperature at its set point by measuring the temperature and acting on the difference. Four parts make up the loop, and their order matters: sensor, controller, final element, and the sign of the feedback. The sensor is a temperature element in the vessel. The sensor measures the temperature continuously and sends the measurement to the controller as a signal. Measurement is the loop's only contact with the process: every later decision rests on the value the sensor reports, and a sensor that reads high or low displaces the whole loop by that error. The controller compares the measured temperature with the set point and calculates a correction from the difference. The controller does not move anything itself; its output is an instruction, sized by the size of the difference. The final element carries out the instruction. In this loop the final element is a valve on the heating medium line: the valve changes the flow of heating medium, and the changed flow changes the heat delivered to the vessel. Feedback closes the loop because the sensor measures the result of the valve's action and the controller acts again on the new difference. The sign of the feedback decides whether the loop settles or runs away. The action must oppose the change that produced it: a temperature above the set point calls for less heating, a temperature below the set point for more. With the opposite sign, a rise in temperature would call for more heating, the next measurement would be higher still, and the loop would drive the vessel away from the set point it exists to hold.

topic: tut:phase:a binary mixture at fixed pressure
fact_base: A tutorial passage explains phase equilibrium for a binary mixture at fixed pressure. The passage states the equilibrium condition in words (equality of chemical potential across phases) before any equation is named. No numerical data are introduced; the passage is conceptual.
input: Phase equilibrium for a binary mixture at fixed pressure is the state in which the two phases coexist without net transfer of either component between them. The equilibrium condition is equality of chemical potential across the phases: for each component, the chemical potential in one phase equals the chemical potential in the other. Net transfer stops at that equality because transfer is driven by a difference in chemical potential; a component moves from the phase in which its chemical potential is higher to the phase in which it is lower, and the movement continues until the difference is gone. Temperature is uniform across the phases in the same state, and the fixed pressure is common to both. Composition is where the two phases differ. Each phase has its own composition, and the equilibrium compositions are set by the chemical-potential equality, not by the overall composition of the mixture. The overall composition decides how much of each phase is present: a mixture rich in the more volatile component holds more of the phase in which that component concentrates. Changing the temperature at the fixed pressure shifts both equilibrium compositions, because the chemical potentials move with temperature and the equality is restored at new values. A mixture whose overall composition lies outside the range between the two equilibrium compositions exists as a single phase, since no pair of phases can satisfy the equality and the overall balance at once. The condition is stated here in words because it is the definition the rest of the subject uses: phase equilibrium is the equality of chemical potential for every component across every phase present, at uniform temperature and at the stated pressure.

input: It is interesting to note that the lifetime values reported for this class of material appear to differ quite considerably between the two groups, and resolving this apparent discrepancy is by no means straightforward. On the one hand, the first group reports values that are, broadly speaking, rather encouraging, whereas on the other hand the second group's results seem to paint a somewhat less optimistic picture overall. A number of factors could arguably be involved here, including the conditions under which the tests were carried out, the way in which the samples were prepared, and the environments to which the materials were exposed during testing. IAST has been used in parts of this work, and the benchmark material features in both studies, which at least provides some common ground for comparison. Nevertheless, it remains genuinely difficult to say with complete confidence which set of values should be regarded as the more representative, because the test conditions differ in ways that are not always fully documented, and the cycling regimes in particular may not be directly comparable. target: The two groups report conflicting lifetime values for the same material class, and the conflict is not resolved by the values themselves. Both studies include the benchmark material, and IAST is used in both to put the comparison on a common basis, so the difference lies in the test conditions rather than in the materials tested. One programme cycles the material under humid feed with short regeneration, the other under dry feed with long regeneration. Lifetime under the first programme is a measure of tolerance to water and to repeated short cycling; lifetime under the second is a measure of capacity retention when regeneration is complete. The numbers are therefore answers to different questions, and neither group is wrong on its own conditions. The preference between them rests on the service the material is being judged for. Where the service feed is humid and the cycle short, the first programme's values govern, because its conditions reproduce the service duty and the second programme never exposes the material to water at all. On that condition, the shorter lifetimes are the design values, and the longer values from the dry programme are an upper bound that the humid service will not reach.
