fact_base: A gravity settler removes activated sludge from a process stream. Design overflow rate is 0.8 m h-1 at a throughput of 283 m3 h-1, giving a plan area of 354 m2. The overflow-rate basis is a vendor rule for this solid; no settling test on the actual slurry has been run.
input: A gravity settler is employed in order to remove activated sludge from a process stream, and the sizing of the unit is carried out on the basis of the overflow rate. The design overflow rate is 0.8 m h-1 at a throughput of 283 m3 h-1, giving a plan area of 354 m2, a figure that is derived by dividing the throughput by the overflow rate. The overflow rate may be understood as the upward velocity of the clarified stream over the plan of the settler, and it follows that solids which settle more rapidly than this rate are retained within the unit, whilst solids that settle more slowly than it are carried out with the clarified stream. The plan area is therefore the quantity that is fixed jointly by the throughput that has to be handled and the rate at which the stream is permitted to rise, and any increase in the throughput, if the rate is to be maintained, has to be matched by a corresponding increase in the area provided. It should nevertheless be appreciated that the overflow-rate basis on which the sizing rests is a vendor rule that is offered for this particular solid, and that no settling test has in fact been run on the actual slurry that the unit will receive. The area that has been derived is consequently no better than the rule from which it proceeds, and the behaviour of the real slurry, whose settling characteristics may differ in either direction from those that the vendor's rule assumes, remains untested at this stage.

Sludge settling varies with the state of the sludge, and a slurry that settles more slowly than the rule assumes leaves the settler loaded with solids the design did not intend to pass. The derived area is therefore the size the rule requires, held at the rule's accuracy: it is the area to build if the vendor basis is accepted, and the settling test that would replace the rule with a measurement has not been run.

subtype: worked example with equation: Fourier conduction
fact_base: A flat stainless steel wall has thickness 150 mm and thermal conductivity $k$ of 16 W m-1 K-1. The temperature difference $\Delta T$ across the wall is 163 K, giving a heat flux $q$ of 17387 W m-2. The calculation is steady and one-dimensional; film resistances are excluded.
input:
For a flat stainless steel wall under steady conditions, the heat flux through the wall is calculated from the following data. The wall has a thickness $\Delta x$ of 150 mm, the material has a thermal conductivity $k$ of 16 W m-1 K-1, and the temperature difference $\Delta T$ across the wall amounts to 163 K. The calculation rests on the assumptions that the process is steady and one-dimensional, which means that the same flux crosses every plane parallel to the faces and that no heat flows along the wall. It is important to note that film resistances are excluded from the analysis, since the stated temperature difference is the difference between the two faces of the wall itself. Fourier's law for one-dimensional conduction through a plane wall takes the following form:

$$q = k \frac{\Delta T}{\Delta x}$$

where $q$ denotes the heat flux, $k$ the thermal conductivity of the wall material, $\Delta T$ the temperature difference across the wall, and $\Delta x$ the wall thickness. The thickness in metres is 0.15 m, and substituting the data then yields $q$ = 16 × 163 / 0.15 = 17387 W m-2. A check of the units confirms consistency, in that a conductivity in W m-1 K-1, multiplied by a temperature difference in K and divided by a length in m, returns a flux in W m-2. The value obtained is the conduction flux for the wall alone: surface films on the two faces would add resistance in series and lower the flux at the same overall temperature difference, while a conductivity that varies with temperature would be evaluated at the mean wall temperature.

subtype: worked example with equation: Stokes settling
fact_base: Glass beads of diameter $d_p$ = 100 micrometres and density 2500 kg m-3 settle in water at 293 K. Stokes' law gives a terminal velocity $v_t$ of 8.19 mm s-1. The estimate requires creeping flow; the particle Reynolds number must be checked before the value is used.
input:
In this example, the aim is to estimate the terminal velocity of glass beads as they settle in water at 293 K. The beads in question have a diameter $d_p$ = 100 micrometres and a density $\rho_p$ = 2500 kg m-3. By terminal velocity is meant the constant velocity that a bead eventually reaches when the drag acting on it comes into balance with its weight net of buoyancy; below that balance the bead continues to accelerate, and above it the bead slows down. It should be emphasised that the estimate rests on the assumption of creeping flow: the drag on the particle is taken to be the viscous drag described by Stokes' law, with no inertial contribution whatsoever, and this condition is stated explicitly here because the result stands or falls with it. Stokes' law, which gives the terminal velocity of a sphere settling under gravity, can be expressed as follows:

$$v_t = \frac{g d_p^2 (\rho_p - \rho)}{18 \mu}$$

where $v_t$ denotes the terminal velocity, $g$ the acceleration due to gravity, $d_p$ the particle diameter, $\rho_p$ the particle density, $\rho$ the density of the liquid, and $\mu$ the viscosity of the liquid. For the stated beads in water at 293 K, Stokes' law gives $v_t$ = 8.19 mm s-1. The velocity is essentially set by the balance that the equation states. The driving term grows with the density difference and with the square of the diameter, whereas the resisting term grows with the viscosity, so that a finer bead settles more slowly and a more viscous liquid slows the settling further, in the proportions the equation gives. The density and viscosity of the water enter at the stated temperature, and any change of temperature moves the result through those two properties alone. It is worth noting that the value is an estimate obtained under the creeping-flow condition, rather than a measured settling rate. Before the value is used in any design context, the particle Reynolds number, formed with the terminal velocity and the bead diameter, must be checked: Stokes' law is valid only where that number confirms creeping flow, and a check that fails means the calculation has to return to a drag relation that covers the transitional regime.

fact_base: A review passage on catalysts for carbon dioxide hydrogenation, in four parts: scope, established results, disagreements, and gaps. The review covers 93 papers from the last 8 years. The disagreements part names the quantity on which reports conflict; the gaps part names the measurement nobody reports.
input:
Scope
This review sets out to cover catalysts for the hydrogenation of carbon dioxide, that is, the conversion of carbon dioxide with hydrogen to products including methanol, methane, dimethyl ether, and higher hydrocarbons. In total, the review covers 93 papers from the last 8 years. Papers are included where a catalyst is tested under flowing carbon dioxide and hydrogen and where both conversion and product selectivity are reported; studies of the water-gas shift reaction alone, and studies that report activity without selectivity, fall outside the review. The catalysts themselves fall into families that recur across the period: copper-based catalysts carried on oxide supports, catalysts based on indium oxide, noble-metal catalysts on oxide carriers, and zeolite-containing combinations that couple methanol formation to further conversion. It is important to note that conditions vary widely across the set. Temperature, pressure, feed ratio, and space velocity are seldom the same in any two papers, and the products targeted differ, so the review compares catalysts within product groups and treats comparisons across groups as comparisons of reported performance under unlike conditions, rather than as rankings of the materials themselves. Characterisation, it should also be noted, is reported unevenly across the set. Most papers support their performance claims with measurements of surface area and of the state of the active phase before and after reaction, but the measurements are not made on a common plan, and a catalyst described in one paper by its preparation alone cannot fairly be set against a catalyst described in another by its working surface. The review therefore records, for each paper, the characterisation actually reported, and does not infer the working state of a catalyst from its preparation where the paper does not measure that state.

Established results
Several results are reported consistently enough across the literature to be regarded as established. Carbon dioxide hydrogenation over copper-based catalysts produces methanol together with carbon monoxide from the reverse water-gas shift reaction, and the split between the two moves with temperature: higher temperature favours carbon monoxide, and methanol selectivity falls as conversion rises. Water is formed in both routes, and water inhibits the reaction on most catalysts tested; papers that remove water, or that feed it deliberately, show the rate and the selectivity responding in the direction that inhibition predicts. Promoters change the performance of a base catalyst in reproducible directions within a family, although the size of the change is specific to the preparation. Supports, moreover, are not inert: the same active metal on different oxide carriers gives different conversions at the same stated conditions, and the difference is attributed across the literature to the interface between the metal and the carrier, to the dispersion the carrier stabilises, and to acid or basic sites the carrier contributes. For indium oxide catalysts, the established picture is one of high methanol selectivity at low conversion, with activity limited by the supply of the surface vacancies the mechanism requires. Zeolite combinations convert the methanol formed on the first function into dimethyl ether or hydrocarbons, and their reported product distributions are set jointly by the two functions and by how closely the two are mixed.

Disagreements
Reports conflict on methanol selectivity at a stated conversion. One set of papers reports selectivity falling steeply as conversion rises, and reads the trend as the reverse water-gas shift overtaking methanol formation along the bed. Another set reports selectivity holding nearly constant across the same conversion range, and reads its result as the two routes running in parallel at rates fixed by the inlet conditions. The conflict is not resolved by the reported conditions, because the two sets differ in how conversion was changed: the first set changed temperature, while the second changed space velocity, and temperature moves the equilibrium and the shift reaction together while space velocity does not. Reports also conflict on the state of the copper surface under reaction, with one group assigning activity to metallic copper and another to copper at the interface with the support oxide, and the conflict rests on measurements made after reaction rather than during it. A third disagreement concerns deactivation: sintering is named as the cause in some reports and the accumulation of surface species in others, and the two are seldom separated, because the measurements that would separate them do not form part of the standard test.

Gaps
The measurement nobody reports is performance over extended time on stream. Tests in the reviewed set are short, and conversion and selectivity are reported at the start of the run or as an average over it; no paper tracks both quantities across a long continuous run under a feed that contains the water the reaction produces, so the deactivation behaviour that decides industrial use is largely absent from the record the review covers. Regeneration is treated in much the same way: a catalyst is sometimes reported as regenerated, but its conversion and selectivity after regeneration are not reported against the fresh values, so recovery is asserted rather than measured. A second gap is the absence of a common test protocol. Because feed composition, pressure, and space velocity are chosen paper by paper, the cross-paper comparisons this review is forced to make carry the condition differences with them, and the literature does not contain the shared-condition dataset that would remove them. Rates, furthermore, are reported on unlike bases, per mass of catalyst in some papers and per mass of active metal in others, which blocks the direct comparison of activity across families.

fact_base: A tutorial passage explains the Nusselt number to second-year students. Definition in words: the Nusselt number is the ratio of convective to conductive heat transfer at a surface. The passage must state what a value near 1 means and what a large value means, without inventing numerical examples.
input: The Nusselt number is a dimensionless group that plays a central role in heat transfer at a surface, and it is typically introduced to second-year students when they first encounter convective transfer. In essence, the Nusselt number can be defined as the ratio of convective to conductive heat transfer at a surface. The numerator of this ratio is the heat that is actually carried away from the surface by the moving fluid, while the denominator is the heat that conduction alone would carry across a stagnant layer of the same fluid, having the same thickness and subject to the same temperature difference. Since both terms are heat fluxes evaluated at the same surface, their ratio has no units, and the group essentially compares two mechanisms rather than measuring either one of them directly. A value near 1 means that the two terms are of the same size. At such a value, the moving fluid removes little more heat than a stagnant layer would conduct, and the surface transfer behaves much as conduction across the layer would behave. A large value, by contrast, means that the convective term is much the larger. The motion of the fluid then carries heat away far faster than conduction across the stagnant layer, and the surface transfer is governed by the flow rather than by the conductivity of the fluid alone. The group is formed from quantities that are held separately in a calculation: a heat transfer coefficient for the surface, a length that fixes the thickness of the comparison layer, and the thermal conductivity of the fluid. Read in that direction, the Nusselt number states how many times over the surface transfer exceeds pure conduction at the same scale. The group is widely used to report surface heat transfer in a form that can be compared across fluids, geometries, and flow rates, and to carry a measured or correlated coefficient from one size of equipment to another of the same shape. It is important to note that the comparison is local to the surface and to the chosen length. A value quoted without its length does not fix the transfer, because the conductive term in the denominator is set by that length.

fact_base: Excerpt content: two groups report conflicting selectivity values for the same material class; the excerpt weighs their test conditions. The excerpt reaches a limited preference and states the condition on which it rests.
input: When it comes to selectivity, the two studies of the benchmark material do not agree with one another, and the disagreement lies in the values that each reports for the same class of material rather than in the materials being compared. The first study measured mixture uptake directly, at the feed composition and pressure of the separation this review covers, and its selectivities are ratios of adsorbed amounts taken from those mixture measurements. The second study, by contrast, measured single-component isotherms and obtained its selectivities from IAST, so that its values inherit every assumption the theory makes about the adsorbed phase, including the mixing behaviour the isotherms are fitted to. When the two sets of values are placed side by side, the mixture values turn out to be the lower of the two, and the gap between the two sets widens as the feed moves away from the composition at which the isotherms were measured. The preference here is for the mixture measurements, on the condition that holds throughout this section: the material is being ranked for the stated separation, at the stated feed, and a value measured on that feed answers the ranking question without an intervening model. The preference is, however, limited to that use. For compositions the second study did not measure, its values are the only values available, and they enter the comparison with the model step stated.

fact_base: An operating-manual chapter for a centrifugal pump, in four sections: start-up, normal operation, alarms, and shutdown. The alarms section lists two alarms and the operator action for each; no other alarms are introduced. The chapter addresses the operator directly and uses imperative verbs for actions.
input:
Start-up
Before the first start of a shift, it is advisable to walk the pump and its lines and to satisfy yourself that everything is in order. You should confirm that the coupling guard is fitted and secure, that the suction and discharge lines are connected as the line-up sheet shows, and that no blanks or blinds remain in the line from maintenance. The lubricant in the bearing housing should be checked by the sight glass; if the level is low, it should be topped up with the specified oil, and the reason for the loss should ideally be found before the pump is run. Where a seal flush is fitted, the flush supply should be opened and flow confirmed at the seal drain. The pump must then be primed. The casing and the suction line are filled with the pumped liquid from the suction vessel, and the casing is vented at the vent point until liquid, rather than air, comes from the vent; it is important to understand that a centrifugal pump started dry or partly full of air does not develop head and runs its seals without liquid. The suction valve is opened fully. The discharge valve is set closed or nearly closed, as the pump's data sheet directs for starting. Where access allows, the shaft should be turned by hand to confirm that it rotates freely; a shaft that will not turn is reported, not forced. The motor is bumped once to check the direction of rotation against the arrow on the casing, with the coupling guard refitted immediately afterwards. The motor is then started. The discharge pressure gauge should be watched as the pump comes up to speed: pressure should rise promptly to the normal discharge band. The discharge valve is opened slowly and the pump brought onto line, with the flow and the suction pressure watched as the valve opens. As the pump settles, the seal should be checked: a small steady leakage at a packed seal is to be expected, while a mechanical seal should show no visible leakage. You should also listen for cavitation noise, a crackling sound like gravel passing through the casing; if it is heard, the pump should be stopped and the suction condition corrected before running on. Once the pump is steady, the discharge pressure, the flow, and the bearing condition are recorded in the log. The pump should be checked again after a short run at duty. A gland that drips steadily when cold may seal as it warms, and a flange that is dry at start-up may weep as the line reaches temperature; both are findings for the log either way, and neither should be left to be discovered by the next shift.

Normal operation
During normal running, the pump should be kept within its normal band of flow. Careful attention should be paid to the suction vessel level, because the suction condition depends on it: a falling level moves the pump towards cavitation, and the level is the earliest warning the operator gets. The discharge pressure and the flow should be read on each round and compared with the logged values from earlier rounds; a drift in either, at unchanged valve positions, is information about the pump or the line and should be reported, rather than compensated silently by moving valves. The bearing housings should be felt on each round, or their temperature indicators read where fitted; a housing that is warming round by round should be reported before it reaches the alarm. The seal condition should likewise be checked on each round: leakage that grows, or leakage that changes character, is reported the same day. Listening to the pump forms part of the round: new vibration, new noise, or a change in the sound of the flow is a finding. The pump must not be run against a closed or nearly closed discharge valve; at low flow the power the motor delivers turns to heat in the liquid trapped in the casing, and the temperature rises quickly. The suction valve must not be throttled to control flow; flow is controlled at the discharge side, because suction throttling starves the pump and invites cavitation. The pump and its surroundings should be kept clean and clear: a leak that is washed away without being reported removes the evidence the next round depends on. Where a standby pump is fitted on the same duty, a changeover to it should be made on the rota the site keeps, so that both machines are exercised and neither stands long enough to seize or to settle solids in its casing. The changeover is logged, and the pump taken off line is left primed and ready unless work on it is planned. Pressures, flow, and any change found are logged, with the time of the round.

Alarms
Two alarms are fitted to this pump, and no others are introduced in this chapter. The first alarm is low suction pressure. This alarm means that the pump is losing its suction condition: the vessel level is low, the suction line is obstructed, or the liquid is vaporising at the eye of the impeller. On this alarm, the pump should be stopped. The suction vessel level and the suction line are checked, any obstruction found is cleared, the casing is vented, and the pump is reprimed before any restart is attempted. The pump should not be restarted against the alarm in the hope that the condition clears; a pump run in cavitation damages its impeller and its seals, and the damage is done while the condition lasts. The second alarm is high bearing temperature. This alarm means that the bearing is running hotter than its design allows, most often from low or degraded lubricant, misalignment, or a load the bearing is beginning to fail under. On this alarm, the pump should be stopped and the bearing allowed to cool. The lubricant level and its condition are checked, and the cause is looked for before restart; a bearing that has alarmed once and is restarted without a cause found will alarm again, with less margin. Both alarms should be reported in the log with the action taken, whether or not the pump is returned to service. An alarm that recurs after the action has been taken should be treated as a defect report, not a running instruction: the pump is withdrawn, the defect is raised for maintenance, and the alarm history from the log goes with the report.

Shutdown
For a stop to standby, the motor is stopped, the discharge valve is closed, and the pump is left primed and full, ready to start, with the suction valve open. For a planned stop, the flow is first reduced by closing the discharge valve towards the minimum the data sheet allows, and the motor is then stopped. The discharge valve is closed fully, followed by the suction valve. If the pump is to stand idle for a long period, or is to be opened, the casing should be drained through the drain point and vented, so that no liquid is trapped against the seals and no pressure remains in the casing. A pump standing full of a liquid that can crystallise, set, or corrode is drained and flushed before it is left. Where the liquid is hot, the pump should be allowed to cool before it is drained, and drained to the closed drain system, not to the floor. Where the liquid is hazardous, the draining and venting are done under the site permit arrangements, with the same proof of isolation before any joint is broken. The pump must be isolated electrically before any work is done on it, and the isolation locked and tagged; the lock is removed only by the person who fitted it, on completion of the work. Before any joint on the pump is broken, it must be proved that the casing is drained and vented: a joint slackened against trapped pressure or trapped liquid releases both at the fitter. Before the first start of a shift, walk the pump and its lines. Confirm that the coupling guard is fitted and secure, that the suction and discharge lines are connected as the line-up sheet shows, and that no blanks or blinds remain in the line from maintenance. Check the lubricant in the bearing housing by the sight glass; top up with the specified oil if the level is low, and find the reason for the loss before the pump is run. Open the seal flush supply where a flush is fitted, and confirm flow at the seal drain. Prime the pump. Fill the casing and the suction line with the pumped liquid from the suction vessel, and vent the casing at the vent point until liquid, not air, comes from the vent; a centrifugal pump started dry or partly full of air does not develop head and runs its seals without liquid. Bump the motor once to check the direction of rotation against the arrow on the casing, with the coupling guard refitted immediately after. Start the motor. fact_base: Staffing review for a quality laboratory: 16 full-time staff, overtime at 6% of paid hours last year. Replacing half the overtime with one additional hire costs $80k per year fully loaded. Overtime is concentrated in two seasonal peaks; a hire is paid for the full year.
input: This review considers whether the quality laboratory should make an additional hire. The laboratory has 16 full-time staff, and last year overtime ran at 6% of paid hours. A substantial amount of overtime might appear to point towards a need for more staff. However, the workload that produced it is concentrated in two seasonal peaks, and this distribution changes the picture. Replacing half the overtime with one additional hire would cost $80k per year fully loaded, and the hire would be paid for the full year, whereas the peaks occupy only part of that year. The trade-off can be stated in one sentence: $80k committed for twelve months against cover that is needed in two peaks. Even if half the overtime were replaced, overtime would still stand at 3% of paid hours, and the remaining peak load would still fall on the existing staff in the peak weeks themselves. Overtime, by contrast, is bought only in the weeks the peaks occur and stops when they pass, so its cost tracks the demand that causes it. The record behind this assessment is one year of paid hours; a single year does not show whether the peaks are lengthening, and the decision should be reopened if they do. The case for the hire would need demand outside the peaks, which last year's record does not show. On balance, the recommendation is not to add a hire: laboratory management, which holds the decision, should keep the overtime arrangement for the coming year and review the position if overtime outside the peaks begins to grow.

fact_base: A shell-and-tube exchanger heats crude oil in a refinery preheat train. Duty is 1088 kW. Hot stream: 150 °C in, 110 °C out. Cold stream: 30 °C in, 55 °C out. The log-mean temperature difference is 87.3 K and the installed area is 56.7 m2, giving an overall coefficient of 220 W m-2 K-1. Fouling was assessed from a single 90-day run; no cleaning cycle has been completed.
input: A shell-and-tube exchanger forming part of the refinery preheat train is used to heat crude oil, and in the run reported here it operates with a duty of 1088 kW. The hot stream enters at 150 °C and leaves at 110 °C, while the crude enters at 30 °C and leaves at 55 °C. Working from the stream temperatures, the terminal differences come out at 95 K at the hot end and 80 K at the cold end, and the log-mean temperature difference calculated from those two values is 87.3 K. With the installed area of 56.7 m2, the duty and the log-mean difference together give an overall coefficient of 220 W m-2 K-1. It should be understood that this coefficient is the operating value for the run as a whole. It bundles together the two film resistances, the wall, and whatever fouling had accumulated over the course of the run, and no part of it can be separated out by these measurements. The smaller terminal difference stands at the cold end, so the cold end is where a change in either stream temperature moves the driving force most, and where the exchanger reaches its closest approach. Fouling was assessed from a single 90-day run, and no cleaning cycle has yet been completed, so the fouling share of the coefficient cannot be split from the clean value on the basis of this evidence. A second run after cleaning would give that split; on one run the two are necessarily reported together. Overall, the exchanger met the stated duty at the stated temperatures over the run. How the coefficient moves as fouling builds, and what it returns to after cleaning, are both open questions on the basis of a single run, and the reported coefficient should be read as a run-average value at the tested conditions.

fact_base: A viscous liquid of viscosity $\mu$ = 0.001 Pa s flows laminarly through a tube of radius $R$ = 6 mm and length $L$ = 39 m. At a pressure drop $\Delta P$ of 20 kPa the volumetric flow $Q$ is 939.6 L h-1. The Hagen-Poiseuille equation assumes laminar, fully developed flow of a Newtonian liquid.
input:
In this example, the volumetric flow of a viscous liquid through a tube is to be calculated from the Hagen-Poiseuille equation. The liquid has a viscosity $\mu$ = 0.001 Pa s and flows through a tube of radius $R$ = 6 mm and length $L$ = 39 m, at a pressure drop $\Delta P$ of 20 kPa. It is important to appreciate that the equation assumes laminar, fully developed flow of a Newtonian liquid, and these conditions are stated before the equation is introduced because the result carries them with it: a liquid whose viscosity changes with shear rate, or a flow that is still developing from the inlet, falls outside the relation. For laminar flow in a circular tube, the Hagen-Poiseuille equation takes the following form:

$$Q = \frac{\pi R^4 \Delta P}{8 \mu L}$$

where $Q$ denotes the volumetric flow, $R$ the tube radius, $\Delta P$ the pressure drop along the tube, $\mu$ the viscosity, and $L$ the tube length. Converting the radius into metres gives $R$ = 0.006 m, and expressing the pressure drop in pascals gives $\Delta P$ = 20000 Pa, so that substitution yields $Q$ = π (0.006)^4 × 20000 / (8 × 0.001 × 39), and the stated flow is $Q$ = 939.6 L h-1. The fourth power on the radius is the sensitivity that the result carries. The flow responds to the radius far more strongly than to any other datum, so the radius is the measurement on which the result depends, and a small error in the radius returns a flow error four times as large in proportion. The viscosity and the pressure drop enter linearly, so their errors pass into the flow at the same proportion. Finally, the value obtained is the fully developed laminar value. Entrance length is not included in the equation, so a tube in which the developing region makes up a large share of the length will show a higher pressure drop at the same flow, and the equation understates the drop there.

fact_base: A gravity settler removes activated sludge from a process stream. Design overflow rate is 2.19 m h-1 at a throughput of 246 m3 h-1, giving a plan area of 112 m2. The overflow-rate basis is a vendor rule for this solid; no settling test on the actual slurry has been run.
input: A gravity settler is used to remove activated sludge from a process stream. The design overflow rate is 2.19 m h-1 at a throughput of 246 m3 h-1, and the plan area follows from the definition of the overflow rate: the area is simply the throughput divided by the rate, because the overflow rate is the throughput spread over the plan area of the settler. Carrying out that division gives a plan area of 112 m2. The overflow rate is, in effect, the design statement of the separation. Liquid leaves over the weir at a superficial velocity equal to the overflow rate, and solids that settle faster than that velocity are retained and pass to the underflow, whereas solids that settle more slowly leave with the clarified stream in the proportion the two velocities set. It is worth noting that the depth of the settler does not enter the area: separation in a gravity settler is fixed by the plan area and the throughput, and depth serves the storage of settled solids and the steadiness of the flow, rather than the settling condition itself. The basis of the rate is a vendor rule for this solid. No settling test on the actual slurry has been run, so the rate is not a measured property of the sludge the settler will actually treat: flocculation state, solids concentration, and temperature in the actual stream all move the settling velocity, and none of them is fixed by the vendor rule. The plan area of 112 m2 is therefore the area the vendor basis requires, stated at that basis. A settling test on the actual slurry, run across the concentration range the settler will see, is the measurement that would replace the rule with a rate for this stream; until that test is run, the area carries the uncertainty of the vendor rule whole.

subtype: worked example with equation: log-mean difference
fact_base: A countercurrent exchanger cools a process stream from 200 °C to 150 °C with water entering at 30 °C and leaving at 55 °C. The terminal differences are 145 K and 120 K, and the log-mean temperature difference $\Delta T_{lm}$ is 132.1 K. The log-mean value assumes constant overall coefficient and no phase change.
input:
The task here is to calculate the log-mean temperature difference for a countercurrent exchanger in which a process stream is cooled from 200 °C to 150 °C by water entering at 30 °C and leaving at 55 °C. In countercurrent flow, the two terminal differences pair each inlet with the outlet at the same end: at the hot end, 200 °C against 55 °C gives $\Delta T_1$ = 145 K, and at the cold end, 150 °C against 30 °C gives $\Delta T_2$ = 120 K. The log-mean temperature difference is defined by the following expression:

$$\Delta T_{lm} = \frac{\Delta T_1 - \Delta T_2}{\ln(\Delta T_1 / \Delta T_2)}$$

where $\Delta T_{lm}$ denotes the log-mean temperature difference and $\Delta T_1$ and $\Delta T_2$ the terminal differences at the two ends. Substituting the two terminal differences into the expression gives $\Delta T_{lm}$ = 132.1 K. The log-mean value is the mean driving force that the duty equation uses: with a constant overall coefficient, the duty is the product of the coefficient, the area, and this difference, and an arithmetic mean used in its place would overstate the driving force wherever the two terminal differences differ. It should be noted that the value assumes a constant overall coefficient along the exchanger and no phase change in either stream; a stream that condenses or boils holds its temperature along the exchanger and breaks the profile that the definition averages. As a check, the log-mean value lies between the two terminal differences and below their arithmetic mean of 132.5 K, as it must for two unequal positive differences. An exchanger sized on the arithmetic mean would be undersized in the proportion the gap between the two means states.

fact_base: A centrifugal pump moves caustic solution between two vessels at grade. At the duty point the flow is 86 m3 h-1 against a head of 20 m, with pump efficiency 70%. Shaft power at the duty point is 6.7 kW. The motor is rated 15% above this value. Cavitation was not observed in the acceptance test, which ran for 4 h at the duty point only.
input: It is worth considering the performance of the centrifugal pump that moves caustic solution between the two vessels at grade, because the reported figures, taken together, give a fairly complete picture of the intended operating condition. At the duty point, the flow is 86 m3 h-1 against a head of 20 m, with pump efficiency 70%, and the shaft power at the duty point is 6.7 kW. The motor is rated 15% above this value, a margin that is presumably intended to provide a comfortable degree of headroom above the calculated requirement at the selected point. It should also be noted that cavitation was not observed in the acceptance test, which ran for 4 h at the duty point only, and this observation is broadly reassuring as far as it goes. At the same time, the observation is tied to the tested point and to the duration of the test, and it does not in itself say anything about behaviour at other flows or under other suction conditions. The efficiency figure likewise belongs to the duty point, and the wider performance of the pump away from that point is not described by the values given. Overall, the passage presents a single, clearly defined operating point, a motor margin above the shaft power at that point, and an acceptance observation whose reach is limited to the condition actually tested.

The motor is rated 15% above the shaft power; the margin sets the installed rating, and the margin is not a measured efficiency and does not change the duty-point power. Pump efficiency connects the hydraulic power imparted to the liquid with the shaft power drawn at the same point, and the stated value belongs to that point. The vessels stand at grade, and the stated head is the head the pump works against in the reported arrangement. A selection made from the duty point still depends on the system curve of the connecting line, and no second operating point is reported from which that curve could be drawn. Operation away from the duty point is outside the reported result: a centrifugal pump delivers a different flow and head as system resistance changes, and efficiency moves with them. Cavitation was not observed in the acceptance test. The acceptance test ran for 4 h at the duty point only, and the observation is limited to the tested condition. No cavitation statement is made for other flows, other suction conditions, or longer running. The duty figures fix the selection point and the motor margin, and the test result fixes what was seen at that point during acceptance.

fact_base: Excerpt content: a staffing gap of 6 weeks is reported with its cause; the excerpt proposes one mitigation and its owner. The excerpt does not open or close the memo and does not restate its subject line.
input: The staffing position on the document-control side has, unfortunately, become more difficult than had previously been expected, largely because the contract checker who had been carrying the EPC review load left the project before a cleared replacement had been appointed to take over the work. As a result, a staffing gap of 6 weeks is now reported, and during that period the checking sequence for the affected packages cannot be staffed in the way that had originally been planned. It is important to note that the gap is not presented as a general shortage across the whole project; rather, it sits in a specific checking function, and it is the concentration of the work in that function that makes the absence difficult to absorb. In terms of a response, it is proposed that the checking load for the affected packages be redistributed to cleared home-office reviewers for the duration of the gap, and the project board is proposed as the owner of that redistribution, so that the decision and its follow-through rest in one place. This would not remove the underlying shortage, but it would keep the review sequence moving while the replacement is brought into post, and it would avoid each affected package making its own separate arrangement.

Cover of this kind is workable because the home-office reviewers hold the same clearance as the checker who left, and the packages affected are those already in the review sequence rather than new work entering it. Work not yet in the sequence waits for the replacement, and the distinction keeps the mitigation bounded: the redistributed load is the load the gap would otherwise have stalled, and no wider commitment is made. The reported position is therefore a six-week gap in a single function, a named cause, and one mitigation with a named owner.

input: The aim of this worked example is to compute the half-life of a first-order reaction and the fraction remaining after 60 min, using the measured rate constant k = 0.023 min-1 at 323 K, which was obtained from concentration measurements taken every 5 min over 90 min. For a first-order reaction, the half-life t1/2 is fixed by the relation t1/2 = ln(2) / k, and the fraction remaining after a given time is given by exp(-k t), where the rate constant and the time are the quantities that enter. Substituting the measured rate constant into these relations gives a half-life of 30.1 min and a fraction remaining of 0.25 at the stated time. It is worth noting that these relations hold for a first-order reaction only; a reaction of another order follows a different decay law, and the same numerical procedure would not apply. The example is a useful illustration of the way in which, for a reaction of this kind, a single measured constant determines the whole course of the decay, since once the constant is known, the fraction remaining at any time can in principle be obtained from the same pair of relations without further measurement. As a broad internal check, the stated time is close to two half-lives, and the fraction remaining is correspondingly close to one quarter, which is consistent with the computed values.
target: Calculate the half-life of a first-order reaction and the fraction remaining after 60 min. The rate constant k is 0.023 min-1 at 323 K, from concentration measurements every 5 min over 90 min. For a first-order reaction, the half-life t1/2 is fixed by t1/2 = ln(2) / k, and the fraction remaining after time t is exp(-k t). Substitution of the rate constant gives a half-life of 30.1 min. The fraction remaining at the stated time is 0.25. The check is internal: the stated time is close to two half-lives, and one quarter of the material remains, which matches the computed fraction. The relations hold for a first-order reaction only. A reaction of another order follows a different decay law, and neither relation carries over to that case. The two relations are used in sequence: the rate constant first fixes the half-life, and the half-life then gives a direct reading of the fraction at any stated time, because each successive half-life halves what remains. The measurement pattern behind the rate constant matters to the result: readings spread over the full run show whether the decay stays first-order throughout, and a drift in the fitted constant would show in the later readings before it showed in the half-life. The result is therefore a statement about first-order decay at the measured rate constant: a half-life of the stated length, and a quarter of the material remaining after the stated time.

input: The cost position has moved adversely since the previous forecast, and an overrun of 2 weeks is now reported against the current programme allowance. The underlying reason appears to be that rework followed a late change to the installed quantities, and once the installed work had been remeasured, the EPC forecast had to be revised to reflect the quantities actually in place rather than the quantities originally assumed. It is important to note that the overrun is not being attributed to a general loss of productivity across the project as a whole; the movement is concentrated in the packages affected by the change and by the remeasurement that followed it. In response, it is proposed that the remaining work packages be brought into a single re-plan, so that sequence, access, and float are considered together rather than package by package, and the project board is proposed as the owner of that re-plan. Such a re-plan would not undo the rework that has already taken place, but it would give the remaining work a single agreed basis, and it would prevent each package from continuing to plan against assumptions that the remeasurement has already overtaken. It is also the case that, until such a re-plan has been agreed, there is a risk that individual packages will continue to make their own local adjustments, with the result that the overall sequence becomes harder rather than easier to recover, and the movement reported here is better addressed while the remaining work is still capable of being reordered as a whole. The position, in short, is a defined movement against the allowance, arising from a specific change, with a single corrective action proposed in reply.
target: An overrun of 2 weeks is reported against the current programme allowance. Rework followed a late change to the installed quantities, and the EPC forecast was revised after remeasurement of the work in place; the forecast now rests on the quantities installed, not on the quantities originally assumed. The movement is concentrated in the packages affected by the change and the remeasurement. No general loss of productivity across the project is reported, and no part of the overrun is assigned to packages outside the changed work. The mitigation is a single re-plan of the remaining work packages. Sequence, access, and float are settled in the one re-plan rather than package by package, so no package continues to plan against assumptions the remeasurement has overtaken. The project board owns the re-plan. The re-plan does not undo the rework already done, and the overrun already reported is not recovered by replanning alone. What the re-plan changes is the basis of the remaining work: one sequence, one treatment of float, and one owner for departures from the agreed order. Departures after the re-plan are therefore visible as departures from a stated basis, rather than as further drift between packages working to different assumptions. The re-plan also fixes the order in which the affected packages are revisited, so the remeasurement is worked through in a sequence the site teams can staff, rather than arriving as separate demands from separate packages. Float is treated as a project resource in the re-plan: it is held where the remaining risk sits, and it is not left embedded in individual package programmes where it cannot be seen or moved. The reported position is a defined overrun with a named cause, and one mitigation with a named owner.

fact_base: A tutorial passage explains the pump affinity laws for a centrifugal pump at varying speed. The passage states the three proportionalities in words: flow with speed, head with speed squared, power with speed cubed. A worked check is included: doubling speed multiplies power by 8. No other numbers are introduced.
input: The pump affinity laws provide a convenient way of describing how the performance of a centrifugal pump changes when its speed is varied, and they can be summarised in terms of three straightforward proportionalities. Firstly, the flow varies in direct proportion to the speed: if the speed is increased, the flow increases in the same ratio, and if the speed is reduced, the flow falls correspondingly. Secondly, the head varies with the square of the speed, so the head responds more strongly to a change in speed than the flow does. Thirdly, the power varies with the cube of the speed, which means that the power responds more strongly still. A simple worked check helps to make this concrete: if the speed is doubled, the power is multiplied by 8, which follows directly from the cube proportionality. It is worth bearing in mind that these proportional relationships describe the behaviour of a given pump as its speed changes, and they are most naturally applied when comparing operating points of that pump at different speeds. In practice, this is why relatively modest adjustments to speed can be used to trim the duty of a pump, and why, conversely, a decision to run a pump appreciably faster than its original duty point needs to be examined with some care, since the power absorbed rises so much more steeply than either the flow or the head.
target: Doubling the speed of a centrifugal pump multiplies its power by 8. The affinity laws give the three proportionalities behind that check. Flow is proportional to speed: at twice the speed, the same pump delivers twice the flow, and at half the speed, half the flow. Head is proportional to the square of the speed, and head therefore responds more strongly to a speed change than flow does. Power is proportional to the cube of the speed, and power responds more strongly than head. The worked check follows from the cube proportionality alone: a doubling of speed raises the power by the cube of the speed ratio. Read in the other direction, the same proportionalities give the flow, head, and power at a reduced speed from the values at the original speed, with the power falling fastest as speed is reduced. The three proportionalities are not three separate rules: they are one similarity statement read for three quantities, and the steepening from flow to head to power is the content of the laws. A speed change that looks modest against flow is therefore not modest against power, and the check case is the extreme form of that difference. The laws compare operating points of a given centrifugal pump at varying speed. Each proportionality is a ratio statement between two speeds of that pump, and the three statements together fix how flow, head, and power move when the speed is set to a new value.

fact_base: A flat firebrick wall of thickness 150 mm separates two process streams. Thermal conductivity of the wall is 1.1 W m-1 K-1 and the measured temperature difference across it is 281 K. Steady one-dimensional conduction gives a heat flux of 2061 W m-2. Surface (film) resistances are excluded from this estimate; including them lowers the flux.
input: In this example we consider a flat firebrick wall of thickness 150 mm which separates two process streams, and for which the thermal conductivity is 1.1 W m-1 K-1 and the measured temperature difference across the wall is 281 K. Under the assumptions of steady, one-dimensional conduction, the heat flux through the wall is 2061 W m-2. It should be noted that surface (film) resistances are excluded from this estimate, and that including them would lower the flux, since the overall temperature difference would then be shared between the films and the wall itself rather than being applied across the wall alone. The figure quoted is therefore best understood as the flux associated with conduction through the wall material under the stated temperature difference, rather than as a complete description of the heat transfer between the two streams. The example is, of course, an idealised one, in that a real wall in a real installation would be bounded by films whose resistances might well be appreciable in comparison with the resistance of the wall itself, and the temperature difference that is actually measured may require some care in its interpretation if it is measured in the streams rather than at the wall faces. Nevertheless, as an exercise in the application of the conduction relation to a single layer, the example is perfectly serviceable, provided that its limitations are borne in mind when the resulting figure is used. The calculation is, in that sense, deliberately simplified: it treats the wall as the only resistance in the path, it holds the temperature difference at its measured value, and it reports the resulting flux on that basis alone.
target: A flat firebrick wall of thickness 150 mm separates two process streams. Thermal conductivity of the wall is 1.1 W m-1 K-1, and the measured temperature difference across the wall is 281 K. Steady one-dimensional conduction gives a heat flux of 2061 W m-2. The flux is uniform across the wall area under the stated conditions: steady state removes time variation, and one-dimensional conduction removes variation along the wall face, so a single flux value describes the whole wall. Surface (film) resistances are excluded from the estimate. Including the film resistances lowers the flux, because the measured temperature difference would then be shared between the films and the wall rather than applied across the wall alone. The estimate treats the wall as a single homogeneous layer: one conductivity, one thickness, and one temperature difference describe the whole path, and no layer-by-layer construction is attempted. That treatment is what makes the result a property of the wall rather than of the installation. The measured temperature difference is taken as the difference between the two wall faces; a difference measured between the two streams instead would already contain the film effects that the estimate excludes, and the two measurements are not interchangeable. Steady state is part of the same simplification: a wall still warming or cooling distributes the difference differently, and the stated flux belongs to the steady condition. The stated flux is therefore the wall-only value at the stated temperature difference. The direction of the omission is known: the wall-only estimate is an upper value for the flux between the two streams, and any design use of the figure takes it with that limit attached.

fact_base: Goal: compute the diffusive flux of oxygen through a stagnant water film. The diffusive flux J (mol m-2 s-1) is computed from the diffusivity D (m2 s-1) and the concentration gradient dC/dx, where C is concentration (mol m-3) and x is position (m). Fick's first law: J = -D dC/dx; the negative sign states that diffusion runs from high concentration to low concentration. Oxygen in water: D = 1.6 x 10-9 m2 s-1. Concentration falls by 0.4 mol m-3 across a film 0.4 mm thick, so dC/dx = -1000 mol m-4. Worked result: J = 1.60x 10-6 mol m-2 s-1. The law as stated covers a stagnant medium; a moving medium adds convection, which the equation does not include.
input: The goal of this example is to compute the diffusive flux of oxygen through a stagnant water film. The diffusive flux J (mol m-2 s-1) is computed from the diffusivity D (m2 s-1) and the concentration gradient dC/dx, where C is concentration (mol m-3) and x is position (m). Fick's first law states that J = -D dC/dx, and the negative sign indicates that diffusion runs from high concentration to low concentration. For oxygen in water, D = 1.6 x 10-9 m2 s-1. The concentration falls by 0.4 mol m-3 across a film 0.4 mm thick, so dC/dx = -1000 mol m-4. Putting these values into the expression gives J = 1.60x 10-6 mol m-2 s-1. In working through the example, it may help to observe that the film thickness plays its part through the gradient, in that a given fall in concentration, when spread over a greater thickness, corresponds to a gentler gradient and hence to a smaller flux, whereas the same fall concentrated within a thinner film produces a steeper gradient and a larger flux. The diffusivity, for its part, is a property of the particular combination of substances and of the conditions in the film, and it is simply taken as given here. It is important to note that the law as stated covers a stagnant medium; a moving medium adds convection, which the equation does not include, and so the computed flux is the diffusive contribution under the stated conditions rather than a total flux for a moving film.
target: Compute the diffusive flux of oxygen through a stagnant water film. The diffusive flux J (mol m-2 s-1) is computed from the diffusivity D (m2 s-1) and the concentration gradient dC/dx, where C is concentration (mol m-3) and x is position (m). Fick's first law gives J = -D dC/dx; the negative sign states that diffusion runs from high concentration to low concentration. For oxygen in water, D = 1.6 x 10-9 m2 s-1. Concentration falls by 0.4 mol m-3 across a film 0.4 mm thick, thus dC/dx = -1000 mol m-4. Substitution gives J = 1.60x 10-6 mol m-2 s-1. The sign check closes the calculation: the gradient is negative in the direction of falling concentration, and the computed flux is positive in that direction, as the sign convention requires. The film thickness enters through the gradient, not as a separate factor: the same concentration fall across a thicker film gives a weaker gradient and a smaller flux, and across a thinner film a stronger gradient and a larger flux. The diffusivity belongs to the pair of substances and the temperature of the film; the example takes the stated value as given and does not adjust it. What the calculation isolates is the diffusive part of the transport, stated per unit area and per unit time, under a gradient held steady by the conditions at the film faces. Fick's first law as stated holds for a stagnant medium. A moving medium adds convection, which the equation does not include, and the computed value is the diffusive flux under the stated conditions.

subtype: worked example with equation: Arrhenius ratio
fact_base: Rate constants for a food spoilage study were measured at two temperatures. With activation energy $E_a$ of 94 kJ mol-1, raising the temperature from 300 K to 330 K multiplies the rate constant $k$ by 30.76. The estimate holds the pre-exponential factor $A$ constant over the interval.
input: Rate constants for a food spoilage study were measured at two temperatures, and the temperature dependence of the rate constant k can be represented by the Arrhenius equation, which is written as follows: $$k = A \exp\left(-\frac{E_a}{R T}\right)$$ In this expression, the activation energy $E_a$ has a value of 94 kJ mol-1, and on raising the temperature from 300 K to 330 K, the rate constant $k$ is multiplied by 30.76, which is a fairly substantial increase over what is, in absolute terms, a relatively modest temperature interval. It should be noted that this estimate rests on the assumption that the pre-exponential factor $A$ is held constant over the interval considered; if that factor were itself to vary with temperature, the ratio of the rate constants would not be given by the exponential term alone. The result is therefore best read as the change attributable to the activation-energy term under the stated assumption, applied to the particular interval examined in the spoilage study. The practical interest of the result, in the context of a spoilage study, is that a comparatively small excursion in temperature can correspond to a disproportionately large change in the rate at which spoilage proceeds, which is precisely the kind of behaviour that the activation-energy term is intended to capture.
target: Rate constants for a food spoilage study were measured at two temperatures. The Arrhenius equation gives the temperature dependence of the rate constant $k$: $$k = A \exp\left(-\frac{E_a}{R T}\right)$$ With activation energy $E_a$ of 94 kJ mol-1, raising the temperature from 300 K to 330 K multiplies the rate constant $k$ by 30.76. The estimate holds the pre-exponential factor $A$ constant over the interval. Under that condition, the ratio of the two rate constants is set by the exponential term alone, and $A$ cancels in the ratio. The stated factor is therefore the change over the stated interval under the stated assumption, for the spoilage study measured. The size of the factor comes from the activation energy: a high activation energy makes the exponential term steep in temperature, and a reaction with a lower activation energy would show a smaller factor over the same interval. The two measurements therefore do more than fix the rate at the two ends of the interval; with the equation, they characterise the temperature sensitivity of the spoilage process over the range in which the study works, and storage or handling decisions that turn on temperature inherit that sensitivity. No value outside the interval is computed, and the factor is not a property of the reaction independent of the interval: a wider interval, taken from the same equation, gives a larger factor, and a narrower interval a smaller one.

fact_base: Design report for an amine absorber, in four sections: basis, sizing, materials, and risks. Design throughput is 15 t per day and the removal or separation duty is 97% of the key component. Materials are 316L stainless steel for wetted parts; the basis section states this once. The risks section names fouling and turndown as open items; neither is resolved in the report.
input:
Basis

This report sets out the design of an amine absorber for a gas treatment duty, and the basis on which the design rests is as follows. The design throughput is 15 t per day, and the removal duty is 97% of the key component in the feed gas. The materials basis is that wetted parts are in 316L stainless steel, and that statement is made here, in the basis, so that the materials discussion later in the report can refer back to it. The basis also fixes the frame within which the rest of the design is developed: the absorber is to treat the stated throughput continuously, the duty is expressed as a removal of the key component rather than as an outlet specification in absolute terms, and any matter that the design has not been able to settle is not hidden within the sizing but is instead carried openly into the risks section at the end of the report. It is worth noting that the basis does not attempt to fix every operating variable in advance; rather, it fixes the throughput, the duty, and the materials, and it leaves the detailed selection of internals and the detailed circulation arrangements to the sizing discussion, where they properly belong.

Sizing

The sizing of the absorber is governed by the need to bring the gas and the amine solution into sufficiently close and sufficiently prolonged contact for the stated removal to be achieved at the stated throughput. The column diameter is set by the gas and liquid traffic through the vessel: the diameter must be large enough for the traffic to pass without flooding and without excessive entrainment, and the liquid must be distributed over the cross-section so that the whole of the contacting volume is used. The height of the contacting section is set by the separation requirement, since the removal duty can only be met if the gas is exposed to enough contacting stages, or to an equivalent depth of packing, for the key component to transfer from the gas into the solvent to the extent required. The solvent circulation rate is the other principal sizing variable, because a higher circulation gives a greater capacity for the key component per pass, at the cost of a greater regeneration load elsewhere in the process. The sizing adopted is therefore a balance among diameter, height, and circulation, struck at the design throughput. The report does not resolve the behaviour of the column at throughputs well below the design value, and that question is carried forward as an open item rather than being settled here by assertion.

It should perhaps be explained that the sizing discussion proceeds in this way because the variables concerned cannot in practice be chosen independently of one another: a change in the circulation alters the loading of the solvent and the duty of the regeneration section; a change in the diameter alters the velocities of both phases and with them the closeness of contact; and a change in the height alters the pressure cost of passing the gas through the column. The design that is reported is thus a single consistent selection among these variables, and not a collection of separately optimised items.

Materials

The materials requirement is that wetted parts are in the stainless steel grade named in the basis. The parts concerned are those in contact with the amine solution or with the wet gas: the column shell and internals, the liquid distribution arrangements, and the associated wetted pipework and fittings within the battery limit of the report. Amine service is corrosive in character, and the selection reflects the need for the wetted surfaces to resist the solution, the absorbed component, and the products of solvent degradation that accumulate in service. Fabrication requirements follow from the selection: welds in wetted parts are to be made by procedures appropriate to the grade, and the finished surfaces are to be inspected before the equipment is put into service. Parts that are not wetted, such as external supports and cladding, are outside the materials statement, and the report makes no selection for them. The materials position is thus a single requirement, stated once, applied to the wetted boundary of the absorber and its associated items.

Risks

Two open items are named in this report, and neither of them is resolved here. The first is fouling. In amine service, deposits can form on the internals and on the liquid distribution arrangements, and fouling of that kind reduces the effective contacting area and raises the resistance to gas flow through the column. The rate at which fouling might develop in this service is not established by the design work reported here, and no cleaning interval is fixed. The risk is therefore carried as an operating risk: performance is to be watched in service, and a deterioration in removal or in pressure behaviour is to be read as a possible sign of fouling rather than being attributed at once to other causes. The second open item is turndown. The design is struck at the stated throughput, and the behaviour of the column at substantially lower throughputs has not been demonstrated: liquid distribution and wetting of the contacting surface can deteriorate as the liquid rate falls, and the removal duty may not be held at the bottom of the operating range. No turndown ratio is claimed in this report. Both items are left open deliberately. The design as reported is complete at its basis, and the two risks define the limits of what the design has established: fouling governs the durability of the performance in service, and turndown governs the width of the operating range over which that performance can be assumed.
target:
Basis

The design throughput of the amine absorber is 15 t per day, and the removal duty is 97% of the key component in the feed gas. Wetted parts are 316L stainless steel; the grade is stated here, in the basis, and the materials section refers back to this statement. The basis fixes three things: the throughput, the duty expressed as a removal of the key component, and the materials of the wetted parts. Operating variables not fixed by the basis are settled in the sizing, and matters the design has not settled are carried into the risks section rather than absorbed into the sizing. The absorber treats the stated throughput continuously. The duty is a fractional removal, not an outlet concentration: compliance is judged on the share of the key component removed across the column, and the sizing is developed against that measure.

The basis is also the reference for later change: a throughput above the basis value, or a duty above the basis removal, is a new basis and not an extension of this design, because the sizing margins are struck against the stated figures and are not reported as spare capacity.

Sizing

Sizing is governed by contact between the gas and the amine solution: the removal duty is met only if the gas meets enough active solvent, over enough contacting length, at the design throughput. Column diameter is set by the gas and liquid traffic. The diameter must pass the traffic without flooding and without excessive entrainment, and the liquid must be distributed across the whole cross-section so that the contacting volume is used evenly. The height of the contacting section is set by the separation requirement: the gas must be exposed to enough contacting stages, or to an equivalent depth of packing, for the key component to transfer into the solvent to the stated extent. Solvent circulation is the remaining sizing variable. A higher circulation gives a greater capacity for the key component in each pass and is paid for in regeneration load outside the absorber. The adopted sizing is a balance among diameter, height, and circulation, struck at the design throughput. Sizing at the design point does not demonstrate behaviour well below that point, and low-rate behaviour is not settled in this section.

The contacting device is selected within the same balance: internals that give closer contact also give a higher resistance to gas flow, and the pressure cost of the contacting section is part of the sizing judgement, not an afterthought. Liquid distribution receives the same treatment. A distributor that spreads the solvent evenly at the design rate is part of how the height is made effective; height that the liquid does not reach, or that the gas bypasses, does not contribute to the removal. The rich solvent leaving the base of the column and the treated gas leaving the top are the two streams by which the sizing is judged in operation: the removal is read from the gas, and the solvent loading is read from the liquid, and a sizing that satisfies one reading while degrading the other has not met the duty. Regeneration sits outside the absorber, but the circulation chosen here fixes the load that the regeneration section has to carry, and the sizing records that coupling rather than treating the column as an isolated vessel.

Materials

Wetted parts are in the stainless steel grade named in the basis. The wetted boundary covers the column shell and internals, the liquid distribution arrangements, and the wetted pipework and fittings inside the battery limit of the report. Amine service is corrosive: the wetted surfaces meet the solvent, the absorbed component, and the degradation products that accumulate in the circulating solution, and the grade is selected against that exposure. Welds in wetted parts are made by procedures appropriate to the grade, and finished wetted surfaces are inspected before the equipment enters service. Parts outside the wetted boundary, such as external supports and cladding, are not covered by the materials statement, and no selection is made for them in this report. The materials position is one requirement applied to one boundary: the grade named in the basis, for the parts the process fluids touch.

Risks

Fouling and turndown are open items. Neither is resolved in this report. Fouling in amine service deposits material on the internals and on the liquid distribution arrangements; the deposits reduce the effective contacting area and raise the resistance to gas flow. The design work reported here does not establish a fouling rate for this service, and no cleaning interval is fixed. Fouling is carried as an operating risk: a deterioration in removal or in pressure behaviour in service is to be read first as a possible fouling sign, and the cleaning decision rests on that monitoring rather than on a date set at design. The monitoring that carries the fouling risk has to distinguish fouling from the other causes of a falling removal: a change in feed, a change in solvent condition, and a change in circulation can each move the same readings. The report therefore assigns the sign, not the diagnosis: deterioration opens an inspection question, and the inspection settles whether the cause is deposit on the internals or a process change that the design did not predict. Solvent condition is part of the same picture, since a degraded solvent loses capacity and can present, in the operating readings, much like a fouled column. Turndown is the second open item. The design is struck at the stated throughput, and behaviour at substantially lower throughputs has not been demonstrated. As liquid rate falls, distribution and wetting of the contacting surface deteriorate, and the removal duty may not be held at the bottom of the range. No turndown ratio is claimed. The design is complete at its basis, and the two open items mark its limits: fouling governs how long the design performance lasts in service, and turndown governs how far below the design throughput that performance can be assumed to hold.

input: This summary reviews delivery performance at a contract packaging firm which runs 2 plants and has revenue of $74 million per year, drawing on order records for 12 months covering 14591 orders. On-time delivery over the last two quarters was 84%, against a target of 95%, and the shortfall is concentrated rather than evenly spread, since Plant 2 accounts for 61% of late orders. Overtime cost was $2.1 million last year, up 27% on the year before, and the order backlog stands at 4.2 weeks, against 2.1 weeks a year ago, which suggests that the lateness problem is being carried forward rather than cleared. A scheduling system for all plants is quoted at $320k, whereas Plant 2 alone is $133k, and an internal estimate (not a vendor figure) puts the overtime reduction at Plant 2 at 15-20% in the first year. The recommendation under consideration is to install at Plant 2 first and hold the other plants until Plant 2 results are reported, with the operations director owning the scheduling programme. The concentration of the lateness in a single plant is, on the face of the records, the strongest argument for the staged course, since it allows the effect of the system to be observed where the problem is most acute before a decision is taken about the remaining plant.
target: Install the scheduling system at Plant 2 first, and hold the other plants until Plant 2 results are reported; the operations director owns the scheduling programme. Order records for 12 months (14591 orders) give on-time delivery over the last two quarters at 84%, against a target of 95%. The firm runs 2 plants, and revenue is $74 million per year. Lateness is concentrated: Plant 2 accounts for 61% of late orders. Overtime cost was $2.1 million last year, up 27% on the year before. The order backlog stands at 4.2 weeks, against 2.1 weeks a year ago. A scheduling system for all plants is quoted at $320k; Plant 2 alone is $133k. An internal estimate, not a vendor figure, puts the overtime reduction at Plant 2 at 15-20% in the first year. The concentration matters to the choice: a system installed everywhere at once would spend the full quoted sum against a problem that the records place mainly in one plant, and the staged route tests the system where the lateness is generated before any wider commitment is made.
