The sequence spends the smaller sum first and makes the wider installation wait on reported results from the plant where the late orders are concentrated.

fact_base: A single-stage compressor raises air from 2 bar to 9 bar. Inlet temperature is 313 K. For isentropic compression with a heat-capacity ratio of 1.4, the discharge temperature is 481 K. The isentropic estimate excludes mechanical losses; the installed machine's measured discharge temperature is higher.
input:
Compressors are among the most widely used machines in process plants, and the temperature at which the gas leaves a compressor is a figure with far-reaching implications for downstream equipment, for safety, and for energy use. In the case considered here, a single-stage compressor raises air from 2 bar to 9 bar, with the air entering the machine at an inlet temperature of 313 K. If the compression is modelled as isentropic, in other words as a process that is both perfectly adiabatic and perfectly reversible, and if a heat-capacity ratio of 1.4 is adopted for air, the discharge temperature works out at 481 K.

It is important to appreciate the idealisations that sit behind this figure. The model assumes that no heat whatsoever is transferred between the gas and its surroundings during compression, that frictional effects are entirely absent, and that air behaves as an ideal gas whose heat-capacity ratio does not vary across the temperature range involved. Provided those assumptions hold, the discharge temperature is governed solely by the inlet temperature and by the pressure ratio, and matters such as the physical size of the machine, the speed at which it runs, and the detailed design of its valves have no bearing on the outcome.

In practice, however, the position is somewhat different, because the isentropic estimate deliberately leaves mechanical losses out of account. In a real, installed machine there is friction in the bearings and in the seals, and there are irreversibilities as the gas passes through the valves, all of which convert a portion of the shaft work into extra heat within the gas itself. It follows that the measured discharge temperature of the installed machine will be higher than 481 K, in many cases noticeably so, and the estimate should be regarded as an idealised benchmark: valuable as a reference point for preliminary design and for judging the condition of a machine, but not a prediction of the temperature that will actually be observed in service.
target:
A single-stage compressor raises air from 2 bar to 9 bar. The air enters at 313 K, and the discharge temperature on the isentropic estimate is 481 K.

The estimate treats the compression as reversible and adiabatic. No heat crosses the casing during the compression, no friction acts on the gas, and air is treated as an ideal gas with a constant heat-capacity ratio of 1.4 over the whole temperature range. Under those assumptions, the discharge temperature is fixed by the inlet temperature and the pressure ratio. The size of the machine, its rotational speed, its valve geometry, and its clearance volume do not enter the calculation, because none of them alters the end state of an isentropic compression carried out between the same two pressures.

The figure is the discharge temperature of the idealised machine, and it is a lower bound on the temperature the installed machine will reach. The isentropic estimate excludes mechanical losses. In the installed machine, friction in the bearings and seals and the irreversibility of the flow through the valves convert part of the shaft work into heat in the gas, and the measured discharge temperature is higher than 481 K. A measured temperature above the estimate is the expected outcome of the comparison; the estimate and the measurement describe different machines, one idealised and one as built, and a difference between them is not, on its own, evidence of a fault in either.

The estimate is used where the idealised temperature is the quantity the decision needs: a first sizing of the discharge cooler, an early check of the discharge temperature against a limit set by a seal material or a lubricant, and a baseline against which the measured temperature is read when the condition of the machine is assessed. Where the decision turns on the temperature the machine actually reaches in service, the measured discharge temperature displaces the estimate, and the estimate retains only its baseline role.

fact_base: Goal: compute the diffusive flux of oxygen through a stagnant water film. The diffusive flux J (mol m-2 s-1) is computed from the diffusivity D (m2 s-1) and the concentration gradient dC/dx, where C is concentration (mol m-3) and x is position (m). Fick's first law: J = -D dC/dx; the negative sign states that diffusion runs from high concentration to low concentration. Oxygen in water: D = 1.6 x 10-9 m2 s-1. Concentration falls by 0.25 mol m-3 across a film 0.4 mm thick, so dC/dx = -625 mol m-4. Worked result: J = 1.00x 10-6 mol m-2 s-1. The law as stated covers a stagnant medium; a moving medium adds convection, which the equation does not include.
input:
In this example we are going to work through the calculation of the diffusive flux of oxygen through a stagnant water film that is 0.4 mm thick, across which the oxygen concentration falls by 0.25 mol m-3, and the exercise is a useful illustration of how Fick's first law is applied in practice.

The starting point is the definition of the quantities involved. The diffusive flux $J$ (mol m-2 s-1) is obtained from the diffusivity $D$ (m2 s-1) together with the concentration gradient $dC/dx$, where $C$ (mol m-3) is the concentration and $x$ (m) is the position measured across the film. Fick's first law expresses the relationship in the compact form $J = -D dC/dx$, and the negative sign is by no means a mere formality: it captures the essential physical fact that diffusion always proceeds from regions of high concentration towards regions of low concentration, so that when the concentration decreases in the direction of increasing $x$, the resulting flux is positive in that same direction.

Turning to the numbers for oxygen dissolved in water, the diffusivity $D$ takes the value 1.6 x 10-9 m2 s-1. The fall in concentration across the thickness of the film corresponds to a concentration gradient $dC/dx$ = -625 mol m-4, and substituting these values into the law yields a diffusive flux $J$ = 1.00 x 10-6 mol m-2 s-1.

It is worth emphasising the sheer smallness of this flux, which reflects the very low diffusivity of dissolved gases in liquids. Finally, it should be borne in mind that Fick's first law in the form used here is strictly applicable to a stagnant medium; if the medium is moving, convection contributes to the transport as well, and that contribution is simply not included in the equation, so the result obtained here represents the diffusive part of the transport only.
target:
Calculate the diffusive flux of oxygen through a stagnant water film 0.4 mm thick, across which the oxygen concentration falls by 0.25 mol m-3.

The diffusive flux $J$ (mol m-2 s-1) is calculated from the diffusivity $D$ (m2 s-1) and the concentration gradient $dC/dx$, where $C$ (mol m-3) denotes the concentration and $x$ (m) the position across the film. Fick's first law gives the flux as $J = -D dC/dx$. The negative sign states that diffusion runs from high concentration to low concentration: where the concentration falls in the direction of increasing $x$, the gradient is negative and the flux is positive in that direction.

For oxygen in water, the diffusivity $D$ is 1.6 x 10-9 m2 s-1. The stated fall across the stated thickness gives the concentration gradient $dC/dx$ = -625 mol m-4. Substitution into Fick's first law gives $J$ = 1.00 x 10-6 mol m-2 s-1.

The sign check closes the calculation: the gradient is negative, the diffusivity is positive, and the law carries a negative sign, so the flux comes out positive in the direction of falling concentration, as the physical picture requires. The gradient is taken as uniform across the film. That is the stagnant-film picture: the concentration profile is a straight line between the two faces of the film, and the flux the law gives is the flux at every plane in the film, the same at the face where the oxygen enters as at the face where it leaves. A profile that curved would give a gradient varying with position, and the flux would then have to be evaluated at the plane of interest. The magnitude is small because the diffusivity of a dissolved gas in a liquid is small; the same concentration difference across a gas film would drive a far larger flux. Fick's first law as stated holds for a stagnant medium. A moving medium adds convection to the transport, and the equation does not include that term, so the flux calculated here is the diffusive contribution only.

fact_base: A tutorial passage explains representative sampling of a powder blend. The passage covers where samples are taken, how many increments form one sample, and why a single grab sample misleads. No numerical limits are quoted; regulatory limits belong to the site's permit, not to the passage.
input:
When it comes to characterising a powder blend, it is tempting to assume that a material which has been thoroughly mixed will be uniform throughout, so that any small portion can be taken as representative of the whole. In practice, however, this assumption is unreliable, and great care has to be taken over how samples are obtained if the results are to mean anything.

The underlying difficulty is segregation. The particles that make up a blend differ in size and in density, and ordinary handling tends to separate them again: fine particles percolate downwards through the voids between coarser ones during transport and vibration, coarse particles roll outwards to the surface and the edges of a heap, and when a container is discharged the material does not leave uniformly from every region. The composition of the blend therefore varies from place to place, even in a batch that was well mixed to begin with.

For this reason, samples are built up from many increments taken at many points and at many times. Wherever the process permits, increments are cut from a moving stream across its full cross-section, on the grounds that such a cut gathers material that originated from all parts of the bed or vessel. Where the material is stationary, increments are drawn with a sampling thief from positions and depths spread across the whole mass, taking care that easily reached spots near walls and outlets do not dominate. All of the increments are combined into a single composite sample, and the laboratory portion is obtained from it by a splitting method, such as riffling, that does not select by particle size, so that local variations are averaged out.

A single grab sample, by contrast, can be seriously misleading, because it captures the composition of one location at one moment and silently presents it as the composition of the entire batch. The analysis itself may be perfectly accurate, yet the conclusion drawn from it wrong, since the error lies in the sampling rather than in the measurement. This discussion deliberately quotes no numerical limits: any limits that a sampling scheme has to meet are regulatory or contractual in nature, and they are set out in the site's permit rather than in a description of sampling practice.
target:
A powder blend is not uniform at the scale of a scoop. Particles differ in size and density, and handling moves them relative to each other: fine particles settle through voids during transport, coarse particles roll to the surface and to the edges of a heap, and discharge from a container draws material from some regions before others. A sample that is to stand for the whole batch must be built against that segregation.

Samples are therefore taken at many points and at many times rather than at one accessible point. Increments are drawn across the full cross-section of a moving stream where the process allows it, because a stream cut in passing contains material from every part of the bed or container that fed it. Where the material is at rest, increments are taken from distributed positions and depths with a sampling thief, and positions near walls and outlets are not allowed to dominate the set.

The increments are combined into one composite sample, which is then reduced to the laboratory portion by a method that does not select by particle size, such as riffling. Each increment contributes a small part of the whole, so the segregation of any one region is diluted by material from the rest of the batch, and the composite reports the batch average rather than any local composition.

A single grab sample misleads because it reports the composition of the place and moment it was taken from, generalised without warrant to the whole batch. In a segregated blend, that local composition can differ substantially from the batch average, and the error is invisible in the result itself: the analysis can be accurate for the scoop and wrong for the batch. No numerical limits are stated here. The limits a sampling scheme must satisfy are set by regulation or by contract, and they belong to the site's permit, not to the sampling method.

fact_base: A tutorial passage explains the Sherwood number to second-year students. Definition in words: the Sherwood number is the ratio of convective to diffusive mass transfer at a surface. The passage must state what a value near 1 means and what a large value means, without inventing numerical examples.
input:
Students meeting mass transfer for the first time often ask why another dimensionless group is needed, and the Sherwood number answers a practical question: how much does the movement of the fluid actually help? The Sherwood number is defined as the ratio of convective to diffusive mass transfer at a surface. In the numerator stands the rate at which the flowing fluid delivers material to the surface, or carries it away; in the denominator stands the rate at which diffusion alone, acting across a stagnant layer of the same thickness, would transport the material. Because the comparison is made across one and the same layer, the ratio isolates the contribution of the flow itself.

If the value obtained is close to 1, convection is contributing essentially nothing over and above diffusion. The fluid may well be in motion, yet that motion does not thin the layer, and so the transfer is controlled by diffusion across the layer, exactly as it would be in a stagnant film. This limit is the natural benchmark for everything else.

At the other extreme, a large value tells us that convection has taken over. The flow sweeping past the surface maintains only a very thin diffusive layer and constantly renews the fluid in contact with the surface, so that material is transferred far more rapidly than diffusion across the whole layer could achieve, and the observed rate is dictated by the flow pattern and the geometry rather than by the diffusivity alone.

In practice, the Sherwood number earns its keep when a mass-transfer coefficient is required for a geometry and flow arrangement that has never been measured: published correlations give the number in terms of the flow conditions and fluid properties, and the coefficient is back-calculated from it. One caution deserves emphasis: the value is only meaningful together with its basis, since the characteristic length in the definition must match the length used in the correlation, failing which the recovered coefficient will be wrong by the ratio of the two lengths.
target:
The Sherwood number is the ratio of convective to diffusive mass transfer at a surface. The numerator is the rate at which a flowing fluid delivers material to or from the surface; the denominator is the rate at which diffusion alone would move the same material across a stagnant layer of the same thickness. The two rates describe the same transfer across the same layer, so the ratio compares the two mechanisms on one basis, and the comparison is what the number reports.

A value near 1 means that convection adds nothing to the transfer. The fluid may be moving, but its motion does not thin the layer through which the material must diffuse, and diffusion across that layer sets the rate. The stagnant film gives this limit, and the limit is the reference state against which any enhancement by the flow is measured.

A large value means that convection dominates the transfer. Flow past the surface keeps the diffusive layer thin and continually replaces the fluid in contact with the surface, so material crosses far faster than diffusion across the full layer would allow. The rate is then governed mainly by the flow and by the geometry that shapes the flow, and the diffusivity on its own no longer predicts it.

The Sherwood number is used where a mass-transfer coefficient is needed for a geometry and a flow that have not been measured. Correlations report the number as a function of the flow conditions and the fluid properties, and the coefficient is recovered from the number. A reported value is tied to its basis: the length in the definition must be the length the correlation used, or the recovered coefficient is wrong by the ratio of the two lengths.

fact_base: A textbook chapter section on process control, in four parts: principle, equipment, a worked example, and limits. The worked example uses only the numbers given in the principle part; no new data appear later in the chapter. The limits part states where the simple model fails, in plain terms, without new equations.
input:
## Principle

Feedback control rests on a simple idea: measure the variable you care about, compare it with the value you want, and act so as to oppose any difference that appears. This chapter is anchored to one familiar example, the level of liquid in a tank. Liquid flows into the tank at a rate set by the process upstream, and out through a line fitted with a valve the control system can adjust. The material balance fixes the behaviour: whenever the inflow is greater than the outflow the level rises, whenever the outflow is greater the level falls, and only when the two flows are equal does the level remain steady.

The control loop therefore begins with a measurement of the level, which is compared against the set point, the value at which the level is to be maintained. The difference between the two is termed the error, and it is on the basis of this error that the controller decides how to move the outflow valve: if the level is too high, the outflow is increased, and if it is too low, the outflow is reduced. Because the action opposes the deviation that called it forth, the feedback is negative and the loop is self-correcting.

Under proportional control, the change made to the outflow is proportional to the error, with a consequence students often find surprising. If the inflow undergoes a sustained change, the outflow must change by the same amount for balance to be restored, yet under proportional action a changed valve position can only be maintained by a standing error. The level consequently settles away from the set point, at an offset that grows with the disturbance and shrinks as the proportional gain is raised. Integral action overcomes this drawback: while any error persists, the controller keeps moving the valve in the correcting direction, bringing the level back to the set point and eliminating the offset, since the new valve position no longer depends on an error to sustain it.

The simple model sketched above is a deliberately narrow one. It deals with a single measured variable and a single manipulated variable, it supposes that every element responds proportionally and instantaneously, and it ignores delays, limits of travel, and measurement noise altogether. The worked example that follows stays within this idealised picture, and the final part of the chapter turns to the question of where the picture ceases to be a faithful description of a real loop.

## Equipment

A practical loop is built from three functional elements: an instrument that measures, a controller that decides, and a final element that acts.

Measurement of the level is the job of a level transmitter. Depending on the application, a float or displacer may follow the surface directly, or a differential-pressure cell may infer the level from the pressure exerted at the base of the tank; either way, the instrument produces a signal that represents the level across the range over which control is required. This signal is the loop's only window on the process: everything downstream of the transmitter responds to the signal, not to the level itself, so any fault or bias in the measurement is acted upon as though it were real.

The controller accepts the measurement, holds the set point, computes the error, and generates an output signal in accordance with the control action that has been selected, whether proportional, integral, or a combination of the two. Its tuning determines how vigorously a given error is answered and how persistently it is chased.

The final element is a control valve installed in the outflow line, driven by an actuator that converts the controller's output signal into a stem position, working against the forces exerted by the flowing liquid and by the valve's own spring or air supply. Where the actuator by itself cannot hold the stem accurately at the demanded position, a valve positioner is added. The valve is also the point at which the loop's behaviour on failure is fixed in hardware: if the signal or the air supply is lost, the valve travels to its failure position, fully open or fully closed, and the choice between the two is made by asking which failure is safer, an overfilled tank or an empty one, rather than by control considerations.

## Worked example

Consider the tank running steadily, with inflow and outflow equal and the level at the set point. Now let the inflow step up to a higher rate and remain there, as when an upstream unit raises its throughput.

Initially nothing has yet happened to the outflow, so the inflow exceeds it and the level begins to climb. The transmitter detects the rise, an error develops, and the controller, acting proportionally, opens the outflow valve further. The outflow increases towards the new inflow, the climb of the level slackens as the two flows converge, and the level finally settles at a new steady value above the set point, where inflow and outflow are once more equal. The residual error is precisely the error needed to hold the valve at its new opening, exactly the offset the principle predicts under proportional action alone: balance has been restored, but at the wrong level.

Now introduce integral action. As long as the error persists, the controller keeps edging the valve open, the outflow rises beyond the rate that balanced at the elevated level, and the level is drawn back down towards the set point. The movement dies away as the level reaches the set point, because the error that was driving it has disappeared, and the loop comes to rest with the flows again equal, the level at the set point, and the valve held at its new opening by the accumulated integral term rather than by any standing error. The example bears out the principle step by step: the flow balance dictates the level, proportional action alone leaves an offset after a sustained change in the inflow, and integral action removes the offset by sustaining the new outflow without an error to do it.

## Limits

The simple model departs from reality first in its treatment of time. A real measurement is never instantaneous: transmitter, signal, and actuator each take time, and the process develops over time, so that by the moment the loop acts, the level it acts on has already moved. Dead time of this sort limits how aggressively a loop can be tuned, and a controller set up for a brisk response on the simple model will oscillate on the real tank.

The second departure concerns range. A valve can only open so far and can only move so fast, and a disturbance that calls for more outflow than the fully open valve can pass is beyond correction, whatever the tuning. In addition, the characteristic of a real valve is nonlinear, particularly towards the ends of its travel, so that the gain of the loop is not a constant but varies with the operating point to which events have pushed it.

The third departure concerns the boundaries of the problem. The model treats the tank in isolation and the inflow as an external event, whereas in an operating plant that inflow is the outflow of some other unit with a loop of its own, and the two loops interact. The model treats the measurement as though it were the level, whereas a noisy measurement is acted upon as though the level itself were jumping about. And the model assumes a self-regulating process of the kind described, whereas a tank emptied by a pump at a fixed rate integrates the imbalance, and the same settings produce a different response. The simple model, in short, is a statement about a single loop, a single variable, small movements, and an absence of delay, and it is trustworthy only within those conditions.
target:
## Principle

Feedback control holds a chosen variable at a chosen value by acting against its deviations. The example used throughout this chapter is the level of liquid in a tank. Liquid enters the tank at a rate set by the process upstream, and leaves through a line whose flow the control system can adjust. The level is fixed by the balance between the two flows: the level rises while the inflow exceeds the outflow, falls while the outflow exceeds the inflow, and holds steady only while the two are equal.

The control loop measures the level and compares the measurement with the set point, the value the level is to be held at. The difference between the measurement and the set point is the error. The controller acts on the error and moves the outflow so as to reduce the error: a level above the set point calls for more outflow, and a level below it calls for less. The action opposes the deviation that produced it, which is what makes the feedback negative and the loop self-correcting.

Under proportional action, the movement of the outflow is proportional to the error. This has a consequence that the rest of the chapter uses. If the inflow changes and stays changed, the outflow must change by the same amount to restore the balance, and under proportional action a changed outflow is held only by a standing error. The level therefore settles away from the set point, by an offset that grows with the size of the change and shrinks as the proportional gain is raised. Under integral action, the controller keeps moving the outflow for as long as an error stands, at a rate set by the error; the level is then driven back to the set point and the offset is removed, because the outflow can be held at its new value with no error remaining.

The simple model behind these statements is narrow. It treats one measured variable and one manipulated variable, it treats the response of each part of the loop as proportional and immediate, and it says nothing about delays, limits of travel, or noise. The worked example stays inside that model; the closing part states where the model stops describing a real loop.

## Equipment

The loop has three working parts: a measurement, a controller, and a final element.

The measurement is made by a level transmitter. A float or a displacer follows the surface, or a differential-pressure cell infers the level from the pressure at the tank base; in each case the instrument delivers a signal that represents the level over the range the control is required to cover. The measurement is the loop's only knowledge of the process, and every later part of the loop acts on the signal, not on the level itself.

The controller receives the measurement, holds the set point, forms the error, and computes the output signal by the control action selected, proportional, integral, or the two combined. The controller is where the loop's behaviour is set: its tuning decides how large an output change a given error produces and how persistently an error is pursued.

The final element is a control valve in the outflow line, driven by an actuator that takes the controller's output signal and sets the valve opening against the force of the flow and the valve's own spring or air supply. A valve positioner is fitted where the actuator alone cannot hold the stem at the position the signal demands. The valve is also where the loop's safety behaviour is decided in hardware: on loss of signal or air supply the valve moves to its failure position, open or closed, and that position is chosen from the hazard of the tank overfilling or running dry, not from the convenience of control.

## Worked example

Take the tank at a steady level, with inflow and outflow equal and the level at the set point. The inflow then rises to a new, higher rate and stays there, as when an upstream unit raises its throughput.

At first the outflow is unchanged, so the inflow exceeds it and the level rises. The transmitter reports the rise, an error appears, and the controller, acting proportionally, opens the outflow valve. The outflow rises towards the new inflow. As the outflow approaches the inflow, the rise of the level slows, and the level settles above the set point, where the two flows are again equal. The standing error at that level is exactly the error needed to hold the valve at its new opening, and the offset in the level is the offset the principle states for proportional action: the loop has restored the balance, but at a level away from the set point.

Integral action is then added. While the error stands, the controller continues to open the valve slowly, the outflow rises past the rate that balanced at the raised level, and the level falls back towards the set point. The movement stops when the level reaches the set point, because the error that drove it has vanished, and the loop settles with inflow and outflow equal at the set point and the valve held at its new opening by the accumulated integral action. The trace matches the principle at each step: balance of flows fixes the level, proportional action alone leaves an offset after a sustained change in inflow, and integral action removes the offset by holding the new outflow without a standing error.

## Limits

The simple model fails first on time. A real measurement is not immediate: the transmitter, the signal path, and the actuator each take time, and the process itself responds over time, so the loop acts on a level that has already moved on. Dead time of that kind limits how hard the loop can be driven; a controller tuned for a fast response on the simple model will oscillate on the real tank.

The model fails next on range. The valve has a finite travel and a finite rate of movement, and a disturbance large enough to demand more outflow than the fully open valve passes cannot be corrected at any tuning. Near the ends of its travel the valve's characteristic is also nonlinear, so the gain of the loop changes with the operating point the disturbance has moved it to.

The model fails lastly on its boundaries. It treats the tank in isolation, with the inflow as an outside event; in a plant the inflow is another loop's outflow, and the two loops act on each other. It treats the measurement as the level; noise in the measurement is acted on as if it were movement of the level. And it treats the process as self-regulating in the manner stated; a tank whose outflow is fixed by a pump rather than by the level itself integrates the imbalance, and the same control action gives a different response. The model is a statement about one loop, one variable, small movements, and no delays, and it is reliable inside those conditions.

fact_base: A continuous stirred-tank reactor runs a neutralisation that is first order in the limiting reactant. The rate constant is 0.14 min-1 at the operating temperature and the mean residence time is 41 min. Steady-state conversion for an ideal CSTR is 85.2%. The estimate assumes perfect mixing and constant density; tracer tests on the actual vessel have not been run.
input:
This example concerns a continuous stirred-tank reactor in which a neutralisation reaction is carried out, the reaction being first order in the limiting reactant, and the aim is to establish what conversion can be expected when the reactor is operating at steady state. The answer, on the usual idealised analysis, is a steady-state conversion of 85.2%.

By conversion we mean, as always, the fraction of the limiting reactant that is consumed in passing from the feed to the outlet stream. Since the reaction is first order, the local rate of reaction is directly proportional to the local concentration of the limiting reactant. The special feature of the continuous stirred-tank reactor is that vigorous stirring keeps the contents uniform, so that the composition everywhere inside the vessel is the composition of the outlet stream; the rate of reaction is therefore the same at every point in the vessel, and the steady-state material balance can be written in terms of that one rate, which greatly simplifies the analysis compared with a reactor in which the composition changes along the flow path.

The numerical data are as follows. The rate constant $k$ is 0.14 min-1 at the operating temperature, and the mean residence time $\tau$ is 41 min. For the ideal continuous stirred-tank reactor, the conversion $X$ is related to these quantities through the expression $X = \frac{k \tau}{1 + k \tau}$, in which the product $k\tau$ appears as the governing group; that product evaluates to 5.74, and substitution into the expression duly gives the steady-state conversion of 85.2%.

Two assumptions underpin the whole calculation and should be stated plainly. The first is perfect mixing, which is what justifies treating the entire vessel as sitting at the outlet composition; any departure from it means that the simple balance no longer holds exactly. The second is constant density, which allows the mean residence time to be identified with the ratio of the vessel volume to the volumetric throughput. It is worth stressing that these assumptions remain unchecked for the vessel in question, inasmuch as tracer tests on the actual vessel have not been run, so phenomena such as bypassing or the presence of stagnant zones would pass unnoticed, and any of them would tend to reduce the conversion achieved in practice.

Conversion is the fraction of the limiting reactant consumed between the feed and the outlet. For a first-order reaction, the rate at any point is proportional to the concentration of the limiting reactant at that point. In a continuous stirred-tank reactor the vessel contents are uniform and sit at the outlet composition, so the rate is the same everywhere in the vessel, and the steady-state balance on the limiting reactant closes on that single rate rather than on a rate that varies along a flow path.

The product $k\tau$ is 5.74, and substitution gives the steady-state conversion, 85.2%. The figure is a steady-state figure: during start-up the outlet composition is still moving towards its steady value, and the conversion passes through lower values on the way there.

The estimate assumes perfect mixing and constant density. Perfect mixing is the assumption that places the whole vessel at the outlet composition; where mixing falls short, part of the vessel sits nearer the feed composition, the local rate there is higher, and the single-rate balance no longer describes the vessel. Constant density is the assumption that makes the mean residence time the ratio of the vessel volume to the volumetric feed rate. fact_base: Pervaporation is a membrane separation in which a liquid feed contacts one side of a membrane and vacuum on the other side draws the permeating component through as vapour. Flux is the mass permeating per unit membrane area per hour (kg m-2 h-1). The separation factor is the water-to-alcohol ratio in the permeate divided by the same ratio in the feed (dimensionless). Feed: 85 wt% n-butanol in water, at 60 °C. One feed composition was tested; no test ran beyond 500 h. Polymer membrane: flux 2.1 kg m-2 h-1, separation factor 120, flux fell 9% over 500 h. Zeolite membrane: flux 1.2 kg m-2 h-1, separation factor 420, flux unchanged over 500 h within measurement error. Flux, selectivity and stability are seldom reported together for the same membrane.
input:
Pervaporation is an attractive membrane separation technique in which a liquid feed is brought into contact with one side of a membrane while a vacuum applied to the other side draws the component that permeates through the membrane in the form of a vapour. In the study reported here, a polymer membrane and a zeolite membrane were evaluated side by side for the removal of water from a feed consisting of 85 wt% n-butanol in water at 60 °C. Two performance measures are used throughout. The flux is the mass of material permeating per unit membrane area per hour (kg m-2 h-1), and the separation factor is defined as the water-to-alcohol ratio in the permeate divided by the corresponding ratio in the feed.

The headline results can be summarised as follows. The polymer membrane delivers the higher flux but the lower separation factor (2.1 kg m-2 h-1; 120), whereas the zeolite membrane delivers the lower flux but a considerably higher separation factor (1.2 kg m-2 h-1; 420). Long-term stability draws a further distinction between the two materials: the flux of the polymer membrane fell 9% over 500 h of operation, while the flux of the zeolite membrane was unchanged over 500 h, at least within the limits of measurement error.

Taken together, the results present the familiar trade-off between throughput and selectivity. The polymer offers more throughput but less enrichment, and its advantage is eroded to some extent by the decline it exhibits during the test; the zeolite offers less throughput but more enrichment, and it maintains its performance. It should be borne in mind that only one feed composition was investigated and that no test ran beyond 500 h. This matters because flux, selectivity and stability are seldom reported together for one and the same membrane, and it is precisely the combination of all three that determines which material is preferable in practice.

The comparison is a trade-off between throughput and selectivity. Neither membrane dominates: each leads on one measure and trails on the other, and the vacuum duty that drives the separation is common to both. fact_base: A shell-and-tube exchanger heats propylene glycol in a refinery preheat train. Duty is 1377 kW. Hot stream: 180 °C in, 130 °C out. Cold stream: 25 °C in, 50 °C out. The log-mean temperature difference is 117.1 K and the installed area is 40.2 m2, giving an overall coefficient of 293 W m-2 K-1. Fouling was assessed from a single 90-day run; no cleaning cycle has been completed.
input:
The results reported here relate to a shell-and-tube heat exchanger installed in a refinery preheat train, where its duty is to heat propylene glycol. The exchanger operates at a duty of 1377 kW. On the hot side, the stream enters at 180 °C and leaves at 130 °C, while on the cold side the stream enters at 25 °C and leaves at 50 °C. Working from these terminal temperatures, the temperature difference at the hot end is 130 K and at the cold end is 105 K, giving a log-mean temperature difference of 117.1 K. With an installed area of 40.2 m2, the corresponding overall heat-transfer coefficient works out at 293 W m-2 K-1.

This overall coefficient is best understood as a measure of the performance of the exchanger as actually installed, referred to the installed area. It lumps together the resistances of the two fluid films, the resistance of the tube wall, and the resistance due to any fouling that had built up over the course of the run, and it provides the natural starting point for any future rerating exercise or for checking the unit against a revised duty. It is also worth noting that, because the two terminal differences differ considerably from one another, the log-mean value lies well below the hot-end figure, so that anyone sizing an exchanger on the hot-end difference alone would overestimate the effective driving force and end up with too little surface.

As far as fouling is concerned, the assessment rests on a single 90-day run, and it must be emphasised that no cleaning cycle has yet been completed. The reported coefficient accordingly characterises the exchanger over that one run only, and the available data say nothing about the extent to which performance recovers on cleaning, the rate at which fouling re-establishes itself afterwards, or whether the fouling eventually levels off.

A shell-and-tube exchanger in a refinery preheat train heats propylene glycol. The duty is 1377 kW. The hot stream enters at 180 °C and leaves at 130 °C; the cold stream enters at 25 °C and leaves at 50 °C. The terminal temperature differences are 130 K at the hot end and 105 K at the cold end, and the log-mean temperature difference is 117.1 K. On the installed area of 40.2 m2, the overall coefficient is 293 W m-2 K-1.

The coefficient is the installed performance, stated on the installed area. It folds the two film resistances, the tube wall, and whatever fouling had accumulated during the run into a single figure, and it is the figure from which a rerating of the same exchanger, or a check of the exchanger against a changed duty, would start. The duty and the four terminal temperatures fix that figure jointly; no one of them carries it alone. Because the terminal differences are wide apart, the log-mean difference sits well below the hot-end difference; a sizing checked against the hot-end difference alone would overstate the driving force along much of the exchanger and undersize the surface.

Fouling was assessed from a single 90-day run, and no cleaning cycle has been completed. The coefficient therefore describes the exchanger over that one run, from its condition at the start of the run to its condition at the end. The run does not show how far the coefficient recovers when the exchanger is cleaned, how quickly it falls again afterwards, or whether the fouling approaches a plateau. A cleaning interval and a long-run performance figure cannot be read from a single run; the measurement that would settle the fouling behaviour is a further run with a completed cleaning cycle inside it.

fact_base: A single-stage compressor raises air from 2 bar to 9 bar. Inlet temperature is 293 K. For isentropic compression with a heat-capacity ratio of 1.4, the discharge temperature is 450 K. The isentropic estimate excludes mechanical losses; the installed machine's measured discharge temperature is higher.
input:
In this example we consider a single-stage compressor that raises air from 2 bar to 9 bar, the air entering the machine at an inlet temperature of 293 K, and we ask what discharge temperature the standard isentropic analysis predicts. Carrying out that analysis gives a discharge temperature of 450 K.

The analysis rests on the customary idealisations. The compression is treated as though it were both reversible and adiabatic, and air is treated as an ideal gas whose heat-capacity ratio of 1.4 remains constant throughout the process. On the basis of those assumptions, the discharge temperature turns out to depend only on the inlet temperature and on the pressure ratio between discharge and inlet, and practical details such as the dimensions of the machine, the speed at which it runs, and the design of its valves have no influence on the result, since the isentropic end state is fixed by the two pressures alone.

One qualification must, however, be kept firmly in mind: the isentropic estimate makes no allowance at all for mechanical losses. In the installed machine, friction in the bearings and seals and the irreversibilities associated with flow through the valves convert a part of the shaft work into additional heat, and consequently the discharge temperature actually measured on the installed machine will be higher than the estimated value. The estimate is therefore most properly used as a baseline figure, for preliminary sizing of the discharge cooler, for checking against temperature limits imposed by seals or lubricants, and as a reference against which measured temperatures can be compared when the condition of the machine is being assessed.
target:
A single-stage compressor raises air from 2 bar to 9 bar, with an inlet temperature of 293 K. The discharge temperature on the isentropic estimate is 450 K.

The estimate treats the compression as reversible and adiabatic, and air as an ideal gas with a constant heat-capacity ratio of 1.4 over the temperature range. On those assumptions, the discharge temperature is fixed by the inlet temperature and the pressure ratio; the size of the machine, its speed, and the design of its valves do not enter the calculation, because an isentropic end state between two pressures does not depend on the path the machine takes between them.

The isentropic estimate excludes mechanical losses. Friction in the bearings and seals, and the irreversibility of the flow through the valves, convert part of the shaft work into heat in the gas, so the measured discharge temperature of the installed machine is higher than the estimate. The estimated temperature is a baseline: it serves a first sizing of the discharge cooler, a check against temperature limits set by seals or lubricant, and a reference for the measured temperature when the condition of the machine is judged. Where a decision turns on the temperature the machine actually reaches, the measured discharge temperature displaces the estimate. A higher pressure ratio at the same inlet temperature gives a higher discharge temperature; the estimate moves with the duty in that direction, by the relation the assumptions fix.

subtype: worked example with equation: Stokes settling
fact_base: Sand grains of diameter $d_p$ = 100 micrometres and density 2650 kg m-3 settle in water at 293 K. Stokes' law gives a terminal velocity $v_t$ of 9 mm s-1. The estimate requires creeping flow; the particle Reynolds number must be checked before the value is used.
input:
This worked example looks at the settling of sand grains in water at 293 K, a classic application of Stokes' law. The grains in question have a diameter $d_p$ of 100 micrometres and a density of 2650 kg m-3, and applying Stokes' law to them gives a terminal velocity $v_t$ of 9 mm s-1:

$$v_t = \frac{g d_p^2 (\rho_p - \rho)}{18 \mu}$$

The symbols appearing in the equation are to be interpreted as follows: $v_t$ denotes the terminal velocity, $g$ the acceleration due to gravity, $d_p$ the particle diameter, $\rho_p$ the density of the particle material, $\rho$ the density of the water, and $\mu$ the viscosity of the water. It is worth drawing attention to the fact that the velocity depends on the square of the particle diameter, which makes the result highly sensitive to the size adopted for the grains; since a real sand contains a spread of sizes, the finer fraction will settle appreciably more slowly and will remain in suspension correspondingly longer, and the single diameter used in the calculation is in effect standing in for the entire distribution.

Finally, an important caveat must be attached to the result. Stokes' law is strictly valid only for creeping flow, the regime in which viscous forces dominate and inertial effects can be neglected, and for that reason the particle Reynolds number must be checked before the calculated value is relied upon. Should that check show that the settling does not in fact lie in the creeping-flow regime, then the drag experienced by the grain will differ from the drag embodied in the law, and the terminal velocity will need to be redetermined using a drag relation appropriate to the regime actually encountered.
target:

$$v_t = \frac{g d_p^2 (\rho_p - \rho)}{18 \mu}$$

In the equation, $v_t$ denotes the terminal velocity, $g$ the acceleration due to gravity, $d_p$ the particle diameter, $\rho_p$ the density of the particle, $\rho$ the density of the water, and $\mu$ the viscosity of the water. The velocity varies with the square of the diameter, so the estimate rests heavily on the diameter chosen for the grains: a real sand is a distribution of sizes, the finer grains settle more slowly than the stated velocity and remain suspended longer, and the single diameter used here stands for the whole distribution.

Stokes' law holds for creeping flow, the regime in which viscous forces dominate the motion of the fluid around the particle and inertia is negligible. The estimate is conditional on that regime: the particle Reynolds number must be checked before the value is used. If the check places the settling outside creeping flow, the drag on the grain is not the drag the law assumes, and the terminal velocity has to be obtained from a drag relation that covers the regime the check establishes.

fact_base: Capital appraisal for a bottling line: installed cost $1334k, expected net saving $301k per year for 10 years. At a discount rate of 10% the present value of the savings is $1850k and the net present value is $516k. Savings are vendor and utility estimates; no saving has yet been measured on a comparable installation.
input:
This note sets out a capital appraisal for a proposed new bottling line and reaches a clear conclusion: on the figures currently available, the investment is financially attractive, with a net present value of $516k at a discount rate of 10%, the present value of the expected savings being $1850k when set against an installed cost of $1334k.

The savings in question are put at $301k per year for 10 years, and it is the discounting of that stream of savings at the company's discount rate that produces the present value quoted above, the difference between that present value and the installed cost being, by definition, the net present value of the project.

A word of caution is nevertheless in order. The savings figures are not based on any measured performance: they are estimates provided by the vendor and by the utility, and no saving has as yet been measured on a comparable installation anywhere. The appraisal therefore stands or falls with the quality of those estimates, and should the savings actually achieved fall persistently short of the estimate, the net present value would fall correspondingly, a possibility that the appraisal itself does nothing to exclude. The recommendation to proceed accordingly rests on the estimates as they stand, and the first hard evidence will come from savings actually measured on a comparable line.
target:
The bottling line clears its appraisal. The net present value is $516k at a discount rate of 10%: the present value of the expected savings is $1850k, against an installed cost of $1334k.

The appraisal compares two amounts at one date: the cost falls at installation, and the savings arrive over the operating life that follows it. Discounting puts the later savings on the same footing as the present cost, and the surplus of the one amount over the other is the measure on which the decision rests.

The savings behind the appraisal are $301k per year for 10 years, discounted at the stated rate to the present value in the opening. The margin between the present value of the savings and the installed cost is the net present value, and it is positive on the figures as supplied.

The result rests on estimates, not measurements. The savings are vendor and utility estimates, and no saving has yet been measured on a comparable installation, so the evidence base for the finding is the estimates as supplied rather than operating data. A measured saving persistently below the estimate would reduce the net present value, and nothing in the appraisal rules that out. The appraisal supports proceeding on the estimates, and the first measured savings on a comparable line are the evidence that would confirm or overturn it.

fact_base: A review passage on adsorbents for gas drying, in four parts: scope, established results, disagreements, and gaps. The review covers 109 papers from the last 9 years. The disagreements part names the quantity on which reports conflict; the gaps part names the measurement nobody reports.
input:
## Scope

The present review surveys 109 papers published over the last 9 years dealing with adsorbents for gas drying, that is to say, with the removal of water vapour from a gas stream by means of a solid material which takes up the water and is subsequently regenerated so that the process can be repeated in a cyclic fashion. The adsorbents falling within the scope of the review are the silica gels, the activated aluminas, the zeolite molecular sieves, and, increasingly in recent years, a variety of newer porous solids that have been proposed for the same duty. The gases concerned include natural gas, air, and a range of process gases, and the duties extend all the way from relatively modest drying requirements to the extremely low residual water contents demanded by downstream operations such as liquefaction and low-temperature separation. It should be noted at the outset that virtually all of the work reviewed is cyclic in character: the bed adsorbs under one set of conditions and is regenerated under another, whether by heating, by depressurisation, or by purging with dry gas, and it follows that the performance of an adsorbent in this literature is as much a property of the cycle in which it is employed as it is of the material itself.

## Established results

On the broad directions of the principal effects there is, happily, little disagreement. The uptake of water by all of the adsorbents under consideration increases as the partial pressure of water vapour in the gas increases, and decreases as the temperature increases, which is why drying is carried out cold and regeneration is carried out either hot or at reduced pressure. Water is bound strongly at the hydrophilic sites of these materials, far more strongly than the carrier gas, and it is this preferential binding that makes the separation feasible in the first place; by the same token, however, it makes regeneration the energy-intensive step of the cycle, since the water that is most readily adsorbed is inevitably the water that is most difficult to drive off again.

The outline of breakthrough behaviour is equally well established. A bed continues to dry the gas to its outlet specification until such time as the adsorption front reaches the outlet end of the bed, whereupon the water content of the outlet gas rises sharply. The useful capacity of a bed is accordingly the capacity up to breakthrough rather than the equilibrium capacity of the material, and it is eroded by anything that broadens the front, including excessive velocity, maldistribution, and channeling. There is also general agreement that capacity is progressively lost over repeated cycling, owing to contamination of the bed by heavier components present in the gas, to damage caused by liquid water reaching materials that liquid water harms, and to the gradual degradation of the pore structure under repeated heating, and furthermore that this loss is most rapid during the early life of a bed.

## Disagreements

Where the literature becomes considerably less harmonious is in the region of low partial pressure, where reports are in conflict over the equilibrium water uptake, the very quantity that determines how dry a gas a given adsorbent is capable of delivering. Values published for what is nominally the same class of material, at nominally the same temperature, differ from one another by more than the differences between the materials themselves, and rankings of materials constructed from data in this region have a disconcerting habit of reversing from one paper to the next.

A good deal of this conflict appears to arise because the quantity is not, in fact, being measured on material in the same state. Different laboratories regenerate their adsorbents under different conditions before measurement, and a sample that goes into the measurement still carrying residual water will inevitably report a lower uptake than the same sample fully regenerated. Equilibration at low partial pressures is a slow business, and some of the values in the literature are in reality uptakes recorded after a fixed waiting period rather than true equilibrium values. The measurement techniques differ too: gravimetric determinations, uptakes inferred from breakthrough curves, and volumetric measurements do not interrogate the bed in the same state, and each has its own sensitivity to the temperature control on which low-pressure uptake so critically depends. The disagreement is therefore, at least in part, a disagreement about the state of the material being measured, and until preparation and equilibration are reported on a common basis, the values published in this region cannot meaningfully be ranked against one another.

## Gaps

Perhaps the most striking omission in this literature is a measurement that nobody seems to report at all, namely the water uptake retained after extended regeneration cycling. The papers characterise fresh material: they give the equilibrium uptake, the breakthrough capacity, and the behaviour over at most a modest handful of cycles. Yet the quantity that a design actually consumes is the capacity of the bed after it has been regenerated many times over, under genuine plant conditions, exposed to genuine plant gas with all of its contaminants and its full thermal history, precisely the conditions that the laboratory cycle leaves out.

This gap is far from academic, because the established results demonstrate that capacity declines with cycling, and declines fastest early on, which is exactly the territory that a long cycling record would illuminate. In the absence of retained-uptake data over extended cycling, a designer who sizes a bed on the basis of fresh capacity has no way of knowing whether the ageing margin he has allowed is generous or inadequate, and an operator has no way of telling from the literature when the drying performance of a bed will approach its limit. The missing measurement is not a difficult one; it is merely a long one. Until it is reported, the low-pressure disagreement also remains open in practice, since some part of the scatter between papers may well be attributable to the unreported cycling histories of the materials that were measured.

fact_base: Goal: compute the diffusive flux of oxygen through a stagnant water film. The diffusive flux J (mol m-2 s-1) is computed from the diffusivity D (m2 s-1) and the concentration gradient dC/dx, where C is concentration (mol m-3) and x is position (m). Fick's first law: J = -D dC/dx; the negative sign states that diffusion runs from high concentration to low concentration. Oxygen in water: D = 2.1 x 10-9 m2 s-1. Concentration falls by 0.4 mol m-3 across a film 0.4 mm thick, so dC/dx = -1000 mol m-4. Worked result: J = 2.10x 10-6 mol m-2 s-1. The law as stated covers a stagnant medium; a moving medium adds convection, which the equation does not include.
input:
Calculate the diffusive flux of oxygen through a stagnant water film. The film is 0.4 mm thick, and the oxygen concentration falls by 0.4 mol m-3 across it.

The diffusive flux $J$ (mol m-2 s-1) is computed from the diffusivity $D$ (m2 s-1) and the concentration gradient dC/dx, where $C$ denotes concentration (mol m-3) and $x$ denotes position (m). Fick's first law states the relation: J = -D dC/dx. The negative sign states that diffusion runs from high concentration to low concentration.

For oxygen in water, D = 2.1 x 10-9 m2 s-1. The concentration fall across the film gives dC/dx = -1000 mol m-4. Substitution gives J = -(2.1 x 10-9) x (-1000), and thus J = 2.10 x 10-6 mol m-2 s-1.

The sign of the result is the check on the calculation. The gradient is negative because concentration falls as $x$ increases, and the negative sign in Fick's first law returns a positive flux in the direction of increasing $x$, the direction from high concentration to low concentration. Fick's first law as stated holds for a stagnant medium. A moving medium adds convection, which the equation does not include; the value computed here is the diffusive flux alone, for the stated film and the stated concentration fall.

The diffusive flux $J$ (mol m-2 s-1) is computed from the diffusivity $D$ (m2 s-1) and the concentration gradient dC/dx, where $C$ denotes concentration (mol m-3) and $x$ denotes position (m). Fick's first law states the relation: J = -D dC/dx. The negative sign states that diffusion runs from high concentration to low concentration.

For oxygen in water, D = 2.1 x 10-9 m2 s-1. The concentration fall across the film gives dC/dx = -1000 mol m-4. Substitution gives J = -(2.1 x 10-9) x (-1000), and thus J = 2.10 x 10-6 mol m-2 s-1.

The sign of the result is the check on the calculation. The gradient is negative because concentration falls as $x$ increases, and the negative sign in Fick's first law returns a positive flux in the direction of increasing $x$, the direction from high concentration to low concentration. Fick's first law as stated holds for a stagnant medium. A moving medium adds convection, which the equation does not include; the value computed here is the diffusive flux alone, for the stated film and the stated concentration fall.

fact_base: Inventory policy for a spare motor: mean demand 785 units per week, standard deviation 179 units per week, replenishment lead time 8 weeks. Safety stock for a 95% cycle service level is 835 units. Demand is treated as normal and independent between weeks; seasonal peaks are excluded.
input:
For the spare motor, the established policy sets the safety stock at 835 units, determined to support a 95% cycle service level over a replenishment lead time of 8 weeks. The safety stock protects against variability in demand during the lead time, rather than covering average demand, which is handled separately.

The mean demand stands at 785 units per week, with a standard deviation of 179 units per week around that mean. Across the full 8 weeks of the lead time, the average demand comes to some 6280 units in total, and this average requirement is what the cycle stock is there to satisfy. The role of the safety stock, by contrast, is to absorb the fluctuation around that average, because in roughly half of all cycles actual demand runs above the mean, and the 835 units soak up that excess up to the specified service level. Bringing the two elements together, the reorder point works out at 7115 units, which is simply the lead-time demand combined with the safety stock, and ordering at this point should ensure that replenishment arrives in good time in most cycles.

Demand has been treated as normally distributed and as independent from one week to the next. The independence assumption is what allows the weekly variability to be combined across the lead time in the manner assumed; a pattern of linked heavy weeks would fall outside this treatment. Seasonal peaks have been excluded from the demand data behind the figure, so the 95% service level is a statement about the modelled demand only. In a peak season the same stock is drawn on under a demand pattern the figure does not describe, and the cover achieved will be lower than the headline level. The figure remains valid while the demand pattern behind it remains unchanged; a shift in mean demand, in weekly variability, or in the lead time would change the safety stock the service level requires, and the policy figure would then be recalculated from the new values.

fact_base: Excerpt content: a seal replacement takes about 45 min with the unit isolated; the excerpt gives the isolation steps only. The excerpt warns once about stored pressure and does not repeat the warning.
input:
Once the standby pump is in service and carrying the full flow, the duty pump is stopped from the local panel and left selected to hand, so that it cannot be restarted remotely. The discharge valve of the duty pump is closed first, then its suction valve, letting the motor-driven travel complete on each and then shutting both fully by hand to seat them properly. The section of pipework between the two closed valves, together with the pump casing itself, still holds stored pressure after isolation, and for this reason the drain on the casing is cracked open slowly, into the closed drain system, and left open until the flow from it has stopped. The vent at the high point of the casing is then opened and left open as well; if the casing is still blowing at the vent, it is still pressurised, and under no circumstances should any joint on the casing be touched until the vent has run quiet and the local pressure gauge is reading zero.

The casing is drained down fully, and the isolation is proved at the drain, because a drain that flows again after running dry shows that either the suction valve or the discharge valve is passing, in which case the isolation is made again with the second valve on that line before further work goes ahead. The lock and the tag are fitted to each of the closed valves under the PTW arrangements, and the isolation is entered in the isolation register against the duty pump. As a final proof, a start of the duty pump is attempted from the local panel with the isolation in force, and the pump must not turn at all. With the unit isolated and proved in this condition, the seal replacement itself takes about 45 min to complete. The gland follower is then slackened off evenly, a small amount on each stud in turn, with the drain left open underneath the seal housing, so that any liquid that is still held behind the follower will run away to the drain rather than over the hands of the fitter, and the follower is drawn back along the shaft

fact_base: A viscous liquid of viscosity $\mu$ = 0.001 Pa s flows laminarly through a tube of radius $R$ = 6 mm and length $L$ = 40 m. At a pressure drop $\Delta P$ of 7 kPa the volumetric flow $Q$ is 320.6 L h-1. The Hagen-Poiseuille equation assumes laminar, fully developed flow of a Newtonian liquid.
input:
In this worked example, the volumetric flow $Q$ is to be determined for a viscous liquid flowing through a long tube under a specified pressure drop. The tube in question has a radius $R$ of 6 mm and a length $L$ of 40 m, the liquid has a viscosity $\mu$ of 0.001 Pa s, and the pressure drop $\Delta P$ along the tube is 7 kPa. The relationship that connects these quantities is the Hagen-Poiseuille equation, which, it should be noted, rests on the assumptions of laminar, fully developed flow of a Newtonian liquid, and the flow in this case is understood to satisfy those assumptions.

$$Q = \frac{\pi R^4 \Delta P}{8 \mu L}$$

Substituting the values $R$ = 6 mm, $\Delta P$ = 7 kPa, $\mu$ = 0.001 Pa s and $L$ = 40 m into the equation gives the volumetric flow $Q$ as 320.6 L h-1. It is interesting to observe that the radius enters the equation raised to the fourth power, which means that the result is especially sensitive to the radius: a relatively small error in $R$ will shift $Q$ by more than a comparable relative error in any of the other quantities, and it is for this reason that the radius is the measurement that deserves to be checked first of all. The pressure drop, for its part, enters in direct proportion, so the flow that has been obtained here belongs specifically to the stated drop of 7 kPa and not to any other condition. Finally, it should be kept in mind that the computed value is a laminar-flow value from start to finish: the Hagen-Poiseuille equation is valid for laminar, fully developed flow of a Newtonian liquid, and a flow that departs from the laminar condition, or a liquid whose viscosity varies with shear, would fall outside the reach of the equation and of the result that has been derived from it here.
target:
The volumetric flow $Q$ is computed from the tube radius $R$ = 6 mm, the pressure drop $\Delta P$ = 7 kPa, the viscosity $\mu$ = 0.001 Pa s and the tube length $L$ = 40 m. The Hagen-Poiseuille equation assumes laminar, fully developed flow of a Newtonian liquid, and the flow in the tube meets those conditions.

$$Q = \frac{\pi R^4 \Delta P}{8 \mu L}$$

Substitution of $R$ = 6 mm, $\Delta P$ = 7 kPa, $\mu$ = 0.001 Pa s and $L$ = 40 m in the Hagen-Poiseuille equation gives $Q$ = 320.6 L h-1. The equation balances the pressure force along the tube against the viscous resistance of the liquid, and the substitution evaluates that balance for the stated tube and the stated liquid: every quantity in the equation is a property of the tube or of the liquid, and none of them is a property of the flow that results. The flow is stated in litres per hour, the unit of the duty as given, and it is the flow through the whole cross-section of the tube, not a velocity at any point of it. The fourth power of the radius is the term the result rests on: a small error in $R$ moves $Q$ more than the same relative error in any other quantity in the equation, and the radius is the measurement the calculation is checked against first. The value is the laminar value throughout: the Hagen-Poiseuille equation is valid for laminar, fully developed flow of a Newtonian liquid, and a flow that leaves the laminar condition, or a liquid whose viscosity changes with shear, falls outside the equation and outside the result computed from it.

fact_base: An operating-manual chapter for a pressure relief valve, in four sections: start-up, normal operation, alarms, and shutdown. The alarms section lists two alarms and the operator action for each; no other alarms are introduced. The chapter addresses the operator directly and uses imperative verbs for actions.
input:
Start-up

Before any pressure is admitted, it is essential to confirm that the relief valve fitted is the valve called for on the line list, installed with its inlet connected to the protected system and its discharge connected to the discharge line. The direction of flow marked on the valve body is read and checked against the run of the pipework. The inlet and discharge block valves are then opened fully and left secured open, in whatever manner the plant uses for valves that must not be closed in service. A relief valve with a closed block valve on either side protects nothing at all, and no start-up should proceed while either valve remains shut.

The discharge path must be proved clear first. The drain at the low point of the discharge line is opened, the line confirmed to be running free, and the drain closed again. The outlet is confirmed to discharge to its safe location, with the area around it clear of people and temporary equipment. A pressure gauge is fitted at the valve inlet, or the gauge already there is proved, and confirmed to read zero with the system depressurised and to be readable from the operating position.

The operator inspects the valve and its joints, looking for damage in transit or during fitting, for corrosion on the body and the discharge flange, for missing or slack bolts at the joints, and for the maker's cap or seal still in place on the adjusting screw. No gag, blank or clamp is to be fitted to the valve; a gagged valve is effectively a removed valve and is reported as such. Any shipping restraint found is removed.

Pressure is then admitted slowly, raised by the normal start-up route in stages, with the inlet gauge watched as it rises. At each stage the rise is stopped and the joints are walked: a leak at either flange is made good before the pressure is raised further. As the system approaches normal operating pressure, the operator listens at the valve. A valve that simmers or leaks at the seat below its set pressure is reported in the log; the start-up may continue only where the leak is small and the discharge side stays dry, and the valve is then entered for inspection at the next opportunity. At normal operating pressure the inlet reading is recorded in the log, the valve is recorded as in service, and the system is handed over to normal operation.

Normal operation

In normal operation the relief valve stays shut while the pressure in the protected system remains within its normal operating band. The valve opens when the pressure reaches its set pressure and reseats once the pressure has fallen again; between such events it performs no work and requires no handling. The valve is not operated by hand in service, and is never used to control pressure: pressure control belongs to the normal control route of the system, and the valve is protection against the failure of that route.

The inlet pressure gauge is read on each round and the reading entered in the log. A reading trending upward across a shift is reported to the supervisor while the pressure is still inside the normal band; the valve is not the instrument that reports such a trend, and to wait for the valve to lift is to wait too long. Each reading is compared with the normal band, and a gauge that disagrees with the system instruments is changed, with the disagreement recorded.

The valve itself is inspected on the same round. The operator looks for leakage at the body joints and the bonnet, and checks the discharge line downstream: a discharge line that is warm although the system has not lifted the valve, or a hiss at the valve outlet, indicates a valve passing at the seat. Any such sign is noted in the log with the inlet pressure at the time. The operator also confirms that both block valves are still fully open and secured, that the discharge path remains unobstructed, and that nothing has been stored against the valve or under the outlet.

The setting of the valve is not to be touched: spring, adjusting screw and every other part are left alone, and a gag is never fitted to stop a passing valve. Adjustment and internal repair are workshop activities, carried out with the valve removed under the shutdown procedure and tested before it returns. Corrosion, mechanical damage, a broken seal on the adjusting screw, or a valve known to have lifted is reported to the supervisor and entered in the log on the shift on which it is found. After any lift, the operator confirms that the valve has reseated, the discharge line is clear and dry at its drain, and the inlet pressure is back within the normal band; the lift, the recovery pressure, and the state of the valve are recorded in the log.

Alarms

High inlet pressure. This alarm shows that the pressure in the protected system has risen above its normal operating band and is moving toward the set pressure of the valve. The alarm is acknowledged and the inlet gauge at the valve read to confirm the system reading. The pressure is reduced by the normal operating means: the inflow to the protected system is cut, and any heating input is reduced through its normal control route. Throughout, both block valves of the relief valve are kept fully open; no action under this alarm closes a valve between the protected system and its relief valve. If the pressure still rises and the valve lifts, the valve is allowed to discharge: the operator stands clear of the outlet, keeps other people clear, and continues cutting the inflow until the pressure falls and the valve reseats. The alarm, the highest pressure reached, and the action taken are reported to the supervisor and entered in the log. A system that has lifted its relief valve is not returned to full operation until the cause of the rise has been found.

Relief valve discharging. This alarm shows flow in the discharge line, or a high temperature in the discharge line at the valve outlet, and means the valve is open or passing. The first step is to read the inlet pressure gauge. Where the inlet pressure stands at or above the set pressure, the event is treated under the high inlet pressure alarm and the inflow is cut. Where the inlet pressure stands inside the normal operating band, the valve is passing at its seat: it is left in service, neither block valve is closed while the system remains pressurised, and the valve is not gagged. The supervisor and the maintenance group are notified, and the alarm entered in the log with the inlet pressure and the state of the discharge line. Both are monitored for the rest of the shift, and a valve that begins to pass more heavily is reported again at once. The valve stays as the protection of the system until the system can be shut down, and its repair is planned for that shutdown.

Shutdown

The protected system is taken out of service by its normal route and the pressure allowed to fall. The inflow is cut, any heating input stopped, and the system vented through its normal vent path until the inlet gauge at the valve reads zero. The zero is proved at the vent point of the section: a section still blowing at the vent is still pressurised, and the relief valve on such a section is not touched. Throughout the depressurisation the relief valve remains in service with both block valves open, as the protection of the system while pressure remains in it.

Only when the section has been proved depressurised are the inlet and discharge block valves closed. The pipework between the block valves and the valve is drained through the low-point drain, and the trapped section vented at its high point until drain and vent run dry and quiet. The valve and its short pipe runs are now isolated and depressurised, and only in this state is the valve unbolted. It is removed under the permit arrangements for the work, its weight supported as the last bolts come out, and blanks are fitted to the open flanges before the work party leaves the area. The removal, the reason for it, and the state in which the valve left the site are entered in the log. The protected system is not returned to service without a tested relief valve fitted and the start-up section of this chapter carried out on it.
