fact_base: Goal: compute the Reynolds number for water in a pipe and state the flow regime. The Reynolds number Re (dimensionless) is computed from density rho (kg m-3), mean velocity v (m s-1), pipe diameter D (m) and dynamic viscosity mu (Pa s) by Re = rho v D / mu. Water at 293 K: rho = 998 kg m-3, mu = 1.00 x 10-3 Pa s. Pipe diameter D = 0.08 m; mean velocity v = 0.6 m s-1. Worked result: Re = 47900 (computed as 998 x 0.6 x 0.08 / 0.001). Flow is laminar below Re = 2300 and turbulent above Re = 4000; between the two values the regime is transitional and is not assigned by the number alone.
input:
The task in this worked example is to compute the Reynolds number for water flowing in a pipe and, on the basis of that number, to state the flow regime that applies. As will be seen, the result comes out at Re = 47900, which places the flow in the turbulent regime.

The Reynolds number Re (dimensionless) is computed from the density $\rho$ (kg m-3), the mean velocity $v$ (m s-1), the pipe diameter $D$ (m) and the dynamic viscosity $\mu$ (Pa s), according to the relation Re = rho v D / mu. For water at 293 K, the relevant property values are $\rho$ = 998 kg m-3 and $\mu$ = 1.00 x 10-3 Pa s. The pipe diameter $D$ is 0.08 m and the mean velocity $v$ is 0.6 m s-1.

Substituting these values into the relation gives Re = 998 x 0.6 x 0.08 / 0.001 = 47900. In order to assign the regime, the result is compared with the conventional limits: flow is laminar below Re = 2300 and turbulent above Re = 4000, while between the two values the regime is transitional in character and cannot be assigned by the number alone. The computed value stands well above the upper limit, squarely in the turbulent range, and the comparison itself serves as the check on the result: had the value fallen between the limits, the regime would have had to be left open, and had it fallen below the lower limit, the statement would have been reversed. The Reynolds number computed here rests on the mean velocity; the local velocity varies across the pipe, and no local value enters the calculation.

fact_base: 260 pumps run at the plant. Maintenance records for 12 months show 1114 h of unplanned downtime; bearing failures account for 46% of the downtime hours. In a vendor trial on a comparable unit, the sensors cut downtime by 23%; the figure is a vendor figure and was not measured at this plant. A pilot on 17 pumps costs $33k over three months. Spare-part lead times are unchanged by the sensors. The memo recommends the three-month pilot; the reliability engineering group owns the pilot and reports before the March capital review; the decision on full installation is held until the pilot results are reported.
input:

The 23% is, however, a vendor figure and was not measured at this plant; it shows what the sensors achieved on another unit, and the pilot would convert it into a figure meaningful for this one. Spare-part lead times are unchanged by the sensors, and no part of the case rests on faster repair.

fact_base: A gravity settler removes sand from a process stream. Design overflow rate is 0.51 m h-1 at a throughput of 150 m3 h-1, giving a plan area of 294 m2. The overflow-rate basis is a vendor rule for this solid; no settling test on the actual slurry has been run.
input:
The settler sized in this case has a plan area of 294 m2. The area is derived from the design overflow rate and the throughput, and it stands or falls with the overflow rate adopted.

The design overflow rate is 0.51 m h-1 at a throughput of 150 m3 h-1. The plan area follows from the throughput divided by the overflow rate, 150 / 0.51, which yields the stated 294 m2; the overflow rate is the sizing quantity, and the area is whatever the throughput requires at that rate. In operation, sand is removed by gravity settling across that area: the stream passes over the plan area at the design rate, and the sand that settles during the pass is drawn from the bottom of the unit while the clarified stream leaves over the outlet. A larger throughput at the same overflow rate would require the area in direct proportion, and a smaller overflow rate at the same throughput more area in inverse proportion; the stated area belongs to the stated pairing of rate and throughput and to no other.

The overflow rate rests on a vendor rule for this solid. No settling test on the actual slurry has been run, and the figure has not been checked against the behaviour of the sand in the actual stream: particle size distribution, concentration, and the liquid in which the sand is carried all enter a settling test, and none of them enters a vendor rule. The plan area of 294 m2 is therefore the area the vendor basis gives, and a settling test on the actual slurry is the measurement that would confirm or move it.

fact_base: Cost review of a regional delivery route: 771 km per trip at $1.95 per km, 373 trips per year. Annual transport cost is $561k. Costs are carrier invoices for the last 12 months; empty running is included in the trip count.
input:
The regional delivery route under review costs $561k per year. The figure is the invoiced cost of the route as it is currently run, derived from the trip distance, the carrier rate and the trip count.

Carrier invoices for the last 12 months give 771 km per trip at $1.95 per km and 373 trips per year. These three figures together produce the annual cost: the distance per trip and the rate per kilometre between them determine the cost of a single trip, and the trip count then determines how many times that cost is incurred over the course of the year. It should be noted that empty running is included in the trip count, which means that the annual figure in effect pays for the whole of the distance that the route runs, loaded and empty together; the cost of a loaded kilometre on this route is therefore higher than the bare rate per kilometre might suggest, precisely because the empty distance is carried inside one and the same total.

The $561k figure is best understood as a record of what the route actually cost over the period in question, computed on the basis of carrier invoices. It is not a benchmark, and it carries no comparison with anything else: nothing in the figure states what the route should cost, and a saving against it could only properly be claimed from a change in one of the three quantities of which it is composed, namely fewer kilometres per trip, a lower rate per kilometre, or fewer trips per year. Each of those changes amounts to a change to the route itself or to the contract under which it is run, and the annual figure will move only when one of them is actually made. For as long as the route, the rate and the trip count stand exactly as invoiced, the annual transport cost stands at $561k, and the review of the route is, in essence, a review of those three quantities and of nothing else.

fact_base: A continuous stirred-tank reactor runs a neutralisation that is first order in the limiting reactant. The rate constant is 0.273 min-1 at the operating temperature and the mean residence time is 61 min. Steady-state conversion for an ideal CSTR is 94.3%. The estimate assumes perfect mixing and constant density; tracer tests on the actual vessel have not been run.
input:
The steady-state conversion for the neutralisation that is carried out in the continuous stirred-tank reactor comes out at 94.3%. This figure is the ideal-CSTR value corresponding to the stated rate constant and residence time, and it should be understood as carrying with it all of the idealisations that are built into that particular model.

The reaction in question is first order in the limiting reactant. The rate constant is 0.273 min-1 at the operating temperature and the mean residence time is 61 min, and the two quantities enter into the conversion through their product: $k\tau$ = 0.273 x 61 = 16.65. For an ideal CSTR at steady state, the conversion is given by $X = \frac{k\tau}{1 + k\tau}$, where $X$ denotes the conversion and the denominator reflects the dilution of the reacting mixture by the material that is already present in the vessel. Substituting $k\tau$ = 16.65 into this relation gives $X$ = 94.3%. A product $k\tau$ of this magnitude stands well into the flat part of the relation: the conversion is high essentially because the residence time is long in comparison with the rate constant, and a moderate change in either quantity would move the result only slightly.

It is important to note the assumptions on which the estimate rests, namely perfect mixing and constant density. Tracer tests on the actual vessel have not in fact been run, which means that the mixing behaviour of the actual vessel remains unverified: the presence of dead zones or of short-circuiting in the vessel would cause part of the feed to pass through in less than the mean residence time, and would bring the actual conversion down below the ideal value. The 94.3% figure is therefore the conversion of the ideal reactor at the stated conditions, and should be presented as such; the actual vessel can only be measured against it once a tracer test, or a direct measurement at the outlet, has supplied the comparison that is needed.

It is worth being clear that this figure is the finished thickness, with the allowance already included; the pressure-resisting part of the wall is what is left once the allowance has been taken off, and the plate itself is ordered to the finished figure.

fact_base: A tutorial passage explains feedback control through a flow loop on a process vessel. The passage covers the sensor, the controller, the final element and the sign of the feedback, in that order. No tuning numbers are given; the passage explains structure, not settings.
input:
Feedback control, as applied to a flow loop on a process vessel, rests on four elements in a fixed order: the sensor, the controller, the final element, and the sign of the feedback that closes the loop. The structure of the loop, not its settings, is the subject.

The first element is the sensor, which measures the flow in the outlet line of the vessel. A flow element in the line produces a signal that varies with the flow passing through it, and a transmitter conveys that signal to the controller as the measured value of the flow.

The controller compares the measured flow with the set point, the flow at which the loop is to be held. The difference between the two is the error, and it is on the error that the controller acts: a measured flow below the set point calls for more flow, whereas a measured flow above it calls for less. The controller output is a signal rather than a flow; it specifies by how much the final element is to move, in the direction determined by the sign of the loop.

The final element is the control valve in the line. The valve receives the controller output and changes the flow itself: it opens to pass more flow and closes down to pass less. The valve is the only element that touches the process stream, and the correction reaches the vessel only through its movement.

Finally, the sign of the feedback is negative. A rise in the measured flow brings about an action that reduces the flow, while a fall brings about one that raises it; the loop opposes the change that called it into action, and that opposition holds the flow at the set point against disturbances in the line. Feedback of the opposite sign would reinforce a change and drive the flow away from the set point; a loop built with that sign would not control the flow at all.

fact_base: A food plant uses 1978 MWh of electricity per year in refrigeration. A heat-recovery retrofit is projected by the equipment vendor to save 14% of that use, a derived saving of 277 MWh per year at the vendor figure. Capital cost is $399k. At an electricity price of $0.11 per kWh, the derived annual saving is $30k and the derived simple payback is 13.3 years. The saving figure is a vendor projection and was not measured at this plant; refrigeration load in the summer peak month was not modelled. The recommendation is a metered trial on one of the three refrigeration lines before any capital decision. The plant engineer owns the trial.
input: A food plant currently uses 1978 MWh of electricity per year in refrigeration, and a heat-recovery retrofit has been proposed as a way to reduce that consumption. According to the equipment vendor's projections, the retrofit is expected to save 14% of the annual use, which corresponds to a derived saving of 277 MWh per year at the vendor figure. The capital cost of the installation is $399k. At an electricity price of $0.11 per kWh, the derived annual saving works out to $30k, giving a derived simple payback of 13.3 years. It is worth noting, however, that the saving figure is a vendor projection and was not measured at this plant, and refrigeration load in the summer peak month was not modelled. On balance, it would seem prudent to recommend a metered trial on one of the 3 refrigeration lines before any capital decision is taken, so that the projected performance can be validated under real operating conditions. The plant engineer owns the trial and will oversee its execution and reporting. A trial of this kind also has the advantage of isolating the retrofit's effect from everything else that influences refrigeration demand, such as changes in output or product mix, which a whole-plant comparison would inevitably mix together. Until metered evidence of that kind is available, the projected saving should be treated as an estimate rather than as a demonstrated result, and any decision should be framed accordingly.
target: The recommendation is a metered trial on one of the 3 refrigeration lines before any capital decision; the plant engineer owns the trial. The food plant uses 1978 MWh of electricity per year in refrigeration. A heat-recovery retrofit is projected by the equipment vendor to save 14% of that use. At the vendor figure, the saving is derived as 277 MWh per year. Capital cost is $399k. At an electricity price of $0.11 per kWh, the derived annual saving is $30k and the derived simple payback is 13.3 years. The saving figure is a vendor projection and was not measured at this plant. Refrigeration load in the summer peak month was not modelled, and the payback inherits that gap: the annual use is an average over the year, and a load concentrated in the peak month would change the hours over which recovered heat can be used. The trial meters one line through a full production cycle and compares metered use with the same line's earlier use at matched output. A capital decision taken before the trial would rest on the vendor figure alone. The trial result, not the projection, is the figure a capital case can use. Metering one line also separates the retrofit's effect from changes in production: output, product mix and ambient conditions all move refrigeration use, and a whole-plant comparison would gather those movements into the same figure. The trial's metered comparison holds them apart by following a single line at matched output. Until that comparison exists, the projected saving remains a vendor's estimate attached to a payback that the plant has not tested.

fact_base: A vapour-compression unit serves an ice rink, evaporating at 0 °C and condensing at 45 °C. The Carnot coefficient of performance between these temperatures is 6.07; the installed unit achieves 2.49. The achieved value is from the manufacturer's test at full load; part-load performance is not stated.
input: The vapour-compression unit in question serves an ice rink, evaporating at 0 °C and condensing at 45 °C. Between these two temperatures, the Carnot coefficient of performance is 6.07, which represents the theoretical maximum that any refrigerator operating between the same reservoirs could achieve. In practice, the installed unit achieves 2.49, a figure that comes from the manufacturer's test at full load; part-load performance is not stated. This difference illustrates the various irreversibilities that are inevitably present in real equipment, including losses in the compressor, in the expansion process, and in the heat exchangers themselves. It is also worth bearing in mind that, because the rink's load varies over the season, the full-load figure may not be representative of everyday operation, and overall efficiency in service could differ appreciably from the tested value. Figures of this kind are nevertheless useful, because they allow the machine's performance to be judged against the best that the temperature levels permit, rather than against an arbitrary standard. At the same time, the absence of part-load data means that any broader judgement about the unit's performance across a full season would go beyond what the available evidence can support, and such a judgement should be made only with that limitation clearly in mind.
target: A vapour-compression unit serves an ice rink, evaporating at 0 °C and condensing at 45 °C. The Carnot coefficient of performance between these temperatures is 6.07. The installed unit achieves 2.49. The achieved value is from the manufacturer's test at full load; part-load performance is not stated. The gap between the two values is the loss the cycle carries in compression, throttling and heat transfer: the Carnot value assumes reversible operation throughout, and the installed unit departs from that limit at each step. Because the achieved value holds at full load only, it does not describe the unit across a season in which the rink load varies. A comparison at part load would need test data the manufacturer has not given. The figures fix the unit's standing at the tested point: less than half of the reversible limit, with the untested range left open. The two temperatures fix the comparison: both values belong to the same pair of reservoirs, and the Carnot figure is the ceiling the pair sets. Any real machine working between the same reservoirs sits below that ceiling, because its processes depart from reversibility in ways the tested figure summarises but does not itemise. The manufacturer's test therefore gives the unit's position relative to the limit at the load where the test was run. It gives nothing about how that position changes as the load falls, and a seasonal judgement would need measurements the present statement does not contain.

fact_base: Pricing case for a contract cleaning service: price $83 per unit, variable cost $45 per unit, fixed costs $391k per year. Break-even volume is 10289 units per year; current volume is 7850 units per year. Volume figures are last year's actuals; the effect of the price on volume is not estimated.
input: This pricing case concerns a contract cleaning service. The service is priced at $83 per unit, while the variable cost is $45 per unit, and the fixed costs amount to $391k per year. Working through these figures, the break-even volume is 10289 units per year. Current volume, however, is only 7850 units per year, which means the service is presently operating below its break-even point. It should be noted that the volume figures are last year's actuals, so they may not fully reflect current trading conditions. Furthermore, the effect of the price on volume is not estimated, which is an important caveat: in practice, changing the price would be expected to change the volume sold, and that response is not captured anywhere in this analysis. Taken together, the figures suggest that the current pricing and cost structure leaves the service short of covering its fixed costs at recent volumes. For the time being, then, the case identifies a shortfall at recent volumes, while leaving open how it might best be closed, since the information needed to judge the effect of a price change is not available in the material presented here.
target: Break-even volume for the contract cleaning service is 10289 units per year; current volume is 7850 units per year. The service is priced at $83 per unit against a variable cost of $45 per unit, and fixed costs are $391k per year. At the current volume the service runs below break-even: each unit contributes the difference between price and variable cost toward the fixed costs, and the volume on hand does not cover them. The volume figures are last year's actuals. The effect of the price on volume is not estimated, and the break-even figure inherits that limit: a price change that moved volume would move the volume at which the service covers its costs, by an amount the present figures cannot give. On last year's volumes the gap is the distance between the two stated volumes, and closing it requires volume growth at the stated price or a change in the cost figures themselves. The statement is a position at stated prices and costs, not a forecast: volumes from a past year are set against a break-even computed from the same figures, and the distance between them is the finding. A decision on price would need the missing response of volume to price; a decision on costs would need figures the case does not give. Within the case as stated, the service's present volume does not carry its fixed costs, and that is the whole of what the figures establish.

fact_base: A defect-reduction project on a filling line cut the reject rate from 4.2% to 2% over one quarter. At 193k units per year the change avoids about 4246 rejected units per year. The quarter included a planned shutdown; rates are not adjusted for it.
input: A defect-reduction project was carried out on a filling line, and over the course of one quarter it succeeded in cutting the reject rate from 4.2% to 2%. At 193k units per year, this change avoids about 4246 rejected units per year, which represents a meaningful improvement in the line's performance. It is worth noting, however, that the quarter in question included a planned shutdown, and the rates are not adjusted for it. This means the comparison is not entirely clean: the shutdown may have influenced the measured rates in ways that have not been separated out, and the annual saving is calculated as though the quarterly rates applied across the whole year at the stated volume. Nevertheless, the direction of the change is clear, and the project demonstrates that sustained attention to reject rates can deliver substantial benefits in avoided waste over time. Even so, the reported change is substantial, and the project illustrates the value of measuring reject performance carefully before and after an intervention of this kind. Further monitoring over a longer period, ideally including quarters without interruptions, would help to establish whether the improved rate can be sustained in ordinary operation, and would give a much firmer basis for projecting the annual benefit with confidence.
target: A defect-reduction project on a filling line cut the reject rate from 4.2% to 2% over one quarter. At 193k units per year the change avoids about 4246 rejected units per year. The quarter included a planned shutdown; the rates are not adjusted for it. The avoided figure is computed on the annual volume at the two quarterly rates, and the shutdown sits inside that computation unadjusted: production lost to the shutdown is not separated from production over which the rates were measured. The comparison therefore states what the rate change is worth on a full year at the stated volume, with the shutdown's effect on the quarterly rates left unquantified. Whether the lower rate holds over a longer run is a separate measurement; the passage states the quarter's result and the annual figure derived from it, and nothing about later quarters. The rates themselves are the project's evidence: each was measured over the quarter on the line as it ran, and the rate change is the difference between them. Stating the annual figure on the annual volume converts a quarterly rate into an annual count, and the conversion assumes the quarter's rates stand for the year. That assumption is the limit the shutdown qualifies. A quarter without a shutdown, measured on the same line, would test whether the lower rate is the line's ordinary performance or partly an artefact of the stopped period. The project as reported does not separate those two readings, and the passage does not separate them either. What the passage states is the measured change and its annual equivalent at the stated volume, bounded by the shutdown that the quarter contained.

fact_base: A tutorial passage explains absolute and relative error through a pressure measurement. Worked figures: reading 261 units, tolerance 1% of reading, so the absolute error is 2.61 units. The passage distinguishes error from uncertainty and does not merge the two terms.
input: When a pressure measurement is made, the reading that is obtained is never perfectly exact, and it is helpful to have a clear vocabulary for describing how far it might be from the true value. The absolute error is the size of the difference between the reading and the actual value, expressed in the same units as the measurement itself. The relative error, by contrast, expresses that difference as a proportion of the reading, often as a percentage. For example, consider a pressure reading of 261 units with a tolerance of 1% of reading; the absolute error is then 2.61 units. It is important to distinguish error from uncertainty, two terms that are often used interchangeably in everyday speech. Error attaches to a particular reading, whereas uncertainty describes the range within which the value is believed to lie, taking into account all of the influences on the measurement. Keeping these concepts separate helps to avoid confusion when measurement quality is being discussed or specified. In practice, the distinction matters whenever a specification is written or a result is reported. If a figure described as an error is in fact an uncertainty, a reader may try to check it against a single reading and find that it does not reconcile; conversely, if an uncertainty is reported as though it were an error, the measurement may appear better characterised than it really is in practice. Careful usage therefore protects both the writer and the reader of measurement results, and it costs nothing beyond the discipline of choosing the right term.
target: A pressure reading carries an error as well as a value, and this passage sets out the two forms the error takes. Absolute error is defined as the size of the difference between the reading and the value it stands for, stated in the units of the measurement. Relative error is defined as the absolute error divided by the reading, stated as a fraction or a percentage of the reading. Take a pressure reading of 261 units with a tolerance of 1% of reading. The tolerance fixes the absolute error at 2.61 units. The relative error is the tolerance itself, because the tolerance was stated as a percentage of the reading. Error is not uncertainty. Error is the difference attached to a single reading; uncertainty is the range within which the value is placed when the measurement is reported, and it gathers every contribution the measurement carries, not the tolerance alone. Merging the two terms hides which quantity a figure states. A figure labelled as an error can be checked against a single reading and its tolerance; a figure labelled as an uncertainty cannot be reduced to that check, because it rests on the whole measurement, and the passage keeps the two apart throughout. The worked figures show the distinction in use. A tolerance stated as a percentage of the reading gives the relative error directly, and the absolute error follows from the reading it qualifies: change the reading and the absolute error changes with it, while the relative error stays where the tolerance put it. Neither figure says how the reading was obtained, what instrument carried it, or what else bears on it; those matters belong to the uncertainty of the measurement, which is stated separately when it is stated at all. Keeping the vocabulary apart keeps each figure answerable to its own check: the error to the reading and its tolerance, the uncertainty to the measurement as a whole.

fact_base: Goal: compute the half-life of a first-order reaction and the fraction remaining after 60 min. For a first-order reaction the rate constant k (min-1) fixes the half-life t1/2 (min) by t1/2 = ln(2) / k, and the fraction remaining after time t (min) is exp(-k t). Measured rate constant: k = 0.069 min-1 at 323 K, from concentration measurements every 5 min over 90 min. Worked results: t1/2 = 10 min; the fraction remaining after 60 min is 0.02 (dimensionless), both computed from the stated relations. The relations hold for a first-order reaction only; a reaction of another order follows a different decay law.
input: The goal of this worked example is to compute the half-life of a first-order reaction and the fraction remaining after 60 min. For a first-order reaction, the rate constant $k$ fixes the half-life through the relation in which the half-life equals the natural logarithm of two divided by $k$, and the fraction remaining after a time $t$ is given by exp(-−$k$ $t$). The measured rate constant is $k$ = 0.069 min⁻¹ at 323 K, obtained from concentration measurements taken every 5 min over 90 min. Working through the calculation, the half-life comes out at 10 min, and the fraction remaining after the stated time is 0.02, dimensionless. It should be remembered that these relations hold for a first-order reaction only; a reaction of another order follows a different decay law altogether, so the same formulas cannot simply be applied to other kinetic schemes. The results show how quickly the reactant is consumed under the stated conditions. It is also worth observing that the half-life of a first-order reaction does not depend on how much reactant is present at the start, which is one of the features that makes this case particularly instructive. The fraction remaining after any given time can likewise be obtained directly from the same exponential relation, provided that the time and the rate constant are expressed in consistent units. Students should nevertheless be careful not to carry these convenient properties over to reactions of other orders, where the half-life generally does depend on the starting concentration and the decay follows a different mathematical form altogether.
target: Calculate the half-life of a first-order reaction with rate constant $k$ = 0.069 min⁻¹ at 323 K, and the fraction remaining after 60 min. The rate constant was obtained from concentration measurements every 5 min over 90 min. For a first-order reaction, the half-life is the natural logarithm of two divided by $k$. Substitution of the stated rate constant gives a half-life of 10 min. The fraction remaining after a time $t$ is exp(-−$k$ $t$), with $k$ and $t$ in matching units. At the stated time the fraction remaining is 0.02, dimensionless. The check is the half-life count: the elapsed time is a whole number of half-lives, and repeated halving of the starting concentration reaches the stated fraction. The relations hold for a first-order reaction only; a reaction of another order follows a different decay law, and neither result transfers to it. The half-life is a property of the rate constant alone for this order: it does not depend on the starting concentration, and the fraction remaining at any stated time follows from the same relation. The measurement base matters to the result: the rate constant came from concentrations followed over a stated interval at stated spacing, and the half-life and the remaining fraction are computed from that constant, not measured directly. A rate constant from a different temperature would give different results, because the constant is a property of the reaction at the temperature of the measurement. The fraction remaining is stated without units because it is a ratio of concentrations, and the half-life carries the time unit of the rate constant. Both results are read off the same two relations, and the closing check ties them together: the time asked about is a multiple of the half-life, and the fraction is the value repeated halving predicts. The example's figures are therefore read as a pair: a time that characterises the decay, and a fraction that states its extent at the time asked about.

fact_base: Performance of a natural-draft tower at a chemical site was logged over one summer month. Mean wet-bulb temperature was 18 °C, the approach was 3 K and the range was 9 K. Performance outside the logged month, in particular at winter wet-bulb temperatures, was not measured.
input: The performance of a natural-draft tower at a chemical site was logged over one summer month. During that period, the mean wet-bulb temperature was 18 °C, the approach was 3 K, and the range was 9 K. The approach describes how close the leaving water temperature comes to the wet-bulb temperature, while the range describes the temperature fall the water experiences as it passes through the tower. Together, these figures give a useful picture of how the tower performed under the conditions that prevailed during the logging period. It is important to note, however, that performance outside the logged month was not measured, in particular at winter wet-bulb temperatures. Because a natural-draft tower depends on buoyancy-driven air flow, and because ambient conditions vary considerably between summer and winter, the summer results cannot simply be assumed to hold throughout the year. The choice of a summer month is itself relevant, since summer is when cooling duty is usually at its most demanding and when the wet-bulb temperature is at its highest. Performance recorded then represents the tower working under its most testing ambient conditions, although it cannot by itself reveal how the tower behaves across the rest of the year. Operators considering these results should therefore treat them as a characterisation of summer behaviour, and should be cautious about extrapolating them to the colder months, when both the heat load on the tower and the properties of the incoming air will be quite different in several respects. Results recorded in this way are most useful when they are read together with the conditions under which they were obtained, as this account sets out to do.
target: Performance of a natural-draft tower at a chemical site was logged over one summer month. Mean wet-bulb temperature was 18 °C, the approach was 3 K and the range was 9 K. The approach is the difference between the leaving water temperature and the wet-bulb temperature; the range is the fall in water temperature across the tower. The two figures describe different parts of the tower's duty: the approach states how closely the cooled water comes to the limit the air sets, and the range states the cooling the water undergoes. Performance outside the logged month was not measured, in particular at winter wet-bulb temperatures. A natural-draft tower's driving force depends on the density difference the heated air creates, and that difference changes with the season; the summer figures therefore do not describe winter operation. The logged month fixes the tower's standing under summer conditions, and no figure in the passage extends beyond it. The logged month is the whole of the evidence. Within it, the wet-bulb temperature is a mean, and the approach and range are stated as the tower's performance over the same period; the passage does not give daily extremes, and no figure here describes the hottest days of the month. The tower is a natural-draft unit, so its air flow is set by the buoyancy of the warmed air rather than by a fan, and its performance follows the weather more closely than a mechanical-draft tower's would. For that reason the season is not a detail of the record but a condition of the figures: the same tower at winter wet-bulb temperatures would draw air differently, cool the water against a different limit, and return figures that this record cannot supply. The passage therefore reports a summer standing, complete for the month logged and silent beyond it. Nothing in the record is carried over to those conditions.

fact_base: Pervaporation is a membrane separation in which a liquid feed contacts one side of a membrane and vacuum on the other side draws the permeating component through as vapour. Flux is the mass permeating per unit membrane area per hour (kg m-2 h-1). The separation factor is the water-to-alcohol ratio in the permeate divided by the same ratio in the feed (dimensionless). Feed: 85 wt% n-butanol in water, at 60 °C. One feed composition was tested; no test ran beyond 500 h. Polymer membrane: flux 2.1 kg m-2 h-1, separation factor 240, flux fell 7% over 500 h. Zeolite membrane: flux 1.2 kg m-2 h-1, separation factor 560, flux unchanged over 500 h within measurement error. Flux, selectivity and stability are seldom reported together for the same membrane.
input: Pervaporation is a membrane separation technique in which a liquid feed contacts one side of a membrane, while a vacuum applied on the other side draws the permeating component through as a vapour. Two quantities are commonly used to characterise performance. Flux is the mass permeating per unit membrane area per hour (kg m-2 h-1), and the separation factor is the water-to-alcohol ratio in the permeate divided by the same ratio in the feed, a dimensionless quantity. In the tests described here, the feed was 85 wt% n-butanol in water, at 60 °C. Only one feed composition was tested, and no test ran beyond 500 h. The polymer membrane achieved a flux of 2.1 kg m-2 h-1 with a separation factor of 240, although its flux fell 7% over 500 h. The zeolite membrane, by contrast, achieved a flux of 1.2 kg m-2 h-1 with a separation factor of 560, and its flux was unchanged over 500 h within measurement error. Flux, selectivity and stability are seldom reported together for the same membrane, which makes direct comparisons of this kind relatively uncommon. Results of this kind are valuable precisely because the three quantities are reported side by side for the same membranes under the same conditions. A membrane chosen on flux alone would look different from one chosen on selectivity or on stability, and in practice the operator's priorities will determine which of these matters most for a given duty. The comparison is nevertheless confined to the feed composition and the duration actually tested, and it should not be extended to other feeds or to longer campaigns without further evidence of the same kind.
target: Pervaporation is a membrane separation in which a liquid feed contacts one side of a membrane and vacuum on the other side draws the permeating component through as vapour. Flux is the mass permeating per unit membrane area per hour (kg m-2 h-1). The separation factor is the water-to-alcohol ratio in the permeate divided by the same ratio in the feed, and is dimensionless. The feed was 85 wt% n-butanol in water, at 60 °C. One feed composition was tested; no test ran beyond 500 h. The polymer membrane gave a flux of 2.1 kg m-2 h-1 and a separation factor of 240; its flux fell 7% over 500 h. The zeolite membrane gave a flux of 1.2 kg m-2 h-1 and a separation factor of 560; its flux was unchanged over 500 h within measurement error. The polymer membrane passes more mass and separates less; the zeolite membrane separates more and holds its flux. Flux, selectivity and stability are seldom reported together for the same membrane, and the comparison is limited to the one feed composition and the stated duration. The two membranes divide the reported quantities between them: the polymer leads on flux, the zeolite leads on separation factor and on stability. No single ranking follows from the figures without a weighting the abstract does not supply, because the quantities answer different questions: flux states the area a duty would need, the separation factor states the enrichment a pass achieves, and the change over the test states how long either figure can be relied on. The feed and the duration bound every figure in the comparison. A different feed composition would change the driving force across each membrane, and a longer test would extend the stability statement beyond the point where the present evidence stops. Within those bounds, the comparison states what each membrane did on the same feed over the same period. The abstract reports the two membranes on equal terms and leaves the choice between them to the duty.

fact_base: Pricing case for a contract cleaning service: price $77 per unit, variable cost $44 per unit, fixed costs $143k per year. Break-even volume is 4333 units per year; current volume is 2343 units per year. Volume figures are last year's actuals; the effect of the price on volume is not estimated.
input: The figures in this case describe a contract cleaning service and its current pricing position. The service is priced at $77 per unit, while the variable cost is $44 per unit, and the fixed costs amount to $143k per year. Working through these figures, the break-even volume is 4333 units per year. Current volume, however, is only 2343 units per year, which means the service is presently operating well below its break-even point. It should be noted that the volume figures are last year's actuals, so they may not fully reflect current trading conditions. Furthermore, the effect of the price on volume is not estimated, which is an important caveat: in practice, changing the price would be expected to change the volume sold, and that response is not captured anywhere in this analysis. Taken together, the figures suggest that the current pricing and cost structure leaves the service a long way short of covering its fixed costs. The position will therefore need attention, whether through higher volumes, lower costs, or some combination of the two, and the case provides a clear statement of the gap that any such response would have to address.
target: At 2343 units per year, current volume sits below the break-even volume of 4333 units per year. The service is priced at $77 per unit against a variable cost of $44 per unit, and fixed costs are $143k per year. At the current volume the service runs below break-even: each unit contributes the difference between price and variable cost toward the fixed costs, and the volume on hand covers less than the fixed costs require. The volume figures are last year's actuals. The effect of the price on volume is not estimated, and the break-even figure inherits that limit: a price change that moved volume would move the covering volume with it, by an amount the present figures cannot give. On last year's volumes the shortfall is the distance between the two stated volumes, and it stands as the gap the service has to close at the stated price and costs. The case as stated leaves the remedy open: the figures identify the shortfall but carry nothing that prices a response to it. Volume growth at the stated price, a lower fixed-cost base, or a lower variable cost would each move the position, and the case gives no basis for ranking those routes against one another. What the case settles is the present position on last year's volumes: the service does not cover its costs, and the distance to covering them is stated in full.

fact_base: A tutorial passage explains absolute and relative error through a flow measurement. Worked figures: reading 286 units, tolerance 0.5% of reading, so the absolute error is 1.43 units. The passage distinguishes error from uncertainty and does not merge the two terms.
input: A flow reading, like any measurement, is never perfectly exact, and a clear vocabulary helps in describing how far it might lie from the true value. The absolute error is the size of the difference between the reading and the actual value, expressed in the same units as the measurement itself. The relative error expresses that same difference as a proportion of the reading, often as a percentage. For example, consider a flow reading of 286 units with a tolerance of 0.5% of reading; the absolute error is then 1.43 units. It is important to distinguish error from uncertainty, two terms that are frequently used interchangeably in everyday speech. Error attaches to a particular reading, whereas uncertainty describes the range within which the value is believed to lie, taking into account all of the influences on the measurement. Keeping the concepts separate avoids confusion when measurement quality is discussed or specified in practice. Specifications and reports both depend on the distinction drawn here. If a figure described as an error is in fact an uncertainty, a reader may try to check it against a single reading and find that it does not reconcile; conversely, if an uncertainty is reported as though it were an error, the measurement may appear better characterised than it really is in practice. Careful usage therefore protects both the writer and the reader of measurement results, and it costs nothing beyond the discipline of choosing the right term for the quantity actually being reported in each case. The same care is needed wherever readings are recorded, compared, or passed on to others for use in their own work.
target: Absolute error is defined as the size of the difference between a flow reading and the value it stands for, stated in the units of the measurement. Relative error is defined as the absolute error divided by the reading, stated as a fraction or a percentage of the reading. Take a flow reading of 286 units with a tolerance of 0.5% of reading. The tolerance fixes the absolute error at 1.43 units. The relative error is the tolerance itself, because the tolerance was stated as a percentage of the reading. Error is not uncertainty. Error is the difference attached to a single reading; uncertainty is the range within which the value is placed when the measurement is reported, and it gathers every contribution the measurement carries, not the tolerance alone. A figure labelled as an error can be checked against one reading and its tolerance. A figure labelled as an uncertainty rests on the whole measurement and cannot be reduced to that check. The passage keeps the two terms apart, because merging them hides which quantity a reported figure states. The worked figures show the distinction in use. A tolerance stated as a percentage of the reading gives the relative error directly, and the absolute error follows from the reading it qualifies: change the reading and the absolute error changes with it, while the relative error stays where the tolerance put it. Neither figure says how the reading was obtained, what instrument carried it, or what else bears on it; those matters belong to the uncertainty of the measurement, which is stated separately when it is stated at all. A reported figure can therefore be read for exactly what it is: an error figure answers to the reading and its tolerance, and an uncertainty figure answers to the measurement as a whole, and the vocabulary used here keeps those two answers distinct throughout.

fact_base: A food plant uses 2365 MWh of electricity per year in refrigeration. A heat-recovery retrofit is projected by the equipment vendor to save 12% of that use, a derived saving of 284 MWh per year at the vendor figure. Capital cost is $514k. At an electricity price of $0.12 per kWh, the derived annual saving is $34k and the derived simple payback is 15.1 years. The saving figure is a vendor projection and was not measured at this plant; refrigeration load in the summer peak month was not modelled. The recommendation is a metered trial on one of the three refrigeration lines before any capital decision. The plant engineer owns the trial.
input: Refrigeration at a food plant uses 2365 MWh of electricity per year, and a heat-recovery retrofit has been put forward as a means of reducing that consumption. The equipment vendor projects that the retrofit would save 12% of the annual use, which corresponds to a derived saving of 284 MWh per year at the vendor figure. The capital cost is $514k. At an electricity price of $0.12 per kWh, the derived annual saving amounts to $34k, giving a derived simple payback of 15.1 years. It should be noted, however, that the saving figure is a vendor projection and was not measured at this plant, and refrigeration load in the summer peak month was not modelled. In light of these uncertainties, a metered trial on one of the 3 refrigeration lines is recommended before any capital decision is taken. The plant engineer owns the trial and will report its findings. The length of the payback underlines why a trial is attractive in this case: committing the full capital sum on the strength of a projection alone would expose the plant to a long recovery period if the saving turned out to be smaller than expected in practice. A metered trial, by contrast, tests the central assumption directly and at a fraction of the cost, and it produces evidence from the plant's own lines under the plant's own operating conditions, which is the evidence a capital decision of this kind ought properly to rest on.
target: Before any capital decision, a metered trial on one of the 3 refrigeration lines is recommended; the plant engineer owns the trial. The food plant uses 2365 MWh of electricity per year in refrigeration. A heat-recovery retrofit is projected by the equipment vendor to save 12% of that use. At the vendor figure, the saving is derived as 284 MWh per year. Capital cost is $514k. At an electricity price of $0.12 per kWh, the derived annual saving is $34k and the derived simple payback is 15.1 years. The saving figure is a vendor projection and was not measured at this plant. Refrigeration load in the summer peak month was not modelled, and the payback inherits that gap: the annual use averages the year, and a load concentrated in the peak month would change the hours over which recovered heat can be used. The trial meters one line through a full production cycle and compares metered use with the same line's earlier use at matched output. A capital case built on the projection alone would carry the vendor figure as its central number; the trial replaces that figure with a measured one. The payback is long at the stated price, and the trial is the step that tests whether the plant's own figure supports it. Metering a single line also separates the retrofit's effect from movements in output and product mix, which a whole-plant comparison would gather into one figure. A measured saving near the projection would give the capital case a plant figure in place of a vendor figure; a measured saving well below it would close the case at the trial's cost rather than the retrofit's, and either outcome is cheaper to learn before the capital is committed.

fact_base: Excerpt content: the analogy between the transfer processes is stated, then qualified by the case where it fails. The excerpt works one short numerical check with numbers given inside the excerpt itself. The excerpt assumes the chapter's earlier definitions and adds none.
input: ...the analogy can also be tested against the measurements from the packed bed, where the Reynolds number is 20000. Taking $f$ = 0.0064 from the pressure-drop measurements, the Chilton-Colburn analogy gives $j_D$ = $f$/2 = 0.0032, and this value is found to be in good agreement with the mass transfer measured in the bed, within the usual scatter of such data. Results of this kind are frequently cited in support of the analogy, because they suggest that the same surface processes govern both the friction and the transfer. It is important to recognise, however, that the agreement depends on the pattern of the flow. When the flow is directed across a surface rather than along it, form drag contributes to the pressure drop without contributing anything to the transfer at the surface, and the two quantities that the analogy equates are no longer measuring the same thing. Under those conditions, $f$ reflects both contributions whereas $j_D$ reflects only the transfer, so the analogy will tend to overstate the transfer, and the careful reader will treat values obtained in that geometry with some caution The point is worth emphasising because the failure is not random: it follows from the geometry, and it will appear whenever the flow is arranged in that way, whatever the fluid or the surface material may be....
target: ...where the analogy is applied to a packed bed at a Reynolds number of 20000, the comparison runs as follows. With $f$ = 0.0064 from the pressure-drop measurements, the Chilton-Colburn analogy gives $j_D$ = $f$/2 = 0.0032, and the measured mass transfer agrees with the stated value within the scatter of the bed data. Agreement of that kind is the ground on which the analogy is used for beds of this packing: at the surface, the same exchange sets both the friction and the transfer, and the two factors state it in the same terms. The agreement does not survive a change in the flow pattern. Where the flow meets a surface across its direction, form drag adds a part of the pressure drop that has no counterpart in the transfer at the surface, and the two sides of the analogy separate. In that case $f$ gathers both parts while $j_D$ gathers only the transfer part, and equating them overstates the transfer by the form-drag share. The distinction is one of mechanism: friction at a surface and transfer at the same surface share the near-surface exchange, while form drag arises from the pressure field around the body and has no share in that exchange. That is why the failure is systematic rather than scattered: the analogy does not merely lose accuracy, it assigns to transfer a part of the drop that belongs elsewhere. The analogy is therefore applied where the flow runs along the surface, and a bed or bundle in cross-flow is treated on its own measurements rather than on the analogy's value...

fact_base: A flat stainless steel wall of thickness 12 mm separates two process streams. Thermal conductivity of the wall is 16 W m-1 K-1 and the measured temperature difference across it is 325 K. Steady one-dimensional conduction gives a heat flux of 433333 W m-2. Surface (film) resistances are excluded from this estimate; including them lowers the flux.
input: A flat stainless steel wall with a thickness of 12 mm separates two process streams, and the goal here is to estimate the heat flux passing through it. The thermal conductivity of the wall material is 16 W m⁻¹ K⁻¹, while the measured temperature difference across the wall is 325 K. Under conditions of steady, one-dimensional conduction, the heat flux through a plane wall increases in proportion to the temperature difference and decreases in inverse proportion to the thickness of the wall, and applying this relationship to the values given yields a heat flux of 433333 W m⁻². It is important to note that this estimate deliberately excludes the surface, or film, resistances on either side of the wall. Because those resistances would act in series with the resistance of the metal itself, including them would lower the overall flux, since a portion of the temperature difference would then be consumed across the fluid films instead of across the wall. The figure should therefore be understood as the value for conduction through the metal alone, under the simplifying assumptions of a linear temperature profile, constant conductivity, and negligible edge losses and contact resistance at the faces of the wall.
target:
Calculate the heat flux through a flat stainless steel wall of thickness 12 mm that separates two process streams. The wall has thermal conductivity 16 W m⁻¹ K⁻¹, and the measured temperature difference across the wall is 325 K. Steady one-dimensional conduction through a plane wall gives a heat flux proportional to the temperature difference and inversely proportional to the thickness; for a thin metal wall the temperature profile is taken as linear, and the flux is uniform over the wall area. Substitution of the stated values gives a heat flux of 433333 W m⁻².

The estimate excludes surface (film) resistances on the two faces of the wall. Film resistances act in series with the conduction resistance, and including them lowers the flux, because part of the temperature difference then falls across the fluid films rather than across the metal. The stated flux is the conduction-only value for the wall itself, and a figure for the stream-to-stream transfer would sit below it by an amount set by the two film coefficients, which the estimate does not use. The calculation treats the conductivity as constant over the temperature range of the wall; a conductivity that varies with temperature would change the profile from linear to curved and would change the flux at the same terminal temperatures. Heat loss through the edges of the wall is neglected, as is any contact resistance at the faces.

fact_base: Performance of a natural-draft tower at a chemical site was logged over one summer month. Mean wet-bulb temperature was 27 °C, the approach was 4 K and the range was 5 K. Performance outside the logged month, in particular at winter wet-bulb temperatures, was not measured.
input:
Over the course of one summer month, the performance of a natural-draft cooling tower located at a chemical site was carefully logged. During this period, the mean wet-bulb temperature was 27 °C. The approach, which is essentially the difference between the temperature of the water leaving the tower and the wet-bulb temperature, came to 4 K, which means that the leaving water temperature was 31 °C. The range, which describes the fall in water temperature as the water passes through the tower, was 5 K, so the entering water temperature was 36 °C.

It is worth noting that a natural-draft tower has no fan: instead, air is drawn through the fill purely by buoyancy, because the air inside the tower becomes warmer, more humid and therefore less dense than the air outside, and the considerable height of the tower turns this density difference into a driving pressure. As a result, the performance of the tower is closely tied to the weather, and in particular to the wet-bulb temperature of the ambient air. The approach shows how close the tower came to the wet-bulb limit, while the range shows how much cooling each unit of circulating water received during the month that was actually observed.

Importantly, performance outside the logged month was not measured at all. In winter, when wet-bulb temperatures are much lower, the driving force, the air flow and the water-side behaviour would all be different, and icing at the air inlet could become an issue, so the summer figures should not be extrapolated to winter conditions or treated as a year-round characterisation of the tower.
target:
Performance of a natural-draft cooling tower at a chemical site was logged over one summer month. The mean wet-bulb temperature over the month was 27 °C. The approach, the difference between the leaving water temperature and the wet-bulb temperature, was 4 K, and the leaving water temperature was therefore 31 °C. The range, the fall in water temperature across the tower, was 5 K, and the entering water temperature was 36 °C.

A natural-draft tower has no fan. Air moves through the fill because the air inside the tower, warmed and humidified by the water, is less dense than the air outside, and the height of the tower converts that density difference into a driving pressure. The air flow the tower can draw is set by the weather and by the heat load together, and the water temperatures the tower reaches follow the wet-bulb temperature of the entering air. The approach is the margin the tower holds above that limit: no cooling tower can cool water below the wet-bulb temperature, and the approach states how close the leaving water came to it during the logged month. The range states the cooling done to each unit of water circulated, and with the circulation rate it fixes the heat the tower rejected.

The logged month is a summer month, and the record describes summer operation. Performance outside the logged month was not measured. At winter wet-bulb temperatures the driving force, the air flow and the water-side behaviour all change, and the tower may also face icing at the air inlet, a condition the summer record does not cover. No winter approach or range is stated, and none is inferred from the summer figures. The record supports statements about the tower at the wet-bulb temperatures and loadings of the logged month; a design or guarantee figure for the year would need measurements across the seasons the tower is required to serve.

fact_base: A tutorial passage explains feedback control through a level loop on a process vessel. The passage covers the sensor, the controller, the final element and the sign of the feedback, in that order. No tuning numbers are given; the passage explains structure, not settings.
input:
Feedback control is an approach in which a process variable is held at a desired set value by continuously measuring the variable and then adjusting a flow in response to that measurement. In a level loop on a process vessel, the variable of interest is the liquid level, and the loop passes through the sensor, the controller and the final element, with the sign of the feedback determining how the loop behaves.

The sensor measures the level in the vessel and converts that measurement into a signal that can be used by the rest of the loop. The measurement must genuinely represent the level in the part of the vessel the control is responsible for, and it must move when the level moves; if the sensor reads a stagnant tapping or a coated probe, it reports a level that the vessel does not really have, and every other part of the loop then acts on that false value.

The controller receives the measurement and compares it with the set value. The difference between the measurement and the set value is the error, and the controller forms its output from the error, indicating how much correction is required and in which direction. The controller itself does not move anything in the process; its output is an instruction passed to the final element.

The final element carries out the instruction. In a level loop, the final element is commonly a control valve on the outlet line or on the inlet line, and it changes the flow through the vessel, which in turn changes the rate at which the level rises or falls. The level itself responds through the inventory in the vessel, because any flow imbalance integrates into a change in level.

Finally, the sign of the feedback is negative in a properly working level loop. When the level is above the set value, the loop produces an action that brings the level down, and when the level is below the set value, it produces an action that raises it, so the response always opposes the disturbance that created it. With the opposite sign, a rising level would trigger action that raises the level even further, and the loop would drive the vessel either to empty or to overflow.
target:
Feedback control holds a process variable at a set value by measuring the variable and adjusting a flow in response to the measurement. In a level loop on a process vessel, the variable is the liquid level, and the loop runs through the sensor, the controller and the final element, with the sign of the feedback closing the loop.

The sensor measures the level in the vessel and turns the measurement into a signal. The measurement must represent the level in the part of the vessel the control is responsible for, and it must move when the level moves; a sensor that reads a stagnant tapping or a coated probe reports a level the vessel does not have, and every later part of the loop then acts on a false value.

The controller receives the measurement and compares it with the set value. The difference between the two is the error, and the controller forms its output from the error: the output states how much correction the loop calls for, and in which direction. The controller itself moves nothing in the process; its output is an instruction to the final element.

The final element carries out the instruction. In a level loop the final element is commonly a control valve on the outlet line or on the inlet line, and it changes the flow through the vessel, which changes the rate at which the level rises or falls. The level responds through the inventory in the vessel: a flow imbalance integrates into a level change, and the loop acts on that change through the sensor.

The sign of the feedback is negative in a working level loop. A level above the set value produces an action that brings the level down, and a level below the set value produces an action that raises it; the response opposes the disturbance that created it. With the opposite sign, a rising level would call for action that raises the level further, and the loop would drive the vessel to empty or to overflow.

fact_base: Goal: compute the diffusive flux of oxygen through a stagnant water film. The diffusive flux J (mol m-2 s-1) is computed from the diffusivity D (m2 s-1) and the concentration gradient dC/dx, where C is concentration (mol m-3) and x is position (m). Fick's first law: J = -D dC/dx; the negative sign states that diffusion runs from high concentration to low concentration. Oxygen in water: D = 2.1 x 10-9 m2 s-1. Concentration falls by 0.25 mol m-3 across a film 0.8 mm thick, so dC/dx = -312 mol m-4. Worked result: J = 6.56x 10-7 mol m-2 s-1. The law as stated covers a stagnant medium; a moving medium adds convection, which the equation does not include.
input: The goal of this worked example is to compute the diffusive flux of oxygen through a stagnant water film. The diffusive flux $J$ (mol m⁻² s⁻¹) is computed from the diffusivity $D$ (m² s⁻¹) and the concentration gradient d$C$/d$x$, where $C$ is the concentration (mol m⁻³) and $x$ is the position (m). Fick's first law states that $J$ = −$D$ d$C$/d$x$, and the negative sign indicates that diffusion runs from regions of high concentration to regions of low concentration. For oxygen in water, $D$ = 2.1 × 10⁻⁹ m² s⁻¹. The concentration falls by 0.25 mol m⁻³ across a film that is 0.8 mm thick, which gives d$C$/d$x$ = −312 mol m⁻⁴. Substituting these values into the law gives a worked result of $J$ = 6.56 × 10⁻⁷ mol m⁻² s⁻¹. It is important to note that the law as stated here covers a stagnant medium only; in a moving medium, convection would also be present, and the equation as written does not include that contribution, so the total flux in a moving medium would be higher wherever the flow runs in the direction of the gradient. The film is assumed to be stagnant throughout, and the diffusivity is treated as constant across it, so a single gradient describes the whole film from one face to the other.

The negative sign states that diffusion runs from high concentration to low concentration. For oxygen in water, $D$ = 2.1 × 10⁻⁹ m² s⁻¹. The concentration falls by 0.25 mol m⁻³ across a film 0.8 mm thick, thus d$C$/d$x$ = −312 mol m⁻⁴. Substitution gives $J$ = 6.56 × 10⁻⁷ mol m⁻² s⁻¹.

The gradient is the concentration fall divided by the film thickness, and its negative sign records that concentration decreases as position increases across the film. The film is treated as stagnant and the diffusivity as constant across it, so the gradient is uniform and the flux is the same at every plane in the film. As a check, the flux falls to zero when the gradient falls to zero, and it doubles when the gradient doubles; the linear form of Fick's first law gives both behaviours. Fick's first law as stated holds for a stagnant medium; a moving medium adds convection, which the equation does not include, and the flux then exceeds the diffusive value wherever the flow runs in the direction of the gradient.

fact_base: A gravity settler removes activated sludge from a process stream. Design overflow rate is 0.94 m h-1 at a throughput of 139 m3 h-1, giving a plan area of 148 m2. The overflow-rate basis is a vendor rule for this solid; no settling test on the actual slurry has been run.
input:
A gravity settler removes activated sludge from a process stream. The design overflow rate is 0.94 m h⁻¹ at a throughput of 139 m³ h⁻¹, giving a plan area of 148 m². The overflow rate is the throughput divided by the plan area, and the area follows from the rate the design adopts: a solid that settles at the overflow rate is removed, and a solid that settles more slowly leaves with the clarified stream. The sizing therefore rests on the overflow rate, and the overflow rate rests on the settling behaviour of the sludge.

The settler separates by density difference under gravity, with the feed introduced so that the upward velocity of the liquid stays below the settling velocity of the flocs to be removed. Residence time, inlet distribution and sludge withdrawal all bear on performance, but none enters the area figure, which the overflow-rate method fixes from the throughput alone.

The basis used here is a vendor rule for this solid. No settling test on the actual slurry has been run, so the rate has not been checked against the material the settler will treat; a slurry whose flocs settle more slowly than the vendor rule assumes would need a larger area at the same throughput, and the stated area holds only as long as the vendor rule describes the actual sludge.
