fact_base: 260 pumps run at the plant. Maintenance records for 12 months show 1356 h of unplanned downtime; bearing failures account for 51% of the downtime hours. A sensor set for all 260 pumps is quoted at $449k installed, plus $60k per year. In a vendor trial on a comparable unit, the sensors cut downtime by 28%; the figure is a vendor figure and was not measured at this plant. A pilot on 19 pumps costs $32k over three months. Spare-part lead times are unchanged by the sensors. The memo recommends the three-month pilot; the reliability engineering group owns the pilot and reports before the March capital review; the decision on full installation is held until the pilot results are reported.
input: This memo considers the question of whether maintenance sensors should be installed on the pumps at the plant, where 260 pumps are currently in operation. Maintenance records covering a period of 12 months show a total of 1356 h of unplanned downtime, and a closer look at those records reveals that bearing failures account for 51% of the downtime hours, which suggests that bearing condition is a particularly important part of the overall picture. A sensor set covering all 260 pumps has been quoted at $449k installed, together with a further $60k per year. In a vendor trial carried out on a comparable unit, the sensors were reported to cut downtime by 28%, although it should be noted that this figure is a vendor figure and was not measured at this plant. As an alternative to immediate full installation, a pilot on 19 pumps would cost $32k over three months. It should also be noted that spare-part lead times are unchanged by the sensors. By comparison, full installation would commit $449k immediately, plus a further $60k per year, in return for a downtime reduction that has not yet been demonstrated at this plant. On balance, this memo recommends the three-month pilot; the reliability engineering group owns the pilot and will report before the March capital review, and the decision on full installation is held until the pilot results have been reported and considered.
target:
The reliability engineering group should run the three-month pilot of the maintenance sensors on 19 pumps, and report before the March capital review; the decision on full installation is held until the pilot results are reported.

Maintenance records for 12 months show 1356 h of unplanned downtime across the 260 pumps at the plant, and bearing failures account for 51% of the downtime hours. A sensor set for all 260 pumps is quoted at $449k installed, plus $60k per year. In a vendor trial on a comparable unit the sensors cut downtime by 28%; the figure is a vendor figure and was not measured at this plant. The pilot costs $32k over three months, against a full installation at $449k plus $60k per year whose downtime saving at this plant is unmeasured. Spare-part lead times are unchanged by the sensors, and the pilot does not alter them.

The pilot pumps are drawn from the population that produced the recorded downtime, so the trial measures the failure modes the records identify rather than a selected subset. Bearing failures dominate the downtime hours, and bearing condition is what the sensors monitor; the pilot therefore tests the sensors against the plant's largest downtime source. The report to the capital review states the downtime change on the pilot pumps over the trial, the false-alarm rate the maintenance crews worked under, and any downtime the sensors themselves caused. The pilot tests the vendor figure on plant equipment and plant failure history; the full-installation decision takes the pilot's measured downtime change as its evidence.

fact_base: Pervaporation is a membrane separation in which a liquid feed contacts one side of a membrane and vacuum on the other side draws the permeating component through as vapour. Flux is the mass permeating per unit membrane area per hour (kg m-2 h-1). The separation factor is the water-to-alcohol ratio in the permeate divided by the same ratio in the feed (dimensionless). Feed: 85 wt% isopropanol in water, at 60 °C. One feed composition was tested; no test ran beyond 500 h. Polymer membrane: flux 2 kg m-2 h-1, separation factor 180, flux fell 6% over 500 h. Zeolite membrane: flux 1.1 kg m-2 h-1, separation factor 560, flux unchanged over 500 h within measurement error. Flux, selectivity and stability are seldom reported together for the same membrane.
input: Pervaporation is a membrane separation process in which a liquid feed is placed in contact with one side of a membrane, while a vacuum applied on the other side draws the permeating component through the membrane as a vapour. In this context, flux refers to the mass permeating per unit membrane area per hour (kg m⁻² h⁻¹), and the separation factor is defined as the water-to-alcohol ratio in the permeate divided by the same ratio in the feed, and is therefore dimensionless. In the work described here, two membranes were compared using a feed of 85 wt% isopropanol in water at 60 °C. The polymer membrane achieved a flux of 2 kg m⁻² h⁻¹ with a separation factor of 180, although its flux fell by 6% over 500 h. The zeolite membrane, by contrast, achieved a flux of 1.1 kg m⁻² h⁻¹ with a separation factor of 560, and its flux remained unchanged over 500 h within measurement error. It is worth noting that only one feed composition was tested, and no test ran beyond 500 h. The figures for the two membranes were obtained on the same feed, and the stability figures cover the same test duration for each membrane, so the comparison between them is a direct one. Overall, flux, selectivity and stability are seldom reported together for the same membrane, which makes comparisons of this kind less complete than they might otherwise be.
target:
Pervaporation separates a liquid mixture through a membrane: the liquid feed contacts one side of the membrane, and vacuum on the other side draws the permeating component through as vapour. Flux denotes the mass permeating per unit membrane area per hour (kg m⁻² h⁻¹), and the separation factor denotes the water-to-alcohol ratio in the permeate divided by the same ratio in the feed. A polymer membrane and a zeolite membrane were compared on a feed of 85 wt% isopropanol in water at 60 °C, both run under the same arrangement, so the comparison is between the membrane materials and not between test conditions.

The polymer membrane gave a flux of 2 kg m⁻² h⁻¹ and a separation factor of 180, and its flux fell 6% over 500 h. The zeolite membrane gave a flux of 1.1 kg m⁻² h⁻¹ and a separation factor of 560, and its flux was unchanged over 500 h within measurement error. The zeolite membrane is the more selective and the more stable of the two; the polymer membrane passes more mass per unit area. The ranking by flux and the ranking by separation factor run in opposite directions, and a selection between the membranes turns on which quantity the separation duty values.

Each membrane's figures were obtained on that feed, and the stability figures cover the same test duration for both membranes. One feed composition was tested, and no test ran beyond 500 h; flux, selectivity and stability are seldom reported together for the same membrane, and the comparison states all three for these two membranes at the tested composition.

fact_base: Energy assessment of a brewery, in four sections: current use, refrigeration, steam, and recommendation. Electricity use is 3690 MWh per year; refrigeration takes the largest share. A heat-recovery retrofit is projected to save 18% of electricity use, a derived saving of 664 MWh per year, at a capital cost of $166k. At $0.12 per kWh the derived annual saving is $79704 and the derived simple payback is 2.1 years. Steam figures are from one winter month and are flagged as seasonal in the recommendation.
input:
Current use

Electricity use at the brewery comes to 3690 MWh per year. Of this total, refrigeration accounts for the largest share, ahead of packaging, the brewhouse, compressed air and the general services of the site. The annual figure is simply the sum of the metered supplies to the site, and it forms the base against which all of the savings discussed in this assessment are measured. Broadly speaking, electricity serves two kinds of duty in a brewery. The first is direct process duty, covering drives for pumps, mills, conveyors and packaging machinery, together with the air compressors that supply instrument and process air. The second is thermal duty delivered electrically, most notably refrigeration, where electricity is used to move heat rather than to make it. This distinction is important, because the measures that reduce the two kinds of duty are quite different: drive duty can be reduced through motor efficiency, scheduling and the elimination of idle running, whereas refrigeration duty responds to temperature settings, heat ingress and the recovery of the heat that the refrigeration plant rejects. It is also worth noting that use is not level throughout the year, since production campaigns concentrate brewing and packaging into part of the year and refrigeration load rises with ambient temperature, so the annual figure is really an average over peaks and quieter periods.

Refrigeration

Refrigeration is the largest single user of electricity at the brewery. Its duties include fermentation temperature control, the cooling of wort after the boil, cold storage of finished product, and the cooling of the glycol and water circuits that serve the cellar and the packaging hall. Fermentation releases heat as the yeast works, and the temperature of each vessel has to be held within a narrow band by removing that heat as it appears, so the load tends to follow the brewing programme rather than the weather alone, although warmer weather does add heat leakage into every cold space and raises the temperature at which the plant must reject its heat. All of the heat collected by the refrigeration system is ultimately rejected at its condensers, and this rejected heat is the largest low-temperature heat stream on the site. Where a suitable use exists for heat at or below the condensing temperature — for example, preheating water for cleaning or for the brewhouse — recovering heat from the condenser circuit can displace fuel or electricity that would otherwise be needed for the same duty, and it is on this recovery that the retrofit considered here is based. In addition, refrigeration settings themselves offer savings that require no capital at all: pressures set by habit rather than by duty, cold-room doors and insulation in poor repair, and defrost cycles run on a timer rather than on need all increase the electricity consumed per unit of cooling, and all of them can be corrected through normal maintenance.

Steam

Steam serves the thermal duties of the brewhouse and the packaging line, including mashing and wort boiling, pasteurisation, keg and bottle washing, and cleaning in place of vessels and pipework. Steam is raised in the site boiler house and distributed to the various duties, and the losses of the system are found in distribution, in condensate that is not returned, and in the standing losses of plant that is kept hot against intermittent use. The steam figures used in this assessment are taken from one winter month. A winter month, however, carries the space-heating load of the buildings and the highest heat losses from distribution, and it does not include the production peak of the brewing season, so it cannot be regarded as a representative sample of the year. As a result, steam use per unit of production, boiler efficiency across the year, and the value of condensate return in other seasons cannot be derived from a single winter month, and no annual steam figure is stated. What the month does show is the pattern of the duties: which users take steam continuously, which take it in batches, and where the standing losses occur. Measures such as condensate return, insulation repair and the scheduling of batch duties are identified by that pattern, but their savings are not quantified here, and a project on the steam system would need metering over a full production cycle before its case could be stated in money terms.

Recommendation

A heat-recovery retrofit is projected to save 18% of electricity use, which corresponds to a derived saving of 664 MWh per year, at a capital cost of $166k. At $0.12 per kWh, the derived annual saving is $79704, and the derived simple payback is 2.1 years. The retrofit would recover heat from the refrigeration condensers into the water services that currently draw on the steam system and on direct heating, and its saving falls on the electricity account because recovered heat displaces heated duty identified in the current-use survey and because the refrigeration plant rejects its heat more cheaply when part of that heat is drawn off usefully. It should be noted that the payback is a simple payback: it is obtained by dividing the capital cost by the annual saving, and it takes no account of maintenance, of the life of the equipment, or of possible changes in the electricity price, so it should be read as a screening figure rather than as a full investment appraisal. The recommendation is that the retrofit should proceed to detailed design, at which stage the condenser tie-ins, the water temperatures that each duty can accept, and the controls needed to keep refrigeration stable while heat is drawn off can be fixed and priced. The steam figures behind this assessment are from one winter month and are seasonal, so no steam saving is claimed in the recommendation, and the steam measures identified earlier stand as work whose value remains unquantified until steam metering covers a production cycle.

subtype: worked example with equation: first-order decay
fact_base: A peroxide initiator decomposes by first-order kinetics with rate constant $k$ = 0.142 min-1. After 116 min the fraction remaining $C / C_0$ is 0. The rate constant was measured at one temperature; no activation energy is available.
input:
A peroxide initiator decomposes according to first-order kinetics, with a rate constant $k$ of 0.142 min⁻¹. For a first-order process, the fraction of the initiator remaining after a given time can be described by the following relationship:

$$\ln\frac{C}{C_0} = -k t$$

In this expression, the fraction remaining is the concentration at time $t$ expressed relative to the initial concentration, and $k$ is the rate constant. After 116 min, the fraction remaining works out to 0, which essentially means that, at the precision with which the value is stated, the decomposition is effectively complete. It should be noted that first-order kinetics means that the rate of decomposition at any given moment is proportional to the amount of initiator that is still present, so the fraction that survives a given time depends on the elapsed time and the rate constant together, rather than on how much initiator was charged at the beginning. The rate constant was measured at one temperature only, and no activation energy is available, which means that the constant cannot reliably be transferred to another temperature: at a higher temperature the initiator would decompose more quickly, but by how much cannot be determined from the information available here. As a limiting check, at very short times the fraction remaining should still be close to its initial value, and the exponential form does indeed give that behaviour, while at long times the fraction tends towards zero, which is consistent with the value stated above for the longest time considered here.

$$\ln\frac{C}{C_0} = -k t$$

where the fraction remaining is the concentration at time $t$ divided by the initial concentration, and $k$ denotes the rate constant. After 116 min the fraction remaining is 0, at the precision of the stated value: the exponential has fallen below the precision at which the fraction is reported.

First-order kinetics means the rate of decomposition at any instant is proportional to the amount of initiator still present. The proportion that survives a given time therefore depends on the elapsed time and the rate constant together, and not on how much initiator was charged at the start. In polymerisation practice the initiator is chosen so that its decomposition rate matches the temperature of the reactor; an initiator that decomposes too slowly leaves the reaction starved of radicals late in the batch, and one that decomposes too fast spends itself early. Neither behaviour can be assessed for this initiator at reactor temperature from the stated constant, because the constant belongs to its measurement temperature and the temperature dependence is not given. The closing check is the limiting behaviour: at short times the fraction remaining is close to its initial value, and the exponential form gives that behaviour, while at long times the fraction tends to zero, which the stated result reaches within its precision.

fact_base: Excerpt content: two groups report conflicting selectivity values for the same material class; the excerpt weighs their test conditions. The excerpt reaches a limited preference and states the condition on which it rests.
input: The selectivity values reported for the benchmark material differ markedly between the two groups, and the difference is large enough that it cannot be dismissed as routine scatter between laboratories. Both groups studied the same material class, yet the conditions under which their measurements and calculations were carried out were not equivalent, and this lack of equivalence is central to how the disagreement should be read. One set of results rests on single-component measurements combined with IAST calculations, whereas the other rests on measurements made with gas mixtures, in which the components compete for the same adsorption sites. Mixture behaviour is, arguably, the more demanding test, because competition between components is present in the measurement itself rather than introduced afterwards through a model. At the same time, mixture measurements are harder to control, and small differences in feed composition or in the approach to equilibrium can shift the reported values in ways that are difficult to trace afterwards. On balance, a limited preference for the mixture-based values seems reasonable, although the preference is by no means unconditional. It holds only where the mixture measurements were made at compositions close to the separation task of interest and where equilibrium was demonstrated rather than assumed, and it should not be extended beyond those conditions without further evidence.

fact_base: A flat stainless steel wall of thickness 20 mm separates two process streams. Thermal conductivity of the wall is 16 W m-1 K-1 and the measured temperature difference across it is 399 K. Steady one-dimensional conduction gives a heat flux of 319200 W m-2. Surface (film) resistances are excluded from this estimate; including them lowers the flux.
input:
In this worked example, we consider a flat stainless steel wall with a thickness of 20 mm that separates two process streams, and the aim is to estimate the heat flux passing through the wall under steady one-dimensional conduction. The thermal conductivity of the wall material is 16 W m⁻¹ K⁻¹, and the measured temperature difference across the wall is 399 K, so the hotter stream loses heat through the metal to the colder stream at a rate set by these quantities together with the wall thickness. Expressed in metres, the thickness is 0.020 m, and the conduction relation makes the flux proportional to the conductivity and to the temperature difference, and inversely proportional to the thickness, so that a thinner wall or a more conductive metal would pass a larger flux for the same imposed difference. Putting the stated values into the relation gives a heat flux of 319200 W m⁻². It is important to note that this figure is an estimate for the metal wall alone. Surface (film) resistances on the two faces of the wall have been excluded from the estimate, and including them would add resistance in series with the wall, so the flux calculated on the same overall basis would be lower than the figure obtained here. The result therefore describes conduction through the wall itself, under the stated conditions, and it should not be read as the flux for the complete path between the two streams, which would have to account for the films as well.

Two features of the result follow from the form of the relation itself. The flux acts in the direction from the hotter face towards the colder face, because the temperature difference that drives the conduction is imposed across the wall in that direction. The flux also responds in proportion to its drivers: a larger temperature difference across the same wall would produce a proportionally larger flux, while a wall of greater thickness, with every other quantity unchanged, would produce a smaller flux, in inverse proportion to the thickness.
target:
A flat stainless steel wall of thickness 20 mm separates two process streams. Thermal conductivity is 16 W m⁻¹ K⁻¹ and the measured temperature difference across the wall is 399 K. The example estimates the heat flux through the wall for steady one-dimensional conduction. Expressed in metres, the thickness is 0.020 m. The conduction relation makes the flux proportional to the thermal conductivity and to the temperature difference, and inversely proportional to the thickness. A thinner wall, or a more conductive metal, passes a larger flux at the same temperature difference. Substitution of the stated values gives a heat flux of 319200 W m⁻². The estimate covers the metal wall alone. Surface (film) resistances at the two faces are excluded, and film resistance acts in series with the wall. Including the films lowers the flux calculated on the same overall basis. The figure therefore describes conduction through the wall itself under the stated conditions. The complete path between the two streams includes the films, and a flux for the complete path is a different quantity from the wall flux reported here.

The relation behind the figure has three parts. Thermal conductivity measures how readily the metal conducts heat. The temperature difference drives the conduction, and the flux acts from the hotter face towards the colder face. The thickness resists the conduction. Covariation follows the same relation. A larger temperature difference across the same wall gives a proportionally larger flux. A wall of a more conductive metal gives a larger flux at the same difference and thickness. A thicker wall gives a smaller flux, in inverse proportion to the thickness. The stated figure is checked against the relation in that form: thermal conductivity, temperature difference and thickness together fix the flux, and no other property of the two streams enters the wall calculation. Properties of the streams enter only through the films at the faces, and the films are excluded from the estimate. The wall figure and a figure for the complete path therefore answer different questions, and the two are not interchanged.

fact_base: Excerpt content: two groups report conflicting selectivity values for the same material class; the excerpt weighs their test conditions. The excerpt reaches a limited preference and states the condition on which it rests.
input:
The benchmark material is also the subject of a disagreement over selectivity that the published values, taken at face value, do not resolve. Two groups have reported values for the same material class that differ substantially, and it would be misleading to average them or to treat the spread as ordinary experimental noise, because the groups did not obtain their numbers in the same way. In one case, the reported selectivity was predicted from measurements on the separate pure components, with IAST used to estimate how the components would behave together in the adsorbed phase; the prediction therefore inherits the assumptions built into that treatment, including the treatment of mixing in the adsorbed phase itself. In the other case, selectivity was measured with mixtures directly, so that competition between the components for adsorption sites was part of the observation rather than an assumption added during the analysis. Direct mixture measurement is closer to the conditions of an actual separation, which counts in its favour, but it is also exposed to drift in feed composition and to doubt about whether equilibrium had genuinely been reached when the measurement was taken. Weighing these considerations, the mixture-based values deserve a limited preference, since the effect that decides the separation is present in the measurement. The preference is, however, conditional in an important respect: it rests on the mixture measurements having been made at feed compositions close to the intended separation and on equilibrium having been demonstrated, and where either of those conditions is absent the preference loses its basis.

For a reader, the practical consequence is that the test conditions have to be reported beside each value, since a figure from one route cannot be placed directly against a figure from the other without them.
target:
Selectivity values for the benchmark material differ substantially between the two groups, and the published values do not resolve the disagreement at face value. Averaging the values would mislead: the groups did not obtain their numbers in the same way, and the spread is not ordinary experimental noise. One group predicted selectivity from measurements on the separate pure components, using IAST to estimate how the components behave together in the adsorbed phase. A prediction of that kind inherits the assumptions of the treatment, including the treatment of mixing in the adsorbed phase. The other group measured selectivity with mixtures directly. Competition between the components for adsorption sites was part of the observation, not an assumption added during the analysis. Direct mixture measurement stands closer to the conditions of an actual separation. Mixture measurement carries its own weaknesses: feed composition can drift during a run, and equilibrium at the point of measurement can be in doubt. The mixture-based values carry a limited preference, because the effect that decides the separation is present in the measurement itself. The preference rests on two conditions. Feed compositions in the mixture measurements must lie close to the intended separation, and equilibrium must be demonstrated. Where either condition is absent, the preference loses its basis, and the two sets of values stand unresolved.

Test conditions therefore belong beside each reported value. A selectivity figure without its route of measurement, its feed basis and its equilibrium evidence cannot be placed against a figure obtained by the other route. The disagreement is a disagreement about values obtained under different conditions. The disagreement is not a contradiction between two measurements of the same state.

fact_base: An amine absorption unit was tested at pilot scale on gas from a cement kiln. Over 90 days at 11 t of carbon dioxide per day, the unit captured 88% of the carbon dioxide in the treated gas. Steam demand was 3.7 gigajoules per tonne of carbon dioxide captured; solvent loss was 1.8 kg per tonne captured. Beyond 90 days, the effect of kiln dust on the solvent is untested.
input:
This passage reports the results of a pilot-scale test of an amine absorption unit treating gas from a cement kiln, a source whose gas composition and dust loading might be expected to raise questions about how well a capture unit performs outside a cleaner test setting. The unit was operated over 90 days at a rate of 11 t of carbon dioxide per day, and over that period it captured 88% of the carbon dioxide in the treated gas, which can be regarded as a substantial capture fraction sustained over a test of meaningful length rather than a brief demonstration. The associated utility and solvent figures were also recorded: steam demand was 3.7 gigajoules per tonne of carbon dioxide captured, and solvent loss was 1.8 kg per tonne captured, both of which are relevant to the operating cost of the process at larger scale. It should nevertheless be kept in mind that the test has a clear limit. Beyond the test period, the effect of kiln dust on the solvent remains untested, so questions about longer-term solvent behaviour, and about any gradual change in performance that dust exposure might bring about, cannot be answered from these results and would require a longer campaign in which the solvent itself was monitored as the exposure accumulated.

Operating on gas drawn from an actual cement kiln, rather than on a prepared gas of fixed composition, also exposes the unit to the variation of a real source, and the results carry that exposure with them. Kiln operation changes as raw feed and burning conditions change, and the gas reaching the unit reflects those changes in its dust burden and in the load placed on the solvent. A capture fraction held across such variation, over the full duration of the test, is in this respect a stronger result than the same fraction held on a steady prepared gas for a short run, and the solvent loss figure, recorded across the whole campaign, likewise reflects contact with the real gas rather than with a clean substitute.
target:
An amine absorption unit was tested at pilot scale on gas from a cement kiln. Over 90 days at 11 t of carbon dioxide per day, the unit captured 88% of the carbon dioxide in the treated gas. Capture at that fraction was sustained over the full test period, not held for a brief demonstration. Steam demand was 3.7 gigajoules per tonne of carbon dioxide captured. Solvent loss was 1.8 kg per tonne captured. Steam demand and solvent loss set much of the operating cost of the process at larger scale, and both were recorded on the same basis, per tonne captured. The test period sets the limit of the results. Beyond the test period, the effect of kiln dust on the solvent is untested. Longer-term solvent behaviour, and any gradual change in performance under continued dust exposure, cannot be read from the pilot results. A longer campaign, with the solvent monitored as exposure accumulates, is the measurement that would settle the question. The pilot results support the capture fraction, the steam demand, and the solvent loss at the stated rate and duration. Claims about solvent life under kiln dust stand outside the pilot results.

Gas drawn from an actual cement kiln varies as raw feed and burning conditions change. Dust burden and the load placed on the solvent vary with the kiln. A capture fraction held across that variation, over the full test period, is a stronger result than the same fraction held briefly on a prepared gas of fixed composition. The solvent loss figure belongs to the same picture. Solvent loss was recorded across the whole campaign, under contact with the real gas. A clean substitute gas would give a loss figure for different conditions. Performance figures from the pilot are therefore figures for kiln gas as fired, with its variation included. The figures are not figures for a smoothed feed, and a design that treats the kiln gas as steady takes on a variation the pilot results do not support.

subtype: worked example with equation: log-mean difference
fact_base: A countercurrent exchanger cools a process stream from 160 °C to 120 °C with water entering at 40 °C and leaving at 65 °C. The terminal differences are 95 K and 80 K, and the log-mean temperature difference $\Delta T_{lm}$ is 87.3 K. The log-mean value assumes constant overall coefficient and no phase change.
input:
A countercurrent exchanger is used to cool a process stream from 160 °C to 120 °C, with cooling water entering at 40 °C and leaving at 65 °C, and the quantity required for sizing calculations of this kind is the log-mean temperature difference, denoted $\Delta T_{lm}$, which accounts for the fact that the local temperature difference between the two streams is not the same at the two ends of the exchanger. At the end where the water leaves, the difference between the streams is 95 K, while at the end where the water enters, the difference is 80 K, and the appropriate mean of these two terminal differences, for an exchanger of this type, is given by the relation $$\Delta T_{lm} = \frac{\Delta T_1 - \Delta T_2}{\ln(\Delta T_1 / \Delta T_2)}$$ in which the two terminal differences appear in the numerator and inside the logarithm. Evaluating the relation with the terminal differences stated above gives the log-mean temperature difference as 87.3 K. It is worth noting that this value rests on particular assumptions: the log-mean value assumes a constant overall coefficient along the exchanger and no phase change in either stream, and where those conditions do not hold the single log-mean figure no longer describes the exchanger in the same way.

The arithmetic mean of the two terminal differences would not serve the same purpose. Along the length of the exchanger, the local difference changes from one end to the other, and the contribution of each part of the surface to the heat transferred depends on the local difference at that part, so a mean that weights the two ends in the logarithmic way set out above is the mean that matches how the exchanger actually transfers heat. The resulting figure is then the temperature difference that, together with the surface area and the overall coefficient, sets the duty of the exchanger, which is why the log-mean value, rather than either terminal difference on its own, is the quantity carried into sizing work.
target:
A countercurrent exchanger cools a process stream from 160 °C to 120 °C with water entering at 40 °C and leaving at 65 °C. The local temperature difference between the streams differs at the two ends of the exchanger, and the log-mean temperature difference $\Delta T_{lm}$ is the mean used for sizing. At the end where the water leaves, the terminal difference is 95 K. At the end where the water enters, the terminal difference is 80 K. The log-mean temperature difference is calculated from the two terminal differences by $$\Delta T_{lm} = \frac{\Delta T_1 - \Delta T_2}{\ln(\Delta T_1 / \Delta T_2)}$$ Substitution of the two terminal differences gives $\Delta T_{lm}$ as 87.3 K. The value lies between the two terminal differences. The log-mean value assumes a constant overall coefficient along the exchanger and no phase change in either stream. Where the overall coefficient varies along the exchanger, or where a stream changes phase, a single log-mean figure does not describe the exchanger in the same way, and the exchanger is treated in sections instead.

An arithmetic mean of the two terminal differences does not serve the same purpose. The local difference changes along the length of the exchanger. Each part of the surface transfers heat in proportion to the local difference at that part. The logarithmic mean weights the two ends in the way the surface actually transfers heat. The log-mean temperature difference then sets the duty of the exchanger together with the surface area and the overall coefficient. The two assumptions mark the scope of the single figure. A constant overall coefficient means one value is used along the whole length. No phase change means each stream changes temperature by sensible heat alone from one end to the other, and the two terminal differences describe the ends completely.

fact_base: A contract packaging firm runs 3 plants; revenue is $82 million per year. Evidence base: order records for 12 months, 11777 orders. On-time delivery over the last two quarters was 89%, against a target of 95%. Overtime cost was $1.8 million last year, up 23% on the year before. The order backlog stands at 4.2 weeks, against 1.5 weeks a year ago. Plant 2 accounts for 62% of late orders. A scheduling system for all plants is quoted at $286k; Plant 2 alone is $151k. An internal estimate (not a vendor figure) puts the overtime reduction at Plant 2 at 15-20% in the first year. The recommendation under consideration: install at Plant 2 first, hold the other plants until Plant 2 results are reported. The operations director owns the scheduling programme.
input: Install the scheduling system at Plant 2 first. That is the recommendation under consideration, and the other plants are held until results from Plant 2 are reported. The firm runs 3 plants and revenue is $82 million per year, so the delivery problem is not a marginal one for a business of this size. The evidence base is the order records for 12 months, covering 11777 orders, and those records show on-time delivery over the last two quarters at 89%, against a target of 95%. Late delivery is concentrated rather than evenly spread: Plant 2 accounts for 62% of late orders. Overtime cost was $1.8 million last year, up 23% on the year before, and the order backlog stands at 4.2 weeks, against 1.5 weeks a year ago, which suggests that the present way of working is absorbing pressure through overtime rather than clearing it. A scheduling system for all plants is quoted at $286k; Plant 2 alone is $151k. An internal estimate, which is not a vendor figure, puts the overtime reduction at Plant 2 at 15–20% in the first year. The pattern matters for the choice being considered. Because the late orders sit mainly at one plant, a system installed everywhere at once would spend the full quoted amount before any site had shown whether the overtime saving is real. A staged start limits the initial commitment to the plant where the problem is largest, and it gives the operations director a reported result, drawn from the firm's own orders, on which the later decision can rest. The operations director owns the scheduling programme, and the decision is whether to accept the staged route, with Plant 2 as the test case, before committing the remaining plants.
target:
Install the scheduling system at Plant 2 first, and hold the other plants until Plant 2 results are reported. The evidence base is order records for 12 months (11777 orders). On-time delivery over the last two quarters was 89% against a target of 95%. The firm runs 3 plants with revenue of $82 million per year, and late orders are concentrated: Plant 2 accounts for 62% of late orders. Overtime cost was $1.8 million last year, up 23% on the year before. The order backlog stands at 4.2 weeks, against 1.5 weeks a year ago. Present working absorbs pressure through overtime rather than clearing the backlog. A scheduling system for all plants is quoted at $286k, and Plant 2 alone is $151k. An internal estimate, not a vendor figure, puts the overtime reduction at Plant 2 at 15–20% in the first year. Concentration of late orders drives the staging. A system installed everywhere at once commits the full quoted cost before any site has shown whether the overtime saving is real. A staged start limits the initial commitment to the plant with the largest share of the problem. Extension then rests on a reported result from the firm's own orders. The operations director owns the scheduling programme. The decision is whether to accept the staged route before the remaining plants are committed.

The staged route also fixes the order of spending. The smaller quoted amount is committed first. The larger extension is considered only after the reported saving at Plant 2 is known, and the remaining plants enter the programme on the strength of a measured result rather than on the strength of the estimate alone.

fact_base: Excerpt content: the schedule float is set at 16% and the excerpt defends that figure against a lower alternative. The excerpt refers to the project's cost table by section name and does not repeat its figures.
input: The schedule float for the upgrade project has been set at 16%, and the figure has been questioned on the ground that a lower allowance would present a tighter and more ambitious programme. That argument is understandable, but it overlooks what the float is there to do. The float is not spare time added for comfort; it is the allowance that stands between the planned sequence of work and the point at which slippage in one activity begins to consume the dates of the activities that follow it. Several of the activities on the critical path have durations that cannot be fixed with precision at this stage, because they depend on interfaces between work packages and on approval steps that lie outside the direct control of the project team. If the float were set lower, the first significant slippage would exhaust the allowance, and every subsequent delay would move the completion date directly, leaving the steering group to recover time by compressing work that is already planned tightly. The cost consequences of such compression are set out in the cost table in the Costs section, and they are not repeated here; the point for the schedule is that recovery after the float has gone is bought at a price, whereas the float itself costs nothing until it is used. Retaining the stated figure keeps a single, visible allowance under the control of the steering group, rather than distributing hidden padding through individual activity durations, where it would be spent without being tracked. For those reasons the float should stay as set, and the steering group is asked to endorse the figure when the programme is reviewed.
target:
The schedule float for the upgrade project is set at 16%, and the figure stands against a lower alternative. Float is the allowance between the planned sequence of work and the point where slippage in one activity begins to consume the dates of the activities after it. Float is not spare time added for comfort. Several activities on the critical path have durations that cannot be fixed with precision at this stage. Critical-path activities depend on interfaces between work packages and on approval steps outside the direct control of the project team. A lower float is exhausted by the first significant slippage. Every later delay then moves the completion date directly, and the steering group must recover time by compressing work already planned tightly. The cost of such compression is set out in the cost table in the Costs section and is not repeated here. Recovery after the float has gone is bought at a price; the float itself costs nothing until it is used. A single visible allowance, held under the control of the steering group, is also easier to protect than padding distributed through individual activity durations, where allowance is spent without being tracked. The float stays as set, and the steering group is asked to endorse the figure at the programme review.

The defence of the figure is practical. Float that is visible can be allocated deliberately, activity by activity, as risks materialise. Float that has been designed out cannot be recovered except by compression of the work or by movement of the completion date, and both routes are decided under pressure, after slippage has already occurred.

subtype: worked example with equation: first-order decay
fact_base: A drug in solution decomposes by first-order kinetics with rate constant $k$ = 0.111 min-1. After 93 min the fraction remaining $C / C_0$ is 0. The rate constant was measured at one temperature; no activation energy is available.
input:
A drug in solution decomposes by first-order kinetics, which means that the rate of loss of the drug at any moment is proportional to the amount of the drug still present, and the concentration ratio follows the relation $$\ln\frac{C}{C_0} = -k t$$ where the rate constant $k$ for this decomposition is 0.111 min⁻¹. The question addressed here is how much of the drug remains after 93 min. Because the exponent in the relation is the product of the rate constant and the elapsed time, and that product is large for the time considered, the exponential term falls to a very small value, and the fraction remaining after the stated time is 0, at the precision of the stated value. In other words, for practical purposes the decomposition is essentially complete within the period considered, even though the first-order relation itself never quite reaches zero in a mathematical sense. One limitation of the result should be kept in mind: the rate constant was measured at one temperature, and no activation energy is available, so the calculation cannot be extended to other temperatures, where the rate constant would in general be different and the time for decomposition would change accordingly.

The result can also be read directly from the size of the exponent. When the product of the rate constant and the time is small, a substantial fraction of the drug survives in solution; when the product is large, very little survives, and the stated case falls firmly in the second of those two regimes, which is why the reported fraction is so small.
target:
A drug in solution decomposes by first-order kinetics: the rate of loss at any moment is proportional to the amount still present. The concentration ratio is given by $$\ln\frac{C}{C_0} = -k t$$ The rate constant $k$ is 0.111 min⁻¹. After 93 min, the fraction remaining is 0, at the precision of the stated value. The exponent is the product of the rate constant and the elapsed time, and the product is large at the stated time. The exponential term is therefore very small, and decomposition is complete for practical purposes within the period considered. The first-order relation itself approaches zero without reaching it; the stated fraction is a rounded value, not an exact zero. The rate constant was measured at one temperature, and no activation energy is available. The calculation is limited to the measured temperature. At another temperature the rate constant differs, the time for decomposition changes with it, and no figure for another temperature can be obtained from the stated data.

The size of the exponent decides the outcome in general. A small product of rate constant and time leaves a substantial fraction of the drug in solution. A large product leaves very little. The stated case falls in the second regime, and the fraction remaining is minute before rounding. Presentation of the result depends on precision: a value carried to more decimal places would show a small residue, while the value at the stated precision is the figure reported here.

fact_base: Inventory policy for a resin grade: mean demand 570 units per week, standard deviation 99 units per week, replenishment lead time 2 weeks. Safety stock for a 95% cycle service level is 231 units. Demand is treated as normal and independent between weeks; seasonal peaks are excluded.
input:
This case concerns the inventory policy for a resin grade, and specifically the level of safety stock that should be held to protect the cycle service level against variation in demand during the replenishment lead time. Demand for the grade averages 570 units per week, with a standard deviation of 99 units per week, and the replenishment lead time is 2 weeks, so the exposure that the safety stock has to cover is the variation in demand that can accumulate over that lead time rather than over a single week. For a 95% cycle service level, the safety stock is 231 units. The figure rests on the assumptions built into the calculation: demand is treated as normal and independent between weeks, which is what allows the weekly variation to be combined over the lead time in the way the calculation requires. Seasonal peaks are excluded from the treatment, and that exclusion matters in practice, because a policy sized on the stated demand pattern will not necessarily provide the same service level during a seasonal peak, when demand is systematically higher than the average pattern on which the safety stock figure was based. The stated figure therefore applies to the demand conditions described, and it should be revisited if the pattern of demand, or the lead time itself, changes.

The service level referred to is a cycle service level, which is to say the standard the policy sets for meeting demand during a replenishment cycle from stock, and the safety stock is the buffer that stands between ordinary variation in demand and a stock-out during the period in which a replenishment order is outstanding and cannot yet be drawn upon.
target:
Inventory policy for a resin grade sets safety stock at 231 units for a 95% cycle service level. Mean demand is 570 units per week, with a standard deviation of 99 units per week. Replenishment lead time is 2 weeks. Safety stock covers variation in demand over the lead time, not variation in a single week: demand fluctuations accumulate across the full period between ordering and delivery, and the stock must absorb the accumulated fluctuation if the service level is to be held. Demand is treated as normal and independent between weeks. The normal treatment sets the form of the calculation, and independence between weeks sets how weekly variation combines over the lead time. Seasonal peaks are excluded. A policy sized on the stated demand pattern does not necessarily give the same service level during a seasonal peak, when demand stands systematically above the average pattern. The safety stock figure applies to the demand conditions stated. A change in the pattern of demand, or in the lead time, changes the exposure the stock has to cover, and the figure is then set again from the new conditions.

The service level is a cycle service level: the standard set for meeting demand during a replenishment cycle from stock. Safety stock is the buffer between ordinary variation in demand and a stock-out during the period when a replenishment order is outstanding and cannot yet be drawn upon. Demand in some cycles exceeds the mean, and demand in others falls below the mean. The buffer is sized for the cycles in which demand runs high while delivery is still awaited.

fact_base: A tutorial passage explains representative sampling of a gas emission. The passage covers where samples are taken, how many increments form one sample, and why a single grab sample misleads. No numerical limits are quoted; regulatory limits belong to the site's permit, not to the passage.
input:
Emissions sampling has one central requirement that is easy to state but easy to get wrong in practice: the sample that is analysed must represent the emission as a whole, because every conclusion drawn from the analysis will be applied to the whole gas stream and not merely to the portion that happened to enter the sampling line. Where samples are taken is the first decision. The sampling position should be at a location where the gas is well mixed, since a sample drawn from a poorly mixed region may reflect a local pocket of gas rather than the stream average, and positions close to disturbances that disturb the flow, or where deposits accumulate, carry the same risk. The second point concerns how a sample is built up. A single sample is formed from a number of increments, which are small portions collected at intervals over the sampling period and combined before analysis, so that the sample reflects conditions across the period rather than at one instant of it. This matters because a single grab sample, taken at one moment and analysed on its own, can mislead in either direction: the emission varies as operating conditions vary, concentrations are not uniform across the duct, and a moment that is convenient for sampling may be quite untypical of the emission over the period the result is meant to describe. A sample built from increments taken at a representative position does not remove all uncertainty, but it matches the quantity being reported, which is the emission over a period, rather than the state of the gas at a single point in space and time.

The increments also need to be spread across the operating cycle of the source, because an emission that follows a process cycle will present different concentrations at different stages of that cycle, and increments clustered in a quiet stage would understate the emission just as surely as increments clustered in a peak stage would overstate it, even if every individual increment were collected and analysed correctly.
target:
A sample of a gas emission must represent the emission as a whole. Every conclusion from the analysis is applied to the whole gas stream, not to the portion that entered the sampling line. Sampling position is the first decision. Samples are taken where the gas is well mixed. A sample drawn from a poorly mixed region reflects a local pocket of gas, not the stream average, and positions close to flow disturbances, or where deposits accumulate, carry the same risk. Sample construction is the second decision. One sample is formed from a number of increments: small portions collected at intervals over the sampling period and combined before analysis. A combined sample reflects conditions across the period. A single grab sample misleads. Emission strength varies as operating conditions vary, concentration is not uniform across the duct, and a moment convenient for sampling can be untypical of the emission over the period the result describes. A grab sample can therefore sit above or below the period average, with nothing in the sample itself to show the direction of the error. Increments taken at a representative position match the sample to the quantity reported: the emission over a period, not the state of the gas at a single point in space and time.

Increment timing carries the same requirement. Increments are spread across the operating cycle of the source. An emission that follows a process cycle presents different concentrations at different stages of the cycle. Increments clustered in a quiet stage understate the emission. Increments clustered in a peak stage overstate the emission. Correct collection and analysis of each increment do not repair a biased spread. The sampling line also draws from the main body of the gas. A stagnant pocket near a wall or a dead leg gives increments from gas that is not moving with the stream, and increments of that kind misrepresent the emission however carefully the later stages are handled. Position, increment spread and sample construction act together: a defect in any one of them passes into the reported result.

fact_base: Excerpt content: the analogy between the transfer processes is stated, then qualified by the case where it fails. The excerpt works one short numerical check with numbers given inside the excerpt itself. The excerpt assumes the chapter's earlier definitions and adds none.
input: The analogy between the transfer processes, expressed in its most familiar form by the Chilton-Colburn analogy, draws together momentum transfer, heat transfer and mass transfer by setting the transfer factors for heat and mass alongside the friction factor for the flowing fluid, the suggestion being that the same surface behaviour governs all three. In the case of mass transfer the analogy takes $j_D$ to be equal to $f/2$, and a short check illustrates the kind of use that is made of it: for a surface at which $f$ has the value 0.008, the analogy gives $j_D$ as 0.004, a prediction obtained directly from the friction behaviour without a separate mass-transfer measurement. The analogy is, however, an analogy and not an identity, and there is a well-recognised case in which it breaks down. Where the friction factor contains a substantial contribution from form drag, as it does for flow across a bluff body, part of $f$ arises from pressure forces that have no counterpart in heat or mass transfer at the surface, and the equality with the transfer factors, which respond only to the surface shear contribution, can no longer be expected to hold.
target:
The Chilton-Colburn analogy sets the transfer factors for heat and mass transfer alongside the friction factor for the flowing fluid. One surface behaviour is taken to govern momentum, heat and mass transfer together. For mass transfer, the analogy gives $j_D$ equal to $f/2$. A short check shows the use made of the relation: at a surface where $f$ is 0.008, the analogy gives $j_D$ as 0.004, obtained from the friction behaviour with no separate mass-transfer measurement. The analogy is not an identity, and one case marks where the analogy fails. Where $f$ contains a substantial contribution from form drag, as in flow across a bluff body, part of $f$ comes from pressure forces. Pressure forces of that kind have no counterpart in heat or mass transfer at the surface. The transfer factors respond to the surface shear contribution alone. An equality between the friction term and a transfer factor cannot be expected in that case.

The check also shows the character of an analogy prediction. A value obtained from the analogy is an estimate tied to the friction measurement. The standing of the estimate rests on the case at hand falling inside the conditions where surface shear alone governs both the friction and the transfer at the surface.

fact_base: A tutorial passage explains absolute and relative error through a pressure measurement. Worked figures: reading 100 units, tolerance 2% of reading, so the absolute error is 2 units. The passage distinguishes error from uncertainty and does not merge the two terms.
input:
When a pressure measurement is reported, two different questions can be asked about its quality, and keeping them apart is the starting point for understanding measurement error. The first question is how far the reading might be from the true value, and this is the province of error. In the worked figures used here, the reading is 100 units and the tolerance is 2% of reading, so the absolute error is 2 units: the reading may depart from the true value by that amount, expressed in the same units as the measurement itself. The relative error expresses the same departure as a fraction of the reading, which makes it dimensionless and allows errors on measurements of very different sizes to be compared with one another on a common basis. Error, in this sense, belongs to a particular measurement: it is the difference between the reading and the true value, even though in practice the true value is not known exactly and the error is therefore stated as a bound rather than as a known difference. Uncertainty is a different term and should not be merged with error. Uncertainty describes the range within which the value is believed to lie, together with the doubt that attaches to the measurement as a whole, taking account of the instrument and the conditions of use. A report that mixes the two terms, using error where a range is meant or uncertainty where a difference is meant, leaves the reader unable to tell what has actually been stated about the measurement.

The distinction also affects how a specification or a tolerance on an instrument should be read. A tolerance stated as a percentage, as in the worked figures, ties the permitted departure to the size of the reading, so the same instrument is held to a tighter absolute departure at a small reading than at a large one, and a reader who treats the percentage as a fixed absolute amount will misjudge the measurement at one end of the range or the other.

fact_base: An amine absorption unit was tested at pilot scale on gas from a cement kiln. Over 90 days at 12 t of carbon dioxide per day, the unit captured 92% of the carbon dioxide in the treated gas. input: It is important to note that amine absorption technology has recently been evaluated at pilot scale on gas originating from a cement kiln, and the findings of this evaluation provide valuable insights into how the process performs under real-world operating conditions. Over a period of 90 days, during which the unit handled 12 t of carbon dioxide per day, the system successfully captured 92% of the carbon dioxide present in the treated gas, underscoring the effectiveness of the approach in this setting. In terms of energy requirements, the steam demand was found to be 3.5 gigajoules per tonne of carbon dioxide captured, a figure that reflects the considerable energy needed to regenerate the solvent on an ongoing basis so that it can be returned to the absorber for further use. Furthermore, the solvent loss was measured at 1.6 kg per tonne of carbon dioxide captured, highlighting the importance of careful solvent management in maintaining efficient, sustainable, and cost-effective operation over time. It should also be noted that questions remain regarding the longer-term behaviour of the solvent in this environment. Beyond 90 days, the effect of kiln dust on the solvent is untested, and further investigation will ultimately be needed in order to fully understand how dust carried over from the kiln might impact solvent condition and, in turn, overall performance during extended periods of operation. Overall, the results demonstrate the significant potential of the process, while also pointing towards areas where additional research could further strengthen confidence going forward.
