An amine absorption unit treated gas from a cement kiln at pilot scale. Over 90 days at 12 t of carbon dioxide per day, the unit captured 92% of the carbon dioxide in the treated gas. Steam demand was 3.5 gigajoules per tonne of carbon dioxide captured. Solvent loss was 1.6 kg per tonne of carbon dioxide captured.

The capture figure is a fraction of the carbon dioxide in the treated gas. Gas that did not pass through the unit is outside the stated result, and the figure says nothing about kiln output as a whole. Steam demand is the heat supplied to release the captured carbon dioxide from the solvent and return the solvent to the absorber. A demand stated per tonne captured ties the energy cost to output rather than to operating time, and units of different size can be compared on that basis. Solvent loss is stated on the same basis. Solvent leaves a working unit with the treated gas and the captured stream, and by degradation in service; the loss figure is the make-up needed to hold the solvent inventory during the test. Neither figure is a design value. Both were measured on kiln gas at pilot scale, under the gas composition and dust load of the test period.

Beyond 90 days, the effect of kiln dust on the solvent is untested. Dust reaches the solvent with the gas, and a longer run could change solvent condition in ways a test of this length does not show. The capture, steam, and solvent figures are stated for the tested period, and no figure is given for extended operation.

fact_base: An operating-manual chapter for a pressure relief valve, in four sections: start-up, normal operation, alarms, and shutdown. The alarms section lists two alarms and the operator action for each; no other alarms are introduced. The chapter addresses the operator directly and uses imperative verbs for actions.
input:
Start-up

The pressure relief valve that is the subject of this chapter is an extremely important item of safety equipment, since it protects the equipment to which it is fitted against the potentially serious consequences of excessive pressure. Under normal circumstances the valve remains closed, but if the pressure within the protected equipment should rise to the set pressure, the valve will open automatically, allowing fluid to be discharged until such time as the pressure has fallen back to a more acceptable level, at which point the valve will close again. This chapter describes the procedures for the start-up, the normal operation, the alarm response, and the shutdown of the valve.

Prior to start-up, a thorough inspection of the valve and of the associated equipment should be carried out. The valve body, the inlet and outlet flanges, and the discharge line should be examined carefully for any evidence of damage, corrosion, or previous leakage. It should be confirmed that the discharge line is completely clear along the whole of its length and terminates at the designated safe discharge point, with no cap, plug, or closed valve situated anywhere along the path. Where an inlet isolation valve has been fitted, it should be verified that this valve is fully open and secured in the open position. The pressure gauge on the protected equipment should be checked to ensure that it is readable and has not become isolated from the equipment it serves. Any defects identified should be reported before pressurisation is commenced.

The pressure in the protected equipment should then be raised slowly, in accordance with the normal start-up procedure that applies to that particular equipment, and the pressure gauge should be observed closely while this is being done. As the normal operating pressure is approached and reached, it should be confirmed that the relief valve remains firmly shut, with no discharge at the outlet and no leakage at the flange joints. Once the equipment has settled down at its normal operating pressure, an entry should be made in the operating log recording that the valve is in service, that the inlet is open, and that the discharge path has been proved to be clear.

In the event that the valve is found to be leaking or discharging at normal operating pressure during the start-up, no attempt should be made to adjust it. The spring, the adjuster, and any seals on the valve should be left strictly alone. If the discharge continues, the pressure should be reduced, the supervisor should be informed, and the valve should be left for examination under a maintenance permit,.

Normal operation

During normal operation, the relief valve remains shut, and the protected equipment operates at a pressure below the set pressure of the valve

During each round, the valve and its joints should be inspected visually for leakage, corrosion, and mechanical damage, and the operator should listen out for any hissing sound that might indicate that the valve is passing. The discharge outlet should be examined for any discharge that should not be present, and also for deposits, staining, or icing that might indicate that a discharge has taken place at some point since the previous round. All findings should be recorded in the operating log, including quiet rounds, as evidence that the required watch has been kept.

The area in the vicinity of the valve and of the discharge outlet should be kept clear at all times. No materials should be stored against the discharge line, and nothing should be hung from the valve or from its associated pipework. The valve should not be painted, and particular care should be taken to avoid painting the spring housing or the nameplate, because paint applied to the moving and venting parts of a relief valve can trap moisture against the metal surfaces and can also conceal the corrosion that inspections are intended to detect.

There are three prohibitions that apply throughout the whole of normal operation. The inlet isolation valve should never be closed while the protected equipment remains pressurised, because an isolated valve protects nothing. The discharge outlet should never be plugged, capped, or blanked for any reason whatsoever, even where a passing valve is causing inconvenience. The set pressure should never be adjusted by the operator, because adjustment and bench testing are maintenance activities carried out under permit with the valve removed. Any valve that is passing, leaking at a joint, or showing signs of damage should be reported to the supervisor during the same shift, and the report should be entered in the operating log.

Alarms

There are two alarms on the protected equipment that are relevant to the relief valve, and the actions that are required in response to each of these alarms are described under the appropriate headings below. Neither alarm calls for work on the relief valve mechanism itself; the actions required are concerned instead with the pressure within the equipment and with the positioning of personnel in the area.

High pressure in the protected equipment

This alarm indicates that the pressure in the protected equipment has risen towards the set pressure, and that the relief valve may consequently be about to lift. Before any action is taken, the reading should be confirmed by reference to the local pressure gauge. The pressure should then be reduced by the normal means available for the equipment, which may involve cutting the feed, the heat input, or the inflow responsible for raising the pressure. Personnel should keep well clear of the discharge outlet, and if the pressure continues to rise, personnel should withdraw from the area in the vicinity of the discharge, the supervisor should be informed, and the valve should be allowed to perform its intended function. After the pressure has fallen and the valve has reseated, the event should be recorded in the operating log, and the valve should be reported for inspection.

Discharge at the relief valve outlet

This alarm indicates that the relief valve has lifted, or is passing heavily, with the result that fluid is being discharged. All personnel should keep well clear of the discharge outlet and of any area that the discharge can reach, and it should be confirmed, by reference to the pressure gauge, that the pressure within the protected equipment is falling. No attempt should be made to close, block, or throttle the discharge, and the valve should not be approached while a discharge is in progress. If the pressure is not falling, the supervisor should be informed immediately and the emergency procedure for the protected equipment should be followed. Once the discharge has stopped and the pressure is steady, the lift should be recorded in the operating log, together with the cause where this is known, and the valve should be reported for examination.

Shutdown

It should be borne in mind that the relief valve remains in service until such time as the protected equipment has been fully depressurised, and that the shutdown of the equipment does not in itself provide any justification for isolating the valve at an earlier stage. The valve continues to guard the equipment for as long as any pressure remains within it, including pressure that builds up again from heat or a leaking isolation.

The pressure should be reduced in accordance with the normal shutdown procedure for the protected equipment, and the pressure gauge should be monitored until the reading demonstrates that the equipment has been fully depressurised, a state that should be proved by the vent or drain before any isolation is touched. Only at this stage, and only where the valve is to be removed for bench testing or replacement, should the inlet isolation valve be closed. The drain or vent between the protected equipment and the valve should be opened, and it should be proved that no pressure remains trapped within the short length of pipe between the closed isolation and the valve before any attempt is made to loosen a flange bolt.

The removal of the valve is a maintenance activity and is carried out under permit, so that the part played by the operator is essentially that of the hand-over. An entry should be made in the operating log to the effect that the valve has been removed, identifying the equipment that it guarded and the state in which the equipment has been left, and any open flange left behind by the removal should be blanked Equipment from which the relief valve has been removed should not be repressurised until a valve has been restored to service on it, or an approved alternative protective arrangement is in place.

In summary, then, the valve guards pressurised equipment and is proved at start-up with its inlet open and its discharge path clear; during normal operation it is watched carefully and is otherwise left entirely alone; its two alarms call for the reduction of pressure and for the clearance of the discharge area; and it remains in service at shutdown until the protected equipment has been proved to be free of pressure.
target:
Start-up

A pressure relief valve guards the equipment it is fitted to against pressure above the limit the equipment is built to withstand. The valve opens when the pressure in the protected equipment reaches the set pressure, discharges fluid until the pressure has fallen, and closes again. This chapter covers start-up, normal operation, alarm response, and shutdown for the valve

Before start-up, walk round the valve and the protected equipment. Inspect the valve body, the inlet and outlet flanges, and the discharge line for damage, corrosion, and signs of past leakage. Confirm that the discharge line is clear along its whole run and ends at the safe discharge point, with no cap, plug, or closed valve in the path. Confirm that the inlet isolation valve, where one is fitted, is fully open and secured open. Check that the pressure gauge on the protected equipment is readable and is not isolated from the equipment it serves. Report any defect you find before the equipment is pressurised; a relief valve with a blocked discharge or a closed inlet gives no protection at all.

Raise the pressure in the protected equipment slowly, by the normal start-up procedure for that equipment. Watch the pressure gauge as the pressure rises. As the equipment reaches its normal operating pressure, confirm that the relief valve remains shut: no discharge at the outlet, no sound of passing fluid, and no leakage at the flange joints. Check each joint in turn and deal with any leak by the procedure for the protected equipment, not by work on the relief valve. When the equipment is steady at its normal operating pressure, record in the operating log that the valve is in service, the inlet is open, and the discharge path has been proved clear.

If the valve leaks or discharges at normal operating pressure during start-up, do not adjust it. Do not touch the spring, the adjuster, or any seal on the valve. Reduce the pressure if the discharge continues, inform the supervisor, and leave the valve for examination under a maintenance permit. A valve that cannot stay shut at normal pressure is not in service, whatever its position on the equipment.

Normal operation

In normal operation the relief valve is shut and the protected equipment runs below the set pressure. Your duty in this state is watchkeeping. The valve needs no adjustment, no operation, and no routine movement from you, and any interference with it reduces the protection it gives.

On each round, look at the valve and its joints for leakage, corrosion, and mechanical damage. Listen for the hiss that shows the valve is passing. Look at the discharge outlet for discharge that should not be there, and for deposits, staining, or icing that show discharge has taken place since the last round. Read the pressure gauge on the protected equipment and compare the reading with the normal operating band for the equipment. Record what you find in the operating log, including rounds on which nothing unusual is found: a log entry that shows a quiet round is evidence that the watch was kept.

Keep the area round the valve and the discharge outlet clear. Store no material against the discharge line, and hang nothing from the valve or its pipework. Protect the valve from knocks during lifting work and cleaning work nearby, and report any damage at once. Do not paint the valve, and in particular do not paint the spring housing or the nameplate. Paint on the moving and venting parts of a relief valve can hold moisture against the metal and can hide the corrosion that an inspection is meant to find.

Three prohibitions govern the whole of normal operation. Never close the inlet isolation valve while the protected equipment is pressurised; an isolated relief valve protects nothing. Never plug, cap, or blank the discharge outlet for any reason, including a passing valve that is making a nuisance of itself. Never adjust the set pressure; adjustment and bench testing belong to maintenance, under permit, with the valve off the equipment. A valve that passes, leaks at a joint, or shows damage is reported to the supervisor the same shift, and the report is entered in the operating log

Alarms

Two alarms on the protected equipment concern the relief valve. The action for each alarm is set out under its heading. No other alarm in this chapter calls for work on the relief valve itself, and in both cases your work is on the pressure and on people's positions, never on the valve mechanism.

High pressure in the protected equipment

Pressure in the protected equipment has risen towards the set pressure, and the relief valve may be about to lift. Confirm the reading on the local pressure gauge before acting on it. Reduce the pressure by the normal means for the equipment: cut the feed, the heat input, or the inflow that is raising the pressure, as the procedure for the equipment directs. Keep clear of the discharge outlet and keep other people clear of it. If the pressure continues to rise, withdraw from the area round the discharge, inform the supervisor, and let the valve do its work. When the pressure has fallen and the valve has reseated, record the event in the operating log and report the valve for inspection before the equipment is returned to unrestricted service.

Discharge at the relief valve outlet

The relief valve has lifted, or is passing heavily, and fluid is discharging. Keep yourself and all other personnel clear of the discharge outlet and of the area the discharge reaches. Confirm from the pressure gauge that the pressure in the protected equipment is falling. Do not attempt to close, block, or throttle the discharge, and do not approach the valve while it is discharging. If the pressure is not falling, inform the supervisor at once and follow the emergency procedure for the protected equipment. When the discharge has stopped and the pressure is steady, record the lift in the operating log, with the cause if it is known, and report the valve for examination; a valve that has lifted is inspected before its next period of service is relied on.

Shutdown

The relief valve stays in service until the protected equipment is fully depressurised. Shutdown of the equipment is not a reason to isolate the valve early: the valve guards the equipment for as long as any pressure remains in it, including pressure that builds up again from heat or from a leaking isolation after the main pressure source has been cut.

Reduce the pressure by the normal shutdown procedure for the protected equipment. Watch the pressure gauge until the reading shows that the equipment is fully depressurised, and prove the state by the vent or drain on the equipment before any isolation is touched. Only then, and only where the valve is to be removed for bench testing or replacement, close the inlet isolation valve. Open the drain or vent between the protected equipment and the valve, and prove that no pressure is trapped in the short length of pipe between the closed isolation and the valve before any flange bolt is loosened

Removal of the valve is a maintenance task and is done under permit. Your part is the hand-over: enter in the operating log that the valve has been removed, which equipment it guarded, and the state the equipment has been left in. Blank any open flange that removal leaves behind. Equipment from which the relief valve has been removed is not to be repressurised until a valve is back in service on it, or an alternative protective arrangement approved for the purpose is in place.

The chapter in restatement: the valve guards pressurised equipment and is proved at start-up with its inlet open and its discharge clear; in normal operation it is watched and left alone; its two alarms call for pressure reduction and for clearance of the discharge area; and it stays in service at shutdown until the equipment is proved free of pressure.

fact_base: An operating-manual chapter for a pressure relief valve, in four sections: start-up, normal operation, alarms, and shutdown. The alarms section lists two alarms and the operator action for each; no other alarms are introduced. The chapter addresses the operator directly and uses imperative verbs for actions.
input:
Start-up

It should be understood at the outset that the pressure relief valve covered by this chapter is a vitally important protective device, and that the operator in charge of the protected equipment has charge of the valve as well. The function of the valve is to open automatically when the pressure reaches the set pressure, to discharge fluid until the pressure has fallen, and subsequently to reseat itself, without any intervention on the part of the operator. The instructions in this chapter, which relate to start-up, normal operation, alarms, and shutdown, are designed to ensure that the valve remains capable of performing this function, and they should be followed in the sequence presented, the sequence being discontinued at any point where a check is not satisfied until the fault has been reported and cleared.

Attention should be directed first of all to the discharge side. The discharge line should be traced from the valve outlet to the safe discharge point, and it should be established that the line is open along the whole of its length, free from caps, plugs, blanks, and shut valves, and sound at every joint. Attention should then be turned to the inlet side, where, where an inlet isolation valve has been fitted, that valve should be opened fully and secured open. The valve body and both flanges should be examined for damage, distortion, corrosion, and staining indicative of past leakage, and the pressure gauge on the protected equipment should be checked to ensure that it is readable, undamaged, and live on the equipment rather than shut off from it.

The protected equipment should be brought up to pressure slowly, in accordance with its own start-up procedure, the operator standing where the gauge can be observed and the outlet heard. When the normal operating pressure has been reached, the equipment should be held steady and the state of the valve confirmed, there being no discharge at the outlet, no hissing sound indicative of passing fluid, and no leakage at either of the flanges. An entry should then be made in the operating log, recording that the inlet is open, the discharge line proved, and the valve shut at the normal operating pressure.

If the valve is found to be passing or lifting during the course of this initial pressurisation, no attempt should be made to coax it back by hand, and the spring and adjuster should be left entirely untouched. The pressure should be brought down if the discharge fails to stop, and the valve should be reported to the supervisor so that it can be examined under permit, the equipment remaining without its full protection until the valve has been passed fit.

Normal operation

Under normal operating conditions, the relief valve is to be found in the shut condition, fitted to equipment that is live, with the equipment being operated at a pressure below the set pressure of the valve. The responsibility of the operator under these circumstances is essentially to ensure that any change in the condition of the valve is noticed at an early stage, as with a valve becoming audible, a joint staining, or an outlet showing signs of flow.

The valve should be included in every round. The pressure gauge on the protected equipment should be read and the reading noted against the normal operating band for the equipment, while the valve, its flanges, and the first length of discharge line are inspected for leakage, corrosion, and damage from nearby work. The outlet should be listened at for passing and examined for the marks a discharge leaves behind, including deposits, staining, and icing. The round should be written up in the operating log regardless of whether or not anything of note has been found, so that a record exists of the watch kept.

It is essential that the valve is not given any work to do during normal operation. The valve should not be cracked open in order to test it, it should not be eased with a lever, and it should not be used to control the equipment pressure, since it is a protective device, not a control valve, and a hand-opened valve may not reseat correctly. The ground round the valve and the discharge outlet should be kept clear, for access and for a discharge to escape safely, and paint should be kept off the valve entirely, the nameplate remaining readable and the spring housing free of paint that might trap moisture. Any damage, corrosion, leakage, or passing that is discovered should be reported to the supervisor on the same shift.

Three rules are applicable throughout the whole of the operating period. The inlet isolation valve is not to be closed while pressure is held within the protected equipment. The discharge outlet is not to be obstructed, even merely to silence a passing valve. The set pressure is not to be altered, and no instruction to alter it is to be accepted other than under a maintenance permit with the valve removed from the plant, the three rules together ensuring that, should the pressure rise beyond the limit, the valve is connected, unobstructed, and set as it was set on the test bench.

Alarms

Two alarms fitted on the protected equipment involve the relief valve, each with its own course of action. In neither instance does the action that is required involve work being carried out on the valve itself, the relevant tools being the gauge, the normal means of cutting the pressure at its source, and the withdrawal of personnel from the discharge area.

Protected equipment pressure high

This alarm indicates that the pressure in the protected equipment has climbed towards the set pressure, and that the valve may lift at any moment. The alarm should first be checked against the local pressure gauge. The pressure should then be cut at its source by the normal means applicable to the equipment, the inflow, the firing, or the feed driving the pressure up being stopped. The discharge outlet area should be cleared and kept clear, and if the pressure continues to climb, personnel should move out of the line of the discharge, the supervisor should be informed, and the valve should be left to lift and reseat without interference. After the pressure has fallen and become steady, the event should be logged and the valve reported for inspection.

Relief valve discharging

This alarm indicates that fluid is passing out of the discharge, whether from a full lift of the valve or from the valve passing heavily. Personnel near the outlet should be moved away from the discharge and kept away, and the pressure gauge on the protected equipment should be watched, a satisfactory lift being characterised by a falling pressure. The valve should not be approached, no attempt should be made to shut it, and the discharge should not be blocked to stop the noise or the loss. If the pressure fails to fall, the supervisor should be informed without delay and the emergency procedure for the equipment followed. After the discharge has ended and the valve has reseated, the lift should be logged and the valve reported for examination before it is relied upon again.

Shutdown

The relief valve should be retained in service for the whole of the shutdown, until such time as the protected equipment has been proved to be empty of pressure. The work of the valve is not completed merely because the pressure source has been cut off, since heat soak or a passing isolation can cause the pressure to rise again, and it is against such eventualities that the valve continues to protect for as long as it remains connected and unobstructed.

The pressure should be run down in accordance with the shutdown procedure for the protected equipment, and the equipment proved empty of pressure, first on its gauge and secondly at its vent or drain, before the valve isolation is touched. In cases in which the valve is to be removed for the purposes of bench testing or renewal, the inlet isolation valve should be closed only after this proof has been obtained, following which the drain or vent between the isolation and the valve should be opened and that length proved empty, that short length being proved as carefully as the vessel itself. No flange bolt should be loosened until both proofs have been made and recorded.

The valve itself is removed under a maintenance permit, the duty of the operator concluding with the hand-over. The removal should be logged, together with the equipment that the valve guarded and its proved state, and the open flange that remains following the removal should be blanked. Equipment standing without its relief valve is not to be pressurised, and no start-up should be permitted on such equipment until a proved valve has been fitted once again or a protective arrangement that has been approved for the purpose has been installed in its place.

In summary: the discharge and the inlet are to be proved before pressure is raised, the valve watched and left alone in operation, its two alarms answered by cutting the pressure and clearing the discharge area, and the valve kept in service at shutdown until the equipment is proved empty.
target:
Start-up

You have charge of the pressure relief valve whenever the equipment it protects is in your care. The valve is the last protection on that equipment: it opens at the set pressure, discharges until the pressure falls, and reseats itself, all without action from you. The start-up, normal operation, alarm, and shutdown instructions in this chapter keep the valve able to do that work. Follow them in the order given, and stop the sequence at any point where a check fails, until the fault has been reported and cleared.

Start with the discharge side. Walk the discharge line from the valve outlet to the safe discharge point and satisfy yourself that the line is open along its whole length, free of caps, plugs, blanks, and shut valves, and sound at every joint. Move then to the inlet: where an inlet isolation valve is fitted, open it fully and secure it open. Examine the valve body and both flanges for damage, distortion, corrosion, and staining from past leaks. Last, check the pressure gauge on the protected equipment: it must be readable, undamaged, and live on the equipment, not shut off from it by a closed cock.

Bring the protected equipment up to pressure slowly, by its own start-up procedure, and stand where you can see the gauge and hear the valve outlet as the pressure rises. At the normal operating pressure, hold the equipment steady and confirm the state of the valve: no discharge at the outlet, no hiss of passing fluid, no leak at either flange. Enter the start-up in the operating log, noting that the inlet is open, the discharge line proved, and the valve shut at the normal operating pressure.

A valve that passes or lifts during this first pressurisation is not to be coaxed back by hand. Keep your hands off the spring and the adjuster, bring the pressure down if the discharge does not stop, and report the valve to the supervisor for examination under permit. The equipment is without its full protection until the valve has been passed fit, and the log entry must say so.

Normal operation

Normal operation for the relief valve is a shut valve on live equipment. The equipment runs below the set pressure, and the valve waits. Your task in this state is to notice change early: a valve that was tight and becomes audible, a joint that was dry and begins to stain, an outlet that was cold and shows signs of flow.

Make the valve part of every round. Read the pressure gauge on the protected equipment and note the reading against the equipment's normal operating band. Look over the valve, both flanges, and the first length of discharge line for leakage, corrosion, and damage done by passing work. Listen at the outlet for passing, and look for the marks that discharge leaves behind it: deposits at the outlet, staining, eroded paint, icing on cold service. Write the round up in the operating log whether or not anything was found, so that the record shows the watch kept on the valve as plainly as on any other item of the plant.

Do not give the valve work to do in normal operation. Do not crack it open to test it, do not ease it with a lever, and do not use it to control the equipment pressure; it is a protective device, not a control valve, and a valve opened by hand may not reseat on its seat afterwards. Keep the ground round the valve and the discharge outlet clear for access and for a discharge to escape safely. Keep paint off the valve entirely: the nameplate must stay readable and the spring housing must stay free of paint that traps moisture. Report damage, corrosion, leaks, and passing to the supervisor on the shift on which you find them.

Three rules bind you for the whole period of operation. You do not close the inlet isolation valve while the protected equipment holds pressure. You do not obstruct the discharge outlet, even to silence a passing valve. You do not alter the set pressure, and you accept no instruction to do so outside a maintenance permit with the valve off the plant. Each rule protects the same point: when the pressure rises beyond the limit, the valve must be connected, open-mouthed, and set as it was set on the test bench.

Alarms

Two alarms fitted on the protected equipment involve the relief valve, and each has its own action. In neither case is the action work on the valve. Your tools are the pressure gauge, the normal means of cutting the pressure at its source, and the withdrawal of people from the discharge area.

Protected equipment pressure high

The pressure in the protected equipment has climbed towards the set pressure and the valve may lift at any moment. Check the alarm against the local pressure gauge first. Then cut the pressure at its source by the normal means for the equipment: stop the inflow, the firing, or the feed that is driving the pressure up. Clear the discharge outlet area and keep it clear. If the pressure still climbs, get out of the line of the discharge, tell the supervisor, and leave the valve to lift and reseat on its own. Once the pressure is down and steady, log the event and report the valve for inspection; it has worked near its limit and is checked before the equipment runs unrestricted again.

Relief valve discharging

Fluid is passing out of the discharge, either from a full lift or from a valve passing heavily. Move yourself and anyone near the outlet away from the discharge and keep them away. Watch the pressure gauge on the protected equipment: a healthy lift shows the pressure falling. Do not go to the valve, do not try to shut it, and do not block the discharge to stop the noise or the loss. If the pressure does not fall, tell the supervisor at once and follow the emergency procedure for the equipment. After the discharge ends and the valve has reseated, log the lift and report the valve for examination before it is trusted for a further period of service.

Shutdown

Keep the relief valve in service for the whole of the shutdown until the protected equipment is proved empty of pressure. The valve's work is not finished when the pressure source is cut: heat soak, a passing isolation, or liquid warming in a shut vessel can raise the pressure again, and the valve guards against each of them for as long as it stays connected and unobstructed.

Run the pressure down by the shutdown procedure for the protected equipment. Prove the equipment empty of pressure on its gauge and again at its vent or drain before you touch the valve's isolation. Where the valve is to come off for bench testing or renewal, close the inlet isolation valve only after that proof. Open the drain or vent in the pipe length between the isolation and the valve, and prove that length empty as well: it is short, it is easy to overlook, and it holds pressure exactly as the vessel did. Loosen no flange bolt on the valve until both proofs have been made and recorded.

The valve itself comes off under a maintenance permit; your duty ends with the hand-over. Log the removal, the equipment the valve guarded, and the proved state of that equipment. Blank the open flange that the removal leaves. Treat equipment standing without its relief valve as equipment that must not be pressurised, and allow no start-up on it until a proved valve is fitted again or a protective arrangement approved for the purpose has been installed in its place.

In restatement: prove the discharge and the inlet before pressure is raised, watch the valve and leave it alone while the equipment runs, answer its two alarms by cutting the pressure and clearing the discharge area, and keep it in service until the protected equipment is proved empty at shutdown.

fact_base: Goal: compute the diffusive flux of oxygen through a stagnant water film. The diffusive flux J (mol m-2 s-1) is computed from the diffusivity D (m2 s-1) and the concentration gradient dC/dx, where C is concentration (mol m-3) and x is position (m). Fick's first law: J = -D dC/dx; the negative sign states that diffusion runs from high concentration to low concentration. Oxygen in water: D = 2.1 x 10-9 m2 s-1. Concentration falls by 0.2 mol m-3 across a film 0.5 mm thick, so dC/dx = -400 mol m-4. Worked result: J = 8.40x 10-7 mol m-2 s-1. The law as stated covers a stagnant medium; a moving medium adds convection, which the equation does not include.
input:
In this example, we will work through the calculation of the diffusive flux of oxygen through a stagnant water film, which is a classic application of Fick's first law of diffusion. Fick's first law essentially tells us that the diffusive flux $J$ (mol m⁻² s⁻¹) can be obtained from the diffusivity $D$ (m² s⁻¹) together with the concentration gradient $dC/dx$, where $C$ denotes the concentration (mol m⁻³) and $x$ denotes the position (m), and the relationship is expressed as $J$ = -$D$ $dC/dx$. It is worth noting that the negative sign in this expression is very important, because it indicates that diffusion naturally proceeds from regions of high concentration towards regions of low concentration, in other words down the concentration gradient rather than up it.

Turning now to the specific values for this particular case, the diffusivity of oxygen in water is given as 2.1 × 10⁻⁹ m² s⁻¹, which is a relatively small value, as one might expect for a dissolved gas. The concentration, meanwhile, falls by 0.2 mol m⁻³ across a film that is 0.5 mm thick, which means that the concentration gradient works out to $dC/dx$ = -400 mol m⁻⁴. Substituting these values into the equation therefore gives $J$ = -(2.1 × 10⁻⁹ m² s⁻¹)(-400 mol m⁻⁴) = 8.40 × 10⁻⁷ mol m⁻² s⁻¹, with the two negative signs effectively cancelling one another out. Finally, it should be emphasised that Fick's first law, as stated here, applies to a stagnant medium; a moving medium would additionally involve convection, which the equation does not include, and so the treatment would need to be extended accordingly in such situations, giving a final flux of 8.40 × 10⁻⁷ mol m⁻² s⁻¹ for the stagnant case considered here.
target:
This worked example computes the diffusive flux of oxygen through a stagnant water film, and the result is a flux of 8.40 × 10⁻⁷ mol m⁻² s⁻¹. The flux follows from Fick's first law applied to the diffusivity of oxygen in water and the concentration gradient across the film.

Fick's first law relates the diffusive flux $J$ (mol m⁻² s⁻¹) to the diffusivity $D$ (m² s⁻¹) and the concentration gradient $dC/dx$, where $C$ is concentration (mol m⁻³) and $x$ is position (m). The law is written $J$ = -$D$ $dC/dx$. The negative sign states that diffusion runs from high concentration to low concentration: the flux is directed down the gradient, against the direction in which concentration rises.

For oxygen in water, $D$ is 2.1 × 10⁻⁹ m² s⁻¹. The concentration falls by 0.2 mol m⁻³ across a film 0.5 mm thick, and the gradient is therefore $dC/dx$ = -400 mol m⁻⁴. The gradient is a single value because the fall is spread over the film thickness; a thicker film at the same concentration fall would give a smaller gradient and a smaller flux.

Substitution in Fick's first law gives $J$ = -(2.1 × 10⁻⁹ m² s⁻¹)(-400 mol m⁻⁴) = 8.40 × 10⁻⁷ mol m⁻² s⁻¹. The two negative signs cancel, and the flux is positive in the direction from the concentrated side of the film to the dilute side. The check is the size as well as the sign: a very small diffusivity keeps the flux small even under a steep gradient.

Fick's first law holds for a stagnant medium. A moving medium adds convection, which the equation does not include, and the flux in a moving film is the sum of the diffusive flux computed here and a convective part that the stated law does not give.

fact_base: Capital appraisal for a bottling line: installed cost $1673k, expected net saving $350k per year for 12 years. At a discount rate of 6% the present value of the savings is $2934k and the net present value is $1261k. Savings are vendor and utility estimates; no saving has yet been measured on a comparable installation.
input: This capital appraisal examines a proposed bottling line and brings together the key financial figures that are relevant to the investment decision. The installed cost of the line is $1673k, while the expected net saving has been estimated at $350k per year for 12 years, reflecting anticipated reductions in operating expenditure once the line is in service. When these savings are discounted at a discount rate of 6%, the present value of the savings amounts to $2934k, and once the installed cost is taken into account, the resulting net present value is $1261k, which is positive and therefore indicates that the discounted savings are expected to exceed the initial outlay. It is important to note, however, that the savings underpinning this appraisal are based on vendor and utility estimates, and no saving has yet been measured on a comparable installation. This means that a considerable degree of uncertainty inevitably attaches to the figures, and stakeholders should be aware that if the realised savings turn out to be lower than estimated, the present value of the savings, and consequently the net present value, would also be lower than the values presented here.
target:
Capital appraisal of a bottling line gives a net present value of $1261k. The installed cost is $1673k, and the expected net saving is $350k per year for 12 years. At a discount rate of 6%, the present value of the savings is $2934k. The net present value is the present value of the savings minus the installed cost, and a positive value means that the discounted savings exceed the cost by the stated amount.

Net present value places savings arising in different years on one basis. Discounting reduces a saving in a later year relative to the same saving in an earlier year, because money available earlier can earn a return in the interval. The discount rate is the rate used for that reduction, and the same rate is applied to every year of the appraisal period. The installed cost falls at the start and is not discounted.

The savings are vendor and utility estimates. No saving has yet been measured on a comparable installation, and the appraisal inherits the uncertainty of the estimates: a realised saving below the estimate lowers the present value of the savings, and the net present value falls with it. The stated net present value is therefore a figure computed from estimates, not a measured return, and it holds only while the estimated savings hold.

subtype: worked example with equation: Fourier conduction
fact_base: A flat stainless steel wall has thickness 20 mm and thermal conductivity $k$ of 16 W m-1 K-1. The temperature difference $\Delta T$ across the wall is 326 K, giving a heat flux $q$ of 260800 W m-2. The calculation is steady and one-dimensional; film resistances are excluded.
input:
In this worked example, we will calculate the heat flux passing through a flat stainless steel wall, which is a straightforward application of Fourier's law of heat conduction. Fourier's law relates the heat flux $q$ (W m⁻²) to the thermal conductivity $k$ (W m⁻¹ K⁻¹), the temperature difference $\Delta T$ (K) across the wall, and the wall thickness $\Delta x$ (m), as follows:

$$q = k \frac{\Delta T}{\Delta x}$$

where $q$ represents the heat flux, $k$ represents the thermal conductivity of the material, $\Delta T$ represents the temperature difference across the wall, and $\Delta x$ represents the thickness of the wall. For the particular wall under consideration here, the thermal conductivity of the stainless steel is 16 W m⁻¹ K⁻¹, and the temperature difference across the wall is 326 K. The wall itself has a thickness of 20 mm, which can equivalently be expressed as 0.02 m. Substituting these values into the equation gives $q$ = 16 × 326 / 0.02 = 260800 W m⁻², which is a relatively large heat flux, largely because the wall is quite thin in comparison with the substantial temperature difference that is being maintained across it. It is important to note that this calculation is based on steady, one-dimensional conditions, and that film resistances have been excluded from the analysis, so the result should be understood as describing conduction through the wall alone rather than the overall heat transfer process including the fluid films on either side.
target:
A flat stainless steel wall separates two fluids, and the worked quantity is the heat flux through the wall under steady conditions. Fourier's law for one-dimensional conduction relates the heat flux $q$ (W m⁻²), the thermal conductivity $k$ (W m⁻¹ K⁻¹), the temperature difference $\Delta T$ (K) across the wall, and the wall thickness $\Delta x$ (m):

$$q = k \frac{\Delta T}{\Delta x}$$

where $q$ is the heat flux through the wall, $k$ is the thermal conductivity of the stainless steel, $\Delta T$ is the temperature difference across the wall, and $\Delta x$ is the wall thickness. The temperature falls in the direction of heat flow, and the flux is the heat transferred per unit area of wall in unit time.

For the stated wall, $k$ is 16 W m⁻¹ K⁻¹ and $\Delta T$ is 326 K. The thickness is 20 mm, which is 0.02 m. Substitution gives $q$ = 16 × 326 / 0.02 = 260800 W m⁻².

The calculation is steady and one-dimensional. Film resistances are excluded: the stated flux is the conduction flux through the wall alone, and resistance in the fluid films on the two faces is not included in the result. The flux is large because the wall is thin and the temperature difference across it is large relative to the thickness. A thicker wall of the same steel at the same temperature difference would give a smaller flux in inverse proportion to the thickness, and the stated value is a check on that proportion: doubling the thickness halves the flux. The result describes conduction through the metal only, at the stated temperatures, with no allowance for the films.

subtype: worked example with equation: friction loss
fact_base: Water at 293 K flows in a horizontal pipe. The density $\rho$ is 998 kg m-3. Mean velocity $v$ is 2.2 m s-1, pipe diameter $D$ is 0.08 m, pipe length $L$ is 22 m and the Darcy friction factor $f$ is 0.02. The friction pressure drop is 13.3 kPa.
input:
In this example, we will determine the pressure drop due to friction for water flowing through a horizontal pipe, making use of the well-known Darcy-Weisbach relationship. The water is at a temperature of 293 K, and the relevant properties and dimensions are as follows: the density $\rho$ is 998 kg m⁻³, the mean velocity $v$ is 2.2 m s⁻¹, the pipe diameter $D$ is 0.08 m, the pipe length $L$ is 22 m, and the Darcy friction factor $f$ is 0.02. The friction pressure drop is expressed by the following equation:

$$\Delta P = f \frac{L}{D} \frac{\rho v^2}{2}$$

where $\Delta P$ denotes the friction pressure drop (Pa), $f$ denotes the Darcy friction factor, $L$ denotes the pipe length (m), $D$ denotes the pipe diameter (m), $\rho$ denotes the density of the water (kg m⁻³), and $v$ denotes the mean velocity (m s⁻¹). Substituting the values listed above into this equation gives $\Delta P$ = 0.02 × (22 / 0.08) × 998 × 2.2² / 2 = 13.3 kPa. It is worth noting that, because the pipe is horizontal, there is no change in elevation to take into account, and the calculated pressure drop therefore represents the effect of friction alone. This result illustrates the considerable influence that friction can have on the pressure required to maintain flow through a pipe of appreciable length, a consideration that should be borne in mind whenever the flow through the pipe is increased.
target:
Water at 293 K flows in a horizontal pipe, and the worked quantity is the pressure drop caused by friction along the pipe. The density $\rho$ is 998 kg m⁻³, the mean velocity $v$ is 2.2 m s⁻¹, the pipe diameter $D$ is 0.08 m, the pipe length $L$ is 22 m, and the Darcy friction factor $f$ is 0.02. The friction pressure drop $\Delta P$ is given by:

$$\Delta P = f \frac{L}{D} \frac{\rho v^2}{2}$$

where $\Delta P$ is the friction pressure drop (Pa), $f$ is the Darcy friction factor, $L$ is the pipe length (m), $D$ is the pipe diameter (m), $\rho$ is the density of the water (kg m⁻³), and $v$ is the mean velocity (m s⁻¹). The ratio $L/D$ counts the pipe length in diameters, and the term in $\rho$ and $v$ is the velocity head, the kinetic energy per unit volume of the moving water. Friction converts part of that energy along each diameter of length, and the friction factor states the part converted.

Substitution gives $\Delta P$ = 0.02 × (22 / 0.08) × 998 × 2.2² / 2 = 13.3 kPa. The pipe is horizontal, and no elevation change enters the stated figure: the pressure drop given is the friction drop alone. The check is the proportion: at the same velocity and diameter, a pipe twice as long gives twice the friction drop, because the length enters the relation to the first power. The velocity enters squared, and a modest rise in velocity raises the drop much more strongly, which is the main sensitivity in the stated result.

fact_base: A tutorial passage explains absolute and relative error through a flow measurement. Worked figures: reading 319 units, tolerance 2% of reading, so the absolute error is 6.38 units. The passage distinguishes error from uncertainty and does not merge the two terms.
input: When measurements are being discussed, the concept of error is one that frequently arises, and it is helpful to understand clearly what is meant by the term and how it can be expressed. Essentially, the error of a measurement can be thought of as the difference between the reading that is obtained and the true value that the reading is intended to represent. This difference can be expressed in two main ways. The absolute error is simply the magnitude of the difference, expressed in the same units as the measurement itself, whereas the relative error is obtained by dividing the absolute error by the reading, and is commonly expressed as a percentage of the reading. To illustrate these ideas, it is useful to consider a simple flow measurement example. Suppose that a reading of 319 units has been obtained, and that the applicable tolerance is 2% of reading. On this basis, the absolute error amounts to 2% of 319 units, which works out to 6.38 units. It is also important to appreciate the distinction between error and uncertainty, two terms that are sometimes used rather loosely as though they were interchangeable. In fact, they are not the same thing at all: error relates to a specific reading and the difference between that reading and the underlying value, while uncertainty is a broader concept that is concerned with the range within which the value might reasonably be expected to lie, taking into account the instrument and the method that have been used. Keeping these two concepts separate helps to ensure that measurement results are interpreted correctly and communicated clearly.
target:
A measurement error is the difference between a reading and the value that the reading stands for. The error is a property of a single reading: the instrument gives one number, the quantity has one value, and the error is the gap between them. Error is stated in two forms. The absolute error is the size of the difference, in the units of the measurement itself. The relative error is the absolute error divided by the reading, and is a pure ratio, often written as a percentage of the reading. The two forms answer different questions. The absolute error states how far the reading may be out on the scale in use; the relative error states how large that deviation is against the size of the quantity measured, and relative errors can be compared across instruments and scales where absolute errors cannot.

A flow measurement makes the distinction concrete. A reading of 319 units carries a tolerance of 2% of reading. The absolute error is 2% of 319 units, which is 6.38 units. The tolerance grows with the reading, because a percentage of reading is being applied: the same instrument at a larger flow would carry a larger absolute error at the same relative error, and at a smaller flow a smaller one. A tolerance stated as a percentage of reading therefore fixes the relative error and lets the absolute error follow the reading.

Error is not uncertainty. Error attaches to a particular reading as the difference between that reading and the value behind it, a value that is in practice unknown, which is why error is estimated from a tolerance rather than observed directly. Uncertainty describes the measurement as a whole: it states the range within which the value may lie, given the instrument and the method, and it can be attached to a procedure before any single reading is taken. The two terms are not merged here. The worked figure is an error, computed from a stated tolerance on a stated reading, and it makes no claim about the range that an uncertainty statement would give.

subtype: worked example with equation: radiative exchange
fact_base: A blackened plate at 600 K faces surroundings at 290 K. Its emissivity $\varepsilon$ is 0.9. Net radiative heat flux $q$ is 6.3 kW m-2, with the Stefan-Boltzmann constant $\sigma$ = 5.67 x 10-8 W m-2 K-4. The estimate treats both surfaces as large and parallel; view factors for the real geometry are not included.
input:
In this example, we will estimate the net radiative heat flux from a blackened plate that is situated facing extensive surroundings. The plate is at a temperature of 600 K, while the surroundings are at 290 K, and the emissivity $\varepsilon$ of the plate surface is 0.9. The net radiative heat flux $q$ can be calculated from the following relationship:

$$q = \varepsilon \sigma (T_1^4 - T_2^4)$$

where $q$ represents the net radiative heat flux (W m⁻²), $\varepsilon$ represents the emissivity, $\sigma$ represents the Stefan-Boltzmann constant, $T_1$ represents the temperature of the plate (K), and $T_2$ represents the temperature of the surroundings (K). The Stefan-Boltzmann constant $\sigma$ has a value of 5.67 × 10⁻⁸ W m⁻² K⁻⁴. Substituting the given values into the equation gives $q$ = 0.9 × 5.67 × 10⁻⁸ × (600⁴ − 290⁴) = 6.3 kW m⁻². It should be noted that this estimate is based on the assumption that both surfaces can be treated as large and parallel; view factors appropriate to the real geometry have not been included in the calculation, and the result should therefore be interpreted with that particular limitation in mind whenever it is applied to the actual installation in practice. The strong dependence on temperature is also worth emphasising, since the fourth-power relationship means that the temperature of the hotter surface has a particularly pronounced effect on the resulting flux.
target:
A blackened plate at 600 K faces surroundings at 290 K, and the worked quantity is the net radiative heat flux leaving the plate. The plate has emissivity $\varepsilon$ of 0.9. The net radiative heat flux $q$ is given by:

$$q = \varepsilon \sigma (T_1^4 - T_2^4)$$

where $q$ is the net radiative heat flux (W m⁻²), $\varepsilon$ is the emissivity of the plate, $\sigma$ is the Stefan-Boltzmann constant, $T_1$ is the plate temperature (K), and $T_2$ is the temperature of the surroundings (K). The flux is a difference of two emission terms: the plate emits according to its own temperature, the surroundings emit according to theirs, and the net flux is what remains after the incoming part is subtracted. Emissivity scales both parts for a surface that emits and absorbs below the black-body rate.

The Stefan-Boltzmann constant $\sigma$ is 5.67 × 10⁻⁸ W m⁻² K⁻⁴. Substitution gives $q$ = 0.9 × 5.67 × 10⁻⁸ × (600⁴ − 290⁴) = 6.3 kW m⁻². The fourth power makes the flux sensitive to the plate temperature: the hotter surface dominates the difference, and a small rise in plate temperature raises the net flux far more than the same rise in the surroundings.

The estimate treats both surfaces as large and parallel. View factors for the real geometry are not included, and a plate facing a smaller or angled surroundings would exchange radiation at a rate the stated figure does not describe. The stated flux holds for the large parallel arrangement and the stated temperatures. No other exchange path is included in the figure.

fact_base: Excerpt content: a seal replacement takes about 28 min with the unit isolated; the excerpt gives the isolation steps only. The excerpt warns once about stored pressure and does not repeat the warning.
input:
Once the standby pump has been brought into service and is running satisfactorily, it becomes possible to proceed with the replacement of the seal on the duty pump, a task that takes about 28 min with the unit isolated. Before any work on the seal itself is commenced, the duty pump must be isolated in accordance with the arrangements set out under the PTW. The suction valve should be closed first, followed by the discharge valve, and both valves secured with the locks and tags provided. The casing drain should then be opened so that the liquid within the casing can run to the closed drain until the flow has stopped.

It is important to be aware that stored pressure may remain trapped inside the casing even after both valves have been shut, and the casing vent should be cracked open slowly, with personnel standing clear of the vent opening, until no further flow or hissing is present, before any attempt is made to loosen the casing bolts.

During the parting of the seal faces, both the drain and the vent should be left open, and the coupling should not be approached until rotation has stopped completely. Throughout this period, the discharge gauge of the standby pump should be watched carefully, because that pump is carrying the area on its own until the duty pump has been reassembled and brought back into operation alongside
target:
With the standby pump running and proved on load, attention turns to the seal on the duty pump. The replacement takes about 28 min with the unit isolated, and the isolation is made before any seal part is touched. Close the suction valve of the duty pump first, then the discharge valve, and fit the locks and tags that the PTW requires on both valves. Open the casing drain and let the liquid in the casing run to the closed drain until the flow stops.

Stored pressure can remain trapped in the casing after both valves are shut. Crack the casing vent slowly, stand clear of the vent opening, and wait until no further flow or hiss is present before a single casing bolt is loosened.

Leave the drain and the vent open while the seal faces are parted. Keep clear of the coupling until rotation has stopped and the stop has been confirmed at the casing. Watch the standby pump discharge gauge while the duty pump stands open, and report any fall at once through the PTW holder, since the running pump carries the area alone until the duty pump is returned to service and its valves are reopened in the reverse order, suction last checked against
